boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange
On December 1, 1950, the Baltimore Bullets traded Dick Mehen to the Boston Celtics for Kenny Sailors and Brady Walker. Baltimore's transaction page, Boston's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same three-player exchange. Boston was moving two reserves who had combined for only 27 Celtics appearances before the trade, while Baltimore sent out a frontcourt player who had been part of its own rotation. The deal is notable because Boston did not keep Mehen for long; eighteen days later, the Celtics sent him to Fort Wayne for Bob Harris, creating a clear downstream branch from the original transaction.

Baltimore Return
Baltimore received substantially more immediate playing time from the two-player package. Kenny Sailors appeared in 50 games for the Bullets in 1950-51, averaging 9.5 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.8 assists. Brady Walker appeared in 49 games and averaged 7.5 points, 6.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists. Neither became a star, but together they supplied nearly 100 player-games and filled meaningful guard and frontcourt roles for a Baltimore team that lacked depth. Their combined production makes the Bullets' return much larger than the limited Boston value they had produced before the trade.

Boston Return
Dick Mehen's direct Boston tenure was brief. He played seven games for the Celtics, averaging 6.3 points, 3.7 rebounds and 1.6 assists. Boston then moved him to the Fort Wayne Pistons on December 19 for Bob Harris. Harris became the more durable part of Boston's asset chain, appearing in 44 games that season at 5.5 points and 5.6 rebounds per game. That downstream conversion matters because it prevents the Celtics' side from being evaluated as only seven Mehen games. Boston did extract a second useful player from the asset it acquired, even though the original target did not stay.

Hindsight Comparison
Baltimore still comes out ahead because Sailors and Walker produced more combined service and stronger immediate rotation value than Boston received from Mehen and the first Harris season. The Celtics deserve credit for turning a short-lived acquisition into another contributor, which narrows the gap considerably. This is not a case where one side received nothing. Baltimore simply got the better volume and role value from two players who both remained active for the balance of the season, while Boston had to make another trade to recover useful depth.

Final Verdict
Bullets Win, B+/B-. Baltimore receives the B+ because Sailors and Walker combined for 99 regular-season games with useful scoring, rebounding and playmaking. Boston receives the B- because Mehen lasted only seven games, but the Celtics salvaged the asset by converting him into Bob Harris, who contributed 44 games that season. The exchange favored Baltimore, but Boston's downstream trade keeps it from becoming a lopsided result.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
On December 8, 1950, the Baltimore Bullets sold Don Otten's player rights to the Fort Wayne Pistons for cash. Baltimore's transaction page, Fort Wayne's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same sale. Baltimore had acquired Otten's rights from the Washington Capitols on November 29, so the Bullets held the asset for only nine days. Otten appeared in two Baltimore games during that window, totaling 11 points and three rebounds. The reviewed public sources do not preserve the amount Fort Wayne paid, which means Baltimore's financial return cannot be measured directly.

Fort Wayne Return
Otten immediately became a much more useful player for the Pistons. He appeared in 49 Fort Wayne games during 1950-51 and averaged 8.4 points, 6.0 rebounds and 0.8 assists. He also played three playoff games, adding 9.7 points and 6.3 rebounds per game in Fort Wayne's first-round series against Rochester. Otten returned for seven regular-season games in 1951-52 before the Pistons released him in November. Across the two seasons, Fort Wayne received 56 regular-season games plus a short playoff contribution from the cash purchase.

Baltimore Return
Baltimore received cash after only a brief look at Otten. The Bullets had gone from acquiring his rights on November 29 to selling them on December 8, so the transaction functioned almost like a rapid asset flip. That may have made practical financial sense, but the missing sale amount prevents the return from being valued. There is no documented player, pick or later transaction directly tied to the payment. Baltimore therefore has a tangible but opaque financial return, while Fort Wayne's basketball return is visible in Otten's 49-game role that season.

Hindsight Comparison
Fort Wayne clearly received more traceable value. Otten became a regular center, played nearly three quarters of the 1950-51 schedule for the Pistons and contributed in the playoffs. Baltimore's two-game stint with him before the sale was negligible, and the cash return cannot be compared numerically. The result still belongs in the minor-to-moderate category because Otten was released less than a year later and did not become a long-term Pistons fixture. Even so, 56 regular-season games and playoff minutes are enough to establish a clear realized-value edge.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, B+/C. Fort Wayne receives the B+ because an undisclosed cash purchase produced 56 regular-season games over two seasons and a useful 1951 playoff contribution. Baltimore receives a C because the Bullets quickly monetized an asset they had held for only nine days, but the payment is unknown and no downstream basketball value is documented. The legacy record understated how much playing value Fort Wayne actually received from Otten.

philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Exchange
On December 10, 1950, the Syracuse Nationals sold Belus Smawley's player rights to the Baltimore Bullets for cash. Syracuse's transaction page, Baltimore's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same sale. Smawley was already a proven professional scorer, having averaged 15.5 points for St. Louis in 1948-49 and 13.7 in 1949-50. His role had fallen after joining Syracuse: he appeared in 16 games for the Nationals in 1950-51 and averaged 7.8 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists. The reviewed public sources do not preserve Baltimore's purchase price.

Baltimore Return
Smawley immediately regained a larger scoring role with the Bullets. He played 44 games for Baltimore during the rest of 1950-51 and averaged 13.8 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.8 assists while shooting .389 from the field and .859 at the line. That made him one of the team's most productive perimeter scorers alongside Red Rocha and gave Baltimore far more direct value than a short reserve stint. Smawley returned for 11 additional games in 1951-52 before his NBA career ended, bringing the Bullets' total return to 55 regular-season appearances across two seasons.

Syracuse Return
Syracuse received cash and moved on from a veteran whose role had already contracted. The Nationals finished 32-34 and reached the Eastern Division semifinals, so the sale did not remove a central piece from a contending rotation. The limitation is the missing dollar figure. Without the amount, Syracuse's financial return cannot be measured against the 607 points Smawley scored for Baltimore in the remainder of 1950-51 or traced to a later roster asset. The Nationals still received something tangible, but the surviving record does not support a stronger claim about its value.

Hindsight Comparison
Baltimore's advantage is clear because Smawley became a productive scorer immediately after the purchase. His 13.8 points per game with the Bullets nearly doubled his 7.8-point Syracuse average from earlier in the same season, and he played 44 games after the deal rather than serving as a brief replacement. Syracuse had a rational reason to monetize a veteran who was playing a smaller role, but the unknown cash amount leaves the Nationals without measurable basketball value on the other side. This is a meaningful Baltimore win within the context of an early cash transaction, even though Smawley's stay lasted only two partial seasons.

Final Verdict
Bullets Win, A-/C. Baltimore receives the A- because the cash purchase produced 55 games across two seasons and immediately added a 13.8-point scorer to the rotation. Syracuse receives a C because the Nationals monetized a reduced-role veteran and remained competitive, but the payment is unknown and no downstream player or pick value is documented. The transaction had a much stronger realized basketball return for Baltimore than the legacy even-grade suggested.

los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange
On December 11, 1950, the Minneapolis Lakers sold Ed Beach's player rights to the Tri-Cities Blackhawks for cash. Minneapolis' transaction page, Tri-Cities' transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same sale. Beach had been Minneapolis' fifth-round pick in the 1950 NBA Draft, 59th overall, and had already appeared in 11 games for the Lakers before the transaction. Tri-Cities Return
The Blackhawks received almost no realized basketball value from the purchase. Minneapolis received cash for a player who had been used sparingly on a defending-champion roster. Beach's 11 Lakers appearances produced only 22 total points, and the club remained strong after moving him, finishing 44-24 and reaching the Western Division Finals. Because the payment amount is unknown, the Lakers' financial return cannot be measured precisely. Even so, the franchise converted a marginal roster asset into compensation rather than carrying a player who was not part of the main rotation.

The Lakers hold the narrow edge because the Blackhawks' return was limited to one scoreless game. This is not a major historical win: the cash amount is unknown, Beach was a fifth-round rookie, and neither side gave up a meaningful long-term asset. Still, the realized comparison is straightforward. Minneapolis received financial value and lost almost no production, while Tri-Cities paid for rights that generated only one NBA appearance. The surviving record supports a modest Lakers advantage rather than the legacy even-grade.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
On December 13, 1950, the Tri-Cities Blackhawks traded Noble Jorgensen and cash to the Syracuse Nationals for Ed Peterson. Tri-Cities' transaction page, Syracuse's transaction page, the league transaction log and executive records for Ben Kerner and Leo Ferris all identify the same exchange. Jorgensen had averaged 11.2 points and 5.1 rebounds in 22 Tri-Cities games that season. Peterson had averaged 4.7 points and 2.2 rebounds in 17 games for Syracuse. The cash amount was not preserved, but its direction is clear: Tri-Cities sent the payment together with Jorgensen.

Tri-Cities Return
Peterson gave the Blackhawks a respectable short-term return. He appeared in 36 games after the trade and averaged 7.8 points, 6.9 rebounds and 1.6 assists. His rebounding role was especially useful for a team that needed frontcourt size, and his scoring improved from the smaller role he had occupied in Syracuse. The limitation is duration. Those 36 games were the last regular-season appearances of Peterson's NBA career, so Tri-Cities did not receive a multi-season player or a later trade asset from the deal.

Syracuse Return
Jorgensen became a larger and much more durable piece for the Nationals. He played 41 games for Syracuse in the remainder of 1950-51, averaging 9.3 points, 5.5 rebounds and 1.6 assists. He then stayed for two more full seasons, appearing in 66 games in 1951-52 and 70 in 1952-53. Across his Syracuse tenure after the trade, Jorgensen played 177 regular-season games. He also participated in the playoffs in each of those seasons. Syracuse received that multi-year center production plus an undisclosed cash payment.

Hindsight Comparison
Tri-Cities received a useful player, so this is not a one-sided transaction in the sense of one team getting nothing. Peterson played 36 games and rebounded well. Syracuse still owns the stronger return because Jorgensen was productive immediately and remained part of the rotation for three seasons. The 177-game Syracuse tenure creates a large durability gap, and the cash component moves in the same direction rather than offsetting it. That combination makes the Nationals' advantage clearer than the legacy grade suggested.

Final Verdict
Nationals Win, A-/C+. Syracuse receives the A- because Jorgensen produced 177 regular-season games across three seasons and the Nationals also received cash. boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange
On December 19, 1950, the Fort Wayne Pistons traded Bob Harris to the Boston Celtics for Dick Mehen. Boston's transaction page, Fort Wayne's transaction page, the 1950-51 league transaction log and Red Auerbach's executive record all identify the same player-for-player exchange. Mehen had been in Boston for only seven games after arriving from Baltimore on December 1. Harris had appeared in 12 Fort Wayne games that season. The trade therefore moved two players who were already being treated as movable rotation pieces rather than long-term franchise anchors.

Boston Return
Harris became a useful frontcourt rebounder for the Celtics. Basketball-Reference credits him with 44 Boston games in 1950-51 at 5.5 points, 5.6 rebounds and 1.3 assists per game. He later made brief appearances for Boston in three additional seasons, so the Celtics did receive continuing roster value beyond the first year. Harris was never a major scorer, but he supplied more immediate games than Mehen had given Boston and fit as depth behind the club's more prominent frontcourt players.

Fort Wayne Return
Mehen gave the Pistons 43 games during the rest of 1950-51, averaging 6.5 points, 2.8 rebounds and 1.2 assists. The more important value came after the season. On May 31, 1951, Fort Wayne traded Mehen, Howie Schultz and cash to the Tri-Cities Blackhawks for Frankie Brian. Brian became an All-Star for Fort Wayne in 1951-52, appearing in 66 games and scoring 1,051 points, then remained a major part of the Pistons the following season. Mehen therefore served as both a usable player and a direct component in acquiring a much more valuable guard.

Hindsight Comparison
Boston's side was respectable. Harris gave the Celtics 44 games immediately and remained available for later short stints. Fort Wayne's side still separates because Mehen's value did not end with his 43-game Pistons run. Converting him into part of the Frankie Brian package created a second, much larger return that directly followed from the asset acquired in this trade. That downstream path is the kind of traceable conversion that matters in a hindsight review and was not captured by the legacy grade.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, A-/B-. Fort Wayne receives the A- because Mehen supplied 43 games and then helped bring All-Star Frankie Brian to the Pistons in the next major transaction. Boston receives the B- because Harris was a useful rebounder who played 44 games in 1950-51 and made later brief appearances for the Celtics. Both sides received real value, but Fort Wayne's downstream Brian conversion gives the Pistons the stronger historical return.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
On February 3, 1951, the Tri-Cities Blackhawks traded Kleggie Hermsen to the Boston Celtics for Harry Boykoff. Tri-Cities' transaction page, Boston's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log all identify the same one-for-one exchange. The archive stores Hermsen under his given name, Clarence Hermsen, while Basketball-Reference uses the familiar Kleggie Hermsen name. Boykoff had played 32 Boston games at 6.3 points and 4.2 rebounds before the swap. Hermsen had appeared in 48 Tri-Cities games at 8.0 points and 6.8 rebounds.

Tri-Cities Return
Boykoff gave the Blackhawks 16 games over the remainder of the season. He averaged 7.8 points, 5.3 rebounds and 1.3 assists, which was a modest scoring increase from his Boston role. That production was useful, but it was also the end of Boykoff's NBA career. He did not return the next season and created no documented downstream trade value for Tri-Cities. The Blackhawks therefore received a short-term center who helped for several weeks without becoming a lasting roster asset.

Boston Return
Hermsen played 23 games for Boston in 1950-51, averaging 6.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 0.9 assists. He did not play in 1951-52, then returned for four brief Celtics appearances in 1952-53 before finishing the season with Indianapolis. Boston's return was hardly transformative, but it lasted longer than Boykoff's Tri-Cities stint and produced more total regular-season games. The later four-game return also shows the Celtics retained some control of the asset beyond the initial season.

Hindsight Comparison
The gap is small because both players were short-term contributors with similar rebounding numbers. Boykoff was slightly more productive as a scorer after the trade, while Hermsen gave Boston more games and a longer connection to the roster. Neither side turned the player into a major later asset, and neither return changed the trajectory of the franchise. The surviving record therefore supports only a slight Boston edge, based primarily on duration and total service rather than a dramatic difference in quality.

Final Verdict
Celtics Edge, C+/C. Boston receives the C+ because Hermsen provided 23 games immediately and four more in a later stint, giving the Celtics the longer realized return. Tri-Cities receives a C because Boykoff produced 16 respectable games but never appeared in the NBA again. The deal remained minor for both sides, and the source-backed record does not support the stronger Hawks-win label carried by the legacy review.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange
On February 12, 1951, the Boston Celtics sold John Mahnken's player rights to the Indianapolis Olympians for cash. Boston's transaction page, Indianapolis' transaction page, the 1950-51 league transaction log and Red Auerbach's executive record all agree on the sale. Mahnken had been a regular Boston center, appearing in 46 games before the transaction and averaging 5.2 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.5 assists. The reviewed sources do not preserve the cash amount, so Boston's financial return cannot be measured directly.

Indianapolis Return
Mahnken appeared in 12 regular-season games for Indianapolis after the purchase. His role and production dropped sharply, to 2.3 points, 2.9 rebounds and 0.8 assists per game while shooting .170 from the field. He also appeared in all three of the Olympians' playoff games against Minneapolis, averaging 1.3 points, 3.7 rebounds and 3.0 assists. That gives Indianapolis a real but limited on-court return. The acquisition did not become a long-term roster piece for the Olympians.

Boston Return
Boston received cash for a player who had been part of the rotation but whose role could be replaced. The amount is unknown, which prevents a precise financial grade. Mahnken then appears back on Boston's 1951-52 roster for 60 games and again for 69 games in 1952-53. The reviewed Basketball-Reference transaction logs do not show how he returned to the Celtics, so that later Boston service should not be credited as a documented downstream return from this sale. It does, however, underline how temporary the Indianapolis acquisition proved to be.

Hindsight Comparison
Indianapolis bought a veteran center and received 12 regular-season games plus a short playoff stint. Boston received an undisclosed cash payment and gave up only a partial-season contribution. Neither side produced a major asset outcome from the transaction itself. Because Mahnken's Indianapolis production was limited and the Olympians did not retain him into the next season, the slight edge goes to Boston for monetizing the rights. The unknown cash amount keeps that advantage modest rather than decisive.

Final Verdict
Celtics Edge, C+/C. Boston receives the C+ because it converted a veteran's rights into cash while Indianapolis received only 12 low-production regular-season games. The Olympians receive a C because Mahnken did contribute depth and appeared in the playoffs, but the acquisition did not last. The later return of Mahnken to Boston is noted without assigning transaction value because the reviewed logs do not document how that move occurred.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
On February 15, 1951, the Baltimore Bullets sold Ken Murray's player rights to the Fort Wayne Pistons for cash. Fort Wayne's transaction page and the 1950-51 league transaction log identify the same sale. Murray had been one of Baltimore's more productive rookies, appearing in 52 games and averaging 13.7 points, 5.5 rebounds and 2.9 assists. The reviewed public sources do not preserve the cash amount, so Baltimore's financial return cannot be measured against the playing value Fort Wayne later received.

Fort Wayne Return
Murray joined the Pistons for the final 14 regular-season games of 1950-51. He averaged 9.9 points, 4.9 rebounds and 3.8 assists, giving Fort Wayne immediate backcourt production even though his scoring efficiency dipped from Baltimore. He then missed the 1951-52 and 1952-53 NBA seasons while serving in the U.S. Army. Murray returned to Fort Wayne in 1953-54 and appeared in 49 more games. Across those two Pistons seasons, the original cash purchase produced 63 regular-season appearances.

Baltimore Return
Baltimore received cash for a player who had been an active part of its rotation. The sale therefore carried more opportunity cost than many early rights transactions involving fringe players. Murray had scored 712 points in 52 Bullets games before the move. The problem for hindsight grading is that the amount paid by Fort Wayne is unknown, and no later player or draft asset can be traced directly to that payment in the reviewed record. Baltimore's return was tangible but opaque.

Hindsight Comparison
Fort Wayne holds the advantage because the Pistons received useful immediate production and later regained Murray after his military service. The two-year absence limits the continuity of the return, but it does not erase the 63 total games Fort Wayne ultimately received from the purchased rights. Baltimore may have received a reasonable cash price, yet the surviving record cannot quantify it. The comparison therefore favors the Pistons without treating the deal as a franchise-changing acquisition.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, B+/C. Fort Wayne receives the B+ because Murray contributed 14 games immediately, returned after military service and ultimately gave the Pistons 63 regular-season appearances. Baltimore receives a C because the Bullets monetized a productive rookie, but the sale price is unknown and no downstream basketball asset is documented. The source-backed record supports a stronger Fort Wayne advantage than the legacy minor-deal grade suggested.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange
On April 26, 1951, the Fort Wayne Pistons traded Bill Sharman to the Boston Celtics for the rights to Chuck Share. Boston's transaction page, Fort Wayne's transaction page, the 1950-51 league transaction log and Carl Bennett's executive record all agree on April 26, correcting the legacy April 27 intake date. Share had been the first overall pick in the 1950 NBA Draft but spent 1950-51 outside the NBA. Sharman had played 31 games for the Washington Capitols before that franchise folded and his rights reached Fort Wayne through the dispersal process.

Boston Return
Sharman immediately became a major Celtics piece. He played 63 games in 1951-52 and averaged 10.7 points, then grew into one of the league's premier guards. Basketball-Reference lists him as an eight-time All-Star, seven-time All-NBA selection, four-time NBA champion and Hall of Famer, with a career average of 17.8 points. His shooting and free-throw accuracy complemented Bob Cousy in the backcourt and made him part of the core that moved Boston from a rising team into the league's dominant late-1950s franchise.

Fort Wayne Return
Share was not a throwaway return. He debuted with Fort Wayne in 1951-52 and played 63 games, then 67 in 1952-53 and 21 more in 1953-54. That gave the Pistons 151 regular-season games from a young center before they converted him again. On December 21, 1953, Fort Wayne traded Share to the Milwaukee Hawks for Max Zaslofsky. Zaslofsky then appeared in 45 Pistons games that season and averaged 11.0 points. The downstream conversion materially improves Fort Wayne's side of the original deal.

Hindsight Comparison
Fort Wayne received legitimate multi-season value and a useful second asset, which makes a low grade inappropriate. Share became a long NBA player and later won a championship with the Hawks, while the Pistons extracted 151 games and then Zaslofsky from him. Boston still wins decisively because Sharman became a Hall of Fame guard and a central member of four championship teams. The gap is about ceiling and historical impact, not whether Fort Wayne received anything. This is a strong return for the Pistons that happened to be exchanged for one of the foundational players of the Celtics dynasty.

Final Verdict
Celtics Win, A+/B+. Boston receives the A+ because Sharman became an eight-time All-Star, four-time champion and Hall of Fame cornerstone. Fort Wayne receives the B+ because Share produced 151 Pistons games and was later traded directly for Max Zaslofsky, who supplied another productive stint. Both franchises extracted value, but Sharman's decade-level impact and championship role give Boston the overwhelming historical advantage.

summary: On May 31, 1951, the Tri-Cities Blackhawks traded Frankie Brian to the Fort Wayne Pistons for Dick Mehen, Howie Schultz and cash, correcting the legacy May 4 date. Brian became the best long-term asset in the deal: he played five seasons for Fort Wayne, made the 1952 All-Star team and averaged 15.9 points that first season. Mehen gave the Hawks 65 games at 10.8 points and 4.3 rebounds in 1951-52, while Schultz was returned before playing for the franchise. Tri-Cities received useful short-term production and cash, but Fort Wayne got the longer, higher-impact return.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Tri-Cities, Fort Wayne and league transaction logs all place the deal on May 31, 1951: the Blackhawks sent Frankie Brian to Fort Wayne for Dick Mehen, Howie Schultz and cash. That corrects the legacy May 4 date in the legacy archive entry. Brian had just completed an All-NBA Second Team season for Tri-Cities, averaging 16.8 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.9 assists across 68 games. Fort Wayne therefore acquired a proven high-usage guard rather than a speculative piece, while Tri-Cities received two veterans plus undisclosed financial consideration.

Fort Wayne Return
Brian immediately justified the acquisition. In 1951-52 he played all 66 games for Fort Wayne, averaged 15.9 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.5 assists, and made the All-Star team. He remained with the Pistons for five seasons and appeared in 306 regular-season games for the franchise, averaging 10.1 points over that span. His role declined later, but the longevity matters: Fort Wayne converted one transaction into several years of backcourt production and received Brian's best post-Tri-Cities season immediately after the trade.

Tri-Cities Return
Mehen became a major part of the renamed Milwaukee Hawks in 1951-52. He appeared in 65 games, averaged 10.8 points, 4.3 rebounds and 2.6 assists, and logged more than 35 minutes per game. Schultz, however, did not produce the same return. Basketball-Reference lists him outside the NBA in 1950-51, and executive records note that his rights were later returned to Fort Wayne before Minneapolis acquired him in October 1951. The cash amount is not preserved. Tri-Cities therefore received one substantial season from Mehen, an unclear short-lived rights component in Schultz and an unquantified financial payment.

Hindsight Comparison
The Hawks' side was better than a simple loss because Mehen delivered a full season of starter-level minutes and double-digit scoring. Still, Brian's five-year Fort Wayne tenure created more durable value, and his first Pistons season included an All-Star selection while nearly matching his Tri-Cities scoring. The cash consideration could narrow the gap, but the amount is unknown and cannot be credited beyond acknowledging it existed. Schultz also failed to become a Hawks contributor. The surviving record supports a Fort Wayne win, though not an overwhelming one because Mehen was genuinely useful in Milwaukee.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, A-/B. Fort Wayne receives the A- because Brian became an immediate All-Star and stayed five seasons, producing 306 regular-season games for the franchise. The Hawks receive a B because Mehen supplied 65 games of starter-level production and the package also included cash, even though Schultz never became part of the on-court return. The corrected May 31 date and the realized player outcomes make Fort Wayne the stronger side of a trade that still gave Tri-Cities useful short-term value.

Brian had just completed an All-NBA Second Team season for Tri-Cities, averaging 16.8 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.9 assists across 68 games. Fort Wayne therefore acquired a proven high-usage guard rather than a speculative piece, while Tri-Cities received two veterans plus undisclosed financial consideration.

Fort Wayne Return
Brian immediately justified the acquisition. In 1951-52 he played all 66 games for Fort Wayne, averaged 15.9 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.5 assists, and made the All-Star team. He remained with the Pistons for five seasons and appeared in 306 regular-season games for the franchise, averaging 10.1 points over that span. His role declined later, but the longevity matters: Fort Wayne converted one transaction into several years of backcourt production and received Brian's best post-Tri-Cities season immediately after the trade.

Tri-Cities Return
Mehen became a major part of the renamed Milwaukee Hawks in 1951-52. He appeared in 65 games, averaged 10.8 points, 4.3 rebounds and 2.6 assists, and logged more than 35 minutes per game. The Hawks' side was better than a simple loss because Mehen delivered a full season of starter-level minutes and double-digit scoring. Still, Brian's five-year Fort Wayne tenure created more durable value, and his first Pistons season included an All-Star selection while nearly matching his Tri-Cities scoring. The cash consideration could narrow the gap, but the amount is unknown and cannot be credited beyond acknowledging it existed. Schultz also failed to become a Hawks contributor. The surviving record supports a Fort Wayne win, though not an overwhelming one because Mehen was genuinely useful in Milwaukee.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, A-/B. Fort Wayne receives the A- because Brian became an immediate All-Star and stayed five seasons, producing 306 regular-season games for the franchise. The Hawks receive a B because Mehen supplied 65 games of starter-level production and the package also included cash, even though Schultz never became part of the on-court return. Superseded malformed legacy record. Don Otten's move to Milwaukee belongs to a November 1951 free-agent signing after Fort Wayne released him. Dike Eddleman's move to Fort Wayne belongs to the February 11, 1952 Art Burris-and-cash trade. The July 1, 1951 Otten-for-Eddleman swap should not be treated as a completed NBA trade.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Syracuse acquired Red Rocha from the Baltimore Bullets for Fred Scolari and Alex Hannum on July 14, 1951, correcting the legacy July 15 date. Rocha became an All-Star immediately, averaging 12.9 points and 8.3 rebounds while playing all 66 games in 1951-52, and he ultimately gave the Nationals four productive seasons around a one-year retirement, including the 1955 championship run. philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Exchange
On July 14, 1951, the Syracuse Nationals traded Alex Hannum and Fred Scolari to the Baltimore Bullets for Red Rocha. Syracuse's transaction page, Baltimore's transaction page and the 1951-52 league transaction log all agree on July 14, correcting the legacy July 15 intake date. This was a substantial veteran exchange rather than a minor reserve move. Scolari had averaged 13.4 points in 1950-51, Hannum had started 63 games for Syracuse, and Rocha had just completed an All-Star season in Baltimore. Each side was dealing from proven NBA talent.

Syracuse Return
Rocha became one of Syracuse's core frontcourt players. In 1951-52 he played all 66 games, averaged 12.9 points, 8.3 rebounds and 1.9 assists, and made the All-Star team. He followed with 69 games in 1952-53, then returned after sitting out 1953-54 to play 72 games for the 1954-55 championship Nationals and another 72 in 1955-56. Across those four Syracuse seasons he supplied 279 regular-season games, plus substantial playoff work, including 12.4 points per game over 11 postseason games during the 1955 title run. That longevity gives Syracuse a durable return well beyond the first year.

Baltimore Return
Baltimore's side was also productive, especially immediately. Scolari played 64 games for the Bullets in 1951-52, averaged 14.6 points, 4.7 assists and 3.3 rebounds, and made the All-Star team. Hannum appeared in 35 Baltimore games at 7.7 points, 5.5 rebounds and 2.1 assists. On January 18, 1952, Baltimore sold Hannum's player rights to Rochester, creating an additional financial return even though the amount is not preserved. The Bullets therefore received one full All-Star season from Scolari, half a season from Hannum and some later cash value from Hannum's rights.

Hindsight Comparison
The trade is much closer than the legacy A-versus-D grading suggested. Baltimore received excellent first-season value, and Scolari's 14.6-point All-Star year was arguably the strongest immediate scoring return in the deal. Syracuse wins the longer comparison because Rocha remained a productive center for four Nationals seasons and was part of the 1955 championship team. His 279 regular-season Syracuse games outweigh Baltimore's shorter combined tenure, even after crediting the Hannum rights sale. The correct historical framing is a good return for both sides with a meaningful durability advantage for Syracuse.

Final Verdict
Nationals Win, A-/B+. Syracuse receives the A- because Rocha became an immediate All-Star, stayed productive across four seasons and contributed to the 1955 championship. Baltimore receives the B+ because Scolari delivered an All-Star season, Hannum provided useful frontcourt minutes, and the Bullets later monetized Hannum's rights. Syracuse ultimately received the more durable franchise value, but Baltimore's return was substantial enough that this should not be treated as a one-sided trade.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
On September 25, 1951, the Minneapolis Lakers sold Kevin O'Shea's player rights to the Milwaukee Hawks for cash. Milwaukee's transaction page and the 1951-52 league transaction log agree on the September 25 date, correcting the legacy September 21 intake record. O'Shea had been Minneapolis' first-round pick in 1950 and appeared in 63 games as a rookie, averaging 4.3 points, 2.0 rebounds and 1.6 assists. The Lakers moved his rights before the 1951-52 season, and the reviewed public sources do not preserve the amount Milwaukee paid.

Milwaukee Return
O'Shea became a regular part of a rebuilding Hawks rotation. He appeared in 43 games for Milwaukee at 6.0 points, 2.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists while averaging 25.0 minutes. His efficiency was limited, but the playing time shows that the Hawks received more than a token roster piece. The return also had a downstream component. On February 3, 1952, Milwaukee sold O'Shea's player rights to Baltimore, where he finished the season with 22 games at 8.7 points and 3.2 assists. The amount of Milwaukee's later sale is also unknown, but it means the Hawks extracted both playing value and a second cash transaction from the rights.

Minneapolis Return
Minneapolis received cash for a player who had been useful but not central during his rookie season. The Lakers went on to win the 1952 NBA championship without O'Shea, so moving his rights did not create an obvious competitive gap. The missing sale amount prevents a precise financial comparison, and there is no documented draft pick or later player directly tied to the payment. The Lakers' return is therefore tangible but opaque: they monetized a former first-round pick who was no longer part of their championship rotation.

Hindsight Comparison
Milwaukee has the slightly stronger realized-value case because O'Shea gave the Hawks 43 games before his rights were sold again. That second sale means the original cash purchase was not a dead-end asset even though O'Shea did not become a long-term Hawk. Minneapolis deserves credit for converting a non-core player into money while remaining a championship team, which keeps the gap narrow. With both cash amounts undisclosed, the safest conclusion is a modest Milwaukee edge based on the visible on-court service and traceable downstream transaction rather than a large win.

Final Verdict
Hawks Edge, B-/C+. Milwaukee receives the B- because O'Shea supplied 43 games of rotation minutes and the franchise later sold his rights to Baltimore. Minneapolis receives the C+ because the Lakers monetized a player outside their championship core, but the payment cannot be measured. The trade produced useful short-term value for Milwaukee without becoming an important long-term franchise transaction.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
On October 10, 1951, the Fort Wayne Pistons sold Howie Schultz's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers for cash. Fort Wayne, Minneapolis and league transaction logs all record the same sale. Those sources also flag an unusual piece of provenance: Schultz had been sent to Tri-Cities with Dick Mehen and cash in the May 31, 1951 Frankie Brian trade, but his rights were evidently returned to Fort Wayne before the October transaction. The reviewed public record does not explain the return mechanism or preserve the amount Minneapolis paid, so the safest treatment is to document the known rights sale without inventing an intermediate transaction.

Minneapolis Return
Schultz became a regular frontcourt reserve immediately. He played all 66 regular-season games for Minneapolis in 1951-52, totaling 268 points, 246 rebounds and 102 assists. That works out to 4.1 points, 3.7 rebounds and 1.5 assists per game while averaging just under 20 minutes. He also appeared in 12 playoff games as the Lakers won the 1952 championship. Schultz returned for 40 more regular-season games in 1952-53, adding 91 points and 80 rebounds during another championship season. Across the two years, Minneapolis received 106 regular-season appearances plus postseason depth from the purchased rights.

Fort Wayne received cash for a player who had not appeared for the Pistons since 1949-50 and had spent 1950-51 in the NPBL. The amount is not preserved in the transaction logs, and no player or draft asset can be traced directly from the payment. Selling the rights therefore may have been practical roster management, especially after the confusing May 31 rights movement, but the surviving record provides no measurable basketball return for Fort Wayne. The Pistons did not lose an active 1951-52 contributor because Schultz was not on their playing roster at the time of the sale.

Hindsight Comparison
Minneapolis gets the stronger realized-value result. Schultz was not a star and his scoring role was small, but 106 regular-season games across two championship seasons is meaningful depth from an undisclosed cash purchase. Fort Wayne's return may have had financial value, yet the missing amount makes it impossible to compare directly with two years of roster service. The unusual rights history also argues against overstating the transaction; Schultz had already been moved once that offseason and apparently returned. Even with that caveat, the Lakers received the only documented on-court value from the October sale.

Lakers Win, B+/C. Minneapolis receives the B+ because Schultz supplied 106 regular-season games and postseason depth across consecutive championship seasons. Fort Wayne receives a C because the Pistons monetized rights to a player outside their active rotation, but the cash amount is unknown and no downstream basketball asset is documented. The result is a clear Lakers win in realized value without turning a reserve acquisition into a franchise-changing move.

The Exchange
RealGM records the Boston Celtics acquiring Dick Dickey's draft rights from the Baltimore Bullets on August 1, 1951. That date is repeated in Boston's 1951-52 transaction history and is consistent with Dickey signing a Celtics contract on September 1. The legacy TradeVerdicts intake placed the transaction on October 23 and described Boston sending cash. The August 1 rights transfer is independently corroborated, but the reviewed external transaction source does not identify what Baltimore received. TradeVerdicts therefore corrects the date and rights classification while retaining the legacy cash return only as an unconfirmed legacy detail rather than presenting the amount or structure as independently established.

Boston Return
Dickey became a reserve guard for the Celtics in 1951-52. Basketball-Reference credits him with 45 regular-season games, 9.8 minutes per game, 2.8 points, 1.8 rebounds and 1.1 assists. He also appeared in all three Boston playoff games against New York, averaging 10.3 minutes. His role was clearly secondary on a team led by Bob Cousy and Ed Macauley, but the Celtics did receive actual NBA service from a player whose rights they acquired before the season. Dickey became a free agent after the year and did not play another NBA season, so the value stopped after one campaign.

Baltimore Return

The legacy Boston source says the Bullets received cash, while RealGM confirms a trade but does not specify consideration. With no amount preserved and no traceable downstream player or pick identified, Baltimore's return cannot be graded as though a known financial value existed. The Bullets at least converted rights to a player who had not joined their roster into some form of consideration according to the legacy archive record.

Hindsight Comparison
Boston's advantage is modest and entirely based on realized player service. Forty-five games from a reserve guard is useful, but Dickey averaged fewer than ten minutes and less than three points per game, and the asset disappeared after one season. Baltimore never received on-court value from Dickey, but the uncertainty around the consideration prevents a hard loss grade. The date repair is more important than the verdict: the supported transaction belongs on August 1, before Dickey's September signing, not on October 23 after the season was already approaching.

Slight Celtics Edge, B-/C+. Boston receives the B- because the rights acquisition produced 45 regular-season games and three playoff appearances from a usable reserve. Baltimore receives a C+ because the Bullets moved rights to a player who never played for them, but the consideration cannot be independently measured from the reviewed public sources. The deal helped Boston at the margins without becoming a long-term roster win.

The legacy Boston intake record describes an October 23, 1951 transaction in which the Celtics supposedly acquired Charlie Black from the Baltimore Bullets for cash. The surviving team and player records do not support that transaction. Boston's 1951-52 roster does not include Black, and the Celtics' transaction history has no matching October 23 acquisition. Baltimore's 1951-52 transaction history likewise contains no sale of Black to Boston. The absence is especially important because both franchises have other October transactions documented in the same surviving ledgers.

Black's actual 1951-52 path points somewhere else. RealGM records him signing with the Milwaukee Hawks on November 20, 1951, and later becoming a free agent after the Hawks waived him in December. The appropriate archival treatment is therefore supersession: keep the legacy archive entry privately so its source history is not lost, but remove it from player-query relationships, hindsight grading and any future public/indexable candidate set.

Final Resolution
Superseded malformed legacy record. Charlie Black's supported 1951-52 transaction is his November 20 signing with Milwaukee, followed by 13 Hawks games and a December exit. The October 23, 1951 Baltimore-to-Boston cash trade should not be treated as a completed NBA transaction.

The Exchange
Syracuse drafted John McConathy fifth overall in the 1951 NBA Draft, but he never played for the Nationals. RealGM's player transaction history and Milwaukee Hawks transaction ledger both record the Hawks acquiring McConathy's draft rights from Syracuse on September 1, 1951, the same date he signed his Milwaukee contract. That conflicts with the legacy TradeVerdicts intake, which used October 30 and described the return as cash. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse and league transaction pages do not list the later rights transfer, so the strongest surviving date evidence is the matching RealGM player and team records. The canonical route is therefore repaired to September 1, while the exact consideration remains unresolved.

Milwaukee Return
McConathy made his NBA debut on November 3 and appeared in 11 games for the 1951-52 Hawks. He averaged 1.3 points, 1.8 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 9.6 minutes per game, shooting .138 from the field. His entire NBA career consisted of those 11 appearances. RealGM records Milwaukee placing him on waivers December 1 and his becoming a free agent December 3. The Hawks therefore received a real but very small basketball return from the rights acquisition: 106 minutes, 14 points, 20 rebounds and eight assists before the relationship ended.

Syracuse Return
The precise Syracuse return cannot be established confidently from the reviewed public record. The legacy Atlanta/Hawks intake called the transaction a cash sale, but the more specific RealGM histories simply describe Milwaukee acquiring McConathy's draft rights in a trade and do not identify the consideration. Rather than convert the legacy cash field into a factual claim, the source-backed review treats Syracuse's side as unresolved consideration. The Nationals still avoided losing an active contributor because McConathy never appeared for them, but any attempt to assign a dollar value or downstream asset would go beyond the available evidence.

The realized basketball stakes were minor. Milwaukee obtained an NBA player, but McConathy lasted only 11 games and produced little statistically. Syracuse surrendered rights to a first-round pick who never became part of its rotation, and the exact return is not preserved in the stronger public sources. That supports an effectively even hindsight result. The important correction is archival rather than evaluative: September 1 is better supported than October 30, and the consideration should be described as unresolved instead of asserting cash as settled fact.

Even Trade, C/C. Milwaukee receives a C because McConathy reached the NBA but contributed only 11 low-minute games before being waived. Syracuse also receives a C because it moved rights to a player who never appeared for the club, while the return cannot be measured confidently. The source-backed record supports a minor, essentially even transaction with a corrected September 1 date.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Baltimore sold Walt Budko's player rights to the Philadelphia Warriors on November 5, 1951. The legacy TradeVerdicts record used November 3, but Basketball-Reference's league-wide, Baltimore and Philadelphia transaction logs all agree on November 5. Philadelphia received a usable rotation forward for the full 1951-52 season: Budko played 63 regular-season games, averaged 4.0 points, 3.7 rebounds and 1.4 assists, and added three playoff appearances. Baltimore received cash, but the surviving public sources reviewed here do not preserve the amount, so the hindsight verdict should avoid pretending the Bullets' return can be precisely valued.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange
Baltimore and Philadelphia completed the Walt Budko transaction on November 5, 1951. Basketball-Reference's 1951-52 league transaction log, Baltimore team log and Philadelphia team log all place the sale on that date, making the legacy November 3 route a straightforward archival error. The same sources describe Baltimore selling Budko's player rights to the Warriors. That wording supports retaining cash as Baltimore's consideration, but no reviewed source provides a dollar figure. Budko was already a known NBA player rather than an untested draft stash: he had spent the previous three seasons with Baltimore and had even served as the Bullets' interim head coach during the 1950-51 season.

Philadelphia Return
The Warriors received one full season of useful depth. Budko appeared in 63 of Philadelphia's 66 regular-season games in 1951-52, logging 1,126 minutes. He averaged 4.0 points, 3.7 rebounds and 1.4 assists in 17.9 minutes per game, shot .404 from the field and produced 1.5 win shares. He also appeared in all three of Philadelphia's playoff games against Syracuse. This was not star-level production, but it was real rotation value from a midseason cash acquisition, and Budko remained available throughout essentially the entire season. He became a free agent after the season, so there was no long downstream asset chain.

Baltimore Return
Baltimore received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the transaction records reviewed for this pass. That limitation matters. A cash sale can be completely rational for a club moving a veteran it no longer plans to use, but without the amount there is no defensible way to compare the financial return to Budko's 1,126 minutes for Philadelphia. The Bullets also had direct knowledge of Budko after three seasons as a player and his short interim coaching stint, so this was not a case of unknowingly discarding an unproven prospect who later broke out elsewhere.

Hindsight Comparison
Philadelphia clearly received the more measurable basketball return because Budko played 63 games and contributed to a playoff team. Baltimore's side is real but economically opaque. That makes an extreme grade split hard to justify. The original D+/F framing treated the unknown cash return as nearly worthless, which overstates what the surviving evidence can prove. A neutral middle grade better reflects the record: Philadelphia bought a year of rotation minutes, while Baltimore monetized rights to a veteran it was prepared to move.

Final Verdict
Even Trade, C/C. Philadelphia obtained modest but useful one-season production. Baltimore received cash of unknown amount and surrendered a player who did not become a long-term asset for the Warriors. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's league-wide 1951-52 transaction log, Baltimore team log and Milwaukee team log agree that the Bullets sold Red Owens' player rights to the Hawks on December 26, 1951. That evidence resolves an identity issue in the legacy Atlanta-side intake, which labeled the player Jim Owens. Basketball-Reference identifies Red Owens as James L. Owens and lists Jim and Jamie among his nicknames, so the older record was pointing to the correct person under a less common name rather than a different player. The transaction date and cash-sale structure are supported; the dollar amount is not preserved in the reviewed sources.

Milwaukee Return
Owens joined Milwaukee after playing 19 games for Baltimore earlier in the season. He appeared in ten games for the Hawks, averaging 28.5 minutes, 8.0 points, 3.1 rebounds and 3.2 assists. He shot .308 from the field and .615 from the foul line in that Milwaukee segment. The playing-time figure matters more than the raw game count because Owens immediately occupied a real rotation role for a club that finished 17-49. His stint still had a hard ceiling: those ten games were the final NBA appearances of his career, so Milwaukee did not create a multi-year asset or any later trade chain from the purchase.

Baltimore Return
Baltimore received cash. Basketball-Reference explicitly describes the move as a sale, which is enough to preserve cash as the consideration, but none of the reviewed transaction pages provide an amount. That prevents a precise economic comparison with Owens' ten-game Milwaukee contribution. The Bullets had already used Owens in 19 games that season and moved him after obtaining direct on-court value, so this was not a prospect giveaway. The available evidence supports treating Baltimore's return as real but unquantified rather than assigning it near-zero value by default.

Hindsight Comparison
Milwaukee received the more visible basketball asset, but the realized value was short-lived. Owens played 285 minutes for the Hawks and then exited the NBA after the season. Baltimore converted the remainder of his rights into cash, with the amount lost to the surviving public record. Those facts do not support a strong directional verdict. A source-backed evaluation should acknowledge Milwaukee's ten games without pretending that an unknown cash payment was worthless.

Final Verdict
Even Trade, C/C. Milwaukee acquired a usable guard for ten games and 285 minutes. Baltimore received cash for a player whose NBA career ended that season. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Rochester sold Joe McNamee to the Baltimore Bullets on December 28, 1951, one day earlier than the legacy TradeVerdicts route. RealGM's Baltimore transaction history, McNamee player profile and league roster-turnover record all agree on December 28, and Basketball-Reference shows McNamee in Baltimore's lineup the next day. Baltimore received 34 regular-season games from the forward after the move, with McNamee averaging 4.5 points, 3.3 rebounds and 1.1 assists in 17.0 minutes per game. Rochester received cash, but the reviewed public record does not preserve the amount.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
The surviving transaction evidence supports December 28, 1951 as the date Rochester sent Joe McNamee to Baltimore for cash. RealGM's Baltimore transaction history, McNamee's player transaction page and its 1951-52 roster-turnover ledger all independently place the acquisition on December 28. That is also consistent with Basketball-Reference's December 29 Baltimore box score, which already lists McNamee in uniform for the Bullets. The legacy TradeVerdicts route used December 29, so the canonical date is corrected by one day. Rochester had drafted McNamee 10th overall in 1950 and used him for 84 games across his first two NBA seasons before the sale.

Baltimore Return
McNamee gave Baltimore a real rotation contribution after the transaction. His 1951-52 split with the Bullets covers 34 games and 577 minutes, or 17.0 minutes per appearance. He averaged 4.5 points, 3.3 rebounds and 1.1 assists while shooting .325 from the field and .636 from the foul line. Those numbers are modest, but they are more substantial than the brief stints attached to several neighboring early-1950s cash transactions in the archive. McNamee also appeared for Baltimore immediately after the trade, removing any doubt that the transaction produced usable on-court value rather than only dormant rights. He became a free agent after the season, so the value did not extend into a long asset chain.

Rochester Return
Rochester received cash, but the amount is not available in the reviewed public sources. That means the Royals' side cannot be valued with the same precision as Baltimore's 577 minutes. The context still matters: McNamee had fallen to a limited role in Rochester, appearing in 24 games that season while averaging only 4.9 minutes and 0.6 points. Moving a marginal rotation player for cash was therefore a plausible roster decision for a club that finished first in the Western Division and reached the division finals. The absence of a recorded dollar figure argues against treating Rochester's return as worthless.

Hindsight Comparison
Baltimore received the more visible basketball return, but it was a half-season depth acquisition rather than a franchise-changing move. McNamee played 34 games for the Bullets and then left the NBA after the season. Rochester converted a player it was barely using into an unknown cash return while continuing a 41-win season. The realized outcomes are close enough that a directional winner would overstate the evidence. The archival correction is more important than the grade: December 28 is the best-supported transaction date, not December 29.

Final Verdict
Even Trade, C/C. Baltimore obtained 577 minutes of usable forward depth from McNamee. Rochester received cash for a player whose role had nearly disappeared and whose NBA career ended months later. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Milwaukee sent Dike Eddleman to Fort Wayne on February 11, 1952 for Art Burris and cash. Basketball-Reference's team transaction logs give the same date and structure: Fort Wayne traded Burris plus cash for Eddleman, while Milwaukee records the inverse transaction. Those sources also resolve the main identity defect in the legacy TradeVerdicts record. The Atlanta-side intake labeled the outgoing player Thomas Eddleman, but the verified player was Dike Eddleman. Before the move, Eddleman had played 50 games for Milwaukee that season, while Burris had appeared in 29 games for Fort Wayne.

Fort Wayne Return
Eddleman gave the Pistons useful value across two seasons. He played 16 games after the trade in 1951-52, totaling 288 minutes, 104 points, 37 rebounds and 23 assists. He then returned for 69 games in 1952-53, adding 1,571 minutes, 615 points, 236 rebounds and 104 assists. That produced 85 regular-season games for Fort Wayne after the exchange. Eddleman was no longer at his earlier peak, but the Pistons acquired a real rotation forward and retained him through the following season instead of receiving a short rental.

Milwaukee Return
Burris' Milwaukee stint was much shorter. He appeared in 12 games for the Hawks, averaging 22.4 minutes, 5.6 points, 4.2 rebounds and 1.3 assists. Those 12 games were the final NBA appearances of his career. Milwaukee also received cash, which prevents the transaction from being treated as a one-for-one player swap. The reviewed transaction pages do not state the amount, however, and no later player or draft asset can be traced to those proceeds from the surviving record.

Hindsight Comparison
Fort Wayne received the stronger documented basketball value. Eddleman's 85 post-trade games substantially outlasted Burris' 12-game Milwaukee run, and the Pistons did not have to surrender another player beyond Burris. Milwaukee's cash return was legitimate but unquantified, so it deserves neutral credit rather than being assumed worthless. The evidence supports a moderate Pistons win rather than an extreme grade gap.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, B/C. Fort Wayne receives a B for turning Burris and cash into 85 games from Eddleman across two seasons. Milwaukee receives a C for 12 games from Burris plus an undisclosed cash payment. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange
Boston sold the player rights to Clarence Henry 'Kleggie' Hermsen to Indianapolis on November 17, 1952. Basketball-Reference records the sale on both team transaction pages and in the league-wide 1952-53 ledger. The source-backed review also fixes an important data classification. Hermsen was not a 1952 draft-rights asset; he was a 29-year-old veteran who had already played four games for the Celtics that season after returning from a year away from the league. The canonical player identity remains Clarence Hermsen with Kleggie Hermsen as the verified alias.

Indianapolis Return
The Olympians received very little on-court value. Hermsen appeared in six games after the sale and logged only 40 total minutes. He made four field goals, scored 10 points, grabbed 12 rebounds and recorded four assists. Basketball-Reference credits him with minus-0.3 win shares in that Indianapolis stint. He did not appear in another NBA season after 1952-53. This was therefore a short final stop for a veteran rather than a developmental rights acquisition that later paid off.

Boston Return
Boston received cash, but the reviewed transaction logs do not preserve the amount. That prevents a precise financial valuation and argues against assigning an unusually strong grade to the Celtics. Boston converted a marginal active-roster asset into cash without surrendering meaningful future NBA production.

The transaction favors Boston modestly. Indianapolis bought the final six games of Hermsen's NBA career and received almost no positive statistical value. The old even-trade label understates how little Indianapolis ultimately received, while an extreme Celtics grade would overstate an unknown cash amount.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Milwaukee sent Mark Workman to Philadelphia for Don Sunderlage on November 19, 1952. The Milwaukee, Philadelphia and NBA transaction logs all describe a direct player-for-player trade. That requires two corrections to the legacy record: no cash is listed by the verified sources, and Sunderlage was not a 1952 draft-rights asset. Philadelphia had drafted him ninth overall in 1951, but he missed both 1951-52 and 1952-53 while serving in the military. Milwaukee acquired his player rights while he was away, then waited for his return. Workman, meanwhile, had been the first overall pick in the 1952 draft and had already appeared in five games for the Hawks.

Milwaukee Return
Sunderlage did not play immediately because his military service continued through the 1952-53 season. The payoff arrived one year later. In 1953-54 he appeared in 68 games for Milwaukee, averaged 32.8 minutes, 11.2 points, 3.3 rebounds and 2.8 assists, and was selected to the NBA All-Star Game. Basketball-Reference credits him with 762 points in that season. For a team that had traded away the No. 1 pick after only five games, receiving a full All-Star-caliber season from Sunderlage was a meaningful recovery of value.

Philadelphia Return
Workman became a rotation player for the Warriors but did not develop into the kind of cornerstone usually associated with the first overall pick. He played 60 games for Philadelphia in 1952-53, logging 1,001 minutes while averaging 5.3 points, 3.1 rebounds and 0.6 assists. His shooting percentage was .320, and Basketball-Reference credits his entire two-year NBA career with negative win shares. Workman did not return to Philadelphia the following season; he played 14 games for Baltimore in 1953-54 and then left the NBA.

Hindsight Comparison
The verified record gives Milwaukee the stronger return. Workman's Philadelphia tenure was longer in immediate availability, but Sunderlage's delayed debut produced the best season either player delivered after the exchange. He became an All-Star and handled a much larger role, while Workman's 60-game Warriors stint remained modest and was his only season with the club. Removing the unsupported cash component also makes the trade easier to evaluate: this was Workman for Sunderlage, not Workman for Sunderlage plus additional consideration.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, B+/D+. Milwaukee receives a B+ for turning five games of Workman into an eventual 68-game All-Star season from Sunderlage. Philadelphia receives a D+ because Workman produced one modest season and no durable Warriors tenure. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Fort Wayne Return
Phillip immediately became a major part of the Pistons. He played 57 games after the sale in 1952-53, averaging 37.7 minutes, 10.0 points, 4.9 rebounds and 5.0 assists while producing 5.6 win shares. Philadelphia Return
Philadelphia received cash. The reviewed transaction records do not state the amount, so the Warriors deserve credit for actual consideration without assigning an invented dollar value. He remained a high-minute guard, continued to earn league honors and became part of the Pistons' strongest run of the era. The surviving record therefore shows much more measurable basketball value on Fort Wayne's side.

Fort Wayne acquired a Hall of Fame guard who gave the club 262 regular-season games, three All-Star selections and meaningful playoff value. Philadelphia received an unknown cash payment and no traceable player or draft asset from the transaction. The uncertainty around the payment deserves restraint, but it does not erase the scale of Phillip's subsequent production.

Pistons Win, A-/D+. Fort Wayne receives an A- for acquiring four productive seasons from Phillip, including three All-Star selections and two NBA Finals runs. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Milwaukee traded Don Boven, Pete Darcey and George McLeod to Baltimore on January 2, 1953 for Stan Miasek and Dave Minor. Basketball-Reference's 1952-53 league transaction ledger gives that exact five-player structure. The source-backed review also fixes a serious identity defect in the legacy TradeVerdicts record: the third outgoing Hawk was George McLeod, a 1952 Milwaukee draft pick, not George McCloud. The bad spelling had incorrectly attached the 1953 transaction to the much later NBA player George McCloud. That false edge is removed and reassigned to a new canonical George McLeod identity.

Milwaukee Return
Miasek and Minor both became meaningful rotation players for the Hawks during the remainder of the season. Miasek appeared in 40 Milwaukee games, averaging 11.0 points and 7.7 rebounds. Minor also played 40 games, averaging 32.7 minutes, 8.0 points, 5.3 rebounds and 2.6 assists. Together they supplied 80 post-trade appearances and filled substantial roles for a Milwaukee team trying to stabilize its lineup. Neither player remained in the NBA beyond 1952-53, so the value was concentrated in that season, but it was real and immediate.

Baltimore Return
Baltimore's three-player package produced much less direct on-court value. Boven played 23 games for the Bullets, averaging 14.3 minutes and 4.6 points, before Baltimore moved him again on February 16. McLeod made his NBA debut after the trade and appeared in 10 games, totaling 85 minutes and 12 points; those were the only NBA games of his career. Darcey had already appeared in 12 games for Milwaukee, but Basketball-Reference credits him with no Baltimore appearances after the transaction and no later NBA season. Boven's ability to be included in the later Fort Wayne trade adds some secondary value, but the immediate return was still limited.

Hindsight Comparison
Milwaukee received the stronger realized package. The Hawks got 80 combined games from two veterans who both handled regular rotation roles, while Baltimore received 33 combined appearances from Boven and McLeod plus a non-playing Darcey. Boven's subsequent trade value keeps Baltimore's side from being a complete miss, yet it does not offset the larger body of useful production Milwaukee received immediately. The source-backed evidence supports a moderate Hawks advantage rather than the legacy even-grade treatment.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, B/C. Milwaukee receives a B for 80 combined games of useful production from Miasek and Minor. Baltimore receives a C for limited direct production from Boven and McLeod, no post-trade NBA appearances from Darcey and some residual value through Boven's February move. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Fort Wayne traded Jack Kerris and Ralph O'Brien to the Baltimore Bullets for Fred Scolari and Don Boven on February 16, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, Baltimore and league transaction logs all show a straight four-player exchange; the legacy TradeVerdicts record incorrectly added cash to Baltimore's return. Scolari played 16 games for Fort Wayne to finish 1952-53 and another 64 in 1953-54, while Boven added 17 regular-season games and eight playoff appearances. perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Fort Wayne sent Jack Kerris and Ralph O'Brien to Baltimore on February 16, 1953 for Fred Scolari and Don Boven. Basketball-Reference lists the same four-player trade on the Fort Wayne and Baltimore transaction pages and in the league-wide 1952-53 ledger. That source agreement exposes the key legacy defect: no cash is listed as part of the deal. The unsupported cash asset is removed from the canonical record so the exchange is evaluated strictly as Kerris and O'Brien for Scolari and Boven.

Fort Wayne Return
Scolari supplied the most durable post-trade value. He played 16 games for Fort Wayne to finish 1952-53, logging 505 minutes, then returned for 64 games and 1,589 minutes in 1953-54. Boven added 17 regular-season games after the trade, with 377 minutes, 104 points and 58 rebounds, and he appeared in eight playoff games during Fort Wayne's postseason run. Together, Scolari and Boven gave the Pistons 33 regular-season appearances immediately after the exchange, while Scolari's next full season extended the return to 97 combined regular-season games.

Baltimore Return
Kerris played 17 games for Baltimore after the trade, logging 442 minutes with 95 points, 88 rebounds and 48 assists. O'Brien appeared in 14 games and 182 minutes, scoring 72 points with 20 rebounds and 17 assists. Both players finished their NBA careers with Baltimore at the end of the season. The Bullets therefore received 31 combined regular-season games and no later NBA value from the package. Removing the unsupported cash component also leaves no additional consideration to narrow the difference.

Hindsight Comparison
Fort Wayne received the stronger realized return. The immediate 1952-53 playing-time difference was not enormous, but Scolari's 64-game 1953-54 season gave the Pistons a second year of rotation value that Baltimore did not receive from Kerris or O'Brien. Boven also contributed during the 1953 playoffs. Baltimore's package was useful for the final weeks of the season, but both incoming players exited the NBA afterward. The source-backed evidence supports a moderate Pistons advantage rather than the legacy even-trade grade.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, B/C. Fort Wayne receives a B for Scolari's two-season return plus Boven's regular-season and playoff contribution. Baltimore receives a C for 31 combined games from Kerris and O'Brien with no subsequent NBA value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Why This Record Is Superseded
The legacy Atlanta and Boston rows describe a July 1, 1953 transaction in which Milwaukee supposedly sent Jack Nichols to Boston for cash. The authoritative 1953-54 transaction record does not support that event. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee Hawks, Boston Celtics and league-wide transaction pages all identify the Nichols transaction as a November 29, 1953 five-for-one trade. Boston sent John Azary, Fred Eydt, Tom Lillis, J.C. Maze and Paul Unruh to Milwaukee and received Nichols. None of those sources records a July cash sale between the same clubs.

The season record independently conflicts with the legacy date. Nichols played 15 games for Milwaukee in 1953-54 before joining Boston, then appeared in 60 Celtics games after the November trade. A July 1 transfer would place him on Boston before the season began and cannot be reconciled with those 15 Milwaukee appearances. The surviving evidence therefore does not point to a simple one-day or one-month date typo. It points to an erroneous extra record that reduced the real November package to Nichols-for-cash.

Canonical Transaction
TradeVerdicts already contains the November 29 transaction as nba-trade-19531129-cad95c0931cb. That record carries the complete six-player asset structure from both the Atlanta and Boston source intakes: Milwaukee sent Nichols and received Azary, Eydt, Lillis, Maze and Unruh. Preserving a second July transaction would double-count Nichols' move to Boston and create a false player relationship. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.

Final Resolution
Record Superseded. The July 1, 1953 Nichols-for-cash listing should not be treated as a completed NBA trade and receives no hindsight winner or grades. The verified transaction is the November 29, 1953 five-for-one Milwaukee-Boston exchange, which remains in the chronology for its own source-backed analysis. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.

summary: Baltimore traded Don Barksdale to the Boston Celtics on August 27, 1953 for Jim Doherty, Herm Hedderick, Mo Mahoney, Vernon Stokes and cash. boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange
Baltimore sent Don Barksdale to Boston on August 27, 1953 for Jim Doherty, Herm Hedderick, Mo Mahoney, Vernon Stokes and cash. Basketball-Reference's Baltimore, Boston and league-wide transaction logs all list that date and package, so the legacy August 28 route is corrected by one day. The source-backed review also normalizes two player names from the old intake: Francis Mahoney is the player known in the NBA record as Mo Mahoney, and Herman Hedderick is Herm Hedderick. Boston was acquiring a proven frontcourt player who had just made the 1953 All-Star team for Baltimore.

Boston Return
Barksdale gave the Celtics two full seasons of useful frontcourt play. He appeared in 63 games in 1953-54, averaging 21.6 minutes, 7.3 points and 5.5 rebounds, then played all 72 games in 1954-55 while averaging 10.5 points and 7.6 rebounds. Across the two seasons he totaled 135 regular-season appearances and averaged 9.0 points and 6.6 rebounds for Boston. The production was below his Baltimore All-Star peak, but the Celtics received a legitimate multi-year rotation starter from a package built mostly around fringe or future players.

Baltimore Return
The Bullets received very little measurable NBA production from the four players. Mahoney appeared in two Baltimore games and did not score. Hedderick remained in military service throughout 1953-54 and later played only five NBA games, all for New York in 1954-55. Basketball-Reference lists Doherty and Stokes as drafted players but credits neither with an NBA appearance. Baltimore also received cash, and the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public record. That financial consideration deserves credit, but it cannot erase the large difference in realized playing value.

Hindsight Comparison
Boston acquired the only durable NBA contributor in the transaction. Barksdale supplied 135 games over two seasons, while Baltimore's four-player return produced only Mahoney's two Bullets appearances and no later Baltimore value from the other three players. The undisclosed cash payment prevents an extreme bottom grade for the Bullets, but the documented basketball outcome remains heavily tilted toward Boston.

Final Verdict
Celtics Win, A-/D+. Boston receives an A- for turning four marginal rights/player assets and cash into two productive seasons from a recent All-Star. Baltimore receives a D+ because the cash return was real but unquantified and the four players produced almost no NBA value for the Bullets. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Minneapolis sold Lew Hitch's player rights to Milwaukee on October 27, 1953. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Lakers, Hawks and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts record classified Hitch as 1953 draft rights, but that is not historically possible: the Lakers drafted him in 1951, and he had already played 131 regular-season games across two Minneapolis seasons before this transaction. The canonical asset is therefore repaired to a veteran player-rights/direct-player sale.

Milwaukee Return
Whatever the later rights bookkeeping, Milwaukee received substantial immediate basketball value. Basketball-Reference credits Hitch with all 72 Hawks games in 1953-54, including 2,452 minutes. He averaged 34.1 minutes, 8.0 points, 9.6 rebounds and 2.0 assists, giving a 21-win Milwaukee team one of its heaviest workloads. Hitch's 3.3 win shares were also the strongest single-season total of his career to that point. The October sale therefore gave Milwaukee far more than a speculative or unused right; it put a veteran frontcourt player into a major role for the season.

Minneapolis Return
Minneapolis received cash, but the reviewed public transaction pages do not preserve the amount. The Lakers had already captured two championship seasons from Hitch before selling his rights, so this was not a case of giving away an untested player. The cash return has real but unquantifiable value. The record also becomes complicated because Basketball-Reference separately lists Milwaukee trading Hitch back to Minneapolis for Bobby Watson on December 21 even though its player statistics credit Hitch's entire 1953-54 season to Milwaukee. That inconsistency argues against pretending the downstream rights path is fully resolved.

Hindsight Comparison
The October transaction itself favors Milwaukee because the Hawks obtained a full 72-game season and a large frontcourt workload from Hitch, while the Lakers' cash return cannot be measured. The later December transaction entry is preserved as a separate source-backed record and should not be used to erase the value Milwaukee clearly received during 1953-54. The uncertainty is enough to keep the grade gap moderate rather than extreme.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, B/C. Milwaukee receives a B for acquiring a veteran who played all 72 games and averaged more than 34 minutes per game in 1953-54. Minneapolis receives a C for legitimate but undisclosed cash after already receiving two championship seasons from Hitch. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
