los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange
Minneapolis traded Jim Fritsche to Baltimore for cash on November 11, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Bullets and league-wide transaction pages all record the same deal. Fritsche had been the ninth overall pick in the 1953 draft, but the defending-champion Lakers used him for only two games and eight total minutes before moving him. Baltimore was buying a young frontcourt player with first-round pedigree, while Minneapolis chose immediate financial consideration instead of carrying him as a developmental piece.

Baltimore Return
Fritsche became a regular part of the Bullets' rotation almost immediately. He appeared in 66 Baltimore games during 1953-54, totaling 1,213 minutes, 280 points, 217 rebounds and 73 assists. His per-game line of 18.4 minutes, 4.2 points and 3.3 rebounds was modest, but it was meaningful availability for a club that needed bodies and developmental minutes. Baltimore also retained enough asset value to move Fritsche again on October 26, 1954, when the Bullets traded him to Fort Wayne for Ken Murray. That second transaction gives the original acquisition value beyond one season of minutes.

Minneapolis Return
The Lakers received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public transaction records. That prevents a precise financial comparison. Minneapolis had already made the decision quickly: Fritsche played only two games and eight minutes for the Lakers before the trade. Because the club was defending a championship and had a veteran-heavy frontcourt, converting a little-used rookie into cash was understandable. Still, the surviving record does not show another player, pick or identifiable downstream asset tied to the payment.

Hindsight Comparison
Baltimore received the stronger measurable basketball return. Fritsche supplied 66 games and more than 1,200 minutes in the season immediately after the trade, then retained enough value to be exchanged again the next fall. The Lakers' side was real but economically opaque. Fritsche never became a major NBA player, so the gap should remain moderate rather than dramatic, but the Bullets clearly extracted more documented roster value from the transaction.

Final Verdict
Bullets Win, B-/C. Baltimore receives a B- for one full season of usable rotation depth plus a later trade asset. Minneapolis receives a C for legitimate but undisclosed cash after giving up a rookie it had barely used. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Baltimore sent Max Zaslofsky to Milwaukee on November 25, 1953 for Bob Houbregs. Basketball-Reference records the same player-for-player exchange on both team transaction pages and in the league-wide 1953-54 ledger. Zaslofsky was a proven veteran scorer who had already made an All-Star team and led the BAA in scoring earlier in his career. Houbregs was the third overall pick in the 1953 draft and only 21 years old, so Baltimore was trading established production for a younger frontcourt piece.

Baltimore Return
Houbregs immediately handled a major role for the Bullets. He appeared in 59 Baltimore games during 1953-54, logging 1,804 minutes with 544 points, 329 rebounds and 114 assists. He averaged more than 30 minutes per game after the trade and remained with Baltimore for 10 games in 1954-55 before the franchise folded. His later NBA career continued elsewhere, but Baltimore's direct return was still substantial: the Bullets received most of a season of starter-level minutes from a rookie with meaningful upside.

Milwaukee Return
Zaslofsky's direct Milwaukee stint was short but productive. He appeared in nine games, averaging 33.2 minutes and 15.1 points. More importantly, the Hawks retained his asset value. On December 21 they traded Zaslofsky to Fort Wayne for Chuck Share. Share then played 47 Milwaukee games that season and 69 in 1954-55 before remaining with the franchise after its move to St. Louis. He became the club's regular center for years and was part of the 1958 NBA championship team. That downstream conversion is the largest long-term outcome attached to the original exchange.

Hindsight Comparison
Baltimore received useful immediate value from Houbregs, so this was not a one-sided failure. The Bullets got 59 games and heavy minutes from a young frontcourt player. Milwaukee, however, turned Zaslofsky into both short-term scoring and the trade asset that produced Share, whose multi-year run became part of the Hawks' rise into a championship contender. The downstream chain creates a clear Milwaukee advantage while still recognizing that Baltimore's return was real.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, A-/B-. Milwaukee receives an A- because Zaslofsky produced immediate scoring and then directly became Chuck Share, a long-term franchise center and 1958 champion. Baltimore receives a B- for acquiring a rookie who supplied 59 games and major minutes before the original Bullets franchise folded. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Milwaukee sent Jack Nichols to Boston on November 29, 1953 for John Azary, Fred Eydt, Tom Lillis, J.C. Maze and Paul Unruh. Basketball-Reference records that exact package on the Hawks, Celtics and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages, and the Red Auerbach and Ben Kerner executive ledgers independently preserve the same exchange. The structure looks large because Boston sent five names, but the source-backed review has to distinguish roster rights from actual NBA production. Nichols was the only player in the package who produced measurable post-trade NBA minutes.

Boston Return
Nichols appeared in six Celtics games in 1953-54, seven in 1954-55 and three in 1955-56. Across those three partial seasons he totaled 16 games, 542 minutes, 214 points, 147 rebounds and 64 assists. The role was small, but it was real. Boston received a veteran forward who could fill rotation minutes over several seasons without surrendering a player who later emerged as a meaningful NBA contributor. Nichols' best Boston stretch came immediately after the deal, when he averaged 35.2 minutes and 16.7 points across six games in 1953-54.

Milwaukee Return
Azary, Eydt, Lillis, Maze and Unruh generated no documented NBA regular-season appearances after the trade. Basketball-Reference preserves their draft or player identities, but none became an NBA rotation piece for Milwaukee. That makes the five-player return look much larger on paper than it was in realized basketball value. The Hawks effectively exchanged a veteran who still had some usable NBA minutes for a group of rights and fringe assets that did not translate into league production.

Hindsight Comparison
Boston received the stronger realized return because Nichols was the only asset in the transaction to play another NBA game. At the same time, 16 games across three seasons is too little to treat this as a major win. The Celtics gained useful depth at very low realized opportunity cost, while Milwaukee's five-player package never produced a corresponding NBA contribution. The source-backed result should therefore favor Boston without exaggerating the importance of the trade.

Final Verdict
Celtics Win, B-/D+. Boston receives a B- for acquiring the only post-trade NBA contributor and getting 16 games of usable veteran depth. Milwaukee receives a D+ because none of the five incoming players produced a documented NBA appearance after the exchange. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Milwaukee traded Max Zaslofsky to Fort Wayne on December 21, 1953 for Chuck Share. Basketball-Reference lists the same exchange on the Hawks, Pistons and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages. The move came less than a month after Milwaukee acquired Zaslofsky from Baltimore, so the Hawks effectively converted a veteran scoring guard into a younger center with size and upside. Share had been the first overall pick in the 1950 draft and was still only 26, while Zaslofsky was an established scorer entering the later stage of his career.

Milwaukee Return
Share's role expanded immediately after the trade. He played 47 games for Milwaukee in 1953-54, logging 1,421 minutes with 528 points and 493 rebounds. His averages jumped to 30.2 minutes, 11.2 points and 10.5 rebounds per game, and Basketball-Reference credits him with 4.6 win shares for the Hawks portion of the season. He stayed with the franchise through the move to St. Louis, became a regular center for several years and remained on the roster during the 1958 championship season. That continuity makes him one of the stronger long-term returns in Milwaukee's early transaction history.

Fort Wayne Return
Zaslofsky was not a throwaway return. He appeared in 45 Pistons games in 1953-54, averaging 25.9 minutes and 11.0 points while contributing 495 total points. He then played 70 games for Fort Wayne in 1954-55 at 11.2 points per game and remained on the roster into 1955-56. For a team trying to contend immediately, adding an experienced scorer had clear utility. The Pistons received more short-term perimeter production than Share had been giving them before the deal, and the exchange helped both teams address different roster needs.

Hindsight Comparison
Both sides received real value, but Milwaukee's return aged better. Zaslofsky provided two useful Fort Wayne seasons, while Share became a multi-year starting-caliber center, followed the franchise to St. Louis and remained part of the roster through the 1958 title run. The gap is therefore about longevity and franchise fit rather than one team receiving nothing. Fort Wayne's return deserves a strong grade, but Share's sustained role gives the Hawks the superior realized outcome.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, A/B+. Milwaukee receives an A for acquiring a long-term center who immediately produced 47 strong games and remained with the franchise through its 1958 championship season. Fort Wayne receives a B+ because Zaslofsky supplied substantial scoring over the next two seasons. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Milwaukee traded Lew Hitch to Minneapolis for Bobby Watson on December 21, 1953. Basketball-Reference lists the same transaction on the Hawks, Lakers and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages, and the Ben Kerner and Max Winter executive ledgers preserve the exchange as well. The transaction itself is therefore well supported. The difficult part is the roster chronology that follows. Hitch's 1953-54 line is entirely credited to Milwaukee, and Watson did not appear in an NBA game until the following season. That means the public transaction date should not be treated as proof that both players immediately changed uniforms that night.

Minneapolis Return
Hitch became the more valuable NBA player. Basketball-Reference credits him with 57 Milwaukee games and 17 Minneapolis games in 1954-55, then 69 more Minneapolis games in 1955-56. Across those two Lakers stints after the recorded trade, he supplied regular frontcourt minutes, rebounding and interior depth. His 1954-55 Minneapolis segment produced 17 games, 323 minutes, 98 points and 93 rebounds, and the next season he appeared in 69 games. The chronology is imperfect, but the long-term direction is clear: Hitch eventually returned to Minneapolis and gave the Lakers substantially more NBA production than Watson produced for Milwaukee.

Milwaukee Return
Watson's NBA career was brief. He debuted in 1954-55 and played 63 total games that season, 50 with Minneapolis and 13 with Milwaukee. His Milwaukee segment averaged 12.0 minutes, 2.2 points, 1.8 rebounds and 1.3 assists. He did not play another NBA season. That is a real contribution, but it is a small one, and the same season split that places Watson in both Minneapolis and Milwaukee underscores why the 1953 transaction ledger cannot be read as a complete movement timeline.

Hindsight Comparison
The player-value comparison favors Minneapolis because Hitch had the longer and more productive NBA career after this period, including 86 regular-season games for the Lakers across 1954-55 and 1955-56. Watson's only NBA season produced 13 Milwaukee games. The uncertainty lies in transaction timing, not in which player generated more eventual NBA value. That warrants a Lakers edge, but the grade gap stays moderate because the public records do not fully reconcile when each player's rights and roster status changed hands.

Final Verdict
Lakers Win, B/C+. Minneapolis receives a B for ultimately getting the more useful player and another full season of frontcourt depth from Hitch. Milwaukee receives a C+ because Watson produced only 13 Hawks games and one NBA season overall. Confidence is medium because the verified transaction ledger conflicts with the team-season chronology. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Fort Wayne sold Fred Schaus' player rights to the New York Knicks for cash on December 29, 1953. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, New York and league transaction logs agree on the sale. The legacy TradeVerdicts record classified Schaus as draft rights, but he was an active veteran in his fifth NBA season and had already played 23 games for the Pistons that year. After the sale he played 44 games for New York, logging 1,243 minutes with 387 points, 217 rebounds and 88 assists. Because the cash amount is undisclosed while the Knicks received substantial immediate rotation value, the measurable hindsight return favors New York.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Fort Wayne sold Fred Schaus' player rights to New York on December 29, 1953. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Pistons, Knicks and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts asset called this draft rights, but that classification is historically wrong. Schaus was already a veteran NBA forward in his fifth season and had played 23 Fort Wayne games in 1953-54 before the transaction. The asset is therefore repaired to a veteran player-rights/direct-player sale rather than a draft-rights transfer.

New York Return
Schaus moved directly into a meaningful Knicks role. Basketball-Reference credits him with 44 New York games after the sale, totaling 1,243 minutes, 387 points, 217 rebounds and 88 assists. He averaged 28.3 minutes, 8.8 points, 4.9 rebounds and 2.0 assists in the Knicks segment of the season. New York finished 44-28 and reached the Eastern Division round-robin, so the acquisition supplied useful veteran minutes for a contender rather than merely preserving a future right. Schaus did not remain in the NBA beyond that season, but the immediate return was tangible.

Fort Wayne Return
Fort Wayne received cash, and the reviewed public transaction pages do not preserve the amount. That prevents a precise financial valuation. The Pistons had already received 23 Schaus appearances that season before selling his rights, and the move cleared a veteran from the roster while returning money. The surviving record does not identify another player, draft selection or downstream basketball asset tied to the payment, so the Pistons' side has to be graded conservatively rather than treated as equivalent to New York's documented rotation production.

Hindsight Comparison
The Knicks received the stronger measurable return. Schaus played 44 games and more than 1,200 minutes for New York immediately after the sale, while Fort Wayne's cash return is legitimate but unquantified. This was not a franchise-changing acquisition because Schaus' NBA career ended after 1953-54, but it was clearly more than a speculative rights purchase. The proper hindsight gap is moderate: New York bought one useful stretch of veteran production, while Fort Wayne accepted an undisclosed financial return.

Final Verdict
Knicks Win, B/C. New York receives a B for adding 44 games of useful veteran rotation production at an undisclosed cash cost. Fort Wayne receives a C for a real but unquantifiable cash return after already using Schaus for 23 games that season. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Minneapolis sold Bob Harrison's player rights to Milwaukee on February 2, 1954. Basketball-Reference lists the same sale on the Lakers, Hawks and league-wide 1953-54 transaction pages. Harrison was not an untested prospect: he had already played four full seasons plus 40 games of 1953-54 for Minneapolis, won three NBA championships with the Lakers and remained an active rotation guard. The transaction is therefore best understood as the sale of a veteran player's rights for cash, with the amount not preserved in the reviewed public record.

Milwaukee Return
Harrison immediately became one of Milwaukee's heaviest-minute guards. He played 24 Hawks games to finish 1953-54, averaging 34.3 minutes, 9.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 3.5 assists. He then appeared in all 72 Milwaukee games in 1954-55, averaging 31.9 minutes, 10.1 points, 3.1 rebounds and 3.5 assists. That is substantial realized value from a February cash purchase: the Hawks added an experienced guard who could handle starter-level minutes across the remainder of one season and the entirety of the next.

Minneapolis Return
The Lakers received cash, but the reviewed transaction pages do not disclose the amount. Minneapolis had already extracted considerable value from Harrison before the sale, including three championship seasons and more than four years of regular rotation work. The timing also came during another championship season, so the Lakers were moving an established veteran from a deep roster rather than giving away an unknown asset. Still, the cash cannot be translated into an identifiable player, pick or downstream basketball return in the surviving transaction record.

Hindsight Comparison
Milwaukee received the stronger measurable return because Harrison supplied 96 regular-season games across the remainder of 1953-54 and all of 1954-55, including starter-level minutes and double-digit scoring in the latter season. Minneapolis' financial return was real but opaque. The Lakers' prior success with Harrison reduces the sting of the sale, but prior championships are not part of the post-trade return. The result therefore favors Milwaukee without treating the move as a franchise-changing transaction.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, A-/C. Milwaukee receives an A- for buying a proven guard who immediately played heavy minutes and then appeared in every game the following season. Minneapolis receives a C for a legitimate but undisclosed cash return after already receiving years of championship-era production from Harrison. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Milwaukee traded Don Sunderlage to Minneapolis for Pep Saul on September 18, 1954. Basketball-Reference lists the same exchange on both teams' 1954-55 transaction pages. The players entered from very different points. Sunderlage was 24 and coming off an All-Star rookie season for Milwaukee in which he averaged 11.2 points across 68 games. Saul was 30, a veteran guard and three-time champion with Minneapolis whose role had gradually declined. The swap therefore traded youth and recent peak production for a more experienced but lower-usage guard.

Milwaukee Return
Saul played 65 games for the Hawks in 1954-55, logging 1,139 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 287 points, 134 rebounds and 104 assists, or 17.5 minutes, 4.4 points, 2.1 rebounds and 1.6 assists per game. Those are modest numbers, but he stayed available for nearly the entire season and gave Milwaukee far more total minutes than the outgoing player produced for Minneapolis. The 1954-55 campaign was Saul's final NBA season, so his value was concentrated entirely in that one-year return.

Minneapolis Return
Sunderlage's Lakers stint was much smaller than his All-Star year in Milwaukee. He appeared in 45 games but averaged only 9.0 minutes, 2.5 points, 1.2 rebounds and 0.8 assists. His season totals were 404 minutes, 114 points, 56 rebounds and 37 assists. He did not play another NBA season. Minneapolis therefore acquired the younger player with the stronger recent résumé, but the realized result never matched that upside. His role collapsed, and the trade did not produce a long-term Lakers contributor.

Hindsight Comparison
Milwaukee received the stronger post-trade return because Saul supplied almost three times as many minutes and materially more total production in the only season either player had left in the NBA. That does not make the swap a major win: Saul was a low-usage veteran on a 26-win team, and Sunderlage's Lakers tenure still produced 45 games. But hindsight should follow realized value rather than the players' pre-trade reputations. On that basis, the Hawks got the more useful final-season guard.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, B-/C. Milwaukee receives a B- for 65 games and more than 1,100 minutes from Saul in his final NBA season. Minneapolis receives a C because Sunderlage's younger, All-Star profile translated into only 404 minutes and no later NBA season. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The Exchange
Fort Wayne traded Fred Scolari to Boston on October 16, 1954 for Bob Harris. 'rights to Bob Harris (Anderson)' is not a separate player shell or a draft-rights asset; it is Robert Anderson Harris, the veteran forward Boston had acquired from Fort Wayne in December 1950. The canonical trade is therefore a direct player-for-player exchange.

Boston Return
Scolari played 59 games for Boston in 1954-55, the final season of his career. The legacy wording 'rights to Bob Harris' is therefore better understood as veteran player rights, not a new prospect or draft asset.

Boston received the stronger realized return. Scolari's 59 games and 619 minutes were modest, but they still represent a full season of reserve utility. Fort Wayne received no post-trade NBA appearances from Harris. Because Scolari was at the end of his own career and played a limited role, the result should not be treated as a major organizational win. A moderate Celtics advantage best matches the documented outcome.

Celtics Win, B/C-. Boston receives a B for turning a non-playing veteran-rights asset into 59 games of usable backcourt depth. Fort Wayne receives a C- because Harris did not appear in another NBA game after the trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Baltimore traded Jim Fritsche to the Fort Wayne Pistons for Ken Murray on October 26, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Baltimore, Fort Wayne, league and executive transaction logs agree on the straight player-for-player swap. Fritsche appeared in 16 games for Fort Wayne, totaling 151 minutes, 45 points and 32 rebounds before his NBA career ended. Murray played six games for Baltimore before the Bullets disbanded on November 27, then was selected by Philadelphia in the dispersal draft and played 60 Warriors games. Fort Wayne received slightly more direct post-trade value from the exchange, but the limited minutes on both sides make this a minor result.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Baltimore sent Jim Fritsche to Fort Wayne on October 26, 1954 for Ken Murray. Basketball-Reference records the same trade on the Bullets, Pistons and league-wide 1954-55 transaction pages, and Fred Zollner's executive ledger independently preserves the exchange. Fritsche was a second-year forward who had played 66 Baltimore games the previous season after arriving from Minneapolis. Murray was a veteran guard who had already spent parts of two seasons with Fort Wayne around two years of U.S. Army service. The swap therefore exchanged a younger reserve forward for a more experienced guard.

Fort Wayne Return
Fritsche appeared in 16 Pistons games during 1954-55, logging 151 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 45 points, 32 rebounds and four assists, or 9.4 minutes, 2.8 points and 2.0 rebounds per game. Those were the final games of his NBA career. The contribution was small, but it gave a deep Fort Wayne team another reserve frontcourt option during a season in which the Pistons finished first in the Western Division and reached the NBA Finals.

Baltimore Return
Murray played only six games for Baltimore before the franchise disbanded on November 27. He logged 134 minutes with 56 points, 11 rebounds and 26 assists in those games. After the Bullets folded, Philadelphia selected him in the dispersal draft, and he played 60 Warriors games during the remainder of the season. That later Philadelphia production should not be credited to Baltimore as trade return; it followed the dissolution of the franchise rather than a subsequent Bullets transaction.

Hindsight Comparison
Fort Wayne received the slightly stronger direct return, but the difference is small. Fritsche produced 16 games and 151 minutes for the Pistons, while Murray supplied six games and 134 minutes before Baltimore ceased operations. Neither side retained a durable asset from the exchange. Murray's later 60-game Philadelphia season demonstrates that he still had NBA value, but Baltimore did not realize that value after the franchise folded. A narrow Pistons edge fits the documented outcome without overstating a minor transaction.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, C+/C. Fort Wayne receives a C+ for 16 games of reserve frontcourt depth from Fritsche. Baltimore receives a C for six useful games from Murray before the franchise disbanded. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: Syracuse sold Jackie Moore's player rights to the Milwaukee Hawks on November 1, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse, Milwaukee and league transaction logs agree on the sale, while RealGM confirms Moore went undrafted in 1954 and had signed with Syracuse as a free agent. With Milwaukee receiving almost no direct playing value and Syracuse receiving undisclosed cash, the source-backed result favors the Nationals.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Syracuse sold Jackie Moore's player rights to Milwaukee on November 1, 1954. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Nationals, Hawks and league-wide transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts record treated Moore as a 1954 draft-rights player, but RealGM's transaction history shows that Moore went undrafted and signed with Syracuse as a free agent. He had already made his NBA debut for the Nationals on October 31. The canonical asset is therefore veteran/current player rights rather than draft rights.

Milwaukee Return
Moore appeared in only one game for the Hawks, logging 13 minutes with two points, four rebounds and one assist. Milwaukee eventually placed him on waivers on February 14, 1955. Philadelphia signed him the following day, and his career continued there for three seasons. The later Warriors run included 131 games and a place on the 1956 championship roster, but that value did not accrue to Milwaukee because the Hawks had already relinquished him. The direct Hawks return from the November sale was therefore almost entirely limited to one brief appearance.

Syracuse Return
Syracuse received cash, and the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public record. The Nationals had used Moore for one five-minute appearance before selling his rights, so they converted a player who was not part of their established rotation into immediate consideration. Syracuse then went on to win the 1955 NBA championship without Moore. The unknown amount prevents a precise financial grade, but the transaction cost the Nationals almost no realized on-court value while producing a tangible payment.

Hindsight Comparison
Syracuse received the stronger direct return. Milwaukee bought a young player's rights, used him once, and waived him roughly three and a half months later. Moore later demonstrated that he could be a useful NBA reserve in Philadelphia, but the Hawks did not capture that value. The Nationals' cash return is unquantified, so the gap should remain moderate, but the one-game Milwaukee outcome is too small to support an even grade.

Final Verdict
Nationals Win, C+/D+. Syracuse receives a C+ for converting a marginal roster piece into cash. Milwaukee receives a D+ because Moore produced only one Hawks game before being waived, even though he later became a useful Philadelphia reserve. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Philadelphia sold Gene Shue's player rights to the New York Knicks on November 28, 1954. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, New York and league transaction logs agree on the sale. The legacy TradeVerdicts draft-rights classification was wrong because Shue had already made his NBA debut and played six Warriors games before the transaction. He then appeared in 56 Knicks games in 1954-55 and all 72 in 1955-56, giving New York 128 regular-season games before the Knicks traded him to Fort Wayne for Ron Sobie in April 1956. Philadelphia received undisclosed cash, so New York owns the stronger measurable return without warranting the legacy A/F gap.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange
Philadelphia sold Gene Shue's player rights to New York on November 28, 1954. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Warriors, Knicks and league-wide 1954-55 transaction pages. The source-backed review fixes the most important structural defect in the legacy record: Shue was not a dormant 1954 draft-rights asset by late November. Philadelphia had drafted him third overall that spring, but he had already made his NBA debut on November 13 and appeared in six Warriors games. The November transaction therefore transferred the rights to an active NBA player.

New York Return
Shue immediately became a regular Knicks guard. He appeared in 56 New York games during the remainder of 1954-55 and then played all 72 games in 1955-56. Across those two seasons, the Knicks received 128 regular-season appearances from a young player who was still developing into the guard he would become later in Detroit. New York also preserved residual trade value. On April 30, 1956, the Knicks sent Shue to Fort Wayne for Ron Sobie, so the original cash purchase produced two seasons of playing value plus another NBA player in a later transaction.

Philadelphia Return
Philadelphia received cash, but the reviewed transaction logs do not preserve the amount. That consideration was real and should not be treated as zero. The Warriors also moved Shue before his best NBA seasons, which makes the hindsight cost visible, but his later five-time All-Star run came after New York traded him to Fort Wayne and should not all be credited to the Knicks' side of this transaction. The direct comparison is Philadelphia's undisclosed payment against 128 Knicks games and the later Sobie asset.

Hindsight Comparison
New York received the stronger realized return. Shue gave the Knicks two seasons of regular availability and remained valuable enough to be traded for another player. At the same time, the legacy A/F split overstates the evidence because the cash amount is unknown and Shue's peak seasons occurred after he left New York. A clear but moderated Knicks advantage better separates the value the Knicks actually realized from the larger career value Shue later created elsewhere.

Final Verdict
Knicks Win, B+/C-. New York receives a B+ for 128 regular-season games from Shue plus the later trade return of Ron Sobie. Philadelphia receives a C- for legitimate but undisclosed cash while surrendering a young player who became a durable NBA contributor. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Rochester sold Alex Hannum's player rights to Milwaukee on December 10, 1954. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Royals, Hawks and league-wide 1954-55 transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts record treated Hannum as 1954 draft rights, but that is impossible. He had entered the NBA in 1949 and played six seasons before the transaction, including all 72 games for Rochester in 1953-54. Milwaukee therefore bought the rights to an established veteran forward rather than a developmental prospect.

Milwaukee Return
Hannum stepped directly into the Hawks' rotation. He appeared in 53 Milwaukee games during 1954-55, logging 1,088 minutes and averaging 20.5 minutes, 5.9 points, 4.6 rebounds and 2.0 assists. He returned for 71 games after the franchise moved to St. Louis in 1955-56, adding 1,480 minutes. That gives the Hawks franchise 124 games across the two seasons immediately following the sale. Hannum's later return to St. Louis as a free agent and championship coaching career are historically important, but they are not credited as direct trade value because they followed a separate transaction path.

Rochester Return
Rochester received cash, but the reviewed transaction logs do not preserve the amount. The Royals had received three productive seasons from Hannum before selling his rights, including a full 72-game campaign in 1953-54. Converting a 31-year-old veteran into cash was therefore a defensible roster decision. Still, the surviving record contains no player, pick or later asset chain tied to the payment, while Milwaukee received two seasons of documented rotation production.

Hindsight Comparison
Milwaukee received the stronger measurable return. Hannum supplied 124 games across the next two seasons and remained a regular frontcourt option, while Rochester's cash consideration cannot be quantified. The legacy A-/D+ treatment overstates the separation because Hannum was a useful veteran rather than a star and the cash amount is unknown. A clear but moderate Hawks advantage better reflects what the transaction itself produced.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, B+/C. Milwaukee receives a B+ for acquiring two seasons and 124 games of veteran frontcourt depth. Rochester receives a C for legitimate but undisclosed cash after already receiving three seasons from Hannum. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: New York sold Paul Hoffman's player rights to the Philadelphia Warriors on January 12, 1955. Basketball-Reference's New York, Philadelphia and league transaction logs agree on the sale. Hoffman had played 18 games for the Knicks after arriving from the defunct Baltimore Bullets, then appeared in only 11 games for Philadelphia. He averaged 11.0 minutes, 1.5 points, 1.7 rebounds and 1.4 assists for the Warriors, and those were the final NBA games of his career. Because New York received cash and Philadelphia obtained only a brief low-impact stint, the verified record favors the Knicks, though the undisclosed payment keeps the grade gap modest.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange
New York sold Paul Hoffman's player rights to Philadelphia on January 12, 1955. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Knicks, Warriors and league-wide 1954-55 transaction pages. Hoffman had spent the early part of the season with Baltimore before that franchise folded, then appeared in 18 games for New York. Philadelphia was acquiring an experienced backcourt player with several productive NBA seasons behind him, while the Knicks chose to turn his remaining rights into cash. The public transaction logs do not preserve the amount paid.

Philadelphia Return
Hoffman's Warriors stint was brief and light. He appeared in 11 games, averaging 11.0 minutes, 1.5 points, 1.7 rebounds and 1.4 assists while shooting .241 from the field. Those 11 appearances were the final games of his NBA career. Philadelphia therefore received some immediate depth but no multi-season contribution, no later trade asset and no meaningful long-term rotation value. The acquisition was not worthless, but the realized basketball return was small.

New York Return
The Knicks received cash. Because the amount is unknown, the financial return cannot be measured precisely, but New York surrendered a player who produced only 11 more NBA games. That makes the decision easier to defend than the legacy F grade suggested. The Knicks had already used Hoffman for 18 games and converted his remaining rights into value before his career ended. Nothing in the surviving record indicates that Philadelphia unlocked a meaningful second act.

Hindsight Comparison
The verified outcome leans toward New York. Philadelphia received only a short, low-minute stint before Hoffman's NBA career ended, while the Knicks at least received cash consideration. The unknown payment prevents a dramatic grade gap because the exact economic value is unavailable, but the Warriors did not realize enough on-court value to justify the old claim that they clearly won the transaction. A modest Knicks advantage best fits the surviving evidence.

Final Verdict
Knicks Win, B-/C-. New York receives a B- for converting Hoffman's remaining rights into cash before his career ended. Philadelphia receives a C- for 11 low-impact games with no later NBA value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Philadelphia sold Zeke Zawoluk's player rights to the Rochester Royals on May 12, 1955. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Rochester and league transaction logs agree on the sale. Zawoluk had just completed his third NBA season, appearing in 67 games for the Warriors at 16.7 minutes, 6.4 points and 3.8 rebounds per game. He never appeared in another NBA game after the transaction, so Rochester received no realized on-court value from the rights it purchased. Philadelphia's cash return is undisclosed, but converting a player whose NBA career had ended into consideration gives the Warriors the stronger hindsight outcome.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange
Philadelphia sold Zeke Zawoluk's player rights to Rochester on May 12, 1955. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Warriors, Royals and league-wide 1954-55 transaction pages. Zawoluk had just finished his third NBA season and was still only 24, so Rochester was not purchasing the rights to a long-retired veteran. He had appeared in 67 Philadelphia games in 1954-55 after playing 71 the year before, giving the Royals a reasonable basis to expect usable frontcourt depth. Philadelphia chose cash instead of carrying his rights into another season.

Rochester Return
The expected on-court return never arrived. Basketball-Reference lists Zawoluk's NBA career ending with the 1954-55 Philadelphia season. He has no 1955-56 Rochester line and no later NBA appearance. That makes the transaction easy to separate from deals where a buyer received even a short reserve stint: the Royals acquired rights that produced zero documented NBA games. Zawoluk's earlier career had been respectable, but none of that prior production belongs to Rochester's side of this exchange.

Philadelphia Return
The Warriors received cash. The amount is not preserved in the reviewed transaction logs, so the precise financial return cannot be measured. Still, Philadelphia converted an outgoing player right into consideration and then watched the player leave the NBA without producing another game. That is the strongest possible evidence that the sale did not cost the Warriors future on-court value. The legacy F grade therefore reverses the actual realized outcome.

Hindsight Comparison
Philadelphia received the superior realized return. Rochester paid for player rights that never generated an NBA appearance, while the Warriors received cash for a player whose career ended before the next season. The unknown payment argues against assigning an extreme top grade to Philadelphia because the size of the financial benefit remains unavailable. Even so, the direction of the result is clear: Rochester realized no basketball value from the asset.

Final Verdict
Warriors Win, B/C-. Philadelphia receives a B for converting Zawoluk's remaining rights into cash before his NBA career ended. Rochester receives a C- because the acquired rights produced no NBA appearances. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Fort Wayne acquired the draft rights to Chuck Noble from the Philadelphia Warriors on June 1, 1955. RealGM's Fort Wayne transaction history and Noble's player transaction log agree on the rights transfer, while Basketball-Reference confirms Philadelphia originally drafted Noble in 1954 and that he debuted for Fort Wayne in 1955-56. Noble then spent seven NBA seasons with the Pistons franchise, appearing in 411 games and making the 1960 All-Star team. The legacy archive record lists cash going to Philadelphia, but Basketball-Reference's team and league transaction ledgers omit the June 1 transfer, so the exact consideration carries thinner archival support than the rights acquisition itself. Even with that limitation, Fort Wayne received the clearly stronger realized basketball value.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
RealGM records Fort Wayne acquiring Chuck Noble's draft rights from Philadelphia on June 1, 1955. Noble had been Philadelphia's fourth-round pick in the 1954 draft but spent 1954-55 outside the NBA. Basketball-Reference confirms the Warriors drafted him and that his NBA debut came with Fort Wayne in November 1955. The legacy TradeVerdicts record also carries cash from Fort Wayne to Philadelphia, but Basketball-Reference's 1954-55 and 1955-56 transaction ledgers do not list the June 1 transaction. That source gap means the rights transfer is well supported while the exact consideration deserves a lower-confidence note.

Fort Wayne Return
Noble became an immediate rotation regular once he signed with the Pistons. He played all 72 games in 1955-56, averaging 28.0 minutes, 9.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 3.9 assists. He stayed with the franchise through its move to Detroit and ultimately logged 411 NBA games across seven seasons. Noble's best individual recognition came in 1960, when he was selected to the Western Conference All-Star team. He was never a franchise star, but turning a dormant draft right into a seven-year contributor is substantial realized value.

Philadelphia Return
The Warriors' legacy side of the exchange is cash, but the amount is not preserved and the Basketball-Reference transaction pages do not independently document the June 1 transfer. That prevents a precise evaluation of Philadelphia's consideration. What is clear is the opportunity cost: Noble became a long-term NBA player immediately after Fort Wayne obtained his rights. Philadelphia had already held those rights for more than a year without bringing him into the league, so monetizing them was understandable, but hindsight shows that the player still had considerable value.

Hindsight Comparison
Fort Wayne received the stronger basketball return by a wide margin. Noble produced seven NBA seasons, 411 games and an All-Star selection for the Pistons franchise. Philadelphia's financial return may have had real value, but it is unquantified and not preserved consistently across the reviewed transaction ledgers. The appropriate source-backed conclusion is therefore a clear Pistons win with medium confidence on the full transaction mechanics rather than on Noble's identity or career outcome.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, A-/C. Fort Wayne receives an A- for converting Noble's rights into a seven-year contributor and 1960 All-Star. Philadelphia receives a C for an unquantified financial return on a player it had not signed, while surrendering substantial future NBA value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The Exchange
RealGM records Fort Wayne acquiring Corky Devlin's draft rights from Philadelphia on August 1, 1955. The Warriors had selected Devlin in the second round, 11th overall, only a few months earlier. Basketball-Reference confirms the Philadelphia draft selection and Devlin's Fort Wayne debut in November 1955. Fort Wayne Return
Devlin became a dependable rotation guard immediately. He appeared in 69 games as a rookie, averaging 22.2 minutes, 7.9 points, 2.5 rebounds and 2.0 assists. He played 71 more Fort Wayne games in 1956-57 at 17.5 minutes and 6.7 points per game. Across the two seasons, the Pistons received 140 regular-season appearances and 2,777 minutes, plus 11 playoff games. That included a meaningful role on the 1955-56 team that reached the NBA Finals. Devlin was never an All-Star, but the rights clearly translated into useful multi-season production.

Philadelphia Return
The Warriors' legacy side is cash, with no surviving amount in the reviewed material. Philadelphia therefore received real financial consideration but gave up the rights to a recent second-round pick who immediately became an NBA rotation player elsewhere. The decision was not catastrophic because Devlin's career lasted only three seasons and his ceiling remained that of a useful guard rather than a star. Still, he gave Fort Wayne two full seasons of value that Philadelphia did not recapture in an identifiable player or pick.

Hindsight Comparison
Fort Wayne received the stronger realized return. Devlin played 140 games for the Pistons, appeared in the playoffs and helped provide backcourt depth during a Finals season. Philadelphia's cash return may have been useful, but it is unquantified and the exact transaction is absent from Basketball-Reference's ledger. That source gap lowers confidence in the mechanics, not in Devlin's outcome. The appropriate result is a clear but not overwhelming Pistons advantage.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, B+/C. Fort Wayne receives a B+ for acquiring two full seasons and 140 games of useful rotation play from Devlin. Philadelphia receives a C for an unquantified cash return while surrendering a recent second-round pick who became an immediate NBA contributor. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Fort Wayne traded Monk Meineke to the Rochester Royals for Odie Spears on September 30, 1955. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, Rochester and league transaction logs agree on the straight player-for-player swap. Spears played all 72 games for the Pistons in 1955-56, averaging 19.1 minutes, 6.8 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.7 assists before Fort Wayne waived him the following November. Meineke played 69 games for Rochester at 18.1 minutes, 7.1 points and 4.6 rebounds, then returned to the same franchise after its move to Cincinnati for 67 more games in 1957-58. Both teams received useful value, but Meineke's additional franchise season gives the Royals a modest hindsight edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Fort Wayne sent Monk Meineke to Rochester on September 30, 1955 for Odie Spears. Basketball-Reference records the same swap on both team transaction pages and in the league-wide 1955-56 ledger. Meineke had spent his first three NBA seasons with Fort Wayne and had been the league's first Rookie of the Year in 1952-53. Spears was a veteran forward with seven prior BAA/NBA seasons and had just completed four straight years with Rochester. The deal therefore exchanged two established rotation players rather than prospects or rights.

Fort Wayne Return
Spears gave the Pistons one full, useful season. He appeared in all 72 regular-season games in 1955-56, averaging 19.1 minutes, 6.8 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.7 assists. Fort Wayne won the Western Division and reached the NBA Finals, so Spears' availability came during a contending season. His Pistons tenure ended the next fall, however. Basketball-Reference's 1956-57 transaction log shows St. Louis claiming him on waivers from Fort Wayne on November 15, 1956. The return was therefore meaningful but short.

Rochester Return
Meineke appeared in 69 games for Rochester in 1955-56, averaging 18.1 minutes, 7.1 points, 4.6 rebounds and 1.5 assists. He did not play in 1956-57, then returned when the Royals franchise moved to Cincinnati and played 67 games in 1957-58. Across those two post-trade franchise seasons, he logged 136 games. The second stint was lighter at 11.8 minutes per game, but it still extended Rochester/Cincinnati's return beyond the single season Fort Wayne received from Spears.

Hindsight Comparison
Both teams got legitimate rotation value, which makes the legacy lopsided grading too harsh. Spears contributed all season to a Finals team, while Meineke supplied a similar first-year workload and later returned for another 67 games with the same franchise lineage. That extra season gives Rochester the more durable realized return, but the difference is not large enough for a decisive grade gap. A narrow Royals advantage best matches the documented outcomes.

Final Verdict
Royals Win, B/B-. Rochester receives a B for 136 post-trade franchise games from Meineke across two seasons. Fort Wayne receives a B- for 72 games of useful veteran depth from Spears during a Finals season before losing him on waivers the next year. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: Rochester sold Arnie Risen's player rights to the Boston Celtics on October 26, 1955. Basketball-Reference's Rochester, Boston and league transaction logs agree on the transfer, while the legacy Boston intake identifies cash as the consideration. Risen then played three seasons for Boston, appearing in 174 regular-season games and 23 playoff games. He averaged 8.1 points and 8.1 rebounds in 68 games during 1955-56, then remained an important veteran center on Boston's first championship team in 1956-57. Rochester's cash return is undisclosed, but Boston received the clearly stronger measurable basketball value from a Hall of Fame center who helped bridge the Celtics into their title era.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange
Rochester sold Arnie Risen's player rights to Boston on October 26, 1955. Basketball-Reference records Boston acquiring Risen's rights and Rochester selling them on the same date, while the legacy Boston source preserves cash as the consideration. Risen was no ordinary late-career reserve at the time of the deal. He was a four-time All-Star with Rochester, had been a major part of the Royals' 1951 championship team and remained a productive veteran center. Boston was buying experience and interior depth just before the franchise's championship window opened.

Boston Return
Risen contributed immediately. He played 68 games in 1955-56, averaging 8.1 points and 8.1 rebounds while logging 1,597 minutes. He returned for 43 games in 1956-57 and 63 in 1957-58, giving Boston 174 regular-season appearances across three seasons. His role became smaller as Bill Russell took over the center position, but Risen remained useful veteran depth and appeared in 10 playoff games during Boston's 1957 championship run. He added another 10 playoff appearances in 1958. The Celtics therefore obtained both immediate production and experienced frontcourt support during the transition into their first title era.

Rochester Return
Rochester received cash, but the reviewed records do not preserve the amount. That consideration was real and may have reflected the Royals' decision to move on from a 31-year-old veteran after seven seasons with the franchise. The basketball opportunity cost, however, is visible. Risen still had three NBA seasons left, remained productive enough to play 174 Boston games and became part of a championship roster. The Royals did not receive a player, pick or identifiable downstream basketball asset in the documented exchange.

Hindsight Comparison
Boston received the stronger realized return. Risen was no longer at his Rochester peak, but three seasons of center depth, 174 regular-season games and a role on the 1957 championship team easily outweigh an undisclosed cash return in the measurable basketball record. The unknown payment keeps Rochester from receiving the lowest possible grade, and the trade should not be confused with Boston's later acquisition of Russell as the primary cause of the dynasty. Still, the Celtics clearly extracted substantial value from a player Rochester sold.

Final Verdict
Celtics Win, A-/C. Boston receives an A- for acquiring three useful seasons from a Hall of Fame center who contributed during the franchise's first championship run. Rochester receives a C for legitimate but unquantified cash while surrendering a veteran who still had meaningful NBA value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Minneapolis sold Jim Holstein's player rights to Fort Wayne on November 28, 1955. Basketball-Reference lists the same sale on the Lakers, Pistons and league-wide 1955-56 transaction pages. Holstein had already played three full NBA seasons for Minneapolis, including 62 games in 1954-55, but he had become a modest reserve rather than a major rotation piece. Fort Wayne purchased short-term forward depth while the Lakers chose cash. The amount is not preserved in the reviewed transaction logs.

Fort Wayne Return
Holstein appeared in 27 Pistons games after the transaction, totaling 352 minutes. He averaged 13.0 minutes, 2.7 points, 2.8 rebounds and 1.4 assists while shooting .270 from the field. Fort Wayne won the Western Division and reached the NBA Finals, so even limited reserve minutes had some use during a contending season. The value ended there, however. Basketball-Reference lists 1955-56 as Holstein's final NBA season, leaving the Pistons with no multi-year contribution or downstream trade asset.

Minneapolis Return
The Lakers received cash. Because the amount is undisclosed, their side cannot be valued precisely, but the opportunity cost turned out to be small. Holstein produced only 27 more NBA games after leaving Minneapolis and then exited the league. The Lakers therefore converted the remaining rights to a declining reserve into consideration without surrendering a player who later developed into a durable contributor elsewhere.

Hindsight Comparison
Minneapolis received the stronger realized outcome. Fort Wayne did get real depth during a Finals season, so the transaction was not a complete miss, but 27 low-minute games were the entirety of Holstein's post-trade NBA value. The Lakers' cash return is unquantified yet was exchanged for a player whose career was nearly finished. That supports a modest Lakers advantage rather than the legacy Pistons edge.

Final Verdict
Lakers Win, B-/C. Minneapolis receives a B- for turning Holstein's remaining rights into cash before his NBA career ended. Fort Wayne receives a C for 27 games of reserve help during a Finals season with no later value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: The St. Louis Hawks and Rochester Royals completed a four-player exchange in early January 1956, with St. Louis receiving Jack Coleman and Jack McMahon while Rochester received Dick Ricketts and Chris Harris. RealGM splits the transaction postings across January 8 and January 9, while the legacy Atlanta source record uses January 8; Basketball-Reference's team transaction pages omit the swap even though its season statistics confirm all four players changed teams. Coleman and McMahon became multi-year Hawks contributors and remained with the franchise through the 1958 championship season. Ricketts gave Rochester/Cincinnati 183 games over three seasons, while Harris played 26 Royals games and then left the NBA. Both teams received real value, but St. Louis gained the stronger combined long-term package.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
The legacy Atlanta record describes a January 8, 1956 trade in which St. Louis sent Dick Ricketts and Chris Harris to Rochester for Jack Coleman and Jack McMahon. RealGM's league transaction history supports the four-player structure but splits the postings: Harris is listed as acquired by Rochester on January 8, while Ricketts, Coleman and McMahon are listed on January 9. Basketball-Reference's team transaction pages omit the swap entirely, even though its season splits confirm that all four players changed clubs. The safest source-backed treatment is therefore to preserve the canonical January 8 record while explicitly noting the one-day archival discrepancy.

St. Louis Return
Coleman and McMahon became durable Hawks pieces. Coleman played 41 St. Louis games after the trade in 1955-56 and then 72 games in each of the next two seasons. Across his three Hawks seasons he appeared in 185 regular-season games and remained with the franchise through the 1958 championship. McMahon supplied even more longevity: 36 games after the trade, then 72 games in each of the next three seasons before a final 25-game St. Louis season in 1959-60. Basketball-Reference credits him with 277 regular-season games for the Hawks, and he was part of the 1958 title team.

Rochester Return
Ricketts was a meaningful return rather than a throw-in. The 1955 first overall pick played 39 Rochester games after the deal, then 72 in 1956-57 and another 72 after the franchise moved to Cincinnati in 1957-58. His Royals-family total reached 183 games, with 9.5 points and 6.2 rebounds per game across that run. Harris added 26 games in 1955-56 but did not play another NBA season. Rochester therefore received one legitimate multi-year frontcourt contributor plus a short-term reserve.

Hindsight Comparison
Both clubs extracted real value, which makes the old D+ treatment for Rochester too harsh. The difference is package depth and longevity. Ricketts gave the Royals three useful seasons, but St. Louis received two multi-year contributors whose combined Hawks tenure exceeded 450 regular-season games and included the franchise's 1958 championship season. Coleman remained a productive frontcourt piece, while McMahon became a long-term guard and playmaker. That cumulative return gives the Hawks the stronger outcome without turning the deal into a failure for Rochester.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, A/B. St. Louis receives an A for acquiring two multi-year rotation players who remained through the 1958 championship, while Rochester receives a B for landing Ricketts' three useful seasons plus Harris' brief reserve stint. Confidence is medium on the exact transaction date because surviving ledgers split the four-player posting across January 8-9, but the player movement and realized value are well supported. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Boston acquired the draft rights to Bill Russell from St. Louis on April 30, 1956 for Ed Macauley and the Celtics' rights to Cliff Hagan. NBA.com's 1956-57 season review and Russell history both preserve that structure, and Basketball-Reference records Boston sending Macauley and Hagan to the Hawks for Russell. Two legacy asset details require correction. Russell was the second overall pick in the 1956 draft and had not yet played an NBA game, so Boston received draft rights rather than an active player. Hagan, meanwhile, was Boston's third-round pick in 1953 and spent the next three seasons in U.S. Air Force service before making his NBA debut with St. Louis in 1956-57.

Boston Return
Russell transformed the scale of the Celtics franchise. Boston had never won an NBA championship before his arrival; with him anchoring the defense and rebounding, the Celtics won the 1957 title and ultimately 11 championships in his 13 seasons. Russell won five MVP awards and became the defining defensive player of the league's first great dynasty. The transaction was not merely a star acquisition. It supplied the structural piece Boston's high-scoring roster lacked and created a championship model that dominated the NBA for more than a decade.

St. Louis Return
The Hawks' side was exceptionally strong by ordinary trade standards. Macauley played all 72 games in 1956-57, averaged 16.5 points and made the All-Star team, then remained a productive part of the roster during the 1958 championship season. Hagan debuted after military service, developed into one of the league's best forwards and made five consecutive NBA All-Star teams with the Hawks. In 1957-58 he averaged 19.9 points and 10.1 rebounds, and St. Louis defeated Boston in six games to win the NBA championship. The Hawks therefore converted Russell's rights into two Hall of Fame-caliber players and an actual title, not a failed package.

Hindsight Comparison
The return explains why St. Louis deserves a high grade even though Boston wins decisively. Macauley and Hagan helped produce the Hawks' only NBA championship and Hagan became a long-term star. Russell, however, delivered an unmatched combination of longevity, individual honors and team success. Eleven titles in 13 seasons, five MVP awards and the defensive identity of the Celtics dynasty exceed even the Hawks' excellent outcome. The result is one of the rare trades where the losing side can still be graded as having received championship-level value.

Final Verdict
Celtics Win, A+/A-. Boston receives an A+ for acquiring the centerpiece of 11 championship teams and one of the defining players in NBA history. St. Louis receives an A- because Macauley and Hagan were major contributors, Hagan became a five-time Hawks All-Star and the package helped produce the 1958 championship. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: On April 30, 1956, the New York Knicks traded Gene Shue to the Fort Wayne Pistons for the draft rights to Ron Sobie, whom Fort Wayne had selected seventh overall that day. Basketball-Reference's New York, Fort Wayne and league transaction logs all verify the exchange. The legacy TradeVerdicts record treated Sobie as a direct player and carried a malformed 'Ron Sobie)' label; the asset is corrected to 1956 draft rights and his canonical Basketball-Reference name. Shue became a five-time All-Star and two-time All-NBA guard during his Pistons run before Detroit later traded him back to New York for Darrall Imhoff and cash. Sobie was a useful Knick, appearing in 191 games over four seasons, but Shue's star-level production and later asset conversion give Detroit the stronger return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
New York traded Gene Shue to Fort Wayne on April 30, 1956 for Ron Sobie, whom the Pistons had just selected in the first round of the 1956 NBA Draft. Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Pistons and league transaction pages all record the swap on draft day. The source-backed repair matters because the legacy archive record treated Sobie as an established player. He had not yet appeared in the NBA; Fort Wayne drafted him seventh overall and immediately transferred his draft rights to New York. Shue, by contrast, was an active 24-year-old guard who had played all 72 Knicks games in 1955-56 and averaged 9.2 points.

Fort Wayne Return
Shue developed into one of the franchise's best guards of the era. He played all 72 games in 1956-57, then made five consecutive All-Star teams from 1958 through 1962 while the franchise transitioned from Fort Wayne to Detroit. Basketball-Reference also credits him with two All-NBA selections. His scoring climbed from 10.9 points per game in his first Pistons season to 15.6 in 1957-58 and 17.6 in 1958-59, and he remained a major creator and scorer through 1961-62. Detroit then preserved additional asset value by trading Shue back to New York in August 1962 for Darrall Imhoff and cash.

New York Return
Sobie gave the Knicks a legitimate multi-year return. He played 71 games as a rookie, 55 in 1957-58, 50 in 1958-59 and 15 in 1959-60 before being moved to Minneapolis. Across 191 New York games he logged 3,855 minutes, scored 1,617 points and produced 7.2 win shares. He was a useful guard rather than a failed draft acquisition. That production is why the Knicks deserve more than the legacy D+ grade, even though Sobie never reached Shue's level or longevity.

Hindsight Comparison
Detroit clearly received the superior player. Shue became a five-time All-Star and two-time All-NBA selection during his Pistons tenure, then generated another trade return in 1962. Sobie was useful for New York, but his NBA career lasted four seasons and his role never approached Shue's star-level impact. The exchange therefore belongs in the category of clear Detroit wins where the other club still received meaningful rotation value rather than an empty asset.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, A/B-. Detroit receives an A for acquiring a five-time All-Star, two-time All-NBA guard and later trade asset. New York receives a B- for four seasons and 191 games from Sobie, a solid but much smaller realized return. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Syracuse sold Billy Kenville's player rights to the Fort Wayne Pistons on October 3, 1956. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse, Fort Wayne and league transaction logs all verify the sale. Kenville had been a three-year Nationals guard and a member of the 1955 championship team before the move. He then played 71 games for Fort Wayne in 1956-57, averaging 24.0 minutes, 8.2 points, 4.6 rebounds and 2.4 assists, followed by 35 Detroit games in 1957-58 and another 25 in 1959-60 after a year in the EBA. That 131-game Pistons return is meaningful, while Syracuse's cash payment remains undisclosed. The source-backed outcome favors Detroit, but Kenville was a rotation player rather than a star, so the grade gap remains moderate.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Syracuse sold Billy Kenville's player rights to Fort Wayne on October 3, 1956. Basketball-Reference records the same sale on the Nationals, Pistons and league-wide 1956-57 transaction pages, and Danny Biasone's executive ledger preserves the transaction as well. Kenville was not an unused prospect: he had already played three full NBA seasons for Syracuse, including 70 games during the Nationals' 1955 championship season and all 72 games in 1955-56. Fort Wayne was purchasing an established rotation guard before the season, while Syracuse chose an undisclosed cash return.

Fort Wayne Return
Kenville immediately became a regular part of the Pistons' backcourt. He played 71 games in 1956-57 and logged 1,701 minutes, with 582 points, 324 rebounds and 172 assists. His 24.0 minutes per game were the largest workload of his NBA career. After the franchise moved to Detroit, he appeared in 35 games in 1957-58, spent 1958-59 in the EBA, then returned for 25 more Detroit games in 1959-60. Across his Pistons tenure he totaled 131 regular-season games. That is substantial realized value from a simple cash purchase, even though Kenville never became a top-tier player.

Syracuse Return
The Nationals received cash, and the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public transaction record. That makes the financial return legitimate but impossible to quantify. Syracuse was selling a 25-year-old guard who had averaged 7.4 points in 17.8 minutes the previous season and who still had multiple NBA seasons ahead. The club remained competitive without him, but there is no documented player, pick or other downstream basketball asset attached to the payment.

Hindsight Comparison
Detroit received the stronger measurable basketball return. Kenville supplied a full 71-game season immediately, then remained connected to the franchise for two additional NBA seasons around a one-year EBA absence. Syracuse's cash return prevents the deal from being treated as a severe loss, especially because Kenville was a rotation guard rather than an All-Star-level asset. The value gap is therefore clear but moderate: Detroit bought useful depth and got exactly that.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, B/C. Detroit receives a B for acquiring 131 games of useful guard depth, including a 71-game first season at 24 minutes per game. Syracuse receives a C for real but undisclosed cash while surrendering a player with multiple productive seasons remaining. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The Exchange
Syracuse sold Red Rocha's player rights to Fort Wayne on October 23, 1956. los-angeles-lakers.summary: Minneapolis traded Slater Martin, the draft rights to Jerry Bird and a player to be named later who became Phil Jordon to the New York Knicks on October 26, 1956 for Walter Dukes and the draft rights to Burdette Haldorson. Basketball-Reference's team and league ledgers list Martin, Bird and Jordon for Dukes and Haldorson, while the Knicks media guide preserves the period mechanics as Martin, Bird and a later player for Dukes and Haldorson's rights. Dukes gave Minneapolis a 71-game, 11.2-rebound season before becoming Larry Foust, a two-time Lakers All-Star. New York used Martin for 13 games and then traded him for Willie Naulls, who became a four-time All-Star and long-term Knicks scorer. Both clubs created substantial downstream value, with New York holding the slight hindsight edge.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange
Minneapolis and New York completed a five-asset trade on October 26, 1956. Basketball-Reference records Jerry Bird, Phil Jordon and Slater Martin going to the Knicks for Walter Dukes and Burdette Haldorson. The Knicks' own historical media guide preserves a more precise version of the mechanics: Martin, Bird and a player to be named later went to New York for Dukes and the draft rights to Haldorson. The legacy Lakers record identifies that later player as Jordon on December 28. That treatment also fits the players' status. Bird was Minneapolis' 19th overall pick in 1956 and was in military service; Haldorson had been drafted 25th overall by St. Louis in 1955 and never played an NBA game.

Minneapolis Return
Dukes immediately became the Lakers' starting center. He played 71 games in 1956-57, averaging 26.3 minutes, 10.1 points and 11.2 rebounds. Minneapolis then converted him into another major asset on September 12, 1957, trading Dukes to Detroit for Larry Foust. Foust made the All-Star team in each of his first two Lakers seasons and played 191 regular-season games for Minneapolis before being traded in 1960. Haldorson's rights never produced an NBA appearance, but the Dukes-to-Foust chain gave the Lakers several seasons of high-level center production.

New York Return
Martin's direct Knicks stay lasted only 13 games, but New York preserved his value. On December 12 the Knicks sent him to St. Louis for Willie Naulls. Naulls became a long-term frontcourt star for New York, making four All-Star teams overall and three consecutive All-Star teams from 1960 through 1962 while averaging 21.4, 23.4 and 25.0 points in those seasons. Bird eventually played 11 games for the Knicks in 1958-59 after military service. Jordon appeared in nine New York games in 1956-57 and 12 more in 1957-58 before his rights went to Detroit. The Martin-to-Naulls conversion dominates the Knicks' realized return.

Hindsight Comparison
This is much closer than the legacy Lakers C+ grade suggests. Minneapolis got a full productive season from Dukes and then turned him into Foust, a two-time Lakers All-Star. New York got only a short Martin stint directly, but the subsequent Naulls trade created years of All-Star-level production, while Bird and Jordon added smaller supporting value. Both teams managed the assets well after the initial exchange. New York's downstream return lasted longer and reached a higher offensive peak, giving the Knicks a slight overall advantage rather than a one-sided win.

Final Verdict
Knicks Win, A/A-. New York receives an A because Martin became Willie Naulls, a multi-year All-Star scorer, while Bird and Jordon added smaller value. Minneapolis receives an A- because Dukes produced a strong 71-game season and then became Larry Foust, a two-time Lakers All-Star. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis sold Bob Harrison's player rights to Syracuse on December 2, 1956. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on the Hawks, Nationals and league-wide 1956-57 transaction pages. Harrison had been an established NBA guard for years and made the 1956 All-Star team with St. Louis, but his role collapsed early in 1956-57: he appeared in only 10 Hawks games and averaged 4.8 minutes before the sale. Syracuse was therefore buying a veteran whose current fit had deteriorated, while St. Louis chose cash rather than continuing to carry him.

Syracuse Return
Harrison immediately recovered a substantial role. He appeared in 56 Syracuse games over the rest of 1956-57, averaging 31.5 minutes, 9.9 points, 2.7 rebounds and 2.7 assists. The next season he played all 72 games for the Nationals, adding 25.0 minutes, 7.2 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.3 assists per game. Across those two Syracuse seasons he supplied 128 regular-season appearances and became a steady backcourt contributor on teams that reached the playoffs both years. That is far more than a short emergency stint.

St. Louis Return
The Hawks received cash, but the reviewed public transaction logs do not preserve the amount. That makes the financial return impossible to measure precisely. St. Louis did have a rational basketball reason to move Harrison because his role had nearly disappeared before the sale, and the Hawks were building around a different core. The later outcome shows that Harrison still had useful NBA basketball left, however, so the unknown cash has to be weighed against two full Syracuse seasons of proven production.

Hindsight Comparison
Syracuse received the stronger measurable return. Harrison gave the Nationals 128 games over two seasons and immediately regained starter-level minutes after barely playing in St. Louis. The Hawks' cash return should not be treated as zero, and the undisclosed amount prevents an extreme grade gap. Still, the realized basketball value is clear enough to move this well beyond the legacy even-trade framing. Syracuse bought a veteran at a moment when his prior team had little use for him and extracted two productive seasons.

Final Verdict
Nationals Win, B+/C. Syracuse receives a B+ for acquiring two productive seasons and 128 games from Harrison. St. Louis receives a C for legitimate but unquantified cash after selling a player who still had meaningful rotation value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Basketball-Reference's St. Louis and New York transaction logs agree on the one-for-one exchange. Martin immediately became St. Louis' floor general, making the 1957 All-Star team and All-NBA Second Team, helping the Hawks reach the 1957 Finals, and remaining a key part of the 1958 championship team. Naulls gave New York the longer individual peak, becoming a four-time All-Star and averaging 21.4 points and 14.2 rebounds at his 1959-60 Knicks high point. Both teams received major value, with St. Louis holding a slight hindsight edge because Martin fit directly into a championship core.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis traded Willie Naulls to New York for Slater Martin on December 12, 1956. Basketball-Reference lists the same one-for-one exchange on both team transaction pages and in the Ben Kerner executive ledger. The players were at very different career stages. Martin was 31, already a five-time All-Star and four-time NBA champion with Minneapolis. Naulls was a 22-year-old rookie and the tenth overall pick in the 1956 draft. St. Louis was choosing immediate veteran control for a young frontcourt scorer with substantial upside.

St. Louis Return
Martin's fit was immediate. He played 53 Hawks games in 1956-57, averaging 37.3 minutes, 11.5 points, 4.6 rebounds and 4.3 assists. He made the All-Star team and All-NBA Second Team while St. Louis reached the NBA Finals. The next season he again earned All-Star and All-NBA Second Team honors and helped the Hawks win the 1958 championship. Martin remained a regular through 1959-60 and even served briefly as player-coach in 1957. His value was not simply veteran leadership; he was a high-minute point guard whose arrival aligned directly with the franchise's first two Finals appearances in St. Louis and its championship peak.

New York Return
Naulls was also an excellent acquisition. He played 52 Knicks games as a rookie after the trade, then broke out in 1957-58 with 18.1 points and 11.8 rebounds per game and an All-Star selection. He went on to make four consecutive All-Star teams for New York and became one of the league's premier scoring forwards. At his 1959-60 peak he averaged 21.4 points and 14.2 rebounds. The Knicks therefore received the younger player, more seasons and the stronger individual statistical prime, making any claim of a one-sided St. Louis victory indefensible.

Hindsight Comparison
This is a high-value trade for both clubs. New York received years of All-Star production from Naulls, while St. Louis acquired the veteran point guard who immediately organized a contender and remained central through the 1958 title. Martin's championship-era fit gives the Hawks the transaction's highest-leverage team outcome, but Naulls' sustained star production keeps the gap narrow. The source-backed result is a slight St. Louis edge rather than a decisive win.

Final Verdict
Slight Hawks Edge, A+/A. St. Louis receives an A+ because Martin made immediate All-Star and All-NBA impact, reached two Finals with the Hawks and helped deliver the 1958 championship. New York receives an A for acquiring a 22-year-old who became a four-time Knicks All-Star and high-volume scorer and rebounder. The completed value is tied to Martin’s St. Louis championship role and Naulls’s actual New York scoring, not the trophies or seasons each earned with other franchises.
