boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange
Boston sold Togo Palazzi's player rights to Syracuse on December 29, 1956. Basketball-Reference lists that date on the Celtics, Nationals and league-wide 1956-57 transaction pages. The legacy Boston source record had carried November 29, and that stale date survived in the stored date reference even after the canonical tradeDate was corrected to December 29. This pass aligns the route metadata with the verified transaction date while preserving the original source provenance. Boston was converting a reserve forward into cash; Syracuse was buying a 24-year-old who had already shown he could score in limited minutes.

Syracuse Return
Palazzi's role grew immediately after the sale. He played 42 Syracuse games in 1956-57, averaging 18.6 minutes, 10.7 points and 4.5 rebounds. He then appeared in 67 games in 1957-58 and 71 in 1958-59, remaining a regular part of the Nationals' rotation. Across those first three Syracuse seasons he gave the club 180 regular-season appearances. His scoring settled into the eight-to-nine-point range after the initial burst, but the durability and repeated rotation use make the acquisition much more valuable than a short-term roster patch.

Boston Return
The Celtics received cash, and the amount is not preserved in the reviewed public ledgers. That consideration has real value and should not be treated as zero. Boston also had a crowded roster and was in the opening year of its championship dynasty, so moving a reserve whose role had shrunk was understandable. Palazzi had played 21 Boston games that season before the sale and averaged only 11.1 minutes. The transaction did not derail Boston's title path, but hindsight still shows that the player rights carried several seasons of useful NBA production.

Hindsight Comparison
Syracuse received the stronger measurable basketball return. Palazzi supplied 180 games over three seasons after the transaction and remained a regular contributor, while Boston's cash return cannot be quantified. The gap is meaningful but not franchise-changing because Palazzi was a rotation forward rather than a star and Boston was already positioned to contend without him. A clear Nationals edge with a solid but not extreme grade best matches the documented outcome.

Final Verdict
Nationals Win, B+/C. Syracuse receives a B+ for turning cash into three seasons and 180 games of rotation production. Boston receives a C for legitimate but undisclosed cash after moving a player whose remaining value proved useful elsewhere. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Rochester sold Lew Hitch's player rights to the Philadelphia Warriors on January 4, 1957, not January 5 as the legacy route recorded. Basketball-Reference's Rochester, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers all agree on the January 4 date. golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange
Rochester sold Lew Hitch's player rights to Philadelphia on January 4, 1957. Basketball-Reference lists the same date on the Royals, Warriors and league-wide transaction pages, and the Les Harrison executive ledger independently records the sale. The legacy TradeVerdicts route was dated January 5, so this pass corrects the date and route metadata while preserving the original source lineage. Hitch had joined Rochester as a free agent in July 1956 and played 30 games before the move. Philadelphia was purchasing an experienced reserve big man for the second half of the season.

Philadelphia Return
Hitch played 38 games for the Warriors after the sale, averaging 15.2 minutes, 3.7 points and 3.5 rebounds. He was not a high-impact acquisition, but Philadelphia received regular reserve minutes through the rest of a 37-win season and playoff appearance. Those 38 games were the final appearances of Hitch's NBA career, so there was no downstream multi-year value. The return was nevertheless tangible and considerably more useful than a dormant player right.

Rochester Return
The Royals received cash, but the public ledgers do not preserve the amount. Rochester had already gotten 30 games from Hitch that season and was able to monetize his remaining rights before his career ended. That makes the sale defensible and prevents a low grade. At the same time, because the cash amount is unknown, there is no basis for claiming that it clearly exceeded the value of the 38 reserve games Philadelphia received.

Hindsight Comparison
The deal is close, with a modest Philadelphia edge. The Warriors received half a season of useful depth, while Rochester received real but unquantified financial consideration. Hitch's short remaining career limits the upside on Philadelphia's side, and the Royals did not give away a future starter or long-term asset. The old C-/F split substantially overstated the gap. A mild Warriors advantage better matches the documented outcome.

Final Verdict
Slight Warriors Edge, B-/C+. Philadelphia receives a B- for 38 games of usable reserve frontcourt depth at modest acquisition cost. Rochester receives a C+ for legitimate but undisclosed cash after already using Hitch for 30 games that season. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Fort Wayne traded Mel Hutchins and its 1957 first-round pick, which New York used at No. 2 on Charlie Tyra, to the Knicks on April 3, 1957 for Harry Gallatin, Nat Clifton and Dick Atha. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, New York and league transaction logs agree on the package. The legacy TradeVerdicts record incorrectly classified Atha as draft rights even though he had already played 25 NBA games for New York in 1955-56. Gallatin and Clifton gave the Pistons strong veteran production in 1957-58, while Atha added 18 games. New York received only 18 games from Hutchins but four seasons and 270 games from Tyra. perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Fort Wayne sent Mel Hutchins and its 1957 first-round pick to New York on April 3, 1957 for Harry Gallatin, Nat Clifton and Dick Atha. Basketball-Reference records the same five-asset exchange on the Pistons, Knicks and league-wide transaction pages. The draft pick later became Charlie Tyra at No. 2 overall. One structural problem in the legacy record is clear: Atha was not a draft-rights asset. He had already appeared in 25 games for New York in 1955-56, so the transaction moved his player rights as an established NBA player. This pass converts that asset and its player relationships to direct-player status.

Fort Wayne Return
Gallatin gave the Pistons the strongest immediate return. In 1957-58, the franchise's first season in Detroit, he played all 72 games and averaged 27.6 minutes, 14.9 points and 10.4 rebounds. Clifton added 68 games, 1,435 minutes, 525 points and 403 rebounds in his final NBA season. Atha returned from his lost 1956-57 season to appear in 18 Detroit games. The group was old, but it supplied 158 regular-season appearances in 1957-58 and gave the newly relocated club substantial veteran frontcourt production.

New York Return
Hutchins had been a four-time All-Star with the Pistons, but his Knicks stint was short. He appeared in only 18 games in 1957-58 before his NBA career ended. Tyra became the enduring asset. He played 270 regular-season games for New York across four seasons, including 68 games as a rookie while averaging 17.4 minutes, 7.4 points and 7.1 rebounds. He never became an All-Star, but his multi-year rotation value gave the Knicks a younger and longer-lived return than the veteran package sent to Detroit.

Hindsight Comparison
Both teams received useful value. Detroit got the stronger single-season veteran impact, led by Gallatin's double-double production and Clifton's regular minutes. New York received much less from Hutchins than his reputation suggested, but Tyra supplied four seasons and 270 games. The longevity advantage is enough to nudge the deal toward the Knicks, though the gap is small because Detroit's 1957-58 return was meaningful and immediate. The source-backed result should therefore be a modest New York edge rather than the extreme grades carried by the legacy perspectives.

Final Verdict
Slight Knicks Edge, B+/B. New York receives a B+ because Tyra became a four-year contributor and the club still received a brief Hutchins stint. Detroit receives a B because Gallatin, Clifton and Atha delivered substantial veteran production in the franchise's first Detroit season. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Rochester and Minneapolis transaction logs agree on the full April 17, 1957 package. The Royals sent Bob Burrow, Ed Fleming, Hot Rod Hundley, Monk Meineke and Art Spoelstra to the Lakers for Clyde Lovellette and Jim Paxson. Hundley had just been selected No. 1 overall by Rochester, so the asset was not a vague future right: it was the rights to the top pick in the same day's draft. The historical team names matter here. Rochester moved to Cincinnati for the 1957-58 season, while the Lakers were still in Minneapolis.

Rochester/Cincinnati Return
Lovellette immediately delivered star production. In 1957-58 he played 71 games for Cincinnati and averaged 23.4 points and 12.1 rebounds, finishing 12th in MVP voting. Paxson also gave the Royals 67 games at 9.8 points, 5.2 rebounds and 2.1 assists. The direct return therefore included an elite center season plus a full year of rotation wing play. The Lovellette asset also retained major transaction value. In September 1958 Cincinnati traded him to St. Louis for Gerry Calvert, Wayne Embry, Darrell Floyd, Jim Palmer and Ken Sidle. Embry became the long-term prize of that follow-up deal, playing 603 games across eight Cincinnati seasons and making five straight All-Star teams from 1961 through 1965. That later trade is a separate transaction and its full value should not simply be copied backward, but it proves that the Royals did not exhaust Lovellette's value after one season. Meineke is also a notable wrinkle: although he was included in the package sent to Minneapolis, Rochester/Cincinnati re-signed him as a free agent in November 1957, and he played 67 games for Cincinnati that season. His later return was not compensation from the Lakers and should not be counted as part of this trade.

Minneapolis/Los Angeles Return
Hundley became the durable centerpiece of the Lakers package. He played all six seasons of his NBA career for the franchise, 431 regular-season games in total, and made the All-Star team in 1960 and 1961. His best season was 1959-60, when he averaged 12.8 points, 5.3 rebounds and 4.6 assists. He remained a rotation guard after the franchise moved to Los Angeles and participated in multiple deep playoff runs. Fleming also supplied real value: 170 Minneapolis games over three seasons, including 72 games at 8.8 points and 6.8 rebounds in 1957-58. Spoelstra played 50 games for Minneapolis in 1957-58 and averaged 7.6 points and 5.6 rebounds before finishing the season with New York. Burrow contributed only 14 Lakers games, while Meineke did not produce Lakers regular-season value before returning to Cincinnati. The package was therefore not five equally valuable pieces, but Hundley plus several useful supporting seasons created a long and tangible return.

Hindsight Verdict
The legacy slight Rochester edge underweights Hundley and Fleming, while a Lakers win would underweight how strong Lovellette was immediately and how much transaction value he retained. Rochester received the best single season in the deal and then turned that star into a package that included Embry. Minneapolis received the longest direct player value through Hundley's six seasons and two All-Star selections, plus meaningful Fleming and Spoelstra contributions. Both sides extracted high-level value from different time horizons. An A for each franchise fits better than forcing a winner: Cincinnati/Rochester got elite short-term production and reusable star value, while the Lakers got a six-year guard and multiple supporting contributors. Final verdict: Even Trade.

perspectives.summary: Fort Wayne traded Corky Devlin to the Minneapolis Lakers for Ed Kalafat on May 14, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Fort Wayne, Minneapolis and league transaction logs all verify the one-for-one exchange. Kalafat had just completed his third NBA season, playing 65 games for Minneapolis at 24.9 minutes, 8.5 points and 6.5 rebounds per game, but he never appeared in another NBA game after the trade. Devlin, by contrast, played 70 games for the Lakers in 1957-58 and averaged 17.8 minutes, 6.8 points, 2.5 rebounds and 2.4 assists. Because Minneapolis received the only post-trade NBA production, the realized outcome clearly favors the Lakers.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Fort Wayne traded Corky Devlin to Minneapolis for Ed Kalafat on May 14, 1957. Basketball-Reference records the same exchange on the Pistons, Lakers and league-wide transaction pages, and the Fred Delano and George Mikan executive ledgers preserve it as well. The timing is important: the deal took place after the 1956-57 season. Kalafat had just completed a solid year for Minneapolis, while Devlin had appeared in 71 Fort Wayne games. This was a direct exchange of two established players rather than a speculative rights deal.

Minneapolis Return
Devlin gave the Lakers one more full NBA season. He appeared in 70 games in 1957-58, averaging 17.8 minutes, 6.8 points, 2.5 rebounds and 2.4 assists. He was not a high-impact starter, but 70 games of usable backcourt depth is meaningful realized value from a straight player swap. That 1957-58 season was also the final year of Devlin's NBA career, so the return was concentrated entirely in one season rather than a longer asset chain.

Detroit Return
Kalafat never appeared in an NBA game after the transaction. Basketball-Reference lists his career ending with the 1956-57 Minneapolis season despite the verified May 14 trade to the Pistons. His pre-trade production had been respectable: 65 games, 24.9 minutes, 8.5 points and 6.5 rebounds per game. None of that prior value belongs to Detroit's side of this exchange. In hindsight, the Pistons acquired a player who produced zero regular-season NBA appearances for them.

Hindsight Comparison
Minneapolis received the only post-trade NBA production, making the directional result clear. Devlin supplied 70 games of rotation minutes while Kalafat never played another NBA game. The gap should not be exaggerated into a franchise-changing win because Devlin's Lakers stint lasted one season and his production was modest. Still, an even verdict would understate the difference between a full season of usable depth and no realized on-court return.

Final Verdict
Lakers Win, B/C-. Minneapolis receives a B for acquiring 70 games of rotation backcourt production. Detroit receives a C- because Kalafat never appeared in an NBA game after the trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Syracuse sold George King's player rights to the Cincinnati Royals on August 15, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse, Cincinnati and league transaction logs agree on the sale and show that the legacy TradeVerdicts draft-rights classification was wrong: King was a veteran guard who had already played five NBA seasons for Syracuse and helped the Nationals win the 1955 championship. After sitting out 1956-57, King returned with Cincinnati for 63 games in 1957-58, averaging 36.1 minutes, 9.7 points, 4.9 rebounds and 5.3 assists. The Royals therefore received a full season of starter-level production, while Syracuse's cash return remains undisclosed.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Exchange
Syracuse sold George King's player rights to Cincinnati on August 15, 1957. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on the Nationals, Royals and league-wide 1957-58 transaction pages. The legacy TradeVerdicts record treated King as a draft-rights asset, but that is historically incorrect. He had already completed five NBA seasons for Syracuse from 1951-52 through 1955-56, including the 1955 championship season, before sitting out 1956-57. Cincinnati was therefore buying the rights to an experienced point guard, not an untested draftee.

Cincinnati Return
King returned to the NBA immediately and became one of Cincinnati's highest-minute players. He appeared in 63 games in 1957-58 and averaged 36.1 minutes, 9.7 points, 4.9 rebounds and 5.3 assists. Basketball-Reference credits him with 2,272 minutes, 610 points, 306 rebounds and 337 assists. That is substantial realized value from a cash purchase, especially after King had missed the entire previous season. The Royals did not get a long multi-year run, but they did receive a full season of starter-level backcourt production.

Syracuse Return
The Nationals received cash, and the amount is not preserved in the reviewed transaction logs. Syracuse had already received five productive seasons from King, so selling his rights after a year away from the NBA was understandable roster management. Still, the surviving record shows that King had enough value left to return as a heavy-minute starter for Cincinnati. The financial consideration should be credited as real, but it cannot be measured against the 63 games and 2,272 minutes the Royals actually received.

Hindsight Comparison
Cincinnati received the stronger measurable return. King came back from a season away and immediately played major minutes, averaging more than five assists per game while appearing in 63 contests. Syracuse's unknown cash return keeps this from becoming an extreme grade gap, and the Nationals were not giving away a young player at the start of his career. Even so, the legacy even-trade framing understates the practical value Cincinnati extracted from the rights purchase.

Final Verdict
Royals Win, B+/C. Cincinnati receives a B+ for acquiring a veteran who returned as a 36-minute-per-game starter and supplied 63 games. Syracuse receives a C for legitimate but unquantified cash after moving a player whose NBA career still had one productive season remaining. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit traded Larry Foust to the Minneapolis Lakers for Walter Dukes on September 12, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Minneapolis and league transaction logs all show a straight player-for-player exchange, so the unsupported cash asset in the legacy TradeVerdicts record is removed. Dukes then played six seasons and 422 regular-season games for Detroit, making the 1960 and 1961 All-Star teams. Foust gave Minneapolis 191 games across three seasons, made the 1958 and 1959 All-Star teams and was later traded to St. Louis for Nick Mantis, Willie Merriweather and Chuck Share. Both clubs received major value, with Dukes' longer Detroit tenure giving the Pistons a narrow hindsight edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Detroit sent Larry Foust to Minneapolis on September 12, 1957 for Walter Dukes. Basketball-Reference's Pistons, Lakers and league-wide 1957-58 transaction pages all record the same one-for-one trade. That source agreement exposes the main legacy defect: the legacy TradeVerdicts record added cash to Minneapolis' return even though the authoritative transaction logs and the Lakers' own historical transaction guide show only Foust for Dukes. The unsupported cash asset is removed so the trade is graded as the straight center swap that actually occurred.

Detroit Return
Dukes became a long-term Pistons center. He played all 72 games in each of his first two Detroit seasons, then remained with the franchise through 1962-63. Across six seasons with Detroit he appeared in 422 regular-season games. His 1957-58 season produced 803 points and 954 rebounds, and he followed with 933 points and 958 rebounds in 1958-59. Dukes made the 1960 and 1961 All-Star teams and finished ninth in MVP voting in 1957-58 and eleventh in 1959-60. He was not an efficient scorer by modern standards, but the combination of durability, rebounding and multi-year availability gave Detroit substantial realized value.

Minneapolis Return
Foust was immediately excellent for the Lakers. He played all 72 games in both 1957-58 and 1958-59, averaging 16.8 points and 12.2 rebounds in the first season and 12.3 points and 8.7 rebounds in the second. He made the All-Star team in both years. Foust remained with Minneapolis for 47 games in 1959-60 before the Lakers traded him to St. Louis for Nick Mantis, Willie Merriweather and Chuck Share. The downstream return was modest on the court, but the original acquisition still gave Minneapolis 191 regular-season games and two All-Star seasons from a productive veteran center.

Hindsight Comparison
This was a strong trade for both clubs. Minneapolis received the better immediate peak: Foust was an All-Star in each of his first two Lakers seasons and helped stabilize the frontcourt before Elgin Baylor's arrival changed the franchise's trajectory. Detroit, however, received six seasons and 422 games from Dukes, including two All-Star selections of its own. That longevity advantage outweighs Foust's stronger first two seasons and the limited downstream package Minneapolis received in 1960. The result is a narrow Pistons edge, not the large Lakers advantage carried by one legacy perspective.

Final Verdict
Slight Pistons Edge, A-/B+. Detroit receives an A- for six seasons, 422 games and two All-Star selections from Dukes. Minneapolis receives a B+ for two All-Star seasons, 191 games and a later three-player trade return from Foust. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Dick McGuire from the New York Knicks for its 1958 first-round pick, later used at No. 3 on Mike Farmer. The transaction date is unusually conflicted across historical sources: contemporary September 24, 1957 reporting says Detroit had just obtained McGuire, early Pistons media guides place the move in September, while Basketball-Reference, RealGM and later Pistons guides index it to April 3. TradeVerdicts preserves the September 23 route date but flags the discrepancy rather than pretending the archive is unanimous. McGuire then played 208 games over three Detroit seasons and made the 1958 and 1959 All-Star teams. Farmer gave New York 141 games plus two more in 1960-61 before Cincinnati acquired him. The realized value favors Detroit.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Detroit acquired Dick McGuire from New York for a 1958 first-round pick that became Mike Farmer. The package itself is well established, but the exact date is not. Basketball-Reference and RealGM place the trade on April 3, 1957, alongside the separate Hutchins/Tyra-for-Gallatin/Clifton/Atha transaction. Later Pistons media guides also use April 3. By contrast, a September 24, 1957 Associated Press report says Detroit had just obtained McGuire, and Pistons guides published closer to the period describe the acquisition as a September 1957 move. Pro Sports Transactions lists September 23. Because the disagreement is genuine, this pass preserves the existing September 23 route date and records the conflict instead of silently normalizing one chronology.

Detroit Return
McGuire gave Detroit three productive final NBA seasons. He appeared in 69 games in 1957-58, 71 in 1958-59 and 68 in 1959-60, totaling 208 regular-season games and 5,840 minutes. He averaged 6.6 assists in his first Detroit season and 6.2 in the next, made the Western Conference All-Star team in both 1958 and 1959, and finished eleventh in MVP voting in 1958-59. He later became the Pistons' player-coach, so the acquisition also carried organizational value beyond the box score, although the trade grade here is based primarily on realized playing contribution.

New York Return
The Knicks used the acquired first-round pick on Mike Farmer. Farmer played all 72 games as a rookie in 1958-59 and 67 more in 1959-60, then appeared in two New York games in 1960-61 before moving to Cincinnati. Across his first two Knicks seasons he logged 3,081 minutes, but his advanced production was modest: Basketball-Reference credits 0.1 win shares in 1958-59 and minus-0.1 in 1959-60. Farmer later remained an NBA player for several more seasons, but most of that later value came with Cincinnati and St. Louis rather than New York.

Hindsight Comparison
Detroit received the stronger realized return. McGuire provided 208 games, two All-Star selections and high-level playmaking over three seasons, while Farmer gave New York two full seasons of rotation minutes without approaching McGuire's impact. The Knicks did receive a young first-round player who stayed in the league, so this is not a failed asset conversion. The date conflict lowers confidence in the transaction chronology, not in the asset package or player outcomes.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, A-/B-. Detroit receives an A- for three productive seasons, 208 games and two All-Star selections from McGuire. New York receives a B- for turning the pick into two full seasons of Farmer, but the realized impact was clearly lower. Confidence is medium because period and retrospective sources disagree on whether the transaction belongs to April or September 1957. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Philadelphia sold Larry Costello's player rights to the Syracuse Nationals on October 10, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse, league and Eddie Gottlieb executive transaction ledgers agree on the sale. Costello immediately became an All-Star point guard for Syracuse, playing all 72 games in 1957-58 and averaging 14.9 points, 5.3 rebounds and 4.4 assists. He then made five consecutive All-Star teams with Syracuse from 1958 through 1962, later earned another All-Star selection after the franchise became the Philadelphia 76ers, and finished his playing career on the 1967 championship team. The Warriors received cash, but the long-term basketball value overwhelmingly favored Syracuse.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange
Philadelphia sold Larry Costello's player rights to Syracuse on October 10, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse transaction page, the league-wide 1957-58 ledger and Warriors executive Eddie Gottlieb's transaction record all preserve the move. The Warriors received cash. A later biographical account places the price at $5,000, but the primary transaction ledgers reviewed here do not preserve the amount, so TradeVerdicts treats the financial return as real but unquantified. Costello was 26 and had just returned from military service for a full Warriors season, making this a sale of an established NBA guard rather than a speculative right.

Syracuse Return
Costello became one of the Nationals' defining guards almost immediately. He played all 72 games in 1957-58, logged 2,746 minutes and averaged 14.9 points, 5.3 rebounds and 4.4 assists while making the All-Star team. In 1958-59 he raised his scoring to a career-high 15.8 points per game, averaged 5.4 assists and finished seventh in MVP voting. Costello made five consecutive All-Star teams with Syracuse from 1958 through 1962, earned All-NBA recognition in 1960-61, and remained with the franchise after its move to Philadelphia. He later added a sixth All-Star selection and was part of the 1967 championship roster.

Philadelphia Return
The Warriors received cash and no player or draft asset. The exact amount is not preserved in the Basketball-Reference transaction logs, which limits the precision of the financial comparison. What can be measured is the opportunity cost. Costello had already shown he could handle a full NBA role, and Syracuse received years of starting-caliber point-guard play, repeated All-Star production and eventual championship-era continuity from the purchase. Even a meaningful cash payment would have needed extraordinary non-roster value to match what the Nationals and later 76ers received on the court.

Hindsight Comparison
This is one of the clearest early-NBA cash-sale outcomes in the archive. Syracuse acquired a six-time All-Star who became a long-term franchise floor general, while Philadelphia received only financial consideration. The Warriors did not surrender an unknown prospect; Costello had already returned from military service and played a full season in Philadelphia. The gap in realized basketball value is therefore large even without assigning a precise dollar value to the cash.

Final Verdict
76ers Win, A+/D. Syracuse receives an A+ for acquiring a long-term All-Star point guard whose franchise run extended through the 1967 championship season. Philadelphia receives a D because its cash return was real but the sold player became vastly more valuable on the court. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Tom Marshall's player rights from the Cincinnati Royals for cash on December 10, 1957. Basketball-Reference's Detroit transaction log and Pro Sports Transactions agree on the move, while Marshall's career record shows the legacy TradeVerdicts draft-rights classification was wrong: he was a veteran in his fourth NBA season. Marshall played only nine games for Detroit, averaging 7.3 minutes and 2.3 points, before the Pistons waived him on February 18, 1958. Two days later Cincinnati claimed him back, and he finished the season with 29 additional Royals games. Because Cincinnati received cash and reacquired the player after Detroit's brief trial, the realized outcome favors the Royals.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Detroit acquired Tom Marshall's player rights from Cincinnati on December 10, 1957 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Pistons transaction page records Detroit acquiring Marshall's rights, and Pro Sports Transactions preserves the cash going to the Royals. The legacy TradeVerdicts asset was labeled draft rights, but Marshall had already played three NBA seasons for Rochester/Cincinnati and was 27 years old. The canonical asset is therefore repaired to a veteran player-rights/direct-player transaction rather than a draft-rights move.

Detroit Return
Marshall's Detroit stint was extremely short. Basketball-Reference credits him with nine Pistons games, 66 total minutes, 21 points and eight rebounds. He averaged 7.3 minutes and 2.3 points per game. Detroit waived him on February 18, 1958, only a little more than two months after acquiring his rights. That makes the purchase a low-impact roster trial rather than a transaction that created durable rotation value.

Cincinnati Return
The Royals received cash, although the amount is not preserved in the reviewed transaction sources. More importantly in hindsight, Cincinnati reclaimed Marshall on waivers on February 20, two days after Detroit let him go. Marshall then played 29 additional Cincinnati games in 1957-58. The cash return is therefore paired with the practical fact that the Royals regained the same veteran after Detroit received only nine games from him.

Hindsight Comparison
Cincinnati realized the stronger outcome. Detroit paid cash for a player who lasted nine games, while the Royals received financial consideration and then recovered Marshall during the same season. The exact cash amount is unknown, so the grade should not imply a large financial windfall, but the asset path is unusually unfavorable to Detroit. The source-backed record also makes clear that this was a veteran-rights purchase rather than the draft-rights transaction carried by the legacy shell.

Final Verdict
Royals Win, B+/C-. Cincinnati receives a B+ for receiving cash and later reclaiming Marshall during the same season. Detroit receives a C- for nine low-minute games before waiving the player it had purchased. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: St. Louis traded Dave Plunkett to the Philadelphia Warriors for Walt Davis on January 19, 1958. Basketball-Reference's St. Louis, Philadelphia and league transaction logs all verify the exchange. Plunkett's Basketball-Reference career ends before a Philadelphia season appears, leaving St. Louis with the only documented post-trade NBA value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis sent Dave Plunkett to Philadelphia on January 19, 1958 for Walt Davis. Basketball-Reference records the same exchange on the Hawks, Warriors and league-wide transaction pages, and both franchise executive ledgers preserve it as well. The old Atlanta-source record used 'Buddy Davis,' but Basketball-Reference identifies Buddy as a nickname for Walter Francis Davis. That alias has already been merged into the canonical Walt Davis player shell, and this pass aligns the trade asset itself with that verified identity.

St. Louis Return
Davis gave the Hawks useful depth immediately. He played 26 regular-season games after the trade, totaling 287 minutes, 127 points and 86 rebounds. That works out to 11.0 minutes, 4.9 points and 3.3 rebounds per game. More importantly, he remained on the roster for the postseason and appeared in nine playoff games while St. Louis won the 1958 NBA championship. His playoff role was small, but the Hawks received a real rotation piece during the most successful season in franchise history.

Philadelphia Return
Plunkett had been St. Louis' sixth-round pick in the 1956 draft and had already made his NBA debut before the exchange. Basketball-Reference lists his career length as one rookie season and does not show a 1957-58 Philadelphia line or any later NBA season. The Warriors therefore acquired player rights that produced no documented post-trade NBA contribution. That makes this materially different from a low-minute swap where both teams at least received some floor time.

Hindsight Comparison
St. Louis received the only realized post-trade NBA value and did so during a championship run. Davis was not a major part of the Hawks' core, so the deal should not be inflated into a franchise-changing transaction. Still, 26 regular-season games plus nine playoff appearances are clearly preferable to an incoming player who never appeared for Philadelphia. The source-backed evidence supports a solid Hawks win rather than the legacy even-trade framing.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, B+/D+. St. Louis receives a B+ for acquiring usable depth that remained on the roster through the 1958 championship. Philadelphia receives a D+ because Plunkett produced no documented post-trade NBA games. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Minneapolis traded Art Spoelstra to the New York Knicks for Bo Erias and cash on February 5, 1958. Basketball-Reference's Minneapolis, New York and league transaction logs all verify the package. Erias made his NBA debut four days later and played 18 games for the Lakers, averaging 22.3 minutes, 8.2 points, 4.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists. Spoelstra appeared in 17 games for New York at 12.2 minutes, 3.9 points and 3.0 rebounds per game, and those were the final NBA games of his career. With the better on-court return plus cash, Minneapolis received the stronger realized value.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange
Minneapolis sent Art Spoelstra to New York on February 5, 1958 for Bo Erias and cash. Basketball-Reference records the same package on both team transaction pages, in the league-wide ledger and in the executive transaction records for John Kundla and Fred Podesta. Spoelstra was a fourth-year NBA center who had played 50 games for the Lakers that season before the deal. Erias had not yet appeared in an NBA game, so Minneapolis was exchanging a known reserve for an untested 25-year-old forward plus financial consideration.

Minneapolis Return
Erias debuted for the Lakers on February 9 and immediately became a real rotation piece. He appeared in 18 games over the rest of 1957-58, totaling 401 minutes, 148 points, 83 rebounds and 26 assists. His averages of 22.3 minutes, 8.2 points and 4.6 rebounds were all meaningful for a late-season acquisition. Erias did not play another NBA season, so the return was short-lived, but Minneapolis still received the better individual post-trade production and cash on top of it.

New York Return
Spoelstra played 17 games for the Knicks, averaging 12.2 minutes, 3.9 points, 3.0 rebounds and 0.4 assists. Basketball-Reference lists those 17 New York games as the final NBA appearances of his four-year career. He therefore gave the Knicks some frontcourt depth, but his role was smaller than Erias' role in Minneapolis and there was no later season or downstream trade value to extend the return.

Hindsight Comparison
Both players gave their new teams only the remainder of the 1957-58 season, which keeps this from becoming a major hindsight judgment. The difference is that Erias played more minutes, scored more, rebounded more and came with cash. Spoelstra's New York stint was shorter and represented the end of his NBA career. The source-backed evidence therefore reverses the legacy slight-Knicks framing and supports a clear but modest Lakers advantage.

Final Verdict
Lakers Win, B/C. Minneapolis receives a B for 18 useful Erias games plus cash. New York receives a C for 17 lower-impact Spoelstra games with no later NBA value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
los-angeles-lakers.gradeRationale: The completed outcomes are close enough to treat as broadly comparable. Grades weigh realized player production, identifiable pick conversion, role, timing, contract context and downstream asset use.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: On February 16, 1958, Minneapolis acquired Frank Selvy from St. Louis for the rights to Dick Boushka and Terry Rand. Basketball-Reference, the Lakers' official transaction history and both franchise executive ledgers describe an outright trade, while Pro Sports Transactions preserves the older wording that Selvy was loaned to Minneapolis for the rest of 1957-58. That distinction is noted rather than forced: Selvy played 12 Lakers games after the move, totaling 231 minutes and 76 points, while neither Boushka nor Rand ever appeared in an NBA game. The immediate realized value therefore favors Minneapolis, even with uncertainty about whether Selvy's rights reverted to St. Louis after the season.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange
Minneapolis acquired Frank Selvy from St. Louis on February 16, 1958 for the rights to Dick Boushka and Terry Rand. The transaction is unusually important to describe with source discipline. Basketball-Reference's St. Louis and league logs, John Kundla's executive ledger, Ben Kerner's executive ledger and the Lakers' own all-time transaction history all describe a trade. Pro Sports Transactions instead labels Selvy's movement a loan for the remainder of 1957-58. A later legacy Hawks record also places Selvy back under St. Louis control before a reported October 1958 move to New York. Because the public record does not fully reconcile those mechanics, this review preserves the disagreement rather than silently converting the loan wording into a permanent transfer.

Minneapolis Return
Whatever the rights mechanism, Selvy unquestionably played for the Lakers after February 16. Basketball-Reference credits him with 12 Minneapolis games in 1957-58, totaling 231 minutes, 76 points, 35 rebounds and 19 assists. He averaged 19.3 minutes and 6.3 points in that stint after playing only 7.5 minutes per game in 26 St. Louis appearances earlier in the season. Minneapolis therefore received real late-season rotation value from a player who had barely been used by the eventual champion Hawks. The Lakers later reacquired Selvy from Syracuse in December 1959, but that separate transaction is not credited to this 1958 exchange.

St. Louis Return
Boushka and Rand were legitimate Lakers draft-rights assets, not fabricated names. Minneapolis had selected Boushka in the third round of the 1955 draft and Rand in the second round of the 1956 draft. Neither player, however, produced an NBA appearance after the rights transfer. Basketball-Reference identifies Boushka as an Olympic gold medalist and later AAU player without an NBA game, while Rand also chose the industrial/AAU route and never appeared in the league. St. Louis therefore received two recognizable prospects but no realized NBA minutes from either right.

Hindsight Comparison
The immediate basketball outcome favors Minneapolis because Selvy supplied 12 games and more than 200 minutes while the two rights sent to St. Louis produced no NBA appearances. The uncertain loan-versus-trade mechanics keep the conclusion from being overstated: if Selvy's rights reverted to the Hawks after the season, St. Louis retained future contractual value that a simple permanent-trade label would miss. That uncertainty affects the size of the advantage, not the documented 1957-58 production gap.

Final Verdict
Lakers Win, B/D+. Minneapolis receives a B for acquiring useful late-season guard minutes at the cost of two rights that never became NBA players. St. Louis receives a D+ for two legitimate prospects that produced no NBA appearances, with the grade protected from falling further because the Selvy rights mechanism is not perfectly reconciled across sources. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: St. Louis traded the draft rights to Wayne Embry, Jim Palmer, Darrell Floyd, Ken Sidle and Gerry Calvert to the Cincinnati Royals on August 5, 1958 for Clyde Lovellette, who was delivered as the player to be named later in September. Basketball-Reference's league and Ben Kerner executive ledgers place the agreement on August 5, while the St. Louis and Cincinnati team pages record the completed Lovellette transfer on September 16. Lovellette gave the Hawks four strong seasons, 245 games and two All-Star selections. Cincinnati received even more long-term volume from Embry alone: 603 games across eight seasons and five All-Star selections, plus 87 games from Palmer. The verified hindsight result is a high-value trade for both clubs with a slight Royals edge in total longevity.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis agreed on August 5, 1958 to send the rights to Wayne Embry, Jim Palmer, Darrell Floyd, Ken Sidle and Gerry Calvert to Cincinnati for Clyde Lovellette. Basketball-Reference's league transaction page and Ben Kerner executive ledger use the August 5 date, while the St. Louis and Cincinnati team transaction pages record September 16, the date Lovellette was formally delivered as the player to be named later. The source-backed repair therefore keeps August 5 as the trade date but replaces the malformed 'player to be named later or 1959 second round pick' asset with the actual player, Clyde Lovellette.

St. Louis Return
Lovellette immediately became a major frontcourt scorer for the Hawks. He played 70 games in 1958-59, 68 in 1959-60, 67 in 1960-61 and 40 in 1961-62. Across four St. Louis seasons he appeared in 245 games, averaged 19.3 points and 9.6 rebounds, made the All-Star team in 1960 and 1961, and received MVP votes in 1960-61. He also remained a substantial playoff contributor during a period when St. Louis returned to the NBA Finals in 1960 and 1961. For a contender built around Bob Pettit, acquiring an established All-NBA-level center produced immediate win-now value.

Cincinnati Return
The Royals received the longer-lived package. Embry became their starting center almost immediately and stayed for eight seasons, playing 603 regular-season games from 1958-59 through 1965-66. He made five straight All-Star teams from 1961 through 1965 and became one of the franchise's foundational frontcourt players. Palmer also supplied 87 Cincinnati games across two seasons, including 67 games as a rookie at 10.3 points and 7.0 rebounds per game. Floyd, Sidle and Calvert did not generate comparable NBA value, but Cincinnati did not need them to for the return to succeed because Embry alone became a long-term star-level piece.

Hindsight Comparison
Both clubs realized substantial value, which makes this one of the stronger two-sided trades in the early archive. St. Louis received the better immediate player and four seasons of high-end production during a championship-contending window. Cincinnati received far more longevity through Embry, plus useful early production from Palmer. Lovellette's peak Hawks impact keeps the difference narrow, but Embry's eight-year tenure and five All-Star selections give the Royals the slightly stronger total return.

Final Verdict
Royals Edge, A/A-. Cincinnati receives an A for Embry's eight seasons, five All-Star selections and Palmer's additional 87 games. St. Louis receives an A- for four highly productive Lovellette seasons, two All-Star selections and major playoff value during two Finals runs. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: St. Louis traded Frank Selvy to the New York Knicks on October 22, 1958 for a 1959 second-round draft pick that became Alan Seiden at No. 14 overall. The transaction is preserved in the Knicks' historical media guide, Pro Sports Transactions and RealGM's Selvy timeline even though Basketball-Reference's 1958-59 team and league transaction pages omit it. Selvy then played 68 games for New York in 1958-59, averaging 21.3 minutes and 9.8 points per game. St. Louis used the acquired pick on Seiden, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season career for him. The verified realized value therefore favors New York.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis traded Frank Selvy to New York on October 22, 1958 for a 1959 second-round draft choice. The Knicks' historical media guide explicitly records Selvy arriving from St. Louis for that pick on October 22, and Pro Sports Transactions plus RealGM independently preserve the same move. Basketball-Reference's 1958-59 team and league transaction pages do not list it, so the transaction is kept with a source-gap note rather than pretending every archive agrees. The pick was subsequently used by St. Louis at No. 14 overall on Alan Seiden.

New York Return
Selvy immediately became a useful rotation guard for the Knicks. He appeared in 68 games during 1958-59, averaging 21.3 minutes, 9.8 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists while shooting .385 from the field. New York went 40-32 and reached the Eastern Division playoffs, so the acquired player contributed meaningful regular-season offense to a winning team. Selvy did not become a long-term Knick; he was waived in October 1959 and later resumed his career elsewhere. Even so, one full productive season is substantial realized value for a second-round pick.

St. Louis Return
The Hawks used the acquired 1959 second-round pick on Alan Seiden at No. 14 overall. Seiden was a decorated St. John's guard and a consensus All-American, but Basketball-Reference does not record an NBA regular-season career for him. That means the draft asset generated no measurable NBA production for St. Louis. The selection itself was legitimate value at the time, but hindsight has to distinguish draft pedigree from realized professional return.

Hindsight Comparison
New York received the clear realized advantage. Selvy supplied 68 games and almost 10 points per game in the season immediately after the trade, while the pick St. Louis received became a player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The archival omission on Basketball-Reference lowers confidence in the transaction mechanics slightly, but the Knicks media guide and independent transaction databases align on the date and consideration. The result therefore supports a decisive Knicks edge.

Final Verdict
Knicks Win, B+/D. New York receives a B+ for acquiring a useful one-season rotation scorer for a second-round pick. St. Louis receives a D because the resulting No. 14 selection, Alan Seiden, produced no NBA regular-season value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Philadelphia traded Phil Rollins to the Cincinnati Royals for Vern Hatton on December 16, 1958. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Cincinnati and league transaction logs all verify the straight player-for-player exchange. Hatton appeared in 42 games for Philadelphia to finish 1958-59, then 67 in 1959-60 and 54 in 1960-61, giving the Warriors 163 games across three seasons. Rollins played 21 Cincinnati games after the trade, 72 the next season and 14 more in 1960-61, totaling 107 games for the Royals. Both sides received rotation value, but Hatton's greater volume gives Philadelphia the stronger realized return.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange
Philadelphia sent Phil Rollins to Cincinnati on December 16, 1958 for Vern Hatton. Basketball-Reference lists the same exchange on the Warriors, Royals and league-wide transaction pages, so the basic transaction mechanics are unusually clean for this part of the archive. Both players were young guards early in their NBA careers. Hatton had been Cincinnati's second-round pick that spring and had already played 22 games for the Royals, while Rollins had recently returned from military service and appeared in 23 games for Philadelphia.

Philadelphia Return
Hatton became a multi-season Warriors reserve. He played 42 Philadelphia games over the rest of 1958-59, then 67 in 1959-60 and 54 in 1960-61. Across those three seasons he totaled 163 regular-season appearances, more than 2,100 minutes and 756 points for the Warriors. His efficiency was modest, but he gave Philadelphia dependable backcourt depth over a longer stretch than Rollins ultimately supplied Cincinnati. That durability is the strongest component of the Warriors' return.

Cincinnati Return
Rollins also gave the Royals real rotation value. He appeared in 21 Cincinnati games after the trade, then played all 72 games in 1959-60 and another 14 in 1960-61 before moving on. Across 107 Royals games he logged 1,761 minutes, with 561 points and 302 assists. His 1959-60 season was the centerpiece of the return, when he averaged 17.2 minutes and 3.2 assists per game. Cincinnati therefore received a legitimate guard, not a failed asset.

Hindsight Comparison
The deal was useful to both teams, but Philadelphia received the better total return. Hatton stayed longer and produced 56 more regular-season games for the Warriors than Rollins did for Cincinnati. Rollins had a somewhat larger role per game during his best Royals season, which keeps the grade gap narrow. This is better treated as a modest Warriors edge than as a one-sided transaction or the legacy Kings-favored verdict.

Final Verdict
Warriors Edge, B/C+. Philadelphia receives a B for three seasons and 163 games of backcourt depth from Hatton. Cincinnati receives a C+ for 107 games from Rollins, including one useful full season. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis sent Med Park and Jack Stephens to Cincinnati for Si Green in January 1959. Basketball-Reference's Hawks, Royals, league and executive transaction ledgers all place the deal on January 14 and list only those three players. RealGM uses January 10, which explains the legacy TradeVerdicts date, but the stronger four-ledger agreement supports moving the canonical date to January 14 while retaining the disagreement in audit metadata. The source-backed review also removes an unsupported cash asset and corrects the legacy 'Ned Park' spelling to Med Park, whose full name was Medford R. Park.

St. Louis Return
Green gave the Hawks the larger body of post-trade value. He played 26 St. Louis games to finish 1958-59, then 70 in 1959-60, 76 in 1960-61 and 14 more in 1961-62 before being traded to Chicago. Across those segments he appeared in 186 regular-season games for St. Louis and developed from a reserve into a substantial backcourt contributor. His 1960-61 season was the strongest full Hawks year of the run: 25.9 minutes, 9.2 points, 5.0 rebounds and 3.4 assists per game. He also retained enough value to become part of a later multi-player trade package.

Cincinnati Return
Park was a useful return rather than a throw-in. He played 33 Cincinnati games after the trade in 1958-59, averaging 27.2 minutes, 9.7 points, 4.5 rebounds and 2.4 assists, then appeared in 74 games in 1959-60 at 25.0 minutes, 8.7 points, 4.1 rebounds and 2.9 assists. That produced 107 Royals games over two seasons. Stephens, however, did not add any post-trade NBA value. Basketball-Reference lists his entire NBA career as the 72 games he played for St. Louis in 1955-56, so Cincinnati's realized package is essentially Park's two seasons.

Hindsight Comparison
Both teams received useful NBA production, but St. Louis got more longevity and a player who remained relevant to later roster construction. Green supplied 186 Hawks games over parts of four seasons, compared with Park's 107 Cincinnati games over two seasons and no post-trade NBA appearances from Stephens. Cincinnati's return was respectable enough to avoid a wide grade gap, especially because Park immediately handled substantial minutes. The verified outcome supports a moderate Hawks edge rather than the legacy Royals-favored verdict.

Final Verdict
Hawks Edge, B+/B-. St. Louis receives a B+ for 186 games from Green and a later usable trade asset. Cincinnati receives a B- for 107 productive games from Park, while Stephens produced no post-trade NBA appearances. Confidence is medium-high because the transaction package is well verified but RealGM and Basketball-Reference disagree on the exact January date. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Philadelphia traded Jack George to the New York Knicks for Guy Sparrow on January 27, 1959. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, New York and league transaction ledgers all preserve the same date and one-for-one package, while Eddie Gottlieb's executive ledger independently confirms the Warriors' side. George then played 110 regular-season games for New York over parts of three seasons, averaging 8.2 points and 3.0 assists. Sparrow played only 34 games for Philadelphia over parts of two seasons and averaged 3.4 points and 2.4 rebounds. The realized return clearly favors the Knicks, although George's best NBA years had already come before the trade.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange
Philadelphia sent Jack George to New York for Guy Sparrow on January 27, 1959. The Warriors and Knicks transaction pages, the league transaction ledger and Eddie Gottlieb's executive record all agree on the date and the simple player-for-player structure. No draft pick, cash term or later condition appears in those ledgers, so the source-backed review preserves the legacy package while replacing the thin legacy write-up with a fully sourced retrospective.

New York Return
George gave the Knicks a useful veteran guard after arriving during the 1958-59 season. He played 25 games for New York that year, then 69 in 1959-60 and 16 more in 1960-61. Across 110 Knicks games he averaged 8.2 points, 3.0 assists and 2.8 rebounds while handling a regular backcourt role. His peak honors had come earlier with Philadelphia, including two All-Star selections and an All-NBA Second Team season, so New York did not acquire the prime version of George. Even so, it received more than a season and a half of rotation value from a proven guard.

Philadelphia Return
Sparrow's Warriors tenure was much shorter. He appeared in 23 Philadelphia games after the trade in 1958-59 and 11 more in 1959-60, for 34 total games. His combined Philadelphia line was 3.4 points and 2.4 rebounds per game in 9.3 minutes, and 1959-60 became his final NBA season. Sparrow had been an 11.1-point scorer for New York as a rookie in 1957-58, but that earlier production did not carry over into a substantial Warriors role.

Hindsight Comparison
The gap comes from durability and usable post-trade minutes rather than star-level upside. George stayed with New York for 110 games and remained a regular part of the guard rotation. Sparrow lasted only 34 games with Philadelphia and was out of the NBA after the following season. Because George was already 30 and his All-Star peak predated the trade, the Knicks' advantage should not be inflated into a franchise-changing result. It was still a clear exchange of one declining veteran for another in which New York extracted much more remaining NBA value.

Final Verdict
Knicks Win, B+/C-. New York receives a B+ for 110 games and useful veteran backcourt production from George. Philadelphia receives a C- because Sparrow produced only 34 games and a limited role before his NBA career ended. Confidence is high because multiple Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers agree on the date and package and both players' post-trade production is directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit traded George Yardley to the Syracuse Nationals for Ed Conlin on February 13, 1959. Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Syracuse and league transaction ledgers all use February 13, correcting the legacy February 7 date, and executive ledgers for Nick Kerbawy and Danny Biasone confirm the one-for-one exchange. Yardley played 88 regular-season games for Syracuse over the rest of 1958-59 and all of 1959-60, averaged 19.6 points per game there and made the 1960 All-Star team. Conlin gave Detroit 85 games across parts of two seasons before being traded again in 1960. The Nationals received the stronger realized player, but Detroit still got a useful rotation return rather than an empty asset.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Detroit sent George Yardley to Syracuse for Ed Conlin on February 13, 1959. Basketball-Reference's Pistons, Nationals and league transaction pages all agree on that date, as do the Nick Kerbawy and Danny Biasone executive ledgers. That agreement corrects the legacy February 7 date while preserving the basic one-for-one package. The deal moved a five-time All-Star scorer out of Detroit for a younger wing who had spent his first three seasons with Syracuse.

Syracuse Return
Yardley remained a high-level scorer after the trade. He played 15 regular-season games for Syracuse to finish 1958-59, averaging 16.7 points and 6.9 rebounds, then appeared in 73 games in 1959-60 at 20.2 points and 7.9 rebounds per game. Across 88 Nationals games he averaged 19.6 points and 7.8 rebounds, made the 1960 All-Star team and added a major playoff burst immediately after the trade. He retired from the NBA after the 1959-60 season, so the return was short, but it was high quality.

Detroit Return
Conlin gave the Pistons more ordinary but still usable depth. He played 15 Detroit games after the trade in 1958-59 and 70 more in 1959-60, for 85 regular-season appearances. His role was not comparable to Yardley's star scoring, but Detroit did not lose the asset immediately; Conlin remained in the rotation through the next season before being moved in another trade in 1960. That longevity keeps the Pistons' side above the level of a failed return even though the quality gap is clear.

Hindsight Comparison
Syracuse won the exchange because Yardley continued to perform at an All-Star level and produced nearly 20 points per game across his 88 regular-season appearances with the franchise. Detroit received roughly the same number of games from Conlin, but the impact was materially lower and never approached Yardley's scoring or status. The limited duration of Yardley's Nationals tenure keeps the grade from reaching the very top tier, while Conlin's 85 games prevent Detroit from being treated as receiving no meaningful value.

Final Verdict
Nationals Win, A-/B-. Syracuse receives an A- for 88 high-end games, a 1960 All-Star selection and immediate playoff scoring from Yardley. Detroit receives a B- for 85 games of useful rotation service from Conlin before moving him again in 1960. Confidence is high because five independent Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers agree on the corrected February 13 date and the two-player package. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Detroit sent Phil Jordon to Cincinnati on March 31, 1959 for Archie Dees and Cincinnati's 1959 second-round draft pick. The Pistons, Royals and league transaction pages all list the same package, and the Nick Kerbawy and Pepper Wilson executive ledgers independently match it. The pick became Tom Robitaille at No. 9 overall. The source-backed review preserves the legacy date and assets while replacing the malformed draft-pick text and verifying all three identities.

Cincinnati Return
Jordon became a regular center immediately. He played all 75 Cincinnati games in 1959-60, averaging 27.5 minutes, 13.4 points, 8.3 rebounds and 2.8 assists. He remained with the Royals for 48 games in 1960-61 and averaged 10.9 points and 8.8 rebounds before being traded to New York. Across 123 Cincinnati games he supplied substantially more minutes and scoring than either incoming Detroit asset ultimately generated, giving the Royals a dependable two-season interior player rather than a short-term rental.

Detroit Return
Dees provided useful but lower-volume production for Detroit. He appeared in 73 games in 1959-60 at 9.7 points and 5.4 rebounds per game, then 28 games in 1960-61 at 5.2 points and 3.4 rebounds. His Pistons total was 101 games, 8.4 points and 4.9 rebounds per game. The draft pick added no NBA return: Detroit selected Rice center Tom Robitaille ninth overall in the 1959 draft, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season games for him. That makes Dees effectively the entire realized professional return.

Hindsight Comparison
Detroit received two assets on paper, but Cincinnati received the better realized package. Jordon played 22 more games for the Royals than Dees did for the Pistons, handled a substantially larger role and produced more scoring and rebounding over his Cincinnati tenure. Dees was a credible rotation forward-center and had a productive first Pistons season, so Detroit's side still carried real value. Robitaille's lack of NBA appearances, however, removes the extra leverage that the draft pick might otherwise have provided.

Final Verdict
Royals Win, B+/B-. Cincinnati receives a B+ for 123 games of starting-caliber center production from Jordon across parts of two seasons. Detroit receives a B- for 101 useful games from Dees, with no NBA production from the acquired second-round pick. Confidence is high because five Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers agree on the package and the player and draft records directly document what each asset became. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Cincinnati acquired Hub Reed from St. Louis on November 4, 1959 for a player to be named later, which contemporary reporting and later transaction records identify as the rights to No. 1 overall pick Bob Boozer on December 22. A 1961 Cincinnati media guide and a November 5, 1959 newspaper report confirm Reed joined the Royals at that time, while December reporting confirms Boozer's rights completed the exchange. Reed played 304 regular-season games for Cincinnati across four seasons. Boozer never played for St. Louis; RealGM records his rights returning to Cincinnati on April 15, 1960 before his NBA debut. The realized on-court return therefore favors the Royals, while the archival record carries a transaction-ledger conflict that lowers confidence slightly.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Cincinnati acquired Hub Reed from St. Louis on November 4, 1959 for a player to be named later. A contemporary November 5 newspaper item reports the Reed acquisition on those terms, and Cincinnati's 1961 media guide says Reed joined the Royals on November 4. On December 22, contemporary wire coverage reported that St. Louis received the rights to Bob Boozer, Cincinnati's No. 1 overall pick from the 1959 draft, to complete the earlier Reed transaction. RealGM also records the Hawks' acquisition of Boozer's rights on December 22. Current Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers instead fold Reed into a January 31, 1960 Dave Piontek/Dave Gambee transaction, so the source-backed record preserves the better contemporaneous November/December chronology and explicitly records the ledger conflict.

Cincinnati Return
Reed became a durable Royals rotation big. Basketball-Reference credits him with 69 Cincinnati games in 1959-60, 75 in 1960-61, 80 in 1961-62 and 80 in 1962-63, or 304 regular-season games across four seasons. His Cincinnati aggregate was 6.6 points and 6.0 rebounds per game, with his largest role coming immediately after the trade when he averaged 9.7 points and 8.9 rebounds in 69 games. That is substantial realized value for a player acquired as part of a midseason roster adjustment.

St. Louis Return
Boozer was an extremely valuable prospect, but the Hawks did not turn the acquired rights into any Bob Boozer NBA games. He spent 1959-60 outside the NBA, and RealGM records Cincinnati reacquiring his draft rights from St. Louis on April 15, 1960. Boozer then signed with Cincinnati before the 1960-61 season and ultimately played 269 regular-season games for the Royals through the first 32 games of 1963-64. Because the April rights return is a separate transaction, this record does not credit Boozer's later Cincinnati production as an additional direct asset from the November trade. It does, however, mean St. Louis's original return was temporary rather than the long-term star asset implied by the legacy grade.

Hindsight Comparison
The direct realized value strongly favors Cincinnati. Reed produced four seasons and 304 games for the Royals, including a substantial 1959-60 role immediately after his arrival. St. Louis temporarily controlled the rights to a future productive NBA player but never received a Boozer appearance, and those rights returned to Cincinnati before Boozer entered the league. The exact mechanics of the later rights return are inconsistently represented across modern transaction databases, so it would overstate the evidence to treat Boozer's full Cincinnati career as part of this one trade or to assign a zero-value label to the rights themselves. The safest hindsight conclusion is that Cincinnati received the much stronger on-court outcome from the November exchange.

Final Verdict
Royals Win, A-/C+. Cincinnati receives an A- for 304 games and four seasons of useful frontcourt production from Reed. St. Louis receives a C+ because Boozer's rights were a premium asset with real transaction value, but he never played for the Hawks and the rights returned to Cincinnati before his NBA debut. Confidence is medium-high rather than high because contemporary newspapers, Cincinnati's team media guide and RealGM support the November 4/December 22 structure while current Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers record a conflicting January 31 package. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit sold the player rights to Barney Cable to the Syracuse Nationals on November 10, 1959 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Syracuse, league, Nick Kerbawy and Danny Biasone transaction ledgers all agree on the date and sale structure. Cable then became a real rotation piece for Syracuse: the Nationals' 1962 media guide credits him with 125 regular-season games across two seasons, and Basketball-Reference lists 75 games and 1,642 minutes in 1960-61 alone. Detroit received guaranteed financial consideration, but the public records do not preserve the amount. Because Syracuse extracted two seasons of usable frontcourt depth before losing Cable in the 1961 expansion draft, the realized basketball return gives the Nationals the edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Detroit sold Barney Cable's player rights to Syracuse on November 10, 1959. The Pistons, Nationals and league transaction pages all use the same date, and the Nick Kerbawy and Danny Biasone executive ledgers independently record the sale. That evidence supports the legacy cash-for-player structure and removes the ambiguity created by the old thin summary. The cash amount is not preserved in the public ledgers, so the retrospective grade has to treat Detroit's return as real but unquantified financial value rather than inventing a dollar figure.

Syracuse Return
Cable gave the Nationals substantially more than a short trial. Syracuse's 1962 media guide credits him with 125 regular-season games across two seasons. Basketball-Reference shows that he played 75 games in 1960-61 and logged 1,642 minutes, making him a regular frontcourt rotation piece rather than an end-of-bench acquisition. He also appeared in all three games of Syracuse's 1960 division semifinal against Philadelphia. The Nationals therefore converted cash into two seasons of meaningful depth during a period in which they remained a playoff team.

Detroit Return
Detroit received cash and moved on from a player who had appeared in only 31 games as a rookie in 1958-59. From the Pistons' perspective, monetizing the rights to a reserve forward was a defensible roster decision. The problem for a hindsight comparison is that the cash amount is unknown, while Cable's post-trade basketball value is directly visible. Without a documented premium or another asset attached to the sale, there is no basis for treating Detroit's return as equal to 125 games of rotation production.

Hindsight Comparison
Syracuse wins the realized-value comparison because Cable stayed for two seasons and played a genuine role. Detroit did receive immediate guaranteed consideration, so this is not a lopsided failure for the Pistons. Cable was never a star and Syracuse eventually lost him to Chicago in the 1961 expansion draft without a trade return. Still, the Nationals got much more basketball utility than the legacy write-up suggested, and the known on-court value outweighs an undisclosed cash payment in the absence of evidence that the payment was unusually large.

Final Verdict
Nationals Win, B+/C+. Syracuse receives a B+ for two seasons and 125 regular-season games of usable depth from Cable. Detroit receives a C+ for converting a reserve player's rights into cash, with the unknown amount limiting any stronger retrospective credit. Confidence is high because five Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers agree on the date and structure and the Nationals' own media guide documents Cable's two-season tenure. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: New York sold Ron Sobie's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers on December 1, 1959 for cash. Basketball-Reference's league, Knicks, Lakers, Fred Podesta and Bob Short transaction ledgers all agree on the date and sale structure, while RealGM records the same acquisition under Sobie's longer surname form. The Lakers received almost no realized basketball value: Sobie appeared in one Minneapolis game, played 13 minutes and scored two points, and he never played in the NBA again. New York's cash return is not publicly quantified, but the Knicks converted rights to a player at the end of his NBA career into guaranteed consideration. The verified hindsight result therefore favors New York.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange
New York sold Ron Sobie's player rights to Minneapolis on December 1, 1959 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Lakers and league transaction pages all record the same date and structure. Fred Podesta's New York executive ledger and Bob Short's Minneapolis ledger independently match the transaction, while RealGM lists the player as Ron Sobiezczyk. Those records support normalizing the malformed legacy 'Ron Sobie)' label to Ron Sobie while retaining the longer surname variants as aliases rather than treating them as different players.

Minneapolis Return
The Lakers received almost no on-court return. Sobie appeared in one game for Minneapolis during the 1959-60 season, played 13 minutes, made one field goal and finished with two points, two rebounds and two assists. That became the final game of his four-year NBA career. Minneapolis did reach the Western Division Finals that season, but Sobie did not become a meaningful part of the rotation or playoff run. The transaction therefore produced essentially one brief regular-season appearance for the acquiring club.

New York Return
The Knicks received cash, and the surviving public transaction ledgers do not preserve the amount. That limits how aggressively the financial return can be graded, but the basic outcome is still favorable. New York moved the rights to a player who had already appeared in 191 games for the franchise and was nearing the end of his NBA career, then received guaranteed consideration rather than carrying an asset that generated almost no future league production. No later player or draft obligation was attached to the sale in the verified ledgers.

Hindsight Comparison
This is a straightforward realized-value edge for New York. Minneapolis paid cash for rights that yielded one 13-minute appearance and no later NBA value. New York's return cannot be measured precisely because the cash amount is unknown, so the Knicks should not receive an elite grade for the transaction. Even a modest payment, however, compares favorably with the tiny basketball return the Lakers received. The deal is best understood as a successful rights sale for New York and a low-cost acquisition that simply did not work for Minneapolis.

Final Verdict
Knicks Win, B/C-. New York receives a B for monetizing the rights to a player whose NBA career was effectively over. Minneapolis receives a C- because Sobie produced only one game and 13 minutes after the purchase, though the unknown cash price prevents treating the miss as a major organizational loss. Confidence is high because multiple Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers agree on the date and mechanics and Sobie's post-sale production is directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
los-angeles-lakers.gradeRationale: The Lakers produced a modest realized-value advantage. Grades weigh realized player production, identifiable pick conversion, role, timing, contract context and downstream asset use.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Syracuse sold Frank Selvy's player rights to the Minneapolis Lakers on December 15, 1959 for cash. Basketball-Reference's league, Syracuse, Minneapolis and executive transaction ledgers all agree on the date and sale structure, and RealGM independently records the same move. Selvy then played 352 regular-season games for the Lakers over the rest of his career, made the 1962 All-Star team and became a major guard on the 1962 and 1963 NBA Finals teams. The public ledgers do not preserve the cash amount Syracuse received. The verified hindsight result therefore favors the Lakers by a wide margin, while the undisclosed payment keeps the Nationals' side from being treated as a zero-value return.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange
Syracuse sold Frank Selvy's player rights to Minneapolis for cash on December 15, 1959. Basketball-Reference's Nationals, Lakers and league transaction pages all use that date, and the Danny Biasone and Bob Short executive ledgers independently preserve the same transfer from each front office. RealGM also records Selvy moving from Syracuse to Minneapolis that day. The source-backed review therefore keeps the canonical Philadelphia franchise key but uses the historically correct Syracuse Nationals name in the copy. The cash amount is not available in the public ledgers, so the financial return cannot be measured precisely.

Lakers Return
Selvy became a durable part of the Lakers backcourt almost immediately. He played 43 Minneapolis games after the sale in 1959-60, then 77 games in 1960-61, 79 in 1961-62, 80 in 1962-63 and 73 in 1963-64. That is 352 regular-season games after the transaction, separate from a brief earlier Lakers stint in 1957-58. His best post-sale season came in 1961-62, when he averaged 14.7 points, 5.2 rebounds and 4.8 assists and made the All-Star team. He also appeared in 50 playoff games over those five seasons, including major minutes during the Lakers' 1962 and 1963 runs to the NBA Finals.

Syracuse Return
The Nationals received cash and no player or draft asset appears in the verified transaction ledgers. That makes the return impossible to grade with the same precision as Selvy's on-court production. Syracuse had claimed Selvy on waivers from New York only weeks earlier, so selling his rights did convert a recently acquired veteran into guaranteed consideration. Still, the opportunity cost became substantial once Selvy settled into a five-season Lakers role. The unknown cash amount deserves real weight, but there is no surviving evidence that it approached the basketball value Minneapolis ultimately received.

Hindsight Comparison
Minneapolis received the clearly superior realized basketball return. Selvy became a five-season contributor, made an All-Star team and played deep into the postseason repeatedly, while Syracuse's benefit is limited to an undisclosed cash payment. The deal was not a superstar heist, because Selvy was already 27 and had bounced among several teams, but the Lakers found a stable role for him during the franchise's transition from Minneapolis to Los Angeles. That combination of longevity, playoff usefulness and a relatively simple acquisition cost creates a wide hindsight gap.

Final Verdict
Lakers Win, A-/C+. The Lakers receive an A- for acquiring 352 games, an All-Star season and substantial Finals-era backcourt value for cash. Syracuse receives a C+ because the club did receive guaranteed consideration for a recently claimed veteran, but the amount is unknown and no lasting basketball asset came back. Confidence is high because multiple Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers agree on the date and mechanics and Selvy's Lakers production is directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
los-angeles-lakers.gradeRationale: Frank Selvy became a useful starting and rotation guard for multiple Lakers Finals teams after being acquired for cash.

summary: St. Louis acquired Larry Foust from the Minneapolis Lakers in a transaction Basketball-Reference dates to February 1, 1960. The Hawks sent Chuck Share plus the draft rights to Nick Mantis and Willie Merriweather, while Pro Sports Transactions and a contemporary Lakers chronology also preserve a $10,000 cash payment to Minneapolis.
