atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Minneapolis, St. Louis and league transaction ledgers all date the Larry Foust deal to February 1, 1960, one day later than the legacy Atlanta-source record. The verified core package sent Foust to St. Louis for Chuck Share and the draft rights to Nick Mantis and Willie Merriweather. Pro Sports Transactions and the APBR Lakers chronology also preserve a $10,000 cash payment from St. Louis to Minneapolis. Because the stronger cluster of team, league and chronology sources uses February 1, the source-backed review corrects the canonical date while retaining the cash term supported outside Basketball-Reference.

St. Louis Return
Foust gave the Hawks a useful veteran center for the rest of his NBA career. He played 25 games after the trade in 1959-60, then 68 games in 1960-61 and 57 more in 1961-62. Across those 150 St. Louis regular-season games he scored 1,359 points and grabbed 899 rebounds. His role was no longer the All-Star-level centerpiece it had been earlier in the decade, but he remained a dependable interior contributor on teams that reached the 1960 and 1961 NBA Finals. The immediate return was especially efficient: Foust averaged 10.2 points and 7.3 rebounds in 22.6 minutes during his 25-game finish to the 1959-60 season.

Minneapolis Return
The Lakers received several assets on paper, but very little of the basketball value lasted. Share appeared in only three regular-season games for Minneapolis before his NBA career ended. Mantis played 10 games for the Lakers in 1959-60, totaling 71 minutes and 21 points, then spent the next two seasons outside the NBA before later resurfacing elsewhere. Merriweather never played in an NBA game. The $10,000 cash payment gave Minneapolis guaranteed financial consideration, and that prevents the return from being graded as a complete zero. Still, the three basketball assets produced only 13 Lakers regular-season appearances combined.

Hindsight Comparison
This is one of the clearer veteran-for-depth exchanges in the early archive. St. Louis gave up an aging reserve center, two draft-rights assets with limited or no NBA impact, and cash, then received 150 games from Foust plus meaningful frontcourt minutes on two Finals teams. Minneapolis gained flexibility and some money, but the actual player return barely materialized. Share was at the end of his career, Mantis never became part of the rotation, and Merriweather never reached the league. The difference is not superstar upside; it is simply that one side received three seasons of usable NBA production while the other received almost none.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, A-/C. St. Louis receives an A- for converting expendable depth, two low-impact rights assets and $10,000 into 150 games from Foust and meaningful contributions during consecutive Finals seasons. Minneapolis receives a C because the cash payment had real value, but Share, Mantis and Merriweather produced almost no sustained on-court return. Confidence is high on the player and rights package and on the February 1 date because multiple Basketball-Reference ledgers agree; the $10,000 term is supported by Pro Sports Transactions and the APBR chronology. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: St. Louis traded Bob Ferry to the Detroit Pistons for Ed Conlin on April 16, 1960. Basketball-Reference's Hawks, Pistons and league transaction ledgers all preserve the same date and one-for-one package. Ferry became a four-season Detroit rotation center, playing 312 regular-season games from 1960-61 through 1963-64 and totaling 3,851 points and 1,968 rebounds before he was included in the 1964 Bailey Howell trade with Baltimore. Conlin never appeared in a regular-season game for St. Louis; the Hawks moved him with cash to Philadelphia before the next season began. Although that later move returned Ernie Beck and Woody Sauldsberry, Detroit received the far stronger direct and durable value from the original exchange.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis traded Bob Ferry to Detroit for Ed Conlin on April 16, 1960. The Hawks, Pistons and league Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers all agree on the date and straightforward player-for-player structure. Ferry had just completed his rookie season after St. Louis selected him in the first round of the 1959 draft. Conlin was an established veteran who had arrived in Detroit in the George Yardley trade a year earlier. There is no additional cash or draft component attached to this April transaction in the verified ledgers, so the source-backed review keeps the package simple and judges the result from the players' actual post-trade paths.

Detroit Return
Ferry became a durable rotation center for four full Pistons seasons. He played 79 games in 1960-61, 80 in 1961-62, 79 in 1962-63 and 74 in 1963-64, totaling 312 regular-season appearances. Across those seasons he scored 3,851 points and collected 1,968 rebounds. His strongest scoring season was 1961-62, when he averaged 13.9 points and 6.3 rebounds, and he remained an important frontcourt piece through 1963-64. Detroit later included Ferry in the June 1964 multi-player trade with Baltimore that brought Terry Dischinger, Don Kojis and Rod Thorn to the Pistons, giving his tenure identifiable downstream value beyond the four seasons he played directly.

St. Louis Return
Conlin never played a regular-season game for the Hawks. St. Louis acquired him in April after the 1959-60 season and then traded him on October 17, 1960 with cash to the Philadelphia Warriors for Ernie Beck and Woody Sauldsberry before the next regular season began. That downstream conversion means the Hawks did not simply lose the asset for nothing, and both Beck and Sauldsberry subsequently appeared for St. Louis. Still, Conlin himself provided no on-court return to the Hawks, while the later package came only after St. Louis added cash and moved him again. The direct April exchange therefore produced almost no immediate basketball value for the Hawks.

Hindsight Comparison
Detroit clearly received the more durable asset. Ferry gave the Pistons 312 games, four seasons of frontcourt minutes and later became part of another substantial trade package. St. Louis used Conlin as an offseason bridge asset and converted him before he ever appeared for the club. The Hawks' later Beck-Sauldsberry return deserves recognition, but it should not erase the difference between four years of direct production and a player who never suited up for the acquiring team. Ferry was not an All-Star, yet his reliability, scoring and rebounding make the original one-for-one trade decisively favorable to Detroit.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, A-/C+. Detroit receives an A- for 312 games of useful center production plus downstream trade value from Ferry in 1964. St. Louis receives a C+ because Conlin never played for the Hawks, although the club did convert him into Beck and Sauldsberry before the season began. Confidence is high because multiple Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers agree on the April 16 package and both players' post-trade paths are directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The Warriors, Pistons and league Basketball-Reference transaction pages all use the same date and identify the move as a sale rather than a player-for-player trade. Ohl had been drafted by Philadelphia in 1958 but spent the next two seasons outside the NBA in the NIBL, so the Warriors were monetizing rights to a player who had not yet joined their roster. The surviving public ledgers do not preserve the cash amount, which limits any precise financial judgment on Philadelphia's side. What can be measured is the NBA value Detroit received once Ohl signed.

Detroit Return
Ohl became a major Pistons backcourt piece immediately. He played 79 games as a rookie in 1960-61, 77 in 1961-62, 80 in 1962-63 and 71 in 1963-64. Across four Detroit seasons he totaled 307 regular-season games and 5,137 points. His scoring climbed from 13.3 points per game as a rookie to 17.0 in his second season and 19.3 in 1962-63, when he made his first All-Star team. He was an All-Star again in 1963-64 while averaging 17.3 points. Ohl also handled substantial minutes in Detroit's playoff appearances and became one of the team's primary perimeter scorers during the early 1960s.

Philadelphia Return
The Warriors received cash, but the amount is not available in the team or league transaction records located for this review. That uncertainty deserves some protection in the grade because a rights sale cannot be treated as if Philadelphia literally received nothing. The larger problem is opportunity cost. Ohl was only 24 when he debuted for Detroit and immediately became a regular NBA guard. Philadelphia had Wilt Chamberlain and a competitive roster, but the decision to sell Ohl's rights removed a player who went on to provide four productive Detroit seasons before entering another major transaction. No later player, pick or conditional asset is attached to the Warriors' side in the verified ledgers.

Hindsight Comparison
The realized gap is substantial. Detroit turned cash into 307 games, more than 5,000 points, two All-Star selections and a player valuable enough to be included in the 1964 multi-player trade with Baltimore. Philadelphia received an undisclosed one-time payment. The price could have made sense to the Warriors at the time because Ohl had remained outside the NBA for two years after being drafted, but retrospective value strongly favors Detroit once his career materialized. This is exactly the kind of rights purchase where uncertainty before the transaction and clarity after it point in different directions: the acquisition risk was real, yet the completed outcome was excellent.

Final Verdict
Pistons Win, A+/D+. Detroit receives an A+ for buying the rights to a future two-time Detroit All-Star who delivered 307 games, 5,137 points and downstream trade value. Philadelphia receives a D+ because it received cash but surrendered a young player who became a high-level NBA starter almost immediately after the sale; the unknown payment prevents a harsher grade. Confidence is high because the date and sale structure are corroborated across multiple Basketball-Reference ledgers and Ohl's Detroit production is directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis sold Dave Gambee's player rights to Syracuse for cash on September 22, 1960. The St. Louis, Syracuse and league Basketball-Reference transaction pages all use that date, while the Ben Kerner and Danny Biasone executive ledgers independently preserve the move from each front office. Gambee had originally been a first-round St. Louis pick in 1958, spent only a brief early stint with the Hawks, moved through Cincinnati and returned to St. Louis as a rights asset before this sale. The public ledgers do not identify the cash amount, so the Hawks' financial return cannot be measured precisely.

Syracuse/Philadelphia Return
Gambee immediately became a substantial rotation forward for the Nationals. He played 79 games in 1960-61 and all 80 in 1961-62, when he averaged 16.7 points and 7.9 rebounds. He remained with the franchise through its move from Syracuse to Philadelphia, playing 60 games in 1962-63, 41 in 1963-64, 80 in 1964-65, 72 in 1965-66 and 63 in 1966-67. That is 475 regular-season games across seven seasons for the same franchise. His role diminished over time, but he remained a useful frontcourt option long enough to be part of the 1966-67 Philadelphia championship roster.

St. Louis Return
The Hawks received cash and no later player, pick or conditional asset appears on their side of the verified transaction. That makes the exact return impossible to quantify, and an undisclosed sale price should not be treated as worthless. Still, St. Louis gave up the rights to a 23-year-old forward who immediately became a starter-level scorer for Syracuse. The Hawks were already a strong contender and reached the 1961 NBA Finals without Gambee, so the move did not derail their short-term team success. Retrospectively, however, the cash payment had to be weighed against seven seasons and 475 games of useful production that materialized for the buyer.

Hindsight Comparison
Syracuse received the more durable basketball asset by a wide margin. Gambee gave the franchise two high-volume early seasons, remained productive through the transition to Philadelphia and lasted through the 1967 championship year. St. Louis received a one-time payment whose amount is unavailable. The Hawks' competitive context and the unknown price keep this from being treated as a catastrophic decision, but the realized basketball gap is clear. A cash-only acquisition that produces 475 games and seven seasons of roster continuity is far more valuable in hindsight than a sale with no identifiable downstream basketball asset.

Final Verdict
76ers Win, A-/C+. The Syracuse/Philadelphia franchise receives an A- for purchasing 475 games, seven seasons of frontcourt production and a contributor who remained through the 1967 title season. St. Louis receives a C+ because it received guaranteed cash and remained a contender, but the undisclosed amount cannot offset the long-term value Gambee delivered elsewhere. Confidence is high because multiple Basketball-Reference team, league and executive ledgers agree on the date and sale structure and Gambee's franchise production is directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: St. Louis traded Ed Conlin and cash to the Philadelphia Warriors for Woody Sauldsberry and Ernie Beck on October 17, 1960. Basketball-Reference's Hawks, Warriors and league transaction ledgers all agree on the date and four-part package. Sauldsberry played 83 regular-season games for St. Louis over parts of two seasons, averaging 7.4 points and 6.8 rebounds, while Beck appeared in seven Hawks games before his rights were sold to Syracuse. Conlin became a two-season Philadelphia rotation wing, playing 147 games at 5.8 points and 2.8 rebounds per game. The Hawks received the slightly stronger overall return because Sauldsberry provided comparable short-term value and later remained usable in another trade, while Beck also generated a cash recovery.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis sent Ed Conlin and cash to Philadelphia for Woody Sauldsberry and Ernie Beck on October 17, 1960. The Hawks, Warriors and league Basketball-Reference transaction pages all preserve the same package. Conlin had never played a regular-season game for St. Louis after arriving from Detroit in April, so the Hawks were converting an offseason asset plus cash into two established Warriors. Philadelphia, meanwhile, consolidated two veterans into one younger wing and financial consideration. The surviving public ledgers do not identify the cash amount, which limits how precisely the Warriors' return can be valued.

St. Louis Return
Sauldsberry became the main basketball return for the Hawks. He played 69 games in 1960-61, averaging 7.5 points and 7.1 rebounds in 21.6 minutes, then appeared in 14 more St. Louis games in 1961-62 before being traded to the Chicago Packers. Across 83 Hawks games he averaged roughly 7.4 points and 6.8 rebounds. St. Louis later included Sauldsberry with Joe Graboski and Si Green in the November 1961 trade that brought Barney Cable and Archie Dees back, so he retained some transactional value beyond his direct minutes. Beck's Hawks stay was much shorter: seven games at 2.7 points before St. Louis sold his rights to Syracuse on November 28, 1960, recovering another cash return.

Philadelphia Return
Conlin gave the Warriors more games than either incoming Hawk did individually. He played 77 games in 1960-61 and 70 more in 1961-62, totaling 147 regular-season appearances for Philadelphia. His role was modest but steady: 7.0 points, 3.4 rebounds and 1.6 assists per game in the first season, followed by 4.6 points and 2.2 rebounds in 1961-62. Across the two seasons he averaged about 5.8 points and 2.8 rebounds. Philadelphia also received cash in the original transaction, but the amount is not preserved in the public ledgers located for this review. Conlin left the NBA after the 1961-62 season, so the Warriors did not turn the deal into a long-duration asset.

Hindsight Comparison
The exchange is closer than the old archive grades suggested. Philadelphia received 147 games from Conlin plus cash, while St. Louis received 90 combined games from Sauldsberry and Beck before both were moved again. The difference is that Sauldsberry supplied stronger rebounding and comparable scoring on a per-game basis, then remained part of a later Hawks trade package, while Beck was sold for additional cash after his brief stay. Those secondary conversions give St. Louis a slight realized-value advantage, but Philadelphia's two full seasons of Conlin make a low grade inappropriate. This was a useful asset reshuffle for both clubs rather than a one-sided result.

Final Verdict
Hawks Win, B+/B-. St. Louis receives a B+ for 83 useful Sauldsberry games, a short Beck stint, a later cash sale and continued trade value from Sauldsberry. Philadelphia receives a B- for 147 games of Conlin plus the original cash payment; the unknown amount keeps the Warriors' side from being valued more precisely. Confidence is high on the date, players and cash component because multiple Basketball-Reference ledgers agree, while the exact financial value remains unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange
St. Louis sold Ernie Beck's player rights to Syracuse for cash on November 28, 1960. The St. Louis, Syracuse and league Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers all agree on the date and identify the move as a sale. Beck had only recently reached the Hawks: Philadelphia sent him and Woody Sauldsberry to St. Louis on October 17 for Ed Conlin and cash. Beck then appeared in seven games for the Hawks before St. Louis converted his rights back into cash. The surviving transaction pages do not preserve the amount Syracuse paid, so the Hawks' financial return cannot be measured exactly.

Syracuse Return
Beck's Nationals stint was extremely brief. He appeared in only three regular-season games for Syracuse in 1960-61, averaging 6.7 minutes, 2.3 points and 3.7 rebounds per game. Those were the final NBA games of a career that had begun with Philadelphia in 1953. Syracuse therefore purchased the rights to a veteran who was essentially at the end of his playing life. There was no later player, pick or conditional asset attached to the acquisition, and Beck did not become a multi-season depth piece as the legacy perspective claimed. His direct on-court contribution to the Nationals was three games.

St. Louis Return
The Hawks received cash and no identifiable basketball asset beyond that payment. Because the amount is unknown, the value should not be exaggerated. Still, St. Louis had acquired Beck only weeks earlier, received seven games from him and then recovered financial consideration before his NBA career ended. In other words, the Hawks extracted a small amount of playing value and then monetized the remaining rights. That is a much more efficient outcome than holding the player through the end of his career for three additional games. The move was minor, but it did preserve some value from a fading veteran asset.

Hindsight Comparison
This is a low-impact transaction where the winner is determined more by avoiding dead value than by acquiring meaningful talent. Syracuse paid cash for a player who gave the club three games and then disappeared from the NBA. St. Louis received an undisclosed payment for rights that were close to expiring in practical basketball terms. The unknown price prevents a strong directional grade because the Hawks' return could have been modest, but even a modest payment compares favorably with three short appearances. The source-backed review therefore reverses the legacy Nationals win and treats the deal as a slight St. Louis advantage.

Final Verdict
Hawks Edge, B-/C+. St. Louis receives a B- for turning a veteran it had used for seven games into cash before the player's NBA career ended. Syracuse receives a C+ because the acquisition cost was only cash, but Beck produced just three games and no downstream value. Confidence is high on the date, sale structure and Beck's limited Nationals stint because the team, league and player records agree. The exact cash amount remains unknown, so the grade gap is intentionally narrow. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Detroit sold Ron Johnson's player rights to Los Angeles for cash on December 15, 1960. The Pistons, Lakers and league Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers all agree on December 15, so the source-backed review corrects the legacy December 16 date. Johnson had been Detroit's second-round pick, 12th overall, in the 1960 draft and made six appearances for the Pistons before the sale. The public transaction ledgers do not identify the amount Los Angeles paid. That missing figure limits the precision of Detroit's grade, but Johnson's post-sale production is fully documented and makes the basketball side of the exchange unusually easy to evaluate.

Los Angeles Return
Johnson played only eight regular-season games for the Lakers. He averaged 5.4 minutes, 0.8 points and 1.9 rebounds per game while shooting 15.4 percent from the field. Those eight appearances were also the final NBA games of his career. Los Angeles therefore acquired a 22-year-old recent high draft pick, but the rights never developed into meaningful rotation value. Johnson did not produce a second season, a later trade return or another identifiable asset for the franchise. The Lakers' upside case existed on the transaction date because of his age and draft position, yet the completed outcome was minimal.

Detroit Return
The Pistons received cash after using Johnson for six games. He had averaged 10.0 minutes and 5.2 points in those appearances, so Detroit was not selling a player who had never reached the floor. Still, the club evidently decided quickly that monetizing his rights was preferable to carrying him longer. The exact payment remains unavailable, which prevents the source-backed review from assigning major value to the return. What is clear is that Detroit received guaranteed consideration for a player whose NBA career lasted only eight additional games. In hindsight, that was an efficient exit from an asset that was close to losing all practical basketball value.

Hindsight Comparison
This is a minor transaction with a narrow but defensible Detroit advantage. Los Angeles paid cash for eight games of deep-reserve production and no downstream return. Detroit received an undisclosed payment after six games and avoided holding the rights through the end of Johnson's short NBA career. The Lakers' risk was understandable because Johnson was only months removed from being selected 12th overall, so the result should not be graded like a major scouting failure. The unknown cash amount also prevents a precise value comparison. Even so, the side receiving guaranteed consideration for an asset that soon exited the league realized the better result.

Final Verdict
Pistons Edge, B-/C+. Detroit receives a B- for converting a young but short-lived player asset into cash before his NBA career ended. Los Angeles receives a C+ because the purchase was a reasonable upside bet on a recent 12th overall pick, but Johnson supplied only eight games and no lasting value. Confidence is high on the corrected December 15 date, sale structure and player outcome because the team, league and player records agree. The exact cash amount remains unknown, so the grade gap stays intentionally narrow. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

new-york-knicks.summary: Cincinnati sold Phil Jordon to the New York Knicks on January 18, 1961 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Royals, Knicks and league transaction ledgers all preserve the same date and sale structure. Jordon immediately became New York's starting-caliber center for the rest of 1960-61, averaging 13.1 points and 8.1 rebounds in 31 games, then played 76 more games for the Knicks in 1961-62 at 11.9 points and 6.3 rebounds per game. Across those two seasons he gave New York 107 regular-season games before the Knicks moved him in September 1962. The public ledgers do not preserve the cash amount Cincinnati received. Retrospectively, buying more than a season and a half of useful center production for cash clearly favors New York.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Exchange
Cincinnati sold Phil Jordon to New York for cash on January 18, 1961. The Royals, Knicks and league Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers all agree on the date and identify the move as a sale. Jordon was 27 and already an established rotation big man, so this was not a speculative rights purchase like several earlier archive sales. The public ledgers do not preserve the price New York paid, which prevents a precise financial comparison. The basketball side is much easier to measure because Jordon stepped directly into the Knicks' rotation and produced meaningful minutes immediately.

New York Return
Jordon played 31 games for the Knicks after the sale in 1960-61, averaging 13.1 points, 8.1 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 29.8 minutes per game. That was a larger role than he had held in Cincinnati earlier that season. He returned in 1961-62 and appeared in 76 games, averaging 11.9 points and 6.3 rebounds in 28.9 minutes. Across the two seasons New York received 107 regular-season games from the purchase, including a full season as a regular frontcourt contributor. The Knicks later moved him in September 1962, so his tenure was not long, but the cash purchase produced more than a season and a half of real rotation value.

Cincinnati Return
The Royals received cash and no later player, pick or conditional asset appears on their side of the verified transaction. That guaranteed return mattered because Cincinnati already had Wayne Embry and other frontcourt options, and Jordon was not irreplaceable to the team's structure. The missing cash amount remains the major unresolved variable. A large payment could materially improve the Royals' side of the evaluation, so the grade should not assume the sale had trivial financial value. Even with that caveat, Cincinnati gave up a player who still had 180 NBA games left after the transaction and who immediately played starter-level minutes for New York.

Hindsight Comparison
New York received the stronger realized basketball value. The Knicks bought 107 games of direct production at center, including nearly 30 minutes per game over his first half-season and another 76-game campaign. Cincinnati's return was one-time cash with no documented downstream basketball asset. This was not a franchise-altering deal and Jordon was never an All-Star for New York, but the buyer received exactly the kind of dependable rotation value that makes cash acquisitions worthwhile in hindsight. The unknown sale price keeps the result from becoming a runaway grade, yet the completed on-court record still points clearly toward the Knicks.

Final Verdict
Knicks Win, A-/C+. New York receives an A- for turning cash into 107 games of useful center production across two seasons. Cincinnati receives a C+ because it received guaranteed financial consideration and had roster alternatives, but the public record does not show a basketball asset coming back and Jordon remained productive after the sale. Confidence is high on the date, sale structure and post-trade production because the team, league and player ledgers agree. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

That same day, Chicago sold McNeill's player rights to Philadelphia for cash. The structure is source-closed, but the price is not. That missing amount matters because the Packers were monetizing part of a package they had just acquired, while the Warriors were buying the rights to a young guard with one NBA season already behind him. McNeill joined the Warriors for the 1961-62 season and appeared in 21 regular-season games. He averaged 4.1 points and 2.3 assists in 10.1 minutes per game, shooting 44.7 percent from the field. The role was limited but real. Philadelphia then sold his rights to the Los Angeles Lakers in December 1961, where he played another 29 regular-season games that season. The Warriors therefore received only a short stretch of direct production, but they also recovered an unknown amount of cash when they moved him again. Because that resale price is also unavailable, the full financial path on Philadelphia's side cannot be reconstructed.

Chicago received cash immediately after acquiring McNeill in the Dave Budd trade. That makes the sale part of the Packers' asset management rather than an isolated decision. The expansion team kept Tyra and Budd-related value while converting McNeill into money before he ever played for Chicago. The amount could have been small, moderate or substantial relative to the economics of the era; the public transaction records do not say. new-york-knicks.summary: New York reacquired Dave Budd from the expansion Chicago Packers on May 16, 1961 after losing him to Chicago in the April expansion draft. The Knicks sent the player rights to Charlie Tyra and Bob McNeill. Budd then played four more seasons for New York, appearing in 292 regular-season games from 1961-62 through 1964-65 and averaging 9.5 points and 5.1 rebounds at his post-trade peak in 1962-63. Tyra gave Chicago 78 games in 1961-62 at 6.7 points and 7.8 rebounds per game, while McNeill never played for the Packers because Chicago sold his rights to Philadelphia for cash the same day. The cash amount is unknown, but the direct realized basketball value favors New York clearly.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Exchange
The transaction is best understood as New York reversing part of the 1961 expansion draft. Chicago had selected Dave Budd from the Knicks on April 26, then traded him back to New York on May 16 for the player rights to Charlie Tyra and Bob McNeill. Basketball-Reference's league and team ledgers agree on the three-player structure, and the timing makes the logic unusually clear: the Packers converted an expansion-draft selection into two rights assets, while the Knicks paid to recover a forward they already knew. Chicago immediately sold McNeill's rights to Philadelphia for cash on the same day, so its practical return became Tyra plus an undisclosed cash payment.

New York Return
Budd gave the Knicks four additional seasons after being reacquired. He played 79 games in 1961-62, 78 in 1962-63, 73 in 1963-64 and 62 in 1964-65, totaling 292 regular-season games after the trade. His best post-trade season was 1962-63, when he averaged 9.5 points and 5.1 rebounds in 22.1 minutes per game. He was never a star, but he provided sustained frontcourt depth and remained in the rotation far longer than either player New York surrendered remained with Chicago. Reacquiring a known contributor for four seasons is a strong outcome for a team that had just lost him in the expansion draft.

Chicago Return
Tyra became the direct basketball return. He played all 78 games for the Packers in 1961-62, averaging 6.7 points and 7.8 rebounds in 20.6 minutes per game. That is meaningful one-season value, especially for an expansion roster. McNeill never appeared for Chicago; the Packers sold his rights to Philadelphia for cash on the same day as the Budd trade. The amount is not preserved in the public transaction ledgers, so Chicago's full financial return cannot be quantified. The important point is that the Packers did receive both a usable one-year frontcourt player and a monetized second asset rather than losing Budd for nothing.

Hindsight Comparison
New York still comes out ahead. Budd produced 292 post-trade games across four seasons, giving the Knicks a durable rotation player they had already developed. Chicago got one full season from Tyra and an unknown cash payment for McNeill's rights. That is a respectable expansion-team return, but it did not create comparable long-term basketball value. The cash prevents the gap from becoming extreme because the Packers extracted additional value from McNeill immediately. Even with that caveat, four seasons of Budd outweigh one season of Tyra when the later cash amount is unknown.

Final Verdict
Knicks Win, A-/B-. New York receives an A- for reacquiring 292 games of useful frontcourt production from a player it had lost in the expansion draft. Chicago receives a B- because Tyra supplied 78 games and strong rebounding in the franchise's inaugural season, while McNeill's rights were converted into cash the same day. Confidence is high on the player package, timing and post-trade production; confidence is lower only on the unknown McNeill sale amount. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Philadelphia sold Vern Hatton's player rights to the expansion Chicago Packers on May 31, 1961 for cash. Hatton then played 15 regular-season games for Chicago in 1961-62, averaging 9.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.9 assists in 26.4 minutes per game. Chicago sold his rights back to Philadelphia on November 29, and the Warriors sold them to St. Louis the next day; Hatton finished his NBA career with 25 Hawks games. The public ledgers do not preserve the cash amount in the May sale or the November buyback. Because the same asset generated multiple unpriced cash transactions around only 15 Packers games, the source-backed verdict remains Insufficient Evidence rather than inventing a financial comparison.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange
Philadelphia sold Vern Hatton's player rights to the Chicago Packers for cash on May 31, 1961. Basketball-Reference's league and team ledgers preserve the sale, and the 1961-62 Packers media guide independently places Hatton on Chicago's inaugural roster after the transaction. The challenge is not the direction or player identity; it is the missing price. Philadelphia received cash, but the amount is not published in the sources located for this review. That becomes especially important because Hatton later returned to Philadelphia through another rights sale only six months later.

Chicago Return
Hatton gave the Packers a short but tangible stretch of backcourt production. He appeared in 15 regular-season games for Chicago in 1961-62, averaging 9.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.9 assists in 26.4 minutes per game. Those numbers are meaningful for an expansion team trying to assemble competent veteran minutes. Chicago then sold Hatton's rights back to Philadelphia on November 29, 1961. The amount of that resale is also unavailable. That means the Packers received both 15 games of player value and an unknown cash recovery, but the total economic benefit cannot be reconstructed from the surviving public ledgers.

Philadelphia Return
The Warriors received cash in May, then reacquired Hatton's rights in November before selling them to St. Louis one day later. Hatton never played another regular-season game for Philadelphia after the May transaction. The Warriors therefore used him as a financial and rights asset rather than an on-court contributor during this sequence. Without the May sale price, the November repurchase price and the November 30 sale amount to St. Louis, the financial path is incomplete. Any attempt to assign a precise advantage to Philadelphia would require assumptions about three separate cash terms.

Hindsight Comparison
The basketball side slightly favors Chicago because the Packers actually received 15 games of useful guard minutes before moving Hatton again. The economic side is impossible to settle. Philadelphia may have sold high and repurchased low, or the opposite; Chicago may have recovered most or all of its original cost, or it may not have. The public record does not answer those questions. Because the player contribution was limited to 15 games, it is not large enough to overwhelm the missing financial information the way a multi-year starter or All-Star outcome might. This is therefore a transaction where source completeness should take priority over a forced grade.

Final Verdict
Insufficient Evidence. The May 31, 1961 sale is verified, Hatton's 15-game Packers stint is verified, and his November return to Philadelphia followed by the immediate St. Louis sale is verified. The cash amounts are not. Those missing terms are material to a fair retrospective judgment, so the record remains ungraded with no declared winner. Confidence is high on the chronology and player value, but intentionally limited on comparative transaction value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: This July 1, 1961 Gary Alcorn Detroit-to-Los Angeles cash transaction is retained only as legacy provenance. The supported record shows Alcorn became a free agent from Detroit on July 1, 1960, signed with the Lakers on October 24, 1960, played 20 games for Los Angeles, and was waived on December 15 before becoming a free agent again on December 17. Basketball-Reference's 1960-61 and 1961-62 transaction ledgers do not show a July 1, 1961 Detroit-Lakers trade, and RealGM's player transaction history ends Alcorn's NBA movement with the December 1960 waiver. The Lakers' own alumni record likewise lists only his 1960-61 season. With no corroborating 1961 trade and a chronology incompatible with the legacy archive entry, the record is structurally superseded.
perspectives.analysis:
The legacy Claim
The legacy Detroit record describes a July 1, 1961 transaction in which the Pistons supposedly sent Gary Alcorn to the Los Angeles Lakers for cash. The surviving transaction record does not support that event. Basketball-Reference's Detroit and Los Angeles transaction pages for the surrounding seasons contain no matching July 1961 trade, and the league transaction logs do not list one either. The problem is more than a missing secondary source: Alcorn's documented career chronology places his move to Los Angeles almost a year earlier and by a completely different mechanism.

Supported Chronology
Detroit drafted Alcorn in 1959, and he played 58 games for the Pistons in 1959-60. RealGM records him becoming a free agent from Detroit on July 1, 1960. He then signed with the Lakers on October 24, 1960. Basketball-Reference and the Lakers' own alumni record confirm that he played 20 games for Los Angeles during the 1960-61 season, averaging 1.6 points and 2.5 rebounds in 8.7 minutes per game. The Lakers waived him on December 15, 1960, and RealGM records him becoming a free agent two days later. He never appeared in another NBA game.

Why the 1961 record Fails
A July 1, 1961 Detroit-to-Los Angeles cash trade would require Detroit to control Alcorn again after he had already left the Pistons as a free agent, signed with the Lakers, been waived by Los Angeles and exited the NBA. No source located for this review documents a reacquisition of his rights by Detroit or a second transfer to the Lakers. Basketball-Reference's 1961-62 transaction log has no Alcorn movement, and the Lakers' transaction page for 1960-61 already captures the actual October signing and December waiver. The legacy archive entry therefore conflicts directly with the verified player history rather than merely lacking detail.

Archival Treatment
There is no defensible corrected date or alternate package to substitute. The likely source problem may be a malformed historical intake, a duplicated or shifted date, or an inferred transaction that never occurred. The archive should preserve the record privately so the provenance is not lost, but it should not remain connected to player search, hindsight grading, index candidates or public trade history. Treating it as a real trade would contaminate both Gary Alcorn's timeline and the Detroit-Lakers transaction graph.

Final Resolution
Record Superseded. Gary Alcorn's supported path is Detroit through 1959-60, free agency on July 1, 1960, a Lakers signing on October 24, 20 Los Angeles games, a December 15 waiver and free agency on December 17. No completed July 1, 1961 Detroit-to-Los Angeles cash transaction is supported by the available evidence. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange

St. Louis traded Frank Radovich, Bob McDonald and cash to Philadelphia for Joe Graboski on August 19, 1961. The Hawks, Warriors and league Basketball-Reference transaction pages all preserve the same date and package. Graboski was a veteran forward-center with more than a decade of professional experience, while Radovich was a 1961 second-round pick and McDonald a sixth-round pick whose NBA value had not yet materialized. St. Louis was therefore paying two younger assets plus cash for an established player. The cash amount is not preserved in the public ledgers, so the retrospective comparison has to leave room for an unquantified financial cost.

St. Louis Return

Graboski's direct Hawks tenure was extremely short. He appeared in only three regular-season games for St. Louis in 1961-62, averaging 2.7 points and 3.0 rebounds in 9.3 minutes per game. His value did not end there, however. On November 21, the Hawks included Graboski with Si Green and Woody Sauldsberry in the trade that brought Barney Cable and Archie Dees from the expansion Chicago Packers. Because that later transaction involved five players, it is not possible to isolate an exact dollar-like share of the return attributable to Graboski. Still, he remained a usable veteran trade asset rather than simply disappearing after three games.

Philadelphia Return

Radovich gave the Warriors 37 regular-season games in 1961-62, averaging 2.4 points and 1.4 rebounds in only 4.7 minutes per game. He also appeared briefly in the playoffs, but his NBA career ended after that season. McDonald never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. That leaves Philadelphia with a small amount of low-minute player production plus the unknown cash payment. The cash matters because it was guaranteed value at the time, but the two basketball assets did not develop into rotation pieces with meaningful longevity.

Hindsight Comparison

Neither side produced a major long-term winner from the exchange. Philadelphia received more direct games because Radovich stayed on the roster for 37 appearances, yet those minutes were minimal and McDonald never reached the league. St. Louis received only three Graboski games, but the Hawks were able to reuse him in another multi-player trade within three months. That downstream utility gives the Hawks a modest realized-value advantage, although the unreported cash amount and inability to isolate Graboski's exact share of the later Cable-Dees package keep the gap narrow. This should be graded as a small edge rather than a decisive victory.

Final Verdict

Hawks Edge, B-/C+. St. Louis receives a B- for acquiring the only established veteran in the deal and preserving some downstream trade value despite receiving just three direct games. Philadelphia receives a C+ because Radovich supplied 37 low-minute appearances, McDonald never played in the NBA, and the cash amount is unknown. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes, with the principal uncertainty limited to the financial term and the exact value Graboski contributed to the later Chicago trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Chicago sold Vern Hatton's player rights back to the Philadelphia Warriors on November 29, 1961 for cash, six months after Philadelphia had sold the same rights to the expansion Packers. Hatton had played 15 games for Chicago, averaging 9.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.9 assists in 26.4 minutes per game. Philadelphia did not use him in another regular-season game; the Warriors sold Hatton's rights to St. Louis the next day, and he finished his NBA career with 25 Hawks games. The public transaction ledgers do not preserve either the November 29 cash price or Philadelphia's November 30 resale amount. Because the Warriors' return was essentially an unpriced one-day rights flip and Chicago's return was also unpriced cash, a winner cannot be supported.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange

Chicago sold Vern Hatton's player rights back to Philadelphia for cash on November 29, 1961. The transaction is the middle leg of an unusually compressed rights chain. Philadelphia had sold Hatton to the expansion Packers on May 31. Hatton then played 15 games for Chicago before the Packers returned his rights to the Warriors. One day later, Philadelphia sold the same rights to St. Louis. The league and team transaction ledgers agree on that sequence, but none of the surviving public records located for this review identifies the cash amount Chicago received on November 29.

Chicago Return

The Packers' side is straightforward in structure but difficult to value precisely. Chicago received cash after getting 15 regular-season games from Hatton earlier in the season. During those games he averaged 9.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.9 assists in 26.4 minutes per game, so the original May purchase did produce usable rotation minutes before the rights were sold back. The November 29 payment gave Chicago an additional financial return, but without the amount it is impossible to know whether the Packers recovered most of their original acquisition cost, sold at a profit or accepted a smaller exit payment.

Philadelphia Return

The Warriors reacquired Hatton's rights but did not use him in another regular-season game. On November 30, just one day after getting the rights back, Philadelphia sold them to St. Louis. Hatton then appeared in 25 games for the Hawks, averaging 3.7 points and 1.8 rebounds in 9.2 minutes per game before his NBA career ended. Philadelphia therefore treated the reacquired rights as a short-lived transaction asset rather than a roster addition. The November 30 St. Louis sale also involved cash, but that amount is likewise unavailable. Without both the buyback price and resale price, Philadelphia's one-day arbitrage cannot be measured.

Hindsight Comparison

This record is a good example of why an unknown cash transaction should not be graded solely from player appearances. Chicago got a known 15-game contribution before selling the rights, while Philadelphia received no new on-court value from the November 29 acquisition. But Philadelphia may have made money by reselling the rights the following day, and Chicago may have received meaningful cash when it exited. Because both sides' actual transaction value is concentrated in undisclosed financial terms, the player record does not settle the comparison. Any letter grades would imply precision that the surviving sources do not support.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence. The November 29 Chicago-to-Philadelphia rights sale is verified, Hatton's 15 Packers games are verified, and Philadelphia's November 30 resale to St. Louis is verified. The relevant cash amounts are not. Those missing financial terms are material enough that no winner or team grades should be assigned. Confidence is high on the chronology and player identity but intentionally limited on comparative value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange

Detroit sold Shellie McMillon's player rights to St. Louis for cash on December 1, 1961. The source review corrects the legacy intake date of December 4. Basketball-Reference's Pistons, Hawks and league transaction ledgers all list December 1, and McMillon's own transaction history repeats the same date. The direction and player identity are therefore high-confidence. The only material gap is financial: the public records located for this review do not identify the amount of cash St. Louis paid.

St. Louis Return

McMillon immediately gave the Hawks meaningful frontcourt production. He played 48 regular-season games for St. Louis in 1961-62, averaging 11.8 points and 6.3 rebounds in 21.6 minutes per game while shooting .470 from the field. Those are substantial numbers for a midseason cash acquisition, especially compared with the 5.1 points and 4.6 rebounds he had averaged in 14 Detroit games earlier that season. The Hawks did not merely receive a short bench cameo; they obtained a productive rotation forward for the remainder of the year.

Downstream Value

McMillon's value also survived beyond those 48 games. On June 14, 1962, St. Louis traded him and Al Ferrari to the Chicago Packers for Bill Bridges and Ralph Davis. That later deal was a multi-player package, so McMillon's exact share of the return cannot be isolated. Even so, his inclusion demonstrates that the Hawks retained a tradable asset after already receiving meaningful on-court production. This is stronger realized value than a cash-only acquisition that disappears at season's end.

Detroit Return

The Pistons received cash and no basketball asset. Detroit had used McMillon for three-plus seasons, including 78 games in 1960-61, so moving him during a reduced 1961-62 role was understandable. The unknown cash amount is an important caveat because it may have been meaningful in the early-1960s team economy. However, unlike some rights sales where the acquired player barely appeared, McMillon produced nearly 50 useful games and then remained part of another NBA trade package. That realized value is large enough to support a modest St. Louis edge even without knowing the exact payment.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, B+/C+. St. Louis receives a B+ for acquiring 48 games of productive frontcourt play and preserving downstream trade value into the June 1962 Bridges-Davis deal. Detroit receives a C+ because the Pistons converted a player whose role had diminished into cash, but the amount is unknown and no future basketball asset is documented. Confidence is high on the corrected December 1 date, the player identity and the realized production; confidence is lower only on the financial term and McMillon's precise share of the later multi-player trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange

Boston sold Al Butler's player rights to New York for cash on December 11, 1961. Basketball-Reference's Celtics, Knicks and league transaction ledgers all preserve the same date and transaction structure, while Butler's player page confirms the move. Boston had selected Butler in the second round of the 1961 draft and used him only briefly before selling his rights. The public sources located for this review do not identify the amount of cash New York paid, so the Celtics' financial return cannot be measured precisely.

New York Return

Butler became a major Knicks rotation player almost immediately. He appeared in 54 regular-season games for New York in 1961-62 and averaged 14.7 points, 6.0 rebounds and 3.7 assists in 36.5 minutes per game. Those are substantial numbers for a player acquired during the season for cash. He remained with the Knicks for the next two campaigns, playing 74 games in 1962-63 and 76 in 1963-64. Across three New York seasons, Butler appeared in 204 regular-season games and averaged 10.7 points per game. The acquisition therefore delivered both immediate starting-level minutes and multi-year roster value.

Boston Return

The Celtics received cash and no basketball asset. Boston had only used Butler in five games during 1961-62, where he averaged 6.2 points in 9.4 minutes per game, so selling his rights was understandable from the perspective of a roster that was already deep and championship-caliber. The unknown cash amount is a meaningful caveat because it may have reflected a reasonable price for a player outside Boston's regular rotation. Still, there is no documented downstream basketball asset attached to the payment, and Butler's later Knicks production was far larger than his Boston role suggested.

Hindsight Comparison

This is one of the clearer early-1960s cash-sale outcomes because the acquired player generated enough sustained production to outweigh the uncertainty around an undisclosed payment. New York received more than 200 games across three seasons, including a 1961-62 stretch in which Butler played starter-level minutes and scored nearly 15 points per game. Boston's return may have been financially sensible at the time, but the surviving record gives no evidence that the cash later became a comparable basketball asset. The hindsight edge therefore belongs to New York, though the unknown sale price keeps the Celtics from receiving an especially harsh grade.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A-/C+. New York receives an A- for turning cash into 204 regular-season games and three seasons of meaningful backcourt production. Boston receives a C+ because the Celtics monetized a player they were barely using, but the cash amount is unknown and no future basketball return is documented. Confidence is high on the exact date, player identity and realized production; confidence is lower only on the financial term. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Exchange

Syracuse purchased Joe Graboski's player rights from the Chicago Packers for cash on December 28, 1961. Basketball-Reference's league ledger, both team transaction pages and Graboski's player page all agree on the date and direction. The move came only five weeks after Chicago had acquired Graboski from St. Louis as part of the Barney Cable and Archie Dees trade. That makes this a short holding-period sale for the expansion Packers rather than a long-term roster decision. The public transaction ledgers located for this review do not identify the cash amount Syracuse paid.

Syracuse Return

Graboski gave the Nationals 23 regular-season games after the sale, averaging 5.1 points, 4.6 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 14.0 minutes per game. He also appeared in four playoff games as Syracuse reached the Eastern Division Finals. Those are real minutes from an established veteran, but they are still a limited return. Graboski was 32 and the 1961-62 season became the final NBA campaign of his career, so Syracuse did not acquire multi-year value or a player who remained part of the franchise's later Philadelphia transition.

Chicago Return

The Packers received cash after using Graboski for 12 games. During his Chicago stint he averaged 5.6 points and 3.3 rebounds in 9.8 minutes per game. The expansion club had acquired him on November 21 and moved him again on December 28, meaning Chicago extracted both a brief on-court contribution and an undisclosed financial return from the asset. That is a reasonable outcome for a veteran who was nearing the end of his career. The missing sale price, however, prevents a precise judgment about whether Chicago maximized value.

Hindsight Comparison

The basketball side slightly favors Syracuse because the Nationals received 23 regular-season games and four playoff appearances, but the scale is too small to overwhelm an unknown cash payment. Chicago also received 12 games before the sale, which means the Packers did not simply pay for Graboski and immediately flip him without use. Both clubs received modest, short-term value from the same veteran within a single season. Without the cash amount, assigning a directional winner would create more certainty than the surviving record supports.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence. The December 28 sale is verified, Graboski's 23 Syracuse regular-season games and four playoff appearances are verified, and his identity is secure. The cash amount Chicago received is not. Because the player return was short and the financial term is material, no winner or team grades should be assigned. Confidence is high on the chronology and player outcome but intentionally limited on comparative value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Cincinnati traded Larry Staverman to the Chicago Zephyrs for Dave Piontek on July 13, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Royals, Zephyrs, league and player transaction records all agree on that date and straight player-for-player structure, correcting the legacy June 30 entry that described a player-to-be-named-later or draft-pick mechanism. Piontek played 48 games for Cincinnati in 1962-63, averaging 2.7 points and 2.0 rebounds in 9.5 minutes per game, then left the NBA. Staverman played 33 games for Chicago at 7.2 points and 4.8 rebounds, remained with the franchise into its Baltimore move, and was traded to Detroit in October 1963 for Kevin Loughery. Loughery then became a major long-term Baltimore guard. The realized and downstream value clearly favors the Chicago/Baltimore franchise.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Cincinnati traded Larry Staverman to the Chicago Zephyrs for Dave Piontek on July 13, 1962. The source review corrects two important problems in the legacy intake. First, the transaction occurred on July 13 rather than June 30. Second, it was a direct player-for-player exchange, not a deal involving a player to be named later or a draft pick. Basketball-Reference's Royals, Zephyrs and league transaction pages all preserve the same structure, and both player pages independently repeat it. Staverman had been a Cincinnati draft pick who spent time in the ABL before the trade, while Piontek was a veteran whom Chicago had acquired in the 1961 expansion draft.

Cincinnati Return

Piontek gave the Royals one final NBA season. He appeared in 48 games during 1962-63, averaging 2.7 points and 2.0 rebounds in 9.5 minutes per game. He did not play another NBA season afterward. Cincinnati therefore received usable frontcourt depth, but the return was short and low-minute. There is no documented downstream asset because Piontek's NBA career ended after the season.

Chicago/Baltimore Return

Staverman immediately produced more substantial minutes for the Zephyrs. He played 33 games in 1962-63, averaging 7.2 points and 4.8 rebounds in 18.2 minutes per game. When the franchise moved to Baltimore for 1963-64, Staverman remained with the club for six more games. On October 28, 1963, Baltimore traded him to Detroit for Kevin Loughery. That later conversion is the decisive hindsight factor.

Downstream Value

Loughery became a major Baltimore backcourt piece. Basketball-Reference shows him playing at least 65 games for the Bullets in 1963-64 and then 80, 74, 76, 77, 80, 55 and 82 games over the next seven seasons. His scoring rose as high as 22.6 points per game in 1968-69, with multiple seasons above 18 points per game. The July 1962 acquisition of Staverman therefore eventually produced not just better immediate value than Piontek, but a pathway to a long-term starter and scorer for the same franchise.

Final Verdict

Chicago/Baltimore Wins, A/C+. The future Wizards franchise receives an A because Staverman supplied better immediate production, survived the franchise move and was then converted directly into Kevin Loughery, who became a long-term Baltimore guard. Cincinnati receives a C+ because Piontek provided 48 games of reserve depth but no multi-year or downstream value. Confidence is high because the date, player-for-player structure, player identities and subsequent Staverman-for-Loughery transaction are all independently documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: New York traded Darrall Imhoff and cash to Detroit for Gene Shue on August 29, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Pistons, Knicks, league and player transaction records all agree on the date and structure. Shue then played 78 games for New York in 1962-63, averaging 11.7 points and 3.3 assists in 29.3 minutes per game. Detroit received 103 regular-season games from Imhoff across two seasons before selling his rights to the Los Angeles Lakers in April 1964, plus an undisclosed cash payment. New York also later packaged Shue with Paul Hogue to acquire Bill McGill, who averaged 16.0 points in 68 Knicks games in 1963-64. Because McGill's acquisition also required Hogue, the downstream value cannot be credited entirely to Shue, but the Knicks still received the stronger realized basketball return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

New York sent Darrall Imhoff and cash to Detroit for Gene Shue on August 29, 1962. The transaction is unusually well preserved for the period. Basketball-Reference's Pistons and Knicks pages, the league transaction ledger and both player pages all agree on the date and the basic structure. Detroit received a younger center plus cash, while New York acquired an established guard who had already been one of the Pistons' leading scorers. The cash amount is not identified in the public records located for this review.

New York Return

Shue immediately became a major part of the Knicks' backcourt. He appeared in 78 regular-season games in 1962-63, averaging 11.7 points and 3.3 assists in 29.3 minutes per game. That is a substantial one-season return, especially compared with the limited role Imhoff had held in New York. Shue did not remain with the Knicks long term, but he was still useful as a trade asset. On October 29, 1963, New York sent Shue and Paul Hogue to Baltimore for Bill McGill.

Detroit Return

Imhoff gave Detroit two seasons of frontcourt depth. He played 45 games in 1962-63 at 2.7 points and 3.4 rebounds per game, then 58 games in 1963-64 at 4.8 points and 4.9 rebounds. The Pistons therefore received 103 regular-season games before selling his rights to the Los Angeles Lakers in April 1964. Detroit also received cash in the original transaction. That combination means the Pistons' side had more value than a simple low-production player return, even though the financial terms of both cash transactions are not available.

Downstream Value

The Knicks' later conversion of Shue requires careful treatment because he was traded with Paul Hogue rather than alone. Bill McGill played 68 games for New York in 1963-64 and averaged 16.0 points and 5.9 rebounds in 25.5 minutes per game, so the subsequent transaction clearly produced useful value. However, assigning all of McGill's production to Shue would overstate the original deal because Hogue was a separate outgoing asset. The safer conclusion is that Shue retained enough value to remain part of a productive follow-up trade.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A-/B. New York receives an A- for 78 games of meaningful guard production and retained trade utility. Detroit receives a B because Imhoff supplied 103 games across two seasons, the Pistons also received cash and later sold his rights for another financial return. The Knicks still hold the stronger realized basketball outcome, but the original A/C+ gap was too wide once Detroit's two seasons of Imhoff and the undisclosed cash component are fully recognized. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, player identities and on-court production, with lower confidence only on the cash amounts and the precise share of downstream value attributable to Shue. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Syracuse sold Dick Barnett's player rights to the Los Angeles Lakers on September 5, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Nationals, Lakers and league transaction ledgers agree on the date and sale structure, while contemporary reporting cited in later biographical records places the price at $35,000. Barnett then played three full seasons for Los Angeles, appearing in 232 regular-season games and averaging 16.8 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.7 assists. He scored 18.0 points per game in 1962-63 and 18.4 in 1963-64, becoming a major backcourt contributor alongside Jerry West. In October 1965, the Lakers traded Barnett to New York for Bob Boozer and cash, preserving additional asset value. The realized basketball return clearly favors Los Angeles, even after recognizing that $35,000 was a substantial early-1960s cash payment.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange

Syracuse sold Dick Barnett's player rights to Los Angeles in September 1962. Basketball-Reference's Syracuse, Lakers and league transaction ledgers all list September 5 as the transaction date, while later biographical accounts cite a $35,000 purchase price and identify contemporary Los Angeles Times reporting from September 8. That secondary date discrepancy is best understood as publication timing rather than enough evidence to override the team and league ledgers. The canonical archive therefore keeps September 5 and records the cash amount as a reported figure rather than an unquestioned primary-ledger field.

Los Angeles Return

Barnett immediately became a major Lakers contributor. He played 80 games in 1962-63 and averaged 18.0 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.8 assists in 31.8 minutes per game. He followed with 78 games at 18.4 points in 1963-64 and 74 games at 13.8 points in 1964-65. Across three Los Angeles seasons, Barnett appeared in 232 regular-season games and averaged 16.8 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.7 assists. The Lakers' own alumni history preserves the same three-season scoring average. This was not a speculative rights purchase; it produced a durable high-minute guard on a contender.

Syracuse Return

The Nationals received cash and no basketball asset. A reported $35,000 was substantial for the era and later accounts describe the transaction as a record player-for-money deal at the time, so Syracuse should not be graded as though it gave Barnett away for a trivial payment. The franchise also had a complicated recent relationship with Barnett because he had spent the 1961-62 season in the rival ABL. Converting his rights into a large cash payment had clear practical value even if that value cannot be traced into a later player or pick.

Downstream Value

Los Angeles extracted one more layer of return in October 1965 when it traded Barnett to the New York Knicks for Bob Boozer and cash. Barnett's later Knicks career, All-Star selection and championships should not be credited to the Lakers, because those achievements occurred after the 1965 trade. What does belong in the Lakers' ledger is the fact that three productive seasons did not exhaust the asset: Barnett still carried enough value to return another NBA player plus cash.

Final Verdict

Syracuse receives a C because the Nationals reportedly received $35,000, a meaningful early-1960s payment, but no later basketball asset is documented from the sale. Confidence is high on the transaction direction, Barnett identity and Lakers production, and medium-high on the exact cash figure because it comes through contemporary-report citations rather than the transaction ledgers themselves. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

new-york-knicks.summary: New York acquired Gene Conley from the Chicago Zephyrs for Phil Jordon and the rights to Cliff Luyk on September 10, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Zephyrs, league and player transaction records agree on the date and structure. Conley gave New York 116 regular-season games across two seasons, including 70 games at 9.0 points and 6.7 rebounds in 1962-63. Chicago never used Jordon in a game; 27 days later it traded him to St. Louis for Charlie Hardnett, who became a useful Zephyrs/Bullets frontcourt piece with 78 games at 10.6 points and 7.7 rebounds in 1962-63 and 164 games for the franchise across three seasons. Luyk never played in the NBA. The downstream Hardnett return gives Chicago/Baltimore a modest edge, but New York also received real multi-season value.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Exchange

New York sent Phil Jordon and the rights to Cliff Luyk to the Chicago Zephyrs for Gene Conley on September 10, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Knicks and Zephyrs transaction pages, the league ledger and the player histories all support the same date and structure. The legacy record correctly identified the three named assets but overstated how one-sided the outcome became. Conley was already an established NBA veteran, while Jordon was a veteran center and Luyk was a rights asset who never appeared in the NBA.

New York Return

Conley gave the Knicks two seasons of useful frontcourt depth. He appeared in 70 games during 1962-63, averaging 9.0 points and 6.7 rebounds in 22.1 minutes per game. He returned for 46 games in 1963-64, averaging 4.2 points and 3.4 rebounds in a smaller role. That is 116 regular-season games of realized value. Conley did not become a long-term building block, but he was far from a failed acquisition and provided substantially more than the legacy D+ grade suggested.

Chicago/Baltimore Return

The Zephyrs did not keep Phil Jordon long enough to use him in a game. On October 7, 1962, Chicago traded Jordon to St. Louis for Charlie Hardnett. That conversion is the key to the other side's value. Hardnett played 78 games for Chicago in 1962-63 and averaged 10.6 points and 7.7 rebounds in 21.2 minutes per game. After the franchise moved to Baltimore, he added 66 games in 1963-64 and 20 more in 1964-65. Across those three seasons, the franchise received 164 games from Hardnett. Cliff Luyk never played in the NBA, so his rights add little realized basketball value.

Hindsight Comparison

Chicago/Baltimore ultimately received more durable production because Jordon became Hardnett within a month. Hardnett's first season was stronger than Conley's best New York year, and the franchise received more total games from him than the Knicks received from Conley. Still, the difference is not large enough to justify the original A versus D+ spread. New York got a legitimate rotation player for two seasons, while Chicago/Baltimore turned one outgoing asset into a somewhat better and longer-lasting frontcourt contributor.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win, A-/B+. The Chicago/Baltimore franchise receives an A- because Jordon was quickly converted into Hardnett, who produced 164 games across three seasons and delivered a strong 1962-63 campaign. New York receives a B+ because Conley supplied 116 games and meaningful rebounding production over two seasons. Luyk's rights did not generate NBA value. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, player identities and downstream Jordon-for-Hardnett conversion. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Cincinnati acquired Tom Hawkins from the Los Angeles Lakers for a 1963 second-round draft pick on September 14, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Royals and league transaction ledgers all agree on the date and structure, and the pick later became No. 14 selection Jim King. Hawkins gave Cincinnati four full seasons of durable frontcourt production: 310 regular-season games from 1962-63 through 1965-66, including 79 games at 9.4 points and 6.9 rebounds in his first season and 79 games at 8.4 points and 7.3 rebounds in his fourth. King also became a useful Lakers guard, playing 213 regular-season games over three seasons before Chicago selected him in the 1966 expansion draft. Both teams received real value, but Hawkins' larger workload and four-season continuity give Cincinnati the stronger realized return.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange

Los Angeles traded Tom Hawkins to Cincinnati on September 14, 1962 for a future 1963 second-round pick. Basketball-Reference's Lakers and Royals transaction pages, the league ledger and both player pages all preserve the same structure. The pick became No. 14 overall in the second round, where the Lakers selected Jim King in April 1963. This is therefore a clean player-for-pick comparison with no unresolved cash term or player-to-be-named-later complication.

Cincinnati Return

Hawkins became a durable Royals rotation forward immediately. He played 79 games in 1962-63, averaging 9.4 points and 6.9 rebounds in 21.8 minutes per game. He followed with 73 games in 1963-64, 79 in 1964-65 and 79 in 1965-66. Across those four seasons, Cincinnati received 310 regular-season games before selling his rights back to Los Angeles in September 1966. His role remained substantial throughout the stretch, including 7.3 rebounds per game in his final Cincinnati season. The Royals therefore obtained both volume and continuity from a single future second-round pick.

Los Angeles Return

The Lakers also realized meaningful value from the pick. Jim King played 60 games as a rookie in 1963-64, 77 in 1964-65 and 76 in 1965-66, for 213 regular-season games over three seasons. His role grew from 12.7 minutes per game as a rookie to more than 19 minutes per game in each of the next two seasons, and he averaged 7.5 points with 2.9 assists in 1965-66. King was then selected by the Chicago Bulls in the 1966 expansion draft. That means Los Angeles did not receive a failed pick; it received a useful reserve guard for three seasons.

Hindsight Comparison

The old record treated this as only a slight Cincinnati edge, and that basic direction holds, but the realized production is strong enough on both sides to support better grades than the legacy record assigned. Hawkins played nearly 100 more games for Cincinnati than King did for Los Angeles, handled a larger minute load and provided more consistent frontcourt production. King still gave the Lakers three real rotation seasons, so this is not a case where one side surrendered a productive veteran for a wasted draft asset.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A-/B+. Cincinnati receives an A- for turning a second-round pick into 310 games and four seasons of dependable frontcourt production. Los Angeles receives a B+ because King supplied 213 games and three seasons of useful guard depth before the expansion draft removed him from the roster. Confidence is high because the transaction date, pick identity, player identities and season-by-season production are all directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
los-angeles-lakers.gradeRationale: The counterpart produced a modest realized-value advantage. Grades weigh realized player production, identifiable pick conversion, role, timing, contract context and downstream asset use.

new-york-knicks.summary: This September 16, 1962 New York-Chicago cash transaction for Cliff Luyk is retained only as legacy provenance. Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Zephyrs and league transaction ledgers do not record a September 16 deal. They instead agree that six days earlier, on September 10, New York traded Luyk together with Phil Jordon to Chicago for Gene Conley. The unsupported September 16 record would require Chicago to sell Luyk back to New York almost immediately, yet no team, league or player ledger shows that reversal. new-york-knicks.analysis:
The legacy Claim

The legacy New York record describes a September 16, 1962 transaction in which the Knicks supposedly reacquired Cliff Luyk from the Chicago Zephyrs for cash. The surviving transaction record does not support that event. Basketball-Reference's New York and Chicago transaction pages contain no September 16 exchange, and the 1962-63 NBA league ledger likewise has no such transaction. The conflict is especially clear because the same sources document Luyk moving in the opposite direction only six days earlier.

Supported Chronology

New York drafted Luyk in the fourth round of the 1962 NBA Draft. On September 10, 1962, the Knicks traded Luyk and Phil Jordon to the Chicago Zephyrs for Gene Conley. The Knicks, Zephyrs and league transaction pages all agree on that date and package. Luyk's own Basketball-Reference transaction history also ends with the September 10 trade to Chicago. Unlike Jordon, who was moved again to St. Louis on October 7, Luyk has no subsequent NBA transaction listed. He never appeared in an NBA game.

Why the September 16 record Fails

For the legacy September 16 cash sale to be genuine, Chicago would have had to reacquire cash from New York while returning Luyk's rights less than a week after the Conley trade. That kind of reversal should appear in at least one of the team ledgers, the league transaction log or Luyk's player history. It appears in none of them. More importantly, New York's own 1962-63 transaction page moves directly from the September 10 Conley deal to the December 5 Tom Gola trade, with no September 16 Luyk transaction in between.

Archival Treatment

There is no defensible corrected date or alternate package for this record. The verified September 10 transaction already accounts for Luyk's rights, and the unsupported September 16 entry would double-count his movement between the same franchises. The most likely explanation is a malformed legacy intake or an inferred cash reversal that is not present in the authoritative transaction record. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.

Final Resolution

Record Superseded. Cliff Luyk's supported NBA transaction path is his March 1962 draft selection by New York followed by the September 10, 1962 trade with Phil Jordon to Chicago for Gene Conley. No completed September 16 Chicago-to-New York cash transaction is supported. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
