perspectives.summary: Detroit sold George Lee's player rights to the San Francisco Warriors for cash on September 19, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Pistons, Warriors, league and player transaction records all agree on the date and structure. Lee then gave San Francisco 148 regular-season games across five playing seasons, with his largest role coming immediately in 1962-63: 64 games at 7.0 points and 3.4 rebounds in 18.6 minutes per game. His role declined over the next two years, he spent 1965-66 as an assistant coach rather than a player, and he later returned for brief appearances in 1966-67 and 1967-68. Detroit received an undisclosed cash payment. The player return clearly had real value, but the unknown sale price and mostly reserve-level production keep the Warriors' edge modest.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Detroit sold George Lee's player rights to the San Francisco Warriors for cash on September 19, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Pistons and Warriors transaction pages, the 1962-63 NBA league ledger and Lee's player page all agree on the date and transaction structure. Lee had spent three seasons with Detroit after being drafted in 1959, so this was a sale of an established roster player rather than an untested rights asset. The public transaction ledgers located for this review do not identify the cash amount.

San Francisco Return

Lee immediately became a useful Warriors reserve. He appeared in 64 games during 1962-63, averaging 7.0 points and 3.4 rebounds in 18.6 minutes per game. He followed with 54 games in 1963-64 and 19 in 1964-65. His role declined during those seasons, but the Warriors still received 137 games over the first three years after the sale. Lee then spent 1965-66 as an assistant coach and later returned to the active roster for one game in 1966-67 and ten games in 1967-68. Across all five playing seasons with the franchise after the transaction, he appeared in 148 regular-season games.

Detroit Return

The Pistons received cash and no documented player or draft asset. Selling Lee was understandable because Detroit had already received three seasons from him and was reshaping the roster around younger pieces. The unknown cash amount is material, especially in the early 1960s, and prevents a precise economic comparison. Nothing in the surviving transaction record shows the payment later becoming a traceable basketball asset, but the absence of that downstream link should not be treated as proof that the cash had little organizational value.

Hindsight Comparison

San Francisco received more value than the original C-minus grade suggested. Lee's first Warriors season alone provided 64 games and a real rotation role, and the relationship lasted long enough for him to return as both a coach and later a reserve player. At the same time, most of the later on-court contribution was limited, so this is not a major franchise-changing acquisition. The unknown cash payment also makes a harsh Detroit grade inappropriate.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, B/C+. Golden State receives a B for acquiring 148 regular-season games, including a useful 1962-63 rotation season, from a cash-only transaction. Detroit receives a C+ because the Pistons monetized a player they had already used for three seasons, but the amount is unknown and no later basketball asset is documented. Confidence is high on the transaction date, player identity and realized Warriors production, with lower confidence only on the financial term. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange

Boston sold Gary Phillips' player rights to the San Francisco Warriors for cash on October 18, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Celtics and Warriors transaction pages, the 1962-63 league ledger and Phillips' player page all agree on the date and structure. Boston had selected Phillips ninth overall in the 1961 draft but used him in only eight games as a rookie. The public transaction records located for this review do not preserve the cash amount, so Boston's financial return cannot be measured directly.

San Francisco Return

Phillips immediately became a regular Warriors guard. He played 75 games in 1962-63, averaging 8.1 points, 3.0 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 24.0 minutes per game. His role grew in 1963-64, when he appeared in 66 games and averaged 10.0 points, 3.8 rebounds and 3.1 assists in 30.5 minutes. Phillips then added 73 games in 1964-65 and 67 in 1965-66. Across four seasons after the sale, San Francisco received 281 regular-season games from a player Boston had barely used.

Boston Return

The Celtics received cash and no documented player or draft asset. Boston's decision was understandable in context because Phillips was buried on a championship roster and had played only eight games during his rookie season. Converting unused rights into cash could therefore have been a sensible roster-management decision even though hindsight favors San Francisco. The missing sale price remains important and prevents a precise economic comparison.

Hindsight Comparison

The Warriors clearly realized the stronger basketball value. Phillips was not a star, but two seasons of meaningful rotation minutes followed by two more seasons of reserve depth is far more than a token rights purchase. At the same time, the old record's Celtics-win framing is not supported by the realized production. Boston may have received a reasonable financial payment, but there is no traceable later basketball asset connected to it. The appropriate hindsight result is a moderate Warriors win rather than an extreme one-sided verdict.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, A-/C+. Golden State receives an A- for turning cash into 281 regular-season games and four seasons of backcourt depth, including a 10.0-point, 3.1-assist season in 1963-64. Boston receives a C+ because it monetized a first-round pick it was barely using, but the amount is unknown and no later basketball return is documented. Confidence is high on the date, player identity and Warriors production, with lower confidence only on the financial term. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

new-york-knicks.summary: This legacy record is a real George Kaftan rights sale with the wrong decade and the wrong Bullets franchise attached. New York sold Kaftan's player rights to the original Baltimore Bullets on November 20, 1952, not to the later Chicago/Baltimore/Washington franchise in 1962. Basketball-Reference's Knicks, original Baltimore and league transaction ledgers, Kaftan's player page, and RealGM all agree on the 1952 date and destination. Kaftan then played 23 regular-season games for Baltimore in 1952-53, averaging 5.8 points and 3.3 rebounds in 16.5 minutes per game before becoming a free agent the next summer. The cash amount New York received is not preserved in the sources reviewed, so the corrected record remains Insufficient Evidence rather than forcing a winner.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The legacy Claim

The legacy New York record described a November 20, 1962 cash transaction sending George Kaftan to the "Bullets," which caused the partner franchise to be mapped to the modern Washington Wizards lineage. That chronology cannot be correct. Kaftan's NBA career ended in the early 1950s, and the surviving transaction record places the sale exactly ten years earlier. This is therefore not an unsupported trade; it is a misdated and mis-franchised version of a documented historical sale.

Supported Chronology

Basketball-Reference's 1952-53 Knicks page states that New York sold Kaftan's player rights to the Baltimore Bullets on November 20, 1952. The original Baltimore Bullets page records the acquisition on the same date, and the 1952-53 league transaction ledger repeats the sale. Kaftan's own player transaction history also lists the November 20, 1952 rights sale. RealGM independently records the same movement to the Baltimore Bullets (BAA). Those sources establish both the correct date and the correct franchise identity.

Baltimore Return

Kaftan played 23 regular-season games for the original Baltimore Bullets in 1952-53. He averaged 5.8 points, 3.3 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 16.5 minutes per game. The stint was useful but short. RealGM records Kaftan becoming a free agent from Baltimore on July 1, 1953, and he did not appear in another NBA season. Baltimore therefore received a modest, one-season player return rather than a long-term asset.

New York Return

New York received cash, but the amount is not identified in the team, league or player transaction sources reviewed. That missing financial term is material because Kaftan's Baltimore contribution was only 23 games. The Knicks had already received 113 regular-season games from him across the prior two seasons and moved his rights after that productive period. Selling the rights for cash was a plausible roster decision, but the surviving public record does not allow the value of that payment to be compared precisely with Baltimore's short on-court return.

Franchise Correction

The partner must be the defunct Baltimore Bullets franchise that operated from 1944 through 1954, not the later Chicago Packers/Zephyrs-Baltimore Bullets-Washington Wizards lineage. Treating the 1952 transaction as a Washington-franchise trade would create a false historical connection between two unrelated organizations. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence. The November 20, 1952 date, New York-to-original-Baltimore direction and Kaftan's 23-game Baltimore stint are all well documented. The cash amount New York received is not. Because the realized player return was short and the missing financial term is central to the comparison, no winner or team grades should be assigned. Confidence is high on the corrected chronology and franchise identity. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: New York acquired Tom Gola from the San Francisco Warriors for Willie Naulls and Kenny Sears on December 5, 1962. Basketball-Reference's Warriors, Knicks, league and player transaction records all agree on the date and package. Gola then gave New York 277 regular-season games across four seasons, including 52 games at 12.0 points, 7.1 rebounds and 4.3 assists immediately after the trade. San Francisco received 47 games from Naulls before selling his rights to Boston in September 1963 and 105 games from Sears across the remainder of 1962-63 and 1963-64. Both incoming Warriors contributed, but neither matched Gola's four-season workload or two-way role. New York produced the stronger realized basketball return, while San Francisco still recovered useful short-term depth and a later cash return from Naulls.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange

San Francisco traded Tom Gola to New York on December 5, 1962 for Willie Naulls and Kenny Sears. Basketball-Reference's Warriors and Knicks transaction pages, the league ledger and all three player histories agree on the date and package. The transaction moved one versatile veteran to New York in exchange for two established forwards whose best Knicks seasons were already behind them. That makes the deal more nuanced than a simple one-for-two headcount comparison.

New York Return

Gola immediately became a major Knicks rotation player. He played 52 games after the trade in 1962-63, averaging 12.0 points, 7.1 rebounds and 4.3 assists in 35.5 minutes per game. He followed with 74 games in 1963-64, 77 in 1964-65 and 74 in 1965-66. Across the four post-trade seasons, New York received 277 regular-season games. His scoring declined as he aged, but he continued to rebound, facilitate and fill multiple perimeter and frontcourt roles. The volume and continuity are the core of New York's realized advantage.

San Francisco Return

Naulls gave the Warriors 47 games for the remainder of 1962-63, averaging 11.0 points and 6.7 rebounds in 26.1 minutes per game. Sears played 54 games that season at 6.1 points and 2.6 rebounds, then returned for 51 games in 1963-64 at 3.3 points and 1.8 rebounds. San Francisco therefore received 152 combined regular-season games from the two players. Naulls was then sold to Boston in September 1963, producing an additional financial return, while Sears' NBA career ended after the 1963-64 season.

Hindsight Comparison

The Warriors did not come away empty. Naulls remained a useful scorer and rebounder for half a season, Sears supplied depth for a season and a half, and Naulls retained enough rights value to be sold. But the package was short-lived. Gola stayed with New York for four seasons and played nearly twice as many regular-season games by himself as Naulls and Sears combined for San Francisco. He also handled a much larger role immediately after the trade, including more than 35 minutes per game in the first partial season.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A/B. New York receives an A for acquiring four seasons and 277 games of useful two-way play from Gola. San Francisco receives a B because Naulls and Sears produced real short-term value and Naulls generated a later cash sale, but the combined player return lasted only 152 games. Confidence is high because the transaction structure, all three player identities and the season-by-season production are directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: Boston sold Jack Foley's player rights to the New York Knicks on January 22, 1963 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Celtics, Knicks and league transaction ledgers, along with Foley's player history, all agree on the date and sale structure. Foley had appeared in five games for Boston as a rookie, averaging 6.4 points in 9.2 minutes per game. After the sale he played only six regular-season games for New York, averaging 3.5 points, 1.5 rebounds and 0.8 assists in 6.2 minutes per game, and never appeared in another NBA season. Because Boston's cash return is not identified in the public transaction records and New York received only six games of low-minute production, the evidence does not support a responsible winner or grade.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange

Boston sold Jack Foley's player rights to New York for cash on January 22, 1963. Basketball-Reference's Celtics and Knicks transaction pages, the league ledger and Foley's player page all agree on the date and mechanism. Foley had been Boston's second-round selection in the 1962 NBA Draft and made only five regular-season appearances for the Celtics before the sale. The surviving public transaction records do not state the cash amount New York paid, which becomes important because the player return was extremely short.

New York Return

Foley appeared in six games for the Knicks during the remainder of the 1962-63 season. He averaged 3.5 points, 1.5 rebounds and 0.8 assists in 6.2 minutes per game. Those six appearances were the final NBA games of his career. New York therefore did receive a real roster player rather than merely dormant rights, but the realized value was minimal: six low-minute games with no later NBA season and no documented downstream trade return.

Boston Return

The Celtics received cash after using Foley for five games. During that Boston stint he averaged 6.4 points in 9.2 minutes per game, then moved before the end of his rookie season. Boston's roster was already championship-caliber, so moving a fringe player for financial value was a plausible transaction even without a basketball asset coming back. The problem for hindsight grading is that the amount of cash is unknown. With only six Knicks games on the other side, even a modest payment could be material to the comparison.

Hindsight Comparison

The verified player outcome is too small to overcome the missing financial term. New York got six games and 37 total minutes from Foley, while Boston received an undisclosed payment and had already gotten five games from him. There is no evidence that either side converted the transaction into a meaningful later basketball asset. Calling this a Knicks win because a player changed hands would overstate six games of production; calling it a Celtics win would require assuming the cash was valuable enough to exceed that small return.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence. The January 22, 1963 sale, Foley's identity, his five Boston games and six New York games are all documented. The cash amount is not. Because the player return was extremely limited and the missing financial term is central to the comparison, no winner or team grades should be assigned. Confidence is high on chronology and player outcome, but intentionally limited on comparative value. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange

San Francisco traded Hubie White to Philadelphia for John Windsor on August 14, 1963. The legacy TradeVerdicts record carried August 15, but Basketball-Reference's Warriors and 76ers transaction pages, the league transaction ledger and both player pages all place the deal on August 14. The package itself is straightforward: White, a second-round pick from the 1962 draft who had played 29 games for the Warriors as a rookie, went to Philadelphia; Windsor, a 1962 fifth-round pick whose rights had belonged to the Syracuse/Philadelphia franchise, went to San Francisco.

Philadelphia Return

White appeared in 23 regular-season games for the 76ers in 1963-64. He averaged 3.4 points, 1.8 rebounds and 0.5 assists in 8.5 minutes per game. He did not play another NBA season after that Philadelphia stint, although he later returned to professional basketball in the ABA near the end of the decade. That later ABA career should not be credited as Philadelphia value because the 76ers did not retain or convert his rights into a documented downstream asset. The realized return here is therefore limited to 23 reserve appearances.

San Francisco Return

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange

San Francisco sold Willie Naulls' player rights to Boston for cash on September 4, 1963. Basketball-Reference's Celtics and Warriors transaction pages, the league ledger and Naulls' own player history all agree on the date and mechanism. The legacy TradeVerdicts asset label treated Naulls as "draft rights," but that classification is wrong. Naulls was already a seven-year NBA veteran who had played for St. Louis, New York and San Francisco. The transaction was a sale of an established player's rights, not a transfer of draft rights.

Boston Return

Naulls became a dependable Celtics rotation forward immediately. He played 78 games in 1963-64, averaging 9.8 points and 4.6 rebounds in 18.1 minutes per game. He followed with 71 games at 10.5 points and 4.7 rebounds in 1964-65, then another 71 games at 10.7 points and 4.5 rebounds in 1965-66. Across three seasons Boston received 220 regular-season games of stable bench and rotation production. That is a substantial realized return for a transaction in which the Celtics surrendered no documented player or draft asset.

San Francisco Return

The Warriors received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the public transaction ledgers reviewed for this pass. San Francisco had acquired Naulls from New York in December 1962 as part of the Tom Gola trade, used him for 47 games and then converted his rights into a financial return before the next season. That sequence means the Warriors did receive both on-court production and cash from the Naulls portion of the earlier package. Without the sale amount, however, the financial value cannot be measured against Boston's three seasons of production.

Hindsight Comparison

Boston has the clear basketball edge because 220 games of useful scoring and rebounding materially exceed an unknown cash return unless the payment was unusually large. Still, the legacy F grade for San Francisco is not defensible from the surviving record. A rights sale for cash was a normal transaction mechanism of the era, and the Warriors had already extracted a half-season of value from Naulls before selling him. The source-backed grade should acknowledge Boston's strong result without pretending the undisclosed payment was worthless.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A/C. Boston receives an A for three seasons, 220 games and steady rotation production from Naulls. San Francisco receives a C because the Warriors converted his rights into cash after a useful half-season, but the amount is unknown and no later basketball asset can be traced to the sale. Confidence is high on the date, rights-sale structure, player identity and Boston production, with lower certainty only on the financial term. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Baltimore acquired Kevin Loughery from Detroit for Larry Staverman on October 28, 1963. Basketball-Reference's Pistons, Bullets, league and player transaction records all agree on the date and direct player-for-player structure. Loughery then became a long-term Baltimore guard, playing 589 regular-season games for the franchise from 1963-64 through 1970-71, including five straight seasons of at least 15.9 points per game and a peak of 22.6 in 1968-69. Staverman played only 20 games for Detroit before the Pistons moved him again in a December three-team trade. perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Detroit traded Kevin Loughery to the Baltimore Bullets for Larry Staverman on October 28, 1963. Basketball-Reference's Pistons and Bullets transaction pages, the 1963-64 league ledger and both player histories all agree on the date and direct one-for-one structure. There is no unresolved cash term or draft-pick component in the original transaction, which makes the realized-value comparison unusually straightforward for this era.

Baltimore Return

Loughery became a major part of Baltimore's backcourt almost immediately. He played 65 games for the Bullets in 1963-64 and averaged 9.2 points and 2.8 assists. He followed with 80 games in 1964-65, then 74, 76, 77, 80, 55 and 82 games over the next six seasons. From 1965-66 through 1969-70, his scoring averages were 18.2, 18.2, 15.9, 22.6 and 21.9 points per game. Across 1963-64 through 1970-71, Baltimore received 589 regular-season games before moving him in October 1971.

Detroit Return

Staverman's Detroit stint was brief. He appeared in 20 games during 1963-64, averaging 5.7 points and 3.5 rebounds in 12.8 minutes per game. On December 16, less than two months after the Loughery trade, Detroit included Staverman in a three-team transaction with Cincinnati and New York. The Pistons also sent Johnny Egan to New York and received Donnie Butcher and Bob Duffy from the Knicks. Because Staverman was only one component of that later package, the value of Butcher and Duffy cannot be credited entirely to him.

Downstream Value

Baltimore's return did not end with Loughery's eight-season run. On October 18, 1971, the Bullets traded Loughery and Fred Carter to Philadelphia for Archie Clark and a 1973 second-round pick. Carter was a separate asset, so the entire return cannot be attributed to Loughery alone. Even with that caveat, the fact that Loughery still carried enough value to anchor another substantive NBA transaction after nearly 600 Baltimore games strengthens an already lopsided hindsight result.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win, A+/C. Baltimore receives an A+ for 589 regular-season games, multiple high-scoring seasons and preserved downstream trade value. Detroit receives a C because Staverman contributed only 20 games before becoming one component of a multi-team follow-up transaction. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, player identities and season-by-season production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Bullets, league and player transaction records all agree on October 29. new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Exchange

Baltimore traded Billy McGill to New York for Gene Shue and Paul Hogue on October 29, 1963. The source review corrects the legacy October 28 date. Basketball-Reference's Knicks and Bullets transaction pages, the 1963-64 league ledger and all three player histories agree on October 29. The package itself was accurately preserved: New York received McGill, while Baltimore received Shue and Hogue.

New York Return

McGill gave the Knicks a strong partial season. He played 68 games after the trade and averaged 16.0 points, 5.9 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 25.5 minutes per game. He was not merely depth; he became one of New York's higher-volume scorers during the 1963-64 season. The following October, the Knicks traded McGill to St. Louis for a 1965 second-round draft pick. That later pick became Hal Blevins. Blevins did not create meaningful NBA value, but the trade still shows that New York preserved another asset after receiving McGill's productive season.

Baltimore Return

Shue played 47 games for Baltimore in 1963-64, averaging 4.2 points, 2.0 rebounds and 3.2 assists in 20.5 minutes per game. Hogue appeared in only nine games for the Bullets and totaled seven points in 58 minutes. Neither player returned to the NBA after that season. Shue supplied useful ballhandling and veteran minutes, but this was the final stretch of his playing career. Hogue's Baltimore contribution was minimal.

Hindsight Comparison

The legacy grade treated Baltimore as the clear winner, likely giving too much weight to Shue's earlier career reputation rather than his actual post-trade production. The realized record points the other way. McGill outscored and outproduced both incoming Baltimore players, remained in the Knicks' rotation for 68 games and still carried enough value to be converted into a future second-round pick. Baltimore received 56 combined games from Shue and Hogue, with only Shue holding a meaningful role.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A-/C+. New York receives an A- for acquiring a 16-point-per-game scorer for 68 games and preserving a downstream draft asset. Baltimore receives a C+ because Shue supplied 47 games of veteran guard minutes, but Hogue barely played and both careers ended after the season. Confidence is high because the corrected date, package and player outcomes are directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: This Detroit-side December 15, 1963 record is a duplicate perspective of the three-team Detroit-New York-Cincinnati transaction that the league and all three team ledgers place on December 16. The supported deal sent Johnny Egan from Detroit to New York, Larry Staverman from Detroit to Cincinnati, Bob Boozer from Cincinnati to New York, and Donnie Butcher plus Bob Duffy from New York to Detroit. A separate New York canonical record already represents that multi-team transaction and contains the broader package. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.
perspectives.analysis:
The legacy Detroit record

The Detroit import records a December 15, 1963 three-team transaction involving Detroit, New York and Cincinnati. Its player movements substantially overlap the New York record dated December 16: Donnie Butcher and Bob Duffy move to Detroit, Johnny Egan moves to New York and Larry Staverman moves to Cincinnati. The Detroit version also carries Hub Reed as a later player-to-be-named-later completion. The key question is whether December 15 represents a separate transaction or only a one-day date discrepancy attached to the same deal.

Supported Chronology

Basketball-Reference's Detroit Pistons, New York Knicks and Cincinnati Royals transaction pages all place the core three-team trade on December 16, 1963. The 1963-64 NBA league ledger agrees. Those sources describe Cincinnati sending Bob Boozer to New York, Detroit sending Larry Staverman to Cincinnati, Detroit sending Johnny Egan to New York, and New York sending Donnie Butcher and Bob Duffy to Detroit. No authoritative team or league ledger reviewed for this pass lists a separate December 15 transaction with the same participants.

Why the Rows Are Duplicates

The player movements in the Detroit import are not an adjacent trade with a different package. They are Detroit's perspective on the same multi-team exchange represented by the New York canonical record. Maintaining both as active trades would cause Johnny Egan, Larry Staverman, Donnie Butcher and Bob Duffy to appear as though they changed teams twice on consecutive days. That would also distort trade counts and player relationship surfaces.

Deferred Hub Reed Component

The Detroit ledger records that on May 1, 1964 it acquired Hub Reed's rights from New York and labels that move as completion of the transaction in which New York obtained Johnny Egan. That deferred component belongs with the same Detroit-New York transaction history, but it does not justify a separate December 15 trade record. The May 1 completion can be preserved as a deferred asset note on the surviving canonical transaction after the package is fully reconciled.

Archival Treatment

The New York record nba-trade-nyk-1963-0050 is the better canonical container because it already carries the three-team structure and New York-facing assets, while the Detroit record is a narrower legacy perspective with the wrong date. Detroit's source perspective should be preserved as provenance on the canonical transaction, not as a second active event. Player relationships attached only to this duplicate record should resolve to the surviving December 16 record.

Final Resolution

Record Superseded. The supported transaction date is December 16, 1963, and the surviving canonical record is nba-trade-nyk-1963-0050. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. Its source evidence and deferred Hub Reed context remain useful for completing the canonical three-team record, but the record itself must not surface as a separate trade.

new-york-knicks.summary: New York came out of the December 16, 1963 three-team trade with Bob Boozer from Cincinnati and Johnny Egan from Detroit. Detroit received Donnie Butcher and Bob Duffy from New York, then Hub Reed rights on May 1, 1964 as the deferred completion of the Egan obligation. Cincinnati received Larry Staverman from Detroit. Boozer gave the Knicks 129 games over the rest of 1963-64 and all of 1964-65, while Egan supplied 123 Knicks games before the Walt Bellamy trade. Detroit received useful depth, but New York landed the two strongest immediate returns.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The verified three-team structure is straightforward: Cincinnati sent Bob Boozer to New York; Detroit sent Johnny Egan to New York and Larry Staverman to Cincinnati; New York sent Donnie Butcher and Bob Duffy to Detroit. Basketball-Reference also records the May 1, 1964 transfer of Hub Reed rights from New York to Detroit as completion of the Egan trade. The authoritative league and team transaction ledgers do not list cash in the December 16 package, so the older cash asset has been removed.

New York received the best basketball return. Boozer played 129 Knicks games across the remainder of 1963-64 and the full 1964-65 season, averaging about 15.4 points and 7.9 rebounds over that span. Egan added 123 games before being moved in the Walt Bellamy deal. Detroit still got useful depth: Butcher played 138 Pistons games across parts of three seasons, while Duffy contributed a shorter stint and Reed arrived later as the deferred completion. Cincinnati received Staverman, whose 34 games for the Royals in 1963-64 did not replace Boozer's value.

Final Verdict: Knicks Win. New York earns an A for landing the two most productive immediate pieces. Detroit merits a B- because Butcher provided real multi-season value and the package included Duffy plus the later Reed completion. Cincinnati receives a C- because Staverman's return was modest compared with the player it surrendered.

From the Knicks' perspective, the timing reinforces the grade. Boozer and Egan were usable immediately, while the deferred Reed obligation did not prevent New York from extracting two rotation pieces from the December exchange. Egan's later inclusion in the Walt Bellamy trade also means his value did not end with his 123 Knicks appearances. Detroit's depth return was legitimate and Cincinnati did receive a playable veteran in Staverman, but neither partner matched the combination of direct production and downstream flexibility that New York obtained.

perspectives.summary: Detroit sold Darrall Imhoff's player rights to the Los Angeles Lakers on April 16, 1964. The Lakers turned that cash purchase into four full seasons of frontcourt value: Imhoff played 316 regular-season games for Los Angeles, including 81 games at 10.7 points and 13.3 rebounds in 1966-67 and 82 games at 9.3 points and 10.9 rebounds in 1967-68. His value lasted beyond those seasons because Los Angeles later included him with Jerry Chambers and Archie Clark in the July 1968 trade that brought Wilt Chamberlain from Philadelphia. Detroit's return was cash with no traceable basketball asset, so the realized-value gap is decisive.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Lakers and league transaction ledgers agree that Detroit sold the player rights to Darrall Imhoff to Los Angeles on April 16, 1964. The transaction is therefore better described as a rights sale than as a conventional player-for-player trade. The surviving record does not disclose the cash amount, which limits any precise valuation of Detroit's return but does not obscure what Los Angeles received.

Los Angeles Return

Imhoff became a durable Lakers center immediately after the purchase. He played 76 games in 1964-65 and 77 in 1965-66, averaging 6.6 rebounds in both seasons. His role expanded sharply in 1966-67, when he appeared in 81 games and averaged 10.7 points, 13.3 rebounds and 2.7 assists in 33.6 minutes. He followed with all 82 games in 1967-68 at 9.3 points and 10.9 rebounds. Across four Lakers seasons, that is 316 regular-season games of realized value from a player acquired for cash.

Downstream Value

The return did not end when Imhoff's Lakers tenure did. On July 9, 1968, Los Angeles traded Imhoff, Jerry Chambers and Archie Clark to Philadelphia for Wilt Chamberlain. Imhoff was only one component of that package, so the Chamberlain return cannot be credited to him alone. Still, the fact that he remained valuable enough to be included in one of the era's defining superstar transactions adds meaningful downstream value to an already productive four-year run.

Detroit Return

Detroit received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the public transaction ledgers used here. Without a documented downstream player, pick or other basketball asset tied to that cash, the Pistons' realized return is inherently limited in a hindsight framework. That does not mean the original sale lacked a business rationale; it means the surviving basketball record gives Los Angeles far more measurable value.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A-/D+. Los Angeles receives an A- for 316 games, two high-level rebounding seasons and preserved downstream trade value in the Chamberlain package. Detroit remains at D+ because the return was undisclosed cash with no identifiable basketball asset to compare against Imhoff's production. Confidence is high on the date, rights-sale structure and player identity, while the undisclosed cash amount remains the main limitation.

perspectives.summary: Baltimore and Detroit made their eight-player blockbuster on June 18, 1964, not June 9 as the legacy TradeVerdicts record stated. The Bullets acquired Bob Ferry, Bailey Howell, Don Ohl and the rights to Les Hunter and Wali Jones for Terry Dischinger, Don Kojis and Rod Thorn. Baltimore received the deeper realized return: Howell produced 158 games at star-level scoring and rebounding, Ohl supplied 247 games with three seasons above 18 points per game, and Ferry added 260 games of frontcourt depth. Detroit still received substantial value from Dischinger, who played 452 games for the Pistons around a two-year military absence, plus shorter Kojis and Thorn runs. Baltimore wins, but Detroit's return was far from a failure.
perspectives.analysis:
The Date and Structure

Basketball-Reference's Baltimore, Detroit and league transaction ledgers all place the trade on June 18, 1964. The legacy TradeVerdicts record carried June 9, so the canonical date needs correction. Baltimore sent Terry Dischinger, Don Kojis and Rod Thorn to Detroit. Detroit sent Bob Ferry, Bailey Howell and Don Ohl, plus the rights to 1964 draftees Les Hunter and Wali Jones, to Baltimore. Because Hunter and Jones had been drafted in May but had not yet made their NBA debuts, rights labeling is appropriate for those two assets.

Baltimore Return

Howell immediately became a major Bullets piece, playing 80 games at 19.2 points and 10.9 rebounds in 1964-65 and 78 games at 17.5 points and 9.9 rebounds in 1965-66. Ohl gave Baltimore 247 regular-season games before moving on during 1967-68, including seasons of 18.4, 20.6 and 20.3 points per game. Ferry added 260 games across five seasons as a durable frontcourt contributor. Jones played 77 games as a rookie before leaving the franchise, while Hunter appeared in 24 games. The package therefore produced both star-level impact and considerable depth.

Detroit Return

Detroit's side had real value, especially through Dischinger. He played 80 games at 18.2 points and 6.0 rebounds in 1964-65, then missed two NBA seasons while serving in the military before returning to Detroit. From 1967-68 through 1971-72 he added another 372 Pistons games, giving Detroit 452 regular-season appearances in total after the trade. Kojis contributed 125 games over two seasons, while Thorn played 74 games at 11.0 points, 3.6 rebounds and 2.2 assists in 1964-65. That production makes a low or failing Detroit grade too harsh.

Hindsight Comparison

Baltimore still comes out ahead because it acquired multiple high-end contributors at once. Howell and Ohl were the two strongest immediate pieces, Ferry stayed for five seasons, and the two draft-rights assets added further roster value. Detroit's case rests heavily on Dischinger's long tenure; Kojis and Thorn were useful but brief. The trade therefore deserves a clear Baltimore verdict without pretending Detroit received little in return.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win, A+/B+. Baltimore receives an A+ for the combination of Howell's star production, Ohl's scoring, Ferry's longevity and additional rights value. Detroit earns a B+ because Dischinger became a long-term contributor and Kojis and Thorn added legitimate rotation production. Confidence is high on the corrected June 18 date, player identities and transaction structure. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The Exchange

St. Louis sold Jerry Grote's player rights to Philadelphia on August 26, 1964. Basketball-Reference's St. Louis and Philadelphia team ledgers and the 1964-65 NBA transaction log all agree on the date and rights-sale structure. The amount of cash is not disclosed in those public records, so the transaction cannot be valued as though the Hawks received a known financial return. What can be measured is whether Philadelphia turned the acquired rights into NBA production or a documented downstream asset.

Jerry Grote's Rights

Grote had been selected by St. Louis in the fourth round of the 1962 NBA Draft. His Basketball-Reference player record confirms that the Hawks sold his rights to Philadelphia on August 26, 1964. He did not play a regular-season game for the 76ers. His only NBA action came with the Los Angeles Lakers later in 1964-65, when he appeared in 11 games and averaged 1.3 points, 0.4 rebounds and 0.4 assists in 3.0 minutes per game.

Philadelphia Return

Because Grote's NBA appearances came for Los Angeles rather than Philadelphia, those 11 games should not be credited to the 76ers. The source set used here does not document a later Philadelphia transaction that converted Grote's rights into a player, pick or cash return. Philadelphia therefore acquired a legitimate former fourth-round draft asset, but the measurable NBA value that reached the 76ers from this specific purchase is effectively zero.

St. Louis Return

The Hawks received cash. The amount is unknown, which prevents a strong grade based on financial value alone. Still, St. Louis converted rights to a player who never appeared for the Hawks and would never play for Philadelphia into a realized return. That is enough for a directional edge, but not enough evidence for a major win.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge, C+/D+. St. Louis receives a C+ for monetizing an unused rights asset. Philadelphia receives a D+ because the acquired rights produced no documented 76ers games or traceable downstream basketball value. Confidence is high on the date, player identity and rights-sale structure, while the undisclosed cash amount keeps the verdict modest. new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Date and Structure

New York sold Al Butler's player rights to Baltimore on October 17, 1964. The legacy TradeVerdicts record carried October 16, but Basketball-Reference's Knicks and Bullets transaction pages and the league transaction ledger all use October 17. The source language also matters: this was a sale of player rights, not a conventional player-for-player trade. Butler had already played three seasons for New York, but the asset transferred in 1964 was the club's rights to him.

Baltimore Return

The Bullets did turn those rights into NBA production. Butler appeared in 25 games for Baltimore in 1964-65, averaging 2.4 points, 0.8 rebounds and 0.5 assists in 6.9 minutes per game. It was a small reserve role and his final NBA season, so the return should not be exaggerated. Still, Baltimore acquired an asset that reached the floor and supplied actual rotation minutes.

New York Return

The Knicks received cash. The public transaction ledgers do not disclose the amount, and the source set does not identify a later player, pick or other basketball asset tied to that money. New York had already received several useful seasons from Butler before the sale, so converting his remaining rights into cash was rational. In a realized-value comparison, however, the undisclosed financial return is harder to credit than Baltimore's documented 25 games.

Hindsight Comparison

The gap is narrow. Butler's Baltimore stint lasted only one season and barely 170 total minutes, while New York at least monetized rights it no longer planned to use. That makes a decisive Bullets win too strong, but it also makes the prior Knicks-win framing difficult to support once the acquired rights are connected to Butler's actual Baltimore appearances.

Final Verdict

Slight Bullets Edge, B-/C+. Baltimore receives a B- for turning the purchased rights into 25 NBA games. New York receives a C+ for the undisclosed cash return and sensible asset monetization. golden-state-warriors.summary: Philadelphia acquired Wilt Chamberlain from San Francisco on January 15, 1965 for Connie Dierking, Paul Neumann, Lee Shaffer and cash. The 76ers received 277 regular-season games from Chamberlain before trading him to the Lakers in 1968, including three straight MVP seasons, the 1967 championship and a 68-13 regular season. San Francisco did get usable depth: Neumann played 102 games for the Warriors across 1964-65 and 1965-66, while Dierking contributed 30 games before moving on. Shaffer never played for the Warriors after the deal. Nate Thurmond's later rise belongs to the Warriors' existing roster and cannot be credited as trade compensation, so the realized value still tilts overwhelmingly toward Philadelphia.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange

San Francisco traded Wilt Chamberlain to Philadelphia on January 15, 1965 for Connie Dierking, Paul Neumann, Lee Shaffer and cash. Basketball-Reference's Warriors, 76ers and league transaction ledgers all agree on the date and four-part return. The public transaction logs do not state a cash amount, so the source-backed record should preserve cash without treating the reported figure in older summaries as verified.

Philadelphia Return

Chamberlain immediately gave Philadelphia superstar production. He played 35 games for the 76ers after the trade in 1964-65 at 30.1 points, 22.3 rebounds and 3.8 assists per game. He then played 79, 81 and 82 games in his three full Philadelphia seasons, bringing his post-trade 76ers total to 277 regular-season games. Those seasons included three consecutive MVP awards. In 1966-67, Chamberlain averaged 24.1 points, 24.2 rebounds and 7.8 assists while Philadelphia went 68-13 and won the NBA championship.

San Francisco Return

The Warriors did receive rotation value. Neumann played 36 games after the trade in 1964-65 and 66 more in 1965-66, averaging 14.4 points in the latter season. Dierking played 30 games for San Francisco at 8.0 points and 6.5 rebounds before leaving the franchise. Shaffer did not appear in an NBA game for the Warriors after the trade, so his inclusion did not become realized on-court value. Cash added financial value, but the amount is not disclosed in the core public transaction sources used here.

Context That Should Not Be Counted

Nate Thurmond became a Hall of Fame center for the Warriors and took on a larger role after Chamberlain left, but Thurmond was already on San Francisco's roster before the trade. His development is relevant context for why the Warriors could move on from Chamberlain, yet it is not compensation received from Philadelphia. TradeVerdicts should therefore avoid crediting Thurmond as part of the incoming package.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/F. Philadelphia receives an A+ for acquiring an all-time great in his prime, capturing three MVP seasons and winning the 1967 championship. San Francisco receives an F because the return produced only short-term rotation value and no comparable downstream asset. The grade is about realized trade value rather than whether the Warriors had broader roster reasons to make the move. Confidence is high on the date, package and player outcomes, while the cash amount remains undisclosed. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: San Francisco sold Wayne Hightower's player rights to Baltimore on February 3, 1965 for cash. The Warriors, Bullets and NBA transaction ledgers agree on the rights-sale structure. Hightower then played 94 regular-season games for Baltimore across parts of three seasons, including 27 games immediately after the sale, before the Bullets sold his rights to Detroit in January 1967 for another cash return. San Francisco did receive immediate cash, but the amount is not disclosed in the public transaction records. Baltimore therefore realized both useful frontcourt minutes and a later financial return from the acquired rights, supporting a clear Bullets edge without treating the original Warriors cash return as worthless.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange

San Francisco sold Wayne Hightower's player rights to Baltimore on February 3, 1965. Basketball-Reference's Warriors, Bullets and league transaction ledgers agree on the date and sale structure. The original cash amount is not disclosed, so the source-backed review should not pretend to know its financial size. Hightower was not a prospect who had never reached the league; he had already played 48 games for San Francisco in 1964-65 before the rights sale.

Baltimore Return

Hightower immediately joined the Bullets and appeared in 27 games for Baltimore to finish the 1964-65 season, averaging 6.7 points and 6.4 rebounds in 18.9 minutes per game. He added 24 games in 1965-66 at 7.6 points and 5.5 rebounds, then 43 more Baltimore games in 1966-67 before leaving for Detroit. That gives the Bullets 94 regular-season games of direct post-acquisition value.

Downstream Value

Baltimore did not simply lose Hightower for nothing after those 94 games. His Basketball-Reference transaction history records that the Bullets sold his player rights to Detroit on January 29, 1967. The later cash amount is also undisclosed, but the transaction still demonstrates that Baltimore was able to convert the acquired asset into another realized return after nearly two full seasons of use.

San Francisco Return

The Warriors received cash in the original February 1965 sale. Because no amount is preserved in the core public transaction ledgers, the return cannot be measured against Hightower's production with precision. It was a legitimate realized asset and should not be graded as though San Francisco received nothing. The hindsight disadvantage comes from Baltimore extracting 94 games plus a later rights sale from the same player.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, B/C. Baltimore receives a B for useful multi-season frontcourt depth and a later cash conversion. San Francisco receives a C because it monetized Hightower's rights but surrendered the larger measurable basketball return. Confidence is high on the February 3 date, rights-sale structure and Hightower's Baltimore production; both cash amounts remain undisclosed. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit purchased the player rights to Bill Chmielewski from Cincinnati for cash. The date requires source adjudication: Detroit's own 1966 media guide and RealGM place the acquisition on May 8, 1965, while Basketball-Reference lists December 8, 1965. TradeVerdicts retains May 8 because the near-contemporary Pistons media guide is the strongest team-produced source in the record. Chmielewski, Cincinnati's No. 17 pick in the 1964 NBA Draft, never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Cincinnati therefore converted unused rights into cash, while Detroit paid for an asset that produced no measurable NBA value.
perspectives.analysis:
The Date Conflict

Detroit acquired Bill Chmielewski's player rights from Cincinnati for cash. The transaction date is not uniform across modern databases. Detroit's 1966 media guide lists May 8, 1965, and RealGM also places the deal on May 8. Basketball-Reference's Cincinnati, Detroit and league transaction pages instead list December 8, 1965. Because the Pistons media guide was a team-produced source published close to the transaction, TradeVerdicts retains May 8 while explicitly recording the Basketball-Reference conflict rather than silently treating the date as unanimous.

The Asset

Cincinnati had selected Chmielewski in the second round of the 1964 NBA Draft, 17th overall. His Basketball-Reference player page identifies him as a 6-foot-10 center from Dayton and preserves the Cincinnati draft history. The important realized-value point is that he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Detroit therefore acquired legitimate draft rights, but those rights did not become on-court production.

Cincinnati Return

The Royals received cash. The amount is not disclosed in the source set used here, so the return cannot be assigned a precise financial value. Even so, Cincinnati converted rights to a player who never reached an NBA regular-season floor into an immediate realized asset. That is a better hindsight outcome than simply holding the rights until they expired or became irrelevant.

Detroit Return

Detroit's downside is straightforward: the Pistons paid cash and received no NBA games from Chmielewski. There is no documented downstream player, pick or later trade return attached to those rights in the sources used for this review. That makes the prior slight-Pistons-edge framing difficult to defend.

Final Verdict

Slight Royals Edge, C+/D+. Cincinnati receives a C+ for monetizing an unused draft-rights asset. Detroit receives a D+ because the purchased rights produced no NBA games or traceable downstream basketball return. Confidence is high on the participants and sale structure, but only medium on the exact date because authoritative records conflict. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Date and Structure

Boston sold Joe Strawder's player rights to Detroit on September 15, 1965. The legacy TradeVerdicts record carried September 14, but Basketball-Reference's Celtics, Pistons and league transaction ledgers all use September 15. The source language also identifies a rights sale rather than a conventional player-for-player trade. Detroit therefore purchased the right to bring Strawder into its roster, while Boston received cash whose amount is not disclosed in the public transaction logs.

Detroit Return

The Pistons received much more than a short trial. Strawder played 79 games in 1965-66, averaging 8.6 points and 10.4 rebounds in 27.6 minutes per game. He followed with another 79 games in 1966-67 at 9.5 points and 10.0 rebounds, then 73 games in 1967-68 at 7.5 points and 9.4 rebounds. Across those three seasons, Detroit received 231 regular-season games and a steady rebounding presence from an asset acquired for cash.

Boston Return

The Celtics received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the transaction ledgers used here. Boston did not receive a player or draft pick that can be traced through the deal, so the basketball side of the return is not directly measurable. That does not mean the sale lacked a financial rationale. It means a hindsight trade evaluation has substantially more observable value on Detroit's side.

Hindsight Comparison

Strawder was not a star, but three seasons of near-double-digit rebounding and 231 games is meaningful realized value. Boston's return was immediate financial value of unknown size. Because the cash amount cannot be reconstructed confidently, the grade gap should acknowledge Detroit's strong basketball return without assigning Boston an automatic failing grade.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, B+/C. Detroit receives a B+ for three full seasons of useful frontcourt production from Strawder. Boston receives a C because it monetized the rights but left no traceable on-court asset in the record. Confidence is high on the corrected September 15 date, rights-sale structure and Strawder's Detroit production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: New York acquired Dick Barnett from the Los Angeles Lakers for Bob Boozer on October 14, 1965. Barnett became an eight-season Knick, playing 599 regular-season games and immediately averaging 23.1 points in his first New York season. He remained a major rotation piece through both the 1970 and 1973 championship runs. Boozer gave Los Angeles one productive season, playing 78 games at 12.2 points and 7.0 rebounds before the Lakers lost him to Chicago in the 1966 expansion draft. Both clubs received real value, but New York turned the exchange into years of continuity and two championship-era contributions while Los Angeles received only one season.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange

The Lakers traded Dick Barnett to New York for Bob Boozer on October 14, 1965. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Knicks and league transaction ledgers all agree on the date and direct player-for-player structure. With no picks, cash or deferred rights in the package, the hindsight comparison is unusually straightforward: how much value did each player create for the franchise that acquired him?

New York Return

Barnett became a long-term Knicks fixture immediately. He played 75 games in 1965-66 and averaged 23.1 points, 4.1 rebounds and 3.5 assists in 34.5 minutes per game. He stayed with New York for eight seasons, totaling 599 regular-season games from 1965-66 through 1972-73. His scoring remained in double figures through 1971-72, and he was a substantial rotation piece on the 1969-70 championship team before still contributing during the 1972-73 title season.

Los Angeles Return

Boozer was productive, but his Lakers tenure lasted only one season. He played 78 games in 1965-66, averaging 12.2 points and 7.0 rebounds in 23.7 minutes. That is legitimate frontcourt value and makes the trade more balanced than a one-sided asset dump. The problem for Los Angeles is duration: the Lakers lost Boozer to the Chicago Bulls in the May 1966 expansion draft, ending their return after a single season.

Hindsight Comparison

The Knicks received nearly eight times as many regular-season games from Barnett as the Lakers received from Boozer. More importantly, Barnett's tenure overlapped with the construction and success of New York's championship teams. Boozer's lone Lakers season was useful, but Los Angeles had no downstream asset after the expansion draft. The separation is therefore large even though Boozer himself played well.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A+/B-. New York receives an A+ for 599 Barnett games, high-end scoring in the early years and meaningful contributions to two championship teams. Los Angeles receives a B- because Boozer delivered a productive 78-game season before the expansion draft cut off the return. Confidence is high on the date, structure and player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Cincinnati acquired Connie Dierking and Art Heyman from San Francisco for Bud Olsen and cash on October 20, 1965. Dierking became the deal's defining asset, playing 374 regular-season games for the Royals through the start of 1970-71 and developing into a 16-point, eight-to-nine-rebound frontcourt piece at his peak. Heyman added only 11 Cincinnati games before Philadelphia claimed him on waivers. San Francisco received 95 games from Olsen across two seasons plus undisclosed cash. The Warriors got legitimate reserve value, but Cincinnati secured the only long-term impact player and clearly realized the stronger basketball return.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange

Cincinnati traded Bud Olsen and cash to San Francisco for Connie Dierking and Art Heyman on October 20, 1965. Basketball-Reference's Royals, Warriors and league transaction ledgers all agree on the date and four-part package. The cash amount is not disclosed in the public ledgers, so its value should be preserved but not treated as precisely measurable.

Cincinnati Return

Dierking became the central asset. He played 57 games for Cincinnati in 1965-66 and then 77, 81, 82 and 76 games over the next four seasons. He peaked at 16.4 points and 9.5 rebounds in 1967-68, 16.3 points and 9.0 rebounds in 1968-69, and 16.7 points with 8.2 rebounds in 1969-70. Including one final Cincinnati appearance in 1970-71, the Royals received 374 regular-season games from Dierking. Heyman contributed 11 games before Philadelphia claimed him on waivers in December 1965.

San Francisco Return

Olsen gave the Warriors 55 games in 1965-66 and 40 more in 1966-67, for 95 regular-season appearances. His role was limited: he averaged 3.5 points and 3.3 rebounds in 10.3 minutes after the trade, then 4.3 points and 2.6 rebounds the next season. San Francisco also received cash, but the amount is unavailable in the core transaction sources.

Hindsight Comparison

The Warriors did not come away empty. Ninety-five reserve games plus cash is a real return. Cincinnati nevertheless acquired a player who became a durable multi-season starter and high-level scorer and rebounder. Heyman's brief Royals tenure barely changes the balance; Dierking alone creates the meaningful separation.

Final Verdict

Royals Win, A-/C+. Cincinnati receives an A- for 374 Dierking games and multiple productive prime seasons, with Heyman adding a small short-term piece. San Francisco receives a C+ for 95 Olsen games plus undisclosed cash. Confidence is high on the date, structure and player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia sold Ben Warley's player rights to Baltimore on October 27, 1965 for cash. Warley had appeared in one game for the 76ers that season before the sale, then gave Baltimore 118 regular-season games across 1965-66 and 1966-67. He averaged 5.3 points and 3.8 rebounds in 56 Bullets games immediately after the move, then 6.2 points and 5.2 rebounds in 62 games the next season. Seattle selected him from Baltimore in the 1967 expansion draft, ending the Bullets' return. Philadelphia received undisclosed cash. Baltimore therefore realized two seasons of useful depth, while Philadelphia's financial return cannot be measured precisely.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Exchange

Philadelphia sold Ben Warley's player rights to Baltimore on October 27, 1965. Basketball-Reference's 76ers, Bullets and league transaction ledgers all agree on the date and rights-sale structure. Warley had appeared in one game for Philadelphia in 1965-66 before the transaction, so this was not the sale of an untested draft prospect. The 76ers received cash, but the public transaction records do not disclose the amount.

Baltimore Return

Warley became a useful reserve immediately after the move. He played 56 games for Baltimore in 1965-66, averaging 5.3 points and 3.8 rebounds in 13.7 minutes. He returned for 62 games in 1966-67 and increased his role to 6.2 points and 5.2 rebounds in 16.7 minutes per game. That gives the Bullets 118 regular-season games from the acquired rights across two seasons.

End of the Return

Baltimore's value stopped through the expansion process rather than through a trade return. Warley's Basketball-Reference transaction history shows that the Seattle SuperSonics selected him from the Bullets in the May 1, 1967 expansion draft. He later moved to the ABA, but those later seasons did not produce a Baltimore asset and should not be credited to this transaction.

Philadelphia Return

Philadelphia received cash. Because the amount is undisclosed, it cannot be compared precisely with Warley's two seasons of production. The sale may have made sense as a roster-management decision for a team with greater frontcourt depth, but the measurable basketball return is on Baltimore's side.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, B/C. Baltimore receives a B for 118 games of useful frontcourt depth before the 1967 expansion draft. Philadelphia receives a C for monetizing Warley's rights without a traceable on-court or downstream asset in the public record. Confidence is high on the October 27 date, rights-sale structure and Warley's Baltimore production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: New York acquired 26-year-old Hall of Fame center Walt Bellamy from Baltimore on November 1, 1965 for Jim Barnes, Johnny Egan, Johnny Green and cash. Bellamy gave the Knicks 268 regular-season games, averaged 23.2 points and 16.0 rebounds in his first New York season, and later became part of the package used to acquire Dave DeBusschere. Baltimore received substantial depth rather than an empty return: Egan became a multi-year rotation guard, Green supplied two productive seasons, and Barnes produced a strong first year before being traded for Leroy Ellis.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
New York's official media guide records the November 1, 1965 trade exactly: Walt Bellamy came from Baltimore for Johnny Green, Johnny Egan, Jim Barnes and cash. That source also records Bellamy's later December 19, 1968 move to Detroit with Howard Komives for Dave DeBusschere, which matters as downstream asset value but should not erase the direct production each side received from the 1965 exchange.

New York Return

summary: St. Louis traded John Tresvant and Chico Vaughn to Detroit for Rod Thorn on December 24, 1965. The Hawks received 113 regular-season games from Thorn before Seattle selected him in the 1967 expansion draft. Detroit received the larger immediate return: Vaughn played 88 Pistons games over two seasons, while Tresvant played 169 and developed into a double-digit scorer and strong rebounder. Tresvant also retained downstream value, joining Tom Van Arsdale in the February 1968 trade that brought Happy Hairston and Jim Fox to Detroit. That combination of deeper production and later trade value reverses the legacy Hawks-win framing.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's St. Louis, Detroit and league transaction ledgers agree that the trade occurred on December 24, 1965. St. Louis sent John Tresvant and Chico Vaughn to Detroit for Rod Thorn. The structure is straightforward and the player identities are directly supported by the transaction record.

St. Louis Return

Thorn played 46 games for the Hawks after the trade in 1965-66 and 67 more in 1966-67, giving St. Louis 113 regular-season games. He averaged 8.8 points in both seasons, with 2.4 rebounds and 1.8 assists per game each year. His Hawks tenure ended when Seattle selected him in the May 1, 1967 expansion draft, so St. Louis did not convert him into a later trade return.

Detroit Return

Vaughn gave Detroit 37 games in 1965-66 and 51 in 1966-67, for 88 total Pistons appearances. Tresvant supplied much more. He played 46 Detroit games at 8.3 points and 6.1 rebounds in 1965-66, 68 games at 9.9 points and 7.1 rebounds in 1966-67, and 55 more in 1967-68 at 13.3 points and 9.8 rebounds before being traded. That is 169 Pistons games from Tresvant alone and 257 combined from the two-player return.

Downstream Value

Tresvant's value did not end with his Detroit tenure. On February 1, 1968, the Pistons traded Tresvant and Tom Van Arsdale to Cincinnati for Jim Fox and Happy Hairston. The later package cannot be credited solely to Tresvant, but his inclusion shows that Detroit retained meaningful transactional value from the original 1965 return after already receiving nearly three seasons of production.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A-/B-. Detroit receives an A- for the larger volume of direct production, Tresvant's stronger peak and the later trade value preserved in the 1968 Cincinnati deal. St. Louis receives a B- because Thorn was a useful two-season contributor, but his Hawks tenure ended in the expansion draft and produced no downstream return. Confidence is high on the date, player identities and realized NBA production.

The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's St. Louis, Detroit and league transaction ledgers agree that the trade occurred on December 28, 1965. Detroit sent Joe Caldwell to St. Louis for John Barnhill. The move came only four days after the same franchises completed the Rod Thorn-for-John Tresvant-and-Chico Vaughn trade, but this is a separate one-for-one transaction and should remain a distinct record.

St. Louis Return

Caldwell became a core Hawks player almost immediately. He played 46 games for St. Louis after the trade in 1965-66, then 81, 79, 81 and 82 games over the next four seasons. The Structure

Basketball-Reference's league transaction ledger records that Chicago sold Hank Finkel's player rights to the Los Angeles Lakers on May 11, 1966. The Lakers' own transaction page confirms that they acquired Finkel's rights that day. The legacy TradeVerdicts record treated the asset as a 1966 second-round pick at No. 14, but the 1966 NBA Draft record lists Finkel as the 17th overall pick. Los Angeles Return

Finkel reached the Lakers roster in 1966-67 but played only 27 regular-season games, averaging 1.5 points and 2.4 rebounds in 5.2 minutes per game. He did not become a meaningful Lakers rotation piece. On May 1, 1967, the San Diego Rockets selected him from Los Angeles in the expansion draft, ending the Lakers' direct control of the asset after one season.

Finkel later became a productive player for San Diego and then spent six seasons with Boston, including the Celtics' 1974 championship season. That later career should not be credited to the Lakers because Los Angeles had already lost him in the 1967 expansion draft. The older TradeVerdicts analysis improperly treated his later Boston value as part of the original Lakers return, overstating the deal.

Chicago Return

Chicago received cash, but the public transaction record does not disclose the amount. That prevents precise valuation. The Bulls did give up rights that eventually produced 27 Lakers games, so the Lakers realized more directly measurable basketball value. The gap is still small because Finkel's Los Angeles role was minimal and no downstream Lakers asset survived the expansion draft.

Slight Lakers Edge, C+/C. Los Angeles receives a C+ for turning the purchased rights into 27 NBA games, while Chicago receives a C for the undisclosed cash return. perspectives.summary: Detroit sold Bob Warlick's player rights to San Francisco on September 1, 1966. The Warriors received 81 regular-season games from Warlick across two seasons, including 69 games at 8.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 1967-68. Detroit received undisclosed cash and no traceable downstream basketball asset in the public transaction record. Warlick did not become a major long-term piece, but San Francisco still turned the purchased rights into two seasons of actual rotation value. That supports only a modest Warriors edge rather than a major win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Structure

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, San Francisco and league transaction ledgers agree that Detroit sold Bob Warlick's player rights to the Warriors on September 1, 1966. The public records do not disclose the cash amount, so the transaction is best evaluated as a rights sale with a known basketball return on one side and an unknown financial return on the other.

San Francisco Return

Warlick played 12 games for the Warriors in 1966-67, averaging 3.0 points and 1.7 rebounds in 5.4 minutes per game. His role expanded the next season: he appeared in 69 games in 1967-68 and averaged 8.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 19.1 minutes. That gives San Francisco 81 regular-season games from the acquired rights, with one season of legitimate rotation-level production.

Detroit Return

Detroit received cash, but the amount is not available in the transaction sources used here. There is no documented player, pick or other basketball asset tied to that cash in the source set. The Pistons therefore converted rights they did not intend to use into an immediate financial return, but the value cannot be measured directly against Warlick's 81 Warriors games.

Hindsight Comparison

San Francisco realized more visible basketball value, but the scale remains modest. Warlick was not a star and did not become a long-term Warriors fixture. Detroit's side was not empty; it was simply undisclosed cash. The result therefore belongs in the slight-edge tier rather than the clear-win tier.

Final Verdict

Slight Warriors Edge, B-/C+. San Francisco receives a B- for two seasons and 81 games of useful depth from Warlick. Detroit receives a C+ for monetizing unused rights without a documented basketball return. Confidence is high on the date, player identity and rights-sale structure, with the undisclosed cash amount remaining the primary limitation.

golden-state-warriors.summary: San Francisco traded Guy Rodgers to Chicago on September 7, 1966 for Jim King, Jeff Mullins and cash. The legacy TradeVerdicts record incorrectly carried an extra unidentified draft pick and treated King and Mullins as later players to be named; Basketball-Reference's Warriors, Bulls and league transaction ledgers list the three-part return directly. Chicago received one elite season from Rodgers, who played 81 games in 1966-67 at 18.0 points and 11.2 assists before appearing only four more times for the Bulls. San Francisco received 167 games from King and, far more importantly, ten Warriors seasons from Mullins, including multiple 20-point seasons. The realized return clearly favors the Warriors.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Structure

Basketball-Reference's San Francisco, Chicago and league transaction ledgers agree on the September 7, 1966 structure: the Bulls sent Jim King, Jeff Mullins and cash to the Warriors for Guy Rodgers. The legacy TradeVerdicts record added an unidentified draft pick and treated King and Mullins as later players to be named. Those elements are not supported by the transaction ledgers and should be removed from the canonical package.

Chicago Return

Rodgers gave the expansion Bulls an excellent first season. He played 81 games in 1966-67, averaging 18.0 points, 4.3 rebounds and 11.2 assists in 37.8 minutes. His Chicago tenure was brief, however. He appeared in only four games for the Bulls in 1967-68 before moving to Cincinnati, so Chicago realized 85 regular-season games from the trade.

San Francisco Return

King gave the Warriors 167 games across parts of four seasons, including 54 games at 16.6 points, 4.5 rebounds and 4.2 assists in 1967-68. Mullins became the enduring asset. From 1966-67 through 1975-76 he played ten seasons for San Francisco/Golden State, with six consecutive seasons from 1967-68 through 1972-73 at 17.8 points per game or better and three straight seasons above 20 points from 1968-69 through 1970-71. He remained with the franchise through the 1975-76 season.

Hindsight Comparison

Rodgers was immediately valuable and helped establish Chicago's first NBA team, so the Bulls received a credible return rather than a failed asset. The scale of Mullins's decade-long Warriors tenure changes the comparison. San Francisco received both the best long-term player and additional useful production from King, plus cash. Once the unsupported draft-pick element is removed, the Warriors' advantage is still clear.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, A+/B+. Golden State receives an A+ for Mullins's ten-season tenure, King's multi-season contribution and the cash component. Chicago receives a B+ for Rodgers's outstanding 1966-67 season and 85 total Bulls games. Confidence is high because the date, player package and absence of a draft pick are directly documented by both team ledgers and the league transaction log.

The Structure

San Francisco sent Guy Rodgers to the expansion Chicago Bulls on September 7, 1966 for Jim King, Jeff Mullins and cash. Basketball-Reference's Warriors, Bulls and league transaction ledgers agree on those components. That matters because an older version of the record carried an unidentified draft pick and described King and Mullins as later players to be named. Chicago's Return

Rodgers gave the first-year Bulls exactly the veteran guard play they were seeking. He appeared in 81 games in 1966-67, averaged 18.0 points and 11.2 assists, and led the league in assists. His Chicago value was concentrated almost entirely in that inaugural season, however. Rodgers played only four more games for the Bulls in 1967-68 before moving to Cincinnati, leaving Chicago with 85 regular-season games from the trade. That is meaningful short-term value, especially for an expansion roster, but it was not a long tenure.

King supplied 167 games across parts of four Warriors seasons and reached 16.6 points per game in 1967-68. Mullins became the centerpiece. He spent ten seasons with San Francisco and Golden State from 1966-67 through 1975-76, produced six straight seasons at 17.8 points per game or better from 1967-68 through 1972-73, and topped 20 points per game in three consecutive seasons. The cash component added value without changing the basketball comparison.

Hindsight Comparison

Chicago did not make a pointless trade: Rodgers immediately organized the offense and gave the expansion Bulls a high-level first season. The long-term balance still favors the Warriors by a wide margin. San Francisco received a decade from Mullins plus several useful seasons from King, while Chicago's return was largely compressed into one excellent Rodgers season. The verified package supports the existing A+ for Golden State and B+ for Chicago.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. The Bulls deserve credit for acquiring a veteran who led the league in assists during their inaugural season, but Mullins's ten-year Warriors run is the defining asset. King added another multi-season contributor, and no unsupported draft pick is needed to make the result decisive.

Cincinnati Return

The Royals received cash, but the amount is not listed in the Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers used here. The scale still falls short of a major historical win because Hawkins was a useful role player rather than a franchise-changing piece.

Ellis became the stronger immediate asset, playing 311 regular-season games for the Bullets over four seasons. He averaged 14.9 points and 12.0 rebounds in 1966-67, then 12.4 points and 11.1 rebounds the next year. The realized production therefore favors Baltimore by a clear margin, reversing the legacy Lakers-win framing while still recognizing that Barnes supplied useful frontcourt depth.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Baltimore and league transaction ledgers agree that Los Angeles traded LeRoy Ellis to the Bullets for Jim Barnes on September 22, 1966. This was a straightforward one-for-one player trade, with no documented picks or cash attached.

Baltimore Return

Ellis immediately became a major Bullets frontcourt contributor. He played 81 games in 1966-67 at 14.9 points and 12.0 rebounds per game, then 78 games in 1967-68 at 12.4 points and 11.1 rebounds. He remained with Baltimore for two more seasons, appearing in 80 games in 1968-69 and 72 in 1969-70. That is 311 regular-season games for the Bullets, with two seasons of double-digit scoring and rebounding at a high level.

Los Angeles Return

Barnes played 80 games for the Lakers in 1966-67 and 42 more in 1967-68 before moving to Chicago. He averaged 7.0 points and 5.6 rebounds in his first Lakers season, then 6.2 points and 5.0 rebounds in 17.0 minutes across the 42 games of his second season. That gives Los Angeles 122 regular-season games of useful depth, but not the same workload or peak as Ellis.

Hindsight Comparison

Both teams received actual rotation value, so this is not a one-sided failure. The difference comes from role and duration. Ellis was a starter-level rebounder for Baltimore and remained there for four seasons, while Barnes was primarily a reserve and left Los Angeles during his second season. The completed outcomes make Baltimore's advantage much clearer than the legacy record suggested.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, A/B. Baltimore receives an A for 311 games and two major rebounding seasons from Ellis. Los Angeles receives a B for 122 games of useful frontcourt depth from Barnes. Confidence is high because the date, player identities and direct statistical outcomes are well documented.
