seattle-supersonics.summary: Seattle acquired Dick Snyder from Phoenix for Art Harris on October 26, 1969. Snyder became a long-term SuperSonics starter, playing 387 regular-season games for Seattle through 1973-74 after the trade and producing several strong scoring seasons, including 19.4 points per game in 1970-71. Phoenix received a useful return in Harris, who played 153 games over three Suns seasons and averaged 7.8 points in 76 games immediately after the trade. Harris provided rotation value, but Snyder's five-season Seattle run, larger role and substantially higher production created the clearer realized return.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Exchange

Phoenix traded Dick Snyder to the Seattle SuperSonics for Art Harris on October 26, 1969. Seattle's transaction ledger and the NBA league log agree on the date and one-for-one player exchange. Both players were young guards with established NBA experience, making this a direct roster-value comparison rather than a deal driven by draft picks or undisclosed financial consideration.

Seattle Return

Snyder became a major part of Seattle's backcourt almost immediately. After six early-season games with Phoenix, he played 76 games for the SuperSonics in 1969-70. He scored 1,030 points, averaging roughly 13.6 per game, and added 333 assists while shooting 53.1 percent from the field.

His role grew the following season. Snyder played all 82 games in 1970-71 and scored 1,592 points, an average of 19.4 per game. He followed with 73 games in 1971-72, 82 in 1972-73 and 74 in 1973-74. Across those five Seattle seasons after the trade, he appeared in 387 regular-season games.

Snyder's production stayed useful throughout that run. He scored 1,210 points in 1971-72, 1,132 in 1972-73 and 1,338 in 1973-74. That combination of longevity and starter-level scoring made him far more than a short-term replacement.

Phoenix Return

Harris also gave Phoenix real value. He played 76 games in 1969-70 after arriving from Seattle, averaging 7.8 points, 2.8 assists and 1.9 rebounds in 18.1 minutes. He then appeared in 56 games in 1970-71 at 8.3 points per game and another 21 games in 1971-72.

Across three Suns seasons, Harris played 153 regular-season games. His role was smaller than Snyder's Seattle role, and his efficiency was limited, but Phoenix still received several seasons of rotation minutes. That keeps the Suns' side from being treated as a failed return.

Hindsight Comparison

Both teams received usable players, but the scale differs substantially. Phoenix got 153 Harris games across three seasons. Seattle got 387 Snyder games across five seasons, including a near-20-point scoring year and multiple seasons as a high-minute starter. Snyder produced more games, more minutes and a much larger offensive role.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, A/B-. Seattle receives an A for five seasons of Snyder production and 387 regular-season appearances, including a 19.4-point season. Phoenix receives a B- because Harris gave the Suns 153 games and several years of rotation value, but the return did not approach Snyder's durability or offensive impact. Confidence is high because the trade structure and both players' post-trade records are directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

His Kentucky stint was even shorter: seven games, 52 total minutes and 19 points, with averages of 2.7 points and 1.1 rebounds. The Colonels received a real player but almost no lasting on-court value, while Indiana's cash return is undisclosed. With neither side producing a durable asset, the completed outcome is best treated as an even low-impact transaction.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Exchange

Indiana traded John Fairchild to the Kentucky Colonels for cash on October 28, 1969. The Pacers and Colonels transaction ledgers agree on the date and player-for-cash structure, and the ABA league transaction log records the same move. The cash amount is not reported in the reviewed sources.

Indiana Return

Indiana received cash for a player whose role had already shrunk sharply. Fairchild had played 52 games for the Pacers in 1968-69, averaging 5.5 points in 11.2 minutes, but he appeared in only three Indiana games in 1969-70 before the trade. Across those three games he logged 26 minutes and scored three total points.

The Pacers therefore did not give up a player occupying a large role in their title-season rotation. Indiana went on to finish 59-25 and win the 1970 ABA championship. Fairchild's departure did not remove a meaningful contributor from that run.

Kentucky Return

Kentucky received Fairchild, but the basketball return was extremely small. He played seven games for the Colonels in 1969-70 and logged only 52 minutes. He scored 19 points, grabbed eight rebounds and averaged 2.7 points in 7.4 minutes per game. Basketball-Reference lists those seven Kentucky appearances as the final games of his ABA career.

That makes the trade very different from the legacy description that framed Kentucky as the clear long-term winner. The Colonels did receive a player rather than an uncertain future asset, but the player contributed for only seven games before disappearing from the league.

Hindsight Comparison

Kentucky's realized return was seven games and 52 minutes from Fairchild. Indiana's return was cash, but the amount remains unknown. Because the player side produced almost no lasting value, there is not enough evidence to assign Kentucky a strong advantage simply because the cash figure is unavailable.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C/C. Kentucky receives a C because Fairchild provided only seven games and no durable roster value. Indiana also receives a C because the Pacers monetized a fringe rotation player, but the undisclosed cash amount prevents a stronger realized-value grade. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Fairchild's post-trade production, while the comparative value remains medium because the financial return is unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Erwin Mueller from Seattle on November 1, 1969 for a 1970 second-round pick that became Jake Ford at No. 20. Mueller immediately joined the Pistons' rotation, playing 74 games after the trade and totaling 759 points, 469 rebounds and 199 assists. He remained in Detroit through the early part of 1972-73, giving the Pistons 189 post-trade regular-season games. Ford reached Seattle a year later but played only 31 NBA games across two seasons. The draft pick produced a real player, yet Mueller's longer tenure and much larger role give Detroit the clear realized-value advantage.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Detroit traded its 1970 second-round pick to Seattle on November 1, 1969 for Erwin Mueller. Detroit, Seattle and the NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the date and structure. Seattle later used the pick at No. 20 on Jake Ford, making the draft outcome traceable rather than speculative.

Detroit Return

Mueller had appeared in four Seattle games before the trade, then became a regular part of Detroit's frontcourt. He played 74 games for the Pistons in 1969-70 and logged 2,284 minutes. He scored 759 points, grabbed 469 rebounds and recorded 199 assists, which works out to roughly 10.3 points, 6.3 rebounds and 2.7 assists per game after arriving.

The return lasted beyond one season. Mueller played 52 games for Detroit in 1970-71, adding 312 points and 223 rebounds. He appeared in 42 more games in 1971-72 and 21 in 1972-73 before finishing his career in the ABA. Across those four Detroit seasons after the trade, he played 189 regular-season games.

Seattle Return

Seattle's pick became Jake Ford, selected twentieth overall in the 1970 draft. Ford did reach the NBA with the SuperSonics, but his role was limited. He played five games late in 1970-71 and 26 games in 1971-72, totaling 31 regular-season appearances and 249 minutes for Seattle.

Ford averaged 6.8 points in his five-game rookie sample and 3.5 points in 26 games the following season. He did not become a long-term Seattle rotation player, and those 31 games were the entirety of his NBA career. The pick therefore produced some realized value, but nothing close to the volume Detroit received from Mueller.

Hindsight Comparison

Detroit received 189 regular-season games from Mueller, including a first post-trade season in which he played more than 30 minutes per game and supplied useful scoring, rebounding and passing. Seattle converted the pick into Ford, but Ford appeared in only 31 NBA games and never established a durable role.

The gap is larger than the legacy Slight Pistons Edge label suggests. Detroit did not land a star, but it acquired a multi-season rotation player for a pick whose eventual selection had a very short NBA career.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, B+/C. Detroit receives a B+ for turning a second-round pick into 189 games of frontcourt production, including a substantial 1969-70 role. Seattle receives a C because Ford reached the NBA and contributed briefly, but 31 games and 249 minutes do not approach Mueller's realized Detroit value. Confidence is high because the trade structure, draft outcome and both players' post-trade records are directly documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: New York acquired George Lehmann from the Los Angeles Stars for cash on November 11, 1969. Lehmann immediately became a useful backcourt piece, playing 46 games for the Nets and totaling 344 points, 104 assists and 41 made three-pointers in 679 minutes. New York then recovered additional value by selling him to Miami for cash on February 19, 1970. Los Angeles received an undisclosed payment in the original deal, but the Nets obtained nearly half a season of rotation production plus a later cash return, giving New York the modest hindsight edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Los Angeles traded George Lehmann to the New York Nets for cash on November 11, 1969. The Stars transaction ledger, Nets transaction ledger and ABA league log all agree on the date and player-for-cash structure. The amount New York paid is not reported in the reviewed sources, so the financial side cannot be valued precisely.

New York Return

Lehmann had already shown he could score in the ABA. After signing with Los Angeles in January 1969, he averaged 18.9 points and 5.0 assists across 32 Stars games in 1968-69. His role was smaller early in 1969-70, but New York still acquired a veteran guard with proven league production rather than a fringe roster piece.

With the Nets, Lehmann appeared in 46 games and played 679 minutes. He scored 344 points, handed out 104 assists and made 41 three-pointers. That works out to 7.5 points and 2.3 assists per game in a little under 15 minutes per night. The stint was not star-level, but it provided legitimate rotation value for a team that went 39-45 and reached the ABA playoffs.

New York also recovered something after using Lehmann. On February 19, 1970, the Nets sold him to the Miami Floridians for cash. The amount of that later payment is also undisclosed, so it cannot be used to claim New York fully recouped its original cost. It does, however, mean the Nets received both on-court production and a second financial return before moving on.

Los Angeles Return

Los Angeles received cash and opened backcourt minutes while continuing toward a 43-41 season and an ABA Finals appearance. Because the original payment amount is unavailable, the Stars' return cannot be dismissed. The club also had other guards and creators on the roster, so moving Lehmann was not equivalent to giving away an irreplaceable starter.

Still, the completed basketball side of the transaction favors New York. Los Angeles gave up a player who supplied 46 games for the Nets, and there is no documented player or draft asset coming back to the Stars beyond the cash payment.

Hindsight Comparison

New York obtained 46 regular-season games, 344 points and 104 assists from Lehmann, then converted him back into cash three months later. Los Angeles received only the undisclosed original payment. Without either cash figure, the margin should remain modest, but the Nets have the clearer documented combination of basketball production and asset recovery.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, C+/C. New York receives a C+ for getting a useful half-season guard contribution and later recovering cash when Lehmann was moved to Miami. Los Angeles receives a C because selling Lehmann was defensible and the payment may have had real value, but the amount is unknown and there is no comparable on-court return to measure. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, dates and Lehmann's production, while the size of the hindsight edge stays modest because both cash amounts are undisclosed. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Indiana reacquired Steve Chubin from the New York Nets for cash on November 11, 1969. Chubin gave the Pacers 32 regular-season games, averaging 4.2 points, 1.3 rebounds and 2.2 assists in 11.9 minutes before Kentucky claimed him on waivers in March. New York received an undisclosed cash payment after Chubin had played 39 games for the Nets earlier in 1969-70. Indiana received the only measurable post-trade basketball production, but the short tenure and unknown cash amount keep the hindsight advantage modest rather than decisive.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Indiana reacquired Steve Chubin from the New York Nets for cash on November 11, 1969. The Pacers, Nets and ABA league transaction ledgers all agree on the date and player-for-cash structure. Chubin had already moved between the same organizations before: Indiana acquired him in December 1968 and sent him to New York for Ron Perry on January 31, 1969. The November deal brought him back to Indiana for a financial payment whose amount is not reported.

Indiana Return

Chubin gave the Pacers a real but limited regular-season contribution. He appeared in 32 games for Indiana in 1969-70 and played 381 minutes. He scored 134 points, collected 41 rebounds and handed out 69 assists. That works out to 4.2 points, 1.3 rebounds and 2.2 assists in 11.9 minutes per game.

His efficiency in that small role was respectable. Chubin shot 44.1 percent from the field and 83.3 percent at the line. He was not a major part of Indiana's championship core, and his tenure ended before the postseason: Kentucky claimed him on waivers on March 17, 1970. That distinction keeps the trade from being credited with playoff or championship production it did not actually produce.

New York Return

New York received cash. The Nets had already used Chubin for 39 games during the season before moving him back to Indiana, so the November transaction converted a reserve guard into financial value. The reviewed transaction records do not disclose the amount, making it impossible to compare the payment directly with Chubin's 32-game Indiana contribution.

The Nets therefore should not be treated as receiving nothing. Cash can have meaningful roster value, particularly for a player who was not retained for the full season. At the same time, there is no documented player or draft asset attached to New York's return, so the Pacers have the clearer measurable post-trade outcome.

Hindsight Comparison

Indiana received 32 games and 381 minutes from Chubin before losing him on waivers. New York received an undisclosed cash payment. The Pacers got actual rotation minutes and some playmaking, but Chubin averaged only 4.2 points and did not finish the season with the club.

That makes the legacy slight Indiana edge directionally reasonable while arguing against a large grade gap. The transaction was useful for Indiana at the margins, not a major acquisition, and the unknown cash return prevents a precise financial comparison.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, C+/C. Indiana receives a C+ for 32 games of reserve guard production at a cash-only cost. New York receives a C because converting Chubin into cash was defensible, but the amount is unknown and there is no comparable on-court asset to measure. Confidence is high on the transaction date, structure, playing record and later waiver claim, while the size of the edge remains modest because the cash figure is unavailable. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange

Boston traded Bob Cousy's playing rights to the Cincinnati Royals for Bill Dinwiddie on November 18, 1969. Boston's team ledger, Cincinnati's ledger, the NBA transaction log and the executive records for Red Auerbach and Joe Axelson all describe the same two-asset exchange. None lists the additional unidentified draft pick that appeared in the legacy TradeVerdicts summary. Because the strongest reviewed ledgers consistently omit that pick, it should not be credited to Boston.

Cincinnati Return

Cousy was already Cincinnati's head coach when the Royals acquired his rights. At age 41, he came out of retirement for seven games during the 1969-70 season. His playing role was tiny: 34 total minutes, or 4.9 per game, with averages of 0.7 points, 0.7 rebounds and 1.4 assists.

The return had promotional and coaching context that ordinary player-value analysis does not fully capture. Contemporary historical accounts describe the comeback as an effort to spark the club and attract interest. Even so, the trade itself produced only seven games of on-court value for Cincinnati. Cousy's larger impact on the Royals came from his coaching job, which predated the transaction and therefore should not be counted as trade return.

Boston Return

Dinwiddie did not play in 1969-70 because of a knee injury, so Boston received no immediate production after making the deal. He returned the following season and appeared in 61 games for the Celtics. In 1970-71 he averaged 4.9 points and 3.4 rebounds in 11.8 minutes per game, giving Boston a season of reserve frontcourt depth.

The Celtics also preserved a small amount of downstream value. On October 11, 1971, Boston traded Dinwiddie to Milwaukee for a 1972 sixth-round pick, later used on Wally Rice. That late pick did not become a major NBA asset, but it shows Boston was able to extract another transaction return after receiving 61 games from Dinwiddie.

Hindsight Comparison

perspectives.summary: Los Angeles acquired Happy Hairston from Detroit in late November 1969 for Bill Hewitt, a 1970 third-round pick that became Jim Hayes, a 1973 third-round pick that became Larry Kenon, and cash. The source set disagrees on the exact package and date: Basketball-Reference's team, league and executive ledgers list November 27 and only Hewitt plus the 1970 pick, while Pro Sports Transactions records November 26 and also traces the 1973 pick and cash to the deal. Hairston became the defining realized asset, playing 394 Lakers games over six seasons and starting on the 1972 championship team. Detroit received 175 useful games from Hewitt, but neither drafted player produced for the Pistons.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Detroit and Los Angeles exchanged Happy Hairston for Bill Hewitt and draft compensation in late November 1969. There is a genuine source conflict that should stay visible rather than be silently resolved. Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Lakers, NBA and executive transaction ledgers all date the trade November 27 and list Hewitt plus a 1970 third-round pick. Pro Sports Transactions dates it November 26 and independently traces both the 1970 third-round pick, the Lakers' 1973 third-round pick and cash to the same trade. Because the existing canonical record was built from the broader transaction lineage, the extra 1973 pick and cash remain documented here with that caveat instead of being treated as uncontested.

Los Angeles Return

Hairston became a long-term Lakers starter and the strongest realized asset in the deal by a wide margin. He played 55 games for Los Angeles after the trade in 1969-70, then stayed through 1974-75. Across six Lakers seasons he appeared in 394 regular-season games.

His peak overlapped directly with the Lakers' championship window. Hairston played all 80 games in 1970-71 and averaged 18.6 points and 10.0 rebounds. In 1971-72 he again played 80 games, averaging 13.1 points and 13.1 rebounds for the team that won 69 regular-season games and the NBA championship. He remained a major rebounder after that title season, including 13.2 rebounds per game in 1972-73 and 13.5 in 1973-74. Los Angeles therefore received both durability and high-level frontcourt production from the transaction.Detroit Return

Hewitt supplied Detroit's only substantial on-court return. He played 45 Pistons games after the trade in 1969-70, then 62 in 1970-71 and 68 in 1971-72. That is 175 regular-season appearances over three seasons. His best Detroit year was 1970-71, when he averaged 7.7 points, 7.3 rebounds and 2.0 assists in 27.8 minutes. He remained useful rotation depth the following season before Buffalo claimed him on waivers in October 1972.

The 1970 third-round pick became Jim Hayes at No. 47. Hayes never played for Detroit; his only major-league season came in the ABA with the New York Nets, where he appeared in 47 games in 1970-71. The 1973 third-round selection became Larry Kenon at No. 50. Kenon developed into an excellent professional player, but he signed with the ABA New York Nets and never produced on-court value for Detroit. His later career therefore should not be counted as Pistons trade return simply because Detroit used the draft slot on him.

Detroit also received cash according to the Pro Sports Transactions lineage, but the amount is not reported. That financial return belongs in the asset record while remaining impossible to value precisely.

Hindsight Comparison

Detroit received a respectable three-season contribution from Hewitt plus draft opportunities and an undisclosed financial return. The two picks did not turn into Pistons production: Hayes played in the ABA, and Kenon's outstanding career began with the ABA Nets rather than Detroit.

Los Angeles received six seasons and 394 games from Hairston. More importantly, his best Lakers years came during the club's championship peak, including 13.1 points and 13.1 rebounds per game in 1971-72. The Lakers therefore received the more durable and more consequential realized basketball value.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A+/B. Los Angeles receives an A+ for acquiring a six-year starting frontcourt piece who became a major rebounder and a core contributor to the 1972 championship team. Detroit receives a B for 175 Hewitt games plus two draft opportunities and cash, even though neither draft selection produced for the Pistons. Confidence is high that Hairston, Hewitt and the 1970 pick were exchanged, and high on the realized player outcomes. Confidence is medium on the full original package because strong transaction ledgers disagree with Pro Sports Transactions about the 1973 pick, cash and exact date. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: San Francisco acquired veteran guard Adrian Smith from Cincinnati on December 25, 1969 for a 1970 second-round pick. The pick became Tiny Archibald at No. 19, so the legacy record must treat Archibald as a draft outcome rather than as a player directly traded on Christmas Day. Smith gave the Warriors 66 regular-season games across parts of two NBA seasons, averaging 6.4 points in 45 games after the deal and 5.3 points in 21 games the next year. Cincinnati received the defining long-term asset: Archibald became a franchise star, a six-time All-Star and the 1972-73 NBA leader in both scoring and assists. The realized value strongly favored the Royals/Kings side.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange

San Francisco traded its 1970 second-round pick to Cincinnati for Adrian Smith on December 25, 1969. The Cincinnati and San Francisco transaction ledgers agree on the date and structure, and both identify the pick as the selection later used on Tiny Archibald at No. 19. That distinction corrects the legacy TradeVerdicts asset model: Archibald was not a player sent by the Warriors in 1969. He was the eventual draft outcome of the pick.

Golden State Return

Smith was 33 and already deep into a productive NBA career when the Warriors acquired him. He had been an All-Star and the 1966 All-Star Game MVP in Cincinnati, but his role had declined by 1969-70. After the trade he played 45 games for San Francisco, averaging 6.4 points, 1.9 rebounds and 1.1 assists in 14.1 minutes per game.

He returned for 21 more Warriors games in 1970-71, averaging 5.3 points in 11.8 minutes. That gave San Francisco 66 regular-season appearances across parts of two seasons. Smith was legitimate veteran depth, not an empty return, but the move did not produce a long-term starter or a major postseason-era building block.

Cincinnati Return

The second-round pick became Tiny Archibald, selected 19th overall in the 1970 draft. Archibald immediately played all 82 games as a rookie and developed into the centerpiece of the Royals' backcourt. By 1971-72 he was averaging 28.2 points and 9.2 assists.

His 1972-73 season made the difference in this trade impossible to ignore. Archibald averaged 34.0 points and 11.4 assists, leading the NBA in both categories in the same season. He later became a six-time All-Star, earned five All-NBA selections and entered the Basketball Hall of Fame. Even though his career eventually continued with other franchises, Cincinnati/Kansas City obtained an elite player from the exact pick acquired in this deal.

Hindsight Comparison

San Francisco received 66 games of useful veteran guard play. Cincinnati received the draft asset that became one of the best point guards of his era. The Warriors could not have known the 19th pick would become a Hall of Famer, but TradeVerdicts grades realized value rather than pretending later outcomes were predictable on the transaction date.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A+/D. The Royals/Kings receive an A+ because a second-round pick produced Tiny Archibald and multiple seasons of franchise-level star value. The Warriors receive a D because Smith contributed across two seasons but the return was modest compared with the asset surrendered. Confidence is high on the trade date, pick lineage, draft slot and player production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles acquired John Tresvant's player rights from Seattle on January 23, 1970 in a cash sale. Multiple Basketball-Reference team, league and executive ledgers agree on January 23, correcting the legacy January 21 TradeVerdicts date. Tresvant played 20 Lakers games that season and eight more in 1970-71 before Los Angeles traded him to Baltimore for a 1972 second-round pick that became Paul Stovall. Seattle's cash amount is undisclosed. The Lakers therefore received modest on-court value plus a later draft asset, giving Los Angeles a small realized-value edge without turning the transaction into a major win.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange

Seattle sold John Tresvant's player rights to the Los Angeles Lakers on January 23, 1970. Seattle's transaction ledger, the Lakers' ledger, the NBA league log and Fred Schaus' executive record all agree on January 23. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. The public ledgers describe a sale, which supports cash going to Seattle, but they do not report the amount.

Los Angeles Return

Tresvant joined a Lakers team headed toward the 1970 NBA Finals. He played 20 regular-season games after the acquisition, averaging 5.9 points and 3.2 rebounds in 11.1 minutes while shooting 53.4 percent from the field. The role was limited, but it gave Los Angeles another experienced frontcourt option during the stretch run.

Tresvant returned for eight Lakers games in 1970-71. On November 11, 1970, Los Angeles traded him to Baltimore for a 1972 second-round pick. That pick later became Paul Stovall. Stovall did not create notable NBA value, so the downstream asset should not be exaggerated, but converting Tresvant into another draft choice meant the Lakers extracted something after receiving 28 regular-season appearances from him.

Seattle Return

Seattle received cash. The exact amount is not stated in the reviewed team, league or executive transaction ledgers, which limits any retrospective valuation. The SuperSonics had already received 75 games from Tresvant across parts of the previous two seasons, including 49 games at 12.6 points and 7.4 rebounds in 1969-70 before the sale.

Because the cash value is unknown, Seattle's side cannot be treated as worthless. The team monetized a veteran it was willing to move and did not surrender a player who went on to become a long-term Lakers starter. The lack of a reported price, however, makes the Lakers' documented player use and later draft return easier to measure.

Hindsight Comparison

Los Angeles received 28 regular-season appearances across parts of two seasons, including depth during a Finals season, and later converted Tresvant into a second-round pick. Seattle received an undisclosed cash payment. Neither side produced a franchise-changing result, but the Lakers have the more visible chain of realized basketball value.

Final Verdict

Slight Lakers Edge, B-/C+. Los Angeles receives a B- for useful short-term depth plus the later second-round pick obtained when Tresvant was moved to Baltimore. Seattle receives a C+ because the cash sale may have been sensible, but the undisclosed amount prevents a stronger realized-value case. Confidence is high on the corrected January 23 date, sale structure, Tresvant's Lakers production and downstream trade; the cash amount remains unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Bob Quick and Baltimore's 1970 second-round pick on February 1, 1970 for Eddie Miles and Detroit's 1970 fourth-round pick. The second-rounder became Ken Warzynski, who never played in the NBA, while Baltimore used the fourth-rounder on Bill Stricker, whose NBA career lasted one game for Portland rather than Baltimore. Quick gave Detroit 93 regular-season games over parts of three seasons, including 56 games at 8.0 points and 4.1 rebounds in 1970-71. Miles gave Baltimore 66 games over parts of two seasons, including 63 games at 9.9 points during the Bullets' 1971 Finals run. The realized packages are close enough to support an even verdict.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Detroit and Baltimore completed the trade on February 1, 1970. The Pistons received Bob Quick and Baltimore's 1970 second-round pick. The Bullets received Eddie Miles and Detroit's 1970 fourth-round pick. Detroit and Baltimore transaction ledgers agree on the structure, and both draft outcomes are documented: Detroit used the acquired second-rounder on Ken Warzynski at No. 32, while Baltimore used the fourth-rounder on Bill Stricker at No. 54.

Detroit Return

Quick supplied the meaningful Detroit value. He played 19 Pistons games after the trade in 1969-70, averaging 7.1 points and 3.3 rebounds in 15.6 minutes. His role grew in 1970-71, when he appeared in 56 games and averaged 8.0 points and 4.1 rebounds in 20.5 minutes. He then added 18 Detroit games in 1971-72 before finishing that season in the ABA.

That gives Detroit 93 regular-season appearances from Quick across parts of three seasons. He was not a core scorer, but he became a real rotation forward rather than a short-term roster placeholder. The acquired draft pick did not add comparable value. Ken Warzynski was selected 32nd overall in the 1970 draft, but his Basketball-Reference record contains no NBA games, so the pick produced no realized NBA contribution.

Baltimore Return

Miles provided the stronger single-season peak. He played only three Baltimore games after the trade in 1969-70, but he remained with the Bullets for 63 games in 1970-71 and averaged 9.9 points, 2.7 rebounds and 1.7 assists. Baltimore won the Eastern Conference that season and reached the 1971 NBA Finals, making Miles part of a deeper postseason roster even though the franchise's stars carried the largest share of the load.

The fourth-round pick produced little direct value for Baltimore. Bill Stricker was selected 54th overall in the 1970 draft, but he did not play for the Bullets. His entire NBA career consisted of one game and two minutes for Portland in 1970-71. The pick therefore should remain correctly linked to Stricker without being treated as a meaningful Baltimore return.

Hindsight Comparison

The trade ultimately reduces to Quick versus Miles. Detroit received more regular-season games from Quick, 93 to 66, and kept him across parts of three seasons. Baltimore received the better one-season production from Miles, including 63 games at 9.9 points for a team that reached the Finals. Neither draft pick became a useful NBA player for the acquiring team.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B-/B-. Detroit receives a B- for 93 games of usable wing depth from Quick, while the Warzynski pick produced no NBA value. Baltimore receives a B- for Miles' stronger 1970-71 season and his role on a Finals roster, while the Stricker pick produced no meaningful Bullets return. The two packages created different kinds of modest value without a durable advantage for either side. Confidence is high on the date, four-asset structure, draft outcomes and player production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Atlanta acquired Walt Bellamy from Detroit on February 1, 1970 for cash and future player consideration that was ultimately satisfied by John Arthurs. A complicated pre-draft obligation briefly pointed to Milwaukee's 1970 first-round pick and Gary Freeman, but Detroit did not receive Freeman; Arthurs replaced that route as the player consideration. Bellamy gave Atlanta 338 regular-season games through 1973-74, including four full seasons averaging at least 13 points and 9 rebounds. Arthurs never played an NBA game for Detroit, and the cash amount is undisclosed. The realized return therefore favored Atlanta by a wide margin.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Detroit traded Walt Bellamy to Atlanta on February 1, 1970. The simplest team transaction ledgers describe Bellamy going to the Hawks with John Arthurs eventually going to Detroit. Contemporary and reconstructed transaction histories show why older databases can look more complicated: Atlanta owed Detroit future consideration tied to a pre-draft arrangement involving Milwaukee's 1970 first-round pick. Milwaukee selected Gary Freeman at No. 16 while that obligation was being resolved, but Detroit did not take Freeman. John Arthurs was delivered in June instead. That means Freeman should not remain counted as a separate realized Detroit asset in this trade.

Atlanta Return

Bellamy immediately became Atlanta's starting center. He played 23 games for the Hawks after the trade in 1969-70 and averaged roughly 15.5 points and 13.5 rebounds. He then played all 82 games in 1970-71, averaging about 14.7 points and 12.9 rebounds, and all 82 again in 1971-72 while raising his scoring to roughly 18.6 points per game with 12.8 rebounds.

The production continued. Bellamy appeared in 74 games in 1972-73 and 77 in 1973-74, staying above 13 points and 9 rebounds per game in each season. Across those five Atlanta season segments he totaled 338 regular-season appearances. The Hawks did not acquire a short rental; they acquired several years of high-minute, high-rebound frontcourt production from an established star.

Detroit Return

Detroit received cash plus the future player consideration that became John Arthurs. Arthurs had appeared in 11 games for Milwaukee as a rookie in 1969-70, averaging 3.2 points in a limited role. Basketball-Reference does not record an NBA appearance for Detroit, so his inclusion did not produce measurable Pistons on-court value.

The cash amount is not available in the reviewed transaction sources, so Detroit's financial return should not be treated as zero. The important correction is structural: Gary Freeman was selected by Milwaukee during the attempted fulfillment of the older draft-pick obligation, but Detroit ultimately did not acquire him. Counting both Freeman and Arthurs as separate Pistons returns double-counts the same future-consideration path.

Hindsight Comparison

Atlanta received 338 regular-season games from Bellamy and multiple seasons of starter-level scoring and rebounding. Detroit received an undisclosed cash payment and Arthurs, who never played an NBA game for the Pistons. Once the Freeman draft path is correctly treated as superseded rather than as an additional Detroit asset, the value gap becomes clear.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, A/C. Atlanta receives an A for acquiring more than four seasons of productive center play from Bellamy. Detroit receives a C because the cash consideration may have carried real value and the move reflected the franchise's roster direction, but the player return produced no Pistons games. Confidence is high on Bellamy's destination, production and the ultimate Arthurs consideration; confidence is medium-high on the full mechanics because contemporary summaries preserve the complicated draft-obligation chain differently. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Miami acquired George Lehmann from the New York Nets for cash on February 19, 1970. Lehmann immediately moved from a reserve role in New York into a major Floridians role, playing 25 games at 43.1 minutes, 17.9 points and 5.0 assists per game. Miami then traded him to Carolina in August for Rich Niemann, who supplied 51 games the next season. New York recovered an undisclosed cash payment after getting 46 games from Lehmann earlier that season. With the cash amount unknown, Miami gets only a modest hindsight edge for turning money into meaningful on-court production and a later player return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

New York traded George Lehmann to the Miami Floridians for cash on February 19, 1970. The Nets, Floridians and ABA transaction ledgers all record the same player-for-cash structure, and Pro Sports Transactions independently lists both sides of the deal on the same date. The amount Miami paid is not available in the reviewed sources, so the financial cost cannot be valued precisely.

Miami Return

Lehmann's role changed immediately. He had appeared in 46 games for New York earlier in 1969-70, averaging 7.5 points and 2.3 assists in 14.8 minutes per game. With Miami, he played 25 games and averaged 43.1 minutes, 17.9 points and 5.0 assists. Basketball-Reference credits him with 448 points over that Floridians stint, along with 125 assists and 46 made three-pointers.

That was a short stay, but it was not a marginal one. Lehmann became one of Miami's heaviest-minute guards during the closing portion of the season and produced at a starter level. The Floridians therefore received a measurable basketball return for their cash rather than merely acquiring a reserve who disappeared from the rotation.

Miami also retained some asset value after the season. On August 26, 1970, the Floridians traded Lehmann to the Carolina Cougars for center Rich Niemann. Niemann then played 51 games for the Floridians in 1970-71, averaging 5.6 points and 5.0 rebounds in 12.6 minutes per game. That later exchange should not be treated as if all of Niemann's value belonged to the February transaction, but it does show that Lehmann remained a movable asset after his productive Miami stint.

New York Return

The Nets received cash. Its amount is undisclosed, which prevents a precise comparison with Lehmann's production. New York had acquired Lehmann from the Los Angeles Stars for cash on November 11, 1969, used him for 46 games and then sold him to Miami roughly three months later. That sequence gave the Nets both on-court value before this trade and a financial return when they moved him.

For this specific February transaction, however, New York did not receive a player or draft asset that can be followed through the basketball record. The cash may have been useful and could have matched Miami's valuation of a player the Nets were using only 14.8 minutes per game, so the Nets should not be graded as if they received nothing.

Hindsight Comparison

Miami obtained 25 games of high-minute guard play from Lehmann, then converted him into Niemann before the next season. New York received an undisclosed payment after already extracting 46 games from Lehmann. The unknown cash figure limits the size of any verdict, but the Floridians have the stronger documented realized basketball return from the assets exchanged on February 19.

Final Verdict

Slight Floridians Edge, C+/C. Miami receives a C+ because Lehmann became a productive short-term starter and still had enough value to bring back Niemann in August. New York receives a C because moving a limited-minutes guard for cash was defensible and the payment may have carried real value, but there is no comparable player or draft return to measure. Confidence is high on the date, structure and Lehmann production, while the margin remains modest because the cash amount is unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Buffalo acquired Mike Davis and the 15th pick in the 1970 draft from Baltimore for the ninth pick on March 23, 1970. The No. 15 selection became John Hummer, who immediately started 81 games for the expansion Braves and averaged 11.3 points and 8.9 rebounds as a rookie. Davis added two useful Buffalo seasons. Baltimore used No. 9 on George E. Johnson, but he appeared in only 24 games for the Bullets as a rookie and never developed into a comparable return. In realized value, Buffalo won the exchange clearly.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Exchange

On March 23, 1970, the expansion Buffalo Braves acquired Mike Davis and Baltimore's 1970 first-round pick from the Bullets. Buffalo sent Baltimore its own first-round selection in return. The picks landed six spots apart: Baltimore used the No. 9 choice on George E. Johnson, while Buffalo used No. 15 on John Hummer. Basketball-Reference's league transaction ledger and Baltimore's team ledger record the same structure, and the draft-pick transaction history independently ties both selections to the exchange.

Buffalo Return

Davis gave the Braves an experienced forward immediately. He played 73 games for Buffalo in 1970-71, averaging 22.2 minutes and 11.4 points per game. He remained with the Braves for 62 games in 1971-72 and averaged 9.1 points. For an expansion club building a roster from scratch, 135 regular-season games of rotation scoring represented useful direct value from the veteran portion of the deal.

The draft pick was more valuable. Buffalo selected Hummer 15th overall, and he stepped directly into a large role. As a rookie in 1970-71 he played 81 games, averaged 32.6 minutes, 11.3 points and 8.9 rebounds, and gave Buffalo a durable frontcourt piece. Hummer stayed with the Braves through the 1972-73 season before Buffalo later moved him to Chicago. Basketball-Reference credits him with 327 career NBA games, 6.9 points and 5.3 rebounds per game, so the pick produced several seasons of legitimate NBA value rather than a brief roster look.

Baltimore Return

Baltimore moved up from No. 15 to No. 9 and selected George E. Johnson, a 6-foot-11 center. The higher draft slot made sense as an asset play, but the realized return was limited. Johnson appeared in 24 games for the Bullets as a rookie in 1970-71, averaging 14.0 minutes, 3.9 points and 4.8 rebounds. He finished his NBA career with 136 games and averages of 3.7 points and 5.0 rebounds.

That result was particularly modest beside what Baltimore surrendered. Davis alone gave Buffalo two seasons of usable rotation minutes, while Hummer became a heavy-minute rookie and stayed on the Braves roster for three seasons. Baltimore did not receive another player or pick in the transaction to offset Johnson's smaller contribution.

Hindsight Comparison

The deal is a useful reminder that moving up in the draft does not guarantee the better outcome. Baltimore converted a veteran plus No. 15 into No. 9, but Johnson's Bullets tenure was brief and low-volume. Buffalo moved down six spots, still found a productive frontcourt player in Hummer and received Davis on top of the pick. The Braves therefore realized more games, more minutes and more sustained production from both incoming pieces.

Final Verdict

Braves Win, A-/C. Buffalo receives an A- because the franchise turned the ninth pick into two useful players: Hummer became an immediate high-minute starter and Davis supplied two seasons of rotation scoring. Baltimore receives a C because moving up to No. 9 was a defensible draft-value decision, but Johnson never produced enough for the Bullets to match the outgoing package. Confidence is high on the trade structure, pick outcomes and player production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Its ABA draft ledger also shows that the Stars had selected McMillian in the second round, 15th overall, of the 1970 ABA draft.

McMillian was a valuable basketball player, but that is different from the value of the ABA rights New York acquired. He did not play for the Nets. The NBA's Los Angeles Lakers selected him 13th overall in the 1970 NBA draft, and he began his NBA career that fall. Basketball-Reference lists his NBA debut as October 16, 1970 and credits him with 631 regular-season games over nine seasons.

For this ABA transaction, however, none of that production became a Nets return. New York held rights to a good player who chose the NBA path. TradeVerdicts therefore separates McMillian's career value from the realized value of the rights asset: the player succeeded, but the Nets did not receive his games.

Stars Return

Los Angeles received a future draft pick. The surviving transaction entry does not specify the draft year, round, selection number or player outcome. That gap matters. The Stars at least received a future pick, although the unidentified outcome prevents a complete realized-value comparison.

Final Verdict

Slight Stars Edge, C+/C. Los Angeles receives a C+ for converting McMillian's unused ABA rights into future draft capital. New York receives a C because the rights did not produce a Nets appearance, even though the player himself became a strong NBA contributor. Confidence is medium on the verdict: the March 24 transaction and McMillian's career path are well supported, but the future pick's year, round and eventual outcome remain unresolved in the reviewed records. houston-rockets.analysis:
The Exchange

On April 15, 1970, the San Diego Rockets sold the player rights to Don Kojis to the Seattle SuperSonics. Basketball-Reference lists the move from both team perspectives and in the league transaction log. RealGM also records Seattle acquiring Kojis from San Diego on that date. The reviewed sources establish the transfer, but none publishes the sale price. TradeVerdicts therefore keeps the Rockets' return as cash with the amount unknown.

Seattle Return

Kojis was already an established NBA forward. He had made the All-Star team in 1967-68 and 1968-69 with San Diego, then averaged 15.3 points and 6.9 rebounds in 56 games during 1969-70. Seattle was not buying a speculative prospect. It was acquiring the rights to a veteran who had recently been one of San Diego's leading scorers.

The move produced immediate usable value. Kojis played 79 games for Seattle in 1970-71, averaging 14.6 points, 5.5 rebounds and 27.1 minutes. He remained in the rotation the next season, appearing in 73 games and averaging 11.4 points, 4.6 rebounds and 25.4 minutes. Across the two seasons, that is 152 regular-season appearances and nearly 4,000 minutes from the purchased rights.

Seattle later moved Kojis in August 1972 as part of a separate transaction with Kansas City-Omaha. This verdict does not assign the entire value of that later package back to the 1970 sale because Kojis was bundled with another player. The direct return is already enough to judge the original purchase: Seattle received two seasons of dependable rotation production.

San Diego Return

San Diego received cash. That asset should not be treated as worthless, especially in an era when player sales were a normal roster-management tool. The problem is documentation, not the existence of value. Without a verified sale price, there is no responsible way to compare the financial return with a player contract, draft choice or later on-court production.

That uncertainty is why the Rockets are not given a failing grade. They monetized the rights to a 31-year-old veteran after a season in which he played 56 games. But the surviving basketball record shows exactly what Seattle received, while the cash side cannot be quantified from the reviewed sources.

Hindsight Comparison

Seattle's advantage is the clearest part of the record. The SuperSonics turned the purchased rights into 152 games, 1,989 points and 770 rebounds over two seasons. Kojis was not a franchise-changing acquisition, but he was a regular contributor on teams that improved from 38 wins in 1970-71 to 47 wins in 1971-72.

Final Verdict

Seattle Win, B/C. Seattle receives a B for obtaining two productive veteran seasons for an undisclosed cash price. San Diego receives a C because the club did receive a real asset, but the amount is unknown and there is no documented basketball return to compare with Kojis' Seattle production. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction and player value, but only medium on the overall economic comparison because the sale price remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee acquired Oscar Robertson from the Cincinnati Royals for Flynn Robinson and Charlie Paulk, adding the veteran organizer who completed a 66-win championship team in his first season.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis: Robertson supplied the exact skill Milwaukee needed beside Lew Alcindor: elite ball control, playmaking, rebounding and late-game judgment without requiring the offense to recreate his Cincinnati usage. The Bucks won 66 games and the 1971 championship immediately, while preserving the rest of the young contender. Cincinnati faced legitimate age, contract and relationship pressures, but Flynn Robinson and Charlie Paulk did not become a durable replacement core. The limited cost, perfect fit and immediate title support Milwaukee A-plus, Cincinnati F and an unequivocal Bucks Win.

perspectives.summary: On April 23, 1970, Chicago traded Clem Haskins to Phoenix for Jim Fox and a 1971 second-round pick that became Howard Porter at No. 32 overall. Phoenix received four productive seasons and 319 regular-season games from Haskins, including 17.8 points and 4.7 assists per game in 1970-71. Chicago received 92 games from Fox and 110 from Porter, then used Fox in the November 1971 trade that brought Norm Van Lier back to the Bulls. Van Lier became a three-time All-Star during seven Chicago seasons. Phoenix won the direct player comparison, but Chicago's downstream return through Fox gives the Bulls the stronger long-term outcome.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

On April 23, 1970, the Chicago Bulls traded Clem Haskins to the Phoenix Suns for center Jim Fox and a 1971 second-round draft pick. Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers agree on the date and package. The pick became Villanova forward Howard Porter at No. 32 overall. The source-backed review also resolves the legacy 'Jim Fox / Sonny Fox' identity to NBA center Jim Fox, whose Basketball-Reference identifier is foxji01.

Phoenix Return

Haskins was the best immediate player in the transaction. He had just completed an 82-game Chicago season with 1,668 points and 624 assists. In Phoenix he played 82 games in 1970-71 and averaged 17.8 points, 4.7 assists and 4.0 rebounds. He followed with 79 games at 15.7 points in 1971-72, then remained with the Suns for 77 games in 1972-73 and 81 in 1973-74. That is 319 regular-season games across four Phoenix seasons.

Haskins' role declined after his first two Suns seasons, but Phoenix still received sustained guard production rather than a short rental. Across his four years with the club he logged 8,620 minutes. That direct longevity is the strongest part of the Suns' case and makes the legacy Bulls-win language too simplistic if the evaluation stops at the first transaction.

Chicago Return

Fox gave Chicago a useful first season. He played all 82 games in 1970-71, averaging 9.7 points, 7.3 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 19.9 minutes. He appeared in 10 more Bulls games the following season before Chicago moved him on November 9, 1971. Porter, selected with the acquired second-round pick, played 67 games as a rookie and 43 more in 1972-73. His Chicago role was modest, at 6.0 points per game in his first season and 5.1 in his second, but the pick still produced 110 NBA appearances for the Bulls.

Fox's later trade is what changes the hindsight comparison. Chicago sent Fox and a 1972 second-round pick to Cincinnati for Norm Van Lier and a 1972 third-round pick. Van Lier then played 535 regular-season games across seven Bulls seasons. During that Chicago tenure he made three All-Star teams, earned an All-NBA Second Team selection in 1973-74 and repeatedly appeared on the All-Defensive teams. The 1970 trade did not acquire Van Lier directly, and Chicago had to add another pick in 1971, so the full value of Van Lier cannot be credited to Phoenix's original assets. Fox nevertheless remained a meaningful component of the deal that brought him back.

Hindsight Comparison

If the trade is judged only by direct post-trade games, Phoenix has the stronger side: Haskins delivered 319 Suns games, while Fox and Porter combined for 202 Bulls games. Chicago's package becomes more valuable when the later disposition of Fox is traced. He was not simply lost; he helped form the package for Van Lier, who became a long-term Chicago point guard and one of the league's leading defensive guards of the era. Porter also supplied two seasons from a second-round selection.

The later Van Lier exchange prevents a simple direct-production verdict. Chicago had to attach an additional second-round pick, and it also received a third-round pick, so Van Lier's entire seven-year Bulls career is not attributable to Fox alone. Even with that discount, Fox's retained trade value plus Porter's 110 games pushes Chicago's long-term realized package ahead of Phoenix's very good Haskins return.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, A-/B+. Chicago receives an A- for one useful Fox season, 110 games from the acquired draft pick and the important downstream role Fox played in the trade that brought Norm Van Lier back to Chicago. Phoenix receives a B+ for four productive Haskins seasons and 319 regular-season games, including two years of high-level scoring and playmaking. The gap is narrower than the legacy verdict suggested because Haskins clearly outperformed Fox and Porter on direct value. Confidence is high on the transaction, identities and player production, and medium-high on the final comparative grade because downstream value requires an attribution discount. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

houston-rockets.summary: On May 11, 1970, the San Diego Rockets traded Jim Barnett to the expansion Portland Trail Blazers for Larry Siegfried. Barnett immediately became Portland's second-leading scorer, averaging 18.5 points in 78 games, while Siegfried gave San Diego 53 games and 6.5 assists per game before appearing in only 10 more games for the relocated Houston club. Portland then traded Barnett for three draft picks, including the 1972 second-rounder used on Dave Twardzik. The direct production and retained asset value give Portland the stronger hindsight return, although Siegfried was a useful starting playmaker for one season.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Exchange

On May 11, 1970, the San Diego Rockets traded Jim Barnett to the Portland Trail Blazers for Larry Siegfried. Basketball-Reference's San Diego transaction log and the league transaction ledger agree on the date and the one-for-one player exchange. The trade happened as Portland was assembling its expansion roster, and San Diego had already lost Rick Adelman and Pat Riley to the Trail Blazers in the expansion draft that same day.

Portland Return

Barnett gave the new franchise immediate scoring. In 78 games during Portland's inaugural 1970-71 season, he averaged 18.5 points, 4.8 rebounds and 4.1 assists in 30.4 minutes per game. Only Rookie of the Year Geoff Petrie scored more for the Trail Blazers. Basketball-Reference's trade-partner ledger credits Barnett with 4.7 win shares in those 78 Portland games, compared with 3.7 win shares from Siegfried in his 63 post-trade games for the Rockets franchise.

Portland did not simply lose Barnett after one season. On March 23, 1971, the Trail Blazers traded him to the San Francisco Warriors for three draft choices: a 1971 second-round pick used on Charlie Yelverton, a 1971 third-round pick used on William Smith and a 1972 second-round pick used on Dave Twardzik. The later package cannot be treated as if the original Rockets trade directly delivered all three players, because Portland made a second transaction to create it. Still, Barnett clearly retained substantial trade value after his productive expansion season.
Twardzik became the most important downstream result. Portland drafted him 26th overall in 1972, but he spent four seasons in the ABA before joining the Trail Blazers in 1976. He then played 74 regular-season games for the 1976-77 championship team and all 14 playoff games, averaging 10.9 points and 2.8 assists in 25.3 postseason minutes. That delayed payoff strengthens Portland's long-term side of the ledger, with an attribution discount because Twardzik came from the later three-pick Barnett trade.

San Diego/Houston Return

Siegfried was not a throwaway. The veteran point guard played 53 games for San Diego in 1970-71 and averaged 8.0 points, 3.9 rebounds and 6.5 assists in 31.6 minutes. For a 40-win team, that was real playmaking value. His role declined sharply after the franchise moved to Houston: he appeared in 10 games in 1971-72, averaging 4.8 points and 2.0 assists.

Houston also preserved some downstream value. On November 9, 1971, the Rockets traded Siegfried and Don Adams to Atlanta for Jim Davis and John Vallely. Because Siegfried was bundled with Adams, the return from that later deal cannot responsibly be credited to Siegfried alone. The same attribution rule applied to Barnett's later three-pick trade keeps this comparison from inflating either side.

Hindsight Comparison

The direct comparison favors Portland. Barnett supplied 78 games at 18.5 points per game and was a major offensive piece on the first Trail Blazers roster. Siegfried supplied 63 total games to the San Diego/Houston franchise after the trade, with one useful playmaking season followed by a short 10-game final stint. Portland then converted Barnett into three draft choices, while Houston used Siegfried as one part of a two-player package.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Win, B+/C+. Portland receives a B+ for one strong Barnett season and meaningful retained asset value that eventually included the pick used on Dave Twardzik. Houston receives a C+ because Siegfried was a productive distributor in 1970-71 and still carried some trade value into the following season. The gap is clear without treating every downstream result as a direct product of the original exchange. Confidence is high on the transaction and player production and medium-high on the comparative grade because later transactions require attribution discounts. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: On May 11, 1970, the expansion Buffalo Braves traded veteran Bailey Howell to Philadelphia for Bob Kauffman and a 1971 second-round pick that Buffalo later used on Spencer Haywood at No. 30. Kauffman became the first major star in Braves history, making three straight All-Star teams while averaging 20.4, 18.9 and 17.5 points in his first three Buffalo seasons. Howell gave Philadelphia one productive final NBA season. The Haywood selection never produced a Buffalo appearance because he had already signed with Seattle and remained there after the litigation over his eligibility. Kauffman's four-year Buffalo run still makes the Braves the clear winner.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Exchange

On May 11, 1970, the expansion Buffalo Braves traded Bailey Howell to the Philadelphia 76ers for Bob Kauffman and a 1971 second-round draft pick. Basketball-Reference's league transaction ledger identifies the future pick as No. 30 in 1971, when Buffalo selected Spencer Haywood. The historical franchise is Buffalo even though the canonical TradeVerdicts team key follows the modern Clippers lineage.

Buffalo Return

Kauffman became an immediate centerpiece for the new franchise. In Buffalo's inaugural 1970-71 season he played 78 games, averaged 20.4 points, 10.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists, and made the All-Star team. He followed with 18.9 points and 10.2 rebounds in 1971-72 and 17.5 points with 11.1 rebounds in 1972-73. Kauffman was an All-Star in all three seasons. By 1973-74 his role had fallen to 17.6 minutes per game, but he still appeared in 74 games as the Braves reached the playoffs for the first time.

Across four Buffalo seasons, Kauffman provided 306 regular-season games and three All-Star selections. Buffalo eventually lost him to New Orleans in the 1974 expansion draft, so there was no later trade return to add. The direct value was already substantial: the Braves obtained a frontcourt anchor at age 24 and received his best NBA seasons.
The 1971 pick requires more careful treatment. Buffalo used the acquired second-rounder on Haywood at No. 30. By then Haywood had already signed with Seattle and had played for the SuperSonics after winning the legal fight that challenged the NBA's four-years-out-of-high-school rule. Buffalo drafted him hoping to secure his rights, but Haywood remained with Seattle and never played for the Braves. The pick therefore counts as a verified draft outcome, not as realized Buffalo player production.

Philadelphia Return

Howell was a Hall of Fame forward near the end of his career, not an empty salary slot. At age 34 he played all 82 games for Philadelphia in 1970-71, averaging 10.7 points and 5.4 rebounds in 19.4 minutes. He also appeared in all seven of the 76ers' playoff games. That is useful one-season value, especially from a veteran who had been an important part of Boston's 1968 and 1969 championship teams.

The limitation is duration. Howell's Philadelphia season was his final NBA campaign. The 76ers received a capable rotation forward for one year, while Buffalo received four years of Kauffman with three All-Star appearances. Even after assigning zero on-court value to the Haywood pick, the player-for-player outcome strongly favors Buffalo.

Hindsight Comparison

The clearest comparison is Kauffman's prime against Howell's final season. Kauffman became the leading veteran presence on an expansion roster and produced three consecutive All-Star seasons before helping the franchise reach its first postseason in year four. Howell remained productive in Philadelphia, but his 82 regular-season games and seven playoff appearances were the end of his career.

The Haywood draft outcome adds historical interest without inflating Buffalo's grade. Buffalo did use the acquired pick on a future Hall of Famer, but the selection never became a Braves player because Haywood's Seattle rights survived the dispute. Treating his Seattle career as Buffalo value would be wrong.

Final Verdict

Braves Win, A-/B-. Buffalo receives an A- for acquiring Kauffman's four-year run and three All-Star seasons, with no extra basketball credit assigned for Haywood beyond documenting the draft outcome. Philadelphia receives a B- because Howell gave the club a full, productive final season and playoff minutes, but the return was far shorter and less valuable than Kauffman's Buffalo tenure. Confidence is high because the transaction, draft outcome and player production are well documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
los-angeles-clippers.gradeRationale: Bob Kauffman became Buffalo's first true star and the package also carried the Spencer Haywood future-consideration asset; Bailey Howell was near the end of his career.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix traded Gail Goodrich to the Lakers for Mel Counts on May 20, 1970. Goodrich then played 466 regular-season games across six Lakers seasons, made four All-Star teams, earned 1974 All-NBA First Team honors and led Los Angeles in scoring on the 1972 championship team. Counts was not an empty return: he played 156 Suns games over two seasons, averaged 11.0 points and 6.3 rebounds in his first year, and Phoenix later traded him for a second-round pick and cash. The gap is enormous, but the Suns received more value than the legacy F suggested.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix's official media guide and the Lakers' transaction history record the deal directly: on May 20, 1970, the Suns acquired Mel Counts from Los Angeles for Gail Goodrich. Goodrich had been Phoenix's leading backcourt star after the 1968 expansion draft, averaging 23.8 points as an All-Star in the franchise's first season and 20.0 points with 7.5 assists in 1969-70. The trade sent him back to the franchise that had originally drafted him in 1965.

Los Angeles Return
Goodrich became a championship-level lead scorer. The Lakers' official alumni profile credits him with six more Los Angeles seasons after the trade, four consecutive team scoring titles from 1971 through 1975, All-Star selections in 1972, 1973, 1974 and 1975, and All-NBA First Team in 1974. He played 466 regular-season games in that second Lakers stint. His peak came during the 1971-72 championship season, when he averaged 25.9 points in all 82 games and led the club in scoring as Los Angeles won 69 games, set the 33-game winning-streak record and captured the title. He stayed above 19 points per game in every season of the stint and later had No. 25 retired by the Lakers. That is elite sustained value from a one-for-one acquisition.

Phoenix Return
Counts gave the Suns two useful seasons rather than disappearing immediately. He played 80 games in 1970-71, averaging 11.0 points and 6.3 rebounds in 20.9 minutes, then appeared in 76 games in 1971-72 at 5.2 points and 3.4 rebounds in a reduced role. Phoenix therefore received 156 regular-season games from Counts. In October 1972, the Suns preserved a little more value by sending Counts to Philadelphia for a 1973 second-round pick and cash; that pick became No. 33 Gary Melchionni. The downstream pick was modest, but it means the Phoenix side included both two seasons of frontcourt depth and a small exit return.

Hindsight Verdict
The Lakers win overwhelmingly. Goodrich supplied six seasons, four post-trade All-Star selections, an All-NBA First Team season and championship-leading scoring. That supports an A+ grade. Phoenix cannot be graded as if Counts produced nothing: 156 games, a double-digit scoring first season and a later second-round return are legitimate assets. A C+ captures useful but ordinary value that was nowhere near Goodrich's Hall of Fame-level Lakers run. Final verdict: Los Angeles Lakers Win.

Goodrich played six more seasons in Los Angeles, made four consecutive All-Star teams from 1972 through 1975 and led the Lakers in scoring for four straight seasons. los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange

The Los Angeles Lakers sent Mel Counts to the Phoenix Suns for Gail Goodrich in May 1970. The package itself is unanimous across the reviewed sources, but the exact date is not. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Suns and league transaction ledgers all list May 20, and RealGM also uses May 20. Pro Sports Transactions lists May 21, which matches the existing TradeVerdicts route date. This review preserves the May 21 canonical route and records the one-day source conflict rather than silently changing a live identifier.

Los Angeles Return

Goodrich returned to the franchise that had drafted him in 1965 after Phoenix had selected him in the 1968 expansion draft. His first season back was already productive: 79 games, 17.5 points and 4.8 assists per game in 1970-71. One year later he became the leading scorer on one of the most famous teams in league history. Goodrich averaged 25.9 points in all 82 games for the 1971-72 Lakers, narrowly leading Jerry West in scoring as Los Angeles won 69 games, produced a 33-game winning streak and captured the NBA championship.

The return lasted far beyond that title season. Goodrich made four consecutive All-Star teams from 1972 through 1975 and led the Lakers in scoring for four straight seasons from 1971-72 through 1974-75. He averaged 23.9 points in 1972-73, 25.3 in 1973-74 and 22.6 in 1974-75, then added 19.5 points and 5.6 assists in his final Lakers season in 1975-76. The franchise later retired his No. 25, and Goodrich was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame.
Phoenix Return

Counts gave Phoenix legitimate frontcourt depth rather than disappearing after the trade. He played 80 games in 1970-71, averaging 11.0 points, 6.3 rebounds and 20.9 minutes. In 1971-72 he appeared in 76 more games, although his role fell to 11.9 minutes and 5.2 points per game. Across the two Suns seasons, Counts supplied 156 regular-season appearances and more than 2,500 minutes.

That production keeps Phoenix from receiving a failing grade. Counts was a veteran seven-footer who could score and rebound in a reserve role, and he remained available nearly every night. But Phoenix had just received two strong Goodrich seasons before making the deal, including a 20.0-point, 7.5-assist campaign in 1969-70. Trading that 27-year-old guard for a useful but lower-impact veteran center created a large long-term opportunity cost.

Hindsight Comparison

The direct realized return is decisive. Counts gave Phoenix two useful seasons; Goodrich gave Los Angeles six, four All-Star selections and the highest scoring average on the 1972 champions. In the 1972 postseason he averaged 23.8 points across all 15 games as the Lakers won the title. The Lakers then continued to receive high-volume scoring from him through the middle of the decade.

This is also a case where no elaborate downstream chain is needed to establish the result. The acquired player himself produced the value. Phoenix's return was real, but the difference in role, longevity and championship contribution is too large to call the trade close.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A+/C+. Los Angeles receives an A+ for reacquiring a Hall of Fame guard who became a four-time All-Star during his second Lakers tenure, led the 1972 champions in regular-season scoring and remained a major offensive piece for six seasons. Phoenix receives a C+ for 156 games of useful center depth from Counts, with the grade recognizing that he was productive even though the Suns surrendered the much more valuable player. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes and medium-high overall because the historical transaction ledgers disagree by one day on the date. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

On June 18, 1970, the Denver Rockets traded Larry Jones, Greg Wittman and a 1971 second-round draft choice to the Miami Floridians for Larry Cannon, Don Sidle and Miami's 1971 first-round choice. Basketball-Reference's ABA transaction ledger, Denver transaction log and Floridians transaction log all describe the same six-asset exchange. Pro Sports Transactions resolves the incoming first-round pick as No. 4 in the 1971 ABA draft, used on Ken Durrett, while Denver's outgoing second-round pick remains listed without a verified player outcome.

Denver Return

Cannon produced the best single season on Denver's side. In 1970-71 he played 80 games, averaged 26.6 points, 4.2 rebounds and 5.2 assists, posted 7.2 win shares and made the All-ABA Second Team. That is substantial immediate value from a player who had averaged 11.8 points as a Miami rookie. Cannon did not extend the return into a second Denver regular season, however; he signed with Memphis in October 1971.

Sidle also helped right away. He played 54 Denver games in 1970-71 and averaged 16.1 points and 9.0 rebounds with 4.2 win shares. Denver traded Sidle with Wayne Chapman to Indiana on February 1, 1971 for John Barnhill and Art Becker. That downstream exchange preserved asset value, but Sidle cannot be credited with the entire Barnhill-Becker return because Chapman was part of the package.

The first-round pick became Ken Durrett at No. 4 in the 1971 ABA draft. Denver moved Durrett's rights to Virginia on January 22, 1971 for another 1971 first-round choice and a player to be named later or cash. Pro Sports Transactions identifies that replacement first-rounder as No. 5 Cliff Meely. Meely played in the NBA rather than for Denver in the ABA, so the original Miami pick did not generate realized Denver player production through that branch.
Floridians Return

Jones was the most durable and productive long-term player in the deal. He played all 84 games for the Floridians in 1970-71, averaging 24.3 points, 5.4 rebounds and 4.6 assists in 43.0 minutes. He made the ABA All-Star Game, finished seventh in MVP voting and produced 8.8 win shares. Jones followed with 66 games in 1971-72 at 17.6 points, 4.7 rebounds and 3.2 assists, adding 8.1 win shares. Across two Florida seasons, that is 150 games, 21.4 points, 5.1 rebounds, 4.0 assists and 16.9 win shares per Basketball-Reference.

Wittman contributed only five Floridians games before Miami traded him and a draft choice to Texas for Charlie Beasley on October 26, 1970. His direct production was minimal, and the unidentified Denver second-round pick cannot be assigned an invented player outcome. Florida therefore wins this comparison because of Jones rather than because every piece of its package paid off.

Hindsight Comparison

Denver got real value. Cannon's 1970-71 season was excellent and Sidle supplied another productive frontcourt season before being moved. Combined, those two players gave Denver 134 regular-season games and 11.4 win shares in 1970-71. The problem is duration. Cannon left after one Denver season, Sidle was traded during that same campaign, and the first-round-pick branch did not lead to a player who appeared for Denver.

Jones alone gave Florida 150 games and 16.9 win shares over two seasons, while also delivering an All-Star season and a top-seven MVP finish in the first year. That longer direct return outweighs Denver's two-player burst even before Wittman's small contribution is considered. The original record's slight-Denver-edge framing was therefore too favorable to the Rockets once the realized player outcomes are measured.

Final Verdict

Floridians Win, A-/B+. Florida receives an A- because Jones supplied two strong seasons, 150 games and 16.9 win shares, including an All-Star year immediately after the trade. Denver receives a B+ for Cannon's All-ABA season, Sidle's useful 54-game run and a first-round asset that retained transaction value even though its eventual rights chain did not produce Denver games. Confidence is high on the trade package, direct production and first-round pick identity; the outgoing Denver second-round pick remains an unresolved historical outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
