new-york-knicks.summary: On June 20, 1970, the expansion Buffalo Braves acquired Nate Bowman and the rights to Mike Silliman from the New York Knicks. Basketball-Reference records the return as cash, while Buffalo and later Clippers media guides describe future considerations or a possible future draft choice, so the exact non-player consideration remains historically disputed. Bowman played 44 Buffalo games at 3.1 points and 3.9 rebounds per game; Silliman played 36 at 2.5 points and 1.7 rebounds. Their combined value was modest and lasted one season. With New York surrendering fringe depth for an uncertain non-player return, the fairest hindsight result is an even trade.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Exchange

On June 20, 1970, the defending champion New York Knicks sent Nate Bowman and Mike Silliman to the expansion Buffalo Braves. Basketball-Reference's league ledger, Knicks transaction page and executive records describe Buffalo's return as cash. Contemporary and franchise media guides complicate the paperwork: Buffalo's 1971 guide says Silliman was acquired for future considerations, while a later Clippers franchise guide says Bowman and Silliman came for future considerations or a future draft choice. Pro Sports Transactions preserves still more alternate wording. Those entries describe competing versions of the same return, not four separate assets, so this review consolidates them into one disputed non-player consideration rather than counting each alternative.

Buffalo Return

Bowman gave the new franchise 44 games in 1970-71. He averaged 11.0 minutes, 3.1 points, 3.9 rebounds and 0.9 assists while producing 0.0 win shares in Basketball-Reference's accounting. The role was larger than his final Knicks season only at the margins: Buffalo needed frontcourt bodies, but Bob Kauffman, John Hummer and Cornell Warner handled far more of the meaningful center and forward workload. Bowman left Buffalo as a free agent after the season and played 18 ABA games for Pittsburgh in 1971-72, so the Braves did not receive a downstream trade asset.

Silliman was a different kind of gamble. New York had drafted the West Point forward in 1966, but military service delayed his NBA debut until Buffalo acquired his rights. The Braves' 1971 media guide highlighted his Army career and 1968 Olympic gold-medal captaincy, while also noting a toe operation before his rookie season. He ultimately played 36 games, averaging 10.2 minutes, 2.5 points, 1.7 rebounds and 0.6 assists with 0.3 win shares. He became a free agent after that single NBA season.

New York Return

The Knicks' exact compensation cannot be reproduced with enough certainty to pretend the historical record is cleaner than it is. Basketball-Reference and executive logs say cash. Buffalo's contemporary media guide uses future considerations for Silliman, and the later Clippers franchise guide describes the combined acquisition as future considerations or a future draft choice. No verified player outcome or durable downstream asset was identified from that consideration in this research pass. The archive therefore records a single disputed non-player return and does not convert alternate source wording into multiple assets.

Hindsight Comparison

Buffalo received 80 combined regular-season games and 849 minutes from Bowman and Silliman, but only 0.3 combined win shares. Both were gone after the Braves' inaugural season. New York, meanwhile, moved fringe depth after a championship season and received some form of non-player consideration without giving up a player who became a long-term Buffalo building block.

That makes the original slight-Knicks verdict too confident, but it also does not justify swinging the result toward Buffalo. The Braves got usable roster bodies for year one; the Knicks shed two low-impact assets for compensation whose precise form remains disputed. Neither side created durable realized value from the transaction.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C+/C+. Buffalo receives a C+ for 80 combined games from Bowman and Silliman, but neither player became a lasting piece and their combined impact was minimal. New York receives a C+ for turning fringe depth into a non-player consideration without losing meaningful long-term production. Confidence is medium because the June 20 date and player movement are well documented while the exact return conflicts across historical sources. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

seattle-supersonics.summary: This July 1, 1970 Seattle-Baltimore listing is retained only as legacy source provenance. Seattle had already lost Dorie Murrey to Portland in the May 11, 1970 expansion draft. Portland then traded Murrey to Baltimore on October 22, 1970 for a 1971 second-round pick, which Portland used on Rick Fisher. The July Seattle-Baltimore record is therefore not a separate NBA trade.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Exchange
The legacy Seattle record says the SuperSonics sent Dorie Murrey to the Baltimore Bullets on July 1, 1970 for a 1971 second-round pick. That sequence conflicts with the stronger transaction record. Seattle's 1969-70 ledger records Murrey leaving the franchise in the May 11 expansion draft, and Portland's media guide identifies Murrey as one of the Trail Blazers' expansion selections. Once Portland selected him, Seattle no longer held the player rights described by this July listing.

Documented Transaction
The supported trade occurred after the 1970-71 season had begun. Basketball-Reference's Portland, Baltimore and league transaction ledgers all record Portland sending Murrey to Baltimore on October 22, 1970 for a 1971 second-round draft pick. Harry Glickman's Portland executive log and Jerry Sachs' Baltimore executive log agree on the same structure. Portland's own media guide also records Murrey as acquired from Seattle in the expansion draft and later traded to Baltimore.

Pick Outcome
The 1971 second-rounder became the No. 27 pick, Rick Fisher. Basketball-Reference's 1971 draft register shows Fisher selected by Portland at that slot. He did not appear in an NBA regular-season game, so the pick produced no NBA playing value. Murrey played only two games for Portland before the October trade and then continued his NBA career with Baltimore. Those outcomes belong to the October 22 Portland-Baltimore transaction, not to the malformed July Seattle record.

Final Resolution
Record Superseded. The July 1 Seattle-Baltimore entry is a legacy timing/team attribution error that duplicates the later Portland-Baltimore Murrey trade after Seattle had already lost Murrey in the expansion draft. TradeVerdicts preserves the legacy archive entry privately for provenance but excludes it from canonical hindsight grading and future public/indexable consideration. The October 22 Portland-Baltimore record remains the canonical transaction.

perspectives.summary: Denver traded Walt Piatkowski's ABA rights to Kentucky on July 14, 1970 for future considerations that became Wayne Chapman on October 2. The return produced a clear, if modest, Denver edge. Chapman played 47 games for the Rockets, averaging 10.0 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 22.3 minutes before Denver included him in a February 1971 trade with Indiana. Piatkowski retired for the 1970-71 season and never played for Kentucky, later returning only briefly with the Floridians. Denver therefore realized the only direct playing value from the exchange.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Denver and Kentucky completed a two-stage ABA transaction. On July 14, 1970, the Rockets sent the rights to Walt Piatkowski to the Colonels for future considerations. Denver's team transaction ledger, Kentucky's ledger and the ABA league log all record the same deal. Kentucky's ledger then identifies the future consideration on October 2: Wayne Chapman was sent to Denver. Pro Sports Transactions independently preserves the same July exchange and October completion, so the asset routing and timing are well supported.

Denver Return

Chapman gave Denver actual rotation value. In 47 games for the 1970-71 Rockets, he averaged 22.3 minutes, 10.0 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists. Basketball-Reference records 1,049 minutes and 468 points for his Denver stint. The efficiency was limited, but this was not a token appearance or an unrealized right; Chapman played a regular role for more than half a season. Denver's own 1971 media guide described him as a defensive and outside-shooting depth piece acquired from Kentucky before the season.

Chapman also retained some downstream transaction utility. On February 1, 1971, Denver packaged him with Don Sidle and sent both to Indiana for John Barnhill and Art Becker. Because that was a two-for-two trade, the later return cannot be credited to Chapman alone, but his inclusion confirms that Denver still held a movable player asset after receiving the future consideration. That secondary value is useful context without inflating his direct production.

Kentucky Return

Kentucky received Piatkowski's rights after he had played two seasons for Denver. The timing proved unfavorable. Basketball-Reference records that Piatkowski did not play in 1970-71 because he retired and worked as a teacher. He never appeared for the Colonels. He briefly returned to the ABA in 1971-72, but those six games came with the Floridians, not Kentucky, and therefore did not create realized value for the Colonels from this transaction.

That distinction is important for a rights trade. Piatkowski had been an actual ABA contributor before July 1970, so Kentucky was not acquiring a meaningless name. In hindsight, though, the rights never became a Kentucky roster contribution, while the player sent later as the consideration became an immediate Denver rotation piece.

Hindsight Comparison

The gap is real but not enormous. Chapman scored 468 points in 47 Denver games and remained tradeable into February, which gives the Rockets a concrete return. His poor shooting efficiency and short stay prevent the acquisition from becoming a major win. Kentucky, meanwhile, received no games from Piatkowski and no documented downstream asset from his rights. The Colonels' side therefore falls below an even grade despite Piatkowski's prior ABA track record.

Final Verdict

Denver Nuggets Win, C+/D. Denver receives a C+ for more than half a season of useful rotation minutes from Chapman plus limited residual trade value. Kentucky receives a D because Piatkowski retired for the entire 1970-71 season, never played for the Colonels and later resurfaced only briefly with another ABA club. Confidence is high on the July trade, the October delivery of Chapman and both players' subsequent records. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: The Nets turned a draft choice and undisclosed cash into Billy Paultz, a five-year cornerstone who played 404 games for the franchise, averaged 15.6 points and 11.2 rebounds, made two ABA All-Star teams as a Net and helped New York win the 1974 ABA championship. Virginia's exact draft-pick outcome and cash amount remain unidentified in the surviving transaction records, so its return cannot be fully priced. Even with that limitation, Paultz's sustained production and championship value give the Nets the clear edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

New York acquired Billy Paultz's ABA rights from the Virginia Squires in August 1970 for a draft choice and cash. The surviving records disagree by one day: Pro Sports Transactions dates the exchange August 10, while Basketball-Reference's Nets, Squires and league transaction logs list August 11. The canonical TradeVerdicts record remains dated August 10 because that is the established source route, but the discrepancy is documented rather than silently resolved. All of the sources agree on the substance of the deal: Paultz went to New York, with a draft choice and cash going to Virginia.

Nets Return

Paultz became immediate frontcourt value. As a rookie in 1970-71 he played 83 games and averaged 14.7 points and 11.3 rebounds while shooting 52.4 percent. He stayed with the Nets for five seasons, appearing in 404 games and averaging 15.6 points and 11.2 rebounds for the franchise. He was an ABA All-Star in 1973 and 1975 as a Net, helped New York reach the 1972 ABA Finals and was a major part of the 1974 ABA championship team. The Nets' own historical feature ranks his rebounding among the best in franchise history.

Virginia Return

Virginia received cash plus an unspecified draft choice. Basketball-Reference does not identify the round, year or player outcome, and Pro Sports Transactions likewise leaves the pick details unresolved. That missing information prevents an aggressive low grade for the Squires: an unidentified pick or cash amount could have produced value that the current record cannot trace. The grade therefore reflects documented realized value rather than assuming the return was worthless.

Hindsight Comparison

The identifiable return is overwhelmingly on New York's side. Paultz supplied five seasons of starting-caliber center play, two All-Star selections with the Nets and a championship contribution. He also remained an asset at the end of the run, when New York traded him to San Antonio in September 1975. Virginia's side is much harder to reconstruct because neither the cash amount nor the draft-choice outcome is identified in the available ledgers. That uncertainty narrows how harshly the Squires can be judged, but it does not erase the scale of the value New York actually received.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, B+/C. New York receives a B+ for converting a modestly documented package into five productive seasons from Paultz, including championship and All-Star value. Virginia receives a C because the consideration is confirmed but incompletely traceable; the surviving sources do not support pretending the draft pick or cash had zero value. Confidence is medium because the transaction itself and Paultz's career are well documented while the exact date differs by one day across major ledgers and the Squires' pick outcome remains unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: The Nets acquired Rick Barry from Virginia for a 1971 first-round ABA draft choice and reported cash of roughly $200,000 to $250,000. Barry immediately became an elite scorer, averaging 29.4 and 31.5 points across his two New York seasons, making the ABA All-Star team both years and helping the Nets reach the 1972 ABA Finals. The pick was later routed to Denver and is recorded as the No. 5 selection tied to Cliff Meely. New York wins the value comparison, though Virginia received meaningful cash and premium draft capital.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

New York acquired Rick Barry from the Virginia Squires on September 2, 1970 for a 1971 first-round ABA draft choice and cash. Basketball-Reference's Nets, Squires and league transaction logs agree on the date and basic structure. Pro Sports Transactions identifies the pick as the No. 5 selection and reports the cash at roughly $200,000 to $250,000. Its draft-trade ledger links that selection to Cliff Meely. The cash figure is therefore treated as reported rather than exact.

Nets Return

Barry delivered star production immediately. He averaged 29.4 points, 6.8 rebounds and 5.0 assists in 59 regular-season games in 1970-71, made the ABA All-Star team and finished fifth in MVP voting. In 1971-72 he played 80 games and averaged 31.5 points, 7.5 rebounds and 4.1 assists while making another All-Star team. Brooklyn's own historical coverage still lists 31.5 points per game as the highest single-season scoring average in franchise history. The Nets reached their first ABA Finals in 1972, with Barry as their primary scorer.

Virginia Return

Virginia's return was not empty. The Squires received a premium 1971 first-round pick plus a large cash payment for the era. The pick did not simply disappear from the asset chain: transaction ledgers show Virginia later sent a 1971 first-round choice to Denver in the January 22, 1971 Ken Durrett deal, while the draft-trade ledger traces the Nets-originated No. 5 selection to Cliff Meely. That routing means the original pick had real transaction utility even though Meely did not play for Virginia. The Squires also went 55-29 in 1970-71 after moving Barry, so the franchise remained competitive in the short term.

Hindsight Comparison

The decisive advantage is the level of production New York actually received. Barry supplied two elite scoring seasons, two All-Star selections and a trip to the ABA Finals. The acquisition lasted only two seasons before his contractual situation returned him to Golden State, which keeps this from being an automatic top-tier grade. Virginia, meanwhile, converted a player who did not want to remain with the relocated franchise into premium draft capital and substantial cash. The Squires deserve more credit than a simple star-for-pick summary suggests, but the identifiable on-court return still falls short of Barry's New York impact.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, B+/C. New York earns a B+ because Barry delivered exactly the type of elite production a team hopes to buy with a first-round pick and cash, culminating in the franchise's first ABA Finals appearance. Virginia receives a C because the Squires obtained a valuable first-round asset and meaningful cash, then remained a 55-win team, but the surviving asset chain does not show a direct return comparable to Barry's two seasons in New York. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, Barry's performance and the pick identity; the only material uncertainty is whether the reported cash was $200,000 or $250,000.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange

On September 10, 1970, the San Diego Rockets traded Art Williams to Boston for the Celtics' 1971 fifth-round draft pick. Basketball-Reference records the same transaction on the Celtics, Rockets and league transaction pages, while the executive histories for Red Auerbach and Pete Newell independently preserve the deal. The pick became the No. 78 selection in the 1971 draft, which the Rockets used on Jacksonville forward Greg Nelson.

Celtics Return

Williams was not acquired to become a star, but Boston received far more than a one-season rental. He played 74 games in 1970-71, then 81 in each of the next two seasons and 67 in 1973-74. Across four Celtics seasons he appeared in 303 regular-season games and Basketball-Reference credits him with 11.1 win shares. His best Boston season by raw production was 1971-72, when he averaged 5.1 points, 4.0 assists and 3.2 rebounds in 16.4 minutes per game. He remained part of the roster when the 1973-74 Celtics went 56-26 and won the NBA championship.

Rockets Return

San Diego converted Williams into a late draft asset rather than losing him for nothing. The pick landed at No. 78 overall in the fifth round, and the Rockets selected Greg Nelson out of Jacksonville. Nelson never appeared in an NBA game, so the pick produced no realized NBA playing value. That outcome matters because the comparison is not between Williams and an abstract future pick anymore; the asset can be traced to a specific selection and player. The low round softens the opportunity cost, but the Rockets still moved a useful veteran and received no NBA production from the draft outcome.

Hindsight Comparison

The scale of the deal is modest, yet the result is unusually straightforward. Boston surrendered a fifth-round pick that became a non-NBA player and received four seasons from a dependable reserve guard. Williams was never one of the Celtics' primary scorers, but his 303 games, positive win-share total and role through the 1974 title season represent substantial realized value for the price. San Diego's pick outcome never reached the league. That makes the trade a strong example of a contender extracting practical roster value from a low-cost future asset rather than a franchise-altering blockbuster.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, B+/D+. Boston earns a B+ because a fifth-round pick became four years of useful guard depth, including a place on the 1974 championship roster. The Rockets receive a D+ because the No. 78 pick was correctly preserved and used, but Greg Nelson never played an NBA game and the asset produced no realized league value. Confidence is high: the transaction date, compensation, draft outcome and Williams' Boston production all agree across Basketball-Reference's team, league, executive, player and draft records.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee acquired Lucius Allen and Bob Boozer from Seattle for Zaid Abdul-Aziz and reported cash of $100,000. The Bucks received immediate championship value: Boozer played 80 regular-season games and all 14 playoff games for the 1971 title team, while Allen grew into a productive multi-year guard who averaged 17.6 points and 5.2 assists in 1973-74. Seattle did get real value from Abdul-Aziz, especially his 13.8-point, 11.3-rebound 1971-72 season, so this was not a giveaway. Milwaukee still comes out ahead.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
The Exchange

Milwaukee and Seattle completed the deal on September 17, 1970. Basketball-Reference's team transaction logs record Lucius Allen and Bob Boozer going to the Bucks for Zaid Abdul-Aziz and cash. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same four-part exchange and reports the cash at $100,000. The amount is therefore treated as reported rather than exact, but the player movement itself is well established.

Milwaukee Return

The Bucks received both short-term and longer-term value. Boozer played 80 regular-season games in 1970-71, averaging 9.1 points and 5.4 rebounds, then appeared in all 14 playoff games as Milwaukee won the NBA championship. Allen played 61 games that season and stayed with the Bucks deep into 1974-75. His role expanded quickly: 13.5 points and 4.2 assists per game in 1971-72, 15.5 and 5.3 in 1972-73, then 17.6 and 5.2 in 1973-74. Basketball-Reference credits Allen with 8.2 win shares in that 1973-74 season, when Milwaukee returned to the NBA Finals.

Seattle Return

Seattle's side deserves more credit than a one-sided title-team story would suggest. Abdul-Aziz immediately gave the SuperSonics frontcourt production, averaging 10.9 points and 7.7 rebounds in 61 games in 1970-71. He improved in 1971-72 to 13.8 points and 11.3 rebounds in 58 games before Seattle later moved him to Houston in 1972. The reported $100,000 also had real value, even though a cash payment cannot be translated cleanly into on-court production. Seattle therefore received a useful starting-caliber big man plus money rather than an empty return.

Hindsight Comparison

The separation comes from Milwaukee combining two forms of value. Boozer supplied immediate rotation minutes on a championship team, while Allen developed into one of the Bucks' primary guards and remained productive across several seasons. Seattle received two useful years from Abdul-Aziz and cash, so the transaction did not cripple the franchise or leave it without a basketball return. But Milwaukee's package contributed to the 1971 title immediately and kept producing through another Finals run in 1974. That combination of championship utility and multi-year guard production outweighs Seattle's return without making the deal a historical fleecing.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win, B+/B-. Milwaukee earns a B+ for getting a title-season contributor in Boozer and several productive seasons from Allen at the cost of Abdul-Aziz and reported cash. Seattle receives a B- because Abdul-Aziz was a legitimate rebounder and scorer for two seasons and the cash payment added value, even though the SuperSonics did not receive the same championship or long-term impact. Confidence is high on the player movement and career outcomes; the only meaningful qualifier is that the $100,000 figure is reported rather than independently documented as a precise cash ledger.

perspectives.summary: Denver traded Jeff Congdon to the Utah Stars on September 19, 1970 for a second-round draft choice. Congdon gave Utah 38 games at 7.7 points and 4.1 assists per game before the Stars moved him to the New York Nets in January 1971. The draft-pick return is confirmed as second-round compensation, but the surviving transaction ledgers do not identify the year or eventual player with enough certainty to trace Denver's realized value. The trade therefore remains ungraded.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Denver and Utah transaction logs agree that the Rockets sent Jeff Congdon to the Stars on September 19, 1970 for a draft choice. Pro Sports Transactions narrows that compensation to a second-round pick, but leaves the year and eventual selection unresolved. That distinction matters: the existence and round of the pick are supported, while assigning a specific drafted player would require a link the surviving ledgers do not establish.

Utah Return

Congdon became a useful guard for a strong Stars team. Basketball-Reference credits him with 38 Utah games in 1970-71, averaging 7.7 points, 4.1 assists and 2.3 rebounds in 25.9 minutes. Utah finished 57-27 and went on to win the ABA championship. Congdon did not stay through the playoff run, however. The Stars traded him to the New York Nets on January 7, 1971 for another draft choice and a player to be named later, so Utah's direct return from this September deal lasted only part of the regular season.

Denver Return

Denver's return cannot be evaluated responsibly from the current record. Pro Sports Transactions' 1971 ABA draft ledger shows multiple second-round picks changing hands and explicitly marks some chains as unknown. It does not connect the Congdon consideration to a named Denver selection. The Rockets' own second-round slot in the 1971 ABA draft produced Marv Roberts, but the available sources do not establish that the Utah pick acquired here became that selection. Treating Roberts, Roger Brown, Garry Nelson or another player as the outcome would turn an unresolved chain into a fabricated conclusion.

Hindsight Comparison

Utah clearly received some immediate basketball value: Congdon played regular rotation minutes for 38 games on the eventual ABA champions. Denver clearly received a second-round asset. What is missing is the step needed for a fair hindsight comparison—what Denver ultimately did with that specific pick. Congdon's later move to New York also limits how much long-term value can be assigned to Utah. With one side traceable for only part of a season and the other side's draft outcome unidentified, a winner or letter-grade comparison would imply more certainty than the evidence supports.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence. The transaction itself is verified, the second-round nature of Denver's compensation is supported, and Congdon's Utah production is measurable. The draft year and ultimate player outcome remain unresolved in the available ledgers, however, so Denver's realized return cannot be priced. This record stays intentionally ungraded until a primary or reliable transaction source closes that asset chain. Confidence is high that the trade occurred as described, but low for any value verdict because the decisive draft outcome is still unknown.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Boston, Baltimore and league transaction logs all record the October 2, 1970 move as a sale of Jim Barnes's player rights from the Celtics to the Bullets. Pro Sports Transactions describes the same exchange as Barnes to Baltimore for cash. The sources agree on the structure, but none of the reliable ledgers used here identifies the cash amount. That missing figure limits how aggressively Boston's side can be graded, even though the transaction itself is well established.

Baltimore Return

Barnes did not become a lasting part of Baltimore's rotation. Basketball-Reference credits him with 11 games for the 1970-71 Bullets, averaging 9.1 minutes, 3.4 points, 1.5 rebounds and 0.7 assists. The club waived him on November 13, only six weeks after acquiring his rights. Those 11 appearances were the final NBA games of Barnes's career. Because the Bullets moved on so quickly, the realized basketball return was limited even before considering what they paid.

Boston Return

Boston's return was cash, and the amount remains unknown in the transaction sources. That prevents assigning the Celtics a high grade based on a financial figure that cannot be verified. The practical result is still favorable: Boston received consideration for a player who produced only a short reserve stint in Baltimore and did not play another NBA season. For a minor roster transaction, converting an expendable player asset into cash is a positive outcome even if the exact dollar value is lost to the historical record.

Hindsight Comparison

The comparison is modest rather than dramatic. Baltimore received 11 games of low-minute frontcourt depth and then waived Barnes. Boston received an unquantified cash payment and gave up no future NBA production beyond that brief stretch. That makes the Celtics' side more efficient in hindsight, but the unknown cash amount keeps the gap from being treated like a major win. The transaction is best understood as a low-impact sale in which Boston extracted some value from a player the Bullets did not retain.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, C+/D+. Boston earns a C+ because the team turned Barnes's rights into cash without surrendering meaningful future NBA value. Baltimore receives a D+ because Barnes lasted 11 games before being waived. Confidence is medium-high: the sale, Barnes's Baltimore statistics and the waiver date are all independently documented, while the exact cash amount remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles acquired Pat Riley's player rights from Portland on October 7, 1970 after the expansion Trail Blazers had selected him from San Diego. Contemporary transaction ledgers describe the move as a sale, while a later Lakers media guide calls it a waiver claim. Riley nevertheless produced 296 regular-season games for Los Angeles and played all 15 playoff games during the 1972 championship run. With the cash figure unavailable and Portland receiving no lasting on-court asset from the transaction, the realized basketball value favors the Lakers.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's league and Portland transaction logs describe the October 7, 1970 move as Portland selling Pat Riley's player rights to Los Angeles. The Lakers team transaction page records the acquisition of his rights without naming a return, and Portland's own media guide also says the expansion club sold Riley to the Lakers. A modern Lakers media guide instead labels the move a waiver claim. Because the surviving sources disagree on the transaction mechanism while multiple ledgers support a sale, this record preserves the cash asset already attached to the canonical trade but treats the exact amount as unresolved.

Los Angeles Return

Riley became a real rotation piece rather than a name attached to a transaction ledger. Basketball-Reference credits him with 296 regular-season games for the Lakers, totaling 2,316 points across six listed seasons. His most important team result came in 1971-72. Riley played 67 regular-season games for the 69-win Lakers and appeared in all 15 playoff games, averaging 16.3 minutes and 5.2 points during the championship run. That contribution was not star-level, but it is meaningful realized value for an acquisition made just before the 1970-71 season. His later coaching career is historically famous but is not part of this trade grade.

Portland Return

Portland had selected Riley from the San Diego Rockets in the 1970 expansion draft, then moved his rights to Los Angeles before playing its first regular-season game. The reliable sale descriptions do not identify the amount Portland received. That makes the Trail Blazers' side difficult to value precisely and argues against an especially harsh grade. What can be measured is the opportunity cost: Riley gave Los Angeles several years of reserve production and a role on a championship team, while Portland's return is not traceable to a durable basketball asset in the sources used for this audit.

Hindsight Comparison

The comparison favors Los Angeles without turning the transaction into a franchise-altering steal. Riley was a reserve, not a centerpiece, and the unknown cash amount means Portland may have received reasonable short-term value for a player it did not intend to keep. Still, Los Angeles obtained nearly 300 regular-season games and postseason minutes from Riley, including a championship run, in exchange for consideration whose exact value has not survived in the transaction record. That is enough realized surplus to support the existing Lakers-win framing.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, B/C-. Los Angeles earns a B for turning a modest acquisition into a multi-year rotation player who contributed throughout the 1972 title season. Portland receives a C- because the club monetized an expansion-draft asset but gave up the only clearly measurable long-term basketball value in the exchange. Confidence is medium-high rather than high because the transaction sources conflict between sale and waiver language and the cash amount is not documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Riley nevertheless produced 296 regular-season games for Los Angeles and played all 15 playoff games during the 1972 championship run. With the cash figure unavailable and Portland receiving no lasting on-court asset from the transaction, the realized basketball value favors the Lakers.
analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's league and Portland transaction logs describe the October 7, 1970 move as Portland selling Pat Riley's player rights to Los Angeles. The Lakers team transaction page records the acquisition of his rights without naming a return, and Portland's own media guide also says the expansion club sold Riley to the Lakers. A modern Lakers media guide instead labels the move a waiver claim. Because the surviving sources disagree on the transaction mechanism while multiple ledgers support a sale, this record preserves the cash asset already attached to the canonical trade but treats the exact amount as unresolved.

Los Angeles Return

Riley became a real rotation piece rather than a name attached to a transaction ledger. Basketball-Reference credits him with 296 regular-season games for the Lakers, totaling 2,316 points across six listed seasons. His most important team result came in 1971-72. Riley played 67 regular-season games for the 69-win Lakers and appeared in all 15 playoff games, averaging 16.3 minutes and 5.2 points during the championship run. That contribution was not star-level, but it is meaningful realized value for an acquisition made just before the 1970-71 season. His later coaching career is historically famous but is not part of this trade grade.

Portland Return

Portland had selected Riley from the San Diego Rockets in the 1970 expansion draft, then moved his rights to Los Angeles before playing its first regular-season game. The reliable sale descriptions do not identify the amount Portland received. That makes the Trail Blazers' side difficult to value precisely and argues against an especially harsh grade. What can be measured is the opportunity cost: Riley gave Los Angeles several years of reserve production and a role on a championship team, while Portland's return is not traceable to a durable basketball asset in the sources used for this audit.

Hindsight Comparison

The comparison favors Los Angeles without turning the transaction into a franchise-altering steal. Riley was a reserve, not a centerpiece, and the unknown cash amount means Portland may have received reasonable short-term value for a player it did not intend to keep. Still, Los Angeles obtained nearly 300 regular-season games and postseason minutes from Riley, including a championship run, in exchange for consideration whose exact value has not survived in the transaction record. That is enough realized surplus to support the existing Lakers-win framing.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, B/C-. Los Angeles earns a B for turning a modest acquisition into a multi-year rotation player who contributed throughout the 1972 title season. Portland receives a C- because the club monetized an expansion-draft asset but gave up the only clearly measurable long-term basketball value in the exchange. Confidence is medium-high rather than high because the transaction sources conflict between sale and waiver language and the cash amount is not documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana acquired Warren Jabali from Kentucky on October 13, 1970 for a 1971 first-round pick and cash. Jabali gave the Pacers 62 regular-season games at 11.0 points, 4.8 rebounds and 3.5 assists per game, plus 11 playoff appearances, before Indiana moved him the following September. The draft trail points to Virginia's No. 7 selection of Willie Sojourner, but the surviving transaction database labels that outcome only as probable. With useful short-term production on one side and meaningful draft-plus-cash value on the other, the existing even-trade verdict remains defensible.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Kentucky and league transaction logs agree that the Pacers acquired Warren Jabali on October 13, 1970 for a 1971 first-round draft choice and cash. Indiana's modern media guide uses the same description. That establishes the core exchange cleanly. The more difficult piece is the draft outcome. Pro Sports Transactions traces the pick as probably the No. 7 selection used on Willie Sojourner and shows that selection reaching Virginia through Kentucky, but its own wording is explicitly probabilistic. WrestleVerdicts therefore preserves the existing Sojourner relationship as a probable historical outcome rather than upgrading it to a fully verified pick chain.

Indiana Return

Jabali supplied real short-term value. Basketball-Reference credits him with 62 regular-season games for Indiana in 1970-71, averaging 11.0 points, 4.8 rebounds and 3.5 assists in 25.6 minutes. He also appeared in all 11 of the Pacers' playoff games, averaging 7.8 points and 3.6 rebounds. Indiana reached the ABA Western Division finals before losing to Utah, so Jabali's season included meaningful postseason minutes rather than empty production on a noncompetitive roster. His Pacers tenure was still brief: on September 24, 1971, Indiana sent him to the Floridians for a draft choice and cash.

Kentucky Return

Kentucky's return was less visible on the court but not empty. The Colonels received cash plus Indiana's 1971 first-rounder. The surviving draft-trade ledger identifies that selection as probably No. 7, Willie Sojourner, and records the pick moving to Virginia through Kentucky. That path fits a broader chain in which Kentucky had acquired Jabali from the Washington Capitols in July 1970 for a 1971 first-round pick and cash. Because the exact contractual linkage between those obligations is not fully documented in the sources used here, this audit does not claim Kentucky directly drafted Sojourner or that the Indiana pick definitively satisfied the earlier Washington obligation. The safe conclusion is that Kentucky recovered a first-round asset and cash when it moved Jabali.

Hindsight Comparison

Indiana received the clearest immediate basketball return: a rotation guard who played 62 games and contributed in the postseason. Kentucky received financial consideration and a premium draft asset, but the pick's final identity is only probable in the available transaction database and did not become a Kentucky player. That makes a winner declaration too aggressive. Indiana's one-season use of Jabali was valuable, yet the Pacers paid a first-rounder plus cash and did not retain him beyond the following September. Kentucky, meanwhile, converted a player it had held for only a few months into another first-round asset and cash.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B-/B-. Indiana earns a B- for receiving a useful starter-level guard for a playoff team and later retaining some value by trading him again. Kentucky also earns a B- because a first-round pick plus cash was a meaningful return for a player whose stay in Indiana lasted one season. Confidence is medium because the main transaction is well documented but the pick's eventual No. 7 Willie Sojourner identity remains labeled probable rather than certain. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Kentucky acquired Walt Simon from the New York Nets on October 14, 1970 for a future draft choice. Simon became a four-season Colonels contributor, appearing in 314 regular-season games and averaging 8.9 points, 3.7 rebounds and 2.4 assists for the franchise. He played all 84 games in 1970-71 as Kentucky reached the ABA Finals. The draft choice sent to New York remains unidentified in the surviving transaction ledgers, so the Nets' realized return cannot be fully traced. Even with that uncertainty, Kentucky's multi-year production gives the Colonels the documented edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Nets, Colonels and ABA transaction logs all agree on the core transaction: New York sent Walt Simon to Kentucky on October 14, 1970 for a draft choice. The surviving ledgers do not identify the year, round or eventual player tied to that pick. Pro Sports Transactions' 1971 ABA draft ledger documents several traded selections but does not connect this Simon transaction to a specific New York choice. That missing link is important because it prevents treating the Nets' return as worthless simply because its outcome is not currently traceable.

Kentucky Return

Simon gave the Colonels immediate and durable rotation value. In 1970-71 he played all 84 regular-season games, averaged 7.7 points, 3.8 rebounds and 1.9 assists, and stayed in the rotation as Kentucky advanced through two playoff rounds before losing the ABA Finals to Utah. His value did not end with that first season. Basketball-Reference's franchise totals credit Simon with 314 games across four Kentucky seasons, 2,780 points, 1,152 rebounds and 746 assists. That works out to 8.9 points, 3.7 rebounds and 2.4 assists per game over the full stint. He was not a franchise centerpiece, but four years of useful wing minutes is a strong realized return for an otherwise unspecified future pick.

New York Return

The Nets received a future draft choice, but the current source trail does not identify its year, round or drafted player. The 1971 ABA draft ledger is especially useful because it explicitly traces a number of traded picks involving New York and Kentucky, including other deals from the same period, yet it does not establish a Simon-to-Nets pick chain. That makes this a source gap rather than proof that the selection failed. New York therefore keeps a neutral grade instead of being penalized as though the asset vanished without value.

Hindsight Comparison

The comparison is asymmetric. Kentucky's side can be measured: Simon played 314 games for the Colonels and remained part of competitive teams that reached the 1971 ABA Finals and posted a 68-16 regular-season record in 1971-72. New York's side cannot be measured beyond knowing that a draft choice changed hands. Because the pick outcome is unresolved, the proper conclusion is not that Kentucky won by a landslide. It is that the Colonels banked several seasons of documented production while the Nets' return remains unverified. That supports a clear but restrained Kentucky advantage.

Final Verdict

Colonels Win, B/C. Kentucky receives a B for turning a future pick into four seasons of Walt Simon, including 314 games of dependable rotation production. New York receives a C because the compensation itself is verified but its eventual player outcome is not. Confidence is medium: the transaction and Simon's Kentucky career are well documented, while the exact draft asset remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Matt Guokas from Philadelphia on October 16, 1970 for a 1971 second-round pick that became No. 33 selection Marvin Stewart. Guokas immediately played 78 games for a 51-win Bulls team, averaging 6.6 points and 4.4 assists in 28.3 minutes while also appearing in six playoff games. Philadelphia used the pick exactly as traced, but Stewart never appeared in an NBA game. Chicago later included Guokas in its May 1971 trade for Charlie Paulk, preserving some additional transaction value. The realized return gives the Bulls the clear edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Chicago and Philadelphia's transaction logs agree that the Bulls acquired Matt Guokas on October 16, 1970 for a 1971 second-round draft choice. Both Basketball-Reference and Pro Sports Transactions trace that selection to No. 33 overall, where Philadelphia drafted Nebraska guard Marvin Stewart. The 76ers' own draft history also lists Stewart at No. 33. This is therefore a fully resolved draft chain rather than an inferred pick outcome.

Chicago Return

Guokas became a regular rotation guard immediately. Basketball-Reference credits him with 78 Bulls games in 1970-71, 28.3 minutes per game, 6.6 points and 4.4 assists while shooting 49.3 percent from the field. Chicago won 51 games and pushed the Lakers to seven games in the Western Conference semifinals; Guokas appeared in six playoff games. His Bulls tenure lasted only that season, but he was not simply lost afterward. Chicago sent Guokas and a future pick to Cincinnati in May 1971 for Charlie Paulk, so he retained some transaction utility after supplying a full season of backcourt minutes.

Philadelphia Return

Philadelphia's pick became Marvin Stewart, the 33rd selection in the 1971 NBA Draft. Stewart had just averaged 21.4 points as a Nebraska senior and earned All-Big Eight recognition, so the selection was a defensible second-round swing at the time. The hindsight result is much weaker. Basketball-Reference's 1971 draft ledger records no NBA games, minutes or production for Stewart. That means the 76ers successfully converted Guokas into a real draft asset, but the asset did not generate NBA value after it was exercised.

Hindsight Comparison

This one has more separation than the older reconciled record suggested. Chicago received a player who immediately filled 28 minutes a night on a 51-win team and contributed in the postseason. Philadelphia received the exact pick promised and used it on a productive college guard, but the selection never produced an NBA appearance. Guokas was not a star and did not stay in Chicago beyond one season, which keeps the Bulls grade below the top range. Still, one full year of usable guard play plus residual trade value comfortably exceeds a second-round outcome with no NBA career.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, B-/D+. Chicago receives a B- for turning a second-round pick into 78 games of useful rotation play from Guokas and then carrying some of his value into another trade. Philadelphia receives a D+ because the acquired pick was correctly identified and used on Marvin Stewart, but the selection produced no NBA games. Confidence is high because the transaction, exact draft slot and realized outcomes are all well documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Philadelphia acquired Connie Dierking and Fred Foster from Cincinnati on October 16, 1970 for Darrall Imhoff and a future draft choice. Foster became the strongest documented return, playing 140 games for the 76ers over two seasons and averaging 11.9 points in 1971-72. Dierking added 53 games in his final NBA season. Imhoff gave Cincinnati 43 games across two seasons before moving to Portland, while the draft choice sent with him remains unidentified in the surviving ledgers. Because that pick cannot be fully valued, Philadelphia's edge is meaningful but not overwhelming.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Cincinnati, Philadelphia and league transaction logs all record the same October 16, 1970 deal: the Royals received Darrall Imhoff and a future draft choice while the 76ers received Connie Dierking and Fred Foster. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same four-part structure and, importantly, also leaves the draft choice unidentified. That means the player side of the trade is traceable, but the exact year, round and ultimate outcome of Cincinnati's pick are not. The verdict therefore has to leave room for value that the surviving source chain cannot price.

Cincinnati Return

Imhoff was acquired to help a team that wanted more rebounding and an outlet for Bob Cousy's faster offense. Cincinnati's 1971 media guide described the trade in those terms after the club had been outrebounded through much of the preseason. On the floor, Imhoff played 34 games in 1970-71, averaging 8.1 points and 6.9 rebounds in 24.3 minutes. His Cincinnati run was interrupted and did not develop into a long stay: he appeared in only nine more Royals games in 1971-72 before finishing that season with Portland. The future draft choice could alter the long-term accounting, but no reliable ledger used here identifies what it became.

Philadelphia Return

Philadelphia received two veterans with different value curves. Dierking played 53 games in 1970-71, averaging 5.8 points and 4.3 rebounds in 13.5 minutes, then retired. Foster provided the more durable return. He played 66 games for the 76ers in 1970-71 and another 74 in 1971-72, when his role expanded to 23.0 minutes per game and 11.9 points. That second season is the clearest realized advantage in the deal: Philadelphia got a useful rotation scorer after Foster had been Cincinnati's third-leading scorer the year before the trade.

Hindsight Comparison

The documented player value favors Philadelphia. Dierking and Foster combined for 119 games in the remainder of 1970-71, and Foster stayed productive for another full season. Imhoff supplied useful rebounding in Cincinnati but played only 43 games for the Royals across two seasons. The unresolved draft choice prevents a harsher grade for Cincinnati because an unidentified pick cannot responsibly be assigned zero value. Still, on what can actually be traced, Philadelphia received more usable NBA minutes and the best post-trade season from any player in the exchange.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, B-/C+. Philadelphia receives a B- for getting two rotation players, highlighted by Foster's 11.9-point 1971-72 season. Cincinnati receives a C+ because Imhoff contributed when available and the future draft choice may have carried additional value that cannot currently be identified. Confidence is medium: the transaction and player outcomes are well documented, but the draft asset remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Under a realized-team-value standard, that difference is enough for a Baltimore win without treating Murrey's bench role as more than it was.

Bullets Win, B-/D+. Baltimore receives a B- for turning a second-round pick into two seasons of reserve frontcourt service and postseason depth from Murrey. perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Utah and league transaction logs agree on the core exchange: Utah sent Tom Workman to Denver on January 5, 1971 for a draft choice. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. That means the existence of draft compensation is verified while the exact asset chain remains unresolved.

Denver Return

Workman supplied short-term frontcourt depth. Basketball-Reference credits him with 39 Denver games in 1970-71, averaging 6.1 points, 3.4 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 12.5 minutes while shooting 44.7 percent from the field. He had already played 17 games for Utah that season, so Denver was acquiring a known veteran rather than an untested prospect. His stay did not extend into the next season: the ABA transaction log records Denver waiving him on September 25, 1971.

Utah Return

Utah's return is the unresolved side of the trade. The Stars definitely received a draft choice, but none of the transaction records used here links that choice to a specific selection. Utah's January 1971 transaction history contains several other draft-choice moves around the same period, which makes inference especially risky. Assigning one of those later selections to the Workman deal without a direct source would create a false asset chain.

Hindsight Comparison

Denver received measurable but limited value: 39 regular-season games from a reserve forward-center, followed by a preseason waiver before 1971-72. Utah received an asset whose eventual value cannot currently be identified. That is not enough to declare the draft choice worthless, and it is not enough to claim Utah won simply because Denver's return was brief. A defensible comparison requires the missing pick outcome.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence. The January 5 transaction and Workman's Denver production are verified, but the draft choice's round, year and eventual player remain unresolved. The record therefore stays ungraded rather than converting an unknown draft asset into a guessed value. Confidence is high on the exchange itself and Workman's short Denver stint, but low on any winner determination until the compensation chain can be closed. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: The New York Nets acquired Manny Leaks from the Texas Chaparrals on January 6, 1971 for Ed Johnson and Levern Tart. Leaks immediately became a productive interior scorer for New York, averaging 17.1 points and 9.7 rebounds in 40 games after the trade. Texas received 33 games of 18.9-point scoring from Tart plus eight games from Johnson. The Chaparrals extracted a little more combined short-term production from the two-player package, but Leaks was the best single long-term asset in the exchange, keeping the result to a slight Texas/San Antonio lineage edge rather than a decisive win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's New York and Texas transaction logs match on the January 6, 1971 deal: the Nets sent Ed Johnson and Levern Tart to the Texas Chaparrals for Manny Leaks. The canonical TradeVerdicts franchise mapping uses Brooklyn Nets and San Antonio Spurs lineage identifiers, but the teams at the time were the New York Nets and Texas Chaparrals of the ABA. All three players are directly traceable in the season and player ledgers, so the exchange itself is high-confidence.

Nets Return

Leaks gave New York a strong half-season at center. In 40 games after the trade he averaged 17.1 points, 9.7 rebounds and 1.2 assists while shooting 49.5 percent from the field. That was not empty volume: he logged 1,427 minutes, or 35.7 per game, and gave the Nets a dependable interior scorer and rebounder through the rest of the regular season. He also remained with New York into the next season for nine more games before moving on, so the Nets received more than a brief rental.

Texas Return

Texas split its return between a scoring guard and a reserve center. Tart played 33 games for the Chaparrals after the deal and averaged 18.9 points, 5.8 rebounds and 4.4 assists in 24.9 minutes per game. Johnson appeared in eight games, averaging 6.5 points and 6.0 rebounds in 19.9 minutes. Neither player became a durable multi-year piece for Texas, but together they gave the Chaparrals useful immediate production across two positions. Tart in particular remained a high-usage scorer, while Johnson provided frontcourt depth behind the team's primary bigs.

Hindsight Comparison

The case for Texas is volume rather than star power. Tart and Johnson combined for 41 post-trade appearances in 1970-71, and Tart's scoring rate was higher than Leaks' while Johnson added a second playable body. The case for New York is concentration and quality: Leaks was the strongest rebounder in the deal, shot more efficiently than Tart and stayed in the Nets' rotation into the following season. Those competing advantages make this much closer than a simple two-for-one count suggests. The Chaparrals gained slightly more immediate aggregate production, but the Nets did not give away the clearly superior player.

Final Verdict

Slight Spurs Edge, C+/C. Texas earns the C+ for turning Leaks into two contributors, led by Tart's 18.9 points per game over 33 appearances. New York earns the C because Leaks was productive and efficient enough to keep the exchange close, averaging 17.1 points and 9.7 rebounds in 40 games after arriving. The grade gap stays narrow because Texas' second piece lasted only eight games and neither outgoing player became a lasting franchise fixture. Confidence is high on the transaction and player production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

That evidence reverses the old slight-Nets edge and favors the Squires.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

ProSportsTransactions records a January 22, 1971 exchange in which New York received Virginia's 1971 ABA second-round pick, No. 17, later used on Bob Kissane, while the Squires were owed a player to be named later identified as Bill Bunting. Its draft-trade ledger ties that No. 17 pick directly to the Nets-Squires exchange and names Bunting as the later consideration. Basketball-Reference presents the same basic player-for-pick relationship differently: its New York, Virginia and league transaction logs date Bunting's move to March 15 and describe it as Bunting for a draft choice. Because those reliable sources disagree on the completion date and mechanics, the canonical January 22 identity is preserved while the conflict is stated rather than silently resolved.

Nets Return

The pick became Bob Kissane at No. 17 in the 1971 ABA draft. Kissane was also selected by Phoenix at No. 84 in the 1971 NBA draft, but Basketball-Reference shows no ABA or NBA season for him. That makes New York's realized professional return from the draft asset effectively zero. The pick itself had real optionality at the time, so the grade should not treat it as valueless on transaction day, but hindsight grading has to account for the fact that the selection never turned into on-court production.

Virginia Return

Bunting supplied modest but real rotation value. Basketball-Reference credits him with 33 Virginia games in 1970-71 and 16 more in 1971-72, for 49 games and 551 minutes across two seasons. He scored 162 points and grabbed 106 rebounds for the Squires in that span. His first Virginia season was the useful portion: 33 games, 436 minutes, 142 points, 91 rebounds and a .521 field-goal percentage. That is not star-level value, but it is considerably more realized professional production than the draft outcome New York received.

Hindsight Comparison

The source-date conflict does not change the realized-value comparison. Whether the Bunting completion is treated as January 24 under the ProSportsTransactions chain or March 15 under Basketball-Reference's transaction ledger, Virginia ultimately turned the exchanged draft choice into a player who appeared in 49 Squires games. New York used the No. 17 ABA selection on Kissane and received no ABA or NBA regular-season production from him. The transaction was low-stakes, so the grading gap should remain restrained, but the evidence no longer supports the old Nets edge.

Final Verdict

Squires Win, C+/D+. Virginia receives a C+ for converting a second-round draft asset into two seasons of reserve minutes from Bunting. New York receives a D+ because the acquired pick was legitimate second-round capital but its eventual selection produced no ABA or NBA season. Confidence is medium-high rather than high because the sources disagree on whether the transaction should be dated January 22 with a later PTBNL completion or March 15 as a direct Bunting-for-pick trade. The asset relationship and realized outcomes are well supported. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Larry Brown from the Virginia Squires for cash on January 22, 1971. Across the two Denver seasons he played 110 games and 2,825 minutes. The cash amount is not disclosed in the reliable transaction ledgers, so Virginia's financial return cannot be fully priced, but the known basketball value gives Denver a clear win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Virginia and ABA transaction logs all agree on the January 22, 1971 exchange: the Rockets sent cash to the Squires for Larry Brown. The executive transaction records for Donald Ringsby and Al Bianchi independently preserve the same player-for-cash structure. The amount of cash is not identified in those reliable records, so the financial side has to remain unpriced rather than converted into a guessed dollar value.

Denver Return

Brown gave Denver immediate point-guard stability. In 34 games after the trade he averaged 8.4 points, 6.1 assists and 1.8 rebounds in 23.9 minutes per game. More importantly for realized value, this was not a short rental. Brown returned in 1971-72 and played 76 games, averaging 9.1 points, 7.2 assists and 2.2 rebounds in 26.5 minutes. Across the two Denver seasons he logged 110 games and 2,825 minutes, giving the Rockets a dependable organizer through a transitional stretch of the franchise.

Virginia Return

Virginia's return was cash, which makes this a different type of hindsight comparison from a player-for-player deal. Cash can matter to a franchise, especially in the ABA, but the surviving transaction records used here do not provide the amount or identify a later basketball asset purchased with it. That prevents the archive from assigning the Squires a precise realized-value total. The safe conclusion is narrower: Denver received two seasons of measurable rotation value, while Virginia's documented return is financially real but unquantified.

Hindsight Comparison

Brown's 110 Denver games make the basketball side unusually clear for a cash transaction. He was not a star at this stage, but he handled a large share of the club's playmaking and stayed through the following season. With no sourced cash figure, the analysis should not pretend Virginia received nothing; it should simply separate known court value from unknown financial consideration. On the evidence that can be measured, Denver came away ahead by a meaningful margin.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, B-/D+. Denver receives a B- for acquiring 110 games of useful point-guard play for an undisclosed cash payment. Virginia receives a D+ only as a realized-basketball grade: the club did receive cash, but the amount and any traceable on-court conversion are unavailable in the sources reviewed. Confidence is medium-high because the transaction and Brown's production are well documented, while the cash amount is not. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The Exchange

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded McCoy McLemore to Milwaukee on February 1, 1971 for Gary Freeman, a 1971 second-round pick that became Willie Long at No. 35, and cash. Freeman played only 11 games and 47 minutes for Cleveland before his NBA career ended, while Long chose the ABA and never played for the Cavaliers. McLemore gave Milwaukee 28 regular-season games during its 1971 championship run, appeared in the playoffs, and returned for 10 more games the next season. With the cash amount undisclosed, Cleveland's full return cannot be priced, but the known realized basketball value favors Milwaukee.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland transaction log confirms the February 1, 1971 deal: the Cavaliers sent McCoy McLemore to Milwaukee for Gary Freeman and a 1971 second-round draft pick later used on Willie Long. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. The reliable sources reviewed here do not identify the cash amount, so it is preserved as real but unpriced consideration rather than used to manufacture a precise advantage.

Cleveland Return

Freeman's Cleveland stay was extremely brief. He appeared in 11 games and logged 47 total minutes after the trade, with the 1970-71 season becoming the last NBA season of his career. The draft pick became Willie Long at No. 35 overall, but Long did not join Cleveland. Basketball-Reference records Long's professional debut in the ABA with The Floridians, where he played 75 games as a rookie and averaged 11.7 points and 6.8 rebounds. That ABA production cannot be credited to Cleveland as realized return from the pick. Cleveland also received cash, but the amount remains unknown.

Milwaukee Return

McLemore gave the Bucks more immediate court value than either identified Cleveland asset delivered for the Cavaliers. He played 28 regular-season games for Milwaukee after the trade, averaging 4.7 points and 3.8 rebounds in 14.8 minutes, then remained available during the club's 1971 championship run. He returned for 10 more Milwaukee games in 1971-72 before being moved to Houston. This was not a major acquisition in the context of a team led by Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Oscar Robertson, but McLemore was a real veteran depth piece for a championship roster rather than a purely theoretical asset.

Hindsight Comparison

Cleveland acquired three forms of consideration, but only one produced Cavaliers minutes and that contribution was tiny. Freeman logged 47 minutes, Long chose the ABA, and the cash cannot be valued from the surviving reliable records. Milwaukee, meanwhile, received 38 regular-season games from McLemore across two seasons and had him available during the 1971 title run. The unknown cash keeps the gap from becoming large, but the known basketball production points toward Milwaukee rather than Cleveland.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win, C+/D+. Milwaukee receives a C+ for acquiring a usable veteran reserve who contributed during a championship season and remained into the next year. Cleveland receives a D+ on realized basketball value because Freeman barely played and the Willie Long pick never became a Cavaliers player, though the undisclosed cash prevents treating the return as empty. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction, pick outcome and player production, with the cash amount the principal unresolved variable. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver received John Barnhill, Art Becker, an undisclosed 1972 high draft pick and cash from Indiana for Wayne Chapman and Don Sidle in the February 1971 ABA exchange. Basketball-Reference dates the player swap February 1 and omits the pick and cash, while Pro Sports Transactions dates it February 2 and includes both additional assets. On realized basketball value, Denver came out ahead: Becker became a 1972 ABA All-Star after a strong post-trade finish, Barnhill supplied useful guard minutes, and Indiana received only limited production from Chapman and Sidle.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Indiana and ABA transaction logs agree on the four-player core of the deal: Denver sent Wayne Chapman and Don Sidle to the Pacers for John Barnhill and Art Becker. Those ledgers date the trade February 1, 1971. Pro Sports Transactions preserves a broader February 2 entry in which Indiana also sent Denver a 1972 high draft pick and cash. Because the reliable sources disagree on the exact date and whether the extra consideration belongs in the same transaction record, the canonical February 2 identity is retained while the discrepancy is stated explicitly. The cash is unpriced and the eventual player attached to the high pick remains unresolved.

Denver Return

Becker became the most valuable realized piece. After the trade he played 29 games for Denver at 27.7 minutes per game, averaging 15.2 points and 7.2 rebounds. He then stayed for the full 1971-72 season, appearing in all 84 games, averaging 12.3 points and 5.6 rebounds, and earning an ABA All-Star selection. Barnhill also gave Denver useful immediate production: 24 games at 28.5 minutes per game, with averages of 11.4 points and 3.2 assists before Denver waived him the following September. That is substantial identifiable court value even before assigning anything to the cash or unresolved high draft pick.

Indiana Return

Indiana received much less from the two players it acquired. Chapman appeared in five Pacers games after the trade in 1970-71 and seven more in 1971-72, averaging 2.6 points in 10.9 minutes during the latter season. Sidle played eight Indiana games after the trade, then returned for 27 games in 1971-72 at 14.6 minutes and 6.5 points per game. Those contributions were real, especially Sidle's reserve work the next season, but neither player approached Becker's combination of post-trade scoring, durability and All-Star recognition in Denver.

Hindsight Comparison

The realized-value gap favors Denver without requiring the unresolved draft asset to do any work in the grade. Becker alone produced 113 regular-season games for the Rockets across the remainder of 1970-71 and the full 1971-72 season, and Barnhill added another 24 games of starting-caliber minutes. Indiana's return amounted to a brief Chapman stay and a modest Sidle reserve role. Denver also held the additional upside of cash and a high 1972 draft pick according to Pro Sports Transactions, but the grade does not invent a dollar figure or a drafted-player outcome where the surviving records do not establish one.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, B+/C-. Denver receives a B+ because Becker became an All-Star and productive full-season starter-level piece after the trade, Barnhill supplied useful immediate minutes, and the club also received unpriced cash plus an unresolved high pick in the broader transaction record. Indiana receives a C- because Sidle provided some reserve value and Chapman appeared briefly, but the known basketball return was far smaller. Confidence is medium-high on the player exchange and production, with the February 1 versus February 2 dating conflict and the unresolved high-pick outcome preventing a higher confidence label. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles acquired Flynn Robinson from Cincinnati on March 29, 1971 for a second-round pick that became Joe Bergman, with Pro Sports Transactions also recording cash going to the Royals. Robinson became a valuable reserve on the 1971-72 Lakers championship team, playing 64 games and averaging 9.9 points in 15.7 minutes while helping the club through its historic 33-game winning streak. Bergman never played an NBA regular-season game, so the known realized basketball return strongly favors Los Angeles despite Cincinnati's unpriced cash consideration.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Cincinnati and league transaction logs agree on the March 29, 1971 core exchange: Cincinnati sent Flynn Robinson to Los Angeles for a 1971 second-round pick later used on Joe Bergman at No. 31. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same player-for-pick deal and additionally lists cash going from the Lakers to the Royals. Because the reliable ledgers differ on the cash detail, the canonical record keeps the cash as real but unpriced consideration rather than dropping it or inventing a dollar value.

Lakers Return

Robinson fit one of the best teams in league history. In 1971-72 he appeared in 64 games for the Lakers, averaging 9.9 points, 1.8 rebounds and 2.2 assists in only 15.7 minutes while shooting 49.0 percent from the field. The Lakers' own historical profile describes him as 'Instant Offense' behind Jerry West and Gail Goodrich and connects his reserve scoring directly to the club's 33-game winning streak and first Los Angeles NBA championship. His playoff role was smaller, but he still appeared in seven postseason games during the title run. That is meaningful realized value from a player acquired for a second-round selection and cash.

Cincinnati Return

The Royals used the acquired second-round pick on Joe Bergman at No. 31 overall in the 1971 draft. Basketball-Reference lists Bergman as a Cincinnati selection but shows no NBA regular-season career, so the pick produced no realized NBA minutes for the franchise. Cincinnati also received cash according to Pro Sports Transactions, and that consideration cannot be treated as worthless simply because the amount is unavailable. Still, there is no identified player, later pick or traceable basketball asset attached to the cash in the sources reviewed here.

Hindsight Comparison

The measurable basketball outcome is decisive. Los Angeles received a rotation scorer who appeared in 64 games for a 69-win champion and supplied nearly 10 points per game in limited minutes. Cincinnati used the principal basketball asset it received on a player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The unknown cash keeps the Royals' side from being graded as empty, but it does not erase the gap between a championship contributor and a draft choice with no NBA production. The acquisition also fit the Lakers' immediate competitive window unusually well: Robinson did not need star usage to create value behind West and Goodrich.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A-/D+. Los Angeles receives an A- for turning a second-round pick and cash into a productive reserve on a championship team, including meaningful scoring during the 33-game winning streak season. Cincinnati receives a D+ because Bergman never produced an NBA regular-season appearance, though the cash component remains real and unpriced. Confidence is medium-high because the player, pick and realized outcomes are well established, while Basketball-Reference omits the cash that appears in Pro Sports Transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
los-angeles-lakers.gradeRationale: The Lakers produced a modest realized-value advantage. Grades weigh realized player production, identifiable pick conversion, role, timing, contract context and downstream asset use.

perspectives.summary: Detroit traded Otto Moore to Phoenix on April 2, 1971 for a 1972 first-round pick that became Bob Nash at No. 9. Moore gave Phoenix 81 games of useful center play in 1971-72, then the Suns flipped him to Houston for another 1972 first-round pick, No. 4 Corky Calhoun, who became a multi-season Phoenix rotation player. Nash played only 71 games and 450 minutes for Detroit across two seasons, so the realized and downstream basketball value favors Phoenix despite Detroit receiving legitimate lottery-level draft capital.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Phoenix and league transaction logs agree on the April 2, 1971 structure: the Pistons sent Otto Moore to the Suns for Phoenix's 1972 first-round draft pick, later used on Bob Nash at No. 9 overall. That direct evidence resolves the older legacy wording that described the return only as future considerations subject to contingencies. The source-backed record therefore identifies the asset as the 1972 first-round pick while preserving the original transaction date and player relationship.

Detroit Return

Detroit used the acquired first-rounder on Bob Nash with the ninth pick of the 1972 draft. The pick had real value on transaction day, but Nash's Pistons production was limited. He appeared in 36 games as a rookie, totaling 169 minutes and 43 points, then played 35 games and 281 minutes in 1973-74. Across those two Detroit seasons, Nash logged 71 games and 450 minutes before leaving the franchise. His later NBA production with Kansas City cannot be credited to Detroit's realized return, so the Pistons received a high draft slot but only modest on-court conversion from it.

Phoenix Return

Moore gave Phoenix far more immediate court value than Nash gave Detroit. In 1971-72 he played 81 games and 1,624 minutes, averaging 7.6 points and 6.7 rebounds in 20.0 minutes per game. Phoenix then converted Moore again on April 7, 1972, trading him to Houston for a 1972 first-round pick that became Corky Calhoun at No. 4 overall. Calhoun played all 82 games as a Phoenix rookie and 77 more the next season, giving the Suns 159 games and more than 4,200 minutes across his first two seasons alone. That downstream conversion makes Moore's value to Phoenix extend well beyond his one season on the floor.

Hindsight Comparison

The original trade gave both teams a credible asset, but Phoenix extracted much more realized value. Detroit received a top-ten pick and selected Nash, yet his two Pistons seasons totaled only 450 minutes. Phoenix received a durable rotation center for 81 games and then recycled him into the fourth pick of the same 1972 draft, producing a second multi-season rotation player in Calhoun. This is exactly the type of downstream asset conversion that matters in a retrospective grade: it is traceable, directly sourced and generated by the acquired player rather than by an unrelated later transaction.

Final Verdict

Suns Win, B+/C-. Phoenix receives a B+ for getting a full season of useful center play from Moore and then turning him into the No. 4 pick that produced two substantial Phoenix seasons from Calhoun. Detroit receives a C- because the first-round pick itself was valuable, but Nash produced only a small amount of Pistons court time after being selected ninth overall. Confidence is high because the trade, first-round pick identity, Nash outcome, Moore production and Calhoun downstream chain are all documented in Basketball-Reference transaction and player records. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
