Washington gave the Hawks 253 regular-season games after the trade, including three straight full seasons as a major frontcourt rebounder, before Atlanta moved him to Buffalo in 1975 for a fifth-round pick. Bridges was excellent for Philadelphia in 1971-72, starting 62 games and averaging 13.2 points with 13.5 rebounds, but the 76ers kept him only 74 games before packaging him with Mel Counts for LeRoy Ellis and John Trapp. Because that later return required another player, only partial downstream credit belongs to Bridges. Atlanta holds the stronger realized result.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Atlanta and league transaction logs agree that the 76ers sent Jim Washington to the Hawks on November 19, 1971 for Bill Bridges. The swap is unusually easy to evaluate because both veterans were already established NBA forwards and both produced immediately for their new teams. The larger hindsight question is duration. Bridges had the stronger first-season statistical peak in Philadelphia, while Washington stayed in Atlanta for more than three seasons and gave the Hawks a much longer run of starting-level rebounding.

Atlanta Return

Washington became a durable Hawks frontcourt piece. After the trade he played 67 games in 1971-72, totaling 2,416 minutes while averaging 12.7 points and 9.0 rebounds. He followed with 75 games at 10.4 points and 10.7 rebounds in 1972-73, then 73 games at 10.0 points and 10.1 rebounds in 1973-74. He remained with Atlanta for 38 more games in 1974-75 before the Hawks traded him to Buffalo for a 1976 fifth-round pick later used on Connie White. White never appeared in an NBA game, so the downstream draft asset did not extend the chain. Washington's direct Hawks tenure is still substantial: 253 regular-season games after the trade, plus postseason appearances in 1972 and 1973.

Philadelphia Return

Bridges was outstanding immediately. In 64 games for Philadelphia in 1971-72, he started 62, played 2,210 minutes and averaged 13.2 points and 13.5 rebounds while shooting 50.9 percent. That is better single-season production than Washington delivered for Atlanta in the same year. Bridges returned for ten more 76ers games in 1972-73 before Philadelphia traded him and Mel Counts to the Lakers for LeRoy Ellis and John Trapp. The later deal matters, but it cannot be assigned wholly to Bridges because Counts was a separate outgoing asset. The source-backed grade therefore gives Bridges partial downstream credit rather than treating Ellis and Trapp as if they were acquired for him alone.

Hindsight Comparison

Philadelphia won the first-season production comparison, but Atlanta won the duration comparison by a wide margin. Bridges gave the 76ers 74 regular-season games across parts of two seasons; Washington gave the Hawks 253 after the swap and remained a double-digit rebounder through 1973-74. Washington's later fifth-round return did not become an NBA contributor, yet the long direct tenure is enough to outweigh Bridges's shorter Philadelphia run. The earlier legacy 76ers-win verdict therefore does not survive a team-value review. At the same time, Bridges's excellent 1971-72 season prevents this from being treated as a lopsided Atlanta steal.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, A-/B. Atlanta receives an A- because Washington supplied more than three seasons of starting-level frontcourt value, 253 regular-season games after the trade and two playoff appearances, then still returned a draft asset. Philadelphia receives a B because Bridges immediately became a high-level rebounder and starter, but his 76ers tenure ended after 74 games and the later Ellis/Trapp return came from a two-player package. Confidence is high on the exchange and direct production, with medium-high confidence on the downstream comparison because Bridges shared the outgoing package with Mel Counts. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The first pick became Joby Wright at No. 18 in 1972; he played 77 games for Seattle. The second became Leonard Gray at No. 26 in 1974; Gray gave the SuperSonics 166 games, 5,062 minutes and 2,061 points before a 1976 trade to Washington. seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Philadelphia and league transaction logs agree on the core November 25, 1971 trade: the 76ers acquired Bob Rule for a 1972 second-round pick and a future second-round pick. Pro Sports Transactions identifies the future selection as Philadelphia's 1974 second-rounder, later used at No. 26 on Leonard Gray, and also records cash going to Seattle. The 1972 pick became Joby Wright at No. 18. That makes the Seattle side unusually traceable for a multi-pick early-1970s deal: both draft outcomes are known, and both produced NBA games for the SuperSonics.

Philadelphia Return

Rule gave Philadelphia a strong immediate season. After arriving from Seattle he played 60 games in 1971-72, started 53, logged 1,987 minutes and averaged 17.3 points with 8.0 rebounds. He was no longer the 20-plus-point All-Star-level center he had been before the Achilles injury that cost most of 1970-71, but he remained a substantial offensive piece. Rule appeared only three times for Philadelphia in 1972-73 before the 76ers traded him to Cleveland for Dave Sorenson on November 10. Sorenson then played 48 games for Philadelphia, averaging 5.9 points and 3.6 rebounds in 13.0 minutes. That downstream return extends Philadelphia's value, but only for one additional season.

Seattle Return

Seattle's first acquired pick became Wright, who played 77 games for the SuperSonics as a rookie in 1972-73. He averaged 12.1 minutes, 3.9 points and 2.8 rebounds. Wright did not become a long-term NBA player, but he gave Seattle a full season of reserve frontcourt minutes directly from the trade. The second pick produced much more. Gray, selected No. 26 in 1974, played 75 games as a rookie and 66 more in 1975-76, then 25 Seattle games in 1976-77 before being traded to Washington. Across his Seattle tenure he played 166 games, totaled 5,062 minutes and scored 2,061 points while averaging 12.4 points and 5.9 rebounds. Gray alone therefore delivered more team-controlled duration than Rule did for Philadelphia, and Wright added another 77 games on top of it. Seattle also received cash, whose amount remains unresolved and is not assigned invented value.

Hindsight Comparison

The trade looks much better for Seattle once the second pick is traced correctly. Rule's 17.3-point Philadelphia season was clearly the best single-season result in the deal, and Sorenson added 48 games after Rule was moved. But Seattle received 243 combined regular-season games from Wright and Gray, with Gray developing into a substantial rotation forward for three seasons. That is materially more durable realized value than Philadelphia's one strong Rule season plus Sorenson's reserve year. The old even verdict understated the 1974 pick because Gray's career was not fully incorporated into the legacy comparison. The source-backed record does not need to speculate about hypothetical drafting: it grades the actual players selected with the acquired picks.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, A-/B+. Seattle receives an A- because both acquired second-round picks became NBA contributors, led by Gray's 166 Seattle games and 5,062 minutes, with Wright adding 77 games and cash also included. Philadelphia receives a B+ because Rule supplied a strong 60-game season and later returned Sorenson, who added 48 games. Confidence is high on the player and pick chain; the only unresolved element is the cash amount, which is preserved but left unpriced. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Jim Davis from Houston in December 1971 for the first-round pick that ultimately became No. 4 overall in the 1972 draft. Davis gave the Pistons 282 games across four seasons, mostly as a reserve center. Houston did not actually draft Corky Calhoun with the pick: the Rockets traded it to Phoenix on April 7, 1972 for Otto Moore. Moore then gave Houston 95 games, including an 82-game 1972-73 season averaging 11.7 points and 10.6 rebounds, before the Rockets traded him for Ron Riley. Riley added 178 Houston games across three seasons. That downstream chain gives Houston the stronger realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Pro Sports Transactions dates the Jim Davis deal to December 9, 1971, while Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Houston and league transaction logs list it on December 10. The canonical archive retains the December 9 source date and records the one-day discrepancy rather than pretending the sources are identical. The basketball substance is consistent across them: Detroit acquired Davis, and Houston received Detroit's 1972 first-round pick. That selection eventually became No. 4 overall, but the Rockets did not make the pick themselves.

Detroit Return

Davis gave Detroit four seasons of dependable reserve-center depth. He played 52 Pistons games after the trade in 1971-72, then 73 in 1972-73, 78 in 1973-74 and 79 in 1974-75. Across those four seasons he totaled 282 games, 3,480 minutes, 1,285 points and 1,035 rebounds. His role was modest—generally around 10 to 14 minutes per game—but the duration was real. Detroit received far more than a short rental and kept Davis through the end of his NBA career. That sustained availability is the principal value on the Pistons side.

Houston Return

Houston converted the draft asset before the 1972 draft. On April 7 the Rockets sent the first-round pick to Phoenix for Otto Moore; the Suns then used No. 4 on Corky Calhoun. That distinction fixes the central problem in the legacy archive record: Calhoun was the eventual draft outcome of the asset, not a Houston player. Moore immediately became Houston's starting center, playing all 82 games in 1972-73 and averaging 33.1 minutes, 11.7 points and 10.6 rebounds. He added 13 more Rockets games in 1973-74 before Houston traded him to Kansas City-Omaha for Ron Riley on November 12, 1973.

Riley extended the chain for three more seasons. He played 36 Houston games in 1973-74, 77 in 1974-75 and 65 in 1975-76. Across 178 Rockets games he averaged 17.1 minutes, 4.8 points and 4.5 rebounds. Taken as a continuous asset chain rather than double-counting simultaneous value, Houston turned Davis into one full starting-center season from Moore, another partial Moore season and three seasons of Riley rotation minutes. That is a more useful realized return than simply saying the Rockets received the player later drafted at No. 4.

Hindsight Comparison

Detroit's case is durability: Davis appeared in 282 Pistons games and stayed with the club for four seasons. Houston's case is role quality plus successful asset conversion. Moore alone played nearly as many Houston minutes in 95 games as Davis did in 282 Detroit games, and his 1972-73 double-double season was clearly the best single year produced by either side. Riley then kept the chain alive for another 178 games. The gap is meaningful but not enormous because Davis was genuinely useful for a long stretch and Houston's advantage comes from sequential conversions rather than one star-level acquisition. A B+/B split better reflects that balance than treating the eventual Calhoun selection as if Houston drafted and kept him.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, B+/B. Houston receives a B+ because the first-round asset became Otto Moore, whose 82-game 1972-73 season delivered starting-center production, and Moore then became Ron Riley for another 178 games of rotation value. Detroit receives a B because Davis supplied 282 games of dependable reserve-center service over four seasons. Confidence is high on the asset chain and player production, with the only material source discrepancy being the transaction date: Pro Sports Transactions says December 9, while Basketball-Reference says December 10. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston traded Curtis Perry and its 1972 first-round pick to Milwaukee on December 9, 1971 for Greg Smith and a 1973 third-round pick. Milwaukee used the No. 6 pick on Russ Lee, while Houston used No. 51 on E.C. Coleman. houston-rockets.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Houston, Milwaukee and league transaction logs agree on the December 9, 1971 structure: Houston sent Curtis Perry and a 1972 first-round pick to Milwaukee for Greg Smith and a 1973 third-round pick. The draft outcomes are also explicit. Milwaukee used the acquired first-rounder at No. 6 on Russ Lee, while Houston used the third-rounder at No. 51 on E.C. Coleman. That makes this a useful hindsight trade because every major asset can be traced without guessing at pick lineage or inventing missing consideration.

Milwaukee Return

Perry became the best realized asset in the deal. After playing 25 games for Houston before the trade, he appeared in 50 Bucks games in 1971-72, then 67 in 1972-73 and 81 in 1973-74. He averaged 9.6 rebounds in 1972-73 and 8.7 in 1973-74, giving Milwaukee a durable frontcourt complement around Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. Perry also remained in the rotation during the 1974 playoff run that reached Game 7 of the NBA Finals, including minutes in all seven Finals games. The acquired first-round pick produced less than its draft slot suggested: Lee played 46 Bucks games as a rookie in 1972-73, averaging 6.0 minutes and 2.8 points, but he still represented real additional value from the same package.

Houston Return

Smith gave Houston the stronger half of its immediate return. He played 54 games after the trade in 1971-72, averaging 28.1 minutes, 9.1 points, 6.0 rebounds and 2.9 assists. He appeared in only four Rockets games the following season before Houston traded him to Portland for Stan McKenzie. McKenzie then gave the Rockets 37 games across 1972-73 and 1973-74, so Smith retained a small amount of downstream value after his own Houston tenure ended. Coleman, the No. 51 pick from the deal, added 58 games as a rookie in 1973-74 at 18.5 minutes per game before New Orleans selected him from Houston in the 1974 expansion draft. The Rockets therefore received two useful rotation pieces plus a modest downstream player return, not an empty package.

Asset-Value Comparison

The difference is duration and role. Perry alone produced 198 Milwaukee regular-season games after the trade, plus meaningful playoff minutes on a contender. Houston's direct Smith and Coleman total reached 116 games, and the later McKenzie return added another 37 low-minute appearances. Lee was a disappointing No. 6 pick, but even his 46 Bucks games sit on top of Perry's much larger contribution. Neither side extracted a star from the draft capital. The first-round pick's realized result was modest, while the third-round pick actually became the longer NBA player in Coleman. That draft irony narrows the gap, yet it does not erase Perry's three-season Bucks tenure or his role during Milwaukee's run to the 1974 Finals.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win, A-/B. Milwaukee receives an A- because Perry became a durable multi-year frontcourt contributor and the acquired first-round pick still produced 46 games from Lee. Houston receives a B because Smith supplied a strong partial season, Coleman gave the Rockets 58 useful rookie games and Smith later returned Stan McKenzie in another trade. The result is clearly favorable to Milwaukee without treating Lee's draft slot as if it automatically became star value. Confidence is high because the exchange, both draft outcomes, player production and Smith's downstream trade are all documented in transaction and statistical records. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee agreed on December 13, 1971 to acquire Wali Jones from Philadelphia for a 1974 second-round pick and a player to be named later, completed with John Block on July 28, 1972. Jones gave the Bucks 75 regular-season games across two seasons and nine playoff appearances in 1972 before being waived. Philadelphia received the stronger long-term return. Block started all 48 games he played for the 76ers in 1972-73, averaging 17.9 points and 9.2 rebounds, then was traded for Tom Van Arsdale and the 1974 No. 42 pick used on Harvey Catchings. The separate No. 36 pick was later sent to Portland as free-agent compensation, so Rubin Collins' career is not Philadelphia value.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Agreement and Completion

Pro Sports Transactions records the agreement on December 13, 1971: Milwaukee received Wali Jones, while Philadelphia received a 1974 second-round pick and a player to be named later. Basketball-Reference records the completed transaction on July 28, 1972, when John Block was formally sent to the 76ers with the pick. The date difference is therefore a transaction-mechanics issue rather than a contradiction in the core exchange. The canonical record keeps December 13 as the source-reported agreement date and documents July 28 as the completion date. The pick eventually became No. 36 in the 1974 draft, but Philadelphia did not hold it through draft day.

Milwaukee Return

Jones gave the Bucks useful contender depth. He played 48 regular-season games in 1971-72, totaling 1,030 minutes while averaging 7.5 points and 2.9 assists. He also appeared in nine playoff games that spring, averaging 10.0 points in 22.2 minutes. Jones returned for 27 more regular-season games in 1972-73, bringing his Milwaukee total to 75 games before the Bucks waived him during the season. The return was real and useful, especially for a team already built around established stars, but it was short-lived and produced no later Milwaukee trade asset.

Philadelphia Return

Block immediately became a much larger piece for Philadelphia than Jones was for Milwaukee. In 1972-73 he started all 48 games he played for the 76ers, averaging 17.9 points, 9.2 rebounds and 2.0 assists in 32.5 minutes. He also earned an All-Star selection that season. Philadelphia then converted Block again on January 26, 1973, sending him to Kansas City-Omaha for Tom Van Arsdale and a 1974 third-round pick. Van Arsdale gave the 76ers 117 regular-season games across parts of three seasons, including 19.6 points per game while starting all 78 games in 1973-74. The third-round pick became No. 42 Harvey Catchings, who played 226 Philadelphia regular-season games across his first four seasons and appeared in the playoffs in 1976, 1977 and 1978. That downstream chain gives Block substantial additional realized value beyond his own excellent half-season.

The No. 36 Pick

The other Philadelphia asset also had real transaction value, but not in the way the legacy summary implies. The 1974 second-round pick ultimately became No. 36, where Portland selected Rubin Collins. Philadelphia had already transferred that selection to Portland on September 11, 1972 as compensation after signing veteran free agent Gary Gregor. Collins never played an NBA game, and his career cannot be credited to Philadelphia because the 76ers did not make the selection. The correct source-backed treatment is to preserve the pick as an asset Philadelphia used in a separate roster transaction, without pretending Rubin Collins was a realized Sixers player return.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A/B. Philadelphia receives an A because Block immediately became a 17.9-point, 9.2-rebound All-Star starter and was then converted into Van Arsdale plus the pick used on Catchings, creating years of additional Philadelphia production. The No. 36 pick also carried transaction value as free-agent compensation, though Rubin Collins himself is not credited to the 76ers. Milwaukee receives a B because Jones supplied 75 regular-season games and nine playoff appearances, including useful scoring during the 1972 postseason, before being waived. Confidence is high: the agreement, completion, player production, Block's downstream trade and both draft-pick lineages are documented. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana traded Don Sidle to the Memphis Pros on December 17, 1971 for Larry Cannon. Cannon gave the Pacers 28 regular-season games after the trade, totaling 478 minutes while averaging 6.6 points and 2.6 assists, then missed the entire 1972-73 season because of a blood disorder. He returned for only three Indiana games in 1973-74 before being waived. Sidle produced a slightly larger direct return for Memphis, playing 42 games and 566 minutes while averaging 7.1 points and 3.3 rebounds before San Diego selected him in the 1972 ABA expansion draft. Both returns were short, but Memphis received modestly more realized court value.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Memphis and league transaction logs all record the December 17, 1971 player-for-player trade: the Pacers sent Don Sidle to the Memphis Pros for Larry Cannon. There are no draft choices, cash terms or later-named players to reconcile, so the hindsight comparison can stay focused on what each player actually delivered after the trade. Both players were already established ABA veterans, but neither became a long-term piece for the acquiring club.

Indiana Return

Cannon's role dropped sharply after the move. He had averaged 16.8 points in 26 Memphis games before the trade, then played 28 games for Indiana at 17.1 minutes per game, averaging 6.6 points and 2.6 assists. He totaled 478 minutes and made four starts as the Pacers moved toward a 47-win season and the 1972 ABA championship. The roster context is favorable, but the trade should not be credited with Indiana's team championship as though Cannon drove it; his individual regular-season role was modest. Cannon then missed all of 1972-73 because of a blood disorder, returned for only three Pacers games in 1973-74 and was waived on February 5, 1974.

Memphis Return

Sidle gave Memphis the larger immediate workload. He appeared in 42 games after the trade, totaling 566 minutes while averaging 7.1 points and 3.3 rebounds in 13.5 minutes. He scored 300 points and collected 139 rebounds for a 26-win Pros team. Those numbers are modest, but they exceed Cannon's post-trade Indiana totals in games, minutes and points. Sidle's Memphis tenure also ended quickly: the San Diego Conquistadors selected him in the August 10, 1972 ABA expansion draft, so the Pros received no later trade asset in return.

Hindsight Comparison

This is a small trade with a small gap. Memphis got 42 games and 566 minutes from Sidle; Indiana got 28 games and 478 minutes from Cannon in 1971-72, then three more games two seasons later. Cannon's illness makes the long-term Pacers return especially limited, but it would be misleading to treat that medical development as something Indiana should have perfectly predicted. The source-backed verdict therefore stays narrow. Sidle's one partial season is enough to give Memphis the edge on realized value, while Cannon still provided meaningful reserve minutes to a championship-season roster. Neither player generated a durable downstream asset for the club that acquired him.

Final Verdict

Sounds Win, B-/C+. Memphis receives a B- because Sidle supplied 42 games and a slightly larger minutes-and-scoring contribution before the 1972 expansion draft ended his tenure. Indiana receives a C+ because Cannon provided 28 games in 1971-72 and three more in 1973-74, but illness erased the intervening season and he was eventually waived. Confidence is high because the exchange, direct production, Cannon's missed season and Sidle's expansion-draft exit are all documented. The margin remains modest rather than decisive. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Memphis and league transaction logs all record the December 17, 1971 player-for-player trade: the Pacers sent Don Sidle to the Memphis Pros for Larry Cannon. There are no draft choices, cash terms or later-named players to reconcile, so the hindsight comparison can stay focused on what each player actually delivered after the trade. Both players were already established ABA veterans, but neither became a long-term piece for the acquiring club.

Indiana Return

Cannon's role dropped sharply after the move. He had averaged 16.8 points in 26 Memphis games before the trade, then played 28 games for Indiana at 17.1 minutes per game, averaging 6.6 points and 2.6 assists. He totaled 478 minutes and made four starts as the Pacers moved toward a 47-win season and the 1972 ABA championship. The roster context is favorable, but the trade should not be credited with Indiana's team championship as though Cannon drove it; his individual regular-season role was modest. Cannon then missed all of 1972-73 because of a blood disorder, returned for only three Pacers games in 1973-74 and was waived on February 5, 1974.

Memphis Return

Sidle gave Memphis the larger immediate workload. He appeared in 42 games after the trade, totaling 566 minutes while averaging 7.1 points and 3.3 rebounds in 13.5 minutes. He scored 300 points and collected 139 rebounds for a 26-win Pros team. Those numbers are modest, but they exceed Cannon's post-trade Indiana totals in games, minutes and points. Sidle's Memphis tenure also ended quickly: the San Diego Conquistadors selected him in the August 10, 1972 ABA expansion draft, so the Pros received no later trade asset in return.

Hindsight Comparison

This is a small trade with a small gap. Memphis got 42 games and 566 minutes from Sidle; Indiana got 28 games and 478 minutes from Cannon in 1971-72, then three more games two seasons later. Cannon's illness makes the long-term Pacers return especially limited, but it would be misleading to treat that medical development as something Indiana should have perfectly predicted. The source-backed verdict therefore stays narrow. Sidle's one partial season is enough to give Memphis the edge on realized value, while Cannon still provided meaningful reserve minutes to a championship-season roster. Neither player generated a durable downstream asset for the club that acquired him.

Final Verdict

Sounds Win, B-/C+. Memphis receives a B- because Sidle supplied 42 games and a slightly larger minutes-and-scoring contribution before the 1972 expansion draft ended his tenure. Indiana receives a C+ because Cannon provided 28 games in 1971-72 and three more in 1973-74, but illness erased the intervening season and he was eventually waived. Confidence is high because the exchange, direct production, Cannon's missed season and Sidle's expansion-draft exit are all documented. The margin remains modest rather than decisive. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Cincinnati acquired Fred Taylor from Phoenix on December 24, 1971 for a 1973 third-round pick that became Joe Reaves at No. 42. Taylor gave the Royals 21 games and 214 minutes before his NBA career ended after the season. Phoenix eventually used the pick on Reaves, but he appeared in only seven Suns games and 38 minutes before continuing in the ABA. The direct realized NBA value therefore leans Cincinnati, although both returns were small and short-lived. The trade is better viewed as a slight Royals edge than the inherited even grade because Taylor supplied materially more immediate court time than Phoenix received from the pick outcome.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Cincinnati transaction ledger records the deal on December 27, 1971, with the Royals sending a 1973 third-round pick to Phoenix for Fred Taylor. The legacy source record uses December 24, and RealGM preserves the same late-December transaction. The exact date discrepancy is noted rather than silently normalized because the canonical archive currently carries December 24. What is not disputed is the asset structure: Cincinnati received Taylor and Phoenix received the future third-round selection that became Joe Reaves at No. 42 in the 1973 NBA Draft.

Cincinnati Return

Taylor played 21 games for the Royals after the trade, totaling 214 minutes, 71 points, 37 rebounds and 11 assists. He averaged 10.2 minutes and 3.4 points while shooting 33.3 percent from the field. That was the final NBA stop of his career; Basketball-Reference lists only two NBA seasons overall. The contribution was modest and did not create a long-term Cincinnati asset chain, but it was still a real rotation return at a time when the Royals were cycling through several backcourt and wing options.

Phoenix Return

Phoenix held the pick until the 1973 draft and used it at No. 42 on Joe Reaves. Reaves made the Suns roster but appeared in only seven NBA games, totaling 38 minutes, 16 points and eight rebounds. He then continued the same season in the ABA with Memphis, where his later production did not accrue to Phoenix. The Suns therefore converted the pick into a player who reached the NBA but generated less direct franchise value than Taylor gave Cincinnati after the trade.

Hindsight Comparison

Neither side found a lasting piece. Cincinnati received 21 games and 214 minutes from Taylor; Phoenix received seven games and 38 minutes from Reaves. That is enough to create a small realized-value advantage for the Royals, but not enough for a strong grade gap because both players were near the end or fringe of NBA rotation value. The third-round pick also carried future optionality at the time, so Phoenix's process was reasonable even though the eventual selection produced little.

Final Verdict

Slight Royals Edge, C+/C. Cincinnati receives a C+ for turning a future third-round pick into 21 games of immediate reserve production. Phoenix receives a C because Reaves reached the NBA but played only seven games and 38 minutes for the Suns. Confidence is high on the pick outcome and player production, with a medium-level date caveat because Basketball-Reference lists December 27 while the legacy canonical record uses December 24. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: New York acquired Brian Taylor's ABA rights from Carolina on March 2, 1972. Pro Sports Transactions lists Bill Chamberlain's rights plus a draft pick going to the Cougars, while Basketball-Reference identifies that second piece as Dennis Wuycik, whom Carolina signed in June. Taylor became the 1973 ABA Rookie of the Year, spent four seasons with the Nets, made two All-Star teams and helped win the 1974 and 1976 ABA championships before entering the Tiny Archibald trade package. Wuycik gave Carolina 132 games and an All-Rookie season, but Chamberlain never played for the Cougars. Both sides received value, with New York landing the franchise-level return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Pro Sports Transactions dates the rights exchange to March 2, 1972: Carolina sent Brian Taylor's ABA rights to New York for Bill Chamberlain's rights and a draft pick. Basketball-Reference's team and executive ledgers describe the same March transaction more specifically as Bill Chamberlain and Dennis Wuycik for Taylor. The draft timing explains the wording difference. Carolina selected Taylor in the early portion of the 1972 ABA Draft, New York selected Chamberlain, and Basketball-Reference also credits New York with selecting Wuycik before his rights moved to Carolina. The 1972 ABA draft ledger is incomplete in exact overall ordering, but it identifies Wuycik as a second-round selection and Taylor as a third-round selection. The source-backed archive therefore treats the generic draft-pick asset as the Wuycik rights component rather than inventing an additional unidentified pick on top of the Basketball-Reference package.

New York Return

Taylor became one of the strongest outcomes in the Nets' early transaction history. He signed with New York on July 26, 1972 and immediately won ABA Rookie of the Year after averaging 15.3 points in 63 games. Across four ABA seasons with the Nets he played 271 regular-season games, made two All-Star teams, earned two All-Defensive First Team selections and was part of the 1974 and 1976 championship clubs. He also appeared in 37 playoff games for New York. His value did not end when the ABA folded. On September 10, 1976 the Nets included Taylor with Jim Eakins and two future first-round picks in the package for Tiny Archibald, giving Taylor a traceable downstream role in another major transaction.

Carolina Return

Carolina's return was not empty. Wuycik signed with the Cougars on June 19, 1972 and played 83 games as a rookie, earning ABA All-Rookie recognition while averaging 4.5 points and 2.2 rebounds in 11.7 minutes. He returned for 49 more Carolina games in 1973-74, giving the franchise 132 regular-season appearances plus 15 playoff games across two seasons. That is useful realized depth from the rights package even though his role was much smaller than Taylor's in New York. Chamberlain, the other named asset, never played for Carolina. His 1972-73 ABA season was split between Memphis and Kentucky, so no Cougars production is credited to his rights.

Why the Margin Is Large

This is not a case where a later award alone creates hindsight bias. Taylor's value was sustained across four seasons and two championships. He produced immediately as Rookie of the Year, remained a high-minute guard, earned defensive and All-Star recognition, and still had enough transaction value in 1976 to be included in the Archibald package after the ABA-NBA merger. Carolina did receive a legitimate rotation player in Wuycik, which prevents the return from being graded as a failure. But 132 lower-minute games from Wuycik plus unused Chamberlain rights do not approach Taylor's combination of volume, awards, playoff work and championship contribution.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A+/B. New York receives an A+ because Taylor became an ABA Rookie of the Year, a two-time All-Star and All-Defensive guard, played four seasons for the Nets, contributed to two ABA championships and later carried downstream trade value. Carolina receives a B because Wuycik produced 132 Cougars games and an All-Rookie season, even though Chamberlain never played for the franchise. Confidence is high on the Taylor, Chamberlain and Wuycik identities and their realized production. The only archival caution is terminology: Pro Sports Transactions calls Wuycik's component a draft pick, while Basketball-Reference names Wuycik directly in the rights exchange. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: Boston acquired Paul Silas and cash from Phoenix in the March 1972 Charlie Scott rights deal, with Silas delivered as the future consideration in September. Silas then played four Celtics seasons, made the 1975 All-Star team, earned three All-Defensive selections and helped Boston win the 1974 and 1976 championships. Phoenix also received elite value: Scott became a three-time Suns All-Star, then was traded in 1975 for Paul Westphal and two second-round picks. Westphal became a four-time Phoenix All-Star and four-time All-NBA guard before the Suns converted him into Dennis Johnson. Both sides won, but Phoenix's longer downstream chain creates a slight edge.

Silas then played four Celtics seasons, made the 1975 All-Star team, earned three All-Defensive selections and helped Boston win the 1974 and 1976 championships. Phoenix also received elite value: Scott became a three-time Suns All-Star, then was traded in 1975 for Paul Westphal and two second-round picks. Westphal became a four-time Phoenix All-Star and four-time All-NBA guard before the Suns converted him into Dennis Johnson. boston-celtics.analysis:
The Exchange

Pro Sports Transactions records the core agreement on March 12, 1972: Boston sent Charlie Scott's NBA rights to Phoenix for cash and future considerations, later fulfilled by Paul Silas. Basketball-Reference dates the rights transaction March 14 and says Silas agreed to terms with Boston in September; the Phoenix media guide lists Silas as sent on September 19, while the legacy Boston source record uses September 18. The exact day varies across otherwise consistent transaction ledgers, so the canonical March 12 date is preserved with the discrepancy documented rather than silently rewritten. The basketball substance is clear: Phoenix obtained Scott's rights, Boston eventually received Silas plus cash, and the cash amount is not identified.

Boston Return

Silas gave Boston four high-value seasons. From 1972-73 through 1975-76 he played 325 regular-season games, including 80 or more in every season, and became one of the league's strongest rebounding forwards. He made the 1975 All-Star team, earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition in 1973 and First Team honors in both 1975 and 1976. The championship value is especially important. Boston won the 1974 and 1976 NBA Finals with Silas in the rotation, and he appeared in 60 postseason games across his four Celtics seasons. His role was not decorative: his rebounding and defensive work complemented Dave Cowens and gave the Celtics a durable frontcourt piece through two title runs. When Boston moved Silas in October 1976, the three-team transaction brought Curtis Rowe to the Celtics. Rowe then supplied 183 more regular-season games over three Boston seasons, so Silas also retained some traceable downstream value after the championship years.

Phoenix Return

Scott's Phoenix value was also immediate and substantial. After leaving the ABA he played six late-season games for the Suns in 1971-72, then became a three-time NBA All-Star for Phoenix from 1972-73 through 1974-75. Across those four partial or full Phoenix seasons he appeared in 208 regular-season games and averaged more than 24 points in each of the final three. The rights therefore became a genuine star rather than a speculative asset. Phoenix then preserved that value instead of losing Scott for nothing.

On May 23, 1975 the Suns traded Scott to Boston for Paul Westphal plus Boston's 1975 and 1976 second-round picks. The picks became Jimmy Dan Conner and Butch Feher, but Westphal is the central downstream return. Westphal played five full Phoenix seasons from 1975-76 through 1979-80, appearing in 406 regular-season games, helping the Suns reach the 1976 NBA Finals and making four consecutive All-Star teams from 1977 through 1980. He also earned four straight All-NBA selections, including three First Team honors. Phoenix then traded Westphal to Seattle on June 4, 1980 for Dennis Johnson. That conversion extends the Scott-rights chain well beyond Scott's own scoring peak and makes the original acquisition one of the more productive rights transactions of the era.

Hindsight Comparison

Calling the trade even understates how well both organizations converted the assets. Boston received the more championship-specific direct return: Silas was a core rebounding and defensive contributor on two title teams, played 325 regular-season games and 60 playoff games, then still returned Curtis Rowe in a later three-team trade. Phoenix received the more expansive star-value chain. Scott was a three-time Suns All-Star, then became Westphal and two picks; Westphal produced five high-level seasons, four All-Star selections, four All-NBA selections and a Finals run before becoming Dennis Johnson. Because downstream credit is shared with the later packages rather than assigned entirely to Scott, the margin should remain narrow. Phoenix does not erase Boston's two championships, but the Scott-to-Westphal-to-Johnson path adds enough durable value to move the verdict beyond a pure tie.

Final Verdict

Slight Suns Edge, A+/A. Phoenix receives an A+ for turning Scott's rights into three All-Star seasons from Scott, then Westphal, two second-round picks and eventually Dennis Johnson. Boston receives an A because Silas gave the Celtics four durable seasons, elite rebounding and defense, an All-Star appearance, three All-Defensive selections and major minutes on the 1974 and 1976 championship teams, with Curtis Rowe arriving downstream. Confidence is high on the player identities, production and later trade chains. The only meaningful source uncertainty is the exact transaction date: Pro Sports Transactions uses March 12 and September 18, while Basketball-Reference and Phoenix media guides use March 14 and September 19 for the two stages. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Phoenix and Boston transaction logs resolve the structure more precisely than the legacy generic 'future considerations' wording. Boston sent Charlie Scott to Phoenix on March 14, 1972 for Paul Silas and cash, with Silas agreeing to terms with Boston in September to complete the transaction. Scott was still playing in the ABA when the deal was arranged, so Phoenix was initially acquiring NBA rights rather than an active Celtics roster player. He joined the Suns late in the 1971-72 season and immediately became the centerpiece of their offense.

Phoenix Return
Scott played six Suns games at the end of 1971-72, then became an All-Star in each of his next three full Phoenix seasons. In 1972-73 he played 81 games and averaged 25.3 points, 6.1 assists and 4.2 rebounds. He followed with 25.4 points and 5.2 assists in 52 games in 1973-74, then 24.3 points and 4.5 assists across 69 games in 1974-75. That is three consecutive All-Star scoring seasons from a player acquired as rights. Phoenix also preserved enormous transaction value. On May 23, 1975, the Suns traded Scott to Boston for Paul Westphal plus second-round choices in 1975 and 1976. Westphal became a franchise star in Phoenix. That later trade is a separate evaluation, so its entire outcome should not simply be copied backward, but it proves the Scott asset remained premium when Phoenix eventually moved him.

Boston Return
Silas fit Boston's championship core almost perfectly. He played 80 games in 1972-73, 82 in 1973-74, 82 in 1974-75 and 81 in 1975-76. He was named All-Defensive Second Team in his first Celtics season, All-Defensive First Team in 1975 and 1976, and an All-Star in 1975. His rebounding was especially valuable for a team built around John Havlicek, Dave Cowens and Jo Jo White: Silas collected more than 1,000 rebounds in both 1974-75 and 1975-76. Most importantly, he was a major rotation piece on Boston's 1974 and 1976 NBA championship teams. The Celtics received four full seasons of high-end defense, rebounding and postseason value from the future-consideration component, while the cash piece was secondary.

Hindsight Verdict
This is one of the rare trades where forcing a winner makes the analysis worse. Phoenix received three full All-Star seasons from Scott, then converted him into the package that included Westphal. Boston received four durable Silas seasons, three All-Defensive selections, an All-Star appearance and two championships. The teams extracted different kinds of value but both outcomes were elite relative to the assets they surrendered. The legacy B-/B- grades dramatically undersell the transaction because they ignore Scott's sustained All-Star peak, Silas's championship defense and the fact that Scott remained a premium trade asset. An A+ for Phoenix and an A+ for Boston better reflect the realized outcomes without double-counting the full downstream Westphal career. Final verdict: Even Trade.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired Otto Moore from Phoenix on April 7, 1972 for a first-round pick that became Corky Calhoun at No. 4. Moore immediately gave the Rockets an 82-game, 11.7-point, 10.6-rebound season, then Houston converted him into Ron Riley, who played 178 more Rockets games. Phoenix received 172 games from Calhoun before trading him to the Lakers for two future picks. One was later moved for Phil Lumpkin, who played on Phoenix's 1976 Finals team, and the other became Mike Bratz, who played 239 Suns games and 25 playoff games. Houston won the immediate return; Phoenix built the slightly deeper long-term asset chain.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Phoenix transaction ledger records the April 7, 1972 deal directly: the Suns sent Otto Moore to Houston for a 1972 first-round pick, and Phoenix used that pick three days later at No. 4 on Corky Calhoun. The deal is important to trace from the correct starting point because Houston did not draft Calhoun and trade him afterward. Houston had acquired the first-round pick from Detroit in the Jim Davis transaction, then moved that pick to Phoenix for Moore before the draft. The source-backed comparison therefore starts with Moore versus the No. 4 pick and follows only the later value each club actually converted from those assets.

Houston Return

Moore was the best immediate player in the exchange. In 1972-73 he started all 82 Houston games and averaged 33.1 minutes, 11.7 points and 10.6 rebounds while shooting 48.7 percent. That was the strongest season of his NBA career by minutes and scoring, and it gave a young Rockets roster a full-time center for an entire year. He returned for 13 games in 1973-74 before Houston traded him to Kansas City-Omaha on November 12, 1973 for Ron Riley. Riley then became a longer-lived Rockets reserve: 36 games in 1973-74, 77 in 1974-75 and 65 in 1975-76, for 178 regular-season games. He also appeared in eight playoff games during Houston's 1975 run. That gives the Rockets a clear two-stage chain: one high-volume Moore season plus a useful three-year Riley return rather than only the 95 regular-season games Moore himself played in Houston.

Phoenix Return

Calhoun gave Phoenix more direct games than Moore gave Houston, although at a lower individual level. He played all 82 games as a rookie, then 77 in 1973-74 and 13 more for the Suns in 1974-75. Across those 172 Phoenix games he was a regular wing and rebounder, with his best Suns season coming in 1973-74 at 8.2 points and 5.3 rebounds per game. Phoenix then traded Calhoun to the Lakers on November 27, 1974 for a 1976 second-round pick and a 1977 third-round pick. The first of those picks did not simply expire: Phoenix moved it to Portland in June 1975 for Phil Lumpkin. Lumpkin played 34 regular-season games and 17 playoff games for the 1975-76 Suns, including the team's run to the NBA Finals. The second pick became Mike Bratz at No. 66 in 1977. Bratz then played 80, 77 and 82 games in his first three Phoenix seasons, giving the Suns 239 regular-season games and 25 playoff games before leaving the franchise. Those are smaller roles than Moore's peak Houston season, but the Calhoun asset kept producing usable roster value for years after Calhoun himself was gone.

Hindsight Comparison

Houston's side is stronger at the top. Moore immediately supplied an 82-game double-double season, and Riley added 178 games plus a small playoff role after Moore was moved. That is a productive return for a single first-round pick, especially because Moore's 1972-73 season carried more individual weight than any one Phoenix season from Calhoun, Lumpkin or Bratz. Phoenix's advantage is depth and duration. Calhoun gave the Suns 172 games, then his trade returned two future picks. One was converted into Lumpkin and helped the 1976 Finals roster; the other became Bratz, who supplied three full seasons and 25 playoff appearances. The downstream chain therefore exceeds the original Calhoun tenure instead of ending with it. The difference is not large enough for a decisive verdict because Houston also preserved Moore's value by acquiring Riley. But once the later conversions are included, Phoenix finishes with the broader and longer-lived asset tree.

Final Verdict

Slight Suns Edge, B+/B. Phoenix receives a B+ for getting 172 games from Calhoun, then converting him into the future assets that produced Lumpkin and Bratz, including 42 combined Phoenix playoff appearances from those two downstream players. Houston receives a B because Moore gave the Rockets an excellent full 1972-73 season and then became Riley, who played 178 more regular-season games plus eight playoff games for Houston. Confidence is high on the trade, draft outcome and both downstream chains. The verdict reverses the inherited slight Houston edge because the earlier grade stopped too close to the first player comparison and did not fully credit what Phoenix later extracted from Calhoun. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston traded Elvin Hayes to the Baltimore Bullets on June 23, 1972 for Jack Marin. A legacy Houston source also listed future considerations, but Basketball-Reference's team and league transaction logs show only the player-for-player exchange, so the extra consideration remains unresolved and is excluded from the realized-value grade. Hayes then spent nine seasons with the Bullets franchise, made repeated All-Star and All-NBA teams and helped Washington win the 1978 NBA championship. Marin gave Houston one All-Star season and 128 regular-season games before being traded again. The scale and duration of Hayes's production make Baltimore the clear winner.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Houston transaction log records the June 23, 1972 deal as Elvin Hayes to Baltimore for Jack Marin, and the league transaction ledger matches that two-player structure. Houston's legacy source packet also carried a question-marked future-considerations line. Because the authoritative transaction logs do not identify an additional asset, the source-backed record preserves that line only as unresolved provenance rather than treating it as a real player, pick or cash return. That keeps the retrospective comparison centered on value the sources can actually trace.

Houston Return

Marin was not a throw-in. He arrived as a 1972 All-Star and immediately produced another All-Star season for Houston in 1972-73, playing 81 games and scoring 1,496 points. He remained with the Rockets for 47 more games in 1973-74 before Houston packaged Marin and Matt Guokas to Buffalo for Kevin Kunnert and Dave Wohl on February 1, 1974. In total, Marin gave Houston 128 regular-season games, 1,998 points and a useful veteran wing presence. His later trade also generated two younger players, but that downstream value was shared with Guokas, so this review does not credit the entire Buffalo return to Marin alone.

Baltimore Return

Hayes became a franchise pillar. He played for the Baltimore, Capital and Washington Bullets from 1972-73 through 1980-81, pairing with Wes Unseld on a team that repeatedly reached the playoffs. In his first season after the trade he played 81 games, averaged 21.2 points and 14.5 rebounds, made the All-Star team and earned second-team All-NBA honors. The following season he was again an All-Star, second-team All-NBA and second-team All-Defense. His best team payoff came in 1978: Washington won the championship, Hayes led the entire postseason with 457 points and also led the playoffs in win shares. He remained a high-minutes frontcourt anchor through multiple deep postseason runs.

Durability and Team Control

The gap is not just peak quality. Hayes supplied nine seasons of team-controlled production after the trade while Marin lasted fewer than two full seasons in Houston. Hayes's Washington tenure included the 1975 Finals, the 1978 championship and a return to the Finals in 1979. Marin's Houston work was useful enough to keep the Rockets side from receiving a failing grade, especially because he was an All-Star immediately after arrival. But the length of Hayes's tenure, his repeated league honors and the championship impact create a much larger realized return.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, A+/B. Washington receives an A+ because Hayes delivered nine seasons of elite durability, repeated All-Star and All-NBA recognition and direct championship value. Houston receives a B because Marin gave the Rockets 128 games, an All-Star season and enough value to remain part of a later trade package. The unresolved future-considerations notation is not priced or assumed. Confidence is high on the core exchange and the realized player outcomes, and medium only on whether any undocumented additional consideration ever changed hands. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Fred Foster from Portland for Terry Dischinger on July 31, 1972. The canonical record also carries Philadelphia as a team because Portland had acquired Foster from the 76ers earlier that same day for a 1973 second-round pick, but Basketball-Reference lists those as two separate transactions rather than one three-team trade. Foster gave Detroit 63 games, 1,460 minutes and 8.7 points per game before moving on. Dischinger also played 63 games for Portland, but only 970 minutes and 6.1 points per game before retiring. perspectives.analysis:
Transaction Structure

Basketball-Reference's Detroit transaction log is direct: the Pistons sent Terry Dischinger to Portland on July 31, 1972 for Fred Foster. Portland's own transaction page shows why the legacy canonical record became confusing. Earlier that same day, the Trail Blazers had acquired Foster from Philadelphia for a 1973 second-round pick that became Allan Bristow, then immediately sent Foster to Detroit for Dischinger. The league transaction ledger lists the Philadelphia-Portland and Detroit-Portland moves as two separate trades. This source-backed pass therefore treats Philadelphia as same-day provenance attached to Foster, not as a participant in the direct Dischinger exchange.

The cash amount is not identified in the surviving transaction ledgers, so Indiana's return remains unpriced. Mount gave Kentucky 61 regular-season games in 1972-73, averaging 14.9 points and 3.2 assists in 29.2 minutes, then played 18 more games for the Colonels the following season. That combination of one useful full season, a partial second season and a downstream return gives the Colonels a clear but modest hindsight edge over an unresolved cash payment.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Kentucky and league transaction logs all agree that the Colonels acquired Rick Mount from the Pacers on July 31, 1972 for cash. Pro Sports Transactions records the same player-for-cash structure. None of the surviving sources identifies the dollar amount, and there is no reliable evidence tying Indiana's payment to a later player, draft pick or transaction. The source-backed archive therefore treats the Pacers' consideration as a real but unpriced financial asset rather than inventing a basketball outcome.

Kentucky Return

Mount became a meaningful rotation guard immediately. In 1972-73 he played 61 games for Kentucky, logged 1,780 minutes and averaged 14.9 points, 2.3 rebounds and 3.2 assists while shooting 45.9 percent from the field. He was fourth on the Colonels in scoring behind Dan Issel, Artis Gilmore and Louie Dampier, giving a 56-win team additional perimeter offense. Kentucky reached the ABA Finals that spring and lost a seven-game series to the same Indiana club that had sold Mount. Mount also appeared in 19 playoff games, adding useful minutes during that run.

Second Season and Downstream Value

Mount remained with Kentucky for 18 games in 1973-74 before the Colonels traded him to the Utah Stars on January 9, 1974. Basketball-Reference lists the return as a draft choice and cash, while Pro Sports Transactions says the pick may have become Sammy High at No. 28 in the 1974 ABA draft. Because that drafted-player link is explicitly uncertain, this review credits Kentucky only with a verified downstream pick-and-cash return, not with a specific player outcome. Even without assigning a name to the pick, that later transaction extends the realized value beyond Mount's 79 regular-season games for the Colonels.

Indiana Return

Indiana's side is harder to quantify. Cash can be strategically useful, especially in the ABA's unstable financial environment, but a retrospective grade cannot safely treat an unknown amount as equal to a productive guard plus a later draft asset. The Pacers also remained an elite team without Mount and won the 1973 ABA championship, beating Kentucky in seven games. That team success matters as context because Indiana clearly did not need Mount to remain a contender, but it does not convert the unidentified cash into traceable roster value.

Final Verdict

Colonels Win, B+/C. Kentucky receives a B+ because Mount delivered 79 regular-season games across two seasons, scored nearly 15 points per game in his full Colonels season, contributed to a Finals run and later generated another pick-and-cash return. Indiana receives a C because it received legitimate cash consideration, but the amount and any downstream use remain unresolved. Confidence is high on the trade structure and Mount's Kentucky production, and medium on the total Pacers return because the cash cannot be priced. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Indiana and Dallas transaction logs agree that the Chaparrals acquired Bob Netolicky on July 31, 1972 for a draft choice and cash. The ABA league ledger records the same structure, and Pro Sports Transactions likewise leaves the draft pick unidentified. No reliable source ties that first pick to a drafted player, and the cash amount is not preserved. The source-backed archive therefore treats both Indiana assets as real but unresolved rather than assigning them an invented draft outcome or dollar value.

Dallas Return

Netolicky became one of the most heavily used players in the league. He played all 84 games for Dallas in 1972-73, logged 3,409 minutes and averaged 18.7 points, 10.1 rebounds and 2.8 assists while shooting 48.3 percent. His 40.6 minutes per game led the Chaparrals, and he finished second on the team in scoring behind Rich Jones while leading the club in rebounds. Dallas still finished only 28-56, so the acquisition did not transform the team competitively, but the individual return was far more substantial than the low-impact label in the legacy review suggests.

San Antonio Continuation

The franchise moved to San Antonio for 1973-74, and Netolicky stayed for the first 19 games of that season. He averaged 12.1 points and 5.3 rebounds in 25.7 minutes while shooting 51.3 percent. That brings the franchise's direct return from the original trade to 103 regular-season games. The Spurs then sent Netolicky back to Indiana in November 1973. Indiana's own media guide says the Pacers reacquired him in exchange for cash and a draft pick. That later transaction gives San Antonio another traceable asset return, although the pick and cash are again not identified well enough to price independently.

Indiana Return

Indiana's first trade return remains the weakly documented side. A draft choice plus cash had real value, and the Pacers were able to remain a contender after moving Netolicky; they won the 1973 ABA championship. But the initial pick cannot be tied to a drafted player, and the cash amount is unknown. The later decision to reacquire Netolicky does not retroactively identify the 1972 return because the 1973 transaction required Indiana to send another pick and cash. The safest hindsight treatment is therefore to give Indiana credit for receiving two legitimate assets without pretending their realized basketball value is known.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win, A-/C+. Dallas/San Antonio receives an A- because Netolicky delivered 103 games, including an 84-game season at 18.7 points and 10.1 rebounds, then generated another pick-and-cash return when he was traded back to Indiana. Indiana receives a C+ because it obtained a draft choice and cash but neither initial asset can be traced to a verified player or amount. Confidence is high on Netolicky's production and the transaction structure, but medium on the Pacers' total realized return because the pick remains unidentified. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver transferred Bill Newton's ABA rights to Indiana for cash around August 1, 1972. Pro Sports Transactions marks the date as approximate, while Denver's legacy archive entry uses August 1; the source-backed record preserves that date with the timing caveat. Newton reached the Pacers roster and appeared in 24 regular-season games plus four playoff games during Indiana's 1973 ABA championship season, but he logged only 117 regular-season minutes and scored 58 points. Denver's cash amount is unknown. Indiana therefore received slightly more traceable basketball value, but the small role and unpriced cash keep this firmly in minor-transaction territory.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

The legacy Denver record says the Rockets sold the ABA rights to Bill Newton to Indiana for cash on August 1, 1972. Pro Sports Transactions shows the same rights-for-cash exchange and labels the date approximate. Basketball-Reference's Indiana transaction page does not separately list the rights purchase, but Newton appears on the Pacers' 1972-73 roster and the broader league transaction trail is consistent with Indiana controlling him by the start of the season. Because the exact cash amount is missing, Denver's side is treated as a verified but unpriced financial return.

Indiana Return

Newton reached the court, which makes the rights asset more concrete than many draft-rights transactions. He appeared in 24 regular-season games for Indiana in 1972-73, starting twice and totaling 117 minutes. He scored 58 points, grabbed 47 rebounds and averaged 2.4 points and 2.0 rebounds in 4.9 minutes. Those numbers show a deep reserve rather than a rotation regular. He also appeared in four playoff games, totaling seven minutes as Indiana went on to win the 1973 ABA championship. Newton's contribution to that title team was therefore real but very small.

Denver Return

Denver received cash and no identified player or draft asset. The lack of a reported amount prevents any strong claim about whether the Rockets gained or lost financially. Cash sales were common in the ABA and could carry meaningful business value, but this archive grades realized basketball value rather than inventing purchasing-power assumptions. There is no source-backed evidence that the payment was later converted into a specific player, pick or transaction. Denver therefore gets credit for a legitimate return, but not for a downstream basketball outcome that cannot be traced.

Scale of the Result

The older D/C- grading was too punitive for such a small exchange. Newton played only 117 regular-season minutes, so Indiana did not obtain a major competitive asset. At the same time, those minutes and four playoff appearances are more traceable than an unspecified cash payment. The correct hindsight gap is narrow: Indiana wins because the rights actually became an ABA player on a championship roster, while Denver's return remains financial and unpriced. Neither side should be pushed toward an extreme grade.

Final Verdict

Slight Pacers Edge, C+/C. Indiana receives a C+ because Newton's rights converted into 24 regular-season appearances and four playoff games, even though his role was minimal. Denver receives a C because it received legitimate cash consideration but the amount and any later use are unresolved. Confidence is medium-high on the exchange itself and Newton's Pacers production, with a small timing caveat because Pro Sports Transactions labels the August 1 date approximate. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit traded Jimmy Walker to Houston for Stu Lantz on August 1, 1972. Walker gave the Rockets 81 games, 3,079 minutes and 18.0 points per game in 1972-73, then appeared three more times before Houston moved him to Kansas City-Omaha for Matt Guokas. Lantz gave Detroit 101 games across two seasons, averaging 9.6 and 8.9 points, and played seven postseason games during the Pistons' 52-win 1973-74 season before New Orleans selected him in the 1974 expansion draft. Both clubs received useful production, but Walker's heavier workload and downstream Guokas return give Houston a modest hindsight edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Houston and league transaction logs all record the August 1, 1972 player-for-player trade: Detroit sent Jimmy Walker to the Rockets for Stu Lantz. Executive transaction histories for Edwin Coil and Ray Patterson independently preserve the same direction. There are no draft picks, cash payments or conditional pieces to reconcile, making this one of the cleaner early-1970s canonical records in the archive. The source-backed comparison can therefore focus directly on each player's production and any traceable downstream return.

Houston Return

Walker supplied the stronger immediate season. In 1972-73 he played 81 games, logged 3,079 minutes and averaged 18.0 points, 3.3 rebounds and 5.5 assists in 38.0 minutes. He was coming off a Detroit All-Star season and remained a high-volume Houston guard rather than collapsing into a reserve role. The Rockets were only 33-49, so the acquisition did not create team success, but Walker delivered substantial individual production and more than three thousand minutes. He appeared in three more Houston games at the start of 1973-74 before the Rockets traded him to Kansas City-Omaha on October 29, 1973 for Matt Guokas.

Downstream Houston Value

Guokas did not become a long-term Rocket, but the asset chain continued. On February 1, 1974 Houston packaged Guokas with Jack Marin and acquired Kevin Kunnert and Dave Wohl from Buffalo. Because Marin was a major second outgoing piece, this review assigns Walker only partial credit for that later return rather than treating Kunnert and Wohl as if they came entirely from Walker. The important point is that Walker produced a full high-minute season and still retained enough transaction value to help Houston make another deal.

Detroit Return

Lantz's Detroit tenure was longer in games but lighter in role. He played 51 games in 1972-73, totaling 1,603 minutes while averaging 9.6 points, 3.4 rebounds and 2.7 assists. In 1973-74 he played 50 more games and 980 minutes, averaging 8.9 points. Detroit improved to 52-30 that second season, and Lantz also appeared in all seven playoff games against Chicago, averaging 12.0 points in 32.4 minutes. That postseason contribution gives the Pistons side more weight than a simple regular-season box-score comparison would suggest.

End of the Asset Chain

Detroit did not receive a trade return when Lantz left. The New Orleans Jazz selected him from the Pistons in the May 20, 1974 expansion draft. Expansion losses are part of roster management rather than ordinary trade value, but for hindsight purposes the selection ended Detroit's direct control of the asset without bringing back a player or pick. Houston, by contrast, had already converted Walker into Guokas before Walker left the Rockets. That difference breaks an otherwise competitive comparison.

Final Verdict

Slight Rockets Edge, B+/B. Houston receives a B+ because Walker gave the club an 81-game, 18-point, 5.5-assist season and then returned Matt Guokas in a later trade. Detroit receives a B because Lantz supplied 101 regular-season games and meaningful minutes in the Pistons' 1974 playoff series, but his tenure ended in the expansion draft without a compensating asset. Confidence is high because the core exchange, production totals and later transactions are well documented. The result is much closer than a star-name comparison suggests, but Houston owns the better realized-value chain. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Seattle and Cincinnati/Kansas City-Omaha documented this deal differently. The Kings' media guide dates the core agreement to August 9, 1972: Don Kojis to Cincinnati for Jim Fox and future considerations. Basketball-Reference records the completed exchange on October 9 as Fox and Dick Gibbs to Seattle for Kojis and Pete Cross, while Gibbs did not actually move to Seattle until May 14, 1973. On realized value, Seattle won clearly. Fox became a three-season starting center, Gibbs added 71 games in 1973-74, and Seattle reclaimed Cross on waivers after only three Kings games. Kojis gave Kansas City-Omaha one 77-game reserve season.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
Reconciling the Dates

The source record requires a two-stage interpretation rather than pretending every ledger uses the same date. Sacramento's franchise media guide says the August 9, 1972 agreement sent Don Kojis from Seattle to Cincinnati for Jim Fox and future considerations. Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Kansas City-Omaha and league transaction logs record October 9 as the completed four-player exchange: Fox and Dick Gibbs to Seattle for Kojis and Pete Cross. The timing around Gibbs confirms why 'future considerations' is the safer August description. Kansas City-Omaha did not acquire Gibbs's rights from Houston until November 2, and RealGM records Gibbs finally moving to Seattle on May 14, 1973. The canonical August date is therefore retained as the franchise-reported agreement date, with October 9 and May 14 documented as completion milestones.

Seattle Return: Jim Fox

Fox alone makes the Seattle side strong. In 1972-73 he played 74 games, logged 2,439 minutes and averaged 11.4 points, 11.2 rebounds and 2.4 assists while shooting 51.5 percent. He ranked third on the SuperSonics in minutes per game behind Spencer Haywood and Dick Snyder and became the club's primary center. Fox stayed productive in 1973-74 with 78 games, 11.3 points and 9.2 rebounds, then added 75 more games in 1974-75 at 9.0 points and 6.5 rebounds. Across three Seattle seasons he supplied 227 regular-season games and more than six thousand minutes of dependable frontcourt work.

Seattle Return: Dick Gibbs and Pete Cross

Gibbs arrived later as the future-consideration piece. After Kansas City-Omaha acquired him from Houston, Seattle received him on May 14, 1973. He then played 71 games for the SuperSonics in 1973-74, totaling 1,528 minutes and 766 points while averaging roughly 10.8 points. That is meaningful second-wave value on top of Fox's production. Seattle also effectively got Pete Cross back. Cross played only three games and 24 minutes for Kansas City-Omaha before the Kings waived him, and Seattle claimed him on December 6, 1972. He then appeared in 26 more Sonics games that season. Cross's later role was tiny, but the waiver claim sharply reduces the lasting cost of including him.

Kings Return

Kojis was a useful veteran but no longer the All-Star scorer he had been in San Diego. He played 77 games for Kansas City-Omaha in 1972-73, averaging 8.5 points and 2.6 rebounds in 16.1 minutes. That was the final season of his NBA career. Cross, meanwhile, produced no points in three Kings appearances before being waived back to Seattle. The Kings therefore received one season of reserve-forward production and almost nothing from the center component, while surrendering a starting center who remained productive for three seasons and later delivering Gibbs as the future consideration.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, A-/C+. Seattle receives an A- because Fox supplied 227 games over three seasons, Gibbs added a productive 71-game season, and Cross returned on waivers after barely contributing to Kansas City-Omaha. The Kings receive a C+ because Kojis did play 77 games and provided legitimate reserve scoring, but his career ended after that season and Cross contributed almost nothing. Confidence is high on realized player outcomes and on the August franchise-media-guide agreement, with medium-high confidence on the exact completion chronology because Basketball-Reference records the four-player transaction on October 9 while Gibbs did not reach Seattle until May 1973. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Baltimore sold Dorie Murrey's player rights to Chicago for cash on August 9, 1972. The transaction is independently preserved by Baltimore, Chicago and league transaction logs, but the cash amount is not reported. Murrey had already played his final NBA game during the 1971-72 season, and he never appeared for the Bulls after they acquired his rights. That leaves Chicago with no realized NBA playing return from the purchase, while Baltimore at least converted an inactive rights asset into cash. The unpriced payment keeps the hindsight gap modest rather than turning this into a major win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Baltimore, Chicago and league transaction logs agree on the August 9, 1972 structure: the Bullets sold Dorie Murrey's player rights to the Bulls. The executive records for Jerry Sachs and Pat Williams preserve the same transaction from each front office, while Pro Sports Transactions records Baltimore receiving cash and Chicago receiving Murrey. No source located for this review identifies the dollar amount. The source-backed archive therefore treats Baltimore's consideration as a verified but unpriced financial return.

Why Chicago Bought Rights

Murrey had been a useful reserve before this deal, but the timing matters. Baltimore had acquired him from Portland in October 1970, and he played 120 regular-season games for the Bullets across 1970-71 and 1971-72. His last NBA season was 1971-72, when he appeared in 51 games and averaged 2.2 points and 2.5 rebounds in 8.3 minutes. Chicago was not acquiring an active 1972-73 rotation player on August 9; it was purchasing his NBA rights after his Baltimore playing tenure had ended. That distinction makes the old archive grade, which treated Murrey as a lasting Bulls contributor, unsupported.

Chicago Outcome

Murrey never appeared in an NBA game for Chicago. His Basketball-Reference career record ends with Baltimore in 1971-72, and the Bulls' 1972-73 roster contains no Murrey appearance. The rights purchase therefore produced zero realized NBA games, minutes, points or rebounds for Chicago. There is also no source-backed evidence in the reviewed transaction trail that Chicago later traded those rights for a player, pick or cash return. The Bulls may have had a speculative reason for controlling the rights, but hindsight grading cannot award production that never reached the court.

Baltimore Return

Baltimore's return was cash, and that is the only reason the Bullets receive the better grade. The amount is unknown, so the archive cannot claim the payment materially improved the roster or finances. Still, selling rights to a player who never returned to the NBA created a traceable return from an asset that otherwise produced no post-trade basketball value. That is modest asset management value, not a major personnel victory. Unlike the prior placeholder analysis, the comparison does not assume an unreported cash figure or assign Chicago value simply because Murrey had contributed for Baltimore before the transaction.

Final Verdict

Slight Bullets Edge, C+/D+. Baltimore receives a C+ because it converted Murrey's inactive NBA rights into cash, even though the amount and downstream use remain unresolved. Chicago receives a D+ because the purchased rights never became a Bulls appearance and no later return has been identified. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and zero-game Chicago outcome, but only medium on the total financial value because the payment is unpriced. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
