indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana acquired Don Buse's ABA rights from the Virginia Squires for cash in August 1972, with the canonical archive retaining August 10 while Basketball-Reference lists the transaction only as August ?. The cash amount is not reported. Buse immediately joined the Pacers, played 77 games as a rookie for the 1972-73 ABA champions, and developed into an elite defensive guard and playmaker. By 1976-77, after the merger, he was an NBA All-Star who led the league in both assists and steals. Virginia's unpriced cash return cannot approach that documented basketball value in hindsight.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Pacers and ABA transaction ledgers agree that Indiana sent cash to the Virginia Squires for Don Buse in August 1972. The important source conflict is the day: the canonical import carries August 10, while Basketball-Reference lists the trade under August ? and then records Indiana signing Buse on August 15. The archive therefore keeps the established canonical date but does not present that day as independently verified. No reviewed source supplies the cash amount, so Virginia's consideration remains real but unpriced.

Immediate Pacers Return

Buse joined Indiana immediately and played 77 games as a rookie in 1972-73, averaging 5.4 points, 2.9 assists and 1.4 steals in 19.3 minutes. The Pacers went 51-33 and won the ABA championship, and Buse appeared in 14 playoff games during that title run. He was not yet the team's central star, but the rights purchase already produced a useful rotation guard on a champion in its first season. That alone gives Indiana a concrete return that cannot be matched to any identified basketball asset on Virginia's side.

Development Into a Star

The long-term payoff made the transaction exceptional. Buse grew from reserve guard into one of the ABA's best defenders and playmakers. By 1974-75 he was an All-Defensive First Team selection. In 1975-76 he started all 84 games, averaged 12.5 points, 8.2 assists and 4.1 steals, earned All-Star and All-ABA recognition, and again made the All-Defensive First Team. His 689 assists led the ABA. Indiana had acquired the rights to that production for an undisclosed cash payment four years earlier.

NBA Merger Value

The value survived the ABA-NBA merger. In 1976-77 Buse started 76 of 81 games for the NBA Pacers, averaged 8.0 points, 8.5 assists and 3.5 steals, made the NBA All-Star team and the All-Defensive First Team, and led the entire NBA in both assists and steals. Basketball-Reference credits him with 685 assists and 281 steals that season. That combination matters for hindsight grading because the transaction did not merely buy a short ABA stint; it secured a guard who remained elite after the league context changed.

Virginia Return

Virginia received cash, but the amount is unknown and no reviewed source ties it to a later player, pick or traceable basketball return. That does not make the consideration literally worthless, and the archive does not invent a dollar value or assume the Squires spent it poorly. It does mean the measurable comparison is dramatically one-sided. Indiana received five seasons of Buse before trading him to Phoenix in 1977, including an ABA championship season, multiple All-Defensive selections and league-leading playmaking and steals production. Virginia's side has no comparable documented basketball asset.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, A/F. Indiana receives an A because a cash purchase of player rights produced a championship contributor who developed into an ABA All-Star, All-ABA guard, repeated All-Defensive selection and then an NBA All-Star who led the league in assists and steals. Virginia receives an F because its return is only an unpriced cash payment with no identified downstream basketball asset in the reviewed record. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction structure and career outcome, with the exact August day preserved as a source-date caveat. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Seattle and league transaction logs all record the same August 23, 1972 exchange: the Cavaliers sent Butch Beard to the SuperSonics for Lenny Wilkens and Barry Clemens. Wilkens was the transaction's defining asset. At age 35 in 1972-73 he played 75 games for Cleveland, averaged 39.6 minutes, 20.5 points, 4.6 rebounds and 8.4 assists, made the All-Star team and finished 16th in MVP voting. He immediately became the Cavaliers' primary organizer rather than a fading-name acquisition. In 1973-74 he added 74 games at 16.4 points and 7.1 assists in 33.6 minutes. Clemens supplied useful depth alongside the star return. He appeared in 72 games in 1972-73, averaging 6.5 points and 2.9 rebounds in 15.5 minutes while shooting 51.6 percent from the field. Clemens was not a franchise-changing player, but his rotation minutes matter because Cleveland did not merely swap Beard for Wilkens one-for-one; it also received a second veteran who stayed in the rotation for the same two-season window.

Beard was coming off an All-Star season with Cleveland, but his Seattle role dropped sharply. In 1972-73 he played 73 games and averaged 6.6 points, 2.4 rebounds and 3.4 assists in 19.2 minutes. Those are useful guard minutes, not a failed acquisition, and Seattle did retain transaction value after the season. On July 25, 1973, the SuperSonics traded Beard to Golden State for Walt Hazzard. Cavaliers Win, A-/C+. perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Jim Cleamons from the Los Angeles Lakers for a 1974 second-round pick on August 31, 1972; that pick became No. 21 Billy Knight. Cleamons developed from a reserve into Cleveland's starting point guard, played 377 regular-season games across five seasons, made the 1976 All-Defensive Second Team and averaged 13.8 points in 13 playoff games during the Cavaliers' 1976 Eastern Conference Finals run. When he left for New York in 1977, Cleveland received Walt Frazier as free-agent compensation. Knight became an excellent pro but never played for the Lakers, leaving Cleveland with the much stronger realized franchise return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Los Angeles and league transaction logs agree on the August 31, 1972 structure: the Cavaliers sent a 1974 second-round draft pick to the Lakers for Jim Cleamons. Those same records identify the selection as No. 21 Billy Knight. Pro Sports Transactions carries older uncertainty language around whether the undisclosed pick was that exact selection, but its 1974 draft ledger also notes an Associated Press attribution calling Knight the Los Angeles pick from Cleveland. With multiple independent transaction records now aligning, this review upgrades the asset from a probable linkage to a verified second-round pick that became Knight.

Cleamons' Cleveland Growth

Cleamons was a little-used Lakers rookie before the trade, but Cleveland turned the acquisition into five seasons of increasing responsibility. He played 80 games in 1972-73 and 81 in 1973-74, then became a full-time lead guard. In 1974-75 he averaged 11.9 points and 5.1 assists in 74 games. The next season he started all 82 games, averaged 12.2 points, 5.2 assists and 1.5 steals, and made the NBA All-Defensive Second Team. By the end of 1976-77, Cleamons had played 377 regular-season games for Cleveland and scored 3,532 points.

Playoff and Team Value

The 1975-76 season is the strongest evidence that Cleveland received more than accumulated regular-season minutes. The Cavaliers went 49-33, won their division and reached the Eastern Conference Finals. Cleamons played all 13 postseason games, averaged 38.7 minutes, 13.8 points, 5.5 rebounds and 4.7 assists, and remained one of the club's primary perimeter players. That postseason role, combined with his All-Defensive selection, turns the acquisition into a core-team result rather than a simple depth win.

The Lakers' Pick Outcome

Los Angeles used the acquired pick on Billy Knight at No. 21 in the 1974 NBA Draft. Knight became an excellent professional player, but not for the Lakers. Indiana had also drafted him in the ABA and signed him in July 1974. He played his first three professional seasons with the Pacers, including an ABA All-Star season and a 1976-77 NBA All-Star season, before Indiana traded him to Buffalo in 1977. The Lakers therefore made a strong talent evaluation with the Cleveland pick but received no realized Lakers games, points or later trade return from Knight in the source trail reviewed here.

Downstream Cleveland Return

Cleveland's value chain continued after Cleamons left. In October 1977 he signed with the New York Knicks as a veteran free agent, and the Cavaliers received Walt Frazier as compensation. Frazier then played 51 games for Cleveland in 1977-78 at 16.2 points, 4.1 rebounds and 4.1 assists, followed by 12 more games the next season. That compensation is not credited as if it were guaranteed by the 1972 trade, but it is a real downstream return generated by Cleveland retaining Cleamons through his veteran-free-agent departure.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A/D+. Cleveland receives an A because one second-round pick produced 377 Cleamons regular-season games, an All-Defensive selection, a major role in the 1976 conference-finals run and later Walt Frazier compensation. Los Angeles receives a D+ because the pick became the highly productive Billy Knight, validating the scouting value of the selection, but Knight never played for the Lakers and the reviewed record shows no realized Lakers return from his rights. Confidence is high on the transaction, pick identity and Cleamons outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: New York acquired Art Becker from the expansion San Diego Conquistadors for cash on September 14, 1972. Becker had been an ABA All-Star the previous season, but his Nets stay was brief: eight games, 46 minutes and 2.9 points per game before New York traded him to Dallas on December 4. That second deal returned a draft choice and cash. San Diego's original cash receipt is unpriced, so its value cannot be measured directly. New York still turned the purchase into short-term depth plus a later pick-and-cash return, giving the Nets the better documented asset chain without making this a major win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, San Diego Conquistadors and league transaction logs agree on the September 14, 1972 exchange: New York sent cash to San Diego for Art Becker. Pro Sports Transactions records the same two-sided movement and identifies Becker as having reached San Diego in the August expansion draft from Denver. The amount of cash is not reported in the reviewed sources, so the Conquistadors' return has to remain unpriced. That uncertainty matters because this was not a player-for-player swap; the Nets can be graded on Becker's realized production and later resale value, while San Diego's financial return cannot be translated into invented roster value.

Why Becker Had Value

Becker was not a random camp body. He had played 84 games for Denver in 1971-72, averaging 12.3 points and 5.6 rebounds in 26.1 minutes, and Basketball-Reference credits him with an ABA All-Star selection that season. San Diego selected him in the August 10 expansion draft, then moved him to New York just over a month later. The Nets were therefore buying a veteran forward with recent starting-level production, even though his role would shrink sharply once he joined a roster built around Rick Barry, Bill Melchionni and the newly signed Brian Taylor.

New York's Direct Return

Becker's direct Nets production was minimal. He appeared in eight games in 1972-73, logged only 46 minutes and averaged 2.9 points and 0.8 rebounds. He never became a meaningful part of Lou Carnesecca's rotation, and New York did not keep him long enough for the acquisition to influence the club's season in a substantial way. If the transaction ended there, paying cash for eight low-minute appearances would be a weak return regardless of Becker's prior reputation. The important part of the hindsight case is what New York did next.

The Dallas Flip

On December 4, 1972, less than three months after acquiring Becker, the Nets traded him to the Dallas Chaparrals for a draft choice and cash. Basketball-Reference's Nets, Dallas and ABA transaction ledgers all preserve that structure, and Pro Sports Transactions independently lists the same return. The reviewed sources do not identify the draft selection or the cash amount, so the archive does not assign downstream player value to the pick. Even with that limitation, New York converted a player who had produced only eight games for the club into two new forms of consideration. That makes the original cash purchase more defensible than Becker's stat line alone suggests.

San Diego's Side

San Diego received cash and gave up a player it had acquired through the expansion draft only weeks earlier. Because the dollar amount is unknown, there is no reliable way to say whether the Conquistadors made a strong financial sale or merely cleared a roster spot. Becker never played a regular-season game for San Diego, so the franchise did not surrender realized on-court production from its own 1972-73 roster. That keeps the San Diego grade respectable rather than punitive. The problem for the Conquistadors in a hindsight comparison is that New York later recovered a draft choice and additional cash while also getting Becker's brief eight-game stint.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, B-/C. New York receives a B- because the initial cash purchase produced very little direct basketball value but was successfully recycled into a later draft choice and cash return. San Diego receives a C because it converted an expansion-draft player into cash before the season, but the amount is unreported and no downstream basketball asset can be traced from that payment. Confidence is medium-high on the transaction structure, Becker's eight-game Nets tenure and the December resale, with the grade gap held in check by the unresolved cash values and unidentified Dallas draft choice. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Williams never appeared in a regular-season game for the Warriors; Golden State waived him on October 9, and he spent 1972-73 outside the NBA before returning with Seattle the next season. Because New York received a real but unresolved future asset while Golden State received zero NBA games, the Knicks hold a modest hindsight edge rather than a major win.
analysis:
The Exchange

Pro Sports Transactions records the September 19, 1972 exchange as New York sending Milt Williams to Golden State for an undisclosed draft pick or future draft consideration in the 1973 draft. RealGM independently records Williams moving from the Knicks to the Warriors that day. Basketball-Reference's team transaction pages are less complete for this specific exchange, so the specialist transaction database and RealGM supply the strongest direct evidence for the trade mechanics. The exact draft round, pick number and eventual selected player remain unresolved, which prevents this archive from assigning New York a specific draft outcome.

Golden State's Intended Return

Williams had a small NBA résumé before the deal. He appeared in five games for New York in 1970-71 and ten for Atlanta in 1971-72 after the Hawks claimed him from the Knicks on waivers. New York later reacquired his rights before sending him to Golden State. The Warriors were therefore acquiring a veteran fringe point guard rather than a proven rotation player. That can still have practical roster value in training camp, but hindsight grading depends on what actually reached the regular-season court.

Zero Warriors Games

Golden State received no regular-season production from Williams. RealGM and Pro Sports Transactions both record the Warriors waiving him on October 9, 1972, less than three weeks after the trade and before the regular season began. Basketball-Reference lists Williams as playing in another professional league during 1972-73, and he does not appear on Golden State's 47-35 roster. The Warriors reached the Western Conference Finals without him. For this transaction, Golden State's realized return is therefore zero NBA games, minutes, points or assists.

Williams' Later Career

Williams did return to the NBA, but not through Golden State. Seattle signed him in October 1973, and he played 53 games for the SuperSonics in 1973-74, averaging 3.1 points and 1.9 assists in 9.5 minutes. He later appeared briefly in the ABA. Those later games confirm that Williams still had professional ability, but they cannot be credited to the Warriors because Golden State had already waived him and received no compensation when he left. Hindsight grading must follow the asset chain actually retained by each team.

New York's Unresolved Consideration

The Knicks' return is harder to value. Pro Sports Transactions labels it an undisclosed draft pick or future draft consideration in the 1973 draft, but the reviewed sources do not resolve the round, selection number or player produced by that consideration. The archive therefore does not attach one of New York's 1973 picks to this deal without evidence. That uncertainty caps the Knicks' grade: they clearly received a contractual asset, but the realized basketball payoff cannot be measured with the same precision as a known draft selection.

Final Verdict

Slight Knicks Edge, D/C. Golden State receives a D because Williams never played a regular-season game for the Warriors and was waived before opening night. New York receives a C because the Knicks obtained future draft consideration, but the exact 1973 asset and downstream player remain unidentified. The gap stays modest because an unresolved future consideration cannot be treated as a successful draft return merely because Golden State received zero games. Confidence is medium-high on the player movement and waiver, but only medium on New York's complete return because the pick identity is still unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston sold John Gianelli's player rights to New York for cash on September 19, 1972, only months after drafting him 20th overall. Gianelli then played 303 regular-season games for the Knicks across five seasons, appeared in 22 playoff games, and contributed seven postseason appearances to New York's 1973 championship run. He later became a full-time starter, averaging 10.3 points and 8.6 rebounds in 1974-75. In December 1976 the Knicks included Gianelli and cash in the trade for Bob McAdoo and Tom McMillen. Houston's payment is unreported, leaving New York with the clearly stronger realized return.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Houston, New York and league transaction logs agree on the September 19, 1972 structure: Houston sold John Gianelli's player rights to the Knicks. Pro Sports Transactions records New York receiving Gianelli and Houston receiving cash, while Ray Patterson's executive history preserves the same sale from the Rockets side. Houston had selected Gianelli 20th overall in the 1972 draft but moved his rights before he played an NBA game. The cash amount is not reported, so the source-backed archive treats Houston's consideration as verified but unpriced rather than inventing a financial value.

Immediate Championship Value

Gianelli joined a veteran Knicks contender and began as a reserve center. In 1972-73 he played 52 regular-season games, averaged 3.5 points and 2.9 rebounds in 9.9 minutes, and supplied 516 minutes behind Willis Reed and Jerry Lucas. New York went 57-25 and won the NBA championship. Gianelli appeared in seven playoff games and scored 25 points in 55 minutes during that run. His rookie contribution was modest, but the acquisition already produced usable depth on a championship roster in the first season.

Growth Into a Starter

The value expanded quickly after the title season. Gianelli played 70 games in 1973-74 and started 41, averaging 7.3 points and 4.9 rebounds. In 1974-75 he started 79 of 80 games and averaged 10.3 points, 8.6 rebounds and 2.0 assists in 35.0 minutes. He returned for all 82 games in 1975-76, starting 51 and averaging 9.3 points and 6.7 rebounds. Those are not star-level numbers, but they turn a cash purchase of draft rights into several years of dependable starting-center production.

Total Knicks Production

Before the Knicks traded him in December 1976, Gianelli had accumulated 303 regular-season appearances for New York. He scored 2,481 points and collected 1,912 rebounds in those games. He also played 22 postseason games for the Knicks across 1973, 1974 and 1975. That multi-year body of work matters more than the championship label alone. New York did not simply buy a fringe rookie who happened to be on a title roster; it acquired a center who grew into a regular starter and remained under team control for more than four seasons.

Downstream Trade Value

Gianelli still carried transaction value when his Knicks tenure ended. On December 9, 1976, New York traded Gianelli and cash to Buffalo for Bob McAdoo and Tom McMillen. Because the Knicks also sent money, the archive does not pretend Gianelli alone purchased an All-Star scorer and another center. Still, he was a named outgoing player in a major trade that brought McAdoo to New York, so the original 1972 rights purchase retained a measurable downstream asset role after 303 regular-season games of direct production.

Houston's Side

Houston received cash after using the 20th pick on Gianelli. No reviewed source identifies the sale price or connects the proceeds to a later player, pick or transaction. Cash has legitimate organizational value, especially for a franchise deciding not to carry a rookie, but a hindsight archive cannot assign specific basketball production to an unpriced payment. Houston therefore gets credit for monetizing the rights rather than losing Gianelli for nothing, yet that return cannot approach five Knicks seasons, a championship bench role, multiple starting years and later trade utility.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A/C. New York receives an A because a cash purchase produced 303 regular-season games, 22 playoff appearances, a role on the 1973 championship team, two seasons with heavy starting responsibility and a later place in the Bob McAdoo trade. Houston receives a C because it converted Gianelli's rights into cash, but the amount and downstream use are unknown. Confidence is high on the transaction and Gianelli's Knicks production, but only medium on Houston's financial value because the payment is unpriced. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver and Carolina recorded a September 20, 1972 cash agreement involving Wayne Hightower, but the deal did not become a completed player transaction. Basketball-Reference and Pro Sports Transactions preserve the agreed exchange, while later biographical reporting states Denver coach Alex Hannum voided it after Hightower reported late to training camp; Hightower's contract returned to Carolina and Denver did not send the money. Hightower appears only on Denver's preseason roster and played zero 1972-73 regular-season games. This record is therefore retained as a source-reconciled voided transaction, with no winner and no basketball return credited to either side.
perspectives.analysis:
The Recorded Agreement

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Carolina and ABA transaction ledgers all record a September 20, 1972 exchange in which the Rockets sent cash to the Cougars for Wayne Hightower. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same direction, and Alex Hannum's executive record also lists Denver trading cash for Hightower. Taken alone, those ledgers make the move look like a completed cash purchase. The source-backed review found an important second layer, however: later biographical reporting says the arrangement was voided before Hightower joined Denver for the regular season. The archive therefore keeps the dated transaction record but no longer grades it as a completed trade.

Why the Deal Was Voided

Hightower was coming off an abbreviated 1971-72 season with Carolina, where he played only 13 games after a blood-clot issue had disrupted the previous year. Biographical sourcing reports that Carolina agreed to sell him to Denver, but Hightower arrived late to the Rockets' preseason training camp. Hannum then voided the transaction. The same account says Hightower's contract was returned to Carolina and Denver refused to send the agreed cash. That detail changes the evaluation completely: neither the player asset nor the financial consideration became a realized post-transaction return.

Denver Roster Evidence

Denver's 1972-73 roster supports the voided-deal account. A historical Rockets roster archive lists Hightower only under the preseason section rather than among regular-season players. Basketball-Reference's team page likewise shows no Hightower appearance for the 47-37 Rockets. Denver's regular-season frontcourt included Julius Keye, Dave Robisch, Byron Beck, Marv Roberts and others, but Hightower logged zero games, minutes, points or rebounds. The absence is not a small sample produced by injury after the trade; it is consistent with the contract never becoming part of Denver's regular-season roster.

Carolina's Position

Carolina's transaction page records the sale, but the later voiding means the Cougars did not ultimately receive the agreed cash according to the biographical account. Hightower also did not return to the 1972-73 Carolina roster. The historical record therefore describes a failed transfer rather than a conventional one-sided deal. Carolina had attempted to monetize the contract and Denver had attempted to acquire veteran frontcourt depth, yet the agreement unraveled before either side realized the intended asset. No reviewed source identifies a later compensation mechanism that replaced the voided arrangement.

How the Archive Treats It

The canonical record remains useful because multiple transaction ledgers preserve September 20 as an agreement date. Removing it entirely would hide a real historical event in the transaction record. Treating it as an ordinary completed trade would be worse, because that would falsely imply Denver paid cash and acquired Hightower for basketball purposes. The correct source-backed treatment is to preserve the record, flag the deal as voided before completion, mark Hightower as a zero-game Denver preseason presence, and mark the cash as agreed but unpaid. No downstream value should be assigned to either asset.

Final Verdict

No Completed Trade. Denver receives no grade because Hightower's contract was returned and he played zero regular-season games for the Rockets. Carolina receives no grade because the agreed cash was not ultimately sent according to the voided-deal reporting. Confidence is medium-high: the September 20 agreement is strongly corroborated by transaction ledgers, and the zero-game roster outcome is clear, while the voiding mechanics rely on later biographical reporting rather than a surviving team transaction note. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded Steve Hawes' rights to Houston on September 22, 1972 for a 1973 third-round pick that became No. 41 James Lister plus cash. Multiple Basketball-Reference team, league and executive ledgers support September 22, correcting the legacy September 21 date; Houston's own media guide also confirms cash was included. Lister never played an NBA game, while Hawes eventually gave Houston 61 games after two seasons in Italy. The Rockets then traded Hawes for John Johnson, extending the asset chain through 147 Houston games and several later second-round picks. Houston holds the clear hindsight edge.
perspectives.analysis:
Date and Trade Structure

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Houston and league transaction logs all place the Steve Hawes trade on September 22, 1972. Nick Mileti's Cleveland executive ledger and Ray Patterson's Houston ledger use the same date. The legacy archive carried September 21, matching a RealGM roster-history entry, so this review corrects the canonical date to September 22 while preserving September 21 as an alternate recorded date. Basketball-Reference describes the return as Houston's 1973 third-round pick, later No. 41 James Lister. Houston's official media guide adds cash to the Rockets' outgoing package, supporting the fuller Cleveland-side asset record already present in the archive.

Cleveland's Return

The draft component became James Lister, a 6-foot-10 center from Sam Houston State selected 41st overall in 1973. Basketball-Reference's Cleveland draft history shows Lister with no NBA games or statistical line. He therefore produced no regular-season value for the Cavaliers. Cleveland also received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the reviewed sources, so the financial return remains real but unpriced. That prevents an F-level grade, yet there is no traceable player production from the draft asset to pair with the unknown payment.

Hawes Takes the Long Route

Houston did not receive immediate NBA production. Hawes spent 1972-73 and 1973-74 playing professionally in Italy, then made his NBA debut with the Rockets in October 1974. Once he arrived, the rights acquisition became useful. Hawes appeared in 55 games during 1974-75, averaging 5.9 points and 5.0 rebounds in 16.3 minutes. He played six more Houston games in 1975-76. Across those two seasons, the Rockets received 61 regular-season appearances, 907 minutes, 335 points and 293 rebounds from a player whose rights had cost a third-round pick and cash.

The John Johnson Conversion

The strongest part of Houston's return came when the Rockets converted Hawes into another productive player. On November 13, 1975, Houston traded Hawes to Portland for John Johnson. Johnson then played 67 games for the Rockets in 1975-76 and 79 in 1976-77, plus one game at the start of 1977-78, for 147 Houston regular-season appearances. He averaged 9.7 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.9 assists in his first Houston season and 9.3 points the next year. That downstream production makes the original Hawes-rights purchase more valuable than Hawes' own 61 games alone.

Further Downstream Assets

Houston later moved Johnson and continued extracting value. In June 1977 the Rockets traded him to Boston for second-round picks that became Larry Moffett and Buster Matheney; Johnson returned to Houston in October while the Rockets kept those picks. Moffett played 20 Houston games. Houston then traded Johnson to Seattle on October 22, 1977 for two more second-round picks, later used on Paul Mokeski and Billy Williams. Mokeski played 12 games for Houston before continuing a long NBA career elsewhere. The full chain therefore includes direct Hawes production, 147 Johnson games and multiple draft assets, even though not every pick became a useful Rockets player.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, A-/C. Houston receives an A- because the corrected September 22 transaction ultimately produced 61 Hawes games, a productive conversion into John Johnson, 147 more Houston games and several later second-round assets. Cleveland receives a C because it obtained cash and the pick that became James Lister, but the cash amount is unknown and Lister never played in the NBA. Confidence is high on the corrected date, player movement and draft conversion, while the exact cash value remains unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: Cleveland traded Steve Hawes' rights to Houston on September 22, 1972 for a 1973 third-round pick that became No. 41 James Lister plus cash. Multiple Basketball-Reference team, league and executive ledgers support September 22, correcting the legacy September 21 date; Houston's own media guide also confirms cash was included. Lister never played an NBA game, while Hawes eventually gave Houston 61 games after two seasons in Italy. The Rockets then traded Hawes for John Johnson, extending the asset chain through 147 Houston games and several later second-round picks. Houston holds the clear hindsight edge.
analysis:
Date and Trade Structure

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Houston and league transaction logs all place the Steve Hawes trade on September 22, 1972. Nick Mileti's Cleveland executive ledger and Ray Patterson's Houston ledger use the same date. The legacy archive carried September 21, matching a RealGM roster-history entry, so this review corrects the canonical date to September 22 while preserving September 21 as an alternate recorded date. Basketball-Reference describes the return as Houston's 1973 third-round pick, later No. 41 James Lister. Houston's official media guide adds cash to the Rockets' outgoing package, supporting the fuller Cleveland-side asset record already present in the archive.

Cleveland's Return

The draft component became James Lister, a 6-foot-10 center from Sam Houston State selected 41st overall in 1973. Basketball-Reference's Cleveland draft history shows Lister with no NBA games or statistical line. He therefore produced no regular-season value for the Cavaliers. Cleveland also received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the reviewed sources, so the financial return remains real but unpriced. That prevents an F-level grade, yet there is no traceable player production from the draft asset to pair with the unknown payment.

Hawes Takes the Long Route

Houston did not receive immediate NBA production. Hawes spent 1972-73 and 1973-74 playing professionally in Italy, then made his NBA debut with the Rockets in October 1974. Once he arrived, the rights acquisition became useful. Hawes appeared in 55 games during 1974-75, averaging 5.9 points and 5.0 rebounds in 16.3 minutes. He played six more Houston games in 1975-76. Across those two seasons, the Rockets received 61 regular-season appearances, 907 minutes, 335 points and 293 rebounds from a player whose rights had cost a third-round pick and cash.

The strongest part of Houston's return came when the Rockets converted Hawes into another productive player. On November 13, 1975, Houston traded Hawes to Portland for John Johnson. Johnson then played 67 games for the Rockets in 1975-76 and 79 in 1976-77, plus one game at the start of 1977-78, for 147 Houston regular-season appearances. Houston later moved Johnson and continued extracting value. perspectives.analysis:
Why the 1972 record Fails

The legacy archive record claims Cleveland sent Lenny Wilkens to Portland on September 24, 1972 for a draft pick and cash. That cannot be reconciled with the season record. Cleveland had acquired Wilkens and Barry Clemens from Seattle for Butch Beard on August 23, 1972. Wilkens then played 75 regular-season games for Cleveland in 1972-73, averaging 20.5 points and 8.4 assists while making the All-Star team. He remained with the Cavaliers for 74 more games in 1973-74. A Portland transfer in September 1972 would be incompatible with those documented Cleveland seasons.

Transaction Ledgers

Basketball-Reference's 1972-73 Cleveland transaction page lists the August 23 Wilkens acquisition, the August 31 Jim Cleamons trade, the September 22 Steve Hawes deal and later Cleveland moves. It does not contain a September 24 Wilkens transaction. The 1972-73 Portland transaction page likewise has no acquisition of Wilkens. The league-wide 1972-73 transaction ledger also lacks such a deal. Those omissions align with the player statistics showing Wilkens active for Cleveland throughout the next two seasons.

The Real Portland Transaction

The actual move occurred more than two years later. Basketball-Reference's 1974-75 Cleveland page records October 7, 1974 as the date Cleveland sold Wilkens' player rights to Portland. Portland's 1974-75 ledger records the same acquisition. RealGM also places the move on October 7, 1974, and historical biographical accounts describe Wilkens joining Portland as player-coach for his final NBA playing season. That verified event already exists in this archive as nba-trade-cle-1974-0018.

Asset Mismatch

The false 1972 record also claims Cleveland received both a draft pick and cash. The verified 1974 Basketball-Reference entries describe a sale of Wilkens' rights, not a September 1972 pick-and-cash exchange. No reviewed 1972 source identifies the draft asset attached to this legacy archive entry, and no Cleveland draft outcome can be responsibly linked to it. Preserving those assets as realized 1972 returns would create a fictional branch in the transaction tree.

Archive Treatment

The correct action is structural rather than evaluative. This record should not receive a winner, grades or hindsight value because the dated transaction did not occur. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results. Its player, pick and cash assets are marked as invalid for realized-value analysis, and the record points to the verified October 7, 1974 canonical transaction. The false September 1972 route is also removed from the launch-eligibility candidate set.

Final Resolution

Record Superseded. No team receives a grade. The verified Lenny Wilkens-to-Portland transaction is the October 7, 1974 sale already stored as nba-trade-cle-1974-0018. Confidence is high because Wilkens' Cleveland game logs, both teams' transaction ledgers and the league chronology all contradict a September 24, 1972 Portland move while independently supporting the 1974 sale.

perspectives.summary: Detroit traded Howie Komives to Buffalo on September 29, 1972 for the Braves' 1973 second-round pick, which became No. 20. Detroit never used the selection on Mike D'Antoni; on November 9 it sent that pick to Kansas City-Omaha for John Mengelt. Mengelt then played 291 regular-season games for the Pistons across four seasons, averaging 10.3 points per game over that span. Komives gave Buffalo 67 games at 6.1 points and 3.6 assists before leaving after one season. The pick-to-Mengelt conversion makes Detroit the clear long-term winner.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Buffalo and league transaction ledgers agree on the September 29, 1972 trade: the Pistons sent Howie Komives to the Braves for Buffalo's 1973 second-round pick. Pro Sports Transactions identifies that selection as No. 20, the pick later used on Mike D'Antoni. Edwin Coil's Detroit executive record confirms the same transaction. A later Pistons media guide lists the date as September 30, one day later than the league and team ledgers; this archive keeps September 29 as the canonical date because the contemporaneous transaction logs agree there.

Buffalo's Return

Komives was 31 and had already played four seasons in Detroit after his earlier Knicks career. Buffalo got a useful veteran point guard for one season. He appeared in 67 games in 1972-73, averaging 6.1 points, 3.6 assists and 1.8 rebounds in 21.9 minutes. That production had real roster value for a young Braves team featuring Bob McAdoo and Randy Smith, even though Buffalo finished 21-61. Komives did not remain part of the club's later rise; he left before the 1973-74 season and signed with Kansas City-Omaha as a free agent.

Detroit Did Not Draft D'Antoni

The most important chain correction is that Detroit never used the acquired pick on D'Antoni. On November 9, 1972, the Pistons traded the same Buffalo second-round selection to Kansas City-Omaha for John Mengelt. Basketball-Reference's Detroit transaction ledger explicitly connects the No. 20 pick to that Mengelt trade. Kansas City-Omaha later used the selection on D'Antoni in the 1973 draft. D'Antoni therefore belongs in the draft lineage of the asset, but he should not be credited as a Detroit player return from the Komives trade.

Mengelt's Detroit Value

The pick conversion produced substantially more on-court value for Detroit than Komives produced in Buffalo. Mengelt played 67 games for the Pistons in 1972-73, then 77 in 1973-74, 80 in 1974-75 and 67 in 1975-76. Across those four seasons, Detroit received 291 regular-season games. Mengelt averaged 10.5 points in his first Pistons season, 8.8 in the next, 11.0 in 1974-75 and 10.7 in 1975-76. He was not a star, but he became a durable rotation scorer who stayed useful for several seasons.

End of the Chain

Detroit eventually sold Mengelt's player rights to Chicago on November 18, 1976. The reviewed transaction logs do not report a cash amount, so that final financial return cannot be quantified. The important point is that the original Buffalo pick had already produced four years and 291 games of direct Pistons value before the asset left the roster. Buffalo's side, by contrast, produced one season and 67 games from Komives, with no documented downstream compensation when he departed.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A-/B-. Detroit receives an A- because the second-round pick was converted into John Mengelt, who supplied 291 games and four seasons of rotation scoring before his rights were later sold. Buffalo receives a B- because Komives gave the Braves 67 games of competent veteran point-guard play, but the return lasted only one season and did not create a retained downstream asset. Confidence is high on the trade, pick lineage and Mengelt conversion. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia acquired Dale Schlueter from Portland for Dave Wohl on October 2, 1972. Schlueter played 78 games for the 76ers that season, averaging 5.4 points and 4.5 rebounds in 14.6 minutes, then Philadelphia traded him to Atlanta for Don May on February 1, 1973. May added 82 games for Philadelphia across the rest of 1972-73 and 1973-74. Portland received only 22 games from Wohl before waiving him on December 6, when Buffalo claimed him. Philadelphia's direct production and second trade return give the 76ers the stronger realized value.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, Portland and league transaction pages agree that the 76ers traded Dave Wohl to the Trail Blazers for Dale Schlueter on October 2, 1972. The swap was a direct player-for-player move with no pick or cash component in the reviewed ledgers. Both players were established role players: Schlueter was a veteran center who had averaged 11.7 points and 10.6 rebounds for Portland the previous season, while Wohl was a second-year point guard coming off 79 games for Philadelphia as a rookie. That makes the trade straightforward to evaluate through the production each team actually retained.

Schlueter in Philadelphia

Schlueter became one of the more durable players on a historically bad 76ers team. He appeared in 78 games during 1972-73, started ten, and averaged 5.4 points, 4.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 14.6 minutes. He totaled 1,136 minutes and 354 rebounds. Philadelphia went 9-73, so his individual contribution did not translate into team success, but the trade still produced a full season of reliable center minutes. For a one-for-one exchange, that volume alone already exceeded what Portland received from Wohl.

Wohl's Short Portland Stay

Wohl played only 22 games for the Trail Blazers. He averaged 5.4 points and 3.1 assists in 17.9 minutes and logged 393 total minutes. Portland then waived him on December 6, 1972, barely two months after the trade. Buffalo claimed him immediately. Wohl went on to play 56 games for the Braves during the same season and remained an NBA guard for several more years, but Portland received no compensation for that later career because its relationship with him ended on waivers. The Blazers' realized return is therefore limited to those 22 appearances.

Philadelphia Converts Schlueter Again

Philadelphia extracted a second return from Schlueter instead of simply letting him leave. On February 1, 1973, the 76ers traded him to Atlanta for Don May. May played 26 games for Philadelphia over the remainder of 1972-73 and averaged 11.9 points and 5.5 rebounds in 23.2 minutes. He returned for 56 games in 1973-74, giving the 76ers 82 regular-season appearances across two seasons after the Schlueter conversion. That downstream value extends the original Wohl trade well beyond Schlueter's own Philadelphia games.

How Much the Team Context Counts

Neither side turned this trade into a competitive breakthrough. Philadelphia's 1972-73 season remains the worst full-season record in franchise history, and Portland also missed the playoffs. The grade therefore should not treat Schlueter's 78 games or May's later production as star-level value. Still, hindsight grading is about realized asset value, not team reputation alone. Philadelphia received a playable center, then used that center to acquire another rotation player. Portland received a guard it waived after 22 games.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, B+/D+. Philadelphia receives a B+ because Schlueter supplied 78 games and the club then converted him into Don May, who added 82 more Philadelphia appearances across two seasons. Portland receives a D+ because Wohl gave the Blazers only 22 games before being waived for no return. Schlueter became one of the more durable players on a historically bad 76ers team. He appeared in 78 games during 1972-73, started ten, and averaged 5.4 points, 4.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 14.6 minutes. He totaled 1,136 minutes and 354 rebounds. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Date Correction and Trade Structure

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, New York and league transaction ledgers all place the Eddie Mast trade on October 9, 1972. Richie Guerin's Atlanta executive record and Red Holzman's New York record use the same date. The legacy archive carried October 7 from an older legacy source, so this review corrects the canonical trade date to October 9 while retaining the old date as a superseded source value. The basketball structure is straightforward: Atlanta received Mast, and New York received Atlanta's 1973 second-round pick, later used at No. 28 on Pat McFarland.

Atlanta's Return

Mast had barely played for the Knicks, appearing in only 12 regular-season games across 1970-71 and 1971-72. Atlanta gave him a larger role after the trade. In 1972-73 he appeared in 42 games, logged 447 minutes, scored 119 points and collected 136 rebounds. That works out to 2.8 points and 3.2 rebounds in 10.6 minutes per game. The Hawks went 46-36 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals, so Mast's contribution was limited to reserve frontcourt depth rather than a major rotation role. Still, 42 actual NBA appearances represent a measurable return from the transaction.

New York's Draft Asset

The Knicks held the second-round pick through the 1973 draft and used it on McFarland with the 28th overall selection. That identifies the pick outcome precisely, but it does not create NBA production for New York. McFarland never appeared in an NBA game. Basketball-Reference lists his professional career entirely in the ABA: 67 games for the Denver Rockets in 1973-74, 70 for the Denver Nuggets in 1974-75 and 11 for the San Diego Sails in 1975-76. Those games cannot be credited to the Knicks because New York never received NBA service or a later trade return from the drafted player.

Why the Pick Still Has Some Value

A second-round selection is not worthless simply because the selected player never appeared for the drafting team. New York acquired a real draft asset and exercised it on a player who proved capable of playing 148 professional ABA games. The hindsight grade therefore should not treat the Knicks' side as if it received literally nothing on transaction day. But realized-value grading follows what the franchise ultimately obtained from the asset. In New York's case, no NBA games, minutes, points, trade return or compensatory pick are documented from McFarland.

Mast's Limited Ceiling

Atlanta's advantage also needs to stay modest. Mast did not become a long-term Hawk. His 42-game 1972-73 season was his only year in Atlanta and his final NBA season. He played only 447 minutes, and no later transaction converted him into another player or pick. The Hawks therefore received useful roster depth rather than a lasting asset chain. That makes this a small win, not a franchise-changing trade. The comparison comes down to 42 documented NBA games on one side versus a second-round pick that produced zero Knicks appearances on the other.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge, B-/D+. Atlanta receives a B- because Mast supplied 42 regular-season games and useful reserve minutes on a 46-win playoff team. New York receives a D+ because the pick became McFarland, who never played in the NBA or generated a documented Knicks trade return, though the club did acquire and exercise a legitimate second-round asset. Confidence is high on the corrected October 9 date, the pick outcome and the player production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Kansas City-Omaha acquired Toby Kimball from Milwaukee on October 9, 1972 for a 1973 fourth-round pick that became No. 59 Clyde Turner plus cash. Kimball gave the Kings 67 games that season, averaging 3.5 points and 2.9 rebounds in 9.6 minutes, before Kansas City-Omaha sold his rights to Philadelphia the following September. Milwaukee used the pick on Turner, who never played an NBA game, while the cash amount is not preserved in the reviewed sources. The Kings receive a slight hindsight edge because they realized one season of rotation value.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Kansas City-Omaha and league transaction pages agree that the Kings acquired Toby Kimball from the Bucks on October 9, 1972 for a 1973 fourth-round pick that later became No. 59 Clyde Turner. Pro Sports Transactions adds a second Milwaukee asset: cash. A 1973 Kansas City-Omaha media guide independently describes Kimball as acquired from Milwaukee for a draft choice and cash, which supports keeping both pieces in the canonical ledger. The payment amount is not reported, so Milwaukee's financial return is verified but unpriced.

Kansas City-Omaha's Return

Kimball was a 30-year-old veteran frontcourt reserve when the Kings acquired him. He played 67 games in 1972-73, averaging 3.5 points and 2.9 rebounds in 9.6 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 643 minutes, 236 points and 191 rebounds. Those numbers are modest, but they are genuine NBA production from a fourth-round pick-and-cash package. On a 36-46 team, Kimball functioned as a low-minute reserve behind the club's heavier frontcourt options rather than as a core starter.

Milwaukee's Draft Return

The draft component did not become NBA production for the Bucks. Milwaukee used the acquired selection on Minnesota forward Clyde Turner with the 59th pick in the 1973 draft. The Bucks' draft history shows no NBA games or statistical line for Turner. That leaves the cash payment as Milwaukee's only realized return that can be credited with certainty. Because the amount is unknown, it cannot be converted into a basketball-equivalent value or treated as a major offset to Kimball's 67 games.

Kimball's Next Move

Kansas City-Omaha did not keep Kimball beyond one season. On September 28, 1973, the Kings sold his player rights to Philadelphia. Basketball-Reference records the sale, and Kimball then played 75 games for the 76ers in 1973-74. Those Philadelphia games do not count as Kansas City-Omaha production, but the sale shows the Kings retained some residual contractual value after receiving a season of direct play. The sale price is not preserved in the reviewed transaction pages, so the downstream cash cannot be quantified.

Hindsight Comparison

This is a small transaction rather than a franchise-changing one. Kansas City-Omaha received one year of usable reserve minutes and later sold the player's rights. Milwaukee received a fourth-round selection that produced no NBA games plus an unpriced cash component. The cash keeps the Bucks from receiving a failing grade, but the basketball ledger favors the Kings because Kimball actually appeared in 67 games and the club still had an asset to sell when his season ended.

Final Verdict

Slight Kings Edge, B-/C+. Kansas City-Omaha receives a B- for 67 games of reserve frontcourt production and a later rights sale. Milwaukee receives a C+ because the Bucks obtained cash and the No. 59 pick, but Clyde Turner never played in the NBA and the payment cannot be valued precisely. Confidence is high on the player movement, pick identity and Kimball production, with moderate uncertainty around the unreported cash amounts. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Counts played seven games for the 76ers before being packaged with Bill Bridges for Leroy Ellis and John Trapp. Philadelphia gets the hindsight edge because the pick remained useful trade currency while Gregor's Bucks stay lasted 88 minutes.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
The Direct Trade

Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers all place the exchange on October 10, 1972: the Bucks sent a 1973 second-round pick to the 76ers for Gary Gregor. Wayne Embry's executive ledger records the same deal. The pick later became No. 33, used by Phoenix on Gary Melchionni. Pro Sports Transactions also records cash moving from Milwaukee, and a historical Bucks media guide independently includes cash, though that guide labels the draft choice as a 1974 second-rounder. Because the team, league and same-day Phoenix chain consistently identify the asset as a 1973 second-round pick, the archive keeps 1973 as the canonical year and preserves the cash as a verified but unpriced secondary component.

Gregor's Milwaukee Stay

Milwaukee received almost no lasting NBA value from Gregor. He appeared in nine games for the Bucks, totaling 88 minutes, 27 points, 32 rebounds and nine assists. His averages were 3.0 points and 3.6 rebounds in 9.8 minutes. Pro Sports Transactions records Milwaukee waiving him on November 15, barely five weeks after the trade. Gregor then joined the New York Nets of the ABA in December and played 40 games there during 1972-73. Those ABA games demonstrate that he still had professional value, but they cannot be credited to Milwaukee after the Bucks released him.

Philadelphia's Same-Day Pick Conversion

Philadelphia did not keep the pick until draft night. On the same date, the 76ers traded a 1973 second-round selection to Phoenix for veteran center Mel Counts. The Philadelphia and Phoenix transaction ledgers both identify that selection as the pick later used on Gary Melchionni, linking Milwaukee's outgoing draft asset to the Suns transaction. Pro Sports Transactions describes the activity as a three-club transaction, while Basketball-Reference presents the Milwaukee-Philadelphia and Philadelphia-Phoenix exchanges as separate trades. For this archive, Milwaukee's canonical record remains bilateral, with Phoenix treated only as downstream pick lineage rather than a direct Bucks counterparty.

Counts and the Next Trade

Counts played only seven games for Philadelphia, logging 47 minutes and scoring ten points. His direct production was therefore even smaller than Gregor's Milwaukee stint. The difference is that Philadelphia retained transactional value. On November 2, the 76ers packaged Counts with Bill Bridges and sent them to the Los Angeles Lakers for Leroy Ellis and John Trapp. Because Bridges was a substantial part of that later package, the original Milwaukee pick cannot be credited with all of Ellis and Trapp's value. It can, however, be credited with helping Philadelphia obtain Counts, who remained a named asset in a subsequent trade less than a month later.

Why Melchionni Is Not a Philadelphia Return

The legacy asset label says the pick became Gary Melchionni, which is useful for draft-lineage identification but can be misleading if read as Philadelphia player production. Phoenix held the selection at draft time and chose Melchionni 33rd overall in 1973. He never played for Philadelphia as a result of this transaction. The source-backed record therefore keeps his name attached to the pick only as the final selection identity and marks the real Philadelphia return as the pick's same-day conversion into Counts. That distinction prevents downstream draft identity from being double-counted as 76ers on-court value.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, B/D+. Philadelphia receives a B because the second-round pick and cash gave the club immediate trade flexibility: the pick was rerouted for Counts, and Counts remained part of another trade three weeks later. The grade stops well short of elite because Counts contributed only seven Philadelphia games and cannot be assigned the full value of the later Bridges package. Milwaukee receives a D+ because Gregor played just nine games and 88 minutes before being waived. Confidence is high on the player movement, pick identity and same-day Phoenix routing, with moderate uncertainty on the cash detail because the supporting records disagree on the pick year even while agreeing that cash was included. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Dennis Awtrey from Philadelphia on October 18, 1972 for a 1973 second-round pick that became No. 32 Caldwell Jones plus cash. Awtrey gave the Bulls 147 regular-season games across two seasons before New Orleans selected him in the 1974 expansion draft. Philadelphia used the pick on Jones, who spent three seasons in the ABA before joining the 76ers in 1976. Jones then played 482 regular-season games for Philadelphia, earned two All-Defensive First Team selections, reached three NBA Finals, and became part of the 1982 trade for Moses Malone. That downstream return makes Philadelphia the clear winner despite Chicago receiving a useful center.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Philadelphia and league transaction pages agree that the Bulls acquired Dennis Awtrey on October 18, 1972 for a 1973 second-round pick later used on Caldwell Jones. Pro Sports Transactions and Chicago's official historical media guide add cash to the Bulls' outgoing package. The draft-trade ledger identifies the selection as No. 32. That pick itself had earlier reached Chicago from New York in the Charlie Paulk deal, but the relevant value chain here begins when Chicago sent it to Philadelphia for Awtrey. The cash amount is not reported, so it remains verified but unpriced.

Awtrey's Chicago Value

Awtrey immediately became a useful Bulls rotation center. He played 79 games for Chicago in 1972-73, totaling 1,650 minutes while averaging 4.7 points, 5.5 rebounds and 2.8 assists. He returned for 68 games in 1973-74. Across the two seasons Chicago received 147 regular-season appearances from a dependable defensive big on teams that won 51 and 54 games. That is legitimate value, and it is enough to keep the Bulls' grade above the low marks suggested by a simple comparison with Jones' eventual career.

Chicago's Asset Ends in the Expansion Draft

The Bulls did not receive a trade return when Awtrey's Chicago tenure ended. On May 20, 1974, the New Orleans Jazz selected him from Chicago in the NBA expansion draft. That means Chicago's realized chain from the 1972 deal stops after two seasons and 147 games. Awtrey later continued his NBA career with Phoenix, Boston and Seattle, but those later games belong to other franchises. His Bulls stint was useful and competitive, yet it did not create a downstream player or draft asset for Chicago when he left.

Philadelphia Drafts Caldwell Jones

Philadelphia used the acquired second-round selection on Caldwell Jones with the 32nd pick of the 1973 draft. Jones did not immediately join the NBA; he began his professional career in the ABA and played there through the 1975-76 season. He entered the 76ers' lineup in 1976-77 and immediately became a major defensive frontcourt piece, starting 57 games and averaging 8.1 rebounds with 2.4 blocks. The delayed arrival matters for timing, but it does not erase the connection between Philadelphia's acquired pick and the player it selected.

Six Seasons of 76ers Production

Jones played 82, 80, 78, 80, 81 and 81 regular-season games for Philadelphia from 1976-77 through 1981-82, a total of 482. He became a full-time starter for much of that span and made the NBA All-Defensive First Team in both 1980-81 and 1981-82. He also played on Philadelphia teams that reached the NBA Finals in 1977, 1980 and 1982. Jones was not a high-volume scorer, but his rebounding and rim protection supplied sustained value that dwarfed the two-season Chicago return.

The Moses Malone Conversion

Philadelphia extracted one more major layer from the asset. On September 15, 1982, the 76ers traded Jones and a 1983 first-round pick to Houston for Moses Malone after the Rockets matched Philadelphia's offer sheet. Jones alone did not purchase Malone, and the first-round pick became Rodney McCray, so the original 1973 second-round selection should not be credited with the entire trade. It was nevertheless one of the two named assets Philadelphia surrendered to acquire the reigning MVP, who immediately became the centerpiece of the 1982-83 championship team.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/B. Philadelphia receives an A+ because one second-round pick produced Caldwell Jones, 482 regular-season games, two All-Defensive First Team selections, three Finals runs and a later role in the Moses Malone acquisition. Chicago receives a B because Awtrey was a useful two-season center who played 147 games for strong Bulls teams, but the asset chain ended when New Orleans selected him in the expansion draft. The unpriced cash adds value to Philadelphia without changing the direction of the result. Confidence is high on the trade, pick identity, player production and downstream Malone transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Gar Heard and Seattle's 1973 third-round pick from the SuperSonics for Kenny McIntosh on October 20, 1972. Heard immediately played 78 games for the Bulls, averaging 10.3 points and 5.7 rebounds, while the pick became No. 39 Martin Terry, who never appeared in an NBA game. McIntosh gave Seattle 131 games across parts of three seasons, including 69 games at 7.4 points and 5.2 rebounds in 1973-74. Chicago then included Heard with Kevin Kunnert in a 1973 trade that returned John Hummer and two second-round picks. The Bulls hold a modest hindsight edge, but Seattle received real multi-season value.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Seattle and league transaction pages agree on the October 20, 1972 structure: the Bulls sent Kenny McIntosh to the SuperSonics for Gar Heard and Seattle's 1973 third-round pick. Chicago used that selection at No. 39 on Arkansas guard Martin Terry. The trade therefore gave Chicago one immediate rotation player plus a draft asset, while Seattle received a young forward who had played only 46 games for the Bulls. The reviewed sources do not add cash or another hidden component, so the canonical ledger remains a straightforward player-for-player-and-pick transaction.

Heard's Chicago Season

Heard became useful immediately. After appearing in only three games for Seattle at the start of 1972-73, he played 78 for Chicago. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,535 minutes, 807 points and 447 rebounds, or 10.3 points and 5.7 rebounds in 19.7 minutes per game. Chicago went 51-31 and reached the Western Conference semifinals. Heard was not a featured star, but his scoring rate and rebounding gave the Bulls much more immediate production than the player they surrendered produced for Seattle that season. He also appeared in two playoff games before the Bulls' postseason ended.

The Martin Terry Pick

The draft asset added little realized value. Chicago selected Martin Terry with the 39th pick in the 1973 draft. Basketball-Reference lists Terry as a Chicago draft choice but shows no NBA statistical line. The pick therefore produced zero NBA games for the Bulls. That prevents the extra selection from turning the trade into a major draft win, yet it still matters that Chicago received an additional asset on top of a productive player. The source-backed ledger marks Terry as a verified zero-game draft outcome rather than treating the third-round pick as unresolved.

McIntosh in Seattle

Seattle received more longevity from McIntosh than the original shorthand suggests. He played 56 games for the SuperSonics in 1972-73, averaging 4.5 points and 4.0 rebounds in 19.7 minutes. He then appeared in 69 games in 1973-74 and increased his role to 29.8 minutes, 7.4 points and 5.2 rebounds per game. McIntosh played six more Seattle games in 1974-75. In all, the SuperSonics received 131 regular-season appearances, 3,262 minutes, 783 points and 598 rebounds. He was a legitimate rotation player, which keeps Seattle's grade respectable despite Heard's stronger per-game impact.

Heard's Downstream Value

Chicago did not simply lose Heard for nothing after one season. On September 10, 1973, the Bulls traded Heard and 1973 first-round pick Kevin Kunnert to Buffalo for John Hummer plus second-round picks in 1974 and 1975. That package later produced Leon Benbow with the 1974 pick, while Hummer played 18 Chicago games before being traded to Seattle for another 1975 second-round pick. Heard cannot be credited with the entire Buffalo return because Kunnert was a meaningful co-asset, so the archive treats the downstream value as supporting evidence rather than assigning all later players and picks to this 1972 trade.

Hindsight Comparison

The direct comparison is closer than the old A-/C shorthand implied. Heard gave Chicago 78 games at 10.3 points and 5.7 rebounds, while McIntosh gave Seattle 131 games and stayed in a larger role for most of 1973-74. Chicago's advantage comes from receiving the more productive player immediately, adding a draft pick at no extra player cost, and retaining enough value in Heard to use him in another multi-asset trade the next year. Seattle's side was useful but did not produce a comparable downstream transaction in the reviewed record.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, A-/B. Chicago receives an A- because Heard supplied a strong 78-game season, the Bulls also received the No. 39 pick, and Heard remained a tradable asset in the 1973 Buffalo deal. Seattle receives a B because McIntosh played 131 games across parts of three seasons and provided legitimate rotation minutes, even though his scoring efficiency and overall impact were lower. Martin Terry's zero-game outcome limits Chicago's draft bonus, and the Kunnert component prevents over-crediting Heard for the later Buffalo package. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, player production, draft identity and immediate downstream transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Portland, league and executive transaction logs agree that the Cavaliers traded Charlie Davis to the Trail Blazers on October 24, 1972 for Portland's 1974 third-round pick. Cleveland later used that selection at No. 38 on Clarence "Foots" Walker. Portland's official historical media guide adds cash to the Blazers' outgoing package, matching the cash asset preserved in the legacy archive entry. Because the amount is not reported, the archive credits Cleveland with receiving cash but does not assign it a numerical basketball value. The draft pick remains the transaction's decisive asset.

Portland's Charlie Davis Return

Davis immediately joined the Portland rotation. He played 69 games for the Trail Blazers in 1972-73, logging 1,333 minutes while averaging 8.9 points, 1.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists. Basketball-Reference credits him with 612 points that season. His role collapsed the next year: Davis appeared in only eight games in 1973-74, totaling 90 minutes and 31 points. Portland's media guide records the club waiving him on October 30, 1973. In all, the Blazers received 77 regular-season games, 1,423 minutes and 643 points before the player asset left without a trade return.

Cleveland Waits for the Pick

Cleveland had to wait until the 1974 draft to realize its main return. The Cavaliers selected Walker 38th overall out of West Georgia. He immediately made the NBA roster and played 72 games as a rookie in 1974-75. Walker averaged only 4.2 points and 2.7 assists in 14.9 minutes, but the early role demonstrated that the third-round pick had already become a usable rotation guard rather than a speculative asset that never reached the league. He then appeared in 81 games during Cleveland's 1975-76 breakthrough season.

Six Seasons of Cavaliers Value

Walker remained with Cleveland through 1979-80. His Cavaliers game totals were 72, 81, 62, 81, 55 and 76, or 427 regular-season appearances across six seasons. His role grew over time. He averaged 5.6 assists in 1977-78, 5.8 in 1978-79 and 8.0 in 1979-80, when he also scored 9.4 points per game in 31.9 minutes. He was never an All-Star, but a third-round pick producing six seasons and eventually handling full-time point-guard duties represents unusually strong realized value for the draft slot.

Different Types of Return

Portland's side should not be dismissed. Davis gave the Blazers one full season of legitimate scoring and another short stint before his release. A 77-game return is meaningful for a player acquired with a third-round pick and cash. The difference is duration. Cleveland transformed that same pick into 427 games, multiple seasons of rotation minutes and several years of starting-level point-guard responsibility. The unpriced cash only adds to Cleveland's side rather than being needed to create the advantage.

Downstream Context

Walker's Cleveland value continued until September 24, 1980, when the Cavaliers traded him to New Jersey. His later Nets production is not part of this direct return, but the fact that Cleveland still had a movable player asset after six seasons reinforces the durability of the original pick. Davis, by contrast, was waived by Portland after eight games in his second Blazers season. The transaction therefore produced both more direct games and a longer asset life for Cleveland.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A/B-. Cleveland receives an A because Portland's third-round pick became Foots Walker, who supplied 427 regular-season games over six seasons and developed into the club's primary point guard by the end of the decade; the unpriced cash is additional value. Portland receives a B- because Davis contributed 77 games and one useful scoring season, but he was waived before the end of 1973 and produced no retained downstream asset. Confidence is high on the pick identity, player production and transaction date; the only material uncertainty is the cash amount, which the official Portland media guide confirms without pricing. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

houston-rockets.summary: Portland acquired Greg Smith from Houston for Stan McKenzie on October 27, 1972. Smith became a multi-season Trail Blazers rotation forward, playing 195 regular-season games for Portland from 1972-73 through one appearance in 1975-76 and averaging 7.4 points and 5.2 rebounds in his first Blazers season. McKenzie played 37 games for Houston across parts of two seasons, averaging 2.9 points in only 8.1 minutes, before the Rockets waived him on November 9, 1973. Portland receives the clear hindsight edge because Smith supplied far more games, minutes and retained roster value.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Houston, Portland and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 27, 1972 trade: the Rockets sent Greg Smith to the Trail Blazers for Stan McKenzie. Ray Patterson's Houston executive record and Harry Glickman's Portland executive record preserve the same two-player structure. No draft choice, cash payment or future consideration appears in the reviewed primary transaction logs. The source-backed record therefore remains a direct player-for-player exchange. The Smith identity is the 1947-born Western Kentucky forward, not the later NBA center with the same common name.

Portland's Immediate Return

Smith arrived after playing four games for Houston in 1972-73 and immediately became a regular member of Portland's rotation. He appeared in 72 games for the Trail Blazers that season, averaging 7.4 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 21.8 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,569 minutes, 533 points and 375 rebounds for Portland in that first season alone. Those totals already exceed the entire Houston production McKenzie would provide after the exchange, and Smith remained with the Blazers for several more seasons.

Three More Seasons in Portland

Smith played 67 games for Portland in 1973-74 and another 55 in 1974-75, then made one final appearance in 1975-76. Across his Portland tenure, he totaled 195 regular-season games. His role diminished after the first season, but he still supplied 878 minutes in 1973-74 and 519 in 1974-75. Portland finally waived him on November 7, 1975. The move produced no trade return, yet the Blazers had already received roughly three full seasons of rotational value from a player acquired straight up for McKenzie.

Houston's McKenzie Return

McKenzie had been a much larger scorer for Portland before the trade, averaging 13.5 points across his first three Trail Blazers seasons. That history gave Houston a reasonable basis for the deal, but the fit did not carry over. He played 26 games for the Rockets in 1972-73, averaging 3.3 points in 7.2 minutes. He returned for only 11 games in 1973-74, averaging 1.8 points in 10.2 minutes. Houston's total return was 37 regular-season appearances, 299 minutes and 106 points.

The Asset Chain Ends Quickly for Houston

Basketball-Reference's 1973-74 Houston transaction page records the Rockets waiving McKenzie on November 9, 1973. That ended Houston's asset chain a little more than a year after the original trade. Unlike several neighboring archive transactions in which a player was later flipped for another asset, McKenzie did not generate a documented draft pick or player return when his Rockets tenure ended. His later professional career therefore does not add downstream value to Houston's side of this exchange.

Why the Legacy Grades Were Too Harsh

The legacy Houston perspective had both teams in the D range, while the Portland perspective called the trade roughly even. The source-backed production record supports a wider gap. Portland received 195 games and multiple seasons from Smith; Houston received 37 low-minute games from McKenzie. Smith's Portland role was not star-level, and his efficiency and minutes declined after 1972-73, so the transaction does not justify an elite grade. It does, however, represent a useful straight-up roster win for the Blazers.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win, B+/D+. Portland receives a B+ because Greg Smith supplied 195 regular-season games over parts of four seasons, including a productive 72-game first year after the trade. Houston receives a D+ because McKenzie appeared in only 37 games, scored 106 points and was waived in November 1973 without a documented downstream return. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, player identities, production totals and exit dates. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Detroit and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 31, 1972 trade: the Hawks sent Don Adams to the Pistons for Detroit's 1973 second-round pick. Edwin Coil's Detroit executive record confirms the same structure. Atlanta later used the selection at No. 27 on Villanova guard Tom Ingelsby. No cash, future consideration or additional player appears in the reviewed transaction logs, so the canonical record remains a direct player-for-pick deal.

Adams Immediately Becomes a Detroit Regular

Adams had played only four games for Atlanta in 1972-73 before the trade. With Detroit, his role expanded sharply. He appeared in 70 games that season, averaging 9.3 points, 6.0 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 25.7 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,798 minutes, 649 points and 419 rebounds for the Pistons after the move. The production was not star-level, but Detroit converted one future second-round pick into an established frontcourt rotation player almost immediately.

His Best Pistons Season

Adams became even more important in 1973-74. He played 74 games and averaged 10.3 points, 6.1 rebounds and 1.9 assists in 31.1 minutes. Detroit went 52-30 and reached the Western Conference semifinals, and Adams also appeared in seven playoff games at 36.6 minutes per contest. That season is the strongest evidence for Detroit's side of the trade: a second-round asset produced starter-level minutes on one of the league's better teams.

A Third Season Before the Waiver

Adams remained with Detroit for 51 games in 1974-75, averaging 5.9 points and 4.8 rebounds in 27.0 minutes. On February 18, 1975, the Pistons waived him. His Detroit tenure therefore ended without a trade return, but by then the club had already received 195 regular-season appearances across parts of three seasons. The absence of a downstream asset limits the ceiling on Detroit's grade, yet the quantity of direct play comfortably exceeds a typical second-round outcome.

Atlanta Uses the Pick on Tom Ingelsby

The Hawks used the acquired selection on Tom Ingelsby with the 27th pick of the 1973 draft. Ingelsby played 48 games for Atlanta in 1973-74, averaging 2.7 points, 0.9 rebounds and 0.8 assists in 8.3 minutes. His total NBA production for the Hawks was 398 minutes and 129 points. He did not appear for Atlanta again after that rookie season; his later professional games came in the ABA with the Spirits of St. Louis and San Diego Sails. Those games cannot be credited to the Hawks' side of this transaction.

Comparing the Realized Returns

Atlanta did at least turn Adams into a real NBA player rather than a failed draft pick. Ingelsby reached the league and supplied 48 games, which keeps the Hawks from receiving the lowest possible grade. The difference is scale. Adams gave Detroit more than four times as many regular-season games, thousands more minutes and two seasons of substantial frontcourt responsibility. The 1973-74 Pistons also used him in a serious playoff rotation, while Ingelsby's Atlanta role never grew beyond limited reserve minutes.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A-/C. Detroit receives an A- because Adams produced 195 regular-season games, a 10.3-point season and meaningful playoff minutes after being acquired for one second-round pick. Atlanta receives a C because No. 27 pick Tom Ingelsby reached the NBA but supplied only 48 games and one limited season for the Hawks before leaving the league. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, pick identity, player production and Adams' 1975 waiver. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
