houston-rockets.summary: Kansas City-Omaha acquired Dick Gibbs' player rights from Houston on November 2, 1972 in a cash sale. Gibbs then played 66 games for the Kings that season, totaling 733 minutes and 207 points while averaging 3.1 points and 1.4 rebounds. Houston had used him for only one two-minute appearance in 1972-73 before selling the rights. The reviewed transaction ledgers do not preserve the cash amount, so Houston's return cannot be priced. Kansas City-Omaha gets the hindsight edge because the rights immediately became a full season of usable reserve minutes, while the Rockets' financial return remains unquantified.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Rights Sale

Basketball-Reference's Houston, Kansas City-Omaha and league transaction ledgers agree on the core event: on November 2, 1972, the Rockets sold Dick Gibbs' player rights to the Kings. Joe Axelson's executive record also lists Kansas City-Omaha acquiring the rights that day. The legacy archive entry correctly treats Houston's return as cash, but none of the reviewed ledgers reports a dollar amount. The source-backed record therefore keeps the payment as verified but unpriced instead of assuming it was trivial or assigning a modern equivalent.

A Complicated Rights Trail

Gibbs appears in another transaction only a few weeks earlier. On October 9, Kansas City-Omaha's ledger says the Kings traded Jim Fox and Dick Gibbs to Seattle for Pete Cross and Don Kojis. Seattle's transaction page records the same deal. The November 2 Houston-to-Kansas City-Omaha entry is specifically phrased as an acquisition of Gibbs' player rights, and Gibbs then actually played for the Kings rather than Seattle during the remainder of 1972-73. The reviewed sources do not explain every contractual step between those entries, so this archive does not collapse them into a speculative three-team transaction.

Gibbs' Kansas City-Omaha Production

The on-court outcome is clear. Gibbs played 66 games for Kansas City-Omaha in 1972-73, logging 733 minutes. He scored 207 points, grabbed 94 rebounds and recorded 61 assists. His averages were 3.1 points, 1.4 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 11.1 minutes per game. That is modest production, but it represents a full season of reserve availability from a player whose rights were purchased for cash rather than a draft pick or rotation player.

Houston's Side

Houston had almost no 1972-73 on-court return from Gibbs before the sale. Basketball-Reference credits him with one Rockets appearance, two minutes and no points that season. His larger Houston contribution had come the year before, when he played 64 games in 1971-72, but those games predate the November 1972 transaction and should not be counted as value retained after the sale. Houston's realized return from this specific move is the cash payment, and the absence of a reported amount prevents a precise comparison in financial terms.

What Happened Next

Gibbs played 71 games for Seattle in 1973-74, but the reviewed Kansas City-Omaha transaction page for that season does not list a corresponding transfer from the Kings to the SuperSonics. Because the documentary chain is incomplete, those Seattle games are not credited as a downstream Kansas City-Omaha asset return. The source-backed evaluation stops with the 66 Kings games directly supported by the 1972-73 roster and transaction records, while flagging the later Seattle appearance as unresolved disposition rather than inventing a missing transaction.

Final Verdict

Slight Kings Edge, B-/C+. Kansas City-Omaha receives a B- because the acquired rights produced 66 games and 733 minutes of immediate reserve value. Houston receives a C+ because it converted a lightly used player-rights asset into cash, but the amount is unknown and therefore cannot be credited as a major return. The edge is intentionally modest: Gibbs was a reserve, not a core player, and the later path to Seattle is not fully documented in the reviewed transaction logs. Confidence is high on the November 2 rights sale and Gibbs' Kings production, with moderate uncertainty around the cash amount and subsequent rights disposition. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles traded LeRoy Ellis and John Trapp to Philadelphia on November 2, 1972 for Bill Bridges and Mel Counts. Bridges became a major rebounding piece for the 60-win Lakers, playing 154 regular-season games across parts of three seasons after the trade, while Counts added 104 games before Los Angeles sent him to New Orleans for future considerations. Philadelphia received 261 post-trade games from Ellis, including three seasons as a regular starter, plus 39 games from Trapp. The realized value is unusually balanced: the Lakers received immediate contender help, while the 76ers received the longest-lasting single player.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Four-Player Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Lakers, 76ers and league transaction ledgers agree on the November 2, 1972 structure: Los Angeles sent LeRoy Ellis and John Trapp to Philadelphia for Bill Bridges and Mel Counts. Pete Newell's Lakers executive record confirms the same four-player exchange. No draft choices, cash or future considerations were part of the original deal. That makes this one of the cleaner early-1970s comparisons in the archive: two veteran frontcourt pieces went each direction, and all four had immediately measurable professional outcomes.

Bridges Becomes the Lakers' Main Return

Bridges supplied the largest immediate impact for Los Angeles. He played 72 regular-season games for the Lakers in 1972-73, averaging 9.8 points and 10.9 rebounds in 34.6 minutes. He also appeared in 17 playoff games as Los Angeles returned to the NBA Finals. Bridges stayed for 65 games in 1973-74 and another 17 in 1974-75, giving the Lakers 154 regular-season appearances after the trade. Los Angeles waived him on December 6, 1974, so his asset chain ended without a trade return, but the club had already received two full seasons plus part of a third.

Counts Adds Depth and a Small Downstream Asset

Counts played 59 games for the Lakers in 1972-73, averaging 5.0 points and 4.0 rebounds in 10.4 minutes. He returned for 45 games in 1973-74. That gives Los Angeles 104 regular-season games from Counts after the deal and 258 combined games from Bridges and Counts. On June 12, 1974, the Lakers traded Counts to the expansion New Orleans Jazz for future considerations. The reviewed transaction record does not identify what those considerations ultimately became, so the archive records the downstream return without assigning it extra realized player value.

Ellis Gives Philadelphia Four Seasons

Philadelphia's best asset was Ellis. He immediately became a starter and played 69 games for the 76ers in 1972-73, averaging 13.7 points and 10.8 rebounds. He then started all 81 of his appearances in 1973-74, averaging 9.9 points and 11.0 rebounds. Ellis played all 82 games in 1974-75 and another 29 in 1975-76. In total, Philadelphia received 261 regular-season games from him after the trade. That longevity and sustained starting role is the strongest argument for the 76ers' side even though the first Philadelphia team was historically poor.

Trapp's Shorter Philadelphia Stay

Trapp added 39 NBA games for Philadelphia in 1972-73, starting 11 and averaging 10.7 points in 21.9 minutes. He later played 24 games for Denver in the ABA during the same season, so his 76ers contribution did not extend beyond that initial NBA stint. Those later ABA games cannot be credited to Philadelphia. The Trapp portion of the return was therefore brief, but combined with Ellis it pushed Philadelphia's direct player-game total to 300, slightly above the Lakers' 258 from Bridges and Counts.

Context Changes the Raw Totals

Simply counting games would lean toward Philadelphia, but the competitive context pulls the comparison back toward Los Angeles. Bridges immediately became a high-minute rebounder for a 60-win Lakers team that reached the 1973 NBA Finals, while Counts provided reserve center depth. Philadelphia received more long-term regular-season volume, especially through Ellis, but the 76ers won nine games in 1972-73 and remained in a rebuild. The trade did not create a major downstream draft asset for either side: Bridges was eventually waived, Counts returned only unspecified future considerations, and Ellis and Trapp did not produce a documented trade return in the reviewed chain.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B+/B+. Los Angeles receives a B+ because Bridges and Counts combined for 258 regular-season games, with Bridges supplying immediate starting-caliber rebounding on a Finals team and Counts later returning future considerations. Philadelphia receives a B+ because Ellis alone produced 261 games across four seasons, including three seasons as a regular starter, while Trapp added 39 more games. The Lakers got the stronger immediate contender fit; the 76ers got the longer-lasting single asset and more total games. Neither side produced enough downstream value to create a clear hindsight winner. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics and player production, with only the unidentified future considerations from the Counts-to-New Orleans deal left unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Bob Rule from Philadelphia for Dave Sorenson on November 10, 1972. Rule played 75 regular-season games for the Cavaliers across parts of two seasons, including 26 games at 7.2 points and 4.0 rebounds in 1973-74 before Cleveland waived him on December 1, 1973. Sorenson played 48 games for the 76ers that season, averaging 5.9 points and 3.6 rebounds in 13.0 minutes, and did not play another NBA season. Cleveland receives the modest hindsight edge because Rule supplied more games and a larger second-season role, though neither side created downstream trade value.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers agree on the November 10, 1972 deal: the Cavaliers sent Dave Sorenson to the 76ers for Bob Rule. The transaction is a simple one-for-one player swap with no draft choices or cash attached in the reviewed logs. That makes the comparison unusually direct. Both players were frontcourt veterans whose roles had diminished from earlier peaks, and neither would generate a later trade asset for the team acquiring him.

Rule's First Cleveland Season

Rule had appeared in only three games for Philadelphia before the trade. He then played 49 games for Cleveland in 1972-73, averaging 2.9 points and 2.2 rebounds in 9.0 minutes. The raw production was limited, but the Cavaliers at least received a regular reserve who remained available through most of the season. Rule's first Cleveland stint totaled 441 minutes, which already represented more team continuity than Philadelphia ultimately received beyond the remainder of that same season from Sorenson.

A Larger Role in 1973-74

Rule returned for 26 games in 1973-74 and saw his role expand to 20.8 minutes per night. He averaged 7.2 points, 4.0 rebounds and 1.8 assists, scoring 187 points in 540 minutes. Those 26 games were the strongest part of Cleveland's return. Rule was no longer the high-scoring Seattle center he had been earlier in his career, but he gave the Cavaliers a useful reserve stretch in a season when frontcourt depth remained thin. Across both Cleveland seasons, he appeared in 75 regular-season games.

Sorenson in Philadelphia

Sorenson had played ten games for Cleveland before the trade and then appeared in 48 for Philadelphia. He averaged 5.9 points, 3.6 rebounds and 0.6 assists in 13.0 minutes while shooting .456 from the field. Basketball-Reference credits him with 626 minutes and 283 points for the 76ers. Those numbers were respectable for a reserve on a rebuilding team, and his per-minute production was not dramatically worse than Rule's. The difference is that 1972-73 became Sorenson's final NBA season, so Philadelphia's return stopped after those 48 games.

Neither Side Creates a Second Asset

Cleveland waived Rule on December 1, 1973. He later signed with Milwaukee as a free agent in July 1974, meaning the Cavaliers received no player, pick or cash return when his Cleveland tenure ended. Sorenson likewise did not create a documented 76ers trade return after his Philadelphia season. Because both asset chains end without a compensating transaction, the comparison should stay focused on direct games, minutes and role rather than speculative later value.

Why the Edge Is Modest

The legacy perspectives disagreed sharply, with one side treating Rule as a decisive Cleveland win and another calling the exchange only slightly favorable to Philadelphia. The source-backed production falls between those extremes. Rule gave Cleveland 75 games and a useful 26-game second season. Sorenson gave Philadelphia 48 games and one decent reserve season. Rule's advantage is real, but neither player became a long-term starter, major trade chip or playoff centerpiece for the acquiring club.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, B/C+. Cleveland receives a B because Rule supplied 75 games across two seasons and expanded into a 20.8-minute role before being waived. Philadelphia receives a C+ because Sorenson provided 48 games and useful reserve scoring, but his NBA career ended after that season and the 76ers received no downstream asset. Confidence is high on the one-for-one trade mechanics, player production and Rule's December 1973 waiver. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers agree that the Suns acquired Walt Wesley on November 22, 1972 for a 1973 second-round pick later used on Allan Hornyak. Pro Sports Transactions adds cash to Phoenix's outgoing package and identifies the pick as No. 26. Jerry Colangelo's executive record confirms the pick-for-Wesley structure. Because Basketball-Reference omits the cash while the specialist transaction database records it explicitly, the source-backed record keeps the cash but marks the amount unpriced rather than treating the discrepancy as grounds to remove it.

Wesley's Direct Phoenix Production

Wesley played 45 games for Phoenix in 1972-73 after appearing in 12 for Cleveland. His role was limited: 8.1 minutes per game, 3.2 points and 2.5 rebounds. Basketball-Reference credits him with 364 minutes, 144 points and 113 rebounds as a Sun. Those totals alone would make the trade modest. The important part of Phoenix's outcome came after the season, when the club retained enough value in Wesley to convert him into multiple future draft assets rather than simply losing him for nothing.

Phoenix Converts Wesley Again

On October 9, 1973, Phoenix traded Wesley to the Capital Bullets for third-round picks in 1974 and 1975. The 1974 selection became No. 49 Earl Williams, and the 1975 selection became No. 54 Bayard Forrest. This downstream deal is directly linked in the Phoenix transaction ledger and Jerry Colangelo's executive record. It gives the original 1972 transaction a second stage: Phoenix received 45 Wesley games, then turned the same player into two draft selections.

The Two Downstream Draft Picks

Williams played 79 regular-season games for Phoenix after being selected in 1974. Forrest later played 139 regular-season games for the Suns. Together they supplied 218 games. Neither became a star, and third-round selections carry inherently limited expected value, but both reached the NBA and contributed real minutes. That downstream production is much more than the original Hornyak selection produced for Cleveland and transforms Phoenix's side from a one-season rental into a multi-year asset chain.

Cleveland's Draft Return

Cleveland used the acquired second-round pick on Ohio State guard Allan Hornyak with the 26th selection in the 1973 draft. Basketball-Reference lists him as a Cavaliers draft choice but shows no NBA games or statistical line. Hornyak therefore produced zero NBA games from the pick. The cash component still has economic value, and its unknown amount prevents treating Cleveland's return as literally zero. Without a documented price, however, it cannot offset hundreds of realized NBA games on Phoenix's side with any precision.

Why the Old Even Grade Missed the Chain

The legacy Phoenix perspective called the trade roughly even because it compared Wesley's modest 45-game Suns stint with Hornyak's failed draft outcome and unpriced cash. That stops the asset chain too early. Phoenix did not waive Wesley; it traded him for two picks, and both selected players reached the NBA for the Suns. source-backed evaluation must include that documented downstream conversion while avoiding the opposite error of crediting Phoenix with unrelated later moves.

Final Verdict

Suns Win, A-/C. Phoenix receives an A- because Wesley provided 45 games and was then converted into two third-round selections that became Earl Williams and Bayard Forrest, who combined for 218 Suns games. Cleveland receives a C because Hornyak never played in the NBA and the cash amount remains unknown, though the verified payment keeps the return from being treated as empty. Confidence is high on the trade, draft identity and Wesley's later Capital deal, with only the cash amount unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The Exchange

Halliburton's Philadelphia Run

Halliburton played 31 games for Philadelphia after the trade. Basketball-Reference credits him with 549 minutes, 294 points, 82 rebounds and 68 assists, equal to 17.7 minutes, 9.5 points, 2.6 rebounds and 2.2 assists per game. He did not start a game, but his scoring rate was useful for a 76ers roster that needed playable guards. The team itself finished 9-73, so Halliburton's production did not change the season's direction. It was still real, immediate NBA value directly tied to the acquired asset.

Atlanta Uses the Pick

The Hawks selected Princeton guard Ted Manakas with the 36th pick of the 1973 draft. Basketball-Reference and NBA.com both identify him as Atlanta's third-round selection. Atlanta signed him before the 1973-74 season but waived him in October. Basketball-Reference's Hawks transaction log records the October 8 waiver, and RealGM places his free-agent date two days later. He therefore produced zero regular-season games for Atlanta. The pick did reach the NBA, but not for the team that acquired it in this trade.

Manakas' Later Five Games Do Not Count for Atlanta

Kansas City-Omaha signed Manakas as a free agent on November 16, 1973. He appeared in five games for the Kings, averaging 2.4 points in 9.0 minutes. Those five games confirm that Manakas was an NBA-caliber fringe roster player, but they are not downstream Atlanta value because the Hawks had already waived him and received no player or pick in return. The source-backed chain therefore stops Atlanta's realized return at zero Hawks games from the No. 36 selection.

Halliburton's Value Was Short but Direct

Philadelphia's side is not a major long-term success. Halliburton's NBA career ended after the 1972-73 season, so the 76ers received only those 31 post-trade games. There is no documented later trade return to extend the asset chain. That limits Philadelphia's grade. Still, a half-season reserve guard scoring 9.5 points per game is materially more realized value than a draft pick whose selected player was waived before appearing for Atlanta.

The legacy archive entry treated the transaction as even because both outcomes were modest. That framing missed the team-specific distinction between a player who actually contributed for Philadelphia and a drafted player who never appeared for Atlanta. Manakas' five Kansas City-Omaha games cannot be credited back to the Hawks. Once the asset chain is restricted to value realized by each acquiring team, Philadelphia has the clearer return even though neither side found a long-term rotation piece.

Atlanta receives a D+ because the No. 36 pick became Manakas, whom the Hawks waived before he played an NBA game for them. His later five games with Kansas City-Omaha are excluded from Atlanta's return because he signed there as a free agent. Confidence is high on the transaction, pick identity, Halliburton production, Atlanta waiver and later Kansas City-Omaha signing. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Kansas City-Omaha acquired John Block from Philadelphia on January 26, 1973 for Tom Van Arsdale and a 1974 third-round pick that became No. 42 Harvey Catchings. Block gave the Kings 107 regular-season games before New Orleans selected him in the 1974 expansion draft. Van Arsdale played 117 games for Philadelphia and averaged 19.6 points in 1973-74, while Catchings played 251 games for the 76ers before becoming part of a later trade package. Philadelphia also turned Van Arsdale into Clyde Lee and another third-round pick in 1974, giving the 76ers the stronger direct and downstream return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Kansas City-Omaha, Philadelphia and league transaction logs agree on the January 26, 1973 structure: the Kings acquired John Block for Tom Van Arsdale and a 1974 third-round pick. Joe Axelson's executive record confirms the same package, and Pro Sports Transactions traces the pick to No. 42 Harvey Catchings. This is therefore a three-asset comparison rather than a simple veteran swap. Kansas City-Omaha received the best player Philadelphia had at that moment, but the 76ers received an established scorer plus a future pick that became a long-term NBA big man.

Block's Two-Part Kings Tenure

Block joined Kansas City-Omaha after averaging 17.9 points and 9.2 rebounds in 48 games for the 76ers. His role fell immediately with the Kings, where he played 25 games in 1972-73 and averaged 9.0 points and 4.8 rebounds in 19.3 minutes. He returned for all 82 games in 1973-74, averaging 8.7 points and 4.7 rebounds in 21.7 minutes. That gives the Kings 107 regular-season games from Block, including a full season of dependable rotation work. He was useful rather than a failed acquisition.

The Expansion Draft Ends Kansas City-Omaha's Chain

On May 20, 1974, Kansas City-Omaha lost Block to the expansion New Orleans Jazz. The Kings did not receive a player or draft choice in exchange. Block later moved from New Orleans to Chicago for Rick Adelman, but that transaction belongs to the Jazz's asset chain, not Kansas City-Omaha's. For this trade, the Kings' realized return therefore stops at 107 Block games. That is a meaningful return for one transaction, but it has a firm endpoint after only a season and a half.

Van Arsdale Becomes Philadelphia's Primary Scorer

Van Arsdale immediately took a much larger role than Block had with Kansas City-Omaha. He started all 30 of his Philadelphia games in 1972-73 and averaged 17.7 points, 6.2 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 34.3 minutes. In 1973-74 he started all 78 games and averaged 19.6 points, 5.0 rebounds and 2.6 assists. He added nine games in 1974-75. In total, the 76ers received 117 regular-season games from Van Arsdale, and his 1973-74 scoring season alone supplied more offensive production than Block ever provided after the trade.

Van Arsdale Also Produced a Second Return

Philadelphia did not simply lose Van Arsdale when his role ended. On November 8, 1974, the 76ers traded him to Atlanta for Clyde Lee and a 1975 third-round pick that became No. 39 Jimmie Baker. Lee then played 71 games for Philadelphia in 1974-75 and 79 more in 1975-76, giving the 76ers 150 games of additional frontcourt value from Van Arsdale's downstream trade. Baker never played an NBA game for Philadelphia, but the pick still represents another realized asset generated from the original Van Arsdale return.

The Third-Round Pick Becomes Harvey Catchings

The 1974 third-round pick had even greater staying power. Philadelphia selected Catchings at No. 42. He played 37 games as a rookie, 75 in 1975-76, 53 in 1976-77, 61 in 1977-78 and 25 in 1978-79 before a February trade to New Jersey. That is 251 regular-season games for the 76ers. Catchings was primarily a defense-and-rebounding center, but he started 68 games in 1975-76 and remained in the rotation for five seasons. A third-round pick becoming a multi-year NBA big man is a strong draft outcome regardless of scoring totals.

Catchings' Later Trade Adds Context, Not Full Credit

On February 7, 1979, Philadelphia traded Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash to New Jersey for Eric Money and Al Skinner. Because Catchings was only one component of that package, the entire Money-Skinner return cannot be assigned to the 1973 Kings trade. The transaction still proves that the Catchings asset retained trade utility after 251 Philadelphia games. That downstream durability is the opposite of Kansas City-Omaha's Block chain, which ended when the expansion draft removed him without compensation.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/B. Philadelphia receives an A+ because Van Arsdale produced 117 games and a 19.6-point season, later returned Clyde Lee plus another draft pick, and the original third-round pick became Catchings for 251 more 76ers games. Kansas City-Omaha receives a B because Block was genuinely useful across 107 games, including a full 82-game season, but the Kings lost him in the expansion draft and received no downstream return. Confidence is high on the trade structure, pick identity, direct production and documented follow-on transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Detroit and league transaction logs agree on the April 13, 1973 structure: the Hawks sent George Trapp to the Pistons for Detroit's 1973 first-round pick. Richie Guerin's executive record confirms the same deal. Atlanta used the acquired selection on Houston big man Dwight Jones. The legacy archive entry labels him as the No. 6 pick, but Basketball-Reference's draft and Atlanta transaction pages place Jones ninth overall. The source-backed record corrects the pick slot while preserving the underlying player identity. No cash or secondary asset appears in the reviewed trade logs.

Jones Gives Atlanta Three Productive Seasons

Jones played 74 games as a rookie in 1973-74, averaging 8.0 points and 6.1 rebounds in 19.6 minutes. His role expanded the next season. In 75 games during 1974-75 he averaged 10.4 points and 9.3 rebounds in 27.8 minutes, giving Atlanta a legitimate frontcourt rebounder from the acquired pick. Jones then appeared in 66 games in 1975-76 and averaged 10.1 points with 7.9 rebounds. Across those three Hawks seasons he totaled 215 regular-season games. That is strong direct value from a first-round selection obtained for one veteran forward.

Trapp Becomes a Durable Detroit Rotation Forward

Detroit also received real value. Trapp played all 82 games in 1973-74, scoring 765 points while averaging 9.3 points and 3.8 rebounds in 18.2 minutes. He followed with 78 games in 1974-75 and 76 more in 1975-76. Trapp appeared in six games at the start of 1976-77 before Detroit waived him on October 20, 1976. His Pistons total was 242 regular-season appearances, more games than Jones played for Atlanta. The old D grade therefore understates the return badly: Detroit received three full seasons of dependable rotation availability.

Peak Value Favors Jones

The difference is role and production rather than longevity. Jones developed into a larger rebounder and scorer, peaking at 10.4 points and 9.3 rebounds per game for Atlanta. Trapp's best Detroit scoring season was 9.3 points, and his rebounding stayed under four per game during each Pistons season. Trapp was useful, but Jones occupied a more valuable frontcourt role and was still only 24 when Atlanta moved him. That makes the direct player comparison lean toward the Hawks despite Detroit receiving 27 more regular-season games.

Atlanta Retains Trade Utility in 1976

On June 7, 1976, Atlanta traded Jones and the No. 1 pick in the 1976 draft to Houston for Gus Bailey, Joe Meriweather and the No. 9 pick. perspectives.summary: Cleveland sent John Johnson, Rick Roberson and the 1973 first-round pick that became No. 15 Barry Parkhill to Portland on April 24, 1973 for the No. 2 pick used on Jim Brewer and the No. 37 pick used on Jim O'Brien. Brewer became a six-season Cavaliers regular, playing 462 games and earning two All-Defensive Second Team selections. The deal produced substantial value on both sides and remains best treated as broadly even.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Portland and league transaction records agree on the April 24, 1973 structure. Cleveland sent John Johnson, Rick Roberson and its 1973 first-round pick to Portland. The Trail Blazers sent the second overall pick plus a third-round pick. Cleveland used those selections on Jim Brewer at No. 2 and Jim O'Brien at No. 37; Portland used the incoming first-rounder on Barry Parkhill at No. 15. Bill Fitch's executive record independently confirms the package. This was a major roster-and-draft exchange, not a simple pick swap.

Brewer Becomes Cleveland's Long-Term Core Return

Brewer immediately made the Cavaliers and played all 82 games in each of his first three seasons. He then appeared in 81 games in 1976-77, 80 in 1977-78 and 55 more in 1978-79 before being traded. That is 462 Cleveland regular-season games. His offensive numbers were modest, but his rebounding and defense became central to the roster. Brewer averaged 10.9 rebounds in 1975-76, started all 82 games and earned All-Defensive Second Team honors. He repeated the defensive honor in 1976-77. He also played 17 playoff games for Cleveland across the 1976 and 1977 postseasons.

The Third-Round Pick Adds No Cleveland NBA Games

Cleveland used the No. 37 pick on Maryland forward Jim O'Brien. O'Brien never appeared in an NBA game for the Cavaliers. His professional games came in the ABA, including time with Kentucky and San Diego, so those games cannot be credited to Cleveland. The second Cleveland asset therefore produced zero NBA games for the acquiring team. The strength of the Cavaliers' return rests overwhelmingly on Brewer rather than on the quantity of picks received.

John Johnson Gives Portland High-Level Immediate Production

Portland received the best established player in the trade. Johnson played 69 games in 1973-74 and averaged 16.4 points, 7.5 rebounds and 4.1 assists. He followed with 80 games in 1974-75 at 16.1 points, 6.3 rebounds and 3.0 assists, then played nine more Portland games in 1975-76. In all, the Trail Blazers received 158 regular-season games from Johnson, with a 16.0-point scoring average across his Portland tenure. His direct production was considerably larger offensively than Brewer's, even though Brewer lasted much longer in Cleveland.

Johnson Also Produces Steve Hawes

Portland retained value when Johnson left. On November 13, 1975, the Trail Blazers traded him to Houston for Steve Hawes. Hawes played 66 games for Portland that season, averaging 7.2 points and 7.3 rebounds in 20.6 minutes. The downstream transaction matters because Portland did not simply lose Johnson after 158 games; the original 1973 asset still produced another useful rotation big man. Hawes later left Portland, but the Johnson-to-Hawes exchange extends the direct trade tree beyond Johnson's own playing time.

Roberson Adds Another Productive Season and Return

Rick Roberson also contributed immediately. He played 69 games for Portland in 1973-74, averaging 13.5 points and 10.2 rebounds in 29.9 minutes. On September 16, 1974, Portland traded Roberson to the expansion New Orleans Jazz for Barry Clemens and a 1976 second-round pick that became Major Jones. Clemens subsequently played for Portland, and the second-round pick became another roster asset. As with Johnson, Roberson therefore produced both direct games and a documented downstream return rather than ending as a sunk asset.

Parkhill Never Joins Portland

The No. 15 pick did not add NBA value for the Trail Blazers. Portland drafted Virginia guard Barry Parkhill, but he chose the ABA and played for the Virginia Squires and Spirits of St. Louis instead. His 173 ABA games are part of his professional career but not realized Portland value. That weakens one piece of the Trail Blazers' package and is the main reason the trade does not become a clear Portland win despite Johnson and Roberson's immediate production.

Brewer Retains Some Cleveland Trade Value

Cleveland also moved Brewer before his asset chain ended. On February 15, 1979, the Cavaliers traded Brewer and future considerations to Detroit for Earl Tatum. Because future considerations were bundled with Brewer, the entire Tatum return cannot be assigned to Brewer alone. The transaction still shows that Brewer remained a tradeable asset after 462 regular-season games and multiple playoff runs. That retained value helps offset Portland's two documented downstream player trades.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, A-/A-. Cleveland receives an A- because Brewer supplied 462 regular-season games, two All-Defensive Second Team seasons and meaningful playoff minutes, while remaining tradeable in 1979. Portland also receives an A- because Johnson and Roberson combined for 227 immediate games at much higher scoring rates and both later generated additional assets. Parkhill never played for Portland and O'Brien never played for Cleveland, effectively canceling the lesser draft outcomes. Brewer provided the longest single-team value; Portland received the stronger immediate veteran production and more branching downstream value. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, draft identities, direct production and major follow-on transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State acquired Butch Beard from Seattle on July 25, 1973 for veteran guard Walt Hazzard, who was also known as Mahdi Abdul-Rahman. Beard played 161 regular-season games for the Warriors across two seasons, averaging 12.8 points and 4.2 assists while appearing in all 82 games for the 1974-75 NBA champions, then played all 17 postseason games during the title run. Hazzard played 49 games for Seattle in 1973-74 at 3.8 points and 2.5 assists per game, and that season ended his NBA career. Golden State receives the clear hindsight edge.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Golden State, Seattle and league transaction ledgers all record the same July 25, 1973 exchange: the Warriors sent Walt Hazzard to the SuperSonics for Butch Beard. Seattle executive Bill Russell's transaction record independently confirms the deal. Hazzard had adopted the name Mahdi Abdul-Rahman, which explains why the legacy asset and internal player identifier use different versions of the same player's name. The source-backed record keeps one identity and records both names rather than treating them as separate players. No cash or draft choice appears in the trade.

Beard Immediately Becomes a Major Warriors Guard

Beard played 79 games for Golden State in 1973-74 and averaged 10.2 points, 4.9 rebounds and 3.8 assists in 27.0 minutes. He shot 51.2 percent from the field, an efficient mark for a guard in that era. The Warriors missed the playoffs, but Beard established himself as one of their primary backcourt pieces. His 2,134 minutes were among the heavier workloads on the roster, giving Golden State a much larger first-season return than Seattle received from Hazzard.

The Championship Season Defines the Trade

Beard's second Warriors season is the central value in the deal. He appeared in all 82 regular-season games for the 1974-75 team, averaging 12.8 points, 4.2 assists, 3.9 rebounds and 1.6 steals in 30.7 minutes while shooting 52.8 percent. Golden State won 48 games, then went 12-5 in the playoffs and swept Washington in the NBA Finals. Beard played all 17 postseason games, averaging 9.1 points, 4.2 rebounds and 3.1 assists in 26.4 minutes. He was not the team's star, but he was a core guard throughout a championship season.

Hazzard's Seattle Return Is Short

Seattle received a veteran with a much longer résumé, including an All-Star season for the original SuperSonics in 1967-68. His second Seattle stint was far smaller. Hazzard played 49 games in 1973-74, averaging 3.8 points, 2.5 assists and 1.2 rebounds in 11.7 minutes. Basketball-Reference lists no later NBA season for him. That makes the transaction a one-season, low-minute return for Seattle compared with two full seasons and a championship role for Golden State.

Beard's Downstream Trade Has to Be Handled Carefully

Golden State moved Beard on May 29, 1975, trading him to Cleveland with a 1975 first-round pick and a 1975 second-round pick for Dwight Davis. That deal proves Beard remained a tradeable asset after the championship. It would be wrong, however, to credit the full Davis return to Beard because Golden State also surrendered two draft choices. The source-backed evaluation therefore treats the Cleveland trade as retained-asset evidence rather than assigning all of Davis' later Warriors value to this 1973 exchange.

Why the legacy Grades Were Too Close

The inherited B+/B split understated the gap. Seattle did receive a real NBA contributor, but only for 49 games at 11.7 minutes per night. Golden State received 161 regular-season games, 4,655 regular-season minutes, a full championship season and 17 playoff appearances. Beard also remained valuable enough to be included in a subsequent multi-asset trade. The difference is not merely team success; it is direct availability, role, production and asset life.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, A/D+. Golden State receives an A because Beard supplied two full seasons, became a high-minute backcourt contributor and played every game of the 1974-75 championship run before retaining trade value in 1975. Seattle receives a D+ because Hazzard supplied 49 low-minute games and 186 points in what became the final season of his NBA career. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, the Walt Hazzard/Mahdi Abdul-Rahman identity, both players' production and Beard's later Cleveland transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Hazzard played 49 games for Seattle in 1973-74 at 3.8 points and 2.5 assists per game, and that season ended his NBA career. Golden State receives the clear hindsight edge.
analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Golden State, Seattle and league transaction ledgers all record the same July 25, 1973 exchange: the Warriors sent Walt Hazzard to the SuperSonics for Butch Beard. Seattle executive Bill Russell's transaction record independently confirms the deal. Hazzard had adopted the name Mahdi Abdul-Rahman, which explains why the legacy asset and internal player identifier use different versions of the same player's name. The source-backed record keeps one identity and records both names rather than treating them as separate players. No cash or draft choice appears in the trade.

Beard Immediately Becomes a Major Warriors Guard

Beard played 79 games for Golden State in 1973-74 and averaged 10.2 points, 4.9 rebounds and 3.8 assists in 27.0 minutes. He shot 51.2 percent from the field, an efficient mark for a guard in that era. The Warriors missed the playoffs, but Beard established himself as one of their primary backcourt pieces. His 2,134 minutes were among the heavier workloads on the roster, giving Golden State a much larger first-season return than Seattle received from Hazzard.

The Championship Season Defines the Trade

Beard's second Warriors season is the central value in the deal. He appeared in all 82 regular-season games for the 1974-75 team, averaging 12.8 points, 4.2 assists, 3.9 rebounds and 1.6 steals in 30.7 minutes while shooting 52.8 percent. Golden State won 48 games, then went 12-5 in the playoffs and swept Washington in the NBA Finals. Beard played all 17 postseason games, averaging 9.1 points, 4.2 rebounds and 3.1 assists in 26.4 minutes. He was not the team's star, but he was a core guard throughout a championship season.

Hazzard's Seattle Return Is Short

Seattle received a veteran with a much longer résumé, including an All-Star season for the original SuperSonics in 1967-68. His second Seattle stint was far smaller. Hazzard played 49 games in 1973-74, averaging 3.8 points, 2.5 assists and 1.2 rebounds in 11.7 minutes. Basketball-Reference lists no later NBA season for him. That makes the transaction a one-season, low-minute return for Seattle compared with two full seasons and a championship role for Golden State.

Beard's Downstream Trade Has to Be Handled Carefully

Golden State moved Beard on May 29, 1975, trading him to Cleveland with a 1975 first-round pick and a 1975 second-round pick for Dwight Davis. That deal proves Beard remained a tradeable asset after the championship. It would be wrong, however, to credit the full Davis return to Beard because Golden State also surrendered two draft choices. The source-backed evaluation therefore treats the Cleveland trade as retained-asset evidence rather than assigning all of Davis' later Warriors value to this 1973 exchange.

Why the legacy Grades Were Too Close

The inherited B+/B split understated the gap. Seattle did receive a real NBA contributor, but only for 49 games at 11.7 minutes per night. Golden State received 161 regular-season games, 4,655 regular-season minutes, a full championship season and 17 playoff appearances. Beard also remained valuable enough to be included in a subsequent multi-asset trade. The difference is not merely team success; it is direct availability, role, production and asset life.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, A/D+. Golden State receives an A because Beard supplied two full seasons, became a high-minute backcourt contributor and played every game of the 1974-75 championship run before retaining trade value in 1975. Seattle receives a D+ because Hazzard supplied 49 low-minute games and 186 points in what became the final season of his NBA career. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, the Walt Hazzard/Mahdi Abdul-Rahman identity, both players' production and Beard's later Cleveland transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: The New York Nets acquired Julius Erving and Willie Sojourner from the Virginia Squires on July 31, 1973 for George Carter, Kermit Washington's ABA rights and cash. Erving then played all 252 Nets regular-season games across the ABA's final three seasons, won three straight league MVP awards and led New York to championships in 1974 and 1976. Sojourner added 161 games over two seasons. Virginia got an excellent 80-game season from Carter, but Washington never played for the Squires and the cash amount is unreported. The Nets receive an overwhelming hindsight win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, Virginia Squires and league transaction ledgers agree on the July 31, 1973 structure: Virginia sent Julius Erving and Willie Sojourner to New York for George Carter, Kermit Washington and cash. Roy Boe's Nets executive record and Al Bianchi's Squires executive record preserve the same package. Washington had just been selected fifth overall by the Los Angeles Lakers in the 1973 NBA draft, so Virginia acquired his ABA rights rather than a player who was under contract to join the Squires. The reviewed sources do not preserve the cash amount, leaving that component verified but unpriced.

Erving Changes the Nets Immediately

Erving transformed New York in his first season. He played all 84 games in 1973-74 and averaged 27.4 points, 10.7 rebounds and 5.2 assists while winning the ABA MVP. The Nets improved from 30-54 the previous year to 55-29 and won the ABA championship. Erving then played all 84 games again in 1974-75 and all 84 in 1975-76, winning the league MVP in each season. Across the three years New York received 252 consecutive regular-season appearances from the best player in the league.

Two Championships and Three MVPs

The postseason return is even more important than the regular-season durability. Erving led the Nets to the 1974 championship in his first year with the club, then to another title in 1976, the ABA's final season. Basketball-Reference lists him as playoff leader in both championship runs, and his 1975-76 regular-season line reached 29.3 points, 11.0 rebounds and 5.0 assists per game. A transaction that produces three MVP seasons and two league titles is not merely a strong star acquisition; it changes the competitive history of the franchise.

Sojourner Adds Real Supporting Value

Sojourner was not a throw-in who disappeared. He played 82 games for New York in 1973-74 and 79 in 1974-75, giving the Nets 161 regular-season appearances across two seasons. In the first championship year he averaged 5.6 points and 4.1 rebounds in 16.0 minutes and appeared in the postseason. New York waived him in October 1975, so his direct asset chain ended before the second championship season, but the initial trade still produced two usable players rather than Erving alone.

Virginia's Best Return Was George Carter

Carter gave the Squires substantial short-term production. In 1973-74 he played 80 games and averaged 19.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and 1.7 assists in 35.2 minutes. He also averaged 20.8 points across five playoff games, which happened to come against the Nets. Virginia later traded Carter and Mike Barr to the Memphis Sounds for Glen Combs and Mike Jackson in August 1974. That means Carter retained some downstream transaction value after his strong Squires season, even though Virginia did not keep him long enough to build a multi-year core around the return.

Washington's Rights Never Become Squires Production

Washington is important to distinguish from Carter. The Lakers drafted him fifth overall in 1973, and Basketball-Reference shows him beginning his NBA career with Los Angeles that fall. He played 45 games for the Lakers in 1973-74 and never appeared for Virginia. The Squires therefore received an ABA rights asset that produced zero direct games. Whatever strategic leverage those rights may have represented at the time, the reviewed transaction history does not show Virginia converting them into a later player or pick.

The Cash Cannot Close the Gap

Virginia also received cash, which mattered for a financially strained ABA club, but the amount is not identified in the reviewed ledgers. This archive does not invent a figure or convert an unknown payment into fictional player value. Carter's 80-game season plus the later Memphis trade give Virginia a real return, and the cash keeps the package from being treated as empty. None of those assets, however, approaches three Erving MVP seasons, two championships and 252 games from a franchise-defining player.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A+/C+. New York receives an A+ because Erving delivered 252 regular-season games, three consecutive ABA MVP awards and championships in 1974 and 1976, while Sojourner added 161 games over two seasons. Virginia receives a C+ because Carter supplied an excellent 80-game scoring season and later trade utility, plus unpriced cash, but Washington's ABA rights produced zero Squires games and the package did not replace the superstar value sent away. Confidence is high on the trade mechanics, player production and Washington's zero-game Squires outcome, with only the cash amount unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Mike Green's ABA rights from Indiana on August 7, 1973 for an unidentified draft choice. Green immediately became a productive Rockets center, playing 79 games as a rookie and 81 more in 1974-75, when he averaged 17.4 points and 9.2 rebounds and made the ABA All-Star team. Denver then included Green with Mack Calvin and Jan van Breda Kolff in the July 1975 trade that brought back George Irvine and David Thompson's rights. The Pacers' draft return remains unresolved in the reviewed record, giving Denver the clear hindsight win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Rights Trade

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Indiana and league transaction pages agree that the Pacers traded Mike Green to the Denver Rockets on August 7, 1973 for a draft choice. Denver also signed Green that day. Indiana had selected him in the ABA's 1973 special-circumstance draft, while Seattle had taken him fourth overall in the NBA draft. The reviewed ABA transaction ledgers do not identify the year, round or eventual player attached to Denver's outgoing pick, so this archive preserves the pick as verified but unresolved rather than inventing a draft lineage.

Immediate Denver Production

Green gave Denver substantial value from the start. As a rookie in 1973-74 he played 79 games, averaging 11.4 points, 7.4 rebounds and 1.6 blocks in 20.9 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 904 points, 584 rebounds and 126 blocks. Remember the ABA also notes that Green was named to the ABA All-Rookie Team. A draft-choice purchase of rights producing a full rookie season at that level is already a favorable realized return even before the second year is considered.

All-Star Growth in 1974-75

Green's second Denver season raised the value considerably. He appeared in 81 games for the renamed Nuggets and averaged 17.4 points, 9.2 rebounds and 2.1 blocks in 31.6 minutes while shooting 54.2 percent from the field. He made the ABA All-Star team as Denver went 65-19, the best record in the Western Division. Across his two Denver seasons, Green supplied 160 regular-season games and developed from a rookie rotation center into one of the club's more productive frontcourt players.

The David Thompson Trade

Denver then converted Green into part of a much larger asset package. On July 14, 1975, the Nuggets traded Mack Calvin, Mike Green and Jan van Breda Kolff to Virginia for George Irvine and David Thompson. Thompson had been drafted by the Squires but signed with Denver and immediately became the 1975-76 ABA Rookie of the Year and a franchise-defining star. Green alone did not purchase Thompson; Calvin and van Breda Kolff were meaningful co-assets. Still, Green's inclusion in that transaction demonstrates that the 1973 rights acquisition retained major downstream trade value after two productive seasons.

Indiana's Unresolved Pick

Indiana's side is much harder to grade because the draft choice cannot be traced in the reviewed sources. The Pacers' 1973-74 transaction page records the trade but does not identify the pick year or player, and the league transaction log is equally general. Specialist historical summaries note that Indiana had drafted Green and that he signed with Denver, but they do not supply a later draft conversion. Without a verified outcome, the archive cannot credit the Pacers with a player who may or may not have resulted from the pick.

Hindsight Comparison

The asymmetry is therefore unusually large. Denver received 160 games, an All-Star season and a player who remained valuable enough to be part of the Thompson acquisition. Indiana received a real draft asset, but no reviewed source connects it to a realized player, another trade or cash return. That does not mean the pick had no value at the time; it means the surviving source trail does not support a concrete hindsight return comparable with Green's documented production.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A-/D+. Denver receives an A- because Green supplied 160 games, made the 1975 ABA All-Star team and later became part of the package that brought David Thompson's rights to Denver. The grade stops short of A+ because Green shared that downstream package with Calvin and van Breda Kolff and did not become the sole source of Thompson's value. Indiana receives a D+ because it did receive a draft choice, but the year, round and eventual outcome remain unresolved in the reviewed record. Confidence is high on Green's acquisition, production and downstream trade, with low confidence only on the Pacers' untraced pick. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: The Capital Bullets traded Stan Love to the Lakers on August 23, 1973 for Los Angeles' 1974 second-round pick, which became No. 22 Truck Robinson; the Lakers' official media guide and draft-trade records also identify cash in the package. Love played 81 NBA games for Los Angeles across parts of two seasons before being waived in February 1975. Robinson played 199 regular-season games for Washington, growing to 16.0 points and 8.9 rebounds before becoming part of a 1977 first-round-pick swap that returned Tom Henderson and the No. 4 pick used on Greg Ballard. Washington holds the clear hindsight edge.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Los Angeles, Capital and league transaction ledgers agree that the Bullets sent Stan Love to the Lakers on August 23, 1973 for a 1974 second-round draft pick that became No. 22 Truck Robinson. Bob Ferry and Pete Newell's executive logs preserve the same player-for-pick structure. The Lakers' official historical media guide and Pro Sports Transactions' 1974 draft-trade ledger add cash considerations from Los Angeles. Because the payment amount is not reported, the source-backed archive keeps the cash as verified but unpriced rather than assigning it a speculative value.

Love's Lakers Production

Love joined Los Angeles after two seasons with the Bullets. He played 51 games for the Lakers in 1973-74, averaging 5.6 points and 3.3 rebounds in 13.7 minutes. He returned for 30 NBA games in 1974-75 and increased to 7.2 points in 14.4 minutes. That gives Los Angeles 81 regular-season appearances and 1,129 minutes from the direct player return. Love was useful reserve depth, but he never became a high-minute rotation cornerstone or long-term starter for the Lakers.

The Lakers' Asset Chain Ends

Los Angeles' official media guide records the club waiving Love on February 10, 1975. He then played 12 ABA games for the San Antonio Spurs during the same season, but those games belong to another franchise and cannot be credited to the Lakers. Los Angeles received no documented player, pick or cash return when Love left. The original 1973 asset chain therefore ends after 81 Lakers games, which is a respectable but limited outcome for surrendering a second-round pick and cash.

Washington Drafts Truck Robinson

The Bullets used the acquired selection on Leonard 'Truck' Robinson with the 22nd pick in the 1974 draft. He immediately reached the NBA and played 76 games as a rookie. Robinson appeared in all 82 games in 1975-76, averaging 11.2 points and 6.8 rebounds, then played 41 more Washington games in 1976-77 and raised his averages to 16.0 points and 8.9 rebounds in 32.4 minutes. In all, the Bullets received 199 regular-season appearances before moving him in January 1977.

Robinson Becomes Part of a Premium Pick Swap

Washington retained substantial value when Robinson left. On January 20, 1977, the Bullets traded Robinson and their 1977 first-round pick, later No. 14 Tree Rollins, to Atlanta for guard Tom Henderson and Atlanta's first-round pick, later No. 4 Greg Ballard. Robinson alone did not purchase Henderson and the higher selection; Washington also surrendered a first-round pick. Still, his inclusion as the principal established player in a seven-slot draft move shows that the original 1974 second-round asset remained valuable after nearly three seasons of direct production.

Why the Downstream Context Matters

Ballard and Henderson became useful Washington players, but the archive does not assign their full careers to this 1973 trade because the Bullets' own No. 14 pick was a meaningful co-asset in the Atlanta exchange. The safer hindsight treatment is to credit Robinson with retained trade utility rather than with every later game Ballard and Henderson played. Even without that downstream conversion, 199 Washington games and Robinson's growth into a 16-point, nine-rebound player already exceed Love's 81-game Lakers return.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, A-/C+. Washington receives an A- because one second-round pick became Truck Robinson, who supplied 199 regular-season games, developed into a starter-level frontcourt player and remained valuable enough to anchor the player side of a later first-round pick swap. The unpriced cash adds modest value. Los Angeles receives a C+ because Love gave the Lakers 81 games of reserve production but was waived without a downstream return. Confidence is high on the transaction, pick identity, player production and 1977 Robinson trade, with only the cash amount unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired John Tresvant from the Capital Bullets on September 4, 1973 for a future draft pick; the Bulls' official historical transaction guide also records cash in the package. Tresvant never appeared in a regular-season game for Chicago. He was waived on October 1 and did not play in the NBA again. The future pick remains unidentified in the reviewed team, league and executive ledgers, and the cash amount is unreported. Washington therefore receives a modest hindsight edge because it converted a departing veteran into two assets, while Chicago realized zero regular-season production.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Capital and league transaction ledgers agree that the Bullets sent John Tresvant to the Bulls on September 4, 1973 for a future draft pick. Dick Motta and Bob Ferry's executive records preserve the same player-for-pick structure. Chicago's official historical media guide adds cash to the Bulls' outgoing package. The reviewed sources do not identify the pick year, round or eventual player, and they do not report the cash amount. The source-backed archive therefore treats both Washington assets as real but unresolved rather than assigning a speculative draft outcome or financial value.

Tresvant Never Plays a Regular-Season Game for Chicago

Tresvant was a veteran frontcourt player entering what would have been his tenth NBA season. He had played 55 games for Baltimore in 1972-73, averaging 3.8 points and 2.8 rebounds in 9.8 minutes. Chicago acquired him shortly before training camp, but the move never produced a regular-season appearance. Basketball-Reference's career record ends with Baltimore in 1972-73, and historical roster material lists Tresvant only with Chicago during the 1973 preseason. The Bulls therefore received no games, minutes, points or rebounds from the direct player asset.

A One-Month Bulls Stay

RealGM's transaction timeline records Chicago waiving Tresvant on October 1, 1973, less than four weeks after the trade. He became a free agent on October 3 and did not return to an NBA regular-season roster. That makes the realized Chicago side unusually simple: the Bulls paid a future pick and cash for a player they carried through part of the preseason but never used in a regular-season game. There is no documented downstream trade return because Tresvant left on waivers.

Washington's Future Pick Is Still Unresolved

The Capital Bullets clearly received a future draft choice, but the surviving transaction ledgers do not connect it to a specific Washington selection. Bob Ferry's executive log lists the September 4 trade without a year or round. The 1973-74 Capital transactions page does the same, and the league ledger remains equally general. Because several later Washington draft selections arrived through other documented trades, assigning one of them to Tresvant without direct evidence would create a false asset chain. The pick is therefore preserved as verified but unresolved.

The Cash Component

Chicago's own historical transaction guide states that the Bulls obtained Tresvant for cash and a future draft choice. That source supports retaining cash in the canonical package even though Basketball-Reference omits the financial detail. No reviewed source supplies the dollar amount or shows how Capital used the proceeds. The archive can therefore credit Washington with an additional asset but cannot elevate the return based on an unknown payment. This is a case where the direction of the hindsight result is clearer than the exact size of the value received.

Why the Edge Is Modest Rather Than Huge

Washington gave up a 33-year-old reserve whose NBA career was about to end and received two forms of consideration. Chicago, meanwhile, got zero regular-season production. That supports a Bullets edge, but the future pick cannot be traced and the cash cannot be priced, so there is no basis for an elite Washington grade. The correct source-backed treatment distinguishes 'better than zero' from a proven high-value return. It also avoids penalizing Chicago as if the Bulls had surrendered a known premium pick when the evidence does not establish that.

Final Verdict

Bullets Edge, B-/D. Washington receives a B- because it converted Tresvant into a future draft choice and cash rather than losing him for nothing, even though neither asset can be fully valued from the surviving record. Chicago receives a D because Tresvant never played a regular-season game for the Bulls and was waived within a month. Confidence is high on the transaction, zero-game Chicago outcome and waiver date, but only medium on Washington's realized value because the pick identity and cash amount remain unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Philadelphia acquired Toby Kimball from the Kansas City-Omaha Kings on September 28, 1973, sending cash instead of a roster player or draft selection. He did not become an elite scorer and he was not a first-choice starter, but he helped absorb a substantial share of the team's frontcourt possessions and rebounding work. The Sixers finished 25-57 in 1973-74 and missed the playoffs, so Kimball did not transform Philadelphia's fortunes. Kansas City-Omaha may have welcomed the financial flexibility, but that benefit cannot be compared precisely with a season of reserve minutes when the payment is unavailable. Philadelphia's narrow edge rests on Kimball's actual acquired-team production. The assessment remains a modest one because neither club gained a long-term centerpiece.

sacramento-kings.analysis:
The 76ers Purchased a Veteran Rebounder in September 1973

Philadelphia acquired Toby Kimball from the Kansas City-Omaha Kings on September 28, 1973, sending cash instead of a roster player or draft selection. The transaction is documented in both clubs' 1973-74 registers. The franchise now called the Sacramento Kings was known as Kansas City-Omaha at the time, a distinction worth keeping in the historical explanation even though the site's canonical team identifier uses its modern successor. Kimball had already played in the NBA for several teams and could provide stability for a Sixers frontcourt rebuilding from an exceptionally poor prior season. The cash amount is not documented by the available ledgers.

Kimball Became a Regular in Philadelphia's Frontcourt

Kimball provided much more than an end-of-bench appearance. During 1973-74 he played in 75 regular-season games for the 76ers, starting once and logging 1,592 minutes. His Philadelphia totals were 559 points and 552 rebounds, translating to 7.5 points and 7.4 rebounds per outing in 21.2 minutes. He did not become an elite scorer and he was not a first-choice starter, but he helped absorb a substantial share of the team's frontcourt possessions and rebounding work. Those figures are specifically from his Philadelphia stint rather than accomplishments with older franchises.

The Kings Took Money and Freed a Reserve Spot

Kansas City-Omaha received cash in the 1973 exchange, not a player whose subsequent points or games can be credited to the franchise. Kimball had been a reserve for the Kings during 1972-73, appearing in 67 games with much lighter usage than he would see in Philadelphia. Trading him removed a veteran from their roster and returned money, but the reported records do not establish a dollar amount or a later downstream basketball asset purchased with the proceeds. The Kings therefore receive credit for the documented financial return, not an imaginary draft selection or another team's future production. The absence of a known cash valuation keeps the verdict cautious.

Useful Depth Was a Better Traceable Return Than Undisclosed Cash

The Sixers finished 25-57 in 1973-74 and missed the playoffs, so Kimball did not transform Philadelphia's fortunes. His 75 games and 552 rebounds nonetheless represent measurable playing value from a cash acquisition, especially on a roster still trying to become competitive after its 9-73 season. Kansas City-Omaha may have welcomed the financial flexibility, but that benefit cannot be compared precisely with a season of reserve minutes when the payment is unavailable. Philadelphia's narrow edge rests on Kimball's actual acquired-team production. The assessment remains a modest one because neither club gained a long-term centerpiece.

Final Verdict

Slight 76ers Edge. Philadelphia earns C+ for 75 games, 559 points and 552 rebounds from Toby Kimball after the September 1973 cash purchase. Kansas City-Omaha gets C for the undisclosed cash it received without a traceable basketball addition. Neither side obtained a foundational star, but the Sixers' one-year frontcourt value is verified.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Moved Christian for Two Draft Opportunities

The Hawks traded Bob Christian to the Phoenix Suns in October 1973, receiving rights associated with the 1976 second round and 1977 third round. The later selections were linked with Bob Carrington and Eddie Johnson, respectively. This was an era when draft rounds extended well beyond the modern two-round format, so a third-round choice was a legitimate asset. Atlanta chose future selection flexibility rather than keeping Christian as an immediate frontcourt player.

The Exact Pick Record Requires Historical Care

Contemporary transaction summaries and Basketball-Reference's team histories identify both incoming picks, while an older draft-rights ledger included a caveat about the additional Carrington selection. The distinction shouldn't be erased simply to present an artificially certain chain. The No. 49 Eddie Johnson selection is also an identity problem for readers unfamiliar with different players who shared that name. It should not be merged with an unrelated later NBA guard's career.

Phoenix Obtained an Immediate Player

Christian had NBA experience as a center and offered Phoenix a current frontcourt option rather than an unknown future rookie. That could be worthwhile for a team that wanted help before the next several draft cycles. His previous statistics for other franchises are not production acquired by the Suns, however. The transaction's practical comparison is between one veteran player and a couple of conditional, lower-round opportunities that Atlanta might use or later redirect.

The Inherited Atlanta Advantage Is Modest

The Hawks receive B+ for taking multiple draft chances while Phoenix gets C for the immediate veteran. Nothing in the original ledger establishes that Carrington or Johnson became franchise stars for Atlanta through this exact exchange. Nor should the trade be portrayed as the source of every later player named Eddie Johnson. Its historical interest comes from the different ways two teams valued draft selections and an established center in the 1970s.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for the 1976 second-round and 1977 third-round rights connected with Bob Carrington and Eddie Johnson, adding two draft opportunities for Bob Christian. Phoenix gets C for receiving Christian as a current center. The imported ledger's caveat about an early source and the Eddie Johnson identity should remain visible rather than be replaced by unsupported career-credit claims.

perspectives.analysis:
Phoenix Preferred Two Future Draft Chances

On October 9, 1973, Phoenix traded veteran center Walt Wesley to the Capital Bullets for two future third-round selections. The 1974 choice later appeared at No. 49, associated with Earl Williams, and the 1975 selection at No. 54 with Bayard Forrest. This transaction happened when the NBA draft extended well beyond two rounds, so third-round rights were legitimate prospects rather than modern undrafted-free-agent invitations. Phoenix opted to create two new chances to find frontcourt talent rather than commit another roster season to Wesley, who already had several years of league experience.

Washington Pursued Immediate Center Depth

The Bullets, indexed under the modern Washington Wizards franchise lineage, acquired Wesley as a veteran interior option. They were not receiving an unproven college player or an extra draft selection. The club's established lineup could use him in practices and roster combinations without waiting through two future drafts. His previous seasons elsewhere should not be treated as fresh Capital Bullets performance, however, and the transaction itself did not guarantee a prominent long-term starting role. The relevant return was the player on his new contract, set against the two picks Washington relinquished.

Third-Round Rights Did Not Guarantee NBA Careers

Earl Williams and Bayard Forrest provide names and slots for the selections Phoenix acquired, but those historical draft identities require separate roster verification. A player being selected at No. 49 or No. 54 didn't establish that he became a regular Suns center. The value of the package was the pair of attempts to identify talent or use the rights in another personnel agreement. Counting both picks as fully successful drafted starters would overstate the return. At the same time, treating third-round selections as nonexistent because today's draft only has two rounds would erase genuine 1970s capital.

The Suns Had a Slightly Broader Set of Options

The Suns ended the trade with two separate future selections while Washington gained a known center who could serve its immediate roster. Neither club obtained a top overall draft pick, and Wesley was a useful veteran rather than a dominant star by 1973. Phoenix has the stronger asset count, especially because its draft rights were held in different years. A measured Suns win captures those development opportunities without borrowing Williams's or Forrest's entire later careers. Washington's choice remains reasonable for a contender trying to staff its frontcourt with established professional experience.

Final Verdict

Suns Win on draft flexibility. Phoenix earns B for two third-round selections, which later corresponded to 1974 No. 49 Earl Williams and 1975 No. 54 Bayard Forrest. The Capital Bullets, historically grouped under Washington's franchise record, get C+ for veteran Walt Wesley. The Suns' incoming rights weren't automatically two productive NBA roster players.

houston-rockets.summary: On November 12, 1973, Houston traded Otto Moore to the Kansas City-Omaha Kings for Ron Riley. Moore played 65 regular-season games for the Kings that season, averaging 3.2 points and 3.1 rebounds. Riley logged 36 Houston games and 421 minutes after the swap. Kings Win, Kings C, Rockets D-; the team's present-day Sacramento slug refers to its Kansas City-Omaha era.
houston-rockets.analysis:
An In-Season Exchange of Two Reserve Big Men

Houston sent Otto Moore to the Kansas City-Omaha Kings on November 12, 1973 and received Ron Riley. Both receiving-team transaction ledgers and the league's season-wide record agree on the date and direct player-for-player structure. Kansas City-Omaha was the Kings franchise's geographic identity at the time, although the site's canonical slug uses the current Sacramento successor. The Rockets were testing an alternative frontcourt reserve after Moore's early-season appearances, while the Kings acquired a more experienced center. There is no documented draft pick, cash component or later compensating condition, so the grades turn on what each player actually provided to his acquiring team.

Riley Gave Houston a Short Run of Bench Minutes

Riley appeared in 36 regular-season games for Houston in 1973-74, accumulating 421 minutes. He averaged 3.4 points and roughly 3.4 rebounds while playing about 11.7 minutes per game, a limited reserve role rather than dependable starter production. His 12 earlier Kansas City-Omaha games occurred before the November transaction and do not count toward the Rockets' gain. Houston finished below the playoff line, and Riley had no postseason run for the Rockets that could extend the result. The exchange was not a productive long-term solution to the franchise's center rotation, even if it supplied some immediate playing time.

Moore Appeared in 65 Kings Games

Moore played 65 games for Kansas City-Omaha after moving from Houston, averaging 3.2 points and 3.1 rebounds in about ten minutes a night. The point average was only marginally lower than Riley's Rockets mark, yet Moore was active for nearly twice as many games. That additional availability gave the Kings a longer period of usable frontcourt cover across the season. Moore's earlier Houston seasons, including his much larger pretrade role, cannot be credited to the Kings. The useful historical return is his 65 actual appearances in their uniform, rather than the reputation or aggregate career statistics he carried into the deal.

Durability Is the Best Available Distinction

This was a minor transaction at a time when both teams were revising their benches. Neither player became a central playoff performer for his new team, and neither provided top-tier scoring. Kansas City-Omaha nonetheless received more games of steady reserve availability, while Houston used Riley less frequently and for fewer total minutes. The difference supports a modest edge for the Kings, not a claim that the deal altered either franchise's trajectory. Treating each player's pretrade production as acquired value would distort the comparison. The two separate team-season splits are enough to explain why the teams' historical grades are not equal.

Final Verdict

Kings Win. Kansas City-Omaha earns C for 65 regular-season appearances from Otto Moore after the November 1973 exchange. Houston receives D- for Ron Riley's 36 games and 421 minutes. Neither was a major contributor, but the Kings obtained the more sustained frontcourt reserve return without surrendering a pick or cash.

indiana-pacers.summary: The ABA's Indiana Pacers brought back Bob Netolicky from the San Antonio Spurs in November 1973, giving up a draft choice and cash. Netolicky returned to a franchise where he had helped win titles and played 56 games that season, averaging 9.1 points and 5.9 rebounds. The Spurs received compensation for an established forward-center, but Indiana got the more visible basketball return.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Brought Back a Former ABA Champion

In November 1973, the Indiana Pacers reacquired Bob Netolicky from the San Antonio Spurs for a draft choice and cash. The center-forward had helped Indiana win earlier ABA championships before leaving for the franchise then known as the Dallas Chaparrals. Bringing him home meant the Pacers knew his strengths and personality, while the Spurs accepted compensation rather than keeping him in their own frontcourt. This was an American Basketball Association deal, not an NBA trade decades after the leagues merged.

Netolicky Returned to Indiana's Playing Rotation

Netolicky appeared in 56 Pacers games during the 1973-74 ABA season, averaging approximately 9.1 points and 5.9 rebounds. He was no longer the centerpiece of the club's offense, but he provided experienced minutes for a team with an established championship core. The Pacers reached the playoffs that season, although Netolicky was injured and did not contribute in that postseason. The result therefore deserves credit for regular-season playing depth without treating his earlier Indiana titles as achievements created by the 1973 reacquisition.

A Protested Spurs-Pacers Game Gained an Unusual Twist

The trade created a remarkable historical footnote. Netolicky had played for San Antonio in a November 14 meeting with Indiana that later became the subject of a protested finish. The league ordered a brief portion replayed before the clubs' next meeting, by which time Netolicky belonged to the Pacers. He thus took part in the same game under two different team affiliations. That anecdote shows the timing and unusual circumstances of his move but doesn't replace the more important question of on-court value.

The Compensation Was Less Tangible Than the Player

San Antonio received a draft opportunity and money, assets that could help future planning without immediately filling frontcourt minutes. Indiana instead brought back a veteran who actually played much of the season in a reserve role. The Spurs' decision to accept compensation was rational, particularly if they intended to restructure their roster, but the immediate receiving-team value favored the Pacers. The matching of historical ABA identities and the later NBA franchise name should not obscure which club actually acquired Netolicky.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win. Indiana earns B for reacquiring Bob Netolicky, who supplied 56 ABA regular-season appearances and valuable veteran frontcourt depth. San Antonio receives C+ for the draft right and cash rather than an immediately usable replacement. Netolicky's earlier championships remain part of his past, not a new accomplishment attributed to this transaction.
