atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Date Correction

The strongest available transaction records agree that Atlanta sold John Tschogl's player rights to Philadelphia on August 29, 1974. Basketball-Reference's Hawks page, 76ers page and 1974-75 NBA league ledger all use that date, and William Wilcox's executive transaction record independently matches it. The legacy August 28 date is therefore corrected rather than preserved as an unexplained one-day discrepancy. The transaction structure is simple: Philadelphia acquired Tschogl's rights and Atlanta received cash. The amount of cash is not stated in the reviewed ledgers.

What Philadelphia Actually Received

Tschogl did reach the NBA with the 76ers, so this was not a rights purchase that produced zero games. He appeared in 39 games during the 1974-75 season and started 14. Basketball-Reference credits him with 625 minutes, an average of 16.0 per game, along with 3.1 points, 2.8 rebounds and 0.8 assists. He was therefore more than a one-week roster experiment, but he was also not a large rotation piece on a team that finished below .500. His playing time and production stayed in a reserve range.

The Value Ended After One Season

Tschogl did not establish a multi-year NBA career after the sale. The 1974-75 Philadelphia season is the only NBA line in his Basketball-Reference record. That sharply limits the realized basketball value of the rights Atlanta sold. Philadelphia did not later trade him for a traceable pick or player that would extend the asset chain. The rights produced one partial season of depth and then stopped producing measurable NBA value.

Atlanta's Side Is Real but Unpriced

Atlanta received cash, and a source-backed history should not treat cash as zero merely because the amount is missing. Clubs used cash sales to monetize draft rights and roster claims that they did not intend to carry. The problem for retrospective grading is that the reviewed team, league and executive records do not disclose the payment. Without an amount, there is no defensible way to compare Atlanta's financial return with Philadelphia's 625 minutes of reserve play. Assuming that any NBA appearance automatically beats an unknown cash payment would create a systematic bias against the selling team.

Why the legacy 76ers Edge Is Too Strong

The legacy archive entry labeled the transaction a slight Philadelphia edge. That conclusion is plausible at a glance because Tschogl did play for the 76ers. Yet the actual return was modest and short-lived. Thirty-nine games at 16 minutes per night is meaningful enough to record, but not large enough to overpower an undisclosed financial return with confidence. There is also no postseason or downstream asset value to widen the gap. The best-supported conclusion is therefore to preserve both known outcomes without forcing a winner.

Final Resolution

Insufficient Evidence. Philadelphia acquired a usable reserve for one season; Atlanta received verified but unpriced cash. The date and player outcome are high-confidence facts, while the economic value of Atlanta's side is the missing variable that prevents a fair grade. Both team grades and the aggregate partner grade remain null rather than creating artificial precision. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Verified Rights Sale

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Buffalo and NBA league transaction pages all record the same August 29, 1974 move: Atlanta sold Dale Schlueter's player rights to the Buffalo Braves. The Hawks received cash, but the reviewed records do not disclose the amount. That distinction matters for grading. The sale itself is fully supported, while the exact financial value is not. Schlueter was already an established NBA center by this point, so Buffalo was purchasing rights to a known veteran rather than taking a chance on an untested draft prospect.

Buffalo Gets a Full First Season

Schlueter immediately became a regular reserve for the 1974-75 Braves. He appeared in 76 regular-season games, averaging 12.7 minutes, 3.5 points, 3.5 rebounds and 1.4 assists. Those numbers do not make him a star, but availability has real value for a team that reached the playoffs. Schlueter also appeared in six postseason games. Buffalo therefore received a complete season of frontcourt depth from a transaction that cost only an undisclosed cash payment and no documented player or draft pick.

A Second Season Extends the Return

The acquisition continued to produce value in 1975-76. Schlueter played 71 games, averaging 10.9 minutes, 2.5 points and 3.2 rebounds. He again appeared in the postseason. Across the two seasons after the sale, Buffalo received 147 regular-season games before the club waived him on October 20, 1976. Phoenix later signed him in December, which ends the original Buffalo asset chain because the Braves did not receive compensation when he left.

Why Modest Production Can Still Win a Trade

Schlueter's per-game statistics were limited, but retrospective trade value is not restricted to stars. A reserve center who remains available for nearly every game across two playoff seasons supplies replacement value, lineup flexibility and roster stability. Buffalo did not have to spend another player or draft asset to obtain that production. The purchase therefore created a larger documented basketball return than a typical cash-rights transaction where the acquired player never appears or lasts only a few weeks.

Atlanta's Cash Cannot Be Ignored

Atlanta did receive legitimate compensation. Cash had practical value and could support payroll, operations or later transactions even when no direct asset chain is visible. The source-backed archive does not treat an undisclosed payment as zero. perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Nate Thurmond from Golden State on September 3, 1974 for Clifford Ray, a 1975 first-round pick that became No. 14 Joe Bryant, and cash. Thurmond gave the Bulls 80 regular-season games and 13 playoff appearances in 1974-75 as Chicago reached the Western Conference Finals, but his Chicago tenure lasted less than two seasons. Golden State received the larger long-term return. Ray became the starting center on the 1975 NBA championship team and remained a Warriors regular for five seasons, while the Bryant rights were later sold to Philadelphia for additional cash. The Warriors receive the hindsight win because the package supplied immediate championship-level frontcourt value and several years of durable production beyond Thurmond's shorter Chicago run.
perspectives.analysis:
The September 3 Blockbuster

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Golden State and NBA league transaction ledgers agree that the Bulls acquired Nate Thurmond on September 3, 1974. Chicago sent Clifford Ray and its 1975 first-round pick, later No. 14 Joe Bryant, to the Warriors. Chicago's historical transaction material and Pro Sports Transactions also preserve cash as part of the outgoing package. This source-backed record is the canonical container for the deal. A separate Golden State import represents the same transaction from the opposite perspective and should not remain active as a second trade.

Thurmond Was Still a High-Level Defender

Chicago did not receive an empty-name veteran. Thurmond played 80 games in 1974-75, averaging 34.5 minutes, 7.9 points, 11.3 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 2.4 blocks. His scoring had declined from his peak San Francisco years, but his rebounding, passing and interior defense fit a veteran Bulls team built around Bob Love, Chet Walker and Jerry Sloan. Chicago won 47 games and reached the Western Conference Finals. Thurmond appeared in all 13 playoff games and remained an important defensive piece even as his offensive role stayed limited.

Golden State Gets Clifford Ray at the Perfect Time

Ray immediately became central to Golden State's frontcourt. He played all 82 regular-season games in 1974-75, averaging 30.7 minutes, 9.4 points and 10.6 rebounds. In the postseason he appeared in all 17 games and averaged 9.8 rebounds as the Warriors won the NBA championship. Golden State defeated Chicago in seven games in the Western Conference Finals before sweeping Washington in the Finals. Ray's contribution therefore was not only durable regular-season value; it arrived in the exact season the Warriors won the title.

Ray's Value Lasted Far Beyond the Championship

The return did not end in June 1975. Ray remained with Golden State through the 1978-79 season, giving the Warriors five full seasons after the trade. His role changed over time, but the club received hundreds of games from a starting-caliber center who was younger than Thurmond and fit the emerging roster. That longevity creates the largest separation in the hindsight comparison. Chicago received a strong first Thurmond season, while Golden State received a championship starter and multi-year continuity.

The Joe Bryant Pick Added Another Asset

Chicago's 1975 first-round pick became No. 14 Joe Bryant. Golden State did not ultimately develop Bryant itself; the Warriors sold his rights to Philadelphia in September 1975. That means the draft component generated another financial return rather than direct Warriors games. The exact cash amount from Philadelphia is not needed to establish the trade's direction because Ray alone produced extensive on-court value, but Bryant's rights show that Golden State also retained additional optionality beyond the player-for-player portion.

Chicago's Shorter Thurmond Window

Thurmond remained with Chicago into 1975-76, but the Bulls' competitive window closed quickly. The team eventually moved him to Cleveland in November 1975. His Chicago stint was meaningful, especially the 1975 playoff run, and a fair grade should reflect that rather than treating the deal as a failure. The issue is relative value: the Bulls paid a younger starting center, a first-round pick and cash for a veteran whose strongest Chicago contribution was concentrated in one season.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, A+/B. Golden State receives an A+ because Ray became the starting center on the 1975 champions and remained with the franchise for five seasons, while the first-round pick retained additional value through Bryant's rights sale. Chicago receives a B because Thurmond played 80 games, supplied elite rebounding and defense, and helped the Bulls reach the 1975 Western Conference Finals. This was not a one-sided disaster; it was a strong short-term return beaten by a championship-producing long-term package. Confidence is high on the date, package and realized player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Why This record Exists

The TradeVerdicts intake process collected historical transactions from multiple team perspectives. That can produce two records for one event when each club's source package describes the same trade independently. This Golden State record is one of those cases. Its asset ledger contains Clifford Ray, Chicago's 1975 first-round pick that became Joe Bryant, cash and Nate Thurmond. The Chicago record nba-trade-chi-1974-0039 contains the same package with the same teams and date. Those are not adjacent moves or separate stages; they are two source views of one September 3, 1974 transaction.

The Authoritative Transaction Record

Basketball-Reference's Chicago Bulls, Golden State Warriors and NBA league transaction pages all describe one September 3 deal. Chicago acquired Nate Thurmond. Golden State acquired Clifford Ray and Chicago's 1975 first-round pick, which became No. 14 Joe Bryant. Chicago's historical transaction material and Pro Sports Transactions also preserve cash as part of the consideration sent to Golden State. None of the reviewed sources records a second same-day trade between the clubs involving the same four assets.

Why Two Active Rows Would Be Wrong

If both imports remained active, Thurmond would appear to move from Golden State to Chicago twice, Ray would appear to move from Chicago to Golden State twice, and the same 1975 first-round pick would be counted twice. Player relationship pages, team-pair histories, transaction totals and retrospective grading would all be distorted. The correct archive treatment is to preserve one canonical transaction and keep the other record only as provenance showing that an independent source batch captured the same event.

Which record Should Survive

The Chicago record is the better canonical container because it is already positioned in the chronology as this review and carries the reconciled package, including the cash component supported by Chicago-specific historical material. It now contains the full source-backed analysis of Thurmond's Bulls value, Ray's championship contribution and the Joe Bryant rights. The Golden State import adds useful corroboration, but it does not represent a distinct economic event that deserves another verdict.

Preserving the Golden State Evidence

Superseding this record does not mean deleting it or discarding its source trail. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. That provenance is useful when auditing how the archive was assembled and when validating the surviving canonical record. What changes is only its status as an independent trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Final Resolution

This Golden State record receives no winner and no grades because grading it separately would score the same transaction twice. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. Confidence is high because the team and league ledgers agree on the single transaction structure and the asset overlap is exact. Treating the duplicate as provenance also preserves every legacy identifier needed for future reconciliation without allowing those identifiers to create a second trade page, second grade or duplicate player-movement history.

Correcting the Transaction Date

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta Hawks, Golden State Warriors and NBA league transaction ledgers all place the Steve Bracey rights sale on September 9, 1974. William Wilcox's executive record is consistent with that chronology. The inherited September 4 date is therefore corrected. The deal itself is straightforward: Atlanta transferred Bracey's player rights to Golden State and received cash. No reviewed source identifies the amount, so the archive can verify the transaction without pretending that the financial return is known.

Bracey Reaches Golden State's Roster

Golden State did receive actual NBA value from the purchased rights. Bracey appeared in 42 regular-season games in 1974-75 and averaged 8.1 minutes, 3.2 points and 1.2 assists. His role was clearly at the back of the rotation rather than among the core guards. The Warriors had a deep roster built around Rick Barry, Jamaal Wilkes and a balanced supporting cast, so Bracey's contribution was mostly reserve minutes. Still, a rights purchase that becomes 42 NBA appearances has more value than a transaction where the acquired player never reaches the roster.

He Was Present for the Championship Run

Golden State won the 1975 NBA championship, and Bracey appeared in four postseason games. That should be recorded, but it should not be exaggerated. Four playoff appearances in a small role are not equivalent to the contributions made by Clifford Ray, Wilkes, Barry or the other regular rotation players. The championship context raises the historical interest of the transaction, not the numerical weight of Bracey's individual return. A source-backed grade should distinguish between being on a title roster and materially driving the title.

The Asset Chain Ends Quickly

Bracey's NBA career ended after the 1974-75 season. There is no multi-year Warriors tenure and no later Golden State trade that converts him into a draft pick or another player. The rights therefore produced one partial regular season and four playoff appearances before the measurable asset chain stopped. That is enough to avoid describing the acquisition as worthless, but it remains a relatively small basketball return.

Atlanta's Cash Is the Missing Variable

Atlanta received cash for rights it did not use. The payment could have been modest, but the reviewed sources do not say. Historical cash transactions are especially vulnerable to bad retrospective grading because modern databases usually preserve the player movement while omitting the dollar figure. Treating that missing figure as zero would systematically favor the acquiring team even when the acquired player supplied only marginal minutes. Here, Bracey's 42-game reserve role is not large enough to overcome that evidentiary gap.

Final Resolution

Insufficient Evidence. Golden State received one season of limited reserve production and four playoff appearances from Bracey; Atlanta received verified but unpriced cash. The date correction and player outcome are high-confidence, but the value comparison is not. No winner or grades are assigned. This is a stronger historical result than the legacy Hawks Win label because it separates what the sources actually establish from what they leave unknown. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Golden State did receive actual NBA value from the purchased rights. Bracey appeared in 42 regular-season games in 1974-75 and averaged 8.1 minutes, 3.2 points and 1.2 assists. The Warriors had a deep roster built around Rick Barry, Jamaal Wilkes and a balanced supporting cast, so Bracey's contribution was mostly reserve minutes. Still, a rights purchase that becomes 42 NBA appearances has more value than a transaction where the acquired player never reaches the roster.

Golden State won the 1975 NBA championship, and Bracey appeared in four postseason games. That should be recorded, but it should not be exaggerated. Four playoff appearances in a small role are not equivalent to the contributions made by Clifford Ray, Wilkes, Barry or the other regular rotation players. The championship context raises the historical interest of the transaction, not the numerical weight of Bracey's individual return. A source-backed grade should distinguish between being on a title roster and materially driving the title.

The Asset Chain Ends Quickly

Bracey's NBA career ended after the 1974-75 season. There is no multi-year Warriors tenure and no later Golden State trade that converts him into a draft pick or another player. The rights therefore produced one partial regular season and four playoff appearances before the measurable asset chain stopped. That is enough to avoid describing the acquisition as worthless, but it remains a relatively small basketball return.

Atlanta's Cash Is the Missing Variable

Atlanta received cash for rights it did not use. The payment could have been modest, but the reviewed sources do not say. Historical cash transactions are especially vulnerable to bad retrospective grading because modern databases usually preserve the player movement while omitting the dollar figure. Treating that missing figure as zero would systematically favor the acquiring team even when the acquired player supplied only marginal minutes. The date correction and player outcome are high-confidence, but the value comparison is not. No winner or grades are assigned. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Fatty Taylor from the Virginia Squires on September 4, 1974 for Darrell Elston and a 1975 first-round ABA draft pick that became No. 10 Mel Bennett. Taylor gave Denver 76 regular-season games and appeared throughout the Nuggets' 1975 playoff run before Denver traded him back to Virginia for Chuck Williams in October 1975. Virginia received two substantial player-seasons from the original return: Elston played 72 games at 8.3 points per game in 1974-75, and Bennett played 75 games at 12.1 points and 7.0 rebounds in 1975-76. The Squires get the hindsight edge because the pick became a real rotation forward in addition to Elston's full season, while Denver's Taylor return was strong but shorter.
perspectives.analysis:
The September 4 Package

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Virginia and ABA league transaction ledgers all agree on the September 4, 1974 structure. Denver sent rookie guard Darrell Elston and a first-round draft choice to the Virginia Squires for veteran point guard Fatty Taylor. Carl Scheer's executive transaction record independently preserves the same package. The first-rounder is important because the 1975 ABA draft record identifies Virginia's No. 10 selection of Mel Bennett as coming from Denver. This is therefore a three-asset trade for hindsight purposes, not merely Taylor for Elston.

Taylor Immediately Helps a 65-Win Denver Team

Taylor gave Denver exactly the kind of veteran guard depth the new Larry Brown group could use. He appeared in 76 regular-season games in 1974-75 and averaged 8.4 points, 4.4 assists and 2.9 rebounds in 26.6 minutes. Denver's depth chart places him behind Mack Calvin at point guard but still credits Taylor with 2,018 minutes, the sixth-highest total on the roster. The Nuggets went 65-19, won the ABA Western Division and reached the Western Division Finals. Taylor also appeared in all 13 playoff games, so the acquisition produced immediate value on a contender rather than only regular-season depth.

Virginia Gets a Full Season from Darrell Elston

Elston was not a throw-in. The 22-year-old guard played 72 games for Virginia in 1974-75 and averaged 26.0 minutes, 8.3 points, 2.8 assists and 2.3 rebounds. The Squires were one of the ABA's weakest teams, but trade grading should separate a player's realized contribution from the club's overall record. Elston logged 1,869 minutes and became a regular part of Virginia's backcourt. His ABA tenure did not extend into 1975-76, limiting that branch to one season, but it was still a meaningful first half of the return.

The Pick Becomes Mel Bennett

Virginia's second asset matured a year later. The 1975 ABA draft record lists Bennett as the No. 10 overall selection by the Squires from Denver. Virginia signed him in June 1975, and he became a substantial frontcourt contributor immediately. Bennett played 75 games in 1975-76 and averaged 12.1 points and 7.0 rebounds in 29.2 minutes. The depth chart credits him with more than 2,100 minutes at power forward. That production matters because it means the first-round pick was not theoretical value; the Squires turned it into one of their more heavily used players in the franchise's final season.

Denver Extends Taylor's Value Once

Denver did preserve some downstream value when it moved Taylor back to Virginia on October 21, 1975 for Chuck Williams. Williams later appeared in 21 games for Denver in 1976-77 before the Nuggets included him with Gus Gerard in the December trade for Jim Price. Because Gerard was also part of that later package, Price's full value cannot fairly be assigned to the original Taylor acquisition. The direct Taylor-for-Williams step is still legitimate downstream value and keeps Denver's side above an ordinary one-season rental. Taylor's return to Denver in August 1976 does not extend this chain because Denver paid Philadelphia a new 1977 second-round pick to reacquire him.

Why Virginia Holds the Hindsight Edge

Denver's side worked. Taylor was a regular guard on a 65-win team and participated in a deep playoff run, then returned another veteran guard when Denver traded him away. The difference is volume. Virginia received 72 games from Elston and then 75 games from Bennett, with Bennett carrying a larger scoring and rebounding role than either Elston or Taylor. The Squires' financial and franchise collapse after 1975-76 prevented a longer asset chain, but that does not erase the production already realized from the Denver pick.

Final Verdict

Squires Win, A-/B+. Virginia receives an A- because Elston supplied a full 72-game season and the acquired first-round pick became Bennett, who delivered 75 games of 12.1-point, 7.0-rebound production. Denver receives a B+ because Taylor gave the Nuggets 76 games, meaningful minutes on a 65-win contender and 13 playoff appearances, then was converted into Chuck Williams. Both clubs received useful value, but Virginia realized two substantial player-seasons from the package. Confidence is high on the transaction date, the No. 10 Bennett pick and the player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix traded Clem Haskins to Washington on September 6, 1974 for Dave Stallworth and Washington's 1975 second-round pick, later No. 35 Allen Murphy. The Suns' own transaction history records the pick rights as completing the Haskins deal on October 10, the same day Phoenix waived Stallworth. Stallworth never played a regular-season game for Phoenix, and Murphy chose the ABA's Kentucky Colonels after Phoenix drafted him, so the acquired package produced no Suns games. Washington received 125 regular-season games from Haskins over two seasons plus 18 playoff appearances, including 13 during the Bullets' 1975 Finals run. Washington wins the hindsight comparison because its reserve guard produced two seasons of real value while Phoenix's two acquired assets never appeared for the Suns.
perspectives.analysis:
The Verified September 6 Deal

Phoenix, Washington and the NBA league transaction ledgers all record the same September 6, 1974 exchange. The Suns sent Clem Haskins to the Bullets and received Dave Stallworth plus Washington's 1975 second-round draft choice. Bob Ferry's Washington executive record and Jerry Colangelo's Phoenix executive record independently preserve the same package. Phoenix's historical media guide adds a useful detail: on October 10 the Suns waived Stallworth and formally acquired the rights to Washington's 1975 second-rounder to complete the Haskins deal. The pick later became No. 35 overall Allen Murphy.

Stallworth Never Reached the Phoenix Regular Season

Stallworth had been a useful veteran earlier in his career, but Phoenix received no regular-season production from him. The Suns waived him on October 10, before their 1974-75 regular season began. He became a free agent and signed with the New York Knicks later that month, where he appeared briefly before being waived again in November. Because he never played a regular-season game for Phoenix and the Suns did not receive compensation when he left, the Stallworth branch of the return ended without realized on-court or downstream trade value.

The Draft Pick Became Allen Murphy

Phoenix did use Washington's second-round choice. The 1975 NBA Draft ledger shows the Suns selecting Louisville guard Allen Murphy at No. 35 overall. That verifies the legacy pick outcome and gives the transaction a traceable draft branch. The problem for Phoenix is that Murphy never played for the Suns. He instead joined the Kentucky Colonels in the ABA for 1975-76, appearing in 29 games as a reserve. After the ABA season and the merger period, Murphy signed with Chicago as a free agent in August 1976, and the Bulls later traded him to the Lakers. Those later moves were not Phoenix transactions, so they do not create downstream value for the Suns' 1974 asset chain.

Haskins Gives Washington Two Useful Seasons

Haskins was already 31 when Washington acquired him, but he still supplied two seasons of dependable reserve play. In 1974-75 he appeared in 70 regular-season games, averaging 10.0 minutes and 4.0 points. Washington reached the NBA Finals, and Haskins appeared in 13 playoff games. He returned in 1975-76 for 55 more regular-season games, raising his scoring to 6.4 points in 13.4 minutes, and he appeared in five more playoff games. Across the two seasons, the Bullets received 125 regular-season games and 18 postseason appearances.

The Role Was Modest, but the Value Was Real

Haskins was not a star in Washington. His usage had fallen sharply from his Phoenix peak, and he played behind the Bullets' primary guards. That limits Washington's grade and keeps this from being treated like a franchise-changing steal. Still, two seasons of available NBA depth on playoff teams is materially more than zero Phoenix appearances from either acquired asset. The comparison is especially direct because Stallworth was waived almost immediately and Murphy never signed with the Suns. There is no need to inflate Haskins' role to establish the direction of the trade.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, A-/D+. Washington receives an A- because Haskins delivered 125 regular-season games and 18 playoff appearances across two seasons, including a reserve role on the 1975 NBA Finals team. Phoenix receives a D+ because Stallworth never played a regular-season game for the Suns and the acquired No. 35 pick became Murphy, who chose the ABA and never appeared for Phoenix. The Suns correctly converted the pick into a real prospect, but neither branch produced team value. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, October 10 completion detail, draft outcome and player histories. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix sent Neal Walk and a 1975 second-round pick to expansion New Orleans on September 16, 1974 for Dennis Awtrey, Nate Hawthorne, Curtis Perry and New Orleans' 1976 first. Perry became a four-year Suns starter-level rebounder, Awtrey supplied four seasons at center, Hawthorne played two years, and Phoenix converted the first into the 1975 No. 16 pick used on Ricky Sobers. New Orleans got 37 Walk games and used the second-rounder with Steve Kuberski to acquire the 1975 No. 7 pick that became Rich Kelley, so its return was not empty.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix and New Orleans transaction logs confirm the September 16, 1974 trade: the Suns sent Neal Walk and a 1975 second-round pick to the expansion Jazz for Dennis Awtrey, Nate Hawthorne, Curtis Perry and New Orleans' 1976 first-round pick. The legacy asset label says that first 'became Adrian Dantley.' That is only the end of the draft chain, not Phoenix's realized outcome. On May 29, 1975, Phoenix traded the 1976 first to Buffalo for the 1975 No. 16 pick, which the Suns used on Ricky Sobers. Buffalo later used the 1976 No. 6 selection on Dantley. The source-backed record therefore has to credit Phoenix with the Sobers conversion, not Dantley's Hall of Fame career.

Phoenix Return
Curtis Perry became the largest direct player return. He played 239 games over four Phoenix seasons and averaged 11.5 points and 9.5 rebounds for the club. In 1974-75 he averaged 13.4 points and 11.9 rebounds; in 1975-76 he averaged 13.3 and 9.6 and then added 12.7 points and 7.7 rebounds across 19 playoff games during the Suns' run to the NBA Finals. Dennis Awtrey supplied four full Phoenix seasons from 1974-75 through 1977-78. He played 82 games in his first Suns year, 74 in the Finals season, 72 in 1976-77 and 81 in 1977-78, providing durable center minutes and rebounding. Nate Hawthorne played 129 Suns games across 1974-75 and 1975-76, averaging roughly six points per game in a reserve role. The draft asset became Ricky Sobers through the Buffalo swap. Sobers played 78 games as a rookie in 1975-76, averaged 9.2 points, and was a meaningful playoff guard with 13.0 points per game across 19 postseason games. He then averaged 13.6 points in 79 games for Phoenix in 1976-77 before the Suns traded him to Indiana. Phoenix therefore received four different contributors to the 1976 Finals roster from the original package, an unusually broad realized return.

New Orleans Return
Walk remained productive but briefly. He played 37 Jazz games in 1974-75, averaging 9.9 points, 7.1 rebounds and 2.7 assists, before New Orleans packaged him with Jim Barnett to the Knicks for Henry Bibby and a 1975 first-round pick that later became Bill Robinzine. That later transaction was not generated by Walk alone, so its full value cannot be credited backward. The 1975 second-round pick also retained transaction value. On October 8, 1974, New Orleans sent that pick, which eventually became No. 22 Clyde Mayes, plus Steve Kuberski to Milwaukee for Russ Lee and a 1975 first-round pick. The Jazz used that No. 7 pick on Rich Kelley. Again, Kuberski was part of the cost, so Kelley's entire career cannot be assigned to this trade, but the second-rounder clearly helped New Orleans upgrade its draft capital. Kelley became a useful long-term NBA center and played 75 and 76 games in his first two Jazz seasons. The New Orleans side therefore deserves more credit than the legacy D grade, even though its value was more indirect and required additional assets.

Hindsight Verdict
Phoenix still wins decisively. Perry, Awtrey and Hawthorne supplied hundreds of regular-season games, and the first-round asset was converted into Sobers. Perry, Awtrey, Hawthorne and Sobers all appeared for the 1975-76 Western Conference champions, tying the trade directly to the franchise's first Finals run. New Orleans received only half a season of Walk, but it successfully recycled both Walk and the incoming second-rounder into later packages. That keeps the Jazz return from being a failure even if those downstream deals required other assets and should not be fully backfilled here. An A+ for Phoenix reflects the breadth, durability and Finals relevance of the realized package without miscrediting Adrian Dantley. A B- for New Orleans reflects Walk's useful short stint and preserved transaction value while acknowledging the enormous direct value surrendered. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Mickey Johnson from Portland on September 18, 1974 for a 1975 third-round pick that became No. 50 Gus Gerard. Johnson became a major long-term Bulls contributor, playing four seasons in Chicago and averaging 15.3 points with 9.4 rebounds in 1975-76, 17.3 and 10.2 in 1976-77, then 18.3 and 9.1 in 1977-78. Portland used the pick on Gerard, but he was already playing in the ABA and never appeared for the Trail Blazers. Because Chicago converted one third-round pick into several seasons of starter-level production while Portland received no direct NBA games from Gerard, the Bulls hold the clear hindsight advantage.
perspectives.analysis:
The Verified September 18 Trade

Chicago, Portland and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the basic structure: the Bulls sent their 1975 third-round pick to Portland and received Mickey Johnson. Dick Motta's executive record independently confirms the same deal. The legacy archive entry's wording, 'Wallace Johnson / Mickey Johnson,' is an identity artifact rather than evidence of two different players. Basketball-Reference identifies Mickey Johnson as Wallace Edgar Johnson, Portland's 1974 fourth-round pick. The canonical player entity is therefore Mickey Johnson, with the alias-only shell removed from this transaction.

Johnson Quickly Became More Than a Throw-In

Johnson's rookie season was modest. He appeared in 38 games for Chicago in 1974-75 and averaged only 7.7 minutes, 3.8 points and 2.5 rebounds. The trade's value becomes obvious one year later. In 1975-76 he played 81 games and averaged 15.3 points, 9.4 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 29.5 minutes. He remained a major frontcourt player in 1976-77, averaging 17.3 points and 10.2 rebounds, then followed with 18.3 points and 9.1 rebounds in 1977-78. That multi-season production turns a late draft-pick exchange into one of the better low-cost acquisitions in this portion of the archive.

Chicago Received Several Years of Starting-Caliber Value

The Bulls did not merely get a useful reserve. Johnson became one of their top rebounders and scorers as the roster moved away from the early-1970s core. Basketball-Reference's franchise pages show him leading Chicago in win shares in 1975-76 and remaining a high-minute contributor in the next two seasons. He also appeared in Chicago's 1977 playoff series. The exact role shifted with the roster, but the broader outcome is stable: Chicago received hundreds of regular-season games and multiple seasons of substantial production from a player acquired for a third-round pick.

Portland's Pick Became Gus Gerard

Portland used the acquired 1975 third-round selection at No. 50 on Gus Gerard. Gerard had already begun his professional career in the ABA with the Spirits of St. Louis, where he averaged 15.7 points and 7.8 rebounds in 1974-75. He remained in the ABA through the 1975-76 season, later playing for Denver. After the ABA-NBA merger he reached the NBA with Denver and Buffalo, but he never played a regular-season game for Portland. His later NBA career was real, yet it does not count as Trail Blazers return because Portland did not realize those games.

Why the Pick Should Still Receive Some Credit

Portland's side was not literally worthless. Turning a third-rounder into the rights to a player good enough to become a seven-year professional had option value, even if the Trail Blazers never converted those rights into direct NBA production. Gerard's later career demonstrates that the selection itself was not a bad talent evaluation. Hindsight grading, however, must distinguish player quality from franchise return. The relevant question is what Portland received from the transaction, and the reviewed record shows no Blazers games or downstream trade value from Gerard's rights.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, A+/C. Chicago receives an A+ because one third-round pick produced four seasons of Mickey Johnson, including three consecutive years with starter-level scoring and rebounding. Portland receives a C because the pick became a legitimate professional in Gus Gerard, but he never played for the Trail Blazers and no verified downstream Portland asset is attached to his rights. Confidence is high on the date, Johnson identity and No. 50 pick chain. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: The Zelmo Beaty-to-Los Angeles transaction has a genuine source conflict that prevents a clean franchise attribution. Golden State's legacy archive record and the 1975 draft-trade ledger say the Warriors sent Beaty to the Lakers for the 1975 No. 20 pick later used on Gus Williams. Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Lakers and league transaction ledgers instead credit Atlanta with trading Beaty to Los Angeles on September 24, while the Lakers' official media guide dates the acquisition to October 3 and also lists cash. Golden State had acquired Beaty's NBA rights from Atlanta in 1970 and signed him on September 25, 1974. Until those conflicting records can be reconciled, this record remains Source Conflict / Insufficient Evidence with no winner or grades.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Why This record Cannot Be Graded Normally

The legacy Golden State record treats September 24, 1974 as a straightforward Warriors-Lakers trade: Golden State sends Zelmo Beaty and receives the Lakers' 1975 second-round pick, later No. 20 Gus Williams. Pro Sports Transactions preserves that exact draft-pick chain. Several other authoritative records disagree. Basketball-Reference's Atlanta Hawks page, Los Angeles Lakers page and league-wide transaction ledger all say Atlanta traded Beaty to Los Angeles on September 24 for the same pick. The Lakers' official media guide attributes the acquisition to Atlanta as well, but dates it October 3 and adds cash considerations. That is too much disagreement to hide behind a single confident narrative.

The 1970 Rights Trade Complicates Atlanta's Attribution

Four years earlier, Atlanta had traded Beaty's NBA rights to the San Francisco Warriors for a 1970 first-round pick and future consideration. That first-rounder became Pete Maravich, and the future consideration eventually became Clyde Lee. TradeVerdicts already has that February 2, 1970 transaction source-backed and reconciled. Because Golden State possessed Beaty's NBA rights after that deal, a 1974 record saying Atlanta directly traded Beaty again requires explanation. It may reflect a rights reversion, a clerical convention, or a database reconstruction issue, but none of the reviewed sources explicitly explains the mechanism.

Golden State's Own Ledger Shows a September 25 Signing

Basketball-Reference's 1974-75 Golden State transaction page does not list a September 24 trade. Instead it records the Warriors signing Beaty on September 25, one day after the disputed transaction date. The ABA league ledger says Utah waived Beaty on September 20 and Golden State signed him on September 25. RealGM describes the sequence as Beaty signing with Golden State as part of an eventual sign-and-trade to the Lakers. Those records support Golden State involvement, but they still do not reconcile why Atlanta appears as the seller in Basketball-Reference's NBA ledger and the Lakers' own historical guide.

The Gus Williams Pick Is Real

The downstream draft asset is not in doubt. Golden State selected Gus Williams with the 20th pick of the 1975 NBA draft. The draft-trade ledger traces that Lakers-origin second-round pick to the Beaty transaction. Williams then played two seasons for Golden State, making the All-Rookie First Team before later becoming a star in Seattle. If the pick legally belonged to Golden State through this Beaty move, it was a strong return. The unresolved issue is not whether Williams became No. 20; it is which franchise should be credited as the Beaty seller and exactly when the transfer occurred.

Beaty's Lakers Outcome Is Also Clear

Beaty did play his final professional season with Los Angeles. He appeared in 69 regular-season games in 1974-75 and averaged 5.5 points and 4.7 rebounds in 17.6 minutes. That gives the Lakers a measurable one-season return. The conflict therefore does not erase the player outcome. It prevents the archive from assigning the opposing return to Golden State with enough confidence to grade a Warriors-Lakers trade page as though the chain were fully settled.

Final Resolution

Source Conflict / Insufficient Evidence. The Beaty-to-Lakers move and the Lakers-origin No. 20 Gus Williams pick are both well documented, but the transaction's selling franchise and exact date conflict across otherwise credible sources. Golden State's rights history and September 25 signing support its involvement; Atlanta and Lakers transaction ledgers attribute the trade to Atlanta; the Lakers media guide gives October 3 and adds cash. No winner or team grades are assigned until the legal transaction chain is reconciled. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland sold Lenny Wilkens' playing rights to Portland on October 7, 1974 for cash. Wilkens had already been hired as Portland's head coach in May, so the coaching role should not be credited to this transaction. The rights purchase gave the Trail Blazers his final NBA playing season: 65 games at 6.5 points, 3.6 assists and 17.9 minutes per game. Cleveland received a verified cash payment, but the amount is not preserved in the reviewed record. Portland gets the hindsight edge because it obtained a full season of useful veteran guard depth, while Cleveland's financial return cannot be measured precisely.
perspectives.analysis:
The Verified October 7 Rights Sale

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Portland and league-wide transaction ledgers agree on the structure and date: Cleveland sold Lenny Wilkens' playing rights to Portland on October 7, 1974. The Trail Blazers' historical material also preserves the rights transfer for cash. This was not a conventional player-for-player trade or a free-agent signing with draft compensation. Cleveland controlled Wilkens' NBA playing rights after his two seasons with the Cavaliers and monetized those rights when Portland wanted him available as a player.

The Coaching Job Predated the Transaction

One important correction to the legacy analysis is that Portland did not acquire Wilkens' coaching services through the October rights sale. The Trail Blazers hired him as head coach on May 24, 1974, more than four months earlier. He therefore entered training camp already responsible for the team from the bench. The October transaction only resolved his ability to continue playing. That distinction matters for hindsight grading because Portland's later 38-44 coaching record was not purchased from Cleveland and should not inflate the value of the rights transaction.

Portland Still Received Real On-Court Value

Even after separating the coaching role, the acquired playing rights produced a useful season. Wilkens appeared in 65 games in 1974-75 and averaged 17.9 minutes, 6.5 points, 3.6 assists and 1.8 rebounds. At age 37 he was no longer the All-Star-level guard who had led the league in assists earlier in his career, but he remained a dependable secondary ball-handler behind Portland's younger core. His 1,161 minutes are a meaningful realized return from a cash-only acquisition, especially because no player or draft choice left Portland in the transaction.

It Was His Final NBA Playing Season

The Portland season also marked the end of Wilkens' 15-year NBA playing career. He did not create a later player trade asset for the Trail Blazers, and the club did not receive compensation when his playing career ended. That limits the transaction to one season of direct court value. The acquisition should therefore be graded as useful rather than transformative. Portland received a veteran contributor for 65 games, not a long-term starter or a multi-year asset chain.

Cleveland's Cash Is Real but Unpriced

Cleveland's side should not be treated as zero. The Cavaliers sold rights to a 37-year-old player they no longer planned to use and received cash rather than carrying an inactive asset. That is rational roster management. The problem for retrospective grading is that the reviewed sources do not disclose the payment amount. Without a figure, the archive cannot compare the cash precisely with Portland's 1,161 minutes of veteran guard play. Still, the known on-court return is substantial enough to support a modest Portland edge while keeping Cleveland's grade respectable.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Win, B/C+. Portland receives a B because the rights purchase produced 65 games of reliable veteran guard depth in Wilkens' final NBA season. Cleveland receives a C+ because it converted unused playing rights into cash, but the amount is unknown and there is no traceable downstream basketball asset. The coaching role is explicitly excluded from the trade valuation because Portland had hired Wilkens months before the sale. Confidence is high on the date, transaction structure and playing outcome, with uncertainty limited to the cash amount. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee traded Russ Lee and its 1975 first-round pick to the expansion New Orleans Jazz on October 8, 1974 for Steve Kuberski and New Orleans' 1975 second-round pick. The first-rounder became No. 7 Rich Kelley, who gave the Jazz four productive seasons before the franchise moved to Utah and was then traded for Bernard King, John Gianelli and Jim Boylan. Milwaukee's No. 22 pick became Clyde Mayes, who played 65 games for the Bucks, while Kuberski played 59 Milwaukee games before being claimed on waivers the next season. New Orleans produced far more direct and downstream value, so the modern Utah Jazz franchise receives the hindsight win.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
The Verified October 8 Transaction

Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, New Orleans and league transaction ledgers agree on the structure and date. The Bucks sent Russ Lee and their 1975 first-round pick to the expansion Jazz for Steve Kuberski and New Orleans' 1975 second-round pick. Wayne Embry's Milwaukee executive record and Bill Bertka's New Orleans executive record independently match the package. The archive maps the historical New Orleans Jazz to the modern Utah Jazz franchise key, so the transaction remains under utah-jazz even though every contemporary source uses New Orleans.

Russ Lee Was a Short-Term Jazz Piece

The legacy archive entry called him Russell Lee, but the verified player identity is Russ Lee, Basketball-Reference ID leeru01. New Orleans used him in only 15 regular-season games in 1974-75. He averaged 9.3 minutes, 4.3 points and 2.1 rebounds, then the Jazz waived him on November 27. Lee therefore supplied little direct value and did not create a later trade asset. His part of the package matters mostly because it accompanied the first-round pick that became the trade's dominant Jazz return.

Rich Kelley Became the Difference Maker

New Orleans used Milwaukee's 1975 first-round pick at No. 7 on Rich Kelley. He immediately became a productive center, playing 75 games as a rookie and averaging 7.0 points, 7.0 rebounds and 2.1 assists. His role grew each season. Kelley played 76 games in 1976-77, all 82 in 1977-78 and 80 in 1978-79. In that final New Orleans season he averaged about 15.7 points and 12.8 rebounds, giving the franchise 313 regular-season games across four years from the acquired pick.

Kelley's Value Continued After the Move to Utah

The franchise moved to Utah in 1979, and Kelley still carried trade value. On October 2, the Jazz sent him to New Jersey for Bernard King, John Gianelli and Jim Boylan. That downstream return should not be credited entirely as if the original Milwaukee pick alone created every later win, but it demonstrates that Kelley remained a substantial asset after four productive seasons. The trade therefore generated both direct on-court value and a later three-player return for the Jazz franchise.

Milwaukee Received Useful but Limited Depth

Steve Kuberski appeared in 59 games for Milwaukee in 1974-75 and averaged 2.8 points and 2.1 rebounds in 8.8 minutes. The Bucks kept him into the next preseason, but Buffalo claimed him on waivers on October 16, 1975. Milwaukee's draft return was No. 22 Clyde Mayes. Mayes played 65 games for the Bucks in 1975-76, averaging 4.4 points and 4.0 rebounds in 14.6 minutes. He did not become a long-term Milwaukee rotation piece, and his later NBA appearances came with other franchises.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win, A+/C+. The Jazz franchise receives an A+ because Milwaukee's first-round pick became Rich Kelley, who supplied four productive seasons and later brought back Bernard King, John Gianelli and Jim Boylan. Russ Lee added only 15 games, but the pick outcome alone makes the return excellent. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Verified November 8 Trade

Atlanta, Philadelphia and the NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the November 8, 1974 structure. The Hawks sent Clyde Lee and their 1975 third-round pick to the 76ers for Tom Van Arsdale. William Wilcox's Atlanta executive record and Pat Williams' Philadelphia record independently preserve the same deal. The pick became No. 39 in the 1975 draft, where Philadelphia selected Jimmie Baker. The legacy archive entry uses Jim Baker, but Basketball-Reference's player record identifies him as Jimmie Baker Jr.; the source-backed record retains Jim Baker as an alias while linking the draft outcome to the verified player identity.

Van Arsdale Immediately Became a Major Atlanta Scorer

Van Arsdale had appeared in nine games for Philadelphia before the trade, averaging 14.0 points. His role expanded sharply in Atlanta. He played 73 games for the Hawks in 1974-75 and averaged 18.9 points, 3.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists in 35.2 minutes. That was not reserve value; he became one of Atlanta's principal offensive players. He returned for 75 games in 1975-76, averaging 10.9 points and 2.6 assists. Across the two post-trade seasons, Atlanta received 148 games from a veteran wing who was still capable of carrying substantial offensive responsibility.

Atlanta Also Preserved Downstream Value

The Hawks did not lose Van Arsdale for nothing when his Atlanta tenure ended. On June 16, 1976, they traded him to the Buffalo Braves for Ken Charles, Dick Gibbs and cash. The later return does not automatically make every component of that Buffalo package equal to the original 1974 acquisition, but it proves Van Arsdale still had trade value after two seasons in Atlanta. That downstream conversion separates the Hawks' side from a simple two-year rental and adds another layer of realized value to the original transaction.

Clyde Lee Gave Philadelphia Real Frontcourt Production

Philadelphia's return should not be minimized. Lee played 71 games for the 76ers after the trade in 1974-75, starting 35 and averaging 32.1 minutes, 5.8 points and 9.7 rebounds. He remained with the club for 79 games in 1975-76, contributing another 5.7 rebounds in 18.0 minutes per game. That is 150 regular-season appearances over two seasons from a useful veteran big man. The first season in particular gave Philadelphia a substantial rebounding presence while the roster was still being rebuilt around younger players.

The Jimmie Baker Pick Added Little NBA Value

Philadelphia used Atlanta's third-round pick at No. 39 on Jimmie Baker. Baker did play professionally, appearing in five ABA games for Kentucky during 1975-76, but he never recorded an NBA regular-season game for the 76ers. The pick therefore added draft optionality without adding direct Philadelphia NBA production. In a close comparison between Van Arsdale and Lee, that unused draft outcome is not enough to erase Atlanta's advantage in scoring impact and Van Arsdale's later trade return.

Hawks Win, A/B+. Atlanta receives an A because Van Arsdale produced 148 games, delivered high-level scoring immediately after the trade and was later converted into Ken Charles, Dick Gibbs and cash. Philadelphia receives a B+ because Lee supplied 150 useful games and strong rebounding across two seasons, but the third-round pick did not become an NBA contributor for the 76ers. This was a productive trade for both sides rather than a lopsided failure; Atlanta's edge comes from Van Arsdale's stronger offensive impact and retained asset value. los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles acquired Lucius Allen from Milwaukee on November 8, 1974 for Jim Price. Both teams received substantial value. Allen played 210 regular-season games for the Lakers across three seasons, including 19.5 points and 5.7 assists per game immediately after the trade, then was dealt to Kansas City for Ollie Johnson and two 1978 draft picks. Price played 127 games for Milwaukee across parts of three seasons and was later traded to Buffalo for a 1977 first-round pick that Milwaukee packaged with Swen Nater to obtain the No. 3 pick used on Marques Johnson. Los Angeles gets a slight hindsight edge because Allen produced the larger direct role and a broader downstream return, but Milwaukee also created major value.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Verified November 8 Swap

Basketball-Reference's Los Angeles, Milwaukee and league transaction ledgers agree on the November 8, 1974 structure: the Lakers acquired Lucius Allen and sent Jim Price to the Bucks. Wayne Embry's Milwaukee executive record independently preserves the same player-for-player trade. There were no draft picks or cash in the original exchange, so the retrospective comparison begins with two guards whose direct production can be measured cleanly before following what each club later received when it moved them again.

Allen Became a Major Lakers Guard Immediately

Allen stepped into a large role in Los Angeles. He played 56 games for the Lakers after the trade in 1974-75 and averaged 19.5 points, 5.7 assists and 4.4 rebounds in 35.9 minutes. He returned for 76 games in 1975-76 at 14.7 points and 4.7 assists, then 78 games in 1976-77 at 14.6 points and 5.2 assists. That is 210 regular-season games over three seasons, with starter-level usage throughout most of the run. The first post-trade season alone supplied more offensive creation than the legacy B-minus grade suggested.

Los Angeles Preserved Downstream Value

On June 1, 1977, the Lakers traded Allen to Kansas City for Ollie Johnson plus 1978 first- and second-round picks. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Kings and league transaction ledgers all preserve that package, with the draft assets later associated with Purvis Short and Ron Carter. The Lakers should not be credited with those players' careers simply because the picks later became their selections, but the package proves Allen still carried substantial transaction value after three productive Los Angeles seasons. That downstream return raises the value of the original acquisition beyond Allen's direct box-score production.

Price Was Productive for Milwaukee Too

Jim Price also gave his new team substantial immediate value. He played 41 games for Milwaukee after the trade in 1974-75 and averaged 14.9 points, 5.4 assists and 3.8 rebounds in 37.3 minutes. He then played 80 games in 1975-76 at 11.7 points and 4.9 assists before appearing in six more games for the Bucks in 1976-77. Across the Milwaukee portion of his career, Price produced 127 regular-season appearances and handled a meaningful share of the club's backcourt creation. That direct return supports a high grade even though Allen's Lakers tenure was longer.

Price's Downstream Pick Helped Milwaukee Reach Marques Johnson

Milwaukee traded Price to Buffalo on November 2, 1976 for a 1977 first-round pick that became No. 13 Tate Armstrong. On June 7, 1977, the Bucks packaged Swen Nater and that same first-round asset to Buffalo for the No. 3 pick, which Milwaukee used on Marques Johnson. It would be incorrect to attribute Johnson's later Bucks career entirely to Price because Nater was also a major part of the exchange. Still, the Price-derived first-rounder clearly contributed to obtaining one of Milwaukee's most important late-1970s players.

Final Verdict

Slight Lakers Edge, A+/A. Los Angeles receives an A+ because Allen gave the club 210 games of high-minute guard production and later returned Ollie Johnson plus two draft assets. Milwaukee receives an A because Price supplied 127 productive games and was converted into a first-round pick that became part of the package used to acquire the No. 3 Marques Johnson selection. Both franchises extracted major value from the same one-for-one trade. The Lakers' edge comes from Allen's larger direct body of work and broader downstream package, not from Milwaukee receiving a poor return. Confidence is high on the original exchange and the major downstream transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The Verified November 11 Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, New Orleans and league transaction ledgers agree on the November 11, 1974 deal: the Bulls sent Rick Adelman to the expansion Jazz for John Block. Dick Motta's Chicago executive record and Bill Bertka's New Orleans record independently preserve the same one-for-one swap. The archive maps the historical New Orleans Jazz to the modern Utah Jazz franchise key, so the source-backed verdict is stored under utah-jazz even though every contemporary record properly identifies New Orleans.

Block Helped a Contender Immediately

John Block had played only four games for New Orleans before the trade, but Chicago gave him a steady frontcourt role. He appeared in 50 regular-season games for the Bulls in 1974-75 and averaged 17.6 minutes, 8.1 points and 4.3 rebounds while shooting 47.3 percent. Chicago won 47 games, finished first in the Midwest Division and reached Game 7 of the Western Conference Finals. Block was not one of the team's stars, but he supplied useful scoring and rebounding depth during a deep playoff season.

Chicago's Return Was Mostly a One-Season Asset

Block's Chicago value was concentrated in that first year. He appeared in only two games for the Bulls in 1975-76, totaling seven minutes, and that season became the end of his NBA career. That does not erase the value of 50 useful appearances for a contender, but it limits the long-term return. There was no later Chicago trade package or draft asset created from Block, so the Bulls' side can be evaluated almost entirely from his direct 1974-75 production.

Adelman Gave New Orleans a Short-Term Backcourt Piece

Rick Adelman played 28 games for the Jazz after the trade and averaged 21.9 minutes, 6.3 points, 2.5 assists and 2.0 rebounds. He was not a long-term building block for an expansion team that was still changing personnel rapidly, but he gave New Orleans a credible veteran guard during the franchise's difficult first season. His direct Jazz production was smaller than Block's Chicago contribution, so the New Orleans side needs its downstream transaction to justify the overall edge.

Adelman Became Part of the Nate Williams Deal

On February 1, 1975, New Orleans traded Adelman and Ollie Johnson to Kansas City-Omaha for Nate Williams. Williams immediately averaged 14.3 points in 35 games for the Jazz, then played 81 games in 1975-76, 79 in 1976-77 and 27 more in 1977-78 before moving on. The Jazz should not receive full credit for Williams as though Adelman alone bought him, because Ollie Johnson was also part of the package. perspectives.summary: Utah acquired Stew Johnson from San Diego and moved him to Memphis on November 9, 1974, with the Memphis leg returning a draft choice and cash. Two legacy Denver imports incorrectly dated the moves November 19 and assigned Utah's role to Denver. Memphis received the clearest basketball value: Johnson played 72 regular-season games for the Sounds, averaged 17.8 points and 6.1 rebounds, and made the 1975 ABA All-Star team. Utah's consideration is real but cannot be fully valued because the reviewed ledgers do not identify the draft choice or cash amount. The corrected Memphis transaction therefore remains Insufficient Evidence rather than forcing a winner against an unresolved Utah return.
perspectives.analysis:
Correcting the Legacy Denver Import

The authoritative transaction ledgers do not support a Denver-Memphis Stew Johnson trade on November 19, 1974. Basketball-Reference's Utah Stars, Memphis Sounds and ABA league pages all place the transaction on November 9 and identify Utah as the team sending Johnson to Memphis for a draft choice and cash. The Denver record is therefore retained as the original import identifier but its canonical date, teams and package are corrected to the supported Utah-Memphis transaction.

Memphis Received a Proven ABA Scorer

Johnson had been an established ABA forward before the move and immediately became one of Memphis' leading scorers. He played 72 regular-season games for the Sounds in 1974-75 and averaged 17.8 points, 6.1 rebounds and 1.7 assists while shooting 44.7 percent from the field. He also appeared in all five Memphis playoff games, averaging 14.4 points, and earned an ABA All-Star selection. That is substantial realized value from a midseason acquisition rather than a short-term roster claim.

The Utah Return Is Documented but Unresolved

Utah clearly received two forms of consideration: a future draft choice and cash. The problem is that the reviewed transaction pages do not identify the draft year, round, overall selection, eventual player or cash amount. Pro Sports Transactions' 1975 ABA draft ledger does not attach a specific 1975 selection to this Johnson deal. A source-backed archive should therefore preserve the assets without inventing a player outcome or treating the unknown cash as zero.

The Same-Day San Diego Leg Matters

Utah did not hold Johnson as an on-court player. On the same November 9 date, San Diego sold Johnson to the Stars for cash, and Utah then sent him to Memphis. The ABA league ledger lists both moves together. That sequence shows Utah was functioning as the middle team in a same-day asset chain. It also makes a simple box-score comparison misleading: Utah's value came from the financial and draft consideration it received, not from Johnson games in a Stars uniform.

Why the Draft Asset Cannot Be Backfilled

The 1975 ABA draft included multiple Memphis and Utah selections, but none of the reviewed draft-trade records ties a specific one to this transaction with enough confidence. Assigning a later player solely because the pick belonged to one of the teams would create a false relationship edge. Until a stronger primary or specialist source names the exact selection, the asset must remain an unresolved draft choice.

Final Resolution

Insufficient Evidence. Memphis unquestionably received a high-value season from Johnson, including 72 games and an All-Star appearance. Utah unquestionably received a draft choice and cash, but neither asset can be priced or traced to a specific basketball outcome from the reviewed evidence. No winner or team grades are assigned because that missing information could materially change the comparison. Confidence is high on the corrected November 9 date, Utah-Memphis teams, Johnson identity and Memphis production; uncertainty is confined to Utah's draft and cash return. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
Correcting the Second Legacy Denver Import

The second Stew Johnson record contains the same core source error as the Memphis record. Basketball-Reference's San Diego, Utah and ABA league transaction pages all state that the San Diego Conquistadors traded Johnson to the Utah Stars for cash on November 9, 1974. Denver was not involved, and the date was not November 19. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.

Johnson Had Been Productive in San Diego

Stew Johnson was a known ABA scorer rather than an expendable end-of-bench player. He had made the 1973 and 1974 ABA All-Star teams with San Diego and opened 1974-75 by playing nine games for the Conquistadors. Basketball-Reference credits him with 13.1 points and 4.1 rebounds per game in those nine appearances, or 21.5 points and 7.3 rebounds per 36 minutes. San Diego therefore sold the rights to a productive veteran, but the amount of cash it received is not disclosed in the reviewed ledgers.

Utah Never Used Johnson on the Court

The Stars did not acquire Johnson for a playing stint. The same November 9 transaction ledger shows Utah sending him directly to Memphis for a draft choice and cash. Johnson does not appear on Utah's 1974-75 roster or statistical register. That zero-game outcome might look poor in isolation, but it would be misleading to call the acquisition a failed rental because Utah converted the player immediately into other consideration rather than losing him for nothing.

The Same-Day Conversion Creates the Valuation Problem

Utah's transaction can only be judged fairly by comparing the cash it sent San Diego with the draft choice and cash it received from Memphis. Neither side of that financial comparison is fully known. The San Diego sale price is undisclosed, the Memphis cash amount is undisclosed, and the future draft choice has not been traced to a specific selection with sufficient confidence. Without those values, the middle leg could have represented a gain, a loss or simply the execution of a broader set of obligations.

San Diego's Return Is Equally Hard to Grade

San Diego definitely received cash and gave up a player who went on to produce an All-Star season for Memphis. That establishes opportunity cost, but it does not establish that the sale was poor. ABA clubs frequently used cash transactions for financial and roster reasons, and an unknown payment cannot responsibly be scored as negligible. There is no later player or pick asset on San Diego's side to supply an independent basketball measure.

Final Resolution

Insufficient Evidence. The source-backed record can confidently correct the date to November 9, replace Denver with the Utah Stars, and document that Johnson moved onward to Memphis the same day. It cannot confidently compare San Diego's unknown cash return with Utah's unknown purchase price and unresolved downstream draft-and-cash package. No winner or grades are assigned. Confidence is high on the transaction identity and Johnson's direct statistics, while the unresolved financial terms prevent a directional verdict. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles acquired Corky Calhoun from Phoenix on November 27, 1974 for 1976 second- and 1977 third-round picks. Calhoun gave the Lakers 133 regular-season games across two seasons, averaging 5.0 points and 4.1 rebounds after the trade in 1974-75 and 5.4 points with 4.5 rebounds in 1975-76 before being waived. Phoenix converted the 1976 second-rounder into Phil Lumpkin, who played 34 regular-season games and all 17 playoff games during the Suns' 1976 Finals run. The retained 1977 third-rounder became Mike Bratz, who played 239 regular-season games and 25 playoff games for Phoenix over three seasons. The Suns therefore created the stronger long-term return.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Verified November 27 Package

Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Suns and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the November 27, 1974 exchange. Los Angeles received Corky Calhoun, while Phoenix received the Lakers' 1976 second-round pick and 1977 third-round pick. Jerry Colangelo's executive transaction record independently preserves the same package. The two draft assets followed very different paths, which is important for hindsight grading: Phoenix traded the 1976 selection before draft night but kept and used the 1977 pick itself.

Calhoun Gave Los Angeles Two Useful Seasons

Calhoun immediately entered the Lakers' rotation after playing only 13 games for Phoenix that season. He appeared in 57 Los Angeles games in 1974-75, averaging 22.3 minutes, 5.0 points and 4.1 rebounds. In 1975-76 he played 76 games and averaged 23.9 minutes, 5.4 points and 4.5 rebounds. That is 133 regular-season games of dependable wing and forward depth across two seasons. The production was modest, but Calhoun was a real rotation player rather than a fringe acquisition.

The Lakers' Asset Chain Ends With a Waiver

Los Angeles did not turn Calhoun into a later player or draft return. The 1976-77 league transaction ledger records the Lakers waiving him in October 1976. Portland then became the beneficiary of his next productive seasons, but those games cannot be credited to Los Angeles because the Lakers received no compensation when he left. The original trade therefore produced exactly the two Lakers seasons Calhoun played and no documented downstream asset beyond them.

Phoenix Converted the 1976 Pick Before the Draft

The first Lakers pick did not become Jacky Dorsey for Phoenix. On June 9, 1975, the Suns sent the 1976 second-round selection to Portland for Phil Lumpkin. Portland later moved the pick to New Orleans, which ultimately used No. 26 on Dorsey. For Phoenix's side of this trade, Lumpkin is the relevant realized return. He played 34 regular-season games for the 1975-76 Suns and appeared in all 17 playoff games as Phoenix reached the NBA Finals. His regular-season role was small, but the pick clearly became usable roster value on a Finals team.

Mike Bratz Made the Third-Round Pick the Difference

Phoenix kept the Lakers' 1977 third-rounder and selected Mike Bratz at No. 66. Bratz then played 80 regular-season games as a rookie, 77 in 1978-79 and all 82 in 1979-80. His scoring rose from 4.7 points per game to 8.1 and then 8.5, and he appeared in 25 playoff games across those three seasons. In total, the third-round pick produced 239 Phoenix regular-season games before Bratz was lost to Dallas in the 1980 expansion draft. That sustained rotation value is the largest single return in the original transaction.

Final Verdict

Suns Win, A+/B+. Phoenix receives an A+ because the two picks became two separate useful assets: the 1976 second-rounder was converted into Lumpkin for the 1976 Finals run, while the 1977 third-rounder became Bratz for 239 regular-season games and 25 playoff appearances. Los Angeles receives a B+ because Calhoun supplied 133 useful games over two seasons, but the Lakers waived him without a downstream return. The trade was not a failure for Los Angeles; Phoenix simply extracted more total and postseason value from the two draft assets. Confidence is high on the package, Calhoun tenure, pick routing and Bratz outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Howard Porter from New York in late December 1974 for a 1975 first-round pick that eventually became No. 10 Bill Robinzine. Basketball-Reference's team and league ledgers date the transaction December 24, while Pro Sports Transactions lists December 26. Porter gave the Pistons 202 regular-season games across parts of four seasons, including 13.2 points and 5.9 rebounds per game in 1976-77, before Detroit included him in a larger trade with New Jersey. New York did not draft Robinzine; the Knicks used the pick with Henry Bibby to acquire Jim Barnett and Neal Walk from New Orleans. Detroit gets a slight hindsight edge because Porter supplied the stronger directly attributable return, while New York's downstream value was bundled with another meaningful asset.
perspectives.analysis:
Reconciling the December Date

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, New York and NBA league transaction pages all date the Howard Porter trade to December 24, 1974. Edwin Coil's Detroit executive record and Red Holzman's New York executive record agree. Pro Sports Transactions' 1975 draft-trade ledger instead lists December 26. The package is otherwise consistent: Detroit received Porter, while New York received Detroit's 1975 first-round pick, later identified as the No. 10 selection that ultimately became Bill Robinzine. The source-backed record uses December 24 as the canonical date and preserves the two-day source conflict in audit metadata rather than hiding it.

Porter Became a Multi-Year Detroit Rotation Player

Porter had played only 17 games for the Knicks before the trade. His role expanded immediately in Detroit, where he appeared in 41 games in 1974-75 and averaged 10.6 points and 5.3 rebounds while shooting 50 percent from the field. He then played 75 games in 1975-76 and 78 in 1976-77, when he averaged 13.2 points and 5.9 rebounds. Porter appeared in eight more Detroit games in 1977-78 before being traded. That gives the Pistons 202 regular-season games of directly attributable value from the original acquisition.

Detroit Also Retained Some Downstream Value

On November 7, 1977, Detroit included Howard Porter, Kevin Porter and cash in a trade with New Jersey for Al Skinner plus 1978 and 1979 second-round picks. Because Howard Porter was only one component of the outgoing package, the entire Nets return cannot be credited to the 1974 transaction. It still demonstrates that Porter remained a tradeable asset after nearly three years in Detroit. A source-backed evaluation can acknowledge that continuing value without pretending the later package belonged entirely to him.

New York Used the Pick Rather Than Drafting Robinzine

The legacy archive entry makes it look as though the Knicks simply received Bill Robinzine. That is not what happened. On February 1, 1975, New York sent Henry Bibby and Detroit's first-round pick to the New Orleans Jazz for Jim Barnett and Neal Walk. The pick continued moving: New Orleans later sent it to Kansas City-Omaha, which ultimately used No. 10 on Robinzine. Robinzine's productive NBA career therefore belongs to the later Kings outcome, not directly to the Knicks. For New York, the relevant realized value is the pick's role in the Barnett-Walk package.

The Knicks' Return Was Real but Mixed With Henry Bibby

Barnett and Walk both contributed to New York, and Walk ultimately played 123 regular-season games for the Knicks. The difficulty is attribution. New York did not exchange the Detroit pick by itself; Henry Bibby was part of the package sent to New Orleans. Crediting all of Barnett and Walk to the pick would overstate the value created by the Porter trade, while ignoring the downstream transaction would understate it. The safest retrospective treatment is to recognize that the pick retained meaningful trade value but not assign the full later player package solely to this transaction.

Final Verdict

Slight Pistons Edge, A/B+. Detroit receives an A because Porter supplied 202 regular-season games, became a meaningful scorer and rebounder, and retained some later trade value. New York receives a B+ because the first-round pick was valuable enough to help acquire Barnett and Walk, but the Knicks had to add Henry Bibby, making the downstream return only partly attributable to the Porter deal. Bill Robinzine should not be counted as direct Knicks production because New York never used the pick on him. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes, with medium-high confidence on the exact transaction date because of the December 24 versus December 26 source conflict. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
