los-angeles-clippers.summary: Buffalo acquired veteran forward Jim Washington from Atlanta on January 8, 1975 for a 1976 fifth-round pick that became No. 82 Connie White. Washington played 42 regular-season games for the Braves after the trade, averaging 4.2 points and 4.7 rebounds in 16.0 minutes, then appeared once more for Buffalo in 1975-76 before his NBA career ended. Atlanta held the pick through the 1976 draft and selected White, a California guard, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season statistics for him. The modern Clippers franchise therefore receives the hindsight win: Buffalo obtained 43 games of actual NBA production while Atlanta's draft return never reached an NBA regular-season game.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Verified January 8 Transaction

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Buffalo and NBA league transaction ledgers agree that the Hawks traded Jim Washington to the Buffalo Braves on January 8, 1975 for a 1976 fifth-round draft pick. The later draft record identifies that selection as No. 82, which Atlanta used on Connie White. The archive maps historical Buffalo to the modern Los Angeles Clippers franchise key, so the source-backed record remains under los-angeles-clippers even though every contemporary transaction source correctly names the Braves. The package is unusually straightforward: one veteran player for one future fifth-round selection.

Washington Supplied Immediate Frontcourt Depth

Washington joined a Buffalo team that finished 49-33 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. After the trade he appeared in 42 regular-season games, averaging 16.0 minutes, 4.2 points and 4.7 rebounds while shooting 47.5 percent from the field. His per-36 rebounding rate was 10.5, which reflects the skill that had kept him in NBA rotations throughout the previous decade. He was not a featured scorer for Buffalo, but he provided experienced frontcourt minutes during a winning season and gave the club real on-court value from an otherwise distant fifth-round pick.

His Buffalo Tenure Was Brief

The limitation is duration. Washington played only one additional game for Buffalo in 1975-76, logging seven minutes, and that was the final NBA regular-season appearance of his career. The Braves therefore received 43 games in total from the transaction and did not preserve a meaningful later trade asset. That keeps the return from earning an elite grade even though it clearly beats a pick that never produced NBA minutes. The value is best described as useful short-term depth rather than a transformational acquisition.

Atlanta Waited Until the 1976 Draft

The Hawks' consideration did not convey for more than a year. Atlanta retained the fifth-rounder and used it on Connie White with the 82nd overall selection in the 1976 NBA Draft. The Hawks' transaction page and franchise draft history both preserve that outcome. White was a 6-foot-4 guard from California, and Basketball-Reference lists him as Atlanta's fifth-round selection. Because the pick did turn into a named player, the relationship should remain explicit rather than being left as generic future consideration.

White Never Produced NBA Regular-Season Value

Basketball-Reference's player page contains White's draft information but no NBA season statistics, and Atlanta's franchise draft table likewise shows no NBA games for the No. 82 selection. That means the Hawks realized no regular-season production from the draft asset. A late-round pick still carries some optionality at the moment of the trade, so the return should not be graded as though Atlanta received literally nothing. In hindsight, however, the option did not convert into an NBA roster contribution.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, B+/D+. Buffalo receives a B+ because Washington supplied 42 useful games during a 49-win season plus one final appearance the next year. His role was limited and the tenure was short, so the return stops below the A range. Atlanta receives a D+ because the fifth-round pick was retained and used on a real prospect, but White never played an NBA regular-season game. The outcome is clear without exaggerating Washington's impact: Buffalo converted a low future pick into immediate rotation depth, while Atlanta's eventual selection produced no NBA minutes. Confidence is high on the transaction date, package, Washington statistics and White draft outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

new-york-knicks.summary: New York acquired Jim Barnett and Neal Walk from the New Orleans Jazz on February 1, 1975 for Henry Bibby, Detroit's 1975 first-round pick and cash. The pick had come to New York in the Howard Porter trade and ultimately became No. 10 Bill Robinzine, but New Orleans did not use it in the draft. The Jazz moved the selection to Kansas City-Omaha for Ron Behagen and a 1976 second-rounder that became Major Jones. Bibby played 107 regular-season games for New Orleans, while Behagen added 126 more across two seasons. Barnett and Walk combined for 222 Knicks games. Both clubs received useful value, but New Orleans created the deeper asset chain and earns the hindsight edge.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The February 1 Package Is Well Documented

Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Jazz and NBA transaction ledgers agree on the core February 1, 1975 exchange: New York received Jim Barnett and Neal Walk, while New Orleans received Henry Bibby and Detroit's 1975 first-round pick. The official Jazz media guide and Pro Sports Transactions add one more piece that Basketball-Reference omits: cash from New York to New Orleans. The Detroit pick had reached the Knicks in the Howard Porter trade, so this transaction continues the same asset chain already established in the source-backed archive.

New York Received Two Rotation Players

Barnett played 28 games for the Knicks after the trade in 1974-75 and another 71 in 1975-76, giving New York 99 regular-season games. His role was modest by that stage of his career, but he still averaged 6.5 points in the first partial season and 5.9 the next year. Walk gave the Knicks more frontcourt volume. He played 30 games after the trade, all 82 in 1975-76 and 11 more in 1976-77, for 123 regular-season games in New York. His best Knicks season was 1975-76, when he averaged 7.4 points and 4.7 rebounds in 16.3 minutes.

Bibby Became a Useful Jazz Guard

perspectives.analysis:
The February 1 Trade Is Straightforward

Basketball-Reference's Kansas City-Omaha, New Orleans and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the February 1, 1975 exchange. The Kings sent Nate Williams to the Jazz and received Rick Adelman plus Ollie Johnson. No draft choice or cash belongs to the original transaction, which makes the first stage of the comparison unusually direct. The historical team keys in the archive map Kansas City-Omaha to the modern Sacramento Kings franchise and New Orleans to the modern Utah Jazz franchise, but the analysis preserves the contemporary team names when describing what happened.

Adelman Was a Short-Term Piece

Rick Adelman had just arrived in New Orleans from Chicago in November 1974. After moving to Kansas City-Omaha, he appeared in 18 regular-season games and averaged 6.7 minutes and 1.7 points. Those were the final NBA games of his playing career. Adelman later became far more important as an NBA coach, but that coaching career cannot be credited to this player transaction. For trade-value purposes, the Kings received only the 18 games he actually played after the deal.

Ollie Johnson Supplied the Real Kings Return

Ollie Johnson was the durable piece. He played 30 games for Kansas City-Omaha after the trade in 1974-75, then 81 games in 1975-76 and another 81 in 1976-77. That is 192 regular-season games for the franchise, including a 1975-76 season in which he averaged 10.1 points and 4.4 rebounds in 26.2 minutes. Combined with Adelman's 18 games, the Kings received 210 regular-season appearances from the two incoming players. Johnson was a legitimate multi-year rotation forward and keeps the Kings side from being graded as a poor outcome.

Johnson Still Had Trade Value in 1977

On June 1, 1977, Kansas City sent Johnson, a 1978 first-round pick and a 1978 second-round pick to the Lakers for Lucius Allen. That later move shows Johnson retained value, but the full Allen return cannot responsibly be assigned to Johnson because two draft picks were also in the package. A source-backed archive should record the continuing asset chain without pretending one component purchased the entire downstream player. The original deal therefore gets credit for Johnson's direct Kings production and only limited qualitative credit for his later inclusion in a larger trade.

Williams Became the Best Player in the Deal

Nate Williams immediately took on a larger scoring role in New Orleans. He played 35 games after the trade in 1974-75 and averaged 14.3 points, then appeared in 81 games in 1975-76 at 12.8 points and 79 games in 1976-77 at 12.3 points. He added 27 more Jazz games in 1977-78 before being traded. Across those four partial seasons, Williams played 222 regular-season games for New Orleans. His scoring role and durability made him the strongest directly attributable basketball asset on either side of the transaction.

New Orleans Also Preserved Downstream Value

The Jazz did not simply lose Williams when his role ended. On January 5, 1978, New Orleans traded him to Golden State for a 1978 second-round pick that became No. 35 Tommie Green. Green did not become a meaningful NBA player for the Jazz, so the later pick did not add major realized production. It still matters that Williams remained tradeable after 222 games. New Orleans received both the best direct player outcome and an additional asset at the end of the tenure.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win, A/B+. New Orleans receives an A because Williams gave the franchise 222 regular-season games, three consecutive double-figure scoring seasons after the trade and a later second-round pick. Kansas City receives a B+ because Johnson supplied 192 useful games and Adelman added 18 more, but the combined package never matched Williams' offensive role or downstream value. The Kings side was productive enough that this is not a lopsided deal; the Jazz simply received the best player and kept value alive longer. Confidence is high on the date, package, direct production and downstream transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

boston-celtics.analysis:
A Rare Trade That Worked for Both Teams

Basketball-Reference's Boston, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers agree on the May 23, 1975 structure: Boston acquired Charlie Scott and sent Paul Westphal plus two second-round picks to Phoenix. The first pick was No. 36 in 1975 and became Jimmy Dan Conner. The second was No. 33 in 1976 and became Raymond 'Butch' Feher. Unlike many historical transactions in this archive, the principal players on both sides produced immediate, high-level value, making the correct retrospective question less about finding a loser and more about measuring championship impact against a longer star-level prime.

Scott Solved an Immediate Boston Need

Scott stepped directly into Boston's starting lineup in 1975-76. He played all 82 regular-season games and averaged 17.6 points, 4.4 rebounds and 4.2 assists while logging 35.5 minutes per game. In the playoffs he appeared in all 18 games and averaged 15.4 points as the Celtics won the 1976 NBA championship. That title matters enormously in trade evaluation. Boston did not merely add regular-season scoring; it acquired a starting guard who contributed throughout a championship run in his first season with the club.

Scott's Boston Value Extended Beyond One Championship

He remained with the Celtics for parts of two more seasons, playing 43 games in 1976-77 and 31 more for Boston in 1977-78 before being traded to the Lakers. That gives Boston 156 regular-season games from Scott. His later Celtics production never matched the championship year, but the acquisition still delivered more than a one-season rental. The strongest case for Boston's grade remains simple: the trade helped create a title-winning starting five immediately, which is one of the clearest forms of realized value any contender can receive.

Westphal Became the Best Long-Term Player in the Deal

Phoenix turned Westphal from a valuable Boston reserve into a franchise star. He played 82 games in 1975-76, averaged 20.5 points and 5.4 assists, and helped lead the Suns to the first NBA Finals appearance in franchise history. Over his first Phoenix stint he played 406 regular-season games. From 1976-77 through 1979-80 he made four straight All-Star teams and four straight All-NBA teams, including three First Team selections. His peak was longer and individually stronger than Scott's Boston tenure.

Westphal Also Preserved Major Downstream Value

Phoenix's return did not stop when Westphal's first Suns stint ended. On June 4, 1980, the Suns traded him to Seattle for Dennis Johnson. Johnson then became a major Phoenix guard himself and made the 1981 All-Star team during his time with the club before later becoming part of another significant transaction chain. It would be excessive to assign every later Johnson outcome directly to the 1975 trade, but the swap clearly shows that Westphal retained substantial asset value after five high-level seasons in Phoenix.

The Two Draft Picks Were Secondary

The 1975 No. 36 pick became Jimmy Conner, who never played an NBA regular-season game. He did appear in 24 ABA games for Kentucky in 1975-76, but that did not create Phoenix NBA value. The 1976 No. 33 pick became Butch Feher, who played 48 games for the Suns as a rookie and averaged 5.2 points in 10.1 minutes. Feher supplied legitimate depth for one season, but the picks were clearly supporting pieces compared with Westphal.

Final Verdict

Slight Suns Edge, A+/A. Phoenix receives an A+ because Westphal became a four-time All-Star and four-time All-NBA player in his first Suns stint, led the franchise to the 1976 Finals and later returned Dennis Johnson. Boston receives an A because Scott became an immediate championship starter, played 156 regular-season games for the Celtics and delivered exactly the kind of short-term impact a contender seeks. The draft picks add modest extra value to Phoenix but are not the reason for the verdict. This is a two-sided success with Phoenix holding the stronger long-term outcome. Confidence is high on the date, package, player production and draft outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.analysis:
The May 28 Deal Was Cancelled

The legacy archive entry describes Detroit acquiring Earl Williams from Phoenix for Willie Norwood, with a conditional 1976 draft pick tied to Norwood's physical. That package appears in historical transaction material, but the authoritative later ledger resolves the key question: the May 28 transaction was cancelled. Basketball-Reference's 1975-76 Detroit transaction page states that Williams was originally traded for Norwood on May 28, 1975 but that the trade was cancelled. The league-wide 1975-76 transaction ledger repeats the same explanation. That means there is no completed May 28 exchange to grade.

No Player Production Should Be Assigned to the Proposed Swap

A cancelled transaction must not be evaluated as though the players changed teams. Earl Williams did not become a Piston in May, and Willie Norwood did not become a Sun through this proposal. Assigning Williams' later Detroit games to the May transaction would create a false chain, while assigning Norwood's later career to Phoenix would be even more misleading because he never joined the Suns. perspectives.summary: Kansas City-Omaha acquired Detroit's 1975 first-round pick from New Orleans on May 28, 1975 for Ron Behagen and Kansas City's 1976 second-round pick. The Kings used No. 10 on Bill Robinzine, who played 314 regular-season games for the franchise across four seasons and became a durable rotation forward. Behagen gave New Orleans 126 games over two seasons, including 11.5 points and 8.4 rebounds per game in 1975-76. The second-round pick later became No. 20 Major Jones, but New Orleans had already committed that future consideration to Portland in the earlier Rick Roberson trade, so Portland—not the Jazz—made the selection. Kansas City gets the hindsight edge, while New Orleans still received meaningful immediate value.
perspectives.analysis:
The Pick Chain Starts Before This Trade

The first-round pick Kansas City acquired had already moved twice. Detroit originally owned the 1975 No. 10 selection, sent it to New York for Howard Porter, and the Knicks then moved it to New Orleans in the February 1 Jim Barnett-Neal Walk trade. On May 28, New Orleans sent that same pick to Kansas City-Omaha for Ron Behagen and a 1976 second-round pick. Basketball-Reference's Kings and Jazz transaction pages and Pro Sports Transactions all preserve the package. The Kings used No. 10 the next day on Bill Robinzine.

Robinzine Gave Kansas City Four Full Seasons

Robinzine immediately became a useful frontcourt piece. He played 75 games as a rookie in 1975-76 and averaged 8.0 points and 4.7 rebounds. He played another 75 games the next season, all 82 in 1977-78 and all 82 again in 1978-79. That is 314 regular-season games for the Kings franchise in four seasons. His scoring climbed into double figures and his rebounding remained useful throughout the run. A first-round pick becoming a four-year rotation forward is a strong realized return even without All-Star honors.

Behagen Was a Real Return for New Orleans

New Orleans did not give away the pick for nothing. Ron Behagen played 66 games for the Jazz in 1975-76 and averaged 11.5 points, 8.4 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 26.3 minutes. He returned for 60 games in 1976-77 at 8.6 points and 7.2 rebounds. Across those two seasons, Behagen gave the Jazz 126 regular-season games and substantial frontcourt production. His first year in particular was good enough that the deal cannot be treated as a one-sided failure for New Orleans.

The Major Jones Pick Was Already Owed to Portland

The legacy archive entry makes the 1976 second-round pick look like a simple future Jazz selection that became Major Jones. The chain is more complicated. New Orleans had traded Rick Roberson to Portland in September 1974 for Barry Clemens, future consideration, and cash. The Jazz later used the Kansas City second-rounder acquired in this Behagen trade to satisfy that future-consideration obligation. Portland ultimately held the No. 20 pick and drafted Major Jones. The official Jazz media guide explicitly describes the pick as sent to Portland under the earlier Roberson transaction.

That Means Major Jones' NBA Career Is Not Jazz Production

Major Jones eventually played six NBA seasons, but he did not do so for New Orleans. Portland drafted him, and his NBA debut came later with Houston after several seasons in other professional leagues. The Jazz should receive transaction value for acquiring an asset that helped satisfy an existing obligation, but Jones' later NBA statistics cannot be credited to New Orleans. This is an important distinction between a pick's final draft identity and the actual realized production a franchise received from the asset.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A/B+. Kansas City receives an A because the acquired No. 10 pick became Robinzine, who supplied 314 regular-season games over four full seasons. New Orleans receives a B+ because Behagen delivered 126 productive games and the 1976 second-rounder had real value as the asset used to complete the prior Portland obligation. The Jazz did not actually receive Major Jones' NBA production, so that career is not counted in their grade. Kansas City gets the edge through the longer directly attributable player return. Confidence is high on the May 28 package, pick chain and player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Sale Is Preserved Best in the Draft-Trade Ledger

Pro Sports Transactions records a May 29, 1975 exchange in which Seattle sent cash to Atlanta for the Hawks' second-round pick, No. 21 overall. The same specialist database repeats the deal in its transaction-search results. Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Seattle and league transaction pages do not list the cash sale itself, although they do confirm that Seattle selected Bruce Seals with the 21st pick that day. Because the specialist source supplies the missing ownership chain while the draft outcome is independently verified, the source-backed record can preserve the trade with medium-high confidence rather than pretending every database carries identical historical detail.

Seattle Turned the Pick Into an Immediate Rotation Player

Seals arrived with professional experience from the ABA and stepped directly into a substantial Seattle role. He played 81 games in 1975-76 and averaged 30.1 minutes, 11.8 points and 6.3 rebounds. That was not marginal second-round production. He also appeared in six playoff games during Seattle's postseason run. The next season he again played 81 games and averaged 11.0 points and 4.4 rebounds. In 1977-78 he added 73 games at 7.8 points and 3.1 rebounds. Across those three seasons, Seattle received 235 regular-season games from the acquired pick.

Seals' First Two Seasons Carry Most of the Value

The strongest part of the return came early. Seals was a significant rotation forward in both 1975-76 and 1976-77, averaging double figures in scoring each year. His role declined in the third season, but he still played 73 games. That gives Seattle both volume and useful peak production from a second-round selection. Even without a star-level outcome, a three-year contributor who played more than 2,400 minutes as a rookie represents a strong conversion of a purchased draft asset.

Atlanta's Return Was Cash, but the Amount Is Unknown

The Hawks received cash rather than a player or future draft asset. The reviewed specialist source does not provide the amount, and the major team transaction ledgers omit the sale entirely. That prevents a precise financial comparison. Cash can have legitimate value to a franchise, especially when ownership and roster economics differ from modern conditions, but a historical grade should not invent a dollar figure or assume the payment was trivial. Atlanta therefore receives credit for monetizing the pick while carrying a lower-confidence valuation than Seattle's measurable player return.

The Missing Entry in Basketball-Reference Matters

The omission from Basketball-Reference is worth preserving in the audit trail because it limits certainty about transaction mechanics, not about who drafted Seals. Seattle's 1975 draft record clearly shows Seals at No. 21, and Pro Sports Transactions explicitly traces that pick from Atlanta to Seattle for cash. The appropriate response is not to erase the transaction or overstate confidence; it is to retain the specialist chain, cite the independent draft confirmation, and mark the cash amount as unresolved.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, A-/C+. Seattle receives an A- because the purchased second-round pick became Seals, who supplied 235 regular-season games and two double-figure scoring seasons. Atlanta receives a C+ because it converted the pick into cash, but the amount is unknown and no further basketball asset can be traced from the payment. The result is a clear realized-basketball advantage for Seattle without pretending the Hawks received nothing of value. Confidence is medium-high because the pick outcome is verified while the sale mechanics rely primarily on the specialist transaction ledger. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded Dwight Davis to Golden State on May 29, 1975 for Butch Beard, the No. 15 pick used on John Lambert and the No. 33 pick used on Mel Utley. Pro Sports Transactions describes Beard as future consideration delivered June 4, while Basketball-Reference lists him directly in the May 29 package. Lambert became the durable piece, playing 263 regular-season games for Cleveland across his first four seasons. Beard appeared in 15 Cavaliers games before being waived, and Utley never played an NBA regular-season game. Davis gave Golden State 105 games over two seasons. Cleveland gets the hindsight edge because Lambert's multi-year contribution outweighed Davis' shorter Warriors tenure.
perspectives.analysis:
The Core Package Is Consistent

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland and league ledgers list one May 29, 1975 transaction: Dwight Davis to Golden State for Butch Beard, a first-round pick later used on John Lambert and a second-round pick later used on Mel Utley. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same asset chain but treats Beard as future consideration delivered June 4. That timing difference does not change the economic package; Beard, Lambert and Utley all belong to Cleveland's return.

Lambert Supplied the Long-Term Value

Cleveland used the No. 15 pick on John Lambert. He played 54 games as a rookie, 63 in 1976-77, 76 in 1977-78 and 70 in 1978-79. That is 263 regular-season games across four seasons before he later continued his career elsewhere. Lambert was mostly a reserve, but he became a dependable frontcourt body rather than a failed first-round selection. His role grew from 6.2 minutes per game as a rookie to roughly 14 minutes in each of his third and fourth seasons.

Beard Was Useful but Brief

Butch Beard arrived after serving as a rotation guard on Golden State's 1975 championship team. Cleveland used him in 15 games in 1975-76, where he averaged 6.5 points and 3.0 assists in 17.0 minutes. The Cavaliers then waived him in February 1976. Beard therefore added real short-term guard depth but did not become a lasting Cleveland asset. His value helps the package, yet Lambert is the primary reason Cleveland comes out ahead.

Utley Added No NBA Production

The No. 33 pick became Mel Utley, a St. John's guard. Basketball-Reference records the draft selection but no NBA regular-season statistics. Utley therefore represents draft optionality that did not convert into league production. That outcome limits how much credit Cleveland receives for the second-round piece and prevents the deal from becoming a runaway grade despite the three-asset return.

Davis Gave Golden State Two Seasons

Golden State still received a legitimate player. Davis appeared in 72 games in 1975-76, averaging 4.2 points and 3.1 rebounds in 12.0 minutes. He also played 11 playoff games that spring. The next season he appeared in 33 games at 4.8 points and 2.9 rebounds. Across the two seasons, Davis produced 105 regular-season games for the Warriors. That is useful reserve value, but it was shorter and smaller than Lambert's Cleveland tenure.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A-/B. Cleveland receives an A- because Lambert provided four seasons and 263 games, Beard added 15 games of veteran guard depth, and the club also held a second-round lottery ticket even though Utley never reached an NBA game. Golden State receives a B because Davis gave the Warriors 105 games and some playoff minutes, but his role never became large enough to overcome Cleveland's longer player return. Confidence is high on the package, draft identities and direct production; the only source wrinkle is whether Beard is described as part of the May 29 trade or future consideration delivered June 4. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The No. 33 pick became Mel Utley, a St. John's guard. Basketball-Reference records the draft selection but no NBA regular-season statistics. That outcome limits how much credit Cleveland receives for the second-round piece and prevents the deal from becoming a runaway grade despite the three-asset return.

Both sides did very well. Dantley won 1977 Rookie of the Year after averaging 20.3 points and 7.6 rebounds for Buffalo, then was packaged with Mike Bantom for Billy Knight. Sobers played 157 regular-season games for Phoenix, helped the Suns reach the 1976 NBA Finals and was later traded straight up for Don Buse, who gave Phoenix 245 games and three consecutive All-Defensive First Team seasons. Phoenix gets the slight hindsight edge because the Sobers-to-Buse chain produced more sustained franchise value.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Pick Swap Is Straightforward

Buffalo and Phoenix transaction ledgers, the NBA league record and Pro Sports Transactions all agree on the May 29, 1975 exchange. Buffalo sent the No. 16 pick in the 1975 draft to Phoenix for one of the Suns' 1976 first-round selections. Phoenix immediately used No. 16 on Ricky Sobers. One year later Buffalo used the acquired Phoenix pick at No. 6 on Adrian Dantley. The Suns' historical media guide independently describes the same swap from Phoenix's side, making the transaction mechanics unusually well documented for a draft-pick-only trade from this era.

Dantley Gave Buffalo Elite Rookie Value

Buffalo's pick outcome was excellent. Dantley played 77 games in 1976-77, started 76 of them and averaged 20.3 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.9 assists while shooting 52 percent from the field. He won NBA Rookie of the Year. A single season at that level is far more valuable than the legacy A-minus grade suggested, especially because the Braves acquired him without surrendering an existing rotation player. His Buffalo tenure was short, but it was high-end production from the moment he arrived.

Buffalo Converted Dantley Into Another High-Level Player

On September 1, 1977, Buffalo traded Dantley and Mike Bantom to Indiana for Billy Knight. Knight then played 53 games for the Braves in 1977-78 and averaged more than 20 points per game before the franchise's move to San Diego. Knight was later included in the large August 1978 Boston trade. Because Bantom was part of the Dantley-for-Knight package, the full value of Knight cannot be credited solely to the 1975 Phoenix pick. Still, the move proves Dantley retained major trade value after his Rookie of the Year season.

Sobers Was a Real Two-Year Suns Contributor

Phoenix also received more than a placeholder. Sobers played 78 games as a rookie in 1975-76, averaging 9.2 points, 3.3 rebounds and 2.8 assists. He appeared in 19 playoff games during the Suns' run to the 1976 NBA Finals and averaged 13.0 points in the postseason. Sobers improved in 1976-77, playing 79 games and averaging 13.6 points and 3.0 assists. That gives Phoenix 157 regular-season games plus a meaningful playoff run before the club converted him into another asset.

The Sobers-to-Buse Chain Was Exceptionally Productive

Phoenix traded Sobers to Indiana on September 6, 1977 for Don Buse. Buse then started all 82 games for the Suns in both 1977-78 and 1978-79 and played 81 more in 1979-80. He earned All-Defensive First Team honors in each of those three Phoenix seasons. That is 245 regular-season games of elite defensive guard play created directly from Sobers. Unlike Buffalo's Dantley-to-Knight transaction, Phoenix did not have to add another player to acquire Buse, so the downstream attribution is much cleaner.

Why Phoenix Gets the Narrow Edge

Buffalo won the star-quality portion of the pick swap. Dantley was immediately the best individual player produced by the transaction and his Rookie of the Year season was outstanding. Phoenix, however, created a longer uninterrupted chain: two Sobers seasons, a Finals run and then three full Buse seasons with first-team All-Defense recognition. Buffalo's later Knight value is meaningful but partly depends on adding Bantom, which makes it less attributable to Dantley alone. The difference is enough to move the historical verdict away from the legacy claim of a clear Buffalo win.

Final Verdict

Slight Suns Edge, A+/A. Phoenix receives an A+ because Sobers contributed 157 games and a Finals run, then was traded one-for-one for Buse, who added 245 games and three straight All-Defensive First Team seasons. Buffalo receives an A because the acquired pick became Dantley, the 1977 Rookie of the Year, and Dantley retained enough trade value to help acquire Knight. Both franchises extracted major value. The Suns' advantage comes from the longer, cleaner downstream asset chain rather than from Dantley being a poor outcome. Confidence is high on the pick identities, player outcomes and downstream Sobers-to-Buse transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: The New York Nets traded Larry Kenon to the San Antonio Spurs for Swen Nater on June 3, 1975. The legacy archive record incorrectly included cash; Basketball-Reference's ABA league ledger and both franchise transaction pages show the Kenon-Nater deal as a straight player swap, while cash belonged to a separate same-day Mike Gale transaction. Kenon became a cornerstone in San Antonio, averaging 20.7 points and 10.3 rebounds over five seasons and making three All-Star teams. Nater gave New York 43 games at 8.7 points and 10.3 rebounds before being traded with Billy Schaeffer for Jim Eakins. San Antonio wins decisively because Kenon delivered far more sustained star-level value.
perspectives.analysis:
The First Correction Is the Package

New York and San Antonio made two separate transactions on June 3, 1975. Basketball-Reference's ABA league ledger lists them independently: the Nets sold Mike Gale to San Antonio for cash, and in a second move the Nets traded Larry Kenon to the Spurs for Swen Nater. Roy Boe's Nets executive record and John Begzos' Spurs record repeat the same separation. The legacy this review record had pulled cash into the Kenon-Nater exchange, creating a false three-asset package. That cash item is removed from this trade and remains attributable only to the separate Mike Gale transaction that follows in the chronology.

Kenon Became a Long-Term San Antonio Star

Kenon was already an ABA All-Star with New York before the trade, but San Antonio received the prime of his career. Contemporary Spurs history summarizes his five-season run at roughly 20.7 points and 10.3 rebounds per game. He made three All-Star teams during that span and became one of the franchise's core scorers and rebounders alongside George Gervin. The transaction therefore produced exactly the kind of durable high-end return that retrospective grading should reward: immediate performance, multiple seasons of continuity and major-team relevance.

The Spurs' Competitive Window Benefited Directly

Kenon's value was not isolated to box-score accumulation. He remained part of San Antonio through the franchise's transition from the ABA into the NBA and helped the Spurs reach the 1979 Eastern Conference finals, where they came within one game of the NBA Finals. That does not make every team success his alone, but it confirms that the trade acquired a player who remained central throughout one of the franchise's earliest strong NBA periods. The fact that he stayed for five seasons also eliminates the attribution problems that often appear in short rental trades.

Nater Was Useful but Short-Lived in New York

The Nets did receive a real player. Nater appeared in 43 games for New York in 1975-76 and averaged 8.7 points and 10.3 rebounds in 23.6 minutes. His per-36 rebounding rate was 15.6, so the move clearly gave the Nets a strong glass presence. The limitation was duration. On January 27, 1976, New York traded Nater and Billy Schaeffer to the Virginia Squires for Jim Eakins. Nater therefore did not remain through the entire Nets title run and did not create a long direct tenure comparable to Kenon's in San Antonio.

The Eakins Return Adds Some Nets Value

Jim Eakins played 34 regular-season games for the Nets after the January trade and was on the roster that won the 1976 ABA championship. Because Billy Schaeffer was bundled with Nater, Eakins cannot be credited entirely to the original Kenon trade, just as multi-asset downstream deals elsewhere in the archive are not assigned to one component. The branch still matters: New York extracted some continuing value from Nater rather than losing him for nothing. It is not enough to close the enormous gap created by Kenon's five seasons of star production.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win, A+/B-. San Antonio receives an A+ because Kenon became a five-season franchise pillar, averaged approximately 20 points and 10 rebounds, made three All-Star teams and helped anchor a contender through the ABA-to-NBA transition. New York receives a B- because Nater provided 43 strong rebounding games and then contributed to the package that brought back Eakins, but the tenure was short and the downstream return required another player. The cash error is removed because authoritative transaction ledgers place that payment in the separate Mike Gale sale. Confidence is high on the June 3 date, straight player-for-player structure and realized outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: The New York Nets sold Mike Gale to the San Antonio Spurs for cash on June 3, 1975, in a transaction separate from the same-day Larry Kenon-for-Swen Nater trade. Gale became a long-term Spurs guard, playing 414 regular-season games across the club's final ABA season and first five NBA seasons while providing steady ball-handling and perimeter defense. San Antonio later included Gale with a 1982 first-round pick in the December 1980 trade that brought back Ron Brewer. New York's cash return is verified but the amount is not preserved, limiting the precision of the Nets grade. San Antonio still gets the clear hindsight win because six seasons of rotation value are directly documented.
perspectives.analysis:
Separating the Two June 3 Transactions

Basketball-Reference's San Antonio and New York transaction ledgers list two distinct June 3, 1975 deals. In one, New York traded Larry Kenon for Swen Nater. In the other, the Nets sold Mike Gale to the Spurs for cash. Roy Boe's executive record preserves the same separation. That distinction is important because the legacy archive had previously blurred the cash into the Kenon-Nater transaction. This review removed the cash from that record; this review now preserves it only where the authoritative ledgers place it: in the Gale sale.

Gale Immediately Became a Full-Season Spurs Guard

Gale played 78 games for San Antonio in the final ABA season of 1975-76. He averaged 6.8 points, 3.1 assists and 2.7 rebounds while appearing in every regular-season role the club needed from its backcourt. The Spurs then entered the NBA with Gale still in the rotation. In 1976-77 he played all 82 games and averaged 10.3 points, 5.8 assists and 2.3 steals, turning the cash purchase into an immediate NBA starter-level return rather than a short-term depth move.

The Value Continued for Years

Gale remained in San Antonio for 70 games in 1977-78, 82 in 1978-79 and 67 in 1979-80. He appeared in 35 more games for the Spurs in 1980-81 before being traded in December. Across the ABA and NBA portions of his San Antonio tenure, that is 414 regular-season games. His scoring role fluctuated, but his minutes, assists and steals show a guard who remained usable across multiple coaches, league structures and roster iterations. That durability is the central reason the original cash purchase grades so well for the Spurs.

San Antonio Also Retained Downstream Trade Value

On December 19, 1980, San Antonio traded Gale and a 1982 first-round pick to Portland for Ron Brewer. The first-round pick later became Ricky Pierce, so Brewer cannot be credited to Gale alone; the draft asset was an important component of the package. Still, Gale remained valuable enough to be included in a meaningful NBA trade more than five years after San Antonio acquired him for cash. The downstream deal therefore supports, but does not dominate, the verdict on the original transaction.

New York's Financial Return Is Unpriced

The Nets did receive real consideration. The transaction ledgers explicitly say San Antonio sent cash, so New York converted Gale into financial value instead of waiving him or losing him without return. The problem is that the reviewed sources do not preserve the amount. Without that figure, the archive cannot compare the payment directly with Gale's six seasons of Spurs service or assign a precise economic win-loss calculation. The grade should recognize the verified sale while keeping confidence below the level used for trades where both sides' basketball assets are fully measurable.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win, A+/C+. San Antonio receives an A+ because a cash purchase produced 414 regular-season games across the ABA-to-NBA transition, including several seasons of substantial guard minutes, and Gale retained some trade value through December 1980. New York receives a C+ because it monetized the player through a verified cash sale, but the amount is unknown and there is no traceable basketball asset on the Nets side. The verdict is clear on realized court value while the financial comparison remains incomplete. Confidence is medium-high because the transaction structure and Gale outcome are well documented but the cash amount is not. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Lumpkin played 34 regular-season games and all 17 playoff games for the 1975-76 Suns team that reached the NBA Finals, then Phoenix waived him in October 1976. Portland never used the acquired pick on Jacky Dorsey: one year later the Trail Blazers sent that No. 26 selection to New Orleans for a 1977 second-rounder that became No. 28 Kim Anderson. Anderson eventually played 21 regular-season games for Portland. Phoenix gets a modest hindsight edge because Lumpkin contributed during a Finals run, while Portland's converted draft return produced only a short NBA stint.
perspectives.analysis:
The June 9 Trade Is Straightforward

Basketball-Reference's Phoenix, Portland and NBA league transaction ledgers agree that the Suns acquired Phil Lumpkin on June 9, 1975 and sent Portland a 1976 second-round pick. Harry Glickman's executive record independently preserves the same trade. The legacy archive entry correctly identifies that original pick as the selection that ultimately became No. 26 Jacky Dorsey, but that shorthand hides an important downstream transaction: Portland did not make the Dorsey selection. The Trail Blazers moved the pick before the 1976 draft.

Lumpkin Contributed During Phoenix's Finals Season

Lumpkin played 34 regular-season games for Phoenix in 1975-76. His role was small—10.9 minutes per game, 2.1 points and 1.4 assists—but he remained on the roster through the postseason. Basketball-Reference records 17 playoff appearances as the Suns defeated Seattle and Golden State before losing to Boston in the 1976 NBA Finals. Lumpkin averaged only eight postseason minutes per game, so he should not be credited as a major driver of the Finals run. He was still a real bench contributor on a conference-championship team, which gives Phoenix measurable realized value from the deal.

Phoenix's Return Ended After One Season

The Suns did not preserve a later asset through Lumpkin. Phoenix waived him on October 15, 1976, before the next regular season began. He never played another NBA game. That limits the Suns' side to one season of reserve minutes and the playoff appearances attached to the 1976 run. The trade therefore cannot receive a high grade simply because the team reached the Finals; Lumpkin's individual role was limited, and Phoenix did not recover a player or draft asset when his tenure ended.

Portland Converted the Pick Before Draft Night

On June 3, 1976, Portland traded the acquired second-round pick to the New Orleans Jazz for New Orleans' 1977 second-round selection. New Orleans then used No. 26 on Jacky Dorsey. This matters for attribution. Dorsey's later NBA career should not be counted as Portland production, because the Trail Blazers had already exchanged his draft slot for a different future pick. The correct Portland branch is the 1977 selection received from New Orleans.

Portland used the New Orleans second-rounder at No. 28 in the 1977 draft on Kim Anderson. Anderson spent the 1977-78 season outside the NBA, then played 21 regular-season games for Portland in 1978-79. He averaged 3.0 points and 2.1 rebounds in 10.7 minutes. That is a legitimate downstream return from the original Lumpkin trade, but it remained a small one. The Trail Blazers effectively converted a 1976 second-rounder into a 1977 second-rounder and eventually received 21 games of reserve production.

Final Verdict

Suns Win, B+/C+. Phoenix receives a B+ because Lumpkin gave the club 34 regular-season games and 17 playoff appearances during a Finals season, even though his role was limited and ended after one year. Portland receives a C+ because the Trail Blazers intelligently moved the 1976 pick forward and eventually used the replacement selection on Kim Anderson, but Anderson produced only 21 NBA games for Portland. Jacky Dorsey's career is preserved as the final identity of the original No. 26 pick without being falsely credited as Portland production. Confidence is high on the transaction date, draft-pick chain and realized outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles acquired Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Walt Wesley from Milwaukee on June 16, 1975 for Elmore Smith, Brian Winters, Dave Meyers and Junior Bridgeman. The Lakers received 14 seasons and 1,093 regular-season games from Abdul-Jabbar, who won three MVP awards in Los Angeles and became the center of five championship teams. Milwaukee still extracted an exceptional rebuilding package: Bridgeman played 711 games for the Bucks, Winters 582 and Meyers 281, while Smith later helped Milwaukee acquire two first-round picks. The Bucks return deserves a strong grade, but the Lakers win because one trade delivered a franchise pillar whose production, awards and championship impact lasted through 1989.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The June 16 Blockbuster Has a Clean Four-for-Two Structure

Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Bucks and NBA league transaction ledgers all agree on the June 16, 1975 package. Los Angeles sent Elmore Smith, Brian Winters, Dave Meyers and Junior Bridgeman to Milwaukee for Kareem Abdul-Jabbar and Walt Wesley. Pete Newell's Lakers executive record and Wayne Embry's Milwaukee record independently match the same six-player exchange. The legacy summary's reference to future consideration is therefore removed: the reviewed authoritative records support a four-player Bucks return, not an additional unresolved asset.

Abdul-Jabbar Became a Fourteen-Year Lakers Institution

Abdul-Jabbar played 1,093 regular-season games for Los Angeles from 1975-76 through 1988-89 and scored 24,176 points for the franchise. He won the NBA MVP award in each of his first two Lakers seasons and again in 1979-80. The Lakers did not immediately become champions—his first season ended at 40-42—but the trade gave the franchise an elite center years before Magic Johnson arrived. That continuity is central to the verdict because Los Angeles did not acquire a short-window superstar. It acquired a player who remained productive across multiple roster eras.

The Championship Payoff Eventually Became Historic

Abdul-Jabbar was the starting center for Lakers championship teams in 1980, 1982, 1985, 1987 and 1988. He was already 32 when the first of those titles arrived and remained on the roster through the entire five-title Showtime run. The 1985 championship was particularly notable because Los Angeles finally beat Boston in the Finals, with Abdul-Jabbar still functioning as a major contributor. A retrospective trade grade should not pretend one player single-handedly caused five championships, but a 14-season Hall of Fame tenure at the center of that run is extraordinary realized value from one transaction.

Walt Wesley Was Incidental to the Lakers Return

Wesley played only one regular-season game for Los Angeles in 1975-76. That makes the deal's Lakers value overwhelmingly attributable to Abdul-Jabbar rather than a balanced two-player return. Keeping Wesley in the source-backed record is still important because he was part of the verified package, but his four points and seven minutes for the Lakers do not materially affect the outcome. The trade can be evaluated accurately without inflating the secondary asset.

Milwaukee's Return Was Much Better Than a Typical Forced-Star Package

The Bucks received two players who became long-term franchise fixtures. Junior Bridgeman played 711 regular-season games for Milwaukee, placing him among the franchise's all-time leaders in appearances. Brian Winters played 582 Bucks games and was an All-Star in his first Milwaukee season. Those are not consolation pieces. They formed part of the bridge from the Abdul-Jabbar era into the competitive Don Nelson teams that followed.

Meyers and Smith Added More Real Value

Dave Meyers played all 281 games of his NBA career for Milwaukee, averaging 11.2 points and 6.3 rebounds across four active seasons before retiring. Elmore Smith also contributed before becoming part of another valuable transaction. In January 1977 Milwaukee sent Smith and Gary Brokaw to Cleveland for Rowland Garrett plus 1977 and 1978 first-round picks that became Ernie Grunfeld and George Johnson. Because Brokaw was also included, those downstream picks cannot be credited solely to Smith, but the move demonstrates that the fourth major piece of Milwaukee's return still carried trade value.

Why the Lakers Still Win Clearly

Milwaukee did about as well as a team with reduced leverage could reasonably hope to do: two long-term rotation pillars, a productive forward in Meyers and another tradeable big man in Smith. That return merits an A-range grade rather than the weaker mark often attached to the deal simply because Abdul-Jabbar became a Lakers icon. The separation comes from ceiling. Los Angeles received 1,093 games, three MVP awards and a player central to five championships. Milwaukee received a deep rebuilding package, but none of the individual pieces approached that level of franchise-changing impact.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A+/A. Los Angeles receives an A+ because Abdul-Jabbar delivered fourteen seasons, three Lakers MVP awards and a central role on five championship teams. Milwaukee receives an A because Bridgeman, Winters and Meyers combined for enormous long-term roster value and Smith retained downstream trade value. The Bucks did not fail in extracting a return; the Lakers simply acquired one of the most valuable long-term star outcomes in league history. Confidence is high on the exact package, player identities and realized outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana sold Jim Lee's ABA playing rights to San Antonio on June 24, 1975 for cash, eight days after the Pacers used San Antonio's own No. 18 second-round pick on the Syracuse guard. That pick had originally reached Indiana in the 1974 Donnie Freeman trade. Lee never appeared in an ABA or NBA regular-season game for the Spurs, and the reviewed secondary roster record later places him with the Baltimore Claws before that franchise folded in preseason. Indiana therefore gets the hindsight edge for converting unused draft rights into cash, although the payment amount is unknown and keeps the Pacers grade modest rather than treating the sale as a major win.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The June 24 Rights Sale Completes an Unusual Pick Loop

Indiana's transaction ledger and Pro Sports Transactions agree that the Pacers sold Jim Lee's ABA rights to San Antonio for cash on June 24, 1975. The path to that sale began almost a year earlier. In July 1974 Indiana sent Donnie Freeman to the Spurs for cash and San Antonio's 1975 second-round pick. The Pacers used that pick at No. 18 on Lee in the 1975 ABA draft, then sold the rights back to the same San Antonio franchise eight days after draft day. The source-backed record therefore treats this review as the final step of a previously verified asset chain rather than an isolated cash transaction.

Lee Was a Legitimate Two-League Draft Prospect

Lee was a 6-foot-2 guard from Syracuse and was selected in both major professional drafts in 1975. Indiana used the No. 18 ABA pick on him, while Cleveland selected him in the fifth round at No. 79 of the NBA draft. Basketball-Reference preserves the Cleveland selection and identifies Lee as a Syracuse guard. The dual selections show that the rights had genuine prospect value at the moment Indiana sold them, even though Lee never established a top-league regular-season career. That context prevents the San Antonio side from being treated as a nonsensical acquisition simply because the eventual statistical return was zero.

San Antonio Did Not Receive Regular-Season Production

The realized outcome is much less favorable for the Spurs. perspectives.summary: Denver acquired George Irvine and the ABA rights to David Thompson from the Virginia Squires on July 14, 1975 for Mack Calvin, Mike Green and Jan van Breda Kolff. The centerpiece was Thompson. He immediately became Denver's franchise star, averaging 26.0 points as a rookie in 1975-76, earning ABA All-Star and All-ABA honors, then carrying into the NBA after the merger and eventually reaching the Hall of Fame. Irvine also contributed 150 regular-season games across two Denver seasons. Virginia received accomplished veterans, especially Calvin and Green, but the Squires folded after the 1975-76 season and could not realize comparable long-term value. Denver wins decisively because the trade delivered a generational player plus useful secondary production.
perspectives.analysis:
The July 14 Blockbuster Is Straightforward

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Virginia and ABA transaction ledgers agree that Denver acquired George Irvine and the rights to David Thompson on July 14, 1975, sending Mack Calvin, Mike Green and Jan van Breda Kolff to the Squires. The timing is essential: Atlanta had selected Thompson first overall in the 1975 NBA draft, but Denver controlled the ABA route that ultimately secured his professional services. This was therefore not an ordinary veteran swap. It was a bet that Thompson could become the face of Denver basketball.

Thompson Immediately Justified the Price

Thompson's 1975-76 rookie season made the deal's direction obvious almost immediately. He averaged 26.0 points, 6.3 rebounds and 3.7 assists for Denver, made the ABA All-Star team and earned All-ABA First Team honors. He remained with the franchise through the ABA-NBA merger and became one of the NBA's most explosive scorers. In 1977-78 he averaged 27.2 points and finished third in NBA MVP voting. Thompson later entered the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame. No other asset in this transaction approached that combination of peak value, franchise importance and longevity.

Irvine Added Real Secondary Value

George Irvine was not merely attached to Thompson's rights. He gave Denver two useful seasons, appearing in 76 games in 1975-76 and 74 more in 1976-77. His scoring role was modest, but 150 regular-season appearances strengthened the return beyond the star acquisition. That matters for grading because Denver did not simply trade three rotation players for one prospect; it received one of the era's most important young stars plus a functional veteran wing who helped bridge the ABA and NBA versions of the franchise.

Virginia Received Proven Talent

The Squires did receive meaningful players. Mack Calvin had just made the 1975 ABA All-Star team for Denver and finished third in MVP voting. Mike Green was also a 1975 ABA All-Star and had produced two strong Denver seasons. Jan van Breda Kolff had played all 84 games for Denver in 1974-75. On paper, Virginia was acquiring immediate veteran competence in exchange for rights and a role player. The problem is that the franchise's financial instability and short remaining life prevented those assets from generating a durable return comparable to Thompson.

The Squires' Collapse Limits the Realized Return

Virginia finished 15-68 in 1975-76 and folded before the ABA-NBA merger. Calvin, Green and van Breda Kolff therefore could not become long-term Squires assets. Their careers continued elsewhere, but those later seasons do not count as Virginia return once the franchise ceased operations. The trade should not be graded as though the Squires received worthless players; Calvin and Green in particular were high-level ABA veterans. Hindsight evaluation, however, must use realized franchise value, and the short runway of the Squires sharply limits what their side produced.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A+/C+. Denver receives an A+ because Thompson became a franchise-defining superstar and Hall of Famer while Irvine added 150 useful games. Virginia receives a C+ because it acquired three established players, including recent All-Stars Calvin and Green, but the franchise collapsed after one season and could not convert that talent into lasting value. The grade gap reflects realized organizational outcome rather than dismissing the quality of the veterans sent to Virginia. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, Thompson rights chain and player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Jimmy Foster from the Spirits of St. Louis on July 30, 1975 for a draft choice. Basketball-Reference's Denver, Spirits and ABA transaction ledgers agree on the player movement and date, while Pro Sports Transactions describes Denver's return as future considerations or a draft pick with the exact selection unresolved. Foster played 48 regular-season games for Denver in 1975-76, totaling 148 points and 47 assists in a reserve role, and the Nuggets waived him on October 5, 1976. Because Denver's on-court return is measurable but the exact St. Louis draft asset cannot be identified, the trade remains Insufficient Evidence rather than forcing a directional grade.
perspectives.analysis:
The July 30 Transaction Is Verified

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Spirits of St. Louis and league transaction pages all record the same July 30, 1975 move: the Nuggets acquired Jimmy Foster and sent a draft choice to St. Louis. Pro Sports Transactions independently records Foster moving from the Spirits to Denver, but labels the return as future considerations or a draft pick with the exact round and player outcome unresolved. The source-backed archive therefore treats the transaction itself as secure while preserving the compensation uncertainty.

Foster Gave Denver One Season of Reserve Guard Depth

Foster appeared in 48 regular-season games for the 60-win Nuggets in 1975-76. Basketball-Reference credits him with 352 minutes, 148 points and 47 assists, or 3.1 points and 1.0 assist per game. He was not a major part of the rotation, but he did provide backcourt depth during Denver's final ABA season and appeared on a team that reached the ABA Finals. His direct value is therefore modest but real.

The Tenure Ended Before Denver's Second NBA Season

Denver carried Foster into the post-merger period but waived him on October 5, 1976. He did not produce a later trade return for the Nuggets. That limits Denver's realized asset chain to one ABA season of reserve minutes. The acquisition should not be treated like a hidden high-value transaction simply because Foster appeared on a 60-win team; his role was limited and his advanced metrics were poor.

St. Louis' Return Cannot Be Traced Reliably

The critical missing piece is the draft choice. Basketball-Reference does not identify the year, round or player outcome in the transaction line. Pro Sports Transactions likewise leaves the asset unresolved rather than connecting it to a specific later selection. Without a traceable draft slot, the archive cannot determine whether the Spirits realized a player, sold the pick, transferred it before the draft or lost the asset when the franchise ceased operations after the season.

The Spirits' End Does Not Automatically Make the Pick Worthless

St. Louis was not included in the ABA-NBA merger after the 1975-76 season, but that fact alone cannot be used to erase the value of an unidentified draft choice. The asset may have conveyed before the franchise stopped operating, or it may have been incorporated into another transaction. source-backed grading should not substitute franchise closure for evidence about a specific pick chain. The correct approach is to preserve the uncertainty rather than assume the return disappeared.

Final Resolution

Insufficient Evidence. Denver received a known player and realized 48 games of reserve production from Foster before waiving him in October 1976. St. Louis received a verified draft-related asset, but the exact selection and downstream outcome remain unidentified in the reviewed records. That asymmetry is not enough to justify a Nuggets win because the unknown draft return could have had value beyond Foster's modest role. Confidence is high on the date and Foster outcome, but only medium on the compensation details. Additional draft documentation would be required before a directional verdict could be justified. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The July 30 Trade Is Clear

Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Washington and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the basic exchange: the Braves received Dick Gibbs, and the Bullets received Buffalo's 1976 first-round pick. Bob Ferry's executive record confirms the same deal. Pro Sports Transactions adds cash to Washington's side, a detail omitted from Basketball-Reference. The pick later became the 13th selection in the 1976 NBA draft, where Washington chose Mitch Kupchak. The archive therefore keeps the cash as an undisclosed secondary asset while treating the first-round pick as the dominant return.

Gibbs Gave Buffalo One Reserve Season

Gibbs played 72 regular-season games for Buffalo in 1975-76, totaling 866 minutes and 335 points. He averaged 4.7 points and 1.5 rebounds in 12.0 minutes per game. That is legitimate depth on a 46-win playoff team, but it is not a high-impact return for a future first-round pick. Gibbs had already been a larger scorer in Seattle two seasons earlier, yet Buffalo used him almost exclusively as a reserve. He did not become a long-term Braves asset and did not create a later trade return.

Kupchak Immediately Outperformed the Cost

Washington used the acquired pick at No. 13 on Mitch Kupchak in 1976. He played all 82 games as a rookie and averaged 10.4 points and 6.0 rebounds while shooting 57.2 percent from the field. His role expanded in 1977-78, when he averaged 15.9 points and 6.9 rebounds in 67 games. Kupchak became a core frontcourt contributor for a Bullets team that won the 1978 NBA championship and returned to the Finals in 1979. The pick therefore produced both immediate regular-season value and postseason relevance at the highest level.

Washington Kept the Asset for Multiple Seasons

Kupchak remained with Washington through 1980-81. Injuries reduced portions of his later Bullets tenure, but the broader value chain is straightforward: the franchise received several seasons from a first-round talent who became an important part of its championship-era rotation. That is far more durable than Gibbs' one Buffalo season. Even without assigning any value to the cash component, the realized basketball return strongly favors Washington.

The Cash Makes an Already Strong Return Better

Pro Sports Transactions records cash moving from Buffalo to Washington along with the first-round pick. The amount is not preserved, so the archive should not pretend to know its financial significance. It still matters directionally because Washington did not merely receive a premium draft asset for Gibbs; the specialist transaction ledger indicates additional consideration as well. Since the pick alone became Kupchak, the verdict does not depend on pricing the cash.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, A+/C. Washington receives an A+ because the Buffalo pick became Kupchak, a multi-year frontcourt contributor and member of the 1978 championship team, with additional undisclosed cash also listed in the specialist ledger. Buffalo receives a C because Gibbs supplied 72 games of reserve depth on a playoff team but only one season of modest production and no downstream asset. The gap is large without overstating Gibbs' shortcomings: Buffalo obtained a usable player, while Washington turned his departure into a championship-era building block. Confidence is high on the date, pick outcome, Gibbs production and Kupchak career path. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The August 8 Trade Is Fully Traceable

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta and NBA transaction ledgers agree that the Hawks acquired Connie Hawkins from the Lakers on August 8, 1975 for a 1976 third-round pick. The draft record later identifies that selection as No. 36, which Los Angeles used on Rutgers guard Mike Dabney. Unlike several nearby 1975 transactions with unresolved future consideration, this asset chain is complete enough to grade directly: one veteran player went to Atlanta, one named draft pick went to Los Angeles, and both outcomes can be measured.

Hawkins Still Had Useful NBA Value

Hawkins was 33 and well past the peak that made him one of basketball's most celebrated forwards, but Atlanta still received a genuine rotation player. He appeared in 74 games in 1975-76, logged 1,907 minutes and averaged 8.2 points, 6.0 rebounds and 2.9 assists. He shot 44.7 percent from the field and started 25 games. On a rebuilding Hawks team, those minutes represented real veteran production rather than a ceremonial final season.

The Atlanta Season Was Hawkins' NBA Finale

The 1975-76 campaign was Hawkins' final NBA season. He did not create a downstream trade return for Atlanta, so the value chain ends with those 74 games. That prevents the Hawks' grade from reaching the very top tier despite the famous name involved. The transaction should be evaluated on what Atlanta actually received in 1975-76, not on Hawkins' earlier ABA and Phoenix accomplishments or his later Hall of Fame induction. Even on that narrower basis, the Hawks got meaningful value for a third-round selection.

Los Angeles Used the Pick on Mike Dabney

The Lakers retained Atlanta's third-rounder and selected Dabney 36th overall in the 1976 NBA draft. Basketball-Reference identifies him as a 6-foot-4 guard from Rutgers and confirms the Lakers as the drafting team. The draft decision therefore gives Los Angeles a definite asset outcome rather than an unresolved pick. The problem for the Lakers is what happened next: Dabney's Basketball-Reference page contains draft information but no NBA regular-season statistical line.

No Lakers NBA Production Came From the Pick

Because Dabney never logged an NBA regular-season game, the Lakers realized no measurable on-court return from the acquired selection. A third-round pick still had option value when the trade was made, and selecting a legitimate college guard was not inherently irrational. Hindsight grading, however, focuses on realized franchise value. Atlanta received 74 games and nearly 1,900 minutes from Hawkins; Los Angeles received no NBA games from the player chosen with the pick.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, A-/D+. Atlanta receives an A- because one third-round pick produced a full season of useful veteran forward play, including 74 games and substantial minutes. The grade stops below A or A+ because Hawkins' Atlanta tenure lasted only one season and produced no later asset. Los Angeles receives a D+ because the pick was used on a real prospect but did not yield an NBA regular-season appearance. Confidence is high on the August 8 date, the No. 36 pick chain and both player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Washington acquired Dave Bing and Detroit's 1977 first-round pick on August 28, 1975 for Kevin Porter. Bing gave the Bullets 146 regular-season games across two seasons, including an All-Star 1975-76 campaign with 16.2 points and 6.0 assists per game. Porter was productive when available for Detroit, playing 108 games before a November 1977 multi-player trade, including 10.2 assists per game in 19 appearances in 1975-76 and 81 games the next season. The first-round pick never became a Washington draft selection: the Bullets sent it to Atlanta in January 1977 as part of the Truck Robinson-Tom Henderson pick swap, and the Hawks used it at No. 14 on Tree Rollins. Washington still holds the hindsight edge because it received the stronger direct veteran return plus meaningful retained value from the first-round asset.
perspectives.analysis:
The August 28 Structure Is Clear

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Washington and league transaction ledgers agree on the core exchange: Detroit sent Dave Bing and a 1977 first-round pick to the Washington Bullets for Kevin Porter on August 28, 1975. The legacy archive record had incorrectly flattened the future pick into a traded player named Tree Rollins. That is not what happened. Washington received a draft asset, not Rollins' playing rights, and the distinction is important because the Bullets moved that pick before the 1977 draft. This repair restores the first-round pick as the actual asset and preserves Rollins only as its eventual selection outcome.

Bing Gave Washington Two Useful Seasons

Bing immediately remained a high-level NBA guard after leaving Detroit. He played all 82 regular-season games for Washington in 1975-76, averaging 16.2 points and 6.0 assists in 35.9 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with an All-Star selection, the 1976 All-Star Game MVP award and a sixth-place finish in league MVP voting. He returned for 64 games in 1976-77, averaging 10.6 points and 4.3 assists in a reduced role. Across the two Washington seasons, Bing supplied 146 regular-season appearances before his career moved to Boston. That direct return alone gave the Bullets dependable veteran value from the player side of the trade.

Porter Was Productive but His Detroit Tenure Was Shorter

Detroit did not come away empty-handed. Porter was already one of the league's premier passers, and in his first Pistons season he averaged 12.6 points and 10.2 assists across 19 games. In 1976-77 he appeared in 81 games and averaged 8.9 points and 7.3 assists in 26.1 minutes. He then played eight more Detroit games in 1977-78 before the Pistons packaged Kevin Porter, Howard Porter and cash to New Jersey for Al Skinner and two future second-round picks. Because Kevin Porter was only one component of that later package, this verdict credits him with retained trade utility without assigning the entire Skinner-and-picks return to the 1975 transaction.

The First-Round Pick Did Not Stay in Washington

The largest correction concerns the future first-rounder. On January 20, 1977, Washington traded Truck Robinson and the Detroit-origin first-round pick to Atlanta for Tom Henderson and Atlanta's own 1977 first-round selection. The Bullets later used the Atlanta pick at No. 4 on Greg Ballard. The Hawks kept the Detroit-origin choice and selected Tree Rollins at No. 14. The 1977 draft record confirms Rollins as an Atlanta selection. Washington therefore cannot receive evaluative credit for Rollins' long NBA career; he was drafted by a later holder. What Washington can receive is credit for carrying the Detroit pick forward as one of two meaningful assets in the January swap.

Washington's Downstream Credit Must Stay Proportional

The Robinson-Henderson exchange prevents a simplistic claim that Detroit's pick alone produced Henderson and Ballard. Washington also surrendered Truck Robinson, an established frontcourt player, while Atlanta sent both Henderson and its higher first-round choice. The defensible treatment is the same provenance rule used elsewhere in the archive: record the full factual chain, but grade only value the team directly received or demonstrably retained when it moved the asset. Detroit's first-rounder helped Washington execute a later trade, yet Ballard's entire career cannot be assigned to this 1975 deal. That keeps the verdict source-backed rather than inflating downstream value.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, A-/B-. Washington receives an A- because Bing produced 146 regular-season games, remained an All-Star in the first season and the acquired first-round pick retained enough value to be used in a later first-round swap. Detroit receives a B- because Porter was a productive distributor, supplied 108 regular-season games over parts of three seasons and still had enough value to be included in a later multi-asset trade. The gap comes from Washington receiving both the stronger direct veteran run and an additional first-round asset. Confidence is high on the August 28 transaction structure, Bing and Porter production, and the 1977 pick chain. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired veteran forward Fred Foster from Cleveland on September 5, 1975 for a 1976 eighth-round pick. The Bulls waived Foster on October 22 before he appeared in a regular-season game for Chicago. Cleveland used the acquired selection at No. 123 on Wisconsin forward Dale Koehler in the 1976 NBA draft, but Koehler never recorded an NBA regular-season appearance. The trade therefore produced no realized NBA game value for either side. Cleveland at least converted a veteran it was ready to move into a draft asset, while Chicago took a short preseason look at Foster, but neither outcome developed into a lasting franchise return. The source-backed verdict remains even.
perspectives.analysis:
The September 5 Exchange Is Fully Traceable

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Cleveland and league transaction ledgers all record the same structure on September 5, 1975: the Bulls acquired Fred Foster and sent the Cavaliers a 1976 eighth-round draft pick. Bill Fitch's executive transaction record confirms the Cleveland side of the deal, while Dick Motta's executive record confirms Chicago's. Cleveland's draft history later identifies that exact selection as the No. 123 pick used on Dale Koehler. Unlike transactions in this era involving unspecified future considerations, the complete pick outcome is known.

Foster Never Reached a Bulls Regular-Season Game

Chicago received an established NBA player rather than an unproven prospect. Foster had already played eight NBA seasons, including 131 games for Cleveland across 1973-74 and 1974-75. The Bulls nevertheless did not keep him into the regular season. Chicago's transaction ledger and the league ledger both show the club waiving Foster on October 22, 1975. His Basketball-Reference career page lists 1975-76 as a season in which he did not play after being traded to and waived by Chicago. The direct Bulls return therefore produced zero regular-season games, minutes or points.

Cleveland Converted the Veteran Into a Draft Asset

The Cavaliers did preserve some option value by taking a future pick instead of simply waiving Foster themselves. On June 8, 1976, Cleveland used the acquired eighth-round selection on Wisconsin forward Dale Koehler at No. 123 overall. The Cavaliers' transaction ledger, franchise draft record and the 1976 NBA draft page all identify Koehler at that slot. In process terms, Cleveland successfully converted a veteran roster decision into a real draft choice. That is better asset management than receiving nothing at all, even though the later result still needs to be judged on what actually reached the NBA.

Koehler Produced No NBA Regular-Season Return

Koehler's Basketball-Reference page confirms the draft information but contains no NBA regular-season statistical line. The 1976 draft table likewise shows no NBA games or seasons for him. That means Cleveland's acquired pick did not turn into measurable NBA production. Because the archive grades realized franchise value rather than the abstract possibility attached to a late pick, the Cavaliers cannot receive a high grade merely for having converted Foster into an eighth-round selection. The pick existed, was exercised and is fully traceable, but it produced no NBA game value.

Neither Side Created a Downstream Asset Chain

Chicago waived Foster without receiving documented compensation, so the Bulls' branch ends in October 1975. Cleveland's branch ends when Koehler failed to reach an NBA regular-season game. There is no later trade return, retained player right or compensation chain to extend either side's value. This makes the transaction unusually simple to grade despite the complete historical documentation: one side received a veteran who never played for the club, and the other received a draft pick that never produced an NBA player.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C/C. Chicago receives a C because Foster cost only an eighth-round pick, but he never appeared in a Bulls regular-season game and was waived roughly seven weeks after the trade. Cleveland also receives a C because the Cavaliers converted Foster into a legitimate draft asset and used it at No. 123 on Koehler, yet the selection produced no NBA regular-season return. Neither franchise realized enough value to justify a meaningful hindsight edge. Confidence is high on the transaction date, waiver date, draft-pick identity and lack of NBA production from the two direct outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
