perspectives.summary: New York acquired Rich Jones, Chuck Terry, Bob Warren and rookie center Kim Hughes from San Antonio on September 8, 1975 for Billy Paultz. Paultz became an ABA All-Star immediately and gave San Antonio 83 games, 16.5 points, 10.4 rebounds and 4.1 assists per game in 1975-76 before continuing as a long-term Spurs center. The Nets, however, received multiple championship contributors: Jones averaged 13.2 points in 83 games, Hughes averaged 8.2 points and 9.2 rebounds in all 84 games, Terry played 66 games, and Warren was flipped two weeks later for Tim Bassett, who played all 84 games. New York won the final ABA championship that season, then retained several of those assets into the NBA. The package gives the Nets the stronger total hindsight return despite Paultz's excellent Spurs tenure.
perspectives.analysis:
The September 8 Trade Is Fully Documented

Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, San Antonio Spurs and ABA transaction ledgers all identify the same exchange: New York sent Billy Paultz to San Antonio for Rich Jones, Chuck Terry, Bob Warren and Kim Hughes. The Roy Boe and John Begzos executive transaction records independently preserve the deal from each franchise's side. The legacy archive entry was dated September 7, but the authoritative transaction ledgers consistently list September 8, 1975, so the source-backed repair corrects the transaction date while preserving the same five-player structure.

Paultz Was Immediately Excellent for San Antonio

San Antonio received far more than a short-term rental. Paultz played 83 games in 1975-76 and averaged 16.5 points, 10.4 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 3.0 blocks in 35.6 minutes. He made the ABA All-Star team and became one of the Spurs' major frontcourt pieces alongside George Gervin and Larry Kenon. His value did not end with the ABA season: Paultz remained with the franchise into its NBA years, making this a durable return rather than a one-season outcome.

New York Received Two Immediate High-Minute Contributors

Rich Jones and Kim Hughes became important pieces immediately. Jones played 83 games for the 1975-76 Nets, averaging 13.2 points and 5.2 rebounds in 29.2 minutes. Hughes appeared in all 84 games, averaged 8.2 points and 9.2 rebounds, and later earned All-Rookie recognition. Both also played throughout the postseason as New York won the final ABA championship. That direct production alone makes the package much stronger than the old summary suggested.

Terry Added Depth and Warren Became Tim Bassett

Chuck Terry supplied another 66 regular-season appearances for New York in 1975-76 and remained with the franchise for the first NBA season. Bob Warren never became a Nets regular because New York traded him to the San Diego Sails on September 22 for Tim Bassett. Bassett then played all 84 regular-season games and 13 playoff games for the champion Nets, averaging 6.3 rebounds in the postseason. The archive should not pretend Warren alone created Bassett's entire later career value, but this is a direct one-for-one downstream conversion and therefore belongs in the original asset chain.

The Championship Context Matters Without Deciding the Trade by Itself

New York finished 55-29, defeated San Antonio in a seven-game ABA semifinal and then beat Denver for the 1976 ABA championship. The championship does not automatically make every incoming player more valuable, but Jones, Hughes, Terry and Bassett all supplied real regular-season or postseason minutes on that title team. San Antonio also benefited heavily from Paultz, who was an All-Star and productive starter. This is therefore a strong return on both sides rather than a case where one team received value and the other did not.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A+/A. New York receives an A+ because the four-player package produced two major rotation players, additional depth, a direct Warren-to-Bassett conversion and substantial championship-season value, with several assets continuing into the NBA. San Antonio receives an A because Paultz was immediately an ABA All-Star, averaged a double-double with strong passing and rim protection, and remained a long-term Spurs center. The margin is narrower than the old grading suggested, but the combined volume and downstream value of New York's package gives the Nets the stronger hindsight return. Confidence is high on the corrected September 8 date, the five-player structure and the principal player outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Philadelphia acquired the rights to 1975 first-round pick Joe Bryant from Golden State on September 12, 1975 after the Warriors sold his rights for cash. Bryant never played for Golden State, but he became a four-season rotation forward for the 76ers, appearing in 287 regular-season games from 1975-76 through 1978-79 and scoring 1,849 points. He also remained with Philadelphia through its 1977 run to the NBA Finals. Golden State received cash, but the amount is not preserved in the standard transaction record, so the basketball return cannot be measured beyond noting that the Warriors monetized a player they had drafted No. 14. Philadelphia wins in hindsight because the rights produced several years of NBA value while Golden State's return is unpriced cash.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The September 12 Transaction Is a Sale of Draft Rights

Basketball-Reference's Golden State, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers all record the same event on September 12, 1975: the Warriors sold the player rights to Joe Bryant to the 76ers. The legacy archive record was dated September 11, so the source-backed repair corrects the date by one day. Golden State had selected Bryant with the 14th pick of the 1975 NBA draft, but he never appeared in a Warriors regular-season game before the rights sale.

Bryant Became an Immediate Philadelphia Rotation Player

Bryant debuted for Philadelphia in 1975-76 and played 75 regular-season games, averaging 7.4 points and 3.7 rebounds in 16.0 minutes. That is already more realized basketball value than Golden State received on the court from the transaction because the Warriors' side consisted entirely of cash. Bryant did not need years of development before contributing; he entered the rotation as a rookie and remained with the club for four consecutive seasons.

The Rights Produced Four Seasons of Team Value

Across 1975-76 through 1978-79, Bryant played 287 regular-season games for Philadelphia and scored 1,849 points. His role fluctuated, but he remained a useful reserve forward throughout the period. In 1977-78 he appeared in 81 games, and in 1978-79 he played 70 more. The value chain is direct: Philadelphia bought the rights and then received the player's entire first four NBA seasons before his career moved elsewhere.

Bryant Also Contributed During a Finals Run

Philadelphia reached the 1977 NBA Finals in Bryant's second season. The 76ers won 50 games, captured the Atlantic Division and advanced through Boston and Houston before losing to Portland in six games. Bryant was a reserve rather than a centerpiece, so the verdict should not inflate his role, but the purchased rights did remain part of a conference-championship roster. That gives the asset postseason context in addition to regular-season longevity.

Golden State's Cash Return Cannot Be Properly Priced

The surviving Basketball-Reference transaction language identifies the move as a sale, which establishes that Golden State received cash, but the standard ledger does not preserve the amount. The archive therefore should not pretend the cash was trivial or assign a fabricated dollar value. The Warriors may have had legitimate roster and financial reasons to monetize Bryant's rights after a championship season, but hindsight grading can only compare the known outcomes: unpriced cash on one side and 287 Philadelphia games from a first-round player on the other.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A/C-. Philadelphia receives an A because a cash purchase of Bryant's draft rights produced four NBA seasons, 287 regular-season games and 1,849 points, with the player also remaining on the roster during the 1977 Finals run. Golden State receives a C- rather than an F because the Warriors did receive cash and the amount is unknown, making it inappropriate to call the return worthless. The basketball-value gap still favors Philadelphia clearly. Confidence is high on the corrected September 12 date, the rights-sale structure, Bryant's draft position and his Philadelphia production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: New York acquired Tim Bassett from the San Diego Sails on September 22, 1975 for Bob Warren. Bassett immediately played all 84 regular-season games for the Nets, averaged 6.3 rebounds, appeared in all 13 playoff games and helped New York win the final ABA championship. He then remained with the franchise through its first three NBA seasons, including 76 games and 8.4 rebounds per game in 1976-77. Warren played 10 games for San Diego before the Sails ceased operations in November, averaging 10.1 points and 5.9 rebounds, and that became the final season of his professional career. New York wins clearly because Bassett produced championship-season depth plus several additional years, while Warren's San Diego return ended after ten games.
perspectives.analysis:
The September 22 One-for-One Trade Is Clear

Basketball-Reference's New York transaction ledger records the Nets trading Bob Warren to the San Diego Sails for Tim Bassett on September 22, 1975. The two-player structure also fits the direct downstream chain from New York's September 8 Billy Paultz trade, because Warren had arrived from San Antonio only two weeks earlier. This record therefore represents a separate one-for-one transaction while preserving the fact that Warren was an incoming asset from the prior deal.

Bassett Became an Immediate Championship Contributor

Bassett played all 84 regular-season games for New York in 1975-76, averaging 4.8 points and 6.3 rebounds in 21.3 minutes. He also appeared in all 13 playoff games and collected 93 postseason rebounds as the Nets defeated San Antonio and Denver to win the final ABA championship. Bassett was not the star of that team, but the combination of availability, rebounding and playoff minutes gave New York a direct and useful return immediately after the trade.

The Value Continued After the ABA-NBA Merger

Bassett remained with the franchise when the Nets entered the NBA. In 1976-77 he played 76 games, averaged 9.0 points and 8.4 rebounds, and logged more than 2,400 minutes. He then played 65 games in 1977-78 and all 82 games in 1978-79. That gives New York multiple seasons of durable frontcourt value from a player acquired for someone who had not yet played a Nets regular-season game.

Warren Was Productive but San Diego's Window Was Extremely Short

Warren did provide legitimate production for the Sails. He played 10 of the club's 11 games, averaging 10.1 points, 5.9 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 26.5 minutes. The problem was structural rather than individual: San Diego ceased operations after an 11-game start, so the franchise could not retain or build on the return. Warren's 1975-76 Sails stint was also the final season of his eight-year professional career.

The Franchise Survival Difference Decides the Hindsight Gap

A transaction involving a folding team requires care because San Diego's inability to create long-term value was not caused by Warren. Even so, realized-value grading still measures what each franchise actually received. New York got a full championship season from Bassett and then carried him into the NBA for three more seasons. San Diego got ten productive games from Warren before the team disappeared. That is a large outcome gap even after giving Warren full credit for playing well in the brief Sails schedule.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A/C-. New York receives an A because Bassett played every regular-season game for the 1976 ABA champions, contributed throughout the playoffs and remained a multi-year NBA rotation player after the merger. San Diego receives a C- because Warren was productive in ten games, but the return ended when the Sails ceased operations and produced no further franchise value. The verdict does not blame Warren for the team's collapse; it simply reflects the duration and depth of the realized returns. Confidence is high on the date, one-for-one structure, Bassett's New York production and Warren's ten-game San Diego stint. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles acquired Ron Williams from Milwaukee on September 23, 1975 for a 1976 fifth-round pick that became No. 77 James Rappis. The legacy archive entry incorrectly labeled Williams as Fritz Williams, so the source-backed repair restores the correct player identity. Williams appeared in nine regular-season games for the Lakers, averaging 4.9 points and 2.3 assists in 17.6 minutes, and those games became the final NBA appearances of his career. Milwaukee used the pick on Rappis, but he never recorded an NBA regular-season appearance. Neither side created meaningful long-term value, yet Los Angeles at least received nine games from a veteran guard while Milwaukee's draft outcome produced no NBA minutes. The Lakers hold a narrow hindsight edge rather than a decisive win.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The September 23 Exchange Is Clear, and the legacy Identity Was Wrong

Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Bucks and league transaction ledgers all record the same transaction on September 23, 1975: Los Angeles sent Milwaukee a 1976 fifth-round pick for Ron Williams. Pete Newell's executive record confirms the Lakers side. The legacy archive entry incorrectly displayed the incoming player as Ron Williams with Fritz Williams in parentheses and attached the Fritz Williams player identity. That is an archive identity error. The actual player was Ron Williams, the veteran guard who had already spent two seasons with Milwaukee after five years with the Warriors.

Williams Gave Los Angeles Nine Games

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Archie Clark from Seattle on September 25, 1975 for a 1978 first-round pick. Clark gave the Pistons 79 regular-season games, averaging 7.6 points and 2.8 assists, plus nine playoff appearances before Detroit waived him in July 1976. Seattle did not ultimately make the No. 7 selection itself: in November 1977 the SuperSonics packaged the Detroit-origin first-round pick with a 1979 second-rounder to Portland for Wally Walker. Portland used the pick on Ron Brewer. Walker became a useful Seattle rotation forward, playing 68 games and 20 playoff games in 1977-78, then 60 games and 13 playoff games on the 1979 championship team. Seattle wins in hindsight because the acquired pick retained substantial trade value and helped produce a multi-year contributor, while Clark lasted one Detroit season.
perspectives.analysis:
The September 25 Trade Is Clear

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Seattle and league transaction ledgers agree on the structure: the Pistons sent a 1978 first-round pick to the SuperSonics for Archie Clark on September 25, 1975. Oscar Feldman's Detroit executive record and Bill Russell's Seattle record confirm the same deal. The legacy archive entry was dated September 24 and mislabeled Seattle under the modern Oklahoma City franchise name in its prose. The source-backed repair corrects the transaction date while preserving the franchise key used by the archive.

Clark Gave Detroit One Useful Season

Archie Clark played 79 regular-season games for Detroit in 1975-76 and averaged 7.6 points, 2.8 assists and 1.7 rebounds in 20.1 minutes. He also appeared in all nine of the Pistons' playoff games, averaging 8.0 points in 21.3 minutes. Clark was no longer the All-Star-level scorer he had been earlier in the decade, but he was a legitimate veteran rotation player on a playoff team. Detroit's return therefore deserves more credit than a low-end rental grade.

The Detroit Pick Stayed Valuable for Seattle

Seattle held the acquired first-round pick for more than two years. On November 11, 1977, the SuperSonics traded that Detroit-origin 1978 first-rounder and a 1979 second-round pick to Portland for Wally Walker. This distinction matters because Seattle never used the first-rounder to draft Ron Brewer. Portland became the later holder and selected Brewer at No. 7 in 1978. The archive should record Brewer as the eventual pick outcome but should not assign his NBA career directly to Seattle.

Walker Produced Real Downstream Value

The defensible downstream credit is Wally Walker. After the November 1977 trade, Walker played 68 regular-season games for Seattle in 1977-78 and all 20 playoff games during the SuperSonics' run to the NBA Finals. He returned for 60 regular-season games in 1978-79 and appeared in 13 playoff games as Seattle won the NBA championship. Walker remained with the franchise into 1979-80. Because Seattle also surrendered a second-round pick in the Walker trade, the Detroit first-rounder cannot receive full credit for Walker's entire tenure, but it was a major component of the acquisition.

Detroit's Branch Ended Quickly

Clark's Pistons tenure ended after the 1975-76 season. Detroit waived him on July 28, 1976, and he did not play another NBA regular-season game. That leaves the Pistons with one season of useful veteran depth and playoff minutes but no later trade return or retained asset. Seattle, by contrast, carried the first-round value forward and converted it into part of a package for a younger rotation player who contributed across multiple playoff runs.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, A-/B. Seattle receives an A- because a first-round pick acquired for a veteran nearing the end of his career retained enough value to help acquire Wally Walker, who contributed to the 1978 Finals run and 1979 championship. The grade stops short of an A or A+ because Seattle also surrendered a 1979 second-round pick in the Walker trade and did not itself draft Ron Brewer. Detroit receives a B because Clark gave the Pistons 79 regular-season games and nine playoff appearances, a useful one-season return even though the team waived him the next summer. Confidence is high on the September 25 date, Clark's Detroit production and the pick's later use in the Walker trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Dan Issel from the financially troubled Baltimore Claws on October 8, 1975 for Dave Robisch and cash. Basketball-Reference records the cash component without an amount, while contemporary ABA histories commonly report $500,000; the source-backed archive therefore preserves the verified cash asset but avoids treating the amount as independently established by the primary transaction ledger. Issel immediately played all 84 games for Denver, averaged 23.0 points and 11.0 rebounds, made the ABA All-Star team and helped the Nuggets reach the final ABA Finals. He then remained a franchise cornerstone through the NBA transition. Robisch never played a regular-season game for Baltimore because the Claws folded before opening night; San Diego selected him in the dispersal draft, then Indiana acquired him after the Sails also folded. Denver wins overwhelmingly in realized franchise value.
perspectives.analysis:
The October 8 Deal Happened During the Claws' Collapse

Basketball-Reference's Denver and ABA transaction ledgers record Denver sending Dave Robisch and cash to the Memphis/Baltimore franchise for Dan Issel on October 8, 1975. The transaction note explains that the Memphis Sounds had become the Baltimore Claws and that the Claws never played a regular-season game that season. The legacy archive entry's basic player structure is therefore correct, but the opposing franchise should be understood historically as Baltimore rather than as an active Memphis team.

Issel Became an Immediate Denver Star

Issel played all 84 regular-season games for Denver in 1975-76 and averaged 23.0 points, 11.0 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 34.0 minutes. He made the ABA All-Star team and then averaged 20.5 points and 12.0 rebounds across 13 playoff games as Denver reached the final ABA Finals. This was not a speculative acquisition that needed years to mature. The return became elite immediately and arrived at exactly the moment Denver was preparing to move from the ABA into the NBA.

The Value Extended Far Beyond the Final ABA Season

Issel stayed with Denver after the merger and remained one of the franchise's defining frontcourt players for the rest of his career. Basketball-Reference lists a 15-year professional career, seven All-Star selections and Hall of Fame induction, with the Denver portion spanning the club's final ABA season and many NBA seasons. The source-backed verdict does not need to assign every later team accomplishment to this trade; simply retaining a high-level scorer and rebounder through the league transition creates enormous realized value.

Robisch Never Produced a Baltimore Regular-Season Return

Baltimore's side cannot be graded like a normal player-for-player exchange because the Claws folded before the regular season. Robisch therefore never logged a regular-season game for the franchise that acquired him. On October 21, San Diego selected Robisch in the Baltimore dispersal draft. He played all 11 games the Sails completed, then Indiana selected him in the November 12 dispersal draft after San Diego also ceased operations. Robisch went on to have a substantial career, but those later games belonged to San Diego, Indiana and other franchises, not Baltimore.

The Cash Component Matters, but Its Exact Amount Is Not Required to Grade the Basketball Outcome

The authoritative Basketball-Reference transaction ledger identifies cash as part of Denver's outgoing package but does not state an amount. Historical ABA accounts often describe the payment as $500,000 and connect it to Baltimore's earlier obligation in the Issel acquisition from Kentucky. The archive can preserve that context in research notes without pretending the standard transaction ledger independently verifies the figure. Even treating the cash as meaningful consideration, Baltimore never converted either Robisch or the cash into a sustainable on-court return before the franchise disappeared.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A+/D. Denver receives an A+ because Issel immediately delivered an All-Star 23-and-11 season, helped the Nuggets reach the ABA Finals and remained a long-term franchise cornerstone through the NBA transition. Baltimore receives a D rather than an F because it did receive Robisch plus cash and the cash had real economic value, but the franchise folded before Robisch could play a regular-season game and therefore realized no durable basketball return. Confidence is high on the October 8 transaction, Issel's Denver production, Baltimore's collapse and Robisch's dispersal path. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: The legacy October 10, 1975 New York Nets-Virginia Squires record is not a supported trade. Basketball-Reference's ABA league, Utah Stars and Virginia Squires transaction ledgers agree that Utah waived Gerald Govan on September 17 and Virginia claimed him on waivers on October 10. The New York Nets transaction ledger contains no Govan transaction on that date and no future-draft-pick exchange involving him. Govan then played 24 games for Virginia, averaging 5.7 points, 6.7 rebounds and 2.3 assists, before the Squires waived him on December 16. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.
perspectives.analysis:
The October 10 Movement Was a Waiver Claim, Not a Nets Trade

Basketball-Reference's 1975-76 ABA transaction ledger states that the Virginia Squires claimed Gerald Govan on waivers from the Utah Stars on October 10, 1975. Virginia's team transaction page records the same claim, and Utah's page records the same player leaving through waivers. Those three ledgers agree on both the mechanism and the clubs involved. None places the New York Nets in the transaction. The legacy archive entry therefore cannot be repaired simply by changing a draft-pick detail; its entire trade structure is unsupported.

Utah Had Already Waived Govan in September

The Utah Stars waived Govan on September 17, more than three weeks before Virginia claimed him. That chronology matters because a waiver claim does not create a trade package and does not require the claiming club to send a player or draft asset to another team. The legacy record's future draft pick was therefore not merely unresolved. It was attached to a transaction type that did not happen. Treating the draft-pick language as unverified would still leave a false Nets-Squires exchange in the archive, so the safer correction is structural supersession.

New York's Transaction Ledger Has No Matching October 10 Deal

The 1975-76 New York Nets transaction log lists the club's September Billy Paultz and Bob Warren trades, the October 16 Ed Manning deal with Indiana, later waivers, and the January 27 transaction with Virginia involving Swen Nater, Billy Schaeffer and Jim Eakins. It does not list an October 10 Gerald Govan trade or a future draft pick received from Virginia. That absence is especially persuasive when combined with the affirmative Utah and Virginia waiver records, because the correct transaction is already documented elsewhere rather than merely missing from one team page.

Govan Did Play for Virginia, but That Does Not Validate the legacy Package

Govan's 1975-76 player record confirms 24 games for the Squires. He averaged 5.7 points, 6.7 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 27.4 minutes, and Virginia's roster page carries the same 24-game line. The Squires later waived him on December 16. Those facts explain why the legacy archive record may have looked plausible: Govan genuinely ended up in Virginia. The error was assigning that roster move to New York and inventing a reciprocal draft-pick asset. His Virginia production belongs to the waiver claim, not to a Nets trade verdict.

The Correct Archive Treatment Is Superseded Provenance

TradeVerdicts keeps malformed historical imports when they are useful for explaining how a bad record entered the archive, but they should not remain eligible for a graded trade history, player-history links or verdict. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results. The unsupported future-pick asset is explicitly labeled as a legacy claim rather than a real draft asset, and the Nets-to-Virginia player movement is marked unsupported.

Final Verdict

Record Superseded. No winner and no team grades are assigned because there was no verified Nets-Squires trade to evaluate. Confidence is high: the ABA league ledger, Utah Stars ledger and Virginia Squires ledger independently align on a September 17 Utah waiver followed by Virginia's October 10 claim, while New York's transaction history contains no corresponding deal. Govan's 24 Virginia games and December 16 waiver are also directly supported. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Chuck Williams from Virginia on October 21, 1975 for Fatty Taylor, only hours after the Squires selected Williams from the collapsed Baltimore Claws in the dispersal draft. Williams became an immediate starting-caliber guard for the Nuggets, playing 79 games in the final ABA season while averaging 11.0 points and 4.7 assists, and he was part of Denver's run to the 1976 ABA Finals. He stayed through the NBA transition, then Denver packaged him with Gus Gerard to Buffalo for Jim Price in December 1976. Taylor gave Virginia 76 games at 8.2 points, 5.3 assists and 4.5 rebounds, but the Squires finished 15-68 and folded after the season. Denver wins in hindsight because Williams produced more competitive value and retained downstream trade utility, while Virginia received one useful season from Taylor before the franchise ceased operations.
perspectives.analysis:
The October 21 Transaction Is Unusually Well Documented

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Virginia and ABA transaction ledgers all record the same exchange: Denver sent Fatty Taylor to the Squires for Chuck Williams on October 21, 1975. Carl Scheer's Denver executive record and Jack Ankerson's Virginia record repeat the deal. The timing adds important context. Earlier that day Virginia selected Williams from the Baltimore Claws in the dispersal draft after the Claws folded before playing a regular-season game. The Squires then immediately moved him to Denver for Taylor.

Williams Became a Major Part of Denver's Final ABA Team

Williams played 79 regular-season games for Denver in 1975-76, averaging 11.0 points, 4.7 assists and 2.7 rebounds in 32.0 minutes. Basketball-Reference also marks him as an ABA All-Star that season. Denver finished with the league's best regular-season record and reached the final ABA Finals, so Williams' value was not empty-volume production on a losing club. He was a substantial guard on a contender during the exact season when the franchise was preparing to enter the NBA.

Taylor Was Productive for Virginia, but the Team Had No Future

Fatty Taylor also gave his new club legitimate minutes. He played 76 games for Virginia and averaged 8.2 points, 5.3 assists, 4.5 rebounds and 2.7 steals in 32.7 minutes. Those numbers make the old C-minus Denver grade too harsh on the deal's balance because Virginia did receive a real starting guard. The problem is organizational context: the Squires went 15-68, missed the playoffs and disappeared after the season. Taylor's one year therefore produced no retained franchise value beyond the final Virginia campaign.

Denver Retained Williams Through the ABA-NBA Transition

Williams remained with the Nuggets when the ABA clubs entered the NBA. He appeared in 21 games for Denver in 1976-77 before the club traded him and Gus Gerard to Buffalo for Jim Price on December 15, 1976. That later deal means Williams generated a second layer of value beyond his strong 1975-76 season. The original October trade should not receive full credit for Price because Gerard was also part of the package, but Williams was a real component of the acquisition and therefore carried measurable downstream utility.

The Trade Also Illustrates Denver's Rapid Guard Reconfiguration

Denver's later moves add an unusual wrinkle. In August 1976 the Nuggets reacquired Fatty Taylor from Philadelphia for a 1977 second-round pick after the Virginia franchise had disappeared. Taylor then played 79 NBA games for Denver in 1976-77. That later reacquisition is a separate transaction and should not be credited to the Squires side of this October deal, but it shows that Denver still valued Taylor. The key point for this review is narrower: on October 21, 1975 Denver exchanged one useful veteran guard for another who immediately became an All-Star-level contributor and later retained trade value.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A-/B. Denver receives an A- because Williams delivered 79 games, 11.0 points and 4.7 assists for an ABA Finals team, earned All-Star recognition, stayed through the NBA transition and later helped form the package for Jim Price. Virginia receives a B because Taylor was genuinely useful, starting most of the Squires' final season and supplying playmaking, rebounding and defensive activity. The gap comes from team context and retained value rather than from Taylor failing individually. Confidence is high on the transaction, both players' 1975-76 production and Williams' later Buffalo trade. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The legacy Pick Round and Cash Claim Were Wrong

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta Hawks, Seattle SuperSonics and NBA league transaction ledgers all record the October 22, 1975 exchange as Herm Gilliam to Seattle for a 1976 third-round draft pick. Bill Russell's Seattle executive record repeats the same structure. None of those authoritative ledgers includes cash. This review therefore corrects two material import errors: the No. 46 selection was a third-round pick, not a second-rounder, and the extra cash asset is removed rather than preserved as an unsupported part of the package.

Gilliam Gave Seattle a Full Rotation Season

Herm Gilliam appeared in 81 regular-season games for the 1975-76 SuperSonics, averaging 8.5 points, 2.7 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 20.3 minutes. He was no longer the 14-point starting guard he had been in Atlanta two years earlier, but he remained a durable veteran contributor. Seattle therefore converted a third-round pick into immediate usable depth for essentially an entire season, a much stronger realized outcome than the old database wording captured.

Atlanta Used the Pick on Larry Cooke at No. 46

Atlanta retained the pick and used it in the 1976 NBA draft on Larry Cooke, a Virginia Tech guard selected 46th overall. The Hawks' transaction page, the league draft table and Cooke's Basketball-Reference profile all align on that identity. Cooke never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The pick outcome is therefore fully traceable but produced no major-league playing value for Atlanta, making this one of the cleaner historical comparisons in the 1975 chronology.

Seattle Still Had a Small Downstream Asset After the Season

Gilliam did not simply leave Seattle as a free agent. Bill Russell's executive ledger records the SuperSonics selling his player rights to Portland on September 2, 1976. The standard transaction record does not provide a sale amount in the material reviewed here, so the source-backed grade does not assign a specific dollar value. The sale nevertheless confirms that Seattle retained at least some transactional value after Gilliam's 81-game season rather than receiving a one-year return that vanished without compensation.

Gilliam's Portland Championship Is Not Seattle Value

Gilliam later played 80 regular-season games for Portland in 1976-77 and was part of the Trail Blazers' championship roster, but those games belong to Portland, not Seattle. This distinction is important because a downstream player path can easily inflate a trade grade if later production is attributed to the wrong franchise. Seattle's realized return stops at Gilliam's 1975-76 SuperSonics season plus whatever economic value came from the later rights sale. That is already enough to win the trade without borrowing his Portland accomplishments.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, B+/D+. Seattle receives a B+ because a third-round pick produced 81 games of useful veteran rotation play and a later rights sale. The grade stays below A territory because Gilliam was a complementary player and Seattle kept him for only one season. Atlanta receives a D+ because the Hawks did obtain the exact draft asset promised and used it at No. 46, but Larry Cooke never played an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high on the package correction, Gilliam's Seattle production and the Cooke draft outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles acquired the player rights to Cornell Warner from Milwaukee on October 22, 1975 in a cash sale. Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Bucks and league transaction ledgers all describe the move as Milwaukee selling Warner's rights; the standard record does not state the cash amount. Warner immediately became a major Lakers frontcourt contributor, playing 81 games in 1975-76 and averaging 7.3 points, 8.9 rebounds and 31.0 minutes. He returned for 14 more games the following season before leaving Los Angeles. Milwaukee received cash but no player or draft asset that can be traced into later basketball value from this transaction. The Lakers win in hindsight because a cash-only acquisition produced 95 regular-season games and one season of near-nine-rebound starting-level production.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
This Was a Player-Rights Sale, Not a Draft-Rights Trade

Basketball-Reference's Los Angeles Lakers, Milwaukee Bucks and NBA league transaction ledgers agree that Milwaukee sold the player rights to Cornell Warner to Los Angeles on October 22, 1975. The legacy archive entry broadly captured the cash-for-rights structure, but its asset type labels the return as draft rights. Warner was already an established NBA player with two Milwaukee seasons behind him, so this review corrects the asset to player rights and preserves the cash consideration without inventing an amount.

Warner Immediately Became a Major Lakers Rebounder

Warner played 81 games for Los Angeles in 1975-76 and averaged 7.3 points, 8.9 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 31.0 minutes. Only Kareem Abdul-Jabbar averaged more rebounds for the club. Warner's 722 total rebounds and 2,512 minutes make the acquisition materially different from a speculative rights purchase. Los Angeles converted cash into a high-usage frontcourt role for almost an entire season, and the production arrived immediately rather than requiring a development period.

The Lakers Also Retained Warner Into the NBA's 1976-77 Season

Warner returned for 14 games in 1976-77, averaging 3.9 points and 4.9 rebounds in 12.1 minutes. His role diminished sharply, so the second season adds only modest value, but it pushes the Los Angeles return to 95 regular-season appearances across two years. The core of the grade remains the 1975-76 season, when Warner played 31 minutes per game and supplied the rebounding support around Abdul-Jabbar on a team that improved to 40 wins.

Milwaukee's Return Is Real but Economically Opaque

The Bucks received cash, and a cash return should not be treated as zero. The problem for a retrospective basketball archive is that the standard transaction ledgers reviewed here do not state the amount, and no player or draft asset emerged from the deal that can be followed through a later transaction chain. That makes Milwaukee's realized basketball value impossible to quantify with the same precision as Warner's games and production. The grade therefore gives Milwaukee credit for completing a sale rather than pretending the cash had no value, but it does not award unsupported downstream value.

Warner's Milwaukee Tenure Provides Important Context

Milwaukee was not giving up an unknown reserve. Warner had played 67 games for the Bucks in 1973-74 and 79 in 1974-75, averaging 7.0 points and 8.2 rebounds across his two Milwaukee seasons. His 1974-75 workload reached 31.9 minutes per game. Selling his rights therefore represented a real roster decision, not merely clearing an inactive name. Los Angeles correctly identified that Warner could still handle a substantial role and immediately gave him one of the heaviest frontcourt workloads on the team.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, B+/C. Los Angeles receives a B+ because a cash purchase delivered 81 games at 31 minutes per night in the first season, 8.9 rebounds per game and 95 total appearances across two seasons. The grade stays below A territory because Warner's second Lakers season was brief and the acquisition did not create a long multi-year asset chain. Milwaukee receives a C because the Bucks did receive cash, but the amount is not preserved in the standard transaction record and no traceable basketball asset came back. Confidence is high on the transaction type and Warner's production, while the unreported cash amount is explicitly left unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee acquired veteran center Jim Fox from Seattle on October 22, 1975 for a 1976 second-round pick that became No. 19 Bayard Forrest. The legacy archive entry incorrectly added cash; Basketball-Reference's Bucks, SuperSonics, league and executive transaction ledgers all show the exchange as Fox for the pick only. Fox gave Milwaukee 70 games in 1975-76, averaging 3.9 points and 3.4 rebounds in 13.1 minutes, plus three playoff appearances. Seattle used the pick on Forrest, then traded Forrest to Phoenix in March 1977 for a 1979 second-round pick. That pick later joined another second-rounder in Seattle's acquisition of John Johnson, who became a regular on the 1978 Finals team and 1979 championship team. Seattle wins in hindsight because the draft asset retained and compounded value well beyond Fox's one useful reserve season in Milwaukee.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
The Verified Package Was Jim Fox for One Second-Round Pick

Milwaukee, Seattle, the NBA league transaction ledger, Wayne Embry's executive record and Bill Russell's executive record all align on the same October 22, 1975 structure: the Bucks received Jim Fox and Seattle received a 1976 second-round draft pick. None of those ledgers lists cash. This review therefore removes the legacy cash component from the verified package and simplifies the pick language to what the primary records actually support. The pick was later used at No. 19 on Bayard Forrest.

The Pick Had Come to Milwaukee Through the Atlanta Penalty

Milwaukee's 1974-75 transaction ledger shows that on June 5, 1975 the Bucks received two 1976 second-round picks from Atlanta as a league remedy tied to the Hawks' earlier signing of Milwaukee draft pick Julius Erving. Basketball-Reference identifies those two picks as the selections later used on Alex English and Bayard Forrest. By October, Milwaukee moved the Forrest pick to Seattle for Fox. That provenance is important because the legacy phrase about the most favorable Bucks pick is unnecessary and is not how the authoritative October transaction ledgers describe the deal.

Fox Gave Milwaukee One Useful Reserve Season

Jim Fox played 70 games for the 1975-76 Bucks, averaging 3.9 points and 3.4 rebounds in 13.1 minutes. He also appeared in all three games of Milwaukee's first-round playoff series against Detroit. The production was modest compared with his earlier Seattle seasons, but it was real roster value for a Milwaukee team in transition after the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar trade. Fox should not be treated as a failed acquisition simply because his role had shrunk; the Bucks received a durable veteran backup for the entire regular season.

Seattle Turned the Pick Into Bayard Forrest and Then Another Pick

Seattle selected Bayard Forrest with the No. 19 pick in the 1976 draft. Forrest never played a regular-season game for the SuperSonics, but that did not end the asset chain. On March 18, 1977 Seattle traded Forrest to Phoenix for a 1979 second-round pick. The transaction record identifies that future pick as the one later used on Paul Mokeski after Seattle sent it onward. Forrest himself later played 139 NBA games for Phoenix, but those Suns games are not credited to Seattle; Seattle's realized value is the replacement draft asset it received for him.

The Forrest Pick Helped Seattle Acquire John Johnson

On October 22, 1977 Seattle sent the Phoenix-derived 1979 second-round pick and a 1980 second-round pick to Houston for John Johnson. Because two picks were required, the original Fox trade deserves only partial credit for Johnson rather than full credit for the entire acquisition. Even with that discount, the downstream value is substantial. Johnson played 76 games for Seattle in 1977-78 as the SuperSonics reached the NBA Finals, then started all 82 games in 1978-79 and averaged 11.0 points, 5.0 rebounds and 4.4 assists for the NBA champions.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, A-/C+. Seattle receives an A- because a single second-round pick retained value through multiple transactions and became part of the package for a starting forward on consecutive Finals teams, including the 1979 champion. The grade stops short of a full A because the Johnson acquisition also required another second-round pick. Milwaukee receives a C+ because Fox supplied 70 regular-season games and three playoff appearances as a dependable reserve, but the Bucks surrendered the more durable asset and received no comparable downstream return. Confidence is high on the corrected package, Fox's Milwaukee production, Forrest's No. 19 selection and the later Forrest-to-Phoenix and Johnson transactions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

seattle-supersonics.summary: The legacy October 23, 1975 Seattle-side Spencer Haywood record duplicates the New York Knicks transaction record dated October 24 and should not remain a separate trade. Basketball-Reference's Knicks, SuperSonics and NBA transaction ledgers, along with Knicks executive Eddie Donovan's record, all place the completed transaction on October 24: New York acquired Spencer Haywood while Seattle received Gene Short and a conditional 1979 first-round pick that became No. 6 James Bailey. Contemporary reporting published October 30 describes the announcement as occurring Thursday afternoon and reports additional cash, explaining how an October 23 date could enter a secondary archive. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
Two legacy archive entrys Describe One Haywood Transaction

The Seattle import and the New York import contain the same core package: Spencer Haywood moved to the Knicks, while Gene Short and a future first-round pick moved to the SuperSonics. The pick later became the No. 6 selection used on James Bailey. The only major structural difference is the date, with the Seattle record showing October 23 and the Knicks record showing October 24. There is no evidence of two separate Haywood transactions between the clubs on consecutive days.

Basketball-Reference Supports October 24 as the Completed Transaction Date

Basketball-Reference's 1975-76 New York Knicks transaction page lists the trade on October 24, as does Seattle's team transaction page. The NBA league transaction ledger and Eddie Donovan's executive history also use October 24. Those independently maintained Basketball-Reference surfaces agree on the effective transaction date and package. That makes the Knicks-side October 24 record the stronger canonical record for TradeVerdicts.

The October 23 Date Is Still Explainable as Announcement Provenance

A contemporary Black World article dated October 30 says the Haywood trade was announced Thursday afternoon. October 23, 1975 was a Thursday, while October 24 was Friday. That gives the earlier import date a plausible origin: it may reflect the public announcement rather than the completed league transaction entry. The same article describes the return as rookie Eugene Short plus cash estimated at $1.5 million, while later transaction databases also describe the conditional 1979 first-round component. Preserving the duplicate as provenance keeps that historical wrinkle without creating a second trade page.

Gene Short and Eugene Short Are the Same Player

Basketball-Reference identifies Gene Short as Eugene Short Jr., the Knicks' No. 9 pick in the 1975 draft. Seattle's legacy archive entry uses Gene Short, while the Knicks import uses Eugene Short. That naming variation does not create a different asset. Short played only seven games for Seattle before being waived on November 24, and the Knicks signed him as a free agent two days later. This review therefore treats the two names as identity variants inside the same transaction history.

The Conditional Pick Also Confirms the Duplicate

The future first-round asset is not merely similar between the two rows. Both identify a 1979 conditional first-round pick that ultimately became James Bailey at No. 6. Seattle used that selection on Bailey in the 1979 draft. Matching player movement, matching future-pick outcome and matching counterpart clubs make the duplicate diagnosis decisive even before considering the one-day date discrepancy.

Why Supersession Is Better Than Date Correction Alone

Simply changing the Seattle record from October 23 to October 24 would leave two canonical records with the same clubs, players and draft-pick outcome. That would duplicate the transaction across public records, player histories and historical counts. Supersession is therefore the safer structural repair. It preserves the original Seattle import for audit history, records why its date differed, and directs all reader-facing evaluation to one canonical transaction without erasing the provenance that produced the duplicate.

Final Verdict

Record Superseded. No winner or grades are assigned to the October 23 Seattle import because evaluating it independently would double-count the same Spencer Haywood transaction. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. Confidence is high because the team, league and executive ledgers align on October 24 and the contemporary October 23 announcement context explains rather than contradicts the earlier provenance date.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Portland obtained Golden State's rights to Steve Jones on October 23, 1975, while the Warriors received a 1976 sixth-round selection later associated with No. 91 Dwayne Barnett. The original ledger uses the spelling Duane Barnett and questions Steve Jones's 1964 draft-rights chain; contemporary franchise transaction listings corroborate the exchange itself. The inherited Blazers Win grades Portland C and Golden State D+.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Portland Acquired Jones's Veteran Rights

The Trail Blazers acquired Steve Jones from Golden State on October 23, 1975, giving Portland access to a player whose professional experience extended beyond the transaction's immediate roster context. The Warriors obtained a sixth-round choice in the 1976 NBA Draft instead of another established player. The deal took place when the league draft contained considerably more rounds than the modern format. A sixth-round selection was a legitimate right but generally offered far less certainty than an early selection.

The Sixth-Round Selection Had an Identifiable Outcome

Golden State's compensation became associated with the No. 91 selection used on Dwayne Barnett in 1976. The original imported ledger spelled his first name Duane, whereas the Warriors' historical transaction and draft listings use Dwayne. That distinction isn't evidence of a separate player; it is a source spelling correction that should remain visible to anyone tracing the pick. A draft selection also didn't guarantee Barnett would provide major NBA minutes for the club.

Jones's Earlier Rights History Has an Unresolved Detail

The imported source describes Jones as a player whose rights may have originated with a Golden State predecessor's 1964 draft selection, but the exact historical draft listing isn't reconciled in the underlying record. The October 1975 transfer is corroborated by both Warriors and Blazers transaction logs, so the uncertainty shouldn't be used to deny the exchange altogether. At the same time, it would be misleading to invent a detailed continuous rights chain without a complete contemporary roster or draft document.

The Original Grades Reflect an Uneven Exchange

Portland receives C under the inherited model for obtaining Jones's rights, while Golden State gets D+ for a late 1976 choice. Neither grade implies an incoming perennial All-Star, and the older draft's extended structure limits what can be expected from No. 91. The transaction is best understood as a modest rights-for-draft-option move. Its value as an archive entry comes from accurately identifying the teams, player, sixth-round compensation and still-unresolved original rights provenance.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win. Portland earns C for acquiring Steve Jones's player rights, while Golden State receives D+ for the 1976 sixth-round selection linked to Dwayne Barnett. The historic transaction is independently recorded by both franchises, but the inherited Steve Jones 1964 rights origin remains uncertain. The late draft pick didn't by itself ensure substantial Warriors playing production.

new-york-knicks.summary: New York acquired Spencer Haywood from Seattle on October 24, 1975 for rookie Gene Short, a conditional 1979 first-round pick that became No. 6 James Bailey, and cash reported contemporaneously at about $1.5 million. Haywood played 210 regular-season games for the Knicks across parts of four seasons, averaging 17.1 points and 8.6 rebounds, including 19.9 points and 11.3 rebounds in his first year. Short lasted only seven games with Seattle before being waived, but the conditional pick conveyed and Bailey gave the SuperSonics 159 games, highlighted by 14.0 points and 7.4 rebounds in 1980-81. The large reported cash payment also materially strengthens Seattle's side even though Basketball-Reference's standard transaction ledger omits the amount. In hindsight, the exchange is broadly even: New York received the better immediate star production, while Seattle converted an outgoing veteran into cash plus a useful lottery pick.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
October 24 Is the Canonical Completed Transaction Date

Basketball-Reference's New York Knicks, Seattle SuperSonics and NBA transaction ledgers all record the Spencer Haywood trade on October 24, 1975. Eddie Donovan's Knicks executive history uses the same date and package. A contemporary Black World report says the trade was announced Thursday afternoon, which was October 23, explaining the date on the duplicate Seattle import superseded in this review. For the canonical archive, October 24 is the stronger completed-transaction date because the team, league and executive records all align there.

The Package Included Gene Short and a Conditional 1979 First

New York sent Gene Short, the No. 9 pick in the 1975 draft, plus a future first-round pick. Later transaction references describe the pick as conditional on Short failing to remain with Seattle for a specified period. He appeared in only seven SuperSonics games and was waived on November 24. The Knicks signed him as a free agent two days later. The condition therefore triggered, and Seattle ultimately held New York's 1979 first-round selection, which landed at No. 6.

Contemporary Reporting Supports a Large Cash Component

Basketball-Reference's standard transaction ledger does not list cash, so this review does not treat the dollar figure as league-ledger data. A Black World report published October 30, 1975 says the Knicks sent rookie Eugene Short and cash estimated at $1.5 million for Haywood. Later historical accounts repeat a $1.5 million figure. Because the amount was reported contemporaneously rather than reconstructed decades later, the archive preserves it as reported cash with an explicit source caveat rather than deleting it or presenting it as an undisputed official amount.

Haywood Gave New York Four Seasons of High-Level Production

Haywood immediately became a full-time Knicks starter. In 1975-76 he played 78 games and averaged 19.9 points and 11.3 rebounds in 37.1 minutes. He remained productive through parts of four seasons in New York, totaling 210 regular-season appearances and averaging roughly 17 points and nine rebounds for the club. The Knicks reached the playoffs once during that span, so the acquisition did not create a sustained contender, but the on-court return was far beyond a short rental or declining-name acquisition.

Seattle's Pick Became James Bailey at No. 6

The conditional first conveyed in 1979 and Seattle selected Rutgers forward James Bailey sixth overall. Bailey played 67 games as a rookie, then made a major jump in 1980-81 by appearing in all 82 games and averaging 14.0 points, 7.4 rebounds and 1.7 blocks in 31.0 minutes. Across his Seattle tenure he played 159 regular-season games before moving on. That production gives the future pick substantial realized value even though Bailey never reached Haywood's star level.

Gene Short Added Almost No Seattle Value

Short's part of the return was brief. He averaged 1.9 points in seven Seattle games before the club waived him one month after the trade. New York then brought him back as a free agent, and he played 27 additional games for the Knicks before his NBA career ended. His limited Seattle stay is still important because it activated the conditional-pick mechanism, but his own playing contribution should not be mistaken for a meaningful part of Seattle's realized return.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B+/B+. New York receives a B+ because Haywood supplied 210 games of strong frontcourt production and was immediately a near-20-point, double-digit-rebound starter. Seattle also receives a B+ because the SuperSonics obtained a reported major cash payment and a conditional first that became James Bailey, who produced a strong 1980-81 season and 159 Seattle games. Short himself added little, and neither side turned the transaction into sustained championship-level value during the relevant window. Confidence is high on the player movement, October 24 effective date, conditional pick outcome and player production; the cash amount remains explicitly reported rather than official-ledger confirmed. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired John Johnson from Portland on November 13, 1975 for Steve Hawes. The legacy archive entry attached the unrelated name Howard Getty to Johnson, so this review removes that identity error and restores the simple one-for-one structure documented by both teams and the NBA transaction ledger. Johnson gave Houston 147 regular-season games across parts of three seasons, including 67 games at 9.7 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.9 assists in 1975-76, and later generated multiple second-round picks through a Boston transaction and a second Houston exit to Seattle. Portland received 66 games of 7.2 points and 7.3 rebounds from Hawes, then packaged Hawes with Geoff Petrie for the ABA dispersal pick used on Maurice Lucas, a central member of the 1977 championship team. Portland wins in hindsight because Hawes became part of a championship-level downstream acquisition, though Houston also extracted substantial value from Johnson.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The November 13 Trade Was a Straight One-for-One Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Houston, Portland and NBA league transaction ledgers all record the same November 13, 1975 move: Houston sent Steve Hawes to Portland for John Johnson. Ray Patterson's Houston executive record confirms the exchange. The legacy archive entry's John Johnson parenthetical identifying him as Howard Getty is unsupported and incorrect. This review removes that extra identity and ties the incoming player to the verified John Johnson Basketball-Reference record.

Johnson Gave Houston Two Productive Seasons of Rotation Value

John Johnson played 67 games for Houston after the trade in 1975-76 and averaged 9.7 points, 4.4 rebounds and 2.9 assists in 22.2 minutes. He returned for 79 games in 1976-77 at 9.3 points, 3.4 rebounds and 2.1 assists, then appeared once more for Houston in 1977-78. Across his Houston regular-season tenure, Basketball-Reference's trade-partner table credits him with 147 games and 9.4 points per game. He was a legitimate multi-year rotation forward rather than a short-term rental.

Houston Also Recycled Johnson Into Draft Assets

On June 9, 1977 Houston traded Johnson to Boston for 1977 and 1978 second-round picks. Boston later sold Johnson's rights back to Houston on October 18 while Houston kept those draft picks. Four days later, Houston traded Johnson again, this time to Seattle for 1979 and 1980 second-round picks. The unusual sequence means Johnson generated both on-court production and repeated transactional value. Not every later pick outcome became important, so the original 1975 trade should not receive exaggerated credit, but Houston clearly extracted more than just Johnson's 147 games.

Hawes Was Immediately Useful in Portland

Steve Hawes played 66 games for Portland after the trade and averaged 7.2 points, 7.3 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 20.6 minutes. He supplied needed frontcourt depth alongside Bill Walton and Lloyd Neal and produced 3.4 win shares for the Trail Blazers. Portland therefore received a meaningful player return even before the downstream transaction that ultimately makes this trade especially valuable in hindsight.

Portland Used Hawes in the Maurice Lucas Acquisition

On August 5, 1976 Portland traded Hawes and Geoff Petrie to Atlanta for the second selection in the ABA dispersal draft. The Trail Blazers used that position on Maurice Lucas. Because Petrie was also required, Hawes cannot receive full credit for Lucas, but he was one of the two named outgoing players that secured the dispersal slot. Lucas then became a major frontcourt piece for Portland's 1977 NBA championship team. That direct downstream conversion is much more consequential than Hawes' one-season box-score line alone.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win, A-/B+. Portland receives an A- because Hawes supplied 66 useful games and then became half of the player package used to acquire the dispersal pick that produced Maurice Lucas, a core player on the 1977 championship team. The grade stops short of A or A+ because Geoff Petrie was also essential to that later deal. Houston receives a B+ because Johnson gave the Rockets 147 regular-season games and later produced several second-round assets through additional transactions. Both sides did well, but Portland's championship-level downstream conversion creates the stronger hindsight return. Confidence is high on the one-for-one structure, player identities, direct production and the Hawes-to-Lucas chain. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Seattle acquired the player rights to Mike Bantom from Phoenix on November 22, 1975 in a cash sale. Basketball-Reference's Suns, SuperSonics and NBA transaction ledgers agree on the sale structure but do not state the cash amount. Bantom immediately became a useful Seattle forward, playing 66 games in 1975-76 at 8.4 points and 5.6 rebounds per game, then returning for 44 more games in 1976-77 at 7.5 points and 4.2 rebounds. That gave the SuperSonics 110 regular-season appearances and more than 2,200 minutes from a cash-only acquisition. Phoenix received cash but no traceable player or draft asset from the transaction. Seattle wins in hindsight because it converted an unquantified cash payment into two seasons of real rotation value.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The November 22 Move Was a Rights Sale

Basketball-Reference's Phoenix Suns transaction page states that Phoenix sold the player rights to Mike Bantom to Seattle on November 22, 1975. Seattle's transaction page records the same acquisition, and the NBA league ledger describes the same rights sale. The legacy archive entry correctly captured the broad cash-for-player structure, but this review makes the rights language explicit and avoids inventing a sale amount that the standard ledgers do not provide.

Bantom Immediately Rebounded From a Small Phoenix Role

Bantom had played only seven games for Phoenix at the start of 1975-76, averaging 3.0 points in 9.7 minutes. After the sale he appeared in 66 games for Seattle and averaged 8.4 points, 5.6 rebounds and 1.5 assists in 22.8 minutes. He also produced 2.8 win shares for the SuperSonics. That is a meaningful first-year return for a transaction in which Seattle did not surrender a player or draft pick.

Seattle Received a Second Season of Rotation Value

Bantom returned in 1976-77 and played 44 more games for Seattle. His role declined to 18.1 minutes per game, but he still averaged 7.5 points and 4.2 rebounds while shooting 48.8 percent from the field. Across the two seasons, Seattle received 110 regular-season games from Bantom. The total workload matters because the transaction was not a brief rental or a player who failed to report; it produced sustained frontcourt depth across two roster cycles.

Phoenix's Return Was Economic Rather Than Basketball-Specific

Phoenix received cash, and that consideration should not be treated as worthless. The problem for a hindsight basketball grade is that the amount is not stated in the standard Basketball-Reference transaction records reviewed here, and no player or draft asset returned to Phoenix that can be followed through a later basketball chain. Bantom had been the No. 8 pick in the 1973 draft and had averaged 12.5 points and 6.7 rebounds for Phoenix in 1974-75, so the Suns were selling the rights to a player who had already demonstrated rotation value.

The Later Career Does Not Need to Be Borrowed to Make Seattle's Case

Bantom later produced a strong 33-game run for the New York Nets in 1976-77 and continued his career with Indiana, Philadelphia and other teams. Those later games should not be credited to Seattle unless a verified transaction return links them back to the SuperSonics. The source-backed grade does not need that extra reach. Seattle's own 110 games, 923 points and substantial rebounding output are enough to establish the value of the original rights purchase.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, B+/C. Seattle receives a B+ because an unquantified cash payment produced 110 regular-season games, one full 66-game post-trade season and useful frontcourt production over two years. The grade stops below A territory because Bantom was a rotation player rather than a star and no major downstream Seattle asset is assigned to the transaction. Phoenix receives a C because cash had real economic value, but the amount is not preserved in the standard ledger and no traceable basketball asset came back. Confidence is high on the rights-sale structure and Bantom's Seattle production, while the cash amount remains explicitly unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Nate Thurmond and Rowland Garrett from Chicago on November 27, 1975 for Steve Patterson and rookie Eric Fernsten. Thurmond became the transaction's decisive asset. He played 65 regular-season games for the Cavaliers after the trade, then averaged 8.4 points, 11.2 rebounds and 2.8 blocks across all 13 playoff games as Cleveland reached the 1976 Eastern Conference Finals. He returned for 49 more games the next season. Garrett supplied 41 games in 1975-76 and 29 more in 1976-77. Chicago received 52 games from Patterson at 3.2 points and 3.8 rebounds plus 33 games from Fernsten at 2.8 points and 2.1 rebounds; neither created a comparable downstream asset. Cleveland wins clearly because Thurmond gave the Cavaliers high-impact interior defense and playoff value during the franchise's breakthrough season.
perspectives.analysis:
The November 27 Four-Player Exchange Is Fully Verified

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Cleveland and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the same structure: the Bulls sent Nate Thurmond and Rowland Garrett to the Cavaliers for Steve Patterson and Eric Fernsten. The four-player construction in the legacy archive entry is correct. This review focuses on fixing the thin analysis, adding verified player identities and grading the realized value rather than treating every roster appearance as equivalent.

Thurmond Was the Deal's Transformative Piece

Nate Thurmond played 65 regular-season games for Cleveland after the trade and averaged 4.6 points, 5.3 rebounds and 1.3 blocks in 17.4 minutes. Those regular-season numbers look modest, but his postseason role was much larger. Thurmond appeared in all 13 playoff games, averaged 28.8 minutes, 8.4 points, 11.2 rebounds and 2.8 blocks, and gave Cleveland an experienced defensive center during the franchise's run to the Eastern Conference Finals. That playoff workload is the central reason the Cavaliers' side grades so well.

Cleveland Also Retained Thurmond and Garrett Into 1976-77

Thurmond returned for 49 more regular-season games in 1976-77, averaging 5.5 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.7 blocks in 20.3 minutes. Garrett played 41 games for Cleveland immediately after the trade and another 29 the next season before moving to Milwaukee. Garrett's role was small, but he still gave the Cavaliers additional roster depth beyond Thurmond. The combination produced two seasons of value rather than a single playoff rental.

Chicago Received Two Rotation Bigs but Little Lasting Value

Steve Patterson played 52 games for the Bulls after the trade, averaging 3.2 points and 3.8 rebounds in 15.0 minutes. Eric Fernsten appeared in 33 games, averaging 2.8 points and 2.1 rebounds in 7.8 minutes. Both contributed real regular-season minutes, so Chicago's return should not be graded as if the Bulls received nothing. The problem is scale: neither player approached Thurmond's postseason impact, and neither developed into a lasting Chicago asset. Patterson left the NBA after the season for Italy, while Fernsten's later NBA career unfolded elsewhere.

The Team Context Strengthens Cleveland's Hindsight Case

Cleveland finished 49-33 and reached the 1976 Eastern Conference Finals, the breakthrough postseason remembered as the franchise's first deep playoff run. Thurmond was not the Cavaliers' leading scorer, but his 375 playoff minutes and 117 rebounds made him a major part of the rotation. Chicago, meanwhile, fell to 24-58 after having reached the conference finals the year before. A trade should not receive full credit or blame for team records, yet the actual roles matter: Cleveland acquired a player who materially participated in a long playoff run while Chicago received two reserves on a rebuilding season.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A/C+. Cleveland receives an A because Thurmond delivered 65 regular-season games, a major 13-game playoff run at 11.2 rebounds and 2.8 blocks per game, and another 49 games the next season, with Garrett adding depth across parts of two years. Chicago receives a C+ because Patterson and Fernsten combined for 85 regular-season appearances after the trade and filled rotation minutes, but neither matched Thurmond's impact or produced meaningful downstream value. Confidence is high on the four-player package and the principal outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Jack Marin from the Buffalo Braves on November 27, 1975 for the Bulls' 1977 first-round pick. Marin gave Chicago 121 regular-season games across the rest of 1975-76 and 1976-77, including 67 games at 11.0 points per game immediately after the trade. Buffalo did not simply wait to draft Tate Armstrong with the pick. The Braves traded the selection to Milwaukee in November 1976 for Jim Price, then moved Price to Denver for Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams. The same No. 13 pick later returned to Buffalo in the June 1977 Swen Nater/No. 3 pick exchange and was then sent back to Chicago for a second-round pick; Chicago ultimately selected Armstrong. Because Buffalo converted the original pick into useful players while Marin gave Chicago two solid seasons, the source-backed hindsight result is much closer than the legacy archive entry suggested, with a slight edge to the Bulls.
perspectives.analysis:
The Original Deal Was Marin for Chicago's 1977 First-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Buffalo and NBA transaction ledgers agree on the November 27, 1975 structure: Buffalo sent Jack Marin to the Bulls for Chicago's 1977 first-round draft choice. The pick ultimately landed at No. 13 in the 1977 draft and Tate Armstrong was selected there, but Buffalo did not hold the pick continuously until draft night. That distinction is important because the legacy archive entry made Armstrong look like a direct Braves draft return when the actual asset chain was more complicated.

Marin Gave Chicago 121 Regular-Season Games

Marin immediately stepped into a real role for the Bulls. He played 67 games after the trade in 1975-76, averaging 11.0 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 24.3 minutes. He returned for 54 games in 1976-77 and averaged 6.8 points in 16.1 minutes. Across the two Chicago seasons he supplied 121 regular-season appearances and more than 2,400 minutes. He was not a star by that stage of his career, but Chicago received dependable veteran wing production rather than a short rental.

Buffalo Converted the Pick Into Jim Price, Then Gerard and Williams

On November 2, 1976 Buffalo traded the 1977 first-round pick to Milwaukee for Jim Price. Price played 20 games for the Braves before Buffalo moved him to Denver on December 15 for Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams. Gerard then appeared in 41 Buffalo games that season, while Williams played 44. That chain gave the Braves 105 combined regular-season appearances from Price, Gerard and Williams during 1976-77. The original pick therefore produced tangible roster value even before the asset later returned to Buffalo.

The No. 13 Pick Later Returned to Buffalo and Then Back to Chicago

Milwaukee held the pick until June 7, 1977, when the Bucks sent Swen Nater and the No. 13 selection to Buffalo for the No. 3 pick that became Marques Johnson. Three days later Buffalo traded the No. 13 pick back to Chicago for the No. 24 second-round pick that became Larry Johnson; a secondary draft-transaction ledger also reports $150,000 cash going to Buffalo. Chicago then used No. 13 on Tate Armstrong. Because Buffalo had to surrender the No. 3 pick to reacquire No. 13, that later return cannot be credited solely to the 1975 Marin transaction, but it explains why Armstrong was ultimately a Bull rather than a Brave.

Armstrong's Career Should Not Be Treated as Buffalo's Direct Realized Outcome

Armstrong played 92 NBA games, all for Chicago, averaging 3.8 points per game across two seasons. His modest career is relevant to the value of the No. 13 selection, but Buffalo never rostered him. The Braves' directly traceable basketball return from the original asset was the Price-to-Gerard-and-Williams chain, plus whatever value Buffalo received when the reacquired No. 13 pick was moved back to Chicago. That makes the transaction more competitive than a simple Marin-versus-Armstrong comparison.

Final Verdict

Slight Bulls Edge, B+/B. Chicago receives a B+ because Marin gave the club 121 regular-season games and meaningful veteran production over parts of two seasons without requiring another player in the original package. Buffalo receives a B because the first-round pick became a useful trade asset: it brought back Jim Price, who was then converted into Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams, producing substantial 1976-77 roster value. The later No. 13 pick loop is documented but not over-credited because Buffalo spent the No. 3 selection to reacquire it. Confidence is high on the original transaction, Marin's Chicago production and the pick's documented path through Milwaukee and back to Chicago. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana acquired Tom Owens from the Kentucky Colonels on December 3, 1975 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Pacers, Colonels and ABA transaction ledgers agree on a cash-only deal; the legacy future-considerations claim is unsupported and is removed from the verified package. Owens played 16 games for Indiana, averaging 6.5 points and 4.3 rebounds in 15.2 minutes while shooting 51.2 percent. The stay was brief. Basketball-Reference records Indiana selling Owens to San Antonio for cash in January 1976, so the Pacers recovered an economic asset after receiving several weeks of frontcourt depth. Because neither cash amount is preserved in the standard transaction ledgers, the financial side cannot be measured precisely. The source-backed result remains a slight Indiana edge: the Pacers received 16 useful games and later converted Owens back into cash, while Kentucky's return is documented only as an undisclosed cash payment.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Verified December 3 Package Was Tom Owens for Cash

Basketball-Reference's Indiana Pacers transaction page states that Indiana traded cash to Kentucky for Tom Owens on December 3, 1975. Kentucky's transaction page records the mirror image, and the ABA league ledger uses the same structure. None of those standard ledgers includes future considerations. This review therefore removes the legacy future-considerations language from the verified package and retains cash as the only confirmed outgoing asset from Indiana.

Owens Gave Indiana a Short but Legitimate Rotation Stint

Owens appeared in 16 games for the Pacers after the trade. He averaged 6.5 points, 4.3 rebounds and 0.7 blocks in 15.2 minutes while shooting 51.2 percent from the field and 80.0 percent from the line. In a limited role, that is useful frontcourt production rather than an empty roster transaction. Indiana was not acquiring a long-term starter, but Owens supplied real minutes during the final ABA season and gave the club another experienced center option.

The Pacers Recycled Owens Back Into Cash

Basketball-Reference's Indiana and San Antonio transaction logs record a January 1976 sale of Owens to the Spurs for cash. That means Indiana did not simply spend cash for 16 games and lose the asset for nothing. The Pacers received several weeks of production and then recovered another cash return. The exact amounts paid to Kentucky and received from San Antonio are not listed in the standard transaction records, so the two cash legs cannot be compared dollar for dollar. The grade must stay conservative rather than assuming Indiana made or lost money on the resale.

Kentucky's Return Cannot Be Overstated Without a Cash Figure

The Colonels received cash and had already used Owens for 19 games earlier in 1975-76. Selling a reserve center for cash may have been sensible roster management, especially for a club that was also reshaping its frontcourt through the Caldwell Jones and Maurice Lucas transaction later that month. Still, there is no traceable player or draft asset coming back from the Owens sale itself. In a realized-value model, an undisclosed cash return has to be acknowledged but cannot be treated as equal to a documented player contribution without evidence.

Owens' Later San Antonio Production Belongs to the Next Transaction

After leaving Indiana, Owens played 39 games for the Spurs and averaged 5.8 points and 4.0 rebounds in 13.8 minutes. Those games demonstrate that he still had rotation value, but they belong to San Antonio's acquisition rather than Indiana's December deal with Kentucky. The Pacers should receive credit for recognizing a usable player, getting 16 games from him and preserving some residual value through the later cash sale, not for the production he delivered after he left.

Final Verdict

Slight Pacers Edge, B-/C+. Indiana receives a B- because a cash-only acquisition produced 16 games of efficient reserve-center work and was later converted back into cash. Kentucky receives a C+ because the Colonels did receive confirmed cash, but the amount is not preserved in the standard ledger and no basketball asset can be traced from the return. The grade gap remains small because the entire Indiana tenure lasted only 16 games and both cash figures are unresolved. Confidence is high on the December 3 cash-for-Owens structure and his Indiana production. The unsupported future-considerations claim is explicitly excluded. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
