perspectives.summary: Chicago traded Matt Guokas to the Kansas City Kings on December 8, 1975 for a 1976 third-round pick and a 1977 second-round pick. The Bulls used the 1976 selection at No. 37 on Lars Hansen, who stayed in Europe and never played for Chicago; after being drafted again by the Lakers, Hansen eventually played 15 NBA games for Seattle. Chicago used the 1977 selection at No. 30 on Steve Sheppard, who played 64 games for the Bulls as a rookie and averaged 4.3 points and 2.0 rebounds. Guokas played 38 games for Kansas City in 1975-76, averaging 2.2 points in 13.6 minutes, and that was his final NBA season. Basketball-Reference's trade-partner ledger credits Chicago with 0.8 future win shares from the deal and Kansas City with minus-0.1. The picks did not become stars, but Sheppard's 64-game Chicago contribution gives the Bulls the better realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
The December 8 Package Was Guokas for Two Draft Picks

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Kansas City and NBA transaction ledgers agree on the same exchange: the Bulls sent Matt Guokas to the Kings for a 1976 third-round pick and a 1977 second-round pick. Chicago later used the selections at No. 37 on Lars Hansen and No. 30 on Steve Sheppard. The legacy archive entry had the basic structure right, so this review focuses on the draft outcomes and the actual contribution each side received.

Guokas Gave Kansas City 38 Games in His Final NBA Season

Matt Guokas appeared in 38 games for Kansas City after the trade, averaging 13.6 minutes, 2.2 points, 1.2 rebounds and 1.1 assists. Basketball-Reference credits him with minus-0.1 win shares for the Kings. The veteran guard had been a useful rotation player earlier in his career, but by 1975-76 his role had narrowed substantially. He did not play another NBA season after the Kansas City stint, so the Kings received no multi-year return from the transaction.

The Lars Hansen Pick Produced No Chicago NBA Games

Chicago selected Lars Hansen No. 37 in the 1976 draft. Hansen remained in Italy during 1976-77 and 1977-78, and the Lakers drafted him again in 1977. His eventual NBA debut came with Seattle in 1978-79, when he played 15 games. Because he never played for Chicago, those Seattle games are not credited to the Bulls. The 1976 pick therefore produced no realized NBA contribution for Chicago despite eventually identifying an NBA-caliber player.

Steve Sheppard Supplied the Bulls' Real Return

The second pick became Steve Sheppard at No. 30 in 1977. Sheppard played 64 games for Chicago as a rookie in 1977-78, averaging 10.9 minutes, 4.3 points and 2.0 rebounds while producing 0.8 win shares. He later played 42 games for Detroit, but those games belong to a separate transaction path. For this deal, the important point is that Chicago turned one of the two picks into a full season of usable bench minutes, exceeding the brief final-season production Kansas City received from Guokas.

The Difference Is Real but Not Large

Basketball-Reference's Chicago-Kansas City trade-partner table summarizes the realized output neatly: Guokas gave Kansas City 38 games and minus-0.1 win shares, while Sheppard gave Chicago 64 games and 0.8 win shares. Hansen adds no Chicago games. That is enough to create an edge for the Bulls, but not enough to turn a two-pick package into a major win. Neither selection became a long-term Chicago starter, and Guokas still filled a short-term roster role for Kansas City.

Final Verdict

Slight Bulls Edge, B-/C+. Chicago receives a B- because the two draft picks yielded 64 Bulls games from Steve Sheppard, with Lars Hansen producing no Chicago NBA games. Kansas City receives a C+ because Matt Guokas appeared in 38 games but had a small role and finished his NBA career after the season. The 0.8-to-minus-0.1 future win-share comparison supports Chicago's edge while also showing that neither side captured a major asset. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, draft outcomes and direct NBA production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The December 18 Transaction Was a Cash Sale

Basketball-Reference's Denver Nuggets, Spirits of St. Louis and ABA league transaction pages all record the same December 18, 1975 move: Denver sent cash to St. Louis for Gus Gerard. This review therefore preserves the cash consideration but does not invent a dollar figure or assign financial value that cannot be verified.

Gerard Immediately Became a Useful Denver Rotation Forward

Gerard played 60 regular-season games for Denver after the trade in 1975-76. He averaged 9.9 points, 5.0 rebounds and 2.0 assists in 19.8 minutes while shooting 43.4 percent from the field. The minutes and production are meaningful for a midseason cash purchase: Denver received a regular rotation forward rather than a fringe reserve or a short emergency stint, and Gerard remained available throughout the stretch run.

Gerard appeared in all 13 of Denver's playoff games after the acquisition. His postseason role shrank to 10.9 minutes per game, but he still contributed 4.6 points and 2.5 rebounds while the Nuggets advanced through the ABA playoffs. That postseason availability adds value beyond the regular-season line and confirms that Gerard remained part of Denver's working rotation during the final ABA postseason.

Gerard Returned After the ABA-NBA Merger

Denver retained Gerard for the franchise's first NBA season. He played 24 games in 1976-77, started 21, scored 240 points and produced 1.1 win shares in 456 minutes before being traded in December. Combining the two Denver seasons gives the club 84 regular-season games from the original cash acquisition, with useful production on both sides of the league merger. That durability makes the original legacy C-minus grade too low for the realized return.

Denver Later Used Gerard in the Jim Price Package

On December 15, 1976 Denver traded Gerard and Chuck Williams to Buffalo for Jim Price. Because Williams was also required, the original Gerard purchase cannot receive full credit for Price. Still, Gerard retained enough value to function as half of the outgoing player package one year after Denver bought him for cash. Price then played 55 games for Denver in 1976-77. That downstream use strengthens the acquisition without turning it into a one-player chain.

Denver receives a B+ because an undisclosed cash payment produced 84 regular-season games across the ABA and NBA, 13 playoff appearances, an ABA All-Star selection and partial downstream value in the Jim Price trade. The grade stops below A territory because Gerard was a rotation-level forward and Chuck Williams was also needed to acquire Price. perspectives.summary: The New York Nets acquired Jim Eakins from the Virginia Squires on January 27, 1976 for Swen Nater and Billy Schaeffer. The legacy archive entry treated Virginia as a clear winner, but the realized outcome is much closer. Eakins played 34 regular-season games for New York at 6.2 points and 3.5 rebounds, then appeared in all 13 playoff games during the Nets' 1976 ABA championship run, averaging 6.8 points and 6.0 rebounds in 21.6 minutes. Nater gave Virginia 33 games at 11.3 points and 9.8 rebounds, while Schaeffer added 31 games at 6.6 points and 2.9 rebounds. The Squires received more regular-season production, but Eakins became a real postseason rotation center on a championship team. The source-backed verdict is a slight Nets edge rather than the legacy blowout for Virginia.
perspectives.analysis:
The January 27 Three-Player Package Is Verified

Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, Virginia Squires and ABA league transaction ledgers all record the same January 27, 1976 exchange: New York sent Swen Nater and Billy Schaeffer to Virginia for Jim Eakins. This review also corrects the legacy Bill Schaeffer label to the Basketball-Reference identity Billy Schaeffer. There is no cash or draft component in the authoritative ledger, so the evaluation can focus directly on what the three players produced after the trade.

Eakins Became a Championship Rotation Center for the Nets

Eakins played 34 regular-season games for New York after the trade, averaging 6.2 points, 3.5 rebounds and 0.6 blocks in 13.6 minutes while shooting 50.3 percent from the field. His role expanded in the playoffs. He appeared in all 13 postseason games, averaged 21.6 minutes, 6.8 points and 6.0 rebounds, and was part of the rotation as the Nets defeated San Antonio and Denver to win the final ABA championship. That postseason contribution materially changes the hindsight value of the deal.

Virginia Received the Best Regular-Season Player in Nater

Swen Nater was clearly the strongest regular-season performer in the package after the trade. He played 33 games for Virginia and averaged 11.3 points, 9.8 rebounds and 1.1 assists in 23.5 minutes while shooting 49.8 percent. Nater had already been a major rebounder in the ABA, and his Squires production confirms that he remained a starting-caliber interior player. If the trade were judged only by regular-season box-score output, Virginia would have the stronger case.

Schaeffer Added Another 31 Games for the Squires

Billy Schaeffer also contributed immediately, playing 31 games for Virginia at 6.6 points and 2.9 rebounds in 16.7 minutes. His role was smaller than Nater's, but the two outgoing Nets combined for 64 Squires appearances after the deal. That is substantial short-term volume and prevents the transaction from being graded as a New York landslide. Virginia received two usable players, not one star plus a throw-in who never appeared.

The Championship Context Breaks the Near Tie

New York gave up the better regular-season package, but Eakins filled a role that mattered during the most important games of the season. He played every playoff game and increased his rebounding from 3.5 per game in the regular season to 6.0 in the postseason. The Nets did not acquire a star, yet they acquired a center who could handle more than twenty playoff minutes per night on the team that won the ABA title. That kind of direct postseason utility is a legitimate realized outcome and should not be erased by Nater's superior regular-season averages.

Final Verdict

Slight Nets Edge, B+/B. New York receives a B+ because Eakins supplied 34 regular-season games and then became a 21.6-minute postseason rotation center across all 13 games of the 1976 ABA championship run. Virginia receives a B because Nater was the best regular-season player in the transaction and Schaeffer added useful depth, combining for 64 Squires appearances. The margin is intentionally narrow: the Squires won the regular-season production comparison, while the Nets received the more consequential postseason result. Confidence is high on the package and direct 1975-76 outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Phoenix acquired Gar Heard and Buffalo's 1976 second-round pick from the Braves on February 1, 1976 for John Shumate. The legacy archive entry incorrectly added a 1978 second-round pick going to Buffalo; Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Phoenix and NBA transaction ledgers all show only Shumate for Heard plus the 1976 second-rounder. Phoenix used that pick at No. 30 on Al Fleming, who did not play for the Suns. Heard became the decisive return, playing 162 regular-season games for Phoenix over parts of three seasons and all 19 playoff games during the Suns' 1976 NBA Finals run, averaging 13.9 points and 10.4 rebounds in that postseason. Shumate was excellent for Buffalo too, giving the Braves 124 regular-season games and nine 1976 playoff appearances before becoming part of a later multi-asset deal with Detroit. Phoenix holds a slight hindsight edge, but both teams received substantial value.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Verified Package Was Shumate for Heard and One 1976 Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Buffalo Braves, Phoenix Suns and NBA league transaction ledgers agree on the February 1, 1976 structure: Buffalo sent Gar Heard and a 1976 second-round pick to Phoenix for John Shumate. The pick became No. 30 Al Fleming. None of those authoritative ledgers includes the legacy 1978 second-round pick that was labeled as No. 41 Jerome Whitehead. This review therefore removes that unsupported asset from the verified package and disconnects Whitehead from this trade's player-history linkage.

Heard Became a Major Part of Phoenix's 1976 Finals Run

Gar Heard played 36 regular-season games for Phoenix after the trade, averaging 12.4 points and 9.9 rebounds in 33.9 minutes. His postseason role was even more important. Heard appeared in all 19 Suns playoff games, averaged 13.9 points, 10.4 rebounds, 2.1 steals and 1.9 blocks, and helped Phoenix reach the NBA Finals. That immediate two-way playoff production is the strongest single realized outcome in the deal.

Phoenix Kept Heard for Two More Seasons

Heard returned for 46 games in 1976-77 and 80 in 1977-78, giving Phoenix 162 regular-season appearances across parts of three seasons from the original transaction. His scoring declined after the Finals run, but he continued to rebound, defend and play substantial minutes. The extra longevity separates the return from a short postseason rental and gives Phoenix a strong multi-year case even before considering the draft pick.

The Al Fleming Pick Produced No Suns Games

Phoenix used the acquired second-round pick at No. 30 on Al Fleming in the 1976 draft. Fleming did not play for the Suns and is listed as not playing after being waived in 1976-77. He later reached the NBA with Seattle in 1977-78, but those games are not Phoenix value. The pick therefore adds draft optionality to the transaction but no realized Suns production. Heard, not Fleming, carries the Phoenix grade.

Shumate Was an Excellent Buffalo Return

John Shumate immediately became a major Braves frontcourt player. He appeared in 32 games after the trade at 12.2 points and 9.8 rebounds, then played 74 games in 1976-77 at 15.1 points and 9.5 rebounds and another 18 in 1977-78. He also averaged 14.1 points and 8.6 rebounds across nine playoff games in 1976. Buffalo therefore received 124 regular-season games of strong production, making this a competitive trade rather than a one-sided Phoenix win.

Shumate Retained Some Downstream Trade Value

On November 23, 1977 Buffalo included Shumate, Gus Gerard and a 1979 first-round pick in a larger deal with Detroit for Marvin Barnes and two 1978 draft picks. Because Gerard and a first-rounder were also required, this review gives Shumate only partial downstream credit. The later package still shows that he retained trade value after nearly two productive Braves seasons. It also reinforces why Buffalo's side remains close to Phoenix's despite Heard's superior longevity and deeper 1976 playoff run.

Final Verdict

Slight Suns Edge, A-/B+. Phoenix receives an A- because Heard delivered 162 regular-season games, three seasons of frontcourt value and a major 19-game playoff run to the 1976 NBA Finals. The No. 30 pick produced no Suns games, so the grade is driven by Heard rather than draft luck. Buffalo receives a B+ because Shumate gave the Braves 124 regular-season games, strong scoring and rebounding, nine playoff appearances and partial downstream trade value. The margin stays narrow, but Heard's longer Phoenix tenure and much deeper 1976 postseason role break the tie. Confidence is high on the corrected package and direct outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Portland acquired New Orleans' 1977 second-round pick on June 3, 1976 for a 1976 second-round pick. The Jazz used Portland's outgoing selection at No. 26 on Jacky Dorsey, who played in the Eastern Basketball Association in 1976-77 and never appeared in a regular-season game for New Orleans. Portland used the incoming pick at No. 28 on Kim Anderson. Anderson stayed in Italy for 1977-78, then joined the Trail Blazers in 1978-79 and played 21 games, averaging 3.0 points and 2.1 rebounds in 10.7 minutes. Dorsey eventually reached the NBA with Denver, Portland and Houston, but those later games were not New Orleans value. The trade was low-impact on both sides, yet Portland holds a slight hindsight edge because its acquired pick produced 21 actual games for the club while New Orleans' selection produced none for the Jazz.
perspectives.analysis:
The June 3 Deal Was a Straight Second-Round Pick Swap

Basketball-Reference's Portland Trail Blazers, New Orleans Jazz and NBA league transaction ledgers all record the same exchange: Portland sent its 1976 second-round pick to New Orleans for the Jazz's 1977 second-round pick. New Orleans used the 1976 selection at No. 26 on Jacky Dorsey, while Portland later used the 1977 selection at No. 28 on Kim Anderson. The legacy structure is correct; this review adds the actual player outcomes and distinguishes later NBA careers from value realized by the teams that owned the picks.

New Orleans Selected Jacky Dorsey but Received No NBA Games

The Jazz selected Dorsey No. 26 in the 1976 draft. Basketball-Reference lists him as playing in the Eastern Basketball Association rather than the NBA in 1976-77, and he never appeared in a regular-season game for New Orleans. Dorsey did eventually reach the NBA in 1977-78, but his first games came with Denver and later Portland. Those appearances demonstrate that the pick identified an NBA-caliber player, yet they cannot be credited to the Jazz because New Orleans did not realize that production.

Portland Waited a Year for Kim Anderson

Portland used the incoming 1977 second-round pick at No. 28 on Kim Anderson. Anderson spent 1977-78 playing professionally in Italy rather than joining the Trail Blazers immediately. He reached Portland in 1978-79 and appeared in 21 games, averaging 3.0 points, 2.1 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 10.7 minutes. The production was limited and his field-goal percentage was only 31.2 percent, but the pick did eventually generate real NBA minutes for the team that acquired it.

The Later Dorsey Career Does Not Reverse the Jazz Outcome

Dorsey played 11 NBA games across Denver and Portland in 1977-78 and later appeared for Houston. Those games matter to his career history but not to the realized return from this New Orleans trade. A draft pick's hindsight value should follow the team that actually retained and used the player, not automatically inherit every game the drafted player later produced elsewhere. That rule prevents the Jazz from receiving credit for Dorsey's Denver, Portland or Houston appearances after he failed to play for New Orleans.

The Difference Remains Small Because Anderson's Portland Role Was Small

Portland's 21 games from Anderson are enough to separate the outcomes, but not enough to make this a major win. Anderson totaled only 224 minutes in his lone Trail Blazers season and scored 63 points. New Orleans received no direct NBA games from Dorsey, but the Jazz did secure a second-round prospect one year earlier than the pick they surrendered. The swap therefore remains a low-value transaction where the grade gap should be compressed rather than inflated.

Final Verdict

Slight Blazers Edge, C+/C. Portland receives a C+ because the 1977 No. 28 pick eventually produced 21 Trail Blazers games from Kim Anderson, even though the contribution was modest and delayed by a season in Italy. New Orleans receives a C because the 1976 No. 26 pick became Jacky Dorsey, who never played an NBA regular-season game for the Jazz. Dorsey's later NBA career belongs to other teams and does not erase that zero-game New Orleans outcome. Confidence is high on the pick swap and draft outcomes. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

summary: Atlanta and Houston completed a major pre-draft exchange on June 7, 1976. The Hawks sent Dwight Jones and the No. 1 pick, which Houston used on John Lucas Jr., for Gus Bailey, Joe Meriweather and the No. 9 pick, which Atlanta used on Armond Hill. Both teams extracted real value. Lucas played all 82 games in each of his first two Houston seasons, averaging 11.1 points and 5.6 assists as a rookie and 12.4 points and 9.4 assists in 1977-78. Jones added 237 Houston games across three seasons. Atlanta received 74 games of 11.1 points and 8.1 rebounds from Meriweather in 1976-77, while Hill immediately became a long-term backcourt piece and played 324 games over his first four Hawks seasons. Bailey never appeared for Atlanta. The realized returns are strong enough on both sides that the source-backed verdict remains an even trade rather than forcing a winner.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Package and Draft Outcomes Are Fully Verified

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta and Houston transaction records agree on the June 7, 1976 structure: Atlanta sent Dwight Jones and the 1976 No. 1 pick to Houston for Gus Bailey, Joe Meriweather and the No. 9 pick. Houston used No. 1 on John Lucas Jr.; Atlanta used No. 9 on Armond Hill the next day. This review preserves that five-asset structure and attaches the direct player and draft-outcome identities.

Houston Received a Starting Guard and a Durable Big

Lucas played all 82 games as a rookie, averaging 11.1 points, 5.6 assists and 1.5 steals in 30.9 minutes while earning All-Rookie recognition. He returned in 1977-78 and again played all 82 games, this time averaging 12.4 points and 9.4 assists. Dwight Jones supplied frontcourt depth across three Houston seasons, appearing in 74 games in 1976-77, 82 in 1977-78 and 81 in 1978-79. The Rockets therefore received immediate help from both the established player and the premium pick.

Atlanta Turned the No. 9 Pick Into a Multi-Year Point Guard

Armond Hill played 81 games as a rookie and averaged 5.0 assists, then started all 82 games in both 1977-78 and 1978-79. He added 79 more games in 1979-80, giving Atlanta 324 appearances over his first four seasons alone. Hill was not the same caliber of prospect as the No. 1 selection, but he became a stable backcourt piece for several years and gave the Hawks substantial realized value from the pick swap.

Meriweather Was Also a Strong Immediate Return

Joe Meriweather played 74 games for Atlanta in 1976-77 and averaged 11.1 points, 8.1 rebounds and 1.1 blocks in 27.9 minutes. He produced 4.8 win shares before moving on the next season. Gus Bailey did not play for Atlanta and was waived, so the Hawks' player return is driven overwhelmingly by Meriweather rather than Bailey. Even so, Meriweather plus Hill created a productive two-part return that balances much of Houston's Lucas-and-Jones package.

The Trade Worked for Both Sides for Different Reasons

Houston received the best single draft slot and turned it into a guard who immediately played major minutes, while also adding a useful veteran big. Atlanta moved down eight spots but landed Hill and added a starting-caliber center in Meriweather. The draft-position gap is real, yet the Hawks converted their lower pick well enough that the practical results remained competitive rather than one-sided.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, A-/A-. Houston receives an A- for two full seasons of major Lucas production plus three years of Dwight Jones frontcourt minutes. Atlanta receives an A- because Armond Hill became a multi-year starter and Joe Meriweather delivered a strong 74-game season immediately after the trade. Bailey contributed no Atlanta games, which keeps the Hawks from grading higher, while Lucas leaving Houston after only two seasons prevents the Rockets from separating decisively. Confidence is high on the package, draft outcomes and first-stage realized production. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired the player rights to Fatty Taylor from Philadelphia on August 5, 1976 for a 1977 second-round pick that became No. 43 Herm Harris. The deal gave Denver an immediate rotation guard for its first NBA season. Taylor played 79 regular-season games in 1976-77, averaging 3.8 points, 2.7 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.7 steals in 19.6 minutes while appearing in all but three games for a 50-win Nuggets team. Philadelphia used the pick on Harris, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Taylor was waived by Denver in October 1977, so the Nuggets did not receive a multi-year asset, yet one full season of usable backcourt minutes clearly outweighs a draft selection that produced no NBA games. The source-backed verdict remains a Denver win.
perspectives.analysis:
The August 5 Structure Is Fully Verified

Basketball-Reference's Denver and Philadelphia transaction ledgers agree that the Nuggets sent a 1977 second-round pick to the 76ers for Fatty Taylor on August 5, 1976. Carl Scheer's executive record confirms the same exchange, and Denver's own media guide lists Taylor as an August 5 acquisition for the pick that became Herm Harris. Pro Sports Transactions independently traces the selection to No. 43 in the 1977 draft.

Denver Received a Real Rotation Guard Immediately

Taylor played 79 regular-season games for Denver in 1976-77 and averaged 19.6 minutes, 3.8 points, 2.7 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.7 steals. He was no longer the high-usage ABA guard he had been earlier in the decade, but he still gave the Nuggets a steady defensive and ball-handling option throughout their first NBA season. Denver finished 50-32 and first in the Midwest Division, and Taylor was available almost every night.

The Postseason Contribution Was Minimal but the Regular Season Was Not

Taylor appeared in only one playoff game and logged a single minute, so this review does not inflate his value by treating him as an important postseason piece. The trade's Denver case rests on the 79-game regular-season body of work. That distinction matters because the acquisition was useful without being transformative. Denver still received a full regular-season rotation player for the price of one future second-round selection. Taylor filled a role for one season, then Denver waived him in October 1977.

Philadelphia's Pick Became Herm Harris at No. 43

The 76ers used the acquired second-round pick on Herm Harris, a 6-foot-5 forward from Arizona, with the 43rd overall selection in the 1977 NBA draft. Basketball-Reference's draft page lists no NBA seasons or games for Harris. In a realized-value model, the pick therefore produced no NBA on-court return for Philadelphia. The draft choice still had legitimate option value when acquired, but hindsight grading must reflect what actually materialized in NBA competition.

The Rights Language Is Historically Accurate

Secondary transaction records often describe Denver as acquiring Taylor's draft rights because Philadelphia had originally selected him in the 12th round of the 1969 NBA draft even though he built his career in the ABA. RealGM and Denver's historical records both preserve that rights-based framing. Taylor then signed with Denver on the same August 5 date and entered the Nuggets' 1976-77 roster, so the practical outcome is straightforward: Denver converted the rights into an active player immediately.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, B/D+. Denver receives a B because one second-round pick produced 79 games of dependable rotation play during a 50-win season, including useful passing and steal production, even though Taylor lasted only one NBA season with the club and barely played in the postseason. Philadelphia receives a D+ because the pick became Herm Harris at No. 43 and Harris never played an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, Taylor's Denver production and the draft outcome. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
Buffalo and Milwaukee Exchanged Different Draft Opportunities

On August 5, 1976, the Buffalo Braves acquired the rights to the seventh selection of the ABA dispersal draft from Milwaukee. That position was associated with Bird Averitt. The Bucks received an ordinary 1977 NBA second-round selection that later became No. 27 Glenn Williams. The dispersal mechanism was created after the ABA-NBA merger and isn't interchangeable with a regular NBA amateur draft. Milwaukee preferred a future traditional draft opportunity, while Buffalo used its acquisition to evaluate an available professional who had played in the rival league. The modern Clippers franchise index covers the Braves' actual transaction.

Averitt Was a Known ABA Scorer

Averitt had professional experience and a reputation for scoring in the ABA before he entered the merger dispersal process. Buffalo's willingness to use a high dispersal slot reflected interest in a player closer to NBA readiness than an unknown 1977 second-round prospect. Yet a player's previous ABA points weren't NBA minutes with the Braves, and the future roster return had to be established after the acquisition. Moving this asset didn't give Milwaukee Averitt's established professional career. It gave the Bucks a different opportunity to select someone from the following year's amateur draft.

Milwaukee's Selection Became a Specific 1977 Pick

The incoming Bucks second was ultimately identified with the twenty-seventh selection in the 1977 draft, associated with Glenn Williams. That concrete position is a traceable benefit of choosing the future draft route. It did not guarantee a star, but it offered more predictable conventional NBA draft mechanics than acquiring an ABA dispersal right. By contrast, Buffalo took the immediate risk of a professional it could bring into its developing roster. Tracking the actual names prevents the agreement from being reduced to two anonymous draft picks without historical context.

Milwaukee Receives a Narrow Developmental Edge

The Bucks obtained a future second-round right that could support roster rebuilding, while Buffalo took a faster approach through Averitt. Neither side secured a franchise-defining selection, and later team success depended on many unrelated transactions. The result slightly favors Milwaukee given the ordinary draft right and the limited direct NBA impact that can be firmly attributed to Buffalo's dispersal acquisition. This is a modest result: the Bucks did not gain several firsts, and the Braves were not irrational to pursue a familiar professional scorer during the merger transition.

Final Verdict

Slight Bucks Edge. Milwaukee receives C+ for the 1977 No. 27 second-round position eventually associated with Glenn Williams. Buffalo, counted under the Clippers franchise lineage, receives C for the No. 7 ABA dispersal draft rights associated with Bird Averitt. Neither right is treated as an assured NBA starter, and Averitt's ABA résumé isn't Buffalo NBA production.

Atlanta's own historical media guide records Hawes and Petrie arriving from Portland in the same transaction period, while the dispersal-draft ledgers identify the No. 2 right as the Portland return.

Portland Return
Lucas changed the Trail Blazers immediately. NBA.com's 1976-77 season review says his toughness, rebounding and scoring helped propel a franchise that had never posted a winning season to the championship. Portland's own alumni history notes that Lucas led the team in scoring, minutes, field goals, free throws and offensive rebounds in his first season. He averaged 20.2 points and 11.2 rebounds in 1976-77, made the All-Star team, finished ninth in MVP voting and then averaged 19.7 points and 10.7 rebounds across the six-game Finals victory over Philadelphia. He was an All-Star in each of his first three Portland seasons and became such an important franchise figure that the club later retired No. 20. That is championship-level, franchise-defining realized value from a single dispersal selection.

Atlanta Return
The Hawks did not come away empty. Petrie had been a two-time Portland All-Star and former Rookie of the Year, but his knee injury ended his playing career and he never appeared in a game for Atlanta. Hawes, however, became a durable frontcourt piece. He played 44 games in 1976-77, then 75, 81, 82, 74 and 49 games over the next five seasons, for 405 Hawks regular-season games in total. His best Atlanta season came in 1977-78, when he averaged 12.7 points and 9.2 rebounds, and he remained a useful big through 1981-82. That six-season return is far more valuable than a token consolation package and keeps Atlanta well above the failing-grade range even though it missed on the star outcome.

Hindsight Verdict
Portland wins decisively because Lucas became an immediate All-Star, helped deliver the franchise's only NBA championship and supplied elite two-way frontcourt value during the club's breakthrough. An A+ fits both the peak and the direct team result. Atlanta earns a B rather than the legacy C because Hawes provided six seasons and 405 games of legitimate NBA production. Petrie's injury eliminated the second half of the player package, and no amount of useful Hawes value can match the title-level impact of Lucas, but the Hawks still received a meaningful long-term contributor. Final verdict: Portland Trail Blazers Win.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Phoenix acquired Tom Van Arsdale from Buffalo on August 25, 1976 for a 1977 second-round pick that became No. 27 Glen Williams. Basketball-Reference's Suns, Braves and league transaction ledgers all confirm the player-for-pick exchange and do not list cash; Pro Sports Transactions separately reports cash, so this review preserves that only as a secondary-source note rather than a primary-ledger asset. Van Arsdale played 77 games for Phoenix in 1976-77, averaging 5.8 points, 2.4 rebounds and 0.9 assists in 18.5 minutes. The incoming pick did not remain with Buffalo: Pro Sports Transactions traces it to Milwaukee as the second-rounder connected to the Braves' earlier August 5 Bird Averitt dispersal-pick trade. Milwaukee used No. 27 on Glen Williams, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Phoenix gets the slight hindsight edge because it received a full season of rotation value while the pick itself produced no NBA player value.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Verify Van Arsdale for a 1977 Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Phoenix and NBA transaction pages all record the same August 25, 1976 exchange: the Braves sent Tom Van Arsdale to the Suns for a 1977 second-round draft pick that later became Glen Williams at No. 27. Those primary-style transaction ledgers do not list cash. Pro Sports Transactions does list cash, so this review does not erase the secondary report, but it removes cash from the verified primary package and records the discrepancy explicitly.

Van Arsdale Gave Phoenix One Full Rotation Season

Van Arsdale played 77 games for the Suns in 1976-77, averaging 18.5 minutes, 5.8 points, 2.4 rebounds and 0.9 assists while shooting 43.3 percent from the field. He was 33 and no longer the high-scoring wing he had been earlier in his career, but Phoenix still received a dependable veteran who appeared in all but five games. That is meaningful realized value for a future second-round selection.

Buffalo Did Not Use the Pick on Glen Williams

The draft outcome needs a careful chain. Basketball-Reference shows Milwaukee selecting Glen Williams with the No. 27 pick in 1977. Pro Sports Transactions traces that exact selection back through Buffalo: the Braves had agreed on August 5, 1976 to send Milwaukee a 1977 second-rounder in the Bird Averitt dispersal-pick transaction, then acquired Phoenix's second-rounder from the Van Arsdale deal on August 25. The same pick is identified as the one that ultimately went to Milwaukee. This review therefore does not present Williams as a Buffalo draft choice.

The Bird Averitt Connection Is Real but Should Be Discounted

Bird Averitt played 75 games for Buffalo in 1976-77 and averaged 7.9 points in 15.1 minutes. That is useful roster value, but the Braves had already completed the Averitt transaction twenty days before acquiring Phoenix's pick. The later Van Arsdale trade appears to have supplied the draft asset that fulfilled that prior obligation, not to have independently caused the Averitt acquisition. For hindsight grading, Buffalo receives some asset-management credit without assigning all 75 Averitt games directly to this review.

The Pick's Draft Outcome Added No NBA Production

Milwaukee used No. 27 on Glen Williams of St. John's. Basketball-Reference lists him as a 1977 second-round selection but shows no NBA regular-season games. That limits the realized basketball value of the pick itself. The selection had option value when Phoenix surrendered it, and Buffalo was able to use that asset within a broader obligation, but there is no NBA playing career from Williams to add to the return.

Final Verdict

Slight Suns Edge, B/B-. Phoenix receives a B because Van Arsdale supplied 77 regular-season games and steady veteran rotation minutes for the direct cost of a future second-round pick. Buffalo receives a B- because the pick retained real transactional value and is traced to the earlier Bird Averitt obligation, but the No. 27 draft outcome produced no NBA games and the link to Averitt is indirect rather than a fresh August 25 acquisition. Confidence is high on the player-for-pick structure and direct production; the cash component remains secondary-source-only. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Portland traded LaRue Martin to Seattle on September 2, 1976 for future considerations. Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Portland and league transaction ledgers agree on that exchange and separately list Seattle's sale of Herm Gilliam's player rights to Portland on the same date, so Gilliam is not part of the Martin package. An archival report quoting Seattle coach and general manager Bill Russell says the consideration was a conditional 1977 draft pick that would transfer only if Martin made the opening-day roster. RealGM shows Seattle waived Martin on October 12 and he became a free agent two days later; Basketball-Reference shows his NBA career ending with Portland in 1975-76. Because Martin never appeared in a regular-season game for Seattle, the condition did not trigger and Portland received no exercised pick. The completed value is therefore effectively even and minimal.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Martin Trade and the Gilliam Sale Were Separate Transactions

Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Portland and NBA transaction ledgers all list two distinct September 2, 1976 moves between the same clubs. Seattle sold the player rights to Herm Gilliam to Portland, and Portland separately traded LaRue Martin to Seattle for future considerations. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Bill Russell's Seattle executive record preserve the same separation. This review therefore evaluates only Martin for future considerations and does not fold Gilliam into the exchange.

The Future Consideration Was Conditional on Martin Making the Team

The standard Basketball-Reference ledgers do not identify the future consideration by round, but an archival Portland account of a September 3 report quotes Russell clarifying that Seattle had not traded a first-round pick. Russell said the consideration would be a 1977 draft pick and that it was conditional on Martin making Seattle's opening-day roster. That detail resolves the legacy "not exercised" note: the draft asset existed only if the roster condition was satisfied.

Seattle Waived Martin Before the Regular Season

RealGM records Seattle acquiring Martin on September 2, placing him on waivers on October 12 and Martin becoming a free agent on October 14. Basketball-Reference's career page lists four NBA seasons, all with Portland, ending in 1975-76. Martin therefore produced zero regular-season games, minutes or points for Seattle. The SuperSonics took a low-cost look at a former No. 1 overall pick, but the basketball return from the transaction was zero.

Portland's Return Also Finished at Zero

Because Martin did not make Seattle's opening-day roster, the conditional 1977 pick never became an exercised Portland asset. No draft selection or player outcome should be assigned to the Trail Blazers from this transaction. Herm Gilliam did appear in 18 games for Portland in 1976-77, but that value came from the separate same-day rights sale and cannot be used to improve Portland's grade on the Martin deal.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, D/D. Seattle receives a D because Martin never played a regular-season game for the SuperSonics and was waived before opening day. Portland also receives a D because the conditional 1977 draft consideration did not trigger, leaving the Trail Blazers with no realized asset from this specific exchange. The transaction was inexpensive for Seattle and allowed Portland to move on from Martin, so neither side warrants an F, but neither side generated measurable on-court or draft value from the deal itself. Confidence is high on the transaction, the separate Gilliam sale, Martin's waiver and the zero-game outcome; the exact round of the conditional 1977 pick remains unspecified.

seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Gilliam Rights Sale Was Separate From the LaRue Martin Trade

Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Portland and NBA transaction ledgers list two distinct September 2, 1976 transactions between the clubs. Seattle sold the player rights to Herm Gilliam to Portland, while Portland separately sent LaRue Martin to Seattle for future considerations. Gilliam Became a Real Rotation Piece in Portland

Gilliam had already played for Seattle in 1975-76 before the rights sale. With Portland in 1976-77, Basketball-Reference credits him with 80 regular-season games and 1,665 minutes. He averaged 9.3 points, 2.5 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 20.8 minutes per game while shooting 43.8 percent from the field. The conservative approach is to give Seattle some value without equating the unknown cash with Gilliam's documented NBA production.

Seattle receives a C because it converted Gilliam's rights into financial consideration, but the amount is unverified and there is no player or draft asset to trace forward. perspectives.analysis:
The Primary Record Shows McNeill for a 1977 Third-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Kansas City, New York and NBA transaction ledgers all record the September 9, 1976 exchange as Larry McNeill to the Nets for a 1977 third-round draft pick. The Nets' own historical media guide says the same thing and identifies the eventual selection as Bill Paterno. None of those primary-style records lists cash. Pro Sports Transactions does preserve a UPI-based note that cash was also included, while also flagging conflicting reporting around the transaction date. This review therefore keeps the cash report visible as secondary evidence but does not treat it as a fully verified primary-ledger asset.

McNeill Gave New York Only a Brief Regular-Season Return

McNeill had been a useful Kansas City reserve and part-time starter before the trade, appearing in all 82 games in 1975-76. His New York stint was much shorter. Basketball-Reference credits him with eight Nets games, 93 total minutes, 60 points and 26 rebounds in 1976-77. On a per-game basis he averaged 7.5 points and 3.3 rebounds in 11.6 minutes. That is real realized value, but the sample is too small to treat the acquisition as a successful long-term rotation move.

The Nets Waived Him in December

Basketball-Reference's league and Nets transaction pages show New York waiving McNeill on December 13, 1976. RealGM independently records the same waiver, followed by free agency two days later. He did not return to the Nets. Golden State signed him on February 24, 1977, so his later 16-game Warriors stint belongs to a separate free-agent transaction and cannot be credited to New York here. This review grades only the eight games the Nets actually received from the September trade.

Kansas City Used the Pick on Bill Paterno at No. 45

The pick outcome is fully traceable. Kansas City selected Notre Dame forward Bill Paterno with the first pick of the third round, No. 45 overall, in the 1977 NBA Draft. Basketball-Reference's Kings transaction log and Paterno player page both identify that selection. Paterno has no NBA regular-season statistical record, so the pick produced no realized NBA playing value for Kansas City. The draft asset had option value when acquired, but its completed on-court outcome was zero.

The Cash Report Does Not Create a Measurable Kings Advantage

Pro Sports Transactions says a UPI report included cash in addition to the third-rounder. Because the amount is not identified and the Basketball-Reference ledgers plus the Nets' historical media guide omit cash entirely, this review discounts that component heavily. It is reasonable to preserve the possibility that Kansas City received some financial consideration, but there is not enough verified information to price it or use it to overturn the direct basketball comparison.

Final Verdict

Slight Nets Edge, C+/C. New York receives a C+ because McNeill at least produced eight regular-season games and 93 minutes before being waived. Kansas City receives a C because the acquired third-round pick became Bill Paterno, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game; the secondary cash report adds some possible transaction value but cannot be measured confidently. The margin is intentionally small. Confidence is high on the player-for-pick structure, McNeill's Nets production and the Paterno draft outcome, while the cash component remains secondary-source-only.

perspectives.summary: Kansas City traded Tiny Archibald to the New York Nets on September 10, 1976 for Jim Eakins, Brian Taylor and two future first-round picks that became No. 2 Otis Birdsong in 1977 and No. 2 Phil Ford in 1978. The Kings received immediate production from both veterans, then landed two premium guards: Birdsong became a three-time All-Star and 1981 All-NBA Second Team selection during four Kansas City seasons, while Ford won 1979 Rookie of the Year and made All-NBA Second Team as a rookie. Archibald still gave New York 34 games at 20.5 points and 7.5 assists, and the Nets preserved major exit value by trading him to Buffalo in 1977 for George Johnson and two first-round picks. One of those picks later became part of a Knicks settlement package; the other became Cliff Robinson, whom New Jersey eventually traded back to Kansas City for Birdsong. Kansas City owns the stronger hindsight return, but New York's downstream recovery makes the legacy failing grade far too harsh.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange Is One of the Deepest Packages of the Merger Era

Basketball-Reference's Kansas City, New York and league transaction ledgers agree on the September 10, 1976 structure. The Kings sent Tiny Archibald to the Nets for Jim Eakins, Brian Taylor, New York's 1977 first-round pick and its 1978 first-round pick. Those selections became Otis Birdsong at No. 2 in 1977 and Phil Ford at No. 2 in 1978. Joe Axelson's Kansas City executive ledger and Roy Boe's Nets ledger record the same package. Unlike several nearby 1976 trades, there is no material source conflict over the core assets.

Brian Taylor Was an Immediate High-Level Return

Taylor gave Kansas City 72 games in 1976-77 and immediately became one of the club's best guards. He averaged 17.0 points, 4.4 assists and 2.8 steals in 34.6 minutes while shooting 50.4 percent from the field, and he earned NBA All-Defensive Second Team honors. That is substantial direct value before the draft picks even enter the equation. Kansas City then used Taylor in a May 1977 package with another first-round pick to acquire Tom Burleson and a second-round selection, so Taylor also retained transaction value beyond his one Kings season. Because that later deal contained another premium asset, this review credits the downstream return only partially.

Jim Eakins Added a Full Season of Frontcourt Depth

Eakins was less valuable than Taylor but still produced a complete NBA season. He appeared in all 82 games for Kansas City in 1976-77, averaging 6.0 points and 4.4 rebounds in 16.3 minutes. His role was modest, yet it matters in a trade that already delivered two future No. 2 picks. The Kings did not have to wait for the draft assets to mature before receiving useful rotation minutes from the incoming veterans.

Otis Birdsong Became a Multi-Year Kansas City Star

The 1977 first-round pick became Birdsong at No. 2 overall. Across four Kansas City seasons he played 308 regular-season games and developed from a 15.8-point rookie into one of the league's top scoring guards. He made the All-Star team in 1979, 1980 and 1981, averaged 24.6 points in 1980-81 and earned All-NBA Second Team honors that season. In June 1981 Kansas City traded Birdsong and a second-round pick to New Jersey for Cliff Robinson, adding another traceable asset conversion after four strong seasons of production.

Phil Ford Made the Second First-Rounder Pay Off Immediately

The 1978 first-round pick also landed at No. 2, where Kansas City selected Phil Ford. Ford played 79 games as a rookie, averaged 15.9 points and 8.6 assists, won Rookie of the Year and made All-NBA Second Team. He remained the Kings' starting-level point guard beyond that first season. Two consecutive No. 2 selections turning into Birdsong and Ford is the central reason Kansas City's hindsight grade reaches the top tier: the draft portion of the return produced two major backcourt pieces rather than merely retaining theoretical pick value.

Archibald Still Produced Star-Level Numbers for the Nets

New York's direct return was shortened, not empty. Archibald played 34 games in 1976-77 and averaged 20.5 points and 7.5 assists in 37.6 minutes. Basketball-Reference lists his next season as missed because of an Achilles injury, but the Nets had already moved him before that 1977-78 season began. On September 1, 1977 New Jersey traded Archibald to Buffalo. The Nets' historical media guide identifies the return as George Johnson, Houston's 1978 first-round pick and Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick. That distinction is important: Archibald did not simply leave New York for nothing.

New Jersey Recovered Substantial Downstream Value

The two Buffalo-trade picks continued to produce value, although not in a straight line. The Houston-origin 1978 first was the No. 4 selection later used on Micheal Ray Richardson, but New Jersey did not make that pick. In June 1978 the Nets packaged it with another 1979 first in a settlement with the Knicks and received Phil Jackson plus the No. 13 pick that became Winford Boynes, so only part of that later return belongs to the Archibald asset chain. Buffalo's 1979 first stayed with New Jersey and became No. 11 Cliff Robinson. Robinson averaged 13.6 points as a rookie and 19.5 in his second season. In June 1981 the Nets traded Robinson to Kansas City for Birdsong and a second-round pick, bringing one of the original Kings assets back to New Jersey through the Archibald exit chain.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A+/A-. Kansas City receives an A+ because the return produced a full season from Taylor, 82 games from Eakins, four high-level Birdsong seasons and a Rookie of the Year/All-NBA start from Ford. New York receives an A- rather than the legacy F because Archibald was still a 20-point, seven-assist player in his 34 Nets games and, more importantly, retained enough market value to bring back Johnson and two first-round assets. One of those picks became part of a later settlement package and the other became Robinson, who eventually brought Birdsong back to the Nets. The Kings still generated the deeper direct return and the best combined draft outcome, but the source-backed asset chain shows that both franchises realized substantial value.

The Houston-origin 1978 first was the No. 4 selection later used on Micheal Ray Richardson, but New Jersey did not make that pick. In June 1978 the Nets packaged it with another 1979 first in a settlement with the Knicks and received Phil Jackson plus the No. 13 pick that became Winford Boynes, so only part of that later return belongs to the Archibald asset chain. Buffalo's 1979 first stayed with New Jersey and became No. 11 Cliff Robinson. Robinson averaged 13.6 points as a rookie and 19.5 in his second season. In June 1981 the Nets traded Robinson to Kansas City for Birdsong and a second-round pick, bringing one of the original Kings assets back to New Jersey through the Archibald exit chain.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A+/A-. Kansas City receives an A+ because the return produced a full season from Taylor, 82 games from Eakins, four high-level Birdsong seasons and a Rookie of the Year/All-NBA start from Ford. New York receives an A- rather than the legacy F because Archibald was still a 20-point, seven-assist player in his 34 Nets games and, more importantly, retained enough market value to bring back Johnson and two first-round assets. One of those picks became part of a later settlement package and the other became Robinson, who eventually brought Birdsong back to the Nets. The Kings still generated the deeper direct return and the best combined draft outcome, but the source-backed asset chain shows that both franchises realized substantial value.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree This Was a Cash Rights Sale

Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, New York and NBA transaction pages all record the same September 10, 1976 structure: the Braves sold the player rights to Jim McMillian to the Knicks. The New York page describes the acquisition of McMillian's rights, while the Buffalo and league ledgers explicitly use the word "sold." No player or draft pick is listed going back to Buffalo. The legacy cash asset is therefore directionally correct, but the reviewed records do not state an amount. This review keeps the financial return unpriced rather than inventing a figure.

McMillian Became an Immediate Knicks Starter

McMillian was not merely an end-of-bench veteran. In 1976-77 he played 67 games, started 60 and averaged 32.2 minutes, 9.9 points, 4.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists while shooting 46.4 percent from the field. New York finished 40-42, so the acquisition did not create a major team-level jump, but the Knicks received more than 2,100 regular-season minutes from him in the first year alone. That is substantial realized value for a transaction whose only documented outgoing consideration is cash.

The Second Season Added Durability and Playoff Minutes

McMillian returned for 81 games and 63 starts in 1977-78. He averaged 8.5 points, 3.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 24.4 minutes, giving New York another full season of wing depth. The Knicks reached the 1978 playoffs, and McMillian started all six postseason games, averaging 8.8 points and 3.5 rebounds in 22.3 minutes. Across the two regular seasons, New York received 148 games and 123 starts. The scoring role had declined from McMillian's Buffalo years, but the volume of usable NBA minutes is clear.

New York Also Recovered a Compensatory Pick

McMillian became a restricted veteran free agent after the 1977-78 season. Portland signed him in December 1978, and Basketball-Reference records New York receiving a 1979 second-round pick as compensation. The Knicks used that selection at No. 34 on San Diego State forward Kim Goetz. Goetz never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so the downstream draft outcome added no on-court value, but the Knicks still extracted a second asset after two seasons of McMillian production. That preserved value strengthens the acquisition even though the pick itself did not hit.

Buffalo's Return Cannot Be Valued Beyond the Cash Proceeds

The Braves' side is straightforward but difficult to quantify. Buffalo converted McMillian's rights into cash and did not surrender a draft asset or player in addition to those rights. Cash has legitimate franchise value, yet the amount is not disclosed in the reviewed transaction ledgers and there is no basketball asset to trace forward. This review therefore does not assign Buffalo a failing grade simply because New York got useful production, but it also cannot credit an unknown financial return as if it matched 148 games and later pick compensation.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, B+/C. New York receives a B+ because McMillian supplied two full seasons of meaningful minutes, 123 starts and six playoff starts, then generated a 1979 second-round compensation pick when he left for Portland. The pick became Kim Goetz and produced no NBA games, which keeps the return below the highest grades. Buffalo receives a C because it obtained cash in a documented rights sale without taking back a basketball obligation, but the amount is unverified and cannot be compared directly with McMillian's realized production. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and player outcome, with only the cash valuation remaining unknown.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Tom Kropp from Washington on September 13, 1976 for a 1977 third-round pick that became No. 57 Steve Puidokas. Basketball-Reference's Bulls, Bullets and league transaction ledgers all identify the player-for-pick exchange; Chicago's official historical media guide describes Kropp as acquired for future considerations, a broader label that is compatible with the later-identified draft choice. Kropp played 53 regular-season games for Chicago in 1976-77, totaling 480 minutes and 174 points while shooting 48.0 percent from the field, then appeared for two minutes in one playoff game. The Bulls waived him in October 1977. Washington used the pick on Puidokas, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game and instead continued his professional career in Europe. Chicago gets a slight hindsight edge because the acquired player produced one season of real bench minutes while the third-round selection produced no NBA games.
perspectives.analysis:
The Ledgers Resolve the Future Considerations as a Third-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Washington and league transaction pages all record the September 13, 1976 exchange as Tom Kropp to the Bulls for a 1977 third-round draft pick. Chicago's official historical media guide uses the broader phrase "future considerations" for the same acquisition. Those descriptions are not mutually exclusive: the league and team transaction ledgers identify the specific draft asset that later satisfied the consideration. This review therefore keeps the pick as the verified outgoing Chicago asset rather than leaving the return unresolved.

Kropp Gave Chicago One Useful Bench Season

Kropp was a fringe Washington player before the trade, appearing in 25 games but only 72 total minutes for the Bullets in 1975-76. Chicago gave him a much larger role. In 1976-77 he played 53 games and 480 minutes, scoring 174 points while shooting 48.0 percent from the field. His per-game line was modest at 3.3 points, 0.9 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 9.1 minutes, but the Bulls received a full season of usable reserve minutes rather than an empty roster transaction.

His Chicago Tenure Ended After One Season

The return did not develop into a long-term rotation piece. Basketball-Reference credits Kropp with only two minutes in one 1977 playoff appearance, and Chicago's official media guide records the Bulls waiving him on October 17, 1977. RealGM independently lists the waiver and his move to free agency two days later. Kropp never appeared in another NBA regular-season game. That ceiling keeps Chicago's grade below the stronger historical trades where a low draft pick produced multiple seasons or a starter-level role.

Washington Used the Pick on Steve Puidokas

The Bullets kept and exercised the acquired third-rounder. Basketball-Reference's 1977 draft ledger shows Washington selecting Washington State center Steve Puidokas at No. 57 overall, and the Bullets transaction page lists the same selection. Puidokas never recorded an NBA regular-season appearance. Contemporary Washington Post draft coverage described him as a productive four-year college center, but his professional career continued outside the NBA. The pick therefore had legitimate option value on draft night without creating realized NBA production for Washington.

The Margin Should Stay Narrow

Chicago did not acquire a major contributor, and Washington did receive a real draft asset rather than nothing. The distinction is realized outcome: Kropp supplied 53 games and nearly 500 regular-season minutes, while Puidokas supplied no NBA games. That supports a Bulls edge, but not the legacy B+ grade. A third-round pick in this era carried enough uncertainty that one season of reserve play is a modest win rather than a major value event.

Final Verdict

Slight Bulls Edge, B-/C. Chicago receives a B- because Kropp delivered 53 regular-season games and useful bench minutes for the cost of a third-round pick, even though he was gone before the next season began. Washington receives a C because the acquired pick was fully exercised at No. 57 but Steve Puidokas never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high on the transaction and draft outcome. The source wording differs only in specificity: Chicago's media guide says future considerations, while the Basketball-Reference ledgers identify the consideration as the 1977 third-round pick.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Ted McClain from the New York Nets in mid-September 1976 for a 1978 third-round pick that became No. 62 Dave Batton, a 1978 fourth-round pick that became No. 84 Walter Jordan, and cash. RealGM dates the trade September 14, while Basketball-Reference and Denver's official media guide list September 15; this review preserves the canonical September 14 date while documenting that one-day source conflict. McClain became a substantial part of Denver's first NBA team, playing 72 regular-season games, 2,002 minutes and averaging 8.2 points and 4.5 assists, then appearing in all six playoff games. After he left for Buffalo as a veteran free agent, Denver also received a 1978 third-round compensation pick that became Hollis Copeland. New Jersey exercised both original picks, but Batton and Jordan never played a regular-season game for the Nets. Denver gets the clear hindsight edge because McClain supplied a full season and playoff role while the Nets' draft return created no direct New Jersey production.
perspectives.analysis:
The Package Is Verified, With a One-Day Date Conflict

Basketball-Reference's Denver, New York and league transaction ledgers record the Nuggets sending 1978 third- and fourth-round picks to the Nets for Ted McClain on September 15, 1976. Denver's official franchise history also uses September 15 and explicitly adds cash to the package. RealGM dates McClain's acquisition one day earlier, September 14, matching the canonical TradeVerdicts record. This review preserves September 14 as the canonical date but treats the package itself as high confidence: McClain for the two identified picks plus cash.

McClain Became a Major Rotation Guard for Denver

McClain immediately took on a real role in Denver's first NBA season. He appeared in 72 regular-season games and logged 2,002 minutes, averaging 8.2 points, 4.5 assists, 3.2 rebounds and 1.5 steals in 27.8 minutes per game. Denver won 50 games and finished first in the Midwest Division. McClain was not the team's star, but he was a genuine rotation guard on one of the league's better teams rather than a short-term roster flier.

He Also Played Meaningful Postseason Minutes

Denver's season ended in a six-game conference semifinal loss to Portland, and McClain appeared in all six games. He averaged 28.3 minutes, 7.3 points, 4.5 assists and 1.7 steals in the series. Those postseason minutes strengthen the realized return because they show his regular-season role carried into the playoffs. The Nuggets received exactly the kind of immediate veteran depth a contending team could use during the ABA-to-NBA transition.

Denver Recovered a Pick When McClain Left

McClain's Denver tenure lasted one season, but his departure still produced an additional asset. Buffalo signed him as a veteran free agent in October 1977 and sent Denver a 1978 third-round pick as compensation. The Nuggets used that selection at No. 46 on Hollis Copeland. Copeland did not play a regular-season game for Denver and was later an NBA player with New York, so this review does not credit his 93 career games as Nuggets production. Even so, the compensation shows Denver retained some asset value after already receiving a full season from McClain.

New Jersey's Two Picks Produced No Nets Games

The Nets used Denver's original 1978 third-round pick at No. 62 on Dave Batton and the fourth-rounder at No. 84 on Walter Jordan. Both eventually reached the NBA, but neither played a regular-season game for New Jersey. Batton did not debut until 1982 and finished with 58 career games. Jordan spent two seasons outside the NBA before playing 30 games for Cleveland in 1980-81. Those later careers belong to other teams. For this trade, the Nets' draft return created option value but no direct on-court production.

The Cash Helps New Jersey but Is Not Priced

Denver's official media guide explicitly says cash accompanied the two picks. Basketball-Reference's transaction ledgers omit the cash component, and the amount is not identified in the reviewed record. This review therefore recognizes cash as a documented part of the package without assigning it a speculative dollar value. It raises the Nets' return above a pure two-pick miss, but it cannot offset a full season and playoff role from McClain on realized basketball value alone.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, B+/C. Denver receives a B+ because McClain played 72 games, logged more than 2,000 regular-season minutes, contributed throughout the playoffs and later generated a third-round compensation pick when Buffalo signed him. New Jersey receives a C because it obtained two real draft assets plus documented cash, but Dave Batton and Walter Jordan produced no Nets regular-season games and the cash amount is unknown. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes; the only structural uncertainty is whether the transaction should be dated September 14 or September 15, 1976.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia acquired Henry Bibby from the New Orleans Jazz on September 17, 1976 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, New Orleans and league transaction ledgers all identify the move as a cash sale; the amount is not stated in the reviewed record. Bibby became an immediate starting guard for a contender, playing 245 regular-season games across three Philadelphia seasons and starting 200 of them. He averaged 10.2 points and 4.4 assists in 81 games in 1976-77, then played all 19 playoff games as the 76ers reached the NBA Finals. He followed with 82-game seasons in both 1977-78 and 1978-79, including 12.2 points per game in the latter year, and appeared in 38 total playoff games for Philadelphia. New Orleans received cash but no traceable player or draft asset. Philadelphia gets the clear hindsight edge because an unpriced cash acquisition produced three durable seasons, heavy starting minutes and repeated playoff contribution.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Transaction Is a Straight Cash Sale in the Primary Ledgers

Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia, New Orleans and NBA transaction pages all record the September 17, 1976 move as the Jazz selling Henry Bibby to the 76ers. The legacy TradeVerdicts structure is therefore correct: Philadelphia received Bibby and New Orleans received cash. The reviewed transaction ledgers do not identify the amount. This review keeps the financial return unpriced rather than creating a speculative value for the Jazz.

Bibby Immediately Became Philadelphia's Starting Point Guard

The acquisition had an instant basketball effect. Bibby played 81 games in 1976-77, started 80 and averaged 32.6 minutes, 10.2 points, 4.4 assists and 3.4 rebounds. Philadelphia won 50 games and the Atlantic Division. In the playoffs Bibby appeared in all 19 games, averaging 36.4 minutes and 11.1 points as the 76ers won the Eastern Conference before losing the NBA Finals to Portland. That first season alone made the cash purchase a meaningful competitive return.

The Value Continued for Two More Full Seasons

Bibby's Philadelphia tenure was not a one-year peak. He played all 82 games in 1977-78, started all 82 and averaged 30.7 minutes with 10.3 points and 5.6 assists per game. He appeared in all 10 playoff games. In 1978-79 he again played all 82 regular-season games, starting 38 as rookie Maurice Cheeks took over more of the point-guard role. Bibby still averaged 12.2 points, 4.5 assists and 31.0 minutes, then appeared in all nine postseason games. Across the three seasons, Philadelphia received 245 regular-season games and 38 playoff appearances.

The Acquisition Bridged Two Different 76ers Backcourts

Bibby's role also had timing value. In 1976-77 and 1977-78 he handled the primary starting point-guard assignment for teams built around Julius Erving, George McGinnis and Doug Collins. By 1978-79, Cheeks had arrived and immediately started all 82 games, but Bibby remained a high-minute guard rather than becoming disposable depth. That transition allowed Philadelphia to keep veteran ballhandling and scoring while bringing a younger long-term point guard into the lineup.

New Orleans' Return Cannot Be Traced Beyond Cash

The Jazz moved a player who had appeared in only 12 games for them after arriving from New York during the prior season. Receiving cash for a veteran outside the club's long-term core has legitimate financial value, but the amount is not reported in the reviewed source set and there is no incoming player or draft asset to follow. The Jazz therefore receive credit for a documented sale without being treated as if an unknown cash payment matched three seasons of playoff-caliber guard production.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A-/C. Philadelphia receives an A- because Bibby gave the club 245 regular-season games, 200 starts and 38 playoff appearances over three seasons, including a starting role on the 1977 Finals team. New Orleans receives a C because the Jazz obtained cash without taking back another basketball obligation, but the amount is unknown and there is no traceable on-court or draft return. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Bibby's production. The only unquantified element is the cash consideration.

perspectives.summary: Denver's official franchise history and the historical Clippers/Buffalo franchise media guide agree that Denver traded Claude Terry to Buffalo on September 21, 1976 for future considerations. RealGM also records Terry's acquisition by Buffalo in a trade that day. Basketball-Reference preserves a conflicting path, listing Buffalo signing Terry as a free agent on October 21, so this review keeps the official-franchise-history structure but lowers confidence and removes the legacy unsupported claim that Denver received a 1977 draft pick. Terry played 33 regular-season games and 304 minutes for Buffalo, scoring 116 points while averaging 3.5 points in 9.2 minutes per game. Buffalo later sold his player rights to Atlanta on February 1, 1977 for an undisclosed amount. No player, draft selection or other realized basketball asset can be traced from Denver's future considerations. Buffalo therefore gets a narrow hindsight edge for receiving modest bench production and later recovering an unpriced financial return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Official Franchise Histories Say Terry Went to Buffalo for Future Considerations

Denver's official franchise history lists the September 21, 1976 transaction as Claude Terry to Buffalo for future considerations. The historical Clippers media guide, which preserves the Buffalo Braves' transaction history, independently records the same date and structure. RealGM likewise lists Buffalo acquiring Terry from Denver in a trade on September 21. Those records resolve the core package more clearly than the legacy archive entry. This review therefore removes the unsupported 1977 draft-pick language and records Denver's return only as future considerations whose eventual form remains unresolved.

Basketball-Reference Preserves a Conflicting Transaction Path

Basketball-Reference does not list the September 21 trade on the Denver, Buffalo or league transaction ledgers. Its Buffalo page instead says the Braves signed Terry as a free agent on October 21, 1976. That conflict cannot simply be ignored. Two official franchise histories and RealGM agree on the September 21 trade, so TradeVerdicts keeps that date and structure as the canonical interpretation, but confidence is medium rather than high. The disagreement also reinforces why this review should not invent a draft pick or pretend the future consideration has been fully traced.

Terry Gave Buffalo 33 Games of Bench Minutes

Terry's Buffalo stint was modest but real. Basketball-Reference credits him with 33 games, 304 minutes and 116 points for the 1976-77 Braves. He averaged 9.2 minutes and 3.5 points per game while adding 28 rebounds, 33 assists and 11 steals. That is not starter-level or long-term value, but it is enough to distinguish Buffalo's return from an empty roster transaction. Terry provided several months of usable reserve minutes before the club moved his rights again.

Buffalo Recovered Another Financial Return When Terry Left

The historical Buffalo/Clippers record says the Braves sold Terry to Atlanta on February 1, 1977. Basketball-Reference also records Buffalo selling Terry's player rights to the Hawks on that date. The amount is not identified in the reviewed sources, so this review does not assign a speculative dollar value. Still, Buffalo received 33 games from Terry and then converted his rights into another financial return. That downstream sale adds a little value to the acquisition even though the cash cannot be compared precisely with a player or draft asset.

Denver's Future Consideration Cannot Be Traced

The reviewed records do not identify a player, draft pick or other basketball asset that Denver ultimately received from the future-considerations clause. The legacy archive entry's 1977 draft-pick language is therefore removed rather than carried forward as an unresolved guess. Denver still receives credit for a documented consideration in the official franchise histories, but without a traceable realization there is no basis to grade the Nuggets as though they received a usable draft asset.

Final Verdict

Slight Braves Edge, C+/C. Buffalo receives a C+ because Terry delivered 33 regular-season games and 304 minutes, then generated another unpriced financial return when his rights were sold to Atlanta. Denver receives a C because the official franchise histories document future considerations, but the reviewed record does not reveal what those considerations became. The edge stays narrow because Terry's role was small and the downstream cash amount is unknown. Confidence is medium because Basketball-Reference conflicts with the September 21 trade structure preserved by the two franchise histories and RealGM.
