perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Golden State's NBA rights to Willie Wise on September 24, 1976 for a 1977 fourth-round draft pick. Denver's own franchise history and Basketball-Reference show Wise signing with the Nuggets three days earlier, on September 21; Pro Sports Transactions then traces the rights settlement to Golden State and identifies the compensation pick as No. 87 in the 1977 draft. Golden State used that selection on Leartha Scott, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Wise, by contrast, played 75 games for Denver in 1976-77, totaling 1,403 minutes and averaging 8.2 points, 3.4 rebounds and 1.9 assists. He also appeared in all six of Denver's playoff games before being included with Paul Silas and Marvin Webster in the May 1977 trade that brought Tom Burleson, Bob Wilkerson and a second-round pick from Seattle. Denver gets the clear hindsight edge because the rights acquisition produced a full season of rotation value while Golden State's fourth-round return produced no NBA games.
perspectives.analysis:
The Rights Settlement Followed Denver's Signing of Wise

Denver's official franchise history and Basketball-Reference both record the Nuggets signing Willie Wise as a free agent on September 21, 1976. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the complementary draft-rights transaction three days later: Golden State sent Wise's NBA rights to Denver for a 1977 fourth-round pick. That sequence is plausible because Wise had originally been drafted by the Warriors before spending his prime in the ABA. This review therefore treats September 21 as the player signing and September 24 as the separate rights settlement rather than collapsing the two dates into one transaction.

The Fourth-Round Pick Became No. 87 Leartha Scott

The draft chain is specific. Pro Sports Transactions identifies Denver's outgoing 1977 fourth-rounder as the selection Golden State eventually used at No. 87. Basketball-Reference's 1977 draft ledger and Warriors draft history confirm Leartha Scott at that exact slot. Scott never recorded an NBA regular-season appearance. Golden State did receive and exercise a real draft asset, so the return was not empty at the transaction stage, but its realized NBA production was zero.

Wise Became a Useful Denver Rotation Forward

Wise played 75 regular-season games in Denver's first NBA season, totaling 1,403 minutes and 616 points. He averaged 18.7 minutes, 8.2 points, 3.4 rebounds and 1.9 assists while shooting 46.2 percent from the field. Denver won 50 games and finished first in the Midwest Division. Wise was no longer the All-ABA star he had been earlier in the decade, but the Nuggets received a full season of reliable rotation minutes for the price of a fourth-round pick.

The Value Carried Into the Playoffs

Wise appeared in all six games of Denver's 1977 playoff series against Portland. He averaged 17.7 minutes, 7.5 points and 4.7 rebounds in the postseason. Those are modest numbers, but they show that his regular-season role survived into a playoff rotation rather than disappearing when the games became more important. That gives Denver a stronger realized return than a simple end-of-bench rights acquisition.

Wise Also Remained Part of Denver's Trade Inventory

On May 24, 1977, Denver sent Wise, Paul Silas and Marvin Webster to Seattle for Tom Burleson, Bob Wilkerson and a 1977 second-round pick. Because Wise was only one part of a three-player package, this review does not assign the entire Seattle return to him. The later deal still demonstrates that Wise retained transaction utility after his Denver season. Golden State's No. 87 pick did not create a comparable downstream NBA asset.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, B/C. Denver receives a B because Wise supplied 75 regular-season games, meaningful rotation minutes and six playoff appearances before remaining part of a larger trade package. Golden State receives a C because the Warriors converted Wise's NBA rights into a legitimate fourth-round pick and exercised it at No. 87, but Leartha Scott never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is medium because the September 24 rights settlement is documented most specifically by the draft-pick transaction chain, while Denver and Basketball-Reference separately record Wise's September 21 free-agent signing.

Denver's official franchise history and Basketball-Reference both record the Nuggets signing Willie Wise as a free agent on September 21, 1976. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the complementary draft-rights transaction three days later: Golden State sent Wise's NBA rights to Denver for a 1977 fourth-round pick. That sequence is plausible because Wise had originally been drafted by the Warriors before spending his prime in the ABA. This review therefore treats September 21 as the player signing and September 24 as the separate rights settlement rather than collapsing the two dates into one transaction.

The Fourth-Round Pick Became No. 87 Leartha Scott

The draft chain is specific. Pro Sports Transactions identifies Denver's outgoing 1977 fourth-rounder as the selection Golden State eventually used at No. 87. Basketball-Reference's 1977 draft ledger and Warriors draft history confirm Leartha Scott at that exact slot. Scott never recorded an NBA regular-season appearance. Golden State did receive and exercise a real draft asset, so the return was not empty at the transaction stage, but its realized NBA production was zero.

Wise Became a Useful Denver Rotation Forward

Wise played 75 regular-season games in Denver's first NBA season, totaling 1,403 minutes and 616 points. He averaged 18.7 minutes, 8.2 points, 3.4 rebounds and 1.9 assists while shooting 46.2 percent from the field. Denver won 50 games and finished first in the Midwest Division. Wise was no longer the All-ABA star he had been earlier in the decade, but the Nuggets received a full season of reliable rotation minutes for the price of a fourth-round pick.

The Value Carried Into the Playoffs

Wise appeared in all six games of Denver's 1977 playoff series against Portland. He averaged 17.7 minutes, 7.5 points and 4.7 rebounds in the postseason. Those are modest numbers, but they show that his regular-season role survived into a playoff rotation rather than disappearing when the games became more important. That gives Denver a stronger realized return than a simple end-of-bench rights acquisition.

Wise Also Remained Part of Denver's Trade Inventory

On May 24, 1977, Denver sent Wise, Paul Silas and Marvin Webster to Seattle for Tom Burleson, Bob Wilkerson and a 1977 second-round pick. Because Wise was only one part of a three-player package, this review does not assign the entire Seattle return to him. The later deal still demonstrates that Wise retained transaction utility after his Denver season. Golden State's No. 87 pick did not create a comparable downstream NBA asset.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, B/C. Denver receives a B because Wise supplied 75 regular-season games, meaningful rotation minutes and six playoff appearances before remaining part of a larger trade package. Golden State receives a C because the Warriors converted Wise's NBA rights into a legitimate fourth-round pick and exercised it at No. 87, but Leartha Scott never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is medium because the September 24 rights settlement is documented most specifically by the draft-pick transaction chain, while Denver and Basketball-Reference separately record Wise's September 21 free-agent signing.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Acquired Randy Denton for a Later Pick

In October 1976, the Atlanta Hawks received big man Randy Denton from New York. The Knicks obtained a 1977 second-round selection later associated with the No. 26 position and Glen Gondrezick. Atlanta chose to add a current frontcourt player before the season, while New York accepted an opportunity to select a younger prospect months later. Denton's existing professional background made him a more immediate option than a future pick, but his career beforehand did not count as new Hawks production. The agreed compensation was one draft right rather than a package of first-round capital.

Denton Was a Roster Option Rather Than a Cornerstone

Denton offered size and prior experience that Atlanta could evaluate in practices and games as it managed a changing lineup. He wasn't acquired as the clear face of the franchise, and his future service with the Hawks needed to be earned after the transaction date. The practical benefit was having an available center or forward instead of hoping a future second-round prospect would become playable. New York no longer had that immediate player option but was free to find a better fit in the next draft. Neither return guaranteed long-term NBA starting minutes.

The Knicks' Second Turned Into a Specific Prospect Opportunity

New York's incoming 1977 selection is tracked at No. 26 in historical draft records, associated with Glen Gondrezick. The position gave the Knicks an identifiable opportunity near the beginning of the second round rather than an uncertain later-round claim. His eventual career must still be traced through which franchise actually held his rights and put him on the floor, because the selected name alone doesn't guarantee his New York service. The team paid for this chance by surrendering Denton. A draft position with practical scouting value could outlast the usefulness of a marginal current veteran.

A Modest Knicks Edge Reflects Future Flexibility

The Knicks converted a supporting big man into a second-round selection that offered another path to a useful roster player. Atlanta acquired Denton as a near-term option, but did not secure a premium future asset through the trade. The difference is modest: the draft right had no guaranteed NBA payoff, and Atlanta's interest in immediate frontcourt depth was reasonable. The return is best graded through what was actually transferred and when, not by giving either team unrelated later franchise achievements. New York receives a narrow preference for preserving developmental flexibility.

Final Verdict

Slight Knicks Edge. Atlanta Hawks earns C+; New York Knicks earns B-. The Knicks converted a supporting big man into a second-round selection that offered another path to a useful roster player. Atlanta acquired Denton as a near-term option, but did not secure a premium future asset through the trade. perspectives.summary: Chicago traded Allen Murphy to the Los Angeles Lakers on October 4, 1976 for a future draft pick. Basketball-Reference's Bulls, Lakers and league transaction ledgers all agree on that structure, and the Lakers' official media guide independently lists the same transaction. None of the reviewed authoritative records identifies the pick's year, round or eventual player, so this review removes the legacy placeholder language and leaves the draft outcome unresolved. Murphy's Los Angeles return was extremely small: he appeared in two regular-season games for 18 total minutes, scoring five points, and the Lakers waived him on November 2, less than a month after the trade. Chicago unquestionably received a real future-pick asset, but no traceable selection or player can be credited to the Bulls from the current evidence. With only two Lakers games on one side and an unidentified draft outcome on the other, the most defensible hindsight result is an even, low-value trade rather than forcing a directional winner.
perspectives.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree on Murphy for a Future Draft Pick

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Los Angeles and NBA transaction pages all record the October 4, 1976 exchange the same way: the Bulls sent Allen Murphy to the Lakers for a future draft pick. Bill Sharman's Lakers executive record and Jon Kovler's Chicago record repeat that package, while the Lakers' official all-time transaction history independently confirms the future-pick wording. The legacy archive entry is therefore directionally correct, but its question-mark placeholders can be replaced with a cleaner description of what the record actually establishes.

The Pick's Year and Outcome Remain Unresolved

The authoritative transaction sources do not identify a year, round, protection condition or eventual draftee for the future pick. Unlike many surrounding deals, Basketball-Reference does not attach a later selection to this transaction. The reviewed draft-trade sources also do not provide a supported player chain for the Murphy pick. That absence does not prove the pick was cancelled or never exercised. This review therefore records a future draft pick with an unresolved outcome and does not invent a year or player for Chicago.

Murphy Played Only Two Games for the Lakers

Los Angeles received almost no on-court return. Basketball-Reference credits Murphy with two games and 18 total minutes for the 1976-77 Lakers. He scored five points, collected four rebounds and did not record an assist. Those appearances were his only NBA games that season and his only games for Los Angeles. The Lakers had acquired a young guard with ABA experience, but he never established a role in Jerry West's rotation.

Los Angeles Waived Him Less Than a Month Later

The Lakers' transaction ledger and official franchise history both record Murphy being waived on November 2, 1976. That ended his Los Angeles tenure just 29 days after the trade. Murphy did not create a later Lakers trade return or compensation asset. His two games and 18 minutes therefore represent the complete realized basketball value Los Angeles received from the original transaction.

Chicago's Asset Has Option Value but No Traceable Realization

A future draft pick carried real value even when its exact slot was not known on trade day, so Chicago cannot be graded as though it received nothing. The problem is retrospective attribution: without a verified year, round or selected player, TradeVerdicts cannot credit the Bulls with production that may belong to an unrelated pick. The responsible grade recognizes the existence of the asset while stopping short of assigning an invented downstream outcome.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C/C. Chicago receives a C because the Bulls converted Murphy into a legitimate future draft asset, but the reviewed record does not establish what that pick became. Los Angeles also receives a C because Murphy produced only two games and 18 minutes before being waived less than a month after the trade. Neither side generated enough verified realized value to justify a directional edge. Confidence is high on the October 4 package and Murphy's brief Lakers stint but medium on the complete pick chain, so the record's overall confidence is medium.

perspectives.summary: This October 5, 1976 Portland-New Orleans record is not a supported transaction. The legacy archive record says Portland reacquired Sidney Wicks from the Jazz for cash and then credits him with the 1976-77 championship season, but the authoritative Portland, Boston and NBA transaction ledgers show Wicks remaining with Portland through the 1975-76 season before Portland sold his player rights to Boston on October 12, 1976. Wicks then played all 82 regular-season games for the Celtics in 1976-77, not for Portland. No reviewed source supports an October 5 Portland-New Orleans Wicks transaction, and the record is superseded by the existing canonical October 12 Portland-Boston record nba-trade-19761012-63d71dffa22a. No independent winner or grades are assigned because keeping this record active would invent a transaction and double-count Wicks's 1976 transfer.
perspectives.analysis:
The October 5 Portland-New Orleans Transaction Is Unsupported

The legacy archive entry claims Portland acquired Sidney Wicks from the New Orleans Jazz on October 5, 1976 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Portland transaction ledger contains no such move. The league-wide 1976-77 transaction ledger also has no Portland-New Orleans Wicks transaction on October 5. Instead, both sources record Portland selling Wicks's player rights to the Boston Celtics on October 12. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Red Auerbach's Boston executive record preserve that same October 12 transaction.

Wicks Was a Portland Player Before the Boston Sale

The legacy analysis says Portland "reacquired" Wicks from New Orleans one month earlier, but the career record makes that impossible. Wicks played the first five seasons of his NBA career with Portland, including 79 games for the Trail Blazers in 1975-76. There is no intervening Jazz season or New Orleans roster stint to reacquire him from. The false October 5 record appears to have inverted or contaminated a transaction relationship rather than preserving a real economic event.

The 1976-77 Production Belongs to Boston

The legacy archive entry compounds the transaction error by crediting Wicks with 79 starts and 15.1 points per game for Portland's 1976-77 championship team. Basketball-Reference shows Wicks playing all 82 regular-season games for Boston that season, averaging 15.1 points and 10.0 rebounds in 32.2 minutes. He also appeared in all nine Celtics playoff games. Portland won the 1977 championship without Wicks. Leaving the false record active would therefore assign another team's production to Portland.

The Real Transaction Already Exists in TradeVerdicts

TradeVerdicts already contains canonical record nba-trade-19761012-63d71dffa22a, dated October 12, 1976, between Boston and Portland. That record correctly represents Boston acquiring Wicks's player rights from the Trail Blazers. The October 5 Portland-New Orleans import adds no distinct transaction, no distinct asset chain and no valid player movement. Retaining it as an active candidate would create duplicate Wicks transfer history and distort team-pair counts.

Why the Bad Import Should Be Preserved but Superseded

The record still has provenance value because it documents how the original Portland batch introduced the error. Deleting it outright would make the historical cleanup harder to audit later. The superseded entry is retained for provenance but excluded from graded results. That preserves the source history without allowing the false Portland-New Orleans transaction to surface as an independent trade.

Final Resolution

Record Superseded. Canonical trade: nba-trade-19761012-63d71dffa22a. No winner and no grades are assigned. Confidence is high because the Portland, Boston and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 12 rights sale, the executive records agree, and Wicks's 1976-77 Boston statistics directly contradict the legacy Portland championship claim. This review therefore removes this October 5 record from the active source-backed candidate path while preserving it as provenance for the original import error.

summary: Boston acquired Sidney Wicks's player rights from Portland on October 12, 1976 for cash. Basketball-Reference's Portland, Boston and league transaction ledgers all identify the move as a rights sale, while Harry Glickman and Red Auerbach's executive records preserve the same transaction. The reviewed sources do not state the cash amount. Wicks gave Boston two full seasons of substantial frontcourt production: 163 regular-season games, 5,055 minutes, 2,321 points and 1,497 rebounds. He averaged 15.1 points and 10.0 rebounds in 82 games in 1976-77, then 13.4 points and 8.3 rebounds in 81 games in 1977-78. He also appeared in all nine of Boston's 1977 playoff games. In August 1978, Wicks remained one piece of the four-player package Boston sent to San Diego in the larger Tiny Archibald trade. Portland received an unpriced cash return. Boston gets the clear hindsight edge because the cash purchase produced two durable seasons plus continued trade utility.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree on an October 12 Rights Sale

Basketball-Reference's Portland, Boston and NBA transaction pages all record the same October 12, 1976 move: Portland sold the player rights to Sidney Wicks to the Celtics. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Red Auerbach's Boston record independently preserve that structure. This review therefore treats the transaction as Wicks's rights for cash and does not repeat the false October 5 Portland-New Orleans record that has now been superseded. The cash amount is not identified in the reviewed ledgers.

Wicks Immediately Became a Major Boston Frontcourt Piece

Wicks played all 82 regular-season games for Boston in 1976-77 and logged 2,642 minutes. He averaged 15.1 points, 10.0 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 32.2 minutes per game while shooting 45.8 percent from the field. That was not fringe production from an aging name. Wicks was one of Boston's highest-minute frontcourt players and delivered a full season of double-figure scoring and double-figure rebounding after the cash acquisition.

The First Season Also Carried Into the Playoffs

Boston reached the 1977 postseason and Wicks appeared in all nine playoff games. He averaged 29.0 minutes, 13.1 points and 9.2 rebounds while shooting 51.9 percent from the field. The Celtics beat San Antonio in the opening round before losing a seven-game conference semifinal to Philadelphia. Wicks's role therefore survived into the postseason rather than disappearing when the rotation tightened.

The Value Continued for a Second Full Season

Wicks remained a substantial part of Boston's 1977-78 team even as the Celtics fell out of the playoffs. He played 81 games and another 2,413 minutes, averaging 13.4 points, 8.3 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 29.8 minutes. Across the two Boston seasons, the rights purchase produced 163 regular-season games, 5,055 minutes, 2,321 points and 1,497 rebounds. That volume is enough to make the acquisition materially better than a short-term cash flier.

perspectives.summary: Denver traded Rudy Hackett to the New York Nets on October 18, 1976 for a future draft pick. Basketball-Reference's Denver, New York and league transaction ledgers agree on that structure, while Carl Scheer's and Roy Boe's executive records preserve the same exchange. The reviewed sources do not identify the year, round or eventual player attached to the future pick, so this review leaves the draft asset unresolved rather than inventing an outcome. Hackett played only one regular-season game for New York, logging eight minutes and two points, before the Nets waived him on October 29. Indiana signed him in November, confirming that New York received no downstream compensation when his brief tenure ended. Denver therefore gets the modest hindsight edge because it converted a September free-agent signing into draft consideration, while the Nets received only one game of realized value.
perspectives.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree on Hackett for a Future Draft Pick

Basketball-Reference's Denver Nuggets, New York Nets and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same October 18, 1976 exchange: Denver sent Rudy Hackett to New York for a future draft pick. Carl Scheer's executive transaction record and Roy Boe's Nets record independently preserve that structure. RealGM also lists Hackett as a New York trade acquisition on the same date. No reviewed source adds cash or a second player to the package.

The Draft Pick Cannot Be Traced Responsibly

The transaction ledgers stop at the phrase "future draft pick." They do not identify a year, round, protection, overall selection or player outcome. Pro Sports Transactions likewise lists the pick as unknown. This review therefore preserves the draft asset without assigning it to a later Denver selection. That matters because a hindsight archive should not turn an unidentified future consideration into a named player simply because Denver later owned other picks.

Hackett Played One Game for the Nets

Hackett's New York tenure was extremely short. Basketball-Reference credits him with one Nets regular-season appearance in 1976-77: eight minutes, two points and three rebounds. The Nets waived him on October 29, only eleven days after the trade. That gives New York a measurable basketball return, but it is about as small as an acquired player's realized value can be.

New York Did Not Preserve a Downstream Asset

After the waiver, Hackett became a free agent and signed with Indiana in November. The Pacers used him in five games before waiving him in December. Because New York received no player, pick or compensation when Hackett left, none of his later Indiana activity belongs to the Nets side of this trade. New York's attributable return ends with the single game he played for the franchise.

Denver Turned a Short-Term Signing Into Draft Consideration

RealGM records Denver signing Hackett in September 1976 before moving him roughly six weeks later. The Nuggets therefore converted a recent free-agent addition into a future draft asset without giving up another documented basketball piece in this transaction. The unidentified pick keeps the return from earning a strong grade, because its eventual use cannot be verified, but the exchange still left Denver with more traceable asset value than New York received on the court.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, C+/D+. Denver receives a C+ because it converted Hackett into a future draft pick, but the pick's year, round and eventual outcome remain unresolved in the reviewed sources. New York receives a D+ because Hackett appeared in only one game before being waived and generated no downstream return. The deal is minor rather than disastrous for the Nets, yet one eight-minute appearance is too little to justify an average grade. Confidence is high on the transaction and Hackett's one-game tenure, but medium on the complete asset chain because the future pick cannot be identified.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Buffalo acquired Moses Malone from Portland on October 18, 1976 for a 1978 first-round pick that became No. 3 Rick Robey. Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Portland and league ledgers agree on the pick-for-Malone structure; Pro Sports Transactions additionally reports $232,000 cash, so this review keeps the cash as secondary-source evidence rather than presenting it as primary-ledger fact. Malone played only two games for Buffalo before the Braves traded him to Houston six days later for two first-round picks. One became part of Buffalo's George Johnson acquisition and the other later helped acquire Tiny Archibald. Portland also extracted major downstream value: the incoming No. 3 pick was packaged with Johnny Davis to move up to No. 1 in 1978, where the Blazers selected Mychal Thompson, who played 551 games for Portland. Both teams converted the transaction into substantial later value, with Portland's long Thompson tenure giving the Blazers the slight hindsight edge.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Verify Malone for the 1978 First-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Portland and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same October 18, 1976 exchange: the Braves sent their 1978 first-round pick to Portland for Moses Malone. The pick later landed at No. 3 and became Rick Robey. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Bob MacKinnon's Buffalo record preserve the same structure. Those primary ledgers do not list cash. Pro Sports Transactions reports an additional $232,000 payment from Buffalo, so this review records that amount as secondary-source evidence without treating it as part of the primary-ledger consensus.

Buffalo Held Malone for Only Six Days

Malone's direct Buffalo production was almost nonexistent. Basketball-Reference credits him with two Braves games and six total minutes before the next transaction. That small sample should not be mistaken for the value Buffalo actually captured, because the Braves did not waive him or lose him for nothing. On October 24, they traded Malone to Houston for a 1977 first-round pick and a 1978 first-round pick. The proper hindsight chain therefore follows those two assets rather than grading Buffalo only on Malone's two appearances.

The First Houston Pick Became George Johnson

Buffalo moved the 1977 first-rounder to Golden State in January 1977 for George Johnson. Johnson immediately became a starting center for the Braves, appearing in 39 games with 39 starts and averaging 10.3 rebounds while providing rim protection. Golden State ultimately used the pick on Wesley Cox. For Buffalo, Johnson is the realized return attributable to that branch of the Malone resale rather than Cox's later career.

The Second Houston Pick Stayed Alive in the Tiny Archibald Package

The 1978 first-rounder acquired from Houston was the pick that later became No. 4 Micheal Ray Richardson. Buffalo did not simply use that selection. In September 1977 the Braves sent George Johnson, that 1978 first and their 1979 first-round pick to the Nets for Tiny Archibald. Because the Archibald trade contained three outgoing assets, this review does not credit the entire Archibald return to the Houston pick alone. It does show that the second first-rounder retained substantial trade utility long after Buffalo's six-day ownership of Malone ended.

Portland Turned the No. 3 Pick Into the No. 1 Pick

Portland's incoming 1978 first-rounder became even more valuable before draft night. On June 8, 1978, the Trail Blazers sent Johnny Davis and the No. 3 pick that became Rick Robey to Indiana for the No. 1 pick. Portland used that selection on Mychal Thompson. The original Buffalo pick was therefore not merely a theoretical top-three asset; it was a central component in Portland's move to the first overall selection.

Mychal Thompson Supplied Seven Seasons of Portland Value

Thompson played 551 regular-season games for Portland from 1978-79 through 1985-86, totaling 18,913 minutes, 9,215 points and 4,878 rebounds. He missed 1979-80 with a leg injury but otherwise became a long-term starting-caliber frontcourt piece. Portland later included Thompson with Larry Krystkowiak in the 1986 trade for Steve Johnson. Johnny Davis was also required in the 1978 pick swap, so this review does not pretend the entire Thompson career came from the Malone trade alone. Still, the No. 3 pick was indispensable to reaching No. 1 and generated the strongest durable player outcome in this asset tree.

Final Verdict

Slight Blazers Edge, A+/A. Portland receives an A+ because the first-round pick obtained for Malone became the key draft asset in the move from No. 3 to No. 1, producing 551 Mychal Thompson games and seven seasons of frontcourt value. Buffalo receives an A because acquiring Malone for one future first and reported cash created an immediate asset arbitrage: six days later the Braves turned him into two first-rounders, one of which became George Johnson and the other remained part of the later Tiny Archibald package. Buffalo's handling of Malone after October 18 belongs to the downstream chain rather than erasing the quality of the acquisition. Confidence is high on the pick-for-Malone structure and all traced basketball assets; the reported $232,000 cash remains secondary-source-only.

analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Verify Malone for the 1978 First-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Portland and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same October 18, 1976 exchange: the Braves sent their 1978 first-round pick to Portland for Moses Malone. The pick later landed at No. 3 and became Rick Robey. Harry Glickman's Portland executive record and Bob MacKinnon's Buffalo record preserve the same structure. Those primary ledgers do not list cash. Pro Sports Transactions reports an additional $232,000 payment from Buffalo, so this review records that amount as secondary-source evidence without treating it as part of the primary-ledger consensus.

Buffalo Held Malone for Only Six Days

Malone's direct Buffalo production was almost nonexistent. Basketball-Reference credits him with two Braves games and six total minutes before the next transaction. That small sample should not be mistaken for the value Buffalo actually captured, because the Braves did not waive him or lose him for nothing. On October 24, they traded Malone to Houston for a 1977 first-round pick and a 1978 first-round pick. The proper hindsight chain therefore follows those two assets rather than grading Buffalo only on Malone's two appearances.

The First Houston Pick Became George Johnson

Buffalo moved the 1977 first-rounder to Golden State in January 1977 for George Johnson. Johnson immediately became a starting center for the Braves, appearing in 39 games with 39 starts and averaging 10.3 rebounds while providing rim protection. Golden State ultimately used the pick on Wesley Cox. For Buffalo, Johnson is the realized return attributable to that branch of the Malone resale rather than Cox's later career.

The Second Houston Pick Stayed Alive in the Tiny Archibald Package

The 1978 first-rounder acquired from Houston was the pick that later became No. 4 Micheal Ray Richardson. Buffalo did not simply use that selection. In September 1977 the Braves sent George Johnson, that 1978 first and their 1979 first-round pick to the Nets for Tiny Archibald. Because the Archibald trade contained three outgoing assets, this review does not credit the entire Archibald return to the Houston pick alone. It does show that the second first-rounder retained substantial trade utility long after Buffalo's six-day ownership of Malone ended.

Portland Turned the No. 3 Pick Into the No. 1 Pick

Portland's incoming 1978 first-rounder became even more valuable before draft night. On June 8, 1978, the Trail Blazers sent Johnny Davis and the No. 3 pick that became Rick Robey to Indiana for the No. 1 pick. Portland used that selection on Mychal Thompson. The original Buffalo pick was therefore not merely a theoretical top-three asset; it was a central component in Portland's move to the first overall selection.

Mychal Thompson Supplied Seven Seasons of Portland Value

Thompson played 551 regular-season games for Portland from 1978-79 through 1985-86, totaling 18,913 minutes, 9,215 points and 4,878 rebounds. He missed 1979-80 with a leg injury but otherwise became a long-term starting-caliber frontcourt piece. Portland later included Thompson with Larry Krystkowiak in the 1986 trade for Steve Johnson. Johnny Davis was also required in the 1978 pick swap, so this review does not pretend the entire Thompson career came from the Malone trade alone. Still, the No. 3 pick was indispensable to reaching No. 1 and generated the strongest durable player outcome in this asset tree.

Final Verdict

Slight Blazers Edge, A+/A. Portland receives an A+ because the first-round pick obtained for Malone became the key draft asset in the move from No. 3 to No. 1, producing 551 Mychal Thompson games and seven seasons of frontcourt value. Buffalo receives an A because acquiring Malone for one future first and reported cash created an immediate asset arbitrage: six days later the Braves turned him into two first-rounders, one of which became George Johnson and the other remained part of the later Tiny Archibald package. Buffalo's handling of Malone after October 18 belongs to the downstream chain rather than erasing the quality of the acquisition. Confidence is high on the pick-for-Malone structure and all traced basketball assets; the reported $232,000 cash remains secondary-source-only.

perspectives.summary: Philadelphia acquired Julius Erving's player rights from the New York Nets on October 20, 1976 in a cash sale. Basketball-Reference's Nets, 76ers and league transaction ledgers agree on the cash-only structure but do not state an amount. Secondary reports differ on the financial figure, so this review records the commonly cited $3 million transaction amount as reported rather than primary-ledger fact. The basketball outcome is unambiguous: Erving spent all 11 of his NBA seasons with Philadelphia, playing 836 regular-season games, winning the 1981 NBA MVP, reaching the Finals in his first season, and helping the 76ers win the 1983 championship. New York received no player or draft asset to trace forward from the sale. The business circumstances explain why the Nets needed liquidity after the ABA-NBA merger, but they do not balance the basketball return. Philadelphia receives the maximum hindsight grade; New York receives an F for surrendering a prime franchise superstar for cash alone.
perspectives.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Confirm a Cash Sale

Basketball-Reference's New York Nets, Philadelphia 76ers and NBA transaction ledgers all agree on the October 20, 1976 transaction: New York sold the player rights to Julius Erving to Philadelphia. Roy Boe's executive record preserves the same structure. No player or draft pick is listed going back to the Nets. This review therefore treats the exchange as Erving for cash rather than importing a basketball asset that the primary ledgers do not support.

The Cash Amount Is Reported Differently Across Secondary Sources

The primary transaction ledgers do not publish a dollar figure. Pro Sports Transactions lists a reported $3 million cash payment, while contemporary and retrospective wire reports sometimes describe larger figures when discussing the broader acquisition and contract package. Those references are not necessarily measuring the same thing. This review keeps the asset label at reported $3 million cash with an explicit secondary-source qualifier and does not present the amount as a settled primary-source fact. The grade does not depend on choosing among those financial reports because the Nets received no traceable player or draft asset.

Philadelphia Got Eleven Seasons of Elite Production

Erving's Philadelphia tenure is one of the clearest realized-value outcomes in the archive. Basketball-Reference credits him with 836 regular-season games for the 76ers, totaling 28,677 minutes, 18,364 points, 5,601 rebounds, 3,224 assists, 1,508 steals and 1,293 blocks. He averaged 22.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 3.9 assists over those eleven seasons. This was not a short peak followed by replacement-level years; Philadelphia acquired a franchise centerpiece who remained productive through the end of his NBA career.

Erving Immediately Took Philadelphia to the Finals

The return started in year one. Erving played all 82 regular-season games in 1976-77 and scored 1,770 points before appearing in 19 playoff games and scoring 518 more. Philadelphia reached the NBA Finals in his first season. The 76ers did not win that series, but the immediate Finals run shows how quickly the acquisition changed the team's ceiling and eliminates any need to rely only on later-career hindsight.

The 1981 MVP and 1983 Championship Define the Peak

Erving's Philadelphia tenure eventually produced the league's highest individual honor and the franchise's defining team result of the era. He won the 1980-81 NBA Most Valuable Player award after averaging 24.6 points, 8.0 rebounds and 4.4 assists over 82 games. Two seasons later he remained a major scorer and all-around contributor on the 1982-83 championship team. Philadelphia therefore received both sustained star production and the kind of peak outcomes that justify an A+ trade grade.

New York Received No Traceable Basketball Asset

The Nets' side is different from a normal star trade because there is no pick tree or player package to evaluate. The cash consideration had real business value, especially in the financially difficult period immediately after the ABA-NBA merger, but it did not create a traceable on-court asset in this transaction. New York went from controlling the rights to a 26-year-old superstar to receiving financial consideration only. Business context can explain the decision without converting the basketball outcome into a balanced exchange.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/F. Philadelphia receives an A+ because Erving delivered eleven NBA seasons, 836 regular-season games, an MVP award, an immediate Finals run and a central role on the 1983 championship team without costing the 76ers a player or draft pick. New York receives an F because the Nets surrendered a prime franchise superstar for cash and received no basketball asset that can be traced into future value. The reported dollar amount varies by secondary source and is not needed to reach the hindsight verdict. Confidence is high on the transaction structure, Erving's Philadelphia production and the absence of an incoming player or pick for New York.

summary: Boston, Denver and Detroit completed a three-team trade on October 20, 1976: the Celtics sent Paul Silas to the Nuggets, Denver sent Ralph Simpson to the Pistons, and Detroit sent Curtis Rowe to Boston. Basketball-Reference's team, league and executive ledgers agree on that exact routing, which corrects the incomplete legacy asset ledger that omitted Simpson. Rowe gave Boston 183 regular-season games over three seasons plus nine playoff starts in 1977. Silas played 81 games for Denver, averaging 7.5 rebounds, before becoming part of a larger May 1977 package sent to Seattle. Simpson gave Detroit 109 games across two seasons, then the Pistons traded him back to Denver for Jim Price and a 1979 first-round pick that became No. 15 Phil Hubbard. Hubbard played 196 games for Detroit before a later trade. Detroit therefore created the strongest downstream value, while all three teams received legitimate NBA rotation production.

Basketball-Reference's team, league and executive ledgers agree on that exact routing, which corrects the incomplete legacy asset ledger that omitted Simpson. boston-celtics.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Lock the Three-Team Routing

Basketball-Reference's Boston, Denver, Detroit and NBA transaction ledgers all preserve the same October 20, 1976 structure. Boston sent Paul Silas to Denver. Denver sent Ralph Simpson to Detroit. Detroit sent Curtis Rowe to Boston. Red Auerbach's, Carl Scheer's and Oscar Feldman's executive records repeat that routing. This review therefore repairs the canonical asset ledger by adding Simpson as Denver's outgoing asset and Detroit's incoming asset instead of leaving Detroit with an empty return.

Curtis Rowe Gave Boston Three Seasons of Real Value

Rowe became an immediate Celtics rotation piece. He played 79 games in 1976-77, totaling 2,190 minutes, 800 points and 563 rebounds. Boston reached the playoffs, and Rowe started all nine postseason games, including the seven-game conference semifinal against Philadelphia. He then played 51 games in 1977-78 and 53 more in 1978-79. Across the three Boston seasons, Rowe appeared in 183 regular-season games and supplied more than 1,400 points and 1,000 rebounds. The return was not star-level, but it was far stronger than the old C-minus grade implied.

Paul Silas Helped Denver Immediately

Silas played 81 games for the Nuggets in 1976-77 and averaged 7.5 rebounds in 24.2 minutes. He also appeared in all six Denver playoff games. That gave the Nuggets a veteran frontcourt contributor during a 50-win season. Denver did not simply lose Silas after one year: on May 24, 1977, the Nuggets included him with Marvin Webster and Willie Wise in the trade that brought Tom Burleson, Bob Wilkerson and a second-round pick from Seattle.

Denver's Downstream Return Must Be Shared Across a Larger Package

The Seattle trade created additional value, but this review does not assign the entire return to Silas because Webster and Wise were also outgoing assets. Denver then moved Burleson and the acquired second-rounder to Kansas City for Brian Taylor and a 1977 first-round pick that became Tom LaGarde. That downstream chain shows Silas retained trade utility after his Denver season, but the multi-player package prevents treating LaGarde or Taylor as a one-for-one Silas return.

Ralph Simpson Produced for Detroit and Then Became Another Package

Simpson played 77 games for Detroit in 1976-77, averaging 11.0 points, then appeared in 32 more Pistons games the following season at 10.6 points per game. Detroit therefore received 109 regular-season games from the player it acquired in the three-team deal. On February 1, 1978, the Pistons traded Simpson back to Denver for Jim Price and a 1979 first-round pick. That second transaction is where Detroit's side of this review separates from the others.

The Simpson Exit Produced Jim Price and Phil Hubbard

Price played 34 games for Detroit after the February 1978 trade, averaging 11.5 points and 3.0 assists. More important for the long-term asset chain, the 1979 first-round pick became No. 15 Phil Hubbard. Hubbard played 64 games for Detroit as a rookie, 80 in 1980-81 and 52 more before his 1981-82 move, giving the Pistons 196 regular-season games from the draft asset created by Simpson's exit. Detroit received useful production from Simpson first and then converted him into another player plus a first-round pick that produced several additional seasons of value.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A/B+/B. Detroit receives an A because Simpson supplied 109 games and then became Jim Price plus the first-round pick used on Phil Hubbard, extending the transaction's value well beyond the original player. Denver receives a B+ because Silas contributed to a 50-win team for 81 games and retained value in the later Seattle package, although that downstream return cannot be credited to Silas alone. Boston receives a B because Rowe delivered 183 regular-season games and nine playoff starts across three seasons. All three teams received meaningful basketball value; Detroit simply created the strongest verified downstream chain. Confidence is high on the three-team routing and the traced player outcomes.

perspectives.summary: Los Angeles acquired the NBA rights to Dwight “Bo” Lamar in October 1976 for future consideration that became the Lakers' 1978 second-round pick, No. 38 Lew Massey. This transaction carries a source discrepancy that this review preserves instead of hiding: Basketball-Reference's league and Lakers ledgers describe Indiana sending Lamar to Los Angeles for future considerations, while official Lakers media guides and the historical draft-pick chain identify Detroit as the rights holder and trace the consideration to the 1978 No. 38 pick. Lamar played 71 regular-season games for the Lakers, averaging 7.1 points and 2.5 assists, then appeared in all 10 of their 1977 playoff games. Detroit later included the No. 38 pick in the Marvin Barnes trade with Buffalo; Buffalo eventually returned that pick to Los Angeles for Tom Abernethy, and the Lakers selected Massey, who never played an NBA regular-season game. The Lakers receive the better hindsight grade because Lamar supplied a full season of usable rotation minutes.
perspectives.analysis:
The Sources Disagree on Which Franchise Sent Lamar to Los Angeles

this review has an important source conflict. Basketball-Reference's 1976-77 NBA and Lakers transaction ledgers say the Indiana Pacers traded Bo Lamar to Los Angeles for future considerations on October 20, 1976. Bill Sharman's executive record repeats Indiana. Official Lakers media guides, however, state that Los Angeles acquired Dwight "Bo" Lamar from Detroit for future consideration, and the 1978 draft-pick transaction chain ties Detroit to the Lakers' future second-round selection. Because the canonical record represents the Detroit rights transaction, this review keeps that record but explicitly preserves the disagreement rather than pretending every source says the same thing.

The Future Consideration Became the No. 38 Pick

The historical 1978 draft-pick chain identifies the consideration as the Lakers' second-round pick, eventually No. 38. Pro Sports Transactions cites contemporary draft reporting that the choice originally belonged to Los Angeles and had been traded for Bo Lamar. Detroit later sent that pick, along with Marvin Barnes and another draft asset, to Buffalo in November 1977. Buffalo then traded the No. 38 pick back to Los Angeles for Tom Abernethy on June 7, 1978.

Lamar Gave the Lakers a Full Rotation Season

Whatever the rights-routing ambiguity, Lamar's Los Angeles outcome is clear. Basketball-Reference credits him with 71 regular-season games in 1976-77. He averaged 16.4 minutes, 7.1 points and 2.5 assists while shooting 40.6 percent. The Lakers won 53 games and finished first in the Pacific Division. Lamar was not a star, but 71 appearances and more than 1,100 minutes represent legitimate rotation value from an acquisition made immediately before the season.

He Also Appeared Throughout the 1977 Playoffs

Lamar played in all 10 Lakers playoff games in 1977. His role shrank to 10.9 minutes per game and 3.3 points, but Los Angeles used him in both postseason rounds as the club beat Golden State before losing to Portland in the Western Conference Finals. That playoff participation reinforces that the Lakers received more than an expendable camp body from the transaction.

Detroit Used the Pick in a Larger Marvin Barnes Package

Detroit did not simply hold the future second-rounder until draft night. On November 23, 1977, the Pistons sent Marvin Barnes, the No. 38 pick and a 1978 fourth-round pick to Buffalo for Gus Gerard, John Shumate and a 1979 first-round pick that later became Roy Hamilton. That gives the Lamar consideration real transactional utility. This review does not assign the full Gerard-Shumate-Hamilton return to the second-rounder, however, because Barnes and another pick were also necessary outgoing assets.

The Pick Eventually Returned to Los Angeles and Produced No NBA Games

Buffalo subsequently sent the No. 38 selection back to the Lakers for Tom Abernethy. Los Angeles used the pick on UNC Charlotte guard Lew Massey. Basketball-Reference lists Massey as the No. 38 selection but shows no NBA regular-season statistics. That terminal outcome prevents Detroit's original consideration from receiving a strong standalone grade even though the pick had value as part of the Barnes package.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, B/C+. Los Angeles receives a B because Lamar played 71 regular-season games, contributed useful reserve scoring and appeared in all 10 playoff games during a 53-win season. Detroit receives a C+ because the future consideration became a real second-round asset and was used in the larger Marvin Barnes package, but the pick eventually returned to Los Angeles and became Lew Massey, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is medium rather than high because Basketball-Reference attributes Lamar's October 20 transfer to Indiana while Lakers media guides and the traced draft-pick chain identify Detroit's rights involvement.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired 21-year-old Moses Malone from Buffalo on October 24, 1976 for Houston's 1977 and 1978 first-round picks. The primary transaction ledgers agree on the package. Malone became Houston's franchise centerpiece, winning the 1979 and 1982 NBA MVP awards, leading the Rockets to the 1981 NBA Finals and producing six seasons of elite rebounding and scoring before leaving for Philadelphia. Buffalo also received strong asset value rather than empty picks. The 1977 first-rounder was traded to Golden State for George Johnson, who immediately started at center for the Braves. The 1978 first-rounder later became part of the package used to acquire Tiny Archibald from the Nets. Because that second branch was bundled with George Johnson and Buffalo's own 1979 first, the full Archibald return cannot be credited to Houston's pick alone. Houston wins the deal decisively on superstar impact, but Buffalo's two-first return earns a strong grade.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree on Two First-Round Picks for Malone

Basketball-Reference's Houston, Buffalo and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same October 24, 1976 package. Houston sent its 1977 first-round pick and 1978 first-round pick to Buffalo for Moses Malone. The two selections later landed at No. 18 in 1977 and No. 4 in 1978. This is a clean two-pick transaction; no cash or additional player is needed to explain the canonical package.

Houston Acquired a Franchise Center Before His Prime

Malone was only 21 and had played two NBA games for Buffalo when Houston acquired him. He immediately appeared in 80 Rockets games in 1976-77, totaling 2,500 minutes and 1,071 rebounds while averaging 13.5 rebounds per game. Houston won 49 games and reached the Eastern Conference Finals in his first season. The early return alone already exceeded what most first-round packages produce.

The Trade Produced Two Houston MVP Seasons

The acquisition became extraordinary as Malone developed. In 1978-79 he played all 82 games, averaged 24.8 points and 17.6 rebounds, and won the NBA Most Valuable Player award. In 1981-82 he averaged 31.1 points and 14.7 rebounds and won MVP again. Those were not awards earned after leaving Houston; they were direct outcomes of the player acquired in this trade.

Malone Also Led Houston to Its First NBA Finals

In 1980-81 Houston reached the NBA Finals with Malone as the center of the team. He played 21 postseason games that spring, averaging 26.8 points and 14.5 rebounds while carrying a 40-42 Rockets team through the Western Conference bracket. Houston lost to Boston in the Finals, but the playoff run gives the trade a franchise-level postseason outcome in addition to the regular-season awards.

Buffalo Converted the 1977 Pick Into George Johnson

Buffalo did not simply wait for Houston's 1977 pick to become Wesley Cox. On January 18, 1977, the Braves sent that first-rounder to Golden State for George Johnson. Johnson played 39 games for Buffalo that season, starting all 39 and averaging 10.3 rebounds. Golden State later used the No. 18 selection on Cox. For Buffalo's side of this review, Johnson is the realized return from that pick branch.

The 1978 Pick Became Part of the Tiny Archibald Package

Houston's 1978 first-rounder eventually landed at No. 4, where Micheal Ray Richardson was selected, but Buffalo did not use the pick itself. In September 1977 the Braves included George Johnson, the Houston 1978 first and Buffalo's 1979 first in the deal for Tiny Archibald. The pick therefore retained major trade utility. This review does not assign Archibald's entire value to that one selection because two other meaningful assets were included in the package.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, A+/A-. Houston receives an A+ because Malone delivered six seasons of franchise-center production, two MVP awards and the 1981 NBA Finals run after being acquired at age 21. Buffalo receives an A- because two first-round picks were a substantial return and both were converted into useful downstream assets: the 1977 pick became George Johnson, while the 1978 pick remained valuable enough to help complete the Tiny Archibald package. Houston still wins by a wide margin because the realized value of a multi-time MVP in his prime exceeds even a well-used pair of first-round picks. Confidence is high on the package and the traced asset branches.

Toney spent his entire eight-year NBA career with the 76ers, made two All-Star teams, started all 81 games he played for the 1982-83 champions and averaged 18.8 points in that postseason. The pick therefore became a championship-level core guard while Bennett's Pacers return stayed limited. Philadelphia wins the deal decisively on realized value.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree on Bennett for Indiana's 1980 First

Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Philadelphia and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same November 2, 1976 exchange. The Pacers sent their 1980 first-round pick to the 76ers for Mel Bennett. No additional player or cash component appears in those ledgers. The future selection ultimately landed at No. 8 overall, where Philadelphia drafted Andrew Toney.

Bennett Gave Indiana Two Limited Seasons

Bennett played 67 games for Indiana in 1976-77 and another 31 in 1977-78. He started only once across those 98 appearances. His first Pacers season produced 4.7 points and 3.5 rebounds per game in 13.6 minutes; the second fell to 2.4 points and 3.0 rebounds in 9.2 minutes. The acquisition supplied frontcourt depth, but not enough production or tenure to match the value of a future top-ten first-round pick.

The Pick Matured Into No. 8 Overall

Philadelphia waited more than three seasons for the asset to convey. In the 1980 NBA Draft, the 76ers used the eighth overall selection on Andrew Toney out of Louisiana. That matters for hindsight grading because the transaction did not merely create theoretical draft value. The exact pick transferred by Indiana turned into a player who immediately entered Philadelphia's rotation and remained with the franchise for his entire NBA career.

Toney Became a Two-Time All-Star

Toney played 468 regular-season games for Philadelphia and scored 7,458 points. He made the All-Star team in 1983 and 1984. His peak arrived during the franchise's championship window rather than years after the original trade had lost relevance, making the draft-pick return a direct and durable payoff from Philadelphia's decision to move Bennett.

The 1983 Championship Makes the Value Gap Wider

On the 1982-83 title team, Toney started all 81 regular-season games he played and averaged 19.7 points. He then averaged 18.8 points across 12 playoff games. Philadelphia swept the Lakers in the NBA Finals, and Toney scored 23 points with nine assists in the clinching Game 4. He was not a peripheral roster piece; he was one of the central guards on a championship team.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/F. Philadelphia receives an A+ because a reserve forward with limited future value was converted into the No. 8 pick and then into a two-time All-Star who became a core starter on the 1983 champions. Indiana receives an F because Bennett produced only 98 games, one start and modest bench production before leaving the NBA for two seasons, while the surrendered first became a franchise-level championship asset. This grade uses realized value rather than assuming Indiana itself would have drafted Toney. Confidence is high on the package, pick identity and player outcomes.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Buffalo acquired Jim Price from Milwaukee on November 2, 1976 for the Braves' 1977 first-round pick. Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Milwaukee and league transaction ledgers agree on the one-player-for-one-pick package. Price played only 20 games for Buffalo before the Braves sent him to Denver for Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams, extending Buffalo's return beyond the short Price stint. Milwaukee held the first-rounder until June 1977, then packaged it with Swen Nater to reacquire Buffalo's higher first-round pick. That upgraded selection became No. 3 Marques Johnson, a five-time All-Star and three-time All-NBA player. Because Nater was a substantial part of the later swap, this review credits the original pick as an important contributor rather than the sole source of Johnson's value. Milwaukee gets the stronger hindsight result, while Buffalo still recovered useful rotation value.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree on Price for Buffalo's 1977 First

Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Milwaukee and NBA transaction ledgers all record the same November 2, 1976 exchange. Buffalo sent its 1977 first-round pick to Milwaukee for Jim Price. The selection ultimately landed at No. 13. No additional player or cash component is needed to explain the canonical trade.

Price Stayed in Buffalo for Only 20 Games

Price's Braves stint was brief. He appeared in 20 games, averaging 5.3 points and 1.9 assists in 16.7 minutes per game. On December 15, only six weeks after the Milwaukee deal, Buffalo moved him again. The short stay limits the direct value of the acquisition, but it does not end the asset chain.

Buffalo Flipped Price for Two Rotation Players

The Braves sent Price to Denver for Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams. Gerard played 41 games for Buffalo in 1976-77, while Williams appeared in 44 games that season and 73 more in 1977-78. Williams became a regular backcourt contributor, averaging 5.7 assists per 36 minutes in 1977-78. That secondary return keeps Buffalo's side from being judged as 20 games of Price and nothing else.

Milwaukee Used the Pick as Trade-Up Currency

Milwaukee did not simply make the No. 13 selection. On June 7, 1977, the Bucks sent Swen Nater and the acquired No. 13 pick back to Buffalo for the Braves' own higher first-rounder. That incoming pick became No. 3 overall. The original Buffalo selection therefore became part of a direct draft-night value upgrade.

The No. 3 Pick Became Marques Johnson

Milwaukee used the third pick on Marques Johnson. Johnson went on to make five All-Star teams and three All-NBA teams, and Basketball-Reference credits him with a 20.1-point career scoring average. His Milwaukee tenure became one of the strongest outcomes tied to the 1977 draft. This review does not assign all of that value to the No. 13 pick because Nater was a major outgoing asset in the trade-up.

Nater's Value Prevents Over-Crediting the Pick

Nater had averaged 13.0 points and 12.0 rebounds for Milwaukee in 1976-77 before the Bucks included him in the June trade. He then averaged 15.5 points and 13.2 rebounds for Buffalo in 1977-78. That production matters when grading the downstream branch. The No. 13 pick helped Milwaukee reach Johnson, but the trade-up required a productive starting center as well.

Final Verdict

Bucks Edge, A-/B-. Milwaukee receives an A- because turning Price into a first-round asset and then using that asset in the package that produced No. 3 Marques Johnson created excellent long-term value. Buffalo receives a B- because Price himself lasted only 20 games, but his resale brought back Gus Gerard and Chuck Williams, with Williams contributing across two seasons. The gap favors Milwaukee, though the later Johnson outcome cannot be credited to the original pick alone. Confidence is high on the package and downstream transaction chain.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles traded Mack Calvin to San Antonio on November 16, 1976 for the Spurs' 1977 first-round pick plus cash. Basketball-Reference's team and executive ledgers verify Calvin for the first-rounder, while the Lakers' own media guide and Pro Sports Transactions also record the cash component. Calvin played 35 games for San Antonio before the Spurs waived him in February 1977. The Lakers used the No. 15 pick on Brad Davis, who appeared in 38 games for Los Angeles across two seasons before being waived in October 1978. Davis later built a 15-year NBA career, but almost all of that value came after leaving the Lakers and is not credited back to this trade. San Antonio gets a narrow hindsight edge from Calvin's stronger immediate production, while the pick and cash keep the Lakers' return respectable.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Verify Calvin for San Antonio's 1977 First

Basketball-Reference's Lakers, Spurs and executive transaction ledgers agree on the core November 16, 1976 exchange: Los Angeles sent Mack Calvin to San Antonio for the Spurs' 1977 first-round pick. The selection became No. 15 overall and was used on Brad Davis. Basketball-Reference does not list cash in its transaction line, but the Lakers' official media guide and Pro Sports Transactions both add cash considerations from San Antonio. This review therefore records the cash component with that source distinction rather than treating every ledger as identical.

Calvin Gave San Antonio 35 Games

Calvin had played only 12 games for the Lakers before the trade. With San Antonio he appeared in 35 games. Basketball-Reference's trade-partner summary credits him with 8.8 points and 3.0 assists per game for the Spurs, along with 0.7 win shares. That is useful short-term guard production, but the tenure ended quickly. San Antonio waived Calvin in February 1977, and Denver claimed him shortly afterward.

The Lakers Used the Pick on Brad Davis

Los Angeles kept the incoming first-rounder through the 1977 draft and selected Davis at No. 15. Davis played 33 games for the Lakers as a rookie and five more in 1978-79. Across his 38 Lakers games, the trade-partner ledger credits 2.7 points and 2.4 assists per game with 0.4 win shares. The pick therefore produced an NBA player, but not a long Lakers tenure.

Davis' Long Career Belongs Mostly to Other Teams

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired the player rights to John Mengelt from Detroit on November 18, 1976 in a cash sale. Basketball-Reference's Bulls, Pistons and league transaction ledgers all record Detroit selling Mengelt's rights to Chicago. Mengelt then became a useful multi-year Bulls reserve, playing 253 regular-season games across four seasons and scoring 2,386 points. He appeared in 61 games immediately after the 1976 transaction, then played 81 games in 1977-78 and 75 in 1978-79 while averaging double figures in both seasons. Detroit received cash rather than a basketball asset, and the amount is not specified in the primary ledgers used for this review. Chicago therefore earns the stronger hindsight result: the Bulls converted a financial outlay into several seasons of rotation production without surrendering a player or draft pick.
perspectives.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Describe a Sale, Not a Player-for-Player Trade

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Detroit and NBA transaction pages all record the same November 18, 1976 move. Detroit sold the player rights to John Mengelt to Chicago. That wording is important because it defines the package more precisely than a generic "Mengelt for cash" label. Chicago did not surrender a player or draft choice; Detroit received financial consideration for Mengelt's rights.

Mengelt Immediately Entered Chicago's Rotation

Mengelt played 61 games for the Bulls in 1976-77 after arriving in November. He averaged 8.3 points and 1.9 assists in 19.3 minutes per game. Chicago finished 44-38 and reached the playoffs, where Mengelt appeared in all three games of the first-round series against Portland and averaged 12.7 points. That gave the Bulls useful immediate value from a transaction that cost no basketball asset.

His Best Bulls Seasons Followed

The return improved in 1977-78. Mengelt appeared in 81 games, averaged 10.3 points and 2.9 assists, and shot 48.1 percent from the field. He followed with 75 games and an 11.0-point average in 1978-79. Those were not star seasons, but they are exactly the type of durable rotation production that makes a cash acquisition worthwhile in hindsight.

Chicago Ultimately Received 253 Games

Mengelt remained with the Bulls through 1979-80. Across four Chicago seasons he played 253 regular-season games and scored 2,386 points. His role declined in the final season, when he appeared in 36 games, but the cumulative return still far exceeded a short rental. The player-rights purchase produced several years of usable guard depth.

Detroit's Return Was Financial

Detroit's side is harder to measure because the transaction ledgers used here do not specify the cash amount. Cash can have real organizational value, especially for a player a team no longer intends to keep, but it does not create an identifiable on-court or draft branch for retrospective grading. This review therefore avoids inventing a dollar figure or downstream basketball return that the source record does not establish.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, B+/C. Chicago receives a B+ because a cash outlay produced 253 games, two double-figure scoring seasons and immediate playoff rotation value without costing a player or draft pick. Detroit receives a C because selling Mengelt generated financial value but removed a player who subsequently supplied several useful seasons to Chicago. The gap is meaningful rather than franchise-changing, so the grade stops short of an elite result. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Mengelt's realized Chicago production.

perspectives.summary: Chicago traded Bob Love to the New York Nets on November 30, 1976 for the Nets' 1977 second-round pick plus cash. Basketball-Reference's Bulls, Nets, league and executive ledgers verify the pick-for-Love core package, while the Bulls' official transaction history and Pro Sports Transactions also preserve the cash component. Love gave New York only 13 games before the Nets waived him, averaging 10.1 points in 17.5 minutes per game. Chicago used the No. 23 selection on Mike Glenn, but the Bulls waived Glenn in December 1977 before he made his NBA debut; his productive 10-year career began elsewhere and is not credited back to Chicago. The Bulls therefore converted Love into draft optionality and cash without receiving on-court value from the selected player, while the Nets received a brief veteran contribution. The realized result is close to even.
perspectives.analysis:
The Core Transaction Is Bob Love for a 1977 Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, New York Nets, league and executive transaction ledgers all agree on the November 30, 1976 core exchange. Chicago sent Bob Love to the Nets for New York's 1977 second-round pick, which became No. 23 overall. The Bulls' official all-time transaction history and Pro Sports Transactions add cash to the Nets' outgoing package. This review keeps that cash component while distinguishing the sources that actually record it.

Love's Nets Tenure Lasted 13 Games

Love had been one of the defining Bulls scorers of the previous decade, but by the time of this trade he was 34. With New York he appeared in 13 games, averaging 10.1 points, 2.9 rebounds and only 17.5 minutes. The Nets did receive immediate veteran offense, but the relationship ended quickly. Love was waived in January 1977 and finished the season with Seattle.

Chicago's Pick Became Mike Glenn

The incoming second-rounder landed at No. 23 in the 1977 draft. Chicago used it on Mike Glenn out of Southern Illinois. Glenn eventually played 593 NBA games across ten seasons and finished with a 54.2 percent career field-goal rate, so the selection itself identified a legitimate long-term NBA player.

The Bulls Did Not Receive Glenn's NBA Career

That career cannot be credited to Chicago. The Bulls waived Glenn on December 8, 1977, six days before his NBA debut with Buffalo. He never appeared in a regular-season game for Chicago. The pick therefore had real draft value at the moment of the trade, but its realized on-court return to the Bulls was zero. This review credits Chicago for obtaining and exercising the No. 23 asset, not for the production Glenn later supplied to Buffalo, New York or Atlanta.

The Cash Keeps Chicago's Side From Being Empty

The official Bulls media guide and Pro Sports Transactions both record cash in addition to the pick, although the amount is not specified in the sources used here. That financial consideration matters because the pick did not become Chicago production. At the same time, an unspecified cash payment cannot be treated as though it created a known player or draft branch.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C+/C+. The Nets receive a C+ because Love supplied only 13 games before being waived, but those games at least produced immediate NBA rotation value. Chicago also receives a C+ because the Bulls obtained a top second-round pick plus cash, yet the selected player was waived before his NBA debut and produced no Chicago games. The transaction created optionality for the Bulls and short-term production for the Nets without a durable franchise return on either side. Confidence is high on the package and the realized player outcomes.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee acquired Fred Carter from Philadelphia on December 8, 1976 for the Bucks' 1977 and 1978 second-round picks. Carter gave Milwaukee 47 games that season, averaging 8.3 points in 18.6 minutes, but his NBA career ended after the year. Philadelphia used the 1977 pick at No. 25 on Wilson Washington, who played only 14 games for the 76ers. The 1978 pick became far more important: Philadelphia selected Maurice Cheeks at No. 36. Cheeks immediately started all 82 games as a rookie, became a four-time All-Star and five-time All-Defensive selection, helped the 76ers win the 1983 championship and was later inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame. Because that franchise-level return came directly from one of the two picks acquired for a short Carter stint, Philadelphia owns the decisive hindsight advantage.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree on Two Second-Round Picks for Carter

Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers record the same December 8, 1976 package. The Bucks sent their 1977 and 1978 second-round selections to the 76ers for Fred Carter. The first pick landed at No. 25 in 1977 and the second at No. 36 in 1978. No extra player or financial component is needed to explain the transaction.

Carter Gave Milwaukee One Short Veteran Stint

Carter was 31 and had already spent most of his career in Philadelphia when the trade happened. He played 47 games for Milwaukee in 1976-77, averaging 8.3 points and 2.2 assists in 18.6 minutes per game. He gave the Bucks real rotation minutes, but the return ended there. The 1976-77 season was Carter's final NBA season.

The 1977 Pick Became Wilson Washington

Philadelphia used the first incoming pick at No. 25 on Wilson Washington. His 76ers tenure was brief. Washington played 14 games for Philadelphia, totaling 19 points and 14 rebounds before continuing his career with the Nets. That branch of the trade did not produce meaningful long-term value for the 76ers.

The 1978 Pick Became Maurice Cheeks

The second pick changed the entire evaluation. Philadelphia used the No. 36 selection in 1978 on Maurice Cheeks. He started all 82 games as a rookie, averaged 5.3 assists and 2.1 steals, and immediately became a core guard. Cheeks remained a long-term Philadelphia starter rather than a prospect whose best years arrived elsewhere.

Cheeks Became a Championship-Era Franchise Piece

Cheeks eventually made four All-Star teams, earned five All-Defensive selections and entered the Basketball Hall of Fame. In 1982-83 he started 79 regular-season games for the championship 76ers, averaged 12.5 points and 6.9 assists, and earned first-team All-Defensive honors. The 1978 second-round pick therefore became a direct championship contributor and one of the most productive players ever selected in that draft range.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/C+. Philadelphia receives an A+ because two second-round picks produced one low-impact player and one Hall of Fame point guard who became a starter from day one, anchored multiple Finals-level teams and helped win the 1983 championship. Milwaukee receives a C+ because Carter provided 47 useful games, but the veteran rental lasted only one season and cost the pick that became Cheeks. This is not a criticism of knowing the future in 1976; it is a realized-value grade. Confidence is high on the package, draft identities and player outcomes.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Buffalo traded Bob McAdoo and Tom McMillen to New York on December 9, 1976 for John Gianelli and cash, reported contemporaneously at $2.5 million. McAdoo immediately gave the Knicks elite production, averaging 26.7 points and 12.7 rebounds in 52 games after the trade, then 26.5 points in an All-Star 1977-78 season. McMillen added 56 games in 1976-77. New York later converted McAdoo into three 1979 first-round picks plus Tom Barker. Buffalo did recover more than Gianelli's 57 games: in September 1977 the Braves moved Gianelli to Milwaukee for a 1979 first-rounder, which later became part of another trade package, and additional cash is reported in secondary transaction records. That downstream salvage and the large original cash payment improve Buffalo's grade, but they do not match prime McAdoo production plus New York's eventual resale return.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Confirm McAdoo and McMillen for Gianelli and Cash

Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, New York and league transaction ledgers agree on the December 9, 1976 structure. The Braves sent Bob McAdoo and Tom McMillen to the Knicks for John Gianelli and cash. Contemporary Associated Press reporting placed the cash at $2.5 million. The exact financial context matters because Buffalo was not simply exchanging two players for Gianelli; ownership economics were a major part of the transaction.

McAdoo Was Still a Prime-Age Star

McAdoo was 25 and only one season removed from three straight scoring titles. After the trade he played 52 games for New York in 1976-77, averaging 26.7 points, 12.7 rebounds and 39.1 minutes. In 1977-78 he played 79 games, averaged 26.5 points and 12.8 rebounds, made the All-Star team and finished tenth in MVP voting. That is immediate star-level production rather than value that appeared years later.

McMillen Added Useful Rotation Value

Tom McMillen was not a throw-in with no NBA contribution. He appeared in 56 games for the Knicks in 1976-77, starting 22 and averaging 9.4 points and 5.7 rebounds. His New York tenure was short, but the Knicks received meaningful frontcourt minutes from both incoming players in the first season of the deal.

New York Later Recovered Major Asset Value for McAdoo

The Knicks did not lose McAdoo for nothing when the relationship ended. In February 1979 they traded him to Boston in a package that produced three 1979 first-round picks plus Tom Barker. Those picks became Bill Cartwright at No. 3, Larry Demic at No. 9 and Sly Williams at No. 21. This review does not assign all of the later players' career value to the Buffalo trade, but the resale package demonstrates that McAdoo retained substantial transaction value after more than two seasons of elite New York production.

Buffalo Did Create a Downstream Branch From Gianelli

The Braves received 57 games from Gianelli in 1976-77. On September 2, 1977, Buffalo traded him to Milwaukee for a 1979 first-round pick; Pro Sports Transactions also records cash in that later deal. The first-rounder eventually became No. 10 Roy Hamilton, but Buffalo moved the pick again in the November 1977 Marvin Barnes transaction. Because that later deal bundled multiple players and picks, this review credits Gianelli's branch for producing another first-round asset without assigning the entire Barnes package to this trade.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A+/C+. New York receives an A+ because McAdoo delivered prime superstar production, McMillen added useful depth and McAdoo later returned a major draft package. Buffalo receives a C+ rather than an F because the reported $2.5 million cash payment was substantial, Gianelli contributed 57 games and his resale generated another first-round asset. The financial and downstream context makes the Braves' return real, but the basketball-value gap remains wide. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes, with the cash amount identified as a contemporary report rather than a Basketball-Reference figure.
