seattle-supersonics.summary: Seattle traded Leonard Gray to Washington on December 13, 1976 for Nick Weatherspoon in a straight one-for-one forward swap. Weatherspoon gave the SuperSonics 51 games after the trade, scoring 652 points and grabbing 404 rebounds while averaging 12.8 points and 7.9 rebounds. Gray played 58 games for Washington, scoring 347 points and averaging 6.0 points and 3.2 rebounds, then appeared in eight playoff games as the Bullets reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. Gray missed the entire 1977-78 season with injury and never returned to an NBA regular-season game. Seattle waived Weatherspoon in September 1977, so neither side received a long-term franchise piece. The realized gap still favors Seattle because Weatherspoon supplied substantially more regular-season scoring and rebounding during the shared 1976-77 window.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree on a Straight Player Swap

Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Washington and league transaction pages all record the same December 13, 1976 deal. The SuperSonics sent Leonard Gray to the Bullets for Nick Weatherspoon. There were no draft picks or cash components in the recorded package, making this review a direct comparison of the two forwards' realized value after the exchange.

Weatherspoon Became a Productive Seattle Regular

Weatherspoon had appeared in only 11 games for Washington before the trade. In Seattle he played 51 games, totaling 652 points and 404 rebounds. That works out to 12.8 points and 7.9 rebounds per game, and Basketball-Reference credits him with 2.8 win shares during the Seattle portion of the season. He was not a star, but he immediately became a meaningful rotation scorer and rebounder.

Gray Gave Washington More Games but a Smaller Role

Gray played 58 regular-season games for the Bullets after arriving from Seattle. He totaled 347 points, 186 rebounds and 69 assists, averaging 6.0 points and 3.2 rebounds in 17.2 minutes per game. Washington went 48-34 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. Gray also appeared in eight playoff games, though his postseason role was limited to 6.5 minutes and 1.5 points per game.

The Longer-Term Return Vanished on Both Sides

Neither team turned the trade into a durable multi-season asset. Gray did not play in 1977-78 because of injury and never returned to an NBA regular-season game. Seattle kept Weatherspoon through the end of the 1976-77 season but waived him on September 28, 1977. He continued his career with Chicago and later San Diego, so those later seasons are not credited to the SuperSonics.

The Timing Makes Seattle's Edge Clear but Modest

Seattle received fewer games than Washington, but Weatherspoon's 51-game stretch was much more productive. He more than doubled Gray's points per game and delivered over twice as many rebounds per game. Washington can still point to 58 regular-season appearances and a small playoff contribution, which keeps the trade from becoming a one-sided failure. The difference is mainly the quality of the one-season rotation value each club received.

Final Verdict

Seattle Edge, B/C+. Seattle receives a B because Weatherspoon produced 51 solid games with 12.8 points and 7.9 rebounds per night before the relationship ended. Washington receives a C+ because Gray supplied 58 games and appeared in the playoffs, but his role was smaller and injury ended his NBA career after that season. With no picks or downstream assets attached, the comparison stays focused on those direct 1976-77 results. Confidence is high on the package and player outcomes.

perspectives.summary: Houston traded Dave Wohl to the New York Nets on January 8, 1977 for the Nets' 1978 fourth-round pick. Basketball-Reference's Houston, Nets, league and executive ledgers all place the transaction on January 8, correcting the canonical record's prior January 7 date. Wohl played 37 games for the Nets after the trade, averaging 7.4 points and 3.4 assists, then returned for 10 games in 1977-78 before being waived in November. Houston used the No. 67 pick on Jackie Robinson in the 1978 draft, but the Rockets waived Robinson on October 11, 1978 before he made his NBA debut. Robinson later played 22 NBA games for other teams, so that production is not credited to Houston. The Nets therefore received the only direct NBA production created by the transaction, giving Brooklyn's franchise the modest hindsight edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Correct the Date to January 8

Basketball-Reference's Houston, New York Nets, NBA league and executive ledgers all record the Dave Wohl trade on January 8, 1977. The existing canonical record used January 7. This review corrects the stored date while preserving the stable canonical trade ID. The package itself is straightforward: Houston sent Wohl to the Nets for New York's 1978 fourth-round pick.

Wohl Immediately Became a Nets Rotation Guard

Wohl had appeared in only 14 Houston games before the trade in 1976-77. With the Nets he played 37 games, averaging 25.0 minutes, 7.4 points and 3.4 assists. He totaled 275 points and 127 assists in that post-trade stretch. The Nets were a struggling team, but the transaction still produced a regular rotation player rather than a brief end-of-bench appearance.

He Added a Small Second Season

Wohl returned after the franchise moved to New Jersey in 1977-78. He appeared in 10 more games, adding 35 points and 13 assists before the Nets waived him on November 19, 1977. That gives the franchise 47 regular-season games from the acquisition. The second season was minor, but it confirms the return lasted beyond the closing months of 1976-77.

Houston's Pick Became Jackie Robinson

The fourth-round selection conveyed at No. 67 in the 1978 draft. Houston selected Jackie Robinson from UNLV. Basketball-Reference's draft record shows Robinson eventually played 22 NBA games over three seasons, so the pick did identify a player capable of reaching the league.

Robinson Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Houston

The important realized-value distinction is that Robinson's NBA career did not occur with the Rockets. Houston waived him on October 11, 1978, months before his March 1979 NBA debut. His later 22-game career therefore belongs to other teams for franchise-value purposes. This review credits Houston for the draft selection but not for production the Rockets never received.

Final Verdict

Nets Edge, C+/C. The Nets receive a C+ because Wohl supplied 47 regular-season games and became a usable rotation guard immediately after the trade. Houston receives a C because the fourth-rounder became an NBA player, but Robinson was waived before debuting and produced zero Rockets games. The difference is modest because Wohl's tenure was not long or high-impact, yet the Nets clearly received more realized basketball value from the direct exchange. Confidence is high on the corrected date, package, draft identity and player outcomes.

Smith became the centerpiece of Cleveland's return, playing 141 regular-season games across three seasons and averaging 10.5 points, 7.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks for the Cavaliers. perspectives.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Confirm a Two-Player Package for Garrett and Two Firsts

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Milwaukee and league transaction ledgers all record the January 13, 1977 exchange the same way. Cleveland sent Rowland Garrett plus its 1977 and 1978 first-round picks to Milwaukee for Gary Brokaw and Elmore Smith. The first-round picks later became No. 11 Ernie Grunfeld in 1977 and No. 12 George Johnson in 1978.

Smith Gave Cleveland Three Seasons of Real Frontcourt Value

Smith was the strongest direct asset Cleveland received. He played 36 games for the Cavaliers after the trade in 1976-77, averaging 8.7 points, 6.4 rebounds and 2.1 blocks. He followed with 81 games in 1977-78 at 12.5 points, 8.4 rebounds and 2.2 blocks, then appeared in 24 more games in 1978-79. Across his Cleveland tenure he played 141 regular-season games and averaged 10.5 points, 7.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks.

Brokaw Was a Shorter-Term Secondary Return

Brokaw played 39 games for Cleveland after the deal, averaging 7.2 points and 3.0 assists. The Cavaliers traded him to Buffalo for future considerations in October 1977. Because the primary ledgers do not identify a concrete later player or pick emerging from those future considerations, this review credits Cleveland for Brokaw's 39 games and acknowledges the subsequent transaction without inventing a downstream asset.

Garrett Was the Smallest Milwaukee Piece

Garrett played 33 games for the Bucks after the trade, averaging 4.7 points and 2.2 rebounds. The 1976-77 season was his final NBA season. His direct value therefore does little to separate the packages, which puts most of Milwaukee's case on the two first-round picks.

Grunfeld Became a Useful Two-Year Buck

Milwaukee used the No. 11 pick in 1977 on Ernie Grunfeld. He played 73 games as a rookie and all 82 in 1978-79, improving from 6.9 to 10.3 points per game. After 155 Milwaukee games, the Bucks traded Grunfeld and a 1980 second-round pick to Kansas City for Richard Washington in October 1979. This review credits Grunfeld's direct Milwaukee service and notes that he retained transaction value, without assigning the entire later Washington return to him because Milwaukee also sent a pick.

Johnson Added Another First-Round Rotation Piece

The 1978 first-rounder became George Johnson at No. 12. Johnson played 67 games for Milwaukee as a rookie, averaging 6.2 points and 5.4 rebounds. The Bucks sold his player rights to Denver in October 1979. That gives Milwaukee another season of direct production plus a later transactional return, although the financial amount is not specified in the primary source used here.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win, B+/B-. Milwaukee receives a B+ because two first-round picks became legitimate NBA rotation players who combined for 222 Bucks games, with Grunfeld also retaining later trade value. Cleveland receives a B- because Smith was a productive three-year center and Brokaw added a short guard stint, so the Cavaliers did receive meaningful basketball value. The difference comes from Milwaukee turning both premium picks into useful players while Garrett's limited tenure did not undermine the package. Confidence is high on the trade structure, draft outcomes and direct player production.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Buffalo traded its 1977 first-round pick to Golden State on January 18, 1977 for center George Johnson. The pick landed at No. 18 and became Wesley Cox, who played 74 games across two Warriors seasons while averaging 4.6 points and 2.8 rebounds. Johnson immediately started all 39 of his games for Buffalo after the trade and averaged 7.6 points, 10.3 rebounds and 2.7 blocks. The Braves then used Johnson as one component of the September 1977 package that acquired Tiny Archibald from the Nets, along with 1978 and 1979 first-round picks. Because Johnson supplied stronger direct production and retained meaningful trade utility, Buffalo's franchise received the better realized return. Golden State did convert the pick into an NBA player, which keeps the Warriors' side from being empty, but Cox's two-year role was limited.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Transaction Is a Straight Johnson-for-First Swap

Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Golden State and league transaction ledgers all record the January 18, 1977 deal the same way. The Braves sent their 1977 first-round pick to the Warriors for George Johnson. The pick became No. 18 overall and Golden State used it on Wesley Cox in the 1977 draft.

Johnson Immediately Became Buffalo's Starting Center

Johnson had played 39 games for Golden State before the trade, mostly in a reserve role. Buffalo changed his usage immediately. He started all 39 of his Braves games after the deal and averaged 27.1 minutes, 7.6 points, 10.3 rebounds and 2.7 blocks. That is meaningful direct value from a midseason acquisition, especially because his rebounding and rim protection were substantially larger contributions than his scoring average suggests.

Johnson Also Retained Trade Utility

Buffalo did not keep Johnson into the next season. On September 1, 1977, the Braves traded him with their 1978 and 1979 first-round picks to the New Jersey Nets for Tiny Archibald. Johnson therefore remained a useful transaction asset after his 39-game Buffalo stint. This review does not credit Buffalo with Archibald's entire value because Johnson was only one of three outgoing assets, but his inclusion in that package is legitimate downstream evidence that the Braves had not exhausted his value.

Cox Became a Two-Year Warriors Reserve

Golden State selected Cox at No. 18 in 1977. He played 43 games as a rookie and 31 more in 1978-79, giving the Warriors 74 regular-season games in total. Cox averaged 4.6 points and 2.8 rebounds for his career while playing roughly 11 minutes per game. He was a real NBA return from the pick, but he never became a major rotation piece and his NBA career ended after those two Warriors seasons.

The Direct Comparison Favors Buffalo

The Braves received only half a season of Johnson before moving him again, but those 39 games included starting-center production at 10.3 rebounds and 2.7 blocks per night. Golden State received more total games from Cox, yet in a much smaller role. The later Archibald package adds modest extra value to Buffalo's side because Johnson was still useful enough to be included in a major trade.

Final Verdict

Braves Edge, B/C+. Buffalo receives a B because Johnson provided strong starting-center production immediately and retained downstream trade utility. Golden State receives a C+ because the first-round pick became Cox, who supplied 74 games but only limited reserve production over two seasons. The outcome is a clear Buffalo edge rather than a franchise-altering result, and the grading avoids assigning Archibald's full later value to Johnson alone. Confidence is high on the package, pick identity and direct player outcomes.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Confirm a Player-and-First-Round-Pick Swap

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Washington and league transaction ledgers agree on the January 20, 1977 structure. Atlanta sent Tom Henderson and its 1977 first-round pick to Washington for Truck Robinson and Washington's 1977 first-round pick. The Bullets' incoming pick became No. 4 Greg Ballard. Atlanta's incoming pick became No. 14 Tree Rollins.

Robinson Was Excellent Immediately for Atlanta

Robinson played 36 games for the Hawks after the trade and produced star-level numbers: 806 points and 462 rebounds, or 22.4 points and 12.8 rebounds per game. He did not remain in Atlanta after the season. New Orleans signed Robinson as a veteran free agent in August 1977, and the Hawks received Ron Behagen and cash as compensation. That gives Atlanta both a high-end half-season and a legitimate downstream return.

Rollins Became the Long-Term Atlanta Anchor

The No. 14 pick became Tree Rollins, whose value dwarfed a typical mid-first-round outcome. Rollins spent eleven seasons with Atlanta, developed into one of the league's premier shot blockers, led the NBA in blocks in 1982-83 and earned two All-Defensive selections. The trade therefore gave the Hawks both immediate star production from Robinson and a durable defensive center from the pick.

Henderson Became Part of Washington's Championship Backcourt

Henderson played 41 games for Washington after the trade in 1976-77, then 75 games in 1977-78 and 70 in 1978-79. That is 186 regular-season games for the Bullets. More important than the raw total, he played 21 postseason games during Washington's 1978 championship run and averaged 9.6 points and 5.0 assists in those playoffs. His contribution was not merely regular-season depth.

Ballard Became an Eight-Year Washington Fixture

Washington used the No. 4 pick on Greg Ballard. He played 76 games as a rookie on the 1978 championship team and remained with the franchise through 1984-85. Across eight Washington seasons he appeared in 643 regular-season games, growing from a reserve into a full-time starting forward and double-figure scorer. The pick produced far more than a short rookie-contract contribution.

Henderson Created One More First-Round Asset

Houston signed Henderson as a veteran free agent in July 1979. Under the compensation rules of the era, Washington received a 1980 first-round pick that became No. 14 Wes Matthews. This review credits that specific compensation because it was directly tied to Henderson's departure, while avoiding any unrelated later asset chains.

Final Verdict

Bullets Edge, A+/A. Atlanta receives an A because Robinson delivered an elite half-season, Rollins became a long-term defensive anchor, and Robinson's departure produced compensation. Washington receives an A+ because Henderson and Ballard both contributed to the 1978 championship, Ballard supplied eight seasons and 643 games, and Henderson later generated another first-round pick. This is a high-value trade for both teams; Washington's championship impact and extra draft return create only a narrow hindsight advantage. Confidence is high on the package, draft identities and realized outcomes.

perspectives.summary: The New York Nets acquired Mike Bantom from Seattle on January 27, 1977 for the Nets' 1979 fourth-round pick plus cash, according to the Nets' own media guide. That pick became No. 73 James Donaldson. Basketball-Reference encodes the draft-asset side as New York selling Donaldson's rights to Seattle, while RealGM independently records Bantom joining the Nets that day. Bantom gave New York an excellent 33-game stretch, scoring 614 points and grabbing 285 rebounds, but he left as a veteran free agent after the season. Seattle waited for the pick to convey, then received three NBA seasons from Donaldson: 232 regular-season games from 1980-81 through 1982-83, including consecutive 82-game seasons. Donaldson also retained trade value when Seattle included him in the 1983 Tom Chambers package. The Sonics therefore earn the stronger long-term result, although Bantom's immediate production keeps New York's return useful.
perspectives.analysis:
The Nets Media Guide Preserves the Full Package

The clearest package source is the New Jersey Nets' historical media guide. It records that New York obtained Mike Bantom from Seattle on January 27, 1977 in exchange for the Nets' 1979 fourth-round pick, which became James Donaldson, plus cash. Pro Sports Transactions preserves the same media-guide account while flagging conflicting historical descriptions. Basketball-Reference's team and league ledgers record New York selling the rights attached to Donaldson to Seattle on that date, and Bantom's player ledger records Seattle selling his rights to New York. Taken together, the sources support the canonical Bantom-for-pick-and-cash package while explaining why individual ledgers describe the two sides as sales.

Bantom Was Excellent for 33 Nets Games

Bantom played 33 games for New York after the transaction. He totaled 614 points and 285 rebounds, which works out to 18.6 points and 8.6 rebounds per game, while logging 33.8 minutes. That was strong immediate production for a Nets team going through a difficult first NBA season.

The Nets Did Not Keep Him Beyond the Season

Bantom became a veteran free agent after the season and signed with Buffalo on September 1, 1977. New Jersey received a future fourth-round pick as compensation. Because the primary compensation ledger used here does not identify the eventual selection, this review credits the Nets with the existence of that downstream draft asset without inventing a player outcome.

The Fourth-Round Pick Became James Donaldson

Seattle's incoming 1979 fourth-round pick landed at No. 73 and became James Donaldson. Donaldson spent 1979-80 playing professionally in Italy before joining the SuperSonics in 1980-81. He appeared in 68 games as a rookie, then played all 82 games in both 1981-82 and 1982-83. Across those three Seattle seasons he logged 232 regular-season games.

Donaldson Became a Useful Seattle Center

His role grew each year. Donaldson averaged 5.3 points and 4.5 rebounds in 1980-81, 8.1 points and 6.0 rebounds in 1981-82, then 8.9 points and 6.1 rebounds in 1982-83. The late fourth-round pick therefore became a durable rotation center rather than a player who never reached the roster.

He Also Retained Downstream Trade Value

In August 1983 Seattle included Donaldson, Greg Kelser, Mark Radford and two draft picks in the trade that brought back Tom Chambers, Al Wood and additional picks from San Diego. The pick became No. 7 Bernard King. King was immediately an elite scorer for New Jersey, averaging 24.2 points and 9.5 rebounds as a rookie and 21.6 points the next season. Hillman later added 45 Nets games at 13.1 points and 7.5 rebounds. Indiana also received real value. Williamson averaged 20.7 points in 30 games that season and 19.1 in 42 games the next year before the Pacers traded him back to New Jersey for Bob Carrington plus 1980 and 1981 second-round picks. The 1980 pick became Louis Orr, who played 162 useful Pacers games. New Jersey still owns the stronger peak-value return because King became a top-line scorer, but Indiana's downstream branch makes this far closer than a one-sided loss.
perspectives.analysis:
The February Date Comes From the Team Media Guides

The historical ledgers require care. Indiana's official media guide records February 1, 1977 as the date the Pacers acquired John Williamson from the Nets for Darnell Hillman and a first-round pick. The Nets' own historical media guide separates the mechanics: New York traded Williamson on February 1 for Indiana's 1977 first-round pick and a player to be named, then received Hillman in April to complete the deal. Basketball-Reference lists the completed transaction under April. This review preserves February 1 as the parent-trade date while treating Hillman's April delivery as part of the same exchange.

The First-Round Pick Became Bernard King

New Jersey used the No. 7 pick on Bernard King. His impact was immediate. King played 79 games as a rookie and averaged 24.2 points and 9.5 rebounds, finishing third in Rookie of the Year voting. He followed with all 82 games in 1978-79 and scored 1,769 points, or 21.6 per game. Across two Nets seasons he played 161 games and scored 3,678 points.

Hillman Added Another Useful Nets Piece

Hillman did not join the Nets until the following season, but he supplied real frontcourt production once he arrived. In 1977-78 he played 45 games for New Jersey and averaged 13.1 points and 7.5 rebounds. The Nets then traded him to Denver in January 1978 for a 1979 second-round pick that became Clint Richardson. Because Hillman directly produced that pick, this review credits the draft asset as downstream value without assigning unrelated later moves to him.

Williamson Was a High-Volume Indiana Scorer

The Pacers did not receive a marginal player. Williamson played 30 games after the trade in 1976-77, started 28 and averaged 20.7 points. He returned for 42 more Pacers games in 1977-78 and averaged 19.1 points. Across the two partial seasons he scored 1,424 points in 72 regular-season games.

Indiana Then Recycled Williamson Into Three More Assets

On January 27, 1978, Indiana traded Williamson back to New Jersey for Bob Carrington, a 1980 second-round pick and a 1981 second-round pick. Carrington played 35 games for the Pacers that season. The 1980 pick became Louis Orr, who played all 82 games as a rookie and 80 more in 1981-82 while averaging 10.5 and 11.5 points. The 1981 pick became Brian Jackson, who did not play an NBA regular-season game. That downstream package materially improves Indiana's side of the original evaluation.

King's Nets Tenure Was Great but Not Permanent

New Jersey traded King in October 1979 with Jim Boylan and John Gianelli to Utah for Rich Kelley. This review does not credit the full Kelley return to King because two other players were included. The trade still demonstrates that King's value had not disappeared after his two high-scoring Nets seasons.

Final Verdict

Nets Edge, A/B+. New Jersey receives an A because the No. 7 pick became an immediate 20-plus-point scorer in King, while Hillman added 45 productive games and another second-round asset. Indiana receives a B+ because Williamson was a 20-point scorer for 72 games and his resale produced Carrington plus the pick that became Louis Orr, a useful two-year Pacers forward. King's peak scoring gives the Nets the stronger realized return, but Indiana's downstream value makes the gap moderate rather than overwhelming. Confidence is high on the assets and outcomes, with the parent date anchored to the team media guides.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Describe a Player-Rights Sale

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Buffalo and NBA transaction pages agree on February 1, 1977. Buffalo sold Claude Terry's player rights to Atlanta. The Braves had signed Terry as a free agent on October 21, 1976, so the February transaction converted a player the club had held for a little more than three months into financial consideration.

The Cash Amount Is Not Identified in the Primary Ledgers

Atlanta's canonical record represents the outgoing side as cash, which is consistent with Basketball-Reference's sale language. The amount is not specified in the primary transaction ledgers used for this review. That means Buffalo receives credit for a real financial return, but the grade does not invent a dollar value or treat the cash as though it became a later player or draft asset.

Terry Immediately Received a Larger Atlanta Role

Terry had played 33 games for Buffalo in 1976-77, averaging 9.2 minutes and 3.5 points. After the sale, he appeared in 12 games for Atlanta and averaged 20.1 minutes and 9.3 points while shooting 54.0 percent from the field. The Hawks therefore received more immediate on-court use from him than Buffalo had been getting before the transaction.

His Second Atlanta Season Was Smaller

Terry returned for 27 games in 1977-78, but his role dropped to 6.1 minutes per game and 2.2 points. Across the two Atlanta seasons he appeared in 39 regular-season games, played 407 minutes and scored 171 points. Those totals establish a genuine but limited basketball return.

There Is No Major Downstream Asset Chain

Terry's NBA career ended after the 1977-78 season. Atlanta did not turn him into a documented later player or draft pick in the source set used here. Buffalo's side is similarly limited to the sale proceeds. This review therefore remains a narrow comparison between two seasons of modest Atlanta production and an unspecified cash return.

Final Verdict

Hawks Edge, B-/C+. Atlanta receives a B- because a cash-only acquisition produced 39 games, including a productive 12-game stretch immediately after the sale, without costing a basketball asset. Buffalo receives a C+ because selling Terry created financial value and removed a player who had been playing only 9.2 minutes per game for the Braves, but the unidentified cash amount cannot be credited with a known basketball outcome. The gap is small and the stakes are low. Confidence is high on the transaction structure and Terry's Atlanta production, while the precise cash value remains unknown.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Phoenix acquired Bayard Forrest's rights from Seattle on March 18, 1977 for the Suns' 1979 second-round pick, with Pro Sports Transactions also recording cash going to Seattle. Forrest remained unsigned for the rest of 1976-77, then played 139 regular-season games for Phoenix across the next two seasons, totaling 569 points and 565 rebounds before a back injury wiped out 1979-80 and ended his NBA career. Seattle did not use the incoming pick itself. The No. 42 selection eventually became Paul Mokeski after the SuperSonics bundled that pick with a 1980 second-rounder to Houston for John Johnson in October 1977. Johnson then played 333 regular-season games for Seattle, including all 82 games as a starter on the 1979 championship team. Because the Forrest-derived pick was only one component of the Johnson package, Seattle receives partial downstream credit rather than Johnson's full value. That still gives Seattle the stronger realized result.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Core Package Was Forrest for a 1979 Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers agree on the March 18, 1977 core exchange. Phoenix sent its 1979 second-round pick to Seattle for Bayard Forrest. Pro Sports Transactions' 1979 draft ledger also records cash going from Phoenix to Seattle. The cash amount is not specified in the sources used for this review.

Forrest Did Not Play Until the Following Season

Forrest had been Seattle's second-round selection in the 1976 draft but did not play in the NBA during 1976-77. His Phoenix career began in 1977-78. He appeared in 64 games that season, averaging 13.9 minutes, 4.2 points and 3.9 rebounds. He also appeared in one playoff game.

His Second Suns Season Was More Durable

Forrest played 75 games in 1978-79, averaging 16.6 minutes, 4.0 points and 4.2 rebounds. He appeared in 14 playoff games as Phoenix reached the Western Conference Finals, including the seven-game series against Seattle. Across two regular seasons with the Suns, Forrest totaled 139 games, 569 points and 565 rebounds.

A Back Injury Ended the Phoenix Return

Basketball-Reference lists Forrest as missing the entire 1979-80 season with a back injury. He never returned to an NBA regular-season game. Phoenix therefore received two seasons of reserve-center production and meaningful playoff availability, but no longer-term asset branch.

Seattle Reused the Incoming Pick Before the Draft

The 1979 second-rounder later landed at No. 42, where Paul Mokeski was selected. Mokeski never played for Seattle because the SuperSonics had already traded the pick. On October 22, 1977, Seattle sent that 1979 second-rounder plus a 1980 second-round pick to Houston for John Johnson. Pro Sports Transactions' draft ledger confirms the Phoenix-to-Seattle and Seattle-to-Houston chain.

Johnson Became a Major Seattle Rotation Piece

Johnson played 76 games for Seattle in 1977-78, then started all 82 games in 1978-79 as the SuperSonics won the NBA championship. He remained with Seattle through 1981-82, totaling 333 regular-season appearances across five seasons. Because the Forrest-derived pick was only one of two second-rounders used to acquire Johnson, this review does not assign all of Johnson's production to this transaction. The pick still had clear downstream utility as one half of a successful trade package.

Final Verdict

Sonics Edge, B+/B. Seattle receives a B+ because the incoming second-round pick and cash retained enough value for the pick to become part of the John Johnson acquisition, which supported a championship core. Phoenix receives a B because Forrest supplied 139 games and 15 playoff appearances across two seasons before injury ended his career. The Seattle edge is meaningful but not overwhelming because the Johnson return required an additional second-round pick. Confidence is high on the core trade, Forrest's production and the pick's downstream path, while the cash amount remains unspecified.

perspectives.summary: Denver and Seattle completed a six-asset trade on May 24, 1977. The Nuggets received Tom Burleson, Bob Wilkerson and the 1977 second-round pick that became No. 30 Steve Sheppard; Seattle received Paul Silas, Marvin Webster and Willie Wise. Denver quickly recycled two incoming assets, sending Burleson and the Sheppard pick to Kansas City the next day for Brian Taylor and the No. 9 pick used on Tom LaGarde. Wilkerson then played 236 regular-season games for Denver across three seasons. Seattle's side had the higher peak. Silas played all 82 games in three consecutive seasons and was part of the 1979 championship team. Webster played all 82 games in 1977-78 and 22 playoff games during Seattle's run to the NBA Finals, then his 1978 free-agent departure triggered an arranged compensation exchange that brought Lonnie Shelton and the 1979 first-round pick used on Vinnie Johnson. Seattle gets the stronger hindsight grade.
perspectives.analysis:
The Core Package Is Fully Confirmed

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Seattle and league transaction ledgers all record the May 24, 1977 exchange the same way. Denver sent Paul Silas, Marvin Webster and Willie Wise to Seattle for Tom Burleson, Bob Wilkerson and Seattle's 1977 second-round pick, which became No. 30 Steve Sheppard. The structure is unusually useful for hindsight analysis because nearly every major asset produced either direct playing time or a traceable downstream branch.

Denver Immediately Recycled Burleson and the Pick

The Nuggets did not hold Burleson or the Sheppard pick through the draft. One day later Denver traded both to Kansas City for Brian Taylor and a 1977 first-round pick that became No. 9 Tom LaGarde. That means Burleson and the incoming second-rounder should be evaluated together as one downstream package rather than as separate Denver tenures. Taylor played 39 regular-season games for Denver in 1977-78, while LaGarde played 77. The two incoming assets therefore became another useful two-player package almost immediately.

Wilkerson Was the Long-Term Denver Piece

Bob Wilkerson became the clearest direct return for the Nuggets. He played 81 games in 1977-78, 80 in 1978-79 and 75 in 1979-80. Across those three seasons he appeared in 236 regular-season games for Denver and scored 2,358 points. He also played 16 playoff games for the Nuggets over the first two seasons. Denver therefore received both durable direct production and a successful next-day asset conversion.

Silas Became a Three-Year Seattle Rotation Mainstay

Paul Silas played all 82 games in each of his first three Seattle seasons, giving the SuperSonics 246 regular-season appearances from 1977-78 through 1979-80. He also appeared in 54 playoff games during that stretch. Most importantly, Silas was part of the 1978-79 championship team and appeared in all 17 playoff games during Seattle's title run.

Webster Powered the 1978 Finals Run

Marvin Webster played all 82 regular-season games for Seattle in 1977-78 and then appeared in 22 postseason games as the SuperSonics reached the NBA Finals. His playoff workload included every game of the first round, conference semifinals, conference finals and seven-game Finals. Webster left after the season as a veteran free agent, but that departure produced another traceable branch.

The Webster Compensation Branch Added More Value

When Webster signed with the Knicks in September 1978, Seattle and New York completed an arranged compensation exchange. Seattle sent a 1981 first-round pick to New York and received Lonnie Shelton plus a 1979 first-round pick that became Vinnie Johnson. Shelton immediately played 76 regular-season games and 17 playoff games for the 1979 champions. Johnson later played 119 regular-season games for Seattle across two seasons. This review credits that compensation branch while also acknowledging that Seattle surrendered a future first-round pick to complete it.

Wise Was the Smallest Seattle Asset

Willie Wise played only two games for Seattle before being waived in November 1977. His minimal contribution does not materially change the evaluation.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, A+/A. Denver receives an A because Wilkerson supplied 236 games and the Burleson-Sheppard branch quickly became Taylor plus LaGarde. Seattle receives an A+ because Silas provided three full seasons and championship value, Webster helped drive a Finals run, and Webster's departure produced Shelton and the pick used on Vinnie Johnson through a documented compensation exchange. Both teams extracted real value, but Seattle's combination of Finals impact, a championship contributor and downstream compensation gives it the stronger realized outcome. Confidence is high.

Kansas City received 169 games from Burleson and later received a 1981 second-round compensation pick when he signed with Atlanta. That pick became No. 29 Eddie Johnson, who played 483 games and scored 9,027 points for the Kings franchise through 1986-87. The second-round-pick side has conflicting historical ownership ledgers, so this review does not credit Kansas City with Steve Sheppard's Chicago career. Kansas City still wins on realized value.
perspectives.analysis:
The Core Trade Is Clear, but the Second-Round Pick Needs a Source Note

Denver, Kansas City and the NBA transaction ledgers agree on the May 25, 1977 framework: Denver sent Tom Burleson plus a 1977 second-round pick and received Brian Taylor plus Kansas City's 1977 first-round pick. The first-rounder became No. 9 Tom LaGarde. The second-rounder is commonly attached to No. 30 Steve Sheppard in the transaction ledger, but Chicago's own history lists the Bulls as the team that drafted Sheppard and Sheppard's player ledger traces a prior Kansas City-to-Chicago future-pick obligation from 1975. This review preserves that conflict and does not award Sheppard's NBA production to the Kings.

Taylor Was Valuable but Short-Lived in Denver

Brian Taylor played 39 games for Denver in 1977-78 and earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition. His direct tenure was short, but it retained downstream value. Taylor later signed with San Diego as a veteran free agent, and Denver received two 1979 second-round picks as compensation. Those picks became Lawrence Butler and Gary Garland. Butler never produced NBA regular-season value for Denver, but Garland played 78 games for the Nuggets in 1979-80.

LaGarde Produced One Season and Another First-Round Asset

Denver used the No. 9 pick on Tom LaGarde. He played 77 regular-season games as a rookie and appeared in nine playoff games during Denver's run to the 1978 Western Conference Finals. In June 1978 the Nuggets traded LaGarde to Seattle for a 1978 first-round pick that became No. 17 Rod Griffin. Griffin was drafted by Denver but never played an NBA regular-season game, so the LaGarde branch generated draft capital without a later NBA player return.

Burleson Gave Kansas City Three Seasons

Tom Burleson played 76 games for Kansas City in 1977-78, 56 in 1978-79 and 37 in 1979-80. That is 169 regular-season appearances and 1,884 points across three seasons. His role declined over time, but the Kings received substantially more direct service from him than Denver received from either Taylor or LaGarde individually.

Burleson's Departure Produced the Biggest Downstream Asset

Atlanta signed Burleson as a veteran free agent in July 1980. Kansas City received a 1981 second-round pick as compensation, and that pick became No. 29 Eddie Johnson. Johnson immediately became a major franchise asset. He played 74 games as a rookie, then 82 games in each of the next five seasons spanning Kansas City and Sacramento. Across those six franchise seasons he appeared in 483 regular-season games and scored 9,027 points, including three consecutive seasons above 19 points per game from 1982-83 through 1984-85.

The Sheppard Ledger Conflict Stays Uncredited

The canonical trade record and several transaction pages associate the outgoing second-round pick with Sheppard, but Chicago's draft history shows the Bulls selecting him at No. 30 and his player ledger contains an older Kansas City-to-Chicago pick transaction. los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles traded Lucius Allen to Kansas City on June 1, 1977 for Ollie Johnson plus the Kings' 1978 first- and second-round picks. The Lakers never used the first-rounder on Purvis Short themselves: six weeks later they sent that pick and cash to Golden State as veteran-free-agent compensation for Jamaal Wilkes. Wilkes became a core Lakers scorer on the 1980 and 1982 championship teams. Johnson also became a downstream asset before playing for Los Angeles, going to Atlanta for Lou Hudson, who gave the Lakers 160 games and 1,891 points across two seasons. The second-round pick became No. 26 Ron Carter, who played 46 Lakers games. Kansas City received useful immediate production from Allen, who played 108 games across two seasons and averaged 11.9 points and 4.7 assists in 1977-78, but his NBA career ended after 1978-79. The Lakers' three-branch return produced far more lasting value.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Agree on a Three-Asset Lakers Return

Basketball-Reference's Los Angeles, Kansas City and league transaction ledgers all record the June 1, 1977 exchange the same way. The Lakers sent Lucius Allen to the Kings for Ollie Johnson, Kansas City's 1978 first-round pick and Kansas City's 1978 second-round pick. The draft slots later became No. 5 Purvis Short and No. 26 Ron Carter, but the first-round branch requires an important correction: Los Angeles did not draft Short.

The No. 5 Pick Became Part of the Jamaal Wilkes Compensation Package

On July 11, 1977, the Lakers signed Jamaal Wilkes as a veteran free agent from Golden State. Los Angeles sent cash and the 1978 first-round pick acquired in this trade to the Warriors as compensation. Golden State later used that pick on Short. This review therefore does not credit Short's Warriors career to the Lakers. It credits the pick as one component of the compensation package that brought Wilkes to Los Angeles.

That downstream use was enormously valuable. Wilkes immediately played 51 games for the Lakers in 1977-78 and earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition. He then played all 82 games in 1978-79, 1979-80 and 1981-82, with 81 games in 1980-81. In the 1980 championship run he averaged 21.3 points in the six-game NBA Finals against Philadelphia. Two years later he averaged 19.7 points in another six-game Finals win over Philadelphia. Because cash was also part of the free-agent compensation, this review treats Wilkes as a major shared downstream return rather than assigning every ounce of his Lakers value to the pick alone.

Johnson Turned Into Two Full Seasons of Lou Hudson

Ollie Johnson never played a regular-season game for Los Angeles after the trade. On September 30, 1977, the Lakers sent him to Atlanta for Lou Hudson. Hudson then appeared in all 82 games in 1977-78, averaging 13.7 points, and played 78 more games in 1978-79 at 9.8 points. Across two Lakers seasons he totaled 160 regular-season games and 1,891 points. The Johnson branch therefore produced a meaningful veteran return even though Johnson himself never suited up for the Lakers.

The Second-Round Pick Produced a Lakers Reserve

Los Angeles kept the 1978 second-round pick and selected Ron Carter at No. 26. Carter played 46 regular-season games for the Lakers in 1978-79 and appeared twice in the playoffs. His role was modest, but the pick produced actual roster value rather than expiring unused.

Allen Gave Kansas City One Strong Season and a Short Second Year

Allen started the trade's other side with a useful 1977-78 season. He played 77 games for Kansas City, averaging 11.9 points and 4.7 assists in 27.9 minutes. He returned for 31 games in 1978-79 at 5.1 points and 1.4 assists, then his NBA career ended. Basketball-Reference lists no later Allen transaction producing another Kansas City player or draft asset, so this review stops the branch there.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A+/B-. Los Angeles receives an A+ because all three incoming branches created realized value: the first-round pick helped secure Wilkes, Johnson became two productive Hudson seasons, and the second-rounder became Carter. Kansas City receives a B- because Allen supplied 108 games and a useful first season, but there was no comparable downstream asset after his short tenure. The gap is large without pretending the Lakers directly drafted Short or that the Wilkes compensation consisted of the pick alone. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: This June 7, 1977 Cleveland-Buffalo record is not a supported NBA transaction. The legacy archive record says Cleveland sent Jim Cleamons to Buffalo for John Gianelli and a 1977 first-round pick, but the Cavaliers, Braves and league transaction ledgers record no such exchange. Cleamons remained a Cleveland player until October 10, 1977, when he signed with New York as a veteran free agent and the Cavaliers received Walt Frazier as compensation. Gianelli likewise remained with Buffalo until September 2, 1977, when the Braves traded him to Milwaukee for a 1979 first-round pick that became Roy Hamilton. Cleveland's 1977 draft history contains no first-round selection; its first pick was No. 33 Eddie Jordan in round two. Buffalo's documented June 7 move was its separate first-round-pick exchange with Milwaukee. The legacy Cleamons-Gianelli-pick record is therefore retained only as provenance and receives no winner or grades.
perspectives.analysis:
The June 7 Cleveland-Buffalo Trade Does Not Appear in the Primary Ledgers

The legacy archive entry claims Cleveland traded Jim Cleamons to the Buffalo Braves on June 7, 1977 for John Gianelli and a 1977 first-round pick. Basketball-Reference's Cleveland transaction log does not contain that move. Buffalo's transaction log does not contain it either, and the league-wide 1976-77 transaction ledger has no Cleveland-Buffalo transaction involving Cleamons or Gianelli on June 7.

Cleamons Stayed With Cleveland Until October

Cleamons's own transaction history directly contradicts the legacy trade. Basketball-Reference records his 1972 move from the Lakers to Cleveland, then no transaction until October 10, 1977. On that date the New York Knicks signed Cleamons as a veteran free agent and sent Walt Frazier to Cleveland as compensation. The Knicks' team ledger and the 1977-78 league ledger independently record the same free-agent compensation transaction. A June sale to Buffalo would be incompatible with Cleveland still owning Cleamons's veteran-free-agent compensation rights in October.

Gianelli Stayed With Buffalo Until September

Gianelli's transaction history creates the same contradiction on the other side. The Knicks had traded Gianelli and cash to Buffalo for Bob McAdoo and Tom McMillen on December 9, 1976. He remained a Braves asset through the summer. On September 2, 1977, Buffalo traded Gianelli to Milwaukee for a 1979 first-round pick that became Roy Hamilton. Milwaukee's transaction ledger and the 1977-78 league ledger both preserve that September move. There is no intervening Cleveland transaction.

The Claimed 1977 First-Round Pick Cannot Be Reconciled

Cleveland's draft history shows no Cavaliers first-round selection in the 1977 draft. The team's first listed choice was Eddie Jordan at No. 33 in round two. los-angeles-clippers.summary: Buffalo moved the 1977 No. 3 pick to Milwaukee on June 7, 1977 for Swen Nater and the first-round pick that would land at No. 13. The Bucks used No. 3 on Marques Johnson, who played 524 regular-season games for Milwaukee across seven seasons, made four All-Star teams and earned three All-NBA selections before retaining major trade value in the 1984 package for Terry Cummings, Craig Hodges and Ricky Pierce. Buffalo also received substantial value. Nater played 78 games for the Braves and 348 more after the franchise moved to San Diego, giving the franchise 426 games of elite rebounding production before he was included with Byron Scott in the 1983 Norm Nixon trade. Buffalo did not keep the No. 13 pick: three days after this deal it sent that pick to Chicago for No. 24 Larry Johnson, whose NBA career lasted four Braves games. Milwaukee still owns the stronger peak and long-term return, but Buffalo's Nater branch makes this far better than a lopsided loss.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The June 7 Package Is Fully Confirmed

Buffalo, Milwaukee and the league transaction ledgers agree on the core exchange. The Braves sent the 1977 first-round pick that became No. 3 Marques Johnson to Milwaukee. The Bucks sent Swen Nater plus the first-round pick that became No. 13 Tate Armstrong to Buffalo. The trade happened three days before the draft, so the pick identities were not yet actual drafted players when the teams exchanged them.

Buffalo's No. 13 Pick Became a Different Asset Before the Draft

The stale version of this record credits Buffalo with Tate Armstrong as though the Braves drafted and kept him. They did not. On June 10, Buffalo traded the No. 13 pick to Chicago for a second-round pick. Chicago then drafted Armstrong at No. 13, while Buffalo used the incoming second-rounder at No. 24 on Larry Johnson. Armstrong's own transaction history confirms the full chain from Buffalo to Milwaukee, back to Buffalo, then to Chicago.

Johnson provided almost no NBA return. Basketball-Reference's 1977 draft ledger lists him as Buffalo's No. 24 selection, and his player page records only four regular-season games, 38 minutes and six points before his NBA career ended in 1977-78. This review therefore credits Buffalo with the actual Johnson outcome rather than Armstrong's Chicago career.

Nater Was a Major Franchise Return

Nater supplied far more value. He played 78 games for Buffalo in 1977-78 and averaged 15.5 points and 13.2 rebounds in 35.6 minutes per game. After the franchise moved to San Diego, he stayed for six more seasons and appeared in 348 Clippers games. Across the Buffalo and San Diego portions of the same franchise, that is 426 regular-season games.

His rebounding remained a defining part of his value. He averaged 8.9 rebounds in 1978-79, then continued as a major frontcourt piece through the early 1980s. Basketball-Reference's franchise split lists 348 San Diego appearances alone, on top of the 78 Buffalo games from his first season after the trade.

Nater Also Retained Downstream Trade Value

On October 10, 1983, San Diego traded Nater and the rights to Byron Scott to the Lakers for Norm Nixon, Eddie Jordan and two future second-round picks. The Clippers then used those two picks in another trade for Ricky Pierce one week later. Nater clearly remained part of a valuable package, but this review does not assign the whole Nixon or Pierce return to him because Byron Scott and other assets were also involved.

Marques Johnson Became Milwaukee's Franchise Star

Milwaukee used the No. 3 pick on Marques Johnson. He played 80 games as a rookie, then 77, 77, 76, 60, 80 and 74 over the next six seasons. That is 524 regular-season games in seven Bucks seasons. Johnson made four All-Star teams during that run and earned All-NBA First Team in 1979-80 plus All-NBA Second Team in 1980-81 and 1981-82. He also became the central scorer on the teams that restored Milwaukee to sustained playoff contention after the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar era.

Johnson's Value Extended Into a Major 1984 Trade

Milwaukee did not lose Johnson for nothing. On September 29, 1984, the Bucks traded Johnson, Junior Bridgeman, Harvey Catchings and cash to the Clippers for Terry Cummings, Craig Hodges and Ricky Pierce. Johnson was one piece of a multi-asset outgoing package, so this review does not credit the entire incoming trio to him. His inclusion nevertheless demonstrates that the No. 3 pick still carried major transaction value seven years after the original Buffalo deal.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win, A+/A-. Milwaukee receives an A+ because the No. 3 pick became a seven-year franchise star with four All-Star selections, three All-NBA honors and substantial later trade value. Buffalo receives an A- because Nater gave the franchise 426 games across Buffalo and San Diego, including elite first-season rebounding, and remained part of a major 1983 trade package. The recast No. 13 pick produced only four NBA games from Larry Johnson, which limits that branch. Buffalo received a very good return; Milwaukee simply converted the premium draft slot into the best player and the stronger peak outcome. Confidence is high.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston traded John Johnson to Boston on June 9, 1977 for two second-round picks, then somehow kept the picks and regained Johnson's rights before the next season. The first pick became No. 34 Larry Moffett, who played 20 Rockets games. The second became No. 28 Buster Matheney, who never played an NBA game. On October 18, Boston sold Johnson's rights back to Houston while the Rockets retained both picks. Four days later Houston sent Johnson to Seattle for two more second-round picks. Those became No. 42 Paul Mokeski and No. 43 Billy Williams. The Houston ledger explicitly notes that Johnson returned to the Rockets while Houston kept the draft picks from the June 9 trade. The amount of cash Boston received is not listed in the cited ledgers, so this review does not invent a dollar value or treat the return as zero.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The legacy archive entry is dated June 9, 1977, but Buffalo, Los Angeles and the league transaction ledgers all place the deal on June 10. The Braves sent a 1977 third-round pick to the Lakers for Johnny Neumann. Los Angeles used the pick at No. 46 on James Edwards, who immediately played 25 Lakers games at 14.8 points and 7.2 rebounds per game. In December, the Lakers packaged Edwards with Earl Tatum and cash for Adrian Dantley and Dave Robisch; Dantley then played 116 regular-season games for Los Angeles across the next two seasons, though that full downstream value cannot be assigned to Edwards alone. Buffalo received no post-trade regular-season games from Neumann. los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Authoritative Ledgers Put the Trade on June 10

The legacy archive record carries a June 9, 1977 date, but the Buffalo, Los Angeles and league transaction ledgers all list the exchange on June 10. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

The package itself is clear. Buffalo sent a 1977 third-round pick to Los Angeles for Johnny Neumann. The Lakers used the pick at No. 46 on James Edwards.

Edwards Immediately Produced for Los Angeles

Edwards was not a throwaway third-round selection. As a 22-year-old rookie, he played 25 Lakers games before the December trade, averaging 14.8 points and 7.2 rebounds in 28.9 minutes. He scored 370 points and grabbed 180 rebounds in that short Los Angeles stint.

That alone creates far more realized value than Buffalo received from Neumann after the June transaction. Edwards also retained meaningful trade value almost immediately.

The Edwards Branch Helped Bring Adrian Dantley and Dave Robisch

On December 13, 1977, the Lakers traded Edwards, Earl Tatum and cash to Indiana for Adrian Dantley and Dave Robisch. This review does not assign the entire Dantley-Robisch return to Edwards because Tatum and cash were also outgoing assets. Edwards was nevertheless one of the named pieces in the package and had already established himself as a productive rookie.

Dantley then gave Los Angeles major scoring production. He played 56 regular-season games for the Lakers in 1977-78 at 26.5 points per game and another 60 in 1978-79 at 19.4 points. Across those two seasons he appeared in 116 regular-season games for Los Angeles. Robisch added frontcourt depth as part of the same return. The downstream package therefore reinforces the value of the No. 46 pick without requiring this review to pretend Edwards alone purchased Dantley.

Neumann Never Played a Post-Trade Game for Buffalo

Neumann's history is unusual because Buffalo had already signed him in September 1976, played him in four games, waived him in November and watched the Lakers sign him nine days later. The June 1977 transaction brought him back to the Braves, but he did not appear in a Buffalo regular-season game after that reacquisition.

On October 18, 1977, Buffalo traded Neumann to Indiana for a 1978 third-round pick. The Pacers used Neumann in 20 games before waiving him in December, but those games belong to Indiana rather than Buffalo.

The Replacement Pick Produced No NBA Value

Buffalo used the 1978 third-round pick at No. 48 on Mike Santos. His Basketball-Reference page records the draft transaction but no NBA regular-season career. The Neumann branch therefore ends with no post-trade Buffalo games from Neumann and no NBA games from the replacement pick.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A-/F. Los Angeles receives an A- because a third-round pick became a productive rookie who averaged 14.8 points and 7.2 rebounds in 25 Lakers games and then served as one component of the Dantley-Robisch trade. Buffalo receives an F because Neumann produced no post-trade Braves games and the pick acquired for him became a player with no NBA regular-season appearances. The only caution is downstream attribution: Dantley's full Lakers production cannot be credited to Edwards alone because Tatum and cash were also part of that December package. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: Chicago moved up from the 1977 No. 24 pick to No. 13 by sending Buffalo the second-round slot plus $150,000 in cash. Basketball-Reference confirms the pick-for-pick exchange, while Pro Sports Transactions supplies the cash component. The Bulls used No. 13 on Tate Armstrong, who played 92 games across two Chicago seasons and scored 350 points. Armstrong then retained downstream value in 1979 when Chicago sent him with cash to San Antonio as veteran-free-agent compensation for Coby Dietrick. Dietrick played 235 regular-season games for the Bulls across three seasons, although this review does not credit all of that return to Armstrong because cash was also part of the compensation. Buffalo used No. 24 on Larry Johnson, whose entire NBA career consisted of four Braves games, 38 minutes and six points. The Braves also received the documented $150,000, but the player outcome was minimal. Chicago gets the stronger realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Pick Exchange Is Confirmed, and the Cash Comes From a Separate Ledger

Chicago, Buffalo and the league transaction logs all agree on the June 10, 1977 pick swap. The Bulls sent the second-round pick that became No. 24 Larry Johnson to the Braves and received the first-round pick that became No. 13 Tate Armstrong.

Those Basketball-Reference ledgers do not list cash. Pro Sports Transactions' 1977 draft-pick ledger adds the financial term, recording that Chicago also sent $150,000 to Buffalo. This review preserves that source distinction instead of presenting the cash as though every ledger independently reported it.

Armstrong Gave Chicago Two Seasons of Direct Production

Chicago used the No. 13 pick on Armstrong. He played 66 games as a rookie in 1977-78, averaging 4.3 points in 10.8 minutes. He returned for 26 games in 1978-79. Across his two Bulls seasons, Armstrong appeared in 92 regular-season games, logged 975 minutes, scored 350 points and handed out 105 assists.

That is modest first-round production, but it is still substantially more on-court value than Buffalo received from the player attached to the No. 24 pick.

Armstrong Also Retained Some Downstream Value

Chicago later used Armstrong in a veteran-free-agent compensation transaction. In 1979 the Bulls signed Coby Dietrick from San Antonio and sent Armstrong plus cash to the Spurs as compensation. Basketball-Reference and the Bulls' own historical transaction record both preserve that exchange.

Dietrick then became a useful Chicago rotation big. He played 79 games in 1979-80, 82 in 1980-81 and 74 in 1981-82, for 235 regular-season games across three Bulls seasons. He scored 1,138 points and grabbed 816 rebounds during that span.

This review does not assign the entire Dietrick return to Armstrong because the compensation package also included cash. The later transaction still demonstrates that Armstrong retained enough value to function as a named component in acquiring a veteran who gave Chicago three seasons.

Buffalo's No. 24 Pick Produced Almost Nothing

The Braves used the incoming second-round pick on Larry Johnson, the Kentucky guard born in 1954. His player ledger records only four NBA regular-season games, all for Buffalo in 1977-78. He played 38 total minutes, scored six points and was waived twice during the season.

Johnson's transaction history also confirms the exact pick chain. Buffalo had originally sent this future second-round pick to Chicago in 1974, then reacquired it in the Armstrong trade and drafted Johnson at No. 24. There was no meaningful later NBA player value from the pick.

The $150,000 Keeps Buffalo's Grade From the Bottom

Buffalo did receive a real financial asset. The $150,000 should not be erased simply because the player outcome failed. At the same time, there is no source-supported basketball conversion that lets this review trace that cash into another player or pick. It therefore counts as financial value without inventing a downstream roster branch.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, B+/D+. Chicago receives a B+ because No. 13 became 92 Armstrong games and Armstrong later remained useful in a compensation package that helped bring Dietrick, who played 235 Bulls games. Buffalo receives a D+ because No. 24 produced only four Johnson games, with the documented $150,000 providing the main remaining value. The gap is meaningful, but Chicago did not receive a star and the later Dietrick branch was not created by Armstrong alone. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix traded Dale Schlueter to Portland on July 15, 1977 for a 1978 fourth-round pick that became No. 88 Wayne Smith. Phoenix's contemporary media guide adds a conditional term: if Schlueter remained on Portland's active roster on December 1, the Suns would receive a third-round pick instead. Pro Sports Transactions records that conditional third as not exercised, while Basketball-Reference lists only the fourth-round pick. Portland received limited but real NBA production. Schlueter appeared in 10 Trail Blazers games in 1977-78, totaling 109 minutes, before retiring on April 24, 1978. Phoenix used No. 88 on Smith, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season career for him. Neither side generated meaningful long-term value, and the conditional pick created no second asset. Portland gets the slight edge because Schlueter at least supplied 10 games; the overall return was small for both teams.
perspectives.analysis:
The Basic Trade Is Confirmed Across Team and League Ledgers

Phoenix, Portland and the 1977-78 league transaction logs all record the July 15, 1977 exchange. The Suns sent Dale Schlueter to the Trail Blazers and received Portland's 1978 fourth-round pick. That pick eventually became No. 88 Wayne Smith.

The ordinary Basketball-Reference transaction pages stop there. A Phoenix media guide and Pro Sports Transactions preserve an additional conditional term that explains why the legacy archive entry contains a second draft-pick asset.

The Conditional Third-Round Pick Never Activated

Phoenix's 1979 media guide says the Suns would receive Portland's third-round pick instead of the fourth-rounder if Schlueter was on the Trail Blazers' active roster as of December 1, 1977. Pro Sports Transactions records the same condition and marks the conditional third-round pick as not exercised.

This review therefore treats the conditional pick as a contingent term, not as a second realized asset. The cited records establish that Phoenix ultimately received the fourth-round pick and did not receive a third-round selection from this condition. The exact roster-status mechanics behind the failed condition are not independently reconstructed here.

Schlueter Produced Ten Portland Games

Schlueter did make regular-season appearances for Portland in 1977-78. Basketball-Reference records 10 games and 109 minutes, with 25 points, 21 rebounds and 18 assists. He was a deep reserve rather than a meaningful rotation piece.

Portland's transaction log later records Schlueter's retirement on April 24, 1978. There is no subsequent player or draft return tied to his departure, so the Blazers' branch ends with those 10 games.

Phoenix's Pick Became Wayne Smith

The Suns kept the fourth-round pick and used it at No. 88 in the 1978 draft on Wayne Smith. Phoenix's draft ledger and Smith's player page both confirm the selection.

Smith never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Basketball-Reference lists him as a drafted rookie without an NBA playing career. That means Phoenix realized no on-court NBA value from the pick.

This Was a Low-Impact Exchange on Both Sides

Schlueter had previously played 39 games for Phoenix in 1976-77, but those Suns games occurred before the trade and are not part of Portland's return. Likewise, Smith's college background cannot substitute for NBA production that never materialized.

The difference between the teams is therefore narrow and based on actual realized service. Portland received 10 games from an aging veteran; Phoenix received a draft selection that produced no NBA games. The unused conditional third does not change the outcome.

Final Verdict

Blazers Edge, D+/F. Portland receives a D+ because Schlueter provided 10 regular-season games before retiring, a small but tangible return for a fourth-round pick. Phoenix receives an F because the realized pick became a player with no NBA regular-season appearances and the conditional upgrade was not exercised. The trade is low impact overall, so the grade gap should not be mistaken for major franchise value. Confidence is high.

Houston, Portland and the 1977-78 league transaction logs all list the August 10, 1977 trade as Tom Owens for Robin Jones. None of those Basketball-Reference ledgers mentions cash. Pro Sports Transactions separately records the same date and teams with Jones plus cash going to Houston for Owens.

This review therefore preserves the cash component while keeping the source distinction explicit. The amount is not stated in the cited transaction record, so the archive does not invent a dollar figure or assign a speculative roster conversion to it.

Owens Became a Four-Year Portland Contributor

The basketball outcome was much clearer. Owens played all 82 games for Portland in 1977-78, averaging 10.1 points and 6.6 rebounds. His role expanded dramatically in 1978-79, when he started all 82 games and averaged 18.5 points, 9.0 rebounds and 3.7 assists.

He remained productive for two more seasons. Owens played 76 games in 1979-80 at 16.4 points and 7.5 rebounds per game, then appeared in 79 games in 1980-81 at 10.6 points and 5.8 rebounds. Across those four Portland seasons he totaled 319 regular-season games, 4,437 points and 2,310 rebounds.

That direct return alone makes the trade far more valuable for Portland than the legacy preliminary grades suggested.

Owens Then Produced a Premium Future Pick

Portland retained trade value when Owens's playing tenure ended. On June 5, 1981, the Trail Blazers traded him to Indiana for a 1984 first-round pick. Basketball-Reference identifies that pick as the selection later used on Sam Bowie at No. 2 overall.

The Bowie outcome is complicated historically because injuries limited his Portland career, but the realized value was still substantial. Bowie played 139 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers, starting 101, and totaled 1,457 points and 1,122 rebounds. This review credits that direct draft result without importing later narratives about players Portland could have selected instead.

Jones Had a Very Short Houston Tenure

Robin Jones played 12 regular-season games for Houston in 1977-78, averaging 2.2 points and 1.2 rebounds in 5.5 minutes. The Rockets waived him on December 5, 1977, and his NBA career ended.

No later Houston player or draft asset is tied to Jones's departure in the cited transaction ledgers. His branch therefore stops with those 12 games.

The Cash Is Real but Not Traceable Further

Pro Sports Transactions gives Houston an additional asset in the form of cash. That keeps the Rockets' return from being evaluated as Jones alone. However, without an amount or a documented later conversion, the cash cannot be converted into invented on-court value for hindsight grading.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win, A+/D. Portland receives an A+ because Owens gave the franchise 319 productive regular-season games, including a 1,520-point season, then became the 1984 first-round pick used at No. 2 on Bowie. Houston receives a D because Jones lasted 12 games and was waived, with unspecified cash as the only remaining value. The source disagreement over whether the player ledgers display cash does not alter the basketball outcome; it only limits how precisely Houston's financial return can be valued. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded Tiny Archibald to Buffalo on September 1, 1977 and received center George Johnson plus two first-round picks. The legacy archive entry had omitted Buffalo's 1978 first, so this review restores the missing asset from the Nets, Braves and league transaction ledgers. Johnson played 240 regular-season games for New Jersey across three seasons. The 1978 pick became the No. 4 slot later used on Michael Ray Richardson, but the Nets traded that pick with another 1979 first to New York for Phil Jackson and the No. 13 pick used on Winford Boynes; Jackson and Boynes combined for 208 Nets games. Buffalo's 1979 first became No. 11 Cliff Robinson, who played 133 Nets games before being traded for Otis Birdsong and a second-round pick. Archibald never played a regular-season game for Buffalo because an Achilles injury cost him all of 1977-78, and his rights were later included in a multi-asset trade to Boston. The realized return decisively favored the Nets.
perspectives.analysis:
The legacy archive entry Was Missing an Entire First-Round Pick

New Jersey, Buffalo and the league transaction ledgers all record the September 1, 1977 deal the same way: the Nets sent Tiny Archibald to the Braves for George Johnson, Buffalo's 1978 first-round pick and Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick.

The legacy canonical record contained Johnson and the 1979 first but omitted the 1978 first entirely. This review repairs that structural error before grading the trade. The missing asset eventually became the No. 4 slot in the 1978 draft, where Michael Ray Richardson was selected after the pick changed hands again.

George Johnson Gave the Nets Three Full Seasons

Johnson immediately became New Jersey's starting-caliber interior anchor. He played 81 games in 1977-78 at 8.7 points, 9.6 rebounds and 3.4 blocks per game. He followed with 78 games in 1978-79 and 81 more in 1979-80.

That is 240 regular-season Nets games from one of the three incoming assets. When Johnson left for San Antonio as a veteran free agent in 1980, New Jersey also received a 1981 first-round compensation pick that became No. 18 Ray Tolbert. This review does not need that later branch to make the original return valuable, but it reinforces that Johnson retained asset value after his playing tenure.

The 1978 First Became a Trade-Up Currency Asset

New Jersey did not directly draft Richardson with Buffalo's 1978 first. On June 8, 1978, the Nets sent that pick plus their own 1979 first-rounder to the Knicks for Phil Jackson and the 1978 No. 13 pick that became Winford Boynes.

Jackson played 75 regular-season games for New Jersey over two seasons. Boynes played 133 Nets games and scored 1,191 points. Because another 1979 first was also outgoing, this review does not assign the entire Jackson-Boynes return to Buffalo's 1978 pick. The important point is that the restored asset was real premium trade currency, not an unused draft entry.

The 1979 First Became Cliff Robinson and Then Otis Birdsong

Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick landed at No. 11 and became Cliff Robinson. Robinson played 70 games for New Jersey as a rookie and 63 more in 1980-81, scoring 2,180 points across those two seasons.

In June 1981 the Nets traded Robinson to Kansas City for Otis Birdsong and a second-round pick. Birdsong became a long-term New Jersey guard, giving the Robinson branch substantial additional downstream value. That branch alone is far more productive than the single pick line in the legacy summary suggested.

Archibald Never Played for Buffalo

The Braves acquired a Hall of Fame-level guard, but the realized Buffalo outcome was brutal. Archibald missed the entire 1977-78 season with an Achilles injury, so Buffalo received zero regular-season games from him.

After the franchise moved to San Diego, the Clippers traded Archibald in August 1978 as part of a much larger package with Marvin Barnes, Billy Knight and two second-round picks to Boston for Kevin Kunnert, Kermit Washington, Sidney Wicks and Freeman Williams. Archibald therefore retained trade value, but this review cannot attribute that whole return to him because five assets went to Boston.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A+/D+. New Jersey receives an A+ because the club got 240 Johnson games, a premium 1978 first that helped produce Jackson and Boynes, and a 1979 first that became Robinson and later Birdsong. Buffalo receives a D+ because Archibald produced no Braves games and only later contributed as one component of a multi-asset Boston trade. The missing 1978 first materially changes the canonical record and makes the Nets' advantage much larger than the legacy archive entry showed. Confidence is high.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana sent Billy Knight to Buffalo on September 1, 1977 for Adrian Dantley and Mike Bantom. Knight gave the Braves immediate star production, averaging 22.9 points and 7.2 rebounds in 53 games and making the 1978 All-Star team. Indiana still extracted the larger team-specific return. Dantley played only 23 Pacers games, but averaged 26.5 points and 9.4 rebounds before being moved with Dave Robisch to the Lakers for James Edwards, Earl Tatum and cash. Bantom became the durable core of the deal, playing 240 regular-season games for Indiana across three seasons while averaging 15.4 points, 8.0 rebounds and 3.4 assists over that span. Buffalo later included Knight in the large August 1978 Boston trade with Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes and two second-round picks, so the full return from that deal cannot be credited to Knight alone. Buffalo got an excellent season; Indiana got three years of Bantom plus a valuable Dantley downstream branch.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Original Exchange Is Straightforward

Indiana, Buffalo and the league transaction ledgers all record the same September 1, 1977 deal: the Pacers sent Billy Knight to the Braves for Adrian Dantley and Mike Bantom. There is no draft-pick or cash ambiguity in the cited ledgers, so this review starts from a stable three-player transaction.

Buffalo Got an Immediate All-Star Season From Knight

Knight was already one of Indiana's best scorers before the trade, and he remained highly productive in Buffalo. He played 53 regular-season games for the Braves in 1977-78, averaging 22.9 points, 7.2 rebounds and 3.0 assists in 40.7 minutes. He also made the 1978 All-Star team.

That is a strong direct return. Buffalo did not merely acquire a famous name; it received one of the league's most productive forwards for most of a season.

Knight also retained transaction value when the franchise moved to San Diego. On August 4, 1978, the Clippers sent Knight, Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes and two second-round picks to Boston for Kevin Kunnert, Kermit Washington, Sidney Wicks and Freeman Williams. Because Knight was only one of five outgoing assets, this review does not assign that entire Boston package to him.

Bantom Became Indiana's Durable Return

The most important Pacers asset was Bantom. He played all 82 games in 1977-78, starting 78 and averaging 15.3 points, 7.4 rebounds and 2.9 assists. He followed with 81 games in 1978-79 at 17.0 points and 9.3 rebounds, then played 77 games in 1979-80 at 14.0 points, 7.0 rebounds and 4.3 assists.

Across those three Indiana seasons, Bantom appeared in 240 regular-season games. That kind of multi-year availability and production gives the Pacers a much longer realized return than Buffalo received from Knight before the franchise's next major reshuffle.

Dantley Added Elite Short-Term Production and a Downstream Trade Branch

Dantley's Pacers stay was brief but spectacular. He played 23 games, started all 23 and averaged 26.5 points, 9.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists in 41.2 minutes.

On December 13, 1977, Indiana traded Dantley and Dave Robisch to the Lakers for James Edwards, Earl Tatum and cash. Edwards became a productive young center for Indiana and Tatum played a regular role that season. This review does not credit the entire return to Dantley because Robisch was also outgoing, but Dantley was clearly one of the central pieces used to create that second asset cycle.

The Teams Both Got Real Value, but Indiana Got More of It

Buffalo's side should not be downgraded simply because Knight stayed only one season. His 53 games were high-level, All-Star-caliber production. The problem is that Indiana received both a productive three-year starter in Bantom and a 23-game scoring burst from Dantley before recycling Dantley into another useful package.

Final Verdict

Pacers Edge, A/B+. Indiana receives an A because Bantom produced 240 games over three seasons and Dantley added elite short-term production plus meaningful downstream trade value. Buffalo receives a B+ because Knight was excellent, made the All-Star team and remained part of a later blockbuster package, but his direct Braves tenure lasted only 53 games. The trade was productive for both teams; Indiana's advantage comes from depth and duration rather than Buffalo receiving a weak player. Confidence is high.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Buffalo traded John Gianelli to Milwaukee on September 2, 1977 for the Bucks' 1979 first-round pick. The legacy archive entry described the asset as a 1979-or-1980 first and also listed cash, but Buffalo, Milwaukee and the league transaction ledgers all specify a 1979 first and do not show cash; this review removes the unsupported cash term.
