The Bucks later packaged Gianelli with the 1979 first-round pick used on Calvin Natt to acquire Harvey Catchings from New Jersey, so that downstream return cannot be credited to Gianelli alone. Buffalo did not keep Milwaukee's first until draft night. On November 23, 1977, the Braves sent the pick with Gus Gerard and John Shumate to Detroit for Marvin Barnes plus 1978 second- and fourth-round picks. Detroit ultimately used the 1979 selection at No. 10 on Roy Hamilton. Milwaukee gets the slight realized-value edge.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The source-backed Package Is Gianelli for a 1979 First

Buffalo, Milwaukee and the 1977-78 league transaction ledgers all agree on the September 2, 1977 exchange: the Braves sent John Gianelli to the Bucks for Milwaukee's 1979 first-round pick. The legacy archive entry described the draft asset as a 1979-or-1980 first and also included cash.

The authoritative Basketball-Reference ledgers used for this review specify 1979 and do not list cash. No independent source in this review verified a cash component, so the canonical record is repaired to the documented one-for-one package rather than preserving an unsupported financial asset.

Gianelli Gave Milwaukee Two Full Seasons

Gianelli immediately became a dependable Bucks rotation big. He played all 82 games in 1977-78, logging 2,327 minutes and producing 693 points, 509 rebounds and 192 assists. He returned for all 82 games in 1978-79, adding 584 points, 408 rebounds and 160 assists.

Across the two seasons, Milwaukee received 164 regular-season games, 1,277 points, 917 rebounds and 352 assists. That is not star production, but it is substantial realized service for a future first-round pick.

Gianelli Also Retained Some Trade Value

On May 31, 1979, Milwaukee traded Gianelli and a separate 1979 first-round pick, later used on Calvin Natt, to New Jersey for Harvey Catchings. The move gives Gianelli a downstream branch, but it has to be handled carefully because the Bucks also surrendered a first-round selection.

This review therefore records the Catchings transaction as evidence that Gianelli still had trade value without assigning the entire return to him alone.

Buffalo Quickly Recycled the Milwaukee First

The Braves did not hold Milwaukee's 1979 first through the 1979 draft. On November 23, 1977, Buffalo sent Gus Gerard, John Shumate and the Bucks' first-round pick to Detroit for Marvin Barnes, a 1978 second-round pick later used on Lew Massey and a 1978 fourth-round pick later used on Larry Harris.

That package shows the Milwaukee first had useful market value, but three assets went to Detroit. This review cannot credit Barnes and both incoming picks solely to the first-rounder.

Detroit eventually retained the 1979 selection and used it at No. 10 on Roy Hamilton. Hamilton's later NBA production belongs to Detroit and Portland, not Buffalo, because Buffalo had traded the pick away more than a year before the draft.

The Difference Is Modest but Real

Milwaukee's return is easier to measure: 164 Gianelli games and two full seasons of rotation production. Buffalo's return is more indirect. The first-round pick became part of a November package that helped the Braves acquire Barnes and two draft choices, but the pick shared that transaction with Gerard and Shumate.

Final Verdict

Bucks Edge, B+/B. Milwaukee receives a B+ because Gianelli provided two complete seasons of useful frontcourt minutes and later remained a named component in another trade. Buffalo receives a B because the 1979 first was a valuable asset and helped support the Barnes package, but its specific downstream value is diluted by the two additional players Buffalo sent in that deal. This was not a lopsided transaction; Milwaukee simply received the clearer direct return. Confidence is high on the documented player-for-pick package and the downstream transactions.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana traded Don Buse to Phoenix for Ricky Sobers on September 6, 1977. Both guards produced real value, but Phoenix received the longer and more durable return. Sobers started all 160 games he played for Indiana across two seasons, averaging 18.2 points and 7.4 assists in 1977-78 and 17.3 points and 5.6 assists in 1978-79. He was then sent to Chicago as veteran-free-agent compensation after Indiana signed Mickey Johnson. Buse played 245 regular-season games for Phoenix across three seasons, starting 164 and earning All-Defensive First Team recognition in each season. In November 1980 Phoenix traded Buse back to Indiana for 1981 and 1982 second-round picks. The Suns later sent those two picks, plus a separate first-round swap concession, to Indiana for Dudley Bradley. Indiana got the better scorer for two years; Phoenix got three seasons of elite perimeter defense plus downstream draft value, giving the Suns a modest overall edge.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Trade Was a Straight Guard-for-Guard Swap

Indiana and Phoenix both list the September 6, 1977 deal identically: Don Buse went to the Suns and Ricky Sobers went to the Pacers. The league transaction ledger matches those team records. There are no picks, cash terms or conditions to reconcile at the original transaction point.

Sobers Gave Indiana Two High-Usage Starting Seasons

Sobers immediately became a full-time Pacers starter. In 1977-78 he played 79 games, started all 79 and averaged 18.2 points, 7.4 assists, 4.1 rebounds and 2.2 steals in 38.2 minutes. He followed with 81 starts in 1978-79, averaging 17.3 points and 5.6 assists.

Across the two seasons, Sobers played 160 regular-season games for Indiana and started every one of them. That is substantial direct value, especially for a team that had just moved Billy Knight one week earlier and was remaking its backcourt and scoring structure.

Sobers's Indiana tenure ended in July 1979 when he was sent to Chicago as veteran-free-agent compensation after the Pacers signed Mickey Johnson. This review treats that as a real asset-use event, but not as a conventional one-for-one trade return. Indiana's acquisition of Johnson required the compensation mechanism, so Sobers still carried value even though the transaction structure differs from a normal trade.

Buse Gave Phoenix Three Seasons and Elite Defense

Phoenix received the longer direct tenure. Buse played 82 games in 1977-78, 82 in 1978-79 and 81 in 1979-80, for 245 regular-season Suns games. He started 164 of those games and averaged roughly eight points with strong playmaking while taking the tougher defensive assignments.

More importantly, Basketball-Reference lists Buse as All-Defensive First Team in all three Phoenix seasons. In 1977-78 he averaged 4.8 assists and 2.3 steals; in 1978-79 he averaged 4.3 assists and 1.9 steals; in 1979-80 he averaged 4.0 assists and 1.6 steals. His scoring was lower than Sobers's, but his defensive impact and three-year availability gave Phoenix a different kind of sustained value.

Phoenix Then Turned Buse Into Two Second-Round Picks

On November 25, 1980, Phoenix traded Buse back to Indiana for a 1981 second-round pick that became Al Leslie and a 1982 second-round pick that became Jose Slaughter.

The Suns did not simply use both selections. On June 8, 1981, Phoenix sent those same two picks back to Indiana for Dudley Bradley while also relinquishing an option to swap first-round picks with the Pacers in 1983. Because that extra concession was part of the Bradley transaction, this review does not assign all of Bradley's value to the Buse-derived picks. Still, the picks clearly extended Buse's asset life beyond his 245 Phoenix games.

The Difference Is Longevity and Defensive Value

Indiana can make a strong case from offensive production alone. Sobers was the better scorer and higher-volume creator during the first two seasons after the trade. Phoenix's case is broader: Buse gave the Suns three full seasons, three All-Defensive First Team selections and then returned two second-round picks.

Final Verdict

Suns Edge, A-/B+. Phoenix receives an A- because Buse delivered 245 games, three All-Defensive First Team seasons and two later second-round assets. Indiana receives a B+ because Sobers delivered 160 starts with high-end scoring and playmaking over two seasons before being used as compensation in the Mickey Johnson signing. Both teams got substantial value, but Phoenix's extra season, defensive honors and downstream picks create the modest separation. Confidence is high.

Indiana got the better scorer for two years; Phoenix got three seasons of elite perimeter defense plus downstream draft value, giving the Suns a modest overall edge.
analysis:
The Trade Was a Straight Guard-for-Guard Swap

Indiana and Phoenix both list the September 6, 1977 deal identically: Don Buse went to the Suns and Ricky Sobers went to the Pacers. The league transaction ledger matches those team records. There are no picks, cash terms or conditions to reconcile at the original transaction point.

Sobers Gave Indiana Two High-Usage Starting Seasons

Sobers immediately became a full-time Pacers starter. In 1977-78 he played 79 games, started all 79 and averaged 18.2 points, 7.4 assists, 4.1 rebounds and 2.2 steals in 38.2 minutes. He followed with 81 starts in 1978-79, averaging 17.3 points and 5.6 assists.

Across the two seasons, Sobers played 160 regular-season games for Indiana and started every one of them. That is substantial direct value, especially for a team that had just moved Billy Knight one week earlier and was remaking its backcourt and scoring structure.

Sobers's Indiana tenure ended in July 1979 when he was sent to Chicago as veteran-free-agent compensation after the Pacers signed Mickey Johnson. This review treats that as a real asset-use event, but not as a conventional one-for-one trade return. Indiana's acquisition of Johnson required the compensation mechanism, so Sobers still carried value even though the transaction structure differs from a normal trade.

Buse Gave Phoenix Three Seasons and Elite Defense

Phoenix received the longer direct tenure. Buse played 82 games in 1977-78, 82 in 1978-79 and 81 in 1979-80, for 245 regular-season Suns games. He started 164 of those games and averaged roughly eight points with strong playmaking while taking the tougher defensive assignments.

More importantly, Basketball-Reference lists Buse as All-Defensive First Team in all three Phoenix seasons. In 1977-78 he averaged 4.8 assists and 2.3 steals; in 1978-79 he averaged 4.3 assists and 1.9 steals; in 1979-80 he averaged 4.0 assists and 1.6 steals. His scoring was lower than Sobers's, but his defensive impact and three-year availability gave Phoenix a different kind of sustained value.

Phoenix Then Turned Buse Into Two Second-Round Picks

On November 25, 1980, Phoenix traded Buse back to Indiana for a 1981 second-round pick that became Al Leslie and a 1982 second-round pick that became Jose Slaughter.

The Suns did not simply use both selections. On June 8, 1981, Phoenix sent those same two picks back to Indiana for Dudley Bradley while also relinquishing an option to swap first-round picks with the Pacers in 1983. Because that extra concession was part of the Bradley transaction, this review does not assign all of Bradley's value to the Buse-derived picks. Still, the picks clearly extended Buse's asset life beyond his 245 Phoenix games.

The Difference Is Longevity and Defensive Value

Indiana can make a strong case from offensive production alone. Sobers was the better scorer and higher-volume creator during the first two seasons after the trade. Phoenix's case is broader: Buse gave the Suns three full seasons, three All-Defensive First Team selections and then returned two second-round picks.

Final Verdict

Suns Edge, A-/B+. Phoenix receives an A- because Buse delivered 245 games, three All-Defensive First Team seasons and two later second-round assets. Indiana receives a B+ because Sobers delivered 160 starts with high-end scoring and playmaking over two seasons before being used as compensation in the Mickey Johnson signing. Both teams got substantial value, but Phoenix's extra season, defensive honors and downstream picks create the modest separation. Confidence is high.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Buffalo traded Ernie DiGregorio to the Lakers on September 7, 1977 for future considerations. The legacy archive entry labeled that return as possible cash, but the Lakers, Braves, league and executive transaction ledgers all use only “future considerations,” so this review removes the unsupported cash characterization. DiGregorio played 25 regular-season games for Los Angeles, averaging 3.9 points and 2.8 assists in 13.3 minutes per game. The Lakers waived him on January 30, 1978, and Boston signed him as a free agent two days later. No cited ledger identifies what Buffalo ultimately received from the future-considerations clause, so that side remains unresolved rather than being scored as confirmed cash or a specific draft asset. Los Angeles at least received a half-season of reserve guard service, but the return was short-lived. The Lakers receive the modest edge on documented realized value, with medium confidence because Buffalo’s consideration outcome is still unidentified.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Package Is Future Considerations, Not Verified Cash

The Lakers, Buffalo Braves, league transaction log, Bill Sharman executive ledger and Norm Sonju executive ledger all record the September 7, 1977 transaction the same way: Buffalo sent Ernie DiGregorio to Los Angeles for future considerations.

The legacy archive entry had converted that phrase into “undisclosed considerations (cash?),” but none of the authoritative ledgers reviewed for this review identifies cash. That distinction matters. “Future considerations” can later become cash, a draft asset, player rights or another agreed return, but the cited record does not establish which outcome occurred here.

This review therefore changes the asset type from cash to future consideration and labels the downstream outcome unresolved. The review does not invent a payment amount or a later asset.

DiGregorio Gave the Lakers 25 Games

Los Angeles received a recognizable former Rookie of the Year, but the actual Lakers tenure was brief. DiGregorio appeared in 25 regular-season games in 1977-78 and averaged 13.3 minutes, 3.9 points, 2.8 assists and 0.9 rebounds.

The team did get usable reserve minutes, especially at point guard, but his role was limited. Basketball-Reference lists 332 total Lakers minutes, 98 points and 71 assists. That is real production, though not enough to create a large transaction win by itself.

The Lakers Waived Him in January

Los Angeles waived DiGregorio on January 30, 1978. Boston signed him as a free agent on February 1, and he played 27 games for the Celtics to finish the season.

Because the Lakers waived him rather than trading him, there was no downstream Lakers asset return to attach to this transaction. Their realized value from the deal is therefore almost entirely those 25 games of reserve production.

Buffalo's Return Is Still Unresolved

Buffalo's side is harder to score because the original consideration was deferred and the reviewed transaction ledgers do not identify the eventual fulfillment. The Braves' 1977-78 ledger continues to label the September 7 return simply as future considerations even while later entries identify concrete picks, cash sales and player transactions in detail.

That is a reason to preserve uncertainty rather than assume Buffalo received nothing. A missing downstream identification is not proof that the consideration had zero value.

At the same time, TradeVerdicts grades realized, traceable outcomes. Without a verified cash amount, pick or player connection, Buffalo cannot receive full credit for an asset that remains unspecified in the source record.

Final Verdict

Lakers Edge, C-/D+. Los Angeles receives a C- because it obtained 25 games and modest reserve production before waiving DiGregorio in January. Buffalo receives a D+ on documented realized value because the future consideration is real but unresolved in the cited ledgers. The grade gap is intentionally small, and confidence is medium rather than high because Buffalo's eventual return could not be identified. This review's main repair is factual: future considerations should not be rewritten as confirmed or probable cash without source support.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Atlanta traded Bill Willoughby to Buffalo on September 13, 1977 for a 1978 second-round pick. Willoughby gave the Braves 56 regular-season games that year, averaging 6.7 points and 3.9 rebounds in 19.3 minutes. Atlanta did not keep the pick until the draft. On October 5, 1977, the Hawks sent it to Portland for rookie guard Rich Laurel. Atlanta released Laurel on November 28 before he appeared in an NBA game for the Hawks; Milwaukee later signed him, and he played only 10 NBA games. Portland kept the second-rounder and used it at No. 24 on Keith Herron, whose NBA career lasted 124 games, but that production belongs to Portland and later teams rather than Atlanta because the Hawks had already moved the asset. Buffalo therefore received the only meaningful direct on-court value from the original trade, while Atlanta’s pick briefly functioned as trade currency but produced no Hawks games.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Original Deal Was Willoughby for One Second-Round Pick

Buffalo and Atlanta both record the September 13, 1977 transaction the same way: the Braves acquired Bill Willoughby and the Hawks received Buffalo's 1978 second-round pick. The league ledger matches those team records.

The pick eventually became No. 24 in the 1978 draft and was used on Keith Herron, but Atlanta did not make that selection. That downstream distinction is the key to grading this review accurately.

Willoughby Gave Buffalo 56 Games

Willoughby was only 20 years old during the 1977-78 season and immediately entered Buffalo's rotation. He played 56 games for the Braves, averaging 19.3 minutes, 6.7 points and 3.9 rebounds. Basketball-Reference lists 1,079 total minutes, 376 points and 219 rebounds.

Those numbers are modest, but they are real first-season value from a second-round-pick acquisition. Buffalo was in the middle of a major roster overhaul and received a young forward who could absorb meaningful minutes immediately.

The franchise moved to San Diego after the season, and Willoughby did not play in 1978-79 after being waived. This review therefore does not inflate the Buffalo return into a long multi-season run. The realized Braves portion is the 56-game 1977-78 season.

Atlanta Recycled the Pick Before the Draft

On October 5, less than a month after the original trade, Atlanta sent Buffalo's 1978 second-round pick to Portland for Rich Laurel. Portland's transaction ledger and Harry Glickman's executive record identify the same pick, later used at No. 24 on Herron.

That means the Hawks did extract market value from the asset before draft night. The original second-rounder was not wasted or forgotten.

The problem is what Atlanta received for it. Laurel never played a regular-season game for the Hawks. Atlanta released him on November 28, 1977. Milwaukee signed him on December 2, and his entire NBA career consisted of 10 games for the Bucks.

Herron's NBA Career Belongs to Portland's Branch

Portland retained the pick and selected Herron at No. 24 in 1978. Herron eventually played 124 NBA games over three seasons.

That outcome confirms the pick itself had legitimate draft value, but TradeVerdicts does not credit Herron's production back to Atlanta because the Hawks had traded the pick away for Laurel. The correct Atlanta outcome is the Laurel conversion, not Herron's later career.

Final Verdict

Braves Edge, B-/D+. Buffalo receives a B- because Willoughby supplied 56 games and useful rotation minutes at age 20. Atlanta receives a D+ because the second-round pick had real trade value, but the Hawks converted it into Laurel and released him before he played a game for them. The gap is meaningful without being enormous: Buffalo did not acquire a long-term star, but it received far more realized team-specific value than Atlanta ultimately produced from the asset cycle. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: Buffalo sold the player rights to Bird Averitt to New Jersey on September 16, 1977. The Buffalo and league transaction ledgers explicitly describe the move as a sale, confirming cash consideration even though no cited source states the amount. Averitt played 21 regular-season games for the Nets, averaging 8.3 points and 3.2 assists in 19.5 minutes before New Jersey waived him on December 12. The later twist belongs outside the original asset chain: Buffalo signed Averitt as a free agent on January 31, 1978, and he then played 34 games for the Braves, but that reacquisition was not part of the September sale. New Jersey therefore received a short but measurable rotation return, while Buffalo received cash of unknown amount. With no traceable downstream cash use, the Nets hold only a modest edge on documented realized basketball value rather than a decisive win.
perspectives.analysis:
This Was a Rights Sale, Not a Conventional Player Trade

Buffalo's transaction ledger says the Braves sold the player rights to Bird Averitt to the New Jersey Nets on September 16, 1977. The league transaction log uses the same “sold the player rights” language. New Jersey's ledger records that it acquired Averitt's rights but does not specify the payment amount.

That is enough to establish cash consideration while still preserving uncertainty about the amount. This review therefore keeps the cash asset but labels it as an unspecified rights-sale payment rather than treating the transaction as a normal player-for-player exchange.

Averitt Gave New Jersey 21 Games

Averitt appeared in 21 regular-season games for the Nets in 1977-78. He averaged 19.5 minutes, 8.3 points, 3.2 assists and 1.6 rebounds. Basketball-Reference lists 409 total minutes, 174 points and 68 assists.

Those numbers are modest, but they are more than a purely administrative rights acquisition. New Jersey received actual rotation minutes from the player it purchased.

The Nets Waived Him in December

New Jersey waived Averitt on December 12, 1977. There was no trade return attached to that departure, so the Nets' direct asset cycle ends after those 21 games.

That short tenure keeps the grade restrained. The Nets did not turn the purchased rights into a long-term starter or a later draft asset.

Buffalo Later Re-Signed Averitt, but That Is a Separate Event

The unusual historical wrinkle is that Buffalo signed Averitt as a free agent on January 31, 1978. He then played 34 regular-season games for the Braves, averaging 9.5 points and 3.8 assists.

This review does not credit those 34 games as a direct return from the September sale. Buffalo reacquired him through a later free-agent signing after New Jersey had waived him. The sequence is still worth documenting because it shows that the Braves ultimately regained the player, but the later roster move is not the consideration that New Jersey paid in September.

Buffalo's Cash Return Cannot Be Fully Valued

The Braves definitely received a sale payment, but no amount is identified in the cited Buffalo, New Jersey, league or executive records. There is also no source-backed downstream transaction connecting that payment to a later player or draft asset.

TradeVerdicts therefore records the cash as real but unquantified. That prevents both extremes: Buffalo should not be treated as receiving nothing, and the unknown payment should not be inflated into a major return.

Final Verdict

Nets Edge, C+/C. New Jersey receives a C+ because Averitt produced 21 games and useful reserve scoring before being waived. Buffalo receives a C because it received a confirmed cash payment of unknown amount and later independently re-signed Averitt, though that free-agent return is not part of the original sale. The separation is limited, and confidence is high on the transaction structure but naturally lower on the exact value of Buffalo's cash because the amount is not preserved in the cited record.

This Was a Rights Sale, Not a Conventional Player Trade

Buffalo's transaction ledger says the Braves sold the player rights to Bird Averitt to the New Jersey Nets on September 16, 1977. The league transaction log uses the same “sold the player rights” language. New Jersey's ledger records that it acquired Averitt's rights but does not specify the payment amount.

That is enough to establish cash consideration while still preserving uncertainty about the amount. This review therefore keeps the cash asset but labels it as an unspecified rights-sale payment rather than treating the transaction as a normal player-for-player exchange.

Those numbers are modest, but they are more than a purely administrative rights acquisition. New Jersey received actual rotation minutes from the player it purchased.

The Nets Waived Him in December

New Jersey waived Averitt on December 12, 1977. There was no trade return attached to that departure, so the Nets' direct asset cycle ends after those 21 games.

That short tenure keeps the grade restrained. The Nets did not turn the purchased rights into a long-term starter or a later draft asset.

summary: Atlanta traded longtime star Lou Hudson to the Lakers on September 30, 1977 for Ollie Johnson. Johnson gave the Hawks one full season, appearing in all 82 games and averaging 8.5 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.5 assists in 20.8 minutes. Atlanta waived him on October 4, 1978, so the Hawks received no later trade return. Hudson was older at 33, but Los Angeles still received two productive seasons. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Package Was a Straight One-for-One Swap

Atlanta, Los Angeles and the league transaction ledger all record the September 30, 1977 deal the same way: the Hawks sent Lou Hudson to the Lakers for Ollie Johnson. There were no picks, cash terms or later considerations attached to the original exchange.

That makes this review a relatively simple realized-value comparison. The question is how much useful basketball each team received before the asset cycle ended.

Johnson Gave Atlanta One Full Season

Johnson played all 82 games for the Hawks in 1977-78. He averaged 20.8 minutes, 8.5 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.5 assists while shooting 47.2% from the field and 85.4% from the line.

That was a legitimate rotation season, not a negligible return. Johnson gave Atlanta dependable availability and enough scoring to contribute to a young Hawks roster that was being rebuilt around players such as John Drew and Tree Rollins.

The problem is duration. Atlanta waived Johnson on October 4, 1978, before the next regular season began. Chicago signed him later that month. Because the Hawks waived him instead of trading him, there was no downstream Atlanta asset return from the original deal.

Hudson Still Had Two Productive Lakers Seasons

Hudson was 33 when Los Angeles acquired him, so this was not a trade for his All-Star prime. Even so, he immediately gave the Lakers more production than Johnson gave Atlanta.

Hudson played all 82 games in 1977-78, averaging 27.8 minutes and 13.7 points while shooting 49.7%. He also added 2.4 assists and 2.3 rebounds per game. In the playoffs, he appeared in three games and averaged 11.7 points.

He returned for 78 regular-season games in 1978-79. His role declined to 21.6 minutes, but he still averaged 9.8 points and shot 51.7%. He then played six more playoff games.

Across the two seasons, Hudson appeared in 160 regular-season Lakers games and nine playoff games. Basketball-Reference lists an 11.8-point average across his Los Angeles tenure.

The Age Risk Did Not Hurt Los Angeles

The trade could have backfired if Hudson's decline had accelerated immediately. Instead, the Lakers got two useful seasons from an older scorer while giving up a younger forward who lasted only one season in Atlanta.

Neither side created a downstream trade tree. Johnson was waived by Atlanta, and Hudson finished his NBA career after the 1978-79 season. That leaves the direct production comparison as the decisive evidence.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A-/B-. Los Angeles receives an A- because Hudson delivered 160 regular-season games, efficient scoring and two playoff appearances. Atlanta receives a B- because Johnson gave the Hawks a complete 82-game rotation season, but the team waived him before year two and received no later asset return. The Lakers' advantage comes from both higher production and twice the team-specific longevity. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded its 1981 and 1983 first-round picks to Philadelphia on October 3, 1977 for Terry Furlow. Furlow gave the Cavaliers 102 regular-season games across two seasons and was then traded to Atlanta for Butch Lee plus a 1983 first-round pick that eventually became No. 11 Derek Harper. Cleveland later packaged that Atlanta pick with Bill Robinzine and a 1986 first to Dallas, so Harper's career is not a Cavaliers return. Philadelphia converted Cleveland's 1981 first into Lionel Hollins, who played 190 regular-season games for the 76ers and started 81 games in 1981-82. The Cleveland 1983 first became the No. 3 pick and was sent with Caldwell Jones to Houston for Moses Malone. That pick cannot receive full credit for Malone because Jones was also outgoing, but it was premium currency in a championship-defining transaction. Philadelphia clearly won the realized asset cycle.
perspectives.analysis:
Two Future Firsts Were the Price for Furlow

Cleveland and Philadelphia transaction ledgers agree on the October 3, 1977 package: the Cavaliers sent their 1981 and 1983 first-round picks to the 76ers for Terry Furlow.

Those picks eventually landed at No. 4 in 1981 and No. 3 in 1983. That makes the original cost look enormous in hindsight, but this review follows how each asset was actually used rather than pretending Philadelphia simply drafted Al Wood and Rodney McCray.

Furlow Gave Cleveland Two Seasons and a Later Trade Return

Furlow played 53 games for Cleveland in 1977-78, averaging 8.9 points in 15.6 minutes. He played another 49 Cavaliers games in 1978-79 and averaged 13.3 points in 22.7 minutes.

That produced 102 regular-season games of direct value. Cleveland then traded Furlow to Atlanta on January 31, 1979 for Butch Lee and Atlanta's 1983 first-round pick.

Lee played 33 Cleveland games that season at 11.5 points and 3.8 assists, then only three more games for the Cavaliers in 1979-80. The acquired 1983 first eventually became the No. 11 pick used on Derek Harper, but Cleveland did not keep it. On October 30, 1980, the Cavaliers sent that pick, Bill Robinzine and a 1986 first-round pick to Dallas for Richard Washington and Jerome Whitehead. This review therefore does not credit Harper's career to Cleveland.

Philadelphia Turned the 1981 First Into Lionel Hollins

The first Cleveland pick did not remain with Philadelphia until the 1981 draft. On February 8, 1980, the 76ers traded it to Portland for Lionel Hollins.

Hollins became a substantial Philadelphia contributor. He played 27 regular-season games after the trade, then 82 games in 1980-81 and 81 in 1981-82. Across those three seasons he played 190 games for the 76ers and started 120, averaging 10.5 points and 4.1 assists during his Philadelphia tenure.

Philadelphia later traded Hollins to San Diego in October 1982 for a 1983 fourth-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick. The Cleveland 1981 first therefore produced both three seasons of useful guard play and a small downstream return.

The 1983 First Became Part of the Moses Malone Deal

The second Cleveland first became an even more important asset. On September 15, 1982, Philadelphia sent Caldwell Jones and the 1983 first-round pick that became No. 3 Rodney McCray to Houston for Moses Malone.

That does not mean the Cleveland pick alone “became Moses Malone.” Jones was a meaningful outgoing player, and the transaction was part of Malone's restricted-free-agent process. But the No. 3 pick was unquestionably premium currency in the deal that brought Malone to Philadelphia.

Malone then became the 1982-83 MVP and the centerpiece of the 76ers' championship season. This review records the connection without assigning the entire championship value to one draft asset.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/C. Philadelphia receives an A+ because the two picks produced a three-season Hollins run plus a premium No. 3 asset used in the Malone acquisition. Cleveland receives a C because Furlow gave the Cavaliers 102 games and generated Lee plus another future first, but Cleveland's downstream conversion of that first was limited and required additional assets. The 76ers' side created much greater team-specific value over multiple stages. Confidence is high.

perspectives.analysis:
The source-backed Package Is One-for-One

Portland, Atlanta and the league transaction ledgers all record the October 5, 1977 deal the same way: the Hawks sent their newly acquired 1978 second-round pick to the Trail Blazers for Rich Laurel. Harry Glickman's executive ledger matches that package.

The legacy archive entry also included “future considerations,” but none of those authoritative records contains an additional consideration. This review removes the unsupported asset rather than preserving an unexplained extra term.

Atlanta Had Just Acquired the Pick

The second-rounder originated in Buffalo. On September 13, Atlanta traded Bill Willoughby to the Braves for Buffalo's 1978 second-round pick. Just 22 days later, the Hawks moved that pick to Portland for Laurel.

That short chain is important because it prevents the pick from being treated as a long-held Atlanta draft asset. Atlanta converted it almost immediately into a player-rights bet.

Laurel Never Played for the Hawks

Portland had drafted Laurel No. 19 overall in the 1977 draft, but he did not make the Trail Blazers' regular-season roster. Atlanta acquired his rights in October and then released him on November 28.

Laurel therefore produced zero regular-season games for the Hawks. Milwaukee signed him on December 2, and he played 10 NBA games for the Bucks, averaging 5.7 minutes and 2.4 points. Milwaukee waived him in January, ending his NBA career.

Those 10 Bucks games do not help Atlanta's trade grade. The Hawks had already released him and received no downstream trade asset.

Portland Used the Pick on Keith Herron

Portland retained the second-round pick and used it at No. 24 in the 1978 draft on Keith Herron. That establishes the pick as a real draft asset rather than a paper return that disappeared before selection.

The realized Portland outcome was still poor. Herron never played a regular-season game for the Trail Blazers. On October 16, 1978, Atlanta claimed him on waivers from Portland.

Herron then played 14 games for Atlanta in 1978-79. He later had a stronger 80-game season with Detroit and finished his NBA career with 124 games, but none of those later games are Portland production.

Atlanta's Later Herron Claim Is Separate

There is an unusual circularity to the transaction chain: Atlanta traded the pick that became Herron, Portland drafted Herron, and Atlanta ultimately claimed him on waivers.

This review keeps those events separate. Atlanta's 14 Herron games came from a 1978 waiver claim, not from the 1977 Laurel transaction. They are useful historical context, but they cannot be retroactively counted as the return for trading the pick.

The Difference Is Asset Control, Not Team Production

Neither side generated meaningful direct team-specific production from the original return. Laurel never played for Atlanta, while Herron never played for Portland.

Portland's advantage is that the Trail Blazers controlled a second-round pick through draft night and selected a player who did establish an NBA career. Atlanta converted the same asset into Laurel and released him before he appeared in a game.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Edge, C-/D. Portland receives a C- because the second-round pick remained a usable draft asset through selection, even though Herron never played for the team. Atlanta receives a D because Laurel produced zero Hawks games and no downstream asset before being released. The gap stays modest because Portland also failed to realize on-court value from its return. Confidence is high on the one-for-one package and downstream chronology.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Bo Ellis from Washington on October 11, 1977 for the Nuggets' 1978 first-round pick, which became No. 18 Dave Corzine. Ellis gave Denver 168 regular-season games across three seasons, totaling 613 points and 482 rebounds while serving mostly as a reserve forward. Washington received the more durable long-term asset. Corzine played 137 regular-season games for the Bullets over two seasons, then was traded to San Antonio in September 1980 for 1981 and 1982 second-round picks that became Claude Gregory and Dwight Anderson. Corzine himself went on to a 13-year NBA career, though only his Washington tenure and the two-pick return belong to the Bullets' realized trade value. Denver received useful frontcourt depth, but Washington converted one future first into two seasons of center play plus two additional draft assets. The source-backed record therefore favors the Bullets without turning a serviceable Denver return into a failure.
perspectives.analysis:
The Original Package Is Fully Verified

Denver's 1977-78 transaction ledger records the October 11 deal as a straight exchange: the Nuggets sent their 1978 first-round pick to Washington for Bo Ellis. The pick became No. 18 in the 1978 draft and Washington used it on Dave Corzine.

There is no cash term or conditional language in the cited team and league ledgers. This review therefore treats the transaction as a clean player-for-first-round-pick swap.

Ellis Gave Denver Three Seasons of Rotation Depth

Ellis played 78 games in 1977-78 and averaged 4.3 points and 3.9 rebounds in 15.6 minutes. He followed with 42 games in 1978-79 and 48 more in 1979-80.

Across those three Denver seasons, Ellis appeared in 168 regular-season games, scored 613 points and grabbed 482 rebounds. His role was modest, but the volume matters. Denver did receive a real NBA player who stayed on the roster for multiple seasons rather than a short-term rental.

Corzine Gave Washington Two Seasons

Washington selected Corzine with the acquired No. 18 pick in 1978. He played 59 games as a rookie and 78 in 1979-80, for 137 regular-season Bullets appearances.

His Washington production was limited by a veteran frontcourt that included Wes Unseld and Elvin Hayes. Corzine averaged 3.0 points and 2.5 rebounds as a rookie, then 2.9 points and 3.5 rebounds in his second season. The direct Washington value was useful depth rather than star-level production.

The Pick Created a Second Asset Cycle

The more important part of Washington's return arrived after those two seasons. On September 26, 1980, the Bullets traded Corzine to San Antonio for a 1981 second-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick.

Those selections later became Claude Gregory and Dwight Anderson. Neither player created major NBA value, so this review does not overstate the downstream branch. Still, the fact that Washington turned Corzine into two more draft assets extends the life of the original 1978 first-round pick beyond his 137 Bullets games.

Corzine's Later Career Belongs Mostly to Other Teams

Corzine developed into a long-term NBA center after leaving Washington and eventually played 13 seasons. That career is useful context for the quality of the original draft selection, but this review does not credit the Bullets with production he delivered for San Antonio, Chicago or other later teams.

The same discipline applies on Denver's side. Ellis's three Denver seasons are the realized return. There is no evidence in the cited records of a later Denver trade branch that would materially increase his value.

Final Verdict

Bullets Edge, B/B+. Denver receives a B because Ellis delivered 168 games of usable frontcourt depth over three seasons. Washington receives a B+ because the acquired first became Corzine, who played 137 games for the Bullets and then returned two second-round picks in a 1980 trade. The difference is modest but source-supported: Washington got a slightly more durable asset chain, while Denver still received meaningful multi-year service. Confidence is high.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Package Is Exactly What the legacy archive entry Says

Atlanta's and Los Angeles' 1977-78 transaction ledgers agree on the October 17, 1977 exchange: the Hawks sent a 1979 fourth-round pick to the Lakers for Tony Robertson. The pick later became No. 79 overall and Los Angeles used it on Ray White.

There is no cash component, condition or additional player in the cited ledgers. This review therefore treats this as a straightforward player-for-future-fourth transaction.

Robertson Gave Atlanta One Useful Rookie Season

Robertson played 63 regular-season games for the Hawks in 1977-78. He averaged 5.9 points, 1.6 assists and 1.2 steals in 14.7 minutes while shooting 44.1 percent from the field.

That is not star-level production, but it is meaningful rotation value for a fourth-round pick two years into the future. He logged 929 minutes, scored 373 points and collected 74 steals for a 41-win Atlanta team that reached the playoffs.

The Hawks did not turn Robertson into another asset. Their 1978-79 transaction ledger shows that he was waived on September 22, 1978. Golden State later signed him as a free agent in February 1979, so his later Warriors games do not belong to Atlanta's realized return.

The Lakers' Pick Became Ray White

Los Angeles held Atlanta's fourth-rounder through the 1979 draft and selected Ray White at No. 79 overall. White appears in the draft record but never logged an NBA regular-season game.

That result gives the Lakers no realized playing value from the pick itself. This review does not penalize Los Angeles for failing to turn a late fourth-rounder into a long-term contributor; most selections in that range were uncertain. But retrospective grading has to count what the asset actually became, and in this case it did not produce NBA minutes.

The Asset Cost Was Very Low for Atlanta

The trade matters because the Hawks converted a distant late-round pick into 63 games of immediate depth. There was no premium first-round value at risk, and the pick did not later become a productive NBA player.

Los Angeles, meanwhile, did create a legitimate future draft asset out of a player it was willing to move. The process was rational even though the eventual selection produced no NBA return.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, B/D+. Atlanta receives a B because Robertson supplied 63 games and nearly 1,000 minutes of useful rookie-season depth for a low-value future pick. Los Angeles receives a D+ because the acquired fourth-rounder did reach the draft and become White, but White never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. This is a clear Atlanta win on realized value without being a major franchise-changing transaction. Confidence is high.

Brokaw played 13 regular-season games for the Braves, totaling 130 minutes and 54 points while averaging 4.2 points and 1.5 assists. Those were the final NBA games of his career. No reviewed source identifies what Cleveland ultimately received from the future-considerations clause, so the Cavaliers cannot be credited with a specific realized asset. Buffalo therefore gets only a narrow documented-value edge: it received a short reserve guard stint, while Cleveland's return remains real but untraceable. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.
perspectives.analysis:
The Transaction Structure Is Clear, but the Return Is Not

Cleveland's 1977-78 transaction ledger says the Cavaliers traded Gary Brokaw to Buffalo on October 17, 1977 for future considerations. Buffalo's ledger records the same exchange from the other side, and the league transaction log matches it.

The historical Clippers media guide also lists Brokaw as acquired from Cleveland for future considerations. None of those sources identifies the consideration as cash, a draft pick or another player. This review therefore removes the question-mark styling from the legacy asset text but does not pretend the missing detail has been solved.

Brokaw Gave Buffalo 13 Games

Brokaw's Braves tenure was brief. He played 13 regular-season games in 1977-78, averaging 10.0 minutes, 4.2 points and 1.5 assists. His total Buffalo line was 130 minutes, 54 points, 20 assists and 12 rebounds.

Those 13 games were the final NBA appearances of his four-year career. That limits the upside of Buffalo's side immediately: the Braves did receive measurable rotation depth, but not a multi-season player or later trade asset.

Cleveland's Future Consideration Cannot Be Traced

The difficult side is Cleveland. The future-considerations clause is documented by multiple sources, so it should not be treated as though the Cavaliers received nothing.

At the same time, TradeVerdicts grades realized and traceable outcomes. No source reviewed for this review identifies a later player, pick, cash amount or other basketball asset as the fulfillment of this specific October 17 clause. Without that link, assigning Cleveland the value of a hypothetical asset would be unsupported.

This is the same discipline used elsewhere in the archive when future-considerations details remain unresolved: acknowledge that a consideration existed, avoid converting uncertainty into zero, but do not give full realized-value credit for an asset whose outcome cannot be identified.

The Broader Brokaw Context Does Not Change the Grade

Cleveland had acquired Brokaw with Elmore Smith from Milwaukee in January 1977 in a much larger trade. Brokaw then played 39 games for the Cavaliers before the Buffalo move. That earlier acquisition is a separate transaction and cannot be used to improve or reduce the grade here.

Likewise, Buffalo's later roster moves do not create a downstream Brokaw branch. His NBA career ended after these 13 Braves games.

Final Verdict

Braves Edge, C-/D+. Buffalo receives a C- because Brokaw delivered 13 documented regular-season games and a small amount of reserve production. Cleveland receives a D+ on documented realized value because the future consideration is unquestionably part of the trade but remains unidentified in the reviewed record. The gap is intentionally small, and confidence is medium rather than high because Cleveland's eventual return could not be traced. This review's main source-backed improvement is precision: future considerations stay future considerations unless a source establishes what they became.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Glenn Hansen from New Orleans on October 18, 1977 for the Bulls' 1978 fourth-round pick, which became No. 75 Jeff Covington. Hansen's Chicago stay was far smaller than the legacy grade suggested: he appeared in only two regular-season games, played four total minutes and went scoreless before his NBA career ended. New Orleans exercised the pick in the 1978 draft on Covington, but Covington never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The transaction therefore produced almost no realized basketball value for either side. Chicago at least received two NBA appearances from Hansen, while the Jazz's draft asset reached selection but generated no NBA minutes. That supports only a tiny Bulls edge, not the previous B+/C+ framing. The source-backed grade is intentionally low because neither asset produced durable rotation value, a downstream trade return or a meaningful second asset cycle.
perspectives.analysis:
The Package Is a Straight Player-for-Fourth-Round Pick

Chicago and New Orleans list the October 18, 1977 transaction identically: the Bulls sent their 1978 fourth-round pick to the Jazz for Glenn Hansen. The league draft-trade record also traces that exact selection to New Orleans, where it became No. 75 overall.

There are no extra players, cash terms or conditions in the reviewed record. This review therefore keeps the legacy package structure and focuses on correcting the realized-value assessment.

Hansen Barely Appeared for Chicago

The biggest issue with the legacy B+ grade is Hansen's actual Bulls production. Basketball-Reference credits him with only two Chicago games in 1977-78 and four total minutes.

He went 0-for-2 from the field, did not score and recorded no rebounds or assists for the Bulls. Hansen also played three games for Kansas City that season, but those minutes came after Chicago and do not belong to the Bulls' return.

His NBA career ended after 1977-78. Chicago therefore received a real player but almost no measurable on-court value from the transaction.

New Orleans Used the Pick on Jeff Covington

The Jazz kept the acquired fourth-rounder through the 1978 draft and selected Jeff Covington at No. 75 overall. The draft record confirms both the slot and the Youngstown State forward.

Covington never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Basketball-Reference lists the draft selection but no NBA career statistics, and the 1978 draft table shows no NBA games or minutes attached to his record.

That means New Orleans received a valid draft asset and exercised it, but the pick produced no realized NBA playing value. There is also no verified downstream trade return attached to Covington in the reviewed sources.

The Difference Between Two Games and Zero Games Is Small

Chicago technically realized more direct NBA production because Hansen appeared twice. But two games and four minutes should not be inflated into a meaningful roster win.

New Orleans, meanwhile, at least retained the flexibility of a future fourth-round selection through draft night. In process terms that asset had value. In retrospective realized-value terms, however, it became a player who never appeared in the league.

This is exactly the kind of low-stakes historical transaction where the grade gap should remain narrow. Neither side surrendered premium capital, and neither side generated a lasting contributor.

Final Verdict

Slight Bulls Edge, D+/D. Chicago receives a D+ because Hansen produced two documented regular-season appearances, even though the contribution was only four minutes and zero points. New Orleans receives a D because the acquired pick was fully exercised at No. 75 but Covington never played an NBA regular-season game. The Bulls edge is technical rather than substantial. Confidence is high on the package, Hansen's Chicago line and the draft outcome.

indiana-pacers.summary: Buffalo traded Johnny Neumann to Indiana on October 18, 1977 for the 1978 third-round pick that became No. 48 Mike Santos. Basketball-Reference's Buffalo, Indiana and league ledgers, plus the Pacers' 1979 media guide, list only the draft pick. Pro Sports Transactions adds future considerations/cash, so this review preserves that term as source-specific and leaves the amount unspecified. Neumann played 20 regular-season games for Indiana, starting once and averaging 4.2 points in 10.8 minutes, before the Pacers waived him on December 22. Buffalo used the third-round pick on Santos, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season career for him. The Braves therefore received no realized on-court value from the draft outcome, although the unspecified consideration prevents the return from being treated as literally zero. Indiana gets the small edge because Neumann at least supplied 20 games; neither side created meaningful long-term value.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Core Trade Is Johnny Neumann for a 1978 Third-Round Pick

Buffalo, Indiana and the league transaction ledgers all record the October 18, 1977 exchange the same way. The Braves sent Johnny Neumann to the Pacers for Indiana's 1978 third-round pick. The pick later landed at No. 48 and became Mike Santos.

Indiana's 1979 media guide independently confirms the same package, describing Neumann as acquired from Buffalo for a 1978 third-round draft choice. That official Pacers source does not mention cash.

The Cash/Future-Considerations Term Is Source-Specific

Pro Sports Transactions' 1978 draft-pick ledger records the No. 48 selection and adds future considerations/cash to Buffalo's return. Because the Basketball-Reference and Pacers media-guide ledgers omit that term, this review does not present the financial component as universally confirmed. It is retained as a source-specific asset with no amount attached.

That distinction matters for grading. Buffalo should receive some credit for a documented additional consideration, but there is no basis to invent a dollar value or trace it into another player.

Neumann Gave Indiana Twenty Games

Neumann appeared in 20 regular-season games for the Pacers in 1977-78, making one start. He averaged 10.8 minutes, 4.2 points and 1.4 assists, totaling 83 points in 216 minutes.

Indiana waived him on December 22, 1977. He did not produce a later Pacers trade asset, and Basketball-Reference lists him outside the NBA the following season. The direct return was therefore brief and limited, but it was real.

The Pick Became Mike Santos

Buffalo kept the pick through the 1978 draft and selected Santos at No. 48. The Braves' transaction ledger lists the selection, while Santos's player page confirms he was drafted in the third round with the fourth pick of that round.

Santos never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. His Basketball-Reference page lists a rookie career length with no NBA game line. The draft branch therefore produced no realized NBA playing value for the Buffalo/San Diego franchise.

This Is a Low-Impact Trade, Not a Hidden Win

The temptation with late-round trades is to overstate small differences. Indiana did receive more measurable basketball production because Neumann played 20 games. Buffalo's pick produced no NBA games, but the Pro Sports Transactions consideration means the Braves' return was not only the failed draft pick.

Final Verdict

Pacers Edge, C/D+. Indiana receives a C because Neumann provided 20 games and a small amount of rotation value before being waived. Buffalo receives a D+ because Santos never played an NBA regular-season game, with the unspecified future-considerations/cash term keeping the grade above a pure no-return outcome. The edge is real but minor. Confidence is high on the player-for-pick structure and moderate on the financial term because it appears in Pro Sports Transactions but not the primary team and league ledgers.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston traded John Johnson to Seattle on October 22, 1977 for two second-round picks. Seattle received the overwhelming direct return: Johnson played 333 regular-season games across five SuperSonics seasons, scored 3,608 points and started all 82 games for the 1978-79 championship team. Houston's 1979 pick became No. 42 Paul Mokeski, who played 12 Rockets games before being traded to Detroit for a 1982 second-round pick. Houston later used that pick in the deal that brought Joe Bryant and No. 42 Jeff Taylor; Bryant and Taylor combined for 125 Rockets games, though the transaction also sent the pick itself to San Diego. The 1980 second-rounder became No. 43 Billy Williams, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Houston did create a useful downstream branch from Mokeski, but Seattle turned Johnson into five seasons of rotation value and a championship starter. The SuperSonics clearly earned the stronger realized outcome.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Seattle Received Five Seasons From John Johnson

Houston and Seattle's transaction ledgers agree on the October 22, 1977 exchange. The Rockets sent John Johnson to the SuperSonics for Seattle's 1979 and 1980 second-round picks. The legacy archive entry's "John Johnson (Howard Getty)" label is a bad source-import artifact; the player in the transaction is John Johnson, and this review normalizes the asset accordingly.

Johnson immediately became a major Seattle rotation piece. He played 76 regular-season games in 1977-78 and appeared in 22 playoff games as the SuperSonics reached the NBA Finals. In 1978-79 he played all 82 games, started all 82, averaged 11.0 points and became a starter on Seattle's NBA championship team.

His value did not end with the title. Johnson played 81 games in 1979-80, 80 in 1980-81 and 14 in 1981-82. Across five Seattle seasons he totaled 333 regular-season appearances and 3,608 points. That is a large realized return for two future second-rounders.

The 1979 Pick Became Paul Mokeski

Houston used the first pick at No. 42 in the 1979 draft on Paul Mokeski. He appeared in 12 regular-season games for the Rockets in 1979-80 before Houston traded him to Detroit on October 7, 1980 for a 1982 second-round pick.

That trade kept the asset chain alive. The 1982 pick eventually landed at No. 32. On June 28, 1982, Houston sent the No. 32 pick to San Diego and received Joe Bryant plus the second-round pick that became No. 42 Jeff Taylor.

Bryant played 81 regular-season games for Houston in 1982-83, starting 56 and averaging 10.0 points. Taylor played 44 Rockets games that season. Because Houston had to send the No. 32 pick to obtain both players, this review credits the Mokeski branch with creating the transaction opportunity rather than pretending the pick itself played those 125 games.

The 1980 Pick Produced No NBA Games

The second Seattle pick became No. 43 Billy Williams in the 1980 draft. Houston selected Williams, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season career. That branch ended without realized on-court value.

Houston's Return Was Better Than the Raw Draft Names Suggest

A simple Mokeski-plus-Williams comparison would underrate Houston because Mokeski still produced a later second-round asset that helped bring Bryant and Taylor. The Rockets therefore did receive more than 12 direct games from the package.

The gap remains large. Seattle received Johnson's five-season tenure, deep playoff participation and a full 82-game starting season on a championship team. Houston's return required multiple later transactions to create modest roster value.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, A/B-. Seattle receives an A because Johnson gave the franchise 333 regular-season games, 3,608 points, multiple playoff runs and a starting role on the 1979 champions. Houston receives a B- because Mokeski's branch eventually helped produce Bryant and Taylor, while Williams never reached an NBA regular-season game. The Rockets preserved some asset value, but Seattle received the durable high-impact player. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey sent Al Skinner and two second-round picks to Detroit on November 7, 1977 for Howard Porter, Kevin Porter and cash. The Nets received strong immediate production: Howard Porter played 55 games at 12.8 points per game, while Kevin Porter played 74 at 16.2 points and a league-leading 10.8 assists in his New Jersey portion of the season. Kevin Porter was then traded back to Detroit for Eric Money, who gave the Nets 47 games at 16.7 points before another trade. Detroit's return proved more durable. Skinner played 69 Pistons games, and the 1978 second-rounder became No. 23 Terry Tyler, who played 574 Detroit games across seven seasons, made the 1979 All-Rookie team and became one of the league's better shot blockers. The 1979 second became Tony Price, who never played for Detroit. The Nets got real short-term value, but Tyler's seven-year Pistons tenure gives Detroit the stronger realized result.
perspectives.analysis:
The Package Is Fully Confirmed

New Jersey, Detroit and the league transaction ledgers all record the November 7, 1977 trade the same way. The Nets sent Al Skinner, their 1978 second-round pick and their 1979 second-round pick to the Pistons. Detroit sent Howard Porter, Kevin Porter and cash to New Jersey. The cited Basketball-Reference ledgers do not state a cash amount, so this review leaves it unspecified.

The Nets Got Two Productive Veterans Immediately

Howard Porter played 55 games for New Jersey after the trade, averaging 12.8 points and 4.8 rebounds in 22.1 minutes. Those 55 games were the final NBA regular-season games of his career.

Kevin Porter provided the larger return. He played 74 Nets games in 1977-78, averaging 16.2 points and 10.8 assists. Across his full two-team season he led the NBA at 10.2 assists per game, and his New Jersey segment was even higher.

The Nets also retained value when Kevin Porter left. On September 8, 1978, New Jersey traded him back to Detroit for Eric Money. Money then played 47 Nets games in 1978-79 at 16.7 points and 5.3 assists before being moved with Skinner to Philadelphia for Harvey Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash. Because Skinner was also in that later package, this review does not assign the entire Philadelphia return to the Kevin Porter branch.

Skinner Was a Useful but Short Detroit Piece

Skinner played 69 games for Detroit after the trade, averaging 7.0 points in 18.5 minutes. The Pistons waived him on September 15, 1978. He signed back with New Jersey six days later, so Detroit's direct Skinner return ended after one season.

Terry Tyler Became the Centerpiece of Detroit's Return

The 1978 second-round pick landed at No. 23 and became Terry Tyler. He played all 82 games in each of his seven Detroit seasons from 1978-79 through 1984-85, totaling 574 regular-season appearances for the Pistons.

Tyler averaged 11.6 points, 6.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks over those seven seasons. He made the 1979 All-Rookie First Team and ranked among the league's leading shot blockers repeatedly. That combination of durability and defense is the largest single realized asset in the trade.

Tyler's 1985 veteran-free-agent departure also created a compensation arrangement involving first-round positioning and a second-round pick. Detroit ultimately selected John Salley at No. 11 in 1986, but the arrangement also sent Detroit's own first-round position to Sacramento, so this review does not credit Salley's entire later career to Tyler alone.

The 1979 Pick Produced No Detroit Games

Detroit used the other second-round pick at No. 29 in 1979 on Tony Price. The Pistons waived him before the season, and he never played a regular-season game for Detroit. Price later appeared in five games for San Diego in 1980-81.

Final Verdict

Pistons Edge, A/B+. Detroit receives an A because Tyler alone supplied 574 games across seven seasons, with Skinner adding another 69. New Jersey receives a B+ because Kevin Porter delivered an outstanding 74-game season, Howard Porter added 55 useful games and the Kevin Porter branch produced Eric Money. The Nets did well in the short term, but Detroit's seven years of Tyler production create the stronger total return. Confidence is high.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Seattle acquired Wally Walker from Portland on November 11, 1977 for a 1978 first-round pick and a 1979 second-rounder. Walker became a durable SuperSonics rotation forward, playing 350 regular-season games across five seasons and contributing to the 1979 NBA championship team. Portland used the first-rounder at No. 7 on Ron Brewer, who played 192 Trail Blazers games and averaged 13.3 points as a rookie and 15.7 in his second season. Portland then traded Brewer to San Antonio in December 1980 for Mike Gale and a 1982 first-round pick that became No. 18 Ricky Pierce, extending the asset branch beyond Brewer's direct tenure. The second-round pick became No. 40 Andrew Fields, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Walker's championship contribution keeps Seattle's return strong, but Portland received a productive lottery-level scorer and then recycled him into another first-round asset. The Blazers get the narrow hindsight edge.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Core Trade Is Fully Confirmed

Portland, Seattle and the league transaction ledgers all record the November 11, 1977 trade the same way. The Trail Blazers sent Wally Walker to the SuperSonics for Seattle's 1978 first-round pick and a 1979 second-round pick.

The first-rounder became No. 7 Ron Brewer. The second-rounder became No. 40 Andrew Fields. There are no cash terms or conditional clauses to reconcile.

Walker Gave Seattle Five Seasons and a Championship Rotation Piece

Walker played 68 games for Seattle in 1977-78 after the trade, averaging 6.5 points and 3.0 rebounds. He returned for 60 games in 1978-79 and was part of the SuperSonics team that won the NBA championship.

His role remained useful beyond the title season. Walker played 70 games in 1979-80, all 82 in 1980-81 and 70 in 1981-82. Across five Seattle seasons, he appeared in 350 regular-season games and averaged 7.3 points and 3.3 rebounds.

Seattle eventually recovered another asset when it traded Walker to Houston in October 1982 for a 1984 second-round pick. This review records that later return without overstating it; Walker's main value had already come through five years of service and a championship run.

Brewer Became Portland's Main Return

Portland used the No. 7 pick on Ron Brewer. He played 81 games as a rookie in 1978-79, averaging 13.3 points, then started all 82 games in 1979-80 and averaged 15.7 points.

Brewer's Portland role declined early in 1980-81, but he still played 29 games before the Trail Blazers moved him. In total he appeared in 192 regular-season games for Portland and provided substantially more scoring per game than Walker did in Seattle.

The Brewer Branch Stayed Valuable

On December 19, 1980, Portland traded Brewer to San Antonio for Mike Gale and a 1982 first-round pick. That pick later became No. 18 Ricky Pierce.

This review does not credit Pierce's entire NBA career to the original Seattle trade, because Portland had to move Brewer to obtain the pick. The chain still matters: the No. 7 selection produced more than two seasons of Brewer and then returned another first-round asset instead of expiring without value.

The Second-Round Pick Did Not Produce NBA Games

Portland used the 1979 second-rounder at No. 40 on Andrew Fields. Basketball-Reference lists Fields as drafted by the Trail Blazers but records no NBA regular-season career. That branch ended without realized NBA playing value.

Final Verdict

Blazers Edge, A/A-. Portland receives an A because the No. 7 pick became a productive scorer for 192 games and was then converted into Gale plus another first-round pick. Seattle receives an A- because Walker gave the club 350 games across five seasons and was part of the 1979 championship roster. The title context makes Seattle's return genuinely valuable, but Portland extracted more reusable asset value from the outgoing picks. Confidence is high.

seattle-supersonics.summary: San Antonio acquired Mike Green from Seattle on November 12, 1977 for 1978 and 1979 second-round picks. Green gave the Spurs 139 regular-season games across two seasons, averaging 7.5 points and 4.7 rebounds, then was traded to Kansas City for the 1980 second-round pick used on Michael Wiley. Wiley added 33 Spurs games. Seattle's 1978 pick became No. 42 Keven McDonald, who never played an NBA regular-season game. The 1979 pick has an unusual route: Basketball-Reference identifies it as the No. 40 Andrew Fields selection and shows Seattle sending that same future pick to Portland one day earlier in the Wally Walker trade. Fields was ultimately drafted by Portland and never played an NBA game. Seattle therefore received a pick that functioned as part of the Walker transaction chain rather than a retained draft asset. That indirect value matters, but San Antonio's 139 Green games plus the Wiley return give the Spurs the stronger realized outcome.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Core Trade Is Consistent Across the Ledgers

San Antonio, Seattle and the league transaction records all list the November 12, 1977 deal the same way. The Spurs sent a 1978 second-round pick and a 1979 second-round pick to the SuperSonics for Mike Green.

The 1978 pick became No. 42 Keven McDonald. The 1979 pick is attached to No. 40 Andrew Fields. That second pick requires special handling because the transaction trail shows Seattle had already promised the same future selection to Portland one day earlier.

Green Gave San Antonio Two Productive Seasons

Green played 63 games for the Spurs after the trade in 1977-78, averaging 7.6 points, 4.8 rebounds and 1.4 blocks in 18.0 minutes. He returned for 76 games in 1978-79 and averaged 7.5 points, 4.7 rebounds and 1.6 blocks.

Across the two seasons, San Antonio received 139 regular-season games. Green was not a star, but he supplied dependable frontcourt minutes over a meaningful two-year stretch.

Green Then Produced Another Draft Asset

On September 13, 1979, the Spurs traded Green to Kansas City for a 1980 second-round pick. San Antonio used that pick at No. 39 on Michael Wiley.

Wiley played 33 regular-season games for the Spurs in 1980-81, averaging 5.7 points in 8.2 minutes. His NBA career continued for one more season in San Diego, but only those 33 San Antonio games belong to this downstream branch.

The 1978 Seattle Pick Produced No NBA Games

Seattle used the 1978 second-round pick at No. 42 on Keven McDonald. Basketball-Reference lists McDonald as drafted by the SuperSonics but records no NBA regular-season career.

That branch therefore produced no direct NBA playing value for Seattle.

The Andrew Fields Pick Was a Routing Asset, Not a Seattle Draft Return

The 1979 pick is more complicated. On November 11, 1977, one day before the Green trade, Seattle sent Portland a 1979 second-round pick along with a 1978 first-rounder for Wally Walker. Basketball-Reference identifies that promised second-rounder as the same No. 40 Andrew Fields pick that San Antonio transferred to Seattle on November 12.

Fields's player transaction history preserves both steps: Seattle sent the future pick to Portland on November 11, then San Antonio sent the same future pick to Seattle on November 12. Portland ultimately drafted Fields at No. 40 in 1979, and Fields never played an NBA regular-season game.

The best source-backed reading is that Seattle acquired the San Antonio second-rounder to satisfy or complete the prior Portland obligation. This review therefore credits the pick as part of the Wally Walker transaction chain rather than pretending Seattle retained and drafted Fields.

That indirect value was meaningful because Walker played 350 regular-season games for Seattle and contributed to the 1979 championship team. The Fields pick was only one component of the Walker package, however; Seattle also sent the first-round pick that became Ron Brewer. This review does not assign Walker's entire value to the San Antonio second-rounder alone.

Final Verdict

Spurs Edge, A-/B. San Antonio receives an A- because Green supplied 139 games over two seasons and then returned the pick used on Wiley, who added 33 more Spurs games. Seattle receives a B because McDonald produced no NBA games, while the Fields pick functioned as one part of the separate Walker acquisition that delivered five seasons and championship value. The Seattle return had legitimate indirect utility, but San Antonio received the clearer and more self-contained production. Confidence is high, with the unusual one-day Fields routing explicitly preserved rather than flattened into a simple draft result.

summary: Atlanta acquired Tom McMillen from New York on November 14, 1977 for the Hawks' 1978 second-round pick. The transaction ledgers agree on the one-for-one package, and the pick became No. 32 John Rudd. McMillen delivered 416 regular-season games for Atlanta across six seasons, averaging 8.5 points and 4.4 rebounds in 21.3 minutes per game during his Hawks tenure. Rudd played one NBA season, appearing in 58 games and totaling 184 points, 167 rebounds and 35 assists. Atlanta also retained downstream value: in July 1983, the Hawks traded McMillen with a 1984 second-round pick to Washington for Randy Wittman. Because another pick was included, that entire return cannot be assigned to McMillen alone. Even without that later branch, six seasons of rotation value for one second-round pick produced a clear Atlanta advantage.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Original Package Is Fully Verified

Atlanta, New York and the league transaction ledgers all record the same November 14, 1977 transaction: the Hawks sent their 1978 second-round pick to the Knicks for Tom McMillen. There are no additional cash terms, protections or players in the cited ledgers.

The pick landed at No. 32 in the 1978 draft and New York used it on John Rudd. That makes this a straightforward realized-value comparison between a known veteran rotation player and the player actually selected with the acquired pick.

McMillen Became a Six-Season Atlanta Rotation Piece

McMillen gave the Hawks immediate and durable frontcourt depth. He played 68 games in 1977-78 after arriving in November, then appeared in 82 games in 1978-79, 53 in 1979-80, 79 in 1980-81, 73 in 1981-82 and 61 in 1982-83.

Across those six Atlanta seasons he played 416 regular-season games. Basketball-Reference credits him with 8.5 points and 4.4 rebounds per game in 21.3 minutes across that Hawks tenure. He was not a franchise star, but the trade did not require star-level production to be valuable. Atlanta spent a second-round pick and received six years of usable NBA minutes.

His first post-trade season was productive enough to make the immediate exchange look good on its own. McMillen averaged 9.9 points and 6.1 rebounds in 68 games for the 1977-78 Hawks. Later seasons moved him more firmly into a rotation role, but he remained available and useful through 1983.

Rudd Had a Much Smaller NBA Footprint

New York used the No. 32 pick on John Rudd out of McNeese State. The 1978 draft ledger shows one NBA season, 58 games, 723 minutes, 184 points, 167 rebounds and 35 assists.

perspectives.summary: Detroit traded Marvin Barnes plus 1978 second- and fourth-round picks to Buffalo on November 23, 1977 for John Shumate, Gus Gerard and Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick. The authoritative Detroit, Buffalo and league ledgers specify a 1979 first, so this review removes the legacy 1979-or-1980 ambiguity. Shumate played 71 Pistons games across two active seasons, including 62 games at 15.5 points and 8.9 rebounds in 1977-78. Gerard played 49 Detroit games, and the first became No. 10 Roy Hamilton, who played 72 games for Detroit. Buffalo received 48 Barnes games before he became part of the large 1978 Boston package. The Braves also traded the incoming second-round pick to the Lakers for Tom Abernethy; when Abernethy signed with Golden State, San Diego received a 1979 second-round compensation pick. The fourth became No. 73 Larry Harris. Detroit's three incoming assets produced the stronger direct return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Retrospective Ledgers Clarify the Package

Detroit, Buffalo and the league transaction ledgers agree on the November 23, 1977 structure: the Pistons sent Marvin Barnes, a 1978 second-round pick and a 1978 fourth-round pick to the Braves for Gus Gerard, John Shumate and Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick.

The legacy archive entry called that first a "1979 or 1980" selection and described Gerard as a player to be named later. The authoritative retrospective ledgers used for this review list Gerard directly and identify the draft asset as a 1979 first. This review normalizes the canonical record to those documented terms while preserving the historical date.

Shumate Was Detroit's Best Immediate Player Return

Shumate played 62 games for Detroit in 1977-78 after the trade and averaged 15.5 points, 8.9 rebounds and 2.0 assists in 35.0 minutes. That is the strongest single-season production generated by either side's direct player return.

He missed the entire 1978-79 season with injury, then returned for nine Detroit games in 1979-80 before being waived. His Pistons total therefore finished at 71 regular-season games, but the first 62 carried substantial value because he was a full-time frontcourt contributor.

Gerard Added Depth, Then Moved On

Gerard played 47 games for Detroit in 1977-78 and two more in 1978-79. He averaged 7.9 points in 17.1 minutes during the first season, then left the Pistons after the brief second-year appearance.

That is modest value compared with Shumate, but it still adds another 49 games to Detroit's return. The deal did not depend on Gerard becoming a star; he functioned as a second usable roster piece behind Shumate.

The 1979 First Became Roy Hamilton

Buffalo's 1979 first-round pick landed at No. 10. Detroit selected Roy Hamilton, who played 72 games for the Pistons as a rookie in 1979-80, averaging 4.6 points and 2.7 assists in 15.5 minutes.

Hamilton's NBA career was short, but the pick did produce another full season of rotation availability. Taken together, Shumate, Gerard and Hamilton generated 192 regular-season Detroit games from the three incoming assets.

Buffalo Got Barnes and Recycled the Second-Round Pick

Barnes gave Buffalo 48 games in 1977-78, averaging 11.8 points and 7.3 rebounds in 28.7 minutes. He was then included in the August 1978 blockbuster that sent Barnes, Tiny Archibald, Billy Knight and two second-round picks to Boston for Kevin Kunnert, Kermit Washington, Sidney Wicks and Freeman Williams.

Because Barnes was only one of five outgoing assets, this review does not assign that full Boston return to him. His inclusion does show that he retained transaction value beyond his 48 Braves games.

The 1978 second-round pick also created a downstream branch. Buffalo sent the pick to the Lakers on June 7, 1978 for Tom Abernethy. The Lakers later used the selection at No. 38 on Lew Massey. Abernethy did not become a long-term Buffalo/San Diego player; after he signed with Golden State as a veteran free agent, the Clippers received a 1979 second-round compensation pick that became Gary Garland.

The fourth-round pick became No. 73 Larry Harris. The 1978 draft ledger does not show an NBA career line for Harris, so that asset did not create comparable realized value.

Final Verdict

Pistons Edge, A-/B. Detroit receives an A- because Shumate supplied a strong 62-game first season, Gerard added 49 games and the 1979 first produced 72 Hamilton games. Buffalo receives a B because Barnes was useful and the second-round pick retained transaction value through the Abernethy and compensation-pick chain, but the direct on-court return was shorter and the fourth-round pick did not develop into an NBA contributor. Confidence is high on the corrected package and its primary downstream branches.
