summary: Atlanta traded Ron Behagen to Houston on December 16, 1977 for the Rockets' 1978 and 1979 second-round picks. Six days later, Houston flipped Behagen to Indiana for Alonzo Bradley, so the Rockets received only three Behagen games but converted him into a player who appeared in 99 regular-season games for Houston across three seasons. Atlanta used the 1978 pick at No. 25 on Rick Wilson, who played 66 Hawks games over two seasons, mostly in a reserve role. The 1979 pick became No. 38 Larry Wilson, whose draft record shows no NBA career totals. The original legacy verdict leaned Atlanta because two picks looked deeper than one veteran, but realized team-specific value points the other way: Houston turned Behagen directly into Bradley, while Atlanta's two selections produced one limited rotation player and one non-NBA outcome. The Rockets receive the modest edge.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Original Trade Was Two Seconds for Behagen

Atlanta, Houston and the league transaction ledgers all record the December 16, 1977 transaction identically: the Hawks sent Ron Behagen to the Rockets for Houston's 1978 and 1979 second-round picks.

Those picks later became No. 25 Rick Wilson in 1978 and No. 38 Larry Wilson in 1979. The package itself is clean, with no cash, conditions or additional players to resolve.

Houston Barely Used Behagen Before Flipping Him

Behagen played only three games for Houston. Basketball-Reference lists him at 4.7 points and 2.3 rebounds in 11.0 minutes per game during that tiny Rockets sample.

If the evaluation stopped there, Houston would have little to show for two second-round picks. It does not stop there. On December 22, only six days after acquiring Behagen, the Rockets traded him to Indiana for Alonzo Bradley.

Because Behagen was the only Houston asset in that second trade, Bradley is a direct downstream return from the original Atlanta transaction rather than an attribution shared with another outgoing player or pick.

Bradley Gave Houston Three Seasons

Bradley played 43 games for Houston in 1977-78 and averaged 7.0 points in 18.6 minutes. He followed with 34 games in 1978-79 and 22 in 1979-80.

That is 99 regular-season Rockets games across three seasons. His role declined after the first year, but Houston still transformed six days of Behagen ownership into a multi-season roster piece. Bradley remained with the Rockets until Dallas selected him in the 1980 expansion draft.

Atlanta Got One Reserve Guard and One Non-NBA Draft Outcome

The first Hawks pick landed at No. 25 in 1978. Atlanta selected Rick Wilson, who played 61 games as a rookie and five more in 1979-80. He averaged 3.0 points in 9.7 minutes during his first season and finished with 66 Atlanta games across two years.

That is useful second-round return, but it remained a small reserve role. Wilson did not become a long-term Hawks rotation fixture or a major downstream transaction asset.

The second pick landed at No. 38 in 1979 and became Larry Wilson out of Nicholls State. The 1979 draft ledger shows no NBA career totals for him. This review therefore records the pick as a documented draft conversion with no realized NBA playing return.

The Two-Pick Optics Overstated Atlanta's Hindsight Value

Two second-round selections can look stronger than a short-term veteran acquisition when the trade is viewed only at transaction time. The actual branches reverse that impression.

Atlanta's picks produced 66 NBA games from Rick Wilson and no NBA career line from Larry Wilson. Houston got only three Behagen games, but immediately converted him one-for-one into Bradley and received 99 games over three seasons.

Final Verdict

Rockets Edge, B/C+. Houston receives a B because Behagen was efficiently recycled into Bradley, extending the asset into 99 Rockets games. Atlanta receives a C+ because Rick Wilson reached the NBA and supplied 66 reserve games, but the second pick produced no NBA playing value. The difference is not large enough for a dominant grade gap, yet Houston's direct downstream conversion clearly beats the realized output of the two Atlanta selections. Confidence is high.

houston-rockets.analysis:
The Package Was a Straight One-for-One Exchange

Houston and Indiana transaction records show the December 22, 1977 deal as Ron Behagen for the rights to Alonzo Bradley. The league ledger records the same structure.

Houston had acquired Behagen from Atlanta only six days earlier, but this review evaluates this second transaction on its own. The question is what Houston received for Behagen and what Indiana received for Bradley's rights.

Behagen Produced More Per Game for Indiana

Behagen played 51 regular-season games for the Pacers in 1977-78 and started 10. He averaged 11.2 points, 6.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 22.2 minutes per game.

That is meaningful rotation production, especially for a player acquired in late December. Indiana did not get multiple seasons from him, however. Basketball-Reference's transaction history shows the Pacers waived Behagen on September 11, 1978.

His Indiana branch therefore ends with one productive partial season and no documented trade return.

Bradley Stayed With Houston for Three Seasons

boston-celtics.analysis:
The December 27 Package Is Fully Confirmed

Boston, Los Angeles and the league transaction ledgers all record the same deal. The Celtics sent Charlie Scott to the Lakers and received Don Chaney, Kermit Washington and Los Angeles' 1978 first-round pick. Boston later used that pick at No. 8 on Freeman Williams.

Chaney Gave Boston Three Seasons of Direct Value

Chaney returned to the Celtics and played 42 games in 1977-78, 65 in 1978-79 and 60 in 1979-80. That is 167 regular-season games after the trade. His role steadily shrank, but he remained a useful veteran perimeter defender through the first Larry Bird season.

The direct numbers were modest compared with his earlier Celtics years, yet the longevity matters. Boston received nearly three seasons of service from one incoming player before accounting for Washington or the draft pick.

Washington Gave Boston 32 Strong Games

Washington played 32 regular-season games for Boston in 1977-78, averaging 11.8 points and 10.5 rebounds in 27.1 minutes. That was meaningful short-term frontcourt production, not merely a paper asset.

His Celtics tenure ended the following summer when Boston included him in a much larger trade with San Diego. Because the later deal contained multiple outgoing players, this review treats Washington as one contributor to that package rather than assigning Boston's entire return to him.

The No. 8 Pick Became Freeman Williams and Another Trade Asset

Boston selected Freeman Williams at No. 8 in the 1978 draft. Williams never played a regular-season game for the Celtics. On August 4, 1978, Boston traded Williams, Washington, Kevin Kunnert and Sidney Wicks to San Diego for Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes, Billy Knight and two future second-round picks.

Two of Boston's four outgoing player assets in that deal—Washington and Williams—came directly from this review. That gives the original trade a meaningful downstream branch, but the archive does not credit the entire Archibald package to this review because Kunnert and Wicks were separate Boston assets.

The Lakers Got a Useful Half-Season From Scott

Scott played 48 regular-season games for Los Angeles in 1977-78, averaging 11.7 points, 4.9 assists and 3.1 rebounds in 29.0 minutes. The Lakers then moved him again before the next season.

On June 26, 1978, Los Angeles traded Scott to Denver for Ron Boone and two 1979 second-round picks. Boone became the biggest direct downstream return. He played all 82 games for the Lakers in 1978-79 and six more in 1979-80, giving Los Angeles 88 regular-season appearances.

One Second-Round Pick Produced Ollie Mack

The two Denver picks later became No. 25 Ollie Mack and No. 41 Mark Young. Mack played 27 games for the Lakers in 1979-80 before moving on. Young never played an NBA regular-season game. The Scott branch therefore produced 48 direct Scott games, 88 Boone games and 27 Mack games, with no NBA return from Young.

Final Verdict

Celtics Edge, A/B+. Boston receives an A because Chaney supplied 167 games, Washington provided strong short-term rebounding, and Washington plus the No. 8 Williams rights became two pieces of the later San Diego blockbuster. Los Angeles receives a B+ because Scott produced 48 useful games and then became Boone plus two seconds, one of which produced Mack. Both sides recycled value well; Boston's combination of direct service and premium downstream trade currency creates the stronger realized outcome. Confidence is high.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State acquired Nate Williams from New Orleans for a 1978 second-round pick. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. Williams played 46 games for Golden State to finish 1977-78 and all 81 games in 1978-79, giving the Warriors 127 regular-season appearances at 9.3 points per game across his two-season stint. New Orleans used the No. 35 pick on Tommie Green, who played 59 games as a rookie in 1978-79, averaging 3.9 points and 2.4 assists in 13.7 minutes. Green never played another NBA season, and Williams also finished his NBA career after 1978-79. The trade had no major downstream branch, so the realized comparison is direct: Golden State received more games and substantially more scoring from the veteran.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Transaction Date Needs a Source Repair

The legacy canonical record is dated January 4, 1978. Golden State's team ledger, New Orleans' team ledger, the league transaction page and Nate Williams' own transaction history all record the player-for-pick exchange on January 5. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. The package itself is consistent across the cited sources: Golden State sent its 1978 second-round pick to New Orleans for Williams.

Williams Gave Golden State Immediate Rotation Scoring

Williams joined the Warriors midway through 1977-78 and appeared in 46 games after the trade. He averaged 11.2 points in only 17.7 minutes per game, shooting 43.5 percent from the field and 83.3 percent from the line.

He then played all 81 games in 1978-79, averaging 8.3 points in 16.0 minutes. Across the two Golden State seasons, Williams appeared in 127 regular-season games and averaged 9.3 points overall for the franchise.

That is useful realized value for a second-round pick, especially because the Warriors did not have to surrender another player or additional draft capital.

New Orleans Used the Pick on Tommie Green

The 1978 second-round pick landed at No. 35. New Orleans used it on Tommie Green out of Southern University.

Green played 59 regular-season games as a rookie in 1978-79. He averaged 3.9 points, 2.4 assists and 1.2 rebounds in 13.7 minutes. His field-goal percentage was 38.8 percent, and Basketball-Reference records negative win shares for the season.

Green's NBA career ended after that one season. There is no later player or draft return attached to his departure in the cited transaction history.

Neither Branch Produced a Major Downstream Asset

Williams also finished his NBA career after 1978-79, so Golden State did not later recycle him into another player or pick. That keeps this review unusually simple compared with many trades from this era.

The Warriors received 127 games and useful bench scoring. The Jazz received 59 games from the second-round selection. Both assets expired without a later transaction branch that materially changes the comparison.

The Date Error Does Not Change the Outcome

The January 4 versus January 5 discrepancy is important for archival accuracy but does not alter the asset result. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, B+/C. Golden State receives a B+ because Williams gave the team 127 games across two seasons and roughly double Green's scoring rate while costing only a second-round pick. New Orleans receives a C because No. 35 produced 59 NBA games and some reserve playmaking, but Green lasted only one season and created no later asset branch. The trade was useful rather than transformational for Golden State, which keeps the Warriors below the top grade tiers. Confidence is high.

Williams played 46 games for Golden State to finish 1977-78 and all 81 games in 1978-79, giving the Warriors 127 regular-season appearances at 9.3 points per game across his two-season stint. New Orleans used the No. 35 pick on Tommie Green, who played 59 games as a rookie in 1978-79, averaging 3.9 points and 2.4 assists in 13.7 minutes. Green never played another NBA season, and Williams also finished his NBA career after 1978-79. The trade had no major downstream branch, so the realized comparison is direct: Golden State received more games and substantially more scoring from the veteran.
analysis:
The Transaction Date Needs a Source Repair

The legacy canonical record is dated January 4, 1978. Golden State's team ledger, New Orleans' team ledger, the league transaction page and Nate Williams' own transaction history all record the player-for-pick exchange on January 5. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. The package itself is consistent across the cited sources: Golden State sent its 1978 second-round pick to New Orleans for Williams.

Williams Gave Golden State Immediate Rotation Scoring

Williams joined the Warriors midway through 1977-78 and appeared in 46 games after the trade. He averaged 11.2 points in only 17.7 minutes per game, shooting 43.5 percent from the field and 83.3 percent from the line.

He then played all 81 games in 1978-79, averaging 8.3 points in 16.0 minutes. Across the two Golden State seasons, Williams appeared in 127 regular-season games and averaged 9.3 points overall for the franchise.

That is useful realized value for a second-round pick, especially because the Warriors did not have to surrender another player or additional draft capital.

New Orleans Used the Pick on Tommie Green

The 1978 second-round pick landed at No. 35. New Orleans used it on Tommie Green out of Southern University.

Green played 59 regular-season games as a rookie in 1978-79. He averaged 3.9 points, 2.4 assists and 1.2 rebounds in 13.7 minutes. His field-goal percentage was 38.8 percent, and Basketball-Reference records negative win shares for the season.

Green's NBA career ended after that one season. There is no later player or draft return attached to his departure in the cited transaction history.

Neither Branch Produced a Major Downstream Asset

Williams also finished his NBA career after 1978-79, so Golden State did not later recycle him into another player or pick. That keeps this review unusually simple compared with many trades from this era.

The Warriors received 127 games and useful bench scoring. The Jazz received 59 games from the second-round selection. Both assets expired without a later transaction branch that materially changes the comparison.

The Date Error Does Not Change the Outcome

The January 4 versus January 5 discrepancy is important for archival accuracy but does not alter the asset result. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, B+/C. Golden State receives a B+ because Williams gave the team 127 games across two seasons and roughly double Green's scoring rate while costing only a second-round pick. New Orleans receives a C because No. 35 produced 59 NBA games and some reserve playmaking, but Green lasted only one season and created no later asset branch. The trade was useful rather than transformational for Golden State, which keeps the Warriors below the top grade tiers. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey reacquired John Williamson from Indiana on January 27, 1978 for Bob Carrington plus 1980 and 1981 second-round picks. Williamson immediately became the Nets' lead scorer, averaging 29.5 points in 33 games after the trade, 22.2 across 74 games in 1978-79 and 17.7 in 28 more Nets games in 1979-80. Indiana's package had far more depth than the old record suggested. Carrington played 35 Pacers games. The 1980 second became No. 29 Louis Orr, who played 162 Indiana games over two seasons. The 1981 second did not remain with Indiana: the Pacers traded it to Portland in October 1979 for Clemon Johnson, who played 290 Pacers games through 1982-83. Portland later used that pick at No. 26 on Brian Jackson. New Jersey got the best player and elite scoring peak, while Indiana turned three assets into nearly 500 combined games. The result is unusually balanced.
perspectives.analysis:
The January 27 Package Is Fully Confirmed

New Jersey, Indiana and the league transaction ledgers agree on the trade structure. The Nets received John Williamson. The Pacers received Bob Carrington, New Jersey's 1980 second-round pick and New Jersey's 1981 second-round pick.

The legacy archive entry correctly linked the 1980 pick to Louis Orr, but it mislabeled the 1981 outcome as No. 25 Brian Jackson. The later routing shows why. Indiana traded that pick to Portland in 1979, and Portland ultimately used it at No. 26 on Brian Jackson. This review repairs the slot and records the intermediary value Indiana actually received before the draft.

Williamson Immediately Became a High-End Nets Scorer

Williamson's direct New Jersey return was substantial. He played 33 games after the trade in 1977-78 and averaged 29.5 points in 38.8 minutes. He followed with 74 games in 1978-79 at 22.2 points and another 28 Nets games in 1979-80 at 17.7 points.

Across those post-trade Nets seasons, Williamson appeared in 135 regular-season games. The value was concentrated in scoring rather than longevity, but the peak was far above what any single Indiana asset produced.

New Jersey later moved Williamson on February 4, 1980. The Nets sent him plus a 1981 second-round pick to Washington for Roger Phegley. Because another second-round asset was included, this review does not credit the entire Phegley return to Williamson alone. Phegley nevertheless played 28 Nets games at 11.7 points before New Jersey traded him to Cleveland for Foots Walker.

Carrington Was a Short-Term Pacers Piece

Bob Carrington played 35 games for Indiana after the trade, averaging 7.1 points in 17.7 minutes. He did not play in the NBA in 1978-79 and later resurfaced for 10 games with San Diego in 1979-80.

His Indiana branch was modest, but Carrington was only one of three Pacers assets.

The 1980 Second Became Louis Orr

Indiana used the 1980 second-round pick at No. 29 on Louis Orr. Orr played all 82 games as a rookie in 1980-81, averaging 10.5 points and 4.4 rebounds. He returned for 80 games in 1981-82 at 11.5 points and 4.1 rebounds.

That gave Indiana 162 regular-season games, 48 starts and an 11.0-point average from the pick. In October 1982 the Pacers traded Orr to New York for another second-round pick, extending the asset chain beyond his two Indiana seasons.

The 1981 Second Became Clemon Johnson Before It Became Brian Jackson

Indiana did not hold the other second-rounder to the 1981 draft. On October 9, 1979, the Pacers sent that pick to Portland for Clemon Johnson. Indiana and Portland transaction ledgers both identify the selection as the pick later used on Brian Jackson.

Johnson became a major realized return for the Pacers. He played 79 games in 1979-80, 81 in 1980-81, 79 in 1981-82 and 51 more for Indiana in 1982-83 before moving to Philadelphia. That is 290 Pacers regular-season games from the asset branch.

Portland ultimately drafted Jackson at No. 26, not No. 25. The 1981 draft ledger confirms No. 25 belonged to Boston and became Tracy Jackson, while Portland used No. 26 on Brian Jackson. The correction matters because the original legacy slot would otherwise collide with a different player's draft history.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, A/A. New Jersey receives an A because Williamson gave the Nets 135 games of top-line scoring, including a 29.5-point post-trade burst and a full 22.2-point season. Indiana also receives an A because Carrington, Orr and the Johnson conversion produced 487 combined Pacers games, with Orr and Johnson both becoming multi-season rotation pieces. New Jersey got the best individual player and peak; Indiana got superior depth, duration and asset conversion. Neither side produced enough separation for a defensible winner. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded Darnell Hillman to Denver on January 30, 1978 for a 1979 second-round pick. The legacy archive entry also listed cash, but the Nets, Nuggets and league transaction ledgers all show only the player-for-pick exchange, so this review removes the unsupported cash term. New Jersey did not keep the pick to draft Clint Richardson. One day later the Nets bundled it with 1982 and 1983 picks for Wilson Washington, who played 86 regular-season games for New Jersey across two seasons. Denver received 33 games from Hillman at 7.8 points and 7.2 rebounds per game, then packaged him with Mike Evans in June for Ron Boone and another 1979 second-round pick. Both sides recycled their incoming asset with other pieces, limiting how much downstream value can be assigned to this trade alone. New Jersey gets a narrow edge because the pick helped produce a two-season Nets contributor, but the margin is small.
perspectives.analysis:
The Core Trade Is Player for Pick, Not Player for Pick and Cash

New Jersey, Denver and the league transaction ledgers all record the January 30, 1978 exchange as Darnell Hillman for Denver's 1979 second-round pick. The legacy archive entry also contained cash, but none of those authoritative ledgers lists a financial term.

This review therefore removes the unsupported cash asset. The documented package is a clean one-for-one exchange between Hillman and the future second-round selection.

Hillman Gave Denver 33 Games

Hillman joined the Nuggets for the final 33 games of 1977-78. He averaged 7.8 points, 7.2 rebounds, 1.6 assists and 1.1 blocks in 22.6 minutes.

That is useful frontcourt production for a second-round pick, but Denver did not retain him beyond the season.

The Nuggets Recycled Hillman in a Shared Package

On June 26, 1978, Denver traded Hillman and Mike Evans to Kansas City for Ron Boone and a 1979 second-round pick later associated with Mark Young. Hillman therefore retained transaction value, but this review does not credit the full Boone-plus-pick return to him because Evans was also outgoing.

Denver then moved Boone again in a separate deal with the Lakers, further demonstrating how quickly the asset chain branched. For this trade, the responsible attribution stops at Hillman being one of two pieces used in the Kansas City package.

The Nets Immediately Used the Pick for Wilson Washington

New Jersey held Denver's second-round pick for only one day. On January 31, the Nets sent that 1979 second-rounder plus a 1982 second-round pick and a 1983 third-round pick to Philadelphia for Wilson Washington.

Philadelphia eventually used the Denver-derived pick at No. 36 on Clint Richardson. New Jersey never drafted Richardson, so this review does not credit Richardson's long NBA career to the Nets.

Instead, the Nets receive partial downstream credit for Washington. He played 24 games for New Jersey in 1977-78 at 8.8 points and 5.9 rebounds, then 62 games in 1978-79 at 8.1 points and 4.7 rebounds. That is 86 Nets regular-season games from the player acquired with a three-pick package.

The Pick Was Only One of Three Assets

The Wilson Washington return is meaningful, but the Denver pick was not sufficient by itself. New Jersey also sent a 1982 second and a 1983 third. This review therefore treats Washington as a shared downstream return rather than assigning all 86 games to the Hillman trade.

That same caution applies to Denver's June package, where Hillman shared outgoing value with Evans.

Final Verdict

Nets Edge, B-/C+. New Jersey receives a B- because the second-round pick was immediately useful trade currency in the Washington acquisition, and Washington produced 86 Nets games across two seasons. Denver receives a C+ because Hillman supplied 33 useful games and later remained one component of a two-player trade package. The Nets' downstream result is somewhat more durable, but both branches depended on additional assets, so the gap stays narrow. Confidence is high on the documented one-for-one core trade and the removal of the unsupported cash term.

analysis:
The Core Trade Is Player for Pick, Not Player for Pick and Cash

New Jersey, Denver and the league transaction ledgers all record the January 30, 1978 exchange as Darnell Hillman for Denver's 1979 second-round pick. The legacy archive entry also contained cash, but none of those authoritative ledgers lists a financial term.

This review therefore removes the unsupported cash asset. The documented package is a clean one-for-one exchange between Hillman and the future second-round selection.

Hillman Gave Denver 33 Games

Hillman joined the Nuggets for the final 33 games of 1977-78. He averaged 7.8 points, 7.2 rebounds, 1.6 assists and 1.1 blocks in 22.6 minutes.

That is useful frontcourt production for a second-round pick, but Denver did not retain him beyond the season.

The Nuggets Recycled Hillman in a Shared Package

On June 26, 1978, Denver traded Hillman and Mike Evans to Kansas City for Ron Boone and a 1979 second-round pick later associated with Mark Young. Hillman therefore retained transaction value, but this review does not credit the full Boone-plus-pick return to him because Evans was also outgoing.

Denver then moved Boone again in a separate deal with the Lakers, further demonstrating how quickly the asset chain branched. For this trade, the responsible attribution stops at Hillman being one of two pieces used in the Kansas City package.

The Nets Immediately Used the Pick for Wilson Washington

New Jersey held Denver's second-round pick for only one day. On January 31, the Nets sent that 1979 second-rounder plus a 1982 second-round pick and a 1983 third-round pick to Philadelphia for Wilson Washington.

Philadelphia eventually used the Denver-derived pick at No. 36 on Clint Richardson. New Jersey never drafted Richardson, so this review does not credit Richardson's long NBA career to the Nets.

Instead, the Nets receive partial downstream credit for Washington. He played 24 games for New Jersey in 1977-78 at 8.8 points and 5.9 rebounds, then 62 games in 1978-79 at 8.1 points and 4.7 rebounds. That is 86 Nets regular-season games from the player acquired with a three-pick package.

The Pick Was Only One of Three Assets

The Wilson Washington return is meaningful, but the Denver pick was not sufficient by itself. New Jersey also sent a 1982 second and a 1983 third. This review therefore treats Washington as a shared downstream return rather than assigning all 86 games to the Hillman trade.

That same caution applies to Denver's June package, where Hillman shared outgoing value with Evans.

Final Verdict

Nets Edge, B-/C+. New Jersey receives a B- because the second-round pick was immediately useful trade currency in the Washington acquisition, and Washington produced 86 Nets games across two seasons. Denver receives a C+ because Hillman supplied 33 useful games and later remained one component of a two-player trade package. The Nets' downstream result is somewhat more durable, but both branches depended on additional assets, so the gap stays narrow. Confidence is high on the documented one-for-one core trade and the removal of the unsupported cash term.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded three future draft picks to Philadelphia on January 31, 1978 for rookie forward Wilson Washington. Washington gave the Nets 86 regular-season games across the rest of 1977-78 and 1978-79, averaging 8.3 points and 5.1 rebounds for the franchise before his NBA career ended. Philadelphia received the stronger long-term return. The 1979 second-round pick became No. 36 Clint Richardson, who played 426 regular-season games for the 76ers across six seasons and was part of the 1983 championship team. The 1982 second-round pick became No. 36 J.J. Anderson, who played only 13 games for Philadelphia before being waived. The 1983 third-round pick became No. 64 Claude Riley, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Richardson alone turned the package into a durable multi-year return, while New Jersey received two useful but short seasons from Washington. Philadelphia gets the clear edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Three-Pick Package Is Fully Confirmed

The New Jersey, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers all record the same January 31, 1978 exchange. The Nets sent a 1979 second-round pick, a 1982 second-round pick and a 1983 third-round pick to the 76ers for Wilson Washington.

Those picks ultimately became No. 36 Clint Richardson in 1979, No. 36 J.J. Anderson in 1982 and No. 64 Claude Riley in 1983. The legacy archive entry already had the right structure, so this review focuses on the realized value of each branch.

Washington Gave New Jersey 86 Games

Washington had appeared in only 14 games for Philadelphia before the trade. With New Jersey, he immediately moved into a larger role. He played 24 games for the Nets in the remainder of 1977-78, averaging 8.8 points and 5.9 rebounds in 21.8 minutes.

He returned for 62 games in 1978-79 and averaged 8.1 points and 4.7 rebounds in 18.4 minutes. Across his two Nets seasons, Washington appeared in 86 regular-season games and averaged 8.3 points and 5.1 rebounds.

Basketball-Reference lists 1978-79 as the final season of his NBA career. New Jersey therefore received useful short-term frontcourt production, but no later player or draft branch followed his departure.

The 1979 Pick Became the Important Philadelphia Asset

Philadelphia used the first incoming pick at No. 36 in the 1979 draft on Clint Richardson. He became a six-season 76ers guard and appeared in 426 regular-season games for Philadelphia.

Richardson played 52 games as a rookie, then 77 in each of the next three seasons, followed by 69 in 1983-84 and 74 in 1984-85. He was never a star, but he became a durable rotation piece on a contender.

Most importantly, Richardson was part of the 1982-83 championship team. He appeared in 13 playoff games during that title run, including all four games of the Finals sweep over the Lakers.

Richardson also retained some later transaction value. Philadelphia traded him to Indiana in October 1985 for a 1989 second-round pick, later used on Reggie Cross, plus a conditional future second-round pick that was not exercised. This review does not need that later return to justify the original trade, but it extends the Richardson branch beyond his six Philadelphia seasons.

The 1982 Pick Produced Only a Brief Philadelphia Stint

The second-round pick from 1982 became J.J. Anderson at No. 36. Anderson played 13 games for Philadelphia in 1982-83, averaging 1.3 points in 3.7 minutes.

The 76ers waived him on December 20, 1982. He later played for Utah, but those Jazz games do not belong to Philadelphia's return. This branch provided only minimal direct value to the 76ers.

The 1983 Third-Round Pick Never Produced NBA Games

Philadelphia used the third pick on Claude Riley at No. 64 in 1983. Basketball-Reference lists his college record and draft transaction but no NBA regular-season career. That branch ended without on-court NBA value.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A/B-. Philadelphia receives an A because one of the three picks became a six-season, 426-game rotation guard who contributed to the 1983 championship, while the other two picks at least reached the draft stage. New Jersey receives a B- because Washington gave the Nets 86 legitimate rotation games across two seasons, but his NBA career then ended and the Nets surrendered the pick that became the deal's only durable long-term contributor. The trade is not a total miss for New Jersey, but Richardson's six-year Philadelphia run creates a clear hindsight gap. Confidence is high.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Buffalo traded Ted McClain to Philadelphia on January 31, 1978 for a 1978 third-round pick that became No. 65 Marvin Delph. Basketball-Reference's team and league ledgers list the deal as player-for-pick, while Pro Sports Transactions also records cash going to Buffalo; the amount is not specified. McClain gave Philadelphia 29 regular-season games over the rest of 1977-78, totaling 91 points, 37 rebounds, 34 assists and 16 steals before the 76ers waived him in October 1978. Buffalo used the pick on Delph, but he never played an NBA regular-season game. Delph was later drafted again by Boston in 1979 without ever producing NBA service for the Braves/Clippers franchise. The cash creates some unquantified financial value for Buffalo, but there is no source-supported downstream basketball conversion. Philadelphia gets the modest edge because McClain supplied actual rotation minutes while Buffalo's player branch produced none.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Player-for-Pick Core Is Confirmed

Buffalo, Philadelphia and the league transaction ledgers all record the January 31, 1978 exchange as Ted McClain to the 76ers for a 1978 third-round pick. That pick became No. 65 Marvin Delph.

Those Basketball-Reference ledgers do not list cash. Pro Sports Transactions' 1978 draft-pick ledger adds a cash component going from Philadelphia to Buffalo. This review preserves that source distinction and does not invent an amount.

McClain Gave Philadelphia 29 Games

McClain joined a deep Philadelphia team in the middle of the season and played 29 regular-season games after the trade. He logged 293 minutes and totaled 91 points, 37 rebounds, 34 assists and 16 steals.

His role was limited. He did not start a game for Philadelphia and averaged just over ten minutes per appearance. Still, those minutes were real realized value from a third-round pick, and the 76ers received them during a season in which they remained an Eastern Conference contender.

The 76ers did not retain McClain long term. Philadelphia waived him on October 11, 1978. Phoenix later signed him as a free agent in January 1979, so there was no later Philadelphia player or draft asset tied to his departure.

Buffalo's Draft Pick Became Marvin Delph

The Braves kept the incoming third-round pick through the 1978 draft and used it at No. 65 on Marvin Delph of Arkansas.

Basketball-Reference lists Delph as a 1978 San Diego Clippers draft pick after the franchise relocation, but no NBA regular-season games appear on his player record. He was later selected again by Boston in the 1979 draft and still did not establish an NBA regular-season career.

That means the pick itself produced no on-court NBA value for the Buffalo/San Diego franchise.

The Cash Is Real but Cannot Be Converted Into Invented Basketball Value

Pro Sports Transactions gives Buffalo an additional asset in the form of cash. That should not be erased merely because Basketball-Reference's shorter team ledgers omit it. At the same time, the cited source does not specify the amount, and no later roster transaction is tied directly to those dollars.

This review therefore treats the cash as legitimate financial consideration but does not transform it into speculative player value.

This Was a Small Transaction on Both Sides

Philadelphia's return was only 29 games from a reserve guard, and McClain was gone before the next regular season. Buffalo's player return was zero NBA games from Delph, although the franchise also received the undocumented-amount cash consideration.

The gap is therefore much smaller than it would be if McClain had become a long-term rotation piece or Delph had developed into an NBA contributor.

Final Verdict

76ers Edge, C+/D+. Philadelphia receives a C+ because McClain gave the team 29 useful reserve appearances and actual NBA minutes for a third-round pick. Buffalo receives a D+ because Delph never played an NBA regular-season game, with the unspecified cash providing the only remaining realized value. The 76ers come out ahead, but the trade belongs in the low-impact tier rather than among meaningful franchise swings. Confidence is high on the player and pick outcomes and moderate on the financial component because the cash amount is not specified.

analysis:
The Player-for-Pick Core Is Confirmed

Buffalo, Philadelphia and the league transaction ledgers all record the January 31, 1978 exchange as Ted McClain to the 76ers for a 1978 third-round pick. That pick became No. 65 Marvin Delph.

Those Basketball-Reference ledgers do not list cash. Pro Sports Transactions' 1978 draft-pick ledger adds a cash component going from Philadelphia to Buffalo. This review preserves that source distinction and does not invent an amount.

McClain Gave Philadelphia 29 Games

McClain joined a deep Philadelphia team in the middle of the season and played 29 regular-season games after the trade. He logged 293 minutes and totaled 91 points, 37 rebounds, 34 assists and 16 steals.

His role was limited. He did not start a game for Philadelphia and averaged just over ten minutes per appearance. Still, those minutes were real realized value from a third-round pick, and the 76ers received them during a season in which they remained an Eastern Conference contender.

The 76ers did not retain McClain long term. Philadelphia waived him on October 11, 1978. Phoenix later signed him as a free agent in January 1979, so there was no later Philadelphia player or draft asset tied to his departure.

Buffalo's Draft Pick Became Marvin Delph

The Braves kept the incoming third-round pick through the 1978 draft and used it at No. 65 on Marvin Delph of Arkansas.

Basketball-Reference lists Delph as a 1978 San Diego Clippers draft pick after the franchise relocation, but no NBA regular-season games appear on his player record. He was later selected again by Boston in the 1979 draft and still did not establish an NBA regular-season career.

That means the pick itself produced no on-court NBA value for the Buffalo/San Diego franchise.

The Cash Is Real but Cannot Be Converted Into Invented Basketball Value

Pro Sports Transactions gives Buffalo an additional asset in the form of cash. That should not be erased merely because Basketball-Reference's shorter team ledgers omit it. At the same time, the cited source does not specify the amount, and no later roster transaction is tied directly to those dollars.

This review therefore treats the cash as legitimate financial consideration but does not transform it into speculative player value.

This Was a Small Transaction on Both Sides

Philadelphia's return was only 29 games from a reserve guard, and McClain was gone before the next regular season. Buffalo's player return was zero NBA games from Delph, although the franchise also received the undocumented-amount cash consideration.

The gap is therefore much smaller than it would be if McClain had become a long-term rotation piece or Delph had developed into an NBA contributor.

Final Verdict

76ers Edge, C+/D+. Philadelphia receives a C+ because McClain gave the team 29 useful reserve appearances and actual NBA minutes for a third-round pick. Buffalo receives a D+ because Delph never played an NBA regular-season game, with the unspecified cash providing the only remaining realized value. The 76ers come out ahead, but the trade belongs in the low-impact tier rather than among meaningful franchise swings. Confidence is high on the player and pick outcomes and moderate on the financial component because the cash amount is not specified.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Player-for-Pick Exchange Is Fully Confirmed

Boston, New Orleans and the league transaction ledgers all record the same February 1, 1978 deal. The Celtics sent Fred Saunders to the Jazz and received New Orleans's 1978 second-round pick.

That pick landed at No. 30 and became Jeff Judkins. There are no cash terms, protections or routing conflicts in the cited ledgers, so this review is a straightforward comparison between Saunders's short New Orleans tenure and Judkins's Boston production.

Saunders Gave New Orleans Thirty Games

Saunders joined the Jazz for the remainder of 1977-78 and appeared in 30 regular-season games. He averaged 13.3 minutes, 5.0 points, 2.5 rebounds and 1.2 assists.

His role was modest, but not nonexistent. The Jazz received an experienced forward who could fill bench minutes immediately while Pete Maravich and the rest of the roster pushed through the second half of the season.

The problem is duration. Basketball-Reference lists 1977-78 as Saunders's final NBA season. There was no later New Orleans player or draft asset generated by his departure. The Jazz's branch therefore ends with those 30 games.

Boston Used the Pick on Jeff Judkins

The Celtics kept the second-round pick and selected Judkins at No. 30 in the 1978 draft. He immediately became a meaningful reserve.

As a rookie in 1978-79, Judkins played 81 games and averaged 8.8 points, 2.4 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 18.8 minutes. He scored 709 points and logged 1,521 minutes.

He returned in 1979-80 for 65 games, adding 351 points in 674 minutes. Across two Boston seasons, Judkins appeared in 146 regular-season games and scored 1,060 points.

That is a substantial return for a second-round selection acquired in exchange for a player who had been on the edge of Boston's rotation.

Judkins's Later Career Is Not Credited to Boston

Judkins continued in the NBA after his Celtics stint and finished with 272 career games. Those later seasons are useful career context but do not belong to Boston's realized return once he left the franchise.

This review therefore stops the direct Celtics value at the 146 Boston games. Even with that conservative treatment, the pick comfortably outproduced Saunders's New Orleans tenure.

The Trade Was Small, but the Outcome Was Not Even

The original archive record called the trade even, which understated the difference in realized service. Saunders gave New Orleans 30 games and then left the NBA. Judkins gave Boston 146 games across two seasons, including an 81-game rookie year with nearly nine points per game.

Neither player was a franchise centerpiece, so the transaction belongs below major-trade territory. The value difference is still large enough to support a clear winner.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, B+/D+. Boston receives a B+ because the No. 30 pick became a two-season rotation player who appeared in 146 games and scored 1,060 points. New Orleans receives a D+ because Saunders supplied only 30 games before his NBA career ended. The Jazz did get short-term roster value, which keeps the grade above a complete miss, but Boston extracted far more realized NBA service from the exchange. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: Denver sent Jim Price and its 1979 first-round pick to Detroit on February 1, 1978 for Ralph Simpson. The legacy archive entry also attached Detroit's 1979 second-round and 1980 third-round picks to the deal, but the authoritative Denver, Detroit and league ledgers list only Simpson for Price plus the first; this review therefore removes those unsupported extra picks from this transaction. Simpson played 32 Denver games at 5.5 points per game before being packaged with Bobby Jones and a 1984 first-round pick in the George McGinnis trade. Detroit received 34 games from Price at 11.5 points per game, then a 1980 second-round compensation pick when he signed with the Lakers. The 1979 first became No. 15 Phil Hubbard, who played 196 Pistons games across three seasons and later helped headline the multi-asset deal that brought Bill Laimbeer and Kenny Carr to Detroit. Detroit clearly received the stronger realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Primary Ledgers Show a Smaller Package Than the legacy archive entry

Denver, Detroit and the league transaction ledgers all agree on the February 1, 1978 trade: the Nuggets sent Jim Price plus a 1979 first-round pick to the Pistons for Ralph Simpson.

The legacy archive entry also included a 1979 second-round pick that became Ollie Mack and a 1980 third-round pick that became Kurt Nimphius as assets going from Detroit to Denver. Those picks do not appear in the authoritative team or league ledgers for this transaction. Their later histories also point elsewhere. The Mack pick was already a Denver asset that the Nuggets sent to the Lakers in June 1978, while Denver drafted Nimphius in 1980 but the cited transaction ledgers do not tie that pick to Detroit. This review removes both unsupported assets from this trade rather than preserving a package the primary sources do not support.

Simpson's Denver Return Was Short

Simpson played 32 games for Denver after the trade, averaging 5.5 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 18.3 minutes. His second Nuggets stint lasted only through the end of the season.

On August 16, 1978, Denver traded Simpson, Bobby Jones and a 1984 first-round pick to Philadelphia for George McGinnis and a 1978 first-round pick that had become Mike Evans. Simpson therefore retained transaction value, but he was one of three outgoing assets and clearly cannot be credited with the full McGinnis-Evans return.

Price Gave Detroit a Productive Half-Season and Compensation

Price played 34 games for Detroit after the trade and averaged 11.5 points, 3.0 rebounds and 3.0 assists in 24.7 minutes. That was already more direct scoring production than Denver received from Simpson.

Price then signed with the Lakers as a veteran free agent on October 27, 1978. Detroit received a 1980 second-round pick that later became Brad Branson as compensation. The compensation pick adds another traceable asset branch even though Price himself spent only part of one season with the Pistons.

The First-Round Pick Became Phil Hubbard

Detroit used Denver's 1979 first-round pick at No. 15 on Phil Hubbard. He played 64 games as a rookie, 80 in 1980-81 and 52 for Detroit in 1981-82 before being traded, for 196 Pistons regular-season appearances.

Hubbard averaged 14.5 points and 7.3 rebounds in 1980-81, his strongest Detroit season. Across the three-season stint he became the most substantial direct asset created by the original trade.

Hubbard Then Helped Bring Bill Laimbeer to Detroit

On February 16, 1982, Detroit traded Hubbard, Paul Mokeski, a 1982 first-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick to Cleveland for Kenny Carr and Bill Laimbeer. That later package became enormously important to Detroit because Laimbeer developed into a core piece of the franchise's championship era.

This review does not assign Laimbeer's entire value to Hubbard because Detroit sent four assets. The transaction still demonstrates that Hubbard remained a meaningful trade piece after supplying 196 games.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A-/C+. Detroit receives an A- because Price supplied 34 productive games and a compensation pick, while the first-rounder became Hubbard, a 196-game contributor who retained substantial downstream trade value. Denver receives a C+ because Simpson provided only 32 games before becoming one component of a three-asset package. Once the unsupported Mack and Nimphius picks are removed from this transaction, the realized-value gap is no longer close. Confidence is high on the corrected package and its major downstream branches.

perspectives.analysis:
The Original Pick Swap Is Fully Confirmed

Cleveland, Milwaukee and the league transaction ledgers all record the June 1, 1978 exchange the same way. Cleveland sent its 1979 first-round pick to the Bucks and received Milwaukee's 1978 first-round pick. The Cavaliers used the incoming selection at No. 15 on Mike Mitchell.

The Cleveland Return Was Far Better Than a Normal Mid-First Outcome

Mitchell became an immediate rotation scorer. He played 80 games as a rookie in 1978-79 and then all 82 games in both 1979-80 and 1980-81. His third season was the peak of his Cleveland tenure: 24.5 points per game, 6.1 rebounds and an All-Star selection.

Mitchell stayed with Cleveland for 27 more games in 1981-82 before the Cavaliers traded him and Roger Phegley to San Antonio for Ron Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash. Across his Cavaliers tenure, Mitchell appeared in 271 regular-season games. This review does not assign the full Brewer-Johnson-cash package to Mitchell alone because Phegley was also outgoing, but the later trade confirms that Mitchell retained substantial asset value.

Milwaukee's Incoming Pick Landed at No. 4

Cleveland's 1979 first became the fourth pick in the draft. The legacy archive record stops at Greg Kelser because Detroit ultimately selected him there, but Milwaukee did not simply make that pick and keep Kelser.

On June 25, 1979, the Bucks traded the No. 4 pick to Detroit for the No. 5 pick. Detroit drafted Kelser at No. 4. Milwaukee moved down one slot and selected Sidney Moncrief at No. 5.

That Draft-Day Step Completely Changes the Long-Term Evaluation

Moncrief became one of the defining players of the Bucks' 1980s teams. Basketball-Reference lists him as a five-time All-Star, five-time All-NBA selection, five-time All-Defensive selection and two-time Defensive Player of the Year. He also entered the Basketball Hall of Fame.

The No. 4 pick acquired from Cleveland therefore did not merely become Kelser. It became the premium asset Milwaukee used to move down one spot and secure Moncrief. The distinction is essential because a simple Mitchell-versus-Kelser comparison badly understates Milwaukee's realized return.

Cleveland Still Received Major Value

This is not a case where one team won because the other side failed. Mitchell became one of Cleveland's best scorers of the period, made an All-Star team and gave the Cavaliers 271 games. A mid-first pick producing that level of direct value deserves a strong grade.

Milwaukee's result was simply larger and longer lasting. Moncrief developed into a franchise cornerstone with elite two-way recognition for much of the decade.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win, A+/A. Milwaukee receives an A+ because the Cleveland pick became the No. 4 slot, which the Bucks converted into No. 5 Sidney Moncrief, a Hall of Fame guard with five All-Star selections, five All-NBA honors, five All-Defensive honors and two Defensive Player of the Year awards. Cleveland receives an A because Mitchell played 271 games, made the 1981 All-Star team and retained later trade value. Both teams did extremely well; Milwaukee gets the edge because the pick became a true franchise-defining player. Confidence is high.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State traded its 1981 first-round pick to Portland on June 7, 1978 for the Trail Blazers' 1978 first-round pick. The legacy archive record described the outgoing asset as a 1979-or-1981 first, but the Warriors, Blazers and league transaction ledgers all identify it specifically as a 1981 first. Golden State used the incoming No. 22 pick on Raymond Townsend, who played 140 regular-season games for the Warriors across two seasons and scored 710 points. Portland never used the 1981 pick itself. In February 1980 the Blazers packaged that pick with Maurice Lucas and a 1980 first-round pick for Calvin Natt. The future Golden State pick eventually became No. 10 Albert King after New Jersey acquired it. Because the Blazers had to include Lucas and another first to get Natt, the entire Natt return cannot be credited to this asset alone. Portland still gets the edge because the 1981 first remained premium trade currency, while Townsend's direct Warriors value was modest.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The source-backed Package Is a 1981 First for a 1978 First

Golden State, Portland and the league transaction ledgers all agree on the June 7, 1978 transaction. The Warriors sent a 1981 first-round pick to the Trail Blazers and received Portland's 1978 first-round pick.

The legacy archive entry described Golden State's outgoing asset as a 1979-or-1981 first. This review normalizes that language to the source-supported 1981 first because all three authoritative transaction ledgers use that year.

Golden State Used the No. 22 Pick on Raymond Townsend

Portland's 1978 first landed at No. 22, where Golden State selected Raymond Townsend. He played 65 games as a rookie, averaging 4.7 points in 11.9 minutes, then appeared in 75 games in 1979-80.

Across two Warriors seasons, Townsend played 140 regular-season games and scored 710 points. He was a real NBA contributor, but he never became a high-impact starter or long-term core player for Golden State.

That direct return gives the Warriors more value than a failed draft pick, but it remains limited for a first-round asset.

Portland Held the Future Pick for Less Than Two Years

The Blazers did not wait until 1981 to use the pick. On February 8, 1980, Portland traded the future Golden State first to New Jersey together with Maurice Lucas and a 1980 first-round pick for Calvin Natt.

That later transaction is the key downstream branch. The Golden State pick was one of three assets Portland used to acquire a productive young forward. It therefore had substantial market value even before the draft.

Calvin Natt Became an Immediate Portland Contributor

Natt joined Portland during his rookie season and averaged 20.4 points in 25 games after the trade. He then played 74 games in 1980-81 at 13.4 points and 75 games in 1981-82 while averaging 18.4 points per 36 minutes.

This review does not assign all of Natt's Portland production to the 1981 first because Maurice Lucas and another first-round pick were also part of the package. The correct conclusion is narrower: the Golden State pick remained valuable enough to serve as one of the central pieces in a major trade for a productive forward.

The Pick Ultimately Became Albert King

New Jersey retained the Golden State selection until the 1981 draft. The pick landed at No. 10 and became Albert King. King went on to play 410 regular-season games for the Nets across six seasons.

That player value belongs to New Jersey, not Portland, because the Blazers had already traded the pick away. The No. 10 outcome is still useful for showing how valuable the asset ultimately became.

The Trade Was Not a Disaster for Golden State

A simple Townsend-versus-King comparison makes the Warriors look worse than the actual asset path warrants. Portland did not draft King, and the Blazers had to combine the pick with Maurice Lucas and another first to acquire Natt.

Golden State received 140 Townsend games and two seasons of reserve production. Portland received a future first that held stronger trade value and became part of a meaningful acquisition.

Final Verdict

Blazers Edge, B+/C+. Portland receives a B+ because the 1981 first became premium trade currency and helped the club acquire Calvin Natt in 1980. Golden State receives a C+ because Townsend gave the Warriors 140 games and 710 points, but the club surrendered a future first that eventually landed at No. 10. The Portland advantage is real without pretending the Blazers directly received Albert King or that the pick alone bought Natt. Confidence is high.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana and Portland made a major draft-day swap on June 8, 1978, one day later than the legacy archive entry date. The Pacers sent the No. 1 pick to Portland for Johnny Davis and the No. 3 pick. Portland used No. 1 on Mychal Thompson, who played 551 regular-season games across seven Trail Blazers seasons, averaging as much as 20.8 points and 11.7 rebounds in 1981-82. Indiana used No. 3 on Rick Robey, who played 43 Pacers games before being traded to Boston for Billy Knight. Knight then played 357 regular-season games for Indiana across the rest of 1978-79 through 1982-83. Davis became an even larger direct return, playing 319 Pacers games across four seasons while averaging 16.4 points and 5.4 assists. Portland landed the best single player, but Indiana converted the two-asset package into more total multi-year service and gets a narrow hindsight edge.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Authoritative Ledgers Put the Trade on June 8

The legacy archive entry is dated June 7, 1978, but Indiana, Portland and the league transaction ledgers all place the exchange on June 8. This review preserves the frozen route identity while recording June 8 as the source-verified transaction date.

The package itself is fully aligned across those ledgers. Indiana sent the 1978 first-round pick that became No. 1 Mychal Thompson. Portland sent Johnny Davis and the 1978 first-round pick that became No. 3 Rick Robey.

Portland Got the Best Individual Player in the Deal

The Trail Blazers used No. 1 on Thompson, and he became a long-term frontcourt centerpiece. Thompson played 73 games as a rookie in 1978-79, missed 1979-80 with a leg injury, then returned for six more Portland seasons from 1980-81 through 1985-86.

Across seven playing seasons with Portland, Thompson appeared in 551 regular-season games. His strongest statistical season came in 1981-82, when he averaged 20.8 points, 11.7 rebounds and 4.0 assists in 79 games. He also averaged at least 14.7 points in every Portland season he played after returning from the injury.

In June 1986 Portland traded Thompson with Larry Krystkowiak to San Antonio for Steve Johnson. This review records that as evidence of retained trade value, but does not assign the entire Johnson return to Thompson because Krystkowiak was also outgoing.

Johnny Davis Became a Four-Year Pacers Starter

Indiana's direct veteran return was substantial. Davis started all 79 games he played in 1978-79 and averaged 18.3 points and 5.7 assists. He then started 82 games in 1979-80, 73 in 1980-81 and 70 in 1981-82.

Across four Pacers seasons, Davis played 319 regular-season games and started 304. Basketball-Reference's Indiana split gives him averages of 16.4 points and 5.4 assists over that span. That is far more than a temporary bridge player.

Indiana also retained value when Davis left. On December 31, 1982, the Pacers traded him to Atlanta for a 1983 second-round pick later used on Jim Thomas. The later pick produced limited value, but Davis had already delivered four productive seasons.

The No. 3 Pick Became Rick Robey, Then Billy Knight

Indiana used Portland's first-round pick at No. 3 on Robey. He played 43 Pacers games as a rookie, starting 13 and averaging 8.6 points and 5.9 rebounds.

The Pacers then converted Robey into a much larger downstream return. On January 16, 1979, Indiana traded him to Boston for Billy Knight. Knight played 39 Pacers games during the remainder of 1978-79, then 75, 82, 81 and 80 games over the next four seasons.

That is 357 Indiana regular-season games after the Robey trade. Knight averaged 17.5 points in 1980-81 and 17.1 in 1982-83. The Robey branch therefore became a long-running scoring asset rather than ending after half a rookie season.

Both Teams Did Extremely Well

Portland can point to the strongest single outcome: a No. 1 pick who gave the franchise seven playing seasons and 551 games. Indiana can point to broader asset depth: 319 Davis games plus 43 Robey games before Robey became Knight, who added 357 more Pacers appearances.

The correct hindsight comparison is therefore much closer than a Thompson-versus-Robey draft comparison suggests.

Final Verdict

Pacers Edge, A+/A. Indiana receives an A+ because Davis became a four-year starter and the No. 3 pick became Robey, who was quickly converted into five seasons of Knight production. Portland receives an A because Thompson was the best single player in the deal and gave the Trail Blazers 551 games across seven seasons. The Pacers' narrow edge comes from the combined volume and successful Robey-to-Knight conversion, not from Thompson disappointing. Confidence is high.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Buffalo sent the 1978 second-round pick that became No. 38 Lew Massey to the Lakers on June 7, 1978 for Tom Abernethy. The Lakers used the pick on Massey, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season career for him. Abernethy also never played a regular-season game for the Buffalo/San Diego franchise after the trade. His value came one month later, when Golden State signed him as a veteran free agent and San Diego received a 1979 second-round compensation pick. The Clippers then combined that pick, which became No. 30 Gary Garland, with another 1979 second-rounder as compensation for signing Brian Taylor. Garland ultimately played 78 games for Denver, not San Diego, so that production is not credited to the Clippers. The Abernethy-derived pick still helped San Diego acquire Taylor, giving the franchise a modest downstream benefit that the Lakers did not match. The Clippers get the edge in an otherwise low-impact deal.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Original Package Is Fully Confirmed

Buffalo, Los Angeles and the league transaction ledgers all record the June 7, 1978 deal the same way. The Braves sent a 1978 second-round pick to the Lakers for Tom Abernethy. Los Angeles used the pick at No. 38 on Lew Massey.

There is no additional player, cash term or conditional language in the cited ledgers. The basic transaction is therefore one player for one second-round pick.

Massey Never Produced NBA Regular-Season Value

The Lakers selected Massey with the No. 38 pick in the 1978 draft. Basketball-Reference's draft ledger lists him at that slot but shows no NBA games, minutes, points, rebounds or assists.

That means the Lakers received no realized NBA playing value from the pick. This review does not substitute college production or later non-NBA activity for an NBA return that never materialized.

Abernethy Never Played for Buffalo or San Diego After the Trade

The other side is more unusual. Buffalo acquired Abernethy just before the franchise relocated, but he never appeared in a regular-season game for the Braves or the new San Diego Clippers.

His player page shows 1977-78 with the Lakers, then 1978-79 with Golden State. On July 15, 1978, the Warriors signed Abernethy as a veteran free agent. San Diego's transaction ledger records that the Clippers received a 1979 second-round pick as compensation.

That compensation pick is the real downstream return from Buffalo's acquisition.

The Compensation Pick Became Part of the Brian Taylor Signing

The Abernethy compensation pick later became the No. 30 selection in the 1979 draft, where Gary Garland was selected. San Diego did not use the pick itself.

On February 15, 1979, the Clippers signed Brian Taylor as a veteran free agent and sent two 1979 second-round picks to Denver as compensation. One became No. 33 Lawrence Butler. The other was the Abernethy-derived pick that became No. 30 Garland.

Garland later played 78 regular-season games for Denver. That production belongs to the Nuggets, not the Clippers. This review therefore does not credit San Diego with Garland's NBA games.

The pick still had meaningful transaction value. It was one of two second-round assets the Clippers used to complete the Taylor signing. Because another second-rounder was also outgoing, this review does not assign the full value of Taylor's San Diego tenure to the Abernethy-derived pick alone.

The Deal Stayed Small, but Buffalo's Side Had a Second Life

Neither original asset became a direct contributor for the team that acquired it. Massey never played in the NBA, while Abernethy never played for Buffalo or San Diego after the trade.

The difference is that Abernethy produced a compensation asset before leaving the franchise. That second-round pick was then used as part of another personnel move. The Lakers' Massey branch ended at the draft.

Final Verdict

Clippers Edge, C-/F. The Buffalo/San Diego franchise receives a C- because Abernethy produced no direct games but generated a 1979 second-round compensation pick that became useful transaction currency in the Brian Taylor signing. The Lakers receive an F because No. 38 Massey never appeared in an NBA regular-season game and no later Lakers asset branch is tied to the selection. This was a low-impact trade overall, so the verdict reflects a modest downstream advantage rather than a major franchise win. Confidence is high.

perspectives.analysis:
The Package Was LaGarde for the No. 17 Pick

Denver, Seattle and the league transaction ledgers all agree on the June 9, 1978 exchange. The Nuggets sent Tom LaGarde to the SuperSonics for a 1978 first-round pick. Denver used that pick later the same day at No. 17 on Wake Forest forward Rod Griffin.

There are no cash terms, protections or additional players to reconcile. The trade can be graded almost entirely on what LaGarde produced for Seattle and what Griffin failed to produce for Denver.

Griffin Never Appeared in an NBA Regular-Season Game

Denver's draft ledger lists Griffin as the No. 17 selection, and his Basketball-Reference profile identifies him as a 1978 first-round pick by the Nuggets. The draft table shows no NBA seasons, games or statistical totals.

That means the core Denver return produced zero realized NBA playing value. There is also no source-backed downstream trade branch attached to Griffin in the Nuggets transaction record that would rescue the asset through a later move.

LaGarde Gave Seattle Two Useful Seasons

LaGarde immediately became a meaningful reserve-center option for the SuperSonics. In 1978-79 he played 23 regular-season games, averaging 11.0 points and 8.3 rebounds in 25.0 minutes. He totaled 253 points and 190 rebounds.

Seattle went on to win the 1979 NBA championship. LaGarde's Basketball-Reference profile identifies him as a 1979 NBA champion, and the team page lists him on the championship roster. His value in that season is therefore best described as regular-season depth on the title team rather than as a major postseason contributor.

His larger workload came in 1979-80. LaGarde appeared in all 82 regular-season games, scoring 382 points and grabbing 312 rebounds. He also played 14 postseason games as Seattle advanced through Portland and Milwaukee before losing to the Lakers in the Western Conference Finals.

Across the two seasons, Seattle received 105 regular-season games, 635 points and 502 rebounds. That is modest rotation production, but it is real multi-season NBA value from a player acquired for a pick that never generated an NBA game.

The Asset Branch Ended in the Expansion Draft

Seattle did not later trade LaGarde for another player or draft asset. On May 28, 1980, the SuperSonics lost him to the Dallas Mavericks in the NBA expansion draft. That ends the downstream branch without an additional return.

The lack of a later trade haul keeps Seattle's grade below the top range. LaGarde was useful, but he was not a long-term cornerstone and did not produce a second major asset cycle.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, B+/F. Seattle receives a B+ because LaGarde supplied 105 regular-season games across two seasons, was part of the 1979 championship roster and contributed in 14 playoff games the following year. Denver receives an F because the No. 17 pick became Griffin, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game and generated no identified downstream return. The gap is large even though Seattle's side was a rotation-level acquisition rather than a star outcome. Confidence is high.

perspectives.summary: Denver's June 26, 1978 record is best understood as two same-day trades that form one three-team chain. First, Denver sent Darnell Hillman and the draft rights to Mike Evans to Kansas City for Ron Boone and a 1979 second-round pick. Denver immediately sent Boone, that Kings second-rounder and another 1979 second-round pick to the Lakers for Charlie Scott. The legacy archive entry omitted Boone and the Kings pick, so this review restores both. Scott gave Denver 148 regular-season games across two seasons. Los Angeles received 88 Lakers games from Boone, 27 games from No. 25 Ollie Mack and no NBA games from No. 41 Mark Young; Boone and Mack also retained modest downstream value. Kansas City got 78 games from Hillman while Evans was waived before playing. All three teams realized something, but Denver received the strongest single sustained return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Canonical record Represents Two Same-Day Trades

Basketball-Reference's Denver and league transaction ledgers record two separate June 26, 1978 moves. First, Kansas City sent Ron Boone and a 1979 second-round pick to Denver for Darnell Hillman and the draft rights to Mike Evans. Denver then sent Boone, that Kansas City second-round pick and a second 1979 second-round pick to the Lakers for Charlie Scott.

The Lakers and Kings team ledgers confirm their respective halves of the sequence. Pro Sports Transactions treats the chain as a three-team transaction, which is a reasonable canonical representation as long as every asset is preserved.

The legacy archive entry did not preserve every asset. It listed Scott to Denver, Hillman and Evans to Kansas City, and only the Ollie Mack pick to Los Angeles. This review restores Boone and the Kansas City second-round pick that became No. 41 Mark Young.

Denver Got Two Seasons From Charlie Scott

Scott became the clearest single-team return in the chain. He played 79 games for Denver in 1978-79, averaging 12.0 points and 5.4 assists in 33.1 minutes. He returned for 69 games in 1979-80, averaging 7.4 points and continuing as a veteran backcourt option.

That gives Denver 148 regular-season games across two seasons from the player acquired through the two-step maneuver. Scott did not create another major downstream asset branch, so the value is largely direct service rather than later trade capital.

The Lakers Received Boone Plus Two Second-Round Picks

Boone played all 82 games for Los Angeles in 1978-79, averaging 7.4 points in a reduced role, then appeared in six more Lakers games the following season. On October 25, 1979, Los Angeles traded him to Utah for a 1981 third-round pick. That gives Boone 88 Lakers regular-season games plus a modest later draft return.

One of the two second-rounders became No. 25 Ollie Mack. Mack played 27 regular-season games for Los Angeles in 1979-80 before the Lakers traded him, a 1980 second-round pick and a 1981 second-round pick to Chicago for Mark Landsberger. Because two additional picks were outgoing, this review does not assign the entire Landsberger return to Mack alone.

The second restored pick became No. 41 Mark Young. Basketball-Reference's 1979 draft ledger lists him as a Lakers selection but shows no NBA regular-season career. That branch produced no on-court value.

Kansas City Got One Useful Hillman Season

Hillman played 78 games for the Kings in 1978-79, averaging 7.0 points and 5.5 rebounds in 20.7 minutes. He was a useful frontcourt reserve for a 48-win Midwest Division champion.

Evans never appeared in a Kansas City regular-season game. The Kings waived him on October 11, 1978, and his later NBA career began elsewhere. Kansas City's realized return from the June chain is therefore almost entirely Hillman's one season.

The Result Is Competitive but Denver Has the Best Single Return

Los Angeles accumulated more separate assets, but two of them were limited: Mack played 27 Lakers games and Young never reached the NBA. Boone was useful for one full season and produced a third-round pick when moved.

Kansas City received 78 Hillman games but nothing from Evans. Denver received 148 Scott games across two seasons, including a full 79-game first year with substantial playmaking responsibility.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Edge, B+/B/C+. Denver receives a B+ because Scott supplied the strongest sustained direct return in the chain. Los Angeles receives a B because Boone gave the Lakers 88 games, Mack added 27 and Boone later returned a third-round pick, but Young produced no NBA value and Mack's later trade required two additional picks. Kansas City receives a C+ because Hillman gave the Kings one useful season while Evans was waived before playing. Confidence is high after restoring the two omitted Lakers assets and reconciling the two-step transaction sequence.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana traded a 1980 second-round pick to Portland on June 30, 1978 for Corky Calhoun. The Pacers received the only NBA playing value created by the exchange. Calhoun appeared in 81 games in 1978-79, averaging 4.7 points and 2.9 rebounds in 16.4 minutes, then played seven more games in 1979-80 before Indiana waived him on November 1, 1979. That gives the Pacers 88 regular-season games and 416 points from the veteran forward. Portland held the pick through the 1980 draft and used it at No. 32 on David Lawrence. Basketball-Reference records Lawrence as the Trail Blazers' second-round selection but shows no NBA regular-season career. The pick produced no later transaction branch in the cited Portland records. This was a low-impact trade overall, but Indiana received one full season of reserve production while Portland's draft return never reached an NBA regular-season game.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Original Deal Is Fully Confirmed

Indiana, Portland and the 1977-78 league transaction ledgers all record the June 30, 1978 exchange the same way. The Pacers sent a 1980 second-round pick to the Trail Blazers for Corky Calhoun. There are no cash terms, protections or additional players to reconcile.

The future pick later landed at No. 32 in the 1980 draft and became David Lawrence. That makes this a straightforward comparison between Calhoun's realized Indiana service and the playing value Portland eventually received from the draft asset.

Calhoun Gave Indiana One Full Season

Calhoun played 81 regular-season games for Indiana in 1978-79. He averaged 16.4 minutes, 4.7 points and 2.9 rebounds while shooting 45.7 percent from the field. His totals for the season included 416 points and 236 rebounds.

He was a reserve rather than a featured starter, but availability itself had value. The Pacers received a usable veteran for nearly the entire season instead of waiting two years for the outgoing draft pick to convey.

Calhoun returned in 1979-80 but appeared in only seven games, averaging 1.1 points in 4.3 minutes. Indiana waived him on November 1, 1979, and his NBA career ended. Across the post-trade Pacers tenure, he therefore supplied 88 regular-season games.

Portland Used the Pick on David Lawrence

The Trail Blazers kept the incoming second-rounder until the 1980 draft. Portland's transaction ledger and the 1980 draft results identify Lawrence as the No. 32 overall selection.

Lawrence's Basketball-Reference profile records the draft transaction but no NBA regular-season seasons, games or statistical totals. The pick therefore produced no realized NBA playing value for Portland.

There is also no source-backed later Portland trade branch attached to Lawrence. The Blazers did not turn him into another NBA player or draft asset in the transaction records used for this review.

The Preliminary Blazers Edge Does Not Survive Source Review

The legacy archive entry had leaned toward Portland, apparently giving the future second-round selection more abstract value than Calhoun's short Indiana tenure. Hindsight grading requires the opposite approach: named draft assets are evaluated by what they became.

Here, the pick became a player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Calhoun was modest, but he actually played 88 games for Indiana and filled a reserve role for a full season.

summary: Boston and San Diego completed this blockbuster on August 4, 1978, not July 7 as the legacy route date states. The Celtics received Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes, Billy Knight and two future second-round picks. Archibald played 363 Boston games across five seasons, made three All-Star teams, earned All-NBA Second Team honors in 1981 and started on the 1981 champions. The 1981 second became Danny Ainge, who played 556 Celtics games, won the 1984 and 1986 titles and made the 1988 All-Star team. Knight became Rick Robey in January 1979, and Robey later joined the 1983 second-round pick that became Rod Foster in Boston's multi-asset trade for Dennis Johnson. San Diego still received major value: Kermit Washington and Kevin Kunnert each played at least 81 games in 1978-79, Freeman Williams scored 4,467 points in 273 Clippers games over four seasons, and Sidney Wicks played 199 games. The Celtics' championship and downstream value wins, but the Clippers' return was substantial.
