boston-celtics.analysis:
The Authoritative Date Is August 4, 1978

Boston, San Diego and the league transaction ledgers all record this transaction on August 4, 1978. The legacy route is frozen under a July 7 date, so this review does not rewrite its archival identifier. It records August 4 as the source-verified transaction date.

The package itself is consistent across the authoritative ledgers. Boston sent Kevin Kunnert, Kermit Washington, Sidney Wicks and Freeman Williams to San Diego. The Celtics received Tiny Archibald, Marvin Barnes, Billy Knight, a 1981 second-round pick that became Danny Ainge and a 1983 second-round pick that later became Rod Foster. The legacy description of Wicks as a later future consideration is not supported by the Basketball-Reference team or league ledgers; they include him directly in the August 4 package.

Archibald Became a Championship Point Guard

Archibald's Boston tenure transformed the trade. He played 69 games in 1978-79, then 80 in both 1979-80 and 1980-81, 68 in 1981-82 and 66 in 1982-83. That is 363 regular-season games.

He made the All-Star team in 1980, 1981 and 1982, earned All-NBA Second Team honors in 1980-81 and was the starting point guard on Boston's 1981 championship team. The Celtics received five years of high-end guard play from a player who had missed the entire previous season with an Achilles injury.

The Ainge Pick Became Another Championship Core Piece

Boston kept the 1981 second-round pick and selected Ainge at No. 31. He played 556 regular-season games for the Celtics from 1981-82 through part of 1988-89. Ainge was on the 1984 and 1986 championship teams and made the 1988 All-Star team.

That outcome alone would make the draft portion of the deal unusually strong for a second-round asset.

Knight and the 1983 Pick Later Converged in the Dennis Johnson Trade

Knight played 40 games for Boston before the Celtics traded him to Indiana for Rick Robey on January 16, 1979. Robey then played 339 regular-season games for Boston and was part of the 1981 championship team.

On June 27, 1983, Boston sent Robey, the 1983 second-round pick from this trade and another 1983 second-rounder to Phoenix for Dennis Johnson, a 1983 first-round pick and a third-round pick. Phoenix used the incoming No. 28 selection on Rod Foster.

That branch requires careful attribution. Both Robey and the Foster pick trace back to the 1978 transaction, but another second-round pick was also outgoing, and Phoenix sent multiple assets back. This review credits the branch as a major shared downstream return without assigning all of Johnson's later Celtics value to either Knight or the Foster pick individually.

Barnes Was the Short Boston Branch

Barnes played 38 games for Boston in 1978-79, averaging 8.1 points and 4.7 rebounds. The Celtics waived him in February 1979. His limited tenure does not materially drive the grade.

San Diego Received a Strong Four-Player Return

The Clippers' side was much better than the legacy C+ grade suggested. Washington played all 82 games in 1978-79 and averaged 11.3 points and 9.8 rebounds. Kunnert played 81 games and averaged 6.5 points and 7.0 rebounds.

Freeman Williams became the best long-term San Diego scorer from the package. He played 273 games across four Clippers seasons and scored 4,467 points, including 18.6 points per game in 1979-80 and 19.3 in 1980-81. Wicks added 199 games across three seasons.

Washington and Kunnert also retained transaction value. In May 1979 San Diego sent both players plus a 1980 first-round pick to Portland as veteran-free-agent compensation after signing Bill Walton. That later return required an additional first-rounder, so this review does not assign Walton solely to the two players.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A+/A-. Boston receives an A+ because Archibald became a five-year championship point guard, Ainge became an eight-season Celtics contributor and two-time champion, and the Knight/Foster branches later helped form the package for Dennis Johnson. San Diego receives an A- because Williams, Wicks, Washington and Kunnert combined for substantial real playing value and two of those assets retained later transaction utility. This was not a one-sided talent giveaway; Boston simply converted its side into multiple championship-era pillars. Confidence is high.

perspectives.analysis:
The Original Package Is Fully Confirmed

Denver, Kansas City and the league transaction ledgers all record the July 10, 1978 transaction the same way. The Nuggets sent a 1981 fourth-round pick to the Kings for the draft rights to Geoff Crompton. The pick later landed at No. 78 and became Kenny Dennard.

Crompton Gave Denver Only a Short Rookie Look

Crompton had been Kansas City's fourth-round selection at No. 70 in the 1978 draft. After Denver acquired his rights, he appeared in 20 regular-season games for the Nuggets in 1978-79. Basketball-Reference lists only 88 total minutes, with 26 points and 19 rebounds.

Denver waived Crompton on April 11, 1979. He later returned to the NBA with Portland, Milwaukee, San Antonio and Cleveland, but those later seasons came after separate signings and trades. They do not create additional return for Denver from this 1978 transaction.

Kansas City Turned the Pick Into Kenny Dennard

The Kings used the 1981 fourth-round pick at No. 78 on Dennard. He played 30 games as a rookie in 1981-82 and 22 more in 1982-83. Across those two Kansas City seasons he appeared in 52 regular-season games, including three starts.

Dennard's production was modest, but Kansas City got more direct service from him than Denver received from Crompton. More importantly, the Kings did not lose Dennard for nothing.

Dennard Produced Another Draft Pick

On September 27, 1983, Kansas City traded Dennard to Denver for a 1985 third-round pick. Denver's transaction ledger confirms the same move from the opposite side. That pick later became No. 66 Michael Adams.

Adams played 18 games for Sacramento in 1985-86 before being waived on December 17, 1985. His later NBA career became far more substantial after he moved on, including an All-Star selection with Washington, but Sacramento did not realize that later value. This review therefore credits only the 18 Kings games tied to the pick outcome.

The Kings Won a Small Trade, Not a Franchise-Changing One

The difference here is quantity of realized value, not star impact. Denver received 20 Crompton games and no downstream asset after waiving him. Kansas City turned the future fourth into 52 Dennard games, then turned Dennard into a third-round pick that produced 18 Adams games.

Final Verdict

Kings Edge, B-/D+. Kansas City receives a B- because the club converted a fourth-round pick into two separate NBA players and 70 total regular-season games across the Dennard and Adams branches. Denver receives a D+ because Crompton appeared in only 20 games before being waived and produced no later Nuggets return. The overall trade is still low impact, so the gap reflects better asset recycling rather than a major talent win. Confidence is high.

summary: Boston traded its 1980 first-round pick to Indiana on July 19, 1978 for Earl Tatum. The legacy archive entry also showed cash moving in both directions, but the Celtics, Pacers and league transaction ledgers all record a straight player-for-pick exchange, so this review removes the unsupported cash entries. Tatum played only three Boston games, but the Celtics flipped him three months later to Detroit for Chris Ford and a 1981 second-round pick. Ford became a four-year Celtic, playing 309 regular-season games and starting 75 games on the 1981 championship team. Indiana held the first until February 1980, then packaged it with Alex English for George McGinnis. McGinnis played 173 regular-season games for the Pacers over parts of three seasons. Because English was also outgoing, this review gives the first-round pick only partial credit for that return. Boston's downstream conversion produced the stronger realized value.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The source-backed Package Is Tatum for a 1980 First

Boston, Indiana and the 1978-79 league transaction ledgers all record the July 19, 1978 deal as a straight exchange: the Celtics sent a 1980 first-round pick to the Pacers for Earl Tatum.

The legacy archive entry included cash going in both directions. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

Tatum Barely Played for Boston but Retained Immediate Trade Value

Tatum appeared in only three regular-season games for the Celtics in 1978-79, averaging 6.7 points in 12.7 minutes. If the branch ended there, Boston's side would be weak.

It did not. On October 19, 1978, Boston traded Tatum to Detroit for Chris Ford and a 1981 second-round pick that became Tracy Jackson. Detroit's transaction ledger independently confirms the same package.

Ford Became the Real Boston Return

Ford played 309 regular-season games for Boston across four seasons. He averaged 15.6 points in 78 games immediately after arriving in 1978-79, then started 73 games in 1979-80.

His most important team value came in 1980-81. Ford played all 82 games, started 75 and averaged 8.9 points and 3.6 assists for the Celtics team that won the NBA championship. He remained with Boston for another 76 games in 1981-82.

The second-round pick became Tracy Jackson. His NBA impact was minimal, but the pick was a separate realized asset on top of Ford. The Tatum branch therefore produced far more value than Tatum's three Boston appearances suggest.

Indiana Recycled the First Before the Draft

The Pacers did not use the acquired first-round pick themselves. On February 1, 1980, Indiana traded Alex English plus the Boston first to Denver for George McGinnis.

Denver later used the pick at No. 23 on Carl Nicks. Nicks never played for Indiana because the pick had already been moved. This review therefore does not credit his NBA career to the Pacers.

The Pick Helped Bring McGinnis, but English Was Also a Major Outgoing Asset

McGinnis played 28 games for Indiana after the trade in 1979-80, then 69 in 1980-81 and 76 in 1981-82. That is 173 regular-season games across parts of three seasons.

The value cannot be assigned entirely to the Boston first-round pick because Alex English was the other outgoing piece, and English was already a productive 26-year-old forward. The pick clearly had first-round trade value, but it was one component of a package rather than a standalone purchase of McGinnis.

Final Verdict

Celtics Edge, A/B. Boston receives an A because three Tatum games quickly became Chris Ford, a four-year Celtic and 1981 championship starter, plus a second-round pick. Indiana receives a B because the first-round pick retained meaningful trade value and helped acquire 173 McGinnis games, but the Pacers also surrendered Alex English in that deal. The source-backed cleanup also removes the unsupported two-way cash entries. Confidence is high.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston traded C.J. Kupec to Milwaukee on July 26, 1978 for the Bucks' 1979 fourth-round pick. The transaction is confirmed by the Rockets, Bucks and league ledgers. Neither side ultimately received NBA regular-season production from the acquired asset. Kupec never appeared in a game for Milwaukee; Basketball-Reference lists his final NBA season as 1977-78 with Houston. The Rockets held the pick until the 1979 draft and used it at No. 76 on Sammy Drummer, but the draft ledger records no NBA career for him. There is also no traceable downstream transaction attached to either asset after the deal. Houston at least retained a live draft asset for nearly a year, but hindsight realized-value grading cannot convert that unused opportunity into on-court production. With zero NBA games on both branches, this review resolves the trade as effectively even and low impact.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Original Exchange Is Unambiguous

Houston, Milwaukee and the 1978-79 league transaction ledgers all record the July 26, 1978 deal the same way. The Rockets sent C.J. Kupec to the Bucks and received Milwaukee's 1979 fourth-round pick.

The pick later landed at No. 76 and became Sammy Drummer. There are no cash terms, protections or secondary assets in the cited ledgers.

Kupec Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Milwaukee

Kupec had already played three NBA seasons before the trade. He appeared in 16 games for the Lakers in 1975-76, all 82 in 1976-77 and 49 for Houston in 1977-78.

His player page lists no 1978-79 Milwaukee season. The transaction history records the July 26 trade to the Bucks, but his NBA career ends after the 1977-78 Rockets season. Milwaukee therefore received the player asset but no regular-season NBA games from him.

There is no later NBA transaction on Kupec's Basketball-Reference history that creates a downstream Bucks return. His branch stops at zero realized Milwaukee games.

Houston Used the Pick on Sammy Drummer

The Rockets kept the fourth-round pick through the 1979 draft and used it at No. 76 on Sammy Drummer out of Georgia Tech.

The 1979 draft ledger lists Drummer at No. 76 but shows no NBA seasons, games, minutes or statistical totals attached to his record. That means the pick produced no NBA regular-season player value.

Unlike some other late-round picks in this archive, there is no source-supported trade of Drummer's rights that creates a second downstream branch. The Houston side therefore also ends at zero NBA games.

The Pick Still Had Interim Asset Value, but Hindsight Production Was Zero

Houston did hold a future draft choice for almost a year, which gave the Rockets more transaction optionality than Milwaukee had once Kupec's NBA career ended. That is real context, but the site's source-backed grading emphasizes realized outcomes rather than theoretical optionality.

By that standard, neither team converted its incoming asset into NBA production. Milwaukee got no Kupec games, and Houston got no Drummer games.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, F/F. Both teams receive an F because neither incoming asset produced an NBA regular-season appearance for the acquiring franchise and neither created a traceable downstream return. Houston's fourth-round pick preserved temporary asset optionality, but the actual No. 76 outcome produced no NBA career. This is a true low-impact transaction rather than a case where one side quietly found long-term value. Confidence is high.

Jura never played an NBA regular-season game for Cleveland; contemporary career histories indicate he returned to Italy. Because the exact future draft choices cannot be verified, this review does not assign Garrett or any other specific pick to Chicago and does not force a hindsight winner. perspectives.analysis:
The Rights Trade Is Real, but the Exact Return Is Not Fully Recoverable

Chicago's official historical transaction log records an August 11, 1978 move sending Chuck Jura to Cleveland for future considerations. RealGM's Cleveland and league transaction histories independently record Cleveland acquiring Jura's draft rights from the Bulls on that date.

The record becomes less certain when the return is broken into individual draft choices. Pro Sports Transactions describes Chicago's consideration as multiple future draft picks and places a possible link to the 1979 No. 47 selection used on Calvin Garrett, but the draft-pick page explicitly labels that connection unconfirmed.

This review therefore preserves the transaction while refusing to convert a possibility into a canonical pick outcome.

Basketball-Reference Does Not Carry the August 1978 Trade

The 1978-79 Bulls, Cavaliers and league transaction pages at Basketball-Reference do not list the Jura transaction. Jura's own Basketball-Reference transaction history records Chicago drafting him No. 45 in 1972 but does not add the later rights move.

That omission does not erase the deal because the Bulls' own media guide and RealGM both support the transaction. It does mean the archive should distinguish a source-supported rights transaction from a fully reconstructed draft-routing chain.

Jura Never Produced an NBA Game for Cleveland

Jura had spent his professional career in Italy after Chicago drafted him in 1972. The Cleveland transaction was an attempt to bring his NBA rights into the Cavaliers organization, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

Contemporary career summaries indicate Cleveland signed him in August 1978 before he ultimately returned to Italy. This review therefore records zero realized NBA games for Cleveland from the rights asset.

Chicago's Future Considerations Cannot Be Safely Assigned to Calvin Garrett

Chicago did use the No. 47 pick in the 1979 draft on Garrett, and the Bulls' draft ledger confirms that selection. The problem is provenance. The best draft-routing source located for this review calls the Jura-to-Garrett connection unconfirmed rather than established.

Assigning Garrett's 166-game NBA career to this trade would overstate the evidence. The same problem applies to any unspecified additional pick within the phrase multiple future draft picks. Without a source-supported identity for the actual conveyed selections, the Chicago branch cannot be graded from realized player output.

Why this review Keeps the record Active but Unscored

This is different from an unsupported legacy transaction. The Chicago rights deal itself is corroborated by the team's official history and independent transaction records. What is missing is enough precision about the return to make a directional hindsight verdict defensible.

Final Resolution

Insufficient Evidence, N/A/N/A. Cleveland acquired Jura's rights but received no NBA regular-season production from him. Chicago received future considerations, probably in draft capital, but the exact pick identities remain unresolved and the commonly suggested Calvin Garrett connection is explicitly unconfirmed in the available draft-routing source. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. Confidence is high that the rights transaction occurred and low on the precise composition of Chicago's return.

perspectives.summary: Philadelphia sent George McGinnis and the 1978 first-round pick used on Mike Evans to Denver on August 16, 1978 for Bobby Jones, Ralph Simpson and a future first-round pick that became No. 10 Leon Wood in 1984. Denver received real short-term value: McGinnis played 121 games for the Nuggets across parts of two seasons, averaged 22.6 points and 11.4 rebounds in 1978-79 and made the 1979 All-Star team. Evans did not play in 1978-79 and did not create immediate Nuggets value from the pick. Philadelphia's return was far more durable. Jones played 617 regular-season games across eight 76ers seasons, earned six straight All-Defensive First Team selections after the trade, won the inaugural Sixth Man of the Year award and helped the 1983 team win the championship. Simpson added 37 games before another trade, while Wood later played 67 Philadelphia games. The 76ers won the long-term value exchange decisively.
perspectives.analysis:
The Five-Asset Package Is Fully Confirmed

Denver, Philadelphia and the league transaction ledgers all record the August 16, 1978 exchange the same way. The Nuggets received George McGinnis and Philadelphia's 1978 first-round pick, which had already become No. 21 Mike Evans. The 76ers received Bobby Jones, Ralph Simpson and a future first-round pick that eventually conveyed in 1984 at No. 10 as Leon Wood.

There is no source conflict over the core package, which makes this review primarily a realized-value comparison.

McGinnis Gave Denver a Strong First Season

McGinnis was still a major player when he arrived. In 1978-79 he played 76 games for Denver and averaged 22.6 points, 11.4 rebounds and 3.7 assists. He made the All-Star team and remained one of the Nuggets' highest-usage players.

He returned for 45 Denver games in 1979-80, averaging 15.6 points, 10.3 rebounds and 4.9 assists. Across the two partial seasons, McGinnis played 121 regular-season games for Denver.

On February 1, 1980, the Nuggets traded him to Indiana for Alex English and a 1980 first-round pick that became Carl Nicks. That later trade gave Denver a major downstream branch, especially through English, but the return cannot be credited solely to this 1978 deal without acknowledging that it required moving McGinnis as a still-valued asset.

The Evans Pick Did Not Provide Immediate Denver Production

Philadelphia's outgoing No. 21 pick became Mike Evans. Basketball-Reference lists Evans as not playing in 1978-79. He later built an NBA career and eventually played several seasons for Denver after separate transactions, but those later Nuggets seasons were not direct uninterrupted production from this draft asset.

This review therefore does not inflate the original pick return by counting later Denver service acquired through different roster mechanisms.

Bobby Jones Became the Defining Asset

Philadelphia's side is dominated by Jones. He played 617 regular-season games for the 76ers across eight seasons. In each of his first six Philadelphia seasons, from 1978-79 through 1983-84, he earned All-Defensive First Team recognition. He also made All-Star teams in 1980-81 and 1981-82.

Jones's role changed without reducing his value. In 1982-83 he came off the bench, won the inaugural Sixth Man of the Year award and remained a major defensive piece on the 65-win Philadelphia team that swept the Lakers in the NBA Finals. That championship contribution gives the trade a team-success component that Denver's return cannot match.

Simpson Added a Short Secondary Branch

Ralph Simpson played 37 games for Philadelphia in 1978-79, averaging 5.5 points in 12.2 minutes. On February 7, 1979, the 76ers traded Simpson, Harvey Catchings and cash to New Jersey for Eric Money and Al Skinner.

Because Catchings and cash were also outgoing, this review records that downstream transaction without assigning the entire Money-Skinner return to Simpson.

The Future First Eventually Became Leon Wood

The final Philadelphia asset took six years to convey. Denver's future first ultimately became the No. 10 pick in the 1984 draft, which Philadelphia used on Leon Wood.

Wood played 38 games for the 76ers as a rookie and 29 more in 1985-86 before moving to Washington, giving Philadelphia 67 direct regular-season appearances from the long-delayed draft branch. His impact was modest, but the pick did produce an NBA rotation player.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/B. Denver receives a B because McGinnis gave the Nuggets 121 games, an All-Star season and enough retained value to headline the later Alex English trade. Philadelphia receives an A+ because Jones delivered eight seasons, elite defense, two All-Star selections, Sixth Man of the Year honors and a championship role, with Simpson and the future Wood pick adding secondary value. Denver received a legitimate short-term star; Philadelphia received the far stronger long-term foundation. Confidence is high.

The Jazz's official media guide says New Orleans received a 1979 second-round pick with considerations. Pro Sports Transactions describes that pick as conditional and questions whether it was exercised, while the available 1979 draft-routing evidence does not identify a specific Jazz selection from the deal. Davis signed with Milwaukee four days later but was waived in October and never played an NBA regular-season game. Because Milwaukee received zero NBA games and the exact New Orleans draft return cannot be tied confidently to a player or pick, this review does not force a hindsight winner. The legacy description is normalized from 'conditional second round pick (not exercised?)' to a source-backed description that preserves both the official media-guide language and the unresolved conveyance status.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
The Rights Trade Is Confirmed, but the Pick Outcome Is Not

New Orleans's official transaction history records that the Jazz traded 1978 fourth-round pick Mel Davis to Milwaukee on September 6, 1978 in exchange for a 1979 second-round pick with considerations. RealGM independently records Milwaukee acquiring Davis's draft rights on the same date.

Pro Sports Transactions supplies a more tentative description. Its Milwaukee transaction ledger calls the return a 1979 conditional second-round pick and includes a question about whether the condition was exercised. That uncertainty is important enough that this review does not convert the pick into a specific player without a stronger routing source.

Davis Never Played an NBA Game for Milwaukee

Davis had been selected by New Orleans at No. 74 in the 1978 draft. Milwaukee acquired his rights, and RealGM records the Bucks signing him on September 10.

The experiment ended quickly. RealGM records Milwaukee waiving Davis in October 1978, and Basketball-Reference's Melvin Davis draft page shows no NBA regular-season career. The Bucks therefore received no realized NBA playing value from the rights acquisition.

New Orleans Clearly Received Draft Consideration in the Agreement

The Jazz media guide is stronger than the legacy question mark on one point: it explicitly says the transaction was for a 1979 second-round pick with considerations. The deal was not simply Davis for nothing.

What the available record does not resolve is which second-round slot, if any, ultimately conveyed. Pro Sports Transactions treats the pick as conditional and possibly unexercised. Milwaukee's 1979 draft history still includes its own second-round selection, but that alone is not sufficient to reconstruct every possible condition, swap or reacquisition.

This review therefore preserves the contractual draft consideration without assigning a fabricated overall number.

Why the Trade Cannot Be Graded Directionally Yet

Milwaukee's branch is known: zero NBA games from Davis and no later Bucks transaction tied to his rights. New Orleans's branch is only partially known: a 1979 second-round consideration existed, but the actual conveyance and player outcome are unresolved in the cited sources.

Treating an unresolved pick as zero would be just as misleading as assigning it to an unverified player. The correct source-backed approach is to distinguish a documented consideration from an unidentified realized outcome.

The Earlier San Antonio Attempt Adds Context but Not Value

The Jazz media guide also records that New Orleans had tried to trade Davis to San Antonio in July 1978 for a 1979 third-round pick with considerations, but that transaction was cancelled when Davis failed to sign with San Antonio. That failed deal helps explain why Davis's rights were still available in September, but it is not part of Milwaukee's trade return and receives no value in this review.

Final Resolution

Insufficient Evidence, N/A/N/A. Milwaukee acquired Davis's rights and received zero NBA regular-season games. New Orleans received a contractual 1979 second-round consideration, but the exact conveyed pick and downstream player remain unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value. Confidence is high on the trade and Davis's zero-game outcome, and low on the final pick conveyance.

perspectives.summary: Detroit reacquired Kevin Porter from New Jersey on September 8, 1978 for Eric Money, and both clubs extracted real value from the swap. Porter played all 82 games for the Pistons in 1978-79, averaged 15.4 points and an NBA-leading 13.4 assists, then left for Washington as a veteran free agent; Detroit received two first-round picks as compensation, one in 1980 and one in 1982. Money gave the Nets 47 games at 16.7 points and 5.3 assists before New Jersey included him with Al Skinner in a February 1979 trade for Harvey Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash. Catchings was later moved for John Gianelli and the 1979 first-round pick used on Calvin Natt, but that downstream branch came from a multi-player package and cannot be credited entirely to Money. Detroit therefore gets the stronger source-traceable return: a league-leading season from Porter plus two directly attributable first-round compensation assets.
perspectives.analysis:
The One-for-One Exchange Is Clear

New Jersey and Detroit list the September 8, 1978 transaction identically: the Nets sent Kevin Porter to the Pistons for Eric Money. The league transaction ledger confirms the same one-for-one swap.

The legacy asset label called Porter "Kevin Porter (Sr.)," but the historical player record is simply Kevin Porter. This review normalizes that name rather than preserving a misleading generational suffix.

Porter Delivered an Elite Passing Season Immediately

Detroit received much more than ordinary rotation production. Porter played all 82 games in 1978-79, started all 82 and averaged 15.4 points, 13.4 assists and 1.9 steals.

The NBA's official 1978-79 season review lists Porter as the league assists leader at 13.4 per game. Basketball-Reference records 1,099 assists in the season. That gives Detroit a full season of high-end direct value from the acquired player even though the Pistons finished 30-52.

Porter Then Produced Two First-Round Compensation Assets

Porter signed with Washington as a veteran free agent on July 12, 1979. Detroit's transaction ledger records two first-round picks as compensation: a 1980 first that eventually landed at No. 13 and a 1982 first that eventually landed at No. 12.

Those picks retained real transaction value even though Detroit did not simply draft both named players. The 1980 first later identified with Rickey Brown was included with another first-round pick in the Bob McAdoo transaction. The 1982 first later identified with John Bagley was included with Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski and a second-round pick in the 1982 deal that brought Kenny Carr and Bill Laimbeer to Detroit.

This review does not assign all of McAdoo or Laimbeer's value to Porter's compensation picks because both were multi-asset packages. It does, however, credit Detroit for preserving two first-round assets directly tied to Porter's departure.

Money Was Productive for New Jersey

The Nets also got useful immediate production. Money played 47 games for New Jersey in 1978-79 and averaged 16.7 points, 5.3 assists and 1.6 steals in 30.5 minutes.

On February 7, 1979, New Jersey traded Money and Al Skinner to Philadelphia for Harvey Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash. Because Skinner was an additional outgoing player, the entire return cannot be assigned solely to Money.

The Money Branch Still Helped Feed a Valuable Nets Chain

Catchings later became the clearest downstream branch from that Philadelphia return. On May 31, New Jersey traded Catchings to Milwaukee for John Gianelli and a 1979 first-round pick that became No. 8 Calvin Natt.

Natt then played 53 games for the Nets as a rookie, averaging 19.7 points and 9.7 rebounds. In February 1980, New Jersey traded Natt to Portland for Maurice Lucas and two first-round picks that became Mike Gminski and Albert King.

That chain became extremely valuable for the Nets, but source-backed grading has to preserve the attribution problem: Catchings was received for Money plus Skinner, not Money alone. This review records the downstream sequence as shared package value rather than pretending every later Nets asset came only from the original Porter-for-Money exchange.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A+/A-. Detroit receives an A+ because Porter supplied a complete 82-game season, led the NBA at 13.4 assists per game and then generated two first-round compensation picks. New Jersey receives an A- because Money was productive for 47 games and participated in a trade package that fed a valuable Catchings-to-Natt downstream chain. The Nets did well, but Detroit's strongest outcomes are more directly attributable to the single incoming asset. Confidence is high.

Watts gave the Rockets 61 regular-season games in 1978-79, averaging 3.7 points and 4.0 assists in 17.1 minutes, and that season proved to be the end of his NBA career. indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana's 1978 signing of Alex English cost the Pacers a 1979 first-round pick sent to Milwaukee as free-agent compensation. Basketball-Reference dates the signing and compensation to June 8, while the legacy October 3 record aligns with a draft-trade ledger that records Milwaukee's agreement not to exercise its right of first refusal. English gave Indiana 135 regular-season games across parts of two seasons, including 16.0 points and 8.1 rebounds per game in 1978-79. The Pacers later traded English with another first-round pick for George McGinnis, so that downstream return is shared-package value. Milwaukee did not draft Calvin Natt with Indiana's pick: the Bucks packaged the pick with John Gianelli for Harvey Catchings, and New Jersey used it at No. 8 on Natt. Catchings then played 372 games for Milwaukee. Indiana gets the edge because English's direct Pacers production was stronger, but Milwaukee realized a durable return from the compensation asset.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Source Record Has a Date Split, but the Economic Exchange Is Clear

Basketball-Reference's 1977-78 Indiana and Milwaukee transaction logs record June 8, 1978 as the date Indiana signed Alex English as a veteran free agent and sent Milwaukee a 1979 first-round pick as compensation.

The legacy canonical record is dated October 3. A separate draft-pick transaction ledger places Milwaukee's agreement not to exercise its right of first refusal on English on that date and ties the same 1979 first-round pick to the agreement. This review preserves the canonical record rather than inventing a second transaction, but records the date split explicitly.

Whichever administrative date is used, the underlying value exchange is the same: Indiana acquired English's services, and Milwaukee acquired Indiana's 1979 first-round pick.

English Gave Indiana 135 Productive Games

English immediately became a major Pacers contributor. In 1978-79 he played 81 games, started 69 and averaged 16.0 points, 8.1 rebounds and 3.3 assists while shooting 51.1 percent.

He remained productive for Indiana in 1979-80. Before the midseason trade he played 54 games, started 15 and averaged 14.9 points, 7.0 rebounds and 2.6 assists.

That gives the Pacers 135 direct regular-season games from the free-agent signing. This review does not credit Indiana for the Hall of Fame career English later built in Denver. Those seasons occurred after he left the Pacers and belong to Denver's side of the later transaction.

Indiana Also Used English in the George McGinnis Trade, but Attribution Is Shared

On February 1, 1980, Indiana traded English and a 1980 first-round pick to Denver for George McGinnis. The additional first matters because McGinnis cannot be treated as a return generated by English alone.

McGinnis nevertheless gave Indiana substantial downstream value from the package. He played 28 games for the Pacers after the trade in 1979-80 and averaged 16.9 points, 10.9 rebounds and 5.1 assists. He followed with 69 games in 1980-81 at 17.6 points, 10.3 rebounds and 4.1 assists, then played 76 more games in 1981-82.

The Pacers therefore received useful downstream production, but this review assigns it only as shared-package context because the separate first-round pick was part of the price.

Milwaukee Did Not Simply Use the Pick on Calvin Natt

The legacy summary says Milwaukee received Calvin Natt. That skips an important transaction.

On May 31, 1979, Milwaukee traded John Gianelli and the Indiana first-round pick to New Jersey for Harvey Catchings. New Jersey, not Milwaukee, then used the pick at No. 8 on Natt.

That means Natt's NBA career is not realized Bucks production from this transaction. Milwaukee's actual downstream return from the pick was its role in the package that acquired Catchings.

Catchings Became a Long-Term Bucks Rotation Player

Catchings played five seasons for Milwaukee from 1979-80 through 1983-84. He appeared in 372 regular-season games for the Bucks and started 45.

His role was mostly defensive and rotational rather than star-level. He played 72 games in his first Milwaukee season, 77 in 1980-81, 80 in 1981-82, 74 in 1982-83 and 69 in 1983-84.

The attribution again requires care because Milwaukee sent Gianelli with the pick. Catchings cannot be credited entirely to Indiana's first-rounder, just as McGinnis cannot be credited entirely to English.

The Pacers Still Hold the Hindsight Edge

Both organizations realized useful value. Milwaukee turned the compensation pick, together with Gianelli, into a player who stayed in the rotation for five seasons. That is a materially better outcome than simply losing English for nothing.

Indiana, however, received 135 direct games from English at a much higher individual level, including a full season as a 16-point, eight-rebound starter. The later McGinnis package adds more value even after discounting it for the extra first-round pick.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, A-/B. Indiana receives an A- because English delivered 135 productive games and then remained part of a package that returned McGinnis. Milwaukee receives a B because the first-round compensation asset retained enough value to help acquire Catchings, who played 372 Bucks games, but Gianelli was also required in that deal. The result is a clear Pacers edge without crediting Indiana for English's Denver prime or pretending Milwaukee directly drafted Natt. Confidence is high.

Golden State held the pick and used it at No. 24 in 1980 on Larry Smith. Smith became a nine-season Warriors fixture, playing 617 regular-season games for the franchise. As a rookie he averaged 9.6 points and 12.1 rebounds and earned All-Rookie recognition, then remained one of the team's primary rebounders through the decade. perspectives.analysis:
The source-backed Exchange Does Not Include Cash

Detroit, Golden State and the 1978-79 league transaction ledger all record the October 9, 1978 trade as Rickey Green to the Pistons for Detroit's 1980 second-round pick.

None of those ledgers includes cash. The legacy canonical record did, so this review removes the unsupported cash asset rather than carrying forward a term that is absent from the strongest transaction sources.

Detroit Got Only 27 Games from Green

Green played 27 regular-season games for the Pistons in 1978-79. He averaged 16.0 minutes, 6.6 points, 2.3 assists and 0.9 steals while shooting 37.9 percent.

Detroit waived him on December 11, barely two months after the trade. Green then spent 1979-80 outside the NBA before resurfacing with Utah and eventually becoming an All-Star-level point guard there.

Those later Jazz seasons do not count as Detroit value. The Pistons received no traceable trade compensation or downstream asset when they waived him.

The Pick Became Larry Smith at No. 24

Golden State kept Detroit's second-round pick through the 1980 draft and used it on Alcorn State forward Larry Smith with the 24th overall selection.

The outcome was dramatically better than a typical second-round return. Smith played 82 games as a rookie, averaged 31.4 minutes, 9.6 points and 12.1 rebounds, and earned All-Rookie recognition.

He followed with 74 games at 11.0 rebounds per game in 1981-82, 49 games at 9.9 rebounds in 1982-83 and 75 games at 9.0 rebounds in 1983-84. His role stayed substantial through the middle of the decade.

Smith Became a Nine-Season Warriors Fixture

Smith remained with Golden State through 1988-89. Across those nine seasons he played 617 regular-season games for the Warriors.

His scoring was never the point of his value. Smith's career was built around rebounding, interior work and durability. He later continued for Houston and San Antonio, but this review credits only the Warriors seasons produced by Detroit's pick.

The contrast with Green's Detroit stint is unusually stark. Detroit acquired a young guard who lasted 27 games and was waived. Golden State turned the outgoing player into a second-round pick, waited through the 1980 draft and found a player who stayed almost a decade.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, A+/D. Golden State receives an A+ because the No. 24 pick became Larry Smith, a 617-game Warriors contributor and elite rebounder whose rookie season alone dwarfed Detroit's realized return. Detroit receives a D because Green supplied 27 modest games before being waived and created no downstream asset. The legacy Pistons-win framing is reversed by the source-backed outcome, and the unsupported cash term is removed. Confidence is high.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State traded Charles Dudley to Chicago on October 10, 1978 for the Bulls' 1979 second-round pick and cash. The Warriors' official media guide supports the canonical October 10 date and includes cash, while Basketball-Reference dates the transaction October 11 and lists only the pick; this review preserves the first-party date and restores the cash term while documenting the source conflict. Dudley played 43 games for Chicago in 1978-79, averaging 2.7 points and 2.7 assists in 15.9 minutes, and was waived before the next season. Golden State used the pick at No. 28 in 1979 on Danny Salisbury, whose draft ledger shows no NBA regular-season career. The cash amount is not identified in the reviewed sources. Chicago therefore gets the modest hindsight edge from receiving actual rotation minutes, but this remained a low-impact transaction.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Warriors' Own Ledger Clarifies the Package

Golden State's official media guide records the trade on October 10, 1978: Charles Dudley to Chicago for a 1979 second-round draft choice and cash.

That first-party record differs slightly from Basketball-Reference. The Bulls, Warriors and league Basketball-Reference ledgers date the trade October 11 and list the second-round pick but omit cash. RealGM agrees with the Warriors on the October 10 date.

This review preserves the canonical October 10 date because it is supported by the Warriors' own historical transaction ledger and RealGM. It also restores cash as a received Golden State asset, but marks the amount unresolved because no reviewed source identifies a figure.

The Pick Is Fully Traceable to Danny Salisbury

The pick itself is not vague future consideration. Golden State's Basketball-Reference transaction log identifies it as Chicago's 1979 second-round pick, and the 1979 draft ledger shows the Warriors using No. 28 on Danny Salisbury.

Salisbury's draft record contains no NBA seasons, games, minutes or statistical totals. His Basketball-Reference player page likewise lists the Golden State selection but no regular-season NBA production.

That means the draft branch produced no realized NBA games for the Warriors. This review still preserves the value of the cash term, but it does not invent a monetary amount or use theoretical pick value as a substitute for realized production.

Dudley Gave Chicago 43 Games

Dudley played 43 games for the Bulls in 1978-79. He averaged 15.9 minutes, 2.7 points, 2.7 assists and 2.0 rebounds.

The role was modest, but it was real rotation service. Chicago received nearly 700 regular-season minutes from the acquired guard.

Dudley did not become a long-term Bull. The 1979-80 league transaction ledger records Chicago waiving him on September 25, 1979, before he appeared in another regular-season game for the franchise.

There is no traceable downstream Chicago return attached to that waiver. Dudley's branch therefore ends with one season and 43 games.

Why Chicago Holds Only a Small Edge

This is not a trade where either side found a major long-term asset. Chicago got one season of reserve point-guard minutes. Golden State converted the pick into a player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

The unresolved cash term keeps Golden State from being treated as receiving literally nothing. Cash had transaction value at the time, but without a documented amount it cannot be translated into a precise retrospective grade.

The source conflict also matters editorially. Basketball-Reference's clean one-for-one listing is incomplete relative to the Warriors' own media guide, while the official guide's October 10 date is corroborated by RealGM. This review therefore records the disagreement instead of silently choosing one source and hiding the other.

Final Verdict

Slight Bulls Edge, C-/D. Chicago receives a C- because Dudley supplied 43 games and 684 minutes of real rotation service before being waived. Golden State receives a D because the No. 28 pick became Salisbury, who produced no NBA regular-season career, while the additional cash return remains unquantified. The difference is real but small, and confidence is medium-high because the on-court outcomes are clear even though the sources disagree on the administrative date and cash term.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Core Exchange Is Clear

Boston and Phoenix agree on the central transaction. On October 11, 1978, the Celtics acquired Dennis Awtrey and sent Phoenix their 1979 second-round pick. The Suns later used that selection at No. 24 on Johnny High.

Basketball-Reference's Boston, Phoenix and league transaction ledgers all record the player-for-pick structure. The Boston source batch preserved in this archive also lists cash going to Phoenix. Because the reviewed public ledgers do not repeat that cash term and no amount is identified, this review keeps the cash asset in the record but labels it unresolved rather than silently presenting it as fully corroborated.

Awtrey Became More Than 23 Boston Games

Awtrey appeared in 23 games for the 1978-79 Celtics and logged 247 minutes. His Boston line was modest: 2.2 points, 2.0 rebounds and 0.9 assists per game.

The more important branch came three months later. On January 17, 1979, Boston traded Awtrey to Seattle for a 1979 first-round pick. Basketball-Reference identifies that pick as the selection later used on Sly Williams at No. 21.

Boston did not make that selection itself. On February 12, the Celtics included the Sly Williams pick with Tom Barker and two other 1979 first-round picks in the package sent to New York for Bob McAdoo.

That means Awtrey's Boston value was not limited to his 23 games. He was converted into a first-round asset that became one component of a larger acquisition. This review records that downstream path without assigning the entire value of McAdoo, or anything that followed McAdoo, solely to the Awtrey branch.

Phoenix Got Four Seasons from Johnny High

Phoenix used the incoming second-round pick on Johnny High at No. 24 in the 1979 draft.

High played four NBA seasons, all with Phoenix, appearing in 274 regular-season games. He averaged 5.1 points, 2.3 rebounds and 1.9 assists for his career and accumulated 4,538 minutes.

The Suns received useful reserve-guard service from a second-round pick. High played all 82 games as a rookie, 81 the next season, then returned for 82 games in 1982-83 and 29 more in 1983-84.

That is a strong realized outcome for the asset Phoenix received. The unresolved cash term may add some transaction value, but no numerical weight is assigned because the amount is not documented in the reviewed public sources.

Why the Result Stays Even

Phoenix has the cleaner direct outcome. The second-round pick became a four-season contributor who played 274 games for the franchise.

Boston's return was less direct but still meaningful. Awtrey supplied 23 games, then became a first-round pick within three months. That pick was subsequently used as one part of the McAdoo package.

It would overstate the record to credit Boston with all of McAdoo's later value, because the Celtics sent multiple other assets in that February transaction. It would also understate the Awtrey branch to stop the analysis after 23 games and ignore the first-round return.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B-/B-. Phoenix gets a B- because the No. 24 pick became Johnny High, a four-season Suns contributor with 274 games. Boston also gets a B- because Awtrey produced short-term center depth and was quickly converted into a 1979 first-round pick that remained useful in a larger trade package. los-angeles-clippers.summary: Philadelphia traded World B. Free to the San Diego Clippers on October 12, 1978 for a 1984 first-round pick. Free immediately became an elite scorer in San Diego, averaging 28.8 points in 78 games in 1978-79 and 30.2 points in 68 games in 1979-80. The Clippers then traded him to Golden State for Phil Smith and another 1984 first-round pick, later used on Lancaster Gordon. Philadelphia held the original Clippers pick for nearly six years and used it at No. 5 in 1984 on Charles Barkley. Barkley played 610 regular-season games over eight Philadelphia seasons, averaging 23.3 points and 11.6 rebounds. Both branches produced substantial value, but the Barkley outcome gives Philadelphia the clear hindsight advantage.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Original Trade Is Fully Traceable

Philadelphia and San Diego transaction ledgers record the same October 12, 1978 exchange. The 76ers sent World B. Free to the Clippers and received San Diego's 1984 first-round pick.

That distant pick did not disappear into a later transaction. Philadelphia retained it until the 1984 draft, when it landed at No. 5 and became Charles Barkley.

Free Became a Star Immediately in San Diego

The Clippers did not miss on the incoming player. Free played 78 games in 1978-79 and averaged 28.8 points, 4.4 assists and 3.9 rebounds in 37.9 minutes. He earned All-NBA Second Team recognition and finished sixth in MVP voting.

He followed with 30.2 points per game over 68 games in 1979-80 and made the All-Star team. Across his two San Diego seasons, Free played 146 regular-season games and averaged 29.4 points.

That is major realized value. Any retrospective grade that treats San Diego as receiving nothing would misrepresent what the club actually got from the deal.

The Clippers Also Created a Downstream Return

On August 28, 1980, San Diego traded Free to Golden State for Phil Smith and a 1984 first-round pick. Smith immediately played 76 games for the 1980-81 Clippers, averaging 16.8 points and 4.9 assists, then appeared in 48 more games the following season.

The first-round pick from Golden State became No. 8 in the 1984 draft and was used on Lancaster Gordon. Gordon played 201 regular-season games for the Clippers over four seasons.

Those later assets strengthen San Diego's side of the original Free branch. This review records them as downstream value rather than stopping the analysis when Free left after two seasons.

Philadelphia's Pick Became Charles Barkley

The original 1978 return ultimately landed even higher in the same 1984 draft. Philadelphia used the Clippers pick at No. 5 on Barkley.

Barkley spent his first eight NBA seasons with the 76ers. He played 610 regular-season games for Philadelphia and averaged 23.3 points, 11.6 rebounds and 3.7 assists. The 76ers' own alumni history notes four All-NBA First Team selections during his Philadelphia tenure.

That realized outcome is extraordinary for an asset acquired almost six years earlier. The value is not theoretical draft capital; it is eight seasons from a Hall of Fame player who became one of the franchise's defining stars.

Why Philadelphia Still Holds the Clear Edge

San Diego's return was genuinely strong. Free delivered two elite scoring seasons, and the Clippers later converted him into Smith plus the pick that became Gordon. That branch produced useful value across multiple players and years.

Philadelphia's branch was simply much larger. Barkley's 610 games, star-level production and long Philadelphia tenure outweigh even the successful Free-to-Smith-and-Gordon chain.

The gap should not turn the Clippers grade into a failure grade. They acquired a player who performed at an All-NBA level and later recovered additional assets. The trade is a hindsight win for Philadelphia because of an exceptional draft conversion, not because San Diego's incoming player disappointed.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/B+. Philadelphia receives an A+ because the 1984 first-round pick became Barkley, who produced eight star-level seasons and 610 games for the franchise. The Clippers receive a B+ because Free became an immediate All-NBA scorer and was later converted into Smith plus the pick used on Gordon. Both sides received substantial realized value, but Philadelphia's long-term return was on a different scale.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Trade Structure Is Straightforward

Boston and Detroit transaction records agree on the October 19, 1978 exchange. The Celtics sent Earl Tatum to the Pistons and received Chris Ford plus a 1981 second-round pick.

The draft asset stayed with Boston long enough to become the No. 25 selection in 1981. The Celtics used it on Notre Dame guard Tracy Jackson.

Ford Became a Four-Year Boston Contributor

Ford played 78 games for Boston immediately after the trade in 1978-79 and averaged 15.6 points, 4.7 assists and 3.3 rebounds. He stayed with the Celtics through 1981-82.

Across four Boston seasons, Ford appeared in 309 regular-season games and started 201. His role changed as the roster improved, but he remained a real rotation piece throughout the transition from a 29-win 1978-79 team to a championship roster.

The most important season is 1980-81. Ford played all 82 games, started 75 and averaged 33.2 minutes. Boston won the NBA championship that season, making Ford a substantial contributor to the title team rather than a fringe roster holdover.

He also continued into 1981-82, playing 76 games and starting 53 before his NBA career ended.

The Extra Pick Produced Limited but Real Value

Boston's second asset became Tracy Jackson at No. 25 in the 1981 draft.

Jackson played 11 games for the Celtics in 1981-82, totaling 66 minutes. On December 9, 1981, Boston sold his player rights to Chicago.

That outcome is modest, and this review does not inflate the pick as if Boston received Jackson's entire three-year NBA career. The direct Celtics value was 11 games plus whatever consideration came from the rights sale, whose amount is not documented in the reviewed Basketball-Reference transaction record.

Detroit Got One Rotation Season from Tatum

Tatum played 76 games for Detroit in 1978-79 after the trade. He logged 1,195 minutes and averaged 7.8 points, 1.6 rebounds and 0.9 assists.

That is meaningful short-term return. Tatum was not a non-factor, and Detroit received substantially more than a few appearances or an unused roster spot.

The difference is duration and role. Tatum's Detroit value is concentrated in one season. Ford gave Boston four seasons, more than 9,000 minutes, 309 regular-season games and a starting role on a championship team.

Why Boston Wins in Retrospect

The Celtics received the best individual asset in Ford and also retained the additional second-round pick long enough to turn it into an NBA player.

Jackson's Boston contribution was small, so the pick is secondary to the grade. Ford carries the case. His 309 games, 201 starts and championship-season role create a much larger realized return than Detroit received from Tatum's 76-game season.

Detroit still deserves credit for receiving a usable rotation guard. The result is not a zero-value loss; it is a clear Boston win created by Ford's longevity and championship relevance.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A-/C+. Boston receives an A- because Ford became a four-year contributor and a regular starter on the 1981 champions, while the extra second-round pick added 11 Jackson games before his rights were sold. Detroit receives a C+ because Tatum supplied 76 useful games in 1978-79 but did not approach Ford's cumulative Boston impact.

He also continued into 1981-82, playing 76 games and starting 53 before his NBA career ended.

The Extra Pick Produced Limited but Real Value

Boston's second asset became Tracy Jackson at No. 25 in the 1981 draft.

Jackson played 11 games for the Celtics in 1981-82, totaling 66 minutes. On December 9, 1981, Boston sold his player rights to Chicago.

That outcome is modest, and this review does not inflate the pick as if Boston received Jackson's entire three-year NBA career. The direct Celtics value was 11 games plus whatever consideration came from the rights sale, whose amount is not documented in the reviewed Basketball-Reference transaction record.

Detroit Got One Rotation Season from Tatum

Tatum played 76 games for Detroit in 1978-79 after the trade. He logged 1,195 minutes and averaged 7.8 points, 1.6 rebounds and 0.9 assists.

That is meaningful short-term return. Tatum was not a non-factor, and Detroit received substantially more than a few appearances or an unused roster spot.

The difference is duration and role. Tatum's Detroit value is concentrated in one season. Ford gave Boston four seasons, more than 9,000 minutes, 309 regular-season games and a starting role on a championship team.

Why Boston Wins in Retrospect

The Celtics received the best individual asset in Ford and also retained the additional second-round pick long enough to turn it into an NBA player.

Jackson's Boston contribution was small, so the pick is secondary to the grade. Ford carries the case. His 309 games, 201 starts and championship-season role create a much larger realized return than Detroit received from Tatum's 76-game season.

Detroit still deserves credit for receiving a usable rotation guard. The result is not a zero-value loss; it is a clear Boston win created by Ford's longevity and championship relevance.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A-/C+. Boston receives an A- because Ford became a four-year contributor and a regular starter on the 1981 champions, while the extra second-round pick added 11 Jackson games before his rights were sold. Detroit receives a C+ because Tatum supplied 76 useful games in 1978-79 but did not approach Ford's cumulative Boston impact.

perspectives.analysis:
A Small Trade with a Clear Asset Trail

Milwaukee's transaction ledger records the October 23, 1978 deal as Otis Howard to Detroit for a 1979 fourth-round pick. The Bucks later used that selection at No. 69 on Eugene Robinson.

There are no complicated protections or later pick reroutes to resolve. The historical question is simply whether Howard's brief Detroit stint produced more value than Milwaukee's eventual draft selection.

Howard Played 11 Games for Detroit

Howard had been a fourth-round Milwaukee pick in the 1978 draft and appeared in three games for the Bucks before the trade.

After arriving in Detroit, he played 11 regular-season games and 91 total minutes. He averaged 4.5 points, 3.1 rebounds and 0.4 assists in 8.3 minutes per game.

Those 11 appearances were the last NBA games of Howard's career. His full NBA record consists of 14 games split between Milwaukee and Detroit in 1978-79.

That limits the upside of Detroit's return, but it does leave the Pistons with measurable on-court production from the asset they acquired.

Milwaukee's Pick Became Eugene Robinson

The incoming fourth-round pick became No. 69 in the 1979 draft. Milwaukee selected Eugene Robinson from Louisiana-Monroe.

Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee draft history lists Robinson at No. 69 but shows no NBA games or statistical record attached to the selection. This review therefore treats the draft return as a used pick that produced no NBA regular-season playing time.

The Bucks did not give up a long-term rotation player to obtain that pick. Howard's Detroit career lasted only 11 games, so Milwaukee's opportunity cost was also small.

Why Detroit Gets Only a Slight Edge

This is not a trade where either side created meaningful franchise value. Detroit received 91 minutes from Howard. Milwaukee received a fourth-round selection that did not produce an NBA player.

The Pistons therefore have the better realized outcome, but the gap is narrow in absolute value. Howard's 11 appearances are enough to beat a zero-game draft result without justifying a strong grade.

The exchange is best classified as a minor Detroit win rather than an important personnel success.

Final Verdict

Slight Pistons Edge, C-/D+. Detroit receives a C- because Howard gave the club 11 games and 91 minutes after the trade. Milwaukee receives a D+ because the fourth-round pick became Eugene Robinson at No. 69 but produced no NBA regular-season games. The difference is real but small.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Scott Lloyd from the San Diego Clippers on October 26, 1978 for a 1981 third-round pick. Lloyd played 67 games for the Bulls that season, totaling 465 minutes and averaging 1.7 points and 1.4 rebounds. San Diego later sent the incoming pick, along with a 1983 third-rounder, to Phoenix as compensation for signing Gar Heard. Heard played 78 games and 1,631 minutes for the Clippers in 1980-81. Phoenix ultimately used the 1981 pick at No. 62 on Sam Clancy, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Because the Clippers' downstream return required another pick and Chicago received only limited reserve production, the retrospective result is effectively even.
perspectives.analysis:
Chicago Received a One-Season Reserve

The Bulls acquired Scott Lloyd on October 26, 1978 after he had appeared in five games for San Diego.

Lloyd played 67 games for Chicago in 1978-79. He logged 465 minutes and averaged 1.7 points and 1.4 rebounds in 6.9 minutes per game.

That is real NBA production, but it is modest. Lloyd did not stay with Chicago beyond the season, spending 1979-80 outside the NBA before later returning with Dallas.

The Pick Did Not Stay with the Clippers

The 1981 third-rounder has a more interesting route than the original record suggests.

San Diego did not use the pick directly. In connection with signing veteran free agent Gar Heard, the Clippers sent this 1981 third-round pick plus a 1983 third-round pick to Phoenix as compensation.

That means the No. 62 Sam Clancy outcome belongs to Phoenix, not directly to San Diego. This review preserves the final draft result for traceability but does not treat Clancy as the Clippers' realized player return.

Heard Was the Downstream Clippers Benefit

Heard played 78 games for San Diego in 1980-81 and logged 1,631 minutes. He averaged 4.8 points, 4.5 rebounds and 1.6 assists in 20.9 minutes.

The original Chicago pick was one component of the compensation package that helped San Diego secure Heard. Because another 1983 third-round pick was also sent to Phoenix, the full value of Heard cannot be assigned to this 1978 trade branch alone.

Still, the pick retained practical transaction value for more than two years after the Lloyd trade. That downstream use keeps the Clippers side from being graded as an empty return.

What Happened to the No. 62 Pick

Phoenix used the selection on Sam Clancy in the 1981 draft. Basketball-Reference lists Clancy at No. 62 but no NBA regular-season games.

That final draft outcome is useful for identifying the asset, but it should not be used to erase the value San Diego extracted earlier by moving the pick in the Heard compensation package.

Why the Result Is Even

Chicago got the cleaner direct return: 67 games from Lloyd. The Clippers got no direct drafted player, but they preserved the pick as a movable asset and later used it as one piece of the compensation required to add Heard.

Neither branch created large long-term value. Lloyd was a low-minute reserve for one season, while Heard's larger 78-game contribution cannot be fully credited to this pick because San Diego also surrendered another third-rounder.

The best retrospective treatment is therefore an even result rather than forcing a winner from two modest branches.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C-/C-. Chicago receives a C- for 67 Lloyd games and 465 minutes. San Diego also receives a C- because the third-round pick retained downstream utility as part of the Gar Heard compensation package, even though the pick itself ultimately became Sam Clancy at No. 62 and produced no NBA games.

new-york-knicks.summary: New York traded Spencer Haywood to the New Orleans Jazz on January 5, 1979 for Joe Meriweather. Meriweather played 106 regular-season games over parts of two Knicks seasons, averaging about nine points and five-and-a-half rebounds, before New York included him in a 1980 three-team trade. Haywood immediately averaged 24.0 points and 9.6 rebounds over 34 games for New Orleans. After the franchise moved to Utah, the Jazz traded Haywood to the Lakers for Adrian Dantley. Dantley then played 461 games across seven Utah seasons and averaged 29.6 points. Meriweather was useful, but the Haywood-to-Dantley conversion gives the Jazz an overwhelming long-term advantage.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Direct Exchange Happened in January 1979

Basketball-Reference lists the trade on January 5, 1979: New York sent Spencer Haywood to New Orleans for Joe Meriweather.

Both players had already appeared for their original teams that season, so the cleanest comparison starts with production after the transaction rather than their full 1978-79 totals.

Meriweather Gave New York Two Useful Partial Seasons

Meriweather played 41 games for the Knicks after the trade in 1978-79. He started 26, averaged 25.7 minutes and produced 9.5 points and 5.5 rebounds per game.

He stayed for 1979-80 and appeared in another 65 games, starting 30. He averaged 9.0 points and 5.4 rebounds in 24.1 minutes.

That gives New York 106 regular-season games from Meriweather across the two seasons. He was a legitimate rotation big rather than a throw-in who disappeared from the roster.

In September 1980, New York included Meriweather and a 1981 first-round pick in a three-team trade that brought Campy Russell from Cleveland. This review records that later use but does not credit the entire Russell return to Meriweather because the Knicks also surrendered a first-round selection.

Haywood Was Excellent Immediately

Haywood played 34 games for New Orleans after the trade. He started 18 and averaged 39.4 minutes, 24.0 points, 9.6 rebounds and 2.1 assists.

That half-season alone was stronger individual production than New York received from Meriweather, but the decisive value came after the franchise relocated to Utah.

On September 13, 1979, the Jazz traded Haywood to the Los Angeles Lakers for Adrian Dantley.

Dantley Turned the Branch into a Franchise-Level Return

Dantley played seven seasons for Utah from 1979-80 through 1985-86. Basketball-Reference's franchise register credits him with 461 regular-season games, 17,899 minutes and 13,635 points for the Jazz.

He averaged 29.6 points, 6.2 rebounds and 3.7 assists over those 461 games. His Utah tenure included multiple All-Star seasons, two scoring titles and two All-NBA selections.

The transaction path is direct enough to count. Utah did not combine Haywood with another premium asset to acquire Dantley; the September 1979 record is Haywood for Dantley.

That makes Dantley a legitimate downstream return from the original Meriweather-for-Haywood trade rather than a distant branch requiring speculative allocation.

Why the Jazz Win by a Wide Margin

New York received useful value. Meriweather gave the Knicks 106 games and more than 2,600 minutes across two seasons, then remained part of a later trade package.

The Jazz received 34 high-level Haywood games and then converted him into seven seasons of Dantley. Dantley's 461 games at 29.6 points per game move the outcome well beyond a normal rotation-player comparison.

The result is a major hindsight win for the Jazz even though the Knicks' incoming player was productive.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win, A+/C. Utah receives an A+ because Haywood produced 24.0 points and 9.6 rebounds over 34 games and was then traded straight up for Adrian Dantley, who became a seven-season franchise star. New York receives a C because Meriweather supplied 106 useful regular-season games before becoming one part of a later three-team package.

Dantley played seven seasons for Utah from 1979-80 through 1985-86. Basketball-Reference's franchise register credits him with 461 regular-season games, 17,899 minutes and 13,635 points for the Jazz.

He averaged 29.6 points, 6.2 rebounds and 3.7 assists over those 461 games. His Utah tenure included multiple All-Star seasons, two scoring titles and two All-NBA selections.

The transaction path is direct enough to count. Utah did not combine Haywood with another premium asset to acquire Dantley; the September 1979 record is Haywood for Dantley.

That makes Dantley a legitimate downstream return from the original Meriweather-for-Haywood trade rather than a distant branch requiring speculative allocation.

Why the Jazz Win by a Wide Margin

New York received useful value. Meriweather gave the Knicks 106 games and more than 2,600 minutes across two seasons, then remained part of a later trade package.

The Jazz received 34 high-level Haywood games and then converted him into seven seasons of Dantley. Dantley's 461 games at 29.6 points per game move the outcome well beyond a normal rotation-player comparison.

The result is a major hindsight win for the Jazz even though the Knicks' incoming player was productive.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win, A+/C. Utah receives an A+ because Haywood produced 24.0 points and 9.6 rebounds over 34 games and was then traded straight up for Adrian Dantley, who became a seven-season franchise star. New York receives a C because Meriweather supplied 106 useful regular-season games before becoming one part of a later three-team package.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
New Orleans' 1978-79 transaction log confirms the January 12, 1979 package: the Jazz sent Truck Robinson to Phoenix for Marty Byrnes, Ron Lee, first-round picks in 1979 and 1980, and cash. The two firsts became No. 20 Larry Knight in 1979 and No. 19 John Duren in 1980. This is a useful hindsight case because the acquisition cost looked enormous in pick count, yet the actual draft outcomes were modest while Robinson remained a high-level starter for Phoenix.

Phoenix Return
Robinson joined a 50-win Suns team in midseason and immediately produced 19.9 points and 10.7 rebounds across 26 regular-season games. In the 1979 playoffs he appeared in all 15 Phoenix games as the Suns beat Portland and Kansas City before losing a seven-game Western Conference Finals to eventual champion Seattle. He then played all 82 games in 1979-80 and remained a major frontcourt piece on a 55-win team. In 1980-81 he again played all 82, started all 82 and averaged 18.8 points, 9.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists for a 57-win Suns club. He made the 1981 All-Star team and finished 19th in MVP voting. Those two complete seasons after the initial 26-game stretch give Phoenix at least 190 regular-season games of direct value before even considering the remainder of his Suns tenure. The trade therefore delivered both immediate playoff help and durable star-level regular-season production.

New Orleans/Utah Return
Byrnes played 36 games for New Orleans after the trade, while Lee played only 17. Neither became a long-term Jazz piece. The draft outcomes were similarly limited. Larry Knight, selected No. 20 in 1979, never played an NBA regular-season game. John Duren, selected No. 19 in 1980 after the franchise moved to Utah, did make the league. He played 40 games as a rookie and 79 games with nine starts in 1981-82, averaging 3.4 points and 2.0 assists in the latter season. That is real rotation value, but it is far below what teams generally hope to obtain from two first-round selections. The cash component cannot be converted into basketball value from the available record. The Jazz therefore paid away their best player in the package and failed to turn either first into a comparable replacement.

Hindsight Verdict
Phoenix wins clearly, but the grading should acknowledge the size of the original gamble. Two first-rounders, two players and cash is a serious acquisition price, so the Suns deserve a high grade because Robinson actually justified it: he strengthened a Western Conference finalist, stayed available, remained a strong scorer and rebounder, and made an All-Star team. New Orleans/Utah deserves some credit for extracting two firsts rather than losing Robinson for a small package, but hindsight grading follows realized value. Byrnes and Lee were brief stays, Knight never played in the NBA, and Duren was a low-minute guard for two Utah seasons. An A for Phoenix captures star production and playoff impact without pretending Robinson became a franchise legend. A D+ for the Jazz recognizes that Duren supplied real games and the trade process generated valuable draft shots, even though those shots produced little. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

summary: Boston traded Billy Knight to Indiana on January 16, 1979 for rookie center Rick Robey. Knight gave the Pacers 357 regular-season games over the next five seasons, including 17.5 points per game in 1980-81 and 17.1 in 1982-83. Robey played 339 regular-season games for Boston, helped the Celtics win the 1981 championship and later became part of the June 1983 package that brought Dennis Johnson plus two draft picks to Boston. Indiana received the better scorer, but Boston extracted more championship and downstream transaction value.

Knight gave the Pacers 357 regular-season games over the next five seasons, including 17.5 points per game in 1980-81 and 17.1 in 1982-83. Robey played 339 regular-season games for Boston, helped the Celtics win the 1981 championship and later became part of the June 1983 package that brought Dennis Johnson plus two draft picks to Boston. Johnson then played 541 games over seven Celtics seasons and started for the 1984 and 1986 champions. boston-celtics.analysis:
The Swap Was Knight for Robey

Basketball-Reference's league and team transaction logs agree on the January 16, 1979 deal. Boston sent Billy Knight to Indiana for Rick Robey.

Both players immediately became useful for their new teams, and unlike many trades in this part of the archive, both sides received multi-season value.

Knight Became a Five-Year Pacers Scorer

Knight played 39 games for Indiana after the trade in 1978-79 and averaged 14.7 points, 4.5 rebounds and 2.2 assists.

He then stayed for four more seasons. His strongest year came in 1980-81, when he played all 82 games, started 70 and averaged 17.5 points and 5.0 rebounds. Indiana reached the playoffs that season.

Across the five post-trade Pacers seasons, Knight appeared in 357 regular-season games. He also averaged 17.1 points in 1982-83, his final Indiana season.

That is a strong direct return. Indiana did not merely get a short-term veteran; Knight remained an important scorer through several roster cycles.

Robey Played 339 Games for Boston

Robey joined Boston as a 22-year-old rookie center and played 36 games after the trade, averaging 12.4 points and 7.2 rebounds.

He stayed through 1982-83. Over that span, Robey appeared in 339 Celtics regular-season games, including all 82 games in both 1979-80 and 1980-81.

His role declined over time, but the most important season was 1980-81. Robey played all 82 regular-season games and 17 playoff games for the Celtics team that won the NBA championship.

That gives Boston a title-season rotation contribution that Indiana's side cannot match directly.

Robey Later Became Part of the Dennis Johnson Package

Boston did not simply lose Robey when his playing role ended. On June 27, 1983, the Celtics sent Robey and two second-round picks to Phoenix.

In return, Boston received Dennis Johnson, a first-round pick that became Greg Kite and a third-round pick that became Winfred King.

This review does not credit the full Johnson return to Robey alone because Boston also included two second-round selections. Robey was nevertheless one of the assets required to complete the deal.

Johnson then played seven seasons and 541 regular-season games for Boston. He started 522 of them and was part of the Celtics teams that won the 1984 and 1986 championships.

That downstream branch materially raises the value of Boston's original Robey acquisition even after accounting for the additional picks the Celtics had to include.

Why Boston Gets the Hindsight Edge

Indiana received the more productive individual scorer from the original one-for-one trade. Knight's 357 games and multiple double-digit scoring seasons make the Pacers side a strong outcome.

Boston received 339 Robey games, a rotation center on the 1981 champions and an asset later used in the package for Dennis Johnson.

The Johnson transaction cannot be treated as if Robey alone bought a Hall of Fame-level guard, but it is still legitimate realized value from the Robey branch. Combined with Robey's championship contribution, that is enough to move Boston ahead.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A/A-. Boston receives an A because Robey contributed to the 1981 championship and later became part of the package that brought Dennis Johnson and two draft picks to Boston. Indiana receives an A- because Knight produced 357 regular-season games over five seasons and remained one of the Pacers' more reliable scorers during that stretch.

summary: Boston traded Dennis Awtrey to Seattle on January 17, 1979 for a 1979 first-round pick plus cash. Awtrey played 40 regular-season games for the SuperSonics and appeared throughout their 1979 championship playoff run, giving Seattle immediate depth on a title team. Boston never used the pick directly: it became the No. 21 selection later associated with Sly Williams, but the Celtics sent it with two other first-rounders and Tom Barker to New York for Bob McAdoo. McAdoo played 20 games for Boston before becoming part of another major asset chain. Seattle got the cleaner direct basketball return; Boston preserved comparable transaction value.

Awtrey played 40 regular-season games for the SuperSonics and appeared throughout their 1979 championship playoff run, giving Seattle immediate depth on a title team. Boston never used the pick directly: it became the No. 21 selection later associated with Sly Williams, but the Celtics sent it with two other first-rounders and Tom Barker to New York for Bob McAdoo.
