boston-celtics.analysis:
The January 17 Deal Was Awtrey for a First and Cash

Boston's transaction log records Dennis Awtrey going to Seattle for a 1979 first-round pick. The league ledger also records the first-rounder as the selection later used on Sly Williams. Boston's source record includes cash coming back as well, but the amount is not documented in the reviewed sources.

Awtrey Joined a Championship Team

Awtrey played 40 regular-season games for Seattle after the trade. He logged 499 minutes and averaged 5.7 points and 7.5 rebounds per 36 minutes, serving as a low-usage reserve center.

The more important context is the postseason. Seattle won the 1979 NBA championship, and Awtrey's playoff game log shows him appearing in 16 of the team's 17 postseason games. His minutes fell as the run progressed, but he was part of the rotation throughout the title path.

That gives Seattle a concrete championship-season return from a player who had appeared in only 23 games for Boston earlier that year.

Boston Used the Pick as Trade Currency

The incoming first-rounder did not become a Celtics draft selection. On February 12, Boston sent that pick, two other 1979 first-round picks and Tom Barker to New York for Bob McAdoo.

McAdoo then played 20 games for Boston and averaged 20.6 points and 7.1 rebounds. The following September, Boston moved McAdoo to Detroit for two 1980 first-round picks.

Those later picks became part of the famous June 1980 trade that brought Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick used on Kevin McHale to Boston. This review does not assign Parish or McHale to this single Seattle pick because the chain required multiple assets at every step.

The important point is narrower: Boston's incoming first-rounder retained real transaction value and was used in a premium package rather than expiring unused.

Why the Result Is Essentially Even

Seattle received the more direct benefit. Awtrey gave the SuperSonics 40 regular-season games and 16 playoff appearances on a championship team.

Boston received less immediate on-court value, but the first-round pick remained a meaningful piece of a larger McAdoo transaction that later fed another major asset chain. The cash amount is unknown, so it cannot be scored.

Neither side clearly separates from the other once the difference between direct championship depth and diluted downstream trade value is respected.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B/B. Seattle receives a B because Awtrey became a real reserve on the 1979 champions. Boston also receives a B because the first-round pick retained premium transaction utility and helped form the package for McAdoo, even though later Parish-McHale value cannot be credited to this pick alone.

summary: Boston traded longtime guard Jo Jo White to Golden State on January 30, 1979 for a 1979 first-round pick. White played 107 regular-season games over parts of two Warriors seasons, averaging 13.8 points and 4.6 assists across that stint, before Golden State sold his rights to Kansas City in September 1980. Boston never used the incoming pick at the draft. Twelve days later, the Celtics bundled it with two other 1979 first-rounders and Tom Barker to acquire Bob McAdoo from New York. The pick retained real transaction value, but White supplied the cleaner direct return, giving Golden State the slight retrospective edge.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Trade Ended White's Boston Tenure

Boston's transaction log and Golden State's matching ledger record the January 30, 1979 exchange: Jo Jo White to the Warriors for a 1979 first-round pick that was later associated with No. 9 Larry Demic.

White had already played 47 games for Boston that season. After the trade, he appeared in 29 games for Golden State and averaged 12.3 points, 4.6 assists and 30.4 minutes.

White Stayed for Another Full Season

The Warriors kept White for 1979-80. He played 78 games, logged 2,052 minutes and averaged 9.9 points and 3.1 assists in 26.3 minutes.

Across his two partial/full Golden State seasons, White appeared in 107 regular-season games and 2,935 minutes. Basketball-Reference's career split credits him with 13.8 points and 4.6 assists per 36 minutes over that Warriors stint.

On September 10, 1980, Golden State sold White's player rights to Kansas City. The reviewed transaction record does not state the cash amount, so this review does not assign a specific additional value to that sale.

Boston Used the Pick Before the Draft

The Celtics did not select Larry Demic themselves. On February 12, only twelve days after acquiring the pick, Boston sent it to New York with two other 1979 first-round picks and Tom Barker for Bob McAdoo.

McAdoo played 20 games for Boston before being traded to Detroit the following September for two 1980 first-round picks. Those picks later became part of Boston's June 1980 trade for Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick used on Kevin McHale.

That downstream history proves the No. 9 pick retained meaningful trade utility, but this review does not credit Parish or McHale to this one branch. Boston needed three first-rounders and Barker to acquire McAdoo, and later transactions required additional assets.

Why Golden State Gets the Slight Edge

The Warriors received two seasons of usable veteran guard play and then retained enough rights value to sell White to Kansas City. Boston received a premium draft asset, but its direct contribution was one component of a larger McAdoo package.

Both sides extracted value. Golden State's 107 games of direct production are easier to isolate than Boston's diluted downstream branch.

Final Verdict

Slight Warriors Edge, B+/B. Golden State receives a B+ for 107 White games across two seasons plus the later rights sale. Boston receives a B because the first-round pick retained premium transaction value and helped acquire McAdoo, while the much larger later Parish-McHale return cannot be assigned to this pick alone.

summary: Atlanta acquired Terry Furlow from Cleveland on January 31, 1979 for rookie guard Butch Lee and a 1983 first-round pick. Furlow played 50 regular-season games for the Hawks across parts of two seasons before Atlanta sent him to Utah for two second-round picks. Lee played 36 games for Cleveland before the Cavaliers later included him with a separate 1982 first-rounder in a Lakers trade. Cleveland also retained the 1983 first until October 1980, when it was packaged with Bill Robinzine and another first-round pick in a Dallas deal. Both branches produced usable value, with Cleveland holding the slightly stronger original asset package.

Furlow played 50 regular-season games for the Hawks across parts of two seasons before Atlanta sent him to Utah for two second-round picks. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Original Package Favored Cleveland on Asset Depth

Atlanta's transaction log confirms the January 31, 1979 trade: Terry Furlow came to the Hawks, while Cleveland received Butch Lee and a 1983 first-round pick.

Furlow Played 50 Games for Atlanta

Furlow appeared in 29 games for the Hawks after the trade in 1978-79. He averaged 9.9 points, 2.8 assists and 19.9 minutes.

He returned for 21 games in 1979-80, averaging 8.4 points and 3.4 assists. That gives Atlanta 50 regular-season games of direct production from Furlow.

On November 23, 1979, Atlanta traded Furlow to Utah for a 1981 second-round pick later associated with Eddie Johnson and a 1982 second-round pick later associated with Ricky Frazier. That extended the Furlow branch beyond his own Hawks minutes.

Lee Gave Cleveland a Shorter Playing Return

Butch Lee played 33 games for Cleveland after the 1979 trade and another three games the following season. His first Cleveland stint produced 782 minutes, 379 points and 126 assists.

On February 15, 1980, Cleveland traded Lee and a separate 1982 first-round pick to the Lakers for Don Ford and a 1980 first-round pick. Because that transaction required the additional 1982 first, this review does not assign its full downstream result to Lee.

The 1983 First Retained Trade Value

Cleveland held the Atlanta first-rounder until October 30, 1980. The Cavaliers then sent it, Bill Robinzine and a 1986 first-round pick to Dallas for Richard Washington and Jerome Whitehead.

Dallas later used the 1983 selection at No. 11 on Derek Harper. That identifies the pick's final draft outcome, but Harper's career belongs to Dallas rather than Cleveland. The proper realized value for Cleveland is the pick's role in the 1980 trade package.

Why Cleveland Gets a Slight Edge

Atlanta received 50 Furlow games and then converted him into two second-round picks. Cleveland received 36 Lee games plus a first-round asset that remained valuable enough to headline part of a later multi-asset deal.

Neither side turned the original trade directly into a long-term star. The difference is that Cleveland received both a usable player and a premium future pick, while Atlanta's later Furlow return was two second-rounders.

Final Verdict

Slight Cavaliers Edge, B+/B. Cleveland receives a B+ for Lee's short playing stint plus the retained first-round asset. Atlanta receives a B for 50 Furlow games and the two second-round picks received when he was later moved to Utah.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded Eric Money and Al Skinner to Philadelphia on February 7, 1979 for Harvey Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash. Money played eight regular-season games for the 76ers and Skinner played five. Catchings and Simpson each played 32 games for the Nets that season, and Catchings then became the key downstream asset: New Jersey traded him to Milwaukee on May 31 for John Gianelli and the No. 8 pick in the 1979 draft, used on Calvin Natt. Natt gave the Nets 53 games at 19.7 points per game before being traded to Portland for Maurice Lucas and two first-round picks. The Nets won the original exchange decisively.
perspectives.analysis:
The February Trade Was Two Players for Two Players and Cash

New Jersey's and Philadelphia's transaction logs agree on the February 7, 1979 exchange. The Nets sent Eric Money and Al Skinner to the 76ers for Harvey Catchings, Ralph Simpson and cash.

Philadelphia Got Very Little Playing Value

Money appeared in eight regular-season games for Philadelphia after the trade. He averaged 6.8 points and 2.8 assists in 16.1 minutes.

Skinner played five games for the 76ers, averaging 3.6 points and 2.2 assists in 9.4 minutes. Those five games were the final NBA appearances of his career.

The pair therefore produced only 13 combined regular-season appearances for Philadelphia. Neither player created a meaningful downstream asset branch for the 76ers.

Catchings and Simpson Both Played 32 Nets Games

Catchings appeared in 32 regular-season games for New Jersey after the trade. He averaged 6.1 points and 6.4 rebounds in 20.6 minutes, giving the Nets immediate frontcourt depth.

Simpson also played 32 games for New Jersey, averaging 6.9 points in 16.5 minutes. He remained with the club into the following season before being waived on November 13, 1979.

The direct playing return already favored New Jersey, but Catchings created the much larger value branch.

Catchings Became the No. 8 Pick

On May 31, 1979, New Jersey traded Catchings to Milwaukee for John Gianelli and a 1979 first-round pick. The Nets used that pick at No. 8 on Calvin Natt.

Gianelli never became a long-term Nets player. Before the next season, New Jersey included him with Jim Boylan and Bernard King in the trade that brought Rich Kelley from Utah. Because Gianelli was only one component of that larger package, this review assigns only partial downstream credit to that branch.

Natt Became the Major Return

Natt played 53 games for New Jersey as a rookie in 1979-80. He averaged 19.7 points and 9.7 rebounds in 38.6 minutes, giving the Nets immediate high-end production from the pick created by the Catchings trade.

On February 8, 1980, New Jersey traded Natt to Portland for Maurice Lucas and two first-round picks. Those selections later became Mike Gminski at No. 7 in 1980 and Albert King at No. 10 in 1981.

Unlike a multi-asset bridge where one branch is hard to isolate, the Natt transaction was a direct one-player exchange for Lucas and the two firsts. That means the Catchings-to-Natt path deserves substantial downstream credit.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A+/D. New Jersey receives an A+ because the club got 64 combined games from Catchings and Simpson, then turned Catchings into the pick used on Natt, who produced immediately and later returned Maurice Lucas plus two first-round picks. Philadelphia receives a D because Money and Skinner combined for only 13 games after the trade and generated no comparable downstream return.

summary: Boston reacquired the player rights to Kevin Stacom from Indiana on February 9, 1979 after the Pacers had signed him as a veteran free agent the previous summer. The Pacers received cash, with the amount unspecified in the reviewed transaction records. Stacom played 24 regular-season games for Boston after the deal, averaging 4.9 points and 1.5 assists in 10.8 minutes. He did not play in 1979-80, was considered retired, and later returned for seven games with Milwaukee in 1981-82. Boston received a modest amount of immediate guard depth; Indiana's cash return cannot be quantified, so the Celtics get a narrow hindsight edge.

Boston Reacquired a Former Celtic

Kevin Stacom had played 55 games for Boston in 1977-78 before signing with Indiana as a veteran free agent in July 1978. The Pacers sent Boston a 1979 third-round pick as compensation for that signing.

On February 9, 1979, Indiana sold Stacom's player rights back to Boston. The Boston ledger records the rights acquisition, while Indiana's ledger describes the transaction as a sale. The reviewed records do not state the cash amount.

Stacom Played 24 Games After the Deal

Stacom appeared in 24 regular-season games for Boston after returning. He averaged 10.8 minutes, 4.9 points and 1.5 assists while shooting 39.1 percent from the field.

That is limited production, but it is real roster value from a transaction in which Boston surrendered only an unspecified cash payment.

There Was No Long Boston Tail

Stacom did not play in 1979-80 and Basketball-Reference notes that he was considered retired while working as an inn manager. He remained out in 1980-81, then returned for seven games with Milwaukee in 1981-82.

Boston therefore received one short late-season stint rather than a multi-year asset. There was no later Celtics trade branch to increase the return.

Indiana's Cash Return Is Unquantified

The Pacers had already gotten 44 games from Stacom before selling his rights. For this February transaction specifically, their return was cash. Because the amount is not documented in the reviewed sources, this review does not assign speculative value to it.

That uncertainty keeps Boston's edge small rather than turning a 24-game reserve stint into a major win.

Final Verdict

Celtics Edge, B-/C. Boston receives a B- because Stacom gave the team 24 games of usable guard depth for an unspecified cash payment. Indiana receives a C because the cash return cannot be evaluated and produced no traceable basketball asset in the reviewed record.

summary: Boston acquired Bob McAdoo from New York on February 12, 1979 for Tom Barker and three 1979 first-round picks that became Bill Cartwright at No. 3, Larry Demic at No. 9 and Sly Williams at No. 21. McAdoo played only 20 games for Boston, but the Celtics moved him to Detroit that September for two 1980 first-round picks. Boston then traded those two picks to Golden State for Robert Parish and the No. 3 selection used on Kevin McHale. New York received a major direct return, led by All-Star center Cartwright plus useful years from Demic and Williams, but Boston's McAdoo branch ultimately produced two franchise pillars and multiple championships.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Knicks Received Three Firsts and a Player

Boston's February 12, 1979 transaction sent Tom Barker and three 1979 first-round picks to New York for Bob McAdoo. The picks became Bill Cartwright at No. 3, Larry Demic at No. 9 and Sly Williams at No. 21.

Cartwright Was the Centerpiece of New York's Return

Cartwright started all 82 games as a rookie, averaged 21.7 points and 8.9 rebounds and made the All-Star team. He remained a major Knicks center through the first half of the 1980s before a foot injury wiped out 1984-85.

Demic also gave New York three full seasons. He played 206 games, including all 82 as a rookie, and started 68 times across his Knicks career.

Williams played 57 games as a rookie, then became a starter in 1980-81 and remained a productive forward into 1981-82. Barker added 22 games immediately after the trade.

The Knicks therefore converted McAdoo into several years of direct roster value, not just draft capital that failed to develop.

McAdoo's Boston Stay Was Brief but Productive

McAdoo played 20 games for Boston after the trade. He scored 411 points, averaging 20.6 points and 7.1 rebounds in 31.9 minutes.

On its own, that would not justify surrendering three first-round picks. The downstream transaction is what transforms Boston's side.

Detroit Sent Boston Two 1980 Firsts for McAdoo

On September 6, 1979, Boston traded McAdoo to Detroit for two 1980 first-round picks. Basketball-Reference notes that the exchange was arranged as compensation connected to Boston's signing of M.L. Carr.

Those picks later landed at No. 1 and No. 13 in the 1980 draft. Boston did not make either selection. On June 9, 1980, the Celtics sent both picks to Golden State for Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick.

Boston Used No. 3 on Kevin McHale

The next day, Boston selected Kevin McHale with the third pick. Parish and McHale became two core pieces of the Celtics teams that won the 1981, 1984 and 1986 NBA championships.

Because the McAdoo-to-Detroit and Detroit-picks-to-Golden-State steps are both direct transactions, this branch has much stronger attribution than a chain that requires several unrelated assets. Boston's McAdoo acquisition is therefore a legitimate upstream part of the Parish-McHale outcome.

New York Still Received an Excellent Package

A hindsight win for Boston does not make the Knicks' return poor. Cartwright became an All-Star-level starting center, Demic supplied 206 games and Williams developed into a productive starter before leaving New York.

The difference is ceiling. Boston turned a 20-game McAdoo stint into two first-rounders and then directly converted those picks into Parish and McHale.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A+/A. Boston receives an A+ because the McAdoo branch produced Parish and the pick used on McHale after two direct follow-up trades. New York receives an A because Cartwright became a long-term starting center and All-Star while Demic, Williams and Barker added substantial immediate roster value.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland sent Jim Brewer to Detroit on February 15, 1979 for future considerations that were completed when the Pistons sent Earl Tatum to the Cavaliers on April 12. Brewer played 25 games for Detroit, then was traded to Portland in September for a 1981 second-round pick. Detroit later used that exact pick to acquire Wayne Robinson from the Lakers, and Robinson played 81 games for the Pistons in 1980-81. Tatum did not appear for Cleveland in 1978-79 but played 33 games the next season before his NBA career ended. Detroit extracted the stronger realized return from Brewer and the downstream second-round asset.
perspectives.analysis:
The February Deal Was Brewer for Future Considerations

Cleveland's and Detroit's transaction ledgers record the February 15, 1979 framework as Jim Brewer plus future considerations for Earl Tatum. Detroit's historical media guide clarifies the sequence more precisely: the Pistons obtained Brewer from Cleveland in February and sent Tatum to Cleveland on April 12 to complete the transaction.

Brewer Played 25 Games for Detroit

Brewer appeared in 25 regular-season games for the Pistons after the trade. He averaged 12.4 minutes, 2.3 points and 4.2 rebounds while providing reserve frontcourt depth.

That direct return was modest, but Detroit preserved value when Brewer left.

The Brewer Branch Produced a Second-Round Pick

On September 18, 1979, Detroit traded Brewer to Portland for a 1981 second-round pick. That selection later became No. 39 Harvey Knuckles, but Detroit did not use the pick at the draft.

On October 1, 1980, the Pistons sent the same 1981 second-rounder to the Lakers for Wayne Robinson. Robinson then played 81 games for Detroit in 1980-81, scoring 643 points and averaging 7.9 points in 19.7 minutes.

Because the Brewer-to-pick and pick-to-Robinson steps are direct one-asset transactions, this review can attribute Robinson's Detroit season to the Brewer branch without relying on a diluted multi-asset chain.

Tatum Arrived Too Late to Play in 1978-79

Tatum was the player Detroit ultimately sent to Cleveland to complete the deal. He did not appear for the Cavaliers before the 1978-79 season ended.

In 1979-80, Tatum played 33 games for Cleveland, totaling 225 minutes and 85 points. He averaged 6.8 minutes and 2.6 points per game. That was the final season of his NBA career.

Why Detroit Wins the Hindsight Comparison

Cleveland received 33 low-minute Tatum appearances and no later trade branch. Detroit received 25 Brewer games, then converted Brewer into a second-round asset that directly became Wayne Robinson and 81 more games.

The original exchange was not a blockbuster, but Detroit created more cumulative roster value from the outgoing player.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, B+/C+. Detroit receives a B+ because Brewer supplied 25 games and then directly became the draft asset used for Wayne Robinson, who played 81 games the following season. Cleveland receives a C+ because Tatum appeared in 33 games at limited minutes and generated no comparable downstream return.

perspectives.analysis:
Milwaukee Bought Five Years of Frontcourt Depth

The May 31, 1979 transaction sent Harvey Catchings to Milwaukee for John Gianelli and a 1979 first-round pick. The Nets used the pick at No. 8 on Calvin Natt.

Catchings was a strong realized return for Milwaukee. He played 72 games in 1979-80, 77 in 1980-81, 80 in 1981-82, 74 in 1982-83 and 69 in 1983-84. That is 372 regular-season games across five Bucks seasons.

He was never a high-volume scorer, but he provided rebounding and interior defense for repeated playoff teams. Basketball-Reference credits him with 33 postseason appearances for Milwaukee over that span.

Natt Became an Immediate Nets Star

New Jersey used the incoming first-round pick on Calvin Natt at No. 8. He played 53 games for the Nets as a rookie and averaged 19.7 points, 9.7 rebounds and 38.6 minutes.

That alone gave the Nets a high-end return from the pick. The larger value came when they moved Natt before the season ended.

Natt Directly Became Lucas and Two Firsts

On February 8, 1980, New Jersey traded Natt to Portland for Maurice Lucas and two first-round picks. The picks became No. 7 Mike Gminski in 1980 and No. 10 Albert King in 1981.

Because that was a direct Natt-for-package trade, this review gives the branch full downstream credit. Gminski became a long-term Nets center, while King also spent multiple seasons with the franchise. Lucas added immediate veteran frontcourt value before leaving after the following season.

Gianelli Also Retained Trade Utility

John Gianelli was not a major long-term Nets player, but he did not disappear from the asset chain. Before the 1979-80 season, New Jersey included him with Jim Boylan and Bernard King in the trade that brought Rich Kelley from Utah.

Gianelli was only one piece of that package, so this review assigns partial credit to that branch rather than treating Kelley as Gianelli's sole return.

Why the Nets Win Despite Catchings' Excellent Milwaukee Tenure

Milwaukee clearly received real value: 372 Catchings games and 33 playoff appearances across five seasons is a strong result for one veteran acquisition.

New Jersey, however, turned the No. 8 pick into Natt's outstanding rookie production and then directly into Lucas plus two first-rounders. That created both immediate production and a larger multi-year asset base.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A+/A. New Jersey receives an A+ for Natt's rookie season and the direct Lucas-Gminski-King return, with Gianelli adding a smaller secondary branch. Milwaukee receives an A because Catchings supplied five durable seasons and meaningful playoff depth.

perspectives.summary: Chicago traded Wilbur Holland to the Jazz on June 22, 1979 for the player rights to Rickey Williams. Neither side realized NBA production from the asset it received. Holland had just completed three productive Bulls seasons but never appeared in another NBA game after the trade. Williams, a 1978 10th-round Jazz pick, did not play for Chicago and spent time outside the NBA before eventually appearing in 44 games for Utah in 1982-83. Because the reviewed records do not establish a Chicago-to-Utah rights return that would connect those later games to this transaction, this review does not credit them to either side. The trade is a low-value draw.
perspectives.analysis:
The Transaction Was Holland for Williams' Rights

The June 22, 1979 league ledger records Chicago sending Wilbur Holland to the New Orleans Jazz for Rickey Williams. By the time the next season began, the franchise had moved to Utah.

Holland Never Played for the Jazz

Holland had been a useful Bulls guard. He played 243 games across three Chicago seasons and averaged 14.7 points during that stint, including all 82 games in both 1977-78 and 1978-79.

The trade did not extend his NBA career. Basketball-Reference lists no regular-season appearances after his 1978-79 Bulls season, so Utah received no realized NBA games from the outgoing Chicago veteran.

Chicago Never Used Williams in an NBA Game

Williams had been a 10th-round Jazz selection in 1978. Chicago acquired his rights in this trade, but he did not make an NBA appearance for the Bulls.

His Basketball-Reference record shows time in another professional league in 1981-82, followed by 44 NBA games for Utah in 1982-83. Those later Jazz games are not credited to Chicago's side because Williams never played for the Bulls.

The Later Utah Stint Is Not a Downstream Return From This Trade

The reviewed transaction ledgers do not document a later Chicago-to-Utah transaction that restores Williams' rights to the Jazz. Without that routing evidence, this review does not invent a downstream branch linking his 1982-83 Utah season back to the 1979 exchange.

That leaves both teams with zero documented NBA games from the asset each directly received. The trade still makes sense as a rights-and-roster bet at the time: Chicago moved on from a veteran who had just completed a full 82-game season, while the Jazz exchanged the rights to a long-shot 10th-round pick. Hindsight simply shows that neither incoming branch turned into usable NBA value for the acquiring club.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, D/D. Chicago receives a D because the Williams rights never produced Bulls NBA value. Utah receives a D because Holland never played for the Jazz after the trade. The later Williams Jazz season is preserved as career context but remains outside the scored transaction branch.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix sent Washington the rights to Steve Malovic on June 22, 1979 for the No. 22 pick in the 1979 draft and a 1980 third-round pick. The first-rounder became Kyle Macy, who gave the Suns five seasons, 393 regular-season games, 178 starts, 4,180 points and 1,555 assists. The third-rounder became John Campbell, who never played in the NBA. Malovic appeared in only one Washington game before moving on. The enormous difference between Macy's five-year Suns return and Malovic's one-game Bullets stint makes this a clear Phoenix win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Phoenix, Washington and league transaction logs all record the June 22, 1979 deal the same way: Washington sent Phoenix its 1979 first-round pick and a 1980 third-round pick for the rights to Steve Malovic. Contemporary Washington Post reporting adds useful context. The Bullets were the defending Eastern Conference champions, had just lost the 1979 NBA Finals, and believed the 6-foot-10 Malovic could help immediately; general manager Bob Ferry said Malovic had already agreed to contract terms. The first-round choice was No. 22 overall only three days later, while the future third became No. 59 in 1980.

Phoenix Return
Phoenix used the No. 22 pick on Kentucky guard Kyle Macy. Macy stayed in college for 1979-80, then joined the Suns and became a durable five-year rotation and starting guard. He played all 82 regular-season games in each of his first four NBA seasons, started 72 games in 1981-82, and later started 52 games in 1984-85. Across his Phoenix tenure he appeared in 393 regular-season games with 178 starts, scored 4,180 points, handed out 1,555 assists and recorded 491 steals. His shooting efficiency was also a real asset: his five Suns seasons included field-goal percentages of .511, .514, .517, .501 and .485, plus elite free-throw shooting. Macy was not a franchise superstar, but he was a long-term NBA guard who gave Phoenix years of rotation stability and significant starting value. The 1980 third-round pick became Clemson forward John Campbell at No. 59. Campbell never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so that second draft asset produced no realized league value. That miss does not change the overall return because the first-round pick alone became a productive five-year Suns player.

Washington Return
Malovic's Washington outcome was almost empty. Basketball-Reference credits him with one Bullets appearance in 1979-80, totaling six minutes and one point. He then played 28 games for San Diego and 10 for Detroit in the same season, finishing his NBA career after 39 total games. Washington therefore traded a first-round pick and a future third for a player who contributed a single regular-season game to the franchise. The move made more sense in process terms than the raw hindsight result suggests because Washington was a veteran contender trying to add immediate frontcourt depth, and Malovic was a 6-foot-10 prospect who had delayed his NBA arrival to preserve college eligibility. Still, TradeVerdicts grades realized value, and the realized Bullets return was negligible.

Hindsight Verdict
Phoenix wins decisively. The Suns converted rights to a player who never became part of their NBA rotation into a first-round pick that produced five full seasons of Kyle Macy plus an additional draft chance. Washington received only one Malovic game. An A for Phoenix reflects the extraordinary asset conversion without inflating Macy into a star he was not. A D for Washington is severe but fair: the Bullets at least acquired a legitimate prospect rather than receiving nothing, yet the first-round pick they surrendered became a useful long-term guard while Malovic's Washington career lasted six minutes. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Denver's 1979 second-round pick and 10th-round pick on June 24, 1979 for cash. The Bulls used the selections on Lawrence Butler at No. 33 and Cortez Collins at No. 197. Neither player appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Butler's Basketball-Reference record lists him as a drafted rookie with no NBA statistics, while Collins likewise has no NBA game record. Denver's only documented return was cash, and the reviewed sources do not state the amount or identify a later basketball asset purchased with it. Chicago therefore gets only a slight hindsight edge for acquiring two draft chances, but the realized basketball value of both sides was minimal.
perspectives.analysis:
Chicago Bought Two Draft Picks for Cash

The June 24, 1979 transaction moved Denver's second-round and 10th-round selections to Chicago for cash. The draft was held the next day, giving the Bulls two additional chances late in the selection pool.

The second-round pick became No. 33 Lawrence Butler. The 10th-round pick became No. 197 Cortez Collins.

Butler Did Not Produce NBA Games

Butler was a 6-foot-3 guard from Idaho State. Basketball-Reference lists him as Chicago's second-round selection at No. 33 but does not list any NBA regular-season statistics.

That means the more valuable of the two incoming picks did not create realized Bulls game value. There is also no documented Bulls trade branch in the reviewed records that converted Butler's rights into another player or pick.

Collins Also Finished With Zero NBA Games

Collins was selected in the 10th round at No. 197 out of Southern Indiana. His Basketball-Reference page likewise contains draft information but no NBA regular-season line.

A 10th-round pick carried very little expected value in 1979, so that outcome is not surprising. It still means Chicago's second incoming asset produced no traceable NBA contribution.

Denver's Cash Return Cannot Be Quantified

Denver received cash rather than a player or future pick. The reviewed transaction sources do not state the amount, and no direct basketball asset is linked to that payment.

This review therefore does not invent a later Nuggets return. Cash has organizational value, but without an amount or documented use it cannot be scored like a player season or conveyed draft pick.

Why Chicago Gets Only a Small Edge

Chicago acquired two draft opportunities and used both of them, which is at least a traceable basketball process. Neither selected player reached an NBA regular-season game, however, so the Bulls did not realize meaningful on-court value.

Denver's cash return is also unmeasurable in basketball terms. The gap is therefore tiny and should not be mistaken for a successful Bulls transaction.

Final Verdict

Slight Bulls Edge, D+/D. Chicago receives a D+ for turning cash into two draft selections, even though neither player produced an NBA game. Denver receives a D because its return was undocumented cash with no traceable basketball branch in the reviewed sources.

Denver received cash rather than a player or future pick. The reviewed transaction sources do not state the amount, and no direct basketball asset is linked to that payment.

perspectives.analysis:
The Draft-Day Swap Was No. 5 Plus Cash for No. 4

Detroit's transaction record shows the Pistons sending the 1979 first-round pick later used on Sidney Moncrief to Milwaukee for the No. 4 pick later used on Greg Kelser. Detroit's source package also records cash going to the Bucks.

Moncrief Became a Milwaukee Franchise Pillar

Milwaukee used the No. 5 pick on Moncrief and kept him for ten seasons. He played 695 regular-season games for the Bucks, fourth-most in franchise history at the current checkpoint.

The peak value was elite. Moncrief made five All-Star teams, five All-NBA teams and five All-Defensive teams. He also won Defensive Player of the Year in both 1982-83 and 1983-84 and was later inducted into the Hall of Fame.

That is the kind of outcome teams hope for when they acquire a premium lottery-level pick: long tenure, two-way star production and repeated postseason relevance.

Kelser Gave Detroit Two Partial Seasons

Kelser played 50 games as a rookie and 25 more in 1980-81. Across those 75 Pistons games, he scored 1,017 points and provided useful wing production, including 14.2 points per game as a rookie.

Knee trouble interrupted his second season and limited the direct Detroit return. On November 23, 1981, the Pistons traded Kelser to Seattle for Vinnie Johnson.

The Kelser Branch Then Became Vinnie Johnson

That follow-up trade substantially changes Detroit's side of the ledger. Johnson played 798 regular-season games for the Pistons, fourth-most in franchise history at the current checkpoint, and became one of the team's most important bench scorers.

Johnson was part of Detroit's back-to-back championship teams in 1989 and 1990. Basketball-Reference credits him with two NBA titles, and his long Pistons tenure means Kelser's downstream value was far greater than Kelser's own 75 games.

This is direct attribution: Detroit traded Kelser alone for Johnson, so Johnson's Pistons value legitimately belongs to the Kelser branch.

Why Milwaukee Still Gets the Edge

Detroit's outcome was excellent once Johnson is included. The Pistons turned the No. 4 selection into Kelser and then directly into an 798-game championship contributor.

Milwaukee still received the better individual cornerstone. Moncrief became a Hall of Famer and one of the best two-way guards of his era, with 695 Bucks games and a long list of major honors.

The cash amount is not documented in the reviewed sources, so it is not assigned independent value.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win, A+/A. Milwaukee receives an A+ for landing Moncrief, a Hall of Fame guard with 695 Bucks games, five All-Star selections and two Defensive Player of the Year awards. Detroit receives an A because Kelser later became Vinnie Johnson in a direct one-for-one trade, producing 798 Pistons games and two championship seasons.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Seattle sold the draft rights to Johnny Moore to San Antonio for cash on June 26, 1979, one day after selecting him 43rd overall. The Spurs signed Moore that summer but waived him before the season, so his later franchise career cannot be treated as uninterrupted direct trade value. San Antonio re-signed him as a free agent on March 9, 1980, and Moore eventually played 519 regular-season games for the Spurs, including several seasons as their starting point guard. Seattle's cash return is undocumented. The same-team reacquisition makes the trade look favorable for San Antonio in hindsight, but the waiver and free-agent break require a more cautious grade than Moore's full career alone would suggest.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
Seattle Sold Moore's Draft Rights for Cash

Basketball-Reference's 1978-79 league ledger records Seattle selling Johnny Moore's player rights to San Antonio on June 26, 1979. Seattle had drafted Moore one day earlier in the second round with the 43rd overall pick.

San Antonio's own transaction history confirms the rights acquisition. A Spurs media guide also records that the team acquired Moore's rights for cash and signed him on July 23.

The Direct Trade Chain Broke Before Moore Played

This transaction needs an important attribution limit. San Antonio waived Moore on October 12, 1979, before he appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

That means Moore's later Spurs career is not a continuous direct return from the June rights purchase. The original trade delivered his rights and a summer contract, but those rights stopped being exclusive once the Spurs waived him.

San Antonio Re-Signed Moore as a Free Agent

On March 9, 1980, the Spurs signed Moore again as a free agent. He did not record an NBA game in 1979-80, but he made the roster the next season and began a long San Antonio career.

Moore eventually played 519 regular-season games for the Spurs. He appeared in 82 games as a rookie in 1980-81, started 78 games in 1981-82 and averaged 9.6 assists that season, then averaged 9.8 assists in 1982-83.

Across his NBA career, Moore finished with 7.4 assists per game. Nearly all of his 520 career games came with San Antonio, with only one regular-season appearance elsewhere.

How Much of That Value Belongs to This Trade?

The answer is not all of it. San Antonio's initial purchase identified Moore as a player worth acquiring and led directly to his first contract, but the team waived him before the season and reacquired him through free agency months later.

That break makes this different from a player who simply remained under team control from the original transaction. This review therefore treats Moore's later career as strong hindsight context, not full direct downstream credit.

Seattle's Side Is Hard to Quantify

The SuperSonics received cash, but the reviewed transaction records do not disclose the amount. Without a documented figure or a later asset tied to the payment, Seattle's realized return cannot be measured beyond the fact that it monetized a second-round draft right.

Final Verdict

Spurs Edge, B-/C. San Antonio receives a B- because the rights purchase helped bring Moore into the organization and the Spurs later re-signed him for a 519-game franchise career, but the waiver/free-agent gap prevents full credit. Seattle receives a C because the cash amount is unknown and no additional documented basketball asset is tied to the sale.

perspectives.summary: Detroit traded Andre Wakefield to Phoenix on August 24, 1979 for a 1981 fourth-round pick. Phoenix waived Wakefield on October 12 before he appeared in a regular-season game for the Suns; he later signed with Utah as a free agent and played eight games there. Detroit kept the pick through the 1981 draft and used it at No. 89 on Don Koonce, but Koonce never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Neither side generated meaningful NBA production from the original exchange. Detroit gets only a narrow hindsight edge because the Pistons at least carried the acquired asset through to a completed draft selection, while Phoenix received zero games from Wakefield.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Exchanged Wakefield for a Fourth-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Detroit and Phoenix transaction logs agree on the August 24, 1979 deal. The Pistons sent Andre Wakefield to the Suns for a 1981 fourth-round pick that eventually became the No. 89 selection.

Phoenix Got No Regular-Season Games From Wakefield

Wakefield had played 71 games for Detroit in 1978-79 after a brief two-game Chicago stint. He scored 172 points for the Pistons and averaged 8.1 minutes.

The Suns did not receive comparable on-court value. Phoenix waived Wakefield on October 12, 1979, before he appeared in a regular-season game for the club.

Wakefield later signed with Utah as a free agent on November 6 and played eight games for the Jazz. Those Utah games do not count as Phoenix trade value because the Suns had already waived him.

Detroit Kept the Pick Until the 1981 Draft

The Pistons retained the incoming fourth-round selection and used it at No. 89 in 1981 on Don Koonce from UNC Charlotte.

Koonce did not appear in an NBA regular-season game. Basketball-Reference lists him as a Detroit fourth-round selection but shows no NBA statistical line, so the pick produced no realized NBA playing value.

Why Detroit Gets Only a Narrow Edge

This is a low-value trade in hindsight. Phoenix received no regular-season games from Wakefield and lost his rights when it waived him. Detroit at least preserved the incoming asset for two years and exercised the pick, but Koonce did not reach the NBA.

The difference between the sides is therefore administrative rather than meaningful competitive value. Detroit completed the draft branch; Phoenix's player branch ended before the season began.

Final Verdict

Slight Pistons Edge, D+/D. Detroit receives a D+ because the fourth-round asset survived to the 1981 draft even though Koonce never played in the NBA. Phoenix receives a D because Wakefield was waived before recording a Suns regular-season appearance.

Basketball-Reference's Detroit and Phoenix transaction logs agree on the August 24, 1979 deal. The Pistons sent Andre Wakefield to the Suns for a 1981 fourth-round pick that eventually became the No. 89 selection.

Phoenix Got No Regular-Season Games From Wakefield

Wakefield had played 71 games for Detroit in 1978-79 after a brief two-game Chicago stint. He scored 172 points for the Pistons and averaged 8.1 minutes.

The Suns did not receive comparable on-court value. Phoenix waived Wakefield on October 12, 1979, before he appeared in a regular-season game for the club.

Wakefield later signed with Utah as a free agent on November 6 and played eight games for the Jazz. Those Utah games do not count as Phoenix trade value because the Suns had already waived him.

Detroit Kept the Pick Until the 1981 Draft

The Pistons retained the incoming fourth-round selection and used it at No. 89 in 1981 on Don Koonce from UNC Charlotte.

Koonce did not appear in an NBA regular-season game. Basketball-Reference lists him as a Detroit fourth-round selection but shows no NBA statistical line, so the pick produced no realized NBA playing value.

Why Detroit Gets Only a Narrow Edge

This is a low-value trade in hindsight. Phoenix received no regular-season games from Wakefield and lost his rights when it waived him. Detroit at least preserved the incoming asset for two years and exercised the pick, but Koonce did not reach the NBA.

The difference between the sides is therefore administrative rather than meaningful competitive value. Detroit completed the draft branch; Phoenix's player branch ended before the season began.

Final Verdict

Slight Pistons Edge, D+/D. Detroit receives a D+ because the fourth-round asset survived to the 1981 draft even though Koonce never played in the NBA. Phoenix receives a D because Wakefield was waived before recording a Suns regular-season appearance.

perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Bought One Season of Guard Depth

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland transaction ledger records the August 24, 1979 deal: the Cavaliers sent a 1981 third-round pick to Portland for Willie Smith. The pick later became the No. 50 selection used on Derek Holcomb.

Smith Played 62 Games for the Cavaliers

Smith had appeared in only 16 NBA games before arriving in Cleveland, including 13 for Portland in 1978-79. The Cavaliers gave him by far the largest role of his NBA career.

He played 62 games in 1979-80 and logged 1,051 minutes. Smith averaged 4.8 points, 4.2 assists and 2.0 rebounds in 17.0 minutes per game while serving as reserve point-guard depth.

Those 62 games were his final NBA season, so the trade did not create a long-term Cleveland piece. It did, however, provide a full year of usable rotation minutes from a player acquired for a future third-round selection.

Portland Used the Pick on Derek Holcomb

The Trail Blazers kept the incoming pick through the 1981 draft and selected Derek Holcomb 50th overall in the third round.

Holcomb never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Basketball-Reference lists the selection in Portland's 1981 draft history but shows no NBA statistical line for him.

That means Portland successfully converted the asset into a player selection but received no realized NBA playing value from the branch.

Why Cleveland Wins the Hindsight Comparison

This is not a franchise-changing trade. Smith's Cleveland tenure lasted one season, and his role was modest. But 62 games, 1,051 minutes and 259 assists are concrete value.

Portland's side produced a third-round selection that never reached the NBA. With no documented downstream transaction attached to Holcomb, there is no later value to offset Smith's season in Cleveland.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, B-/D+. Cleveland receives a B- for a full season of reserve guard production from Smith. Portland receives a D+ because the acquired third-round pick was exercised at No. 50 but produced no NBA regular-season games.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee sold Kevin Restani's player rights to San Antonio on August 31, 1979 for cash. The cash amount is not documented in the reviewed transaction records, making the Bucks' side impossible to quantify beyond the sale itself. San Antonio received immediate rotation value. Restani played all 82 games in 1979-80, averaging 10.7 points and 4.7 rebounds in 24.0 minutes, then appeared in 64 games the next season and 13 more in 1981-82. His Spurs tenure totaled 159 regular-season games before he finished that final NBA season in Cleveland. A three-season rotation return clearly outweighs an undocumented cash payment in hindsight.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee Sold Restani's Rights for Cash

Basketball-Reference lists the August 31, 1979 transaction as Milwaukee selling Kevin Restani's player rights to San Antonio. The Spurs' transaction page records the corresponding rights acquisition.

The reviewed sources do not disclose the cash amount. That means Milwaukee's return can be recognized as a completed sale, but it cannot be assigned a meaningful basketball value or compared to a known player or draft asset.

Restani Immediately Joined the Spurs Rotation

San Antonio got a substantial first season from Restani. He played all 82 games in 1979-80 and logged 1,966 minutes, averaging 10.7 points, 4.7 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 24.0 minutes per game.

The Spurs used him as a real rotation forward rather than end-of-bench depth. Basketball-Reference's depth chart shows him behind Mark Olberding at small forward but with nearly 2,000 minutes and 3.5 win shares.

The Value Continued Beyond One Season

Restani returned for 64 games in 1980-81 and another 13 for San Antonio in 1981-82. Across the three seasons, he appeared in 159 Spurs regular-season games before finishing 1981-82 with Cleveland.

His role declined after the first year, but San Antonio still converted a cash purchase into multiple seasons of usable NBA minutes. That is much more concrete than the typical rights sale in which the acquired player never reaches the rotation.

Why San Antonio Wins the Hindsight Comparison

Milwaukee may have had a sensible roster or financial reason to monetize Restani's rights, and the Bucks had already received 81 games from him in 1978-79. This review does not evaluate that prior Milwaukee season because it occurred before the trade.

After the transaction, San Antonio received 159 games, including a full 82-game season with double-digit scoring. Milwaukee received cash with no documented amount or downstream basketball asset tied to it.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win, A-/C. San Antonio receives an A- for three seasons and 159 regular-season games from Restani, including a 10.7-point first year. Milwaukee receives a C because the team received a real cash return, but the amount is unknown and no later basketball asset can be traced to the sale.

McAdoo still produced 58 games at 21.1 points per game for Detroit in 1979-80, then appeared in only six Pistons games the next season before being waived. Parish played 1,106 Celtics games and McHale 971, with both becoming Hall of Fame pillars of three championship teams. Few downstream branches are more direct or more decisive.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Compensation Deal Sent McAdoo to Detroit

Basketball-Reference records the September 6, 1979 transaction as Boston sending Bob McAdoo to Detroit for two 1980 first-round picks. The exchange was arranged as compensation for Boston's July signing of veteran free agent M.L. Carr.

This review treats Carr as transaction context rather than an incoming trade asset. The assets scored here are McAdoo on Detroit's side and the two first-round picks on Boston's side.

McAdoo Still Gave Detroit a Productive First Season

McAdoo played 58 games for the Pistons in 1979-80 and averaged 21.1 points, 8.1 rebounds and 3.4 assists in 36.2 minutes. He was still a high-level scorer even though Detroit finished with one of the league's weakest records.

The return did not last. McAdoo appeared in only six Detroit games in 1980-81 before the relationship ended. NBA.com's historical profile describes an injury-plagued Pistons stint and notes that Detroit eventually waived him after a grievance dispute.

That leaves Detroit with 64 regular-season games from a star-level scorer, but no long-term asset chain from the transaction itself.

Boston Kept the Two Picks Together

The decisive part of this trade came nine months later. On June 9, 1980, Boston sent exactly those two incoming first-round picks to Golden State.

One was the No. 1 pick later used on Joe Barry Carroll. The other was the No. 13 pick later used on Rickey Brown. In return, Boston received Robert Parish and Golden State's No. 3 pick.

The Celtics then used No. 3 on Kevin McHale. Because both Detroit picks from this exact transaction moved together in the Parish-McHale deal, this review can credit that downstream return directly rather than treating it as a diluted multi-branch outcome.

The Downstream Return Became a Dynasty Core

Parish played 1,106 regular-season games for Boston over 14 seasons. Basketball-Reference's franchise leaderboard places him second in Celtics history in games played.

McHale played all 971 of his NBA regular-season games for Boston. He became a seven-time All-Star, a Hall of Famer and a three-time NBA champion.

Parish and McHale joined Larry Bird as the frontcourt core of Boston's 1981, 1984 and 1986 championship teams. This is not a speculative value chain: the two picks received for McAdoo were the exact outgoing assets used to obtain Parish and the pick used on McHale.

Why Boston Wins by a Huge Margin

Detroit did receive legitimate value. McAdoo remained a 21-point scorer in his first Pistons season, so the return was not empty.

But 64 games of McAdoo cannot approach 2,077 combined Boston regular-season games from Parish and McHale, three championships with both players on the roster and two Hall of Fame careers.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A+/C. Boston receives an A+ because the two first-round picks were directly converted into Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick used on Kevin McHale. Detroit receives a C because McAdoo still supplied one productive scoring season, but the stint lasted only 64 games and the opportunity cost became one of the most valuable downstream returns in NBA trade history.

McAdoo Still Gave Detroit a Productive First Season

McAdoo played 58 games for the Pistons in 1979-80 and averaged 21.1 points, 8.1 rebounds and 3.4 assists in 36.2 minutes. He was still a high-level scorer even though Detroit finished with one of the league's weakest records.

The return did not last. McAdoo appeared in only six Detroit games in 1980-81 before the relationship ended. NBA.com's historical profile describes an injury-plagued Pistons stint and notes that Detroit eventually waived him after a grievance dispute.

That leaves Detroit with 64 regular-season games from a star-level scorer, but no long-term asset chain from the transaction itself.

Boston Kept the Two Picks Together

The decisive part of this trade came nine months later. On June 9, 1980, Boston sent exactly those two incoming first-round picks to Golden State.

One was the No. 1 pick later used on Joe Barry Carroll. The other was the No. 13 pick later used on Rickey Brown. In return, Boston received Robert Parish and Golden State's No. 3 pick.

The Celtics then used No. 3 on Kevin McHale. Because both Detroit picks from this exact transaction moved together in the Parish-McHale deal, this review can credit that downstream return directly rather than treating it as a diluted multi-branch outcome.

The Downstream Return Became a Dynasty Core

Parish played 1,106 regular-season games for Boston over 14 seasons. Basketball-Reference's franchise leaderboard places him second in Celtics history in games played.

McHale played all 971 of his NBA regular-season games for Boston. He became a seven-time All-Star, a Hall of Famer and a three-time NBA champion.

Parish and McHale joined Larry Bird as the frontcourt core of Boston's 1981, 1984 and 1986 championship teams. This is not a speculative value chain: the two picks received for McAdoo were the exact outgoing assets used to obtain Parish and the pick used on McHale.

Why Boston Wins by a Huge Margin

Detroit did receive legitimate value. McAdoo remained a 21-point scorer in his first Pistons season, so the return was not empty.

But 64 games of McAdoo cannot approach 2,077 combined Boston regular-season games from Parish and McHale, three championships with both players on the roster and two Hall of Fame careers.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A+/C. Boston receives an A+ because the two first-round picks were directly converted into Robert Parish and the No. 3 pick used on Kevin McHale. Detroit receives a C because McAdoo still supplied one productive scoring season, but the stint lasted only 64 games and the opportunity cost became one of the most valuable downstream returns in NBA trade history.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles traded Adrian Dantley to Utah on September 13, 1979 for Spencer Haywood. Haywood gave the Lakers a real one-season return, playing 76 regular-season games at 9.7 points and 4.6 rebounds and appearing in 12 playoff games for the 1980 championship team before his tenure ended during the Finals. Dantley became a franchise cornerstone. He played 461 games over seven Utah seasons, averaged 29.6 points, 6.2 rebounds and 3.7 assists, won two NBA scoring titles, made six All-Star teams during his career and eventually entered the Hall of Fame. Utah later retired his No. 4. The Jazz won the deal decisively despite Haywood's useful title-season contribution.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Swap Was Dantley for Haywood

The Lakers and Jazz transaction ledgers record the September 13, 1979 exchange of Adrian Dantley for Spencer Haywood. Both were accomplished forwards, but their post-trade paths diverged sharply.

Haywood Gave Los Angeles a Real Championship-Season Role

Haywood played 76 regular-season games for the Lakers in 1979-80. He averaged 9.7 points, 4.6 rebounds and 20.3 minutes while appearing on the team that finished 60-22 and won the NBA championship.

His contribution continued into the postseason. Basketball-Reference's playoff log shows 12 appearances, including minutes in the Phoenix series, the Western Conference Finals against Seattle and the first two games of the NBA Finals against Philadelphia.

Haywood's Lakers tenure then ended abruptly during the Finals. That makes the return short, but not empty: Los Angeles received a full regular season of rotation play and postseason minutes from a future Hall of Famer on a championship roster.

Dantley Became Utah's Offensive Centerpiece

Dantley's first Utah season immediately showed the difference in ceiling. He played 68 games in 1979-80 and averaged 28.0 points, 7.6 rebounds and 2.8 assists while shooting 57.6 percent from the field.

He stayed with the Jazz through 1985-86. Across seven Utah seasons, Dantley played 461 regular-season games and averaged 29.6 points, 6.2 rebounds and 3.7 assists.

He won the NBA scoring title in 1980-81 at 30.7 points per game and again in 1983-84 at 30.6. NBA.com's Utah history credits him with 13,635 points for the franchise, third in team history behind Karl Malone and John Stockton.

The Long-Term Legacy Widens the Gap

Dantley became one of the defining players of Utah's early Salt Lake City era. He was a six-time NBA All-Star over his career, entered the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2008 and had his No. 4 retired by the Jazz in 2007.

Los Angeles did receive something important in the short term: Haywood was a rotation player on a championship team. That prevents this from being graded like a total miss. But his Lakers stay lasted one season, while Dantley delivered seven years of elite scoring and franchise-level value.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win, A+/B-. Utah receives an A+ for 461 Dantley games, two scoring titles and a Hall of Fame-level franchise tenure. Los Angeles receives a B- because Haywood played 76 regular-season games and 12 playoff games for the 1980 champions, but the short tenure cannot approach the value surrendered.

perspectives.summary: Kansas City acquired Mike Green from San Antonio on September 13, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. Green played 21 games for the Kings, averaging 7.7 points and 5.4 rebounds in 21.9 minutes before his NBA career ended. San Antonio used the No. 39 pick on Michael Wiley, who played 33 regular-season games for the Spurs in 1980-81 at 5.7 points and 1.9 rebounds in 8.2 minutes and appeared briefly in three playoff games. The frozen Kings source batch also lists cash going to San Antonio, but the reviewed Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers do not document an amount, so this review leaves that term unquantified. San Antonio gets a slight realized-value edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Was Green for a Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's league, Kansas City and San Antonio transaction ledgers agree on the September 13, 1979 core exchange. The Kings acquired Mike Green and the Spurs received Kansas City's 1980 second-round pick, later No. 39 overall.

The frozen Kansas City source record also includes cash going to San Antonio. The public transaction ledgers reviewed for this review do not provide a cash amount, so the cash is preserved as an unresolved term and receives no numerical value in the grade.

Green Played 21 Games for Kansas City

Green joined a Kings team that went 47-35 and reached the 1980 playoffs. He appeared in 21 regular-season games, averaging 7.7 points, 5.4 rebounds and 21.9 minutes.

Those 21 games were the final NBA appearances of his career. Green still supplied usable frontcourt minutes, but Kansas City did not receive a multi-season return or a later trade branch from the player.

San Antonio Used the Pick on Michael Wiley

The Spurs kept the second-round pick and selected Michael Wiley at No. 39 in the 1980 NBA Draft. That makes the draft outcome direct rather than speculative.

Wiley played 33 regular-season games for San Antonio in 1980-81. NBA.com lists him at 5.7 points, 1.9 rebounds and 8.2 minutes per game. He also appeared in three playoff games, although his postseason role totaled only five minutes.

San Antonio waived Wiley on October 27, 1981. He then played one more NBA season with San Diego, but that Clippers production does not belong to the Spurs' realized return.

Why San Antonio Gets the Slight Edge

Neither side uncovered major value. Kansas City received 21 games from Green, while San Antonio turned the pick into 33 regular-season Wiley games plus three brief playoff appearances.

The Spurs therefore received a little more direct team service from the primary asset. Any cash would only strengthen San Antonio's side, but this review does not rely on it because the amount is not documented in the reviewed public records.

Final Verdict

Slight Spurs Edge, B-/C+. San Antonio receives a B- for converting the pick into 33 Wiley games and a small playoff contribution. Kansas City receives a C+ for 21 useful Green games, but the return ended after one season and produced no further realized branch.

perspectives.summary: Detroit traded Jim Brewer to Portland on September 18, 1979 for a 1981 second-round pick. Brewer played 67 games for the Trail Blazers in 1979-80, then Portland moved him to the Lakers for a 1984 second-round pick that became Jerome Kersey. Kersey played 831 regular-season games for Portland, second-most in franchise history. Detroit also extracted real value from its pick: the Pistons sent it to the Lakers for Wayne Robinson, who played 81 games for Detroit in 1980-81 at 7.9 points and 3.6 rebounds. Both branches paid off, but Portland's Brewer-to-Kersey chain created the overwhelming long-term advantage.
perspectives.analysis:
The Original Trade Was Brewer for a Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference records Detroit sending Jim Brewer to Portland on September 18, 1979 for a 1981 second-round pick. That selection eventually became No. 39 overall, but Detroit did not make the pick itself.

Brewer Gave Portland One Useful Season

Brewer played 67 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers in 1979-80. He averaged 2.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 15.2 minutes while filling a reserve frontcourt role.

The direct playing return was modest, but Portland did not let the asset expire. On October 8, 1980, the Trail Blazers traded Brewer to the Lakers for a 1984 second-round pick.

That Pick Became Jerome Kersey

Portland kept the 1984 second-rounder and used it at No. 46 on Jerome Kersey. The downstream link is direct: Brewer was the outgoing asset in the trade that brought Portland the exact pick used on Kersey.

Kersey then played 831 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers. Basketball-Reference's franchise leaderboard ranks him second in Portland history in games played, behind only Clyde Drexler.

That transforms what initially looked like a one-year Brewer rental into a long-term franchise asset chain. Kersey became a major part of Portland's core through the late 1980s and early 1990s, including the teams that reached the 1990 and 1992 NBA Finals.

Detroit Converted Its Pick Into Wayne Robinson

Detroit also avoided simply waiting for the 1981 draft. On October 1, 1980, the Pistons traded the incoming second-round pick to the Lakers for Wayne Robinson.

Robinson played 81 games for Detroit in 1980-81 and averaged 7.9 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists in 19.7 minutes. It was his only NBA season, but that is still a substantial one-year return from a second-round asset.

The Lakers later used the pick at No. 39 on Harvey Knuckles. Knuckles therefore belongs to the final draft identity of the pick, not Detroit's realized on-court return. Detroit's value came from Robinson.

Why Portland Wins Clearly

Detroit's side was respectable: 81 Robinson games is a better return than many second-round picks produce. But Portland received 67 Brewer games and then converted Brewer directly into the pick used on Kersey.

Kersey's 831 Portland games dwarf the one-season Robinson return and turn the original transaction into a major Trail Blazers asset-chain win.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Win, A+/B. Portland receives an A+ because Brewer produced a season of depth and then directly became the draft pick used on Jerome Kersey, who played 831 games for the franchise. Detroit receives a B because it turned the second-round pick into 81 games of Wayne Robinson rather than losing the asset at the draft.

Basketball-Reference records Detroit sending Jim Brewer to Portland on September 18, 1979 for a 1981 second-round pick. That selection eventually became No. 39 overall, but Detroit did not make the pick itself.

Brewer Gave Portland One Useful Season

Brewer played 67 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers in 1979-80. He averaged 2.9 points, 3.8 rebounds and 15.2 minutes while filling a reserve frontcourt role.

The direct playing return was modest, but Portland did not let the asset expire. On October 8, 1980, the Trail Blazers traded Brewer to the Lakers for a 1984 second-round pick.

That Pick Became Jerome Kersey

Portland kept the 1984 second-rounder and used it at No. 46 on Jerome Kersey. The downstream link is direct: Brewer was the outgoing asset in the trade that brought Portland the exact pick used on Kersey.

Kersey then played 831 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers. Basketball-Reference's franchise leaderboard ranks him second in Portland history in games played, behind only Clyde Drexler.

That transforms what initially looked like a one-year Brewer rental into a long-term franchise asset chain. Kersey became a major part of Portland's core through the late 1980s and early 1990s, including the teams that reached the 1990 and 1992 NBA Finals.

Detroit Converted Its Pick Into Wayne Robinson

Detroit also avoided simply waiting for the 1981 draft. On October 1, 1980, the Pistons traded the incoming second-round pick to the Lakers for Wayne Robinson.

Robinson played 81 games for Detroit in 1980-81 and averaged 7.9 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists in 19.7 minutes. It was his only NBA season, but that is still a substantial one-year return from a second-round asset.

The Lakers later used the pick at No. 39 on Harvey Knuckles. Knuckles therefore belongs to the final draft identity of the pick, not Detroit's realized on-court return. Detroit's value came from Robinson.

Why Portland Wins Clearly

Detroit's side was respectable: 81 Robinson games is a better return than many second-round picks produce. But Portland received 67 Brewer games and then converted Brewer directly into the pick used on Kersey.

Kersey's 831 Portland games dwarf the one-season Robinson return and turn the original transaction into a major Trail Blazers asset-chain win.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Win, A+/B. Portland receives an A+ because Brewer produced a season of depth and then directly became the draft pick used on Jerome Kersey, who played 831 games for the franchise. Detroit receives a B because it turned the second-round pick into 81 games of Wayne Robinson rather than losing the asset at the draft.

Smith played every game for Cleveland over two seasons, totaling 164 appearances while averaging 17.6 points in 1979-80 and 14.6 in 1980-81. Cleveland then traded Smith to New York for a 1981 first-round pick that was later used as compensation when the Cavaliers signed Scott Wedman. perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Sent Smith to Cleveland for a First

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland acquiring Randy Smith from San Diego on September 21, 1979 for a 1980 first-round pick. The frozen Cavaliers source package also lists cash going to San Diego, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not provide an amount, so this review does not score the cash term.

Smith Gave Cleveland Two Full Seasons

Smith played all 82 games in both of his Cavaliers seasons. In 1979-80 he averaged 17.6 points, 4.4 assists and 3.1 rebounds in 32.6 minutes.

He followed with 14.6 points and 4.4 assists in 1980-81. Across the two seasons, Smith appeared in 164 games for Cleveland and remained a substantial backcourt contributor rather than a short rental.

Cleveland also preserved a downstream asset. On May 20, 1981, the Cavaliers traded Smith to New York for a 1981 first-round pick. That pick was later sent to Kansas City as compensation when Cleveland signed Scott Wedman as a veteran free agent.

Wedman then played 89 games for Cleveland across parts of two seasons. This review treats those games as downstream use of the Smith return, but stops there rather than assigning every later Wedman transaction branch back to this 1979 trade.

San Diego Used the Pick on Michael Brooks

The Clippers kept Cleveland's 1980 first-round pick and selected Michael Brooks at No. 9. Brooks immediately played all 82 games as a rookie, averaging 14.7 points and 5.4 rebounds.

He played all 82 games again in both 1981-82 and 1982-83, averaging 15.6 points and 7.6 rebounds in the first of those seasons and 12.2 points and 6.4 rebounds in the second.

Brooks added 47 games in 1983-84 before knee trouble cost him the next two NBA seasons. His San Diego total was 293 regular-season games, with useful scoring and rebounding production across four years.

Why San Diego Gets the Modest Edge

Cleveland did well. Smith produced 164 games of veteran guard play and was later converted into a first-round asset that helped facilitate the Wedman signing.

San Diego, however, received 293 games from Brooks, including three consecutive 82-game seasons and several years of starter-level production. The unquantified cash would only strengthen the Clippers' side, but the grade does not depend on it.

Final Verdict

Slight Clippers Edge, A-/B+. San Diego receives an A- for turning the pick into 293 Michael Brooks games over four seasons. Cleveland receives a B+ for 164 Randy Smith games plus a meaningful downstream first-round asset, making this a productive deal for both teams despite the Clippers' longer direct return.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey acquired Rich Kelley from Utah on October 2, 1979 for Bernard King, John Gianelli, Jim Boylan and cash in the frozen Nets source package. Kelley played 57 regular-season games for the Nets before being traded to Phoenix for a 1982 first-round pick and a 1983 second-round pick. Utah received only 19 King games and 17 Gianelli games directly, while Boylan never appeared in a Jazz regular-season game. The Jazz then traded King to Golden State for Wayne Cooper and a 1981 second-round pick; Cooper played 71 games for Utah. Both branches retained value, with Utah holding the modest hindsight edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Public Ledgers Confirm the Three-Player Package

Basketball-Reference records New Jersey sending Bernard King, John Gianelli and Jim Boylan to Utah on October 2, 1979 for Rich Kelley. The frozen Nets source package also lists cash going to Utah, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the term without scoring it.

Kelley Gave New Jersey 57 Games and Two Future Picks

Kelley played 57 games for the Nets in 1979-80, averaging 10.0 points, 7.0 rebounds and 2.2 assists in 25.7 minutes. He was not a long-term Net, but the branch did not end when he left.

On February 15, 1980, New Jersey traded Kelley to Phoenix for a 1982 first-round pick and a 1983 second-round pick. The first later became the No. 17 selection associated with Brook Steppe after New Jersey sent it with Mike Woodson to Kansas City for Sam Lacey.

That later deal required Woodson as well, so this review does not assign the full Lacey return to Kelley alone. The important point is that Kelley produced more than half a season of useful center play and was then converted into a first-round asset plus a second.

Utah's Direct Return Was Brief

King played 19 games for Utah and averaged 9.3 points in 22.1 minutes. Gianelli played 17 games, averaging 3.2 points and 3.6 rebounds, before the Jazz waived him on November 28.

Boylan did not appear in a Jazz regular-season game. His Basketball-Reference page lists only his rookie NBA season, so there is no Utah playing return to score from that portion of the package.

King Still Produced a Useful Downstream Return

Utah moved King on September 11, 1980, receiving Wayne Cooper and a 1981 second-round pick from Golden State. Cooper then played 71 games for the Jazz in 1980-81, averaging 6.9 points and 6.2 rebounds in 20 minutes.

The second-round pick was later associated with Ken Green. This review credits Utah with the retained pick value but does not inflate the branch beyond the assets actually received.

Why Utah Gets the Slight Edge

New Jersey did better than the legacy F grade suggests. Kelley gave the Nets 57 games and was later converted into a first-round pick plus a second-round pick. That is a legitimate multi-step return.

Utah received less immediate production from the original players, but King still became Cooper plus another pick. Adding Cooper's 71 games to King and Gianelli's brief Jazz stints gives Utah a little more isolated realized value from the original package.

Final Verdict

Slight Jazz Edge, A-/B+. Utah receives an A- because the King branch became 71 Wayne Cooper games plus a second-round pick, while King and Gianelli also contributed briefly before leaving. New Jersey receives a B+ because Kelley played 57 games and was later converted into a first-rounder and a second-rounder. The cash amount remains unresolved and unscored.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded Jim Chones to the Lakers on October 5, 1979 for Dave Robisch and a 1980 third-round pick later used on Ron Jones. Chones played all 82 regular-season games in each of his two Los Angeles seasons and started throughout the Lakers' 1980 championship playoff run, giving the Lakers 164 games plus a title-season frontcourt piece. Robisch played 93 games for Cleveland before the Cavaliers traded him to Denver for Kim Hughes and two draft picks; Hughes added 45 Cleveland games. Ron Jones did not produce an NBA regular-season return. Cleveland preserved secondary asset value, but Los Angeles received the stronger direct outcome.
perspectives.analysis:
The October 5 Trade Was Chones for Robisch and a Third

Basketball-Reference's league and Cleveland transaction ledgers agree on the package: Jim Chones went to the Lakers, while the Cavaliers received Dave Robisch and a 1980 third-round pick later used at No. 68 on Ron Jones.

Chones Immediately Joined a Championship Rotation

Chones played all 82 regular-season games for Los Angeles in 1979-80. He averaged 10.6 points, 6.9 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 29.2 minutes, giving the Lakers a dependable veteran big beside Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.

The postseason is the decisive part of the return. Chones started throughout the 1980 playoff run and appeared in all 16 games as Los Angeles won the NBA championship. His Game 6 line in Philadelphia included 11 points and 10 rebounds in 43 minutes, illustrating that he was not merely a deep reserve on the title team.

Chones then played all 82 games again in 1980-81, averaging 10.8 points and 8.0 rebounds in 31.2 minutes. That gives the Lakers 164 regular-season games across two seasons plus a substantial contribution to the 1980 championship.

Robisch Gave Cleveland One Full Season and Part of Another

Robisch also produced immediate value. He played all 82 games for Cleveland in 1979-80 and averaged 15.3 points, 8.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 32.6 minutes.

He returned for 11 more Cavaliers games in 1980-81 before Cleveland traded him to Denver on October 31. The Cavaliers received Kim Hughes, a 1981 third-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick.

Hughes played 45 games for Cleveland that season. His role was small, but it gives the Robisch branch a documented downstream playing return in addition to the two draft assets.

The Third-Round Pick Did Not Add NBA Production

Cleveland used the original Lakers third-round pick at No. 68 on Ron Jones. Basketball-Reference records Jones as the Cavaliers' 1980 third-round selection but does not show an NBA regular-season statistical line, so this review does not assign playing value to that pick.

Why Los Angeles Wins the Hindsight Grade

Cleveland received a productive 93-game Robisch stint and then converted him into Hughes plus two draft picks. That is a useful return and prevents the deal from being one-sided.

Los Angeles, however, received 164 Chones games, two complete regular seasons and a starting frontcourt contributor on the 1980 champions. Championship value at that level outweighs Cleveland's shorter direct stint and later secondary assets.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A/B+. Los Angeles receives an A for Chones' 164 regular-season games and his role throughout the 1980 championship run. Cleveland receives a B+ for 93 Robisch games plus the Hughes-and-picks downstream return, while the original third-round selection did not create an NBA playing return.
