Chones Immediately Joined a Championship Rotation

Chones played all 82 regular-season games for Los Angeles in 1979-80. He averaged 10.6 points, 6.9 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 29.2 minutes, giving the Lakers a dependable veteran big beside Kareem Abdul-Jabbar.

The postseason is the decisive part of the return. Chones started throughout the 1980 playoff run and appeared in all 16 games as Los Angeles won the NBA championship. His Game 6 line in Philadelphia included 11 points and 10 rebounds in 43 minutes, illustrating that he was not merely a deep reserve on the title team.

Chones then played all 82 games again in 1980-81, averaging 10.8 points and 8.0 rebounds in 31.2 minutes. That gives the Lakers 164 regular-season games across two seasons plus a substantial contribution to the 1980 championship.

Robisch Gave Cleveland One Full Season and Part of Another

Robisch also produced immediate value. He played all 82 games for Cleveland in 1979-80 and averaged 15.3 points, 8.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists in 32.6 minutes.

He returned for 11 more Cavaliers games in 1980-81 before Cleveland traded him to Denver on October 31. The Cavaliers received Kim Hughes, a 1981 third-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick.

Hughes played 45 games for Cleveland that season. His role was small, but it gives the Robisch branch a documented downstream playing return in addition to the two draft assets.

The Third-Round Pick Did Not Add NBA Production

Cleveland used the original Lakers third-round pick at No. 68 on Ron Jones. Basketball-Reference records Jones as the Cavaliers' 1980 third-round selection but does not show an NBA regular-season statistical line, so this review does not assign playing value to that pick.

Why Los Angeles Wins the Hindsight Grade

Cleveland received a productive 93-game Robisch stint and then converted him into Hughes plus two draft picks. That is a useful return and prevents the deal from being one-sided.

Los Angeles, however, received 164 Chones games, two complete regular seasons and a starting frontcourt contributor on the 1980 champions. Championship value at that level outweighs Cleveland's shorter direct stint and later secondary assets.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A/B+. Los Angeles receives an A for Chones' 164 regular-season games and his role throughout the 1980 championship run. Cleveland receives a B+ for 93 Robisch games plus the Hughes-and-picks downstream return, while the original third-round selection did not create an NBA playing return.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Philadelphia traded Joe Bryant to San Diego on October 5, 1979 for the Clippers' 1986 first-round pick. Bryant gave San Diego 238 regular-season games over three seasons, including all 82 games in 1980-81 and 75 games with 49 starts in 1981-82. Philadelphia held the pick for nearly seven years; it became the No. 1 selection in 1986, but the 76ers traded that pick to Cleveland before the draft for Roy Hinson rather than selecting Brad Daugherty themselves. Hinson then played 105 games for Philadelphia before becoming one component of the 1988 Mike Gminski trade. Philadelphia gets a modest hindsight edge, not the runaway win implied by the legacy archive entry.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Pick Was Valuable, but Philadelphia Did Not Draft Daugherty

Basketball-Reference's 1979-80 transaction ledgers record Philadelphia sending Joe Bryant to San Diego for the Clippers' 1986 first-round pick. The legacy archive entry labels the asset with Brad Daugherty because he was eventually selected No. 1 with that pick.

That label needs context. Philadelphia still controlled the selection in June 1986, but one day before the draft the 76ers traded the No. 1 pick to Cleveland for Roy Hinson. Cleveland then selected Daugherty. This review therefore evaluates Philadelphia's realized return as Hinson and the later Hinson branch, not Daugherty's Cavaliers career.

Bryant Gave San Diego Three Useful Seasons

Bryant played 81 games for the Clippers in 1979-80, averaging 9.3 points and 6.4 rebounds in 28.7 minutes. He followed with all 82 games in 1980-81 and averaged 11.6 points and 5.4 rebounds.

In 1981-82, Bryant played 75 games, started 49 and averaged 11.8 points. Across the three seasons he appeared in 238 regular-season games for San Diego.

That is substantially more direct production than the old F-style framing suggests. The Clippers gave up a future premium asset, but they received three full years of rotation and starting-level forward play in return.

Philadelphia Eventually Converted the Pick into Hinson

On June 16, 1986, Philadelphia traded the No. 1 selection to Cleveland for Roy Hinson. Hinson then played 76 games for the 76ers in 1986-87, starting 58 and averaging 13.9 points, 6.4 rebounds and 2.1 blocks.

He added 29 Philadelphia games the next season before a January 1988 trade sent Hinson, Tim McCormick and a 1989 second-round pick to New Jersey for Mike Gminski and Ben Coleman.

Because McCormick and the second-rounder were also included, this review does not assign the entire Gminski-Coleman return to the original 1979 pick. Hinson's 105 Philadelphia games are the cleanest direct realized outcome.

Why Philadelphia Still Gets the Edge

San Diego received more games from the original player than Philadelphia later received from Hinson. Bryant was a legitimate three-season rotation piece, so the Clippers deserve a strong grade.

Philadelphia, however, turned an outgoing player who had just averaged 7.6 points into an asset that matured into the No. 1 pick and was then converted into a productive starting forward. Hinson also retained enough trade value to become part of another substantial package.

Final Verdict

Slight 76ers Edge, A-/B+. Philadelphia receives an A- because the future first matured into the No. 1 pick and was converted into 105 Hinson games plus later trade utility. San Diego receives a B+ because Bryant delivered 238 games across three seasons. The result is much closer than an evaluation that credits Philadelphia with Daugherty's Cleveland career.
los-angeles-clippers.gradeRationale: Joe Bryant provided modest value, while the first-round pick ultimately became the No. 1 selection used on All-Star center Brad Daugherty.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles traded Irv Kiffin to San Antonio on October 5, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. Kiffin played only 26 NBA games, all for the Spurs, before San Antonio waived him on December 19. The Lakers kept the pick and selected Butch Carter at No. 37. Carter played 54 games for Los Angeles in 1980-81, then was traded to Indiana for a 1982 third-round pick. Los Angeles used that later selection on Hutch Jones, although Jones never played a regular-season game for the Lakers. The original pick therefore produced both on-court value and another asset, giving Los Angeles the clear hindsight win.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Lakers Turned Kiffin into a Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference records Los Angeles sending Irv Kiffin to San Antonio on October 5, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. The selection landed at No. 37 and was used on Butch Carter.

Kiffin's Spurs Tenure Was Brief

Kiffin made his NBA debut with San Antonio and played 26 games. He averaged 3.2 points, 1.5 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 8.2 minutes while shooting 33.3 percent from the field.

San Antonio waived him on December 19, 1979. Those 26 appearances became his entire NBA career, so the Spurs received no longer-term player value from the trade.

Carter Played 54 Games for the Lakers

Los Angeles used the pick on Butch Carter in the 1980 draft. Carter played 54 games as a Lakers rookie in 1980-81, averaging 5.6 points in 12.4 minutes and totaling 672 minutes.

His role was modest, but the pick produced more NBA games than Kiffin gave San Antonio and retained transaction value after Carter's rookie season.

On October 15, 1981, the Lakers traded Carter to Indiana for a 1982 third-round pick. Los Angeles used that selection at No. 54 on Hutch Jones.

Jones Never Played for Los Angeles

Hutch Jones eventually appeared in 13 NBA games, all for San Diego rather than the Lakers. That means this review does not credit Los Angeles with Jones' later Clippers minutes.

The relevant downstream value is that Carter generated another draft asset before leaving Los Angeles. The final selection itself did not create additional Lakers production.

Why Los Angeles Wins Clearly

San Antonio received 26 games from a player who was waived before Christmas and never played another NBA season.

Los Angeles received a second-round pick that became Carter, got 54 games from him and then converted him into another draft pick. The downstream branch did not become a major player, but the Lakers extracted multiple layers of value from an outgoing player who never appeared for them.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, B+/D+. Los Angeles receives a B+ for 54 Carter games plus the later third-round asset. San Antonio receives a D+ because Kiffin lasted only 26 games and was waived less than three months after the trade.
los-angeles-lakers.gradeRationale: The Lakers produced a modest realized-value advantage. Grades weigh realized player production, identifiable pick conversion, role, timing, contract context and downstream asset use.

perspectives.summary: Denver traded Robert Smith to Utah on October 9, 1979 for a 1980 third-round pick and a 1981 second-round pick. Smith played only six games for the Jazz before Utah waived him on October 25, but those six appearances still exceeded Denver's direct NBA return from the two selections. The Nuggets used No. 48 in 1980 on Eddie Lee, who never played an NBA regular-season game, and No. 34 in 1981 on Ken Green, whom Denver waived before the 1981-82 season. perspectives.analysis:
Denver Took Two Picks for a Reserve Guard

Basketball-Reference records Denver sending Robert Smith to Utah on October 9, 1979 for a 1980 third-round pick and a 1981 second-round pick. The selections became No. 48 Eddie Lee and No. 34 Ken Green.

Smith Lasted Only Six Games in Utah

Smith appeared in six games for the Jazz, totaling 73 minutes, 15 points and seven assists. Utah waived him on October 25, just sixteen days after the trade.

That was a very small return, but it was at least measurable NBA production. Smith later continued his career elsewhere, yet this review does not credit those later teams' games to Utah after the Jazz waived him.

The 1980 Pick Produced No Denver Games

Denver used the 1980 third-round pick on Eddie Lee at No. 48. Basketball-Reference lists Lee as drafted by the Nuggets but records no NBA regular-season games.

The selection therefore produced no on-court value for Denver.

The 1981 Pick Also Produced No Denver Games

The second asset landed at No. 34 in 1981 and became Ken Green. Denver drafted Green, then waived him on October 15, 1981 before the regular season.

Green eventually reached the NBA years later and played seven games for New York in 1985-86, but those appearances were not a Nuggets return. Denver received no regular-season games from the second pick either.

Why Utah Gets the Narrow Edge

Denver received two draft opportunities, which gave the original package more theoretical upside. In realized terms, however, neither selection produced a Denver regular-season game.

Utah's side was also poor: Smith lasted only six games and was gone before the end of October. The difference is simply that the Jazz received some direct NBA minutes while Denver's two picks produced none for the Nuggets.

Final Verdict

Slight Jazz Edge, D+/D. Utah receives a D+ for six Smith games before the waiver. Denver receives a D because two draft selections failed to produce a single Nuggets regular-season appearance.

Smith Lasted Only Six Games in Utah

Smith appeared in six games for the Jazz, totaling 73 minutes, 15 points and seven assists. Utah waived him on October 25, just sixteen days after the trade.

indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Bought Four Seasons of Center Depth

Basketball-Reference records Indiana sending a 1981 second-round pick to Portland on October 9, 1979 for Clemon Johnson. Portland eventually used the selection at No. 26 on Brian Jackson.

Johnson Immediately Entered the Pacers Rotation

Johnson played 79 games in 1979-80, averaging 6.0 points, 5.0 rebounds and 1.5 blocks in 19.5 minutes. He followed with 81 games in 1980-81 and 79 games in 1981-82, starting 42 in the latter season.

Johnson added 51 Indiana games in 1982-83 before being traded in February. That gives the Pacers 290 regular-season appearances from the player acquired for one second-round pick.

The production was not star-level, but it was durable. Johnson became a multi-year rotation center and played a much larger role than the outgoing draft asset ever produced for Portland.

Johnson Also Retained Trade Value

On February 15, 1983, Indiana traded Johnson and a 1984 third-round pick to Philadelphia. The Pacers received Russ Schoene, a 1983 first-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick.

This review does not assign the entire Philadelphia package to Johnson because Indiana also included the third-round selection. The important point is that Johnson remained a meaningful trade asset after 290 Pacers games rather than leaving for nothing.

Portland's Pick Did Not Produce NBA Games

The Trail Blazers held the pick and selected Brian Jackson at No. 26 in the 1981 draft. Basketball-Reference lists Jackson as a Portland draft choice but records no NBA regular-season games.

Jackson had a professional career outside the NBA, but those results do not create realized NBA value for Portland in this archive.

Why Indiana Wins Easily

Indiana received four seasons of rotation play, 290 regular-season games and a player who still carried enough value to be included in a later first-round-pick package.

Portland received one second-round selection that produced no NBA games. There is little ambiguity in the realized comparison.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, A-/D. Indiana receives an A- for 290 Johnson games plus later trade utility. Portland receives a D because the No. 26 selection on Brian Jackson produced no NBA regular-season appearances.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee traded Ernie Grunfeld, a 1980 second-round pick and cash to Kansas City on October 9, 1979 for Richard Washington. Washington gave the Bucks 75 regular-season games before Dallas selected him in the 1980 expansion draft. Grunfeld became a three-season Kings rotation player, appearing in 240 games and averaging 12.7 points in 1981-82. Kansas City also converted the incoming second-round pick into Len Elmore, who played 58 games for the Kings before leaving for Milwaukee as a veteran free agent. The cash amount is undocumented in the reviewed public ledgers. Kansas City received the deeper realized return.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Kansas City Received More Than Grunfeld

Basketball-Reference records Milwaukee sending Ernie Grunfeld and a 1980 second-round pick to Kansas City on October 9, 1979 for Richard Washington. The frozen Milwaukee source package also includes cash going to the Kings, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the term without scoring it.

Washington Gave Milwaukee One Season

Washington played 75 games for the Bucks in 1979-80. He averaged 5.9 points, 3.7 rebounds and 0.7 assists in 14.6 minutes while providing frontcourt depth for a 49-win team.

Milwaukee did not retain him beyond that season. Dallas selected Washington from the Bucks in the May 28, 1980 expansion draft. The Bucks therefore received 75 regular-season games from the original trade and no direct downstream asset from his departure.

Grunfeld Became a Three-Year Kings Rotation Player

Grunfeld appeared in 80 games for Kansas City in 1979-80 and 79 more in 1980-81. His role expanded in 1981-82, when he played 81 games, started 11 and averaged 12.7 points and 3.4 assists in 23.4 minutes.

Across those three seasons, Grunfeld played 240 regular-season games for the Kings. He then signed with New York as a veteran free agent in September 1982. This review does not assign a specific compensation value to that departure because the reviewed Kansas City ledger records the compensation generically rather than naming a clear asset.

The Second-Round Pick Became Len Elmore

Kansas City did not use Milwaukee's 1980 second-round pick at the draft. On November 27, 1979, the Kings sent that selection to Indiana for Len Elmore.

Elmore played 58 regular-season games for Kansas City that season, averaging 4.5 points and 4.4 rebounds in 15.8 minutes. When Elmore signed with Milwaukee as a veteran free agent in June 1980, Kansas City received a 1981 second-round compensation pick.

That later compensation adds another branch to the original pick's value, but this review stops short of assigning unrelated later careers to it. The cleanest realized return is Elmore's 58 Kings games plus the fact that his rights generated another draft asset.

Why Kansas City Wins

Milwaukee received a useful one-year reserve in Washington, but his tenure ended after 75 games when he was lost in the expansion draft.

Kansas City received 240 Grunfeld games, 58 Elmore games from the routed second-round pick and an unquantified cash term. Grunfeld alone supplied more than three times Milwaukee's direct game total, and the pick created additional value rather than disappearing.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A-/C+. Kansas City receives an A- for three Grunfeld seasons plus the Elmore branch and preserved cash term. Milwaukee receives a C+ for 75 Washington games before losing him in the expansion draft.

perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Paid a Second-Round Pick for a Proven Guard

Basketball-Reference records Houston trading Mike Newlin to New Jersey on October 12, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. The frozen Nets source package also includes cash, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the cash term without assigning numerical value.

Newlin Immediately Became New Jersey's Lead Scorer

Newlin played 78 games in 1979-80 and averaged 20.9 points, 4.0 assists and 3.4 rebounds in 32.2 minutes. He scored 1,634 points in his first Nets season and led the roster in total scoring.

He was even more productive in 1980-81. Newlin played 79 games, averaged 21.4 points and 3.8 assists, and logged 2,911 minutes. Basketball-Reference's franchise history credits him as the team's leading win-shares player in both of those seasons.

Across the two-year Nets stint, Newlin appeared in 157 regular-season games and scored 3,322 points. He moved to New York for 1981-82, so this review stops the New Jersey return at those two seasons rather than crediting his final NBA year elsewhere.

Houston Used the Pick on John Stroud

The Rockets kept the incoming selection and drafted John Stroud at No. 27 in 1980. Stroud appeared in nine games for Houston as a rookie, totaling 88 minutes and 25 points.

Those nine games became his entire NBA career. Houston therefore received a real drafted player from the asset, but the on-court return was extremely small compared with Newlin's two high-scoring Nets seasons.

The cash term cannot materially change that comparison because its amount is undocumented in the sources reviewed for this batch. It is preserved as part of the canonical package but not used to manufacture value.

Why New Jersey Wins Decisively

The Nets turned one second-round pick and an unquantified cash term into 157 games from a guard who averaged more than 20 points in both seasons. That is unusually strong realized value for the acquisition cost.

Houston turned the pick into nine Stroud games and 88 minutes. The Rockets received little direct basketball value from the transaction after moving a veteran who still had two productive seasons left.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A/D+. New Jersey receives an A for 157 Newlin games and two 20-point seasons. Houston receives a D+ because the No. 27 pick became John Stroud but produced only nine NBA games; the frozen-source cash term remains unquantified.

analysis:
New Jersey Paid a Second-Round Pick for a Proven Guard

Basketball-Reference records Houston trading Mike Newlin to New Jersey on October 12, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. The frozen Nets source package also includes cash, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the cash term without assigning numerical value.

Newlin Immediately Became New Jersey's Lead Scorer

Newlin played 78 games in 1979-80 and averaged 20.9 points, 4.0 assists and 3.4 rebounds in 32.2 minutes. He scored 1,634 points in his first Nets season and led the roster in total scoring.

He was even more productive in 1980-81. Newlin played 79 games, averaged 21.4 points and 3.8 assists, and logged 2,911 minutes. Basketball-Reference's franchise history credits him as the team's leading win-shares player in both of those seasons.

Across the two-year Nets stint, Newlin appeared in 157 regular-season games and scored 3,322 points. He moved to New York for 1981-82, so this review stops the New Jersey return at those two seasons rather than crediting his final NBA year elsewhere.

Houston Used the Pick on John Stroud

The Rockets kept the incoming selection and drafted John Stroud at No. 27 in 1980. Stroud appeared in nine games for Houston as a rookie, totaling 88 minutes and 25 points.

Those nine games became his entire NBA career. Houston therefore received a real drafted player from the asset, but the on-court return was extremely small compared with Newlin's two high-scoring Nets seasons.

The cash term cannot materially change that comparison because its amount is undocumented in the sources reviewed for this batch. It is preserved as part of the canonical package but not used to manufacture value.

Why New Jersey Wins Decisively

The Nets turned one second-round pick and an unquantified cash term into 157 games from a guard who averaged more than 20 points in both seasons. That is unusually strong realized value for the acquisition cost.

Houston turned the pick into nine Stroud games and 88 minutes. The Rockets received little direct basketball value from the transaction after moving a veteran who still had two productive seasons left.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A/D+. New Jersey receives an A for 157 Newlin games and two 20-point seasons. Houston receives a D+ because the No. 27 pick became John Stroud but produced only nine NBA games; the frozen-source cash term remains unquantified.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired George Johnson's player rights from Milwaukee on October 19, 1979 for cash. Johnson immediately became a major Nuggets frontcourt contributor, playing 75 games while averaging 10.2 points, 7.8 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 25.8 minutes. Denver then sold Johnson's player rights back to Milwaukee on May 16, 1980, preserving additional transaction value after the full season of production. Milwaukee's October cash return is not quantified in the reviewed public ledgers, and the later reacquisition was a separate transaction. The realized basketball value therefore favors Denver clearly.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Bought a Starting-Caliber Season for Cash

Basketball-Reference records Milwaukee selling George Johnson's player rights to Denver on October 19, 1979. The public ledgers describe the transaction as a sale but do not provide a dollar amount, so this review preserves the financial nature of the exchange without inventing a cash value.

Johnson Became a Major Nuggets Rotation Player

Johnson played 75 games for Denver in 1979-80 and logged 1,938 minutes. He averaged 10.2 points, 7.8 rebounds, 2.1 assists, 1.1 steals and 0.9 blocks in 25.8 minutes.

Denver's depth chart places him as the primary power forward by minutes. His 3.8 win shares ranked behind only Dan Issel and John Roche among several high-minute Nuggets, making this much more than a rights-only transaction that never reached the floor.

The Return Also Retained Residual Value

On May 16, 1980, Denver sold Johnson's player rights back to Milwaukee. The reviewed public records again do not state the financial terms.

This review does not combine the two cash transactions into a fabricated net figure, but the resale matters qualitatively: Denver received 75 games of useful production and still held enough rights value to execute another sale after the season.

Milwaukee's Return Cannot Be Quantified

The Bucks received cash in October, but no amount appears in the reviewed Basketball-Reference transaction records. Milwaukee also reacquired Johnson's rights in May through a separate sale from Denver.

Because neither cash figure is documented, assigning a precise financial gain or loss to Milwaukee would be speculation. The grade therefore rests primarily on the known realized basketball value and the documented fact that Denver later resold the rights.

Why Denver Wins

Denver received a 75-game frontcourt season from a 23-year-old who averaged double figures and nearly eight rebounds, then retained enough rights value to sell him back.

Milwaukee received an unquantified cash payment in the original transaction. That is real consideration, but without a documented amount it cannot offset a full season of known production on evidence alone.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A-/C. Denver receives an A- for 75 productive Johnson games plus residual rights value. Milwaukee receives a C because the club received cash but the amount is undocumented, preventing a stronger realized-value case.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Kenny Carr from Los Angeles on October 24, 1979 for two second-round picks. Carr played 201 regular-season games for the Cavaliers across parts of three seasons, including 15.2 points and 10.3 rebounds per game in 1980-81, before Cleveland included him with Bill Laimbeer in a 1982 package for Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski and two draft picks. The Lakers used one incoming pick on Wayne Robinson, then traded him for the pick used on Harvey Knuckles, who never played an NBA game. The other pick helped acquire Mark Landsberger, a 206-game Lakers reserve on the 1980 and 1982 champions. Both sides received real value, with Cleveland holding a slight direct-return edge.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Paid Two Seconds for Kenny Carr

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland sending a 1980 second-round pick and a 1981 second-round pick to Los Angeles on October 24, 1979 for Kenny Carr. The selections later became No. 31 Wayne Robinson and No. 28 Gene Banks, but neither pick followed a simple straight-line path for the Lakers.

Carr Gave Cleveland 201 Games

Carr played 74 games for Cleveland after the trade in 1979-80 and averaged 12.3 points and 7.7 rebounds. He followed with 81 games in 1980-81, averaging 15.2 points and 10.3 rebounds.

Carr added 46 games in 1981-82 before the Cavaliers traded him in February. Across the Cleveland stint, he appeared in 201 regular-season games and produced 2,831 points and 1,800 rebounds.

Cleveland also retained transaction value. On February 16, 1982, the Cavaliers sent Carr and Bill Laimbeer to Detroit for Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski, a 1982 first-round pick used on John Bagley and a 1982 second-round pick used on Dave Magley.

This review does not credit that entire package to Carr because Laimbeer was also outgoing. Carr nevertheless remained a legitimate component of a major return after more than two productive Cleveland seasons.

The Wayne Robinson Pick Became Another Pick

Los Angeles kept Cleveland's 1980 second-rounder and selected Wayne Robinson at No. 31. Robinson never played a regular-season game for the Lakers.

Before the 1980-81 season, Los Angeles traded Robinson to Detroit for a 1981 second-round pick that became No. 39 Harvey Knuckles. Robinson then played 81 games for Detroit, but those Pistons games are not Lakers value.

Knuckles was drafted by Los Angeles but never played an NBA regular-season game. That branch therefore produced no direct Lakers games.

The Gene Banks Pick Helped Bring Mark Landsberger

The second Cleveland pick had a different route. On February 13, 1980, Los Angeles sent that 1981 second-rounder, Ollie Mack and another 1980 second-round pick to Chicago for Mark Landsberger.

Landsberger played 206 regular-season games for the Lakers from 1979-80 through 1982-83. He was a reserve on the 1980 and 1982 championship teams.

The full Landsberger return cannot be assigned to the Gene Banks pick because the Lakers also sent Mack and another second-round selection. Still, the pick was a real component of a package that produced four seasons of useful frontcourt depth and two title-team appearances.

Why Cleveland Gets the Slight Edge

The Cavaliers received 201 Carr games, including a double-double season, and later used him as part of a substantial Detroit package. That value is direct and easy to isolate.

The Lakers received a dead-end Wayne Robinson branch but used the other pick as part of the Landsberger trade. Landsberger's 206 games and championship-team role are meaningful, but the return was diluted across a three-asset outgoing package.

Final Verdict

Slight Cavaliers Edge, A-/B+. Cleveland receives an A- for 201 Carr games and retained trade utility. Los Angeles receives a B+ because one pick helped acquire a long-term championship reserve, while the other branch ultimately produced no Lakers regular-season games.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded franchise veteran Bingo Smith to San Diego on October 27, 1979 for a 1980 third-round pick. Smith immediately became a regular Clippers forward, playing 70 games and averaging 11.7 points, 3.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 28.4 minutes. Dallas then selected him from San Diego in the 1980 expansion draft, ending the Clippers' return after one season. Cleveland used the No. 53 pick on Stuart House, who never played an NBA regular-season game. San Diego therefore received the only meaningful realized basketball value from the deal.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Moved a Longtime Veteran for a Third-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland trading Bingo Smith to San Diego on October 27, 1979 for a 1980 third-round pick. The selection later landed at No. 53 and was used on Stuart House.

Smith Gave San Diego a Full Rotation Season

Smith had played only eight games for Cleveland before the trade, but he immediately stepped into a much larger Clippers role. He appeared in 70 games for San Diego and logged 1,988 minutes.

He averaged 11.7 points, 3.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 28.4 minutes. That made him a regular wing contributor rather than a short-term end-of-bench addition.

The Clippers did not keep him beyond the season. Dallas selected Smith from San Diego in the May 28, 1980 expansion draft. This review therefore stops the Clippers return at those 70 games and does not assign any of Smith's later Dallas production to San Diego.

Cleveland Used the Pick on Stuart House

The Cavaliers kept the incoming third-round selection and drafted Stuart House at No. 53 in June 1980.

Basketball-Reference lists House as a Cleveland draft pick but records no NBA regular-season games. The pick therefore produced no direct on-court value for the Cavaliers.

There is no documented downstream NBA transaction branch from House that changes the comparison. Cleveland acquired a draft opportunity, but the realized result was zero games.

Why San Diego Wins

The Clippers received 70 games and nearly 2,000 minutes from Smith before losing him in the expansion draft. Cleveland received one third-round selection that never reached an NBA regular-season floor.

Smith was near the end of his career, so this was not a long-term franchise-changing acquisition. Even so, a full season of double-digit scoring is decisively more realized value than a draft pick that produced no NBA games.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, B+/D. San Diego receives a B+ for 70 useful Smith games in 1979-80. Cleveland receives a D because the No. 53 selection on Stuart House produced no NBA regular-season appearances.

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland trading Bingo Smith to San Diego on October 27, 1979 for a 1980 third-round pick. The selection later landed at No. 53 and was used on Stuart House.

Smith Gave San Diego a Full Rotation Season

Smith had played only eight games for Cleveland before the trade, but he immediately stepped into a much larger Clippers role. He appeared in 70 games for San Diego and logged 1,988 minutes.

He averaged 11.7 points, 3.5 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 28.4 minutes. That made him a regular wing contributor rather than a short-term end-of-bench addition.

The Clippers did not keep him beyond the season. Dallas selected Smith from San Diego in the May 28, 1980 expansion draft. This review therefore stops the Clippers return at those 70 games and does not assign any of Smith's later Dallas production to San Diego.

Cleveland Used the Pick on Stuart House

The Cavaliers kept the incoming third-round selection and drafted Stuart House at No. 53 in June 1980.

Basketball-Reference lists House as a Cleveland draft pick but records no NBA regular-season games. The pick therefore produced no direct on-court value for the Cavaliers.

There is no documented downstream NBA transaction branch from House that changes the comparison. Cleveland acquired a draft opportunity, but the realized result was zero games.

Why San Diego Wins

The Clippers received 70 games and nearly 2,000 minutes from Smith before losing him in the expansion draft. Cleveland received one third-round selection that never reached an NBA regular-season floor.

Smith was near the end of his career, so this was not a long-term franchise-changing acquisition. Even so, a full season of double-digit scoring is decisively more realized value than a draft pick that produced no NBA games.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, B+/D. San Diego receives a B+ for 70 useful Smith games in 1979-80. Cleveland receives a D because the No. 53 selection on Stuart House produced no NBA regular-season appearances.

perspectives.analysis:
Utah Bought a Starting-Caliber Season for a Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference records Denver trading Tom Boswell to Utah on November 20, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. Denver later used that selection at No. 41 on center Jawann Oldham.

Boswell Became an Immediate Jazz Contributor

Boswell played 61 games for Utah after the trade and logged 1,555 minutes. He averaged 11.5 points, 5.4 rebounds and 1.9 assists while shooting 57.3 percent from the field.

That was meaningful rotation value from a player acquired for a second-round selection. He had averaged 11.3 points in 18 Denver games before the trade, so Utah did not receive an end-of-bench reclamation project; it received a productive 26-year-old forward who immediately filled a regular role.

Boswell did not play in the NBA from 1980-81 through 1982-83. He later signed again with Utah in September 1983 and appeared in 38 more games during 1983-84. Because that return came through a new contract several years later, this review does not credit those later games to the 1979 trade.

Denver Got Only Four Games From Oldham

Denver selected Oldham with the No. 41 pick in June 1980. He appeared in four games for the Nuggets, averaging 5.3 minutes, 1.0 point and 1.3 rebounds.

The Nuggets waived Oldham on October 21, 1980. Houston later signed him as a free agent in October 1981, and Oldham went on to play 329 NBA games overall. That later career belongs to other teams; Denver captured only four games from the pick.

Why Utah Wins

Utah received 61 useful games and more than 1,500 minutes from Boswell immediately after the trade. Denver's second-round pick produced four games before the player was waived.

Oldham's later longevity does not change the grade because the Nuggets did not retain him or convert him into another asset. The realized comparison is sharply one-sided.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win, A-/D. Utah receives an A- for obtaining a productive 61-game season from Boswell at the cost of a second-round pick. Denver receives a D because the No. 41 selection produced only four Nuggets appearances before Oldham was waived.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana traded Len Elmore to Kansas City on November 27, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. Elmore played 58 games for the Kings that season, giving Kansas City useful reserve-center minutes before Milwaukee signed him as a veteran free agent. The Kings then received a 1981 second-round compensation pick, later included with Otis Birdsong in the trade for Cliff Robinson. Indiana used the original No. 40 pick on Dick Miller, whose entire NBA career lasted eight games. Kansas City therefore realized substantially more direct and downstream value from the deal.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Kansas City Turned a Second-Round Pick Into a Useful Veteran

Basketball-Reference records Indiana trading Len Elmore to Kansas City on November 27, 1979 for a 1980 second-round pick. Indiana later used the selection at No. 40 on Dick Miller.

Elmore Played 58 Games for the Kings

Elmore appeared in 58 Kansas City games during 1979-80 and logged 915 minutes. He averaged 4.5 points and 4.4 rebounds in 15.8 minutes, giving the Kings a real reserve interior role rather than a brief trial.

The playing return lasted only that season, but the asset chain did not end there. Milwaukee signed Elmore as a veteran free agent in June 1980, and Kansas City received a 1981 second-round pick as compensation.

The Kings later included that compensation pick with Otis Birdsong in the June 1981 trade that brought Cliff Robinson from New Jersey. This review does not assign Robinson's entire return to the Elmore branch because Birdsong was the principal outgoing asset, but the pick remained legitimate transaction currency.

Indiana Got Eight NBA Games From Miller

The Pacers used the No. 40 pick on Miller in the 1980 draft. Basketball-Reference credits him with an eight-game NBA career, all in 1980-81, averaging 1.0 point and 0.9 rebounds.

There is no meaningful later NBA transaction branch attached to Miller in the reviewed sources. The pick therefore produced only those eight appearances for Indiana.

Why Kansas City Wins

Kansas City received 58 games of usable center depth and then a compensation second-round pick when Elmore left. Indiana's return produced eight games from a second-round rookie and no comparable downstream asset.

Elmore was not a star for the Kings, so the grade should not overstate the transaction. The gap comes from basic realized value: Kansas City received both playing time and a later compensation asset, while Indiana received almost nothing on the court.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, B+/D. Kansas City receives a B+ for 58 Elmore games plus the later compensation pick. Indiana receives a D because Dick Miller produced only eight NBA appearances before his career ended.

new-york-knicks.analysis:
Washington Turned a Third-Round Pick Into Immediate Guard Help

Basketball-Reference records New York trading Jim Cleamons to Washington on December 4, 1979 for a 1981 third-round pick. The Knicks later used that selection at No. 57 on Frank Brickowski.

Cleamons Played 57 Games for Washington

Cleamons had appeared in 22 games for New York before the trade. After arriving in Washington, he played 57 games and logged 1,535 minutes.

He averaged 7.8 points, 4.4 assists and 2.3 rebounds in 26.9 minutes. He did not start a regular-season game, but he was a substantial reserve guard and gave the Bullets a real rotation return for a future third-round selection.

Brickowski Never Played for the Knicks

New York kept the pick and drafted Brickowski in the third round of the 1981 draft. He then spent three seasons playing outside the NBA before making his league debut with Seattle in 1984-85.

Seattle signed Brickowski as a free agent. The reviewed transaction records do not show New York converting his draft rights into another NBA asset, so his later 731-game NBA career cannot be credited to the Knicks side of this trade.

For New York, the realized return was therefore a draft selection that produced zero Knicks regular-season appearances.

Why Washington Wins

Washington received 57 games and more than 1,500 minutes from Cleamons during the same season it made the trade. New York received no on-court NBA value from Brickowski and no documented downstream return for his rights.

Brickowski eventually became a long-tenured NBA player, but that future success came after Seattle signed him independently. Hindsight grading has to follow the value the original team actually realized.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, B+/D. Washington receives a B+ for acquiring a productive 57-game reserve guard at the cost of a third-round pick. New York receives a D because the No. 57 selection never produced a Knicks game or a documented NBA transaction return.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired Billy Paultz from San Antonio on January 17, 1980 for John Shumate, a 1980 third-round pick and cash. Paultz played 240 regular-season games for the Rockets through 1982-83 and was a major playoff contributor during Houston's 1981 NBA Finals run, averaging 12.1 points and 7.0 rebounds across 21 postseason games that spring. Shumate gave San Antonio 49 regular-season games over parts of two seasons before being waived, while No. 60 pick LaVon Mercer never played an NBA game. The realized return clearly favored Houston.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Acquired a Multi-Year Frontcourt Piece

Basketball-Reference records the January 17, 1980 trade as John Shumate and a 1980 third-round pick to San Antonio for Billy Paultz. The frozen Houston package also includes cash going to the Spurs, a term corroborated by San Antonio's historical media guide, but no reviewed source gives an amount, so this review does not assign it a numerical value.

Paultz Played 240 Regular-Season Games for Houston

Paultz appeared in 37 Rockets games after the trade in 1979-80, then 81 in 1980-81, 65 in 1981-82 and 57 in 1982-83. That is 240 regular-season games from the original acquisition.

His most valuable stretch came in the 1981 postseason. Paultz played all 21 Houston playoff games and averaged 12.1 points and 7.0 rebounds while the Rockets advanced to the NBA Finals. He was not merely roster depth; he was a substantial frontcourt piece alongside Moses Malone during the franchise's first Finals run.

Houston waived Paultz on April 4, 1983. San Antonio signed him as a free agent two days later, so this review stops Houston's branch at the waiver rather than treating the later Spurs return as another trade asset.

Shumate Gave San Antonio 49 Games

Shumate played 27 games for the Spurs after the trade in 1979-80, scoring 391 points and averaging roughly 14.5 points and 7.9 rebounds. He returned for 22 games in 1980-81, averaging 7.5 points and 4.0 rebounds.

San Antonio attempted to trade Shumate to Seattle in November 1980, but the transaction was voided after a physical issue. The Spurs waived him on December 2, ending the branch after 49 regular-season appearances.

The Third-Round Pick Produced No NBA Games

San Antonio used Houston's 1980 third-round selection at No. 60 on LaVon Mercer. Basketball-Reference records Mercer as a Spurs draft pick with no NBA regular-season career. He instead built a long professional career in Israel.

That means the pick produced no realized NBA on-court value for San Antonio. The cash term remains unquantified.

Why Houston Wins

The Spurs received useful short-term production from Shumate, especially immediately after the trade, but the return ended after 49 games and the draft pick never reached an NBA floor.

Houston received 240 Paultz games plus a meaningful role on a Finals team. The duration and playoff contribution create a clear hindsight advantage even while giving San Antonio credit for Shumate's productive first half-season.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, A/B-. Houston receives an A for four seasons of Paultz value and his 1981 playoff contribution. San Antonio receives a B- for 49 Shumate games, including strong initial production, but the Mercer pick produced no NBA games and the cash amount cannot be scored.

perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Received the Deeper Original Package

Basketball-Reference records the January 24, 1980 trade as Jim McElroy to Atlanta for Ron Lee, a 1980 second-round pick and a 1980 third-round pick. Detroit later used those selections at No. 45 on Brad Branson and No. 64 on Jonathan Moore.

Ron Lee Played 194 Games for Detroit

Lee played 31 games for the Pistons after the trade in 1979-80, averaging 7.3 points, 5.6 assists and 2.7 steals in 25.9 minutes.

He then played all 82 games in 1980-81 and 81 more in 1981-82. That gives Detroit 194 regular-season games from Lee alone, including two full seasons of rotation guard work.

Detroit placed Lee on waivers in October 1982. No later trade return needs to be credited to the branch.

Atlanta Got 105 Games From McElroy

McElroy played 31 Hawks games after the trade in 1979-80, then 54 in 1980-81 and 20 in 1981-82. He averaged 5.5 points and 2.1 assists during the first partial Atlanta season, then 3.8 points in 1980-81 before starting 17 of his 20 games in 1981-82.

Across the three seasons, Atlanta received 105 regular-season appearances. McElroy became a free agent in 1982, so the direct branch ends there.

The Two Draft Picks Added Little On-Court Value

Detroit selected Branson at No. 45, but he played in Italy in 1980-81 and never appeared in a Pistons regular-season game. Historical transaction records show Detroit later moved his negotiating rights to Dallas for future considerations; the reviewed sources do not identify a concrete NBA return that can be isolated for this review.

Jonathan Moore, the No. 64 pick, also never played an NBA regular-season game. The two picks therefore did not add direct Pistons minutes.

Why Detroit Gets the Edge

Atlanta received more than 100 McElroy games and should get credit for a useful multi-season guard. Detroit, however, received nearly twice as many games from Lee, including two near-complete seasons, while also holding two extra draft assets even though those picks did not become contributors.

The trade is not a blowout because the draft outcomes were poor and McElroy was useful. The difference is Lee's much longer realized tenure.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, B+/B-. Detroit receives a B+ for 194 Ron Lee games plus two additional draft assets. Atlanta receives a B- for 105 McElroy games over parts of three seasons.

perspectives.summary: Atlanta acquired 1980 second- and third-round picks from Utah for cash on January 24, 1980, then immediately used both selections with Ron Lee to acquire Jim McElroy from Detroit. perspectives.analysis:
Atlanta Bought Two Picks and Used Them Immediately

The frozen canonical record and Pro Sports Transactions record Atlanta acquiring a 1980 second-round pick and a 1980 third-round pick from Utah for cash on January 24, 1980. The selections later became No. 45 Brad Branson and No. 64 Jonathan Moore.

The cash amount is not documented in the reviewed public sources. That prevents this review from assigning a precise value to Utah's return and lowers confidence relative to an ordinary player-for-player trade.

The Picks Became Same-Day Trade Currency

Atlanta did not hold the picks until the draft. The Hawks immediately sent both selections plus Ron Lee to Detroit for Jim McElroy on the same date.

McElroy then played 31 games for Atlanta in 1979-80, 54 in 1980-81 and 20 in 1981-82. That is 105 regular-season Hawks games from the larger McElroy package.

This review does not credit all 105 games to the two Utah picks because Ron Lee was also a meaningful outgoing player. The proper realized value is narrower: the picks were usable trade currency that helped Atlanta complete a multi-asset acquisition.

The Draft Outcomes Were Weak for Detroit

Detroit used the second-round pick at No. 45 on Branson and the third-round pick at No. 64 on Moore. Neither player appeared in a Pistons regular-season game.

Those later draft outcomes do not erase the picks' value to Atlanta, because the Hawks had already spent them successfully as transaction assets. They do, however, show that the selections themselves did not later become major NBA players for the team that finally drafted them.

Utah's Side Is Harder to Measure

Utah received cash and no player or draft asset in the recorded exchange. Without a documented amount, there is no reliable way to compare the Jazz's financial return directly with Atlanta's basketball use of the picks.

That uncertainty keeps the grade restrained. The Hawks clearly converted the picks into useful trade leverage, but the deal should not be treated like a major basketball win over Utah when the cash consideration is unknown.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge, B-/C+. Atlanta receives a B- because the two picks were immediately useful in the McElroy trade, which produced 105 Hawks games as part of a larger package. Utah receives a C+ because it received cash by design, but the undocumented amount prevents a stronger realized-value grade. Confidence is medium.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded John Williamson and a 1981 second-round pick to Washington on February 4, 1980 for Roger Phegley. Phegley played 28 games for the Nets before New Jersey traded him straight up for Foots Walker, who then played 231 regular-season games for the franchise through 1983-84. New Jersey's Phegley-to-Walker branch produced the clearly stronger realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Acquired Phegley for Williamson and a Second

Basketball-Reference records the February 4, 1980 trade as John Williamson and a 1981 second-round pick from New Jersey to Washington for Roger Phegley. The pick eventually became No. 44 Steve Lingenfelter.

Phegley Played 28 Games, Then Became Foots Walker

Phegley played 28 games for the Nets after the trade, logging 541 minutes and scoring 327 points. He averaged 11.7 points, 2.5 rebounds and 1.1 assists while shooting 48.5 percent.

New Jersey did not simply lose him afterward. On September 24, 1980, the Nets traded Phegley straight up to Cleveland for Foots Walker. Because that was a one-for-one transaction, Walker is a direct downstream return from the Phegley branch.

Walker then played 41 games for New Jersey in 1980-81, 77 in 1981-82, 79 in 1982-83 and 34 in 1983-84. That is 231 regular-season Nets games, including a 54-start season in 1981-82.

Washington Got 39 Games From Williamson

Williamson played 30 games for the Bullets after the trade in 1979-80, averaging 11.6 points in 20.1 minutes. He returned for nine games in 1980-81 before his Washington tenure ended.

That gives the Bullets 39 regular-season appearances from the veteran guard. Williamson was still a useful scorer immediately after the trade, but the tenure was brief.

The Draft Pick Added Seven Bullets Games

Washington retained the incoming second-round selection and used it at No. 44 in the 1981 draft on Steve Lingenfelter. He did not make the Bullets until 1982-83, when he appeared in seven regular-season games.

Washington waived Lingenfelter on December 10, 1982. He later played three games for San Antonio, but those appearances came after Washington had released him and are not part of the Bullets' realized return.

Why New Jersey Wins

Washington received 39 Williamson games and seven later Lingenfelter games. That is real value, but neither branch became a durable rotation asset for the Bullets.

New Jersey received 28 Phegley games and then converted him directly into Walker, who remained with the Nets for four seasons and 231 regular-season games. The straight-swap downstream chain makes the difference decisive.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A-/C+. New Jersey receives an A- for the Phegley production plus the direct Walker conversion that yielded 231 additional games. Washington receives a C+ for 39 Williamson games and seven Lingenfelter appearances, a modest return that never approached the duration of the Nets branch.

Milwaukee Acquired a Veteran Star Center

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded rookie forward Calvin Natt to Portland on February 8, 1980 for Maurice Lucas plus two first-round picks. Lucas gave the Nets 90 regular-season games across parts of two seasons, while the picks became Mike Gminski at No. 7 in 1980 and Albert King at No. 10 in 1981. Gminski played 550 regular-season games for New Jersey across eight seasons, and King added 410 games over six seasons. Portland still received an excellent player: Natt logged 333 regular-season games in five Trail Blazers seasons and scored 5,738 points. The Nets nevertheless turned one young scorer into three long-lasting rotation assets and win the hindsight verdict.
perspectives.analysis:
The Nets Turned Natt Into Lucas and Two Firsts

Basketball-Reference records the February 8, 1980 deal as Calvin Natt to Portland for Maurice Lucas, a 1980 first-round pick and a 1981 first-round pick. The selections later became No. 7 Mike Gminski and No. 10 Albert King.

Lucas Gave New Jersey Immediate Frontcourt Value

Lucas played 22 games for the Nets after the trade in 1979-80, averaging 15.2 points and 9.6 rebounds in 32.2 minutes. He returned for 68 games in 1980-81 and averaged 16.6 points and 9.6 rebounds.

That gives New Jersey 90 regular-season games from the veteran portion of the return. Lucas was not a long-term Net, but the club received productive frontcourt minutes immediately while waiting for the two draft picks to mature.

The 1980 First Became Mike Gminski

New Jersey used the No. 7 pick in the 1980 draft on Mike Gminski. He played 550 regular-season games for the franchise from 1980-81 through the first 34 games of 1987-88.

Gminski developed from a reserve into a full-time starting center, starting 78 games in 1985-86 and 66 in 1986-87. His eight-season Nets tenure gives this branch the largest volume of direct realized value in the trade.

The 1981 First Became Albert King

The second first-rounder came from Golden State originally and landed at No. 10 in the 1981 draft. New Jersey selected Albert King.

King played 410 regular-season games for the Nets across six seasons. He averaged 17.0 points in 1982-83 and remained a regular wing through 1986-87.

Between Gminski and King, the two picks produced 960 regular-season Nets games. Adding Lucas brings the direct New Jersey total from the incoming assets to 1,050 games.

Portland Still Got a Very Good Player

Natt was far from a miss for the Trail Blazers. He averaged 20.4 points in 25 games immediately after the trade and went on to play 333 regular-season games for Portland over five seasons.

Basketball-Reference credits Natt with 5,738 points and 2,297 rebounds as a Trail Blazer. He gave Portland multiple productive seasons and was a legitimate high-level starter rather than a short-term rental.

Why New Jersey Wins the Hindsight Verdict

Portland acquired the best single scorer in the deal and received five productive years from him. That return deserves a high grade.

New Jersey, however, converted one player into a productive veteran plus two first-round selections that became long-tenured rotation players. Gminski and King alone combined for nearly a thousand regular-season games for the franchise, and Lucas added two useful seasons on top of that.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A+/A-. New Jersey receives an A+ for 90 Lucas games, 550 Gminski games and 410 King games from the three incoming assets. Portland receives an A- because Natt produced 333 games and 5,738 points across five seasons. Both teams received substantial value, but the depth and longevity of the Nets return are too large to ignore.

Hollins played 190 regular-season games for the 76ers across parts of three seasons, including all 81 games as a starter in 1981-82. Portland never used the incoming pick directly. philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Philadelphia Bought a Starting Guard for a Future First

Basketball-Reference records the February 8, 1980 trade as Philadelphia sending a 1981 first-round pick to Portland for Lionel Hollins. The frozen canonical source package also lists cash going to Portland, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the term without scoring it.

Hollins Played 190 Games for the 76ers

Hollins played 27 games after the trade in 1979-80, starting 26 and averaging 12.2 points and 4.1 assists. Philadelphia reached the NBA Finals that spring.

He returned for all 82 games in 1980-81 and then played 81 games in 1981-82, starting every one of them while averaging 11.0 points and 3.9 assists. Philadelphia again reached the NBA Finals in 1982.

Across those three regular seasons, Hollins appeared in 190 games for the 76ers. The trade therefore produced multiple years of real rotation and starting value rather than a short rental.

Portland Used the Pick as Trade Currency

The incoming Philadelphia first eventually became the No. 4 selection in the 1981 draft, where Al Wood was selected after the pick changed hands again. Portland did not use it itself.

On June 10, 1980, the Trail Blazers sent the pick and Ronnie Lester to Chicago for Kelvin Ransey and another 1981 first-round pick that later became No. 16 Darnell Valentine.

Ransey immediately became a major Portland contributor, playing 80 games as a rookie at 15.2 points and 6.9 assists, then 78 games in 1981-82 at 16.1 points and 7.1 assists. Valentine later became a multi-year Portland guard after the second pick was exercised.

This review does not assign the full Ransey-Valentine return to Philadelphia's pick because Ronnie Lester was also outgoing and Portland received two assets back. The proper conclusion is narrower: the No. 4 pick was premium trade currency that helped the Blazers restructure their backcourt.

Why Philadelphia Gets the Edge

Portland extracted meaningful market value from the future first and clearly did not waste the asset. The later Ransey-Valentine transaction makes that side stronger than a simple Hollins-for-Al Wood comparison would suggest.

Philadelphia, however, received 190 directly attributable Hollins games, including a full season as a starter on a Finals team. That value is easier to isolate than Portland's multi-asset downstream branch.

Final Verdict

Slight 76ers Edge, A-/B+. Philadelphia receives an A- for three seasons and 190 games of Hollins production. Portland receives a B+ because the first-round pick remained premium trade currency and became part of a productive Ransey-plus-pick transaction, while the unquantified cash term is preserved but not scored.

Portland extracted meaningful market value from the future first and clearly did not waste the asset. The later Ransey-Valentine transaction makes that side stronger than a simple Hollins-for-Al Wood comparison would suggest.

perspectives.analysis:
The Lakers Acquired a Long-Term Reserve

Basketball-Reference records Chicago sending Mark Landsberger to Los Angeles on February 13, 1980 for Ollie Mack plus 1980 and 1981 second-round picks. The frozen Chicago source package also lists cash coming back, but the public transaction ledger does not give an amount, so this review preserves the term without assigning value to it.

Landsberger Played 206 Lakers Games

Landsberger joined Los Angeles for the final 23 regular-season games of 1979-80, then appeared in 69 games in 1980-81, 75 in 1981-82 and 39 in 1982-83. That is 206 regular-season games for the Lakers.

His role was not star-level, but it fit a championship roster. The Lakers' own alumni record credits Landsberger as a key reserve on the 1980 and 1982 championship teams. That gives Los Angeles direct title-era value from the player it acquired.

Mack Gave Chicago a Short Run

Ollie Mack played 23 games for Chicago after the trade in 1979-80, averaging 8.0 points in 22.9 minutes. He appeared in only three Bulls games the following season before being waived on October 23, 1980.

That leaves Mack at 26 regular-season Chicago games. He was useful immediately after the trade, but he did not become a long-term piece.

The 1980 Second Became Sam Worthen

Chicago used the No. 26 selection in 1980 on Sam Worthen. He played 64 Bulls games as a rookie, logging 945 minutes and scoring 235 points.

Worthen did not return for a second Chicago season, so this branch also produced one year of direct value rather than a durable rotation piece.

The 1981 Second Helped Pay for Larry Kenon

Chicago did not use the second future pick itself. On September 12, 1980, the Bulls sent that 1981 second-round pick plus another 1981 second to San Antonio as compensation for signing veteran free agent Larry Kenon.

Kenon played 77 games for Chicago in 1980-81 and 60 more in 1981-82, then five games in 1982-83. Because two second-round picks were sent as compensation, this review does not assign all 142 Kenon games to the pick received from Los Angeles.

San Antonio eventually used the specific selection at No. 28 on Gene Banks. Banks' NBA production belongs to the Spurs, not Chicago, because the Bulls had already transferred the pick.

Why Los Angeles Gets the Edge

Chicago extracted several forms of value: 26 Mack games, 64 Worthen games and a future second that helped facilitate the Kenon signing. That is a respectable package for one reserve big.

Los Angeles, however, received 206 regular-season games from Landsberger across parts of four seasons, including reserve contributions to two championship teams. The Lakers' value is both easier to isolate and tied directly to the club's highest-level results.

Final Verdict

Lakers Edge, A-/B+. Los Angeles receives an A- for 206 Landsberger games and two championship-season contributions. Chicago receives a B+ for Mack, Worthen and a future pick that retained enough value to become part of the Kenon compensation package, with the unquantified cash term preserved but not scored.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded Rich Kelley to Phoenix on February 15, 1980 for a 1982 first-round pick, a 1983 second-round pick and an unquantified cash term preserved in the frozen source package. Kelley played 185 regular-season games for Phoenix across parts of three seasons before the Suns traded him to Denver for the 1982 first-round pick used on David Thirdkill, who added 49 Phoenix games. New Jersey used the first as part of a package for Sam Lacey and later sent the second straight up for Wayne Sappleton. Those branches produced some value, but Phoenix received the stronger direct and downstream return.
perspectives.analysis:
Phoenix Got Three Seasons of Rich Kelley

Basketball-Reference records Phoenix acquiring Rich Kelley from New Jersey on February 15, 1980 for a 1982 first-round pick and a 1983 second-round pick. The frozen canonical Nets source package also lists cash going to New Jersey, but the reviewed public transaction ledgers do not state an amount, so this review preserves the term without scoring it.

Kelley immediately joined the Suns' rotation. He played 23 games after the trade in 1979-80, then 81 games in 1980-81 and 81 more in 1981-82. That is 185 Phoenix regular-season games.

His role was steady rather than star-level. In 1981-82 he started 39 games, averaged 7.9 points, 6.1 rebounds and 3.6 assists, and gave Phoenix a durable interior passer before the club moved him again.

Phoenix Then Turned Kelley Into Another First

On June 21, 1982, the Suns traded Kelley to Denver for a 1982 first-round pick. Phoenix used that No. 15 selection on David Thirdkill.

Thirdkill played 49 games for Phoenix as a rookie in 1982-83. He was only a reserve, but this is a clean one-for-one downstream branch from Kelley: Phoenix received three seasons of Kelley and then recovered another first-round asset when it moved him.

The Nets Routed the 1982 First Before the Draft

New Jersey never selected Brook Steppe. On November 12, 1981, the Nets sent the incoming first-round pick plus Mike Woodson to Kansas City for veteran center Sam Lacey.

Lacey played 54 regular-season games for New Jersey in 1981-82. Because Woodson was also sent to Kansas City, this review does not credit all 54 Lacey games to the Phoenix pick alone. The first-rounder nevertheless had clear trade utility and helped New Jersey acquire immediate frontcourt depth.

The 1983 Second Became Wayne Sappleton

New Jersey also moved the second-round pick before the 1983 draft. On June 19, 1982, the Nets traded that pick straight up to Golden State for Wayne Sappleton.

Sappleton spent the next two seasons in Italy before returning to New Jersey in 1984-85. He played 33 regular-season games for the Nets that season. This branch therefore produced delayed but directly attributable NBA value.

Why Phoenix Gets the Hindsight Win

New Jersey received two useful trade assets plus cash of unknown amount. The first helped acquire Lacey, and the second directly became Sappleton. That is not an empty return.

Phoenix still did better. Kelley gave the Suns 185 games over three seasons, and the club then converted him into a first-round pick that produced 49 Thirdkill games. The Suns' return is larger, more direct and less dependent on multi-asset attribution.

Final Verdict

Suns Win, A-/C+. Phoenix receives an A- for 185 Kelley games plus the later first-round return that became Thirdkill. New Jersey receives a C+ because both picks retained transaction value, but the first was only one component of the Lacey package and the second ultimately produced 33 Sappleton games; the cash amount is unknown and unscored.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded Butch Lee and an unprotected 1982 first-round pick to the Lakers on February 15, 1980 for Don Ford and the 1980 first-round pick used on Chad Kinch. Ford played 106 regular-season games for Cleveland across parts of three seasons, while Kinch added 29 Cavaliers games. Lee played only 11 regular-season games for Los Angeles, but the future first became the No. 1 pick in 1982 and James Worthy. Worthy played all 926 of his NBA games for the Lakers, won three championships, made seven All-Star teams and earned the 1988 Finals MVP. The long-term result is overwhelmingly Los Angeles.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Looked Ordinary in 1980

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland sending Butch Lee and a 1982 first-round pick to Los Angeles on February 15, 1980 for Don Ford and a 1980 first-round pick. At the time, the later pick was two drafts away and there was no guarantee it would become No. 1 overall.

Ford gave Cleveland immediate depth. He played 21 games after the trade in 1979-80, 64 games in 1980-81 and 21 more in 1981-82. That is 106 regular-season Cavaliers games.

Cleveland Used the 1980 First on Chad Kinch

The incoming Lakers pick landed at No. 22 in the 1980 draft, where Cleveland selected Chad Kinch. He played 29 games for the Cavaliers as a rookie, logging 247 minutes and scoring 80 points.

Kinch did not become a long-term piece. Cleveland therefore received 135 combined regular-season games from Ford and Kinch, mostly in reserve roles.

Butch Lee Barely Played for Los Angeles

Lee appeared in 11 regular-season games for the Lakers after the trade, totaling only 31 minutes. He also appeared briefly in three playoff games during the Lakers' 1980 championship run before being released in June.

That part of the Los Angeles return was negligible. The entire historical weight of the trade comes from the future first-round pick.

The 1982 Pick Became James Worthy

Cleveland's 1981-82 season ended with the league's worst record, and the unprotected pick conveyed to Los Angeles. The Lakers won the draft lottery coin-flip era process and used the No. 1 selection on James Worthy.

Worthy spent his entire 12-year NBA career with Los Angeles, playing 926 regular-season games. Basketball-Reference credits him as a seven-time All-Star, three-time NBA champion, two-time All-NBA selection and the 1988 Finals MVP. He was later inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame.

Worthy became a core member of the Showtime Lakers rather than merely a good draft result. The asset Cleveland surrendered turned into one of the defining forwards of the franchise's championship era.

Why This Is a Landslide

Cleveland did receive usable players. Ford's 106 games and Kinch's 29 mean the Cavaliers were not left with literally nothing.

The scale difference is still enormous. Los Angeles received 926 Worthy games, three championship seasons and a Finals MVP from the future first alone. Lee's minimal contribution is irrelevant to the verdict.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A+/C-. Los Angeles receives an A+ because the unprotected first became James Worthy, a Hall of Fame cornerstone of three championship teams. Cleveland receives a C- because Ford and Kinch combined for 135 games but neither produced remotely comparable long-term value.

The Trade Looked Ordinary in 1980

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland sending Butch Lee and a 1982 first-round pick to Los Angeles on February 15, 1980 for Don Ford and a 1980 first-round pick. At the time, the later pick was two drafts away and there was no guarantee it would become No. 1 overall.

Ford gave Cleveland immediate depth. He played 21 games after the trade in 1979-80, 64 games in 1980-81 and 21 more in 1981-82. That is 106 regular-season Cavaliers games.

Cleveland Used the 1980 First on Chad Kinch

The incoming Lakers pick landed at No. 22 in the 1980 draft, where Cleveland selected Chad Kinch. He played 29 games for the Cavaliers as a rookie, logging 247 minutes and scoring 80 points.

Kinch did not become a long-term piece. Cleveland therefore received 135 combined regular-season games from Ford and Kinch, mostly in reserve roles.

Butch Lee Barely Played for Los Angeles

Lee appeared in 11 regular-season games for the Lakers after the trade, totaling only 31 minutes. He also appeared briefly in three playoff games during the Lakers' 1980 championship run before being released in June.

That part of the Los Angeles return was negligible. The entire historical weight of the trade comes from the future first-round pick.

The 1982 Pick Became James Worthy

Cleveland's 1981-82 season ended with the league's worst record, and the unprotected pick conveyed to Los Angeles. The Lakers won the draft lottery coin-flip era process and used the No. 1 selection on James Worthy.

Worthy spent his entire 12-year NBA career with Los Angeles, playing 926 regular-season games. Basketball-Reference credits him as a seven-time All-Star, three-time NBA champion, two-time All-NBA selection and the 1988 Finals MVP. He was later inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame.

Worthy became a core member of the Showtime Lakers rather than merely a good draft result. The asset Cleveland surrendered turned into one of the defining forwards of the franchise's championship era.

Why This Is a Landslide

Cleveland did receive usable players. Ford's 106 games and Kinch's 29 mean the Cavaliers were not left with literally nothing.

The scale difference is still enormous. Los Angeles received 926 Worthy games, three championship seasons and a Finals MVP from the future first alone. Lee's minimal contribution is irrelevant to the verdict.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A+/C-. Los Angeles receives an A+ because the unprotected first became James Worthy, a Hall of Fame cornerstone of three championship teams. Cleveland receives a C- because Ford and Kinch combined for 135 games but neither produced remotely comparable long-term value.

perspectives.summary: Denver sold George Lee Johnson's player rights to Milwaukee on May 16, 1980 for an undisclosed cash payment. Johnson never played a regular-season game for the Bucks after the reacquisition. Four months later Milwaukee packaged his rights with a 1982 second-round pick to Indiana for Mickey Johnson. Mickey then played 164 regular-season games for the Bucks across parts of three seasons, including 158 starts in 1980-81 and 1981-82. Because Milwaukee had to add another second-round asset and Denver's sale price is unknown, the transaction cannot be valued precisely, but the Bucks extracted the stronger identifiable basketball return.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Sold the Rights Back to Milwaukee

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Milwaukee and league transaction ledgers agree on the May 16, 1980 move: Denver sold the player rights to George Lee Johnson to Milwaukee. The public ledgers do not identify the cash amount, so this review preserves Denver's return as undisclosed cash rather than inventing a dollar value.

Johnson Had Already Given Denver One Productive Season

Johnson played 75 games for Denver in 1979-80 before the sale, averaging 10.2 points, 7.8 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 25.8 minutes. Those games belong to Denver's prior October 1979 purchase of his rights, not to the May 1980 transaction being graded here.

For this review, Denver's realized return begins and ends with the cash received on May 16. Because the amount is not documented in the reviewed public sources, the Nuggets side has to be graded conservatively.

Milwaukee Never Put Johnson on the Floor

Johnson did not play a regular-season game for Milwaukee after the reacquisition. His next NBA team was Indiana in 1980-81, where he appeared in 43 games.

That means the Bucks received no direct on-court production from the player rights themselves. The value came from using those rights as part of another trade before the next season began.

The Rights Helped Milwaukee Acquire Mickey Johnson

On September 11, 1980, Milwaukee sent George Johnson and a 1982 second-round pick to Indiana for Mickey Johnson. The Pacers later used that second-round selection in another transaction chain, so the George Johnson rights were not the only price the Bucks paid.

Mickey Johnson became a major Milwaukee rotation player. He played all 82 games and started all 82 in 1980-81, then played 76 games with 71 starts in 1981-82. He added six more Bucks games in 1982-83 before being traded away.

That gives Milwaukee 164 regular-season Mickey Johnson games from the downstream acquisition. This review does not credit all 164 to George Johnson alone because Milwaukee also surrendered the future second-round pick, but the rights clearly carried real trade value.

Why Milwaukee Gets the Slight Edge

Denver monetized an asset it no longer planned to keep, and an undisclosed cash payment could have been useful. The problem for a hindsight grade is that the amount cannot be verified from the public record reviewed here.

Milwaukee's return is easier to identify. The Bucks turned Johnson's rights, plus another second-round pick, into a starting forward who gave them 164 regular-season games across three seasons. Even after discounting for the extra pick, that is meaningful realized value.

Final Verdict

Slight Bucks Edge, B/C+. Milwaukee receives a B because Johnson's rights became part of the package for Mickey Johnson, who played 164 Bucks games. Denver receives a C+ because the club received real cash consideration, but the amount is undocumented and therefore cannot support a higher evidence-based grade. Confidence is medium because the sale price is unknown.

seattle-supersonics.summary: On June 4, 1980, Seattle traded Dennis Johnson to Phoenix for Paul Westphal in a one-for-one exchange of established All-Star guards. Johnson gave the Suns three durable seasons, two All-Star selections, an All-NBA First Team berth and three straight All-Defensive First Team selections. Westphal remained productive in Seattle but a foot injury limited him to 36 games before his Sonics tenure ended after one season.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Phoenix, Seattle and league transaction logs all place the deal on June 4, 1980: Phoenix sent Paul Westphal to Seattle and received Dennis Johnson. The date correction is important because the legacy archive record carried June 3. Both players arrived with major credentials. Westphal had just averaged 21.9 points for Phoenix and made the 1980 All-NBA First Team, while Johnson was coming off a 19.0-point season for Seattle with All-NBA Second Team and All-Defensive First Team honors.

Phoenix Return
Johnson immediately supplied the stronger sustained return. In 1980-81 he played 79 games, averaged 18.8 points, made the All-Star team, earned All-NBA First Team and All-Defensive First Team honors, and helped Phoenix win the Pacific Division. He followed with 80 games, 19.5 points per game, another All-Star appearance and another All-Defensive First Team selection in 1981-82. In 1982-83 he played 77 games, started 74, averaged 14.2 points and 5.0 assists, and again made All-Defensive First Team. That is three seasons of high-level two-way guard play directly realized by Phoenix. Johnson's later championships with Boston confirm his longevity, but they are not credited as Suns value in this transaction.

Seattle Return
Westphal was still a real player, so Seattle did not receive an empty return. He averaged 16.7 points and 4.1 assists in 36 games and was selected as an All-Star in 1980-81. The problem was availability. Basketball-Reference shows only 36 appearances, and contemporary transaction research plus UPI reporting document a right-foot problem that repeatedly removed him from the lineup. He did not play another regular-season game for Seattle after that season. That makes the Sonics return meaningful but brief: one productive partial season from a decorated guard rather than multiple years of dependable top-end play.

Hindsight Verdict
The direct club value favors Phoenix by a wide margin. Johnson gave the Suns 236 regular-season games across three seasons and remained an elite defender throughout that run; Westphal gave Seattle 36 games in one injury-disrupted season. Phoenix receives an A- for converting an outgoing star into a younger guard who immediately produced All-NBA and repeated All-Defensive value. Seattle receives a C- because Westphal still produced at an All-Star level when available, preventing the return from being treated as a total loss. The final verdict is Phoenix Suns Win, based on realized value with later Boston accomplishments excluded from Phoenix's grade.

The condition converted to a second-rounder because Hordges made the Nuggets roster, and Chicago used the No. 32 pick on Mike Olliver.
