perspectives.analysis:
The Condition Converted to a Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference records Chicago trading Cedrick Hordges to Denver on June 9, 1980 for a conditional 1981 draft pick. The condition was straightforward: the pick would become a second-rounder if Hordges made the Nuggets roster and a third-rounder if he did not.

Hordges made the team, so Chicago ultimately received the No. 32 selection in 1981.

Hordges Became a Two-Year Denver Rotation Player

Hordges had been Chicago's third-round pick in 1979 but did not play in the NBA during 1979-80 while maintaining college eligibility.

After Denver acquired his rights, he debuted in 1980-81 and immediately played 68 games. He averaged 8.4 points and 6.7 rebounds in 23.5 minutes, producing 572 points and 458 rebounds.

He returned for 77 games in 1981-82, averaging 6.8 points and 5.1 rebounds. Across the two seasons, Hordges played 145 regular-season games for Denver and logged 2,971 minutes.

That is a useful realized return from a rights-only transaction.

Chicago Used the Pick on Mike Olliver

The conditional pick became the No. 32 selection in the 1981 draft. Chicago used it on Lamar guard Mike Olliver.

Basketball-Reference lists Olliver as a Bulls second-round pick but records no NBA regular-season statistics. The pick therefore produced no direct NBA games for Chicago.

There is no reviewed downstream NBA transaction branch from Olliver that offsets the comparison.

Why Denver Wins

Chicago converted a player it had not yet used into a second-round pick, so the process itself was reasonable. The problem is that the selected player never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

Denver received 145 Hordges games, including a solid rookie season with meaningful rebounding production. That is far more realized value than Chicago extracted from the No. 32 pick.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, B+/D+. Denver receives a B+ for 145 Hordges games across two seasons. Chicago receives a D+ because the No. 32 pick became Mike Olliver, who did not play an NBA regular-season game.

The Authoritative Ledgers Show Peck for a Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Phoenix, league and executive transaction records agree on the June 9, 1980 deal: Dallas sent Wiley Peck to Phoenix for a 1981 second-round pick that later became Elston Turner.

The legacy Dallas source record also contains a generic future-considerations line. None of the reviewed authoritative transaction ledgers lists that extra term, so this review preserves it as an unverified legacy-source detail rather than scoring it.

Peck Never Played for Phoenix

Peck had played 52 games for San Antonio as a rookie in 1979-80 before Dallas selected him in the expansion draft and immediately moved him to Phoenix.

The Suns waived Peck on September 8, 1980. Basketball-Reference records no Phoenix regular-season appearances for him, and his 52-game Spurs season remained his entire NBA playing career.

That leaves Phoenix with zero direct on-court production from the acquired player.

Dallas Used the Pick on Elston Turner

The second-round pick landed at No. 43 in the 1981 draft, where Dallas selected Elston Turner. He immediately became a useful rotation wing.

Turner played 80 games as a rookie, starting 62 and averaging 8.3 points, 3.8 rebounds and 2.4 assists in 25.0 minutes. He followed with 59 games in 1982-83 and 47 more in 1983-84.

That gives Dallas 186 regular-season Turner games across three seasons, including 79 starts and 3,411 minutes. He later continued his NBA career with Denver and Chicago, but this review stops Dallas's realized value at his Mavericks tenure.

Why Dallas Wins Clearly

Phoenix surrendered a second-round pick for a player who never appeared in a regular-season game for the Suns. Dallas turned that pick into three seasons of useful wing depth and a rookie-year starter.

The unverified future-considerations line is not needed to decide the trade. Even grading only the terms corroborated by Phoenix and league records, Dallas received substantially more realized basketball value.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win, B+/F. Dallas receives a B+ for 186 Turner games across three seasons, including 62 rookie starts. Phoenix receives an F because Peck was waived before playing a regular-season game for the Suns.

perspectives.summary: Chicago traded the rights to Calvin Garrett to Houston on June 10, 1980 for a 1982 second-round pick. Garrett played 121 regular-season games for the Rockets across two seasons, including 70 games and 1,638 minutes in 1980-81. Chicago never used the incoming pick directly. Two years later the Bulls sent the No. 38 selection to Golden State for a 1983 second-round pick that became No. 31, later used by Atlanta on Doc Rivers after Chicago surrendered it as compensation for coach Kevin Loughery. Houston received the stronger direct basketball return.
perspectives.analysis:
Houston Acquired Garrett for a Future Second

Basketball-Reference records Chicago sending Calvin Garrett's rights to Houston on June 10, 1980 for a 1982 second-round pick. Garrett had been Chicago's third-round selection in 1979 but did not play during 1979-80 while maintaining college eligibility.

Houston therefore acquired a young player before his NBA debut, while Chicago chose to push the asset two drafts into the future.

Garrett Played 121 Games for the Rockets

Garrett debuted in 1980-81 and appeared in 70 games for Houston. He logged 1,638 minutes and averaged 6.1 points, 3.8 rebounds and 1.9 assists in 23.4 minutes.

He returned for 51 games in 1981-82, including 22 starts, and averaged 4.5 points in 16.8 minutes. Across the two seasons, Garrett gave Houston 121 regular-season games before continuing his career elsewhere.

That is a useful two-year rotation return from a future second-round pick.

Chicago Converted the Pick Again

Houston's 1982 second-rounder landed at No. 38. Chicago did not use it on Wayne Sappleton. On June 23, 1982, the Bulls traded the No. 38 pick to Golden State for a 1983 second-round pick that later became No. 31.

The Warriors selected Sappleton at No. 38. Chicago retained the new 1983 second until June 1983, when the pick was sent to Atlanta as compensation for head coach Kevin Loughery. Atlanta used No. 31 on Doc Rivers.

This review does not credit Rivers' career to Chicago because he never played for the Bulls and the pick was surrendered as coaching compensation. The proper Chicago value is the transaction utility of converting the original pick into a later second-round asset that helped secure a coach.

Why Houston Gets the Edge

Chicago did not waste the incoming pick. It remained useful trade currency for two years and later became part of the cost of hiring Loughery.

Houston's return is still easier to isolate and more substantial on the court: 121 Garrett games over two seasons, including a 70-game rookie year.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, B+/C+. Houston receives a B+ for 121 Garrett games and two seasons of rotation value. Chicago receives a C+ because the second-round pick retained transaction utility but never produced a Bulls player.

perspectives.summary: Chicago and Portland swapped draft rights plus 1981 first-round picks on June 10, 1980. The Bulls received Ronnie Lester and the first that became No. 4 Al Wood; Portland received Kelvin Ransey and the first that became No. 16 Darnell Valentine. Lester played 191 games for Chicago, while the Wood pick was later packaged with another second-rounder in a larger Atlanta deal that brought Orlando Woolridge plus 1982 first- and second-round assets. Portland received 158 high-production Ransey games and 300 Valentine games, then converted both players into additional trade value. The Blazers hold the stronger realized-value edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Was More Than a Rookie-for-Rookie Swap

Basketball-Reference records Chicago sending the rights to Kelvin Ransey and a 1981 first-round pick to Portland for the rights to Ronnie Lester and another 1981 first-round pick. The outgoing Chicago first became No. 16 Darnell Valentine. The incoming Portland first became the No. 4 selection later associated with Al Wood.

Lester Gave Chicago Four Seasons

Lester played only eight games as a rookie, but he became a much larger part of the Bulls in 1981-82. He appeared in 75 games, started 74 and averaged 11.6 points and 4.8 assists.

He followed with 65 games in 1982-83 and 43 more in 1983-84. Across four Chicago seasons, Lester played 191 regular-season games, made 115 starts and logged 4,459 minutes.

That is a useful direct return, especially after the limited rookie season.

Chicago Also Re-Routed the No. 4 Pick

The Bulls never drafted Al Wood themselves. On June 8, 1981, Chicago sent the No. 4 first-round pick plus a 1981 second-round pick to Atlanta. In return, the Bulls received Atlanta's 1981 first-round pick, a 1982 first-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick.

The 1981 first became No. 6 Orlando Woolridge. The 1982 first became No. 7 Quintin Dailey, and the 1982 second became No. 26 Ricky Frazier. Because Chicago also included a second-round pick in the Atlanta trade, this review does not assign the entire Woolridge-Dailey-Frazier package solely to Portland's original first. The pick nevertheless carried substantial downstream trade value.

Portland Got Two Long-Term Guards

Ransey immediately became one of Portland's primary guards. He played 80 games as a rookie and averaged 15.2 points and 6.9 assists, then played 78 games in 1981-82 at 16.1 points and 7.1 assists. Across two seasons, Ransey gave Portland 158 games and 2,470 points.

In June 1982, Portland traded Ransey to Dallas for Wayne Cooper and a 1985 first-round pick. That pick later became the selection used on Terry Porter, although this review does not treat Porter as a one-asset return because Cooper and the first arrived together in the Ransey transaction.

The 1981 first-round pick became Darnell Valentine. Valentine played 300 regular-season games for Portland over five seasons, started 196 and averaged 9.8 points and 5.4 assists for the franchise.

Portland later traded Valentine and a 1988 second-round pick to the Clippers for a 1986 first-round pick and another 1988 second. The 1986 first became the pick used on Arvydas Sabonis, giving the Valentine branch additional transaction value even though another pick was included.

Why Portland Gets the Edge

Chicago did well. Lester played 191 games, and the incoming first-round pick became premium trade currency in the larger Atlanta deal. This was not a failed Bulls transaction.

Portland, however, received 458 combined regular-season games from Ransey and Valentine, including multiple starter-level seasons, then retained downstream trade value from both players. That volume of direct production gives the Blazers the stronger isolated return.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Win, A+/A-. Portland receives an A+ for 158 Ransey games, 300 Valentine games and meaningful later trade branches from both players. Chicago receives an A- for 191 Lester games plus the No. 4 pick's role in the larger Atlanta package that produced several premium assets.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State traded the draft rights to Jeff Ruland to Washington on June 10, 1980 for a 1981 second-round pick that became No. 33 Sam Williams. Ruland spent 1980-81 in Spain, then played 303 regular-season games for Washington over five NBA seasons, averaged at least 18.9 points in four straight years after his rookie season and made the 1984 and 1985 All-Star teams. Williams gave Golden State 141 games across parts of three seasons before moving to Philadelphia. The legacy summary understated the result: Washington received the decisively more valuable player.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Original Deal Was Ruland for a Future Second

Basketball-Reference's Golden State, Washington and league transaction ledgers all record the same June 10, 1980 trade. Golden State sent the rights to second-round pick Jeff Ruland to Washington for a 1981 second-round selection that later became No. 33 Sam Williams.

Ruland did not immediately join the Bullets. He spent 1980-81 playing in Spain, then debuted for Washington in 1981-82.

Ruland Became an All-Star-Level Washington Big

Ruland played all 82 games as a rookie and averaged 14.4 points and 9.3 rebounds in 27.0 minutes. He followed with 79 games in 1982-83 at 19.4 points and 11.0 rebounds, then produced his best season in 1983-84.

That year Ruland played 75 games, started all 75 and averaged 22.2 points, 12.3 rebounds and 3.9 assists in 41.1 minutes. He made the All-Star team and finished ninth in MVP voting.

Ruland was an All-Star again in 1984-85 despite playing only 37 games. He returned for 30 games in 1985-86. Across five Washington seasons, he appeared in 303 regular-season games and scored 5,653 points while functioning as one of the franchise's primary interior players.

Golden State Used the Pick on Sam Williams

The Warriors kept the incoming second-round pick and selected Sam Williams at No. 33 in 1981. Williams became a useful rotation forward.

He played 59 games as a rookie, starting 22, and averaged 6.1 points and 5.2 rebounds. He followed with 75 games in 1982-83 and averaged 8.4 points and 5.2 rebounds.

Williams appeared in seven more Golden State games in 1983-84 before continuing the season with Philadelphia. His Warriors total was 141 regular-season games, 50 starts and 2,665 minutes.

Why Washington Wins Decisively

Golden State did receive a productive NBA player from the future second-round pick. Williams was not a failed selection, and 141 games of frontcourt depth are real value.

Washington's return operated at a completely different level. Ruland became a five-season starter-level centerpiece, twice made the All-Star team and produced multiple seasons near or above 20 points and 10 rebounds per game.

The original legacy summary described Golden State as holding a modest edge, but the source-backed player records do not support that conclusion. Washington received substantially more realized value.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, A+/B. Washington receives an A+ for 303 Ruland games, two All-Star selections and several elite production seasons. Golden State receives a B because Sam Williams supplied 141 useful games and 50 starts, but his value was far below Ruland's Washington tenure.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired T.R. Dunn and Portland's 1983 first-round pick on August 15, 1980 for Denver's 1983 first and a 1984 second. Dunn became a long-tenured defensive specialist for the Nuggets, while the No. 15 pick produced Howard Carter, who played 55 Denver games. Portland's incoming No. 14 pick became Clyde Drexler, who played 867 regular-season games, scored 18,040 points for the Trail Blazers and became a Hall of Famer. The second-rounder also became Steve Colter, who played 159 Portland games. Denver received real value, but Portland captured a franchise cornerstone and wins decisively.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Swapped Dunn and Future Draft Position

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Portland, league and executive transaction records all agree on the August 15, 1980 structure. Denver received T.R. Dunn and Portland's 1983 first-round pick. Portland received Denver's 1983 first-round pick plus a 1984 second-round pick.

The first-round selections eventually landed one spot apart. Portland used Denver's pick at No. 14 on Clyde Drexler, while Denver used Portland's pick at No. 15 on Howard Carter.

Dunn Became a Major Denver Defensive Piece

Dunn immediately played all 82 games in 1980-81 and again in 1981-82. He started 80 games in the second season and became one of Denver's most durable defensive guards.

He played all 82 again in 1982-83 and earned Second-Team All-Defensive honors. Dunn remained a long-term Nugget through most of the 1980s, later returning to Denver after a brief Phoenix stop.

That longevity is why this trade cannot be treated as a complete Denver failure. Dunn gave the Nuggets many seasons of useful defensive value and playoff minutes.

Howard Carter Added Only a Short Denver Return

Denver's incoming first-round pick became No. 15 Howard Carter in 1983. Carter played 55 games for the Nuggets as a rookie, started five and averaged 6.2 points in 12.5 minutes.

He did not become a long-term Denver player. Carter's NBA career lasted only 66 games, with his final 11 appearances coming for Dallas.

Portland Used the No. 14 Pick on Clyde Drexler

The pick Denver surrendered became one of the most valuable draft outcomes in Trail Blazers history. Portland selected Drexler at No. 14 in 1983.

Drexler played 867 regular-season games for Portland across 12 seasons, the most in franchise history. He scored 18,040 points for the Trail Blazers, averaged 20.8 points, 6.2 rebounds and 5.7 assists in his Portland career, and became a perennial All-Star and All-NBA player.

He helped lead Portland to the NBA Finals in 1990 and 1992 and was later inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame. This review credits only his Portland tenure to this branch, not his later Houston championship.

The Second-Round Pick Also Produced Steve Colter

Denver's outgoing 1984 second-round pick became No. 33 Steve Colter. Portland received two useful seasons from him: 78 games as a rookie and 81 games in 1985-86.

Across those two seasons, Colter played 159 Trail Blazers games, started 73 and provided rotation point-guard production. That secondary asset alone added meaningful value beyond the Drexler pick.

Why Portland Wins Decisively

Denver's side was not empty. Dunn became a legitimate long-term defensive contributor, and Carter supplied 55 rookie-season games.

Portland still landed the overwhelming asset. Drexler became a Hall of Fame franchise cornerstone with 867 Portland games and 18,040 points, while Colter added another 159 useful games. The one-slot 1983 draft difference became enormous in hindsight.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Win, A+/B. Portland receives an A+ for the Drexler pick plus two seasons of Colter. Denver receives a B because Dunn provided sustained defensive value and Carter added a short rookie-season return, but that package cannot approach Drexler's franchise impact.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State acquired World B. Free from San Diego on August 28, 1980 for Phil Smith and a 1984 first-round pick. Free played 162 Warriors games across parts of three seasons, scoring 24.1, 22.9 and 22.8 points per game in those yearly stops before Golden State traded him to Cleveland for Ron Brewer. Smith gave the Clippers 124 games before being flipped for Armond Hill and a second-round pick, while the future first became No. 8 Lancaster Gordon, who played 201 games for the franchise. The returns were different in form but comparable in realized value.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Bought High-End Scoring

Basketball-Reference's Golden State, San Diego and league transaction ledgers agree on the August 28, 1980 trade: the Warriors received World B. Free, while the Clippers received Phil Smith and Golden State's 1984 first-round pick.

Free immediately became one of Golden State's primary scorers. He played 65 games in 1980-81 and averaged 24.1 points with 5.6 assists. In 1981-82 he played 78 games, started all 78 and averaged 22.9 points with 5.4 assists.

He opened 1982-83 with another 19 Warriors games at 22.8 points per game. That brought Free's Golden State total to 162 regular-season games across parts of three seasons, all at star-level scoring volume.

The Free Branch Also Returned Ron Brewer

Golden State did not simply lose Free at the end of that run. On December 15, 1982, the Warriors traded him to Cleveland for Ron Brewer.

Brewer played 53 games for Golden State in 1982-83 and another 13 in 1983-84. This review therefore credits 66 additional Warriors games as direct downstream value from the Free branch.

Brewer was not another Free-level scorer, but the transaction extended the life of the original asset rather than ending it at 162 games.

Phil Smith Gave San Diego Two Useful Seasons

Smith played 76 games for San Diego in 1980-81 and averaged 16.8 points, 4.9 assists and 31.3 minutes. He returned for 48 games in 1981-82, starting 39 and averaging 13.2 points with 4.9 assists.

That is 124 regular-season Clippers games from the veteran guard.

On February 16, 1982, San Diego traded Smith to Seattle for Armond Hill and a 1982 second-round pick later associated with Jeff Taylor. Hill played 19 games for the Clippers and started 14.

The incoming second-rounder was later included with Joe Bryant in a Houston trade that returned the pick used on Richard Anderson. Because Bryant was also outgoing, this review does not assign Anderson's full Clippers career to the Smith branch. The important point is that Smith still carried additional trade value after his 124 San Diego games.

The First-Round Pick Became Lancaster Gordon

The other major San Diego asset did not resolve until the 1984 draft. The Clippers used Golden State's first-round pick at No. 8 on Lancaster Gordon.

Gordon played four NBA seasons, all for the Clippers. He appeared in 201 regular-season games and scored 1,125 points, with his largest role coming in 1986-87 when he played 70 games and averaged 7.5 points.

He never became a high-end starter, but 201 games from a future first-rounder are meaningful realized value.

Why the Trade Stays Even

Golden State received the best player in the transaction. Free produced 162 games of high-volume scoring and then turned into 66 more Brewer games.

San Diego received more asset depth. Smith provided 124 useful games, Gordon supplied 201 more, and Smith later brought back Hill plus additional draft currency.

The Warriors won on peak impact. The Clippers won on volume and asset depth. Neither advantage is large enough to create a clear hindsight winner.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, A-/A-. Golden State receives an A- for 162 Free games at roughly 23 points per game across his Warriors tenure plus the later Brewer return. San Diego also receives an A- for 124 Smith games, 201 Gordon games and the additional Smith trade return. The original balanced verdict survives source-backed review.

Brewer was not another Free-level scorer, but the transaction extended the life of the original asset rather than ending it at 162 games.

Phil Smith Gave San Diego Two Useful Seasons

Smith played 76 games for San Diego in 1980-81 and averaged 16.8 points, 4.9 assists and 31.3 minutes. He returned for 48 games in 1981-82, starting 39 and averaging 13.2 points with 4.9 assists.

That is 124 regular-season Clippers games from the veteran guard.

On February 16, 1982, San Diego traded Smith to Seattle for Armond Hill and a 1982 second-round pick later associated with Jeff Taylor. Hill played 19 games for the Clippers and started 14.

The incoming second-rounder was later included with Joe Bryant in a Houston trade that returned the pick used on Richard Anderson. Because Bryant was also outgoing, this review does not assign Anderson's full Clippers career to the Smith branch. The important point is that Smith still carried additional trade value after his 124 San Diego games.

The First-Round Pick Became Lancaster Gordon

The other major San Diego asset did not resolve until the 1984 draft. The Clippers used Golden State's first-round pick at No. 8 on Lancaster Gordon.

Gordon played four NBA seasons, all for the Clippers. He appeared in 201 regular-season games and scored 1,125 points, with his largest role coming in 1986-87 when he played 70 games and averaged 7.5 points.

He never became a high-end starter, but 201 games from a future first-rounder are meaningful realized value.

Why the Trade Stays Even

Golden State received the best player in the transaction. Free produced 162 games of high-volume scoring and then turned into 66 more Brewer games.

San Diego received more asset depth. Smith provided 124 useful games, Gordon supplied 201 more, and Smith later brought back Hill plus additional draft currency.

The Warriors won on peak impact. The Clippers won on volume and asset depth. Neither advantage is large enough to create a clear hindsight winner.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, A-/A-. Golden State receives an A- for 162 Free games at roughly 23 points per game across his Warriors tenure plus the later Brewer return. San Diego also receives an A- for 124 Smith games, 201 Gordon games and the additional Smith trade return. The original balanced verdict survives source-backed review.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State sold Jo Jo White's player rights to Kansas City on September 10, 1980 for an undisclosed cash return. White played 13 games for the Kings, averaging 6.4 points, 2.8 assists and 18.2 minutes before announcing his retirement on November 3. The Warriors received no on-court asset, but they did receive cash for a veteran who had already completed his final Golden State season. Because the sale amount is undocumented, the realized-value gap should stay modest: Kansas City got limited rotation minutes, while Golden State monetized rights it no longer planned to use.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Sold White's Rights

Basketball-Reference records the September 10, 1980 transaction as a sale of Jo Jo White's player rights from Golden State to Kansas City. The Kings transaction ledger confirms the acquisition.

The canonical TradeVerdicts record describes the return as cash. The reviewed transaction sources do not provide the amount, so this review preserves the cash asset but does not invent a dollar value.

White Played 13 Games for Kansas City

White appeared in 13 regular-season games for the Kings. He logged 236 minutes and averaged 6.4 points, 2.8 assists and 1.6 rebounds in 18.2 minutes per game.

That made him a short-term reserve rather than a major rotation addition. He still produced actual NBA minutes, which gives Kansas City a concrete realized basketball return from the purchase.

Contemporary transaction research compiled by the Association for Professional Basketball Research records White announcing his retirement on November 3, 1980. That ended his NBA career and limited the Kings' return to those 13 games.

Golden State Received Cash, but the Amount Is Unknown

The Warriors' side is harder to quantify because the sale price is not documented in the reviewed public ledgers.

Golden State had already received 107 regular-season games from White across parts of the previous two seasons before this transaction. This review does not re-credit those games here because they occurred before the September 1980 sale.

The relevant return is only the cash received for his rights. That is still realized value, but without an amount there is no defensible way to compare it precisely with Kansas City's 13 games.

Why Kansas City Gets Only a Slight Edge

The Kings received measurable on-court production, even if it lasted less than a month of the regular season before White retired.

Golden State converted an asset it no longer intended to use into cash. The unknown sale amount prevents a harsh grade, but it also prevents the Warriors from matching Kansas City's documented playing value on source-backed evidence.

Final Verdict

Slight Kings Edge, C/C-. Kansas City receives a C for 13 games and 236 minutes from a veteran guard before retirement. Golden State receives a C- because the club realized cash value from the rights, but the amount is undocumented and cannot be scored as more than a limited return.

McKinney played 35 games for the Jazz at 8.4 points and 4.5 assists before Utah moved him to Denver for Carl Nicks, who added 40 Jazz games that season. perspectives.analysis:
Dallas Traded a Guard for Two Future Seconds

Basketball-Reference's Utah and league transaction ledgers record the September 11, 1980 trade: Dallas sent Billy McKinney to the Jazz for a 1983 second-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick.

The delayed return meant Dallas had to wait nearly three years before either asset became an NBA player. Utah, by contrast, got immediate rotation minutes from McKinney.

McKinney Played 35 Games for Utah

McKinney appeared in 35 Jazz games in 1980-81 and logged 1,032 minutes. He averaged 8.4 points, 4.5 assists and 2.1 rebounds while shooting 53.2 percent from the field.

That was meaningful backcourt production, but the Jazz did not keep him for the full season. On December 22, Utah traded McKinney to Denver for rookie guard Carl Nicks.

Nicks then played 40 games for the Jazz that season, averaging 6.3 points in 15.4 minutes. This review credits those Utah games as direct downstream value from the McKinney branch.

The 1983 Pick Became Mark West

Dallas held the first incoming pick until the 1983 draft and selected Mark West at No. 30.

West played 34 regular-season games for the Mavericks as a rookie, logging 202 minutes, and also appeared in four playoff games. Dallas waived him in October 1984, so the Mavericks did not capture the long NBA career West later built elsewhere.

That distinction is important. This review scores only the value realized by Dallas, not West's 17-year career after he became a free agent.

The 1984 Pick Became Anthony Teachey

Dallas used the second incoming pick at No. 40 in 1984 on Anthony Teachey.

Basketball-Reference lists Teachey as a Dallas draft pick but records no NBA regular-season career. The pick therefore did not add direct NBA game value for the Mavericks.

Why Utah Gets the Modest Edge

Dallas received two draft opportunities, but the realized NBA return was limited to 34 regular-season games and four playoff appearances from West. Teachey produced no NBA games for the franchise.

Utah received 35 McKinney games with useful point-guard production and then converted him into Nicks, who added another 40 games. The Jazz branch therefore produced more immediate and identifiable team-specific value.

Final Verdict

Slight Jazz Edge, B-/C+. Utah receives a B- for 35 productive McKinney games plus 40 Nicks games after the December trade. Dallas receives a C+ because Mark West supplied limited rookie minutes and a few playoff appearances while the second pick produced no NBA games.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State acquired Bernard King from Utah on September 11, 1980 for Wayne Cooper and a 1981 second-round pick. King played 160 games over two Warriors seasons, averaging 21.9 and 23.2 points while earning a 1982 All-Star berth and All-NBA Second Team honors. Golden State then traded King to New York for Michael Ray Richardson and a fifth-round pick; Richardson was later flipped for Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson. Cooper gave Utah 71 games before being packaged with Allan Bristow for Bill Robinzine, while the second-round selection ultimately became No. 34 Ken Green in Denver. The Warriors captured the overwhelming realized-value advantage.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Acquired an All-NBA Scorer

Basketball-Reference's Golden State, Utah and league transaction ledgers agree on the September 11, 1980 deal: the Warriors received Bernard King, while the Jazz received Wayne Cooper and a 1981 second-round pick associated with No. 34 Ken Green.

King immediately restored his standing as one of the league's best scorers. He played 81 games for Golden State in 1980-81 and averaged 21.9 points while shooting 58.8 percent from the field.

In 1981-82 he played 79 games, started 77 and averaged 23.2 points, 5.9 rebounds and 3.6 assists. He was selected as an All-Star and earned All-NBA Second Team honors.

That gave Golden State 160 regular-season games and 3,604 points from King across two seasons, with the second year carrying genuine league-wide honors.

The King Branch Kept Producing After 1982

Golden State did not lose King for nothing. On October 22, 1982, the Warriors traded him to New York for Michael Ray Richardson and a 1984 fifth-round pick.

Richardson played 33 games for Golden State, starting 25 and averaging 12.5 points, 7.4 assists and 3.1 steals.

On February 6, 1983, the Warriors then traded Richardson to New Jersey for Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson. Floyd became a long-term Golden State guard and a 1987 All-Star, while Johnson played 174 regular-season games for the Warriors across parts of three seasons.

This review treats that as legitimate downstream value because Richardson was received directly for King and then traded directly for Floyd and Johnson. The fifth-round pick is not needed to establish the branch's strength.

Cooper Gave Utah One Useful Season

Cooper played 71 games for Utah in 1980-81 and averaged 6.9 points, 6.2 rebounds and 20.0 minutes.

On August 20, 1981, Utah traded Cooper and Allan Bristow to Dallas for Bill Robinzine. Robinzine then played 56 games for the Jazz in 1981-82.

Because Bristow was also included, this review does not assign the full Robinzine return to Cooper alone. Cooper nevertheless retained enough value to be part of another NBA trade after his Utah season.

The Second-Round Pick Did Not Become a Jazz Player

The transaction ledgers associate the second-round pick with No. 34 Ken Green. Denver ultimately made that selection in the 1981 draft, and Green did not play for Utah.

Green later appeared in seven NBA games for New York in 1985-86, but those games do not count as realized Jazz value. The pick therefore adds no direct Utah on-court return in this retrospective.

Why Golden State Wins Decisively

Utah received a useful season from Cooper and later included him in a package for Robinzine. That is real value, but it is modest.

Golden State received two elite scoring seasons from King, including an All-Star and All-NBA Second Team year, then converted him into Richardson and subsequently Floyd plus Johnson. The downstream branch widened an already large direct-production gap.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, A+/C+. Golden State receives an A+ for 160 King games at elite scoring efficiency, major 1982 honors and a powerful downstream trade branch. Utah receives a C+ for 71 Cooper games and partial later trade value, while the second-round pick produced no direct Jazz NBA games. Confidence is high.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana traded Mickey Johnson to Milwaukee on September 11, 1980 for George Johnson and a 1982 second-round pick. George Johnson played 265 regular-season games over four Pacers seasons, including all 82 games with 64 starts in 1982-83 and all but one game the next year. Indiana used the No. 43 pick on Jose Slaughter, who added 63 games as a rookie. Mickey Johnson gave Milwaukee 164 games across parts of three seasons, started 153 of the first 158 and helped consecutive playoff teams before being packaged with Fred Roberts for Phil Ford and another second-round pick. Indiana gets the slight hindsight edge on total realized team value.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Trade Exchanged Mickey Johnson for George Johnson and a Second

Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Milwaukee and league transaction ledgers agree on the September 11, 1980 deal. The Pacers sent Mickey Johnson to the Bucks for George Johnson and a 1982 second-round pick that later became No. 43 Jose Slaughter.

The date is important because older secondary summaries have occasionally placed the transaction incorrectly. The official team transaction ledgers put it before the 1980-81 season.

George Johnson Gave Indiana Four Seasons

Johnson played 43 games for the Pacers in 1980-81 and averaged 10.6 points with 6.5 rebounds. He added 59 games in 1981-82 in a reduced role.

His largest Indiana season came in 1982-83. Johnson played all 82 games, started 64 and averaged 11.6 points, 6.6 rebounds and 2.7 assists.

He followed by playing 81 games in 1983-84, averaging 13.0 points and 5.7 rebounds. Across the four seasons, Johnson appeared in 265 regular-season games for Indiana.

That is a substantial multi-year direct return rather than a short stopgap.

The Pick Became Jose Slaughter

Indiana used the incoming 1982 second-round selection at No. 43 on Jose Slaughter.

Slaughter played 63 games for the Pacers in 1982-83, mostly in a reserve role. He averaged 3.6 points in 8.2 minutes and started once.

The pick did not produce a long NBA career, but it still added 63 games of realized roster value to the Indiana side.

Mickey Johnson Was Productive for a Contender

Milwaukee also received a strong return. Johnson played all 82 games and started all 82 in 1980-81, averaging 12.5 points, 6.6 rebounds and 3.5 assists for a 60-win Bucks team.

He played 76 games with 71 starts in 1981-82 and averaged 12.9 points and 6.0 rebounds. Johnson then opened 1982-83 with six more Milwaukee games before being traded.

That gives the Bucks 164 regular-season games from Johnson, including 153 starts across his first two seasons. He also participated in Milwaukee playoff runs during the contender window.

Milwaukee Preserved Some Downstream Value

On November 10, 1982, Milwaukee traded Johnson and Fred Roberts to New Jersey for Phil Ford and a 1983 second-round pick later associated with Ted Kitchel.

This review does not assign the full Ford-and-pick return to Johnson because Roberts was also part of the outgoing package. The transaction still shows Johnson retained trade value after his two full Bucks seasons.

Why Indiana Gets the Slight Edge

Milwaukee received the higher immediate role from one player: Johnson started almost every game across two strong seasons and fit a 60-win contender.

Indiana received more total direct games. George Johnson supplied 265 regular-season appearances across four years, and Slaughter added 63 more. That is 328 Pacers games from the original return.

The Bucks' downstream package narrows the gap, but because it also required Roberts, it cannot be credited entirely to Mickey Johnson.

Final Verdict

Slight Pacers Edge, A-/B+. Indiana receives an A- for four seasons of George Johnson plus 63 Slaughter games. Milwaukee receives a B+ for 164 productive Mickey Johnson games during a strong competitive window and partial downstream trade value. Both teams received useful returns, but Indiana's longer control and extra drafted player create the modest edge.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded its 1984 first-round pick to Dallas on September 16, 1980 for Mike Bratz. Bratz gave the Cavaliers 80 games in 1980-81, averaging 10.0 points, 5.7 assists and 1.7 steals, then Cleveland moved him to San Antonio for a 1983 third-round pick. Dallas held the future first until it landed at No. 4 and selected Sam Perkins, who played 471 regular-season games over six Mavericks seasons and appeared in 38 playoff games, including the 1988 Western Conference Finals run. Cleveland got a useful one-year guard; Dallas got a long-term core starter. The hindsight gap is enormous.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Traded a Future First for Mike Bratz

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Dallas and league transaction ledgers agree on the September 16, 1980 deal: the Cavaliers received Mike Bratz and the expansion Mavericks received Cleveland's 1984 first-round pick.

The pick did not resolve for nearly four years, which is important context. Cleveland was not knowingly trading Sam Perkins in 1980. The source-backed grade still measures what the asset ultimately became.

Bratz Gave Cleveland One Full Season

Bratz played 80 games for the Cavaliers in 1980-81 and logged 2,595 minutes. He averaged 10.0 points, 5.7 assists, 2.5 rebounds and 1.7 steals while playing 32.4 minutes per game.

That is real starting-level workload even though the Cavaliers finished 28-54. Bratz was not a zero-value acquisition or a short cameo.

Cleveland also preserved a small downstream asset. On October 28, 1981, the Cavaliers traded Bratz to San Antonio for a 1983 third-round pick later associated with Les Craft.

That later selection did not become meaningful NBA value, but the transaction shows Cleveland recovered something after Bratz's one season.

Dallas Turned the Pick Into Sam Perkins

The future first eventually landed at No. 4 in the 1984 draft, where Dallas selected Sam Perkins.

Perkins immediately played all 82 games as a rookie and averaged 11.0 points with 7.4 rebounds. He then became a full-time starter, playing 80 games in both 1985-86 and 1986-87 and 75 in 1987-88.

Across six Dallas seasons, Perkins appeared in 471 regular-season games. He scored in double figures every year and started 423 games from 1985-86 through 1989-90.

His postseason value also matters. Perkins appeared in 38 playoff games for Dallas, including all 17 games during the Mavericks' 1988 run to the Western Conference Finals.

He left for the Lakers as a free agent after the 1989-90 season, so there is no additional Mavericks trade branch to credit.

Why Dallas Wins by a Huge Margin

Cleveland received useful short-term guard play. Bratz gave the team 80 games, 452 assists and 136 steals in one season, then returned a third-round pick.

Dallas received six seasons from a durable starting forward who became part of the franchise's strongest 1980s teams. The difference is not simply that Perkins had a longer NBA career elsewhere; Dallas itself realized 471 regular-season games and substantial playoff value.

That team-specific return makes this one of the clearest Stepien-era asset losses even after giving Bratz credit for his actual Cleveland production.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win, A+/C. Dallas receives an A+ for turning the future first into six Perkins seasons, 471 regular-season games and 38 playoff appearances. Cleveland receives a C because Bratz supplied one useful 80-game season and a minor downstream pick, but the realized return was nowhere near the premium first-round asset surrendered.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded Roger Phegley to Cleveland on September 24, 1980 for Clarence 'Foots' Walker. Walker played 231 regular-season games over four Nets seasons, including 77 games with 54 starts in 1981-82, and provided steady point-guard distribution through 1983-84. Phegley played 109 Cleveland games across parts of two seasons, highlighted by 14.4 points per game in 1980-81, before the Cavaliers packaged him with Mike Mitchell in a San Antonio trade for Ron Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash. Both teams received useful players, but New Jersey got more isolated long-term value from the one-for-one exchange.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Was Phegley for Foots Walker

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey, Cleveland and league transaction ledgers record the September 24, 1980 swap as Roger Phegley to Cleveland for Foots Walker. The canonical TradeVerdicts record lists him by his given name, Clarence Walker; Basketball-Reference identifies Foots Walker as Clarence Walker.

Walker Became a Four-Year Nets Guard

Walker played 41 games for New Jersey in 1980-81 and averaged 5.7 points with 6.2 assists in 28.6 minutes.

His largest Nets role came in 1981-82. Walker appeared in 77 games, started 54 and averaged 5.9 points with 5.2 assists. He remained with the team for 79 games in 1982-83 and another 34 in 1983-84.

That gives New Jersey 231 regular-season games from Walker across four seasons. He was not a scorer, but he provided sustained point-guard minutes and distribution well beyond the first year of the trade.

Phegley Gave Cleveland Immediate Scoring

Phegley played all 82 games for Cleveland in 1980-81 and logged 2,269 minutes. He averaged 14.4 points, 3.0 rebounds and 2.2 assists while shooting 49.1 percent from the field.

He returned for 27 Cavaliers games in 1981-82, starting eight and averaging 9.2 points. His Cleveland total was therefore 109 regular-season games across parts of two seasons.

That is meaningful direct production, particularly in the first year. Cleveland did not simply acquire a disposable roster piece.

Cleveland Later Used Phegley in a Larger Trade

On December 23, 1981, Cleveland traded Phegley and Mike Mitchell to San Antonio for Ron Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash.

Phegley therefore retained trade value, but this review does not assign the full Spurs return to him. Mitchell was a major outgoing player and the transaction cannot be reduced to a Phegley-only branch.

The proper source-backed credit is narrower: Cleveland received 109 Phegley games and then used him as one component of a multi-player return.

Why New Jersey Gets the Slight Edge

Cleveland received the better short-term scorer. Phegley's 14.4 points per game in 1980-81 gave the Cavaliers more immediate offensive production than Walker ever supplied the Nets.

New Jersey received much more duration. Walker stayed four seasons, played 231 games and remained useful as a primary or reserve point guard into 1983-84.

Because Cleveland's later trade return required Mike Mitchell, that downstream branch cannot erase the direct 122-game gap between Walker and Phegley.

Final Verdict

Slight Nets Edge, B+/B. New Jersey receives a B+ for four seasons and 231 Walker games. Cleveland receives a B for 109 Phegley games, including a productive 82-game first season, plus partial downstream trade value. The exchange was useful to both clubs, but the Nets realized the more durable one-for-one return.

perspectives.analysis:
The legacy archive entry Was Missing Kansas City's Return

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, New York, Kansas City and league transaction ledgers all describe the September 25, 1980 three-team trade the same way.

Cleveland sent Campy Russell to New York and received Bill Robinzine from Kansas City. New York sent Joe Meriweather and its 1981 first-round pick to Kansas City. The legacy canonical record contained only Russell and Robinzine, leaving the Kings with an empty incoming-assets list.

This review restores both missing Kansas City assets before grading the transaction.

Meriweather Gave the Kings Five Seasons

Joe Meriweather immediately became a useful Kansas City center. He played 74 games in 1980-81 and averaged 7.6 points, 5.3 rebounds and 1.1 blocks.

His role changed over time, but he stayed through 1984-85. Meriweather played 18 games in 1981-82, 78 in 1982-83, 73 in 1983-84 and 76 in 1984-85.

That is 319 regular-season Kings games from an asset missing entirely from the legacy archive entry.

The First-Round Pick Became Steve Johnson

Kansas City also received New York's 1981 first-round pick, which landed at No. 7. The Kings selected Steve Johnson.

Johnson played 78 games with 50 starts as a rookie, averaging 12.8 points and 5.9 rebounds while shooting 61.3 percent. He followed with 79 games in 1982-83 at 11.7 points and 62.4 percent shooting.

He added 50 more Kansas City games in 1983-84 before leaving the club. That produces 207 regular-season Kings games from the second restored asset.

Together, Meriweather and Johnson produced 526 Kansas City regular-season games. The missing branch therefore changes the trade's value picture completely.

Campy Russell Was Productive for New York

The Knicks also received a strong direct return. Russell played 79 games and started all 79 in 1980-81, averaging 16.4 points, 4.5 rebounds and 3.3 assists.

He returned for 77 games with 63 starts in 1981-82 and averaged 13.9 points. Knee injuries then cost him the next two NBA seasons.

New York realized 156 regular-season games and two seasons of starter-level forward play from Russell. That is enough for a strong grade even though the Knicks surrendered the deeper long-term package.

Cleveland Received Only Eight Robinzine Games

Robinzine played eight games for Cleveland before the Cavaliers moved him again on October 30, 1980.

He was sent to Dallas with a 1983 first-round pick later used on Derek Harper and a 1986 first-round pick later used on Roy Tarpley. Cleveland received Richard Washington and Jerome Whitehead.

This review does not credit that entire return to Robinzine because the Cavaliers also surrendered two premium first-round picks. The direct Robinzine return was only eight games and 84 minutes.

Why Kansas City Wins

The Kings gave up a veteran forward and received two meaningful assets. Meriweather supplied 319 games, while the first-round pick became Johnson and added 207 more.

New York received two useful Russell seasons and deserves substantial credit. Cleveland's side was weakest because Robinzine barely played before becoming the least valuable identifiable piece of a later package that also included two first-rounders.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A+/A-/D+. Kansas City receives an A+ for 526 combined Meriweather-and-Johnson games from the restored return. New York receives an A- for 156 productive Russell games across two seasons. Cleveland receives a D+ because Robinzine played only eight games and his later trade cannot be credited independently from the two first-round picks Cleveland also surrendered. Confidence is high after repairing the canonical asset omission.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Duck Williams from Utah on October 1, 1980 for future considerations whose details remain unresolved in the reviewed records. Williams never appeared in a regular-season game for the Cavaliers: RealGM records Cleveland waiving him on October 12, with free agency following two days later. Basketball-Reference lists his entire 77-game NBA career with Utah in 1979-80 and no later NBA season. Cleveland therefore realized no on-court return, but Utah's side cannot be graded because the future consideration has not been identified. The trade remains source-backed but inconclusive rather than forcing a winner.
perspectives.analysis:
The Basic Transaction Is Confirmed

Cleveland and Utah transaction records confirm the October 1, 1980 move sending Duck Williams to the Cavaliers. The legacy archive entry lists future considerations going to the Jazz.

That consideration remains the central evidence gap. None of the reviewed public transaction records identifies a player, pick, cash amount or later conveyance that can be tied confidently to the obligation.

Williams Never Played a Cavaliers Regular-Season Game

Williams had played 77 games for Utah in 1979-80, averaging 6.6 points, 2.4 assists and 1.4 rebounds in 21.2 minutes.

His Cleveland tenure ended before the regular season produced any value. RealGM's Cavaliers transaction history records Williams being waived on October 12, 1980 and becoming a free agent on October 14.

Basketball-Reference lists no Cleveland regular-season line and no NBA season after 1979-80. For realized-value purposes, Cleveland's direct return is therefore zero NBA games.

Why the Trade Still Cannot Be Graded Normally

A zero-game return would ordinarily push Cleveland toward a poor grade. The problem is that Utah's incoming consideration is still unknown.

If the future consideration was trivial or never conveyed, the deal might be close to a wash despite Cleveland's zero-game return. If it became a meaningful pick, player or cash payment, the Jazz side could deserve a clear advantage.

The source-backed archive should preserve that uncertainty rather than inventing a value for an unidentified obligation.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence, N/A/N/A. Cleveland's side is now better documented: Williams produced zero Cavaliers regular-season games and was waived within two weeks. Utah's side remains unresolved because the future consideration has not been identified in the reviewed sources.

This review upgrades the record from a vague placeholder review note to a sourced inconclusive verdict. Confidence is high on Williams' Cleveland outcome and low on the missing consideration, so the overall trade verdict remains intentionally ungraded.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired rookie forward Wayne Robinson from the Lakers on October 2, 1980 for a 1981 second-round pick. Robinson played 81 games for the Pistons in his only NBA season, averaging 7.9 points and 3.6 rebounds in 19.7 minutes while logging 1,592 minutes. Los Angeles used the No. 39 pick on Harvey Knuckles, but Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season games for him. The legacy grades had leaned toward the Lakers; the source-backed outcome reverses that conclusion because Detroit received a full season of usable rotation production while the pick produced no NBA games.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Bought a Full Rookie Season for a Second

Basketball-Reference's Detroit transaction ledger records the October 2, 1980 deal: the Pistons acquired Wayne Robinson from the Lakers for a 1981 second-round pick.

The pick ultimately landed at No. 39 and became Harvey Knuckles. That makes the realized-value comparison unusually direct.

Robinson Played 81 Games for Detroit

Robinson appeared in 81 of 82 games during the 1980-81 season. He averaged 7.9 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.4 assists in 19.7 minutes.

His totals were 643 points, 294 rebounds and 112 assists across 1,592 minutes. He was not a star, but he was a real rotation forward on a team that used him almost every night.

That was also Robinson's only NBA season. Because there is no later NBA transaction branch to track, Detroit's return is contained entirely in those 81 games.

The Lakers' Pick Produced No NBA Games

Los Angeles used the acquired second-round selection at No. 39 on Harvey Knuckles out of Toledo.

Basketball-Reference lists Knuckles as the Lakers' 1981 second-round selection but does not record an NBA regular-season appearance for him.

There is no documented Lakers playing return or downstream transaction branch from the pick that offsets Robinson's Detroit season.

Why Detroit Wins

The original legacy archive entry gave the Lakers a modest edge, but the source-backed evidence points in the opposite direction. Detroit received 81 games and nearly 1,600 minutes from Robinson, while Los Angeles received a draft choice that produced zero NBA games.

This is not a franchise-changing win because Robinson's NBA career ended after one season. Even so, one full rotation season is clearly more realized basketball value than a pick with no NBA appearances.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, B+/D. Detroit receives a B+ for Robinson's 81-game rookie season and useful rotation workload. Los Angeles receives a D because the No. 39 selection on Harvey Knuckles produced no NBA regular-season games.

The frozen canonical record is dated October 6, while Basketball-Reference logs the rights sale on October 7; this review preserves the canonical date but records the source discrepancy. milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee Acquired Evans' Rights for Cash

The legacy archive entry dates the transaction October 6, 1980. Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee and San Antonio transaction ledgers both record the player-rights sale on October 7.

This review does not silently rewrite the frozen canonical date. Instead, it records the one-day source discrepancy and grades the assets that are clear: Mike Evans to Milwaukee, cash to San Antonio.

Evans Gave Milwaukee 85 Regular-Season Games

Evans played 71 games for the Bucks in 1980-81, logging 911 minutes. He averaged 4.5 points and 2.4 assists in 12.8 minutes while appearing on a 60-win team.

He also appeared in four playoff games that spring, scoring 25 points in 38 minutes.

Evans returned for 14 more Milwaukee games in 1981-82. Across the two regular seasons, he played 85 Bucks games and totaled 1,107 minutes, 376 points and 189 assists.

Milwaukee waived Evans during the 1981-82 season. Cleveland later signed him as a free agent, so there is no downstream trade return for the Bucks to credit.

San Antonio Received Unquantified Cash

The Spurs' transaction ledger describes the move as a sale of Evans' player rights. The reviewed sources do not state the cash amount.

That matters because cash is real consideration even when it creates no player or draft branch. This review does not treat San Antonio's side as zero value; it simply cannot assign a precise realized basketball equivalent to an undocumented payment.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Paul Mokeski from Houston on October 7, 1980 for a 1982 second-round pick. Mokeski played 119 regular-season games for the Pistons across parts of two seasons, including 80 games and 1,815 minutes in 1980-81, before Detroit included him with Phil Hubbard and two draft picks in the 1982 package for Kenny Carr and Bill Laimbeer. Houston later paired the incoming No. 32 pick with another second-rounder to acquire Joe Bryant and the No. 42 pick used on Jeff Taylor; Bryant and Taylor then played 125 combined Rockets games in 1982-83. Both branches produced real value, with Detroit holding a slight direct-return edge.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Acquired a Rotation Center for a Future Second

Basketball-Reference records the October 7, 1980 trade as Paul Mokeski to Detroit for a 1982 second-round pick. The pick eventually became the No. 32 selection.

Mokeski immediately became a regular part of Detroit's frontcourt rotation. He played 80 games in 1980-81, logging 1,815 minutes while averaging 7.1 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.7 assists.

He added 39 more Pistons games in 1981-82 before being moved in February. That gives Detroit 119 regular-season games and 2,338 minutes from the original acquisition.

Mokeski Also Retained Package Value

On February 16, 1982, Detroit sent Mokeski, Phil Hubbard, a 1982 first-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick to Cleveland for Kenny Carr and Bill Laimbeer.

That trade became enormously important to Detroit because Laimbeer developed into a long-term starter, but this review does not credit Laimbeer to Mokeski alone. Four Detroit assets went to Cleveland.

The narrower source-backed conclusion is still useful: Mokeski was not allowed to walk for nothing. After 119 games, he remained one of the pieces Detroit used in a major frontcourt restructuring.

Houston Later Used the Pick in a Two-Pick Swap

Houston did not select Richard Anderson itself. On June 28, 1982, the Rockets sent the No. 32 pick to San Diego for Joe Bryant and another 1982 second-round pick, No. 42.

San Diego used No. 32 on Anderson. Houston used No. 42 on Jeff Taylor.

Bryant then played 81 games for Houston in 1982-83, starting 56 and averaging 10.0 points, 3.4 rebounds and 2.3 assists. Taylor played 44 Rockets games as a rookie, starting five.

That is 125 combined Houston regular-season games from the later transaction package. However, the Rockets also surrendered a separate second-round pick to complete that deal, so this review does not assign the entire Bryant-Taylor return to Detroit's original No. 32 pick.

Why Detroit Gets the Slight Edge

Both sides created legitimate value. Detroit received 119 direct Mokeski games before using him as one component of the Carr-Laimbeer package. Houston preserved the pick for nearly two years and then used it as one component of a trade that brought Bryant and Taylor.

Detroit's advantage is attribution clarity. Mokeski's 119 games belong entirely to this trade. Houston's later return is real, but it is shared with the additional second-round pick that went to San Diego.

Final Verdict

Slight Pistons Edge, B+/B. Detroit receives a B+ for 119 Mokeski games plus his later use in a major multi-asset trade. Houston receives a B because the No. 32 pick retained meaningful trade value and helped produce Bryant and Taylor, while the full 125-game downstream return cannot be credited to that pick alone.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Bob Wilkerson's player rights from Denver on October 8, 1980 in a cash sale. Wilkerson played 80 regular-season games for the Bulls, averaging 10.0 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.4 assists in 28.0 minutes, then started all six of Chicago's 1981 playoff games. He moved to Cleveland the following season, so the Bulls' realized return ends after one productive year and postseason run. Denver received cash, but the amount is not documented in the reviewed sources. Chicago therefore owns the clearer realized-value win without assigning a precise value to the Nuggets' payment.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Sold Wilkerson's Rights to Chicago

Basketball-Reference records the October 8, 1980 transaction as Denver selling Bob Wilkerson's player rights to the Bulls. Chicago's ledger confirms the acquisition.

The public transaction sources do not state the cash amount. This review therefore preserves Denver's consideration as real but unquantified rather than treating the Nuggets' return as zero.

Wilkerson Played 80 Games for Chicago

Wilkerson became a regular part of the Bulls' 1980-81 rotation. He appeared in 80 games and logged 2,238 minutes, averaging 10.0 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.4 assists in 28.0 minutes.

Chicago finished 45-37 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. Wilkerson started all six playoff games, averaging 9.2 points in 25.3 minutes.

That gives the Bulls both a full regular-season contribution and postseason usage from a player acquired without surrendering another basketball asset.

His Chicago Tenure Lasted One Season

Wilkerson played for Cleveland in 1981-82. The reviewed records do not show Chicago receiving a player, pick or other transaction return when his Bulls tenure ended.

This review therefore stops Chicago's branch after the 1981 playoffs. That keeps the valuation grounded in the 80 regular-season games and six playoff starts actually realized by the Bulls.

Denver's Cash Return Is Unquantified

The Nuggets deliberately converted Wilkerson's rights into cash. That can be a rational roster decision, but the historical ledger does not provide enough information to measure the payment against on-court value.

Without a documented amount or downstream basketball asset, Denver's side cannot match Chicago's production in a realized-basketball comparison.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, A-/C+. Chicago receives an A- for 80 regular-season games, 2,238 minutes and six playoff starts from Wilkerson. Denver receives a C+ because it received cash of unknown size; the missing amount prevents a harsher grade but does not erase Chicago's clear on-court return.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: The Lakers acquired veteran forward Jim Brewer from Portland on October 8, 1980 for a 1984 second-round pick tied to the clubs' draft-option arrangement. Brewer played 149 regular-season games for Los Angeles across two seasons and appeared in eight games during the Lakers' 1982 championship playoff run. Portland used the No. 46 pick on Jerome Kersey, who then played 831 regular-season games over 11 Trail Blazers seasons, scoring 10,067 points and becoming a core member of multiple deep playoff teams. Brewer gave Los Angeles legitimate value, but Kersey makes this a decisive long-term Portland win.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Trade Produced Real Value for Both Teams

Basketball-Reference records Los Angeles acquiring Jim Brewer from Portland on October 8, 1980. The Lakers sent a 1984 second-round pick that ultimately became the No. 46 selection used on Jerome Kersey.

The transaction ledger also describes Portland's option to swap first-round picks as becoming the second-round pick instead. The legacy canonical record carries the option language on both sides, but this review does not count it as an additional independent asset beyond the realized 1984 second-rounder.

Brewer Played Two Full Lakers Seasons

Brewer appeared in 78 games for Los Angeles in 1980-81 and 71 more in 1981-82. Across those two seasons, he totaled 149 regular-season games, 2,073 minutes, 545 rebounds and 104 blocks.

He was a low-usage reserve rather than a major scorer, but he gave the Lakers dependable frontcourt depth.

Brewer also appeared in eight playoff games during the 1982 championship run. That title-season contribution means Los Angeles did not simply surrender a future pick for a player who failed to help.

Portland Turned the Pick into Jerome Kersey

The long-term gap comes from what the 1984 second-rounder became. Portland selected Kersey at No. 46.

Kersey played 831 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers across 11 seasons. Basketball-Reference's Portland franchise totals credit him with 21,760 minutes, 10,067 points, 5,078 rebounds, 1,762 assists and 1,059 steals.

He developed from a second-round project into a long-term starter and rotation pillar during one of the strongest sustained periods in franchise history.

The Option Is Not a Second Kersey Asset

The legacy archive entry contains a Blazers option to swap 1984 draft picks on both the incoming and outgoing sides. Basketball-Reference's transaction language clarifies that the option became the second-round pick instead.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded Dave Robisch to Denver in late October 1980 for Kim Hughes, a 1981 third-round pick that became Mickey Dillard, a 1982 second-round pick later routed to Indiana and unresolved future considerations. The frozen record is dated October 30, while Basketball-Reference records the completed trade on October 31. Robisch played 165 regular-season games for Denver after the deal. Hughes and Dillard combined for 78 Cleveland games, while the 1982 second became one of two picks Cleveland sent Indiana for the right to sign James Edwards; Edwards then played 92 Cavaliers games. The realized value remains broadly even.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Date Has a One-Day Source Discrepancy

The frozen Cleveland record is dated October 30, 1980. Basketball-Reference's Cleveland and Denver transaction ledgers record the completed Robisch-Hughes trade on October 31.

This review preserves the canonical date while noting the discrepancy. The asset package itself is well supported: Dave Robisch to Denver for Kim Hughes, a 1981 third-round pick, a 1982 second-round pick and future considerations.

Robisch Gave Denver 165 Post-Trade Games

Robisch immediately became a useful Nuggets center. He played 73 Denver games after the trade in 1980-81 and averaged 10.4 points and 5.7 rebounds in 23.9 minutes.

He added 12 Denver games in 1981-82, 61 in 1982-83 and 19 in 1983-84. That is 165 regular-season Denver games after the Cleveland trade.

Robisch's role diminished over time, but Denver still received several seasons of actual NBA production rather than a short rental.

Hughes and Dillard Combined for 78 Cleveland Games

Kim Hughes played 45 games for Cleveland in 1980-81. He logged 331 minutes and served mostly as a reserve center.

The 1981 third-round pick became No. 55 Mickey Dillard. Dillard played 33 Cavaliers games in 1981-82, totaling 221 minutes.

Those two assets alone produced 78 Cleveland regular-season games, though neither matched Robisch's Denver workload.

The 1982 Second Helped Cleveland Acquire James Edwards

Cleveland did not use the 1982 second-round pick itself. Pro Sports Transactions traces the No. 40 pick to Indiana after the Cavaliers sent it with a separate 1981 second-round pick in June 1981.

In return, Indiana agreed not to exercise its right of first refusal on veteran free agent James Edwards. Edwards then played 92 regular-season games for Cleveland over two seasons, averaging 16.0 points and 7.4 rebounds across that Cavaliers tenure.

This review does not assign all 92 Edwards games to this one pick because Cleveland also surrendered the separate 1981 second-rounder. The branch still shows that Denver's 1982 pick retained meaningful transaction value.

Future Considerations Remain Unresolved

The Denver media guide and legacy archive entry both reference future considerations, but the reviewed sources do not identify what was ultimately conveyed.

That asset stays unvalued rather than being treated as either zero or a hidden Cleveland bonus.

Why the Deal Remains Even

Denver received the strongest single direct player return: 165 post-trade Robisch games.

Cleveland received 78 direct games from Hughes and Dillard, then used the second-round pick as one component of the compensation that brought Edwards to Cleveland for 92 games of much larger offensive production.

The future-consideration gap and shared Edwards acquisition make a precise edge difficult to defend. Both clubs realized meaningful value through different paths.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B+/B+. Denver receives a B+ for 165 Robisch games across parts of four seasons. Cleveland receives a B+ for Hughes, Dillard and a valuable second-round pick that helped facilitate the Edwards signing, while the unresolved future consideration is not scored.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded Bill Robinzine plus its 1983 and 1986 first-round picks to Dallas on October 30, 1980 for Richard Washington and Jerome Whitehead. Washington played 87 regular-season games for Cleveland across two seasons, while Whitehead appeared in only three. Dallas received 70 productive Robinzine games immediately, then used the No. 11 pick in 1983 on Derek Harper and the No. 7 pick in 1986 on Roy Tarpley. Harper played 872 regular-season games across 12 Mavericks seasons, and Tarpley added 280 games. The two future firsts turn a useful Dallas return into a decisive long-term win.
perspectives.analysis:
Dallas Received the Better Present and the Better Future

The October 30, 1980 trade sent Richard Washington and Jerome Whitehead to Cleveland. Dallas received Bill Robinzine plus Cleveland's 1983 and 1986 first-round picks.

Cleveland Got 90 Combined Games

Washington played 69 games for Cleveland after the trade in 1980-81, averaging 9.9 points and 5.3 rebounds in 21.8 minutes.

He returned for 18 games in 1981-82. Across the two seasons, Washington totaled 87 Cavaliers regular-season appearances.

Whitehead's Cleveland stint was much shorter. He appeared in only three games in 1980-81 before leaving the roster.

That gives Cleveland 90 combined games from the two incoming players. Washington was useful, but the return did not produce a long-term starter or another major downstream asset.

Robinzine Produced Immediately for Dallas

Robinzine played 70 games for the Mavericks after the trade in 1980-81. He averaged 13.9 points and 7.4 rebounds in 27.6 minutes.

That one-season contribution already compares favorably with Cleveland's direct return because Dallas received meaningful starter-level production rather than only depth.

The future picks are what separate the deal.

The 1983 First Became Derek Harper

Dallas kept Cleveland's 1983 first-round pick and selected Derek Harper at No. 11.

Harper became one of the longest-tenured players in franchise history. He played 872 regular-season games across 12 Dallas seasons and averaged 14.4 points and 5.9 assists during his Mavericks tenure.

He was a full-time starter through much of the club's 1980s playoff run and later returned for a second Dallas stint. This review credits that production directly because the pick from this trade became Harper.

The 1986 First Became Roy Tarpley

Dallas also kept Cleveland's 1986 first-rounder and selected Roy Tarpley at No. 7.

Tarpley's career was interrupted repeatedly, but his on-court production was substantial. He played 280 regular-season games for Dallas, averaging 12.6 points and 10.0 rebounds overall.

His best early stretch included 13.5 points and 11.8 rebounds in 1987-88, and he was a major playoff contributor for the Mavericks.

Why Dallas Wins Easily

Cleveland received 87 Washington games and three Whitehead games. Dallas received 70 productive Robinzine games, 872 Harper games and 280 Tarpley games.

The difference is not close in realized value. Dallas got an immediate veteran contributor plus two first-round selections that became major long-term players.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win, A+/C. Dallas receives an A+ for Robinzine, Harper and Tarpley. Cleveland receives a C because Washington gave the Cavaliers two useful seasons, but Whitehead barely played and the two surrendered first-round picks became far more valuable than the incoming package.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State traded Rudy White to Seattle on November 3, 1980 for a 1981 fourth-round pick. White played only 12 regular-season games for Seattle, averaging 3.3 points in 13.8 minutes. Golden State used the No. 76 pick on Lewis Lloyd, who played 89 regular-season games across two Warriors seasons and averaged 9.4 points in 1982-83. When Lloyd later signed with Houston as a veteran free agent, Golden State also received a 1985 second-round compensation pick that became Bobby Lee Hurt. The realized value clearly favored the Warriors.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Deal Was White for a Future Fourth

Basketball-Reference's player transaction record lists the November 3, 1980 trade directly: Seattle sent Golden State a future 1981 fourth-round pick for Rudy White.

The selection ultimately landed at No. 76 in the 1981 draft and became Lewis Lloyd.

White Played Only 12 Seattle Games

White had appeared in four games for Golden State before the trade. After joining Seattle, he played 12 regular-season games and averaged 3.3 points, 0.9 rebounds and 1.5 assists in 13.8 minutes.

Those 12 appearances were the final NBA regular-season games of his career. Seattle therefore received a very small direct return.

The Pick Became Lewis Lloyd

Golden State used the acquired fourth-rounder on Lloyd in June 1981.

Lloyd played 16 games as a rookie in 1981-82, then appeared in 73 games in 1982-83. In that second season he averaged 9.4 points, 3.6 rebounds and 1.8 assists while starting 24 games.

Across the two seasons, Lloyd gave Golden State 89 regular-season games. That is already substantially more realized value than Seattle received from White.

Golden State Also Received Compensation When Lloyd Left

On August 29, 1983, Lloyd signed with Houston as a veteran free agent.

Basketball-Reference's transaction record states that Golden State received a 1985 second-round pick as compensation. That selection was later used on Bobby Lee Hurt.

This review does not need to assign a large value to Hurt to decide the original trade. The compensation pick simply adds another downstream asset to a branch that had already produced 89 games.

Why Golden State Wins

Seattle received 12 low-minute White appearances and no documented downstream NBA asset from him.

Golden State received 89 Lloyd games, including a useful 1982-83 rotation season, and later recovered a second-round compensation pick when Lloyd left for Houston.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, B+/D. Golden State receives a B+ for the Lloyd production and later compensation pick. Seattle receives a D because White played only 12 games before his NBA career ended.

perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Is Clear, but Dallas' Return Is Not

Basketball-Reference's 1980-81 transaction records show Dallas sending Austin Carr to Washington on November 6, 1980.

The Mavericks received future considerations. The reviewed team and league transaction sources do not identify what those considerations ultimately became.

Carr Played 39 Games for Washington

Carr had played eight games for Dallas before the trade. After joining the Bullets, he appeared in 39 regular-season games.

He averaged 4.9 points, 1.3 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 14.9 minutes. The role was small, but Washington received a real veteran guard contribution.

Those 39 games were the final regular-season appearances of Carr's NBA career. There is no later Washington transaction branch from Carr that materially changes the trade.

Dallas' Future Considerations Stay Unresolved

The key evaluation problem is the Dallas side. "Future considerations" can represent cash, a conditional right, a player to be named later or another form of transaction value, but the reviewed records do not specify the outcome here.

This review therefore leaves that asset unresolved. It is not treated as zero, but it also cannot be credited with an invented player, pick or cash amount.

The Known Return Was Small but Real

Carr's 39 Washington appearances came after he had played only eight games for expansion Dallas. The Bullets did not acquire a long-term starter, but they did receive the only traceable NBA playing value attached to the transaction in the reviewed record.

The uncertainty on Dallas' side is important to preserve. A future-considerations clause proves that Dallas did not simply give Carr away, yet source-backed grading has to distinguish a documented but unidentified asset from a player, pick or cash amount that can actually be measured. That is why the Dallas grade stays above a complete zero-return outcome while remaining below Washington's documented 39-game return.

Why Washington Gets Only a Narrow Edge

Washington's return is modest: 39 games from a veteran near the end of his career.

Dallas may have received some useful value through the future-considerations term, but there is not enough documentation to measure it. The fairest source-backed approach is to grade only the known realized return while keeping confidence below high.

Final Verdict

Slight Bullets Edge, C+/D+. Washington receives a C+ for 39 Carr games. Dallas receives a D+ because an incoming asset is documented but unresolved, preventing either a zero-value grade or a stronger realized-value claim.
