perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded Eddie Jordan to the Lakers in November 1980 for a 1982 first-round pick. Jordan played 153 regular-season games for Los Angeles across parts of three seasons, including 58 games for the 1981-82 championship team. The Nets kept the pick and selected Eddie Phillips at No. 21 in 1982, but Phillips played only 48 NBA games, all for New Jersey, while averaging 3.2 points in 8.7 minutes. Both sides received direct value, but the Lakers turned the deal into substantially more useful playing time and a contributor on a title roster.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Was Jordan for a Future First

Basketball-Reference records New Jersey sending Eddie Jordan to Los Angeles in November 1980 for the Lakers' 1982 first-round pick. The team ledgers list November 20, while the frozen canonical record is dated November 19; this review preserves the canonical date while using the source-backed transaction details.

Jordan Immediately Became Lakers Depth

Jordan had played 14 games for New Jersey in 1980-81 before the trade. He then appeared in 60 regular-season games for Los Angeles that season, logging 987 minutes.

His role was smaller than it had been with the Nets, but he remained a useful reserve guard. Jordan returned in 1981-82 and played 58 regular-season games, then appeared in three playoff games for the Lakers team that won the NBA championship.

He stayed for 35 more regular-season games in 1982-83. Across the three post-trade Lakers seasons, Jordan totaled 153 regular-season appearances.

The Pick Became Eddie Phillips

New Jersey held the incoming first-round pick through the 1982 draft.

The selection landed at No. 21, where the Nets drafted Alabama forward Eddie Phillips. Phillips played 48 regular-season games as a rookie in 1982-83, averaging 3.2 points and 1.6 rebounds in 8.7 minutes.

Those 48 games were his entire NBA career. The pick therefore produced a real NBA player, but not the multi-season value normally expected from a first-round asset.

The Comparison Is Direct

This trade does not require a long downstream chain to evaluate. Los Angeles received 153 Jordan games, including a full reserve season on the 1982 championship roster.

New Jersey received 48 Phillips games from the acquired first-round pick. There is no later Nets transaction branch from Phillips that materially closes the gap.

Why Los Angeles Wins

The Lakers gave up a future first, so the original asset cost was meaningful. In hindsight, however, the pick landed late in the round and became a one-season reserve.

Jordan gave Los Angeles more than three times as many regular-season games and remained available through a championship season. That is a much stronger realized return.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A-/C. Los Angeles receives an A- for 153 Jordan games and his place on the 1981-82 championship roster. New Jersey receives a C because the No. 21 pick did reach the NBA, but Phillips produced only 48 games before his career ended.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana reacquired veteran guard Don Buse from Phoenix on November 25, 1980 for 1981 and 1982 second-round picks. Buse played 140 regular-season games for the Pacers across two seasons, including all 82 games with 78 starts in 1981-82 at 9.7 points and 5.0 assists. Phoenix did not make either selection. In June 1981, the Suns sent both picks back to Indiana for Dudley Bradley while also relinquishing a 1983 first-round swap option. Bradley played 64 games for Phoenix in 1981-82. Because Phoenix had to add another concession to convert the picks, Indiana gets the better realized return.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Bought Two Seasons of Don Buse

Basketball-Reference records Indiana sending Phoenix a 1981 second-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick for Don Buse on November 25, 1980.

Buse was returning to the Pacers after three-plus seasons in Phoenix. He immediately gave Indiana a useful veteran backcourt piece.

Buse Played 140 Pacers Games

Buse appeared in 58 games after the trade in 1980-81. He averaged 5.1 points, 2.4 assists and 1.3 steals in 18.9 minutes.

His role grew substantially in 1981-82. Buse played all 82 games, started 78 and averaged 9.7 points, 5.0 assists and 2.0 steals in 30.8 minutes.

Across those two seasons, Indiana received 140 regular-season games. The second year in particular gave the Pacers a full-time starting point guard.

Phoenix Used the Picks as Trade Currency

The two outgoing Indiana picks were associated with No. 37 Al Leslie in 1981 and No. 43 Jose Slaughter in 1982.

Phoenix never actually made either selection. On June 8, 1981, the Suns sent both picks back to Indiana for Dudley Bradley.

Phoenix also relinquished an option to swap first-round picks with Indiana in 1983. That extra concession matters because the two second-rounders alone did not buy Bradley.

Bradley Played 64 Games for Phoenix

Bradley appeared in 64 regular-season games for the Suns in 1981-82, starting three and averaging 5.1 points in 14.6 minutes.

He left Phoenix after that season. This review treats Bradley as downstream value from the two-pick package, but does not credit all 64 games solely to the original Buse trade because Phoenix had to give up the 1983 swap option as part of the Bradley transaction.

Indiana Also Recovered the Picks

The June 1981 Bradley trade returned both second-round picks to Indiana. The Pacers then drafted Al Leslie at No. 37 in 1981 and Jose Slaughter at No. 43 in 1982.

Leslie never played an NBA regular-season game. Slaughter played 63 games for Indiana in 1982-83, averaging 3.6 points in 8.2 minutes.

Those draft outcomes came only after Indiana surrendered Bradley to reacquire the selections, so they are not treated as free extra value from the original Buse deal. They do, however, show that Phoenix's initial pick return was temporary.

Why Indiana Gets the Edge

Indiana received 140 Buse games, including a full season as a 78-game starter. Phoenix converted the picks into 64 Bradley games, but had to add the first-round swap concession to complete that later deal.

The Suns did receive real transaction value. The Pacers simply received more direct, durable production from the original exchange.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, A-/B-. Indiana receives an A- for 140 Buse games and a full starting season. Phoenix receives a B- because the two seconds helped acquire Bradley, but the Suns needed an additional first-round swap concession and Bradley stayed only one season.

In June 1981, the Suns sent both picks back to Indiana for Dudley Bradley while also relinquishing a 1983 first-round swap option. Bradley played 64 games for Phoenix in 1981-82. Because Phoenix had to add another concession to convert the picks, Indiana gets the better realized return.
analysis:
Indiana Bought Two Seasons of Don Buse

Basketball-Reference records Indiana sending Phoenix a 1981 second-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick for Don Buse on November 25, 1980.

Buse was returning to the Pacers after three-plus seasons in Phoenix. He immediately gave Indiana a useful veteran backcourt piece.

Buse Played 140 Pacers Games

Buse appeared in 58 games after the trade in 1980-81. He averaged 5.1 points, 2.4 assists and 1.3 steals in 18.9 minutes.

His role grew substantially in 1981-82. Buse played all 82 games, started 78 and averaged 9.7 points, 5.0 assists and 2.0 steals in 30.8 minutes.

Across those two seasons, Indiana received 140 regular-season games. The second year in particular gave the Pacers a full-time starting point guard.

Phoenix Used the Picks as Trade Currency

The two outgoing Indiana picks were associated with No. 37 Al Leslie in 1981 and No. 43 Jose Slaughter in 1982.

Phoenix never actually made either selection. On June 8, 1981, the Suns sent both picks back to Indiana for Dudley Bradley.

Phoenix also relinquished an option to swap first-round picks with Indiana in 1983. That extra concession matters because the two second-rounders alone did not buy Bradley.

Bradley Played 64 Games for Phoenix

Bradley appeared in 64 regular-season games for the Suns in 1981-82, starting three and averaging 5.1 points in 14.6 minutes.

He left Phoenix after that season. This review treats Bradley as downstream value from the two-pick package, but does not credit all 64 games solely to the original Buse trade because Phoenix had to give up the 1983 swap option as part of the Bradley transaction.

Indiana Also Recovered the Picks

The June 1981 Bradley trade returned both second-round picks to Indiana. The Pacers then drafted Al Leslie at No. 37 in 1981 and Jose Slaughter at No. 43 in 1982.

Leslie never played an NBA regular-season game. Slaughter played 63 games for Indiana in 1982-83, averaging 3.6 points in 8.2 minutes.

Those draft outcomes came only after Indiana surrendered Bradley to reacquire the selections, so they are not treated as free extra value from the original Buse deal. They do, however, show that Phoenix's initial pick return was temporary.

Why Indiana Gets the Edge

Indiana received 140 Buse games, including a full season as a 78-game starter. Phoenix converted the picks into 64 Bradley games, but had to add the first-round swap concession to complete that later deal.

The Suns did receive real transaction value. The Pacers simply received more direct, durable production from the original exchange.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, A-/B-. Indiana receives an A- for 140 Buse games and a full starting season. Phoenix receives a B- because the two seconds helped acquire Bradley, but the Suns needed an additional first-round swap concession and Bradley stayed only one season.

Phoenix later sent both incoming second-round picks back to Indiana for Dudley Bradley while also relinquishing a 1983 first-round swap option; Bradley played 64 Phoenix games. summary: Atlanta traded Armond Hill to Seattle on December 2, 1980 for 1983 and 1984 second-round picks plus cash. Hill played 72 regular-season games for Seattle across parts of two seasons, then was packaged with another second-round pick for Phil Smith, who added 105 SuperSonics games. Atlanta later turned the 1983 second into Johnny Davis, who played 128 Hawks games over two seasons, and routed the 1984 second through Jim Johnstone before Johnstone became part of a multi-asset package for George Johnson. Both branches produced value, but Atlanta's more direct Johnny Davis return and cash give the Hawks a slight edge.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Received Two Future Seconds and Cash

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, Seattle and league transaction ledgers agree on the December 2, 1980 exchange. Seattle acquired Armond Hill. Atlanta received Seattle's 1983 second-round pick, Seattle's 1984 second-round pick and cash.

The cash amount is not identified in the reviewed records, so this review preserves the term without assigning it a dollar value.

Hill Gave Seattle 72 Games

Hill played 51 games for Seattle after the trade in 1980-81, totaling 255 points and 174 assists.

He returned for 21 more SuperSonics games in 1981-82, bringing the direct Seattle return to 72 regular-season appearances.

On February 16, 1982, Seattle traded Hill and a separate 1982 second-round pick to San Diego for Phil Smith. Smith then played 26 games for Seattle in 1981-82 and 79 more in 1982-83.

That gives the Hill branch additional downstream value, but this review does not treat all 105 Smith games as if Hill alone bought them because Seattle also surrendered a second-round pick.

The 1983 Second Became Johnny Davis

Atlanta did not use Seattle's 1983 second-round pick at the draft. On December 31, 1982, the Hawks sent that pick to Indiana for Johnny Davis.

Davis became a substantial Atlanta guard. He played 53 games in 1982-83, starting 33 and averaging 12.9 points and 5.9 assists.

He followed with 75 games and 72 starts in 1983-84, averaging 12.3 points and 4.3 assists. Across the two seasons, Davis gave Atlanta 128 regular-season games.

In August 1984 the Hawks traded Davis to Cleveland for John Garris and Stewart Granger. This review does not need that later branch to establish the value of the original 1983 pick.

The 1984 Second Became Trade Currency

Atlanta also did not directly draft Ben Coleman with Seattle's 1984 second. On June 30, 1982, the Hawks sent that future pick to Kansas City for the draft rights to Jim Johnstone.

Three months later, Atlanta sent Johnstone plus separate 1983 and 1985 second-round picks to San Antonio for George Johnson.

Johnson played 37 regular-season games for Atlanta in 1982-83. Because two additional second-round picks were included in that trade, this review credits only partial downstream value from the Johnstone branch.

Why Atlanta Gets the Slight Edge

Seattle received 72 Hill games and later used Hill with another second-rounder to acquire Phil Smith, who added 105 games. That is a legitimate and useful return.

Atlanta's 1983 pick, however, directly produced 128 Johnny Davis games with heavy starting usage, while the 1984 pick retained enough value to help create another trade branch. The unquantified cash also belongs on Atlanta's side even though it is not scored.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge, A-/B+. Atlanta receives an A- for the Davis return, additional 1984-pick trade utility and cash. Seattle receives a B+ for 72 Hill games plus his role in the later Phil Smith package.

perspectives.summary: Dallas and Denver completed one of the best win-win trades of the era on December 3, 1980, not December 10 as the legacy archive entry had it. The Mavericks sent Kiki Vandeweghe's draft rights plus a 1986 first-round pick to Denver for 1981 and 1985 first-rounders. Vandeweghe played 293 Denver games, made two All-Star teams and became one of the league's elite scorers. Dallas used the 1981 pick on Rolando Blackman, who played 865 Mavericks games, made four All-Star teams and became a franchise cornerstone. Denver's later No. 16 pick became Maurice Martin, who played 69 games. Dallas gets the narrow hindsight edge because Blackman's tenure was longer and more franchise-defining.
perspectives.analysis:
The Canonical Date Needed Repair

Basketball-Reference's Dallas and league transaction ledgers date the trade to December 3, 1980. The legacy canonical record listed December 10, which was Vandeweghe's NBA debut date rather than the transaction date.

This review repairs the trade date to December 3 while preserving the original asset package.

Denver Received Kiki Vandeweghe and a Future First

Denver acquired the draft rights to Kiki Vandeweghe plus Dallas's 1986 first-round pick.

Vandeweghe became the immediate centerpiece. He played 51 games as a rookie, then all 82 games in both 1981-82 and 1982-83, followed by 78 games in 1983-84.

Across four Denver seasons he played 293 regular-season games. He scored 2,186 points in 1982-83 and 2,295 in 1983-84, making the All-Star team in both seasons.

Dallas Got the Pick That Became Rolando Blackman

The most valuable Dallas asset was Denver's 1981 first-round pick. It landed at No. 9, where the Mavericks selected Rolando Blackman.

Blackman played 865 regular-season games for Dallas across eleven seasons. He scored 16,643 points for the franchise, made four All-Star teams and became one of the foundational players of Dallas's first sustained playoff era.

That alone gives Dallas an elite return from a single incoming pick.

The 1985 First Retained Additional Trade Value

Dallas also received Denver's 1985 first-round pick. The pick was later associated with Sam Vincent, but Dallas did not simply use it on Vincent.

On May 1, 1985, Dallas traded that first-rounder to Boston for another 1985 first-round pick and a 1988 second-round pick. The incoming first was the selection later associated with Terry Porter.

This review does not assign Porter's NBA career to Dallas because the pick was part of a later transaction chain and did not become a Dallas player. The important point is that Denver's 1985 first retained premium trade value for years after the original deal.

Denver's 1986 First Became Maurice Martin

Dallas's outgoing 1986 first-round pick landed at No. 16, where Denver selected Maurice Martin.

Martin played 69 regular-season games for the Nuggets over two seasons. He never became a major rotation piece, so this branch added only modest value compared with Vandeweghe himself.

Why Dallas Gets the Narrow Edge

Denver absolutely succeeded. Vandeweghe became a two-time All-Star and elite scorer, giving the Nuggets four high-level seasons.

Dallas, however, landed 865 Blackman games, four All-Star selections and more than a decade of franchise value from the No. 9 pick. The second incoming first also retained real trade utility.

This is not a lopsided deal. It is a strong outcome for both teams, with Dallas winning only because Blackman's longevity and franchise impact exceed Denver's shorter Vandeweghe peak.

Final Verdict

Slight Mavericks Edge, A+/A. Dallas receives an A+ for Blackman's 865 games, four All-Star selections and the additional value retained in the 1985 first. Denver receives an A for Vandeweghe's 293 games, two All-Star seasons and the later Maurice Martin selection.

perspectives.summary: Portland traded Ron Brewer to San Antonio on December 19, 1980 for Mike Gale and a 1982 first-round pick. Gale played 42 Trail Blazers games before Portland flipped him for two second-round picks. The first-rounder was later sent to Detroit for Kenny Carr, who played 316 regular-season games over five Portland seasons and became a major frontcourt contributor. San Antonio got 71 games from Brewer before including him with Reggie Johnson and cash in the package for Mike Mitchell and Roger Phegley. Both sides extracted value, but Portland clearly won because the pick branch became Carr while Gale also generated additional draft assets.
perspectives.analysis:
Portland Received Gale and a Future First

Basketball-Reference records the December 19, 1980 trade as Ron Brewer to San Antonio for Mike Gale and a 1982 first-round pick.

Gale gave Portland 42 regular-season games after the trade, totaling 476 minutes, 179 points and 70 assists.

Portland then moved Gale again on June 8, 1981. Golden State sent back a 1982 second-round pick later used on Audie Norris and a 1985 second-round pick later associated with Mike Smrek.

This review treats those second-rounders as legitimate downstream value from the Gale branch without assigning the later full careers of every player selected to Gale alone.

The First Became Kenny Carr, Not Ricky Pierce for Portland

The legacy archive entry labels the 1982 first as No. 18 Ricky Pierce. That is the final draft outcome after the pick changed hands, not Portland's direct use of the asset.

On June 23, 1982, Portland traded that first-round pick to Detroit for Kenny Carr. Detroit then used No. 18 on Ricky Pierce.

Carr became the major Portland return. He played 316 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers across five seasons, starting 187 of them.

He produced 3,903 points and 2,545 rebounds for Portland, including 82 games in both 1982-83 and 1983-84. In 1983-84 he averaged 15.6 points and 7.8 rebounds while starting 57 games.

Brewer Gave San Antonio 71 Games

Ron Brewer played 46 games for the Spurs after the trade in 1980-81 and another 25 in 1981-82.

That gives San Antonio 71 regular-season games from the original return. Brewer scored 425 points in his first Spurs stint and 444 more in the second.

On December 23, 1981, San Antonio traded Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash to Cleveland for Mike Mitchell and Roger Phegley.

The later Mitchell return matters, but this review does not assign it entirely to Brewer because San Antonio also surrendered Johnson and cash.

Why Portland Wins

San Antonio received a useful scoring guard for 71 games and later used him as part of a package for Mike Mitchell, one of the better scorers of the era.

Portland received 42 Gale games, two later second-round assets from Gale's re-trade and a first-round pick that was converted into Kenny Carr.

Carr's 316 Portland games alone exceed the direct playing value San Antonio received from Brewer, and Gale's later draft return widens the gap further.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win, A+/B. Portland receives an A+ because the first-round branch became 316 Kenny Carr games while Gale also returned two second-round picks. San Antonio receives a B because Brewer gave the Spurs 71 games and remained part of a later multi-asset trade for Mike Mitchell and Roger Phegley.

perspectives.analysis:
The Deal Was McKinney for Nicks

Denver and Utah's transaction ledgers agree on the December 22, 1980 exchange. Denver sent rookie guard Carl Nicks to the Jazz for Billy McKinney.

McKinney Became a Three-Season Denver Guard

McKinney played 49 games for Denver after the trade in 1980-81 and averaged 10.7 points and 4.1 assists.

He returned for 81 games in 1981-82, starting 27 and averaging 10.8 points and 4.2 assists. He then played 68 games with 38 starts in 1982-83, averaging 9.8 points and 4.2 assists.

That gives Denver 198 regular-season games from McKinney across parts of three seasons.

Denver Still Retained Trade Value

On October 4, 1983, Denver traded McKinney to San Diego for Richard Anderson.

Anderson played 78 games for the Nuggets in 1983-84, starting 17 and averaging 8.5 points, 5.2 rebounds and 2.5 assists.

Because McKinney was the only Denver asset in that later trade, Anderson's 78-game season is a clean downstream return from the original McKinney branch.

Nicks Gave Utah Two Useful Seasons

Carl Nicks played 40 games for Utah after the trade in 1980-81, averaging 6.3 points in 15.4 minutes.

He stayed for the full 1981-82 season and appeared in 80 games, averaging 7.4 points and 2.0 rebounds.

That gives the Jazz 120 regular-season games from Nicks over parts of two seasons. He later played nine games for Cleveland, but Utah did not receive a documented transaction return when his Jazz tenure ended.

Why Denver Gets the Edge

Utah received a legitimate rotation guard for 120 games, so this was not a failed trade.

Denver received 198 McKinney games across three seasons, including meaningful starting work, then converted him into Anderson for another 78 games.

That combination gives the Nuggets more direct playing value and a stronger downstream branch without relying on speculative pick chains.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A-/B. Denver receives an A- for 198 McKinney games plus 78 Anderson games from the clean downstream trade. Utah receives a B for 120 Nicks games over parts of two seasons.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Deal Swapped Two 1980 First-Round Rookies

Atlanta and Washington transaction ledgers agree on the January 17, 1981 exchange. The Hawks sent Don Collins to the Bullets for Wes Matthews.

Matthews immediately became Atlanta's primary point guard. He played 34 games after the trade and averaged 12.5 points, 6.2 assists and 32.5 minutes.

Matthews Gave Atlanta 145 Regular-Season Games

Matthews returned for 47 games in 1981-82, starting five, and averaged 6.9 points with 3.0 assists.

He then played 64 games in 1982-83 and averaged 6.9 points with 3.9 assists. Across the three Atlanta seasons, Matthews appeared in 145 regular-season games.

That is a useful multi-year return, even though his role declined after the initial half-season.

Atlanta Later Converted Matthews Into a Second-Round Asset

On October 6, 1983, Atlanta traded Matthews and Kevin Figaro to San Diego for a 1986 second-round pick.

Atlanta eventually used that pick at No. 32 on Cedric Henderson, who played eight NBA regular-season games in his career.

This review does not credit the full Henderson return to Matthews because Figaro was also included in the trade. The branch still shows that Matthews retained some transaction value after his Hawks playing tenure.

Collins Stayed Longer in Washington

Collins played 34 games for Washington after the trade in 1980-81 and averaged 9.8 points.

He then played 79 games in 1981-82, starting 18 and averaging 10.0 points. Collins added 65 games in 1982-83, starting 21 and averaging a career-best 11.8 points.

That gives Washington 178 regular-season games from Collins across parts of three seasons, 33 more than Matthews gave Atlanta.

Washington waived Collins on October 27, 1983. Golden State signed him later that year, so the Bullets did not receive a documented downstream asset when his tenure ended.

Why Washington Gets the Slight Edge

Both teams received productive rotation players for multiple seasons. Matthews had the stronger immediate post-trade role, while Collins provided the longer Washington tenure and more total games.

Atlanta retained a small downstream branch through the 1986 second-round pick, but that later transaction also required Kevin Figaro and ultimately produced only eight NBA games from Cedric Henderson.

Washington's 178 Collins games therefore outweigh Atlanta's 145 Matthews games plus the diluted late pick return by a modest margin.

Final Verdict

Slight Bullets Edge, B+/B. Washington receives a B+ for 178 Collins games across parts of three seasons. Atlanta receives a B for 145 Matthews games and a later shared-asset second-round return.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded Chad Kinch and a 1985 first-round pick to Dallas on February 7, 1981 for Geoff Huston and a 1983 third-round pick. Huston became a four-season Cavaliers point guard, playing 260 regular-season games after the trade and starting 178 over his final three Cleveland seasons. The third-round pick became Larry Anderson, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Dallas received only 12 games from Kinch, but the first-rounder became No. 8 Detlef Schrempf, who played 264 regular-season games and 29 playoff games for the Mavericks before Dallas later packaged him with a second-rounder for Herb Williams. Dallas wins on the premium pick, though Cleveland's Huston return was substantial.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Was a Player Swap Plus a Major Pick Gap

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland sending Chad Kinch and a 1985 first-round pick to Dallas for Geoff Huston and a 1983 third-round pick.

The first-rounder eventually became No. 8 Detlef Schrempf. The incoming Cleveland third-rounder became No. 56 Larry Anderson.

Huston Gave Cleveland Four Seasons of Real Point-Guard Value

Huston played 25 games for Cleveland after the trade in 1980-81. He then became a major part of the Cavaliers' backcourt.

He played 78 games with 43 starts in 1981-82 and averaged 10.3 points with 7.6 assists. In 1982-83 he played 80 games, started 79 and averaged 12.2 points with 6.1 assists.

Huston added 77 games and 56 starts in 1983-84. Across the post-trade Cleveland tenure, he appeared in 260 regular-season games.

That is enough direct value to prevent this from being graded as a catastrophic Cleveland return.

The Third-Round Pick Produced No NBA Games

Cleveland used the No. 56 pick in 1983 on Larry Anderson. Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season games for Anderson.

The Cavaliers later traded Anderson and Les Craft to San Diego for a 1985 second-round pick used on Calvin Duncan. Duncan also played no NBA regular-season games, and Cleveland later moved his rights with Charles Oakley in a larger draft-night trade.

Because both later branches required additional assets, this review does not assign the full downstream results to the original third-round pick.

Dallas Got the Better Long-Term Asset in Schrempf

Chad Kinch played only 12 games for Dallas after the trade and never appeared in another NBA regular-season game.

The 1985 first-rounder was the important asset. Dallas selected Schrempf at No. 8 and received 264 regular-season games over parts of four seasons.

He also appeared in 29 playoff games for the Mavericks, including 15 during the 1988 run to the Western Conference Finals. His biggest individual awards came later with Indiana and Seattle, so this review does not credit those later honors to Dallas.

Dallas Traded Schrempf Before His Peak

On February 21, 1989, Dallas traded Schrempf and a 1990 second-round pick to Indiana for Herb Williams.

That return matters, but Schrempf was not the only outgoing asset. This review therefore treats the Williams trade as a diluted downstream branch rather than pretending Schrempf alone produced the entire return.

Why Dallas Wins Without Erasing Huston's Value

Cleveland received 260 Huston games and several seasons of starting point-guard production. That is a real return and much stronger than the old shorthand grade implied.

Dallas, however, turned the first-round pick into 264 Schrempf games plus meaningful playoff participation before retaining some later trade value. Kinch contributed little, but the premium pick still created the stronger realized outcome.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win, A/B. Dallas receives an A for four seasons of Schrempf, including 29 playoff games, plus a later shared-asset trade return. Cleveland receives a B for 260 Huston games, while the third-round branch produced no direct NBA player value.

Cleveland used the No. 56 pick in 1983 on Larry Anderson. Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season games for Anderson.

The Cavaliers later traded Anderson and Les Craft to San Diego for a 1985 second-round pick used on Calvin Duncan. Duncan also played no NBA regular-season games, and Cleveland later moved his rights with Charles Oakley in a larger draft-night trade.

Because both later branches required additional assets, this review does not assign the full downstream results to the original third-round pick.

Dallas Got the Better Long-Term Asset in Schrempf

Chad Kinch played only 12 games for Dallas after the trade and never appeared in another NBA regular-season game.

The 1985 first-rounder was the important asset. Dallas selected Schrempf at No. 8 and received 264 regular-season games over parts of four seasons.

He also appeared in 29 playoff games for the Mavericks, including 15 during the 1988 run to the Western Conference Finals. His biggest individual awards came later with Indiana and Seattle, so this review does not credit those later honors to Dallas.

Dallas Traded Schrempf Before His Peak

On February 21, 1989, Dallas traded Schrempf and a 1990 second-round pick to Indiana for Herb Williams.

That return matters, but Schrempf was not the only outgoing asset. This review therefore treats the Williams trade as a diluted downstream branch rather than pretending Schrempf alone produced the entire return.

Why Dallas Wins Without Erasing Huston's Value

Cleveland received 260 Huston games and several seasons of starting point-guard production. That is a real return and much stronger than the old shorthand grade implied.

Dallas, however, turned the first-round pick into 264 Schrempf games plus meaningful playoff participation before retaining some later trade value. Kinch contributed little, but the premium pick still created the stronger realized outcome.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win, A/B. Dallas receives an A for four seasons of Schrempf, including 29 playoff games, plus a later shared-asset trade return. Cleveland receives a B for 260 Huston games, while the third-round branch produced no direct NBA player value.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded veteran guard Randy Smith to New York on May 20, 1981 for a 1981 first-round pick. Smith played all 82 games for the Knicks in 1981-82, starting 40 and averaging 10.0 points and 3.1 assists before leaving as a veteran free agent the following fall. Cleveland did not use the No. 17 pick on Kevin Loder. Nineteen days after acquiring it, the Cavaliers sent that exact first-rounder to Kansas City as compensation for signing Scott Wedman. Wedman played 89 Cleveland games, then was traded straight up to Boston for Darren Tillis and a 1983 first-round pick. Cleveland's clean downstream chain gives it the stronger realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Was Smith for a 1981 First

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland trading Randy Smith to New York on May 20, 1981 for a 1981 first-round pick. The selection landed at No. 17 and was later used by Kansas City on Kevin Loder.

That draft name can be misleading if the transaction is evaluated only from the final pick outcome. Cleveland never drafted Loder.

New York Got One Full Season From Smith

Smith played all 82 games for the Knicks in 1981-82 and started 40. He averaged 10.0 points, 3.1 assists and 1.9 rebounds in 24.8 minutes.

That was a useful veteran season, especially because New York received immediate rotation value instead of waiting on a draft choice.

Smith did not play another game for the Knicks. San Diego signed him as a veteran free agent on October 28, 1982. Basketball-Reference notes that New York received compensation, but the public transaction entry does not identify a concrete asset, so this review does not invent or score an unknown return.

Cleveland Immediately Used the Pick on Scott Wedman

On June 8, 1981, only nineteen days after the Smith trade, Cleveland sent the incoming first-round pick to Kansas City as compensation for signing Scott Wedman as a veteran free agent.

That creates a direct downstream branch from the Smith trade. The Cavaliers did not merely hold abstract draft value; they used the exact asset to acquire a proven starting forward.

Wedman played 54 games for Cleveland in 1981-82, starting 39 and averaging 10.9 points with 5.6 rebounds.

He then played 35 games in 1982-83, starting all 35 and averaging 18.1 points and 5.9 rebounds before Cleveland moved him in January. That gives the Cavaliers 89 regular-season games from Wedman.

Wedman Then Produced Another Clean Trade Return

On January 14, 1983, Cleveland traded Wedman to Boston for Darren Tillis and a 1983 first-round pick.

Because Wedman was the only Cleveland asset in that transaction, the incoming Tillis-plus-first package is a legitimate clean downstream return from the original Smith pick branch.

Tillis later went to Golden State straight up for a 1986 second-round pick that became Johnny Newman. Cleveland's 1983 first-rounder was later included with James Edwards in a larger Phoenix trade, so this review does not assign that whole deeper package to the Smith branch.

Why Cleveland Gets the Edge

New York received a complete 82-game season from Smith and got useful veteran guard play immediately. That is a respectable return.

Cleveland transformed the first-rounder into 89 Wedman games, including a strong 18.1-point partial season, then converted Wedman directly into Tillis plus another first-round pick.

The Knicks' unidentified free-agent compensation cannot be scored. Cleveland's documented chain is both longer and stronger.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A-/B. Cleveland receives an A- for converting the first-rounder into Wedman, 89 games of production and a later clean two-asset trade return. New York receives a B for Smith's full 82-game season.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana acquired veteran center Tom Owens from Portland on June 5, 1981 for an unprotected 1984 first-round pick. Owens played 74 games for the Pacers in 1981-82, starting 40 and averaging 10.5 points and 5.0 rebounds, then Indiana traded him to Detroit for a 1984 second-round pick. Portland's incoming first became the No. 2 selection in 1984 and Sam Bowie, who played 139 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers before being packaged with another first-round pick for Buck Williams. The grade does not rely on a Michael Jordan counterfactual: Portland simply received a premium No. 2 asset and the stronger realized value.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Bought One Owens Season With an Unprotected First

Basketball-Reference and Portland executive records identify the June 5, 1981 deal as Tom Owens to Indiana for the Pacers' unprotected 1984 first-round pick.

That pick eventually landed at No. 2. This review evaluates the actual asset and the actual player selected, not a hypothetical Michael Jordan outcome.

Owens Gave Indiana 74 Useful Games

Owens played 74 games for the Pacers in 1981-82 and started 40. He averaged 10.5 points, 5.0 rebounds and 1.7 assists in 21.6 minutes.

That was legitimate rotation and starting value for a team trying to add veteran frontcourt help. Indiana did not get nothing for the pick.

Owens did not stay beyond the season. On September 22, 1982, Indiana traded him to Detroit for a 1984 second-round pick.

The Pacers Preserved a Smaller Downstream Asset

Indiana later sent that second-rounder to Kansas City on September 17, 1983 for Brook Steppe.

Kansas City subsequently included the pick in a larger trade with Chicago, and the Bulls used the No. 43 selection on Greg Wiltjer. Wiltjer never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

For Indiana, the relevant realized branch is Owens' 74 games plus the later ability to convert his rights into another trade asset. That is meaningful, but it is far below the value of the first-rounder surrendered.

Portland's Pick Became No. 2 Sam Bowie

The Pacers' 1984 first became the No. 2 selection. Portland used it on Sam Bowie.

Bowie played 76 games as a rookie in 1984-85, starting 62. He then played 38 games in 1985-86, five in 1986-87 and 20 in 1988-89 after losing extensive time to leg injuries.

Across his Portland tenure, Bowie appeared in 139 regular-season games.

Those injuries prevented the pick from becoming the outcome Portland hoped for, but 139 games from a No. 2 selection still exceeds Indiana's direct return from Owens.

Bowie Later Became Part of the Buck Williams Package

On June 24, 1989, Portland traded Bowie and its own 1989 first-round pick, No. 12, to New Jersey for Buck Williams.

Because Portland included another first-round pick, this review does not attribute the entire Williams return to Bowie. The later transaction does show that the Bowie asset still carried trade value when his Portland tenure ended.

Why Portland Wins Without Using the Jordan Argument

This trade is often remembered because the 1984 pick became No. 2 in the draft that included Michael Jordan. That counterfactual is unnecessary.

Indiana exchanged an unprotected future first for 74 Owens games and a later second-round branch. Portland received an actual No. 2 pick, got 139 Bowie games and later used Bowie as one component of a major veteran trade.

The premium draft asset alone makes the original cost too high for Indiana's realized return.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win, A/C+. Portland receives an A for securing a No. 2 selection, 139 Bowie games and a later shared-asset trade branch. Indiana receives a C+ for one useful Owens season and a smaller downstream second-round asset.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded Cliff Robinson to Kansas City on June 8, 1981 for Otis Birdsong and a 1981 second-round pick. Birdsong became a seven-season Nets guard, playing 375 regular-season games and making the 1984 All-Star team while averaging 15.9 points during his New Jersey tenure. The incoming second-rounder was not used by the Nets; it was immediately routed to Washington to complete the 1980 Roger Phegley trade. Kansas City received 38 Robinson games at 20.2 points and 8.5 rebounds, then traded him for Reggie Johnson, who played 81 Kings games before being moved for cash. Both sides realized value, but Birdsong made this a clear Nets win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Trade Was Robinson for Birdsong and a Second

New Jersey and Kansas City transaction ledgers agree on the June 8, 1981 exchange. The Nets sent Cliff Robinson to the Kings for Otis Birdsong and a 1981 second-round pick.

The pick later became the No. 44 selection associated with Steve Lingenfelter, but that label needs important routing context.

Birdsong Became a Seven-Season Net

Birdsong arrived after an All-NBA Second Team season with Kansas City and immediately became a major part of New Jersey's rebuild.

He played 37 games in 1981-82, then 62 in 1982-83, 69 in 1983-84, 56 in 1984-85, 77 in 1985-86, seven in 1986-87 and 67 in 1987-88.

That is 375 regular-season games for the Nets across seven seasons.

Birdsong averaged 19.8 points in 1983-84 and 20.6 in 1984-85. He made the All-Star team during his New Jersey tenure and became one of the core guards on the Nets teams that reached five consecutive postseasons after the trade.

The Second-Round Pick Was Immediately Routed to Washington

The Nets did not select Steve Lingenfelter with the incoming No. 44 pick.

New Jersey had already promised that exact 1981 second-rounder to Washington in the February 4, 1980 Roger Phegley trade. Contemporary Nets transaction history shows that after obtaining the pick from Kansas City, New Jersey sent it to the Bullets to complete the earlier obligation.

Washington then used No. 44 on Lingenfelter. This review therefore treats the pick as an obligation-clearing asset for New Jersey, not as a drafted player return.

Robinson Gave Kansas City Strong Short-Term Production

Robinson played 38 games for Kansas City in 1981-82, starting 30. He averaged 20.2 points, 8.5 rebounds and 1.6 blocks in 32.3 minutes.

That is a much better direct return than the old shorthand grade suggested. Robinson was a productive 21-year-old forward during his brief Kings tenure.

Kansas City Then Converted Robinson Into Reggie Johnson

summary: Atlanta and Chicago swapped 1981 first-round positions on June 8, 1981, with the Hawks moving to No. 4 for Al Wood and adding the No. 38 second-round pick while the Bulls received No. 6 Orlando Woolridge plus Atlanta's 1982 second-rounder. The attached 1982 first-round swap option was not exercised. Wood played only 19 Hawks games before Atlanta packaged him with Charlie Criss for Freeman Williams, while Clyde Bradshaw never played an NBA regular-season game. Woolridge played 354 regular-season games for Chicago over five seasons and developed into a 20-point scorer. Ricky Frazier never reached the NBA. Chicago won the exchange decisively.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Deal Was More Than a Simple Pick Swap

Atlanta received the No. 4 pick in 1981, the No. 38 pick and Chicago's option involving a 1982 first-round swap. Chicago received the No. 6 pick, Atlanta's 1982 second-rounder and the same contractual swap structure.

The 1982 first-round option was never exercised, so this review assigns it no realized basketball value.

Atlanta Used No. 4 on Al Wood

The Hawks selected Al Wood fourth overall, but his Atlanta tenure was extremely short.

Wood played 19 games for the Hawks in 1981-82, all off the bench. He averaged 4.8 points and 2.3 rebounds in 12.5 minutes.

On January 20, 1982, Atlanta traded Wood and Charlie Criss to San Diego for Freeman Williams. Because Criss was also included, this review does not credit the entire Williams return to Wood.

Williams played 23 Atlanta games after the trade and averaged 4.8 points in 8.2 minutes. The shared downstream branch therefore added only limited realized value.

The Extra Atlanta Second-Rounder Produced No NBA Games

Atlanta used the No. 38 pick on Clyde Bradshaw.

Basketball-Reference lists Bradshaw as a Hawks draft pick but records no NBA regular-season career. That makes the second-round component a zero-game outcome.

Chicago Turned No. 6 Into Five Woolridge Seasons

The Bulls selected Orlando Woolridge sixth overall.

Woolridge played 75 games as a rookie, then 57 in 1982-83, 75 in 1983-84, 77 in 1984-85 and 70 in 1985-86. That is 354 regular-season games for Chicago over five seasons.

His production rose steadily. Woolridge averaged 19.3 points in 1983-84, 22.9 in 1984-85 and 20.7 in 1985-86.

That long starting-caliber tenure is the dominant realized asset in the trade.

Chicago's 1982 Second-Rounder Did Not Add NBA Value

The Bulls used Atlanta's 1982 second-round pick at No. 26 on Ricky Frazier.

Frazier never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The second-round asset therefore does not materially widen Chicago's edge beyond Woolridge.

Why Chicago Wins Decisively

Atlanta received only 19 Wood games, a no-game second-round pick and a diluted later return involving Freeman Williams. The unexercised 1982 swap added nothing.

Chicago received 354 Woolridge games and multiple seasons of high-level scoring from the No. 6 pick. The Bulls' other second-round asset produced no NBA games, but they did not need it to win the deal.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, A/C-. Chicago receives an A for five Woolridge seasons and 354 regular-season games. Atlanta receives a C- because Wood lasted only 19 games, Bradshaw never played in the NBA and the later Wood trade required another outgoing player.

perspectives.analysis:
The Deal Completed Cleveland's Scott Wedman Signing

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland signing Scott Wedman as a veteran free agent on June 8, 1981 and sending Kansas City a 1981 first-round pick as compensation. The frozen canonical package also carries the Kings' right-of-first-refusal consideration and the 1981 second-round pick that became No. 36 Ray Blume back to Cleveland.

The first-round pick had arrived in Cleveland only nineteen days earlier in the Randy Smith trade with New York. Kansas City used it at No. 17 on Kevin Loder.

Wedman Gave Cleveland 89 Games and a Strong Final Half-Season

Wedman played 54 games for Cleveland in 1981-82, starting 39. He averaged 10.9 points, 5.6 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 30.3 minutes.

He returned for 35 games in 1982-83, started all 35 and averaged 18.1 points with 5.9 rebounds.

That gives Cleveland 89 regular-season games from the veteran forward, with the best production coming just before his departure.

Wedman Then Produced a Clean Two-Asset Trade Return

On January 14, 1983, Cleveland traded Wedman straight up to Boston for Darren Tillis and a 1983 first-round pick.

Because Wedman was the only Cleveland asset in that transaction, the Tillis-plus-first package is a clean downstream return from the original Kansas City compensation deal.

This review stops short of assigning every later branch back to Wedman. Tillis was later traded separately, while the first-round pick was eventually bundled with James Edwards in another transaction.

The No. 36 Pick Was Immediately Reused

Cleveland did not draft Ray Blume.

The Cavaliers sent that exact 1981 second-round pick, together with a separate 1982 second-round pick, to Indiana as compensation for signing James Edwards. Indiana then selected Blume at No. 36.

Edwards played 92 Cleveland regular-season games across parts of two seasons, including 77 starts in 1981-82 at 16.7 points and 7.5 rebounds.

This review does not credit all of Edwards' Cleveland value to the No. 36 pick because Cleveland also sent another second-rounder. The important point is that the incoming pick immediately became useful transaction currency rather than expiring unused.

Kansas City Got 147 Games From Kevin Loder

Loder played 71 games as a rookie for Kansas City and averaged 6.9 points. He added 66 games in 1982-83 at 5.1 points per game.

He played 10 more Kings games in 1983-84 before Kansas City waived him on November 22, 1983. That makes 147 regular-season games for the franchise.

Loder later signed with San Diego as a free agent, so Kansas City did not receive a documented transaction return when his tenure ended.

Why Cleveland Gets the Edge

Kansas City turned the first-round pick into three seasons of rotation depth, so the Kings did receive legitimate value.

Cleveland received the better peak player in Wedman, a clean later two-asset trade return from him and a second-round pick that helped complete the James Edwards signing.

The Cavaliers' total branch is stronger even after discounting the Edwards return because another second-round pick was required.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A/B. Cleveland receives an A for 89 Wedman games, the later Tillis-plus-first return and useful transaction value from the No. 36 pick. Kansas City receives a B for 147 Loder games across parts of three seasons.

The Cavaliers' total branch is stronger even after discounting the Edwards return because another second-round pick was required.

perspectives.analysis:
The Compensation Followed Edwards' May 25 Signing

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Indiana and league transaction ledgers date James Edwards' veteran free-agent signing to May 25, 1981. The frozen canonical record uses June 8 for the compensation package, and contemporary draft-history records likewise describe Indiana as acquiring the two picks on June 8 as compensation for that May signing.

This review preserves the canonical record date but makes the underlying signing timeline explicit rather than treating June 8 as the date Edwards first joined Cleveland.

Edwards Gave Cleveland 92 Games

Edwards became Cleveland's starting center immediately. In 1981-82 he played 77 games, started 75 and averaged 16.7 points, 7.5 rebounds and 1.5 blocks in 33.0 minutes.

He returned for 15 more Cavaliers games in 1982-83, starting eight and averaging 12.3 points and 6.4 rebounds.

That gives Cleveland 92 regular-season games from the free-agent acquisition, with the large majority of the value arriving in his first season.

Edwards Also Retained Trade Value

On February 7, 1983, Cleveland traded Edwards and a 1983 first-round pick to Phoenix for Jeff Cook, a 1983 first-round pick and a 1983 third-round pick.

Because Cleveland included another first-round asset, this review does not attribute the entire Phoenix return to Edwards. The transaction still shows that Edwards retained real value when his Cavaliers tenure ended.

Indiana Did Not Keep Ray Blume

Indiana used the No. 36 pick on Ray Blume, but the Pacers traded his draft rights the next day with a separate 1982 second-round pick to Chicago for Mike Olliver.

Olliver never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Since Indiana had to include another future second in the deal, this review does not assign the entire Olliver return to the Blume pick.

Blume later played 49 games for Chicago, but those games belong to the Bulls' side of the later trade, not to Indiana's realized return here.

Guy Morgan Played Only Eight Pacers Games

Indiana used the other incoming pick at No. 40 in 1982 on Guy Morgan.

Morgan appeared in eight regular-season games for the Pacers in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 1.9 points and 2.1 rebounds in 5.8 minutes.

That was his entire NBA career.

Why Cleveland Wins

The Cavaliers received 92 Edwards games and a full season of starting-center production at 16.7 points and 7.5 rebounds per game. He also remained valuable enough to be included in a later first-round-pick exchange with Phoenix.

Indiana's two-pick return produced only eight direct Pacers games from Morgan. The Blume pick became trade currency, but it had to be paired with another second-round pick for a player who never appeared in the NBA.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A-/C. Cleveland receives an A- for 92 productive Edwards games and retained trade value. Indiana receives a C because the compensation package produced only eight direct games plus limited shared downstream utility from the Blume rights.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State acquired veteran guard Mike Gale from Portland on June 8, 1981 for two future second-round picks. Gale started 70 of 75 Warriors games in 1981-82, averaging 5.6 points, 3.5 assists and 1.6 steals before his NBA career ended. Portland used the 1982 pick on Audie Norris, who played 187 Trail Blazers games over three seasons, and the 1985 pick on Mike Smrek. Portland immediately traded Smrek's rights to Chicago for Ben Coleman and Ken Johnson; Johnson then played 64 games for the Blazers while Coleman never appeared for them. Portland's two-pick return produced the stronger realized value.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Bought One Season of a Veteran Starter

Basketball-Reference records Portland trading Mike Gale to Golden State on June 8, 1981 for a 1982 second-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick.

Gale became a regular starter immediately. In 1981-82 he played 75 games, started 70 and averaged 5.6 points, 3.5 assists and 1.6 steals in 23.9 minutes.

That season was his only year with Golden State and the final season of his NBA career. The Warriors therefore received one full year of useful backcourt play but no downstream transaction return.

Portland Used the First Pick on Audie Norris

The 1982 second-round pick landed at No. 37 and became Audie Norris.

Norris played three NBA seasons, all with Portland. His career total was 187 regular-season games, making this the most durable direct asset created by the trade.

He never became a major scorer, but he provided three years of frontcourt depth before becoming a free agent in 1985.

The 1985 Pick Became Mike Smrek

Portland's second incoming pick landed at No. 25 in 1985 and became Mike Smrek.

Smrek never played a regular-season game for the Trail Blazers. On draft night, Portland traded him to Chicago for Ben Coleman and Ken Johnson.

Because Smrek was the only Portland asset in that exchange, this review treats the Coleman-Johnson package as a clean downstream return from this branch.

Ken Johnson Added 64 More Portland Games

Coleman never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for Portland and was waived in November 1985.

Johnson, however, played 64 games for the Trail Blazers in 1985-86. He averaged 4.1 points and 3.8 rebounds in 12.7 minutes.

That turns the Smrek branch into another season of usable depth even though Smrek himself never suited up for Portland.

Why Portland Wins

Golden State received a legitimate short-term starter. Gale played 75 games, started 70 and gave the Warriors steady veteran guard minutes for one season.

Portland converted the two outgoing picks into 187 Norris games plus a Smrek rights trade that yielded 64 Johnson games. Coleman added no Portland games, but the two productive branches still combine for substantially more realized tenure than Gale's one season.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win, A-/B-. Portland receives an A- for 187 Norris games plus a clean Smrek-to-Johnson branch that added 64 more games. Golden State receives a B- for one solid season and 70 starts from Gale, but no value beyond 1981-82.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston reacquired franchise icon Elvin Hayes from Washington on June 8, 1981 for two second-round picks. Hayes played 244 regular-season games over three final Rockets seasons, starting all 82 games in 1981-82 and averaging 16.1 points and 9.1 rebounds before retiring in 1984. Washington used the 1981 pick on Charles Davis, who played 178 Bullets games across parts of four seasons. The 1983 second-rounder was later sent with a separate 1985 second to Chicago as compensation for Ricky Sobers, so its downstream value was shared. Washington received useful depth, but Houston captured the stronger realized return.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Brought Hayes Back for Two Second-Round Picks

Basketball-Reference records Washington trading Elvin Hayes to Houston on June 8, 1981 for a 1981 second-round pick and a 1983 second-round pick.

For Houston, the transaction brought back one of the franchise's defining early stars. Hayes was 35 when the deal happened, so the value case is about productive late-career years rather than a long prime.

Hayes Played 244 More Rockets Games

Hayes started all 82 games in 1981-82. He averaged 16.1 points, 9.1 rebounds and 1.3 blocks in 37.0 minutes.

He remained a major rotation player in 1982-83, appearing in 81 games and starting 43 while averaging 12.9 points and 7.6 rebounds.

Hayes then played another 81 games in 1983-84, mostly as a reserve, before retiring. Across the three-season return stint, he appeared in 244 regular-season games for Houston.

There was no later player trade to extend the Hayes branch because his NBA career ended with the Rockets.

Washington Used the 1981 Pick on Charles Davis

The first incoming second-round pick landed at No. 35 and became Charles Davis.

Davis played 54 games for Washington as a rookie, then 74 in 1982-83 and 46 in 1983-84. He appeared in four more games early in 1984-85 before the Bullets waived him on November 6.

That gives Washington 178 regular-season games from the direct 1981 draft return. Davis never became a high-volume scorer, but he supplied several seasons of bench depth.

The 1983 Pick Became Shared Compensation Currency

Washington did not use the second incoming pick directly.

On January 24, 1983, the Bullets sent that 1983 second-round pick plus a separate 1985 second-round pick to Chicago as compensation for signing veteran free agent Ricky Sobers.

Chicago later used the 1983 selection at No. 25 on Sidney Lowe. Because Washington had to include another second-rounder in the Sobers compensation package, this review does not assign all of Sobers' Bullets value to this single pick.

The important realized point is that the pick retained transaction utility rather than expiring unused.

Why Houston Wins

Washington received a respectable return for an aging star. Davis alone provided 178 games, and the other second-round pick contributed to a later free-agent compensation package.

Houston still received the stronger basketball outcome. Hayes supplied 244 games, remained a full-time starter in the first season and produced two useful veteran years before transitioning to a reserve role.

The gap is not a blowout because Washington extracted real value from both assets. Hayes' direct production, however, is the strongest isolated branch in the deal.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, A/B. Houston receives an A for 244 Hayes games and two productive late-career seasons. Washington receives a B for 178 Charles Davis games plus shared downstream transaction value from the 1983 second-round pick.

The 1983 Pick Became Shared Compensation Currency

Washington did not use the second incoming pick directly.

On January 24, 1983, the Bullets sent that 1983 second-round pick plus a separate 1985 second-round pick to Chicago as compensation for signing veteran free agent Ricky Sobers.

Chicago later used the 1983 selection at No. 25 on Sidney Lowe. Because Washington had to include another second-rounder in the Sobers compensation package, this review does not assign all of Sobers' Bullets value to this single pick.

The important realized point is that the pick retained transaction utility rather than expiring unused.

Why Houston Wins

Washington received a respectable return for an aging star. Davis alone provided 178 games, and the other second-round pick contributed to a later free-agent compensation package.

Houston still received the stronger basketball outcome. Hayes supplied 244 games, remained a full-time starter in the first season and produced two useful veteran years before transitioning to a reserve role.

The gap is not a blowout because Washington extracted real value from both assets. Hayes' direct production, however, is the strongest isolated branch in the deal.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, A/B. Houston receives an A for 244 Hayes games and two productive late-career seasons. Washington receives a B for 178 Charles Davis games plus shared downstream transaction value from the 1983 second-round pick.

Bradley played 64 Suns games before leaving as a veteran free agent. Indiana got no NBA games from No. 37 Al Leslie and 63 games from No. 43 Jose Slaughter, but the relinquished swap became enormous: Indiana's 1983 first landed No. 2 and became Steve Stipanovich, who played 403 Pacers games, while Phoenix's original first landed No. 21. Preserving that premium pick makes Indiana the clear hindsight winner.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Trade Included More Than Two Second-Round Picks

Basketball-Reference records Phoenix acquiring Dudley Bradley from Indiana on June 8, 1981 for a 1981 second-round pick, a 1982 second-round pick and the Suns relinquishing their right to swap 1983 first-round picks with the Pacers.

That last term is the decisive part of the hindsight evaluation. It looked like optional future protection in 1981, but the 1983 draft positions turned it into premium realized value.

Bradley Gave Phoenix One Season

Bradley played 64 games for Phoenix in 1981-82, starting three and averaging 5.1 points, 1.4 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 14.6 minutes.

He left after the season and signed with Chicago as a veteran free agent on October 2, 1982. Phoenix's transaction ledger says the Suns received compensation, but the public Basketball-Reference entry renders that return only as FROM_TRADE rather than identifying a specific asset.

This review therefore does not invent or score an unknown compensation return.

Al Leslie Produced No NBA Games

Indiana used the 1981 second-round pick at No. 37 on Al Leslie.

Basketball-Reference lists Leslie as a Pacers draft pick but records no NBA regular-season statistics. That branch produced no direct NBA playing value.

Jose Slaughter Played 63 Pacers Games

The 1982 second-round pick landed at No. 43 and became Jose Slaughter.

Slaughter played 63 games for Indiana in 1982-83, starting once and averaging 3.6 points in 8.2 minutes. That was his only NBA season.

On its own, the two-pick portion of Indiana's return would have been modest.

The Relinquished 1983 Swap Became the Real Prize

Phoenix also gave up its contractual right to swap first-round picks with Indiana in the 1983 draft.

Indiana's own 1983 first ultimately landed at No. 2. The Pacers used it on Steve Stipanovich, who played all five of his NBA seasons for Indiana.

Stipanovich appeared in 403 regular-season games, started 365 and averaged 13.2 points, 7.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists for his Pacers career.

Phoenix's original 1983 first ultimately landed at No. 21, the pick that became Greg Kite after later transactions. Because Phoenix had surrendered the swap option two years earlier, Indiana retained control of the No. 2 position instead of being exposed to a No. 2-for-No. 21 exchange.

This review treats that protected draft position as realized value of the relinquishment clause, not as a speculative counterfactual player trade.

Why Indiana Wins

Phoenix received 64 games of useful reserve defense from Bradley, and there may have been later free-agent compensation that the public ledger does not identify clearly enough to score.

Indiana received 63 Slaughter games and no NBA production from Leslie. More importantly, the Pacers eliminated a future swap obligation that would have attached to the No. 2 pick in 1983.

The retained pick became Stipanovich and produced 403 games, 365 starts and five seasons of starting-center value. That branch overwhelms the one-season Bradley return.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, A+/C+. Indiana receives an A+ because surrender of the swap right preserved the No. 2 pick that became Steve Stipanovich, in addition to 63 Slaughter games. Phoenix receives a C+ for 64 Bradley games, with unidentified free-agent compensation left unscored.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded veteran scorer Mike Newlin to New York on June 10, 1981 for rookie guard Mike Woodson. Newlin gave the Knicks 76 games and 32 starts in 1981-82, averaging 9.3 points and 2.2 assists in the final season of his NBA career. Woodson played only seven games for the Nets before New Jersey packaged him with a 1982 first-round pick to Kansas City for Sam Lacey. Lacey then played 54 Nets games, but the incoming center cannot be credited entirely to Woodson because the first-round pick was a substantial additional asset. New York produced the clearer direct return.
perspectives.analysis:
New York Received a Full Season from Newlin

Basketball-Reference's Nets and Knicks transaction ledgers agree on the June 10, 1981 trade: New Jersey sent Mike Newlin to New York for Mike Woodson.

Newlin immediately became a useful Knicks rotation guard. In 1981-82 he played 76 games, started 32 and averaged 9.3 points, 2.2 assists and 1.6 rebounds in 19.8 minutes.

That season was the final year of Newlin's NBA career, so New York's realized return is easy to isolate: 76 games and more than 1,500 minutes of veteran backcourt play.

Woodson Played Only Seven Nets Games

Woodson's New Jersey tenure was much shorter. He appeared in seven games in 1981-82, all off the bench, totaling 145 minutes and 83 points.

The Nets did not simply lose him for nothing, however. On November 12, 1981, New Jersey traded Woodson and a 1982 first-round pick to Kansas City for veteran center Sam Lacey.

That later transaction gives the Woodson branch some downstream value, but it was not a one-for-one conversion. The Nets also surrendered a first-round pick, which later became the No. 17 selection used on Brook Steppe.

Lacey Added 54 Nets Games

Lacey played 54 regular-season games for New Jersey after the November deal. He started six and averaged 2.9 points, 1.9 rebounds and 1.4 assists in 12.0 minutes.

Because Woodson was packaged with a meaningful first-round asset, this review treats Lacey as shared downstream value rather than crediting all 54 games to Woodson.

That distinction prevents the Nets side from being overstated. Woodson's direct contribution was only seven games, and the later package required another premium asset to produce Lacey.

Why New York Gets the Edge

New York received the more direct and more substantial isolated return. Newlin played 76 games, started 32 and gave the Knicks a full season of veteran guard minutes.

New Jersey received seven Woodson games plus a partial claim on the later Lacey package. The downstream branch has real value, but the attached first-round pick means it cannot be treated as if Woodson alone bought 54 games of Lacey.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, B/C+. New York receives a B for 76 Newlin games and 32 starts in his final NBA season. New Jersey receives a C+ for seven Woodson games and shared downstream value in the Lacey transaction, but the first-round pick included in that later package limits how much credit belongs to this branch.

perspectives.analysis:
Chicago Turned Olliver's Rights into Two Assets

Basketball-Reference records the June 10, 1981 exchange one day after the draft. Chicago sent the rights to No. 32 pick Mike Olliver to Indiana for the rights to No. 36 pick Ray Blume and a 1982 second-round pick.

The trade is unusually straightforward in hindsight because every branch has a documented NBA outcome.

Olliver Never Played in the NBA

Olliver was drafted by Chicago but traded to Indiana before the season.

Basketball-Reference lists him as a drafted rookie but records no NBA regular-season statistics. He never appeared in a Pacers game and never appeared in the NBA for another franchise.

Indiana therefore received zero realized NBA games from the only incoming asset.

Blume Played 49 Games for Chicago

Blume made Chicago's roster and played 49 games in 1981-82.

He averaged 4.6 points, 1.4 assists and 0.8 rebounds in 11.9 minutes per game. That was his only NBA season.

Blume's role was modest, but even that one year created more direct playing value than Indiana received from Olliver.

The 1982 Pick Became Rod Higgins

Chicago's second incoming asset became the No. 31 pick in the 1982 draft, used on Rod Higgins.

Higgins immediately played all 82 games as a rookie, started 42 and averaged 10.3 points, 4.5 rebounds and 2.1 assists in 26.8 minutes.

He followed with 78 games in 1983-84 and 68 more in 1984-85. Chicago waived him before the 1985-86 season, then brought him back for a short five-game stint in March 1986.

Across those Chicago stretches, Higgins appeared in 233 regular-season games.

No Downstream Complexity Is Needed

This trade does not require speculative routing or partial credit from multi-asset later deals.

Blume's 49 Bulls games and Higgins' 233 Bulls games are direct realized returns from the two incoming assets. Olliver produced zero NBA games for Indiana.

That creates a combined 282 Chicago games against zero Indiana games from the exchanged draft rights.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, A+/F. Chicago receives an A+ for turning Olliver's rights into 49 Blume games plus 233 Higgins games, including a strong Higgins rookie season. Indiana receives an F because Olliver never appeared in an NBA regular-season game and created no documented NBA return.

perspectives.analysis:
The Public Ledger Describes a Sale

Basketball-Reference records New Jersey selling Edgar Jones' player rights to Detroit on June 11, 1981.

The legacy canonical record describes the Nets' return as future considerations or cash. The reviewed public transaction ledgers do not provide a dollar amount, so this review preserves the financial term without inventing a value for it.

Jones Played 97 Games for Detroit

Jones became a useful Detroit reserve and part-time starter in 1981-82. He played 48 games, started 19 and averaged 7.8 points, 4.3 rebounds and 1.9 blocks in 16.7 minutes.

He remained with the Pistons for most of 1982-83, appearing in 49 games and starting 25. That season he averaged 8.3 points, 5.5 rebounds and 1.6 blocks in 21.1 minutes.

Across the two seasons, Jones gave Detroit 97 regular-season games and 44 starts.

Detroit Later Recovered Two Draft Picks

On February 10, 1983, Detroit traded Jones to San Antonio for a 1984 second-round pick and a 1985 third-round pick.

The 1984 selection landed at No. 32 and became Eric Turner. The 1985 selection landed at No. 60 and became Andre Goode.

Basketball-Reference records no NBA regular-season statistics for either Turner or Goode. The picks therefore did not add direct NBA playing value after the Jones tenure ended.

The Nets' Cash Return Is Unquantified

New Jersey's side cannot be treated as zero value because the transaction was a sale and the club received financial consideration.

The problem is that the reviewed sources do not identify the amount or any later basketball asset tied to that payment. This review therefore grades the Nets conservatively rather than pretending the cash can be compared precisely with 97 games of on-court production.

Why Detroit Gets the Edge

Detroit received two seasons of useful frontcourt play from Jones, including 44 starts, and then converted him into two draft selections.

Neither draft pick reached an NBA regular-season floor, so the downstream branch does not transform the deal into a major win. The direct Jones tenure remains the core of Detroit's value.

New Jersey received real financial consideration, but without a documented amount or a basketball branch it cannot match Detroit's identifiable return in a realized-value archive.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, B+/C. Detroit receives a B+ for 97 Jones games, 44 starts and two later draft opportunities. New Jersey receives a C because the cash consideration was real but is not quantified in the reviewed public record.

perspectives.analysis:
The Public Ledgers Show Silas, Yonakor and One Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland acquiring James Silas and Rich Yonakor from San Antonio on June 16, 1981 for a 1982 second-round pick that later became Oliver Robinson.

The frozen Cavaliers source package also includes cash going to San Antonio. Because that term is not shown in the reviewed Basketball-Reference ledgers, this review preserves it as a frozen-source term but does not invent an amount.

Silas Gave Cleveland 67 Games

Silas played 67 games for the Cavaliers in 1981-82 and started 34.

He averaged 11.2 points, 3.3 assists and 1.6 rebounds in 21.6 minutes. For a veteran guard acquired at age 32, that was a meaningful one-season return.

Silas did not play in 1982-83 because of a back injury and never appeared in another NBA game. Cleveland therefore received one useful season rather than a multi-year branch.

Yonakor Never Played for Cleveland

Cleveland acquired Yonakor's draft rights but waived him on October 27, 1981.

San Antonio later signed Yonakor as a free agent on March 8, 1982. He played 10 games for the Spurs, but those appearances came after Cleveland had released him and therefore are not realized Cavaliers value from this trade.

This review credits Cleveland with the acquired rights but zero NBA games from that branch.

San Antonio Used the Pick on Oliver Robinson

The 1982 second-round selection landed at No. 24 and became Oliver Robinson.

Robinson played 35 games for San Antonio in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 2.9 points, 0.6 assists and 0.5 rebounds in 4.2 minutes.

That was his only NBA season.

Why Cleveland Gets the Edge

San Antonio received 35 Robinson games plus an unquantified cash term preserved from the frozen source package.

Cleveland received 67 Silas games, 34 starts and materially larger playing time and production. Yonakor's rights added no Cavaliers games, so the grade does not depend on that asset.

The unknown cash prevents an extreme grade gap, but the documented basketball value still favors Cleveland.

Final Verdict

Slight Cavaliers Edge, B+/C+. Cleveland receives a B+ for 67 Silas games and 34 starts. San Antonio receives a C+ for 35 Robinson games plus an unquantified frozen-source cash term.

new-york-knicks.summary: New York traded the rights to Tom Barker to Portland on August 4, 1981 for a 1982 third-round pick. Barker had last played in the NBA in 1978-79 and never appeared for Portland, so the Trail Blazers received no regular-season games from the acquired rights. New York kept the pick and used No. 57 on Illinois guard Craig Tucker, who also never played an NBA regular-season game. The deal therefore produced zero direct NBA games for either side. With neither asset generating documented downstream NBA value, the fairest retrospective result is an even, low-impact exchange.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Transaction Was Rights for a Third-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Trail Blazers and league transaction ledgers all record the same August 4, 1981 deal. New York sent Tom Barker to Portland for a 1982 third-round pick.

The canonical source record describes Barker as draft rights, which is the correct asset framing for this retrospective because Barker was not an active NBA contributor at the time.

Barker Never Played for Portland

Barker's Basketball-Reference career page lists 98 NBA games over two seasons, with his final NBA appearances coming in 1978-79.

He played for Houston, Boston and New York that season, including 22 Knicks games. He did not return to the NBA afterward.

Portland therefore realized zero NBA regular-season games from the Barker rights acquired in this trade. No reviewed transaction source shows a later NBA asset return from those rights that would change the evaluation.

New York Used the Pick on Craig Tucker

The incoming third-round selection landed at No. 57 in the 1982 draft.

New York used it on Illinois guard Craig Tucker. Basketball-Reference lists Tucker as the No. 57 selection but shows no NBA regular-season statistics.

The Knicks therefore also received zero NBA games from their direct asset.

Why This Is an Even Trade

This is a rare historical trade where the direct NBA outcome is essentially identical on both sides.

Portland acquired rights to a player whose NBA career had already ended. New York acquired a late draft pick that produced a drafted player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

Neither branch generated documented downstream NBA value in the reviewed ledgers. That makes a winner call artificial.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, D/D. Portland receives a D because Barker produced no Trail Blazers games. New York also receives a D because the No. 57 pick on Tucker produced no Knicks or NBA regular-season games. The trade belongs in the even bucket because both realized returns were effectively zero.

New York kept the pick and used No. 57 on Illinois guard Craig Tucker, who also never played an NBA regular-season game. The deal therefore produced zero direct NBA games for either side. With neither asset generating documented downstream NBA value, the fairest retrospective result is an even, low-impact exchange.
analysis:
The Transaction Was Rights for a Third-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Knicks, Trail Blazers and league transaction ledgers all record the same August 4, 1981 deal. New York sent Tom Barker to Portland for a 1982 third-round pick.

The canonical source record describes Barker as draft rights, which is the correct asset framing for this retrospective because Barker was not an active NBA contributor at the time.

Barker Never Played for Portland

Barker's Basketball-Reference career page lists 98 NBA games over two seasons, with his final NBA appearances coming in 1978-79.

He played for Houston, Boston and New York that season, including 22 Knicks games. He did not return to the NBA afterward.

Portland therefore realized zero NBA regular-season games from the Barker rights acquired in this trade. No reviewed transaction source shows a later NBA asset return from those rights that would change the evaluation.

New York Used the Pick on Craig Tucker

The incoming third-round selection landed at No. 57 in the 1982 draft.

New York used it on Illinois guard Craig Tucker. Basketball-Reference lists Tucker as the No. 57 selection but shows no NBA regular-season statistics.

The Knicks therefore also received zero NBA games from their direct asset.

Why This Is an Even Trade

This is a rare historical trade where the direct NBA outcome is essentially identical on both sides.

Portland acquired rights to a player whose NBA career had already ended. New York acquired a late draft pick that produced a drafted player who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

Neither branch generated documented downstream NBA value in the reviewed ledgers. That makes a winner call artificial.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, D/D. Portland receives a D because Barker produced no Trail Blazers games. New York also receives a D because the No. 57 pick on Tucker produced no Knicks or NBA regular-season games. The trade belongs in the even bucket because both realized returns were effectively zero.
