los-angeles-lakers.summary: Los Angeles secured Washington's agreement not to exercise its right of first refusal on veteran free agent Mitch Kupchak, while the Bullets received Jim Chones, Brad Holland, a 1982 second-round pick and a 1983 first-round pick. Kupchak played 173 regular-season games for the Lakers across four seasons, started 26 games in 1981-82 and was part of the 1982 and 1985 championship teams despite major knee injuries. Washington received 59 Chones games, 13 Holland games, 32 Mike Gibson games and then converted the Randy Wittman pick into Tom McMillen, who played 187 Bullets games. Both sides realized substantial value, making an even verdict more accurate than a one-sided grade.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Deal Was Compensation for Kupchak

Basketball-Reference's transaction records show Washington receiving Jim Chones, Brad Holland, a 1982 second-round pick and a 1983 first-round pick as compensation after the Lakers signed Mitch Kupchak as a veteran free agent.

The canonical record frames Los Angeles' incoming asset as Washington agreeing not to exercise its right of first refusal. That is the operative value: the Lakers secured Kupchak's services.

Kupchak Played 173 Lakers Games

Kupchak appeared in 26 games in 1981-82 and started all 26, averaging 14.3 points and 8.1 rebounds before a severe knee injury interrupted his season.

He missed all of 1982-83, returned for 34 games in 1983-84, then played 58 games in 1984-85 and 55 in 1985-86.

Across four Lakers seasons he totaled 173 regular-season games. His role was reduced after the injury, but he still provided useful frontcourt minutes and was on the 1982 and 1985 championship teams.

Washington Received Four Assets

Chones played 59 games for Washington in 1981-82, starting 13 and averaging 3.1 points and 3.1 rebounds in 14.7 minutes.

Holland appeared in 13 games before Washington waived him in December 1981.

The 1982 second-round pick became No. 44 Mike Gibson. Gibson later played 32 games for Washington in 1983-84.

The 1983 First Became a Productive Downstream Branch

Washington used the No. 22 pick in 1983 on Randy Wittman, but did not keep him.

On July 5, 1983, the Bullets traded Wittman's rights to Atlanta for Tom McMillen and a 1984 second-round pick later used on Tony Costner.

McMillen played 62 games for Washington in 1983-84, 69 in 1984-85 and 56 in 1985-86. That is 187 regular-season games, including 21 starts in 1984-85.

Costner did not produce an NBA regular-season career, so this review stops that branch there.

Why Neither Side Clearly Lost

Washington's compensation package produced more total regular-season games when Chones, Holland, Gibson and McMillen are combined.

Los Angeles, however, acquired the player it actually wanted. Kupchak contributed 173 games, returned from a major knee injury and remained part of two championship rosters.

Those are different kinds of realized value. Washington maximized depth and asset conversion; Los Angeles secured a championship-era rotation big.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, A-/A-. Los Angeles receives an A- for 173 Kupchak games and championship-roster value. Washington also receives an A- because the compensation package produced useful short-term players and a first-round branch that became 187 Tom McMillen games. Calling either side a clear loser would overstate the evidence.

summary: Atlanta acquired Rory Sparrow and a 1985 fourth-round pick from New Jersey for a 1982 fourth-round pick. Sparrow immediately became the Hawks' starting point guard, playing and starting 131 regular-season games across parts of two seasons before Atlanta traded him to New York. The 1985 pick became No. 84 John Battle, who then played 416 regular-season games for Atlanta over six seasons. New Jersey used the incoming No. 80 pick on James Griffin, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The Hawks therefore turned one fourth-round pick into both a starting guard and a long-tenured rotation player, producing a decisive Atlanta win.
analysis:
Atlanta Turned One Fourth-Round Pick Into Two NBA Contributors

The canonical record dates the transaction to August 11, 1981, while Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, New Jersey and league ledgers list August 12. The transaction terms match: Atlanta received Rory Sparrow and a 1985 fourth-round pick, while New Jersey received Atlanta's 1982 fourth-round pick.

For the retrospective grade, the one-day source discrepancy does not change the asset comparison.

Sparrow Became Atlanta's Starting Point Guard

Sparrow played all 82 regular-season games for Atlanta in 1981-82 and started all 82. He averaged 10.5 points and 5.2 assists while helping the Hawks return to the playoffs.

He remained Atlanta's starter in 1982-83, appearing in 49 games and starting all 49 before the Hawks traded him to New York on February 12, 1983 for Scott Hastings and cash.

That gives Atlanta 131 regular-season games and 131 starts directly from Sparrow before any downstream return is considered.

The 1985 Pick Became John Battle

The second Atlanta asset became the No. 84 selection in the 1985 NBA Draft.

Atlanta used it on John Battle, who played six seasons with the Hawks from 1985-86 through 1990-91. He appeared in 416 regular-season games for Atlanta and developed from a reserve guard into a larger rotation role, including 48 starts in 1989-90.

Battle's NBA career lasted 10 seasons, but this review credits only his Hawks tenure to this trade.

New Jersey's Pick Produced No NBA Games

The Nets used Atlanta's 1982 fourth-round pick at No. 80 on James Griffin.

Basketball-Reference lists Griffin as a drafted forward but shows no NBA regular-season statistics. The direct New Jersey return therefore produced zero NBA games.

No reviewed downstream transaction branch from Griffin changes that result.

Why Atlanta Wins Decisively

Atlanta received immediate value from Sparrow and long-term value from Battle. Together, the two direct branches produced 547 Hawks regular-season games, with Sparrow supplying 131 starts before being traded again.

New Jersey's lone incoming pick produced no NBA regular-season games.

Even without assigning value to Atlanta's later Sparrow-for-Hastings-and-cash transaction, the realized basketball return is overwhelmingly one-sided.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, A+/F. Atlanta receives an A+ for 131 Sparrow games and starts plus 416 Battle games from the fourth-round pick. New Jersey receives an F because the No. 80 James Griffin selection produced no NBA regular-season games.

perspectives.summary: Dallas acquired Allan Bristow and Wayne Cooper from Utah for Bill Robinzine on August 20, 1981. Bristow played 119 regular-season games for the Mavericks across two seasons, including 54 starts, while Cooper added 76 games and 38 starts in 1981-82 before becoming part of a later trade package. Robinzine played 56 games with nine starts for Utah in what became his final NBA season. Dallas therefore received 195 direct regular-season games and 92 starts against Utah's 56 games and nine starts, producing a clear Mavericks win.
perspectives.analysis:
Dallas Got Two Rotation Pieces for One Veteran

Basketball-Reference's Dallas, Utah and league transaction ledgers all record the August 20, 1981 deal the same way: the Mavericks received Allan Bristow and Wayne Cooper, while the Jazz received Bill Robinzine.

The direct return strongly favors Dallas even before considering any later transactions.

Bristow Supplied Two Seasons of Value

Bristow played all 82 regular-season games for Dallas in 1981-82 and started 54 of them. He averaged 7.0 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.5 assists while functioning as a secondary playmaker on a young Mavericks team.

He returned for 37 more Dallas games in 1982-83, all off the bench. His Mavericks tenure therefore totaled 119 regular-season games and 54 starts.

Cooper Immediately Became a Starting Center

Cooper appeared in 76 games for Dallas in 1981-82 and started 38. He averaged 9.0 points, 7.2 rebounds and 1.4 blocks per game, giving the Mavericks another useful rotation piece from the same transaction.

On June 28, 1982, Dallas later packaged Cooper with a 1985 first-round pick for Kelvin Ransey. Because that later deal also required a valuable first-rounder, this review does not credit the entire Ransey return to Cooper.

Robinzine's Utah Tenure Lasted One Season

Robinzine played 56 regular-season games for the Jazz in 1981-82 and started nine. He averaged 5.8 points and 2.6 rebounds in 11.6 minutes per game.

That season was the last of his NBA career. Utah therefore received 56 games and nine starts from its only incoming player.

Why Dallas Wins

The Mavericks received 195 direct regular-season games from Bristow and Cooper, including 92 starts. Utah received 56 games and nine starts from Robinzine.

Bristow alone more than doubled Robinzine's Utah game total, while Cooper supplied a full season as a useful center and retained enough value to be included in another trade the following summer.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win, A-/D. Dallas receives an A- for obtaining two usable rotation players who combined for 195 games and 92 starts. Utah receives a D because Robinzine produced one limited season and then exited the NBA.

perspectives.summary: Dallas acquired Allan Bristow and Wayne Cooper from Utah for Bill Robinzine on August 20, 1981. Bristow played 119 regular-season games for the Mavericks across two seasons, including 54 starts, while Cooper added 76 games and 38 starts in 1981-82 before becoming part of a later trade package. Robinzine played 56 games with nine starts for Utah in what became his final NBA season. Dallas therefore received 195 direct regular-season games and 92 starts against Utah's 56 games and nine starts, producing a clear Mavericks win.
perspectives.analysis:
Dallas Got Two Rotation Pieces for One Veteran

Basketball-Reference's Dallas, Utah and league transaction ledgers all record the August 20, 1981 deal the same way: the Mavericks received Allan Bristow and Wayne Cooper, while the Jazz received Bill Robinzine.

The direct return strongly favors Dallas even before considering any later transactions.

Bristow Supplied Two Seasons of Value

Bristow played all 82 regular-season games for Dallas in 1981-82 and started 54 of them. He averaged 7.0 points, 4.1 rebounds and 5.5 assists while functioning as a secondary playmaker on a young Mavericks team.

He returned for 37 more Dallas games in 1982-83, all off the bench. His Mavericks tenure therefore totaled 119 regular-season games and 54 starts.

Cooper Immediately Became a Starting Center

Cooper appeared in 76 games for Dallas in 1981-82 and started 38. He averaged 9.0 points, 7.2 rebounds and 1.4 blocks per game, giving the Mavericks another useful rotation piece from the same transaction.

On June 28, 1982, Dallas later packaged Cooper with a 1985 first-round pick for Kelvin Ransey. Because that later deal also required a valuable first-rounder, this review does not credit the entire Ransey return to Cooper.

Robinzine's Utah Tenure Lasted One Season

Robinzine played 56 regular-season games for the Jazz in 1981-82 and started nine. He averaged 5.8 points and 2.6 rebounds in 11.6 minutes per game.

That season was the last of his NBA career. Utah therefore received 56 games and nine starts from its only incoming player.

Why Dallas Wins

The Mavericks received 195 direct regular-season games from Bristow and Cooper, including 92 starts. Utah received 56 games and nine starts from Robinzine.

Bristow alone more than doubled Robinzine's Utah game total, while Cooper supplied a full season as a useful center and retained enough value to be included in another trade the following summer.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win, A-/D. Dallas receives an A- for obtaining two usable rotation players who combined for 195 games and 92 starts. Utah receives a D because Robinzine produced one limited season and then exited the NBA.

perspectives.summary: Kansas City acquired Larry Drew from Detroit on August 26, 1981 for two second-round picks. Drew played 376 regular-season games for the Kings franchise over five seasons, starting 263 and peaking at 20.1 points and 8.1 assists per game in 1982-83. Detroit did not directly draft Dave Magley or Tony Costner with the incoming picks; it rerouted the 1982 pick in the package that brought Bill Laimbeer and Kenny Carr, and later rerouted the 1984 pick in a package that brought Ray Tolbert. The picks retained trade utility, but Drew's long, productive Kings tenure gives Kansas City the stronger realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
Kansas City Bought Five Seasons of Larry Drew

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Kansas City and league transaction ledgers agree on the August 26, 1981 terms. Detroit sent Larry Drew to the Kings for Kansas City's 1982 second-round pick, later No. 28 Dave Magley, and 1984 second-round pick, later No. 34 Tony Costner.

The original canonical record treated Magley as if Detroit directly received the player. That is not what happened. Both incoming assets were draft picks, and Detroit traded each pick before it was exercised.

Drew Became a Long-Term Kings Starter

Drew played 81 games for Kansas City in 1981-82, then moved into a much larger role. In 1982-83 he started 74 of 75 games and averaged 20.1 points and 8.1 assists.

He remained with the franchise through the move to Sacramento in 1985-86. Across five Kings seasons, Drew played 376 regular-season games and started 263.

That is a large direct return for two second-round picks, especially because Drew was only 23 when Kansas City acquired him.

Detroit Rerouted the 1982 Pick

The 1982 second-rounder became the No. 28 selection, which Cleveland ultimately used on Dave Magley.

Detroit had already moved that pick on February 16, 1982. The Pistons sent Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski, a 1982 first-round pick and this second-round pick to Cleveland for Kenny Carr and Bill Laimbeer.

Because the pick was one component of a four-asset package, this review does not credit the entire Laimbeer-Carr return to the Drew trade. It does, however, credit the pick with retaining real transaction value.

Detroit Rerouted the 1984 Pick Too

The second Kansas City pick became No. 34 in 1984, when Washington selected Tony Costner. Detroit never made that selection.

On February 13, 1983, the Pistons sent the 1984 second-rounder and a 1985 second-rounder to Atlanta in a three-team trade that brought Ray Tolbert from Seattle to Detroit. Tolbert played 77 regular-season games for the Pistons across parts of two seasons.

Again, the incoming pick was only one part of the later package, so Tolbert cannot be assigned entirely to this branch.

Why Kansas City Wins

Detroit extracted meaningful trade utility from both second-round picks, which prevents this from being a one-sided failure. One pick helped complete the package for Laimbeer and Carr, while the other helped bring Tolbert.

Kansas City still received the clearest standalone asset. Drew gave the franchise 376 games, 263 starts and multiple seasons as a productive starting point guard.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A/B-. Kansas City receives an A for turning two second-rounders into five productive seasons of Drew. Detroit receives a B- because both picks retained downstream trade value, including use in the Laimbeer-Carr package, but neither pick created a clean direct return comparable to Drew's Kings tenure.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee acquired Geoff Crompton from Portland on September 24, 1981 for a 1982 third-round pick. Crompton played 35 regular-season games for the Bucks in 1981-82, starting once and providing reserve center depth for a 55-win team. Portland used the No. 66 pick on Alabama center Phillip Lockett, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The return was small in scale, but Milwaukee received actual NBA minutes while Portland's pick produced none.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee Turned a Third-Round Pick Into NBA Depth

Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee and Portland transaction ledgers agree on the September 24, 1981 terms. The Bucks received Geoff Crompton, while the Trail Blazers received Milwaukee's 1982 third-round pick.

That pick later became No. 66 overall, where Portland selected Phillip Lockett.

Crompton Played 35 Games for a 55-Win Bucks Team

Crompton appeared in 35 regular-season games for Milwaukee in 1981-82 and made one start. He logged 203 minutes, averaging 0.8 points and 1.2 rebounds in a limited reserve-center role.

The production was modest, but it was real roster value. Milwaukee won 55 games and finished first in the Central Division, so Crompton's contribution came as depth on a contender rather than as empty minutes on a rebuilding team.

His Bucks tenure lasted only that season. Crompton later played for San Antonio and Cleveland, but this review credits only the 35 Milwaukee games produced directly by this trade.

Portland Used the Pick on Phillip Lockett

The Trail Blazers kept the incoming third-rounder and used it with the 66th pick in the 1982 NBA Draft.

Portland selected Alabama center Phillip Lockett. Basketball-Reference's 1982 draft record lists Lockett at No. 66 but shows no NBA regular-season career statistics.

That means the direct Portland branch produced zero NBA games.

Why Milwaukee Wins

This was a low-cost, low-ceiling transaction, so the grade should not be inflated. Crompton was not a major rotation piece and did not become a long-term Buck.

Still, Milwaukee exchanged a third-round pick that ultimately produced no NBA player for 35 games of usable center depth. Portland received the draft asset it wanted, but the realized outcome of that asset was zero NBA appearances.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win, B/F. Milwaukee receives a B because Crompton supplied one season of real NBA depth at minimal acquisition cost. Portland receives an F on realized value because No. 66 pick Phillip Lockett never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

perspectives.summary: The September 25, 1981 Brad Branson rights transaction carries a genuine source conflict. RealGM's Dallas ledger, Branson's player transaction history and Detroit's draft-history page say Detroit sent Branson's draft rights to Dallas; Dallas signed him five days later and waived him on October 26 without an NBA appearance. Basketball-Reference's Dallas, Detroit and league ledgers reverse the direction and describe Dallas selling Branson's rights to Detroit. The canonical source package records Dallas receiving Branson for a future 1984 third-round obligation whose final outcome is not identified. Because Branson produced no Mavericks games and the future-pick branch has no verified NBA return, this review grades the transaction as an even, low-value result while preserving the source disagreement.
perspectives.analysis:
The Sources Disagree on Which Team Received Brad Branson's Rights

this review has a direct source conflict that cannot be responsibly hidden. RealGM's Dallas transaction history says the Mavericks acquired Brad Branson's draft rights from Detroit on September 25, 1981, then signed him on September 30 and waived him on October 26. RealGM's Detroit draft-history page also marks Branson's 1980 draft rights as moving from Detroit to Dallas.

Basketball-Reference records the opposite direction. Its Dallas ledger says the Mavericks sold Branson's rights to Detroit, while the Detroit and league ledgers say Detroit acquired the rights from Dallas. Because the canonical record was built from a source package that follows the Dallas-receives-rights version, this review keeps that record but explicitly records the disagreement and lowers confidence.

Branson Produced No Dallas NBA Games

The realized Dallas outcome is clear regardless of the ledger conflict. Branson did not appear in an NBA regular-season game for the Mavericks.

RealGM records Dallas signing him five days after the rights transaction and placing him on waivers less than a month later. Branson later reached the NBA with Cleveland and Indiana, playing 72 career regular-season games, but those later appearances came after Dallas had released him and are not credited to this trade.

The Future Consideration Has No Verified NBA Return

The canonical package records a 1984 third-round pick or future draft consideration going to Detroit. The pick is not identified in the public transaction ledgers reviewed for this review, and the legacy archive entry already flagged it as probably not exercised.

Because no specific draft selection or downstream player can be tied confidently to that obligation, this review does not invent a return. Detroit receives credit only for obtaining future consideration with an unverified terminal outcome.

Why the Result Is Even

Dallas, under the canonical source version, acquired the rights to a former second-round pick but got no NBA games before waiving him. Detroit received future consideration, but no verified draft or player result can be attached to it.

Neither side generated a durable realized-value advantage. The correct editorial treatment is therefore an even trade with medium confidence, not a forced winner based on an unresolved source-direction dispute.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C/C. Dallas receives a C because the Branson rights produced no Mavericks regular-season games. Detroit receives a C because the future consideration cannot be tied to a verified NBA outcome. Confidence stays medium because Basketball-Reference and RealGM disagree on which franchise received Branson's rights on September 25, 1981.

perspectives.analysis:
The Sources Differ by One Day

this review corrects the package while preserving an explicit date discrepancy. Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Phoenix and league ledgers place the Johnny High trade on September 30, 1981. The Chicago Bulls' official media guide and RealGM list October 1. Because the canonical record already uses October 1 and the franchise source supports it, this review keeps that date but lowers confidence to medium rather than pretending every ledger agrees.

The outgoing Chicago asset also needs correction. It was not a conditional 1982 third-rounder. The primary transaction ledgers identify the consideration as Chicago's 1983 third-round pick, which later became No. 52 Winfred King.

High Never Played for the Bulls

High had been a useful Phoenix guard before the trade, appearing in 163 games across his first two NBA seasons. Chicago did not receive any of that prior production.

The Bulls waived High on October 20, 1981, and he became a free agent two days later. Basketball-Reference lists 1981-82 as a did-not-play season and specifically notes that he had been traded to and waived by Chicago. His direct Bulls return is therefore zero regular-season games.

Phoenix Preserved Value in the Pick

Phoenix held the Chicago third-rounder until June 27, 1983. The Suns then included the pick, Dennis Johnson and a 1983 first-rounder in the trade that brought Rick Robey and two second-round picks from Boston.

This review does not assign the entire Robey package to this one third-round asset because Dennis Johnson and a first-round pick carried far more value. The important point is narrower: the Chicago pick remained a usable transaction asset nearly two years after the High deal.

Boston Used the Pick on Winfred King

The Celtics ultimately exercised the No. 52 selection on Winfred King of East Tennessee State. Basketball-Reference lists King as the fifth pick of the third round but shows no NBA regular-season career.

That terminal draft outcome was zero NBA games. Even so, Phoenix received more than Chicago because the Suns were able to route the pick into a later major transaction while High produced nothing for the Bulls.

Final Verdict

Suns Win, B-/F. Phoenix receives a B- because it converted a player who would soon be out of Chicago into a draft asset that retained trade utility through 1983. Chicago receives an F because High never appeared in a regular-season game for the Bulls. Confidence is medium because authoritative sources differ by one day on the transaction date, although they agree on the player and 1983 third-round pick.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Jeff Judkins from Utah on October 1, 1981 for a 1982 third-round pick that became No. 55 Jerry Eaves. Judkins played 30 regular-season games for the Pistons, made no starts and averaged 2.6 points before leaving after one season. Eaves played all 82 games for Utah as a rookie, averaged 9.3 points and 2.6 assists, then added 80 more games the following year. The Jazz therefore received 162 regular-season games and eight starts from the pick against Detroit's 30 games and zero starts from Judkins, giving Utah a decisive realized-value win.
perspectives.analysis:
Utah Turned a Third-Round Pick Into Two Full Seasons

Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Utah and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 1, 1981 terms. Detroit received Jeff Judkins, while Utah received the Pistons' 1982 third-round pick.

The pick ultimately landed at No. 55, where the Jazz selected Louisville guard Jerry Eaves.

Judkins Gave Detroit One Small Reserve Season

Judkins appeared in 30 regular-season games for Detroit in 1981-82 and made no starts. He played 251 total minutes, averaging 8.4 minutes and 2.6 points per game.

That was the full extent of his Pistons tenure. Judkins played the following season in Portland, so this review credits Detroit only with the 30 games and reserve minutes produced directly after the trade.

Eaves Immediately Played All 82 Games

Utah used the incoming pick on Eaves, and the result was much more substantial. As a rookie in 1982-83 he appeared in all 82 games, started seven and averaged 19.4 minutes, 9.3 points and 2.6 assists.

He scored 761 points in that first season alone. For a third-round pick, getting a full 82-game rookie campaign with regular rotation minutes is already a strong realized return.

He Added Another 80 Games in Utah

Eaves returned for 80 games in 1983-84 and made one start. His scoring role declined to 4.5 points per game, but he still averaged 12.9 minutes and 2.5 assists while remaining part of the Jazz rotation.

That gives Utah 162 regular-season games and eight starts from the acquired pick across two seasons before Eaves moved on.

Why Utah Wins Clearly

Detroit received a short reserve look at Judkins and no long-term return. Utah converted a third-round pick into a guard who played essentially two full seasons, including a productive 82-game rookie year.

The scale of the original transaction was minor, but the gap in realized value is not. Utah received more than five times as many regular-season games and substantially more rotation impact.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win, A-/C-. Utah receives an A- because the No. 55 pick became 162 games of useful backcourt depth, including 9.3 points per game as a rookie. Detroit receives a C- because Judkins played only 30 games, never started and left after one season.

The Bulls' official transaction history says they acquired the rights that day, signed Stotts shortly afterward and waived him on October 12, before the regular season began. perspectives.analysis:
Houston Sold Rights That Produced No NBA Games

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Houston and league transaction ledgers agree on the core October 2, 1981 transaction: Houston sold the NBA rights to Terry Stotts to Chicago. Pro Sports Transactions identifies cash as the return to the Rockets, matching the canonical package.

Stotts had been Houston's No. 38 pick in the 1980 NBA Draft but had not appeared in an NBA regular-season game before the rights sale.

Chicago Signed Him, Then Waived Him Before the Season

The Bulls' official media guide records the October 2 rights acquisition for cash and an October 12 waiver. RealGM adds that Chicago signed Stotts to a multi-year contract on October 4 before placing him on waivers eight days later.

The 1981-82 Bulls regular season did not begin until October 30. Stotts therefore produced zero regular-season games, starts or minutes for Chicago.

Stotts Never Played in the NBA

Basketball-Reference maintains a player page for Stotts because he was drafted, but it contains no NBA regular-season statistical line. His professional playing career continued outside the NBA before he later became a longtime NBA coach.

For this review, that later coaching career is irrelevant to trade value. Chicago acquired player rights, and those rights produced no NBA basketball for the Bulls.

Houston's Return Was Cash

The Rockets received cash rather than a player or pick. The reviewed public sources do not identify the amount, so this review does not attempt to assign a dollar value or treat the return as a major asset.

Still, cash is a realized return. Houston monetized rights it was not using, while Chicago spent cash and then waived Stotts before he appeared in an NBA game.

Why Houston Gets the Edge

The transaction was minor and should be graded accordingly. There is no evidence that the cash materially changed Houston's roster, and the amount is unknown.

The direct comparison remains simple: Houston received cash, and Chicago received zero NBA production. That gives the Rockets the better hindsight outcome even though the transaction itself was small.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, C+/F. Houston receives a C+ because it converted unused draft rights into a tangible cash return. Chicago receives an F because the acquired rights produced zero NBA regular-season games before Stotts was waived. Confidence is high on the transaction mechanics and Chicago outcome, with the unknown cash amount limiting how strongly Houston can be graded.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Paid a Second-Round Pick for Four Seasons of Mike Glenn

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta and league transaction ledgers record the October 12, 1981 mechanism as veteran free-agent compensation. Atlanta signed Mike Glenn and sent New York its 1982 second-round pick, later No. 34 Vince Taylor.

The canonical record describes New York agreeing not to exercise its right of first refusal. That contractual framing is compatible with the compensation result: Atlanta secured Glenn, while the Knicks received the pick.

Glenn Became a Long-Term Hawks Rotation Guard

Glenn played 49 games for Atlanta in 1981-82 and averaged 7.7 points in 17.0 minutes. He returned for 73 games in 1982-83, 81 in 1983-84 and 60 in 1984-85.

Across those four Hawks seasons he appeared in 263 regular-season games and made nine starts. He was never a star, but his efficient reserve scoring gave Atlanta substantially more than a one-year rental.

His best Atlanta value came from reliability. Glenn shot better than 50 percent from the field in each of those Hawks seasons and remained a regular part of the backcourt rotation until moving to Milwaukee.

New York's Pick Became Vince Taylor

The Knicks used the incoming No. 34 selection in the 1982 NBA Draft on Duke guard Vince Taylor.

Taylor appeared in 31 regular-season games for New York in 1982-83, made no starts and averaged 10.4 minutes, 3.1 points and 1.3 assists. Those 31 games were the entirety of his NBA career.

That gives New York a real but limited return from the compensation pick.

Why Atlanta Wins Clearly

Atlanta gave up a second-round pick and received 263 games across four seasons from Glenn. New York turned the pick into 31 games from Taylor.

The difference is not only games played. Glenn supplied repeated rotation value and several seasons of efficient bench scoring, while Taylor's NBA contribution ended after one year.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, A-/D. Atlanta receives an A- for converting a second-round pick into four useful seasons and 263 regular-season games from Glenn. New York receives a D because Taylor played only 31 games and never started before his NBA career ended.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana acquired Butch Carter from the Lakers on October 15, 1981 for a 1982 third-round pick that became No. 54 Hutch Jones. Carter played 229 regular-season games for the Pacers over three seasons, starting 82 and developing from a reserve into a 13.4-point-per-game starter by 1983-84. Los Angeles drafted Jones at No. 54 but waived him before the 1982-83 season, so he never appeared in a Lakers regular-season game. Jones later played 13 NBA games for San Diego, which are not credited to Los Angeles. Indiana therefore turned a third-round pick into three years of rotation and starting value while the Lakers received zero direct NBA games.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Turned a Third-Round Pick Into Three Seasons of Butch Carter

Basketball-Reference's Indiana and Los Angeles transaction ledgers agree on the October 15, 1981 exchange. The Pacers received Butch Carter, while the Lakers received Indiana's 1982 third-round pick.

Los Angeles used that pick at No. 54 on Hutch Jones, whose full name is Willie D. Jones. The canonical record's mixed "Willie Jones / Hutch Jones" wording refers to the same player.

Carter Became a Real Pacers Rotation Piece

Carter played 75 regular-season games for Indiana in 1981-82, averaging 13.8 minutes and 5.9 points. He did not start that season, but he immediately supplied usable bench minutes.

His role grew sharply in 1982-83. Carter played 81 games, started 28 and averaged 10.5 points while shooting 50.1 percent from the field.

By 1983-84 he was a regular starter. Carter appeared in 73 games, started 54 and averaged 13.4 points, 2.8 assists and 2.1 rebounds in 28.0 minutes.

That gives Indiana 229 regular-season games and 82 starts across three seasons from the acquisition.

The Lakers Drafted Hutch Jones but Got Zero Games

Los Angeles used the incoming pick on Hutch Jones in the 1982 draft. The Lakers then waived him on October 25, 1982, before the regular season.

Jones later signed with San Diego and played nine games in 1982-83, then four more in 1983-84. His 13-game NBA career belongs to the Clippers for realized-value purposes because none of those appearances came with the Lakers.

Why Indiana Wins Decisively

Indiana gave up a third-round pick and received a player who grew into a multi-year starter. Carter's 229 games and 82 starts represent substantial direct value from a low-cost asset.

Los Angeles got no regular-season production from the pick. Drafting an NBA-caliber player provides some scouting credit, but waiving him before he played means the Lakers realized zero basketball value from the return.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, A-/F. Indiana receives an A- for three seasons, 229 games and 82 starts from Carter at the cost of a third-round pick. Los Angeles receives an F because No. 54 Hutch Jones was waived before appearing in a Lakers regular-season game.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Washington acquired John Lucas from Golden State on October 19, 1981 for two second-round picks. Lucas played 114 regular-season games for the Bullets across parts of two seasons, starting 53 and averaging 7.0 assists in his first Washington year. Golden State used the 1982 No. 35 pick on Derek Smith, who played 27 games for the Warriors before being waived, and the 1984 No. 30 pick on Steve Burtt, who played 47 Warriors games. The two picks therefore produced 74 Golden State games and zero starts, while Lucas supplied 114 Washington games and 53 starts. The direct realized value favors Washington.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Washington Got the Best Direct Return

Basketball-Reference's Golden State transaction ledger records the October 19, 1981 package clearly. The Warriors sent John Lucas to Washington for two second-round picks, one in 1982 and one in 1984.

Golden State eventually used those choices on Derek Smith at No. 35 in 1982 and Steve Burtt at No. 30 in 1984.

Lucas Became Washington's Starting Point Guard

Lucas played 79 regular-season games for the Bullets in 1981-82 and started 53. He averaged 24.6 minutes, 8.4 points and 7.0 assists while helping Washington finish 43-39 and reach the Eastern Conference semifinals.

He returned for 35 games in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 4.1 points and 2.9 assists. Washington waived him on January 25, 1983.

That gives the Bullets 114 regular-season games and 53 starts from the trade, including one season in which Lucas handled a major portion of the point-guard workload.

Derek Smith Produced 27 Warriors Games

Golden State used the 1982 pick at No. 35 on Louisville wing Derek Smith. He appeared in 27 Warriors games as a rookie, all off the bench, averaging 5.7 minutes and 2.2 points.

The Warriors waived Smith on September 8, 1983. He later became a productive NBA starter with the Clippers, but that later success came after Golden State had released him and cannot be credited to this trade.

Steve Burtt Added 47 More Games

The second incoming pick became No. 30 in the 1984 draft, where Golden State selected Steve Burtt.

Burtt played 47 regular-season games for the Warriors in 1984-85, made no starts and averaged 8.9 minutes and 4.2 points. His later NBA seasons came with other franchises.

Together, the two draft branches produced 74 Golden State games and zero starts.

Why Washington Wins

Golden State did identify two players who reached the NBA, and that gives the picks more value than unused selections. The problem is that neither player produced much for the Warriors themselves.

Washington received 114 games, 53 starts and a full season of starting point-guard play from Lucas. On direct franchise value, that outweighs 74 reserve appearances and no starts from Smith and Burtt combined.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, B+/C+. Washington receives a B+ because Lucas supplied a useful starting season plus additional reserve time. Golden State receives a C+ because both picks became NBA players, but their combined Warriors contribution stayed below Lucas's Washington value and produced no starts.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey signed restricted veteran free agent Ray Williams on October 25, 1981 after New York declined its right of first refusal, with Maurice Lucas going to the Knicks as compensation. Williams played all 82 games for the Nets, started 69 and averaged 20.4 points, 6.0 assists and 2.4 steals while helping a 24-win team improve to 44-38 and reach the playoffs. Lucas played 80 games for New York, started 74 and averaged 15.8 points and 11.3 rebounds. Both were productive one-season starters before moving on, making the realized exchange unusually balanced.
perspectives.analysis:
Both Teams Got One Strong Season

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey transaction ledger records the October 25, 1981 mechanism directly. The Nets signed Ray Williams as a veteran free agent and sent Maurice Lucas to the Knicks as compensation.

The canonical right-of-first-refusal wording describes the same restricted-free-agent process: New York declined to keep Williams, New Jersey secured him, and Lucas became the compensation moving the other way.

Williams Led the Nets in Scoring

Williams played all 82 regular-season games for New Jersey in 1981-82 and started 69. He averaged 20.4 points, 6.0 assists, 4.0 rebounds and 2.4 steals in 33.3 minutes.

He finished as the Nets' leading scorer during a dramatic team improvement. New Jersey rose from 24-58 in 1980-81 to 44-38 and reached the playoffs.

Williams was not a long-term Net. He moved to Kansas City the following season, so this review credits New Jersey with one high-level season rather than his later career.

Lucas Was Equally Important for New York

Maurice Lucas played 80 regular-season games for the Knicks in 1981-82 and started 74. He averaged 15.8 points and 11.3 rebounds while playing 33.4 minutes per game.

Lucas led New York in rebounding and gave the Knicks a durable veteran frontcourt presence. Like Williams, however, his stay lasted only one season; he joined Phoenix for 1982-83.

The Knicks did not reach the playoffs, but Lucas's individual production was substantial and should not be discounted simply because the team finished 33-49.

Why This Is an Even Trade

Williams delivered more scoring and playmaking, and his arrival coincided with a 20-win improvement and playoff berth for New Jersey. Lucas delivered elite rebounding, interior production and nearly the same availability for New York.

Both sides received roughly one full season from a proven starter. Neither retained the player long enough to create a major long-term advantage, and both players performed at a level that justified the unusual compensation mechanism.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, A-/A-. New Jersey receives an A- for an 82-game, 20.4-point season from Williams during a playoff turnaround. New York receives an A- for 80 games, 74 starts and an 11.3-rebound season from Lucas. The strengths were different, but the realized one-season value was balanced enough that forcing a winner would overstate the margin.

perspectives.analysis:
Both Teams Got One Strong Season

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey transaction ledger records the October 25, 1981 mechanism directly. The Nets signed Ray Williams as a veteran free agent and sent Maurice Lucas to the Knicks as compensation.

The canonical right-of-first-refusal wording describes the same restricted-free-agent process: New York declined to keep Williams, New Jersey secured him, and Lucas became the compensation moving the other way.

Williams Led the Nets in Scoring

Williams played all 82 regular-season games for New Jersey in 1981-82 and started 69. He averaged 20.4 points, 6.0 assists, 4.0 rebounds and 2.4 steals in 33.3 minutes.

He finished as the Nets' leading scorer during a dramatic team improvement. New Jersey rose from 24-58 in 1980-81 to 44-38 and reached the playoffs.

Williams was not a long-term Net. He moved to Kansas City the following season, so this review credits New Jersey with one high-level season rather than his later career.

Lucas Was Equally Important for New York

Maurice Lucas played 80 regular-season games for the Knicks in 1981-82 and started 74. He averaged 15.8 points and 11.3 rebounds while playing 33.4 minutes per game.

Lucas led New York in rebounding and gave the Knicks a durable veteran frontcourt presence. Like Williams, however, his stay lasted only one season; he joined Phoenix for 1982-83.

The Knicks did not reach the playoffs, but Lucas's individual production was substantial and should not be discounted simply because the team finished 33-49.

Why This Is an Even Trade

Williams delivered more scoring and playmaking, and his arrival coincided with a 20-win improvement and playoff berth for New Jersey. Lucas delivered elite rebounding, interior production and nearly the same availability for New York.

Both sides received roughly one full season from a proven starter. Neither retained the player long enough to create a major long-term advantage, and both players performed at a level that justified the unusual compensation mechanism.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, A-/A-. New Jersey receives an A- for an 82-game, 20.4-point season from Williams during a playoff turnaround. New York receives an A- for 80 games, 74 starts and an 11.3-rebound season from Lucas. The strengths were different, but the realized one-season value was balanced enough that forcing a winner would overstate the margin.

perspectives.summary: San Antonio acquired Mike Bratz from Cleveland on October 28, 1981 for a 1983 third-round pick that became No. 66 Les Craft. Bratz played 81 regular-season games for the Spurs, started three, averaged 7.7 points and 5.4 assists, and appeared in all nine of San Antonio's 1982 playoff games. Cleveland drafted Craft in 1983 but immediately packaged his rights with Larry Anderson to San Diego for a 1985 second-round pick that became No. 30 Calvin Duncan. Duncan never played in the NBA and was later included with Charles Oakley in another draft-night trade. The pick retained downstream transaction utility, but San Antonio received the much stronger direct basketball return.
perspectives.analysis:
San Antonio Bought a Full Season of Backcourt Depth

Basketball-Reference's San Antonio transaction ledger records the October 28, 1981 trade clearly. The Spurs sent Cleveland a 1983 third-round pick and received Mike Bratz.

That pick eventually became No. 66 Les Craft, but Cleveland did not simply keep Craft as its final return.

Bratz Played 81 Games for a Conference Finalist

Bratz appeared in 81 regular-season games for San Antonio in 1981-82 and started three. He averaged 20.0 minutes, 7.7 points and 5.4 assists while serving as a reserve point guard behind the Spurs' veteran backcourt.

San Antonio finished 48-34, won the Midwest Division and reached the Western Conference Finals. Bratz also appeared in all nine Spurs playoff games, averaging 20.0 minutes and 5.3 assists per game in the postseason.

His San Antonio tenure lasted one season, but it was a complete and useful one.

Cleveland Used the Pick on Les Craft

The Cavaliers exercised the incoming third-round selection at No. 66 in the 1983 NBA Draft and selected Kansas State center Les Craft.

Craft never played a regular-season game for Cleveland. On the same draft day, the Cavaliers packaged his rights with No. 56 pick Larry Anderson and sent both players to San Diego for a 1985 second-round pick.

That means the original Bratz return retained transaction value even though Craft himself never suited up for Cleveland.

The Downstream Pick Became Calvin Duncan

The 1985 second-rounder acquired from San Diego became No. 30 Calvin Duncan.

Cleveland then included Duncan with Charles Oakley in a draft-night trade with Chicago for Keith Lee and Ennis Whatley. Duncan never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

This review does not credit the entire Lee-Whatley return to the Bratz trade because Craft was packaged with Larry Anderson to acquire the 1985 pick, and Duncan was later packaged with Oakley. Those other assets were essential parts of both downstream transactions.

Why San Antonio Wins

The Spurs received 81 regular-season games, three starts and nine playoff appearances from Bratz. Cleveland received a third-round pick that retained some trade utility but never produced a direct Cavaliers game through Craft or Duncan.

The downstream chain prevents Cleveland from receiving a failing grade, but the direct realized basketball value is clearly on San Antonio's side.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win, B+/C. San Antonio receives a B+ for a full season of useful guard depth on a division champion and conference finalist. Cleveland receives a C because the pick retained later transaction utility, but its direct player outcomes produced zero Cavaliers regular-season games.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey purchased Len Elmore's player rights from Milwaukee on November 2, 1981. Basketball-Reference describes Milwaukee as selling the rights, while the legacy source package identifies the consideration as future considerations/cash; the public dollar amount is not specified. Elmore played 155 regular-season games for the Nets across two seasons, starting 70, and averaged 9.1 points and 5.4 rebounds in 1981-82 as New Jersey reached the playoffs. Milwaukee received cash for a player it no longer used, but the Nets obtained two seasons of rotation value and the stronger realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Bought Two Seasons of Len Elmore

Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee, New Jersey and league transaction ledgers all record the November 2, 1981 move as a sale of Len Elmore's player rights from the Bucks to the Nets. The legacy canonical package identifies the return as future considerations in cash.

The public sources reviewed for this review do not specify the dollar amount, so the Milwaukee side cannot be valued precisely. The basketball return to New Jersey is much easier to measure.

Elmore Started 70 Games in His First Nets Season

Elmore appeared in 81 regular-season games for New Jersey in 1981-82 and started 70. He averaged 25.9 minutes, 9.1 points, 5.4 rebounds, 1.1 steals and 1.1 blocks.

The Nets finished 44-38 and reached the playoffs after going 24-58 the previous season. Elmore was not the only reason for that turnaround, but 70 starts and more than 2,100 minutes make him a substantial part of the rotation.

He also appeared in both New Jersey playoff games that spring.

He Added a Second Full Season

Elmore returned for 74 regular-season games in 1982-83. His role shrank to 13.2 minutes per game and he did not start, but he still supplied frontcourt depth for a 49-win playoff team.

Across the two seasons, Elmore played 155 regular-season games for the Nets. He accumulated 983 points and 679 rebounds during that New Jersey tenure.

Milwaukee Received Cash, Not a Player Asset

The Bucks sold Elmore's rights rather than receiving a player or draft pick. That gives Milwaukee a tangible return, but the lack of a public cash figure limits how strongly the outcome can be graded.

Elmore had played 72 games for Milwaukee the previous season, so this was not a meaningless set of rights. The Bucks chose to monetize a veteran they were moving away from, and that decision produced some value even if the amount cannot be reconstructed from the reviewed public record.

Why New Jersey Wins

The Nets received two seasons and 155 regular-season games from Elmore, including 70 starts in his first year. Milwaukee received an unquantified cash return.

Without a known large cash figure, the realized basketball value clearly favors New Jersey. The transaction was not franchise-changing, but it was a useful low-cost acquisition.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, B+/C. New Jersey receives a B+ for two seasons of frontcourt depth, 155 games and 70 starts. Milwaukee receives a C for converting player rights into cash, with the unknown amount preventing a stronger or more exact grade.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee signed veteran free agent Bob Dandridge on November 2, 1981 after Washington relinquished its right-of-first-refusal claim, with the Bullets receiving a 1982 fifth-round pick and cash as compensation in the canonical source package. Dandridge's return to Milwaukee lasted only 11 regular-season games, all off the bench, before the Bucks waived him on November 25. Washington used the No. 112 pick on Jerry Davis, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The draft asset itself produced no basketball value, but Washington still received cash while Milwaukee received only 11 limited games, leaving a slight Bullets edge rather than a major win.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee's Dandridge Reunion Lasted Less Than a Month

Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee and Washington transaction ledgers agree on the core November 2, 1981 restricted-veteran-free-agent mechanism. Milwaukee signed Bob Dandridge, and Washington received the Bucks' 1982 fifth-round pick as compensation.

The legacy canonical package also includes cash going to Washington. The reviewed public transaction ledgers do not provide a dollar amount, so this review preserves the cash component without assigning it a speculative financial value.

Dandridge Played Only 11 Games

Dandridge returned to the franchise where he had spent his first nine NBA seasons, but the reunion was brief. He appeared in 11 regular-season games for Milwaukee in 1981-82, made no starts and averaged 15.8 minutes.

His production was modest: 4.7 points, 1.5 rebounds and 1.2 assists per game while shooting 38.2 percent from the field.

Milwaukee waived Dandridge on November 25, only twenty-three days after signing him. Those 11 games were the final appearances of his NBA career.

Washington's Pick Became Jerry Davis

The fifth-round compensation pick became No. 112 in the 1982 NBA Draft, where Washington selected Detroit Mercy forward Jerry Davis.

Basketball-Reference lists Davis as the No. 112 selection, while RealGM's draft history gives him zero NBA years of service. The pick therefore produced no regular-season games for Washington.

That prevents the draft branch from creating a meaningful basketball advantage by itself.

Cash Separates Two Small Returns

If the transaction consisted only of Dandridge against the fifth-round pick, the realized result would be close to even: 11 low-minute games for Milwaukee versus zero NBA games from the pick for Washington.

The cash component gives the Bullets an additional tangible return. Because the amount is not publicly identified in the reviewed sources, it should not be treated as a large asset or used to justify an aggressive grade.

Why Washington Gets a Slight Edge

Milwaukee received a famous franchise veteran, but the actual 1981-82 return was only 11 reserve games before a waiver. Washington's pick failed to produce an NBA player, yet the Bullets also received cash.

The difference is small, but Washington extracted more realized value from a veteran it was losing anyway.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, C+/C-. Washington receives a C+ because the fifth-round pick produced no NBA games but the cash component gave the franchise a tangible return. Milwaukee receives a C- because Dandridge played only 11 games, never started and was waived before the end of November.

The legacy canonical package also includes cash going to Washington. The reviewed public transaction ledgers do not provide a dollar amount, so this review preserves the cash component without assigning it a speculative financial value.

Dandridge Played Only 11 Games

Dandridge returned to the franchise where he had spent his first nine NBA seasons, but the reunion was brief. He appeared in 11 regular-season games for Milwaukee in 1981-82, made no starts and averaged 15.8 minutes.

His production was modest: 4.7 points, 1.5 rebounds and 1.2 assists per game while shooting 38.2 percent from the field.

Milwaukee waived Dandridge on November 25, only twenty-three days after signing him. Those 11 games were the final appearances of his NBA career.

Washington's Pick Became Jerry Davis

The fifth-round compensation pick became No. 112 in the 1982 NBA Draft, where Washington selected Detroit Mercy forward Jerry Davis.

Basketball-Reference lists Davis as the No. 112 selection, while RealGM's draft history gives him zero NBA years of service. The pick therefore produced no regular-season games for Washington.

That prevents the draft branch from creating a meaningful basketball advantage by itself.

Cash Separates Two Small Returns

If the transaction consisted only of Dandridge against the fifth-round pick, the realized result would be close to even: 11 low-minute games for Milwaukee versus zero NBA games from the pick for Washington.

The cash component gives the Bullets an additional tangible return. Because the amount is not publicly identified in the reviewed sources, it should not be treated as a large asset or used to justify an aggressive grade.

Why Washington Gets a Slight Edge

Milwaukee received a famous franchise veteran, but the actual 1981-82 return was only 11 reserve games before a waiver. Washington's pick failed to produce an NBA player, yet the Bullets also received cash.

The difference is small, but Washington extracted more realized value from a veteran it was losing anyway.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, C+/C-. Washington receives a C+ because the fifth-round pick produced no NBA games but the cash component gave the franchise a tangible return. Milwaukee receives a C- because Dandridge played only 11 games, never started and was waived before the end of November.

perspectives.summary: Kansas City acquired Mike Woodson and a 1982 first-round pick from New Jersey on November 12, 1981 for veteran center Sam Lacey. Woodson became a long-term franchise scorer, playing 387 regular-season games for the Kings across Kansas City and the first Sacramento season, starting 143 and averaging at least 14 points in each full season from 1981-82 through 1985-86. The No. 17 pick became Brook Steppe, who added 62 games and six starts for Kansas City as a rookie. Lacey played only 54 regular-season games for New Jersey with six starts before moving to Cleveland. The Kings received 449 direct franchise games from Woodson and Steppe against 54 from Lacey, producing a decisive Kansas City win.
perspectives.analysis:
Kansas City Received a Long-Term Scorer Plus a First-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and Kansas City records agree on the November 12, 1981 package. The Nets received Sam Lacey, while the Kings received Mike Woodson and a 1982 first-round pick that became No. 17 Brook Steppe.

The pick was conditional on the more favorable of the Lakers and Suns choices available through New Jersey's prior transactions. It ultimately landed in the middle of the first round.

Woodson Became the Centerpiece

Woodson had played only seven games for New Jersey before the trade. In Kansas City he immediately moved into a much larger role, appearing in 76 games in 1981-82 and starting 74 while averaging 16.1 points.

He followed with 81 games and 18.2 points per game in 1982-83. Woodson then played 71 games in 1983-84, 78 in 1984-85 and 81 in the franchise's first Sacramento season in 1985-86.

Across those five Kings seasons, Woodson played 387 regular-season games and started 143. He scored more than 6,000 points for the franchise during that stretch and remained a reliable scoring guard through the move from Kansas City to Sacramento.

Steppe Added Another NBA Player

Kansas City used the No. 17 pick on Georgia Tech guard Brook Steppe.

Steppe played 62 games for the Kings as a rookie in 1982-83, made six starts and averaged 4.0 points in 9.8 minutes. He moved to Indiana the following season, so this review credits only that original Kansas City tenure.

The pick did not become a star, but it still produced a rotation player on top of Woodson's much larger contribution.

Lacey's Nets Tenure Was Brief

Lacey played 54 regular-season games for New Jersey after the trade and started six. He averaged 8.6 points, 5.7 rebounds and 4.0 assists in a reduced role.

He did not return to the Nets the following season, instead finishing his NBA career with Cleveland in 1982-83. New Jersey therefore received less than one full season from the veteran center.

Why Kansas City Wins Decisively

Woodson alone makes the trade heavily favor the Kings. He provided five seasons of scoring value, including several years as one of the franchise's most productive guards.

Steppe's 62 games add another useful branch. Kansas City received 449 direct regular-season games from the two incoming assets, while Lacey produced 54 for New Jersey.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A+/D. Kansas City receives an A+ because Woodson became a five-season franchise fixture and the first-round pick also produced an NBA rotation player. New Jersey receives a D because Lacey's useful but brief 54-game tenure was nowhere close to the value surrendered.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Vinnie Johnson from Seattle on November 23, 1981 for Greg Kelser. Johnson became a 10-season Pistons fixture, playing 798 regular-season games, starting 164, scoring 10,146 points and serving as a central reserve on the franchise's 1989 and 1990 championship teams. Kelser gave Seattle two useful seasons, playing 129 regular-season games with 19 starts before becoming one piece of the 1983 multi-asset trade that brought Tom Chambers and Al Wood to the SuperSonics. Seattle received legitimate value, but Johnson's decade of production and championship impact makes Detroit the overwhelming winner.
perspectives.analysis:
The Canonical Date Needed Correction

The legacy archive entry carried November 21, 1981, but Basketball-Reference's Detroit, Seattle, league and Jack McCloskey transaction ledgers all place the trade on November 23. RealGM independently lists the same November 23 date.

This review therefore corrects the canonical date rather than preserving the earlier value. The package itself is undisputed: Detroit received Vinnie Johnson and Seattle received Greg Kelser.

Johnson Became a Ten-Year Pistons Fixture

Johnson played 67 regular-season games for Detroit in 1981-82 and started 15. He immediately became useful, averaging 7.7 points and 2.4 assists while shooting 49.3 percent from the field.

His role expanded the following season to 82 games and 51 starts, but his long-term value came from becoming one of the defining reserve scorers of Detroit's rise. Across ten Pistons seasons, Johnson played 798 regular-season games, started 164 and scored 10,146 points.

He stayed with the franchise through both championship seasons. Detroit won the 1989 and 1990 NBA titles with Johnson as a core member of the backcourt rotation, and his postseason résumé with the Pistons reached 108 games.

Kelser Gave Seattle Two Solid Seasons

Kelser was not a zero-value return. He played 49 regular-season games for Seattle in 1981-82, started ten and averaged 4.9 points and 3.1 rebounds.

He then appeared in 80 games in 1982-83, made nine starts and averaged 8.3 points and 5.0 rebounds. That gives Seattle 129 regular-season games and 19 starts from Kelser before the franchise moved him again.

For a player who had battled knee trouble in Detroit, two mostly healthy Seattle seasons represent a credible return.

Seattle Later Used Kelser in a Much Larger Trade

On August 18, 1983, Seattle included Kelser with Mark Radford, James Donaldson, a 1984 first-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick in the multi-asset deal that brought Tom Chambers, Al Wood and two draft picks from San Diego.

That downstream move gives Kelser some additional transaction utility. This review does not assign the entire Chambers return to him because the package included several other meaningful players and picks.

The direct comparison is still the cleanest measure: Seattle received two useful seasons from Kelser, while Detroit received a decade from Johnson.

Why Detroit Wins by a Wide Margin

Johnson's 798 Detroit games alone dwarf Kelser's 129 Seattle games. The gap becomes even larger when Johnson's 10,146 Pistons points, 164 starts, 108 playoff games and two championship seasons are included.

Seattle did not get nothing, and Kelser's later inclusion in the Chambers trade keeps the grade above failing. The outcome simply was not close.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A+/C+. Detroit receives an A+ because Johnson became a ten-year franchise fixture and championship rotation cornerstone. Seattle receives a C+ because Kelser supplied two useful seasons and later retained package value, but the direct and historical returns fall far short of Johnson's Pistons career.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey acquired James Bailey from Seattle on November 25, 1981 for Ray Tolbert and a 1984 second-round pick that became No. 39 Danny Young. Bailey played 73 regular-season games for the Nets, all off the bench, before being traded to Houston for two second-round picks. Seattle received 97 regular-season games and two starts from Tolbert, then used the No. 39 pick on Young, who played 235 regular-season games for the SuperSonics across four seasons with 55 starts. Young became a useful backcourt piece and Seattle later spent an expansion-draft asset to protect him. The Sonics' direct player return was clearly stronger, though Bailey's later flip preserved some value for New Jersey.
perspectives.analysis:
Seattle Received Two Useful NBA Players

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and Seattle transaction ledgers agree on the November 25, 1981 package. The Nets received James Bailey, while the SuperSonics received Ray Tolbert and New Jersey's 1984 second-round pick.

That pick eventually landed at No. 39 and became Danny Young.

Bailey Gave New Jersey 73 Games

Bailey played 67 regular-season games for the Nets in 1981-82, all off the bench. He averaged 8.9 points, 5.1 rebounds and 1.1 blocks in 19.2 minutes while shooting 52.3 percent from the field.

He returned for only six games in 1982-83 before New Jersey traded him to Houston on November 10. Across his Nets tenure, Bailey therefore produced 73 regular-season games and zero starts.

New Jersey did not lose the asset for nothing. The Houston trade returned a 1983 second-round pick that became Horace Owens and a 1985 second-round pick that became Yvon Joseph.

Those downstream picks had limited direct NBA outcomes. Owens never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, although New Jersey later included him in the package that acquired Reggie Johnson from Philadelphia. Joseph played one regular-season game for the Nets.

Tolbert Played 97 Games for Seattle

Ray Tolbert appeared in 52 regular-season games for Seattle after the trade in 1981-82 and 45 more in 1982-83. He made two starts across those seasons.

His role was modest, but he gave the SuperSonics 97 games of frontcourt depth before being moved in a three-team transaction in February 1983. Seattle received Steve Hawes in that later structure, although this review does not assign the entire Hawes return to Tolbert because multiple teams and draft assets were involved.

Danny Young Became the More Important Seattle Return

Seattle used the incoming 1984 second-round pick on Wake Forest guard Danny Young at No. 39.

Young appeared in only three games as a rookie, then became a regular rotation player. He played all 82 games in 1985-86 with 29 starts, followed with 73 games and 26 starts in 1986-87, and added 77 games in 1987-88.

That gives Seattle 235 regular-season games and 55 starts from Young across four seasons. His strongest year was 1985-86, when he averaged 6.9 points and 3.7 assists while shooting 50.6 percent from the field.

Seattle valued Young enough that in June 1988 it sent Miami a second-round pick in exchange for the Heat agreeing not to select him in the expansion draft. The SuperSonics waived him later that October, but the protection transaction confirms that he remained a meaningful roster asset deep into his Seattle tenure.

Why Seattle Wins

The direct player accounting strongly favors the SuperSonics. Tolbert and Young combined for 332 Seattle regular-season games and 57 starts. Bailey produced 73 Nets games and zero starts.

New Jersey's later Bailey trade preserved some transaction utility through two second-round picks, which keeps the result from being a severe loss. The downstream player outcomes from those picks, however, were limited.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, B+/C+. Seattle receives a B+ because Tolbert supplied useful depth and the second-round pick became a four-season rotation guard in Young. New Jersey receives a C+ because Bailey was productive in a reserve role and later returned two second-round picks, but the direct realized player value fell well short of Seattle's package.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Sold Jackson's Rights for Cash

Basketball-Reference's Boston, Chicago and league transaction ledgers agree on the December 9, 1981 mechanism. Boston sold the player rights to Tracy Jackson to the Bulls.

The canonical source package records cash as Boston's return. The reviewed public ledgers do not identify the amount, so this review preserves the cash component without assigning it a speculative dollar value.

Jackson Immediately Joined Chicago's Rotation

Jackson had appeared in only 11 games for Boston before the sale. With Chicago, he played 38 regular-season games in the remainder of 1981-82 and logged 412 minutes.

He averaged 4.5 points in 10.8 minutes while shooting 47.3 percent from the field. He did not start, but the Bulls received a usable reserve rather than a set of inactive rights.

His Bigger Contribution Came the Next Season

Jackson returned for 78 games in 1982-83 and made three starts. His role grew to 16.8 minutes per game, and he averaged 6.3 points, 2.3 rebounds and 1.3 assists.

Across the two Chicago seasons, Jackson played 116 regular-season games and scored 662 points. Those two years account for nearly all of his NBA career; he appeared in only two more games, both with Indiana in 1983-84.

Boston Received Cash but No Basketball Asset

The Celtics converted Jackson's rights into cash rather than holding a player who was buried on a deep roster. That is a rational transaction and gives Boston a real return.

The missing public dollar amount limits any attempt to compare the cash precisely with Jackson's production. There is no evidence in the reviewed sources that the payment represented a major asset.

Why Chicago Gets the Edge

Chicago paid cash and received two seasons of reserve value, including a 78-game second season. Boston received an unquantified financial return.

For a minor transaction, 116 regular-season games is a useful realized outcome. It is enough to give the Bulls the clear basketball edge without turning the deal into a major historical win.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, B/C+. Chicago receives a B because Jackson supplied 116 regular-season games and two seasons of rotation depth for a cash-only cost. Boston receives a C+ because it monetized a little-used player, with the unknown cash amount preventing a more exact assessment.

perspectives.summary: Denver sold Ronnie Valentine's player rights to Washington on December 17, 1981 for cash. The Nuggets, Bullets and league transaction ledgers agree on the rights sale, but none of the reviewed public sources identifies the payment amount. Valentine never appeared in a regular-season game for Washington and his NBA career ended with the 24 games he had played for Denver in 1980-81. The Bullets therefore received zero on-court production, while Denver received an unquantified financial return. Because the cash figure is unavailable, the transaction remains Insufficient Evidence rather than receiving a speculative hindsight grade.
perspectives.analysis:
The Transaction Mechanics Are Source-Closed

Basketball-Reference's Denver, Washington and league transaction ledgers all record the same December 17, 1981 event: Denver sold Ronnie Valentine's player rights to the Bullets. Carl Scheer's executive transaction ledger independently records the rights sale on the same date. The basic mechanism is therefore high-confidence.

The Missing Piece Is the Cash Amount

The public sources reviewed for this review do not state how much Washington paid. That missing figure matters because Denver's entire return was financial rather than a player or draft asset. Assigning a letter grade to the Nuggets would require guessing whether the payment was nominal, meaningful or somewhere between. This review does not introduce a dollar estimate that the source record does not support.

Valentine Produced Zero Games for Washington

Valentine had been Denver's No. 51 pick in the 1980 NBA Draft and played 24 regular-season games for the Nuggets in 1980-81. He averaged 3.5 points in 5.1 minutes during that lone NBA season. After Washington acquired his rights, he did not appear in a Bullets regular-season game and never played another NBA game.

The Bullets Still Acquired a Real Asset

Zero games does not mean the acquired rights had no value at the moment of the transaction. Washington paid for the opportunity to control Valentine's NBA rights and evaluate whether he could help the roster. The hindsight result is clear: that opportunity did not convert into an NBA appearance. What cannot be measured from the public record is whether the purchase cost was trivial enough that the failed roster bet should still be considered harmless.

Why the Verdict Stays Insufficient Evidence

The direction of the basketball outcome is easy to describe: Washington received no games. The scale of Denver's return is not. This review therefore separates factual completion from valuation certainty. The transaction is source-closed, the player outcome is source-closed, and the missing sale price is explicitly preserved as the blocker to a letter-grade verdict.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence. Denver received cash for rights that ultimately produced no Washington games, but the public cash amount is unavailable. Washington's on-court return was zero, yet assigning precise grades would imply a valuation of the unknown payment that the evidence cannot support.

perspectives.summary: San Antonio acquired Mike Mitchell and Roger Phegley from Cleveland on December 23, 1981 for Ron Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash. Mitchell became the centerpiece, playing 488 regular-season games for the Spurs through 1987-88 and starting 417, including 57 starts immediately after the trade in 1981-82. Phegley added 116 Spurs games over two seasons. Cleveland received 68 games and 59 starts from Brewer plus 23 games and 22 starts from Johnson, then turned Johnson into Cliff Robinson, who played 180 Cavaliers games with 174 starts over parts of three seasons. Cleveland recovered substantial value, but Mitchell's long run as San Antonio's high-volume scoring forward still gives the Spurs the stronger outcome.
perspectives.analysis:
Mitchell Became the Long-Term Centerpiece

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, San Antonio and league transaction ledgers agree on the December 23, 1981 package. The Spurs sent Ron Brewer, Reggie Johnson and cash to Cleveland for Mike Mitchell and Roger Phegley.

Mitchell had been an All-Star for Cleveland in 1980-81 and immediately became a full-time San Antonio starter. He played 57 regular-season games for the Spurs after the trade in 1981-82, started all 57 and averaged more than 20 points per game.

He then played 80 games in 1982-83, 79 in 1983-84, 82 in 1984-85, 82 in 1985-86, 40 in 1986-87 and 68 in 1987-88. Across that seven-season Spurs stretch, Mitchell appeared in 488 regular-season games and made 417 starts.

San Antonio also reached the Western Conference Finals in each of Mitchell's first two Spurs seasons. His value was not a brief scoring spike; he became a long-term frontcourt fixture.

Phegley Added Useful Depth

Roger Phegley played 54 games for San Antonio in 1981-82 and 62 more in 1982-83. He made five starts across those two seasons.

His role was smaller than Mitchell's, but 116 additional regular-season games meant the Spurs received value from both incoming players.

Brewer Gave Cleveland a Strong Short-Term Scoring Return

Ron Brewer played 47 games for Cleveland after the trade in 1981-82 and started 41. He averaged 19.4 points in 36.7 minutes for a struggling Cavaliers team.

Brewer returned for 21 games and 18 starts in 1982-83 before moving to Golden State. His direct Cleveland total was 68 games and 59 starts.

That is a meaningful return and prevents the trade from being viewed as Cleveland simply giving away an All-Star for nothing.

Johnson Became Cliff Robinson

Reggie Johnson played 23 games for Cleveland after the trade and started 22. On February 16, 1982, the Cavaliers traded him to Kansas City for Cliff Robinson.

Robinson became the strongest downstream Cleveland asset connected to the deal. He played 30 games for the Cavaliers in 1981-82, 77 in 1982-83 and 73 in 1983-84, totaling 180 regular-season games and 174 starts across those parts of three seasons.

He averaged 17.8 points and 10.3 rebounds in 1983-84. That downstream return materially improves Cleveland's side and should be credited to the Johnson branch without pretending Johnson alone created Robinson's full career value beyond Cleveland.

Cash Adds Another Cleveland Component

Cleveland also received cash, but the reviewed transaction records do not identify the amount. The payment therefore receives qualitative credit without a speculative dollar value.

Why San Antonio Still Wins

Cleveland extracted much more value than a simple one-season accounting suggests. Brewer was a productive scorer, Johnson was quickly converted into Robinson, and Robinson became a multi-year starter.

San Antonio nevertheless received the best player and kept him for far longer. Mitchell's 488 Spurs games and 417 starts, combined with Phegley's 116 games, gave San Antonio 604 direct regular-season appearances from its incoming players.

The long-term scoring role, playoff relevance and durability of Mitchell outweigh Cleveland's shorter Brewer return plus the Robinson downstream branch.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win, A+/B. San Antonio receives an A+ because Mitchell became a seven-season scoring fixture and Phegley added two years of depth. Cleveland receives a B because Brewer produced immediately, Johnson became Cliff Robinson, and the cash component added value, but the total return still did not match Mitchell's sustained Spurs impact.
