perspectives.summary: Los Angeles acquired Bob McAdoo from New Jersey on December 24, 1981 for cash and a 1983 second-round pick that became No. 46 Kevin Williams. McAdoo played 224 regular-season games for the Lakers over four seasons and became a major reserve on the 1982 and 1985 championship teams. New Jersey never used the pick itself: in June 1983 the Nets sent it with Fred Roberts to San Antonio as compensation for signing coach Stan Albeck. Albeck went 87-77 over two Nets seasons and reached the playoffs both years, including a 1984 first-round upset of defending champion Philadelphia. The pick therefore retained real transaction utility, but McAdoo's four-year championship contribution gives Los Angeles a decisive win.
perspectives.analysis:
The Pick Did Not Stay With New Jersey

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and league transaction ledgers place the Bob McAdoo trade on December 24, 1981. Los Angeles received McAdoo, while the Nets received a 1983 second-round pick. The legacy canonical package also records cash going to New Jersey; the public amount is not identified.

A crucial downstream correction is required for the pick. New Jersey did not make the No. 46 selection itself. On June 7, 1983, the Nets sent Fred Roberts and that 1983 second-round pick to San Antonio as compensation for signing Stan Albeck as a veteran coach. The Spurs then used No. 46 on Kevin Williams.

McAdoo Became a Four-Year Lakers Reserve

McAdoo joined a loaded Los Angeles roster and accepted a bench role. He played 41 regular-season games in 1981-82 and made no starts, averaging 9.6 points in 18.2 minutes.

His impact rose in the playoffs. McAdoo appeared in all 14 Lakers postseason games during the 1982 title run and averaged 16.7 points, giving the bench a former MVP-caliber scorer without requiring the offense to revolve around him.

He stayed productive for three more seasons. McAdoo played 47 games in 1982-83, 70 in 1983-84 and 66 in 1984-85. Across those four Lakers seasons he appeared in 224 regular-season games and made only one start, a clear illustration of how fully he adapted to a reserve role.

Los Angeles won the championship again in 1985 with McAdoo still in the rotation. His regular-season scoring that year was 10.5 points per game, and he remained part of the postseason frontcourt.

Kevin Williams Was a Spurs Outcome, Not a Nets Player

San Antonio used the transferred No. 46 pick on Kevin Williams. Williams played 19 regular-season games for the Spurs as a rookie before moving on to Cleveland and later other teams.

Those 19 Spurs games cannot be credited to New Jersey as direct player production. The Nets' realized value came from using the pick as one component of the compensation required to sign Albeck.

The Albeck Branch Had Real Organizational Value

Albeck coached New Jersey for two seasons. The Nets went 45-37 in 1983-84 and 42-40 in 1984-85, reaching the playoffs both years.

The 1984 team defeated the defending champion Philadelphia 76ers in the first round before losing to Milwaukee in the conference semifinals. That makes the pick's rerouting more meaningful than a draft choice that simply washed out.

This review does not assign Albeck's entire coaching tenure to the McAdoo pick because Fred Roberts was also part of the compensation package. The pick nevertheless retained clear transaction utility and contributed to acquiring a successful coach.

Cash Adds Another Nets Return

The canonical package includes cash, but the reviewed public transaction sources do not disclose the amount. New Jersey therefore receives qualitative credit for the payment without a speculative dollar valuation.

Why Los Angeles Still Wins Easily

The Lakers received four seasons from McAdoo, 224 regular-season games and important bench scoring on two championship teams. That is a major realized return for a second-round pick and cash.

New Jersey preserved value by rerouting the pick into the Albeck signing, and the coaching result was useful. Even with that downstream credit, the Nets did not receive a basketball asset comparable to McAdoo's direct championship contribution.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A+/C+. Los Angeles receives an A+ because McAdoo became a four-season reserve weapon and contributed to the 1982 and 1985 championships. New Jersey receives a C+ because the pick retained useful transaction value in the Albeck signing and the club also received cash, but the package fell far short of McAdoo's Lakers impact.

summary: Atlanta acquired Freeman Williams from San Diego on January 20, 1982 for Charlie Criss and Al Wood. Williams played only 23 regular-season games for the Hawks and made no starts, but seven months later Atlanta included him with John Drew in the trade that acquired Dominique Wilkins. San Diego received 28 games and 20 starts from Criss plus 105 games and 52 starts from Wood before Wood became part of the 1983 multi-asset Tom Chambers trade with Seattle. The Clippers won the direct player-production comparison, but Williams' role in the Wilkins acquisition gives Atlanta the more consequential downstream outcome. Because John Drew was also essential to that later package, this review credits Williams with transaction utility rather than the entirety of Wilkins' Hall of Fame career.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
San Diego Won the Immediate Production Exchange

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta, San Diego and league transaction ledgers agree on the January 20, 1982 package. Atlanta sent Charlie Criss and Al Wood to the Clippers for Freeman Williams.

On direct post-trade production alone, the deal favors San Diego. Williams played 23 regular-season games for Atlanta, all off the bench, and averaged 4.8 points in only 8.2 minutes.

Criss immediately became San Diego's starting point guard for much of the remainder of the season. He played 28 games for the Clippers, started 20 and averaged 12.9 points and 4.0 assists in 30.0 minutes.

Wood Gave the Clippers a Longer Return

Al Wood played 29 games for San Diego after the trade in 1981-82 and made five starts. He averaged 12.5 points while shooting 51.8 percent from the field.

His role grew substantially in 1982-83. Wood appeared in 76 games, started 47 and averaged 10.9 points, 3.1 rebounds and 1.8 assists.

That gives San Diego 105 regular-season games and 52 starts from Wood, plus 28 games and 20 starts from Criss. Combined, the two incoming players produced 133 Clippers games and 72 starts.

Criss left after the season and signed with Milwaukee. Wood remained one more year before becoming part of a larger transaction.

Wood Later Carried Additional Trade Utility

On August 18, 1983, San Diego included Wood with Tom Chambers, a 1984 third-round pick and a 1987 second-round pick in the multi-asset trade with Seattle that brought James Donaldson, Greg Kelser, Mark Radford, a 1984 first-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick to the Clippers.

That gives Wood additional downstream value, but this review does not assign the full Seattle package to him. Chambers and the draft assets were substantial pieces of the same transaction.

Williams' Atlanta Tenure Was Short but Strategically Important

Williams' direct Hawks production was minimal. He played only 23 games, made no starts and never returned for another Atlanta regular-season appearance.

The importance comes from what Atlanta did next. On September 2, 1982, the Hawks traded John Drew and Williams to Utah for the draft rights to Dominique Wilkins.

Wilkins became one of the defining players in franchise history, eventually playing 882 regular-season games for the Hawks and becoming the franchise's career leader in games played. He was a nine-time All-Star overall, won the 1985-86 scoring title and later entered the Hall of Fame.

This review does not credit the entire Wilkins career to Williams because John Drew was the other major asset in the Utah package. Williams should instead receive strong transaction-utility credit for being one required component of a franchise-altering acquisition.

Why Atlanta Gets the Hindsight Edge

San Diego clearly received more direct value from the January trade. Criss and Wood combined for 133 games and 72 starts, while Williams gave Atlanta only 23 reserve appearances.

The downstream branches change the comparison. Wood later helped San Diego in the Chambers trade, but Williams was part of the package that brought Wilkins to Atlanta. Even with conservative shared-credit treatment, participating in that acquisition carries more long-term franchise consequence than the original 23-game stint suggests.

Final Verdict

Hawks Edge, A-/B+. Atlanta receives an A- because Williams' direct contribution was small but his later use in the Dominique Wilkins trade created exceptional transaction utility. San Diego receives a B+ because Criss and Wood supplied 133 games and 72 starts, and Wood retained later trade value. The margin is not wide enough to treat Wilkins' full career as Williams-only value, but the downstream Atlanta outcome is still the most consequential branch.

indiana-pacers.summary: Philadelphia acquired Mike Bantom from Indiana for cash on January 20, 1982. Bantom played 43 regular-season games for the 76ers, started once and averaged 8.8 points and 5.3 rebounds while shooting 51.0 percent. He then appeared in all 21 Philadelphia playoff games during the team's run to the 1982 NBA Finals. Bantom left the NBA for Italy after the season, so the Sixers received only a half-season plus one postseason from the deal, but that still exceeded Indiana's unquantified cash return in realized basketball value.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Philadelphia Bought Useful Frontcourt Depth for a Finals Run

Basketball-Reference's Indiana and Philadelphia transaction ledgers place the transaction on January 20, 1982. Philadelphia acquired Mike Bantom's player rights from the Pacers, while the canonical source package records cash going back to Indiana.

The reviewed public ledgers do not identify the cash amount, so this review preserves the return without assigning a speculative dollar value.

Bantom Played 43 Regular-Season Games

Bantom joined a Philadelphia team already headed toward the top of the Eastern Conference. He played 43 regular-season games after the trade, started once and averaged 22.8 minutes.

His production was useful for a midseason veteran acquisition: 8.8 points and 5.3 rebounds per game while shooting 51.0 percent from the field.

Philadelphia finished 58-24 and reached the NBA Finals.

He Appeared in Every Playoff Game

Bantom also played in all 21 of Philadelphia's postseason games. He averaged 19.0 minutes, 4.3 points and 3.7 rebounds during the playoff run.

The 76ers swept Atlanta in the opening round, beat Milwaukee and Boston in longer series, then lost the Finals to the Lakers in six games.

Bantom was not a star on that roster, but a 21-game postseason role gives the acquisition more value than a brief regular-season rental would suggest.

The Tenure Ended After One Season

Bantom did not return to the NBA in 1982-83. Basketball-Reference lists him as playing professionally in Italy beginning the next season.

That limits Philadelphia's long-term return to 43 regular-season games and one postseason. He was not part of the 1982-83 championship roster.

Indiana Received Cash

The Pacers' realized return was cash rather than a player or pick. Because the public amount is not identified, this review cannot determine whether the financial return was unusually large.

The basketball comparison is still straightforward: Philadelphia received a productive rotation forward during a Finals run, while Indiana received no subsequent player production from the transaction itself.

Why Philadelphia Wins

The Sixers got exactly the kind of short-term veteran depth a contender can justify buying in January. Bantom contributed immediately in both the regular season and playoffs.

Indiana's cash return keeps the Pacers from a failing grade, but there is no documented player or draft branch to offset Bantom's on-court contribution.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, B+/C. Philadelphia receives a B+ for 43 useful regular-season games and participation in all 21 playoff games during a Finals run. Indiana receives a C for converting Bantom into cash, with the unknown amount preventing a more precise grade.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Date Differs Across Major Sources

this review preserves a documented source-date conflict instead of forcing false precision. RealGM lists Armond Hill as acquired by San Diego on February 12, 1982, matching the canonical record. Basketball-Reference's San Diego, Seattle and league transaction ledgers place the full Hill-for-Phil Smith trade on February 16.

Because the team and league ledgers agree on February 16 while RealGM supports February 12, this review retains the canonical February 12 date but lowers confidence to medium and records the four-day discrepancy explicitly.

San Diego Got a Short Starting Look at Armond Hill

Hill played 19 regular-season games for the Clippers after the trade and started 14. He averaged 25.3 minutes, 4.7 points and 4.3 assists.

He did not return to San Diego the following season. RealGM's roster turnover lists Hill becoming a free agent on July 1, 1982 before later joining Milwaukee.

That makes Hill a useful but short-lived direct return.

The Second-Round Pick Retained Trade Utility

Seattle's 1982 second-round pick was the choice that ultimately became No. 42 Jeff Taylor, but San Diego did not use it on Taylor. On June 28, the Clippers packaged that pick with Joe Bryant and sent both to Houston for the 1982 No. 32 pick that became Richard Anderson.

This review does not credit the full Anderson return to this one pick because Bryant was also required in the package. The correct value is narrower: the acquired second-rounder retained enough transaction utility to help San Diego move up ten spots in the draft.

The canonical source package also includes cash to San Diego. The reviewed public primary ledgers do not specify the amount, so this review preserves the cash component without assigning a speculative dollar value.

Phil Smith Gave Seattle Two Useful Seasons

Smith played 26 regular-season games for Seattle after the trade in 1981-82, started two and averaged 8.2 points. He also appeared in all eight of Seattle's playoff games that spring.

He returned for 79 games in 1982-83, starting 17 and averaging 5.7 points and 2.7 assists.

Across the two seasons, Smith gave the SuperSonics 105 regular-season games and 19 starts. That is substantially more direct team production than Hill's 19 games for San Diego.

Why Seattle Gets the Edge

San Diego did not come away empty. Hill started 14 games, the pick remained useful in a later draft-day trade and the canonical package includes cash.

Seattle still received the stronger direct realized basketball value. Smith stayed for parts of two seasons, played 105 games and remained a usable rotation guard after Hill had already left San Diego.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win, B+/B. Seattle receives a B+ for 105 games and 19 starts from Smith across parts of two seasons. San Diego receives a B because Hill started 14 games and the pick retained downstream transaction value, with cash providing additional but unquantified consideration. Confidence is medium because authoritative sources disagree on the exact trade date and the public primary ledgers do not quantify the cash component.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Bill Laimbeer and Kenny Carr from Cleveland on February 16, 1982 for Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski, a 1982 first-round pick that became No. 12 John Bagley and a 1982 second-round pick that became No. 28 Dave Magley. Cleveland received substantial quantity: Hubbard played 469 regular-season games for the Cavaliers, Bagley 375, Mokeski 51 and Magley 14. Detroit received the defining player. Laimbeer played 937 regular-season games for the Pistons, made 857 starts, became a four-time All-Star and starting center on the 1989 and 1990 championship teams. Carr was later traded one-for-one for the No. 18 pick that became Ricky Pierce. Cleveland built useful depth, but Laimbeer's thirteen-year franchise impact makes Detroit the clear winner.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Acquired the Defining Asset

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, Detroit and league transaction ledgers agree on the February 16, 1982 package. Detroit received Bill Laimbeer and Kenny Carr. Cleveland received Phil Hubbard, Paul Mokeski, Detroit's 1982 first-round pick and a 1982 second-round pick that had originally come from Kansas City.

The first-rounder became No. 12 John Bagley. The second-rounder became No. 28 Dave Magley.

Laimbeer Became a Detroit Cornerstone

Laimbeer played 937 regular-season games for Detroit across thirteen seasons and started 857. He scored 12,665 points and collected 9,430 rebounds for the Pistons.

His value went far beyond longevity. Laimbeer became a four-time All-Star, led the NBA in rebounds in 1984-85 and served as the starting center on Detroit's 1989 and 1990 championship teams.

NBA and Pistons historical material place him among the central players of the Bad Boys era, and his 9,430 rebounds remain the franchise's all-time record. That level of sustained production makes him the transaction's defining asset by a wide margin.

Kenny Carr Also Retained Direct Trade Value

Carr's Detroit stay was brief, but the branch did not simply disappear. On June 23, 1982, Detroit traded Carr one-for-one to Portland for the No. 18 pick in the 1982 draft.

The Pistons used that pick on Ricky Pierce. Pierce played 39 regular-season games for Detroit as a rookie, making one start, before continuing a long NBA career elsewhere.

Because Carr was the sole outgoing asset in that Portland trade, this review can credit the No. 18 pick directly to the Carr branch without the multi-asset attribution problem that affects many downstream chains.

Cleveland Received Real Volume

Phil Hubbard became the largest Cleveland return. He played 469 regular-season games for the Cavaliers across seven seasons and developed into a productive frontcourt scorer, including 15.8 points per game in 1984-85.

John Bagley also became a multi-year contributor. Across five Cleveland seasons he played 375 regular-season games and started 231, becoming the club's primary starting point guard for much of the mid-1980s.

Paul Mokeski added 51 Cleveland games and 19 starts across parts of two seasons. Dave Magley appeared in 14 Cavaliers games as a rookie, all off the bench.

Combined, Hubbard, Bagley, Mokeski and Magley produced 909 regular-season games for Cleveland. That is substantial realized value and prevents the Cavaliers from receiving a poor grade.

Why Detroit Still Wins

Raw game totals make the Cleveland package look competitive, but the quality and franchise importance of those games were very different. Cleveland received multiple useful rotation pieces. Detroit received a player who became a four-time All-Star, franchise rebounding leader and starting center on two championship teams.

Laimbeer's 937 Detroit games alone exceed the total of any individual Cleveland branch, and his postseason and championship importance gives those games much greater leverage. Carr's direct conversion into the Ricky Pierce pick adds another positive branch.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A+/B. Detroit receives an A+ because Laimbeer became a thirteen-year franchise cornerstone and championship starter, while Carr was converted one-for-one into another first-round pick. Cleveland receives a B because Hubbard, Bagley, Mokeski and Magley produced 909 combined regular-season games, including several productive seasons, but none approached Laimbeer's peak, longevity or championship importance.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired 21-year-old Cliff Robinson from Kansas City on February 16, 1982 for Reggie Johnson. Robinson became an immediate Cavaliers starter, playing 180 regular-season games across parts of three seasons with 174 starts and averaging roughly 17 to 18 points per game during that span. Johnson played 81 regular-season games for the Kings across parts of two seasons, starting nine, before Kansas City sold his player rights to Philadelphia for cash in February 1983. Cleveland later packaged Robinson with 1984 first-round pick Tim McCormick for the draft rights to Melvin Turpin, though the full downstream return cannot be credited to Robinson alone. The direct realized value clearly favors Cleveland.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Acquired the Better Young Forward

The Kings' official transaction history and Basketball-Reference records agree on the February 16, 1982 exchange: Kansas City sent Cliff Robinson to Cleveland for Reggie Johnson.

Both players were young frontcourt pieces, but their post-trade roles diverged quickly.

Robinson Became an Immediate Cavaliers Starter

Robinson played 30 regular-season games for Cleveland after the trade in 1981-82 and started 29. He averaged 16.3 points and 9.6 rebounds while playing more than 31 minutes per game.

His role expanded further in 1982-83. Robinson appeared in 77 games, started 75 and averaged 18.0 points and 11.1 rebounds.

He followed with 73 games and 70 starts in 1983-84, averaging 17.8 points and 10.3 rebounds. Across parts of three Cleveland seasons, Robinson therefore produced 180 regular-season games and 174 starts.

That is a substantial direct return from a one-for-one midseason trade.

Johnson Gave Kansas City a Shorter Rotation Return

Reggie Johnson played 31 games for Kansas City after the deal in 1981-82, starting nine and averaging 12.2 points and 6.1 rebounds.

He returned for 50 more Kings games in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 8.6 points and 4.0 rebounds.

That gives Kansas City 81 regular-season games and nine starts from Johnson. The contribution was useful, but it was far smaller than Robinson's Cleveland role in both volume and starting responsibility.

Kansas City Later Sold Johnson's Rights

On February 15, 1983, Kansas City sold Johnson's player rights to Philadelphia. The Kings' official media guide identifies the return as cash.

The reviewed public record does not provide a dollar amount, so this review credits Kansas City with a tangible downstream cash return but does not invent a financial value.

Cleveland Also Retained Trade Utility in Robinson

Cleveland kept Robinson through the 1983-84 season. On June 19, 1984, the Cavaliers packaged him with the No. 12 pick, Tim McCormick, and sent both to Washington for the draft rights to No. 6 pick Melvin Turpin.

Robinson therefore retained substantial transaction value after his three Cleveland seasons. This review does not credit the entire Turpin return to Robinson because McCormick was an essential second asset in that deal.

Why Cleveland Wins

Robinson gave Cleveland 180 games, 174 starts and three seasons of high-volume scoring and rebounding. Johnson gave Kansas City 81 games and nine starts before being sold for cash.

Even after acknowledging Johnson's later cash return, the direct basketball gap is large. Cleveland received a young starter who became one of its primary scorers and rebounders, while Kansas City received a shorter-lived rotation forward.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A-/C+. Cleveland receives an A- for three seasons, 180 games and 174 starts from Robinson plus retained downstream trade value. Kansas City receives a C+ because Johnson supplied 81 games and later brought back cash, but his realized basketball role was much smaller.

The Kings' official transaction history and Basketball-Reference records agree on the February 16, 1982 exchange: Kansas City sent Cliff Robinson to Cleveland for Reggie Johnson.

Both players were young frontcourt pieces, but their post-trade roles diverged quickly.

Robinson Became an Immediate Cavaliers Starter

Robinson played 30 regular-season games for Cleveland after the trade in 1981-82 and started 29. He averaged 16.3 points and 9.6 rebounds while playing more than 31 minutes per game.

His role expanded further in 1982-83. Robinson appeared in 77 games, started 75 and averaged 18.0 points and 11.1 rebounds.

He followed with 73 games and 70 starts in 1983-84, averaging 17.8 points and 10.3 rebounds. Across parts of three Cleveland seasons, Robinson therefore produced 180 regular-season games and 174 starts.

That is a substantial direct return from a one-for-one midseason trade.

Johnson Gave Kansas City a Shorter Rotation Return

Reggie Johnson played 31 games for Kansas City after the deal in 1981-82, starting nine and averaging 12.2 points and 6.1 rebounds.

He returned for 50 more Kings games in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 8.6 points and 4.0 rebounds.

That gives Kansas City 81 regular-season games and nine starts from Johnson. The contribution was useful, but it was far smaller than Robinson's Cleveland role in both volume and starting responsibility.

Kansas City Later Sold Johnson's Rights

On February 15, 1983, Kansas City sold Johnson's player rights to Philadelphia. The Kings' official media guide identifies the return as cash.

The reviewed public record does not provide a dollar amount, so this review credits Kansas City with a tangible downstream cash return but does not invent a financial value.

Cleveland Also Retained Trade Utility in Robinson

Cleveland kept Robinson through the 1983-84 season. On June 19, 1984, the Cavaliers packaged him with the No. 12 pick, Tim McCormick, and sent both to Washington for the draft rights to No. 6 pick Melvin Turpin.

Robinson therefore retained substantial transaction value after his three Cleveland seasons. This review does not credit the entire Turpin return to Robinson because McCormick was an essential second asset in that deal.

Why Cleveland Wins

Robinson gave Cleveland 180 games, 174 starts and three seasons of high-volume scoring and rebounding. Johnson gave Kansas City 81 games and nine starts before being sold for cash.

Even after acknowledging Johnson's later cash return, the direct basketball gap is large. Cleveland received a young starter who became one of its primary scorers and rebounders, while Kansas City received a shorter-lived rotation forward.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A-/C+. Cleveland receives an A- for three seasons, 180 games and 174 starts from Robinson plus retained downstream trade value. Kansas City receives a C+ because Johnson supplied 81 games and later brought back cash, but his realized basketball role was much smaller.

perspectives.analysis:
The Original Deal Was Only the Beginning

Phoenix's media guide and Basketball-Reference transaction records identify the June 21, 1982 trade clearly. Denver received veteran center Rich Kelley, while Phoenix received Denver's 1982 first-round pick.

The Suns used No. 15 on David Thirdkill. Evaluating only Kelley against Thirdkill would make the deal look minor and perhaps Denver-favored. The source-backed downstream chains change the picture dramatically.

Kelley Played 38 Games Before Denver Converted Him Again

Kelley appeared in 38 regular-season games for Denver in 1982-83, all off the bench. He averaged 14.9 minutes, 4.6 points, 4.5 rebounds and 1.6 assists.

On February 7, 1983, Denver traded Kelley one-for-one to Utah for Danny Schayes and cash. Because Kelley was the sole outgoing asset, this review can credit the Schayes branch directly to the original acquisition.

Schayes Became a Long-Term Nugget

Schayes played 32 Denver games immediately after the trade, then remained with the Nuggets for eight seasons in total.

Basketball-Reference credits him with 536 regular-season games and 229 starts for Denver. He became a durable interior rotation player through the 1980s and appeared in 48 playoff games for the franchise.

That downstream conversion transforms Denver's side from a 38-game rental into a long-running positive asset chain.

Phoenix's Pick Became David Thirdkill

Phoenix selected Thirdkill at No. 15 in the 1982 draft. He played 49 regular-season games for the Suns as a rookie, started twice and averaged 4.0 points in 10.6 minutes.

That direct rookie return was modest. Phoenix, however, did not let the asset chain stop there.

Thirdkill Became Two Future Second-Round Picks

On October 17, 1983, Phoenix traded Thirdkill to Detroit for a 1986 second-round pick and a 1987 second-round pick. Thirdkill was the sole outgoing Suns asset, so both picks belong directly to this branch.

The 1986 pick became No. 46 Jeff Hornacek. The 1987 pick became No. 46 Bruce Dalrymple, who did not play in the NBA.

Hornacek Changed the Entire Value of the Trade

Hornacek played 468 regular-season games for Phoenix across six seasons and started 343. He averaged 13.7 points and 5.4 assists across his Suns tenure while shooting 51.0 percent from the field.

He developed into an All-Star and averaged 20.1 points in 1991-92. Phoenix then included Hornacek with Andrew Lang and Tim Perry in the 1992 trade for Charles Barkley.

This review does not credit the entire Barkley return to Hornacek because Lang and Perry were also part of that package. It does credit Hornacek's six high-level Suns seasons and the fact that he remained a major trade asset at departure.

Why Phoenix Gets the Edge Despite Denver's Excellent Return

Denver's branch was genuinely strong. Kelley became Schayes plus cash, and Schayes delivered 536 games and 229 starts over eight seasons.

Phoenix's branch produced fewer raw franchise games if Thirdkill and Hornacek are combined, but the quality of Hornacek's peak was much higher. He became a long-term starter, an All-Star and a 20-point scorer while remaining valuable enough to become a central component in a later superstar trade.

This is not a one-sided outcome. Both teams turned their original asset into much more than the first-year return.

Final Verdict

Suns Win, A+/A. Phoenix receives an A+ because the No. 15 pick became Thirdkill, then directly became the future pick used on Hornacek, who delivered 468 games, 343 starts and All-Star production. Denver receives an A because Kelley was converted one-for-one into Schayes and cash, producing 536 Schayes games and 229 starts across eight seasons. Phoenix wins on peak impact rather than volume.

perspectives.summary: Chicago traded the No. 38 pick in the 1982 draft to Golden State for a 1983 second-round pick. The later player labels in the canonical record are misleading if treated as direct team outcomes: Chicago never drafted Doc Rivers with No. 31, and Golden State never used No. 38 on Wayne Sappleton for itself. The Warriors routed Sappleton's rights to New Jersey for the 1983 No. 43 pick, Pace Mannion, who played 57 games for Golden State. Chicago's No. 31 asset went to Atlanta as compensation when the Bulls hired Kevin Loughery; Loughery coached Chicago for two seasons, going 65-99 and reaching the 1985 playoffs. Chicago extracted the better realized return, but neither side received the star career implied by the draft labels.
perspectives.analysis:
The Draft Labels Need Routing, Not Literal Credit

Basketball-Reference records the June 23, 1982 exchange as Chicago sending a 1982 second-round pick, later No. 38 Wayne Sappleton, to Golden State for a 1983 second-round pick, later No. 31 Doc Rivers.

Those draft labels describe where the picks eventually landed, not which franchise actually received those players. Treating Rivers as a Bulls player from this trade would be incorrect, and treating Sappleton as a Warriors contributor would be equally misleading.

Golden State Routed the Sappleton Rights to New Jersey

Golden State's executive ledger and the Nets' media guide show that the Warriors sent the rights to Sappleton to New Jersey for a 1983 second-round pick. Basketball-Reference dates that rights transaction June 19, four days before the Chicago pick-swap entry, while other draft-trade ledgers place the rights routing around draft week. This review records the chronology discrepancy but follows the consistent asset chain.

The incoming New Jersey pick became No. 43 Pace Mannion in 1983. Mannion played 57 regular-season games for Golden State in 1983-84, made no starts and averaged 2.1 points in 8.2 minutes.

That gives Golden State a real realized player return from the Chicago branch, but only a modest one.

Chicago Did Not Draft Doc Rivers

The No. 31 pick eventually belonged to Atlanta, not Chicago. The Hawks used it on Doc Rivers in the 1983 draft.

Contemporary and later accounts identify the pick as compensation connected to Chicago's hiring of former Hawks coach Kevin Loughery. Rivers himself later recalled that Atlanta received the selection because Loughery left the Hawks for the Bulls.

This review therefore credits Chicago with the coaching return attached to the asset, not with Rivers' NBA career.

Loughery Coached Two Bulls Seasons

Loughery coached Chicago in 1983-84 and 1984-85. His Bulls record was 65-99 across 164 regular-season games.

The first season ended 27-55. The second improved to 38-44 and produced a playoff berth, with Chicago losing 3-1 to Milwaukee in the first round.

That is not star-level value, but it is substantially more organizational use than 57 low-minute games from Mannion.

Why Chicago Wins Without Getting Doc Rivers Credit

The old shorthand makes the trade look like Chicago acquired Rivers while Golden State acquired Sappleton. Neither statement reflects the realized franchise outcome.

Golden State converted the No. 38 branch into Mannion, who played 57 reserve games. Chicago converted the future No. 31 asset into coaching compensation tied to Loughery, who ran the team for two full seasons and reached one postseason.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, B/C+. Chicago receives a B because the acquired pick became compensation in a two-season coaching hire that included a playoff appearance. Golden State receives a C+ because the Sappleton-rights branch became Pace Mannion and 57 reserve games. Rivers' Atlanta career is not credited to Chicago, and Sappleton's later Nets career is not credited to Golden State.

perspectives.summary: Portland acquired Kenny Carr from Detroit on June 23, 1982 for the No. 18 pick in the 1982 draft, which became Ricky Pierce. The original grading overvalued Pierce's later NBA career instead of his Detroit tenure. Carr played 212 regular-season games for Portland across three seasons, starting 113, and averaged double figures in each year. Pierce played only 39 games for Detroit with one start before the Pistons traded him for two future second-round picks and immediately flipped those picks to Phoenix for David Thirdkill. Thirdkill added 46 Detroit games with no starts. Portland therefore received 212 games and 113 starts from Carr against 85 combined Detroit games and one start from Pierce and Thirdkill, making the Trail Blazers the clear realized-value winner.
perspectives.analysis:
Portland Got Three Productive Seasons From Kenny Carr

Basketball-Reference records the June 23, 1982 deal as Detroit sending Kenny Carr to Portland for the Trail Blazers' 1982 first-round pick, later No. 18 Ricky Pierce.

The old shorthand treated Pierce's eventual NBA reputation as if Detroit received all of it. source-backed grading has to stop at the value the Pistons actually realized, including any directly traceable downstream assets.

Carr Became a Major Portland Rotation Forward

Carr played all 82 regular-season games for Portland in 1982-83 and started 26. He averaged 12.0 points and 7.2 rebounds while shooting 50.5 percent from the field.

He returned for all 82 games in 1983-84, starting 57 and averaging 15.6 points and 7.8 rebounds on 56.1 percent shooting.

Carr then played 48 games in 1984-85, starting 30 and averaging 10.4 points and 6.7 rebounds.

Across those three Portland seasons, Carr produced 212 regular-season games and 113 starts. He also gave the Trail Blazers multiple playoff appearances during that span.

Pierce Barely Played for Detroit

Detroit used the No. 18 pick on Ricky Pierce. As a rookie in 1982-83, Pierce appeared in 39 Pistons games, started once and averaged only 6.8 minutes and 2.2 points.

Pierce later developed into an excellent NBA scorer and Sixth Man of the Year, but that success came after Detroit moved him. This review does not credit the Pistons with his Clippers or Bucks career.

Detroit Did Preserve the Asset Through Another Trade

On October 17, 1983, Detroit traded Pierce to San Diego for 1986 and 1987 second-round picks. The Pistons then immediately sent those exact two picks to Phoenix for David Thirdkill.

Because the Pierce trade and Thirdkill acquisition used the same two picks on the same day, the downstream chain is directly traceable.

Thirdkill played 46 regular-season games for Detroit in 1983-84, made no starts and averaged 1.7 points in 6.3 minutes.

That gives Detroit 85 combined regular-season games from the Pierce-to-Thirdkill branch: 39 from Pierce and 46 from Thirdkill, with only one start between them.

Why Portland Wins

Portland received a dependable starting-caliber forward for three seasons. Carr played more than twice as many games as Detroit's entire directly realized branch and started 113 times compared with one Detroit start.

Detroit deserves some credit for preserving Pierce's value long enough to convert him into another player rather than simply losing him. The problem is that Thirdkill also remained a deep reserve, so the chain never approached Carr's actual Portland production.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Win, A-/C+. Portland receives an A- for 212 games, 113 starts and three productive seasons from Carr. Detroit receives a C+ because Pierce and the directly traceable Thirdkill branch produced 85 total games, but almost no starting value. Pierce's later success elsewhere is not credited to the Pistons.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Chicago and Golden State Swapped Second-Round Positions

The June 23, 1982 agreement gave Chicago a 1983 second-round selection and Golden State the 1982 No. 38 choice. The historical draft ledger associates the Warriors' incoming position with Wayne Sappleton and the Bulls' later right with No. 31 Doc Rivers. That future pick was a year away and didn't represent a contracted player in the 1982 trade. Each franchise was moving between different draft years, not exchanging an NBA veteran for a rookie. The later names provide a useful way to follow the asset trail while preserving the original timing.

Rivers's Longer NBA Career Needs Correct Franchise Attribution

Doc Rivers became a useful NBA guard, most notably during years with Atlanta, but his being selected at the position attached to Chicago's original acquired right does not prove all that future production belonged to the Bulls. A draft right may be moved again or its player's rights assigned elsewhere before a debut. Chicago's immediate return was a later No. 31 selection, giving it a chance to make another decision in 1983. That distinction is especially important in retrospective grading because a famous later NBA name can otherwise exaggerate the value one receiving team actually kept.

Golden State Obtained the Earlier Development Opportunity

The Warriors took a 1982 second-round position connected to Wayne Sappleton. A mid-second-round prospect offered more immediate roster evaluation than a choice deferred until the following year, but neither place in the draft was a guaranteed starting role. Golden State could use the rights itself or transfer them in a subsequent agreement, and any basketball production would need to be attributed to the final signing organization. The franchise had a practical reason to prefer a nearer asset while Chicago accepted a delayed chance with potentially different scouting options.

The Draft Order Favors Chicago Only Modestly

Chicago's incoming No. 31 in 1983 was earlier in its draft than the No. 38 position Golden State received in 1982, and the future right proved attached to a recognizable NBA name. But the difference between these selections was still comparatively small, with a full year separating them. Giving the Bulls credit for every game Rivers later played would be a false attribution if he did not join their roster. A moderate Bulls edge captures the acquired draft flexibility and eventual position without manufacturing a long direct NBA return for Chicago.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win. Chicago Bulls earns B; Golden State Warriors earns C+. perspectives.summary: Portland acquired Wayne Cooper and Dallas' 1985 first-round pick for Kelvin Ransey on June 28, 1982. The pick became No. 24 Terry Porter, who played 758 regular-season games for Portland with 613 starts, made two All-Star teams and started for the 1990 and 1992 NBA Finals clubs. Cooper added 161 games and 98 starts in his initial Portland tenure before becoming one piece of the 1984 Kiki Vandeweghe package. Dallas received 76 games and four starts from Ransey, then traded him one-for-one for Foots Walker plus the picks that became Tom Sluby and Bill Wennington. Walker was waived before playing for Dallas, Sluby played 31 games and Wennington 209. Dallas salvaged real downstream value, but Porter's decade-long franchise impact makes Portland the decisive winner.
perspectives.analysis:
Portland Received Both Immediate Help and a Franchise Point Guard

Basketball-Reference and the Dallas media guide agree on the June 28, 1982 structure. Portland sent Kelvin Ransey to Dallas for Wayne Cooper and Dallas' 1985 first-round pick.

That future pick eventually landed at No. 24, where Portland selected Terry Porter.

Wayne Cooper Gave Portland Two Strong Seasons

Cooper played 80 regular-season games for Portland in 1982-83 and started 60. He averaged 9.7 points, 7.6 rebounds and 1.7 blocks.

He returned for 81 games in 1983-84, starting 38 and averaging 9.8 points, 5.9 rebounds and 1.3 blocks.

That gives Portland 161 regular-season games and 98 starts from Cooper during the directly continuous post-trade tenure.

On June 7, 1984, Portland included Cooper with Fat Lever, Calvin Natt and two draft picks in the package for Kiki Vandeweghe. Because four other valuable assets were required, this review records Cooper's retained trade utility but does not credit the entire Vandeweghe return to him.

The First-Round Pick Became Terry Porter

The long-term value came from Dallas' 1985 first-rounder. Portland used No. 24 on Terry Porter.

Porter played 758 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers across ten seasons and started 613. He averaged 14.9 points and 7.0 assists during his Portland career.

He became a two-time All-Star, developed into the franchise's long-term starting point guard and helped Portland reach the NBA Finals in 1990 and 1992.

The pick alone therefore became one of the most productive players in Trail Blazers history.

Ransey Gave Dallas One Useful Season

Kelvin Ransey played 76 regular-season games for Dallas in 1982-83 and started four. He averaged 11.1 points and 3.7 assists.

His Mavericks tenure lasted only that season, but Dallas did not lose the asset for nothing.

Dallas Converted Ransey Into Three More Assets

On August 12, 1983, Dallas traded Ransey to New Jersey for Foots Walker, a 1984 second-round pick and a 1985 first-round pick. Because Ransey was the sole outgoing Dallas asset, this review can credit that entire return directly to the Ransey branch.

Walker never played a regular-season game for Dallas. The Mavericks' official media guide records that they waived him on October 11, 1983.

The 1984 second-round pick became No. 41 Tom Sluby. Sluby played 31 Dallas games in 1984-85, made no starts and averaged 2.4 points.

The 1985 first-round pick became No. 16 Bill Wennington. Wennington played 209 regular-season games for Dallas across four seasons, starting 12.

That downstream recovery changes Dallas' grade materially. Ransey plus Sluby and Wennington produced 316 Dallas regular-season games and 16 starts, even though none became a long-term core player.

Why Portland Still Wins by a Wide Margin

Portland received 161 direct games from Cooper plus 758 from Porter, for 919 regular-season games and 711 starts before considering Cooper's later trade utility. Porter also became a two-time All-Star and the starting point guard on two Finals teams.

Dallas deserves credit for turning Ransey into a useful future first-round pick rather than simply losing him after one year. That makes the original D-level shorthand too harsh.

The gap remains enormous. Wennington was useful depth, but Porter became a decade-long franchise pillar.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Win, A+/B-. Portland receives an A+ for Cooper's two productive seasons and a first-round pick that became Porter. Dallas receives a B- because Ransey produced one useful year and was converted directly into assets that eventually yielded Sluby and Wennington, but the Mavericks still surrendered the transaction's defining player and far more long-term value.

perspectives.analysis:
Dallas Bought Two Full Starting Seasons

Basketball-Reference's Dallas and Milwaukee transaction records identify the June 28, 1982 deal as Pat Cummings to the Mavericks for the No. 27 pick in the 1982 draft.

Dallas used Cummings as a major frontcourt piece immediately. He played 81 regular-season games in 1982-83, started 71 and averaged 12.5 points and 8.2 rebounds.

He returned for all 80 games he played in 1983-84 and started every one. Cummings averaged 13.1 points and 8.2 rebounds while Dallas reached the playoffs for the first time in franchise history.

That gives the Mavericks 161 regular-season games and 151 starts from the acquisition across two seasons.

Milwaukee Used the Pick on Fred Roberts

The Bucks selected BYU forward Fred Roberts at No. 27.

Roberts ultimately had a long NBA career, but Milwaukee did not receive that career. Basketball-Reference lists 1982-83 as a season in which Roberts played in Italy, and his NBA debut came the following year with San Antonio.

He never appeared in a regular-season game for the Bucks.

That distinction matters for a franchise-specific trade grade. Drafting a player who later becomes useful elsewhere is not the same as receiving that value.

Dallas Got the Production It Needed

Cummings was not merely a bench piece. He started 151 games in two seasons, averaged double-figure scoring both years and provided durable frontcourt minutes during the Mavericks' transition from expansion team to playoff club.

The timing adds weight to the return. Dallas was building around Rolando Blackman, Mark Aguirre and Derek Harper, and Cummings supplied stability while that young core matured.

Milwaukee's branch produced no direct basketball return before Roberts' NBA career began elsewhere.

Why Dallas Wins Clearly

The Bucks can receive some scouting credit because Roberts became a legitimate NBA player, eventually lasting 13 seasons. That career, however, was realized by San Antonio, Utah, Boston and other teams, not Milwaukee.

Dallas received 161 games, 151 starts and two full seasons of dependable production. Milwaukee received zero regular-season games from the player selected with the pick.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win, A-/F. Dallas receives an A- because a late first/early second-round-level asset turned into two full starting seasons and immediate playoff-era value. Milwaukee receives an F because Roberts never played an NBA game for the Bucks, regardless of the respectable career he later had elsewhere.

Bryant played 81 regular-season games for the Rockets in 1982-83, starting 56 and averaging 10.0 points. Houston used No. 42 on Jeff Taylor, who added 44 games and five starts as a rookie. houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Received Two NBA Contributors

The June 28, 1982 transaction sent Joe Bryant and San Diego's No. 42 draft pick to Houston for the Rockets' No. 32 selection. Both draft picks became NBA players, which makes the deal more useful to grade through direct franchise production rather than draft reputation.

Houston received immediate value from Bryant plus a second rotation player from the later pick.

Joe Bryant Started 56 Games for Houston

Bryant played 81 regular-season games for the Rockets in 1982-83 and started 56. He averaged 25.4 minutes, 10.0 points, 3.4 rebounds and 2.3 assists.

Houston struggled to a 14-68 record, so Bryant's season did not translate into team success. Still, he was a regular starter and one of the more experienced players on a rebuilding roster.

That was Bryant's only NBA season in Houston and the final NBA season of his playing career before he continued professionally overseas.

Jeff Taylor Added 44 Games

Houston used the No. 42 pick on Texas Tech guard Jeff Taylor.

Taylor appeared in 44 regular-season games as a rookie, started five and averaged 17.6 minutes, 3.6 points and 2.5 assists. He was waived the following season, so his Houston contribution was limited to that one year.

Even so, the pick produced a real rotation player rather than a zero-game branch.

Richard Anderson Gave San Diego One Season

The Clippers used No. 32 on UC Santa Barbara big man Richard Anderson. He played 78 regular-season games for San Diego in 1982-83, made five starts and averaged 5.2 points and 3.5 rebounds.

Anderson later had a six-year NBA career, but only that rookie season belongs to San Diego for this trade. He played for Denver in 1983-84 and never returned to the Clippers.

The direct Clippers return was therefore 78 games and five starts.

Why Houston Wins

Bryant and Taylor combined for 125 regular-season games and 61 starts in Houston. Anderson gave San Diego 78 games and five starts.

The Clippers selected a player who ultimately had the longest NBA career of the three, but most of that career happened elsewhere. Franchise-specific realized value favors the Rockets because Bryant supplied a full starting season and Taylor added another 44 appearances.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, B/C+. Houston receives a B for extracting one season of starting production from Bryant plus 44 games from Taylor. San Diego receives a C+ because Anderson was a useful rookie rotation player, but his later career cannot be credited to the Clippers and the direct return was smaller.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey acquired Wayne Sappleton's draft rights from Golden State on June 29, 1982 for a 1983 second-round pick that became No. 43 Pace Mannion. Sappleton stayed in Italy for two more seasons before finally joining the Nets in 1984-85, when he played 33 regular-season games off the bench. Golden State used the pick on Mannion, who played 57 regular-season games for the Warriors as a rookie in 1983-84 before moving to Utah. Neither side found a starter, but Golden State received more direct games and received them one season earlier, giving the Warriors a modest realized-value edge.
perspectives.analysis:
Both Assets Eventually Reached the NBA

The June 29, 1982 transaction sent Wayne Sappleton's draft rights to New Jersey and a 1983 second-round pick to Golden State. The pick later became No. 43 Pace Mannion.

Neither return became a major rotation fixture for the acquiring team, but both eventually produced NBA games.

Sappleton's Nets Value Was Delayed

Sappleton did not join New Jersey immediately after the rights trade. Basketball-Reference lists him in Italy for both 1982-83 and 1983-84.

He finally appeared for the Nets in 1984-85, playing 33 regular-season games, all off the bench. Sappleton averaged 9.0 minutes, 2.9 points and 2.3 rebounds.

Those 33 games represent the full NBA career attached to New Jersey's acquired rights.

Golden State Used the Pick on Pace Mannion

The Warriors selected Utah forward Pace Mannion at No. 43 in the 1983 NBA Draft.

Mannion played 57 regular-season games for Golden State in 1983-84 and made no starts. He averaged 8.2 minutes and 2.1 points, giving the Warriors modest but immediate bench depth.

Mannion moved to Utah the following season. His later NBA production is not credited to Golden State.

Why Golden State Gets the Edge

New Jersey did realize value from Sappleton, which prevents the trade from being a clear loss. The Nets held his rights through two seasons overseas and eventually received 33 NBA appearances.

Golden State got 57 games from Mannion, and those appearances arrived one season earlier than Sappleton's Nets debut. Neither player started for the acquiring team, so the comparison is mostly about volume and timing rather than high-end impact.

The difference is real but small. Mannion's 57 Warriors games exceed Sappleton's 33 Nets games, yet neither side received a lasting rotation player.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, C+/C. Golden State receives a C+ for turning the future second-round pick into 57 NBA games from Mannion. New Jersey receives a C because Sappleton eventually produced 33 games after two seasons overseas. The Warriors get the modest edge, not a landslide.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey acquired Phil Ford from Kansas City on June 29, 1982 for Ray Williams. Williams became Kansas City's starting point guard in 1982-83, playing 72 regular-season games with 68 starts and averaging 15.4 points and 7.9 assists. Ford appeared in only seven games for the Nets, all starts, before New Jersey traded him to Milwaukee during the season. Although Ford later played meaningful NBA minutes elsewhere, the Nets realized only 163 minutes from him. Kansas City received nearly a full season of starting point-guard production, so the Kings won the direct exchange decisively.
perspectives.analysis:
Kansas City Received a Starting Point Guard

The June 29, 1982 deal exchanged two established guards. New Jersey received Phil Ford, while Kansas City acquired Ray Williams after Williams had just led the Nets in scoring.

The direct returns quickly diverged once the 1982-83 season began.

Williams Started 68 Games for the Kings

Williams played 72 regular-season games for Kansas City and started 68. He averaged 30.1 minutes, 15.4 points, 7.9 assists, 4.5 rebounds and 1.7 steals.

His 569 assists were a major part of a Kings offense that finished among the league's higher-scoring teams. Kansas City went 45-37, a substantial improvement from the previous season's 30-52 record.

Williams stayed only one season before moving to New York, but that one year produced starter-level value across almost the entire schedule.

Ford Barely Played for New Jersey

Ford's Nets tenure was dramatically shorter. He appeared in seven regular-season games, started all seven and played 163 total minutes.

He averaged 6.7 points and 5.4 assists in those appearances. New Jersey then traded Ford to Milwaukee, where he played 70 games and started 56 during the rest of the 1982-83 season.

Those Milwaukee minutes cannot be credited to the Nets. For this trade, New Jersey received seven games and seven starts.

Why Kansas City Wins

Both players were proven NBA guards, so this was not a case where one side took a flyer on an unknown asset. Kansas City simply extracted far more direct use from the player it acquired.

Williams gave the Kings 72 games and 68 starts, while Ford gave New Jersey seven games before being rerouted. Even if the Nets later received something in the Ford-to-Milwaukee transaction, that downstream deal must be evaluated on its own rather than credited automatically here.

The difference in franchise-specific production is too large to call the original exchange balanced.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A-/D-. Kansas City receives an A- for a full season of starting point-guard production from Williams. New Jersey receives a D- because Ford lasted only seven games before another trade, leaving the Nets with very little direct return from this exchange.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
This record Mirrors the Same June 29 Transaction

this review is the Golden State-source canonical record for the same Wayne Sappleton rights transaction represented by the New Jersey-source record. The underlying package is identical: New Jersey acquired Sappleton's rights, and Golden State received the 1983 second-round pick that became No. 43 Pace Mannion.

The duplicate source representation should not produce a different historical verdict. This review therefore uses the same franchise-specific realized-value standard.

Sappleton's Nets Value Arrived Two Years Later

Sappleton remained in Italy for the 1982-83 and 1983-84 seasons after New Jersey acquired his rights.

He finally joined the Nets in 1984-85 and played 33 regular-season games, all off the bench. He averaged 9.0 minutes, 2.9 points and 2.3 rebounds.

Those 33 appearances were the entirety of his NBA career.

Mannion Played 57 Games for Golden State

Golden State used the incoming 1983 second-round pick at No. 43 on Pace Mannion.

Mannion appeared in 57 regular-season games for the Warriors in 1983-84 and made no starts. He averaged 8.2 minutes and 2.1 points before moving to Utah the next season.

His later NBA career belongs to other franchises for trade-value purposes.

Why Golden State Gets the Edge

Neither side received a starter, and neither asset became a long-term piece for the acquiring franchise. New Jersey did eventually get 33 NBA games from Sappleton, which gives the rights real value.

Golden State received 57 games from Mannion, and those games arrived in 1983-84 rather than after two full seasons overseas. The Warriors therefore realized somewhat more direct value from the exchange.

Because the margin is only 24 reserve games and neither player started, this remains a modest win rather than a major one.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, C+/C. Golden State receives a C+ for 57 direct games from Mannion. New Jersey receives a C for 33 later games from Sappleton. This review explicitly reconciles this Warriors-source record with the matching Nets-source transaction rather than creating a contradictory second judgment.

summary: Atlanta acquired Jim Johnstone's draft rights from Kansas City on June 30, 1982 for Seattle's 1984 second-round pick, later No. 37 Ben Coleman. Johnstone never played a regular-season game for Atlanta; the Hawks packaged his rights with 1983 and 1985 second-round picks to San Antonio in September for George Johnson. Kansas City also rerouted the 1984 pick before it was exercised, sending it to Chicago in the 1983 Mark Olberding/Larry Micheaux deal. Chicago eventually used No. 37 on Coleman. Because neither original team received direct NBA games from the terminal player tied to its incoming asset, the edge is modest, but Kansas City preserved a more portable draft asset that remained useful in another trade.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Both Sides Rerouted the Asset They Acquired

Basketball-Reference records the June 30, 1982 trade as Atlanta receiving Jim Johnstone's draft rights from Kansas City for a 1984 second-round pick. The Hawks' official media guide adds an important detail: the pick originally belonged to Seattle and had reached Atlanta in the 1980 Armond Hill trade.

Neither Atlanta nor Kansas City ultimately used its incoming asset as a long-term player piece.

Johnstone Never Played for Atlanta

Kansas City had selected Johnstone at No. 51 in the 1982 draft. Atlanta acquired his rights the next day but never used him in a regular-season game.

On September 27, 1982, the Hawks sent Johnstone, a 1983 second-round pick and a 1985 second-round pick to San Antonio for George Johnson.

Johnstone later appeared in seven games for San Antonio and sixteen for Detroit in 1982-83. Those games cannot be credited to Atlanta because they occurred after the Hawks had traded him again.

His rights did retain transaction value, but they were only one of three outgoing assets in the George Johnson deal. This review therefore does not assign Atlanta the entire value of Johnson.

Kansas City Also Moved the Pick Again

The Kings held the acquired 1984 second-round pick until June 28, 1983. Kansas City then sent the pick to Chicago together with the draft rights to Ennis Whatley and Chris McNealy for Mark Olberding and the rights to Larry Micheaux.

Chicago ultimately exercised the pick at No. 37 in 1984 and selected Ben Coleman.

Coleman did not play in the NBA until 1986-87 after two seasons in Italy, and he never played for Kansas City. His later five-year NBA career belongs to other franchises for direct realized-value purposes.

Why Kansas City Gets a Small Edge

Atlanta and Kansas City both converted the acquired asset into a later transaction instead of direct on-court production. That makes this a much closer comparison than the terminal player names suggest.

The difference is asset portability. Kansas City's second-round pick remained a discrete draft asset that could be packaged in a later deal and ultimately became a useful NBA player after reaching Chicago. Atlanta's Johnstone rights also carried value, but they were moved only months later as one piece of a three-asset package.

No original team received a direct NBA game from Johnstone or Coleman. The Kings' advantage is therefore limited to the continuing value of the pick, not Coleman's later career.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, C+/C. Kansas City receives a C+ because the 1984 second-rounder remained useful in a later trade and eventually became No. 37 Ben Coleman after leaving the Kings. Atlanta receives a C because Johnstone never played for the Hawks and his rights were only one component of a later multi-asset deal. The margin is modest.

new-york-knicks.summary: New York acquired Truck Robinson from Phoenix on July 7, 1982 for Maurice Lucas. Robinson gave the Knicks 148 regular-season games across parts of three seasons, starting 140, and averaged 9.5 points and 8.1 rebounds in his first New York year. Lucas became a much larger Phoenix piece: 215 games across three seasons, 162 starts, an All-Star selection in 1982-83, and averages of 16.5 points and 10.4 rebounds that first season. Both teams received productive veteran forwards, but Lucas delivered more games, more starting value and the higher peak, giving Phoenix the stronger realized return.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
Both Teams Received Starting Forwards

The July 7, 1982 swap was straightforward: New York received Truck Robinson, and Phoenix received Maurice Lucas.

Unlike many historical trades in this archive, both incoming players immediately became regular starters and stayed beyond a single season. The question is therefore not whether either side got value, but which veteran produced more of it.

Robinson Gave New York Two Full Starting Seasons

Robinson played 81 regular-season games for the Knicks in 1982-83, starting 76. He averaged 30.0 minutes, 9.5 points and 8.1 rebounds.

He returned for 65 games in 1983-84 and started 63, averaging 10.8 points and 8.4 rebounds. Robinson also appeared in 18 playoff games across those two seasons, starting all of them.

His final Knicks season was brief: two games and one start in 1984-85.

That gives New York 148 regular-season games and 140 starts from Robinson.

Lucas Became an All-Star in Phoenix

Lucas made an even larger immediate impact. In 1982-83 he played 77 regular-season games, started 71 and averaged 16.5 points, 10.4 rebounds and 2.8 assists.

He earned an All-Star selection that season and received MVP votes. Phoenix got both high-end production and heavy minutes from him right away.

Lucas returned for 75 games and 69 starts in 1983-84, averaging 15.9 points and 9.7 rebounds. He then played 63 more games in 1984-85, starting 22 and averaging 13.4 points and 8.8 rebounds.

Across three Phoenix seasons, Lucas played 215 regular-season games and started 162.

Phoenix Got the Higher Peak and More Volume

Robinson was a useful Knicks starter and helped New York reach the playoffs in both 1982-83 and 1983-84. His return was legitimate enough that this trade cannot be treated as a bad move for New York.

Lucas, however, gave Phoenix 67 more regular-season games, 22 more starts and substantially more scoring. His 1982-83 All-Star season also produced a level of individual recognition Robinson did not match in New York.

The Suns therefore received both the better peak and the longer direct tenure.

Final Verdict

Suns Win, A-/B. Phoenix receives an A- for three productive seasons, 215 games, 162 starts and an All-Star year from Lucas. New York receives a B because Robinson was a durable two-year starter and playoff contributor, but his direct value was lower in both volume and peak impact.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Bill Hanzlik from Seattle on July 20, 1982 for the rights to veteran forward Wally Walker. Hanzlik became a long-term Nuggets fixture, playing 593 regular-season games across eight seasons, starting 33 and earning 1986 All-Defensive Second Team honors. Seattle turned Walker into a 1984 second-round pick three months later; the No. 28 selection became Cory Blackwell, who played 60 regular-season games for the SuperSonics and never started. The Walker rights therefore retained downstream value, but Hanzlik's eight-year Denver tenure and defensive role made the Nuggets the clear realized-value winner.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Turned a Rights Asset Into Eight Seasons

Basketball-Reference's Denver transaction ledger records the July 20, 1982 move as Bill Hanzlik to the Nuggets for the rights to Wally Walker.

Hanzlik had started 76 games for Seattle in 1981-82. Denver acquired him just before his age-25 season and kept him for the rest of his playing career.

Hanzlik Played 593 Games for Denver

Hanzlik appeared in all 82 regular-season games in his first Nuggets season, then 80 in 1983-84 and 80 again in 1984-85. He remained a rotation player through 1989-90.

Across eight Denver seasons, he played 593 regular-season games and started 33. He gave the Nuggets durable wing and forward depth rather than a one-year return.

His best individual recognition came in 1985-86, when he averaged 12.5 points, 4.8 rebounds and 4.0 assists while earning NBA All-Defensive Second Team honors.

Seattle Converted Walker Into a Draft Pick

Wally Walker never played another regular-season game for Seattle after the July 1982 rights transaction. On October 5, the SuperSonics traded Walker to Houston for a 1984 second-round pick.

That later move is important because it means Seattle did not simply receive a dead rights asset. The Walker branch turned into a usable draft selection.

The Pick Became Cory Blackwell

Seattle used the 1984 second-round pick at No. 28 on Wisconsin forward Cory Blackwell.

Blackwell played 60 regular-season games for the SuperSonics in 1984-85, made no starts and averaged 3.4 points in 9.2 minutes. That was his only NBA season.

The downstream return was real, but it was limited to one reserve season.

Why Denver Wins Clearly

Denver received 593 games, eight seasons and an All-Defensive Team year from Hanzlik. Seattle's rights branch eventually produced 60 reserve games from Blackwell.

The SuperSonics deserve credit for converting Walker into another asset, which keeps the trade from looking empty. The scale of Hanzlik's Denver tenure still overwhelms the downstream return.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A-/C+. Denver receives an A- for eight seasons of durable rotation value and one All-Defensive Second Team campaign. Seattle receives a C+ because the Walker rights were flipped into the pick that became Blackwell, but the final realized return was only 60 games and zero starts.

Hanzlik appeared in all 82 regular-season games in his first Nuggets season, then 80 in 1983-84 and 80 again in 1984-85. He remained a rotation player through 1989-90.

Across eight Denver seasons, he played 593 regular-season games and started 33. He gave the Nuggets durable wing and forward depth rather than a one-year return.

Wally Walker never played another regular-season game for Seattle after the July 1982 rights transaction. On October 5, the SuperSonics traded Walker to Houston for a 1984 second-round pick.

The Pick Became Cory Blackwell

Seattle used the 1984 second-round pick at No. 28 on Wisconsin forward Cory Blackwell.

Blackwell played 60 regular-season games for the SuperSonics in 1984-85, made no starts and averaged 3.4 points in 9.2 minutes. That was his only NBA season.

The downstream return was real, but it was limited to one reserve season.

Denver received 593 games, eight seasons and an All-Defensive Team year from Hanzlik. Seattle's rights branch eventually produced 60 reserve games from Blackwell.

The SuperSonics deserve credit for converting Walker into another asset, which keeps the trade from looking empty. The scale of Hanzlik's Denver tenure still overwhelms the downstream return.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A-/C+. Denver receives an A- for eight seasons of durable rotation value and one All-Defensive Second Team campaign. Seattle receives a C+ because the Walker rights were flipped into the pick that became Blackwell, but the final realized return was only 60 games and zero starts.

perspectives.analysis:
San Antonio Consolidated for the Best Player

Basketball-Reference's Chicago and San Antonio transaction ledgers agree on the July 22, 1982 package. The Spurs received Artis Gilmore, while the Bulls received Dave Corzine, Mark Olberding and cash.

This is not a case where Chicago's return disappeared. Corzine became a long-term Bull and Olberding supplied a full season. The evaluation turns on quality versus quantity.

Gilmore Gave San Antonio Five Productive Seasons

Gilmore played 380 regular-season games for the Spurs and started 367. Across those five seasons he scored 6,127 points and remained one of the league's most efficient interior scorers.

He averaged 18.0 points and 12.0 rebounds in 1982-83 while shooting 62.6 percent from the field. San Antonio won 53 games and reached the Western Conference Finals.

Gilmore stayed through 1986-87, giving the Spurs far more than a short veteran rental.

Corzine Became a Durable Bulls Center

Dave Corzine played 556 regular-season games for Chicago from 1982-83 through 1988-89. He started 405 of those games and averaged 9.8 points and 6.3 rebounds across his Bulls tenure.

That is substantial realized value. Corzine gave Chicago seven seasons of center play and remained a regular starter through the early Michael Jordan years.

His longevity is the main reason the Bulls side grades much better than a typical star-for-depth loss.

Olberding Added One More Full Season

Mark Olberding played 80 games for Chicago in 1982-83 and started 31. He averaged 8.7 points and 4.5 rebounds before leaving after the season.

The Bulls also received cash, but the reviewed public sources do not identify the amount. This review preserves the financial component without assigning speculative value.

Why San Antonio Still Wins

Chicago received 636 regular-season games from Corzine and Olberding combined, plus cash. That is a real package with long-term utility.

San Antonio received the clearly superior player. Gilmore's 380 games came with elite efficiency, heavy starting responsibility and immediate playoff impact on a conference finalist.

The trade is therefore not a blowout, but the premium talent and peak value sit on the Spurs side.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win, A/B. San Antonio receives an A for adding five seasons of Hall of Fame-caliber center play and maximizing a contender window. Chicago receives a B because Corzine became a durable seven-year starter, Olberding added a full season and the cash component provided additional value even though the package never matched Gilmore's peak.

perspectives.summary: Portland signed Jeff Judkins as a veteran free agent on August 2, 1982 and sent Detroit a 1984 third-round pick as compensation. Judkins played 34 regular-season games for the Trail Blazers, all off the bench, before Portland waived him on March 22, 1983. Detroit later traded the incoming pick back to Portland for the rights to Pétur Guðmundsson; Guðmundsson did not play an NBA game for Detroit, and Portland used No. 65 on Tim Kearney, who never appeared in the NBA. Detroit preserved transaction utility in the pick, but Portland received the only direct NBA production, giving the Blazers a slight realized-value edge.
perspectives.analysis:
Portland Got the Only Direct NBA Games

Basketball-Reference's Portland transaction ledger records the August 2, 1982 mechanism clearly. Portland signed Jeff Judkins as a veteran free agent and sent Detroit a 1984 third-round pick as compensation.

Judkins played 34 regular-season games for Portland in 1982-83, made no starts and averaged 3.1 points in 9.1 minutes. The Blazers waived him on March 22, 1983.

That is a small return, but it is measurable NBA production.

Detroit Did Not Simply Use the Pick

The canonical record labels the 1984 third-rounder as No. 65 Tim Kearney, but Detroit did not actually make that selection. On August 18, 1983, the Pistons traded the same 1984 third-round pick back to Portland for Pétur Guðmundsson.

That downstream move matters because it changes how Detroit's return should be evaluated. The pick retained transaction value for a year before Detroit rerouted it.

Guðmundsson Produced Zero Detroit Games

Guðmundsson had previously played 68 NBA games for Portland in 1981-82, but he was playing professionally in Iceland during 1983-84 and did not appear for Detroit.

He later returned to the NBA with the Lakers and Spurs, but none of those appearances came with the Pistons. This review therefore credits Detroit with zero direct games from the Guðmundsson branch.

Portland Eventually Drafted Tim Kearney

After reacquiring the pick, Portland used No. 65 in the 1984 NBA Draft on West Virginia center Tim Kearney.

Basketball-Reference's draft record shows no NBA statistics for Kearney, and his player page contains no NBA regular-season line. The terminal draft outcome was therefore zero NBA games.

Why Portland Gets a Slight Edge

Neither side created a durable asset. Portland received 34 low-minute reserve games from Judkins, while Detroit held a third-round pick for roughly a year and used it to acquire rights that produced no Pistons games.

The pick's transaction utility keeps Detroit from receiving a failing grade. Still, Portland received the only realized NBA minutes directly tied to the exchange.

Final Verdict

Trail Blazers Win, C+/C. Portland receives a C+ for 34 reserve appearances from Judkins before moving on. Detroit receives a C because the pick retained downstream trade utility, but neither Guðmundsson nor the eventual No. 65 selection produced any Pistons regular-season games.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey acquired Darryl Dawkins from Philadelphia on August 27, 1982 for a 1983 first-round pick and $700,000 cash. Dawkins played 258 regular-season games for the Nets across five seasons, started 196 and scored 3,687 points, including 81 starts in 1982-83 and 80 in 1983-84. Philadelphia used the No. 17 pick on Leo Rautins, who played 28 regular-season games for the 76ers with three starts and averaged 1.7 points before moving on. The known cash payment gives Philadelphia real value, but Dawkins' multi-year starting production makes the Nets the clear realized-value winner.
perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Paid a First-Round Pick and Cash for a Starting Center

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and Philadelphia transaction records identify the August 27, 1982 package as Darryl Dawkins to the Nets for a 1983 first-round pick and cash. The canonical package specifies the cash at $700,000.

The pick later landed at No. 17, where Philadelphia selected Leo Rautins.

Dawkins Immediately Became New Jersey's Starting Center

Dawkins played 81 regular-season games for the Nets in 1982-83 and started all 81. He averaged 12.0 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.9 blocks while shooting 59.9 percent from the field.

He was even better in 1983-84, starting 80 of 81 games and averaging 16.8 points on 59.3 percent shooting. New Jersey reached the playoffs and upset defending champion Philadelphia in the first round.

That second season alone supplied more top-end basketball value than the draft return ultimately produced for the 76ers.

He Stayed With the Nets for Five Seasons

Injuries reduced Dawkins' availability after 1983-84, but he still remained a meaningful part of New Jersey's frontcourt. He played 39 games in 1984-85, 51 in 1985-86 and six in 1986-87.

Across five Nets seasons, Dawkins appeared in 258 regular-season games, started 196 and scored 3,687 points.

This review credits only his New Jersey production. His prior Philadelphia career and later appearances elsewhere do not affect the Nets' realized return.

Philadelphia's Pick Became Leo Rautins

The 76ers used the No. 17 pick in the 1983 NBA Draft on Syracuse forward Leo Rautins.

Rautins played 28 regular-season games for Philadelphia in 1983-84, started three and averaged 7.0 minutes, 1.7 points, 1.2 rebounds and 1.0 assist.

He played only four more NBA games, all with Atlanta the following season. Philadelphia therefore received just one limited NBA season from the first-round component.

The $700,000 Cash Component Matters

Unlike many historical cash considerations, the amount here is known. Philadelphia received $700,000 in addition to the first-round pick, so its side should not be evaluated as Rautins alone.

The cash provided tangible financial value and raises the 76ers' grade. It still does not produce on-court value comparable to several seasons from a starting-caliber center.

Why New Jersey Wins

The Nets accepted the cost of a first-round pick and substantial cash, but the acquired player immediately became a starter and stayed for five seasons. Dawkins gave New Jersey 258 games and nearly 200 starts.

Philadelphia's draft branch produced 28 games and three starts. Even with the $700,000 payment, the realized basketball gap is too large to call the transaction even.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A-/C+. New Jersey receives an A- for acquiring five seasons of center production, including two high-volume starting years. Philadelphia receives a C+ because it obtained a first-round pick and a meaningful known cash payment, but the selected player produced only 28 games for the franchise.
