He was even better in 1983-84, starting 80 of 81 games and averaging 16.8 points on 59.3 percent shooting. New Jersey reached the playoffs and upset defending champion Philadelphia in the first round.

That second season alone supplied more top-end basketball value than the draft return ultimately produced for the 76ers.

He Stayed With the Nets for Five Seasons

Injuries reduced Dawkins' availability after 1983-84, but he still remained a meaningful part of New Jersey's frontcourt. He played 39 games in 1984-85, 51 in 1985-86 and six in 1986-87.

Across five Nets seasons, Dawkins appeared in 258 regular-season games, started 196 and scored 3,687 points.

This review credits only his New Jersey production. His prior Philadelphia career and later appearances elsewhere do not affect the Nets' realized return.

Philadelphia's Pick Became Leo Rautins

The 76ers used the No. 17 pick in the 1983 NBA Draft on Syracuse forward Leo Rautins.

Rautins played 28 regular-season games for Philadelphia in 1983-84, started three and averaged 7.0 minutes, 1.7 points, 1.2 rebounds and 1.0 assist.

He played only four more NBA games, all with Atlanta the following season. Philadelphia therefore received just one limited NBA season from the first-round component.

The $700,000 Cash Component Matters

Unlike many historical cash considerations, the amount here is known. Philadelphia received $700,000 in addition to the first-round pick, so its side should not be evaluated as Rautins alone.

The cash provided tangible financial value and raises the 76ers' grade. It still does not produce on-court value comparable to several seasons from a starting-caliber center.

Why New Jersey Wins

The Nets accepted the cost of a first-round pick and substantial cash, but the acquired player immediately became a starter and stayed for five seasons. Dawkins gave New Jersey 258 games and nearly 200 starts.

Philadelphia's draft branch produced 28 games and three starts. Even with the $700,000 payment, the realized basketball gap is too large to call the transaction even.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, A-/C+. New Jersey receives an A- for acquiring five seasons of center production, including two high-volume starting years. Philadelphia receives a C+ because it obtained a first-round pick and a meaningful known cash payment, but the selected player produced only 28 games for the franchise.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Acquired a Franchise Cornerstone

The September 2, 1982 transaction sent Dominique Wilkins' draft rights from Utah to Atlanta for John Drew, Freeman Williams and $1 million.

Utah had selected Wilkins third overall in the 1982 draft, but Atlanta turned the rights deal into one of the defining acquisitions in franchise history.

Wilkins Set Atlanta's Franchise Marks

Wilkins played 882 regular-season games for the Hawks across twelve seasons, the most in franchise history. He also scored 23,292 points for Atlanta, another franchise record.

He made nine consecutive All-Star teams from 1986 through 1994 and earned seven All-NBA selections. In 1985-86 he led the league in scoring at 30.3 points per game.

Atlanta reached the playoffs in eight of Wilkins' twelve seasons with the club. The return was not merely individual production; he became the central player of the franchise's strongest sustained 1980s run.

John Drew Gave Utah Real Short-Term Offense

Drew was not an empty return. He played 44 games for Utah in 1982-83 and averaged 21.2 points, then appeared in 81 games in 1983-84 while averaging 17.7.

He added 19 games in 1984-85. Across his Jazz tenure Drew played 144 regular-season games and started 53.

That production gave Utah a credible veteran scorer during the early years after the franchise moved from New Orleans.

Freeman Williams Added Very Little

Williams played only 18 regular-season games for Utah in 1982-83, started three and averaged 5.1 points.

He did not play in the NBA in either of the next two seasons. His branch of the trade therefore provided almost no lasting basketball value to the Jazz.

The $1 Million Payment Was Meaningful

Atlanta also sent $1 million in cash. Historical accounts of the trade consistently note Utah's financial pressure and Wilkins' reluctance to begin his career with the Jazz.

That context explains why Utah accepted a package built around immediate cash and established scoring. This review gives the Jazz credit for the known financial return rather than evaluating the deal as player-for-player only.

Why Atlanta Still Wins by a Huge Margin

Drew was productive, Williams was limited and the $1 million payment was meaningful. None of those assets approached the twelve seasons of elite production Atlanta received from Wilkins.

The Hawks acquired a Hall of Fame-level franchise centerpiece, while Utah received short-term scoring and financial relief without a comparable long-term basketball asset.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, A+/D. Atlanta receives an A+ for acquiring a franchise-record scorer, nine-time All-Star and long-term centerpiece. Utah receives a D because Drew and the cash had legitimate value, but the completed return never came close to matching Wilkins' career in Atlanta.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Tom Owens from Indiana on September 2, 1982 for a 1984 second-round pick that became No. 43 Greg Wiltjer. Owens played 49 regular-season games for the Pistons in 1982-83, started four and averaged 4.2 points and 3.8 rebounds before leaving the NBA for Italy. Indiana used the pick on Wiltjer, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Detroit therefore received the only direct NBA production, although the return was limited to one reserve season. A second legacy Indiana-perspective record represents the same transaction and is retained only as superseded source provenance.
perspectives.analysis:
One Transaction Had Been legacy Twice

The Detroit and Indiana source packages describe the same September 2, 1982 transaction: Detroit received Tom Owens, while Indiana received the Pistons' 1984 second-round pick.

Two canonical-looking rows were created from opposite franchise imports. This review keeps the Detroit-origin record as the active transaction and marks the Indiana-origin record as superseded provenance so the deal is not counted twice.

Owens Played One Season for Detroit

Tom Owens appeared in 49 regular-season games for the Pistons in 1982-83 and started four. He averaged 14.8 minutes, 4.2 points and 3.8 rebounds.

That was the entirety of his Detroit tenure and the final season of his NBA career. Owens then played professionally in Italy.

The return was modest, but Detroit did receive real reserve minutes from the acquired veteran.

Indiana's Pick Became Greg Wiltjer

The 1984 second-round pick landed at No. 43, where Indiana selected Oregon State forward Greg Wiltjer.

Wiltjer never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. He continued his professional career outside the NBA, so the Pacers received no direct NBA games from the draft selection.

This review credits Indiana with the value of having and exercising a second-round pick, but the completed player outcome was zero NBA production.

Why Detroit Gets the Edge

This was a small trade. Owens did not become a long-term Piston, and 49 reserve appearances do not justify an aggressive grade.

Still, 49 NBA games are more realized franchise value than a draft pick whose selected player never appeared in the league.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, C+/C-. Detroit receives a C+ for one season and 49 games of veteran frontcourt depth. Indiana receives a C- because the second-round pick became Greg Wiltjer, who produced zero NBA regular-season games. The duplicate Indiana source record is superseded rather than evaluated as a second transaction.

indiana-pacers.analysis:
Detroit Took a Veteran Center From Indiana

The Pistons acquired Tom Owens from the Pacers in September 1982, seeking an experienced interior player who could supply size and frontcourt minutes. Owens had spent several seasons in professional basketball, making him a more immediate option than a distant second-round selection. Indiana's compensation was a 1984 second-round right that the historical draft ledger associates with Greg Wiltjer at No. 43. The asset comparison was a veteran center against a future opportunity rather than a swap of two established players.

The Second-Round Pick Needed Its Own Draft History

Wiltjer's selection came two years after the original agreement, and that gap matters when judging what Indiana gave up and received. A second-round right in 1982 offered flexibility but didn't guarantee a rookie who would provide dependable NBA minutes. The Pacers could use the selection or move the right through further transactions. Similarly, Owens's earlier production with other franchises was part of Detroit's scouting context, not new Pistons statistics already delivered on the trade date.

The Imported Row Is a Superseded Duplicate

This specific archive entry carries the verdict Superseded Duplicate, meaning it overlaps with another representation of the same underlying transaction. Maintaining a readable historical description still helps identify Owens and the Wiltjer-linked pick, but readers should not infer that Detroit separately acquired Owens twice or Indiana separately received two different 1984 seconds. The archive's private and nonindexable status is appropriate until any duplicate record relationships are fully reconciled, and the source ledger should remain explicit about the overlap.

The Inherited Ratings Aren't a Second Outcome

Detroit's inherited C+ and Indiana's C- can be understood as evaluations attached to the underlying exchange, but they don't establish a second independent event. Owens offered veteran center utility; Indiana took a lower-round draft opportunity. A clean historical record should preserve the date, participants and future pick reference while avoiding inflated trade totals. The verdict is a record-management designation, not a claim that either team had an entirely different professional career outcome from another September transaction.

Final Verdict

Superseded Duplicate. Detroit's inherited C+ relates to veteran center Tom Owens, and Indiana's C- relates to the 1984 second-round right associated with Greg Wiltjer. This archival representation overlaps the original Owens transaction and isn't a separate completed trade. It remains private and should not create another pick or another Owens arrival in transaction counts.

summary: Boston acquired Quinn Buckner from Milwaukee on September 9, 1982 for the rights to retired Celtics legend Dave Cowens. Buckner played 226 regular-season games for Boston over three seasons, started 62 and appeared in 45 playoff games, including all 23 during the Celtics' 1984 championship run. Cowens came out of retirement for Milwaukee and played 40 regular-season games, starting 34 while averaging 8.1 points and 6.9 rebounds, then retired again after the season. Milwaukee received one useful veteran year, but Boston received three seasons of guard depth plus a championship contribution, giving the Celtics the stronger realized return.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Acquired Three Seasons of Useful Guard Depth

Basketball-Reference's Milwaukee transaction ledger records the September 9, 1982 exchange directly: the Bucks sent Quinn Buckner to Boston for Dave Cowens, who had been retired since 1980.

Buckner immediately became a major rotation guard for a title contender, while Cowens gave Milwaukee one final NBA season.

Buckner Played 226 Regular-Season Games for Boston

Buckner appeared in 72 games for the Celtics in 1982-83 and started 56. He averaged 7.9 points, 3.8 assists and 1.5 steals while playing 21.7 minutes per game.

He returned for 79 games in 1983-84 and all 75 games he was available for in 1984-85. Across three Boston seasons, Buckner played 226 regular-season games and started 62.

His role declined over time, but his availability and defensive backcourt depth gave Boston repeated value well beyond the first season.

He Was Part of the 1984 Championship Rotation

Buckner appeared in 23 playoff games during Boston's 1984 title run. He averaged 11.7 minutes in the postseason and served as a reserve behind the Celtics' established starting backcourt.

That championship contribution is not treated as if Buckner were one of the team's primary stars. It still matters because Boston received a dependable playoff rotation player from the trade.

Cowens Gave Milwaukee One Useful Comeback Season

Cowens had not played in either 1980-81 or 1981-82. Milwaukee acquired his rights and convinced him to return for the 1982-83 season.

He played 40 regular-season games, started 34 and averaged 25.4 minutes, 8.1 points, 6.9 rebounds and 2.1 assists. The Bucks won 51 games and reached the Eastern Conference Finals.

Cowens therefore was not an empty return. Milwaukee received legitimate frontcourt minutes from a Hall of Fame veteran during a strong season.

The Difference Is Duration and Championship Value

Cowens retired again after 1982-83, ending Milwaukee's return after 40 regular-season games. Buckner stayed in Boston through 1984-85 and played 226 regular-season games plus 45 playoff games across those three seasons.

The Celtics did not acquire a star, but they received far more durable value and a contributor to a championship team.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A/C+. Boston receives an A for three seasons, 226 regular-season games, 62 starts and meaningful playoff depth during the 1984 championship run. Milwaukee receives a C+ because Cowens supplied one credible comeback season on a 51-win team, but the return lasted only 40 games before he retired again.

Malone immediately won another MVP, averaged 23.5 points and 14.7 rebounds, then led a 65-win Philadelphia team to a 12-1 postseason and the 1983 championship while earning Finals MVP. houston-rockets.analysis:
Philadelphia Turned the Trade Into an Immediate Championship

The September 15, 1982 transaction sent Moses Malone from Houston to Philadelphia for Caldwell Jones and the 76ers' 1983 first-round pick.

Malone arrived as the reigning NBA MVP. In his first Philadelphia season he played 78 games, averaged 23.5 points and 14.7 rebounds, earned another MVP award and made the All-NBA and All-Defensive first teams.

The 76ers finished 65-17 and went 12-1 in the playoffs. Malone averaged 26.0 points and 15.8 rebounds in the postseason and won Finals MVP after Philadelphia swept the Lakers for the championship.

That is essentially the ceiling for an acquisition's immediate impact.

Malone Gave Philadelphia Four Prime Seasons

The trade was not only a one-year championship play. Malone stayed with the 76ers through 1985-86 and played 302 regular-season games across four seasons.

He remained an All-Star and elite rebounder throughout the stint, giving Philadelphia a long-term interior centerpiece alongside Julius Erving, Maurice Cheeks and later Charles Barkley.

His first season carries the most historical weight, but the return continued well beyond 1983.

Caldwell Jones Gave Houston Two Full Starting Seasons

Houston did not receive an empty veteran contract. Jones played all 82 games in 1982-83 and started all 82, averaging 9.5 points and 8.1 rebounds.

He followed with 81 games and 73 starts in 1983-84, averaging 9.9 points and 7.2 rebounds. Across two Rockets seasons, Jones played 163 games and started 155.

That was substantial short-term frontcourt value during a rebuilding period.

The First-Round Pick Became Rodney McCray

The larger Houston asset was the 1983 first-round pick, which landed at No. 3. The Rockets selected Louisville forward Rodney McCray.

McCray played five seasons for Houston from 1983-84 through 1987-88. He appeared in 405 regular-season games and started 361, developing into one of the league's better defensive forwards.

He earned All-Defensive second-team honors in 1987 and first-team honors in 1988. McCray also started throughout Houston's 1986 run to the NBA Finals.

Houston therefore received a legitimate long-term core player in addition to Jones.

Why Philadelphia Still Wins

Houston's return is good enough that labeling the deal a disaster would ignore the actual results. Jones supplied two years of starting-center production, and McCray became a five-year starter, elite defender and contributor to a Finals team.

Philadelphia nevertheless received the decisive asset. Malone was already an MVP, won the award again immediately, transformed a Finals runner-up into a 65-win champion and delivered the franchise's 1983 title as Finals MVP.

The Sixers achieved the transaction's highest possible outcome in the first season and still retained Malone for three more years.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A+/B+. Philadelphia receives an A+ because Malone delivered MVP production and an immediate championship, then remained a star for four seasons. Houston receives a B+ because Jones and McCray created major real value, including 568 combined regular-season games for the Rockets, but even that strong package did not equal acquiring the best player and winning the title immediately.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Got One Reserve Season From George Johnson

The September 27, 1982 deal sent George Johnson from San Antonio to Atlanta for Jim Johnstone plus second-round picks in 1983 and 1985.

Johnson was a veteran defensive center, but his Atlanta return was limited. He played 37 regular-season games in 1982-83, made no starts and averaged 12.5 minutes, 1.7 points, 3.2 rebounds and 1.6 blocks.

He did not play in 1983-84 after refusing to attend Hawks training camp without a guaranteed contract. He later resumed his career with New Jersey, so Atlanta receives credit only for those 37 games.

Johnstone and Lockhart Barely Played for San Antonio

Johnstone appeared in seven regular-season games for the Spurs in 1982-83, all off the bench, averaging 7.7 minutes and 1.0 point. His San Antonio tenure ended quickly.

The 1983 second-round pick landed at No. 35, where San Antonio selected Darrell Lockhart. Lockhart played only two regular-season games for the Spurs, made no starts and was waived on November 4, 1983.

Those two branches produced just nine direct Spurs games.

The 1985 Pick Became a Useful Trade Asset

The legacy archive entry identifies the 1985 second-round pick as No. 31 Manute Bol. That terminal draft result is correct, but it does not mean Bol played for San Antonio.

On January 20, 1984, the Spurs traded the future second-round pick to Golden State for Ron Brewer. Brewer then played 40 games for San Antonio in 1983-84 and nine more in 1984-85, starting five total and averaging 8.7 points in his first Spurs stint.

That gives San Antonio 49 regular-season games from the direct downstream conversion of the pick.

Manute Bol Belongs to the Later Washington Branch

Golden State later moved the pick to Washington, and the Bullets used No. 31 in the 1985 draft on Manute Bol.

This review preserves Bol as the terminal pick identity but does not credit his Washington career to San Antonio. The Spurs had already converted the asset into Brewer more than a year before the draft.

This distinction avoids overstating San Antonio's return while still recognizing that the 1985 pick carried real transaction value.

Why San Antonio Wins Slightly

Atlanta received 37 reserve games from Johnson. San Antonio received seven games from Johnstone, two from Lockhart and 49 from Brewer through the directly traceable second-round-pick conversion.

The total Spurs basketball return was still modest, but it was broader and lasted longer than Johnson's single Atlanta season.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win, B-/C. San Antonio receives a B- because the original player and 1983 pick produced little, but the 1985 pick was successfully converted into 49 games of Ron Brewer. Atlanta receives a C because Johnson supplied useful shot-blocking depth for 37 games but never played a second season for the Hawks.

perspectives.analysis:
New York Turned a Third-Round Pick Into a Starting Guard

The September 30, 1982 transaction sent Ed Sherod from New Jersey to New York for a 1983 third-round pick.

Sherod had not played in the NBA during 1981-82 after spending time in the CBA, but the Knicks gave him a real role immediately.

Sherod Played 64 Games and Started 37

Sherod appeared in 64 regular-season games for New York in 1982-83 and started 37. He played 1,624 minutes, averaging 25.4 per game.

His season totals included 395 points, 311 assists and 96 steals. That works out to 6.2 points, 4.9 assists and 1.5 steals per game.

For the cost of a third-round pick, New York received a legitimate rotation point guard who started more than half of his appearances.

His NBA Career Lasted Only That Season

Sherod did not return to the NBA after 1982-83, so the Knicks did not obtain long-term value.

That limitation keeps the New York grade below the elite range. The trade was still effective because the immediate return was substantial relative to the asset surrendered.

New Jersey's Pick Became Bruce Kuczenski

The Nets used the incoming third-round pick at No. 59 in the 1983 NBA Draft on Connecticut forward Bruce Kuczenski.

Kuczenski played seven regular-season games for New Jersey in 1983-84, made no starts and logged only 28 minutes. He scored 11 points and collected eight rebounds for the Nets.

He later appeared in three games for Philadelphia and five for Indiana, finishing with 15 NBA games total. Those later appearances are not credited to New Jersey.

Why New York Wins Clearly

New Jersey did convert the pick into an NBA player, so the return was not completely empty. Kuczenski's direct Nets contribution, however, was only seven games and 28 minutes.

Sherod gave New York 64 games, 37 starts and more than 1,600 minutes in the same era. Even though his NBA career ended after one season, that is far more direct realized value.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, B+/D. New York receives a B+ for turning a third-round pick into 64 games, 37 starts and useful point-guard production. New Jersey receives a D because Kuczenski reached the NBA but produced only seven Nets games and no starts before moving on.

summary: Atlanta sent veteran center Tom Burleson to Chicago for future considerations in early October 1982, but the surviving public record does not identify what those considerations became. A contemporary UPI report dates the trade October 1, while the canonical record carries October 2 and RealGM records Chicago's acquisition later in the month, so this review preserves the canonical date while flagging the discrepancy. Burleson had missed the entire 1981-82 season with knee problems, never appeared in a regular-season game for Chicago and was waived before the Bulls' season began. Chicago therefore realized zero basketball value, but Atlanta's unresolved return prevents a defensible winner or team grade.
analysis:
The Trade Is Real, but the Return Is Still Unresolved

A contemporary UPI report says Atlanta traded Tom Burleson to Chicago on October 1, 1982 for future considerations. The legacy canonical record uses October 2, while RealGM places Chicago's acquisition later in October.

Those sources agree on the player and future-considerations mechanism but not on the exact transaction date. This review retains the canonical October 2 date for database continuity and explicitly records the discrepancy rather than manufacturing certainty.

Burleson Had Already Missed a Full Season

Burleson's last NBA statistical season before the trade was 1980-81 with Atlanta. He played 31 games that year and averaged 3.3 points and 3.0 rebounds.

UPI reported that he sat out the entire 1981-82 season because of knee problems that had affected him throughout his career.

That context makes the deal fundamentally different from trading an active rotation center. Chicago was acquiring a veteran comeback possibility, not current production.

He Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Chicago

Burleson does not have a 1982-83 statistical line. Basketball-Reference lists his NBA career as ending after the 1980-81 Atlanta season.

RealGM records Chicago acquiring Burleson and then placing him on waivers later in October. The Bulls' historical transaction material also records his waiver before the regular season.

His direct Chicago return is therefore zero regular-season games, starts and minutes.

Atlanta's Future Considerations Cannot Be Valued Reliably

The contemporary UPI report and both legacy team perspectives identify future considerations going to Atlanta, but the reviewed public sources do not specify cash, a pick, a player or a later conversion.

This review does not infer an asset merely to force a grade. Without knowing whether Atlanta ever received material value, assigning the Hawks a letter grade would create false precision.

This Is a Case for Insufficient Evidence

Chicago's side is measurable and poor in hindsight: Burleson never appeared in a regular-season game. The problem is that the other side of the comparison is unknown.

If Atlanta received even modest cash or another tangible consideration, it likely obtained more realized value than Chicago. If the consideration was never exercised, both sides may have received essentially nothing.

The surviving evidence cannot distinguish those possibilities.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence, N/A/N/A. Burleson's zero-game Chicago outcome is verified, but Atlanta's future consideration remains unresolved. The verdict reflects only verified transaction terms and realized team value.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix allowed restricted veteran free agent Dudley Bradley to sign with Chicago on October 2, 1982 and received the Bulls' 1983 third-round pick as compensation. Bradley gave Chicago 58 games, 11 starts and modest reserve production in 1982-83. Phoenix later included the pick, No. 52 overall, in the Dennis Johnson-to-Boston trade; Boston ultimately used it on Winfred King, who never played in the NBA. Chicago received one usable season while Phoenix received a low-value but tradable draft asset, leaving the original compensation deal close to even.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix did not trade an active player contract to Chicago in the usual sense. Dudley Bradley signed with the Bulls as a veteran free agent, and the Suns agreed to waive their right of first refusal in exchange for Chicago's 1983 third-round pick. Phoenix's 1982-83 transaction log records the free-agent move and compensation, while Pro Sports Transactions maps the pick to No. 52 overall in the 1983 draft. That distinction matters because the correct hindsight comparison is one Chicago season of Bradley versus the draft asset Phoenix received, not Bradley versus a player Phoenix drafted directly.

Chicago Return
Bradley played 58 games for the 1982-83 Bulls and started 11. He averaged 3.5 points, 1.8 rebounds and 1.8 assists in 11.8 minutes per game while shooting 51.6 percent from the field. His role was clearly secondary, but it was real NBA rotation value over most of the season. Chicago finished 28-54, so Bradley did not alter the franchise's competitive direction, and he was not retained as a long-term core piece. After that season his career continued in Washington, Milwaukee and New Jersey, meaning Chicago received only the one-year portion of his later NBA longevity.

Phoenix Return
The compensation became the 1983 third-round pick at No. 52. Phoenix did not actually make the selection. On June 27, 1983, the Suns included that pick with Dennis Johnson and the No. 21 first-round choice in the trade that brought Rick Robey and two second-round picks from Boston. Boston ultimately used No. 52 on East Tennessee State guard Winfred King, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. For this Bradley transaction, Phoenix deserves credit for receiving a movable draft asset, not for any later player that another team selected with it. The pick's inclusion in the Johnson-Robey package proves it had some transaction utility, but it was still a third-rounder with limited standalone value. The later Dennis Johnson trade has its own much larger hindsight story and should not be legacy into this grade.

Hindsight Verdict
Neither side created a major advantage from the original free-agent compensation. Chicago obtained a 58-game reserve season from Bradley. Phoenix obtained a low-cost draft chip that was useful enough to include in a later package but ultimately corresponded to a player who never logged an NBA game. Calling Phoenix the loser would ignore the fact that the Suns received exactly the kind of modest compensation expected when declining to retain a veteran reserve. Calling Chicago the clear winner would overstate one season from a player who averaged 3.5 points. An Even Trade with C+ grades reflects two modest but legitimate returns: one year of rotation depth for Chicago and one transferable third-round asset for Phoenix.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired Wally Walker from Seattle on October 5, 1982 for a 1984 second-round pick that became No. 28 Cory Blackwell. Walker played 140 regular-season games for the Rockets across two seasons, starting 77, and scored 1,041 points before being waived in 1984. Seattle used the pick on Blackwell, who played 60 regular-season games as a rookie, made no starts and scored 202 points in what became his only NBA season. The SuperSonics received a real rotation look from the pick, but Houston received more than twice as many games, 77 starts and substantially more production, giving the Rockets the stronger realized return.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Got Two Seasons and 77 Starts From Wally Walker

Basketball-Reference's Houston transaction ledger records the October 5, 1982 exchange: the Rockets acquired Wally Walker from Seattle for a 1984 second-round pick.

Walker immediately became a regular part of Houston's lineup during a rebuilding season.

He Played All 82 Games in 1982-83

Walker appeared in all 82 regular-season games for Houston in 1982-83 and started 59. He played 2,251 minutes and scored 797 points, which works out to 9.7 points per game.

He also supplied 376 rebounds and 153 assists. The Rockets were not a winning team, but Walker gave them dependable wing minutes throughout the season.

Walker returned for 58 games in 1983-84 and started 18. His role declined to 10.6 minutes and 4.2 points per game, but he still added 244 points before his Houston tenure ended.

Across the two seasons, Walker played 140 regular-season games and started 77.

Seattle Used the Pick on Cory Blackwell

The second-round pick conveyed at No. 28 in the 1984 NBA Draft. Seattle selected Wisconsin forward Cory Blackwell.

Blackwell played 60 regular-season games for the SuperSonics in 1984-85, all off the bench. He logged 551 minutes and averaged 3.4 points and 1.6 rebounds.

Those 60 games were the entirety of his NBA career. He did not return to the league after his rookie season.

The Direct Comparison Favors Houston

Seattle did get an NBA player from the pick, so the return was not empty. Blackwell gave the SuperSonics 60 reserve appearances and a full rookie-season look.

Houston received more than twice as many regular-season games from Walker, plus 77 starts and two years of usable rotation minutes. Walker also scored 1,041 points for the Rockets compared with Blackwell's 202 for Seattle.

The transaction was not franchise-changing for either side, but the realized production gap is clear.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, B+/C-. Houston receives a B+ because Walker supplied 140 games, 77 starts and two seasons of rotation value for the cost of a second-round pick. Seattle receives a C- because Blackwell reached the NBA and played 60 games, but he never started and his NBA career ended after that one season.

Walker appeared in all 82 regular-season games for Houston in 1982-83 and started 59. He played 2,251 minutes and scored 797 points, which works out to 9.7 points per game.

He also supplied 376 rebounds and 153 assists. The Rockets were not a winning team, but Walker gave them dependable wing minutes throughout the season.

The second-round pick conveyed at No. 28 in the 1984 NBA Draft. Seattle selected Wisconsin forward Cory Blackwell.

Seattle did get an NBA player from the pick, so the return was not empty. Blackwell gave the SuperSonics 60 reserve appearances and a full rookie-season look.

Four years later Detroit used the No. 27 pick on Dennis Rodman, who played 549 regular-season games for the Pistons, won two Defensive Player of the Year awards, became a two-time rebounding champion in Detroit and helped the franchise win back-to-back NBA championships in 1989 and 1990. Turning a future second-round pick into a Hall of Fame defender and championship cornerstone makes this one of the clearest realized-value wins in the archive.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Waited Four Years for a Franchise-Altering Return

The October 7, 1982 trade was tiny on the day it happened. Cleveland received Steve Hayes, a reserve center, and Detroit received a future second-round pick in the 1986 draft.

The difference in realized value did not become visible until four years later, when the Pistons used the No. 27 selection on Dennis Rodman.

Hayes Gave Cleveland One Reserve Season

Hayes played 65 regular-season games for the Cavaliers in 1982-83 and started three. He averaged 16.3 minutes, 3.6 points and 3.6 rebounds while shooting 47.9 percent from the field.

That was the entirety of his Cleveland tenure. Hayes played the next season in Seattle and later had brief stops with Philadelphia and Utah.

The Cavaliers therefore received a useful but limited one-year reserve return.

Detroit Used No. 27 on Dennis Rodman

Rodman entered the NBA in 1986 and immediately became part of Detroit's rising core. He played 77 games as a rookie and 82 in each of the next five seasons before appearing in 62 during his final Pistons year.

Across seven Detroit seasons, Rodman played 549 regular-season games.

His value went far beyond availability. Rodman developed into one of the league's defining defenders and rebounders, combining elite versatility with a role that fit the Bad Boys era perfectly.

He Became a Championship Cornerstone

Rodman was a central rotation player on Detroit's 1989 and 1990 championship teams. By the second title season he had also become the NBA Defensive Player of the Year.

He repeated as Defensive Player of the Year in 1990-91. Rodman earned first-team All-Defensive honors multiple times with Detroit and became an All-Star.

In 1991-92 he averaged 18.7 rebounds per game and won the first rebounding title of a seven-year league-leading streak. He led the league again in 1992-93, his final Pistons season.

The Pick Produced Hall of Fame Value

Rodman was inducted into the Basketball Hall of Fame in 2011. His full career later included five championships and seven rebounding titles, although this review credits Detroit only with the value produced during his Pistons tenure.

Even limiting the analysis to those seven seasons, Detroit received two championships, two Defensive Player of the Year awards, elite rebounding and 549 games from the acquired pick.

Why Cleveland Loses Decisively

The Cavaliers could not know in 1982 that a future second-round pick would become Rodman. Hindsight grading is about realized results, not perfect predictability.

Hayes gave Cleveland 65 games and three starts. Detroit turned the pick into one of the defining defenders in franchise history and a core player on consecutive championship teams.

There is no close balancing factor.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A+/F. Detroit receives an A+ for converting a future second-round pick into a Hall of Fame defender, two-time Defensive Player of the Year and two-time Pistons champion. Cleveland receives an F because Hayes provided one reserve season before leaving, while the asset surrendered produced extraordinary franchise value.

perspectives.summary: San Diego acquired Ray Blume's player rights from Chicago on October 8, 1982 for a conditional draft pick that would convey only if Blume made the Clippers' roster. He did not. Blume had played 49 regular-season games for Chicago the previous year, but he never appeared in a regular-season game for San Diego and was waived before the 1982-83 season. Because the condition was not satisfied, Chicago never received the draft pick. The direct post-trade result was therefore zero games for the Clippers and no conveyed asset for the Bulls. With neither side realizing basketball value, the transaction belongs in the even tier rather than showing a Clippers edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Conditional Pick Never Conveyed

The October 8, 1982 transaction sent Ray Blume's player rights from Chicago to San Diego. The Bulls were due a conditional draft pick only if Blume made the Clippers' roster.

He did not, so the condition failed and Chicago never received the pick.

Blume Had NBA Experience, but None Came With San Diego

Blume had played 49 regular-season games for Chicago in 1981-82. He made two starts, averaged 11.1 minutes and scored 4.6 points per game.

Those Bulls games occurred before the trade and cannot be credited to San Diego.

Basketball-Reference lists Blume's NBA career as ending after that 1981-82 Chicago season. His career total remains 49 games, all with the Bulls.

San Diego Acquired His Rights but Got Zero Games

The Clippers' transaction ledger records the October 8 acquisition of Blume's player rights.

Blume never appeared in a regular-season game for San Diego. Contemporary transaction records later show him being waived before the 1982-83 season.

The Clippers therefore realized zero regular-season games, starts or minutes from the acquired rights.

Chicago Also Received Zero Realized Value

Because Blume did not make San Diego's roster, the conditional draft pick was not exercised.

That leaves the Bulls with no player, no conveyed draft selection and no known downstream asset from the transaction.

The conditional structure protected San Diego from paying a pick for a player it did not keep, but it also meant Chicago received nothing after Blume failed to stick.

Why the Correct Verdict Is Even

The legacy perspectives leaned toward San Diego because the Clippers acquired the player rights while Chicago's condition failed. Hindsight value should measure what actually materialized.

Neither side received a regular-season player contribution after the trade. Chicago's pick never conveyed, and Blume never played for the Clippers.

A directional winner would therefore overstate a zero-versus-zero outcome.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C-/C-. Chicago receives a C- because the conditional pick never conveyed and produced no asset. San Diego receives a C- because Blume's rights produced zero regular-season games before he was waived. Confidence is high because the condition and player outcome are both directly verifiable.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
San Diego Bought a Very Small Amount of Guard Depth

The October 15, 1982 transaction sent Robert Smith from Milwaukee to San Diego for a 1983 sixth-round pick.

Basketball-Reference's Clippers transaction ledger confirms the pick later became No. 120 Russell Todd.

Smith Played Only Five Games for the Clippers

Smith had already spent several seasons as an NBA reserve before the trade, but San Diego received very little from the acquisition.

He appeared in five regular-season games for the Clippers in 1982-83, made no starts and played 43 total minutes. Smith scored 11 points, collected three rebounds and recorded six assists.

He then moved to San Antonio, where he played seven more games that season. Those Spurs appearances are not credited to the Clippers.

Milwaukee Used the Pick on Russell Todd

The sixth-round selection landed at No. 120 in the 1983 NBA Draft. Milwaukee selected West Virginia forward Russell Todd.

Basketball-Reference lists Todd as a drafted player but provides no NBA regular-season statistical line. He never appeared in an NBA game.

That leaves Milwaukee with zero direct player games from the pick.

The Difference Is Real but Extremely Small

Five games and 43 minutes are not a meaningful rotation return. San Diego should not receive a strong grade simply because Smith reached the floor.

Milwaukee's branch was even smaller because Todd never appeared in the league. The Bucks used the selection, but no NBA production resulted.

The proper hindsight comparison is therefore a narrow Clippers edge rather than a major win.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, C-/F. San Diego receives a C- because Smith produced five games and 43 minutes before leaving, which is tangible but minimal. Milwaukee receives an F because the No. 120 pick became Todd and produced zero NBA regular-season games. Confidence is high because both terminal outcomes are directly documented.

houston-rockets.summary: San Antonio signed veteran free agent Mike Dunleavy on October 16, 1982 after Houston waived its right of first refusal, with the Rockets receiving a 1983 second-round pick as compensation. Dunleavy played 79 regular-season games for the Spurs, started nine and averaged 7.8 points and 5.5 assists for a 53-win team that reached the Western Conference Finals. Houston did not use the pick itself: on November 10 it packaged that selection with another Spurs second-rounder from the Bill Willoughby compensation deal to acquire James Bailey from New Jersey. Bailey then played 142 regular-season games for Houston across two seasons, including 39 starts. Because the Rockets needed both second-round picks to obtain Bailey, the realized value is best treated as broadly even rather than crediting the entire Bailey return to this one transaction.
houston-rockets.analysis:
San Antonio Got a Full Season From Mike Dunleavy

Basketball-Reference's San Antonio and Houston transaction ledgers agree on the October 16, 1982 mechanism. Dunleavy signed with the Spurs as a veteran free agent, and Houston received San Antonio's 1983 second-round pick as compensation after relinquishing its right-of-first-refusal claim.

Dunleavy appeared in 79 regular-season games for San Antonio and started nine. He averaged 20.5 minutes, 7.8 points and 5.5 assists while serving as Johnny Moore's primary reserve at point guard.

The Spurs finished 53-29, won the Midwest Division and reached the Western Conference Finals. Dunleavy also appeared throughout that playoff run, so the compensation arrangement gave San Antonio immediate rotation value on a contender.

Houston Did Not Draft Horace Owens

The incoming pick later became No. 44 in the 1983 draft, but Houston no longer owned it by draft night.

On November 10, 1982, the Rockets sent this pick and the 1985 second-round pick acquired from San Antonio in the Bill Willoughby compensation deal to New Jersey for James Bailey. The Nets later used No. 44 on Horace Owens, who never played in an NBA regular-season game.

That means this review should not describe Owens as a Houston draft result. The pick's value to the Rockets was its role in the Bailey trade.

James Bailey Gave Houston Two Seasons

Bailey played 69 games for Houston in 1982-83, started 39 and averaged 14.1 points and 6.8 rebounds. He returned for 73 more games in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 8.8 points and 4.0 rebounds.

His two-year Rockets total was 142 regular-season games and 39 starts. That is a meaningful return, especially for a rebuilding Houston team.

The attribution limit is important, however. Houston paid two second-round picks to acquire Bailey. The 1983 Dunleavy compensation pick was only one half of that outgoing package, so this review does not credit all 142 Bailey games solely to this transaction.

Why the Trade Is Even

San Antonio received a known one-season contributor: 79 games, nine starts and 5.5 assists per game on a conference finalist.

Houston received a second-round asset that helped acquire a productive frontcourt player, but the asset had to be combined with another second-rounder. The downstream return is real without being fully attributable to the Dunleavy compensation alone.

Both teams therefore extracted useful value from the mechanism, just in different forms and time horizons.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B/B. San Antonio receives a B for 79 games of productive guard depth on a 53-win conference finalist. Houston receives a B because the pick became an important part of the James Bailey package, which produced two seasons of useful frontcourt play, while acknowledging that a second pick was also required to complete that later trade.

houston-rockets.summary: San Antonio signed veteran free agent Bill Willoughby on October 18, 1982 after Houston declined its right of first refusal, with the Rockets receiving a 1985 second-round pick as compensation. Willoughby played 52 regular-season games for the Spurs, all off the bench, averaging 6.1 points and 3.7 rebounds before San Antonio waived him in February. Houston did not keep the pick through the 1985 draft: on November 10, 1982, the Rockets packaged it with the 1983 second-round pick received in the Mike Dunleavy compensation deal to acquire James Bailey from New Jersey. Bailey played 142 regular-season games for Houston across two seasons, including 39 starts. Because two picks were required for Bailey, this review credits this pick with partial downstream value, producing a modest Rockets edge rather than the full Bailey return.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Received a Second-Round Pick for Bill Willoughby

Basketball-Reference's Houston, San Antonio and league transaction ledgers agree on the October 18, 1982 mechanism. Willoughby signed with the Spurs as a veteran free agent, and Houston received San Antonio's 1985 second-round pick as compensation.

That pick is commonly labeled as the selection later used on Yvon Joseph, but Houston did not retain it until the 1985 draft.

Willoughby Gave San Antonio 52 Reserve Games

Willoughby appeared in 52 regular-season games for San Antonio in 1982-83 and made no starts. He averaged 20.4 minutes, 6.1 points and 3.7 rebounds while shooting 46.1 percent from the field.

The Spurs were a 53-win Midwest Division champion and eventually reached the Western Conference Finals. Willoughby therefore supplied real rotation minutes on a contender even though he was not a starter.

His San Antonio stay ended on February 10, 1983, when the Spurs waived him. New Jersey later signed him on March 25, so this review credits only the 52 Spurs games produced directly from this compensation transaction.

Houston Rerouted the Pick Within Three Weeks

On November 10, 1982, Houston traded the 1985 second-round pick together with the 1983 second-round pick received from San Antonio in the Mike Dunleavy compensation transaction to New Jersey for James Bailey.

The Nets ultimately used the 1985 selection at No. 36 on Yvon Joseph. That draft outcome belongs to New Jersey, not Houston, so this review should not score Joseph's NBA career as the Rockets' realized result.

For Houston, the relevant value is that the pick helped complete the Bailey acquisition.

Bailey Produced Two Useful Rockets Seasons

Bailey played 69 regular-season games for Houston in 1982-83, started 39 and averaged 14.1 points and 6.8 rebounds. He returned for 73 games in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 8.8 points and 4.0 rebounds.

His two-year Houston total was 142 games and 39 starts. That is a strong downstream outcome from the two-pick package.

This review does not assign all of Bailey's value to the Willoughby pick. The Dunleavy compensation pick was equally necessary, so the proper conclusion is that this 1985 second-rounder carried meaningful partial transaction value rather than becoming Bailey by itself.

Why Houston Gets a Modest Edge

San Antonio received 52 reserve games and useful regular-season minutes from Willoughby before waiving him. That is a real return, especially on a 53-win team.

Houston received an asset that became half of the package for a player who produced 142 games and 39 starts over two seasons. Even with conservative attribution, the downstream value of the pick slightly exceeds Willoughby's shorter Spurs tenure.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, B/C+. Houston receives a B because the compensation pick became an important part of the James Bailey acquisition without requiring this review to credit the entire Bailey return to one asset. San Antonio receives a C+ for 52 useful reserve games before Willoughby was waived in February.

golden-state-warriors.summary: New York acquired Bernard King from Golden State on October 22, 1982 for Micheal Ray Richardson and a 1984 fifth-round pick. King played 206 regular-season games for the Knicks, became a two-time All-NBA First Team selection and 1985 scoring champion, and averaged 34.8 points during New York's 1984 playoff run. Golden State's return was much better than Richardson's 33-game Warriors stay suggests: the Warriors flipped Richardson to New Jersey in February 1983 for Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson. Floyd then played 374 regular-season games for Golden State, became a 1987 All-Star and developed into the franchise's starting point guard, while Johnson added 174 Warriors games. The fifth-round pick became Scott McCollum, who never played in the NBA. New York still receives the higher grade because King's peak and playoff impact were exceptional, but Golden State's Richardson-to-Floyd/Johnson chain makes this a strong return rather than a lopsided loss.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Bernard King Became an Elite Knick

Basketball-Reference's Golden State and New York transaction ledgers record the October 22, 1982 exchange as Bernard King for Micheal Ray Richardson and a 1984 fifth-round pick.

King immediately became New York's primary scorer. He played 68 regular-season games in 1982-83, 77 in 1983-84, 55 in 1984-85 and six more after returning from his knee injury in 1986-87.

Across those four Knicks seasons he appeared in 206 regular-season games. His peak was extraordinary: 26.3 points per game with All-NBA First Team honors in 1983-84, followed by a league-leading 32.9 points per game and another First Team selection in 1984-85.

The 1984 Playoffs Defined the Return

King averaged 34.8 points per game in the 1984 playoffs. He scored at least 40 points six times in twelve postseason games and helped New York beat Detroit before taking eventual champion Boston to seven games in the Eastern Conference semifinals.

That postseason run is the strongest single competitive outcome produced by either side of the trade.

Richardson's Direct Warriors Tenure Was Short

Richardson played 33 regular-season games for Golden State, started 25 and averaged 12.5 points, 7.4 assists and 3.1 steals.

If the analysis stopped there, this would look like a severe Warriors loss. It should not stop there.

On February 6, 1983, Golden State traded Richardson to New Jersey for Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson. The value of that downstream exchange belongs in the original trade tree because Richardson was the asset used to obtain both players.

Sleepy Floyd Became a Long-Term Warriors Starter

Floyd played 33 Golden State games after the February trade, then 77 in 1983-84, 82 in 1984-85, 82 in 1985-86, 82 in 1986-87 and 18 more before being traded in 1987-88.

That is 374 regular-season games for the Warriors. He became the full-time starting point guard, averaged 19.5 points in 1984-85, 17.2 points and 9.1 assists in 1985-86, and 18.8 points with 10.3 assists during his 1987 All-Star season.

Floyd's development gives Golden State a major realized-value branch that the earlier one-paragraph review understated.

Mickey Johnson Added Three Useful Seasons

Johnson played 30 Golden State games in 1982-83, 78 in 1983-84 and 66 in 1984-85.

His Warriors total was 174 regular-season games. He averaged 15.5 points and 8.2 rebounds after arriving in 1982-83, then remained a double-figure scorer in each of the next two seasons.

The Richardson branch therefore produced both a future All-Star guard and a multi-year frontcourt contributor.

The Fifth-Round Pick Produced Nothing

Golden State used the 1984 No. 110 selection on Pepperdine forward Scott McCollum. Basketball-Reference lists him as a drafted player without an NBA regular-season career.

That branch contributes no realized NBA value.

Why New York Still Gets the Higher Grade

Golden State's outcome was strong: Richardson supplied 33 games and was then converted into Floyd and Johnson, who combined for 548 Warriors regular-season games. Calling that package a failing return is not supportable once the downstream chain is included.

New York still receives the higher grade because King reached a level none of the Warriors assets matched. He made two All-NBA First Teams, won a scoring title at 32.9 points per game and authored a 34.8-point playoff run that pushed the eventual champion Celtics to seven games.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A+/A-. New York receives an A+ for King's elite peak, scoring title and defining 1984 postseason. Golden State receives an A- because Richardson was successfully converted into Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson, producing years of starter-level value and an All-Star season. The Knicks won the top-end outcome, but this was far more competitive than the direct Richardson-for-King framing implies.

King averaged 34.8 points per game in the 1984 playoffs. He scored at least 40 points six times in twelve postseason games and helped New York beat Detroit before taking eventual champion Boston to seven games in the Eastern Conference semifinals.

That postseason run is the strongest single competitive outcome produced by either side of the trade.

Richardson played 33 regular-season games for Golden State, started 25 and averaged 12.5 points, 7.4 assists and 3.1 steals.

If the analysis stopped there, this would look like a severe Warriors loss. It should not stop there.

On February 6, 1983, Golden State traded Richardson to New Jersey for Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson. The value of that downstream exchange belongs in the original trade tree because Richardson was the asset used to obtain both players.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded Brad Branson to Indiana on October 25, 1982 for the Pacers' 1983 second-round pick, later No. 36. Branson played 62 regular-season games for Indiana, started two and averaged 5.5 points before leaving the NBA. Cleveland did not use the pick on Scooter McCray: on June 27, 1983 the Cavaliers sent that selection plus cash to Seattle for veteran forward Lonnie Shelton. Shelton then played 180 regular-season games for Cleveland across three seasons, started 93 and averaged 10.8 points in 79 games during his first Cavaliers season. Because Cleveland had to add cash to acquire Shelton, this review gives the pick partial rather than full credit for that downstream return. Even with that attribution limit, Cleveland extracted more realized value from the asset than Indiana received from Branson.
perspectives.analysis:
Indiana Received One Season From Brad Branson

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland transaction ledger records the October 25, 1982 exchange directly: the Cavaliers sent Brad Branson to Indiana for a 1983 second-round pick.

Branson played 62 regular-season games for the Pacers in 1982-83 and made two starts. He averaged 11.0 minutes, 5.5 points and 2.8 rebounds while shooting 42.5 percent from the field.

Those 62 games were the final NBA appearances of his career. Indiana therefore received one season of reserve frontcourt production and no longer-term branch from the player.

Cleveland Did Not Draft Scooter McCray

The incoming pick ultimately became No. 36 in the 1983 NBA Draft, where Seattle selected Scooter McCray.

That draft label can be misleading if treated as Cleveland's realized player outcome. On June 27, one day before the draft, Cleveland traded the pick to Seattle for Lonnie Shelton.

Basketball-Reference records the pick-for-Shelton transaction, while Pro Sports Transactions also lists cash going from Cleveland to Seattle. Because the Cavaliers added cash, this review cannot assign Shelton's entire later Cleveland career to the Branson pick by itself.

The Pick Helped Bring Lonnie Shelton to Cleveland

Shelton played 79 regular-season games for Cleveland in 1983-84 and started 78. He averaged 26.6 minutes, 10.8 points, 4.8 rebounds and 2.3 assists.

He returned for 57 games and 14 starts in 1984-85, then 44 games and one start in 1985-86.

Across those three Cavaliers seasons, Shelton appeared in 180 regular-season games and started 93. The first season alone gave Cleveland a near full-time starter from a package built around the acquired second-round pick plus cash.

Scooter McCray's Career Belongs to Seattle

Seattle used No. 36 on McCray, who played 53 regular-season games for the SuperSonics across two seasons before later appearing for Cleveland as a free agent in 1986-87.

Those later Cleveland games are not credited to this 1982 trade. McCray reached Cleveland years later through an independent free-agent signing, after the original pick had already been spent in the Shelton transaction.

Why Cleveland Gets the Edge

Indiana obtained 62 reserve games and two starts from Branson. Cleveland converted the second-round pick, together with additional cash, into a veteran who supplied 180 games and 93 starts over three seasons.

The cash component prevents the pick from receiving full credit for Shelton, but the transaction chain still shows that Cleveland preserved and then leveraged the asset for much more roster value than Branson produced in Indiana.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, B/C+. Cleveland receives a B because the acquired second-round pick became a central part of the Lonnie Shelton package and helped produce three seasons of frontcourt value. Indiana receives a C+ for 62 useful reserve games from Branson, with no additional NBA return after his lone Pacers season.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: San Diego acquired Lionel Hollins from Philadelphia on October 27, 1982 for a 1983 fourth-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick. Hollins immediately started 54 of 56 games for the Clippers, averaging 13.5 points, 6.7 assists and 2.0 steals before leaving after one season. Philadelphia used the No. 74 pick on Kalpatrick Wells, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The No. 29 second-rounder was rerouted to Indiana in February 1983 as one piece of a larger package that brought Clemon Johnson to Philadelphia; Johnson then contributed to the 1983 championship team and stayed through 1985-86, but the Sixers also surrendered Russ Schoene and a first-round pick in that deal. The downstream value is therefore only partially attributable to the Hollins pick, leaving a clear Clippers edge.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
San Diego Bought a Starting Point Guard

Basketball-Reference's San Diego and Philadelphia transaction ledgers agree on the October 27, 1982 package. The Clippers acquired Lionel Hollins for a 1983 fourth-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick.

Hollins played 56 regular-season games for San Diego and started 54. He averaged 32.9 minutes, 13.5 points, 6.7 assists and 2.0 steals while handling a major portion of the Clippers' backcourt workload.

His Clippers tenure lasted only one season. Hollins played for Detroit in 1983-84, so this review credits San Diego with the 56 games and 54 starts produced directly after the trade.

The Fourth-Round Pick Produced No NBA Games

Philadelphia kept the 1983 fourth-round selection and used it at No. 74 on Mississippi State forward Kalpatrick Wells.

Basketball-Reference lists Wells as the No. 74 selection but contains no NBA regular-season statistical line for him. That branch therefore produced zero NBA games for Philadelphia.

The Second-Round Pick Was Rerouted Before the Draft

Philadelphia did not keep the 1984 second-round pick until draft night.

On February 15, 1983, the 76ers sent Russ Schoene, a 1983 first-round pick that became No. 23 Mitchell Wiggins and this 1984 second-round pick to Indiana for Clemon Johnson and a 1984 third-round pick that became No. 48 James Banks.

Indiana ultimately used No. 29 on Stuart Gray. His NBA career belongs to the Pacers branch, not Philadelphia.

Clemon Johnson Added Value to a Championship Team

Johnson played 32 regular-season games for Philadelphia after the February trade, started four and averaged 6.8 points and 6.4 rebounds. He then appeared in all 12 playoff games as the 76ers went 12-1 and won the 1983 championship.

Johnson remained with Philadelphia for three additional seasons, giving the Sixers a useful reserve center beyond the title run.

This review cannot credit all of Johnson's value to the Hollins pick. Philadelphia also surrendered Schoene and a 1983 first-round pick, while receiving a third-round pick along with Johnson. The No. 29 asset was only one component of that later package.

Why San Diego Wins

The Clippers received a known starting point guard for one season: 56 games, 54 starts and strong scoring, passing and defensive production.

Philadelphia's fourth-round pick produced no NBA player, while the second-rounder retained enough transaction value to help complete the Johnson trade. That downstream utility keeps the Sixers' return from being empty, but it was not the sole asset that produced Johnson.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, B+/C+. San Diego receives a B+ for a season of starting-level point-guard play from Hollins. Philadelphia receives a C+ because one pick produced no NBA games and the other contributed to a later multi-asset trade that brought a useful championship reserve, but the full downstream return cannot be assigned to this deal alone.

Indiana ultimately used No. 29 on Stuart Gray. His NBA career belongs to the Pacers branch, not Philadelphia.

Clemon Johnson Added Value to a Championship Team

Johnson played 32 regular-season games for Philadelphia after the February trade, started four and averaged 6.8 points and 6.4 rebounds. He then appeared in all 12 playoff games as the 76ers went 12-1 and won the 1983 championship.

Johnson remained with Philadelphia for three additional seasons, giving the Sixers a useful reserve center beyond the title run.

This review cannot credit all of Johnson's value to the Hollins pick. Philadelphia also surrendered Schoene and a 1983 first-round pick, while receiving a third-round pick along with Johnson. The No. 29 asset was only one component of that later package.

Why San Diego Wins

The Clippers received a known starting point guard for one season: 56 games, 54 starts and strong scoring, passing and defensive production.

Philadelphia's fourth-round pick produced no NBA player, while the second-rounder retained enough transaction value to help complete the Johnson trade. That downstream utility keeps the Sixers' return from being empty, but it was not the sole asset that produced Johnson.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, B+/C+. San Diego receives a B+ for a season of starting-level point-guard play from Hollins. Philadelphia receives a C+ because one pick produced no NBA games and the other contributed to a later multi-asset trade that brought a useful championship reserve, but the full downstream return cannot be assigned to this deal alone.

perspectives.analysis:
The Canonical Player Name Needed a Correction

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey transaction ledger identifies the incoming veteran as Mickey Johnson, not Wallace Johnson. The 1982-83 Nets roster confirms Johnson played 42 games for New Jersey after the trade.

This review corrects that asset identity while preserving the rest of the package: New Jersey received Mickey Johnson and the rights to 1982 second-round pick Fred Roberts, while Milwaukee received Phil Ford and New Jersey's 1983 second-round pick.

Mickey Johnson Gave New Jersey 42 Games

Johnson played 42 regular-season games for the Nets, started seven and averaged 23.8 minutes, 13.4 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.4 assists.

His Nets stay lasted only until February 6, 1983, when New Jersey traded Johnson and Sleepy Floyd to Golden State for Micheal Ray Richardson. This review credits only the 42 direct Nets games from this transaction and does not assign the later Richardson return entirely to Johnson because Floyd was a major co-asset.

Fred Roberts Never Played for the Nets

Roberts had been Milwaukee's No. 27 pick in the 1982 draft but spent 1982-83 in Italy. New Jersey held his NBA rights rather than receiving immediate on-court value.

On June 7, 1983, the Nets sent Roberts and another 1983 second-round pick to San Antonio as compensation for signing Stan Albeck as head coach. Roberts therefore produced zero New Jersey regular-season games.

His later 818-game NBA career cannot be credited to the Nets because it began with San Antonio after New Jersey had moved his rights.

Phil Ford Became a Milwaukee Starter

Ford had appeared in only seven games for New Jersey before the trade. With Milwaukee he played 70 regular-season games in 1982-83 and started 56.

He averaged 20.7 minutes, 6.8 points and 3.6 assists while the Bucks went 51-31 and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. That gave Milwaukee a full season of real rotation and starting value.

The No. 41 Pick Became Ted Kitchel

Milwaukee used the 1983 second-round pick on Indiana forward Ted Kitchel at No. 41. Kitchel never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

That means the pick branch itself produced zero direct Bucks games, but Ford's 70-game season still outweighs New Jersey's shorter Johnson return.

Why Milwaukee Wins

New Jersey received 42 games and seven starts from Johnson, plus Roberts' rights, which never turned into a Nets appearance. Milwaukee received 70 games and 56 starts from Ford, while Kitchel produced no NBA games.

The gap is meaningful but not enormous because Johnson was productive during his short New Jersey stay and Roberts retained some transaction utility as a rights asset.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win, B+/B-. Milwaukee receives a B+ for 70 games and 56 starts from Ford at a modest cost, even though Kitchel did not reach the NBA. New Jersey receives a B- because Johnson gave the Nets 42 useful games and Roberts' rights retained value, but neither incoming asset lasted long enough to match Ford's direct Milwaukee contribution.

perspectives.summary: Houston acquired James Bailey from New Jersey on November 10, 1982 for second-round picks in 1983 and 1985. Bailey gave the Rockets 142 regular-season games across two seasons, starting 39 and averaging 14.1 points and 6.8 rebounds in 1982-83. New Jersey used the 1983 No. 44 pick on Horace Owens, who never played an NBA game, and the 1985 No. 36 pick on Yvon Joseph, who appeared in one Nets game for five minutes. perspectives.analysis:
Houston Bought Two Useful Seasons of James Bailey

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey transaction ledger records the November 10, 1982 trade as James Bailey to Houston for two second-round picks: one in 1983 and another in 1985.

The picks eventually became No. 44 Horace Owens and No. 36 Yvon Joseph.

Bailey Immediately Became a Houston Starter

Bailey played 69 regular-season games for the Rockets in 1982-83 and started 39. He averaged 24.9 minutes, 14.1 points and 6.8 rebounds while shooting 49.7 percent.

Houston was a 14-win rebuilding team, so those numbers did not translate into team success. Still, Bailey's role was real: he logged 1,715 minutes and became one of the club's most productive frontcourt players.

He returned for 73 games in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 8.8 points and 4.0 rebounds in 16.1 minutes.

That gives Houston 142 direct regular-season games from Bailey over two seasons, including 39 starts.

The 1983 Pick Became Horace Owens

New Jersey used the No. 44 pick in the 1983 NBA Draft on Rhode Island guard Horace Owens.

Owens never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The Nets later moved his rights with Eddie Phillips to Philadelphia during the 1983 preseason, and Owens was waived before the season.

Because the player never logged an NBA game, this review treats the 1983 pick's direct basketball return as zero.

The 1985 Pick Became Yvon Joseph

The second Houston pick conveyed at No. 36 in 1985, where New Jersey selected Georgia Tech center Yvon Joseph.

Joseph played one NBA regular-season game for the Nets in 1985-86. He logged five minutes, scored two points at the free-throw line and did not start.

That single appearance was his entire NBA career.

Why Houston Wins Clearly

New Jersey turned two second-round picks into one NBA appearance from Joseph and no NBA games from Owens. Houston received two seasons and 142 games from Bailey.

The picks had some transactional and roster flexibility before being exercised, but their realized player value was negligible compared with Bailey's immediate production.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win, A-/D. Houston receives an A- for acquiring 142 games, 39 starts and a productive first season from Bailey at the cost of two second-rounders. New Jersey receives a D because the two selections produced just one direct NBA game between them.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired World B. Free from Golden State on December 15, 1982 for Ron Brewer. Free became the Cavaliers' primary scorer for parts of four seasons, playing 275 regular-season games for Cleveland, starting 247 and averaging 23.0 points. He scored 24.2 points per game immediately after the trade, then remained above 22 points per game in each of the next three Cleveland seasons while helping the franchise return to the playoffs in 1984-85. Brewer played 66 regular-season games for Golden State across parts of two seasons, starting 37 and averaging 11.3 points in 1982-83. The realized value gap strongly favors Cleveland.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Acquired a Multi-Year Primary Scorer

The December 15, 1982 transaction was a straight player-for-player swap: Cleveland received World B. Free, and Golden State received Ron Brewer.

Free immediately became the centerpiece of Cleveland's offense. In 54 games after the trade he started 51 and averaged 24.2 points, 3.7 assists and 1.5 steals in 35.9 minutes.

That was not a short spike. Free remained with the Cavaliers through the 1985-86 season and stayed above 22 points per game in every full Cleveland season.

Four Seasons of High-Volume Production

Free played 75 games in 1983-84 and averaged 22.3 points. He followed with 71 games and 22.5 points in 1984-85, then 75 games and 23.4 points in 1985-86.

Across his Cleveland tenure, he appeared in 275 regular-season games and started 247. His career average with the Cavaliers was 23.0 points per game.

The 1984-85 season also produced the clearest team payoff. Cleveland reached the playoffs, and Free averaged 26.3 points and 7.8 assists in the first-round series against Boston.

Brewer Gave Golden State a Shorter Return

Ron Brewer was a useful NBA guard, not an empty asset. He played 53 games for Golden State in 1982-83, started 34 and averaged 11.3 points.

He returned for 13 games in 1983-84 with three starts before leaving the Warriors. That gives Golden State 66 direct regular-season games and 37 starts from the trade.

Brewer's later NBA production for other teams does not count toward Golden State's realized return.

Why Cleveland Wins Decisively

Cleveland received 275 games, 247 starts and multiple seasons of 22-plus-point scoring from Free. Golden State received 66 games and 37 starts from Brewer.

The difference is not only volume. Free became a franchise-level offensive focal point and was part of Cleveland's return to the postseason, while Brewer was a shorter-term rotation starter.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A+/C. Cleveland receives an A+ because a one-for-one player trade delivered four seasons of elite scoring and 275 games from Free. Golden State receives a C because Brewer was useful, but his 66-game Warriors tenure was far shorter and far less impactful.

summary: Cleveland acquired World B. Free from Golden State on December 15, 1982 for Ron Brewer. Free became the Cavaliers' primary scorer for parts of four seasons, playing 275 regular-season games for Cleveland, starting 247 and averaging 23.0 points. He scored 24.2 points per game immediately after the trade, then remained above 22 points per game in each of the next three Cleveland seasons while helping the franchise return to the playoffs in 1984-85. Brewer played 66 regular-season games for Golden State across parts of two seasons, starting 37 and averaging 11.3 points in 1982-83. The realized value gap strongly favors Cleveland.
analysis:
Cleveland Acquired a Multi-Year Primary Scorer

The December 15, 1982 transaction was a straight player-for-player swap: Cleveland received World B. Free, and Golden State received Ron Brewer.

Free immediately became the centerpiece of Cleveland's offense. In 54 games after the trade he started 51 and averaged 24.2 points, 3.7 assists and 1.5 steals in 35.9 minutes.

That was not a short spike. Free remained with the Cavaliers through the 1985-86 season and stayed above 22 points per game in every full Cleveland season.

Four Seasons of High-Volume Production

Free played 75 games in 1983-84 and averaged 22.3 points. He followed with 71 games and 22.5 points in 1984-85, then 75 games and 23.4 points in 1985-86.

Across his Cleveland tenure, he appeared in 275 regular-season games and started 247. His career average with the Cavaliers was 23.0 points per game.

The 1984-85 season also produced the clearest team payoff. Cleveland reached the playoffs, and Free averaged 26.3 points and 7.8 assists in the first-round series against Boston.

Brewer Gave Golden State a Shorter Return

Ron Brewer was a useful NBA guard, not an empty asset. He played 53 games for Golden State in 1982-83, started 34 and averaged 11.3 points.

He returned for 13 games in 1983-84 with three starts before leaving the Warriors. That gives Golden State 66 direct regular-season games and 37 starts from the trade.

Brewer's later NBA production for other teams does not count toward Golden State's realized return.

Why Cleveland Wins Decisively

Cleveland received 275 games, 247 starts and multiple seasons of 22-plus-point scoring from Free. Golden State received 66 games and 37 starts from Brewer.

The difference is not only volume. Free became a franchise-level offensive focal point and was part of Cleveland's return to the postseason, while Brewer was a shorter-term rotation starter.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, A+/C. Cleveland receives an A+ because a one-for-one player trade delivered four seasons of elite scoring and 275 games from Free. Golden State receives a C because Brewer was useful, but his 66-game Warriors tenure was far shorter and far less impactful.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Both Teams Received Two Useful Seasons

Basketball-Reference's Atlanta transaction ledger records the December 31, 1982 deal as Johnny Davis to the Hawks for Atlanta's 1983 second-round pick, later No. 40 Jim Thomas. The legacy canonical source package also includes cash going to Indiana.

The reviewed public transaction ledger does not identify the cash amount, so this review preserves it as part of Indiana's return without assigning a speculative dollar value.

Davis Became Atlanta's Starting Guard

Davis played 53 regular-season games for Atlanta after the trade in 1982-83 and started 33. He averaged 27.6 minutes, 12.9 points and 5.9 assists.

The Hawks went 43-39 and reached the playoffs. Davis also appeared in all three first-round games against Boston and averaged 17.0 points and 9.0 assists in the series.

He returned for 75 games in 1983-84, starting 72 while averaging 12.3 points and 4.3 assists. Across the two Atlanta seasons, Davis played 128 regular-season games and started 105.

Indiana Turned the Pick Into Jim Thomas

The Pacers used the No. 40 selection in the 1983 NBA Draft on Indiana University guard Jim Thomas.

Thomas played 72 games as a rookie in 1983-84, started 15 and averaged 6.3 points in 16.9 minutes. His role grew substantially in his second season.

In 1984-85 he appeared in 80 games, started 52 and averaged 25.7 minutes, 11.1 points, 3.3 rebounds and 2.9 assists.

That gives Indiana 152 regular-season games and 67 starts from the pick across two seasons.

The Cash Component Adds Real but Unquantified Value

Indiana also received cash. Because the amount is not identified in the reviewed public sources, this review does not let that unknown figure dominate the verdict.

It still matters as a realized asset, particularly because the player returns themselves are close enough to compare rather than one side receiving nothing.

Why This Lands Near Even

Atlanta received the better immediate starter. Davis logged 105 starts, handled a meaningful playmaking role and contributed to a playoff team.

Indiana received more total games from Thomas, watched him grow into a 52-game starter in his second season and also collected cash.

Neither return became a long-term franchise cornerstone, but both generated multiple seasons of usable value.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B/B. Atlanta receives a B for 128 games, 105 starts and two seasons of starting-caliber guard play from Davis. Indiana receives a B for 152 games, 67 starts from Thomas plus an additional cash return whose amount cannot be verified. The strengths differ, but the completed value is too close to force a winner.
