perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Larry Kenon's player rights from Golden State for cash in January 1983. The Warriors' official media guide dates the transaction January 8, while Basketball-Reference's Cleveland and league ledgers list January 10; this review retains the canonical January 8 date and records the discrepancy. Kenon played 32 regular-season games for Cleveland, starting seven and scoring 235 points in 624 minutes before being waived March 21. Golden State received cash, but the amount is not identified in the reviewed public sources. With Cleveland receiving a short veteran stint and the Warriors receiving an unquantified financial return, the completed value remains broadly even.
perspectives.analysis:
The Sources Differ by Two Days

Golden State's official media guide lists the Larry Kenon transaction on January 8, 1983 and says the Warriors traded him to Cleveland for cash. Basketball-Reference's Cleveland and league transaction ledgers place the acquisition on January 10.

This review retains the canonical January 8 date because a franchise media guide directly supports it, but records the two-day discrepancy rather than presenting the date as universally agreed.

Kenon's Cleveland Stay Was Brief

Kenon played 32 regular-season games for the Cavaliers in 1982-83 and started seven. He logged 624 minutes, scored 235 points and collected 117 rebounds.

That works out to roughly 19.5 minutes, 7.3 points and 3.7 rebounds per game. He remained a usable veteran forward, but the role was far smaller than the All-Star-level seasons he had produced earlier in his career.

Cleveland waived Kenon on March 21, 1983. Those 32 games were the final appearances of his NBA career.

Golden State Received Cash

The Warriors had signed Kenon as a free agent in December and used him for only 11 games before moving his rights to Cleveland.

Their return was cash. The reviewed sources establish the transaction mechanism but do not identify the amount, so this review does not invent a dollar value or treat the financial return as unusually large.

Why the Trade Remains Even

Cleveland received a short-term veteran contribution: 32 games, seven starts and 624 minutes before a March waiver. Golden State monetized a player it had signed only weeks earlier.

Neither side created durable roster value. Kenon did provide more measurable basketball production than an unknown cash figure can demonstrate, but the Cavaliers also paid for a player who was out of the league by season's end.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B-/B-. Cleveland receives a B- for a usable 32-game veteran stint at a low asset cost. Golden State receives a B- for converting a brief free-agent addition into cash. Confidence is medium because authoritative sources differ on the exact date and the cash amount is not publicly identified.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Turned the Package Into Five Seasons of Scott Wedman

The January 14, 1983 transaction sent Scott Wedman to Boston for Darren Tillis, Boston's 1983 first-round pick and cash. The first-round choice later became No. 21 Greg Kite.

Wedman immediately shifted from a starting role in Cleveland to a reserve role behind Boston's established frontcourt. That reduced his box-score volume, but it also placed him on a contender where depth had real value.

Wedman Played 271 Regular-Season Games for Boston

Wedman appeared in 40 regular-season games for the Celtics after the trade in 1982-83. He then played 68 games in 1983-84, 78 in 1984-85, 79 in 1985-86 and six in 1986-87.

Across the five-season Boston tenure, he played 271 regular-season games and started 31. His largest late-career role came in 1985-86, when he appeared in 79 games, started 19 and averaged 8.0 points.

Wedman was part of Boston's 1984 and 1986 championship teams. This review does not inflate his individual value because of team success, but contributing rotation minutes to two title teams gives the Celtics a meaningful realized return.

Tillis Gave Cleveland 37 Games

Darren Tillis had played only 15 games for Boston before the trade. He appeared in 37 games for Cleveland during the rest of 1982-83, made four starts and averaged 13.0 minutes, 4.1 points and 3.3 rebounds.

Tillis moved to Golden State the following season. His 72 Warriors games are not credited to Cleveland because they came after his Cavaliers tenure ended.

The First-Round Pick Was Rerouted Before the Draft

Cleveland did not simply exercise the No. 21 pick. On February 7, 1983, the Cavaliers packaged that first-rounder with James Edwards and sent both to Phoenix.

The Cavaliers received Jeff Cook, Phoenix's 1983 first-round pick that became No. 20 Roy Hinson, a 1983 third-round pick that became Derrick Hord and cash. Phoenix later sent the No. 21 pick to Boston in the Dennis Johnson trade, and the Celtics ultimately drafted Greg Kite.

That chain gives Cleveland legitimate downstream asset credit. However, James Edwards was a major co-outgoing piece, so this review does not assign the entire Cook-Hinson-Hord-cash return to the Wedman trade.

Why Boston Wins

Boston received 271 regular-season games and a multi-year championship rotation player. Cleveland received 37 games from Tillis plus cash and a first-round asset that helped facilitate a later multi-asset trade.

The Cavaliers did not get nothing, and the pick's later use keeps their grade above a failure. The direct, attributable basketball value still favors Boston by a wide margin.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A-/C+. Boston receives an A- for five seasons and 271 games from Wedman, including meaningful depth on two championship teams. Cleveland receives a C+ because Tillis was brief, but the cash and first-round pick retained enough transaction value to avoid a poor overall outcome.

perspectives.analysis:
The No. 90 Pick Changed Hands Twice

The January 18, 1983 transaction began when San Antonio signed Coby Dietrick and sent Chicago a 1983 fourth-round pick as compensation for the Bulls' restricted-veteran-free-agent rights.

That pick later landed at No. 90. The important source-backed correction is that Chicago did not simply draft Brant Weidner with it.

Dietrick Played Only Eight Games for San Antonio

Dietrick returned to the Spurs after three seasons in Chicago, but the reunion was extremely short. He appeared in eight regular-season games for San Antonio in 1982-83, made no starts and played only 34 total minutes.

He averaged 4.3 minutes, 0.3 points and 1.0 rebound. San Antonio waived him on February 8, less than a month after the January 18 compensation transaction.

Those eight games were the final appearances of Dietrick's NBA career.

Chicago Reused the Pick for Mike Bratz

On March 8, Chicago sent the same 1983 fourth-round pick back to San Antonio in exchange for guard Mike Bratz.

Pro Sports Transactions explicitly traces the No. 90 asset through both moves: San Antonio first sent the pick to Chicago for the Dietrick rights, then reacquired it from Chicago for Bratz.

Bratz played 15 regular-season games for the Bulls during the rest of 1982-83. He made no starts, averaged 9.3 minutes and 2.6 points, and left for Golden State the following season.

The Spurs Later Drafted Brant Weidner

After reacquiring the pick, San Antonio used No. 90 on William & Mary forward Brant Weidner. Weidner eventually played eight NBA games for the Spurs in 1983-84.

This review does not credit those eight Weidner games to the January 18 Dietrick transaction. San Antonio had to give Chicago Bratz in a separate March 8 trade to get the pick back. Counting Weidner on the original Spurs side would double-count a later asset purchase.

Why Chicago Gets the Slight Edge

The original January 18 deal gave San Antonio eight games from Dietrick. Chicago turned the compensation pick into 15 games from Bratz through the March transaction.

Neither return was substantial, and neither player started a game for the acquiring team. Still, Chicago extracted slightly more direct basketball value from the asset it received.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, C+/C. Chicago receives a C+ because the fourth-round pick was converted into 15 games of Bratz rather than being allowed to expire unused. San Antonio receives a C because Dietrick played only eight games before being waived. The margin is small, and the later Weidner draft outcome belongs to the separate Bratz transaction rather than this one.

summary: Washington signed veteran free agent Ricky Sobers on January 24, 1983 and sent Chicago 1983 and 1985 second-round picks as compensation after the Bulls declined to exercise their right of first refusal. Sobers played 122 regular-season games for the Bullets across two seasons, starting 120 and averaging 15.7 points and 4.9 assists. Chicago used the 1983 No. 25 pick on Sidney Lowe but immediately packaged Lowe with another second-round pick for Mitchell Wiggins, who played 82 games and made 40 starts for the Bulls. The 1985 No. 35 asset was later bundled with Wiggins and another pick for Caldwell Jones. Chicago preserved real transaction value, but Washington received the stronger direct, attributable return.
analysis:
Washington Got Two Starting Seasons From Ricky Sobers

The January 24, 1983 veteran-free-agent transaction is clear across the league and team ledgers. Washington signed Ricky Sobers after Chicago declined its right of first refusal, and the Bullets sent the Bulls second-round picks in 1983 and 1985 as compensation.

Those picks ultimately landed at No. 25 in 1983 and No. 35 in 1985. Their downstream paths are important because Chicago did not simply keep the players eventually selected with both choices.

Sobers Started 120 Games for Washington

Sobers joined Washington midway through 1982-83 and immediately stepped into the starting lineup. He played 41 games that season, started 39 and averaged 15.7 points, 5.3 assists and 1.5 steals in 35.1 minutes.

He returned in 1983-84 and started all 81 games he played. Sobers again averaged 15.6 points, along with 4.7 assists and 1.4 steals.

That gives Washington 122 regular-season games and 120 starts across two seasons, with 1,911 points and 595 assists. He left for Seattle in 1984-85, so later production is not credited to the Bullets.

Chicago Used the First Pick on Sidney Lowe, Then Traded Him

The 1983 compensation pick became No. 25 Sidney Lowe. Chicago drafted Lowe but traded him on draft day with a 1984 second-round pick to Indiana for Mitchell Wiggins.

Wiggins played all 82 games for the Bulls in 1983-84, started 40 and averaged 12.4 points, 4.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists. Those 82 Chicago games are a real downstream return from the Lowe branch.

This review does not assign all of Wiggins to the Sobers compensation pick, however, because Chicago also included a separate 1984 second-round pick in the deal.

The Second Pick Helped Bring Caldwell Jones

Chicago retained the 1985 second-round compensation asset until August 10, 1984. The Bulls then sent Wiggins, that pick and a 1985 third-round pick to Houston for Caldwell Jones.

The No. 35 pick continued through Houston and San Antonio before the Spurs eventually selected Tyrone Corbin. Corbin never played for Chicago, so his later NBA career is not a Bulls return from this transaction.

The pick clearly retained trade utility, but this review again avoids assigning the entire Caldwell Jones return to one asset because Wiggins and another pick were also required.

Why Washington Wins

Chicago did good asset work with both second-rounders. The 1983 pick helped produce a full 82-game season from Wiggins, while the 1985 pick later contributed to another trade package.

Washington still received the stronger cleanly attributable basketball result: 122 games, 120 starts and two seasons of 15-plus-point scoring from Sobers. Chicago's downstream value was meaningful but shared with other outgoing assets at each conversion point.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win, A-/B. Washington receives an A- for two starting seasons and 122 games from Sobers. Chicago receives a B because both compensation picks retained useful transaction value and the Lowe branch helped bring Wiggins, but the Bulls cannot be credited with every later multi-asset return or with Corbin's Spurs career.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey obtained Micheal Ray Richardson from Golden State on February 6, 1983, sending Eric 'Sleepy' Floyd and Mickey (Wallace) Johnson in return. The archived import had used shortened or formal names for the two Warriors acquisitions; those aliases were reconciled with contemporaneous transaction sources. The original record is marked Superseded Duplicate, with inherited Golden State A+ and New Jersey B.
perspectives.analysis:
Golden State Turned Richardson Into Two Players

The Warriors sent guard Micheal Ray Richardson to the New Jersey Nets in February 1983 and obtained Eric Floyd, better known as Sleepy Floyd, plus forward Mickey Johnson. Contemporary news accounts describe the transaction in those terms, while some historical data exports call the second Warriors acquisition Wallace Johnson. Those two Johnson names refer to the same player, not an extra fourth participant. Richardson had played a prominent role as a defensive guard and playmaker, giving the Nets an established talent in exchange for two current roster options.

Sleepy Floyd Became a Major Warriors Contributor

Floyd was still early in his professional career when Golden State acquired him from New Jersey. His later Warriors tenure developed into a significant backcourt contribution, including one of the league's memorable playoff scoring performances in 1987. That later work is relevant because it occurred for the actual receiving club, not because a future draft-rights chain happened to contain his name. Johnson offered another experienced forward option, though his role and duration with Golden State differed from Floyd's. Together they formed a broader return than a one-for-one guard swap.

The Nets Acquired Richardson's Defensive Skills

Richardson arrived in New Jersey with three prior All-Star selections and a reputation for creating turnovers and directing an offense. The Nets were acquiring an active player, not a right to select him in a future draft. The move fit the team's desire for a veteran guard who could contribute immediately. His earlier achievements with New York and Golden State were background for the decision, while the Nets' actual benefit depended on the seasons he subsequently played for the franchise. He wasn't a separate player called Michael rather than Micheal.

One Official Trade, Two Imported Historical Presentations

The imported entry carries the label Superseded Duplicate. Although the original model gives Golden State A+ and New Jersey B, those grades belong to the underlying February 6 deal, not another transaction completed on the same date. The repaired player names make the two-team asset directions easier to recognize and compare with a contemporary newspaper report. Readers should not count a second Richardson departure or an additional Sleepy Floyd acquisition simply because overlapping database rows exist.

Final Verdict

Superseded Duplicate. Golden State's inherited A+ recognizes the acquisition of Eric 'Sleepy' Floyd and Mickey (Wallace) Johnson, while New Jersey receives B for Micheal Ray Richardson. The names and receiving-team directions match contemporary records, but the entry overlaps the same February 1983 exchange in another archive view. It must not create extra trades or phantom player returns.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State traded Micheal Ray Richardson to New Jersey on February 6, 1983 for Sleepy Floyd and Mickey Johnson. Floyd became the centerpiece: he played 374 regular-season games for the Warriors, started 348, made the 1987 All-Star team and helped Golden State reach the 1987 Western Conference semifinals. Johnson added 174 Warriors games and 43 starts across parts of three seasons. Richardson was also productive for New Jersey, playing 208 games with 172 starts and making the 1985 All-Star team before a league suspension ended his NBA career in 1986. The Warriors still received the stronger total return, 548 direct games and 391 starts from two rotation players versus 208 games and 172 starts from Richardson.

Basketball-Reference records the package under the players' familiar basketball names: Sleepy Floyd, whose given name is Eric Floyd, and Mickey Johnson, whose full name is Wallace Edgar Johnson.

A second legacy Nets-origin record describes the same transaction using the legal-name forms Eric Floyd and Wallace Johnson. This review keeps the Golden State record as the active canonical version because its player identities align with the established NBA records, while this review will retain the opposite-source record only as superseded provenance.

Sleepy Floyd Became the Main Prize

Floyd played 33 games for Golden State after the trade in 1982-83 and then became a full-time starter. He appeared in 77 games in 1983-84, 82 in 1984-85, 82 in 1985-86 and 82 again in 1986-87 before adding 18 more games in 1987-88 prior to the Houston trade.

Across that Warriors tenure, Floyd played 374 regular-season games and started 348. He averaged 16.8 points in 1983-84, 19.5 in 1984-85, 17.2 in 1985-86 and 18.8 in his 1987 All-Star season.

His 1986-87 season also helped Golden State reach the Western Conference semifinals. This review does not treat team playoff advancement as solely Floyd's work, but a multi-year starting point guard who became an All-Star clearly represents premium realized value.

Mickey Johnson Added Three Useful Seasons

Johnson joined the Warriors at age 30 but still provided substantial frontcourt production. He played 30 games after the trade in 1982-83, then 78 in 1983-84 and 66 in 1984-85.

That gives Golden State 174 regular-season games and 43 starts from Johnson. He averaged 15.5 points and 8.2 rebounds in his first Warriors stint after the trade, then remained a double-figure scorer in both following seasons.

Johnson later returned to New Jersey, but those later Nets games are not part of Golden State's return.

Richardson Was Productive for New Jersey

New Jersey did not receive an empty return. Richardson played 31 games for the Nets after the trade in 1982-83, then 48 in 1983-84, all 82 in 1984-85 and 47 in 1985-86.

Across those four partial or full seasons, he played 208 regular-season games and started 172. His best Nets season came in 1984-85, when he averaged 20.1 points, 8.2 assists, 5.6 rebounds and 3.0 steals and made the All-Star team.

Richardson's NBA career ended after the league suspended him for substance-abuse violations in 1986. The abrupt ending reduced New Jersey's long-term return, but it should not erase the high-level production he delivered before the suspension.

Why Golden State Wins

The Warriors received both the longer runway of direct games and the deeper two-player package. Floyd became an All-Star starter and Johnson added three seasons of useful frontcourt production.

Combined, Floyd and Johnson produced 548 Golden State regular-season games and 391 starts. Richardson gave New Jersey 208 games and 172 starts, including an All-Star season. That is meaningful value, but the Warriors still finished well ahead in duration, depth and total realized production.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, A+/B. Golden State receives an A+ because Floyd became a long-term All-Star starter and Johnson added 174 useful games. New Jersey receives a B because Richardson produced multiple strong seasons and an All-Star campaign before his suspension, making the Nets' side much better than a failure even though the Warriors clearly won the deal.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland sent James Edwards and the 1983 first-round pick that became Greg Kite to Phoenix on February 7, 1983 for Jeff Cook, a first-round pick that became Roy Hinson, a third-round pick that became Derrick Hord, and cash. Edwards gave Phoenix 224 regular-season games and several productive starting seasons. Cleveland received 129 games from Cook and three strong Hinson seasons, then traded Hinson in 1986 for the No. 1 pick used on Brad Daugherty. That direct production plus the enormous downstream Hinson conversion gives Cleveland the stronger realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Cleveland and Phoenix transaction logs agree on the February 7, 1983 structure. Cleveland sent center James Edwards and a 1983 first-round pick to Phoenix. The Suns sent forward-center Jeff Cook, their 1983 first-round pick, a 1983 third-round pick and cash to Cleveland. The first-round choices landed consecutively: Cleveland's incoming pick became No. 20 Roy Hinson, while Phoenix's incoming pick became No. 21 Greg Kite. The third-rounder became No. 67 Derrick Hord.

Phoenix Return
Edwards was a legitimate return, not a throw-in. He played 16 games for Phoenix immediately after the trade, then became a regular starter. Across the rest of 1982-83 and the next four seasons he appeared in 224 Suns regular-season games and started 186. He scored 1,059 points in 1983-84, 1,044 in 1984-85 and 848 in 1985-86, providing durable interior scoring before his final partial Phoenix season in 1986-87. That is solid multi-year value and keeps Phoenix well above a losing grade. The No. 21 pick also retained transaction value. Phoenix did not draft Greg Kite itself; on June 27, 1983 the Suns sent that pick, Dennis Johnson and the No. 52 third-round pick to Boston for Rick Robey and two second-round choices. That later deal should be judged separately, so this trade receives credit for the first-round asset as a movable chip rather than for Kite's Celtics career.

Cleveland Return
Cook immediately became useful frontcourt depth. He played 30 games with 20 starts for Cleveland after the trade, then 81 games with 21 starts in 1983-84 and another 18 games in 1984-85 before leaving. Hinson became the centerpiece. The No. 20 pick played 80 games with 61 starts as a rookie, then averaged 15.8 points and 7.8 rebounds in 1984-85 and 20.4 points with 8.1 rebounds while starting all 82 games in 1985-86. Across three Cleveland seasons he played 238 games and started 218. Derrick Hord never produced NBA regular-season value, but that miss was minor relative to Hinson and Cook. The decisive downstream development came in June 1986: Cleveland traded Hinson to Philadelphia for the No. 1 pick in the 1986 draft, which became Brad Daugherty. That later conversion was not guaranteed in 1983, but hindsight asset-chain grading cannot ignore that Cleveland turned the most valuable piece acquired here into the first overall selection.

Hindsight Verdict
Phoenix received a good center and a first-round asset, so this is not a case where one side was stripped of value. Edwards gave the Suns multiple productive seasons and meaningful starting minutes. Cleveland nevertheless did better. Cook supplied additional depth, Hinson became a high-scoring full-time starter, and the Cavaliers ultimately converted Hinson into the No. 1 pick. An A+ for Cleveland reflects both the direct player return and the extraordinary downstream preservation of asset value. A B for Phoenix recognizes Edwards' four-plus seasons and the acquired first-round chip without rewarding Phoenix for Greg Kite, whom the Suns never drafted, or importing the separate Dennis Johnson trade's results. Final verdict: Cleveland Cavaliers Win.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Danny Schayes and cash from Utah on February 7, 1983 for Rich Kelley. The source-backed pass corrects the legacy consideration direction: Basketball-Reference's Denver transaction ledger says the Nuggets received Schayes and cash, not an unresolved extra player asset while sending cash to Utah. Schayes played 536 regular-season games for Denver through 1989-90, starting 229 and developing into a multi-year frontcourt fixture. Kelley gave Utah 184 games and 87 starts across parts of three seasons before leaving for Sacramento. Both teams received real value, but Denver got the longer and stronger return.
perspectives.analysis:
The legacy Consideration Direction Needed Repair

The canonical import had Danny Schayes and an unresolved "other considerations" asset going to Denver while showing cash going to Utah. Basketball-Reference's February 7, 1983 Denver transaction ledger records a simpler package: Denver traded Rich Kelley to Utah for Schayes and cash.

This review therefore removes the phantom unresolved-player treatment, converts that consideration to cash moving from Utah to Denver and deletes the duplicate wrong-way cash asset. The public amount is not identified in the reviewed source, so no dollar value is invented.

Schayes Became a Long-Term Nugget

Schayes joined Denver for the final 32 regular-season games of 1982-83 and averaged 9.2 points and 5.8 rebounds in a reserve role. He then remained with the Nuggets through the 1989-90 season.

His role grew substantially. Schayes played all 82 games in 1983-84, then later started 41 games in 1986-87, 74 in 1987-88, 64 in 1988-89 and 22 in 1989-90.

Across his Denver tenure after the trade, he played 536 regular-season games and started 229. His peak Nuggets season came in 1987-88, when he averaged 13.9 points and 8.2 rebounds while starting 74 games.

That is unusually strong realized value from a one-for-one veteran exchange, even before accounting for the cash that also moved to Denver.

Kelley Gave Utah Three Useful Seasons

Rich Kelley was not a throwaway return. He played 32 games for the Jazz after the trade in 1982-83 and started 23, averaging 7.2 points and 7.3 rebounds.

He returned for 75 games and 30 starts in 1983-84, then 77 games and 34 starts in 1984-85. Across those three Utah stints, Kelley played 184 regular-season games and started 87.

Utah later received cash compensation when Sacramento signed Kelley as a veteran free agent in September 1985. This review does not credit that later compensation as part of the original Denver trade because it came from a separate free-agent transaction more than two years later.

Why Denver Wins

Utah received a legitimate starting center for parts of three seasons. Kelley supplied 184 games and 87 starts, so this was not a failed return.

Denver nevertheless received nearly three times as many direct regular-season games from Schayes, more than twice as many starts and seven-plus seasons of frontcourt continuity. The Nuggets also received cash in the original transaction.

The gap is large enough for a clear Denver win without downgrading Utah to a poor grade.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A+/B. Denver receives an A+ for 536 games, 229 starts and multiple years of starting-caliber production from Schayes, plus cash. Utah receives a B because Kelley gave the Jazz 184 games and 87 starts before moving on. Both sides got useful centers, but Denver captured the much larger long-term return.

perspectives.summary: San Antonio acquired Edgar Jones from Detroit on February 10, 1983 for a 1984 second-round pick and a 1985 third-round pick. Jones played 127 regular-season games for the Spurs across parts of three seasons, started 37 and averaged 10.2 points and 5.5 rebounds in 1983-84. Detroit used the No. 32 pick in 1984 on Eric Turner and the No. 60 pick in 1985 on Andre Goode. Neither draft choice appeared in an NBA regular-season game. San Antonio therefore received all of the direct NBA production while Detroit's two selections yielded zero games, reversing the legacy Pistons-leaning verdict.
perspectives.analysis:
San Antonio Got the Only NBA Production

The February 10, 1983 transaction sent Edgar Jones from Detroit to San Antonio for two future draft choices: a 1984 second-round pick and a 1985 third-round pick.

Both selections eventually stayed with Detroit long enough to be exercised, which makes the completed return straightforward to evaluate.

Jones Helped San Antonio Immediately

Jones played 28 regular-season games for the Spurs after the trade in 1982-83 and started three. He averaged 9.6 points, 6.3 rebounds and 1.1 blocks in 22.2 minutes.

San Antonio went 53-29 that season and reached the Western Conference Finals. Jones was a rotation frontcourt piece after arriving rather than a deep-bench acquisition.

He then played 81 games in 1983-84, started 33 and averaged 10.2 points and 5.5 rebounds. Jones added 18 more Spurs games in 1984-85 before moving to Cleveland.

Across his San Antonio tenure, Jones appeared in 127 regular-season games and made 37 starts.

Detroit's 1984 Pick Became Eric Turner

The 1984 second-round selection landed at No. 32. Detroit used it on Michigan guard Eric Turner.

Turner has a Basketball-Reference draft/player record but no NBA regular-season statistical line. The pick therefore produced zero Pistons regular-season games.

That outcome is especially important because the legacy Detroit-side review had treated the pick itself as the lead realized return. This review evaluates what the selection actually became.

The 1985 Pick Became Andre Goode

Detroit's third-round choice in 1985 landed at No. 60 and became Northwestern forward Andre Goode.

Like Turner, Goode has a draft/player record but no NBA regular-season statistical line. The second draft branch also produced zero direct Pistons games.

Detroit therefore converted two future selections into two players who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

Why San Antonio Wins Clearly

The Spurs received a player who contributed immediately, returned for a full 81-game season and gave the club 127 total regular-season appearances with 37 starts.

Detroit's two picks carried transaction-day optionality, but hindsight grading cannot stop at the abstract value of the selections. Once both were exercised, the completed outcomes were zero NBA games from Turner and zero from Goode.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win, B+/F. San Antonio receives a B+ for 127 games and 37 starts from Jones, including a productive full season in 1983-84. Detroit receives an F because both acquired draft picks were exercised on players who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
New York Acquired the Higher-Impact Player

The February 12, 1983 trade sent Rory Sparrow from Atlanta to New York for rookie forward Scott Hastings and cash. The legacy source perspectives disagreed on whether the result was a Knicks win or broadly even, so this review resolves the question through direct realized franchise value.

The cash amount sent to Atlanta is not identified in the reviewed public sources. It remains part of the Hawks' return, but no speculative dollar value is assigned.

Sparrow Became a Long-Term Knicks Guard

Sparrow played 32 regular-season games for New York after the trade in 1982-83 and started nine. He averaged 10.0 points and 5.0 assists in 28.2 minutes while immediately entering the backcourt rotation.

His role expanded sharply in 1983-84. Sparrow appeared in 79 games, started 74 and averaged 10.4 points and 6.8 assists.

He followed with 79 games and 41 starts in 1984-85, 74 games and 74 starts in 1985-86, and 80 games with 30 starts in 1986-87. He then played three more Knicks games in 1987-88 before being traded to Chicago.

Across his New York tenure, Sparrow appeared in 347 regular-season games and started 228. He was never an All-Star, but several seasons of starting or heavy-rotation point-guard work make him a substantial return.

Hastings Gave Atlanta Long-Term Bench Depth

Scott Hastings had played only 19 games for New York before the trade. In Atlanta he appeared in 10 games for the remainder of 1982-83, then 68 in 1983-84, 64 in 1984-85, 62 in 1985-86, 40 in 1986-87 and 55 in 1987-88.

That gives Hastings 299 regular-season games for the Hawks across parts of six seasons. His durability is meaningful, especially because the transaction also brought Atlanta cash.

The limitation is role. Hastings made only nine starts during that Atlanta tenure and generally played reserve minutes. His best Hawks scoring season was still a modest bench contribution compared with Sparrow's multi-year starting workload in New York.

Why New York Wins

The raw games-played gap is not large: 347 for Sparrow versus 299 for Hastings. Role and usage create the larger difference.

Sparrow started 228 games for the Knicks and repeatedly averaged five or more assists while handling major point-guard minutes. Hastings started only nine times for Atlanta and served mainly as frontcourt depth.

The cash component keeps Atlanta's return from being graded harshly, but the amount is unknown and does not erase the clear on-court role advantage New York received.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A-/B. New York receives an A- for more than four seasons of meaningful point-guard play, 347 games and 228 starts from Sparrow. Atlanta receives a B because Hastings supplied 299 games of durable bench depth and the Hawks also received cash. This was a useful deal for both teams, but the Knicks acquired the more consequential basketball asset.

perspectives.summary: In the February 1983 three-team trade, Atlanta sent Steve Hawes to Seattle and received Detroit's 1984 and 1985 second-round picks; Detroit sent those picks to Atlanta and received Ray Tolbert from Seattle; Seattle sent Tolbert to Detroit and received Hawes. Basketball-Reference dates the transaction February 13 while RealGM lists February 12, so this review retains the canonical February 12 date with medium confidence. Hawes gave Seattle 110 games and one start. Tolbert gave Detroit 77 games and no starts. Atlanta's 1985 pick became Lorenzo Charles, who played 36 Hawks games, while the 1984 pick was later packaged with Tom McMillen to acquire Randy Wittman, a multi-year Atlanta starter. That downstream leverage gives the Hawks the best overall return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Three-Team Routing Is Clear Even Though the Date Differs by One Day

Basketball-Reference records the completed transaction on February 13, 1983, while RealGM's league and team histories place it on February 12. The canonical TradeVerdicts record already uses February 12, so this review retains that date and records the one-day disagreement rather than forcing false precision.

The routing itself is consistent across the sources. Atlanta sent Steve Hawes to Seattle and received Detroit's 1984 and 1985 second-round picks. Detroit sent those two picks to Atlanta and received Ray Tolbert from Seattle. Seattle sent Tolbert to Detroit and received Hawes from Atlanta.

Seattle Got Two Useful Years From Steve Hawes

Hawes played 31 regular-season games for Seattle after the trade in 1982-83 and started one. He averaged 5.5 points and 4.3 rebounds in 17.9 minutes.

He returned for 79 games in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 3.7 points and 2.8 rebounds. That gives Seattle 110 regular-season games and one start from the deal.

Hawes was nearing the end of his NBA career, but the SuperSonics still received two seasons of dependable reserve frontcourt minutes.

Detroit Got 77 Reserve Games From Ray Tolbert

Tolbert appeared in 28 regular-season games for Detroit after the trade and averaged 5.1 points and 3.3 rebounds. He then played 49 more games in 1983-84.

Across those two Pistons seasons he appeared in 77 games and made no starts. His role stayed modest, and he left the NBA for several seasons after 1983-84.

Detroit therefore received a real rotation return, but not a long-term starter or premium contributor.

Atlanta's 1985 Pick Became Lorenzo Charles

The 1985 second-round choice landed at No. 41, where Atlanta selected North Carolina State forward Lorenzo Charles.

Charles played 36 regular-season games for the Hawks in 1985-86 and made no starts. He averaged 3.4 points in 7.6 minutes and did not play another NBA season.

That branch alone would not make Atlanta the winner.

The 1984 Pick Became a Valuable Trade Asset

Atlanta did not exercise the other incoming pick itself. On July 5, 1983, the Hawks packaged Tom McMillen and the 1984 second-rounder to Washington for Randy Wittman.

Washington eventually used the pick at No. 34 on Tony Costner, who never played an NBA regular-season game. Atlanta's value came earlier, when the pick helped complete the Wittman trade.

Wittman then became a major Hawks rotation piece and eventual starter. He played 353 Atlanta regular-season games from 1983-84 through 1987-88 alone, including 226 starts over the final four of those seasons.

This review does not credit all of Wittman's Atlanta career to this one second-round pick because Tom McMillen was the other outgoing asset in that later transaction. The correct takeaway is narrower: the acquired pick retained enough value to help Atlanta secure a long-term starter.

Why Atlanta Has the Best Outcome

Seattle received 110 games of reserve Hawes production. Detroit received 77 reserve games from Tolbert. Both returns were useful and defensible.

Atlanta received only 36 direct games from Charles, but the other pick became part of the package that acquired Wittman, whose Atlanta tenure far exceeded the direct value produced by Hawes or Tolbert for their new teams. That downstream transaction utility is enough to preserve the Hawks as the hindsight winner without pretending the pick alone purchased Wittman.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, A-/B/B-. Atlanta receives an A- because one pick produced an NBA player and the other materially helped acquire a multi-year starter. Seattle receives a B for 110 useful reserve games from Hawes. Detroit receives a B- for 77 reserve games from Tolbert after surrendering two second-round choices. Confidence is medium only because authoritative sources disagree by one day on the transaction date.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Both Teams Received Useful but Modest Value

The February 15, 1983 trade sent Rickey Brown from Golden State to Atlanta for a 1984 second-round pick and cash. The pick later landed at No. 35, where the Warriors selected Virginia guard Othell Wilson.

The legacy team perspectives leaned in opposite directions. Atlanta's source called the exchange a slight partner edge, while Golden State's source called it a slight Warriors edge. The completed player outcomes explain why neither side has a decisive advantage.

Brown Gave Atlanta Three Seasons of Frontcourt Depth

Brown played 26 regular-season games for Atlanta after the trade in 1982-83 and made no starts. He averaged 4.7 points and 3.4 rebounds in 11.7 minutes.

He returned for 68 games in 1983-84, starting three, then appeared in 69 games with five starts in 1984-85.

Across his Hawks tenure, Brown played 163 regular-season games and started eight. He was primarily a reserve center, but three seasons of usable depth is a meaningful return from one second-round pick plus cash.

Wilson Had a Larger Starting Role in His One Warriors Season

Golden State used the No. 35 pick on Othell Wilson in the 1984 NBA Draft.

Wilson appeared in 74 regular-season games for the Warriors in 1984-85 and started 23. He averaged 17.0 minutes, 4.4 points, 2.9 assists and 1.0 steal.

He did not play in the NBA in 1985-86 and later returned with Sacramento in 1986-87. This review credits Golden State only with the 74 games and 23 starts produced for the Warriors.

The Cash Amount Is Unknown

Golden State also received cash in the original transaction. The reviewed public sources do not identify the amount, so the cash is treated as a tangible but unquantified part of the Warriors' return.

That component prevents the games-played comparison from being the entire verdict, but it also cannot justify a large Golden State advantage without a documented figure.

Why the Deal Grades Even

Atlanta received more than twice as many direct regular-season games from Brown, but almost all came in a reserve role. Golden State received fewer games from Wilson but substantially more starts and an additional cash component.

Neither player became a long-term starter or major franchise piece. Brown's duration and Wilson's larger one-season role offset each other closely enough that forcing a winner would overstate a small difference.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B/B. Atlanta receives a B for 163 games of multi-year frontcourt depth. Golden State receives a B for 74 games, 23 starts and cash. The teams extracted different kinds of value from a minor transaction, but neither completed return clearly dominates the other.

perspectives.analysis:
The Primary Ledger Does Not Confirm the Cash Component

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Los Angeles and league transaction ledgers agree on the February 15, 1983 core terms: Chicago sent Dwight Jones to the Lakers for a 1985 second-round pick that later became No. 46 Adrian Branch.

The legacy canonical record also includes cash moving to Chicago. That extra financial component is not listed in the Basketball-Reference transaction ledgers reviewed for this review, and RealGM confirms Jones's acquisition without exposing a cash amount. This review therefore preserves the canonical cash asset as unresolved rather than deleting it, while lowering confidence to medium on the full package.

Jones Gave Los Angeles Immediate Frontcourt Depth

Dwight Jones played 32 regular-season games for the Lakers after the trade and made no starts. He averaged 15.3 minutes, 4.9 points and 3.6 rebounds while shooting 47.0 percent from the field.

The Lakers finished 58-24, won the Pacific Division and reached the NBA Finals. Jones also appeared in seven playoff games, totaling 59 postseason minutes.

Los Angeles waived him in August 1983, so the value was short-term. Even so, the Lakers received a real rotation contribution during a conference-championship season.

The Pick Became Adrian Branch

Chicago held the incoming second-rounder until the 1985 draft and used No. 46 on Maryland forward Adrian Branch.

Branch never appeared in a Bulls regular-season game. Chicago waived him on October 7, 1985 before the season, and his NBA debut came later with another franchise.

That means the draft branch produced zero direct Chicago games despite eventually identifying an NBA player.

The Realized Basketball Value Favors Los Angeles

Chicago's pick outcome did not become on-court Bulls value. The unresolved cash component gives the Bulls some possible financial return, but the reviewed primary ledgers do not establish the amount.

Los Angeles received 32 regular-season appearances plus seven playoff games from Jones. The return was limited, but it is still more direct basketball value than Chicago realized from Branch.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, B-/D+. Los Angeles receives a B- because Jones supplied useful reserve minutes during a Finals season before being waived that summer. Chicago receives a D+ because the No. 46 pick produced zero Bulls games; the grade stays above a failing mark because the canonical record also contains an unresolved cash component. Confidence is medium because the public primary ledgers do not confirm that cash term.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana acquired Russ Schoene, Philadelphia's 1983 first-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick on February 15, 1983 for Clemon Johnson and a 1984 third-round pick. Schoene played 31 Pacers games before a back injury and overseas stint. The first-round pick became No. 23 Mitchell Wiggins, whose rights Indiana immediately traded for Sidney Lowe and another second-round pick; Lowe played 78 Pacers games, while that pick was later used to acquire Granville Waiters, who played 140 for Indiana. indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Received Three Separate Value Paths

Basketball-Reference's Indiana, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers agree on the February 15, 1983 package. Indiana received Russ Schoene, Philadelphia's 1983 first-round pick and a 1984 second-round pick. Philadelphia received Clemon Johnson and Indiana's 1984 third-round pick.

The trade was not decided by Schoene alone. Both draft picks created meaningful downstream branches for Indiana, while Philadelphia's third-round pick did not become an NBA player.

Schoene Gave Indiana 31 Games

Russ Schoene played 31 regular-season games for the Pacers after the trade and started five. He logged 520 minutes and scored 243 points.

He missed 1983-84 with a back injury, then played professionally in Italy before returning to the NBA with Seattle. This review therefore credits Indiana only with those 31 Pacers appearances.

The Mitchell Wiggins Pick Became Sidney Lowe and Another Asset

Indiana used the 1983 first-round pick at No. 23 on Mitchell Wiggins, but Wiggins never played for the Pacers. Indiana traded his rights to Chicago on draft day for Sidney Lowe and a 1984 second-round pick.

Lowe played 78 regular-season games for Indiana in 1983-84, including two starts, and averaged 3.4 assists in 15.9 minutes.

Indiana later used the second-round asset from that Wiggins exchange to acquire Granville Waiters from Portland. Waiters played 140 regular-season games for the Pacers across 1983-84 and 1984-85.

This review credits Lowe and Waiters as downstream realized value from the Wiggins branch because both came directly from Indiana rerouting the acquired first-round asset.

Stuart Gray Became the Longest Indiana Return

Philadelphia's 1984 second-round pick landed at No. 29, where Indiana selected UCLA center Stuart Gray.

Gray stayed with the Pacers for five seasons. He played 52 games in 1984-85, 67 in 1985-86, 55 in 1986-87, 74 in 1987-88 and 72 in 1988-89.

That is 320 regular-season games for Indiana, with four starts. The minutes were modest, but five seasons of reserve-center availability from a second-round pick are real franchise value.

Philadelphia Got Four Useful Seasons from Clemon Johnson

Clemon Johnson was not an empty return. After the trade he played 32 regular-season games for Philadelphia in 1982-83, then 80 in 1983-84, 58 in 1984-85 and 75 in 1985-86.

That gives the 76ers 245 regular-season games from Johnson across parts of four seasons, including 16 starts. He was a useful reserve on the 1983 championship team and remained in the rotation afterward.

The Third-Round Pick Produced No NBA Games

Philadelphia used Indiana's 1984 third-round pick at No. 48 on James Banks. Banks never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

That leaves Johnson as the entire realized on-court return on Philadelphia's side.

Why Indiana Gets the Edge

Philadelphia received a useful veteran reserve for several seasons, so this is not a one-sided trade. Johnson's 245 games and championship-season depth deserve real credit.

Indiana, however, accumulated value from every major incoming branch. Schoene supplied 31 games, the Wiggins branch became Lowe and Waiters, and Gray alone played 320 Pacers games over five seasons.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, B+/B-. Indiana receives a B+ for turning the package into several seasons of usable depth across multiple players, especially Gray's five-year run. Philadelphia receives a B- because Johnson provided 245 useful games, but the third-round pick produced no NBA player and the aggregate return did not match Indiana's broader asset tree. Confidence is medium because the grade depends partly on correctly tracing the Wiggins pick through two later transactions rather than only comparing the first set of names.

perspectives.analysis:
Kansas City Sold Johnson's Rights for Cash

Basketball-Reference's Kansas City, Philadelphia and league transaction ledgers describe the February 15, 1983 move as a sale of Reggie Johnson's player rights to the 76ers.

The canonical record correctly records cash going to Kansas City. None of the reviewed public ledgers identifies the dollar amount, so this review does not assign a speculative financial value to the Kings' return.

Johnson Joined a Championship Team

Johnson had played 50 games for Kansas City earlier in 1982-83. After the rights sale, he appeared in 29 regular-season games for Philadelphia and started eight.

He averaged 18.9 minutes, 5.5 points and 3.1 rebounds while providing another frontcourt option behind the 76ers' established stars.

Philadelphia finished 65-17 and swept through the 1983 NBA Finals. Johnson also appeared in six playoff games during that championship run.

The 76ers Preserved Downstream Value

Johnson did not stay in Philadelphia beyond that season. On October 25, 1983, the 76ers traded him to New Jersey for Horace Owens, Eddie Phillips and a 1987 second-round pick that later became Andrew Kennedy.

This review does not assign the entire later value of those assets to the original cash purchase without qualification, but the transaction matters because it shows Philadelphia retained trade utility after receiving 29 regular-season games and championship-season depth from Johnson.

Kansas City's Return Cannot Be Fully Quantified

The Kings received cash rather than a player or draft pick. Selling a player who was leaving the roster created real economic value and should not be treated as zero.

The problem is evidentiary: the reviewed sources do not state the amount. Without a documented large payment, there is no basis to claim the cash outweighed the basketball value Philadelphia received.

Why Philadelphia Gets the Edge

The 76ers obtained 29 regular-season games, eight starts and six playoff appearances from Johnson during a championship season. They then converted him into another multi-asset package before the following season.

Kansas City received an unquantified cash return. That is tangible value, but the known realized outcome is stronger on Philadelphia's side.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, B/C. Philadelphia receives a B because Johnson supplied useful championship-season depth and still carried trade value afterward. Kansas City receives a C because selling the rights produced cash, but the amount is unknown and no additional basketball asset entered the franchise through the documented transaction. Confidence is medium because the cash figure is unresolved.

Johnson did not stay in Philadelphia beyond that season. On October 25, 1983, the 76ers traded him to New Jersey for Horace Owens, Eddie Phillips and a 1987 second-round pick that later became Andrew Kennedy.

This review does not assign the entire later value of those assets to the original cash purchase without qualification, but the transaction matters because it shows Philadelphia retained trade utility after receiving 29 regular-season games and championship-season depth from Johnson.

Kansas City's Return Cannot Be Fully Quantified

The Kings received cash rather than a player or draft pick. Selling a player who was leaving the roster created real economic value and should not be treated as zero.

The problem is evidentiary: the reviewed sources do not state the amount. Without a documented large payment, there is no basis to claim the cash outweighed the basketball value Philadelphia received.

Why Philadelphia Gets the Edge

The 76ers obtained 29 regular-season games, eight starts and six playoff appearances from Johnson during a championship season. They then converted him into another multi-asset package before the following season.

Kansas City received an unquantified cash return. That is tangible value, but the known realized outcome is stronger on Philadelphia's side.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, B/C. Philadelphia receives a B because Johnson supplied useful championship-season depth and still carried trade value afterward. Kansas City receives a C because selling the rights produced cash, but the amount is unknown and no additional basketball asset entered the franchise through the documented transaction. Confidence is medium because the cash figure is unresolved.

Chicago Received a Short Bratz Stint

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, San Antonio and league transaction ledgers agree on the March 8, 1983 terms. The Bulls acquired the rights to restricted free agent Mike Bratz and sent the Spurs a 1983 fourth-round pick.

That selection eventually became No. 90 Brant Weidner.

Bratz Played 15 Bulls Games

Bratz appeared in 15 regular-season games for Chicago to finish the 1982-83 season. He made no starts and averaged 9.3 minutes, 2.6 points and 1.5 assists.

That is a limited return, but it was still immediate NBA rotation value from a fourth-round pick.

Bratz did not remain with Chicago. He signed with Golden State on September 30, 1983 and went on to play all 82 games for the Warriors the following season.

His Later Departure Generated Another Pick

Because Bratz signed with Golden State as a veteran free agent, Chicago received a 1984 fourth-round compensation pick.

The Bulls used that selection at No. 77 on Northeastern forward Mark Halsel. Halsel never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

This review therefore gives Chicago credit for the extra transaction asset created by Bratz's departure, but not for any on-court value from Halsel.

San Antonio's Pick Became Brant Weidner

The Spurs used the original 1983 fourth-round pick at No. 90 on William & Mary forward Brant Weidner.

Weidner appeared in eight regular-season games for San Antonio in 1983-84, made no starts and averaged 4.8 minutes, 1.0 point and 1.4 rebounds.

Those eight games were the entirety of his NBA career.

Why Chicago Has a Small Edge

Neither side found a long-term player. San Antonio received eight games from Weidner, while Chicago received 15 from Bratz and later generated a fourth-round compensation pick when Bratz left.

The compensation pick ultimately produced zero NBA games, so the edge should stay modest. Still, Chicago extracted more total transaction utility from the original fourth-round asset.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, C+/C. Chicago receives a C+ for 15 Bratz games plus a later compensation pick. San Antonio receives a C because Weidner reached the NBA but played only eight games and never started. This is a narrow realized-value win, not a franchise-changing transaction.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey traded Len Elmore to New York on June 22, 1983 for the Knicks' 1984 second-round pick, later No. 41 Tom Sluby. Elmore played 65 regular-season games for the Knicks in 1983-84, started five and appeared in New York's playoff run. The Nets never used the pick themselves: on August 12, 1983 they packaged it with Foots Walker and their 1985 first-round pick for Kelvin Ransey. Ransey became a productive three-year Nets guard, but because the Sluby pick was only one of three outgoing assets this review does not assign his entire New Jersey value to this trade. The Knicks received the clearer standalone return, so New York gets a modest edge.
perspectives.analysis:
New York Received a One-Season Veteran

Basketball-Reference's New York, New Jersey and league transaction records agree on the June 22, 1983 exchange. The Knicks sent their 1984 second-round pick to the Nets and received Len Elmore.

The pick eventually landed at No. 41, but New Jersey did not keep it through the draft.

Elmore Played 65 Games for the Knicks

Elmore appeared in 65 regular-season games for New York in 1983-84 and started five. He averaged 12.8 minutes, 2.4 points and 2.5 rebounds while providing veteran frontcourt depth.

The Knicks finished 47-35, won a first-round playoff series against Detroit and pushed Boston to seven games in the Eastern Conference semifinals.

Elmore's New York tenure lasted only that season. The contribution was limited in scale but direct and easy to measure.

New Jersey Rerouted the Pick Before the Draft

On August 12, 1983, the Nets traded Foots Walker, the acquired 1984 second-round pick and their 1985 first-round pick to Dallas for Kelvin Ransey.

The No. 41 selection ultimately stayed with Dallas, which used it on Tom Sluby. Sluby never played for New Jersey.

That means the Nets' value from the Elmore trade came through the pick's role inside the Ransey package rather than from the player selected at No. 41.

Ransey Was Valuable, but the Pick Was Only One Piece

Ransey played 80 games for New Jersey in 1983-84, 81 in 1984-85 and 79 in 1985-86. He started 94 games across those three seasons and averaged 9.5 points and 6.0 assists in his first Nets year.

This review does not assign all of that production to the Elmore trade. New Jersey also surrendered Foots Walker and a 1985 first-round pick that became Bill Wennington, so those assets were essential to acquiring Ransey.

The proper credit is narrower: the Knicks second-rounder retained enough value to serve as one component of a larger trade for a useful starting guard.

Why New York Gets the Edge

New York received a complete, if modest, season from Elmore. New Jersey received an asset with real trade utility but no direct games, and its downstream value cannot be isolated from the two other pieces in the Ransey package.

That makes the Knicks' return more concrete without making the Nets' side a failure.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, B-/C+. New York receives a B- for 65 regular-season games and usable playoff-season depth from Elmore. New Jersey receives a C+ because the pick became a meaningful component of the Kelvin Ransey trade, but the Nets never used it directly and cannot be credited with Ransey's entire three-year tenure from this one asset alone. Confidence is high on the transaction chain and moderate in the value split, so the overall confidence remains medium.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Acquired a Championship-Era Core Piece

Basketball-Reference's Phoenix transaction ledger records the June 27, 1983 package: Dennis Johnson, the No. 21 pick that became Greg Kite and the No. 52 pick that became Winfred King went to Boston. Phoenix received Rick Robey plus the No. 28 and No. 45 picks, later Rod Foster and Paul Williams.

The trade is remembered for Johnson, and the direct franchise results justify that emphasis.

Johnson Played Seven Seasons and 541 Games for Boston

Dennis Johnson played 541 regular-season games for the Celtics from 1983-84 through 1989-90 and started 522. He averaged 13.4 points and 6.8 assists across those seven seasons while giving Boston a durable two-way guard next to Larry Bird, Kevin McHale and Robert Parish.

His first Celtics season ended with the 1984 NBA championship. Johnson remained a starter when Boston won again in 1986 and was part of four All-Defensive selections as a Celtic: three Second Team honors followed by a First Team selection in 1986-87.

The value was not a short peak. Johnson stayed in Boston through 1990 and started at least 65 games in every Celtics season.

Greg Kite Added Five Years of Reserve-Center Depth

Boston also used the No. 21 pick on Greg Kite. He played 241 regular-season games for the Celtics across five seasons, made eight starts and supplied backup-center minutes on both the 1984 and 1986 championship teams.

Kite was not a major offensive contributor, but 241 games from the first-round pick add real depth value on top of the Johnson return.

The third-round pick became Winfred King, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. That branch produced no direct value.

Phoenix Got Useful Players, but No Comparable Centerpiece

Rick Robey played 111 regular-season games for Phoenix across three seasons and made five starts. His first Suns season produced 61 games and 4 starts before injuries and a smaller role reduced his availability.

Rod Foster was the stronger Phoenix draft outcome. The No. 28 pick played 207 regular-season games for the Suns across three seasons, started 35 and averaged 7.5 points and 2.3 assists.

Paul Williams, selected at No. 45, never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Phoenix therefore received 318 direct regular-season games and 40 starts from Robey and Foster combined.

The Scale of Impact Decides It

Phoenix did not come away empty. Foster became a legitimate rotation guard, and Robey supplied three seasons of center depth.

Boston still gained far more. Johnson alone gave the Celtics 541 games, 522 starts, elite perimeter defense and a starting role on two championship teams. Kite added another 241 games and two championship rosters.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, A+/C. Boston receives an A+ because Johnson became a seven-year championship-era starter and Kite added five seasons of reserve depth. Phoenix receives a C because Robey and Foster combined for 318 games and 40 starts, but the return never approached the long-term or championship value Boston received.

perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Bought Three Seasons of Lonnie Shelton

Basketball-Reference's Seattle and league transaction ledgers record the June 27, 1983 exchange as Lonnie Shelton to Cleveland for a 1983 second-round pick. Seattle used the pick at No. 36 on Scooter McCray.

Contemporary reporting adds the financial component. The Christian Science Monitor described Seattle as receiving cash and the second-round choice, UPI later called the cash amount large, and Pro Sports Transactions lists it as believed to be about $500,000.

Shelton Immediately Became a Cleveland Starter

Shelton played 79 regular-season games for Cleveland in 1983-84 and started 78. He averaged 26.6 minutes, 10.8 points and 4.8 rebounds while finishing 12th in Defensive Player of the Year voting.

He returned for 57 games in 1984-85, starting 14, then played 44 more games in 1985-86.

Across three Cavaliers seasons, Shelton appeared in 180 regular-season games and made 93 starts. His role declined after the first year, but Cleveland still received multiple seasons of real frontcourt production.

Seattle's Pick Became Scooter McCray

The SuperSonics selected Louisville forward Scooter McCray with the No. 36 pick in the 1983 draft.

McCray played 47 games for Seattle as a rookie, started six and averaged 11.1 minutes. He appeared in only six more Seattle games in 1984-85 before his role disappeared.

That gives Seattle 53 direct regular-season games and six starts from the draft branch.

The Cash Component Matters

Seattle did not trade Shelton for the pick alone. The cash payment was described contemporaneously as substantial, and the commonly cited estimate is roughly $500,000.

This review treats that as real return rather than ignoring it. At the same time, the exact amount is not established by the primary statistical ledgers, so the financial component should not be converted into speculative basketball value.

Why Cleveland Wins

Cleveland received 180 games and 93 starts from Shelton, including a near-full first season as a starter. Seattle received 53 low-minute games and six starts from McCray plus cash.

The financial return narrows the gap, but it does not erase the difference in realized on-court production.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, B+/B-. Cleveland receives a B+ for three seasons and 93 starts from Shelton at the cost of a second-round pick and cash. Seattle receives a B- because McCray provided limited NBA production, but the substantial cash component prevents the return from being treated as a poor outcome. Confidence is medium because the cash amount is reported as an estimate rather than an exact disclosed figure.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired the draft rights to Ennis Whatley and Chris McNealy plus a 1984 second-round pick that became No. 37 Ben Coleman from Kansas City for Mark Olberding and the rights to Larry Micheaux. Whatley gave the Bulls 150 regular-season games and 117 starts over two seasons, including 8.3 assists per game as a rookie. Coleman and Whatley later retained trade utility in separate multi-asset deals, but McNealy never played for Chicago. Olberding became a three-year Kings starter, playing 243 games with 207 starts across Kansas City and Sacramento, while Micheaux added 39 games. Direct realized value therefore favors the Kings, though Chicago's downstream asset utility keeps the deal competitive.
perspectives.analysis:
The legacy Perspectives Disagree

Chicago's legacy review called this a clear Bulls win, while the Kansas City perspective gave the Kings a slight edge. The completed player records support the Kings side more strongly once direct franchise value is counted carefully.

Basketball-Reference's Kansas City transaction ledger confirms the June 28, 1983 package: the Kings sent the rights to Ennis Whatley and Chris McNealy plus a 1984 second-round pick to Chicago for Mark Olberding and the rights to Larry Micheaux.

Whatley Was a Real Starting Point Guard for Chicago

Whatley played 80 games for the Bulls as a rookie in 1983-84 and started 73. He averaged 8.4 points and 8.3 assists in 27.0 minutes, giving Chicago a substantial immediate return from the No. 13 draft rights.

He returned for 70 games and 44 starts in 1984-85, averaging 5.0 points and 5.4 assists. Across two Bulls seasons, Whatley totaled 150 regular-season games and 117 starts.

Chicago later packaged Whatley with 1985 first-round pick Keith Lee in the trade that brought Charles Oakley and Calvin Duncan from Cleveland. This review records that downstream utility but does not credit the entire Oakley return to Whatley because Keith Lee was a major part of the package.

The Other Chicago Assets Produced Little Direct Value

Chris McNealy played professionally in Italy before later reaching the NBA with New York. He never appeared in a regular-season game for Chicago.

The 1984 second-round pick became No. 37 Ben Coleman. Coleman also did not play for the Bulls; he spent two seasons in Italy before entering the NBA with New Jersey.

Chicago later packaged Coleman's rights with Ken Johnson for Mike Smrek. Smrek played 38 Bulls games with five starts. Because Coleman was only one piece of that later transaction, this review treats the branch as retained trade utility rather than assigning all of Smrek's value to this deal.

Olberding Became a Three-Year Kings Starter

Mark Olberding immediately moved into the Kansas City starting lineup. He played 81 games and started all 81 in 1983-84, averaging 12.6 points, 7.4 rebounds and 3.2 assists.

He followed with 81 games and 62 starts in 1984-85, then stayed with the franchise through its move to Sacramento and played another 81 games with 64 starts in 1985-86.

That gives the Kings franchise 243 regular-season games and 207 starts from Olberding alone.

Micheaux Added Another 39 Games

Larry Micheaux played 39 regular-season games for Kansas City in 1983-84, all off the bench, averaging 8.5 minutes. He later played for other teams, so only those 39 games count toward this trade.

Together, Olberding and Micheaux produced 282 direct Kings regular-season games and 207 starts.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A-/B+. Chicago received a useful young point guard and preserved some downstream asset value, so this was not a bad trade for the Bulls. Kansas City still received the stronger completed on-court package: three full seasons of Olberding as a starter plus Micheaux's reserve season. The direct-value gap outweighs Chicago's partial downstream trade branches.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Mitchell Wiggins' draft rights from Indiana on June 28, 1983 for Sidney Lowe's rights and a 1984 second-round pick. Wiggins played all 82 games for the Bulls as a rookie, started 40 and averaged 12.4 points before Chicago included him with two draft picks in the 1984 trade for Caldwell Jones. Lowe played 78 games for Indiana with two starts and 3.4 assists per game. The Pacers then traded the incoming second-round pick by itself for Granville Waiters, who added 140 Indiana games and 13 starts over two seasons. Chicago received the better one-season player peak, while Indiana turned both assets into 218 combined direct/downstream games. The completed value remains broadly even.
perspectives.analysis:
The Original Even Verdict Holds Up

Basketball-Reference's Chicago, Indiana and league transaction ledgers agree on the June 28, 1983 exchange. Chicago received the rights to No. 23 pick Mitchell Wiggins. Indiana received the rights to No. 25 pick Sidney Lowe plus Chicago's 1984 second-round pick.

The two sides created value in different ways, which is why a decisive winner would overstate the result.

Wiggins Gave Chicago a Strong Rookie Season

Wiggins played all 82 regular-season games for the Bulls in 1983-84 and started 40. He averaged 25.9 minutes, 12.4 points, 4.0 rebounds and 2.3 assists.

That is the best single-season player performance directly produced by the trade. Chicago received a legitimate rotation scorer immediately rather than waiting on the future pick.

Wiggins did not stay beyond that season. In August 1984, Chicago packaged him with a 1985 second-round pick and a 1985 third-round pick for Caldwell Jones from Houston. This review records that downstream utility but does not assign the full Jones return to Wiggins because two additional picks were required.

Lowe Played 78 Games for Indiana

Sidney Lowe appeared in 78 regular-season games for the Pacers as a rookie and made two starts. He averaged 15.9 minutes, 4.2 points and 3.4 assists.

His Indiana tenure was shorter than Wiggins' Chicago season in impact, but Lowe still supplied a full year of reserve point-guard minutes.

The Future Pick Became Granville Waiters Before Draft Night

Indiana did not keep the 1984 second-rounder until the draft. On August 18, 1983, the Pacers traded that pick by itself to Portland for rookie center Granville Waiters.

Because the pick alone produced Waiters, that downstream branch can be credited directly. Waiters played 78 Indiana games with eight starts in 1983-84, then 62 games with five starts in 1984-85.

That gives the Pacers 140 games and 13 starts from the pick branch, in addition to Lowe's 78 games and two starts.

The Named Draft Outcome Was Victor Fleming

Portland ultimately used the transferred pick at No. 26 in the 1984 draft on Victor Fleming. Fleming never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

For Indiana's realized value, however, the important outcome is Waiters, because the Pacers had already converted the pick directly into him before Portland made the selection.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B/B. Chicago gets credit for Wiggins' 82-game, 40-start rookie season and for retaining some later trade utility. Indiana gets credit for Lowe's 78 games plus 140 games from Waiters through the direct pick-for-player conversion. Chicago had the better individual season; Indiana extracted more total games from the package. Neither advantage is large enough to force a winner.

perspectives.analysis:
Every Named Player Produced Zero Direct Games

Basketball-Reference's Cleveland, San Diego and league transaction ledgers agree on the June 28, 1983 package. Cleveland sent the rights to third-round picks Larry Anderson and Les Craft to the Clippers for a 1985 second-round pick.

The immediate player outcomes were empty on both sides, which makes the downstream use of Cleveland's pick the only meaningful separator.

Anderson Never Reached the NBA

Cleveland drafted Larry Anderson at No. 56 out of UNLV, then moved his rights to San Diego the same day.

Basketball-Reference lists Anderson as a drafted player with no NBA regular-season statistical line. The Clippers therefore received no direct games or starts from his rights.

Craft Also Produced No NBA Games

Les Craft was selected by Cleveland at No. 66. His rights had reached the Cavaliers through the Mike Bratz trade chain and were then packaged with Anderson for the future pick.

Craft likewise never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. San Diego's two incoming rights therefore combined for zero direct NBA games.

Cleveland's Pick Became Calvin Duncan

The 1985 second-round selection landed at No. 30, where Cleveland drafted VCU guard Calvin Duncan.

Duncan never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. If the pick branch ended there, this trade would be an easy even result: zero direct games on both sides.

The Pick Still Had Downstream Transaction Utility

Cleveland did not simply lose Duncan's rights for nothing. On the same 1985 draft day, the Cavaliers packaged Duncan with No. 9 pick Charles Oakley and sent both to Chicago for Keith Lee and Ennis Whatley.

That gives the original San Diego pick some downstream utility. This review deliberately does not credit the entire Lee-Whatley package to Duncan because Oakley was a top-10 pick and the far more substantial asset in the deal.

The distinction matters: the pick retained trade value, but it did not independently create a major return.

Why Cleveland Gets Only a Slight Edge

San Diego received two rights packages that produced no NBA player. Cleveland received a second-round pick that also became a zero-game player, but the pick survived long enough to be included in another NBA transaction.

That is a narrow advantage, not a major win.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win, C+/C. Cleveland receives a C+ because the incoming pick retained enough value to become part of a later trade package even though Calvin Duncan never played in the NBA. The Clippers receive a C because Anderson and Craft produced zero direct games and no verified downstream franchise value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Turned a Veteran and a Second Into a Long-Term Starter

The June 29, 1983 exchange sent Randy Wittman's draft rights from Washington to Atlanta. The Bullets received Tom McMillen and Atlanta's 1984 second-round pick, later No. 34 Tony Costner.

The legacy archive record originally called the outcome even. Completed player production gives Atlanta a clearer advantage.

Wittman Developed Into a Full-Time Hawks Starter

Wittman played 78 regular-season games for Atlanta as a rookie in 1983-84, mostly off the bench. His role increased in 1984-85, when he started 22 of 41 games and averaged 9.9 points.

By 1985-86, Wittman was a regular starter. He appeared in 81 games, started 79 and averaged 12.9 points while shooting 53.0 percent from the field.

He followed with 71 games and 65 starts in 1986-87, then played all 82 games and started all 82 in 1987-88. Across those first five Hawks seasons alone, Wittman totaled 353 regular-season games and 249 starts.

That span also included repeated playoff participation as Atlanta developed into a strong Eastern Conference team.

McMillen Gave Washington Three Useful Seasons

Tom McMillen was already an established veteran when Washington acquired him. He played 62 games for the Bullets in 1983-84, starting five and averaging 9.2 points.

He returned for 69 games and 21 starts in 1984-85, then added 56 games and one start in 1985-86.

Across three Washington seasons, McMillen produced 187 regular-season games and 27 starts. That is meaningful depth and keeps the Bullets side from being graded as a poor return.

The Second-Round Pick Produced No NBA Games

Washington used the incoming 1984 second-rounder at No. 34 on Saint Joseph's center Tony Costner.

Basketball-Reference lists Costner as a drafted player with no NBA regular-season statistical line. His professional career continued outside the NBA, so the pick branch produced zero direct Bullets games.

Why Atlanta Wins

Washington received three useful seasons from McMillen, but the pick added nothing at the NBA level. Atlanta received a younger wing who grew from reserve minutes into a multi-year starting role.

Wittman's first five Atlanta seasons alone produced nearly twice as many games as McMillen's Washington tenure and more than nine times as many starts. His strongest years also aligned with Atlanta's playoff rise.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, A/B. Atlanta receives an A because Wittman became a durable multi-year starter and productive rotation piece for a rising playoff team. Washington receives a B because McMillen gave the Bullets three useful seasons, but Costner produced zero NBA games and the total return did not match Wittman's longevity or starting value.

Minniefield never played for the Nets. New Jersey later used the incoming 1987 pick as part of a multi-asset trade for Reggie Johnson, so that branch retained some transaction utility. perspectives.analysis:
The Swap Is the Only Branch That Produced Direct Dallas Games

Basketball-Reference's league and Dallas transaction ledgers record the June 29, 1983 package as Dirk Minniefield plus a 1987 second-round pick to New Jersey for a 1986 second-round pick and another 1987 second-round pick. The completed draft outcomes show Dallas at No. 26 in 1987 with Steve Alford and the other side of the exchange at No. 43 with Andrew Kennedy.

The legacy archive record describes the 1987 mechanism as Dallas holding the option to take the more favorable second-round position. The realized draft positions are consistent with that description.

Minniefield Never Played for New Jersey

Dallas drafted Dirk Minniefield at No. 33 in 1983 and immediately moved his rights to the Nets. Minniefield spent the next two seasons outside the NBA and did not debut until 1985-86 with Cleveland.

His later NBA career included 222 games, but none came for New Jersey. This review therefore assigns the Nets zero direct regular-season games from the Minniefield branch.

New Jersey's 1987 Pick Retained Some Trade Utility

The Nets did not hold the incoming 1987 second-rounder all the way to draft night. In September 1983, New Jersey included that pick with Horace Owens and Eddie Phillips in the trade that brought Reggie Johnson from Philadelphia.

Philadelphia ultimately used the pick at No. 43 on Andrew Kennedy, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Because the pick was only one part of the Reggie Johnson package, this review records downstream transaction utility without assigning the full Johnson return to this trade.

Milt Wagner Produced Zero Dallas Games

Dallas used the 1986 second-round pick at No. 35 on Louisville guard Milt Wagner. The Mavericks waived Wagner on October 17, 1986, before he appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

Wagner later played 53 NBA games for the Lakers and Heat, but none of that production belongs to Dallas for trade-value purposes.

Steve Alford Produced the Clear Direct Return

Dallas used the favorable 1987 second-round position at No. 26 on Steve Alford. He played 112 regular-season games for the Mavericks across four Dallas seasons, all off the bench, and scored 385 points for the franchise.

Alford was never a major rotation piece, but he is the only asset in the trade tree that produced substantial direct games for either original team.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win, B/C+. Dallas receives a B because the favorable swap position produced 112 direct games from Alford even though Wagner produced none. New Jersey receives a C+ because Minniefield never played for the Nets, but the 1987 pick retained enough value to be included in a later multi-asset trade for Reggie Johnson. The margin is real but modest.

Macklin played only eight regular-season games for the Knicks, made no starts and was out of the NBA after that season.
