new-york-knicks.analysis:
Atlanta Received the Better Player Outcome

The canonical June 29, 1983 package sends Rudy Macklin to New York for Sly Williams and cash. Basketball-Reference's player records make the on-court comparison straightforward even though the public cash amount is not identified.

Both players were former first-round picks whose roles were already shrinking, so this was a secondary roster move rather than a franchise-changing deal.

Macklin Played Only Eight Knicks Games

Rudy Macklin had spent his first two NBA seasons with Atlanta before the trade. In New York, he appeared in only eight regular-season games in 1983-84.

He made no starts, played 65 total minutes and averaged 4.4 points and 1.4 rebounds. Those eight games were the final NBA appearances of his career.

New York therefore received very little direct basketball value from the acquired player.

Williams Gave Atlanta Parts of Two Seasons

Sly Williams appeared in 13 regular-season games for Atlanta in 1983-84 and made one start. His role expanded the following season, when he played 34 games and started 20.

Across the two Hawks seasons, Williams totaled 47 regular-season games and 21 starts. The production was not star-level, but it was materially more useful than Macklin's eight-game Knicks tenure.

Williams later played six games for Boston in 1985-86, which are not credited to Atlanta.

The Cash Component Adds to Atlanta's Side

The canonical source package also sends cash from New York to Atlanta. The reviewed public sources do not establish the amount, so this review does not convert it into a speculative dollar-adjusted grade.

It still counts as a tangible asset. Atlanta received both the more productive player return and cash, while New York's player contribution ended after eight games.

Why the Original Even Grade Changes

The legacy review treated the transaction as broadly balanced, likely because both players were modest historical contributors and the cash figure was unclear.

Completed franchise-specific production creates a wider gap. Williams produced nearly six times as many games for Atlanta as Macklin did for New York and added 21 starts, with cash on top.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win, B+/D. Atlanta receives a B+ because Williams provided 47 games and 21 starts across two seasons and the Hawks also received cash. New York receives a D because Macklin played only eight games, never started and did not appear in the NBA again after 1983-84.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey acquired Kelvin Ransey from Dallas on August 12, 1983 for Foots Walker plus the picks that became Tom Sluby and Bill Wennington. Ransey played 240 regular-season games for the Nets across three seasons and started 94, averaging 9.5 points and 6.0 assists in his first year. Dallas waived Walker before the season; he later re-signed with New Jersey. Sluby played 31 Mavericks games with no starts, while Wennington played 209 Dallas games with 12 starts over four seasons. The two drafted players therefore matched Ransey's 240-game total exactly, but Ransey carried a much larger role and starting burden. The realized franchise value gives New Jersey a modest edge, not Dallas.
perspectives.analysis:
The legacy Dallas-Win Verdict Overstates the Pick Return

Basketball-Reference and the Dallas media guide agree on the August 12, 1983 package. Dallas sent Kelvin Ransey to New Jersey for Foots Walker, a 1984 second-round pick and a 1985 first-round pick.

The completed outcomes are unusual: Ransey played exactly 240 regular-season games for New Jersey, while Tom Sluby and Bill Wennington combined for exactly 240 games for Dallas. The difference is role and impact.

Ransey Started 94 Games for the Nets

Ransey played 80 games for New Jersey in 1983-84 and started 50. He averaged 9.5 points and 6.0 assists in 24.2 minutes as the Nets won 45 games and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals.

He followed with 81 games and 29 starts in 1984-85, then 79 games and 15 starts in 1985-86. Across three Nets seasons, Ransey totaled 240 games and 94 starts.

He also appeared in 11 playoff games for New Jersey across those seasons, starting six. The Nets received a real rotation point guard rather than a short rental.

Foots Walker Produced Zero Dallas Games

Dallas acquired veteran guard Foots Walker in the deal but waived him on October 11, 1983 before the regular season.

New Jersey later re-signed Walker as a free agent, and he played 34 more Nets games. This review does not count those 34 games as a direct trade return because the Mavericks had already waived him and the Nets reacquired him separately.

For Dallas, Walker's branch produced zero regular-season games.

Tom Sluby Added 31 Reserve Games

Dallas used the 1984 second-round pick at No. 41 on Notre Dame guard Tom Sluby.

Sluby played 31 regular-season games for the Mavericks in 1984-85, made no starts and averaged 4.9 minutes. That was his entire NBA career.

Bill Wennington Supplied Four Years of Center Depth

The 1985 first-round pick became No. 16 Bill Wennington. He played 56, 58, 30 and 65 games for Dallas over four seasons, totaling 209 regular-season appearances and 12 starts.

Wennington had a long NBA career, but his later championship years with Chicago are not credited to Dallas. The relevant Mavericks return is four seasons of mostly reserve-center minutes.

Why New Jersey Gets the Edge

Dallas did realize value from both draft picks. Sluby and Wennington combined for 240 games, matching Ransey's Nets total exactly.

Ransey's 94 starts versus 12 combined Dallas starts tell the more important story. He handled regular point-guard responsibility for three playoff-caliber Nets seasons, while Dallas's return was almost entirely bench depth.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, B+/B. New Jersey receives a B+ for 240 games, 94 starts and three years of useful point-guard play from Ransey. Dallas receives a B because the two picks produced 240 games of legitimate depth, but the outgoing package did not generate the stronger franchise-specific role or impact. The legacy Dallas-win framing is replaced by a modest Nets edge.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Golden State's 1986 second-round pick for Darren Tillis on August 16, 1983. Tillis played 72 regular-season games for the Warriors in 1983-84, starting once and providing 730 minutes of reserve-center work. Cleveland used the No. 29 pick on Johnny Newman, who played 59 Cavaliers games as a rookie in 1986-87, made no starts and logged 630 minutes before Cleveland waived him the following November. Newman later became a productive 16-year NBA player, but those Knicks and later-team seasons are not Cleveland trade value. With one reserve season on each side and comparable direct minutes, the completed franchise-specific outcome is best treated as even.
perspectives.analysis:
Career Value Makes This Trade Look More Lopsided Than It Was

The canonical August 16, 1983 transaction is simple: Golden State acquired Darren Tillis and Cleveland received the Warriors' 1986 second-round pick.

That pick became No. 29 Johnny Newman, whose later NBA career was far more substantial than Tillis'. This review does not award Cleveland those later seasons because Newman played them for other franchises.

Tillis Gave Golden State One Full Reserve Season

Darren Tillis appeared in 72 regular-season games for Golden State in 1983-84 and made one start. He played 730 minutes, averaged 3.6 points and 2.6 rebounds, and blocked 60 shots.

That season accounted for nearly all of Tillis' post-trade NBA value. He did not return to the NBA after 1983-84.

For the Warriors, the direct result was 72 games and one start from a reserve center.

Cleveland Waited Three Years for Johnny Newman

The incoming second-round pick did not convey until the 1986 draft, when Cleveland selected Richmond forward Johnny Newman at No. 29.

Newman played 59 regular-season games for the Cavaliers as a rookie, made no starts and logged 630 minutes. He averaged 5.0 points in 10.7 minutes.

Cleveland waived him on November 5, 1987. The Knicks signed him a week later, beginning the much more productive portion of his career.

Later Newman Success Belongs to New York and Other Teams

Newman eventually played 1,159 NBA games and became a multi-year starter, but Cleveland did not realize that value.

Crediting his Knicks, Hornets and later production to this 1983 trade would turn a modest one-season Cavaliers return into a misleading long-term win. The audit therefore stops Cleveland's value at 59 games and zero starts.

The Direct Returns Are Very Close

Golden State received 72 games, one start and 730 minutes from Tillis. Cleveland received 59 games, zero starts and 630 minutes from Newman.

Newman scored a little more per game; Tillis supplied more rebounding and shot-blocking. Neither original team retained its player beyond one useful reserve season.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C+/C+. The Warriors received slightly more games and minutes from Tillis, while Cleveland received a younger scorer from the delayed pick. The differences are too small to justify a winner once Newman's later non-Cleveland career is excluded.

That pick became No. 29 Johnny Newman, whose later NBA career was far more substantial than Tillis'. This review does not award Cleveland those later seasons because Newman played them for other franchises.

Tillis Gave Golden State One Full Reserve Season

Darren Tillis appeared in 72 regular-season games for Golden State in 1983-84 and made one start. He played 730 minutes, averaged 3.6 points and 2.6 rebounds, and blocked 60 shots.

That season accounted for nearly all of Tillis' post-trade NBA value. He did not return to the NBA after 1983-84.

For the Warriors, the direct result was 72 games and one start from a reserve center.

Cleveland Waited Three Years for Johnny Newman

The incoming second-round pick did not convey until the 1986 draft, when Cleveland selected Richmond forward Johnny Newman at No. 29.

Newman played 59 regular-season games for the Cavaliers as a rookie, made no starts and logged 630 minutes. He averaged 5.0 points in 10.7 minutes.

Cleveland waived him on November 5, 1987. The Knicks signed him a week later, beginning the much more productive portion of his career.

Later Newman Success Belongs to New York and Other Teams

Newman eventually played 1,159 NBA games and became a multi-year starter, but Cleveland did not realize that value.

Crediting his Knicks, Hornets and later production to this 1983 trade would turn a modest one-season Cavaliers return into a misleading long-term win. The audit therefore stops Cleveland's value at 59 games and zero starts.

The Direct Returns Are Very Close

Golden State received 72 games, one start and 730 minutes from Tillis. Cleveland received 59 games, zero starts and 630 minutes from Newman.

Newman scored a little more per game; Tillis supplied more rebounding and shot-blocking. Neither original team retained its player beyond one useful reserve season.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C+/C+. The Warriors received slightly more games and minutes from Tillis, while Cleveland received a younger scorer from the delayed pick. The differences are too small to justify a winner once Newman's later non-Cleveland career is excluded.

perspectives.analysis:
Neither Side Got a Regular-Season Game

Basketball-Reference's Detroit and Portland transaction ledgers agree on the August 18, 1983 terms. Detroit received Pétur Guðmundsson, while Portland received the Pistons' 1984 third-round pick.

The pick eventually became No. 65 Tim Kearney.

Guðmundsson Never Played for Detroit

Guðmundsson had already appeared in 68 NBA games for Portland in 1981-82, but he spent 1982-83 outside the NBA in Iceland. Detroit acquired his rights in August 1983.

The Pistons waived him on October 25, 1983. Detroit did not open its regular season until October 28, so Guðmundsson produced zero regular-season games, starts or minutes for the Pistons.

He later returned to the NBA with the Lakers and Spurs, but those seasons came after Detroit had waived him and are not credited to this trade.

Portland's Pick Became Tim Kearney

The Trail Blazers used the incoming third-round pick at No. 65 in the 1984 NBA Draft on West Virginia forward Tim Kearney.

Basketball-Reference's Portland draft history lists Kearney as the No. 65 selection but shows no NBA regular-season career. Portland therefore received zero direct NBA games from the pick.

The draft asset had real optionality at the time of the trade, but hindsight evaluation has to follow what actually happened with it.

Why This Is Even

Detroit acquired a player who never made its regular-season roster. Portland acquired a draft choice that became a player who never appeared in the NBA.

Neither branch produced direct on-court value for the acquiring franchise. Portland can receive some process credit for converting a player it was not using into a future selection, but the pick's realized basketball return was zero.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, C-/C-. Detroit receives a C- because Guðmundsson was waived before the season and produced no games. Portland also receives a C- because the No. 65 pick became Tim Kearney, who never played in the NBA. Confidence is high because the trade, waiver date and draft outcome are all documented in primary statistical transaction records.

Waiters immediately made the Pacers' roster and played 78 games as a rookie, then 62 more for Indiana in 1984-85. indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Bought Two Useful Seasons for One Pick

Basketball-Reference's Indiana and Portland transaction ledgers agree on the August 18, 1983 exchange. The Pacers acquired Granville Waiters, while the Trail Blazers received Indiana's 1984 second-round pick. That selection became No. 26 Victor Fleming in the 1984 NBA Draft.

The trade looks small on the transaction log, but the realized return is not close.

Waiters Immediately Joined Indiana's Rotation

Waiters was a 6-foot-11 center whose NBA rights belonged to Portland after the 1983 draft. Indiana acquired him in August and signed him to a multi-year contract in September, according to the Pacers' own media guide.

He then played 78 games as a rookie in 1983-84, starting eight. Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,040 minutes, 277 points, 227 rebounds and 85 blocks. That is 3.6 points, 2.9 rebounds and 1.1 blocks per game in a reserve role.

Waiters stayed with Indiana for 1984-85 and appeared in 62 more games with five starts. Across the two seasons, he gave the Pacers 140 regular-season games, 1,743 minutes, 476 points, 397 rebounds and 129 blocks.

Those are not star numbers, but they are real rotation value from a player acquired for a single second-round pick.

Portland's Pick Became Victor Fleming

Portland converted the incoming pick into the No. 26 selection in the 1984 draft and used it on Xavier guard Victor Fleming.

The draft record is clear, but the NBA return ends there. Basketball-Reference lists Fleming as Portland's No. 26 selection and shows no NBA regular-season career. He never played an NBA game for the Trail Blazers or any other franchise.

That does not mean Portland's process was irrational. A future second-round pick carried flexibility, and the Blazers were moving the rights to a player they did not need. But this project grades the completed outcome, not only the theoretical value of the asset on trade day.

Why Indiana Wins

Indiana paid a pick that became a non-NBA player and received a center who filled a real role for two seasons.

Waiters was not a cornerstone, but 140 games of reserve-center production is materially better than zero NBA games from the pick. The margin is especially easy to see because the trade has no complicated downstream chain: Waiters' Pacers tenure is the direct return, and Fleming is the direct draft result.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, B-/D. Indiana earns a B- for turning one second-round pick into two seasons and 140 games of usable frontcourt depth. Portland receives a D because the acquired selection became Victor Fleming, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high because the trade terms, Waiters' Indiana production and Fleming's draft outcome are all documented in primary statistical records.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: In August 1983 the San Diego Clippers acquired James Donaldson, Greg Kelser, Mark Radford and future selections from Seattle, while the SuperSonics obtained Tom Chambers, Al Wood and other picks. Chambers became a notable Seattle scorer; the Clippers' pick later linked to Michael Cage also supplied a substantial NBA player. The inherited Even Trade grades both current franchise identities A+.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Moved Chambers for a Broad Package

The San Diego Clippers traded Tom Chambers and Al Wood to Seattle in August 1983, taking James Donaldson, Greg Kelser and a later player to be named, Mark Radford. Draft rights were also exchanged in both directions. The Clippers sought several roster pieces instead of relying on Chambers, while the SuperSonics wanted a forward with scoring potential. The agreement involved more than the two best-known names.

Chambers Became a Real Seattle Scoring Option

Chambers developed into an important offensive player for the SuperSonics before moving elsewhere later in his career. That Seattle production was a tangible return from the trade rather than hypothetical upside. Al Wood supplied additional wing experience, although he was not the central long-term benefit. The draft rights Seattle obtained also had identities, but those later careers should be traced separately rather than used to enlarge Chambers's Seattle totals.

Donaldson and a Pick Gave San Diego Lasting Value

Donaldson offered a useful interior presence, while the Clippers' 1984 first-round selection became associated with Michael Cage, a powerful rebounder who spent substantial NBA time with the franchise. Kelser and Radford were smaller parts of the incoming picture. Another second-round right was tied to Calvin Duncan. The combination provided San Diego with multiple chances to improve its frontcourt instead of receiving only one direct replacement for Chambers.

Two Different Strong Returns Explain the Tie

The inherited A+ grades for both clubs reflect a productive high-end swap rather than identical player roles. Seattle gained a scorer who flourished as a SuperSonic, while the Clippers added players and draft capital, notably Cage. The deal took place when the franchise still played in San Diego and Seattle still had the SuperSonics name. Current franchise identifiers must not erase the history of the 1983 exchange.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. The Clippers receive A+ for a package featuring James Donaldson and the pick later used on Michael Cage. Seattle's franchise, now Oklahoma City, also earns A+ for Tom Chambers's productive SuperSonics tenure, plus Al Wood and draft rights. Both sides secured meaningful assets in a major 1983 exchange.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Houston signed restricted free agent Lewis Lloyd on August 29, 1983 after Golden State declined to match, sending the Warriors a 1985 second-round pick as compensation. Lloyd immediately became a Houston starter and played 278 regular-season games for the Rockets from 1983-84 through 1986-87, including 82 starts and 17.8 points per game in his first season and a major role on the 1986 Finals team. Golden State used the pick at No. 42 on Bobby Lee Hurt, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Houston won the exchange decisively.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Houston Turned Compensation Into a Starting Guard

Basketball-Reference records the August 29, 1983 transaction as a veteran free-agent signing: Houston signed Lewis Lloyd and sent Golden State a 1985 second-round pick as compensation. Golden State's own media guide says the Warriors had chosen not to exercise Lloyd's option, then waived their free-agent rights in exchange for Houston's pick.

The pick eventually became No. 42 Bobby Lee Hurt.

Lloyd Became Immediate Houston Production

Lloyd was not a marginal signing. He started all 82 games for Houston in 1983-84 and averaged 17.8 points, 3.9 assists and 3.6 rebounds while shooting 51.6 percent from the field.

He stayed in the Rockets' rotation for four consecutive seasons. Basketball-Reference credits Lloyd with 82 games in each of his first three Houston seasons and 32 more in 1986-87, for 278 regular-season games in that first Rockets run.

His best Houston season came in 1985-86, when he averaged 16.9 points on 52.9 percent shooting and started all 82 regular-season games. He also started all 20 of Houston's playoff games as the Rockets beat the Lakers in the Western Conference Finals and reached the NBA Finals.

The later suspension that cost Lloyd the 1987-88 and 1988-89 seasons limits the long-term grade, but it does not erase four years of direct production before that point.

Golden State's Pick Produced No NBA Games

Golden State received a future second-round pick for relinquishing its claim on Lloyd. The Warriors used that selection at No. 42 in the 1985 draft on Alabama forward Bobby Lee Hurt.

The draft record lists Hurt with zero NBA seasons and zero regular-season games. Golden State therefore received no on-court NBA return from the compensation pick.

That outcome makes the comparison unusually direct. Houston received a starting guard who produced nearly 300 regular-season games and played a major role on a Finals team. Golden State received a draft asset that never became an NBA contributor.

Why Houston Wins

The Warriors did recover something rather than losing Lloyd for nothing, so the process deserves more credit than a simple waiver. But realized value is the core of the verdict, and the realized value was overwhelmingly on Houston's side.

Final Verdict

perspectives.summary: On September 6, 1983, Cleveland sent a 1987 second-round draft choice to Portland for Linton Townes. Townes did not appear in an NBA game for the Cavaliers; he later made two appearances each for Milwaukee and San Diego in 1983-84. Portland held the pick and selected Lester Fonville at No. 29 in 1987, but Fonville never played an NBA regular-season game. Even Trade, C- each, because neither acquired asset supplied NBA minutes for the receiving club.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Traded a Distant Second for a Portland Reserve

Cleveland acquired young wing Linton Townes from Portland on September 6, 1983, surrendering its 1987 second-round selection. The league's 1983-84 transaction register and the historical ledgers for both teams identify the same direct player-for-pick exchange. Townes had appeared in 55 games for the Trail Blazers the previous season, so there was a modest reason for the Cavaliers to consider him an inexpensive developmental option. The compensation was a future choice four drafts away, meaning Portland was accepting deferred value rather than an immediately usable roster replacement. There was no reported cash or additional player in this transaction.

Townes Did Not Play a Regular-Season Game for Cleveland

The acquired wing never produced a regular-season NBA appearance for the Cavaliers. His 1983-84 NBA record consists of two games with Milwaukee and two with the San Diego Clippers, not Cleveland. Those four appearances together generated eight points over 19 minutes, but all occurred with other employers. His 55 earlier games in Portland also belong to the team trading him away and cannot be retroactively added to Cleveland's received value. The distinction changes the historical assessment: the Cavaliers acquired Townes's rights and an opportunity to evaluate a young player, yet that opportunity did not convert into NBA minutes for their own team.

Portland Used the Pick on Lester Fonville in 1987

The second-rounder became the No. 29 overall selection in the 1987 NBA draft. Both the league's official draft-history database and Portland's historical draft record show the Trail Blazers selected center Lester Fonville from Jackson State at that position. Pro Sports Transactions independently traces the pick to Cleveland's September 1983 transfer. Fonville never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so the pick's documented draft conversion produced no direct playing return for Portland. The choice was still a genuine asset available to Portland on draft night, but it cannot be assigned points, rebounds or seasons of NBA roster use that Fonville did not supply.

Two Real Assets, but Neither Became an NBA Contributor

Portland received a deferred draft opportunity and Cleveland received a young player who had previously reached the league. In retrospect, neither club obtained a contributing NBA player from the exchange. The Cavaliers got no Townes appearances; the Trail Blazers got a draft selection that produced no NBA games from Fonville. An inherited Cavaliers-win grade was therefore difficult to justify using actual receiving-team outcomes. The results are much closer to a low-value draw, though the chronology of the pick still deserves preservation as a genuine transaction rather than an empty record. Modest matching grades recognize the limited returns without inventing a hidden cash figure or a hypothetical alternative draft choice.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Cleveland earns C- because Linton Townes never played an NBA regular-season game for the Cavaliers. Portland also receives C- because its 1987 No. 29 selection, Lester Fonville, never played in the NBA. Both franchises acquired legitimate assets but neither converted the specific return into recorded NBA playing time.

new-york-knicks.summary: A 1983 three-team transaction sent Ray Williams to New York, Vince Taylor and the 1984 first-round selection that became Vern Fleming to Indiana, and cash to the Kansas City Kings franchise. Fleming developed into a long-serving Pacers guard, explaining Indiana's inherited win despite Williams's prior Knicks history. The grades are Indiana A-, New York B- and the Kings C+.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
New York Brought Williams Back to the Backcourt

The Knicks acquired Ray Williams in September 1983 as part of an arrangement involving Indiana and the Kansas City Kings, the franchise now represented as Sacramento in modern databases. Williams was familiar to New York from an earlier stage of his career, and the club wanted another experienced guard. Indiana received Vince Taylor and an incoming first-round draft right. The Kings received cash. Each participant accepted a different asset type rather than trading three equivalent current NBA starters.

Indiana's Pick Became Vern Fleming

The Pacers' incoming first-round selection became the 18th pick in 1984, used on Vern Fleming. Fleming developed into a steady NBA point guard and spent many seasons with Indiana, giving the transaction a direct long-term receiving-team payoff. His later durability matters more here than the pick's modest position near the end of the first round. Taylor offered an additional prospect opportunity, although the draft right became the package's distinctive success. The club gained a guard who could contribute across changing Pacers lineups.

The Knicks and Kings Received Narrower Returns

Williams brought experience back to the Knicks, but New York did not obtain the same length of future starting-guard service Indiana received from Fleming. It would also be misleading to count Williams's earlier Knicks seasons as new production acquired in 1983. The Kings chose cash instead of a young prospect or veteran scorer. That financial return could be useful to the franchise without generating on-court points. The three sides had different immediate objectives, and not all of them depended on development.

A Long-Term Point Guard Explains the Verdict

Indiana's inherited A- rewards Fleming's career in a Pacers uniform, an unusually durable outcome for a later first-round selection. New York's B- recognizes Williams as a recognizable veteran acquisition, while Kansas City's C+ reflects a cash-only return. The contrast makes the transaction an instructive early-1980s example of a future pick becoming more valuable than the veteran guard being traded. Its history should retain the Kings' contemporary Kansas City identity instead of pretending they played in Sacramento that season.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win. Indiana earns A- for Vince Taylor and, more importantly, the 1984 first-round choice used on long-serving guard Vern Fleming. New York receives B- for bringing back Ray Williams, while the Kings franchise gets C+ for cash. The sustained Indiana contribution provides the clearest long-term basketball return.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Kenny Dennard from the Kansas City Kings in September 1983 for a 1985 third-round pick that became No. 66 Michael Adams. Dennard played 43 games for the Nuggets in 1983-84 before Denver waived him in February, giving the Nuggets 413 minutes of reserve frontcourt play. Kansas City/Sacramento later used the pick on Adams, but he appeared in only 18 games and 139 minutes for the Kings before being waived in December 1985. Adams became an excellent NBA point guard later, but almost all of that value came after he left the franchise. On direct realized team value, Denver holds a narrow edge.
perspectives.analysis:
A Famous Name Does Not Automatically Make the Pick the Better Return

Basketball-Reference records the transaction on September 27, 1983: Denver sent a 1985 third-round pick to Kansas City for Kenny Dennard. The Kings' own media guide dates the agreement September 26. The draft pick later became No. 66 Michael Adams.

At first glance, the Adams name can make this look like an easy Kings win. That would credit Sacramento for production Adams created after the Kings had already waived him.

Dennard Gave Denver One Partial Season

Dennard joined the Nuggets for the 1983-84 season and appeared in 43 games. Basketball-Reference credits him with 413 minutes, 90 points, 101 rebounds, 45 assists and 23 steals.

His role was modest: 9.6 minutes per game and no starts. Denver waived him on February 25, 1984, so the acquisition did not become a long-term piece.

Still, those 43 games are direct realized value for the Nuggets.

The Pick Became Michael Adams, But Sacramento Kept Him Briefly

Kansas City held the third-round pick until the franchise's move to Sacramento and selected Michael Adams at No. 66 in the 1985 NBA Draft.

Adams eventually became an NBA All-Star and a highly productive point guard, but not for the Kings. His Sacramento tenure lasted 18 games in 1985-86. He played 139 total minutes, scored 40 points and averaged 2.2 points and 1.2 assists.

The Kings waived Adams on December 17, 1985. Washington later signed him, and his breakthrough seasons came after he reached Denver in 1987.

Those later Denver and Washington seasons should not be retroactively assigned to Sacramento's side of this 1983 trade.

Why Denver Gets the Slight Edge

Neither team extracted much from the assets it directly controlled. Denver received 43 games and 413 minutes from Dennard. Sacramento received 18 games and 139 minutes from Adams before releasing him.

The Kings deserve some process credit for turning an expendable player into a future pick that identified a legitimate NBA talent. But the franchise did not retain that talent long enough to capture the value that made Adams' career notable.

Final Verdict

Slight Nuggets Edge, C/C-. Denver earns a C for receiving one partial season of usable reserve minutes from Dennard. Sacramento receives a C- because the pick became Michael Adams but produced only 18 low-minute games for the Kings before he was waived. Confidence is high because the trade, Dennard's Denver tenure, Adams' draft slot and Adams' Sacramento exit are all documented in team and league transaction records.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Negotiated Around a Contractual Right

The Hawks wanted veteran center Billy Paultz, but San Antonio held a right of first refusal that could affect his free-agent move. In September 1983 the Spurs agreed not to exercise that right, receiving a future second-round selection in compensation. The arrangement gave Atlanta a path toward adding the center, not an incoming player directly sent from the Spurs in a conventional exchange.

The Hawks Wanted an Experienced Center

Paultz brought an extensive professional background and the ability to provide size in the middle. Atlanta viewed the opportunity as one way to fill an immediate roster need without waiting for a young prospect. His earlier playing record explained the attraction but was not production earned in a Hawks jersey through the agreement. The club paid with a draft opportunity to remove an obstacle to acquiring his services.

San Antonio Received a Later Pick

The Spurs' compensation was a 1985 second-round choice later linked to No. 54 Sam Mitchell. Its value came from the future draft option and the freedom to move or use it. Mitchell's later NBA career should not be counted automatically as production for the Spurs, because the rights trail may include other movements. The concrete 1983 transaction was the exchange of a nonmatching commitment for a selection.

This Was a Rights Decision With Unequal Returns

The inherited Spurs B+ rewards draft compensation obtained without sending an active player in this agreement. Atlanta's C+ reflects its ability to pursue a familiar veteran rather than an assured long-term impact player. Both sides had understandable motives: the Spurs converted a contract right into an asset, and the Hawks addressed a positional need. Describing it as a star-for-star trade would distort the actual arrangement.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win. San Antonio receives B+ for the 1985 second-round right later associated with Sam Mitchell after declining to match Atlanta's interest in Billy Paultz. Atlanta earns C+ for gaining access to an experienced center. This was a free-agent rights arrangement with draft compensation, not a guaranteed player-for-player return.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Chicago Let Golden State Pursue Mike Bratz

Chicago's September 30, 1983 agreement allowed Golden State to pursue restricted free agent Mike Bratz without the Bulls invoking their right of first refusal. In exchange, Chicago obtained a 1984 fourth-round draft position that eventually appeared as No. 77, associated with Mark Halsel. The transaction was principally about a contractual matching right rather than a conventional exchange of two signed players. Golden State valued the immediate access to a veteran guard; Chicago accepted a lower-round development chance instead of defending its matching claim. That distinction is essential to accurately describing what moved.

Bratz Brought Experience But Not Guaranteed Peak Production

Bratz had played NBA guard minutes for multiple clubs and could offer ball handling and perimeter offense to the Warriors. His earlier career was evidence that Golden State had targeted someone familiar with league competition, not proof of what he would produce in a new uniform. A right to sign Bratz might also have had different contractual value depending on the player's terms. The agreement did not convey a first-round selection or an established young star to Golden State. It removed a barrier that could otherwise complicate the club's attempt to add a particular veteran.

A Fourth-Round Selection Was Real Compensation in 1984

Chicago received the No. 77-linked fourth-round position in the 1984 draft. The rights associated with Halsel represented a legitimate selection in an era of drafts longer than the modern two rounds, even though a fourth-round choice generally held a lower likelihood of delivering sustained NBA production. The Bulls couldn't assume that selecting a player there would solve a long-term rotation issue. But they converted a contractual right they chose not to exercise into another tangible asset. Any later professional outcomes from Halsel would need to be checked separately from the original compensation.

The Bulls Secured Value for Forgoing Their Option

Chicago gained something for stepping aside and had no obligation to commit further roster resources to Bratz through this transaction. Golden State secured its desired access to a veteran guard while paying a speculative fourth-round pick. That gives Chicago a slight asset-efficiency advantage, without justifying the inherited failing grade for the Warriors. The Warriors had a roster reason for the agreement, and Chicago's low draft position had limited upside. A restrained Bulls-winning assessment fits the small stakes of a free-agent matching-right trade.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win, slightly. Chicago earns C+ for converting its decision not to match Mike Bratz into a 1984 fourth-round choice, later No. 77 Mark Halsel. Golden State gets C for obtaining a clear route to a veteran guard. No existing player contract was traded for Halsel, and the fourth-round position wasn't a guaranteed Bulls rotation contributor.

perspectives.summary: Denver traded Billy McKinney to the San Diego Clippers for Richard Anderson on October 4, 1983. Both players spent the 1983-84 season with their new clubs, but Anderson provided the stronger direct return: 78 games, 17 starts, 1,380 minutes, 663 points and 406 rebounds for Denver, compared with McKinney's 80 games, zero starts, 843 minutes and 311 points for San Diego. Anderson averaged 8.5 points and 5.2 rebounds in 17.7 minutes, while McKinney averaged 3.9 points in 10.5 minutes. The exchange was useful for both sides, but Denver received the more substantial rotation piece.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Won a Straight Player-for-Player Swap

Basketball-Reference's Denver and San Diego transaction logs agree on the October 4, 1983 terms: the Nuggets sent veteran guard Billy McKinney to the Clippers for second-year big man Richard Anderson.

There were no draft picks or later branches to complicate the comparison. Both players joined their new teams immediately, so the trade can be judged almost entirely on their 1983-84 production.

Anderson Became a Real Denver Rotation Big

Anderson had played 78 games as a rookie for San Diego in 1982-83. After the trade, he again appeared in 78 games, this time for Denver, and started 17.

Basketball-Reference credits Anderson with 1,380 minutes, 663 points, 406 rebounds and 193 assists for the Nuggets. He averaged 8.5 points, 5.2 rebounds and 2.5 assists in 17.7 minutes per game.

That is meaningful second-unit production, and the 17 starts show that Denver could use him for more than low-leverage depth. He also appeared in four playoff games when the Nuggets reached the 1984 postseason.

Anderson then left the NBA for two seasons to play in Italy, so Denver did not get a long multi-year return. Even so, the one season it received was productive.

McKinney Gave San Diego Backcourt Depth

McKinney also played almost the full 1983-84 schedule for his new club. He appeared in 80 games for San Diego, but all 80 came off the bench.

His role was smaller than Anderson's. McKinney logged 843 minutes and produced 311 points and 161 assists, averaging 3.9 points and 2.0 assists in 10.5 minutes.

He did not play in the NBA in 1984-85 and later returned for a brief nine-game stint with Chicago in 1985-86, so San Diego's direct return was essentially one reserve season.

Why Denver Gets the Edge

The Clippers did receive legitimate use from McKinney. Eighty games of backup point-guard minutes is not nothing, and this was not a trade where one side received zero value.

The difference is role and production. Anderson played 537 more minutes, started 17 games, scored more than twice as many points and gave Denver size and rebounding. In a one-season-for-one-season comparison, his contribution was materially larger.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, B-/C. Denver earns a B- for turning McKinney into a younger frontcourt player who delivered 78 games, 17 starts and useful all-around production. San Diego receives a C for getting a dependable reserve guard for 80 games but at a much smaller role. Confidence is high because the transaction and both players' post-trade seasons are fully documented in team and player statistical records.

houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Acquired a Waiver of Milwaukee's Matching Rights

On October 5, 1983, Houston reached an agreement under which Milwaukee declined to exercise its right of first refusal on restricted free agent Phil Ford. The Rockets supplied cash and a 1984 sixth-round draft selection to the Bucks. That far-later selection was eventually identified as No. 120, associated with McKinley Singleton. This was not the sale of an already signed Milwaukee player to Houston on a normal player contract. The underlying prize for the Rockets was the ability to pursue Ford without another club invoking the specific matching right it held.

Ford's Existing Reputation Explained Houston's Interest

Ford had been a notable NBA guard earlier in his career and offered a recognizable ball-handling option for Houston. The Rockets' decision to spend cash and lower-round draft capital reflected an immediate personnel objective, not an attempt to acquire an untested late draft prospect. Ford's most celebrated seasons, however, preceded the October 1983 transaction. Those accomplishments could inform scouting but could not automatically be credited as Rockets games or future playoff results. Milwaukee, meanwhile, was willing to move past the contractual claim rather than retain it without compensation.

Milwaukee Received Cash and a Sixth-Round Position

The Bucks turned their right to match an offer for Ford into immediate financial consideration and a sixth-round selection. The eventual No. 120 slot had a traceable draft identity, but McKinley Singleton was a highly speculative asset at that stage of the draft. Calling him an established future Bucks player on the agreement date would distort the return. Still, the cash was genuine compensation and the pick provided an additional possible player-rights route. That combined return was useful for a club that no longer treated Ford as indispensable to its main roster plan.

The Bucks Collected Compensation Without Losing a Current Star

Milwaukee received a defined payment plus a draft opportunity for voluntarily stepping away from an older guard's free agency. Houston gained an option to sign a veteran with known prior NBA ability. The Bucks have a modest advantage because they converted a contractual right into assets while Houston took on uncertainty about Ford's remaining career. But Houston wasn't left empty-handed, and a sixth-round pick alone could not justify a dominant victory claim. This trade is most accurately evaluated through its free-agent rules, not through a mistaken conventional player-for-pick account.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win by a modest financial and draft-rights edge. Milwaukee earns B- for cash and a 1984 sixth-round pick later associated with No. 120 McKinley Singleton. Houston gets C for Milwaukee's decision not to exercise matching rights on Phil Ford. Ford's earlier NBA peak and Singleton's uncertain future aren't counted as guaranteed receiving-team production.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
San Diego Obtained Two Players for a Conditional Second

On October 6, 1983, the San Diego Clippers acquired Wes Matthews Sr. and Kevin Figaro from Atlanta. The Hawks received a conditional second-round selection that later became associated with the 1986 No. 32 position and Cedric Henderson. The 1983 trade therefore gave the Clippers two players they could evaluate immediately while Atlanta accepted the uncertainty of a later draft claim. The transaction was made while the franchise still played in San Diego, so using the modern Los Angeles Clippers index should not suggest the deal happened at its later home venue.

Matthews Offered an Experienced Guard Option

Matthews was an NBA guard with existing experience and could provide depth to a Clippers backcourt that was looking for workable combinations. Figaro offered another player for the club to assess, though neither should automatically be treated as a long-term starter. Receiving two named basketball assets was useful because the team could decide their roles after training camp. The Hawks' previous playing time from Matthews and Figaro, if any, cannot be assigned to San Diego. The relevant contribution is the period after the exchange, including possible later roster moves that would need separate attribution.

Atlanta Banked a Specific Future Draft Chance

The conditional selection ended up in the historical draft ledger as No. 32 in 1986, associated with Cedric Henderson. That is a meaningful second-round position and gives the outgoing-player exchange a traceable later result. It does not by itself establish that Henderson played for Atlanta or became a major Hawks contributor. The future pick also delayed any prospect evaluation compared with San Diego's immediate player acquisitions. Depending on its conditions and possible subsequent transfers, Atlanta could have used the asset differently without altering the original October 1983 agreement.

Two Available Players Tilt the Return Toward San Diego

San Diego received Matthews and Figaro as immediate roster options while Atlanta turned them into a conditional future pick. The Clippers' clearer near-term depth is enough for a limited winning verdict, though neither acquisition established a new franchise cornerstone. Atlanta retained a development opportunity that could turn out differently from either veteran's direct role. Moderate grades are more appropriate than a strong success claim, particularly because the 1986 draft right must be kept separate from every later contract signed by its eventual namesake.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, narrowly. The San Diego Clippers, indexed under today's Los Angeles franchise, receive B- for Wes Matthews Sr. and Kevin Figaro. Atlanta earns C+ for a conditional second that became associated with 1986 No. 32 Cedric Henderson. Neither Matthews's prior career nor a future draft name is counted as guaranteed new receiving-team NBA production.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Lakers acquired the draft rights to Byron Scott and veteran center Swen Nater from the San Diego Clippers on October 10, 1983 for Norm Nixon, Eddie Jordan and two future second-round picks. Scott immediately became a Lakers rotation guard and went on to start for three championship teams, while Nater played only 17 games. San Diego still received real value: Nixon was an All-Star in 1985 and gave the Clippers three strong seasons, and the two picks were flipped a week later for rookie Ricky Pierce. The Lakers nevertheless won because Scott became a long-term championship starter whose peak impact exceeded the Clippers' return.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Lakers Traded an All-Star Guard for Their Next Championship Backcourt Piece

Basketball-Reference's Lakers and San Diego transaction ledgers agree on the October 10, 1983 package. Los Angeles sent Norm Nixon, Eddie Jordan, a 1986 second-round pick and a 1987 second-round pick to the Clippers for Swen Nater and the draft rights to Byron Scott.

The deal is often remembered as Nixon for Scott, but the complete return matters. San Diego received two picks that it moved again only seven days later, and those assets produced Ricky Pierce before being folded into another trade.

Scott Became a Long-Term Lakers Starter

Scott played 74 games as a rookie in 1983-84, started 49 and averaged 10.6 points. He made the All-Rookie team and appeared in 20 playoff games.

His role expanded immediately. Scott averaged 16.0 points in 1984-85 as the Lakers won the championship, 17.0 in the 1986-87 championship season and a career-high 21.7 in 1987-88 as Los Angeles repeated.

He started all 82 games in 1986-87 and 81 in 1987-88. Scott's shooting and transition scoring fit the Showtime Lakers, and he became a stable backcourt partner for Magic Johnson through three title runs.

Nater was only a small part of the return. He appeared in 17 Lakers games in 1983-84, totaling 146 minutes, 58 points and 40 rebounds.

Nixon Gave the Clippers Legitimate Value

San Diego did not lose this trade badly. Nixon started all 82 games in his first Clippers season and averaged 17.0 points and a league-leading 11.1 assists per game.

After the move to Los Angeles, Nixon averaged 17.2 points and 8.8 assists in 1984-85 and was selected to the All-Star Game. He followed with 14.6 points and 8.6 assists in 1985-86.

Major knee and Achilles injuries then cost him the 1986-87 and 1987-88 seasons. Nixon returned for 53 games in 1988-89, but his best Clippers value came in those first three seasons.

The Picks Became Ricky Pierce, Not Hornacek and Dalrymple for the Clippers

The transaction ledger shows San Diego traded both incoming second-round picks to Detroit on October 17, 1983 for Ricky Pierce. That means Jeff Hornacek and Bruce Dalrymple, the players eventually selected with those picks, should not be credited directly to the Clippers.

Pierce gave San Diego 69 games, 35 starts and 685 points as a rookie in 1983-84. The Clippers then included him in the September 1984 trade with Milwaukee that brought Marques Johnson, Junior Bridgeman and Harvey Catchings to Los Angeles.

Eddie Jordan was waived by San Diego on October 17, 1983, so his direct Clippers value was zero.

Why the Lakers Still Win

The Clippers received an All-Star season from Nixon plus additional value through Pierce. That is a strong return and deserves a high grade.

Scott, however, became a long-term starter on three championship teams and remained productive through the Lakers' title window. Championship-level continuity at a premium rotation spot gives Los Angeles the higher realized value.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win, A+/A-. The Lakers earn an A+ because Scott became a decade-long franchise piece and starter on the 1985, 1987 and 1988 champions. The Clippers earn an A- because Nixon delivered three strong seasons and an All-Star berth, while the draft-pick branch produced Pierce and further trade value. Confidence is high because the trade terms, player production and immediate pick re-trade are documented in team transaction records.
los-angeles-clippers.gradeRationale: Norm Nixon remained a productive guard for San Diego, but the Lakers received the rights to Byron Scott, a core starter on multiple championship teams, plus Swen Nater.

perspectives.summary: Utah sold Ben Poquette's player rights to Cleveland for cash on October 14, 1983. Poquette went on to play 248 regular-season games for the Cavaliers over parts of four seasons, with 79 appearances in 1984-85 and 81 in 1985-86. Utah received cash of an undisclosed amount. Cavaliers Win, Cleveland A-, Utah C; the previous Jazz-favored verdict and grade contradicted the source-verified receiving-team value.
perspectives.analysis:
Utah Sold Poquette's Rights After His Long Jazz Tenure

On October 14, 1983, the Utah Jazz transferred forward-center Ben Poquette to the Cleveland Cavaliers for cash. Utah's official historical media guide describes the compensation directly, resolving a placeholder in some later Cleveland transaction registers. Poquette had been an important Jazz starter in previous seasons, including a 1982-83 campaign of 75 appearances and 50 starts. Those older games belong to Utah before the sale and cannot become Cleveland's acquired-team return. The Cavaliers instead paid for the right to add a veteran reserve who still had several NBA seasons of useful frontcourt minutes ahead.

Poquette Became a Regular Cleveland Reserve for Four Seasons

Poquette played 51 regular-season games for Cleveland in 1983-84, logging 858 minutes and 185 points. The following year he appeared in 79 games, totaling 1,656 minutes and 532 points, and in 1985-86 he added 81 appearances. He remained with Cleveland for 37 games of 1986-87 before being moved to Chicago. Across those four Cleveland seasons he totaled 248 regular-season games, a much larger basketball return than a short rental. Although he was mostly a reserve, his recurring use gave the Cavaliers frontcourt continuity while the organization was rebuilding its playing rotation.

Utah Received Money Rather Than a Replacement Player

The Jazz received cash in return for Poquette, not a named player or draft selection. Neither the NBA ledger nor the franchise media guide establishes an amount for the payment, so the financial value cannot be assigned a precise present-day equivalent. Utah may have had reasonable roster or salary motives after years of using Poquette, but those motives are separate from documented post-transaction production. Because the trade did not bring a new player to Utah, it produced no identifiable Jazz on-court return to compare against Cleveland's 248 Poquette appearances. Assigning Utah a high basketball grade in this particular deal would therefore ignore the uneven recorded outcomes.

Cleveland Got More Value Than the Inherited Grades Suggested

Cleveland's return was not a championship centerpiece, but hundreds of appearances from a veteran acquired for undisclosed cash constitute an economical basketball asset. In 1987 the Cavaliers later traded Poquette to Chicago for a future second-round selection, which created a separate downstream asset branch; the original 1983 cash sale should not be mistaken for that later transaction. The source-backed score therefore favors Cleveland directly even without adding speculative value from the later pick. Utah received a documented cash payment that may have been helpful financially, but the archived Jazz-win verdict gave it more credit than the available history supports.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns A- for obtaining Ben Poquette for cash and using him in 248 regular-season games across four seasons. Utah receives C for monetizing the veteran's rights at an undisclosed amount. The old Jazz-favored grade conflicted with the receiving-club totals; this revision credits Cleveland's documented bench production without inventing cash value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Exchanged a Guard for Cash

The Hawks traded guard Keith Edmonson to the Spurs in October 1983, accepting cash instead of another player or a draft selection. Atlanta was preparing its roster for a new season and chose to convert a marginal guard into a financial return. San Antonio took the opposite side: the Spurs could evaluate Edmonson as a potential backcourt option without giving up an established player. Neither club placed a top draft pick or franchise cornerstone into the exchange.

Edmonson Was Not an Established Spurs Star

Edmonson had NBA experience, but the trade did not install him as San Antonio's long-term offensive organizer or a major scorer. The team's potential benefit was a chance to try a guard whose role had been limited elsewhere. His previous minutes in other uniforms cannot be assigned as production for the Spurs simply because his rights changed hands. This was a small personnel decision, and the basketball return needs to be kept in proportion to that modest scale.

Atlanta Received Cash Rather Than a Prospect

The Hawks' compensation was a cash payment. There was no draft pick to track and no incoming player whose later achievements might justify a larger retrospective grade. Cash could support roster management, but it did not deliver direct assists, scoring or defensive minutes. That distinction is important because some historical transaction summaries describe all incoming assets together even when one side received only financial consideration. Atlanta's benefit was narrower but less uncertain than hoping an unproven player would develop.

The Modest Grade Difference Is Understandable

The inherited slight Hawks edge reflects receiving an actual financial return while surrendering a guard who had not become essential. San Antonio took a low-cost chance on Edmonson, which was reasonable without guaranteeing future on-court success. Neither team received enough to make this a major win or loss on basketball grounds. The proper historical account is a cash deal with limited player impact, not an imagined star-for-star swap or a draft-rights chain that never existed.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta gets C+ for converting Keith Edmonson into cash and preserving roster flexibility. San Antonio earns C for receiving the guard without surrendering a major basketball asset, though he did not become an established Spurs centerpiece. The narrow difference reflects the financial return and limited direct playing value rather than a consequential franchise trade.

perspectives.summary: Detroit traded Ricky Pierce to the San Diego Clippers on October 17, 1983 for the 1986 and 1987 second-round picks San Diego had acquired from the Lakers one week earlier. Detroit did not keep either pick: the Pistons immediately sent both to Phoenix for David Thirdkill. Thirdkill played 56 regular-season games for Detroit across 1983-84 and 1984-85, totaling 406 minutes and 106 points before he was waived. Pierce gave San Diego 69 games, 35 starts and 685 points in 1983-84, then became part of the 1984 package for Marques Johnson. The Clippers received the better realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Flipped the Picks the Same Day

Basketball-Reference's Detroit and San Diego transaction ledgers show the October 17, 1983 exchange clearly. Detroit sent Ricky Pierce to the Clippers for a 1986 second-round pick and a 1987 second-round pick.

Those are the same picks San Diego had received from the Lakers in the Byron Scott-Norm Nixon trade one week earlier. More importantly, Detroit did not hold them until the draft.

The Pistons immediately traded both picks to Phoenix for David Thirdkill. That downstream step changes how the trade has to be graded. Jeff Hornacek and Bruce Dalrymple were eventually selected with the picks, but Detroit never controlled those selections at draft time and should not be credited with their later careers.

Pierce Became a Productive Clippers Rookie

Pierce had played only 39 games as a Detroit rookie in 1982-83. After the trade, he took a much larger role for San Diego.

He appeared in 69 games in 1983-84, started 35 and logged 1,280 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 685 points, 135 rebounds and 62 assists. He averaged 9.9 points in 18.6 minutes and shot 47.0 percent from the field.

The Clippers then used Pierce as a trade asset. On September 29, 1984, Los Angeles sent Pierce, Terry Cummings and Craig Hodges to Milwaukee for Marques Johnson, Junior Bridgeman, Harvey Catchings and cash.

Because Pierce was a direct outgoing asset in that later deal, some downstream trade utility belongs to the Clippers side even though the entire Milwaukee return cannot be assigned to Pierce alone.

Detroit's Picks Became David Thirdkill

Detroit sent both incoming picks to Phoenix on the same October 17 date for David Thirdkill.

Thirdkill played 46 games for the Pistons in 1983-84, all off the bench, totaling 291 minutes and 77 points. He returned for 10 more games in 1984-85, including one start, with 115 minutes and 29 points.

That gives Detroit 56 regular-season games, 406 minutes and 106 points from the actual downstream asset it chose.

The Pistons waived Thirdkill on November 29, 1984. His later time with Milwaukee, San Antonio and Boston came after Detroit had moved on and is not part of this trade's realized return.

Why the Clippers Win

Detroit did not receive zero value. Thirdkill provided two short stretches of reserve minutes, and turning two future seconds into a roster player was a legitimate use of the assets.

Pierce's one San Diego season was still clearly stronger. He played more than three times Thirdkill's Detroit minutes, started 35 games and scored more than six times as many points. He also retained enough value to become part of a major trade package the following offseason.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, B+/C-. San Diego earns a B+ for getting 69 games, 35 starts and meaningful scoring from Pierce plus subsequent trade utility. Detroit receives a C- because the two picks were immediately converted into Thirdkill, whose Pistons tenure produced only 56 games and 406 minutes before he was waived. Confidence is high because both October 17 transactions and the players' team-specific production are documented in primary statistical records.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Detroit's 1983-84 transaction log shows a remarkable same-day chain. On October 17 the Pistons traded Ricky Pierce to the San Diego Clippers for 1986 and 1987 second-round picks, then immediately sent those two picks to Phoenix for David Thirdkill. Phoenix's transaction log confirms the other side: Thirdkill for the 1986 second that became Jeff Hornacek and the 1987 second that became Bruce Dalrymple. That sequencing means Detroit consciously converted two future draft shots obtained for Pierce into a young reserve forward. The hindsight comparison is therefore Thirdkill's Detroit value against what Phoenix realized from those exact picks.

Detroit Return
Thirdkill played 46 games for the 1983-84 Pistons, all off the bench. He logged 291 minutes, scored 77 points and averaged 1.7 points in 6.3 minutes per game. He was a fringe rotation player on a 49-win Detroit team that reached the playoffs, not a meaningful part of the club's emerging Isiah Thomas-Bill Laimbeer core. Detroit waived him on November 29, 1984. His later career included Boston's 1986 championship team, but that value belongs to Boston and cannot be credited to Detroit. For TradeVerdicts purposes, the Pistons received one shallow reserve season and nothing durable beyond it.

Phoenix Return
The 1986 second-round pick became one of the great draft values of its era. Phoenix selected Jeff Hornacek at No. 46 overall. He played 80 games as a rookie, then became a regular starter, eventually developing into an efficient scorer and playmaker. By 1988-89 he was averaging 13.5 points and 6.0 assists; in 1989-90 he averaged 17.6 points while shooting 53.6 percent from the field; and by 1991-92 he was an All-Star. Hornacek spent six full seasons with Phoenix and became important enough to headline the outgoing Suns package in the June 1992 trade for Charles Barkley. The Barkley acquisition must be judged separately, but Hornacek's inclusion proves Phoenix preserved major downstream transaction value after already receiving years of direct production. The 1987 second became No. 46 Bruce Dalrymple. Dalrymple never appeared in an NBA regular-season game, so that second asset produced no direct value. Phoenix did not need it to justify the deal because Hornacek's return was already enormous.

Hindsight Verdict
Phoenix wins by a wide margin. Detroit received 46 bench games and 77 points from Thirdkill. Phoenix received a future All-Star, six seasons of substantial guard play and a core asset in a later superstar trade from one of the two second-rounders. An A+ for Phoenix reflects both Hornacek's direct Suns career and his preserved transaction value without crediting Phoenix for Charles Barkley's later production inside this trade. A D for Detroit recognizes that Thirdkill at least occupied a roster spot for one season, but the opportunity cost of surrendering the pick that became Hornacek is overwhelming. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Got the Only NBA Production in the Deal

Basketball-Reference's New Jersey and Philadelphia transaction ledgers agree on the October 25, 1983 terms. The Nets acquired Reggie Johnson and sent Eddie Phillips, Horace Owens and a 1987 second-round pick to the defending champion 76ers.

The trade happened three days before the regular season began, which makes Philadelphia's roster decisions especially important to the outcome.

Johnson Gave the Nets a Full Rotation Season

Johnson joined a New Jersey team that won 45 games and reached the Eastern Conference semifinals. He appeared in 72 regular-season games, started four and logged 818 minutes.

Basketball-Reference credits him with 346 points, 138 rebounds and 40 assists. Johnson averaged 4.8 points and 1.9 rebounds in 11.4 minutes while shooting 49.6 percent from the field.

The role was not large, but it was real. He gave New Jersey frontcourt depth across almost the entire season and appeared on a playoff team that eliminated Philadelphia in the first round.

That 1983-84 season was Johnson's final NBA campaign, so the Nets did not receive a long-term asset. The value is best described as one dependable reserve season.

Philadelphia Cut Both Players Immediately

The 76ers acquired Phillips and Owens on October 25 and placed both on waivers on October 27.

Phillips had played 48 games for New Jersey as a rookie in 1982-83, but he never appeared in a regular-season game for Philadelphia. RealGM's transaction log lists him becoming a free agent on October 31.

Owens, a 1983 second-round pick from Rhode Island, also never played an NBA regular-season game. Philadelphia waived him in the same final roster cut.

That left the future draft pick as the only remaining path for the 76ers.

The Pick Became Andrew Kennedy

Philadelphia held the 1987 second-round pick and used it at No. 43 on Virginia forward Andrew Kennedy.

Basketball-Reference's draft record lists Kennedy with no NBA regular-season career. He never produced a game for Philadelphia.

The three assets Philadelphia received therefore combined for zero NBA regular-season games for the franchise.

Why New Jersey Wins

The Nets did not acquire a star or a multi-year starter, so this is not an elite-grade win. They simply converted two players outside their plans and a future second-rounder into a reserve who helped immediately.

Philadelphia received no realized NBA production from either incoming player or the eventual draft selection. That creates a clear result even though the total stakes were modest.

Final Verdict

Nets Win, B/D. New Jersey earns a B for obtaining 72 games and a full season of useful reserve minutes from Johnson. Philadelphia receives a D because Phillips and Owens were waived before the season and Andrew Kennedy never appeared in the NBA. Confidence is high because the trade, waiver dates, Johnson's Nets statistics and Kennedy's draft outcome are documented in primary transaction and statistical records.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Seattle acquired Reggie King from Kansas City on October 26, 1983 for a 1985 second-round pick. King immediately became a starter, playing 77 games with 42 starts in 1983-84 and another 60 games in 1984-85. Kansas City did not keep the pick until draft night; in February 1984 it included the selection, which eventually became No. 28 Ken Johnson, in the multi-asset package that brought Reggie Theus from Chicago. seattle-supersonics.analysis:
Seattle Bought Two Seasons of Frontcourt Play for One Second-Round Pick

Basketball-Reference's Seattle transaction ledger records the October 26, 1983 trade: the SuperSonics sent Kansas City a 1985 second-round pick for Reggie King.

King had been a regular starter earlier in his Kings career but had moved into a smaller role in 1982-83. Seattle restored him to a meaningful place in the rotation immediately.

King Started 42 Games in His First Seattle Season

King appeared in 77 games in 1983-84 and started 42. He logged 2,086 minutes, scored 602 points and collected 470 rebounds.

That worked out to 7.8 points, 6.1 rebounds and 2.3 assists per game in 27.1 minutes while shooting 52.0 percent from the field. He was a substantial rotation player on a 42-win Seattle team that reached the playoffs.

King stayed for 1984-85 and appeared in 60 more games, starting five. His role shrank to 14.3 minutes per game, but he still gave Seattle another season of usable depth.

Across the two seasons, the SuperSonics received 137 regular-season games from a player acquired for one future second-round pick.

Kansas City Used the Pick as Part of the Reggie Theus Trade

The pick did not simply sit in the Kings' inventory until 1985. On February 15, 1984, Kansas City traded Steve Johnson and three second-round picks to Chicago for Reggie Theus.

Seattle's 1985 second-rounder was one of those picks. It eventually became No. 28 Ken Johnson after the Bulls held the selection.

Theus became a major Kings contributor. He averaged 19.0 points and 7.0 assists in 30 games after the 1984 trade, then remained a high-level starter as the franchise moved to Sacramento.

That downstream value matters, but it cannot all be credited to the single Seattle pick. Kansas City also surrendered Steve Johnson and two other second-round selections in the Theus package.

The Pick Itself Became Ken Johnson

Chicago ultimately used the pick at No. 28 in the 1985 draft on Ken Johnson. He played one NBA season, appearing in 64 games for the Bulls.

Because Kansas City had already traded the selection away, Johnson's Bulls production does not count as Kings realized value. The Kings' credit comes from the pick's role as one piece of the Theus acquisition.

Why Seattle Gets a Slight Edge

Kansas City handled the asset productively. Rather than waiting for a late second-round selection, the Kings used it as part of a package for a proven scorer and playmaker.

Seattle's return is easier to assign directly. King gave the SuperSonics 137 games, 47 starts and two seasons of frontcourt depth for that single pick.

The Kings' downstream branch was valuable but shared among four outgoing assets, so giving the entire Theus return to this pick would overstate its individual contribution.

Final Verdict

Slight SuperSonics Edge, B+/B. Seattle earns a B+ for getting two seasons and 137 games from King at the cost of one second-rounder. Kansas City earns a B because the pick became useful trade currency in the Reggie Theus deal, even though it was only one part of that package. Confidence is high on the transaction chain and King production, with the grade appropriately limiting how much of Theus' value is assigned to this single pick.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana traded Hank McDowell to the San Diego Clippers on October 26, 1983 for a 1988 third-round pick. McDowell immediately gave San Diego 57 games, 611 minutes, 208 points and 155 rebounds in 1983-84. Indiana held the future pick and used it at No. 73 in 1988 on Michael Anderson, but the Pacers waived Anderson before he played a regular-season game; his only NBA season came later with San Antonio. The Clippers therefore received a full season of reserve frontcourt play while Indiana's eventual draft selection produced zero Pacers games, making San Diego the clear winner.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
San Diego Turned a Future Third-Rounder Into Immediate Depth

Basketball-Reference's Indiana transaction ledger records the October 26, 1983 deal: the Pacers sent Hank McDowell to the San Diego Clippers for a 1988 third-round pick.

McDowell had arrived in Indiana only weeks earlier, but the Pacers chose to move him again before the regular season. San Diego kept him for the full 1983-84 campaign.

McDowell Played 57 Games for the Clippers

McDowell appeared in 57 games for San Diego, all off the bench. He logged 611 minutes, scored 208 points and collected 155 rebounds.

That worked out to 3.6 points and 2.7 rebounds in 10.7 minutes per game. The numbers were modest, but he was a usable reserve big for most of the season.

McDowell left the Clippers after that year and later played for Houston and Milwaukee. Those later stops do not count toward San Diego's return, but the Clippers still received one complete season of direct NBA production.

Indiana Waited Five Years for the Pick

The compensation was a distant 1988 third-round selection. The pick ultimately landed at No. 73, where Indiana selected Drexel point guard Michael Anderson.

Anderson did have an NBA career, but not with the Pacers. Indiana placed him on waivers on October 31, 1988, before he appeared in a regular-season game for the franchise.

He later played 36 games for San Antonio in 1988-89, averaging 5.7 points and 4.3 assists. Because those games came after Indiana had waived him, they are not Pacers realized value from this trade.

Why the Clippers Win

Indiana's process was understandable. The Pacers turned a player they were not planning to use into a future draft asset and held that asset until the 1988 draft.

The realized result, however, was zero Pacers games from the pick. San Diego paid that future third-rounder and received 57 games and 611 minutes from McDowell immediately.

This is a modest-stakes trade, so the Clippers' grade should not be exaggerated, but one full reserve season clearly beats a draft selection that never made Indiana's regular-season roster.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, B-/D. San Diego earns a B- for converting a third-round pick into 57 games of useful frontcourt depth. Indiana receives a D because the pick became Michael Anderson, whom the Pacers waived before he played a regular-season game. Confidence is high because the trade, McDowell's Clippers production, Anderson's draft slot and Indiana waiver are all documented in transaction and statistical records.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia traded Mark McNamara to San Antonio on November 4, 1983 for a 1988 second-round pick. McNamara gave the Spurs 82 games across parts of two seasons, including 70 games, 1,037 minutes, 388 points and 317 rebounds in 1983-84. Philadelphia waited nearly five years, selected Everette Stephens at No. 31, then immediately traded Stephens to Indiana for Ron Anderson. Anderson became a major 76ers reserve and scorer, playing 393 games over five seasons and averaging 16.2 points in his first Philadelphia year. San Antonio got useful center depth, but Philadelphia ultimately extracted much more downstream value.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Philadelphia Waited Five Years and Then Turned the Pick Into Ron Anderson

Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia and San Antonio transaction records show the November 4, 1983 deal: the 76ers sent center Mark McNamara to the Spurs for a 1988 second-round pick.

At the time, Philadelphia was moving a young reserve who had played 36 games for the 1983 championship team. San Antonio received immediate frontcourt help. Philadelphia accepted a long wait for its return.

McNamara Gave San Antonio a Productive Reserve Season

McNamara played 70 games for the Spurs in 1983-84, starting three. He logged 1,037 minutes, scored 388 points and grabbed 317 rebounds.

His efficiency stood out. McNamara shot 62.1 percent from the field and averaged 5.5 points and 4.5 rebounds in 14.8 minutes per game.

He returned for 12 more San Antonio games in 1984-85, adding 63 minutes and 33 points before leaving the team. That brings the Spurs' direct return to 82 games across parts of two seasons.

For a future second-round pick, that was a useful outcome.

The Pick Became Everette Stephens

Philadelphia kept the asset until the 1988 draft and used it at No. 31 on Purdue point guard Everette Stephens.

Stephens never played a regular-season game for the 76ers. On October 4, 1988, before the season, Philadelphia traded him to Indiana for veteran forward Ron Anderson.

That second move is the key downstream branch. Because Stephens was the direct outgoing asset acquired from this pick, Anderson's Philadelphia production is legitimate downstream value from the original McNamara trade.

Ron Anderson Became a Long-Term 76ers Contributor

Anderson played all 82 games for Philadelphia in 1988-89, started 12 and averaged 16.2 points and 5.0 rebounds in 31.9 minutes. He finished sixth in Sixth Man of the Year voting.

He stayed productive for several seasons. Anderson appeared in 78 games in 1989-90, 82 in 1990-91, 82 in 1991-92 and 69 in 1992-93.

Across those five seasons, he gave Philadelphia 393 regular-season games and repeatedly supplied double-digit scoring from the wing.

Stephens himself later played 35 games for Indiana and three for Milwaukee, but those games do not count for Philadelphia. The 76ers' realized value came from converting his draft rights into Anderson.

Why Philadelphia Wins

San Antonio made good use of McNamara. Eighty-two games of reserve center play is a respectable return and prevents this from being a poor trade for the Spurs.

Philadelphia's patience produced much more. One distant second-round pick eventually became the trade chip for a player who logged almost 400 games for the 76ers and scored at a high level for multiple seasons.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, A-/B-. Philadelphia earns an A- for turning a 1988 second-rounder into Ron Anderson and five seasons of substantial production. San Antonio receives a B- for getting 82 games and a strong 1983-84 reserve season from McNamara. Confidence is high because the original trade, Stephens draft result, Stephens-for-Anderson trade and both players' team-specific production are documented in transaction and statistical records.
