perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Philadelphia's restricted free-agent rights to Earl Cureton on November 12, 1983 for two future second-round picks and cash. Cureton became a durable Pistons reserve, playing 234 regular-season games across three seasons with 20 starts, 4,566 minutes, 1,376 points and 1,210 rebounds. Philadelphia's 1989 pick became No. 54 Toney Mack, who never played an NBA regular-season game. The 76ers used the 1990 pick as compensation to sign World B. Free in 1986, but Free lasted only 20 Philadelphia games. Detroit received far more direct and sustained value.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Turned Free-Agent Rights Into Three Useful Seasons

Basketball-Reference's Detroit and Philadelphia transaction records show the November 12, 1983 compensation deal. Detroit acquired Philadelphia's agreement not to exercise its right of first refusal on restricted free agent Earl Cureton. The 76ers received Detroit's 1989 second-round pick, its 1990 second-round pick and cash.

Cureton was not a star acquisition, but he became exactly the kind of durable reserve that championship-level teams need.

Cureton Played 234 Games for Detroit

Cureton joined the Pistons immediately and appeared in 73 games in 1983-84. He logged 907 minutes, scored 193 points and collected 287 rebounds.

His role grew in 1984-85. Cureton played 81 games, started once and produced 496 points and 419 rebounds in 1,642 minutes.

He followed with his largest Detroit role in 1985-86, appearing in 80 games with 19 starts. Cureton logged 2,017 minutes, scored 687 points and grabbed 504 rebounds.

Across those three seasons, Detroit received 234 regular-season games, 20 starts, 4,566 minutes, 1,376 points and 1,210 rebounds. That is substantial realized value from a rights-compensation transaction.

The 1989 Pick Became Toney Mack

Philadelphia held the first pick until the 1989 draft and used it at No. 54 on Toney Mack.

Mack never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The selection therefore produced no on-court NBA return for the 76ers.

The 1990 Pick Became Compensation for World B. Free

Philadelphia did not keep the second pick until the 1990 draft. On December 30, 1986, the 76ers sent that future second-round selection to Cleveland as compensation for signing veteran guard World B. Free.

Free's Philadelphia return was brief. He appeared in 20 games, started two and logged 285 minutes. He averaged 5.8 points in 14.3 minutes while shooting 31.7 percent from the field.

Philadelphia waived Free in March 1987. Cleveland later used the pick at No. 52 in 1990 on Stefano Rusconi, but Rusconi's later NBA career does not count for Philadelphia because the 76ers had already surrendered the asset.

The cash portion remains part of Philadelphia's return, but the available record does not establish a value that could bridge the enormous on-court gap.

Why Detroit Wins

The Pistons received three full seasons of rotation frontcourt play. Philadelphia received one draft pick that produced no NBA player and used the other as compensation for a veteran who lasted only 20 games.

Even allowing for the unquantified cash and the process value of holding future picks, the realized basketball return clearly favors Detroit.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win, A-/C-. Detroit earns an A- for acquiring 234 games and three seasons of dependable frontcourt depth from Cureton. Philadelphia receives a C- because Toney Mack never played in the NBA and the second pick produced only a 20-game World B. Free stint before he was waived. Confidence is high because the compensation terms, Cureton's Pistons production, Mack draft outcome and Free transaction are documented in primary statistical records.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Philadelphia acquired Sam Williams from Golden State on November 12, 1983 for a 1984 second-round pick that became No. 45 Gary Plummer. Williams immediately became a useful 76ers reserve, playing 70 games with 12 starts in 1983-84 and 46 more with eight starts in 1984-85. Across two seasons he gave Philadelphia 116 games, 20 starts and 1,863 minutes. Golden State used the pick on Plummer, who played 66 games and 702 minutes as a rookie before leaving the NBA for several seasons. Both sides received usable depth, but Philadelphia got the larger and longer direct return.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Philadelphia Got Two Seasons From Sam Williams

Basketball-Reference records the November 12, 1983 trade as a straight player-for-pick exchange. Philadelphia sent Golden State its 1984 second-round selection for forward Sam Williams.

Golden State later used that pick at No. 45 on Gary Plummer. The deal therefore produced direct NBA rotation players for both teams, which makes the comparison closer than many late-pick trades.

Williams Became a Real 76ers Rotation Forward

Williams joined Philadelphia shortly after the season began and appeared in 70 games in 1983-84. He started 12, logged 1,375 minutes and produced 472 points and 326 rebounds.

He averaged 6.7 points and 4.7 rebounds in 19.6 minutes while shooting 47.7 percent from the field. Williams also appeared in four playoff games for a Philadelphia team trying to defend its 1983 title.

He returned in 1984-85 and played 46 more games with eight starts. His role was smaller, but he still contributed 488 minutes, 144 points and 106 rebounds.

Across the two seasons, Philadelphia received 116 regular-season games, 20 starts and 1,863 minutes from Williams.

Golden State Used the Pick on Gary Plummer

The Warriors held the incoming second-rounder and selected Boston University forward Gary Plummer at No. 45 in the 1984 draft.

Plummer played 66 games for Golden State as a rookie, all off the bench. He logged 702 minutes, scored 250 points and collected 134 rebounds.

He averaged 3.8 points and 2.0 rebounds in 10.6 minutes. Plummer then missed the 1985-86 season with injury and spent several years outside the NBA before returning with Denver in 1992-93.

That later Denver season does not count for Golden State. The Warriors' realized return from the pick is the 66-game rookie season.

Why Philadelphia Gets the Edge

Neither side made a franchise-changing move. Golden State received an NBA player from a second-round pick, which is a legitimate success and deserves a positive grade.

Philadelphia simply received more. Williams played 50 more games, logged more than twice as many minutes and started 20 times across two seasons. The 76ers also got that production immediately rather than waiting until the following draft.

The transaction was useful for both teams, but the scale of direct realized value favors Philadelphia.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, B+/C+. Philadelphia earns a B+ for turning one second-round pick into 116 games and two seasons of rotation frontcourt play. Golden State receives a C+ because Plummer made the roster and contributed 66 games as a rookie but did not become a lasting Warriors piece. Confidence is high because the trade terms, draft result and both players' team-specific production are documented in primary statistical records.

Williams joined Philadelphia shortly after the season began and appeared in 70 games in 1983-84. He started 12, logged 1,375 minutes and produced 472 points and 326 rebounds.

He averaged 6.7 points and 4.7 rebounds in 19.6 minutes while shooting 47.7 percent from the field. Williams also appeared in four playoff games for a Philadelphia team trying to defend its 1983 title.

He returned in 1984-85 and played 46 more games with eight starts. His role was smaller, but he still contributed 488 minutes, 144 points and 106 rebounds.

Across the two seasons, Philadelphia received 116 regular-season games, 20 starts and 1,863 minutes from Williams.

Golden State Used the Pick on Gary Plummer

The Warriors held the incoming second-rounder and selected Boston University forward Gary Plummer at No. 45 in the 1984 draft.

Plummer played 66 games for Golden State as a rookie, all off the bench. He logged 702 minutes, scored 250 points and collected 134 rebounds.

He averaged 3.8 points and 2.0 rebounds in 10.6 minutes. Plummer then missed the 1985-86 season with injury and spent several years outside the NBA before returning with Denver in 1992-93.

That later Denver season does not count for Golden State. The Warriors' realized return from the pick is the 66-game rookie season.

Why Philadelphia Gets the Edge

Neither side made a franchise-changing move. Golden State received an NBA player from a second-round pick, which is a legitimate success and deserves a positive grade.

Philadelphia simply received more. Williams played 50 more games, logged more than twice as many minutes and started 20 times across two seasons. The 76ers also got that production immediately rather than waiting until the following draft.

The transaction was useful for both teams, but the scale of direct realized value favors Philadelphia.

Final Verdict

76ers Win, B+/C+. Philadelphia earns a B+ for turning one second-round pick into 116 games and two seasons of rotation frontcourt play. Golden State receives a C+ because Plummer made the roster and contributed 66 games as a rookie but did not become a lasting Warriors piece. Confidence is high because the trade terms, draft result and both players' team-specific production are documented in primary statistical records.

Brewer gave the Spurs 49 games across parts of two seasons, including 40 games, five starts and 782 minutes in 1983-84. golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Used the Pick as Trade Currency

Basketball-Reference records the January 20, 1984 deal as Ron Brewer from Golden State to San Antonio for a 1985 second-round pick.

Brewer had been a productive NBA scorer earlier in his career, but by 1983-84 his role had diminished. San Antonio still got useful immediate minutes. Golden State chose the longer asset path.

Brewer Played 49 Games for the Spurs

Brewer appeared in 40 games for San Antonio after the trade and started five. He logged 782 minutes, scored 348 points and shot 44.1 percent from the field.

He averaged 8.7 points in 19.6 minutes, giving the Spurs a legitimate reserve scorer for the second half of the season.

Brewer returned in 1984-85 but his role collapsed. He appeared in nine San Antonio games, all off the bench, totaling 81 minutes and 33 points before moving on to New Jersey.

Across the two seasons, San Antonio received 49 regular-season games, five starts, 863 minutes and 381 points.

Golden State Did Not Use the Pick on Manute Bol

The incoming pick ultimately became the No. 31 selection in the 1985 draft, where Washington selected Manute Bol. Golden State had already traded the pick away before draft night.

On June 17, 1985, the Warriors sent this 1985 second-rounder plus a 1987 second-round pick to Washington for veteran forward Greg Ballard.

That distinction matters. Bol's Washington career cannot be credited to Golden State. The Warriors' legitimate downstream return is Ballard, acquired with this pick and one additional second-round selection.

Ballard Gave Golden State Two Productive Seasons

Ballard played 75 games for the Warriors in 1985-86, starting 14. He logged 1,792 minutes, scored 662 points and grabbed 417 rebounds.

He returned in 1986-87 for all 82 games with seven starts, adding 1,579 minutes, 579 points and 340 rebounds. Golden State reached the playoffs that season.

Across the two years, Ballard gave the Warriors 157 games, 21 starts, 3,371 minutes, 1,241 points and 757 rebounds.

Because Golden State also surrendered a 1987 second-round pick in the Ballard trade, only part of that return should be assigned to the San Antonio pick.

Why Golden State Gets the Slight Edge

San Antonio received real value from Brewer, but it was concentrated in 40 useful games after the trade and nine low-minute games the next season.

Golden State's pick became one of two assets used to acquire two full seasons from Ballard. Even discounting the return to account for the second pick, the Warriors extracted a longer and more substantial franchise benefit.

Final Verdict

Slight Warriors Edge, B/B-. Golden State earns a B for converting the pick into meaningful trade currency that helped acquire 157 games from Ballard. San Antonio receives a B- for getting 49 games and one useful partial season from Brewer. Confidence is high on the transaction chain and team-specific production, with the grade deliberately limiting how much Ballard value is assigned to one of two outgoing picks.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Keith Edmonson from San Antonio on January 21, 1984 for a 1984 third-round pick that became No. 57 Joe Binion. Edmonson's Nuggets tenure was brief: 15 games, 101 minutes and 64 points over the rest of the 1983-84 season. San Antonio selected Binion but never received an NBA regular-season game from him; he spent the next two seasons in the CBA and eventually made his NBA debut with Portland in 1986-87. The stakes were small on both sides, but Denver at least received direct NBA minutes, giving the Nuggets a narrow realized-value edge.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Got a Short Bench Stint; San Antonio Got No NBA Games

Basketball-Reference records the January 21, 1984 exchange as Keith Edmonson from San Antonio to Denver for the Nuggets' 1984 third-round pick.

The pick eventually became No. 57 Joe Binion. Neither branch developed into a lasting franchise piece, so this trade is best judged on modest direct production rather than name value or hypothetical upside.

Edmonson Played 15 Games for Denver

Edmonson had appeared in 40 games for San Antonio earlier in 1983-84. After the trade, his Denver role was much smaller.

He played 15 games for the Nuggets, all off the bench, and logged 101 minutes. Basketball-Reference credits him with 64 points, 18 rebounds and seven assists while shooting 48.9 percent from the field.

Edmonson averaged only 6.7 minutes per game, but he did provide actual regular-season depth during a Denver season that ended with a playoff berth.

Those 15 games were the end of his NBA career. He did not return to the league after 1983-84.

San Antonio Used the Pick on Joe Binion

The Spurs kept the third-round selection and used it at No. 57 in the 1984 NBA Draft on North Carolina A&T forward Joe Binion.

Binion did not play for San Antonio. Basketball-Reference lists him as spending 1984-85 and 1985-86 outside the NBA in the CBA.

His NBA debut did not come until February 1987, when he appeared in 11 games for Portland. Those 11 games and 51 minutes belong to the Trail Blazers, not to San Antonio's return from this trade.

The Spurs therefore received zero NBA regular-season games from the pick.

Why Denver Gets the Edge

This is a low-impact result. Denver received only 101 minutes from Edmonson, so the trade cannot earn a strong grade.

San Antonio's pick did identify a player who eventually reached the NBA, but the Spurs never received a game from him. Realized franchise value therefore favors Denver simply because Edmonson actually appeared for the Nuggets.

Final Verdict

Slight Nuggets Edge, C-/D. Denver earns a C- for getting 15 games and 101 minutes from Edmonson at the cost of a third-round pick. San Antonio receives a D because No. 57 Joe Binion never appeared in a Spurs regular-season game. Confidence is high because the trade, Edmonson's Denver totals, Binion's draft slot and his later Portland debut are all documented in primary statistical records.

perspectives.summary: Chicago traded Reggie Theus to Kansas City on February 15, 1984 for Steve Johnson and three second-round picks. Theus became a long-term Kings starter, playing 346 regular-season games through 1987-88 and producing 6,492 points and 2,809 assists. Chicago still extracted substantial value: Johnson played 105 Bulls games before he and the Mike Brittain pick were traded for Gene Banks, who added 145 Bulls games and 1,505 points. Another pick became Ken Johnson and helped bring Mike Smrek, while Greg Wiltjer never reached the NBA. Kansas City/Sacramento won because Theus delivered the best sustained individual return, but Chicago's multi-branch return was far stronger than a simple draft miss.
perspectives.analysis:
Kansas City Paid a Real Package for a Real Starting Guard

Basketball-Reference records the February 15, 1984 trade as Reggie Theus from Chicago to Kansas City for center Steve Johnson and three second-round picks: a 1984 selection that became Greg Wiltjer, a 1985 selection that became Ken Johnson and another 1985 selection that became Mike Brittain.

Theus had fallen out of Chicago's starting lineup in 1983-84, but he was only 26. Kansas City immediately restored him to a major role.

Theus Became a Four-Year Kings Centerpiece

Theus started all 30 games he played for Kansas City after the trade and averaged 15.8 points and 7.0 assists. He then started 80 games in 1984-85 and produced 1,341 points and 656 assists.

The franchise moved to Sacramento in 1985, and Theus remained a fixture. He played all 82 games in 1985-86, averaging 18.3 points and 9.6 assists, then appeared in 79 games in 1986-87 and 73 in 1987-88.

From the trade through the end of 1987-88, Theus played 346 regular-season games for the Kings franchise, nearly all as a starter, with 6,492 points and 2,809 assists.

That is the strongest individual return in the deal by a wide margin.

Chicago Received More Than Draft Picks That Failed

Steve Johnson gave the Bulls immediate center production. He played 31 games with nine starts after the trade, then 74 games with 54 starts in 1984-85.

Across those two seasons, Johnson gave Chicago 105 games and 63 starts. His 1984-85 line alone included 743 points and 437 rebounds.

Chicago then used Johnson as a trade asset. On June 18, 1985, the Bulls packaged Johnson with the Mike Brittain second-round pick from this Theus trade and acquired Gene Banks from San Antonio.

Banks became a substantial Chicago contributor. He played all 82 games in 1985-86, started 33 and scored 895 points. He added 63 games, 39 starts and 610 points in 1986-87.

Because both outgoing pieces in the Banks transaction came directly from the Theus trade, Banks' 145 games and 1,505 Bulls points are legitimate downstream value from this branch.

The Other Picks Had Mixed Outcomes

Chicago used the 1984 second-rounder at No. 43 on Greg Wiltjer, who never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

The Ken Johnson pick became No. 28 in 1985. Chicago immediately traded Ken Johnson and Ben Coleman to Portland for Mike Smrek. Smrek played 38 Bulls games in 1985-86. Because Coleman was an additional outside asset, only part of Smrek's return should be assigned to this pick.

The Mike Brittain pick, meanwhile, never became a Bulls player because it was part of the Banks trade.

Why the Kings Still Win

Chicago did not come away empty. Johnson gave the Bulls two useful seasons, Banks added two more, and the Ken Johnson branch contributed to another roster move. The package created hundreds of games of downstream value.

Theus still provided the best and most sustained return. He was a high-minute starting guard for more than four seasons, carried a large scoring and playmaking load and remained one of the franchise's primary offensive players after the move to Sacramento.

Final Verdict

Kings Win, A/B+. Kansas City/Sacramento earns an A for acquiring 346 games of high-level starting guard production from Theus. Chicago earns a B+ because Johnson, Banks and the draft branches created substantial multi-year value even though no single return matched Theus. Confidence is high because the trade terms, player production and subsequent Johnson/Brittain and Ken Johnson transactions are all documented in team transaction records.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee signed veteran free agent Mike Dunleavy Sr. on March 8, 1984 and sent San Antonio a 1984 fourth-round pick as compensation. Dunleavy played 36 regular-season games for the Bucks across parts of 1983-84 and 1984-85, starting 31 and providing experienced point-guard minutes for two division-winning teams. San Antonio used the pick at No. 90 on Ozell Jones, who played 67 games with six starts in 1984-85 and gave the Spurs 888 minutes, 238 rebounds and 57 blocks. The two sides received different but comparable one-to-two-season rotation value, making the completed outcome effectively even.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Both Teams Converted a Low-Cost Asset Into Rotation Minutes

Basketball-Reference records the March 8, 1984 transaction as a veteran free-agent compensation move. Milwaukee signed Mike Dunleavy Sr., and San Antonio received the Bucks' 1984 fourth-round pick.

The pick became No. 90 Ozell Jones. Unlike many late-round compensation trades, both branches actually produced regular-season NBA minutes for the receiving franchise.

Dunleavy Joined a Contender Immediately

Dunleavy joined Milwaukee late in the 1983-84 season and stepped straight into the starting lineup. He appeared in 17 games, started 12 and logged 404 minutes.

He averaged 11.2 points and 4.6 assists while shooting 55.1 percent from the field and 42.2 percent from three-point range. The Bucks won 50 games, won the Central Division and reached the Eastern Conference Finals.

Dunleavy returned in 1984-85 and started all 19 games he played. He logged another 433 minutes, averaging 8.9 points and 4.5 assists on a 59-win Milwaukee team.

Across the two seasons, Milwaukee received 36 regular-season games, 31 starts and 837 minutes from the signing.

San Antonio Found an NBA Player at No. 90

The Spurs used the compensation pick in the fourth round of the 1984 draft on center Ozell Jones.

Jones made the roster and played 67 games in 1984-85, starting six. He logged 888 minutes, scored 245 points, grabbed 238 rebounds and blocked 57 shots.

He averaged 3.7 points, 3.6 rebounds and 0.9 blocks in 13.3 minutes while shooting 58.9 percent from the field.

Jones left San Antonio after that season and appeared in only three more NBA games, all with the Clippers. Still, getting 67 games from the No. 90 selection was a productive result.

Why This Is Even

Milwaukee received the better short-term offensive role. Dunleavy started 31 of his 36 Bucks games and contributed meaningful playmaking on two strong playoff teams.

San Antonio received more total games and slightly more minutes from Jones, plus legitimate rebounding and rim-protection value from an extremely late draft pick.

Neither return lasted long enough or reached a high enough level to create a decisive edge. The available transaction record also does not establish a cash amount large enough to alter the basketball comparison.

Final Verdict

Even Trade, B-/B-. Milwaukee earns a B- for adding 36 games and 31 starts of useful veteran guard play at a low acquisition cost. San Antonio also earns a B- for converting the compensation pick into 67 games and 888 minutes from Jones. Confidence is high because the signing, compensation pick, draft result and both players' team-specific production are documented in primary statistical records.

perspectives.summary: Denver traded Kiki Vandeweghe to Portland on June 7, 1984 for Fat Lever, Calvin Natt, Wayne Cooper, a 1984 second-round pick that became Willie White and a 1985 first-round pick that became Blair Rasmussen. Portland received 285 games and 6,698 points from Vandeweghe, including a 26.9-point season in 1986-87. Denver received vastly more aggregate value: Lever became a two-time All-Star and All-NBA guard across 474 Nuggets games, Natt was an All-Star in his first Denver season, Cooper became a starting center, Rasmussen played 429 Nuggets games, and White added 82 games. Both sides did well, but Denver won decisively on depth and longevity.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Traded One All-Star Scorer for an Entire Core

The June 7, 1984 deal sent Kiki Vandeweghe from Denver to Portland for Fat Lever, Calvin Natt, Wayne Cooper, Portland's 1984 second-round pick and its 1985 first-round pick.

Vandeweghe was coming off a 29.4-point All-Star season, so Portland was paying for an established scorer in his prime. The Trail Blazers got what they wanted. The Nuggets still extracted one of the deepest multi-asset returns of the decade.

Vandeweghe Gave Portland Elite Scoring

Vandeweghe played 72 games in his first Portland season and averaged 22.4 points while shooting 53.4 percent. He followed with 24.8 points in 1985-86 and a career Portland peak of 26.9 in 1986-87.

He remained with the Trail Blazers through part of 1988-89. Across five Portland seasons, Vandeweghe appeared in 285 regular-season games and scored 6,698 points.

That is major realized value. Portland did not acquire a short-term rental or a fading veteran; it got several years of high-efficiency scoring from the centerpiece it targeted.

Lever Became a Franchise-Level Denver Guard

Fat Lever became the defining asset on Denver's side.

He started all 82 games in his first Nuggets season and averaged 12.8 points, 7.5 assists, 5.0 rebounds and 2.5 steals. By 1986-87 he was averaging 18.9 points, 8.9 rebounds and 8.0 assists while earning All-NBA honors.

Lever made two All-Star teams as a Nugget and earned an All-Defensive selection. Across six Denver seasons from 1984-85 through 1989-90, he played 474 regular-season games.

Denver therefore received a long-term two-way lead guard, not merely a replacement scorer.

Natt and Cooper Made the First-Year Return Even Bigger

Calvin Natt was immediately outstanding. He played 78 games in 1984-85, started 76 and averaged 23.3 points and 7.8 rebounds while making the All-Star team.

Natt followed with 17.7 points in 69 games in 1985-86 before injuries derailed the later part of his Denver tenure. Even with the shortened stay, his first two seasons gave the Nuggets another high-level starter.

Wayne Cooper also became a starting center. In 1984-85 he played 80 games, started 78 and averaged 12.1 points, 7.9 rebounds and 2.5 blocks. His rim protection and size gave Denver another immediate frontcourt piece from the same trade.

The Picks Kept Producing

Denver used the 1984 second-rounder at No. 42 on Willie White. White played 82 Nuggets games across two seasons and provided low-minute guard depth.

The 1985 first-rounder became No. 15 Blair Rasmussen. Rasmussen developed into a long-term Denver center, playing 429 regular-season games for the Nuggets from 1985-86 through 1990-91.

His role grew from reserve minutes to repeated starting assignments. Rasmussen started 45 games in 1987-88 and 55 in 1989-90, giving Denver another multi-year rotation player from the original Vandeweghe package.

Why Denver Wins Despite Portland's Strong Return

Portland deserves a high grade. Vandeweghe delivered nearly 6,700 points and multiple seasons as a 20-plus-point scorer, so calling the Trail Blazers' side a failure would badly misrepresent the outcome.

Denver simply received too much. Lever became an All-NBA, All-Star and All-Defensive guard. Natt made an All-Star team. Cooper became a starting center. Rasmussen supplied six seasons of center depth, and White added another 82 games.

No single Denver asset has to exceed Vandeweghe's Portland scoring for the Nuggets to win. The combined return created multiple starters, awards-level seasons and years of depth across several positions.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A+/A-. Denver earns an A+ for converting one star scorer into Lever, Natt, Cooper, Rasmussen and White, a package that produced enormous multi-year value. Portland earns an A- because Vandeweghe delivered 285 games, 6,698 points and several elite scoring seasons. Confidence is high because the trade terms, draft outcomes and team-specific production are fully documented in statistical records.

He started all 82 games in his first Nuggets season and averaged 12.8 points, 7.5 assists, 5.0 rebounds and 2.5 steals. By 1986-87 he was averaging 18.9 points, 8.9 rebounds and 8.0 assists while earning All-NBA honors.

Lever made two All-Star teams as a Nugget and earned an All-Defensive selection. Across six Denver seasons from 1984-85 through 1989-90, he played 474 regular-season games.

Denver therefore received a long-term two-way lead guard, not merely a replacement scorer.

Natt and Cooper Made the First-Year Return Even Bigger

Calvin Natt was immediately outstanding. He played 78 games in 1984-85, started 76 and averaged 23.3 points and 7.8 rebounds while making the All-Star team.

Natt followed with 17.7 points in 69 games in 1985-86 before injuries derailed the later part of his Denver tenure. Even with the shortened stay, his first two seasons gave the Nuggets another high-level starter.

Wayne Cooper also became a starting center. In 1984-85 he played 80 games, started 78 and averaged 12.1 points, 7.9 rebounds and 2.5 blocks. His rim protection and size gave Denver another immediate frontcourt piece from the same trade.

The Picks Kept Producing

Denver used the 1984 second-rounder at No. 42 on Willie White. White played 82 Nuggets games across two seasons and provided low-minute guard depth.

The 1985 first-rounder became No. 15 Blair Rasmussen. Rasmussen developed into a long-term Denver center, playing 429 regular-season games for the Nuggets from 1985-86 through 1990-91.

His role grew from reserve minutes to repeated starting assignments. Rasmussen started 45 games in 1987-88 and 55 in 1989-90, giving Denver another multi-year rotation player from the original Vandeweghe package.

Why Denver Wins Despite Portland's Strong Return

Portland deserves a high grade. Vandeweghe delivered nearly 6,700 points and multiple seasons as a 20-plus-point scorer, so calling the Trail Blazers' side a failure would badly misrepresent the outcome.

Denver simply received too much. Lever became an All-NBA, All-Star and All-Defensive guard. Natt made an All-Star team. Cooper became a starting center. Rasmussen supplied six seasons of center depth, and White added another 82 games.

No single Denver asset has to exceed Vandeweghe's Portland scoring for the Nuggets to win. The combined return created multiple starters, awards-level seasons and years of depth across several positions.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win, A+/A-. Denver earns an A+ for converting one star scorer into Lever, Natt, Cooper, Rasmussen and White, a package that produced enormous multi-year value. Portland earns an A- because Vandeweghe delivered 285 games, 6,698 points and several elite scoring seasons. Confidence is high because the trade terms, draft outcomes and team-specific production are fully documented in statistical records.

detroit-pistons.analysis: Detroit's June 1984 choice was to consolidate several young frontcourt and draft assets into established veteran Dan Roundfield. analysis: The June 18, 1984 Roundfield trade was a four-asset return for Atlanta, not Dan Roundfield straight across for Cliff Levingston. The Pistons sent Levingston and the NBA rights to Antoine Carr, plus second-round choices ultimately associated with 1986 No. 40 Augusto Binelli and 1987 No. 42 Terence Bailey. Levingston immediately became a Hawks rotation forward: 74 games, 53 starts and 2,017 minutes in 1984-85, then 81 games and 1,945 minutes in 1985-86. Carr also actually played for Atlanta: 62 games in 1984-85, 17 in 1985-86, 65 in 1986-87, 80 in 1987-88 and 78 in 1988-89. Those five seasons add up to 302 Hawks games, so the source editorial's old speculation about whether Carr ever became an Atlanta contributor understated a documented return. Detroit acquired an experienced veteran but received only 56 Roundfield games and 43 starts, 1,492 minutes and 611 points in 1984-85 before he moved to Washington. The two future picks mattered as asset rights, but the actual NBA contributions of Binelli and Bailey must not be silently assigned to the Hawks without the players joining the roster. The contrast between Detroit's one-season Roundfield stint and Atlanta's multi-season Levingston/Carr returns explains the existing Hawks Win and Atlanta A-/Detroit B result without counting Levingston's later Chicago championships for Atlanta or Roundfield's earlier Hawks honors for Detroit.

perspectives.analysis:
A Draft-Day Chain Created Useful Returns for Three Teams

The June 19, 1984 transaction began with Cleveland, Washington and the draft rights to two first-round centers. Cleveland had selected Tim McCormick at No. 12. Washington had selected Mel Turpin at No. 6.

Basketball-Reference records Cleveland sending McCormick's rights and Cliff Robinson to Washington for Turpin's rights. Washington then immediately sent McCormick and veteran guard Ricky Sobers to Seattle for Gus Williams.

That second move means Washington's return from the Cleveland trade was not simply Robinson plus McCormick. McCormick became part of the package that brought Williams, while Seattle gained the young center it wanted.

Turpin Became Cleveland's Starting Center

Mel Turpin played 79 games as a rookie in 1984-85 and started 45. He logged 1,949 minutes, scored 835 points, grabbed 452 rebounds and blocked 87 shots.

His role grew in 1985-86. Turpin appeared in 80 games, started 69 and produced 1,097 points, 556 rebounds and 106 blocks.

He played 64 more Cavaliers games in 1986-87. Across three Cleveland seasons, Turpin produced 223 regular-season games and 2,325 points.

The Cavaliers did not get an All-Star, but they did get three seasons of legitimate center production from the No. 6 rights they acquired.

Washington Received Two Strong Branches

Cliff Robinson gave Washington immediate frontcourt scoring. He played 60 games with 37 starts in 1984-85 and averaged 16.7 points and 9.1 rebounds.

Robinson followed with 78 games, all starts, in 1985-86 and averaged 18.7 points and 8.7 rebounds. Across those two seasons, he gave the Bullets 138 games and 2,463 points before moving to Philadelphia.

The McCormick branch also became productive. Washington packaged McCormick's rights with Ricky Sobers and acquired Gus Williams from Seattle the same day.

Williams became Washington's starting point guard. He played 79 games with 78 starts in 1984-85, averaging 20.0 points, 7.7 assists and 2.3 steals. He added 77 games and 67 starts in 1985-86, averaging 13.5 points and 5.9 assists.

Because Sobers was an additional Washington asset, the entire Williams return cannot be assigned solely to McCormick. Still, McCormick was a central part of the package, so a meaningful share of those 156 games belongs to this trade tree.

Seattle Got the Young Center It Wanted

The SuperSonics made McCormick the centerpiece of their side. Contemporary reporting identified the 6-foot-11 Michigan center as the player Seattle targeted for interior help behind Jack Sikma.

McCormick played 78 games with 27 starts as a rookie, averaging 9.3 points and 5.1 rebounds. He followed with 77 games and 42 starts in 1985-86.

Across two Seattle seasons, McCormick gave the Sonics 155 games and 69 starts before he was traded to Philadelphia in 1986.

Why Washington Gets the Slight Edge

Cleveland received a starting center for three seasons. Seattle received two productive seasons from a young center. Neither result was poor.

Washington received the broadest combination of value: two strong seasons from Robinson plus a key trade chip that helped land Williams, who immediately became a 20-point, 7.7-assist starting guard.

Final Verdict

Slight Wizards Edge, A/A-/A-. Washington earns an A for combining Robinson's 138 games and high-level scoring with a major role in the Williams acquisition. Cleveland earns an A- for 223 games and three seasons from Turpin. Seattle also earns an A- for 155 games and 69 starts from McCormick. Confidence is high because the draft-day transactions and the team-specific production for Turpin, Robinson, Williams and McCormick are all documented in transaction and statistical records.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State traded the draft rights to No. 31 pick Jay Murphy to the San Diego Clippers on June 19, 1984 for veteran center Jerome Whitehead. Whitehead became an immediate Warriors starter, playing 79 games with 78 starts in 1984-85 and remaining with Golden State for four seasons. Across that span he played 305 regular-season games, including 109 starts, and supplied steady center minutes. Murphy played only 37 games and 249 minutes for the Clippers across two seasons, never starting a game, before finishing his brief NBA career in Washington. Golden State won decisively by turning one second-round pick into four years of frontcourt production.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Turned a Second-Round Pick Into a Four-Year Center

The June 19, 1984 draft-day trade was straightforward. Golden State selected Jay Murphy with the No. 31 pick and immediately sent his rights to the San Diego Clippers for Jerome Whitehead.

Whitehead was already an established NBA center. Murphy was a second-round rookie. The gap in realized value became obvious almost immediately.

Whitehead Started 78 Games in His First Warriors Season

Whitehead stepped directly into Golden State's starting lineup in 1984-85. He appeared in 79 games, started 78 and logged 2,536 minutes.

Basketball-Reference credits him with 1,026 points and 622 rebounds that season. He averaged 13.0 points and 7.9 rebounds while shooting 51.0 percent from the field.

The role became smaller in 1985-86, but Whitehead still played 81 games. He added 73 games in 1986-87 and 72 more in 1987-88.

Across four Warriors seasons, Whitehead played 305 regular-season games. Even after his first-year starting role diminished, he remained a durable rotation center and gave Golden State years of usable minutes from a single second-round selection.

Murphy Barely Played for the Clippers

Jay Murphy made the Clippers as a rookie but never developed into a rotation player.

He appeared in 23 games in 1984-85, all off the bench, and logged 149 minutes. He scored 28 points while shooting 16.0 percent from the field.

Murphy returned for 14 games in 1985-86 and logged another 100 minutes. His Clippers tenure therefore ended at 37 games, zero starts and 249 total minutes.

He later played 30 games across two seasons for Washington, but those appearances came after he left the Clippers and do not count as Los Angeles realized value from this trade.

Why Golden State Wins

The Warriors did more than get the better player. They acquired someone who immediately filled a starting position and then remained in the organization for four seasons.

The Clippers received a prospect, but Murphy never became a regular rotation forward. Thirty-seven low-minute games are a very small return for a center who gave Golden State more than 300 games.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win, A-/D. Golden State earns an A- for converting the No. 31 rights into 305 games and four seasons from Whitehead, including a 78-start first year. The Clippers receive a D because Murphy played only 37 games and 249 minutes for the franchise. Confidence is high because the draft-day trade and both players' team-specific production are documented in team transaction and statistical records.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia traded the draft rights to No. 22 pick Tom Sewell to Washington on June 19, 1984 for the Bullets' 1988 first-round pick. Sewell played only 21 games and 86 minutes for Washington in his lone NBA season. Philadelphia held the future first for two years, then included it with Moses Malone, Terry Catledge and a 1986 first-round pick in the 1986 trade that brought Cliff Robinson and Jeff Ruland to the 76ers. Washington ultimately reacquired the pick and used it at No. 12 on Harvey Grant, so Grant's career belongs to Washington's later 1986 transaction, not to Philadelphia's direct return. The 76ers won the 1984 exchange by turning a low-impact rookie into useful first-round trade capital.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Philadelphia Acquired a Valuable Future Asset, Not Harvey Grant Himself

The June 19, 1984 draft-day trade sent Tom Sewell's rights from Philadelphia to Washington for the Bullets' 1988 first-round pick.

The transaction ledger later labels that pick as the selection used on Harvey Grant. That label can be misleading if the later chain is ignored. Philadelphia did not draft Grant and should not receive credit for his Washington career.

The 76ers used the pick as trade currency two years before the 1988 draft.

Sewell Played Only 21 NBA Games

Washington acquired Sewell after Philadelphia selected him No. 22 overall.

His NBA career lasted one season. Sewell appeared in 21 games for the 1984-85 Bullets, never started and averaged only 4.1 minutes per game.

Basketball-Reference credits him with 86 total minutes and 21 points. He shot 25.0 percent from the field and did not return to the NBA after that season.

That makes Washington's direct 1984 return extremely small.

Philadelphia Held the Pick Until the Moses Malone Deal

The 76ers kept the 1988 first-rounder for two years.

perspectives.summary: New York signed restricted free agent Pat Cummings on June 27, 1984 and sent Dallas a 1985 third-round pick that became Leonard Allen and a 1986 second-round pick that became Mark Price as compensation. Cummings gave the Knicks 205 games across four seasons, including 113 starts and 2,246 points. Dallas received no NBA production from either pick: Allen never played in the league, and the Mavericks traded Price's rights to Cleveland on draft night for a 1989 second-round pick that became Jeff Hodge, who also never played an NBA regular-season game. New York won decisively by receiving four years of rotation frontcourt value while Dallas' two compensation branches produced zero Mavericks games.
perspectives.analysis:
The Famous Name in the Draft Chain Does Not Belong to Dallas

The June 27, 1984 compensation transaction followed New York's signing of Pat Cummings. Basketball-Reference records the Knicks sending Dallas a 1985 third-round pick and a 1986 second-round pick in exchange for the Mavericks' decision not to exercise their right of first refusal.

Those picks later became Leonard Allen and Mark Price.

Price became a four-time All-Star, but Dallas did not keep him. The Mavericks traded his draft rights to Cleveland immediately, so Price's Cavaliers career cannot be credited as Dallas realized value.

Cummings Gave New York Four Seasons

Cummings started 63 games for the Knicks in 1984-85 and averaged 15.8 points and 8.2 rebounds. He logged 2,069 minutes and scored 997 points.

He remained a starter for most of his second New York season, appearing in 31 games with 30 starts and averaging 15.7 points and 9.0 rebounds.

Cummings' role shrank in 1986-87 and 1987-88, but he stayed in the rotation. He played 49 games with 11 starts in 1986-87 and 62 games with nine starts in 1987-88.

Across four Knicks seasons, Cummings gave New York 205 regular-season games, 113 starts and 2,246 points. That is substantial direct value from a free-agent signing.

Leonard Allen Never Reached the NBA

Dallas used the 1985 third-round selection at No. 50 on San Diego State forward Leonard Allen.

Allen never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. That branch therefore produced zero direct Mavericks games.

Dallas Traded Mark Price for Another Future Pick

The second-round pick became No. 25 in the 1986 draft. Dallas selected Mark Price, then traded his rights to Cleveland on draft night for a 1989 second-round pick.

Price became one of the best guards of his era with the Cavaliers, but that production belongs to Cleveland. Dallas chose to convert his rights into another draft asset before he played an NBA game.

The 1989 second-rounder became No. 53 Jeff Hodge. Hodge never appeared in an NBA regular-season game.

Dallas therefore received zero NBA games from the full realized chain of both compensation picks.

Why New York Wins

Dallas deserves some process credit for receiving two picks rather than losing Cummings for nothing. The Price selection in particular shows the Mavericks identified major talent.

Realized value is what decides the verdict. New York received four years and more than 200 games from Cummings. Dallas ended the chain with Leonard Allen and Jeff Hodge, neither of whom played an NBA game.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win, A-/D. New York earns an A- for receiving 205 games, 113 starts and four seasons of frontcourt production from Cummings. Dallas receives a D because Allen never reached the NBA and the Price rights were traded for the pick that became Jeff Hodge, who also never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Confidence is high because the signing, compensation picks, Price draft-night trade and final draft outcomes are all documented in team transaction records.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Took Two Prospects in Exchange for Johnny Davis

Atlanta's 1984 agreement with Cleveland sent guard Johnny Davis to the Cavaliers while the Hawks acquired Stewart Granger and John Garris. The original transaction involved three named players, not future picks or a complicated draft swap. Davis brought NBA backcourt experience to Cleveland, whereas Atlanta gained two younger roster candidates to evaluate. The Hawks' decision could provide more options at different positions, but neither prospect's incoming name ensured a successful full-season rotation role. That distinction matters because the quantity of players received shouldn't automatically determine the winner of a trade.

Davis Offered the Cavaliers a More Certain Immediate Return

Johnny Davis had been a professional guard for multiple seasons, making him a more established option than either younger player Cleveland surrendered. He could bring ball-handling experience and a veteran baseline of competence, but his earlier games for other organizations can't be treated as newly produced Cavaliers minutes. Cleveland's front office preferred one identifiable contributor over two developmental possibilities. The cost was surrendering more than one player, which reduced its room to test younger talent. The question for this deal is whether Davis's next season of service justified that narrower roster option.

Atlanta's Return Was a Pair of Basketball Evaluations

Granger and Garris gave Atlanta two opportunities to compete for roles rather than one experienced veteran. Different skill sets could help the Hawks assemble depth without spending a valuable first-round selection. Their future NBA careers still had to be earned after arrival, and neither player should be described as an established Hawks starter on the date of the transaction. Atlanta's asset advantage is therefore about multiple roster options, not an automatic doubling of production. The club's longer-term performance depended chiefly on existing stars and other moves unrelated to this exchange.

A Narrow Hawks Preference Fits the Limited Stakes

Atlanta received two named personnel options while Cleveland acquired a known veteran guard, giving the Hawks a slightly broader evaluation opportunity. The teams were balancing immediate predictability against development flexibility, and both strategies had a recognizable purpose. Neither side gained a premium draft pick or an obvious future All-Star, so the result shouldn't be inflated into a major historical turning point. The slight Hawks edge reflects the number of potential contributors and their youth, with credit still due to Cleveland for targeting a guard with a genuine NBA résumé.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta Hawks earns B-; Cleveland Cavaliers earns C+. perspectives.summary: The August 23, 1984 Mavericks–Nuggets agreement let Denver sign Dallas restricted free agent Elston Turner when the Mavericks declined to exercise their right of first refusal. Denver sent Howard Carter to Dallas as compensation. Carter played just 11 games, 66 minutes and scored nine points for Dallas; Turner played 81 Nuggets games in 1984-85 and 73 more in 1985-86. The documented 154-to-11 appearance gap supports Nuggets Win, Denver B and Dallas C+, without crediting a later separate Denver stint to this arrangement.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Gained Access to Elston Turner

Dallas held a matching right on Turner, who had played 47 Mavericks games in 1983-84. Denver wanted the restricted free agent and offered Howard Carter so Dallas would not exercise that right. Dallas's own 1984-85 transaction ledger dates the exchange August 23, 1984. This was compensation for Dallas declining to match, not a conventional swap of two existing Denver and Dallas player contracts. The contractual distinction explains why Turner's eventual performance belongs in Denver's evaluation.

Carter's Dallas Opportunity Was Brief

Carter had scored 342 points over 55 games for Denver in 1983-84, before this agreement. He did not repeat that role in Dallas: 11 appearances, zero starts, 66 total minutes and nine points in 1984-85. Dallas waived him in December 1984, according to the Mavericks' dated transactions. His previous Denver output should not be counted as a benefit received by Dallas.

Turner's Two Denver Seasons Supplied the Return

Turner immediately appeared in 81 Nuggets games in 1984-85, supplying 414 points, 158 assists and 96 steals. In 1985-86 he added 73 games, 369 points, 165 assists and 70 steals. Those 154 appearances are traceable to Denver's August 1984 decision to secure Turner. His later contracts with Chicago and a later Denver return were separate roster moves, so those games are not added to the first Denver stint.

Verdict: Denver's Sustained Depth Beat Dallas's Short Trial

The Mavericks obtained compensation for letting a restricted free agent go, but Carter's playing contribution was minimal. The Nuggets turned that right-of-first-refusal agreement into two seasons of reliable guard and wing depth. Nuggets Win with Denver B and Dallas C+ is supported by the specific posttransaction minutes, games and defensive production rather than stock arguments about draft picks or hypothetical later trades. The preserved underlying sources include Dallas's official media-guide transaction record and both players' season statistics.

houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Exchanged a Third-Round Right for Hank McDowell

Houston and the Los Angeles Clippers reached an agreement on August 29, 1984 that sent Hank McDowell to the Rockets in exchange for a 1985 third-round draft selection. The historical draft ledger eventually associates that selection with No. 65 Kenny Perry. Houston preferred to take a look at an available frontcourt player before the season, while Los Angeles converted a player it could part with into a future development chance. The Clippers had recently relocated from San Diego, so the change in franchise location is relevant to the date. This deal didn't contain a first-round selection or an established All-Star.

McDowell's NBA Prospects Were Still Being Evaluated

McDowell was a center and forward prospect whose value depended on how the Rockets would use him, rather than his previous draft reputation alone. Houston could examine whether he fit behind its taller frontcourt players and whether he earned rotation minutes. Acquiring his name on an official transaction ledger did not ensure he would become a substantial new NBA scorer. The team gave up a later selection rather than immediate veteran help, so its practical wager was that an existing player's readiness outweighed an uncertain draft slot. His career after the trade must be assessed separately from what Houston hoped to gain.

Los Angeles Held a Traceable 1985 Draft Asset

The Clippers' incoming third-round choice ultimately connects to the No. 65 Kenny Perry position. In 1985, that was a legitimate professional draft round, but it carried limited certainty of a regular-season roster place. The franchise could select a prospect or deal the pick before the draft; either pathway would require following the individual rights chain. Another transaction in September 1984 involving the Clippers and Washington also references a 1985 No. 65 pick, so those related records need careful reconciliation rather than treating two No. 65 positions as different assets. The direct August return is one third-round right.

The Draft Opportunity Slightly Outweighs the Player Experiment

Los Angeles gave up McDowell but gained a pick it could put toward a future roster, whereas Houston received a chance to test the big man's immediate NBA usefulness. Neither side secured a reliable starter and the draft-rights trail is narrower than some later summaries imply. The Clippers receive a modest edge because the recorded selection gave them another developmental option, while McDowell's new Rockets contribution didn't become a major historical story. This is a small trade whose value is better conveyed through its precise pick and player than through unrelated franchise achievements.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win, narrowly. Los Angeles earns C+ for the 1985 third-round selection associated with No. 65 Kenny Perry, while Houston receives C- for Hank McDowell's limited upside as a frontcourt option. A related later No. 65 transaction requires rights-chain reconciliation; the August deal shouldn't be counted as creating two separate picks.

perspectives.summary: On September 14, 1984, Dallas obtained seven-foot center Wallace Bryant from Chicago for a CONDITIONAL 1986 second-round draft choice. Bryant supplied 65 Mavericks games across parts of two seasons and 43 starts before Dallas waived him. Chicago did NOT use the eventual No. 39 pick on Rafael Addison: the Bulls transferred that right to Phoenix in October 1985, along with a separate 1990 second, as compensation in free agent Kyle Macy’s signing. Phoenix selected Addison and received his 1986-87 Suns minutes. The original Even Trade, Dallas B- and Chicago B-, compares Bryant’s limited Dallas playing time with Chicago’s transferable draft asset and its partial contribution to the later Macy transaction.
perspectives.analysis:
September 14, 1984: Chicago Sold a Reserve Center for a Conditional Future Pick
Dallas acquired seven-foot center Wallace Bryant from the Chicago Bulls on September 14, 1984, sending Chicago a conditional 1986 second-round choice. Bryant had made 29 Chicago NBA appearances before the trade; those prior Bulls minutes did not travel to Dallas. The pick was a future paper right in 1984, not already the named No. 39 selection of Rafael Addison. The eventual 1986 draft identity can be tracked without incorrectly assigning the player to the franchise that briefly held the selection. There was no third active player in the original Dallas-Chicago package.

Bryant Gave Dallas an Immediate 65-Game Center Option
Bryant appeared 56 times for the Mavericks during 1984-85, with 35 starts, 860 minutes, 164 total points and 241 rebounds. Dallas played him nine additional times in 1985-86, eight as a starter, before waiving him on November 26, 1985. The resulting direct Mavericks return is 65 games and 43 starts: a brief but tangible backup center contribution. His subsequent eight Clippers games are not additional Dallas NBA production, and his 29 pretrade Chicago appearances cannot be attributed to the Mavericks retroactively. This limits the grade despite some usable frontcourt depth.

Chicago Redirected the Draft Right to Phoenix in 1985
The Bulls did not retain the incoming 1986 second through the following draft. On October 4, 1985, Chicago sent the Dallas-origin choice to Phoenix together with a separate 1990 second-round selection to resolve compensation associated with the Bulls’ signing of free agent Kyle Macy. Chicago therefore converted one 1984 rights asset into part of a two-pick bargaining package. Macy was not acquired solely for Wallace Bryant: the other Chicago second was additional consideration. The distinction makes the later personnel chain credible without multiplying a single future right into a full NBA player career.

Rafael Addison Was a Suns Draft Selection, Not a Bulls Player
The 1986 pick ultimately conveyed as No. 39 and Phoenix selected Rafael Addison. He played 62 NBA regular-season games for the Suns in 1986-87, not for Chicago. Those Phoenix appearances can establish the eventual player identity and value of the pick to its final owner, but they cannot be booked as direct Chicago player performance. The historical transaction record should distinguish Chicago holding the future conditional right for about a year, its use in the Kyle Macy compensation package, and Phoenix exercising that right on Addison later. All three steps belong to different transactions and dates.

Why the B-Minus Tie Is Plausible Without Misallocating Players
Dallas acquired a usable reserve center who started 43 times over 65 games before departing. Chicago accepted future draft flexibility and used the resulting second-round right as one component of an unrelated free-agent compensation agreement. Neither branch independently created a long-term franchise centerpiece, and Chicago cannot claim all of Kyle Macy’s performance by ignoring the separately sent 1990 second. The preserved Even Trade and B- grades for both clubs represent different kinds of modest return: direct player minutes for Dallas, traceable future pick liquidity for Chicago.

Final Verdict
The original September 1984 exchange was Bryant to Dallas for Chicago’s conditional 1986 second-round right. Bryant played 65 Mavericks games. Chicago later included the right in two-pick Kyle Macy signing compensation with Phoenix, which selected Addison at No. 39. Addison’s NBA Suns minutes are not Chicago receiving-team service. The Even Trade, Chicago B-/Dallas B- remains the archival verdict, now grounded in actual asset custody rather than a false implied Bulls Addison tenure.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana acquired former 1983 first-rounder Leo Rautins from Philadelphia on September 14, 1984, sending its 1987 third-round draft choice in return. The Pacers waived Rautins on October 4 before he played an Indiana NBA regular-season game. Philadelphia later used the conveyed choice at No. 57 on Hansi Gnad in 1987, but Gnad never played in an NBA regular-season game for the 76ers. Neither incoming asset supplied its new franchise any NBA minutes. The inherited Slight 76ers Edge (Philadelphia C+, Indiana C) recognizes an exercised later draft right, not a valuable rotation player.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The September 1984 Package: A Former First-Round Player for a Future Third
On September 14, 1984, the Indiana Pacers received Leo Rautins from the Philadelphia 76ers and surrendered their 1987 third-round selection. Philadelphia had picked Rautins No. 17 in 1983, but his only 76ers NBA season produced 28 games and 196 minutes. The future third-rounder did not convey a named NBA player in 1984. It was a draft right whose ultimate selection could be assessed only once the 1987 draft occurred. The package contains that single outgoing right and the incoming former first-round forward, not an extra player or cash.

Rautins Did Not Make Indiana’s Regular-Season Roster
The Pacers waived Rautins on October 4, 1984, twenty days after trading for him. He recorded zero NBA regular-season minutes for Indiana. Atlanta subsequently signed him on October 15 and used him in four games totaling 12 minutes, but those Hawks appearances belong to Atlanta after a separate acquisition. His previous 28 Philadelphia games also predate the Pacers trade. Counting his total NBA career line as an Indiana return would misattribute two other franchises’ playing time to this transaction.

Philadelphia Converted the Right into the No. 57 Selection
In 1987, Philadelphia exercised the Pacers-origin third-round choice at No. 57 to draft Hansi Gnad. The third NBA draft round existed that year, so this was a real selected player, not a pick eliminated by a later league rule or an unexercised future right. Gnad had a substantial basketball career outside the NBA, but the historical 76ers record establishes no NBA regular-season minutes for him. Philadelphia therefore retained and exercised a future selection opportunity, not an on-court Philadelphia contributor.

Why the Inherited Grades Are Nearly Equal
The original verdict is Slight 76ers Edge with Philadelphia C+ and Indiana C. The Pacers lost a legitimate 1987 selection for an evaluation of Rautins that ended before opening night. The 76ers later exercised that right, but the player they picked supplied no verified NBA service. That makes a narrow option-value edge for Philadelphia more defensible than claiming either side landed a rotation player. Neither outcome merits a franchise-changing grade, and no later Atlanta game can be credited to the Pacers.

Final Verdict
September 14, 1984 exchanged Leo Rautins for Indiana’s 1987 third-round right. Rautins never played for the Pacers; the exercised choice became No. 57 Hansi Gnad, who never played for the 76ers. houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Gambled a Fifth-Round Choice on a Former Pacer Guard

On September 17, 1984, Houston acquired Kevin McKenna from Indiana for its 1985 fifth-round draft pick. Both franchises list the same one-player-for-one-pick exchange. McKenna had made 61 appearances for the Pacers in 1983-84, starting 13, and averaged 6.3 points. He was a plausible inexpensive guard candidate for Houston as the club prepared for its first season with Hakeem Olajuwon alongside Ralph Sampson. Indiana was instead collecting a remote draft option rather than holding a player it could use immediately. The clubs' records confirm a fifth-round choice, although a later Pacers media-guide description has been cited with a different draft year and round.

McKenna Was Waived Before Opening Night

The Rockets released McKenna on October 23, 1984, before the regular season began. He did not appear in an NBA game for Houston, even though his previous Indiana work established that he could play at the league level. McKenna later appeared in 29 games for New Jersey in 1984-85, averaging 5.7 points, but none of those Nets minutes can be credited as a Rockets return. Houston had bought a training-camp evaluation with a low draft selection and decided not to carry it into the season. That makes the actual return far more limited than a reader would infer by looking at his NBA career totals.

Indiana's Pick Became Ivan Daniels at No. 111

The compensation selection arrived in the 1985 draft's fifth round, No. 111 overall, and was associated with Ivan Daniels. Pro Sports Transactions traces the choice from Houston to Indiana, corroborating the direction shown in each club's transaction ledger. Daniels did not turn into a Pacers regular-season NBA contributor. The pick itself represented legitimate optional scouting value for Indiana, but there is no basis for assigning it points or minutes that Daniels never produced in the NBA. The late draft position also helps explain the modest practical stakes. The Pacers did not get a guaranteed future rotation player by moving McKenna.

Two Different Assets, the Same Lack of Realized NBA Return

Indiana exchanged a guard who had logged useful minutes the preceding year for the possibility of finding help deep in the 1985 draft. Houston surrendered that distant possibility to test McKenna as an immediately available veteran. Neither wager developed into playing time for the acquiring franchise: the Rockets waived the guard, and the Pacers' fifth-round outcome brought no recorded NBA games. That does not mean the transaction lacked rationale at the time. It means the inherited Pacers-win assessment exceeded the evidence about its actual result. Equal modest grades accurately describe an exchange in which both clubs received optional value but no sustained basketball contribution.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Houston earns C- after waiving Kevin McKenna before he played any Rockets regular-season games. Indiana also receives C- because the acquired fifth-round pick became No. 111 Ivan Daniels, who never contributed NBA minutes for the Pacers. Neither outcome supports a strong historical winner.

The Clippers Used Draft Compensation to Add Bryan Warrick

On September 25, 1984 the Los Angeles Clippers obtained guard Bryan Warrick from the Washington Bullets. Washington received a 1985 third-round draft choice eventually associated with No. 65 Ken Perry. The acquisition offered Los Angeles another perimeter option as it built its roster for the first season after moving from San Diego. Washington, historically filed under the Wizards franchise lineage, preferred an additional draft opportunity rather than continuing with Warrick. No first-round selection or marquee starting guard moved in this agreement, keeping the immediate stakes relatively modest.

Warrick Provided a Player to Assess Immediately

Warrick had collegiate and professional background that gave the Clippers an identifiable prospect rather than a right requiring another draft to exercise. Los Angeles could assess his handle, defense and ability to contribute in limited guard minutes when assembling the new season's roster. That is more direct than a future selection, but the transaction alone did not make him an established NBA starter. The distinction between his previous developmental record and actual Clippers games after September matters. A short tenure or an additional roster decision would narrow the ultimate return without changing the asset actually delivered.

Washington Received a Third-Round Slot, Not a First

The Bullets' incoming draft right corresponded to No. 65 in 1985, when the NBA still conducted additional rounds beyond the modern two. The player identifier appears as Ken Perry in the September record and Kenny Perry in an associated August Clippers transaction, which may reflect the same rights chain. A reliable audit should treat that naming variation as a reason to reconcile the asset, not to count two different future selections. The draft position still gave Washington a legitimate prospect opportunity. Its practical ceiling was limited by the low selection and by any later change in who finally exercised the choice.

A Young Guard Is a Small Advantage Over a Late Draft Slot

The Clippers obtained a guard they could immediately evaluate and the Bullets accepted a more speculative later selection. Warrick offered a direct route to playing time, which supports a modest Clippers advantage, but neither return was decisive for an entire franchise. Washington's third-round pick had real value in the draft format of the time. The grade shouldn't be inflated through Warrick's earlier biography or by double-counting the same 1985 pick through separate agreements. The immediate roster option and the modest value of a third-round selection warrant restrained grades on both sides.

Clippers Win, modestly. Los Angeles earns B- for acquiring Bryan Warrick as a guard option, while the Washington Bullets receive C+ for a 1985 third-round selection associated with No. 65 Ken Perry. los-angeles-clippers.summary: On September 29, 1984, Milwaukee sent four-time Bucks All-Star Marques Johnson, Junior Bridgeman, Harvey Catchings and cash to the newly relocated Los Angeles Clippers. The Bucks received former Rookie of the Year Terry Cummings, guard Craig Hodges and future Sixth Man of the Year Ricky Pierce. Cummings produced 319 Milwaukee appearances across his first four seasons, including an All-NBA and All-Star 1985 campaign. Johnson made the 1986 Clippers All-Star team but a serious neck injury cut his Los Angeles tenure to 157 NBA games. Bucks Win, Milwaukee A+ and Los Angeles C+, reflects sustained documented returns, not a foreseeable injury or invented cash amount.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The September 1984 Package: Three Players Each Way, Plus Cash
The Bucks exchanged Marques Johnson, Junior Bridgeman, Harvey Catchings and cash for Terry Cummings, Craig Hodges and Ricky Pierce from the Clippers on September 29, 1984. Los Angeles had just relocated from San Diego. The Clippers sought a proven lead scorer in Johnson and veteran depth, while Milwaukee added a 23-year-old former Rookie of the Year and two guards. Cash is present in the original asset ledger, but the current preserved sources do not establish a dollar figure, so none can be assigned. All six players are part of this one date; future roster transactions must be considered separately.

Cummings Immediately Became Milwaukee’s Frontcourt Scorer
In his first Bucks campaign, Cummings appeared in 79 games with 78 starts and averaged 23.6 points and 9.1 rebounds, reaching the 1985 NBA All-Star team and All-NBA Second Team. He followed with 82 appearances at 19.8 points per game, 82 at 20.8 and 76 at 21.3 across the next three seasons. Those four Milwaukee seasons yielded 319 games; this is a defined sample rather than a claim about his entire Bucks career. The combination of early award-level offense and four-year availability supplied Milwaukee a lasting return from a player whose value was still developing on trade day.

Johnson Supplied a Real Clippers Peak Before the Neck Injury
Marques Johnson was already a four-time All-Star from his Milwaukee seasons when Los Angeles acquired him. For the Clippers he played 72 games at 16.4 points in 1984-85 and 75 at 20.3 in 1985-86, earning the 1986 All-Star selection. A serious neck injury limited him to ten appearances in 1986-87, leaving 157 total Clippers regular-season games. His former Bucks statistics are not a new Los Angeles return, and his later brief Golden State comeback is another team’s production. The injury explains much of the eventual gap but was not something the 1984 Clippers could know would occur.

Hodges and Pierce Were Two Distinct Milwaukee Returns
Craig Hodges played all 82 Bucks games in 1984-85, including 63 starts, producing 10.6 points and 4.3 assists per night. In 1985-86 his outside shooting reached 45.1 percent on three-point attempts while he averaged 10.8 points. Ricky Pierce developed into a leading reserve scorer and earned Sixth Man of the Year in 1987, giving Milwaukee a second durable backcourt gain from the package. Neither Hodges’s later Chicago championships nor Pierce’s later unrelated signings count as Milwaukee production in 1984. Los Angeles also received legitimate reserve experience from Bridgeman and Catchings, which should not vanish from the comparison just because Johnson and Cummings had higher peaks.

Verdict: Better Milwaukee Duration, Not an All-Knowing 1984 Forecast
The Bucks obtained several strong seasons from Cummings plus active guard contributions from Hodges and Pierce. The Clippers gained Johnson’s productive 1985 and 1986 seasons and two veterans, alongside unquantified cash, but the neck injury sharply reduced his later on-court tenure. The existing retrospective verdict Bucks Win, Milwaukee A+ and Clippers C+ is therefore rooted in actual player value and time controlled by each team. It does not imply that the Clippers were irrational to pursue a four-time All-Star in September 1984 or that the injury was guaranteed.

Final Verdict
The complete original trade moved Johnson, Bridgeman, Catchings and cash to Los Angeles; Cummings, Hodges and Pierce moved to Milwaukee. Cummings supplied 319 Bucks games in the first four seasons alone, Hodges played substantial guard minutes and Pierce became an award-winning reserve. Johnson gave the Clippers 157 games and a 1986 All-Star season before injury. These sourced returns explain Bucks Win, Milwaukee A+ and Clippers C+ without double-crediting other franchises or fabricating any cash value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
A Free-Agent Rights Settlement, Not a Traditional Player Swap

Atlanta and Utah settled Billy Paultz's free-agent move in the fall of 1984. The Hawks held a right of first refusal, while the Jazz signed the veteran center and sent a 1985 third-round selection to Atlanta as compensation. The NBA transaction record dates that signing and compensation to September 28, even though the imported Hawks source file uses October 1. The historical date requires separate reconciliation before anyone silently changes the canonical record. Neither club swapped two playing contracts in a normal trade; Utah received the freedom to sign Paultz, and Atlanta received a future draft choice instead of retaining its matching right.

Utah Received One Final Season of Frontcourt Depth

Paultz arrived near the end of his long NBA and ABA career, so the Jazz were not buying the player who had once been a high-minute starter in San Antonio and Houston. In 1984-85 he appeared in 62 Utah regular-season games without starting, totaling 370 minutes, 82 points and 96 rebounds. Those numbers describe a limited backup center, rather than a difference-making scorer. Still, the Jazz received genuine playing availability from an identifiable veteran they could register for their roster. His earlier NBA and ABA accomplishments do not count as production acquired in this compensation agreement.

Atlanta Turned the Pick Into Sedric Toney

The 1985 third-round compensation selection became No. 59 overall, used by the Hawks on point guard Sedric Toney from Dayton. Atlanta did retain the pick through draft night, but Toney played only three regular-season games for the franchise in 1985-86. In those appearances he logged 24 minutes and five points before his NBA career continued with other clubs. His full 112-game NBA career is not Atlanta's trade return. Nor should this pick be confused with the Jazz's separate Karl Malone first-round selection in 1985. The actual Atlanta result is three appearances from a third-rounder.

Realized Games Favor Utah, Despite Modest Stakes

On receiving-club totals, Paultz supplied 62 games for Utah while the selected player provided three for Atlanta. The Jazz obtained a short-term reserve who could fill frontcourt minutes immediately, whereas the Hawks traded their option to retain a free agent for a draft chance that delivered little NBA playing time. The comparison is not a major win by modern blockbuster standards: Paultz was barely used and the Hawks' third-rounder was always a low-probability investment. But the documented return favors Utah without speculative value for the matching right, an invented contract amount or credit for either player's career outside the franchise.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win. Utah retains B+ for obtaining Billy Paultz and 62 games of veteran frontcourt availability in 1984-85. Atlanta receives C+ for the No. 59 selection of Sedric Toney, who played three Hawks games. The grades are modest historical evaluations rather than star-level value, and the September 28 versus October 1 date discrepancy stays flagged.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Exchanged an Established Championship Guard for a Future Pick

Gerald Henderson had helped the Celtics win the 1984 NBA championship and appeared in 78 regular-season games that year. Boston still had Dennis Johnson and Danny Ainge, giving the front office options at guard. On October 16, 1984, Boston traded Henderson to Seattle for a 1986 first-round choice. The contemporaneous announcement described a future selection, not a guaranteed No. 2 pick: the actual position would depend on Seattle’s subsequent results and the draft process.

Seattle Received a Player Who Could Help Immediately

The SuperSonics received an experienced guard who had made important plays for Boston in its title run. He appeared in NBA games for Seattle after the exchange, providing tangible backcourt production while the Celtics held a future draft asset. Seattle is the historical team in the transaction; the canonical Oklahoma City Thunder Win label is a modern franchise-continuity label, not a claim the Thunder existed in 1984.

The Future Boston Pick Became Len Bias

Seattle’s 1986 first-rounder eventually conveyed the second overall pick to the Celtics. Boston selected University of Maryland forward Len Bias on June 17, 1986. Bias died before ever appearing in an NBA game. That personal tragedy should never be treated as a predictable basketball decision or reduced to an ordinary player-performance failure. Boston had obtained an exceptionally valuable draft opportunity, but the selection yielded zero on-court NBA production for the franchise. Distinguishing the pick’s potential when acquired from its eventual realized return is essential to an honest assessment.

Verdict: Realized Games Favor Seattle, Without Rewriting What Boston Knew

The inherited retrospective verdict is Oklahoma City Thunder Win, with the Seattle franchise graded B+ and Boston B-. Henderson supplied actual guard play; the Celtics received a premium draft choice whose selected player was lost before his professional career began. This comparison is about realized franchise returns and cannot assume anyone anticipated either the No. 2 slot or Bias’s death. Boston’s decision in 1984 is separate from the unforeseen outcome in 1986. Sources: Boston and Seattle 1984-85 transaction ledgers, Boston’s historical media guide, and contemporaneous October 1984 reporting.
