perspectives.summary: On October 22, 1984, Indiana received Bill Garnett and Terence Stansbury from Dallas for a future first-round selection, protected in the top seven of the 1990 NBA draft and otherwise unprotected in 1991. Both players supplied Indiana immediate NBA minutes—145 Garnett and 148 Stansbury appearances—while Dallas waited for the right. The choice became the 1990 No. 14 pick, later used on Travis Mays by Sacramento AFTER Dallas traded the pick away as part of a larger package for Rodney McCray and two seconds. Mavericks Win, Dallas B and Indiana C+, reflects the first-round trade value, not a false claim that Mays played for Dallas.
perspectives.analysis:
An October 1984 Exchange of Two Players for a Conditional First
The Dallas Mavericks sent Bill Garnett and Terence Stansbury to Indiana on October 22, 1984 for the Pacers’ future first-round choice. The protection specified top seven in the 1990 draft; if that condition had prevented the pick from conveying, it would have become unprotected in 1991. Dallas did not receive a known No. 14 pick or the draft rights to Travis Mays on the original date. It held a contingent future asset while Indiana immediately received two young players. The package contained no cash, other first-round selection or third outgoing NBA player.

Indiana Received Nearly 300 Immediate Appearances
Garnett played 145 regular-season games for the Pacers over the next two seasons, and Stansbury appeared in 148. That is 293 combined Indiana games of frontcourt and wing depth. The pair were not long-term franchise cornerstones, but neither can accurately be dismissed as an unused or purely speculative return. Indiana turned distant draft uncertainty into players it could use straight away. Their later NBA seasons for other teams are not additional Indiana benefits from the 1984 swap.

Dallas Held the Draft Right Until It Became No. 14 in 1990
The deferred first eventually resolved as the No. 14 choice in the 1990 NBA draft. The surviving transaction ledger associates that selection with Travis Mays, but DAL did not draft and deploy Mays as a Mavericks guard. Before the actual selection, Dallas packaged the Indiana-origin first with Bill Wennington and another separate 1990 first in a Sacramento trade. The Mavericks acquired Rodney McCray and two second-round picks as consideration in THAT subsequent multi-asset exchange. Mays was selected using the first after the right had moved; crediting him with two Dallas seasons reverses the custody of the draft pick.

The Sacramento Branch Cannot Be Counted Twice
McCray subsequently played 149 Dallas regular-season games, starting 116, across two seasons. That reflects the real usefulness of the 1990 Sacramento deal. Still, the 1984 Pacers-origin first was only one part of the package Dallas gave up alongside Wennington and another first-round pick. Assigning McCray’s entire Dallas return to the Indiana trade would erase the value of those other outgoing assets. The appropriate link is that the six-year-old future right became part of a credible draft-night transaction enabling an experienced starter, not that Dallas directly selected Travis Mays or acquired McCray for the Pacers pick alone.

Why the B/C+ Verdict Is Narrow
The inherited Mavericks Win label and Dallas B versus Indiana C+ grades recognize the deferred draft choice ultimately carrying enough value to contribute to a meaningful NBA rotation asset. Indiana received nearly 300 combined immediate player appearances, and Dallas had to absorb several years of selection uncertainty, so the record does not support a blowout. Dallas’s later trade package contained multiple pieces; the model should acknowledge that mixed causal contribution rather than overassign McCray’s minutes or treating Mays’s time in Sacramento as Dallas production.

Final Verdict
This October 22, 1984 trade was Garnett and Stansbury for a protected future Indiana first. The two players produced 293 Pacers appearances. Dallas retained the selection until it became the 1990 No. 14 right and transferred that right in a later multi-asset Sacramento transaction for Rodney McCray and other draft compensation. Travis Mays was linked to the pick’s eventual use but was not a Mavericks draft/playing return. Preserve original Mavericks Win, Dallas B and Indiana C+ while correcting that asset-history error.

perspectives.summary: On December 18, 1984, Utah acquired reserve forward Fred Roberts from San Antonio for its 1986 and 1988 second-round draft picks, later associated with No. 38 Lemone Lampley and No. 42 Jeff Moe. Roberts contributed 110 Jazz regular-season appearances over parts of two seasons. The Spurs TRADED the 1986 choice to Seattle on October 23, 1985 for Jon Sundvold; they did not draft Lampley themselves. The inherited Even Trade, C for both Utah and San Antonio, weighs actual forward minutes against two tradeable picks and a documented later pick-for-player conversion.
perspectives.analysis:
Utah Received a Veteran; San Antonio Held Two Future Draft Rights
Utah sent its 1986 and 1988 second-round choices to San Antonio for Fred Roberts on December 18, 1984. Roberts had already played 22 games for the Spurs during that NBA season, but none of those pre-trade San Antonio appearances are part of the Jazz return. Both selections were FUTURE draft options on the exchange date. Historical draft records later associate them with No. 38 Lemone Lampley in 1986 and No. 42 Jeff Moe in 1988, but those hindsight names are not two players Utah handed to the Spurs in December. The trade provided immediate Utah frontcourt depth against two decisions San Antonio would make over later seasons.

Roberts Delivered 110 Receiving-Team Utah Games
Roberts played 52 games for the Jazz after arrival in 1984-85, averaging 8.7 points and 2.9 rebounds in 16.8 minutes. He then appeared in another 58 Utah games during 1985-86, with averages of 3.7 points and 1.4 rebounds in a smaller eight-minute role. He did not start a receiving-team game in either season. The combined 110 games supplied real short-term NBA production and explain why calling Utah an automatic loser would be inaccurate. Utah later traded him to Boston on September 25, 1986 for a 1987 third-round choice, giving the Jazz another traceable downstream asset; Roberts’s eventual Celtics/Bucks minutes are separate team returns.

The Lampley Pick Changed Hands Before the 1986 Draft
The Spurs used the future 1986 second-round option in another transaction on October 23, 1985, sending it to the Seattle SuperSonics in exchange for guard Jon Sundvold. The selection subsequently resolved to No. 38 Lemone Lampley, but San Antonio could not both send the pick away in 1985 and draft Lampley with it in 1986. The actual Spurs conversion was the right into Sundvold. Seattle’s later use of the selection is useful to track pick identity, not a reason to allocate Lampley’s career to the Spurs. The second Utah-origin pick later resolved to No. 42 Jeff Moe in 1988, another future right that deserves separate accounting.

Comparing a Reserve Forward with Future Options
Utah received roughly one and a half seasons of NBA forward appearances and later turned Roberts into another pick. San Antonio took two draft choices; it followed the first into the Sundvold transaction, while the other carried a later second-round selection. Neither side obtained a star-level direct return from the initial deal. The comparison is therefore about Utah’s actual short-rotation playing time and San Antonio’s option value and specific follow-on trade, not about later performances by players on unrelated franchises.

Verdict and Grades: Even Trade, C for Each Team
The historical Even Trade verdict with Utah C and San Antonio C is preserved. Roberts’s first 52 Utah games were useful, his following 58 were in a much smaller role, and he did not become a long-term Jazz starter. The Spurs secured two future seconds and used one as consideration for Sundvold instead of retaining the eventual Lampley selection. That leaves a modest balanced exchange without imaginary cash, a fabricated direct Spurs Lampley tenure or undue credit for Roberts’s games after leaving Utah.

Final Verdict
The December 18 exchange was Fred Roberts for Utah’s 1986 and 1988 second-round picks. It produced 110 Jazz regular-season appearances, two San Antonio future options and a documented 1985 Spurs pick-for-Sundvold conversion. The two named 1986/1988 draftees document where the original rights landed, not guaranteed Spurs-playing production. Even Trade and C/C remain appropriate to the recorded returns.

New York Converted Matching-Rights Compensation Into Two Seconds

Boston's February 21, 1985 arrangement involved veteran free agent Ray Williams and the Knicks' decision not to exercise their right of first refusal. New York received two second-round picks, which subsequently appeared as the 1985 No. 47 selection associated with Gerald Wilkins and 1986 No. 47 Michael Jackson. The Celtics obtained freedom to pursue Williams without New York matching, while the Knicks gained two prospect opportunities. This wasn't an ordinary player-for-player trade because Williams's status was governed by free-agent rules. The exact years and selection numbers make the return more concrete than an unspecified consideration.

Gerald Wilkins Became a Productive Knicks Wing

Wilkins's NBA playing career in New York turned the 1985 second-round position into a notable return. His perimeter athleticism and subsequent Knicks seasons made that draft right far more useful than many ordinary late selections. That outcome was not guaranteed at the February 1985 agreement date, and the deal should not be credited for every later franchise improvement. But the named pick provides a clear player with an actual receiving-team record, unlike an undeveloped right whose future performance would have to be guessed. Wilkins's New York tenure is the most consequential historical part of this compensation package.

The Additional 1986 Second Was a Separate Opportunity

The Knicks also secured a 1986 second-round position associated with No. 47 Michael Jackson. The two picks should not be combined into one imagined high selection or treated as a package automatically producing two long-term starters. Jackson's NBA role must be assessed independently rather than being inferred from Wilkins's much stronger subsequent tenure. Boston paid with future opportunities to pursue a veteran whose established professional history wasn't yet its own. The Knicks had room to turn a contractual right into new talent and evaluate the two acquired prospects on their separate timelines.

New York's Proven Draft Return Drives the Verdict

The Knicks gained two discrete draft chances for stepping aside on Williams, including one that led to a valuable NBA contributor in Wilkins. Boston obtained contractual flexibility toward a veteran guard but did not create a comparable lasting roster asset through this particular arrangement. perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix and Portland transaction logs agree on the June 14, 1985 deal: the Suns sent a 1987 second-round choice to the Trail Blazers for Bernard Thompson. Thompson had been Portland's 1984 first-round pick at No. 19 and had just completed a 59-game rookie season. Two years later Portland used the acquired second-rounder at No. 30 overall on LSU forward Nikita Wilson. Because both assets produced NBA results, this is a straightforward realized-value comparison rather than a rights or conditional-pick problem.

Phoenix Return
Thompson immediately became a useful Suns reserve. In 1985-86 he played 61 games with 20 starts, averaged 8.5 points, 2.3 rebounds and 2.2 assists, and shot 48.9 percent from the field. His role declined in 1986-87, when he appeared in 24 games with two starts, but he returned for 37 games and seven starts in 1987-88. Across those three Phoenix seasons he totaled 122 regular-season games, 29 starts, 819 points, 248 rebounds, 201 assists and 83 steals. That is not star production, but it is a meaningful amount of real rotation value for the cost of one future second-round pick. Thompson later played briefly for Houston, so Phoenix received essentially the prime NBA portion of his career after the trade.

Portland Return
The Trail Blazers waited two years for the pick and selected Nikita Wilson at No. 30 in the 1987 draft. Wilson made the 1987-88 roster but appeared in only 15 games, never started, and logged 54 total minutes. He scored 19 points, grabbed 11 rebounds and recorded three assists before his NBA career ended after that one season. Portland therefore converted a recent first-round wing who still had three NBA seasons ahead of him into a second-round selection that produced only 15 low-minute games. The process was defensible—Thompson had been a low-efficiency rookie and a future second was a normal asset for a player outside the core—but the realized outcome was poor.

Hindsight Verdict
Phoenix wins clearly while the stakes remain modest. Thompson was never a foundational Suns player, so an elite grade would overstate the deal. He did, however, give Phoenix 122 games, nearly thirty starts and one genuinely useful 61-game season. Portland's return became a player who barely reached the floor and was out of the NBA after 15 games. A B for Phoenix reflects strong value extraction from a second-round cost. A D+ for Portland recognizes that the Blazers received a legitimate draft asset and made an ordinary second-round bet, but that bet produced almost no NBA value. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Washington traded veteran forward Greg Ballard to Golden State on June 17, 1985 for the 31st pick that became Manute Bol and a 1987 second-rounder subsequently used at No. 36 on Duane Washington. Ballard supplied 157 Warriors games, 3,371 minutes and 1,241 points in two seasons. Bol gave Washington an extraordinary rookie year with 397 blocks in 80 games and remained three seasons. Bullets Win, A+ against Golden State B.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Washington Exchanged Its Team Captain for Two Second-Round Chances

On June 17, 1985, the Washington Bullets sent Greg Ballard to the Golden State Warriors for the No. 31 selection in the next day's NBA draft and an additional 1987 second-round choice. A contemporary Washington Post account confirms both draft assets. Ballard had been a reliable Washington starter and its team captain, making the trade a meaningful personnel change rather than a routine end-of-bench move. Golden State wanted a proven forward; Washington preferred flexibility as it rebuilt its frontcourt around different players.

Ballard Provided Two Full Warriors Seasons of Experience

Ballard was a genuine contributor for Golden State. During 1985-86 he appeared in seventy-five games, logged 1,792 minutes and recorded 662 points and 417 rebounds. He played all eighty-two games the following season, adding 579 points and 340 rebounds in 1,579 minutes. The combined Warriors return was 157 games, 3,371 minutes, 1,241 points and 757 rebounds. Those figures justify a good receiving-team grade. His previous years in Washington, however, do not become additional Golden State value from the trade.

The Thirty-First Pick Became Manute Bol and a Historic Defensive Season

Washington spent its incoming No. 31 pick on Manute Bol, a 7-foot-7 center who had played at Bridgeport. The rookie instantly changed opponents' shots around the basket, appearing in eighty games in 1985-86 and recording 397 blocked shots. He led the league at roughly five blocks a game and earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition. Bol remained with the Bullets for three seasons, providing a degree of defensive impact beyond what most second-round picks deliver. That rookie season alone gave the acquired choice a substantial return.

The Later Pick Was Another Asset, but Bol Decided the Comparison

The second selection in Washington's package ultimately became No. 36 Duane Washington in the 1987 draft. The historical ledger should recognize that incoming right without assigning unrelated NBA games to the Bullets. Golden State's two useful Ballard seasons were far from a failure; he served as a dependable veteran and helped its rotation. Yet Washington turned the first second-round pick into one of the most distinctive shot blockers in NBA history, while also retaining a later choice. That sporting return exceeds the valuable but shorter Ballard stint.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win. Washington earns A+ for Manute Bol's 397-block rookie season and subsequent Bullets center contributions, plus the 1987 second-round choice. Golden State receives B for Greg Ballard's 157 Warriors games, 3,371 minutes, 1,241 points and 757 rebounds. The Warriors found a useful veteran, but Bol's extraordinary immediate defensive impact made the Washington draft return better.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired center Granville Waiters from Indiana on August 1, 1985, giving up its 1987 third-round pick, eventually No. 60 Sean Couch. Waiters appeared in 43 regular-season Rockets games in 1985-86, scoring 27 points with 28 rebounds in 156 minutes. Couch did not play an NBA regular-season game for Indiana. Rockets Win, Houston C-, Indiana D+; the result corrects an inherited Pacers-win grade.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Obtained a Third-String Center for a Distant Draft Pick

The Rockets traded a 1987 third-round selection to Indiana for Granville Waiters on August 1, 1985. Waiters was a reserve center who had spent the 1984-85 season with the Pacers, and Houston was looking for additional big-man cover behind its well-established frontcourt. The timing was notable: the Rockets were preparing for a season built around Hakeem Olajuwon and Ralph Sampson, so Waiters did not need to arrive as a starter to fill a useful spot. Indiana accepted a low pick two drafts away instead of continuing to use its center. Both clubs' contemporaneous transaction histories agree on those terms.

Waiters Appeared in 43 Games on Houston's Finals Team

Waiters played 43 Rockets regular-season games in 1985-86, recording 156 minutes, 27 points and 28 rebounds. He averaged only 3.6 minutes per appearance, so he was a deep reserve rather than a major part of the rotation. Houston nevertheless reached the NBA Finals that year, losing to Boston, and Waiters was on the regular-season roster that supported the run. His minutes should not be confused with the contributions of Olajuwon, Sampson or the other players who carried Houston. The limited but actual NBA appearances matter when comparing this outcome with a draft selection that did not produce league games.

Indiana's Third-Rounder Became Sean Couch

The compensation was the Rockets' 1987 third-round draft choice, which ultimately became No. 60 Sean Couch. The Pacers' transaction register and the historical draft-choice ledger connect the selection to the Waiters trade. Couch did not appear in an NBA regular-season game for Indiana, leaving the Pacers with no on-court return from that eventual choice. A draft pick can be valuable as a scouting opportunity or later trade ingredient, but there is no documented downstream player acquired by Indiana from this particular third-round selection. It would be a mistake to grade the Pacers as if Couch's college career or hypothetical alternatives were NBA performance for the franchise.

A Small but Measurable Rockets Advantage

Indiana traded a veteran center for an inexpensive chance in the 1987 draft. Houston converted that choice into a reserve who at least gave the club 43 appearances and a handful of frontcourt minutes. The outcome was not a transformative transaction for the Rockets or a costly failure for the Pacers; it was a modest bench deal involving a low-probability pick. Yet the older Pacers-win verdict obscured the basic receiving-team record. Waiters played in an NBA uniform for the acquiring club while the pick did not produce a Pacers player. A slight Rockets advantage with low grades reflects that specific outcome without turning roster depth into a claim of postseason heroics.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win. Houston receives C- for 43 games, 156 minutes and 27 points from Granville Waiters in 1985-86. Indiana gets D+ because the acquired 1987 third-round pick became No. 60 Sean Couch, who did not supply NBA minutes for the Pacers. The gap is small but favors actual reserve usage over an unrealized draft selection.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: On August 19, 1985, Los Angeles acquired veteran forward Maurice Lucas from Phoenix for the Lakers’ 1988 and 1989 second-round picks. Lucas played 77 Lakers games in 1985-86, averaging 10.2 points and 7.4 rebounds, before leaving after one season. Phoenix exercised the two picks on No. 50 Steve Kerr in 1988 and No. 52 Greg Grant in 1989. Kerr supplied only 26 Suns games before another trade; his later Bulls/Spurs championships cannot be counted as Phoenix production. Slight Suns Edge, Suns B and Lakers B-, recognizes two exercised future choices against one useful veteran season, not a retrospective gift of Kerr’s entire career.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
An August 1985 Veteran-for-Two-Picks Exchange
The Lakers acquired Maurice Lucas from Phoenix on August 19, 1985 and sent their second-round draft rights for 1988 and 1989 to the Suns. A contemporary August 20 Los Angeles Times report describes Lucas, 33, wanting out of a Phoenix rebuild and Los Angeles seeking frontcourt defense after the 1985 title. Jerry West pursued Lucas as the Lakers adjusted their rotation rather than keeping Bob McAdoo. Neither team sent a first-round pick or a third established player. The official Lakers transactions media guide corroborates the two future seconds. They were rights to future selections in 1985, not an immediate trade of Steve Kerr or Greg Grant, whose NBA draft years were still ahead.

Lucas Contributed to the 1985-86 Lakers Rotation
Lucas played 77 regular-season games for Los Angeles in his one Lakers campaign, averaging 10.2 points and 7.4 rebounds. He added 14 playoff appearances that spring, a credible return from a veteran big obtained for distant second-round choices. His job was to help on the boards and against physical opponents, not to replace Kareem Abdul-Jabbar as the first option. Lucas had an accomplished previous career, but his past Portland championship and Phoenix minutes are not credited as new Lakers returns from the August transaction. He was not on the 1987 and 1988 Lakers championship rosters; those belong to a later, different frontcourt acquisition. The inherited Lakers B- recognizes a helpful one-season piece, not a lasting star.

Phoenix Exercised Both Draft Choices
The first Lakers-origin right conveyed as the No. 50 selection in the 1988 draft, which Phoenix used on Steve Kerr from Arizona. Kerr appeared in 26 games for the Suns during his 1988-89 rookie season and was then traded to Cleveland for another future second-round asset. Phoenix held both the rookie contribution and a traceable next transaction branch, not Kerr’s full fifteen-year NBA career. The second Lakers-origin selection became No. 52 in the 1989 draft, used on Greg Grant, who played 67 Suns games with three starts in his rookie season. These two draft outcomes are directly linked to the 1985 trade; they do not imply either pick had the expected value of a future championship star on the original trade date.

The Famous Kerr Name Can Mislead Retrospective Grades
Kerr later won five titles as an NBA player, but those were achieved with the Chicago Bulls and San Antonio Spurs, not the Phoenix Suns. Counting all five championships and 910 career NBA games as the Suns’ direct return would exaggerate the transaction and obscure the Suns’ modest actual minutes from the No. 50 selection. By the same logic, Lucas’s earlier All-Star career and championship in Portland cannot be counted as Los Angeles contributions. A fair asset chain follows the Suns’ two exercised selections and any verified later pick received for Kerr, and compares those against the 77-game Lucas season in purple and gold.

Verdict: A Small Phoenix Advantage, Not a Famous-Name Rout
Phoenix acquired two second-round options from a contender in exchange for a 33-year-old nearing the end of his career. Both choices were eventually exercised on NBA players, and Kerr’s immediate post-rookie trade continued one branch of draft value. Los Angeles got exactly what it sought from Lucas for one regular season and playoff run. The inherited Slight Suns Edge verdict with Phoenix B and Los Angeles B- is defensible because the Suns converted both distant selections rather than receiving worthless picks. The one-grade-step difference deliberately avoids claiming Los Angeles received nothing or Phoenix held Kerr through his later championship years.

Final Verdict
The August 19, 1985 package was Maurice Lucas for the 1988 and 1989 Lakers second-round picks. Los Angeles received 77 games of veteran frontcourt service; Phoenix later used the selections on No. 50 Steve Kerr and No. 52 Greg Grant. Kerr’s 26 Phoenix games and his later trade, not his subsequent Bulls/Spurs legacy, are the relevant Suns branches. Preserve the original Slight Suns Edge, Phoenix B/Lakers B- and the private/noindex archival scope; distinguish future pick outcomes from players actually exchanged on that August day.

perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Exchanged a Future Third-Round Chance for Wallace Johnson

On August 21, 1985 the New Jersey Nets acquired Wallace Johnson from Golden State while the Warriors received a 1986 third-round selection. That choice eventually appeared as No. 59, associated with Wendell Alexis. Because the NBA draft still extended beyond two rounds, the selection shouldn't be judged as though it carried the modern protections or contract expectations of a second-round pick. The Nets obtained a named player they could assess during the coming season, while Golden State chose a smaller future development option. The team labels here reflect the actual New Jersey Nets of 1985, not the franchise's later Brooklyn home.

Johnson Represented a Short-Term Player Assessment

Wallace Johnson arrived with prior professional basketball experience, but the swap wasn't comparable to acquiring a proven All-Star or a centerpiece for a playoff run. New Jersey's immediate value lay in being able to evaluate him as part of its roster planning. The players already with the Nets remained responsible for most of that franchise's season results. Describing Johnson as a small, identifiable return is more accurate than treating every earlier game on his career line as newly acquired production. If roster records show a modest tenure, it supports a limited evaluation rather than a large historical trade win.

Golden State's Choice Became a Named Draft Slot

The Warriors received a future third-round selection that the historical draft ledger associates with Wendell Alexis at No. 59 in 1986. That established draft identity gives the asset a traceable outcome even without guaranteeing an NBA rotation career. Alexis's later professional work, including time outside the NBA, should not automatically be turned into Warriors regular-season minutes. The original exchange gave Golden State a right to make or move a lower-priority selection, rather than a signed veteran replacement for Johnson. The value depended on subsequent choices and separate personnel decisions.

A Slight Nets Edge Fits the Scale of the Exchange

New Jersey acquired an immediately identifiable player, while Golden State accepted the future uncertainty of a third-round pick. Neither return had the profile of a franchise-altering acquisition, and any assessment should be restrained by the modest stakes. The Nets receive a narrow preference for present-day personnel flexibility, with credit to Golden State for obtaining a legitimate draft asset. Giving Johnson's complete prior career to New Jersey or assuming the Warriors immediately enjoyed Alexis's international success would exaggerate either side. A low-to-moderate grade for both franchises reflects the transaction rather than the clubs' unrelated records.

Final Verdict

Slight Nets Edge. New Jersey earns C+ for acquiring Wallace Johnson as a near-term roster option, while Golden State receives C for the 1986 third-round selection that became No. 59 Wendell Alexis. Both were modest returns, and the draft rights did not guarantee long-term NBA Warriors production. The 1985 franchise was the New Jersey Nets.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
New Jersey Paid a Future Third for an Experienced Forward

The New Jersey Nets acquired veteran forward Mickey Johnson from Golden State on August 21, 1985, sending a 1986 third-round selection to the Warriors. The Nets transaction ledger independently confirms the same date, asset directions and player's name. The relevant choice eventually became No. 59 and was used on Wendell Alexis. Johnson had previously played substantial minutes for Golden State, but those 1982-85 Warriors contributions must be excluded from New Jersey's acquisition value. The Nets were paying a low draft price for a recognizable forward who could immediately join the rotation, rather than buying a long-term star or attaching future cash considerations.

Johnson Played 79 Games for a Playoff Team

Johnson appeared in 79 regular-season New Jersey games in 1985-86 and started four. He totaled 1,574 minutes, 616 points, 332 rebounds and 217 assists, averages of 7.8 points, 4.2 rebounds and 2.7 assists in 19.9 minutes a game. That is meaningful second-unit production for a third-round draft investment. New Jersey finished 39-43 and qualified for the Eastern Conference playoffs, where Johnson appeared in all three games of its first-round series against Milwaukee. His Nets tenure ended after that season, so the direct return is a useful one-year reserve role rather than a multi-season commitment.

Golden State's Pick Became Wendell Alexis at No. 59

Golden State retained the incoming 1986 third-round selection and chose Syracuse forward Wendell Alexis at No. 59 overall. Alexis never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. He subsequently built a distinguished professional career overseas, but his international production was not on-court contribution to the Warriors from the August trade. The pick was a legitimate scouting opportunity, and its eventual outcome should be described accurately, not as a nonexistent Warriors reserve stint. The number also cannot be awarded twice: a separate imported archive entry repeats the same choice while calling the outgoing Nets player Wallace Johnson, a conflicting historical identity that needs its own source-led reconciliation.

One Real NBA Season Beat an Unconverted Draft Pick

New Jersey obtained 79 appearances from the forward it acquired, with useful scoring, rebounding and passing for a playoff roster. Golden State took a future draft chance and selected a player who never suited up in the NBA. The contrast is not subtle when judged by realized team contributions, making the previously inherited Even Trade label difficult to support. The Nets' modest one-year benefit should not be graded like an All-Star acquisition, but it was demonstrably more than the Warriors received on the court. Tracking the name Mickey Johnson also protects the archive from presenting the same No. 59 draft choice as if it were received in two distinct transactions.

Final Verdict

Nets Win. New Jersey earns B for 79 Mickey Johnson games, 616 points, 332 rebounds and 217 assists during the 1985-86 season. Golden State gets D+ because its 1986 No. 59 selection, Wendell Alexis, produced no NBA appearances. A conflicting imported Wallace Johnson entry is flagged separately and is not treated as another genuine pick acquisition.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Dealt Buckner for an Indiana Draft Right

On September 3, 1985, Boston exchanged guard Quinn Buckner with Indiana for a future 1989 second-round selection. The historical draft ledger later associates that position with No. 44 Reggie Cross. The Celtics were maintaining a veteran roster with multiple backcourt choices and could accept a future asset rather than keeping every experienced reserve. Indiana wanted a player whose NBA defensive reputation was already established. This was a veteran-for-later-pick trade, with several years between the original agreement and the selection's ultimate position. Both parties were pursuing different points on their roster timelines.

Buckner Supplied Indiana With a Known Defensive Identity

Buckner's NBA experience, including participation on Boston's championship-era rosters, made him an understandable target for the Pacers. His defensive background and ability to organize a guard unit could help a club seeking veteran habits. Yet Boston's earlier accomplishments were not automatically Indiana victories, and any new impact had to be measured after Buckner's arrival. He was at a later career stage by 1985 and did not guarantee a long run of star minutes. Indiana acquired immediate expertise and a professional roster option instead of waiting through four future draft cycles.

The Celtics' 1989 Pick Had a Long Development Horizon

Boston accepted a second-round right that didn't become a named selection until 1989, where the record associates it with the No. 44 Reggie Cross slot. As with other historical draft rights, the eventual player identity is a ledger outcome, not proof that Cross became a productive Celtics regular. The pick had value because it could be used or reassigned, but its long lead time created uncertainty about Boston's eventual benefit. The Celtics were trading a veteran who had already served their roster for a new opportunity, rather than expecting to replace his defense immediately through the selection.

Both Clubs Acquired Assets Matching Their Priorities

Indiana gained a guard with an established basketball background, while Boston converted a supporting veteran into a future development opportunity. The trade is fairly balanced when the second-round position's uncertainty is weighed against Buckner's late-career status. There is no credible basis for crediting the Pacers with Boston's prior titles or declaring the Celtics winners simply because the pick eventually had a name attached. Neither asset guaranteed multiple new starting seasons. Equal moderate grades reflect a pragmatic exchange of present-day guard experience for longer-dated prospect flexibility.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston earns B- for the future 1989 second-round right associated with No. 44 Reggie Cross; Indiana receives B- for veteran guard Quinn Buckner. Buckner's earlier Celtics championships aren't Indiana results, and Cross's draft-slot identity isn't proof of long-term Celtics NBA output. Both assets answered reasonable needs in 1985.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Secured a Draft Selection for Allowing a Free-Agent Move

On September 26, 1985, the Celtics agreed not to exercise their right of first refusal concerning veteran free agent Ray Williams, allowing the Los Angeles Clippers to pursue him. In exchange, Boston gained a future fourth-round pick in the 1987 draft. The historical ledger later connects that selection to No. 70 Tom Sheehey. The agreement belongs to a period with more than two NBA draft rounds and different contractual matching arrangements than contemporary free agency. Boston was not trading a currently signed center for a first-round selection, and Los Angeles was seeking access to a particular guard rather than purchasing a high lottery prospect.

Los Angeles Wanted Williams's Established NBA Experience

Williams entered the arrangement with recognizable guard skills and years of NBA work behind him. The Clippers could explore adding his ball handling and scoring to a roster that lacked the depth of the league's established contenders. Previous games with New York, Boston or another franchise did not become new Los Angeles production simply because Boston stepped aside in 1985. A free-agent acquisition also required the club to complete separate roster decisions; the matching-rights waiver removed a contractual obstacle but wasn't a guarantee of future star performance. That made the Clippers' benefit immediate in purpose but uncertain in result.

The Celtics' Compensation Became a Fourth-Round Right

Boston's draft claim ultimately appeared as the 1987 No. 70 choice associated with Tom Sheehey. A fourth-round selection was a legitimate developmental right in that historical draft format, but it wasn't comparable to a protected modern first. The Celtics could attempt to scout and sign a late prospect without keeping the matching option attached to Williams. Any subsequent professional playing time by Sheehey would need to be traced to the actual signing team. The right alone didn't mean Boston had instantly replenished its NBA guard rotation or drafted a guaranteed useful player.

A Small Celtics Edge Fits the Original Risk

Boston converted an option it chose not to use into a distinct later draft asset, while the Clippers gained the chance to negotiate for a known veteran. That supports a narrow Celtics advantage, not a sweeping judgment on either team's mid-1980s performance. The 1987 pick carried limited upside due to its round, but it was still compensation rather than nothing. The Clippers' rationale was an immediate need for backcourt experience, yet the right to pursue Williams was not equivalent to acquiring the best years of his prior career. Both returns were small and conditional in different ways.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win, slightly. Boston receives C+ for the 1987 fourth-round position eventually identified as No. 70 Tom Sheehey. Los Angeles receives C- because Boston agreed not to exercise its matching right on Ray Williams. The trade was about a free-agent right, not an existing signed player, and the fourth-round pick was not a guaranteed rotation solution.

Seattle placed Teachey on waivers October 11, before the regular season, and he never appeared in an NBA game for the franchise. perspectives.analysis:
Dallas Traded Teachey's Rights for a Contingent Future Choice

Dallas transferred Anthony Teachey to Seattle on September 27, 1985, receiving only a conditional second-round draft selection in 1989. The condition depended on Teachey earning an extended place on the SuperSonics roster. The Mavericks had picked the Wake Forest forward in the second round of the 1984 draft and signed him to an NBA contract a day before the exchange. Seattle could evaluate a former college prospect without immediately surrendering a guaranteed pick. Unlike a regular player-for-draft-pick deal, the future compensation was not certain to convey, so it should not be described as a selection that Dallas actually made in 1989.

Seattle Released Teachey Before the Season Started

The surviving NBA transaction chronology shows Seattle acquired Teachey on September 27 but placed his contract on waivers on October 11. He became a free agent four days later. The SuperSonics therefore did not receive a regular-season game, start, rebound or point from this acquisition. Their 1985-86 roster includes productive players elsewhere in the frontcourt, but Teachey was not among those who appeared in games. Counting his collegiate work or Dallas's prior draft investment as Seattle's return would overstate the deal. It was effectively a training-camp evaluation that ended before the regular schedule began.

Dallas's Conditional Second Never Became a Documented Pick

Dallas was promised a second-round draft choice in 1989 only if the agreement's roster condition was met. The imported trade record describes that option as not exercised. That fits the brief Seattle tenure, although the exact contractual definition and a corresponding 1989 pick number are not independently established in the available ledgers. Without evidence that the second actually conveyed, the Mavericks cannot be assigned the later NBA career of a hypothetical draft selection. Their actual documented asset was a contingent right with no identifiable draft conversion. It was a reasonable way to recoup some potential value from an unsigned prospect, but the result was limited.

Neither Side Obtained Sustained Basketball Value

The original archived Seattle-win grade implied a substantial receiving-team advantage, despite Seattle waiving the acquired player before opening night. Dallas's conditional pick likewise has no verified on-court outcome and should not receive a favorable grade merely for appearing in the transaction description. Each club effectively tested a low-cost possibility: Seattle with a young forward, Dallas with a contingent draft asset. Both possibilities failed to yield measurable NBA play for the acquiring teams. An even, low-grade assessment is more faithful to the historical outcome while leaving the exact unexercised-condition wording open to further source verification if the original agreement resurfaces.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Dallas gets C- because its conditional 1989 second-round compensation produced no verified draft selection or NBA playing return. Seattle also earns C- because Anthony Teachey was waived before the 1985-86 regular season and never played an NBA game for the SuperSonics. Neither club obtained meaningful realized basketball value, contradicting the earlier Seattle-win grade.

perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Chicago transaction log identifies this as veteran free-agent compensation rather than a conventional player trade. Chicago signed Kyle Macy on October 4, 1985 and sent Phoenix second-round picks in 1986 and 1990. The Phoenix record describes the Suns' side as agreeing not to exercise their right of first refusal on Macy. The picks later became No. 39 Rafael Addison in 1986 and No. 50 Milos Babic in 1990. That structure means the hindsight comparison is one Chicago season of Macy against the direct and downstream value Phoenix created from two second-round assets.

Chicago Return
Macy became the Bulls' primary point guard immediately. He played all 82 games in 1985-86 and started 79, averaging 29.6 minutes, 8.6 points and 5.4 assists while shooting 48.3 percent from the field and 41.1 percent from three. Chicago's season was disrupted by Michael Jordan's foot injury and ended at 30-52, so Macy did not transform the team's record, but he supplied stable full-season guard play when the roster needed it. He left for Indiana after the season, making the Bulls return useful but short-lived.

Phoenix Return
The 1986 second-rounder became Rafael Addison at No. 39. Addison played 62 games with 12 starts as a Phoenix rookie, averaging 5.8 points in 11.5 minutes. He then spent four seasons outside the NBA before returning with New Jersey, so Phoenix received only that one season of his eventual six-year NBA career. The 1990 second-rounder became Milos Babic at No. 50. Phoenix did not retain Babic's rights: on draft night the Suns traded him to Cleveland for the rights to Stefano Rusconi, selected two spots later. Rusconi did not join Phoenix immediately and eventually appeared in only seven Suns games in 1995-96, totaling 30 minutes. The two picks therefore produced one modest Addison season and a rights chain that yielded almost no NBA court value.

Hindsight Verdict
Chicago has the better realized return, but the margin is not large enough for an extreme grade. Macy gave the Bulls one full season as a starting point guard and played every game. Phoenix received two legitimate draft assets, one of which produced a 62-game rookie season from Addison and the other of which remained movable until it became Rusconi's rights. The Suns did not receive nothing; they simply failed to turn either second-round opportunity into durable rotation value. A B for Chicago reflects the immediate 82-game starting return from a free-agent signing. A C+ for Phoenix recognizes that the compensation was reasonable in form and produced some NBA value, but less than Macy gave Chicago directly. Final verdict: Chicago Bulls Win.

perspectives.analysis:
The Jones Signing Required a Draft-Pick Compensation Settlement

Portland signed veteran big man Caldwell Jones as a free agent in October 1985 after his spell with Chicago, sending the Bulls a 1987 second-round selection as compensation for relinquishing their matching rights. Historical ledgers disagree on the effective day: the Basketball-Reference team registers show October 1, while the detailed pick transaction chain uses October 9. That provenance difference is flagged for reconciliation without altering the archived date during an editorial-only repair. It was not an ordinary player-for-player swap. Portland obtained Jones's services directly, whereas Chicago received a future asset it could keep or trade before the 1987 draft.

Jones Played Four Useful Seasons for Portland

Jones gave the Trail Blazers a long run of frontcourt work after his signing. He appeared in 80 regular-season games in 1985-86, then 78 in 1986-87, 79 in 1987-88 and 72 in 1988-89, totaling 309 Portland games. The 1985-86 season included 19 starts and 355 rebounds, while 1987-88 brought 77 starts and 408 rebounds. By then Jones was a veteran role player rather than an offensive star, but Portland used him extensively enough for the signing to create real roster continuity. His previous Philadelphia and Chicago production is excluded from the Trail Blazers' acquired return.

Chicago Traded the Pick Back Before Milwaukee Selected Garland

The future second-rounder eventually became the No. 40 pick in 1987, but Chicago never drafted Winston Garland with it. On June 17, 1986, the Bulls returned that selection to Portland alongside the rights to Larry Krystkowiak and an additional 1992 second-round pick for Steve Colter. Colter appeared in 27 Bulls regular-season games in 1986-87 before leaving the club. Portland then moved the No. 40 selection to Milwaukee on November 11, 1986 for Chris Engler. The Bucks drafted Garland the following summer. His eventual 511-game NBA career does not belong to either original club's realized playing return from this compensation deal.

Portland Received the Stronger Direct Basketball Return

Portland paid a second-round selection and received 309 games from Jones. Chicago obtained a movable pick and used it as only one part of a larger three-asset transaction that brought Colter, so the Bulls have some traceable but limited downstream roster value. Crediting the entire Colter acquisition to this single selection would overlook the other assets Chicago surrendered. The source-supported outcome is more favorable to Portland than the inherited Even Trade verdict suggested, though Chicago did get real flexibility from the compensation. The mismatch between the original teams' draft rights and the eventual Bucks selection also makes it important not to invent Chicago minutes for Garland.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win. Portland earns A- for 309 games of Caldwell Jones frontcourt depth over four seasons. Chicago retains C+ for securing a second-round pick that helped form a larger package for Steve Colter, who played 27 Bulls games. Milwaukee eventually drafted Winston Garland, so his later NBA production is not credited to either original club.

perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Secured Draft-Swap Rights Before the 1986 Selection

On November 20, 1985, Detroit and Sacramento arranged an option involving their 1986 or 1987 first-round selections along with a future second. The exercised rights in the canonical ledger placed Detroit with the 1986 No. 11 choice associated with John Salley and Sacramento with the No. 17 position associated with Harold Pressley. Detroit also obtained a 1987 second associated with No. 28 Rickie Winslow. This was an exchange of contingent draft positions, not Salley and Pressley trading NBA contracts on that date. The outcome can only be evaluated correctly by tracing how the option was used.

Salley Became a Major Part of Detroit's Championship Core

The Pistons used the higher 1986 draft position to obtain Salley, who developed into a durable defensive frontcourt presence alongside the Bad Boys core. He played meaningful minutes during Detroit's late-1980s championship seasons, making this a rare draft-rights exchange with clear long-term receiving-team value. That outcome was not certain when the swap was negotiated, but it is now part of the retrospective record. The Pistons should not credit Salley with teammates' achievements or treat a future right as a guaranteed title, yet his actual Detroit career strongly supports the trade's winning grade.

Sacramento Obtained Pressley Through the Lower First

The Kings' side of the option is associated with the No. 17 selection used for Harold Pressley. He had an NBA career and represented a legitimate drafted prospect rather than an unused placeholder, but he did not produce a Detroit-equivalent championship role for Sacramento. The terms of the 1985 arrangement determined which draft positions could be used and at what date. The Kings did not receive Salley, and Pressley's earlier college achievements should not be counted as NBA production for Sacramento. Keeping the selection numbers apart avoids a common misunderstanding of an option transaction as if the players exchanged teams.

Detroit's Higher Pick Created a Durable Advantage

Detroit obtained the higher first-round slot and another second-round opportunity, with Salley's actual subsequent NBA service making the difference much more concrete than a hypothetical pick valuation. Sacramento received a genuine first-round prospect in Pressley but did not match the Pistons' long-run return. The second-round identity associated with Winslow is part of the draft trail and should not be inflated into a star career. The verdict favors Detroit on a rare combination of original asset advantage and realized player contribution, without suggesting the entire championship era was caused by one option agreement.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win. Detroit earns A because the 1986 draft-swap option yielded No. 11 John Salley, whose actual Pistons defense and championship-era minutes provided long-term value, plus a later second associated with Rickie Winslow. Sacramento receives C for the No. 17 rights associated with Harold Pressley. The agreement involved draft options, not a direct trade of those players' contracts.

perspectives.analysis:
The Deal: Two Centers, No Picks on November 25
Dallas acquired James Donaldson from the Los Angeles Clippers on November 25, 1985 and sent Kurt Nimphius the other way. The original package contained one established NBA center per team; no draft choices or cash were part of that November swap. The outcome depends on what each club received from those players after they changed uniforms, not on unrelated moves added retrospectively.

Donaldson Became a Starting Center and an All-Star
The 1985-86 Mavericks got 69 Donaldson appearances, including 64 starts, and 9.6 rebounds per game. He carried that role into the following season, starting every game in 1986-87, and was named a 1988 NBA All-Star while still with Dallas. That is direct, sustained value from the center acquired for Nimphius. philadelphia-76ers.summary: On January 10, 1986, Philadelphia traded guard Leon Wood to the Washington Bullets for rookie forward Kenny Green. Wood appeared in 39 games for Washington that season, totaling 378 points and 107 assists, while Green contributed 21 Philadelphia appearances in 1985-86 and 19 more the following year. Washington obtained the stronger near-term guard return; Wizards Win, Washington B, Philadelphia C+.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Two Recently Drafted Players Swapped Roles

On January 10, 1986, the Washington Bullets traded rookie forward Kenny Green to Philadelphia for second-year point guard Leon Wood. Contemporary reporting described the Bullets seeking depth and flexibility at guard, while the Sixers acquired a 6-foot-7 forward whose collegiate scoring reputation had not translated into regular NBA starts. Green had been Washington's No. 12 overall selection in 1985, and Wood had gone tenth overall to Philadelphia in 1984. This was a direct exchange of draft investments made only a year apart. The Bullets were the same franchise represented by the site's modern Washington Wizards identifier.

Wood Became a Real Rotation Contributor for Washington

Wood appeared in 39 Washington regular-season games during the remainder of 1985-86, producing 378 points, 107 assists and 743 minutes. He did not start, but his 19.1 minutes a game gave the Bullets a genuine secondary playmaker with more scoring and passing responsibility than a token roster spot. Washington finished 39-43 and reached the postseason, losing to Philadelphia in the first round. The trade did not create a championship run, and Wood's much longer later stint with New Jersey was outside the club's return. The measurable benefit is a substantial fraction of the season with an NBA-capable reserve point guard.

Philadelphia Used Green Sparingly Across Two Seasons

Green provided 21 regular-season appearances after joining Philadelphia in 1985-86, scoring 92 points across 232 minutes without a start. He remained for 1986-87 and appeared in 19 more games, again as a deep reserve, averaging about 3.4 points. That adds up to 40 appearances for the Sixers, but with much less playmaking volume and substantially fewer minutes per game than Wood supplied for Washington. Green's twenty earlier games in a Bullets uniform must not be treated as Philadelphia acquisition value. His situation illustrates how a lottery pick can retain upside on paper while producing only marginal reserve use for the acquiring team.

The Guards' Actual Usage Explains Washington's Advantage

Washington received the player with the clearer immediate role: Wood distributed the ball and scored regularly during a playoff season. Philadelphia got a young forward who occupied a smaller spot in the rotation for portions of two seasons. The raw game count is close only because Green stayed into 1986-87, and it does not reflect his limited minutes or Wood's larger assist contribution. Neither player became a lasting star for the receiving club, so a sweeping franchise verdict would oversell the exchange. The graded advantage instead follows the distinct amounts of usable basketball production that Washington and Philadelphia obtained.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns B for Leon Wood's 39 Bullets games, 743 minutes, 378 points and 107 assists following the January 1986 deal. Philadelphia receives C+ for Kenny Green's 40 games across two seasons in a smaller role. The teams exchanged former lottery picks, but Washington extracted the more useful immediate contribution.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: On January 14, 1986, the Los Angeles Clippers acquired guard Darnell Valentine from Portland for a BOSTON-ORIGIN 1986 first-round draft right, paired with an agreed exchange of 1988 second-round picks and unspecified other considerations. Portland exercised the first at No. 24 on Arvydas Sabonis, who did not play in the NBA until 1995-96 but later contributed 470 Blazers games. The 1988 swaps became No. 26 Rolando Ferreira for Portland (12 NBA games) and No. 45 Tom Garrick for Los Angeles (211 games). Valentine supplied 178 Clippers games. Blazers Win, Portland A+ and Clippers A-, reflects Sabonis’s late but durable return while recognizing genuine Los Angeles guard production.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The January Trade Moved a Boston-Origin First, Not Sabonis Himself
On January 14, 1986, Portland sent Darnell Valentine to the Los Angeles Clippers. The centerpiece was a future 1986 first-round draft choice the Clippers had obtained from Boston months earlier during the September 1985 Bill Walton trade. Los Angeles and Portland also agreed to exchange second-round rights in 1988; the original private archive records additional future considerations but available reporting does not establish terms or a cash figure. Valentine was an NBA guard changing teams immediately; the first-round right was only an option in January, and Arvydas Sabonis had not yet been selected by Portland. Boston was the source of the pick, not a January 1986 third trading club.

The Clippers Received Valentine’s Immediate Playmaking
Valentine had spent four NBA seasons in Portland, where his standing had changed under coach Jack Ramsay. Los Angeles used him in 178 regular-season games after the exchange, averaging 8.4 points and 5.3 assists. That is real receiving-team guard production, not an empty cap contract or a placeholder for Portland’s previous 300 Valentine appearances. The Clippers preferred an established point guard at a time when they could use ballhandling immediately rather than wait for an unknown late first-round selection. The inherited Clippers A- can be debated in hindsight, but the assessment should not omit the on-court service they actually received.

Portland Drafted Sabonis in 1986 and Waited Nine NBA Seasons for Him
Portland exercised the Clippers-origin first at No. 24 in the June 1986 draft, taking Arvydas Sabonis. His international career and the political and contractual realities of the period delayed his arrival in the NBA until 1995-96. The Blazers received zero Sabonis NBA games in the intervening years, so their 1990 and 1992 Finals teams cannot be credited with playing production from him. Once he arrived, he appeared in 470 regular-season Portland games across seven NBA seasons, averaging 12.0 points and 7.3 rebounds. That unusually durable return from the 24th pick supports a high historical grade while acknowledging the nine-year delay and the risk Portland carried.

The 1988 Second-Round Swap Had Two Separate Draft Outcomes
The original exchange also moved future second-round rights in opposite directions. Portland’s side eventually became the No. 26 selection in the 1988 draft, used on Rolando Ferreira, who appeared in 12 Blazers games. Los Angeles received the future pick that became No. 45 Tom Garrick, whose 211 Clippers appearances contributed 5.8 points and 3.6 assists per game. Neither player was already a January 1986 roster piece. The Clippers combined 178 Valentine games with 211 Garrick appearances; Portland eventually received Sabonis’s 470 games plus limited Ferreira minutes. These exact later selections distinguish the real asset chain from a generic list of four names supposedly exchanged on the original date.

Assessing the Long-Term Grade Without Hindsight Shortcuts
Portland’s A+ reflects successfully holding Sabonis’s rights and eventually receiving a center who played a long productive NBA tenure. That retrospective benefit is not evidence it could have used him immediately in 1986. The Clippers’ A- acknowledges sizable combined Valentine and Garrick games, even though neither became the star Sabonis later was for Portland. The future-considerations component has no documented terms in the source ledger and should not be assigned invented player names or cash. The inherited Blazers Win result represents the eventual long-term quality difference, not a conclusion that Los Angeles received no return.

Final Verdict
The January 14, 1986 deal was Valentine for a Celtics-origin first-round draft right and a reciprocal 1988 second-round pick swap, with unspecified future considerations documented but not monetized. Sabonis, Ferreira and Garrick were future selections, not 1986 traded veterans. Los Angeles gained Valentine’s immediate 178 games and later Garrick’s 211; Portland got Ferreira’s 12 and waited until 1995 for Sabonis’s 470 games. Blazers Win, Portland A+ and Clippers A- remain the stored outcome and grades, with every original drafted-player and trade-asset relationship preserved.

Valentine had spent four NBA seasons in Portland, where his standing had changed under coach Jack Ramsay. Los Angeles used him in 178 regular-season games after the exchange, averaging 8.4 points and 5.3 assists. That is real receiving-team guard production, not an empty cap contract or a placeholder for Portland’s previous 300 Valentine appearances. The Clippers preferred an established point guard at a time when they could use ballhandling immediately rather than wait for an unknown late first-round selection. The inherited Clippers A- can be debated in hindsight, but the assessment should not omit the on-court service they actually received.

Portland Drafted Sabonis in 1986 and Waited Nine NBA Seasons for Him
Portland exercised the Clippers-origin first at No. 24 in the June 1986 draft, taking Arvydas Sabonis. His international career and the political and contractual realities of the period delayed his arrival in the NBA until 1995-96. The Blazers received zero Sabonis NBA games in the intervening years, so their 1990 and 1992 Finals teams cannot be credited with playing production from him. Once he arrived, he appeared in 470 regular-season Portland games across seven NBA seasons, averaging 12.0 points and 7.3 rebounds. That unusually durable return from the 24th pick supports a high historical grade while acknowledging the nine-year delay and the risk Portland carried.

The 1988 Second-Round Swap Had Two Separate Draft Outcomes
The original exchange also moved future second-round rights in opposite directions. Portland’s side eventually became the No. 26 selection in the 1988 draft, used on Rolando Ferreira, who appeared in 12 Blazers games. Los Angeles received the future pick that became No. 45 Tom Garrick, whose 211 Clippers appearances contributed 5.8 points and 3.6 assists per game. Neither player was already a January 1986 roster piece. The Clippers combined 178 Valentine games with 211 Garrick appearances; Portland eventually received Sabonis’s 470 games plus limited Ferreira minutes. These exact later selections distinguish the real asset chain from a generic list of four names supposedly exchanged on the original date.

Assessing the Long-Term Grade Without Hindsight Shortcuts
Portland’s A+ reflects successfully holding Sabonis’s rights and eventually receiving a center who played a long productive NBA tenure. That retrospective benefit is not evidence it could have used him immediately in 1986. The Clippers’ A- acknowledges sizable combined Valentine and Garrick games, even though neither became the star Sabonis later was for Portland. The future-considerations component has no documented terms in the source ledger and should not be assigned invented player names or cash. The inherited Blazers Win result represents the eventual long-term quality difference, not a conclusion that Los Angeles received no return.

Final Verdict
The January 14, 1986 deal was Valentine for a Celtics-origin first-round draft right and a reciprocal 1988 second-round pick swap, with unspecified future considerations documented but not monetized. Sabonis, Ferreira and Garrick were future selections, not 1986 traded veterans. Los Angeles gained Valentine’s immediate 178 games and later Garrick’s 211; Portland got Ferreira’s 12 and waited until 1995 for Sabonis’s 470 games. Blazers Win, Portland A+ and Clippers A- remain the stored outcome and grades, with every original drafted-player and trade-asset relationship preserved.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Replaced One Veteran Guard With Another

The Hawks sent Eddie Johnson to the Cleveland Cavaliers in exchange for Johnny Davis during the 1986 All-Star break. Davis had played two earlier seasons in Atlanta and offered a familiar reserve behind Glenn Rivers and the rest of the Hawks' guards. Johnson was a former two-time All-Star whose long Atlanta tenure included much more significant scoring work. The decision traded the outgoing player's offensive pedigree for a different type of backup experience, with each club operating on its existing season's schedule.

Johnson Offered Cleveland a Proven Offensive Background

At the time of the swap, Johnson had averaged 10.5 points in 39 Hawks games that season. Cleveland's struggling roster had reasons to take a chance on a guard capable of generating offense. His past All-Star standing could not guarantee he would reproduce his peak years with the Cavaliers, but it did show that the incoming player had a larger established scoring résumé than the player traded away. Only what Johnson supplied after joining Cleveland belongs in the Cavaliers' direct return, not his earlier Atlanta totals.

Davis Was Familiar but Less Dynamic for the Hawks

Davis had averaged 7.2 points through 38 Cleveland appearances before the transaction, and he arrived as a backup candidate rather than a franchise-changing acquisition. Bringing him back had practical appeal because the coaching staff knew his game and Atlanta was already competing near the top of its division. Still, the exchange cost a guard who had been a major contributor for the franchise for several years. The available evidence supports evaluating Atlanta's benefit as depth and familiarity rather than superior offensive talent.

The Scoring-Pedigree Difference Informs the Verdict

Both participants were in their thirties, so the trade was less about developing a new prospect than balancing the veteran guard rotation. Cleveland obtained Johnson's higher proven scoring level, while Atlanta reacquired a player it could trust in a secondary role. That makes the inherited grade gap understandable even without pretending Johnson revived every part of his former All-Star form for Cleveland. The Cavaliers secured the stronger individual reputation and scoring possibility while the Hawks accepted a more limited replacement.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives B+ for taking on Eddie Johnson, a former two-time Hawks All-Star with greater proven scoring ability. Atlanta gets D+ for a familiar reserve in Johnny Davis, who had a narrower offensive role. The comparison recognizes the actual exchange of veteran guards without crediting either receiving club for seasons each player spent elsewhere.

perspectives.summary: On June 16, 1986, Cleveland acquired Philadelphia’s No. 1 overall NBA draft pick in exchange for Roy Hinson and cash. The following day the Cavaliers selected Brad Daugherty, who played all 548 of his NBA games for Cleveland, made five All-Star teams and averaged 19.0 points and 9.5 rebounds. Hinson was a legitimate veteran addition for Philadelphia—13.9 points and 6.4 rebounds over 76 games in 1986-87—but his 76ers tenure ended after another 29 appearances. Cavaliers Win, Cleveland A+ and Philadelphia D, reflects the much greater sustained return from the transferred draft choice; no unsupported cash figure is assumed.
perspectives.analysis:
The June 16 Exchange and the Draft-Day Clock
Philadelphia transferred its 1986 No. 1 draft selection to Cleveland on June 16, one day before the NBA draft, for forward Roy Hinson and cash consideration. The original ledger contains the first selection, Hinson and cash, without a reliable amount attached to the cash component. Cleveland still had to use the transferred pick: on June 17 it selected Brad Daugherty from North Carolina. That distinction matters because Daugherty was not already an NBA player when Philadelphia sent the draft right. Cleveland’s separate acquisition of Mark Price that summer was not part of the Hinson agreement.

Daugherty Turned the Pick into an Eight-Season Cavaliers Career
Daugherty made 548 regular-season appearances, every one for Cleveland, while averaging 19.0 points, 9.5 rebounds and 3.7 assists. A skilled passing and scoring center, he earned five All-Star selections and finished with 10,389 points and 5,227 rebounds. Cleveland retired his No. 43 in 1997. Injuries curtailed his NBA career, but the pick still returned a franchise-level center for eight seasons. Those results support the inherited Cavaliers A+ without importing unrelated subsequent trades or speculating about players Cleveland might have drafted.

Hinson Supplied Philadelphia Actual Production
The 76ers did not receive an empty contract. Hinson had started all 82 Cleveland games in 1985-86, producing 19.6 points and 7.8 rebounds per game before the deal. He played 76 Philadelphia games the following season, starting 58 and averaging 13.9 points and 6.4 rebounds. Another 29 76ers appearances followed in 1987-88 before he was sent to New Jersey. That return had immediate value, but his later work for the Nets belongs to a separate asset chain, not an extension of his Philadelphia production. Nor can the trade’s unspecified cash amount be treated as a larger return than the first-round selection.

Why Cleveland’s Return Was Far Larger
The key comparison is 548 games and five All-Star selections from Daugherty’s Cleveland career against Hinson’s comparatively short Philadelphia stint. Hinson helped the 76ers during his first season, which is why describing him as a valueless player would misstate the record. But a usable veteran and cash of unknown amount did not compensate the 76ers for surrendering the top pick that became Cleveland’s franchise center. The grade disparity—Cavaliers A+, 76ers D—tracks actual duration and quality of play rather than draft-night name recognition alone.

Final Verdict
Cavaliers Win is the preserved hindsight result for the June 16 exchange. The Cavaliers turned a transferred draft right into eight seasons of Brad Daugherty, while Philadelphia received less than two seasons of Roy Hinson. Mark Price, later Hinson teams and unconfirmed cash figures are excluded from the original package accounting. The source-backed comparison explains the A+/D result without adding invented assets.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta and Los Angeles Swapped Veterans and Draft Rights

Atlanta obtained guard Mike McGee and the rights to Ken Barlow from the Lakers in a June 1986 agreement. Los Angeles received rights to Ron Kellogg and Billy Thompson. McGee was the only named NBA veteran changing teams in this package, while the other assets were rights to players whose next contracts weren't guaranteed. The Hawks were pursuing usable perimeter depth and an additional forward prospect option. The Lakers could refresh their rights inventory without forcing another veteran into a rotation that already had established scoring and playmaking combinations.

McGee Could Be Evaluated in Atlanta Immediately

McGee had contributed NBA minutes in Los Angeles and represented a recognizable outside-scoring option for the Hawks. His arrival allowed Atlanta to test his fit without waiting for a rookie to be selected in a later draft. However, a player bringing NBA experience doesn't mean the receiving team inherits earlier Lakers seasons or playoff achievements. McGee still needed to win minutes and a role alongside Atlanta's established guards and wings. His return should be judged by actual work after the June agreement rather than by career totals spanning different teams.

The Lakers Acquired Two Distinct Rights Claims

Los Angeles received rights to Kellogg and Thompson, two prospects who were not automatically under signed long-term NBA contracts. Such rights could become valuable through negotiations or additional transactions, but claiming immediate NBA production from both would distort the value of the exchange. The Lakers held the option to decide how each prospect fit their personnel plans. The distinction is important because Barlow, the rights asset headed to Atlanta, could likewise carry professional value outside the NBA without necessarily turning into Hawks game statistics.

Asset Flexibility Gives Los Angeles a Narrow Edge

The Lakers took two developmental chances in exchange for McGee and Barlow's rights, while Atlanta obtained a current guard plus a different prospect option. Neither franchise acquired a top-five draft pick or a newly established All-Star. Atlanta's immediate use of McGee had merit, but Los Angeles gained more separate opportunities to evaluate younger talent without an obligation to commit NBA rotation minutes to both. That supports a modest Lakers-winning assessment rather than an overwhelming outcome. Follow-on rights transactions need independent treatment and can't be credited entirely to the original deal.

Final Verdict

Slight Lakers Edge. Los Angeles receives B- for obtaining rights to Ron Kellogg and Billy Thompson, two separate development options. Atlanta earns C+ for veteran Mike McGee and Ken Barlow's rights. A right to negotiate does not guarantee a signed NBA starter, and McGee's pretrade Lakers output isn't newly acquired Hawks performance.

perspectives.analysis:
One Veteran Guard Against a Draft-Rights Player and Two Future Seconds
Chicago acquired Steve Colter from Portland on June 17, 1986 after selecting Montana forward Larry Krystkowiak with the No. 28 pick. The Bulls sent Portland Krystkowiak’s draft rights and their 1987 and 1992 second-round choices for the experienced guard. Colter had started 51 games for Portland in 1985-86, averaging 8.7 points and 3.2 assists, so there was a concrete rationale for a rebuilding Chicago roster under newly appointed coach Doug Collins. The price was not merely a young forward already contracted to the Bulls; it included two longer-dated NBA draft rights whose subsequent custody must be followed separately.

Colter Played Only 27 Bulls Games, Then Moved to Philadelphia
In Chicago, Colter appeared in 27 NBA regular-season games during 1986-87 and started 18. He scored 4.9 points and supplied 3.5 assists per game, but his field-goal shooting was 34.5 percent. The Bulls moved him to Philadelphia within the same season, where he made a further 43 NBA appearances. Those 43 76ers games and his later Washington career do not increase Chicago’s return from the 1986 Portland transaction. The Bulls obtained limited guard relief while relinquishing multiple rights. This short 27-game receiving-team stint supports the inherited Chicago C+ without denying that Colter had been a legitimate starting option in Portland.

Portland Moved Krystkowiak’s Rights Again Within Two Days
Krystkowiak did not play an NBA regular-season game for Portland following the Bulls trade. On June 19 the Trail Blazers included his NBA draft rights AND veteran center Mychal Thompson in a separate exchange with the San Antonio Spurs for Steve Johnson. Portland controlled Krystkowiak’s rights for roughly 48 hours, and their chief immediate benefit was negotiation value in that later multi-asset deal. Johnson’s entire Portland tenure cannot be attributed to Krystkowiak alone while erasing Thompson’s contribution to the package. Krystkowiak subsequently played in the NBA with San Antonio and Milwaukee, which does not make those seasons original Trail Blazers playing returns.

The Two Future Seconds Left Portland Before Their Drafts
Portland sent the incoming 1987 second-round right to Milwaukee on November 11, 1986 for Chris Engler. The Bucks exercised that pick at No. 40 on Winston Garland in the 1987 draft, meaning Garland should not be listed as someone Portland itself drafted and used with the Bulls-origin right. Years later Portland included its inherited 1992 second in an August 1990 transaction with Sacramento involving Danny Ainge and Byron Irvin and additional considerations. The Kings exercised that eventual No. 54 choice on Brett Roberts in 1992; Roberts did not have an NBA regular-season playing career. The pick lines are correctly associated with their future selection names for historical tracking, but those player careers cannot be allocated to Portland court minutes.

Why the Original Portland Grade Is Better Than Chicago’s
Chicago used one of its stronger draft-rights assets and two further second-round opportunities on a guard who appeared in only 27 Bulls games. Portland created at least three transaction branches: Krystkowiak’s rights assisted in the Johnson deal, the first later pick helped obtain Engler, and the second was used in a much later Ainge-related package. Each branch involved additional considerations and cannot be treated as if Portland got three entire NBA careers from the original trade. The inherited Blazers Win, Portland A- against Chicago C+, reflects multi-year transactional flexibility compared with a short guard tenure; it is not proof every eventual player associated with a 1987 or 1992 pick was a Blazer.

Final Verdict
June 17, 1986 was Colter to Chicago for Krystkowiak’s freshly drafted rights plus Chicago’s next two specified second-round choices. Colter supplied 27 Bulls games before a later move. Portland rapidly rerouted the rights with Thompson, later rerouted the 1987 second to Milwaukee and included the 1992 second in a Sacramento deal; Garland and Roberts were the eventual selection names on other clubs’ draft nights. Preserve Blazers Win with Portland A-/Chicago C+ and the exact original protected assets and private/noindex scope.

perspectives.summary: On June 17, 1986, Dallas used the No. 25 NBA draft choice on Georgia Tech guard Mark Price, then traded his draft rights to Cleveland for the Cavaliers’ 1989 second-round selection and unspecified cash or future considerations. The later pick became No. 53 Jeff Hodge. Price delivered nine Cavaliers seasons, 582 appearances, 9,543 points, 4,206 assists and four All-Star selections; Dallas received a much smaller draft return.
