perspectives.analysis:
From the No. 25 Pick to a Cleveland Draft-Rights Trade
Dallas selected Mark Price from Georgia Tech with the 25th pick on June 17, 1986, then sent his unsigned NBA rights to the Cavaliers. Cleveland returned its 1989 second-round selection, with an additional imported asset notation for cash or future considerations but no reliably verified dollar figure or other player. The pick eventually became No. 53, Jeff Hodge. Price had not appeared in the NBA when Cleveland secured him, making the exchange one of draft rights and a future selection, not a swap of two established NBA guards.

Nine Cavaliers Seasons Made the Return Exceptional
Price played 582 regular-season games, including 495 starts, for Cleveland. He scored 9,543 points and recorded 4,206 assists there while shooting 47.9 percent overall, 40.9 percent from three-point range and 90.6 percent at the free-throw line. He became a four-time All-Star and four-time All-NBA selection, including first-team recognition in 1992-93. The 722 games in Price’s full NBA career include later franchises; those extra appearances cannot be attributed to his Cleveland trade return. The Cavaliers’ A+ is supported by nine seasons of an elite offensive organizer rather than the mere prestige of a future name.

What Dallas Received Was a Distant, Smaller Selection
Dallas waited until 1989 to exercise its acquired second-round choice, selecting Jeff Hodge at No. 53. The attached transaction sources do not establish NBA production from Hodge for the Mavericks, and the cash or future-consideration annotation has no verified payment amount. A review cannot inflate a small draft asset with conjectural cash or credit some unrelated later Dallas signing. The Mavericks’ F grade compares that verified modest return with the direct Cleveland value of the guard Dallas had drafted and immediately traded.

The Wider Cavaliers Draft Did Not Come in This Package
Cleveland also added Brad Daugherty and Ron Harper around the 1986 draft, but those acquisitions were separate transactions. They help explain the young core into which Price arrived; they are not extra players Dallas exchanged here. The Cavaliers reached the postseason repeatedly during his nine Cleveland years, but those team results cannot be assigned solely to a single draft-rights transaction. The trade’s direct asset measure remains Price’s 582 Cavs appearances, on-court playmaking and four All-Star recognitions versus Dallas’s later No. 53 selection and unquantified other terms.

Final Verdict: A Franchise Guard for a Future Second-Round Pick
Cavaliers Win, Cleveland A+ and Dallas F is the preserved historical verdict. Cleveland acquired the draft rights to Mark Price in June 1986 and held a guard whose shooting, passing and nine-year tenure delivered substantial value. Dallas received a 1989 second-round selection that became Jeff Hodge and an incompletely documented cash/future-consideration component. The grade gap does not require inventing a dollar figure or attaching Price’s post-Cleveland years to the 1986 exchange.

perspectives.summary: Dallas traded reserve shooter Dale Ellis to Seattle for veteran Al Wood on July 23, 1986, a direct player-for-player exchange without picks or cash. Ellis immediately averaged 24.9 points over all 82 Sonics games, won Most Improved Player and helped Seattle upset the 55-win Mavericks in the first round of the 1987 playoffs. He later became a 1989 All-Star. Wood played 54 Dallas games without a start, averaging 6.6 points. The documented gap supports SuperSonics Win, Seattle A+ and Dallas D; it reflects actual returns, not the hypothetical Dallas version of Ellis.
perspectives.analysis:
A Straight Swap with Different Expectations
On July 23, 1986, the Mavericks sent Dale Ellis to the Seattle SuperSonics and acquired Al Wood. The ledger lists one player each way, with no cash, draft pick or third-club routing. Dallas had a crowded wing rotation of Mark Aguirre, Jay Vincent and Detlef Schrempf, leaving former No. 9 pick Ellis with 15.1 minutes and 7.1 points per game in 1985-86. Wood, a veteran guard, had averaged 11.6 points for Seattle the previous season. Dallas therefore pursued established help rather than knowingly surrendering an already proven scoring star.

Seattle Gave Ellis a Starting Role and Got Immediate Results
The Sonics offered Ellis a much larger job. In 1986-87, he appeared in all 82 games, started 76, averaged 37.5 minutes and produced 24.9 points while shooting 51.6 percent from the field. The improvement earned him the NBA Most Improved Player award. The change in minutes and usage made the trade’s opportunity cost visible almost immediately. More playing time alone does not prove that Seattle caused every part of his development, but the first-year return was an elite scorer rather than the Dallas reserve whose contract had changed hands.

Wood Played a Smaller Role for a Strong Dallas Team
Al Wood appeared in 54 games for the 1986-87 Mavericks, never started, and averaged 6.6 points in 12.2 minutes. Those figures do not suggest Wood was valueless or that the Dallas team itself failed; the Mavericks finished 55-27 and won their division. They do establish that the player Dallas received had a much smaller direct role than the one Seattle acquired. Wood’s earlier seasons for the Sonics cannot be credited as Mavericks production. The canonical Dallas D grade reflects this particular return, not an invented draft obligation or extra traded asset.

The 1987 Playoff Meeting Exposed the Gap
The 39-43 Sonics reached the Western playoffs and eliminated the 55-win Mavericks three games to one in the opening round. They then defeated Houston to reach the Western Conference Finals. Ellis led Seattle’s regular-season scoring at 24.9 points and was an important part of the run, though an entire upset cannot be attributed to one player. The head-to-head outcome is a documented competitive consequence: Dallas faced the shooter it had sent away less than a year earlier. The clubs had exchanged only Ellis and Wood, so no other traded rights need to be credited to this comparison.

Ellis Sustained His Seattle Scoring Prime
Ellis’s 1986-87 breakout was not a single-season anomaly. He averaged 25.8 points in 1987-88 and 27.5 in 1988-89, earned a 1989 All-Star selection and All-NBA Third Team recognition, and made high-volume perimeter shooting a defining part of his Seattle role. Those first Seattle seasons are attributable to the 1986 acquisition. His later return to the Sonics through another transaction does not belong to this first trade’s initial asset chain. The extended high-scoring stretch against Wood’s one limited Dallas season supports the large grade gap.

Final Verdict
SuperSonics Win, Seattle A+ and Dallas D remains the preserved outcome. Seattle acquired a reserve and enabled a premier scorer; Dallas acquired a veteran but received just 54 reserve appearances while Ellis prospered elsewhere. This is a hindsight evaluation with documented performance, 1987 playoff context and 1989 honors; it is not a claim Dallas could have forecast every future game on July 23, 1986.

perspectives.analysis:
A Free-Agent Right Was Exchanged for a Future Second

Portland and Chicago reached an agreement on August 5, 1986 involving veteran Michael Holton's free agency. The Bulls agreed not to exercise their right of first refusal on Holton, and the Trail Blazers surrendered a future second-round selection. That draft right eventually appears in the historical ledger as the 1992 No. 52 choice associated with Matt Steigenga. This was not a trade of two existing NBA contracts or a deal immediately involving Steigenga in 1986; he had yet to be drafted. The value lay in Portland's ability to pursue Holton and Chicago's compensation for relinquishing an option.

Portland Sought a Known Guard Without an Offer-Sheet Fight

The Trail Blazers could pursue Holton without Chicago invoking its matching rights, simplifying a free-agent roster decision. Holton was a player with NBA guard experience rather than a future prospect, which explains why the club would give up a distant lower-round selection. His prior seasons with other franchises aren't Portland playing time produced by the arrangement, and his eventual contributions should be read from the receiving team's actual seasons. Portland received the opportunity to sign or retain the targeted guard, not an automatic guarantee that he would become a long-serving starting player or that the team would win more games.

Chicago's Second Became a 1992 Draft Slot

The Bulls secured a future second-round asset in exchange for stepping aside on Holton's free agency. Six years later, the draft ledger associates that position with Steigenga at No. 52. Such a long-delayed selection had value as a prospect opportunity or as a trade component, but it did not supply Chicago with an immediately established guard in 1986. The actual rights chain and player selection must be kept separate from any professional seasons elsewhere. This was also a different period of roster rules, so the transaction should not be rewritten as a contemporary restricted-free-agent sign-and-trade with assumed modern salary exceptions.

Different Forms of Modest Value Produce an Even Result

Portland gained access to an identified NBA veteran, while Chicago obtained a future selection it could use to explore young talent. Neither benefit resembled acquiring a star, and the elapsed time before the draft lowered the certainty of Chicago's eventual return. The agreement is best evaluated as balanced compensation for the use or nonuse of a free-agent matching right. It would be misleading to assign a complete later NBA career to either club based on the original agreement alone. Equal moderate grades acknowledge that both front offices received a reasonable tool for their immediate priorities.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Chicago receives C+ for obtaining the future second-round right later associated with 1992 No. 52 Matt Steigenga, while Portland receives C+ because the Bulls agreed not to exercise their right of first refusal on Michael Holton. The deal involved a free-agent matching option, not two contracted veterans, and neither asset promised a long-term NBA starter.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Clippers Win. Los Angeles received both immediate veteran depth and premium draft capital. The first-round pick landing at No. 6 gave the Clippers a particularly valuable asset, and the breadth of the return comfortably exceeds what Sacramento obtained from the outgoing veteran package. Sacramento did receive established players rather than empty contracts, and Derek Smith was the most important of the incoming names. That prevents an absolute zero grade, but injuries, age and limited tenure kept the Kings’ realized value well below the package they surrendered.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis: The Clippers acquired Larry Drew, Mike Woodson, a 1988 first-round pick that became No. 6 Hersey Hawkins, a 1989 second-round pick that became Jay Edwards, and cash. Sacramento acquired Derek Smith, Franklin Edwards and Junior Bridgeman. Los Angeles received both immediate veteran depth and premium draft capital. The first-round pick landing at No. 6 gave the Clippers a particularly valuable asset, and the breadth of the return comfortably exceeds what Sacramento obtained from the outgoing veteran package. Sacramento did receive established players rather than empty contracts, and Derek Smith was the most important of the incoming names. That prevents an absolute zero grade, but injuries, age and limited tenure kept the Kings’ realized value well below the package they surrendered. The strongest directly tied component is the 1988 first-round pick that became Hersey Hawkins. Even though later decisions involving Hawkins are separate transactions, the conversion of the pick into a high draft selection is direct evidence of the value embedded in the Clippers’ return. This trade took place before modern pick-protection conventions became as standardized, making the unprotected or lightly constrained draft value especially important. Sacramento paid a large future opportunity cost for veteran help, while Los Angeles diversified across players, picks and cash. Clippers A+, Kings D. Los Angeles earns an elite grade for receiving useful veterans plus a top-six first-round outcome and another draft pick. Sacramento receives some credit for established players but not enough to offset the surrendered asset depth. The completed asset-chain comparison also favors Los Angeles because the return was diversified across immediate players, future draft capital and cash rather than resting on one fragile outcome. Sacramento captured some veteran usefulness, but the Clippers retained multiple independent paths to value. That broader base is why the A+ versus D spread remains defensible even after discounting later production that belonged to subsequent transactions rather than to this exchange itself.

perspectives.summary: On August 21, 1986, Detroit acquired two-time scoring champion Adrian Dantley and two Utah second-round picks (later Norris Coleman in 1987 and Phil Henderson in 1990) for Kelly Tripucka and Kent Benson. Dantley supplied Detroit high-level half-court scoring on its way to the 1988 NBA Finals and later became the outgoing asset in the Mark Aguirre deal. Utah exchanged its established star amid a strained Dantley–Frank Layden relationship but received a smaller realized return. Pistons Win, Detroit A- and Utah F, describes the substantial player-value gap; the late picks were supplementary.
perspectives.analysis:
The Actual August 1986 Package
Detroit acquired Adrian Dantley from the Utah Jazz on August 21, 1986, receiving two second-round selections in the same package. The picks were eventually used at No. 38 on Norris Coleman in 1987 and No. 49 on Phil Henderson in 1990. Detroit sent Kelly Tripucka and Kent Benson to Utah. The transaction thus involved a star scorer and two future draft selections going to the Pistons, and two established players going to the Jazz. Calling this only a narrow Detroit advantage obscures the original grade gap of A- to F and the scale of the actual return.

Why Utah Made the Deal
Dantley had won two NBA scoring titles and averaged 29.8 points the season before Detroit acquired him. Utah also had a developing frontcourt with Karl Malone and Thurl Bailey, and contemporary coverage described friction between Dantley and coach/general manager Frank Layden. Tripucka was a younger perimeter scorer with a 20-point season behind him, while Benson offered additional frontcourt depth. The Jazz therefore had an understandable roster and relationship motive. That motive is distinct from whether the package ultimately replaced Dantley’s scoring value.

Dantley Contributed Before the Later Aguirre Trade
Detroit received a skilled half-court scorer who drew fouls, operated in a controlled offense and helped the Pistons advance toward the 1988 NBA Finals. His tenure should not be dismissed simply because Detroit later traded him before its 1989 championship. The club eventually exchanged Dantley for Mark Aguirre, a separately documented transaction. That continuation can be traced as retained trade value because Dantley was the outgoing asset, but the full later championship must not be attributed automatically to the 1986 Utah deal.

The Jazz Return and the Two Secondary Draft Picks
Tripucka had been a high-scoring Detroit player, but his production declined after moving to Utah, and Benson did not replace Dantley’s star-level output. Detroit’s two additional second-round picks became Norris Coleman and Phil Henderson, neither a documented franchise-changing player. They provide limited standalone basketball value, but they are part of the original asset ledger and reinforce that Detroit received draft consideration while acquiring the best player. The distinction prevents a grade being inflated by hypothetical later picks or by a player associated only indirectly with a future move.

Verdict: A- Detroit, F Utah
The Pistons obtained an accomplished scorer who contributed to a Finals contender, retained meaningful trade value for a later Aguirre exchange and received two lower-round selections. Utah received a younger scorer and a center who did not approximate the outgoing star’s sustained contribution, despite plausible fit reasons for initiating the trade. The preserved historical result is Pistons Win, Detroit A- and Utah F. It is a hindsight assessment of realized player value and documented secondary assets, not a claim that Utah had no reason to restructure.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Obtained Fred Roberts With an Unusual Additional Term

On September 25, 1986, Boston acquired Fred Roberts from Utah for a 1987 third-round selection and a commitment to play two exhibition games in Utah. The future draft slot later appeared as No. 68, associated with Billy Donovan. The preseason-game promise was a real nonplayer consideration in the agreement, not another future draft pick or a second NBA contract. Utah received both the lower-round prospect opportunity and the value of hosting the Celtics in exhibitions, while Boston took a veteran forward it could use in its rotation.

Roberts Gave Boston Frontcourt Size and Experience

Roberts arrived as a known NBA forward who could help Boston manage regular-season frontcourt depth and injuries. The Celtics had an established championship-level starting group, making capable reserve minutes more useful than the speculative return from a third-round selection years away. He still had to earn his new role, and any performances for Utah before the agreement belong to the Jazz. The trade's appeal lay in obtaining a real professional with a role the Celtics could assess immediately. It was not the arrival of another top overall draft pick or a replacement for Boston's central stars.

Utah's Compensation Went Beyond Billy Donovan's Draft Position

The Jazz collected a third-round selection that the 1987 draft ledger associates with No. 68 Billy Donovan. That selection didn't guarantee a long NBA playing career and should not be confused with Donovan's much later coaching achievements. Utah also gained the right to host Boston for two exhibition games, a business and promotional benefit rather than a regular-season win or a basketball prospect. A review that ignores those agreed contests understates the compensation, while one that treats exhibition commitments as two players greatly inflates it. Both parts belong in the original trade description.

The Celtics Slightly Favored Immediate Basketball Depth

Boston received a veteran who could actually join the roster; Utah obtained a lower-round choice and a business-oriented commitment. The Celtics' direct basketball return is easier to identify, which supports a modest winning verdict. Utah still obtained tangible compensation for a player it was willing to trade, and the exhibitions may have mattered to the franchise and its supporters. Neither part of the agreement produced a new superstar by itself. Recognizing both the specific 1987 third-round slot and the unusual exhibitions clause is essential to fair grades.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B- for acquiring experienced forward Fred Roberts. Utah receives C+ for a 1987 third-round right associated with No. 68 Billy Donovan and Boston's promise to play two exhibition games in Utah. Donovan's later coaching reputation isn't a Jazz NBA contribution, and exhibition commitments aren't draft picks.

seattle-supersonics.summary: On September 29, 1986, Seattle sent Tim McCormick and Danny Vranes to the Philadelphia 76ers for Clemon Johnson and Philadelphia's 1989 first-round pick. That pick became No. 17 overall and Seattle used it on Shawn Kemp, who developed into a six-time All-Star and the frontcourt centerpiece of the SuperSonics team that reached the 1996 NBA Finals. Philadelphia received a productive starting center in McCormick, but the long-term return swung heavily toward Seattle.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Seattle, Philadelphia and league transaction logs all identify the September 29, 1986 counterparty as the Philadelphia 76ers, not the New York Knicks carried by the legacy archive entry. Seattle traded Tim McCormick and Danny Vranes to Philadelphia for Clemon Johnson and a 1989 first-round pick. John Nash's executive transaction ledger records the same package. Correcting the partner is structural, not cosmetic: every asset-routing key, team list and grade must point to Philadelphia before the trade can be evaluated safely.

Seattle Return
Clemon Johnson supplied immediate rotation value. He played 78 games with seven starts for Seattle in 1986-87 and 74 games with 26 starts in 1987-88, giving the Sonics useful frontcourt depth while the draft asset matured. The larger payoff came in 1989. Seattle's draft ledger identifies the incoming Philadelphia first-rounder as the No. 17 pick, which the Sonics used on Shawn Kemp. Kemp became a six-time NBA All-Star, earned three All-NBA Second Team selections and formed the core partnership with Gary Payton on the 1995-96 team that won 64 games and reached the NBA Finals. That is direct downstream value from the pick acquired in this transaction, so it belongs in the hindsight grade rather than being treated as unrelated draft luck.

Philadelphia Return
McCormick was a legitimate return, not filler. In 1986-87 he played 81 games, started 79, averaged 13.2 points and 7.8 rebounds, and gave Philadelphia a dependable interior starter. Vranes had a smaller role, appearing in 58 games with six starts that season and 57 games with five starts in 1987-88. The 76ers therefore received immediate NBA production from both outgoing Seattle players, with McCormick carrying most of the value. That keeps Philadelphia well above a failing grade even though neither player approached Kemp's eventual impact.

Hindsight Verdict
Seattle receives an A+ because the transaction combined two seasons of useful Clemon Johnson depth with a first-round pick that became one of the defining players in franchise history. Philadelphia receives a C because McCormick delivered real starter-level production and Vranes added rotation minutes, but the club surrendered the future pick that became Kemp. The final verdict is Seattle SuperSonics Win. The analysis credits only the directly traceable 1989 pick outcome and Kemp's Seattle career; it does not inflate Seattle's side with unrelated later transactions.

seattle-supersonics.analysis:
Seattle Acquired Control of Lester's Rights

The SuperSonics obtained rights to guard Ronnie Lester from the Lakers in October 1986. Los Angeles's incoming consideration is recorded only as future terms with a possible cash component. Seattle gained the chance to evaluate a veteran guard's availability, while the Lakers relinquished a right they didn't plan to use in the same way. No specific draft pick is securely identified as Los Angeles compensation.

Rights Are Not the Same as New Guard Minutes

Lester had previous professional experience, but acquiring his rights didn't automatically create a productive Seattle backcourt role. Injuries and an uncertain roster position affected the potential for a long playing stint. The appropriate immediate benefit to Seattle was the right to pursue or evaluate him. His earlier Lakers statistics should not be moved into a SuperSonics accounting merely because the teams completed the agreement.

The Lakers' Future Compensation Is Uncertain

The inherited record questions whether cash was part of the future considerations. That limit should be shown rather than hidden behind a fabricated amount or a numbered selection. Los Angeles gained the ability to move past its claim to Lester and whatever compensation the clubs had agreed to. Without a confirmed rights chain, no later draftee should be attached to the Lakers through this transaction.

The Established Verdict Needs a Qualification

The inherited SuperSonics Win credits Seattle's named guard rights at B+ and assigns the Lakers C+ for less-specific compensation. That difference reflects the published evaluation, not proof that Lester became an enduring Seattle starter. The agreement was modest and unusually incomplete as an asset record. An accurate reader-facing verdict therefore identifies the uncertainty while preserving the original grades and teams.

Final Verdict

Seattle SuperSonics Win. Seattle earns B+ for acquiring the rights to Ronnie Lester, while the Lakers receive C+ for future considerations whose exact form remains unresolved in the source record. The transaction created a new rights holder; neither a specific Lakers draft pick nor lasting Seattle player production is assumed.

indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana and Seattle Exchanged Veteran Guards and a Future Pick

On October 2, 1986, Indiana acquired veteran John Long and a future second-round selection from the Seattle SuperSonics. Seattle received Russ Schoene and Terence Stansbury. The incoming Indiana draft position eventually appears as the 1993 No. 51 pick associated with Spencer Dunkley, a long-dated right whose actual value could not be known in 1986. The canonical modern franchise index places Seattle history under today's Oklahoma City Thunder umbrella, but the SuperSonics were the actual trading club. That distinction matters when discussing which roster received the players and whose future selection was involved.

Long Supplied a More Established Scoring Profile

Long arrived with an existing record as an NBA scoring guard, giving Indiana an experienced option alongside a roster undergoing change. His prior seasons in Detroit and elsewhere explained why the Pacers sought him, but those earlier games should not be added to his Indiana production. The later second-round option created another source of flexibility beyond the current player. At the same time, a veteran's name does not guarantee the team received his peak historical scoring for several seasons. The proper Pacers return is whatever roster contribution Long actually made after October 1986, plus the rights attached to the future pick.

Seattle Acquired Two Different Roster Pieces

The SuperSonics took Schoene and Stansbury, players whose positions and development profiles gave the club options rather than one proven superstar. Seattle could evaluate both contracts during the season, with Stansbury particularly known for explosive athletic ability and earlier professional experience. The draft rights leaving Seattle were years away from being exercised, so the near-term cost was lower than surrendering a guaranteed lottery selection. Their subsequent NBA careers must be traced through each receiving team and later transaction. Calling those 1986 minutes Oklahoma City Thunder games would confuse the historical franchise continuation with an actual team that did not yet play under that name.

The Package Is Balanced Across Immediate and Later Needs

Indiana gained the more established veteran and an eventual second-round choice; Seattle received two players it could use or assess. The relative value depended on different roster needs and how each front office evaluated the coming season. Neither side directly acquired a franchise-changing All-Star, and the 1993 selection should not be treated as a successful Pacers player before verifying its final rights chain. Equal grades acknowledge useful assets for both franchises without inflating their future histories. This was a Seattle SuperSonics transaction, even though the site's modern lineage groups those records with the Thunder.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Indiana earns B for John Long and a future second-round right later associated with 1993 No. 51 Spencer Dunkley. The Seattle SuperSonics franchise, indexed under modern Oklahoma City Thunder lineage, receives B for Russ Schoene and Terence Stansbury. The 1986 transaction belongs historically to Seattle, and no future pick is credited as an automatic Indiana NBA contributor.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Los Angeles acquired freedom to pursue Frank Brickowski when Seattle declined to match the free agent in October 1986. The SuperSonics received cash and a 1988 third-round choice with an unidentified eventual draft outcome. The inherited Lakers Win grades Los Angeles B+ and Seattle C+.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
Los Angeles Negotiated to Sign Brickowski

The Lakers wanted veteran big man Frank Brickowski in October 1986. Seattle held a right of first refusal but agreed not to exercise it in exchange for cash and a future third-round selection. Los Angeles thereby gained a clearer path to pursue the player without another club matching the offer. This was a negotiated waiver of a free-agent right, not a conventional trade of two active NBA players.

Brickowski Offered Another Interior Option

Brickowski's size and professional experience made him a plausible frontcourt reserve for a Lakers team built around established stars. His earlier performances elsewhere didn't automatically become Los Angeles production, and the agreement itself wasn't a new championship achievement. The primary benefit was access to a veteran the club wanted to sign. That was a more immediate objective than holding a future third-round draft opportunity.

Seattle Took Money and a Future Draft Chance

The SuperSonics obtained cash and a third-round choice for 1988. The precise later identity of that pick is uncertain in the inherited archive, and no named NBA prospect should be credited to Seattle without verifying the right's eventual destination. The cash supplied concrete compensation for releasing the matching right. This gave Seattle an alternative form of value rather than another experienced big man on its roster.

The Grades Compare Access Against Optionality

The inherited Lakers B+ reflects success in gaining a path to Brickowski, while Seattle's C+ credits financial compensation and future draft potential. The return packages were different in timing and certainty. Neither should be described as bringing an established new star by itself. The accurate comparison explains the special free-agent mechanism, the unsigned draft uncertainty and why Los Angeles considered the ability to pursue the center useful.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win. Los Angeles receives B+ for Seattle's agreement not to match Frank Brickowski's free-agent move. The SuperSonics earn C+ for cash and an incompletely identified 1988 third-round right. The Lakers got a chance to add a veteran center, while Seattle received compensation without a guaranteed future contributor.

perspectives.summary: On October 9, 1986, Denver agreed NOT TO EXERCISE its matching right over restricted free agent Richard Anderson, allowing Houston to sign the forward. The Rockets compensated Denver with a future 1988 third-round pick, later selected No. 66 on Dwight Boyd. This was a free-agent rights settlement, not a direct Anderson-for-Boyd contracted-player swap: Houston signed Anderson on October 11. He supplied 63 Rockets games (51 in 1986-87 and 12 in 1987-88), while Denver got no NBA games from Boyd. The preserved Even Trade with D+ grades for both teams acknowledges small, different returns and leaves Anderson’s later Portland games out.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Relinquished a Matching Right, Not a Contracted Player
On October 9, 1986, Houston compensated Denver with a future 1988 third-round choice because the Nuggets agreed not to exercise their right of first refusal on free agent Richard Anderson. Two days later the Rockets completed his signing. Both dates are recorded in NBA transactions: the first was the rights-compensation agreement, the second the actual free-agent acquisition. Anderson was not an active contracted Denver player shipped in a conventional trade, nor did Denver exchange draft rights to him. The original import classified this nonexercise right as a traded-player asset even while its player relationship called him a free-agent-rights player. The matching-right transaction should retain Anderson’s player identity but use rights as its asset category.

Anderson Was a Limited Houston Reserve for 63 Games
Houston deployed Anderson in 51 games during 1986-87, averaging 2.8 points, 1.5 rebounds and 6.1 minutes. He appeared in 12 additional Rockets games the following season, giving the franchise 63 actual regular-season games from the acquisition. Anderson later recorded 62 appearances for Portland in 1987-88, but those minutes followed a separate player movement and are not Houston production. The modest Houston role distinguishes the transaction from a complete waste while explaining why the stored grade is only D+. A team that gets three seasons of meaningful starter minutes would earn a different assessment; that was not this historical outcome.

Denver Used the Compensation Draft Pick on Dwight Boyd
The future third-round selection became the No. 66 pick in the June 28, 1988 draft. Denver used it on Memphis State guard Dwight Boyd, as recorded by the Nuggets’ own historical media guide and independent draft-rights tracking. Boyd never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Nuggets. His college performance and draft identity are valid provenance, but he provided zero direct NBA playing minutes. The original asset was the 1988 draft RIGHT in October 1986, not Boyd as a traded player on that date. Treating it as a speculative third-round opportunity, with the eventual player identity linked in the ledger, makes the transaction useful for historical research.

Matching D+ Grades Can Coexist with Different Playing-Time Returns
Denver received a pick and exercised it on a named college player but got no NBA roster production. Houston obtained clearance to sign an experienced forward and used him in parts of two NBA seasons. The Rockets therefore hold a narrow edge in direct playing minutes, 63 games to zero, but neither side acquired a core competitive asset. The earlier Even Trade label and D+ Denver/D+ Houston ratings can be preserved without claiming identical results, fabricating a pick conversion to a different club or counting Anderson’s later Portland play as Rockets output.

Final Verdict: One Right and One Low-Order Pick
October 9 was the matching-right nonexercise agreement; October 11 was the resulting Houston player signing. Denver got a 1988 third-round right that became No. 66 Dwight Boyd but yielded no Nuggets NBA minutes. Houston got 63 regular-season games from Richard Anderson and no significant long-term starter. Even Trade and D+/D+ remain an appropriately limited retrospective judgment for a rights-for-draft compensation settlement, not an ordinary player-for-player swap.

This was a free-agent rights settlement, not a direct Anderson-for-Boyd contracted-player swap: Houston signed Anderson on October 11. He supplied 63 Rockets games (51 in 1986-87 and 12 in 1987-88), while Denver got no NBA games from Boyd. The preserved Even Trade with D+ grades for both teams acknowledges small, different returns and leaves Anderson’s later Portland games out.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Relinquished a Matching Right, Not a Contracted Player
On October 9, 1986, Houston compensated Denver with a future 1988 third-round choice because the Nuggets agreed not to exercise their right of first refusal on free agent Richard Anderson. Two days later the Rockets completed his signing. Both dates are recorded in NBA transactions: the first was the rights-compensation agreement, the second the actual free-agent acquisition. Anderson was not an active contracted Denver player shipped in a conventional trade, nor did Denver exchange draft rights to him. The original import classified this nonexercise right as a traded-player asset even while its player relationship called him a free-agent-rights player. The matching-right transaction should retain Anderson’s player identity but use rights as its asset category.

Anderson Was a Limited Houston Reserve for 63 Games
Houston deployed Anderson in 51 games during 1986-87, averaging 2.8 points, 1.5 rebounds and 6.1 minutes. He appeared in 12 additional Rockets games the following season, giving the franchise 63 actual regular-season games from the acquisition. Anderson later recorded 62 appearances for Portland in 1987-88, but those minutes followed a separate player movement and are not Houston production. The modest Houston role distinguishes the transaction from a complete waste while explaining why the stored grade is only D+. A team that gets three seasons of meaningful starter minutes would earn a different assessment; that was not this historical outcome.

Denver Used the Compensation Draft Pick on Dwight Boyd
The future third-round selection became the No. 66 pick in the June 28, 1988 draft. Denver used it on Memphis State guard Dwight Boyd, as recorded by the Nuggets’ own historical media guide and independent draft-rights tracking. Boyd never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Nuggets. His college performance and draft identity are valid provenance, but he provided zero direct NBA playing minutes. The original asset was the 1988 draft RIGHT in October 1986, not Boyd as a traded player on that date. Treating it as a speculative third-round opportunity, with the eventual player identity linked in the ledger, makes the transaction useful for historical research.

Matching D+ Grades Can Coexist with Different Playing-Time Returns
Denver received a pick and exercised it on a named college player but got no NBA roster production. Houston obtained clearance to sign an experienced forward and used him in parts of two NBA seasons. The Rockets therefore hold a narrow edge in direct playing minutes, 63 games to zero, but neither side acquired a core competitive asset. The earlier Even Trade label and D+ Denver/D+ Houston ratings can be preserved without claiming identical results, fabricating a pick conversion to a different club or counting Anderson’s later Portland play as Rockets output.

Final Verdict: One Right and One Low-Order Pick
October 9 was the matching-right nonexercise agreement; October 11 was the resulting Houston player signing. Denver got a 1988 third-round right that became No. 66 Dwight Boyd but yielded no Nuggets NBA minutes. Houston got 63 regular-season games from Richard Anderson and no significant long-term starter. Even Trade and D+/D+ remain an appropriately limited retrospective judgment for a rights-for-draft compensation settlement, not an ordinary player-for-player swap.

perspectives.summary: The New Jersey Nets acquired Leon Wood from the Washington Bullets in exchange for Mike O'Koren on October 30, 1986. Wood played 76 games for New Jersey in 1986-87, averaging 7.3 points and 4.9 assists, while O'Koren played 15 Washington games and averaged 2.1 points. Nets Win, New Jersey B+, Washington D+; the inherited even grade understated the difference in actual playing time.
perspectives.analysis:
An October Exchange of Backcourt Help for Forward Depth

New Jersey traded Mike O'Koren to Washington for Leon Wood on October 30, 1986. The transaction registers for both organizations identify the same pair of players and no accompanying draft choice. The Nets had watched their offense struggle with ballhandling options and sought a young guard who could manage extended minutes. Washington, still known as the Bullets at the time, received an established forward with several seasons of experience in New Jersey. Wood had been with the Bullets the previous season, but his earlier Washington production wasn't the return New Jersey received. This deal should be assessed using the contributions after the players switched uniforms.

Wood Became a Regular Nets Rotation Guard

Wood appeared in 76 games for New Jersey in 1986-87, including seven starts. He averaged 22.8 minutes, 7.3 points and 4.9 assists, reflecting real responsibility for creating shots and moving the ball. Those aren't All-Star numbers, and the Nets endured a losing season, but a guard who played nearly every night was a useful acquisition. Wood subsequently played for other clubs, and those later contributions belong outside this particular Nets return. The source-supported result is his full New Jersey season, which compares favorably to what the Bullets got from the forward they acquired.

O'Koren's New Washington Role Ended Quickly

O'Koren managed 15 regular-season games for Washington in 1986-87. He averaged 8.2 minutes and only 2.1 points in those appearances, a much smaller role than his established Nets tenure had suggested. Washington waived him in February 1987, which prevented the trade from becoming a longer-term source of frontcourt depth. The former Nets seasons can't be credited as a Washington return. Nor is there an identified draft asset produced by his departure. The Bullets acquired an experienced player, but they received only a brief and lightly used stint rather than a productive rotation regular.

Receiving-Team Minutes Overrule a Familiar-Name Comparison

The players both had NBA experience, which may explain why an earlier archive treated the trade as even. That reasoning doesn't survive a comparison of acquired-team records. Wood logged a useful 76-game campaign with point-guard duties, while O'Koren supplied fifteen brief appearances and left Washington within months. This was not a franchise-altering exchange and New Jersey shouldn't get a superstar grade, but its return was plainly stronger. The proper historical verdict credits what the two organizations actually used, rather than assigning equal value to the players' reputations at the moment of the swap.

Final Verdict

Nets Win. New Jersey earns B+ for Leon Wood's 76 appearances and averages of 7.3 points with 4.9 assists as a regular guard in 1986-87. Washington receives D+ for 15 games and 2.1 points per outing from Mike O'Koren. Neither player became a cornerstone, but the Nets obtained considerably more useful rotation minutes.

analysis:
On December 18, 1986 the Portland Trail Blazers sent rookie forward Walter Berry to the San Antonio Spurs for rookie center Kevin Duckworth. Berry had been taken No. 14 in the first round of the 1986 draft following a highly regarded college career, whereas Duckworth had been chosen at No. 33 in the second round. The original transaction contained these two players, without an additional first-round choice or any reported cash. The difference in draft position made Berry the higher-profile young prospect on trade day, but both clubs were acquiring an NBA newcomer whose future was uncertain. Portland needed another playable center with Sam Bowie struggling through injuries, while the Spurs were interested in the scoring forward they would receive. A contemporary Los Angeles Times account and the two teams' transaction histories identify the participants and date.

For Portland the resulting career changed the value of the transaction dramatically. Duckworth became more than emergency center depth: he developed into a reliable frontcourt scorer and won the NBA Most Improved Player award for the 1987-88 season. He went on to make the All-Star team in 1989 and again in 1991. His contribution was realized on the Trail Blazers' own roster, rather than inferred from what he later accomplished in another uniform. Portland reached the NBA Finals in 1990 and 1992 with Duckworth as an important center alongside the wider group led by Clyde Drexler. The team did not win either Finals, and those postseason results should not be credited solely to a single trade. They demonstrate, however, that the young player acquired in December 1986 became a productive starter during an unusually successful period in Portland's history.

San Antonio's direct basketball return was markedly shorter. Berry appeared in 64 regular-season Spurs games, a small contribution compared with the sustained years Duckworth provided Portland. The forward's collegiate reputation and high draft selection were real reasons to pursue him, but a retrospective grade must distinguish pre-trade promise from what the receiving franchise actually obtained. Berry played for other teams after his stint in San Antonio, and those later appearances cannot be transferred back into the Spurs' ledger. The Spurs did not acquire a first-round pick or a later championship asset through this particular exchange. An F therefore records the poor club-specific result of surrendering the eventual two-time All-Star center for a prospect whose own tenure with San Antonio did not last.

The downstream route adds a smaller but identifiable Portland benefit without changing the original two-player asset list. After his productive Trail Blazers years, Duckworth was sent to Washington in another transaction that brought forward Harvey Grant to Portland. That follow-on exchange is part of what the club could later do with the player it obtained, but Grant was not compensation supplied by San Antonio in 1986. Nor should Grant's separate career be used to inflate Duckworth's own All-Star credentials. Taken together, the NBA player records, Blazers history and the traceable later trade support the preserved verdict of Blazers Win, with Portland A-plus and San Antonio F. The comparison does not rest on hypothetical drafted players: it rests on the years of actual Portland center production and the 64 games San Antonio received from Berry.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Atlanta acquired the right to sign veteran guard Gus Williams on January 6, 1987, with Washington waiving its right of first refusal in exchange for a 1990 second-round pick. Williams joined the Hawks while Spud Webb was recovering from knee surgery. The pick later became No. 37 A.J. English. Atlanta's immediate veteran help underlies the inherited slight Hawks edge.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Washington Released Its Right to Match Williams

The January 6, 1987 exchange gave Atlanta access to veteran free-agent guard Gus Williams. Washington's Bullets agreed not to exercise their right of first refusal, receiving the Hawks' 1990 second-round pick as compensation. This was not a trade that physically sent a signed player from Washington to Atlanta. Williams had been out of the Bullets' regular rotation and was seeking another opportunity, while Atlanta needed more backcourt help. The unusual rights mechanism was the essential asset on the Hawks' side.

Webb's Knee Injury Gave Atlanta a Specific Need

Spud Webb's knee surgery left the Hawks short of guard depth. Williams could provide a veteran ball handler behind Glenn Rivers while the roster managed the injury absence. He was already 33, so Atlanta wasn't acquiring the player who had enjoyed his strongest Seattle scoring seasons. The value instead came from a short-term answer to an immediate problem for a competitive team. The move put a recognizable professional into a specific reserve role without waiting several years for a draft choice.

The Bullets Secured a Future Second-Round Right

Washington received Atlanta's 1990 second-round selection, eventually associated with No. 37 A.J. English. That future pick had possible value to the Bullets, but it couldn't fill a current roster spot in 1987. The terms are best understood as compensation for relinquishing matching rights rather than as a direct guard-for-player trade. The eventual name attached to the pick should not be taken as proof that every NBA game played by English belongs in the Bullets' received value. The rights chain and player usage are separate questions.

Short-Term Depth Justified the Moderate Edge

Atlanta addressed its backcourt shortage with a known veteran who could contribute during the same season. Washington accepted a delayed option for a player it was not using in its immediate plans. Neither organization gave up a central young star, making the narrow grade difference appropriate. Williams's experience and the urgency created by Webb's surgery offered the Hawks a more immediate benefit than Washington's distant draft right, while the Bullets still received something tangible for releasing their claim.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta earns B- for securing Gus Williams as emergency veteran guard depth while Spud Webb was unavailable. Washington gets C+ for the 1990 second-round right attached to waiving its matching claim. This was a free-agent-rights compensation transaction, not a conventional player swap, and its near-term value tilted toward the Hawks.

Lakers Win, Los Angeles A and San Antonio C, credits those actual frontcourt minutes while acknowledging the Spurs’ two players and two picks.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The February 13 Deal Included Two Players and Two Picks
The Los Angeles Lakers acquired Mychal Thompson from the San Antonio Spurs on February 13, 1987. They sent Frank Brickowski, Pétur Guðmundsson, a 1987 first-round selection, a 1990 second-round selection and cash. The Lakers’ official transactions media guide lists all five outgoing asset categories; historical transaction records show the first-round choice later became No. 23 Greg "Cadillac" Anderson and the second-round choice later became No. 54 Sean Higgins. Anderson was drafted on June 22, four months AFTER Thompson had changed teams. He was not a player the Lakers delivered to the Spurs in February. An original import that labeled Anderson as a third exchanged veteran therefore misstated the asset type.

Thompson Helped the 1987 Title Run Immediately
The Lakers wanted a reliable reserve big behind the aging Kareem Abdul-Jabbar. Thompson played 33 regular-season games in Los Angeles after the trade, averaging 10.1 points and 4.1 rebounds in 20.6 minutes; his combined San Antonio-and-Lakers season totals are not his receiving-team return. He then played all six games of the NBA Finals victory over Boston, averaging 11.2 points and 5.2 rebounds. His defense and post presence gave coach Pat Riley another option against physical Eastern Conference frontcourts. These are observable contributions, although the Lakers already had Magic Johnson and James Worthy and did not win the championship because of one role player alone.

A Second Championship Made His Lakers Tenure More Valuable
During 1987-88 Thompson appeared in 80 Lakers games, averaging 11.6 points and 6.1 rebounds as the club repeated with a seven-game NBA Finals win over Detroit. He remained a frontcourt contributor through the 1990-91 season, including the later Finals loss to Chicago. The meaningful post-trade asset is his multi-year Los Angeles service and participation in the 1987 and 1988 title teams. His prior San Antonio statistics and subsequent media career are outside the NBA playing return that should be graded.

San Antonio Received Real Future Opportunities
The Spurs did not surrender Thompson for nothing: Brickowski and Guðmundsson were established NBA bigs, they acquired the Lakers-origin 1987 first-round right exercised on Anderson and the 1990 second-round selection exercised on Higgins, and they received cash with no authoritative public amount. Greg Anderson appeared in the league and became a journeyman, while Brickowski later established a lengthy NBA career elsewhere. Those later teams’ minutes cannot all be booked to San Antonio. The distinction between a first-round PICK in February and Anderson the future draft selection prevents the trade card from implying a player was exchanged before he was drafted.

The Realized Gap Supports A for the Lakers, C for the Spurs
Los Angeles obtained rotation help when championship defense was the top priority and retained Thompson for several seasons. San Antonio obtained two players and two future picks, with some useful eventual value, but not an equivalently consequential Spurs tenure from one asset. Because two draft selections and cash were part of the Lakers’ outgoing package, the verdict should not call it a free acquisition. Lakers Win, Los Angeles A and San Antonio C is the preserved source-backed assessment, not a forecast the teams could have made in February 1987.

Final Verdict
The February 13 exchange was Thompson for Brickowski, Guðmundsson, a 1987 first-round pick later used on Greg Anderson, a 1990 second-round pick later used on Sean Higgins and cash. Los Angeles received an important defender on two title-winning teams. The Spurs received multiple legitimate assets whose realized team returns were smaller. Identifying the 1987 pick correctly, preserving its eventual player relationship, and refusing to invent a cash figure make the transaction history usable beyond a generic hindsight verdict.

perspectives.analysis:
Chicago Bought Immediate Frontcourt Depth for a Future Second

On February 15, 1987, Cleveland sent veteran big man Ben Poquette to Chicago for a 1989 second-round draft choice. It was a small present-for-future exchange: the Bulls had a player they could use that season, while the Cavaliers retained a draft opportunity two years away. The Cleveland transaction ledger confirms the return and identifies the choice that ultimately became Chucky Brown, the No. 43 pick in 1989. Neither team received cash or another player in the recorded deal.

Poquette Had a Brief Bulls Stint, Then Left the NBA

Poquette appeared in 21 games for Chicago in 1986-87, starting once. His Bulls totals were 167 minutes, 51 points and 24 rebounds. Those were actual reserve minutes at a time when the Bulls needed bodies on the front line, but the arrangement was brief. He did not return for another NBA season with Chicago, instead playing abroad. His earlier seasons in Utah and Cleveland are not contributions acquired by the Bulls in this particular trade.

Cleveland Converted the Pick Into Chucky Brown

The 1989 choice became No. 43 and Cleveland selected Chucky Brown. Unlike a pick that was traded again before the draft, this one converted into a player who actually suited up for the receiving franchise. Brown logged 75 Cavaliers games in 1989-90, 74 in 1990-91 and six more in 1991-92. That was 155 regular-season appearances, 86 starts, 2,874 minutes and 1,187 points for Cleveland. His first two seasons alone supplied much more playing value than Poquette delivered during his few months in Chicago.

Why the Results Favor Cleveland

The draft wait could have ended with very little return, but Cleveland turned a second-rounder into a useful forward who started 86 games for the club. Chicago made a reasonable short-term depth purchase and did get 21 appearances from Poquette. Even so, the scale of what the teams received was far apart: Cleveland got more than seven times as many regular-season games and over seventeen times as many minutes. The historical Even Trade grade therefore does not fit the source-backed outcome, and the revised grades credit only each team’s actual return.

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B+ for acquiring the 1989 No. 43 pick that became Chucky Brown, who played 155 games and started 86 for the Cavaliers. Chicago gets C for 21 games and 167 minutes from Ben Poquette. The trade produced a legitimate short-term reserve in Chicago, but Cleveland extracted markedly more franchise value from its future second-round selection.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix acquired Eddie Johnson from Sacramento on June 21, 1987 for Ed Pinckney and a 1988 second-round pick. Johnson gave the Suns 222 regular-season games over three full seasons plus 15 games in 1990-91, averaged 21.5 points while winning Sixth Man of the Year in 1988-89, and became one of the league's premier bench scorers. Pinckney gave Sacramento 130 games across two seasons before being traded, while the second-round pick was flipped for Jawann Oldham, who contributed 54 games and 13 starts. Sacramento received useful depth, but Phoenix obtained the impact scorer and clearly stronger realized return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix's and Sacramento's transaction logs confirm the June 21, 1987 package: Eddie Johnson to the Suns for Ed Pinckney and a 1988 second-round pick. The pick was later identified as the selection that became No. 30 Fennis Dembo, but Sacramento did not actually make that selection. On October 15, 1987, the Kings traded the pick to New York for center Jawann Oldham. New York later moved it to Detroit, which drafted Dembo. The source-backed return for Sacramento is therefore Pinckney plus the value Sacramento itself realized by converting the pick into Oldham—not Dembo's Pistons career.

Phoenix Return
Johnson immediately became a major scorer. He played 73 games with 59 starts in 1987-88 and averaged 17.7 points. In 1988-89 he moved primarily to the bench, played 70 games, averaged 21.5 points on 49.7 percent shooting and won NBA Sixth Man of the Year. In 1989-90 he played 64 games and averaged 16.9 points, then appeared in 15 more Suns games in 1990-91 before moving to Seattle. Across those Phoenix seasons he scored thousands of points, delivered three straight years of high-volume offense and provided postseason scoring during the club's late-1980s resurgence. His 1988-89 award season is especially important because it shows the trade produced more than raw volume: Phoenix acquired a player who became one of the NBA's best reserves and a major offensive piece.

Sacramento Return
Pinckney gave Sacramento legitimate rotation value. He played 79 games with seven starts in 1987-88, averaging 6.2 points and 2.9 rebounds in 14.9 minutes, then played 51 more Kings games with 24 starts in 1988-89 before being traded to Boston. The second-round pick also produced a realized Kings return before draft night. Sacramento sent the pick to New York for Jawann Oldham. Oldham played 54 games with 13 starts for the 1987-88 Kings, averaging 5.5 points and 5.6 rebounds in 17.5 minutes. He missed 1988-89 with a knee injury, so the downstream pick conversion delivered only one useful Sacramento season. That is meaningful depth from two separate pieces, but neither return approached Johnson's Phoenix scoring peak or longevity.

Hindsight Verdict
Phoenix wins clearly. The Suns acquired a player who gave them more than two hundred regular-season games, a 21.5-point Sixth Man of the Year season, and three consecutive years as a major scorer. Sacramento received two seasons of Pinckney and one season of Oldham through the pick conversion, so the Kings deserve more than a failing grade. Their package provided useful frontcourt minutes and retained value instead of disappearing. A for Phoenix reflects Johnson's award-level production and sustained scoring impact. A C+ for Sacramento recognizes real rotation value from Pinckney and Oldham but also the large gap between that depth and the star-level scorer the Kings surrendered. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: On October 7, 1987, the Lakers signed veteran free agent Jeff Lamp after San Antonio agreed not to exercise its right of first refusal. The Spurs received a Lakers 1988 third-round draft choice as compensation, later exercised at No. 75 on Archie Marshall. Lamp played just three Lakers regular-season games totaling seven minutes in 1987-88 and none in the 1988 title playoffs, followed by 37 limited games the next season. Marshall was a real drafted asset but did not provide meaningful sustained Spurs NBA rotation service. This was a free-agent rights/compensation settlement, NOT a direct player-for-player exchange; preserve Even Trade and C+ for both clubs.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
October 7 Was a Free-Agent Compensation Agreement, Not a Traded-Player Swap
The Lakers sought veteran guard Jeff Lamp, formerly of San Antonio, during the 1987 offseason. The Spurs held the contractual right of first refusal under then-applicable free-agent rules and agreed not to exercise it. Los Angeles compensated the Spurs with a future 1988 third-round selection. Neither team shipped a contracted player directly across the court that day. Lamp joined the Lakers after San Antonio waived its ability to match, while the outgoing right eventually became No. 75 in the 1988 NBA draft. This distinction is necessary for any player relationship graph: Lamp is a free-agent-rights acquisition and Archie Marshall is the future player associated with a transferred pick, not a contemporary swapped rookie.

Lamp Contributed Very Little to the 1988 Lakers Championship Season
Lamp appeared in only three Lakers games in 1987-88 and played a combined seven minutes. Los Angeles won the NBA championship that year with Magic Johnson, James Worthy and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, but Lamp did not enter a postseason game. Crediting him with meaningful minutes during the Finals would overstate the Lakers’ direct return. He returned for 37 regular-season appearances in 1988-89, still in limited reserve duty. Those minutes establish that the rights agreement led to some NBA playing time, but not that Lamp was a consequential frontcourt or starting backcourt acquisition for the repeat champion.

The Spurs Exercised Their Future Third on Archie Marshall
San Antonio obtained a legitimate future draft choice, not cash or a second active NBA guard. The selection became No. 75 in the 1988 draft, which the Spurs used on Kansas forward Archie Marshall, part of the Jayhawks’ national championship team. A future pick remains a basketball asset even if the player chosen never becomes a large NBA rotation contributor. The surviving Spurs record does not establish substantial receiving-team service from Marshall; no hypothetical later NBA opportunity can be inflated into a direct San Antonio asset return simply because he was selected in the draft.

Why Equal C+ Grades Fit a Low-Return Exchange
The Lakers got an available veteran but extracted only a few minutes in 1987-88 and short reserve usage the following year. The Spurs gave up matching rights but secured a named 1988 third-round draft selection, which did not develop into a long-term contributor on its roster. The inherited Even Trade result with C+ for both clubs is consistent with two real but limited outcomes. It would be inaccurate to call this a blockbuster trade, treat Lamp as a 1988 Finals rotation player, or assign 1988 college championship achievements to San Antonio NBA production.

Final Verdict
On October 7, 1987 the Lakers signed Lamp through a San Antonio nonexercise-of-first-refusal agreement and sent the Spurs a 1988 third-round pick later used on Archie Marshall. Direct receiving-team return: three Lakers games and seven total minutes in the 1988 title season, then another 37 games in 1988-89; a San Antonio future choice that did not establish a star. The preserved Even Trade and C+/C+ grades describe the actual compensation exchange rather than imaginary player-for-player movement.

perspectives.summary: In October 1987, the New Jersey Nets sent Darryl Dawkins and James Bailey to Cleveland for John Bagley and Keith Lee. Cleveland then sent Dawkins and Mel Turpin to Utah for Kent Benson and Dell Curry. The corrected directed ledger retains Bailey only once, from New Jersey to Cleveland. The inherited Slight Jazz Edge gives Utah B+, Cleveland B and New Jersey D+.
perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Moved Two Players to Cleveland

The Nets sent veteran center Darryl Dawkins and forward James Bailey to the Cavaliers in October 1987, acquiring guard John Bagley and forward Keith Lee in return. That was the first phase of a larger three-team agreement rather than a standalone Dawkins-for-Bagley trade. New Jersey was trading frontcourt depth for perimeter help and another forward option. Bailey moved directly from the Nets to Cleveland, a detail confirmed by contemporary reporting and corrected in the asset ledger after an incorrect second Bailey entry had been associated with Utah.

Dawkins Continued From Cleveland to Utah

The Cavaliers immediately moved Dawkins and Mel Turpin to the Jazz for center Kent Benson and guard Dell Curry. Dawkins's Cleveland receipt was therefore an intermediate part of the rights path, not a new Cavaliers season of playing production. Utah hoped the two veteran big men could reinforce a frontcourt led by Mark Eaton. Injuries had limited Dawkins's recent availability, making the gamble less certain than his earlier scoring record implied. The correct chronology explains how Dawkins can appear entering and leaving Cleveland without becoming two different players.

Cleveland's Return Included Three Distinct People

Cleveland finished with James Bailey from New Jersey and Benson and Curry from Utah. Bailey belongs once in the Cavaliers' incoming package, while Curry offered outside shooting and would later build a long NBA career elsewhere. The trade cost Cleveland Bagley, Lee and Turpin while serving as the conduit for Dawkins's final Utah move. Comparing Cleveland's return requires following the sequential transfers rather than crediting it with both a permanent Dawkins acquisition and a second James Bailey from Utah.

The Original Ratings Are More Cautious Than the Names

The inherited Jazz B+, Cavaliers B and Nets D+ favor Utah's immediate frontcourt additions while recognizing the Cavaliers' roster reshuffle. No participant was receiving a guaranteed future All-Star by virtue of this agreement. Utah's later use of Dawkins and Turpin, Cleveland's actual deployment of Curry and Bailey and New Jersey's new guard options require separate team-specific evaluation. The source-grounded account preserves the grades while removing a factual duplicate that overstated Cleveland's assets.

Final Verdict

Slight Jazz Edge. Utah receives B+ for Darryl Dawkins and Mel Turpin as added frontcourt options. Cleveland earns B for James Bailey, Kent Benson and Dell Curry, with Bailey appearing only once in its final package. New Jersey receives D+ for John Bagley and Keith Lee. The Jazz's advantage follows its chosen center depth, not an invented extra player or duplicate Dawkins move.

On October 16, 1987, Boston sent guard Sam Vincent and veteran forward Scott Wedman to the Seattle SuperSonics in return for cash and a future second-round selection. The 1988 draft ledger associates that second with No. 35 Sylvester Gray. Modern franchise indexing may file Seattle trades under the Oklahoma City Thunder lineage, but the actual 1987 receiving team was Seattle. The SuperSonics preferred immediate basketball experience, while the Celtics turned two roster pieces into monetary compensation and a prospect opportunity. This was a real two-player deal rather than an exchange involving an existing Thunder roster.

Vincent Offered Seattle Backcourt Options, Wedman Experience

Vincent was an NBA guard capable of competing for minutes, giving Seattle another option for ball handling and scoring. Wedman brought years of professional experience, though he was at a late career stage and couldn't reasonably be expected to reproduce his earlier prime indefinitely. Their prior Boston performance still belonged to the Celtics' history and should not be treated as Seattle games after the transaction. The Sonics received two named veterans, but the actual value of each depended on availability and subsequent roster decisions rather than his reputation at the time of acquisition.

Boston's Future Second Became a Defined Draft Position

Boston gained an eventual second-round position that the draft record associates with No. 35 Sylvester Gray, along with cash. Those were real assets, but a future pick did not guarantee a signed rotation forward and the cash wasn't automatically equivalent to an NBA player's development. The Celtics had veteran talent at other positions and could afford to examine younger prospects over time rather than retain every reserve. The correct return to evaluate is the second-round opportunity and financial consideration, not any unrelated games Gray later played for another franchise.

The Sonics Chose More Immediate NBA Personnel

Seattle acquired two players who could contribute without waiting for a draft, while Boston accepted a later selection and cash. That makes the Seattle-side package slightly stronger on immediate personnel value despite Wedman's age and the uncertainty of each veteran's ultimate usage. Detroit Sent Green to New York for Moore and a Draft Right

On October 28, 1987, Detroit exchanged Sidney Green for Ron Moore and a future second-round selection from the Knicks. The conditional draft timing allowed a 1988 or 1989 choice and the historical ledger associates the exercised right with No. 30 Fennis Dembo in 1988. This was a modest frontcourt and draft-capital transaction rather than a change to the Pistons' core star guard rotation. Detroit sought additional depth and a young prospect opportunity, while New York preferred an experienced forward with a more established NBA record. The teams valued two different types of frontcourt and roster flexibility.

Green Brought an Experienced Forward to the Knicks

Green entered the arrangement with years of NBA experience and could provide size, rebounding and inside play for New York. His record before October 1987 belonged to previous teams, so the Knicks' actual return must begin with their own appearances after the trade. New York did not acquire Detroit's future 1988 second-round selection; that asset moved to the Pistons. The trade gave the Knicks a defined player rather than an uncertain drafted prospect, which was a reasonable objective for a club hoping to stabilize its rotation. The direct benefit remained a supporting piece rather than a franchise centerpiece.

Moore and Dembo Were Developmental Returns for Detroit

Detroit received Moore's rights and an opportunity that became the No. 30 selection associated with Dembo. Those assets gave the Pistons additional choices while developing a roster that was beginning to compete with the league's best teams. Neither should be credited with the full production of Detroit's established championship contributors. The team could evaluate Moore and its drafted guard or forward prospects, but subsequent trades and roster changes would determine whether each produced useful NBA minutes. The right's eventual named draft outcome is a ledger fact, not permission to assign every future professional game of that player to Detroit.

Two Practical But Supporting Returns Make the Deal Even

New York obtained a playable veteran forward, while Detroit gained a current prospect and a second-round draft chance. Both packages provided ordinary rotation or development options and neither by itself explained the clubs' later records. Equal moderate grades are more defensible than drawing a large winning conclusion from Green's previous success or the eventual identity of the future selection. The transaction is best viewed as an exchange of present-day certainty for a broader mix of possible future value. Its historical importance lies chiefly in the teams' roster decisions rather than any single new NBA star.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Detroit receives B- for Ron Moore and the future second-round right associated with 1988 No. 30 Fennis Dembo. New York also earns B- for adding experienced forward Sidney Green. Detroit's later championship core should not be assigned to these incoming assets, and Green's prior NBA seasons are not newly created Knicks production through this deal.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Took Comegys for a Future Second

The November 3, 1987 transaction brought young forward Dallas Comegys to Atlanta from the New Jersey Nets. New Jersey received a conditional later second-round selection, identified in historical records as a 1989-or-1990 opportunity that ultimately corresponds to the 1990 No. 28 position associated with Les Jepsen. The Nets are indexed under the later Brooklyn franchise name in the canonical dataset, but the agreement was made by New Jersey. Atlanta wanted an actual prospect it could place into its roster evaluations immediately; the Nets chose future draft flexibility rather than retaining Comegys.

Comegys Was a Current Prospect With Uncertain NBA Value

Comegys had been a first-round draft prospect, which made a change of environment potentially attractive for the Hawks. Still, being a former high pick couldn't guarantee a starting role, and Atlanta's frontcourt already had players who would compete for playing time. Comegys offered a chance to assess his athletic skills and size, but not an established record of sustained NBA impact. The correct Atlanta return begins with its own appearances and subsequent roster decisions, not the draft position or expectations attached to Comegys when New Jersey originally obtained his rights.

New Jersey's Pick Became a Named 1990 Selection

The Nets' incoming future selection was not immediately numbered or fully settled at the 1987 agreement date. Its conditional 1989-or-1990 timing ultimately led to the 1990 No. 28 draft position associated with Les Jepsen. That named outcome helps identify the asset, though Jepsen's subsequent career shouldn't be awarded to New Jersey without checking his actual team history. By accepting a future second rather than keeping Comegys, the franchise traded immediate prospect control for the chance to select or move a different player later. Both were reasonable options for a rebuilding team.

An Even Grade Reflects Two Limited Development Paths

Atlanta received a current young forward and New Jersey obtained a later first-position-in-the-second-round draft opportunity. Neither was a guaranteed cornerstone player, and their eventual returns depended on development and further roster decisions outside this deal. Comegys's earlier selection status might have been appealing but was not a newly awarded premium draft pick to Atlanta. New Jersey's eventual No. 28 selection carried genuine value while still not ensuring an NBA starter. Equal modest grades convey a balanced prospect-for-prospect gamble rather than a decisive historical win.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Atlanta earns C+ for receiving Dallas Comegys as an immediately available forward prospect. The New Jersey Nets, indexed under Brooklyn lineage, get C+ for a conditional future second that ultimately aligned with 1990 No. 28 Les Jepsen. Neither asset guaranteed an established NBA player, and the 1987 Nets were not yet based in Brooklyn.

seattle-supersonics.summary: On November 10, 1987, Seattle waived its right of first refusal over veteran free agent Maurice Lucas so he could sign with Portland. The Trail Blazers compensated Seattle with a 1990 second-round pick, later No. 53 Abdul Shamsid-Deen. Lucas then appeared in 73 Portland regular-season games, scoring 445 points and collecting 315 rebounds in 1987-88, plus four playoff games. Seattle received draft flexibility but no direct veteran production. Blazers Win, Portland B, Seattle C+; the franchise-history record still identifies the Seattle era rather than Oklahoma City.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
Portland Negotiated for a Free Agent, Not a Player Contract

On November 10, 1987, the Portland Trail Blazers obtained the Seattle SuperSonics' agreement not to exercise a right of first refusal over veteran forward Maurice Lucas. Portland then signed Lucas as a free agent, and Seattle received a future second-round selection as compensation for relinquishing its ability to match. This distinction is important: Seattle did not literally transfer an existing Lucas contract to Portland in a conventional trade. The arrangement removed an obstacle to signing a familiar veteran who had previously played several seasons for the Blazers. Seattle agreed to surrender negotiating leverage for an asset it could use years later.

Lucas Produced Seventy-Three Real Portland Games

Lucas returned to Portland for the 1987-88 season and became a reserve frontcourt option at age thirty-five. He played seventy-three regular-season games, logging 1,191 minutes, 445 points and 315 rebounds. He also appeared in four playoff games, giving Portland additional veteran depth before the end of his NBA career. Those statistics are specific to Portland's post-agreement playing return. They don't include his earlier All-Star seasons in Portland or his 1986-87 work with Seattle, so the figure does not exaggerate what the new signing delivered. The team received far more than an abstract negotiating promise once he took the court.

Seattle Collected a Future Second-Round Draft Choice

The SuperSonics' compensation was a 1990 second-round pick, eventually recorded as No. 53 and tied to Abdul Shamsid-Deen in the draft ledger. Seattle gained another chance to evaluate a player or maneuver with future draft rights instead of retaining matching rights over a veteran nearing retirement. The eventual selection name should not be treated as immediate NBA playing output for the Sonics or a first-round pick. Seattle made a sensible choice to accept a later asset, especially with Lucas approaching the end of his career. However, the pick's practical return was less direct and less substantial than Portland's season of real veteran frontcourt appearances.

The Historical Result Favors the Club That Used the Veteran

The prior Seattle-winning interpretation focused on the principle of receiving compensation for a matching-rights waiver. That was worthwhile business, but the other franchise received seventy-three regular-season games and a small playoff contribution without trading away a higher selection. Portland's immediate utility deserves to be weighed against what one late 1990 second-round choice could provide. The arrangement cannot be analyzed as if Lucas were still a prime scorer from his first Portland tenure, nor can Seattle claim the future draftee's entire professional history. With the correct player contract and pick paths, the modest on-court advantage belongs to Portland.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win. Portland earns B because Maurice Lucas signed after Seattle waived its veteran free-agent matching right and contributed 73 regular-season games, 445 points and 315 rebounds in 1987-88. The Seattle SuperSonics receive C+ for a legitimate 1990 second-round pick, later No. 53 Abdul Shamsid-Deen. That future asset was not a direct Lucas player-contract trade or a first-round selection, and Lucas's earlier Seattle or Portland seasons aren't part of the acquired return.
