golden-state-warriors.summary: On December 12, 1987, Golden State traded Joe Barry Carroll, Sleepy Floyd and cash to Houston for former No. 1 pick Ralph Sampson and young guard Steve Harris. Sampson had helped Hakeem Olajuwon reach the 1986 NBA Finals but was already dealing with serious knee trouble, and his Warriors tenure never restored the dynamic four-time All-Star. Houston received a known scorer in Carroll and multiple useful seasons from Floyd; Golden State gave up two established rotation players for a damaged former superstar and a secondary guard. The original Rockets Win verdict, Houston A- and Warriors D, reflects realized availability and production rather than assuming either club could perfectly foresee Sampson’s health.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
December 1987: Golden State Paid Two Established Starters for a Health Gamble
Golden State sent center Joe Barry Carroll, guard Sleepy Floyd and cash to the Houston Rockets on December 12, 1987 for Ralph Sampson and Steve Harris. The deal was not a two-player exchange and did not include a future pick; every actual original player and the unquantified cash component belong in its accounting. Sampson had been a No. 1 pick, Rookie of the Year and four-time All-Star, and his celebrated shot in the 1986 Western Conference finals helped Houston reach the championship series. But the player available in late 1987 was managing serious knee problems and an increasingly strained relationship with coach Bill Fitch, creating a much different risk profile from his earlier Twin Towers peak.

The Warriors Sought a Transformative Star, Not a Routine Center Rotation
Golden State had seen productive individual seasons from Carroll and Floyd without establishing a sustainable championship contender. Sampson offered unusual seven-foot-four mobility, passing and scoring at his best, while Steve Harris supplied an additional young backcourt piece. That logic was not irrational in isolation: a healthy former franchise center could have changed the Warriors’ roster ceiling more dramatically than another year with the existing starters. The price made the thesis fragile, though. Carroll and Floyd were not expendable players with no NBA value; Houston inherited their already established playmaking and scoring. The Warriors needed Sampson’s knee condition to stabilize enough to replace their combined minutes, and that recovery did not occur.

The Rockets Had Immediate Frontcourt and Backcourt Replacements
Houston chose to build more directly around Hakeem Olajuwon, moving on from the previous two-center concept rather than waiting for an uncertain Sampson rehabilitation. Carroll gave the Rockets an established scorer and center-size option, albeit for a comparatively short tenure. Floyd added veteran ballhandling and scoring depth that remained useful into the 1990s. Contemporary December 13 Los Angeles Times coverage identifies the Carroll-Floyd package; a December 17 Washington Post follow-up treated Houston’s improved lineup stability as the immediate context. Neither incoming player reproduced peak Sampson individually, but the two-player combination spread medical and production risk over positions and supplied real rotation minutes instead of relying on one injured athlete.

Sampson Could Not Regain His Pretrade Warriors Role
Sampson never established the sustained healthy Golden State center role the front office had hoped to purchase. The knee injuries that had interrupted his Houston career continued to limit his availability and athleticism, while a second Warriors season brought more games without the original All-Star performance level. He was eventually moved again. The relevant Golden State return is the injury-limited time actually spent with the franchise, not his pretrade Rockets awards or the 1986 championship run alongside Olajuwon. The Warriors also received Harris as a legitimate separate player, but his contribution did not offset the lost Carroll-Floyd production and cash.

Why the Historical Grade Gap Is Large but Not Absolute
The inherited Rockets Win verdict and Houston A- reflect converting Sampson’s declining but famous rights into two proven NBA veterans and cash. Golden State’s D reflects the gap between trading away two established contributors and receiving far less predictable, much shorter prime-level Sampson production. The grade is not an indictment of all injured-star acquisitions, nor a claim Golden State could predict every medical outcome. Houston also did not win the title simply because of this trade; Olajuwon’s eventual championship teams came after other roster moves. The judgement concerns the years of usable Houston Carroll/Floyd service against the actual Warriors Sampson/Harris return.

Final Verdict
December 12, 1987: Sampson and Harris to Golden State, Carroll and Floyd plus unquantified cash to Houston. Houston gained greater roster reliability and longer guard service while Golden State’s star-level medical wager failed. Source-specific contemporaneous trade reporting and the actual asset ledger support preserving Rockets Win, Houston A- and Warriors D without rewriting Sampson’s earlier greatness or attributing later Rockets championships to players who were no longer on those rosters.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Took Chris Washburn, Golden State Received Foreign Rights

The Hawks acquired center Chris Washburn from Golden State in December 1987 while the Warriors received rights to forward Ken Barlow. Washburn had been a high draft selection whose professional progress was already uncertain, making this a gamble on a second opportunity rather than a conventional exchange of two established starters. Barlow's rights were a different kind of asset: Golden State gained the ability to negotiate with an internationally based prospect without receiving an immediately signed NBA rotation player. Atlanta wanted a physically talented center to evaluate within its existing roster.

Washburn's Potential Didn't Translate Into a Sustained Hawks Role

Washburn's athletic and physical qualities had once made him an attractive prospect, but acquiring those traits didn't restore the status or playing record attached to his original draft position. The Hawks could examine him in their system, yet his NBA contribution after the exchange was limited and did not turn into a long-standing frontcourt role. That short receiving-team tenure is decisive to the retrospective. Golden State's unsuccessful earlier investment in him was already a sunk cost; Atlanta wasn't acquiring all the games and development resources previously spent on the big man.

Barlow Was a Rights Asset Rather Than Instant Production

The Warriors received rights to Ken Barlow, who had played outside the NBA and had a professional career that could not automatically be assigned to Golden State. A right to approach or sign someone is useful, but it isn't the same as several years of an NBA contract. Golden State could preserve the option or later move the asset while it continued rebuilding its frontcourt. The exact eventual use of those rights would require following subsequent transactions; the original exchange alone does not establish that Barlow ever supplied Golden State with regular-season minutes.

A Small Warriors Edge Reflects a Better Risk Position

Atlanta absorbed the uncertainty tied to Washburn's attempted NBA revival, while Golden State converted a distressed player situation into an additional rights claim. Neither outcome amounted to acquiring a lasting star, so an extreme winning grade would overstate the impact. Still, the Warriors' lighter obligation and potential to use Barlow's rights make their side marginally more defensible. Atlanta gained a chance to restart an athletic prospect, but it didn't create a durable frontcourt solution. This trade illustrates how an asset can have modest optional value even if neither received player becomes a major on-court contributor.

Final Verdict

Slight Warriors Edge. Golden State earns C for receiving Ken Barlow's rights after moving on from Chris Washburn. Atlanta gets C- for a center reclamation attempt that did not become a substantial Hawks rotation role. Barlow's overseas career is not Warriors NBA production, and Washburn's original draft reputation was not a guaranteed Atlanta return.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired veteran center James Edwards from Phoenix on February 24, 1988 for Ron Moore and a 1991 second-round pick. Edwards became a rotation fixture on the Pistons teams that reached three straight NBA Finals and won the 1989 and 1990 championships, then remained productive through 1990-91. Phoenix received almost no direct value from Moore, but the second-rounder became No. 46 Richard Dumas, whose explosive 1992-93 rookie season helped the Suns reach the NBA Finals. Dumas gave Phoenix a real payoff, but Edwards' multi-year championship contribution makes Detroit the stronger side.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Detroit and Phoenix transaction logs agree on the February 24, 1988 package: the Pistons received James Edwards and sent Ron Moore plus a future second-round pick. That pick did not convey until 1991, when Phoenix used No. 46 on Richard Dumas. The long delay is central to the hindsight comparison. Detroit received an established veteran immediately for a title push, while Phoenix's most meaningful return arrived more than three years later through the draft.

Detroit Return
Edwards joined a Pistons team already moving toward the top of the Eastern Conference and fit a role Detroit needed: experienced frontcourt scoring behind and alongside Bill Laimbeer and Rick Mahorn, and later as a larger offensive piece as the roster evolved. He appeared in Detroit's 1988 postseason run to the NBA Finals, then remained part of the rotation for the back-to-back championship teams in 1988-89 and 1989-90. He gave Detroit multiple seasons of regular-season and playoff availability rather than a short rental. In 1989-90, Edwards averaged double figures and became an especially useful interior scorer during a championship season. The key grading point is not that he was a franchise star; he was not. It is that Detroit converted a marginal player and a future second into several seasons of dependable frontcourt production during the exact competitive window that produced two titles.

Phoenix Return
Ron Moore was not the value center of the Suns side. His Phoenix stay was brief and did not approach Edwards' Detroit impact. The future second-round pick, however, became much more important. Phoenix selected Richard Dumas at No. 46 in the 1991 draft. After missing the 1991-92 NBA season, Dumas emerged in 1992-93 as one of the league's most productive rookies, averaging roughly 16 points per game in 48 regular-season appearances and starting for stretches on a Suns team that went 62-20 and reached the NBA Finals. He also supplied athletic scoring in the postseason. That is legitimate realized value from the draft asset and prevents the Phoenix grade from falling into the failing range. His Suns tenure was also short and unstable, though, and he never developed into a durable multi-season cornerstone.

Hindsight Comparison
Phoenix deserves substantial credit because the pick was not merely theoretical: it became Dumas, and Dumas contributed to a Finals team. But Detroit received the more durable and better-timed return. Edwards helped three consecutive Finals teams, won two championships with the Pistons and remained useful across several seasons. Dumas' peak was exciting and meaningful, yet much shorter. Moore adds little to Phoenix's side. The trade therefore is not a landslide, but Detroit clearly captured more total realized value and did so during a championship window.

Final Verdict
Detroit Pistons Win. Detroit earns an A because Edwards became a multi-year championship rotation piece and provided strong timing value without costing a premium first-round asset. Phoenix earns a B because the second-round pick became a genuinely productive Finals-team contributor in Richard Dumas, even though the return was delayed and short-lived. The grade does not credit Detroit for Edwards' pre-trade career or Phoenix for anything Dumas did outside the Suns; it measures only realized value tied to this exchange.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix and Cleveland completed one of the rare blockbuster trades that worked extremely well for both teams. The Suns received Kevin Johnson, Mark West, Tyrone Corbin, the 1988 first-round pick used on Dan Majerle and two second-round picks. Cleveland received Larry Nance, Mike Sanders and the 1988 first-round pick used on Randolph Keys. Johnson became Phoenix's long-term All-NBA point guard, Majerle a three-time All-Star and West a durable starting center. Nance became a long-term Cavaliers All-Star and defensive anchor. Phoenix gets the slight hindsight edge because its package produced more total high-end and supporting value, but Cleveland also deserves an elite grade.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
On February 25, 1988, Phoenix and Cleveland made a six-asset-for-three-asset swap that reshaped both franchises. Cleveland received Larry Nance, Mike Sanders and Phoenix's 1988 first-round choice, which became No. 22 Randolph Keys. Phoenix received rookie point guard Kevin Johnson, Tyrone Corbin, Mark West, Cleveland's 1988 first-round pick and two second-round choices. The first became No. 14 Dan Majerle; the seconds became No. 38 Dean Garrett in 1988 and No. 52 Greg Grant in 1989. Both team transaction logs and Phoenix's own historical retrospective preserve the core package, making this unusually clean to evaluate in hindsight.

Phoenix Return
Johnson is the centerpiece. After limited rookie minutes behind Mark Price in Cleveland, he exploded in Phoenix. In 1988-89 he averaged more than 20 points and 12 assists, won Most Improved Player and made All-NBA Second Team. He became a multiple-time All-Star and remained the lead guard of the Suns through most of the 1990s, including the 1993 Finals season. Majerle turned the No. 14 pick into another major hit. He became a three-time All-Star, an elite perimeter defender and one of the franchise's signature players during the same contender era. Mark West supplied the less glamorous but highly valuable middle of the package: years of center minutes, durability and starts during Phoenix's rise. Corbin's Suns stint was shorter, and the two second-rounders produced little lasting Phoenix value, but those misses barely dent the package because Johnson, Majerle and West all became important pieces.

Cleveland Return
Cleveland did not lose this trade in any ordinary sense. Nance joined a young core built around Mark Price, Brad Daugherty and Ron Harper and became one of the franchise's best frontcourt players. He provided high-efficiency scoring, rebounding, shot blocking and All-Star-level defense over many seasons, made additional All-Star teams as a Cavalier and helped Cleveland become a perennial playoff team. Mike Sanders supplied several seasons of wing depth and defensive work. Randolph Keys did not become a comparable long-term asset, so the first-round pick on Cleveland's side added much less than Majerle did for Phoenix. Even so, Nance alone delivered exactly the veteran impact Cleveland wanted and stayed productive long enough to justify an A-level return.

Hindsight Comparison
The distinction is volume and top-end multiplicity. Cleveland obtained one excellent long-term star plus useful support. Phoenix obtained a franchise point guard, another future All-Star and a multi-year starting center in the same transaction. Johnson and Majerle were also central to the club that reached the 1993 NBA Finals, while West provided continuity through the rebuild-to-contender transition. Cleveland's side achieved its competitive purpose, which is why this should never be framed as a mistake. Phoenix simply extracted more total realized value from a wider set of assets.

Final Verdict
Slight Phoenix Suns Edge. Phoenix earns an A+ because Johnson, Majerle and West collectively produced extraordinary long-term value from one trade. Cleveland earns an A because Nance became a durable All-Star and defensive pillar, Sanders contributed useful depth and the deal strengthened an already rising team. The grade credits only what each franchise actually realized from the acquired assets; it does not treat later careers elsewhere as part of the return.

boston-celtics.summary: Boston arranged for expansion Miami not to select Dennis Johnson in 1988, compensating the Heat with a second-round selection associated with Sylvester Gray. The veteran guard stayed with the Celtics; the pick gave Miami a chance to add a younger player. Boston B+, Miami C.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Protected Its Veteran Guard

When Miami entered the league in 1988, established franchises had to expose players to the expansion draft. Boston wanted to retain Dennis Johnson, an experienced defender and playmaker who had been integral to its championship core. The Celtics arranged for the Heat to pass on Johnson, surrendering a second-round selection as compensation. Boston acquired certainty about keeping a veteran rather than receiving a new player from Miami.

Johnson's Continued Celtics Role Was the Prize

Johnson had been an important part of Boston's backcourt for years, providing defense and dependable decision-making. Preventing an expansion selection preserved the option to use him during the next season, which was more immediately valuable to Boston than taking another developmental prospect. His past championships explain the team's motivation but should not be counted as new accomplishments produced by this arrangement. The transaction protected existing talent.

Miami Took a Second-Round Draft Chance

Miami received the draft choice later associated with No. 35 Sylvester Gray. The Heat chose another opportunity to find a young player over selecting the veteran Celtics guard. That pick carried some flexibility for an expansion organization assembling its roster, even without a guaranteed future starter. Gray's later career needs to be evaluated separately from Johnson's Boston playing time. Neither player was directly traded for the other.

The Grades Reward Different Objectives

The inherited Celtics Win awards Boston B+ for preserving an established guard, while Miami gets C for taking an uncertain second-round opportunity. The Heat could rationally prefer a draft asset and avoid a veteran contract, but Boston's known backcourt fit offered the clearer short-term benefit. Calling this a routine Johnson-for-Gray transaction would misrepresent what the clubs agreed to during the expansion process.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston gets B+ for preserving Dennis Johnson through Miami's agreement not to select him in the expansion draft. The Heat receive C for a second-round selection associated with Sylvester Gray. Boston retained a proven veteran, while Miami chose a future prospect opportunity.

perspectives.summary: Charlotte sent expansion-draft selection Mike Brown to Utah for Kelly Tripucka rights on June 23, 1988. Tripucka gave the Hornets 227 regular-season games across three seasons, including 22.6 points a game in the inaugural 1988-89 campaign. perspectives.analysis: The expansion Hornets obtained the rights to Kelly Tripucka from Utah for freshly selected Mike Brown from Chicago. Tripucka gave Charlotte 71 games and 22.6 points a night in 1988-89, 79 games and 15.6 points in 1989-90, and 77 more games in 1990-91: 227 Hornets games, an immediate lead-scorer return. Brown gave Utah a DIFFERENT kind of value: 66 Jazz games in 1988-89 and an unbroken 82-game regular season in four consecutive following years through 1992-93, 394 Utah appearances and 40 total starts. The inherited Utah C- was too low for that five-year availability even though Brown averaged far fewer points per game than Tripucka. Charlotte A- and Utah B- preserve a modest Hornets edge for lead scoring and expansion identity. Tripucka was never a Charlotte All-Star: Larry Johnson first represented the Hornets in 1993; Tripucka had earned his prior All-Star honors while in Detroit.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia traded Albert King for Pete Myers on August 24, 1988. Myers played four games and 40 minutes for the 76ers before his December release; King provided 46 games and 791 minutes for San Antonio. Spurs Win: San Antonio B-, Philadelphia D+.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Philadelphia and San Antonio Exchanged Backcourt Depth for a Wing

The August 24, 1988 transaction sent Pete Myers from the Spurs to Philadelphia, with Albert King heading to San Antonio. Basketball-Reference records the same straight player exchange from each club’s perspective, and RealGM independently confirms the directions. There was no documented pick attached to this trade. The 76ers were testing an additional guard, while the Spurs were taking a wing with multiple NBA seasons behind him. Neither acquisition was a franchise-level investment, making what the players did for their new clubs the useful basis for comparison.

Myers Barely Entered Philadelphia’s Rotation

The 76ers received just four regular-season appearances from Myers in 1988-89. His Philadelphia line was 40 minutes, 14 points, 10 rebounds and two assists with no starts. The transaction ledger also records that Philadelphia waived him on December 15, 1988. Myers then logged 29 games for the New York Knicks that season, but those appearances were not value Philadelphia received from the August exchange. His broader career would stretch well beyond 1988, yet later stops elsewhere cannot rescue a trade judged by his very short stint with the 76ers.

King Became a Usable San Antonio Reserve

King appeared in 46 games for San Antonio in 1988-89 and started 11 of them. Across 791 minutes he supplied 327 points, 140 rebounds and 79 assists, averaging 7.1 points in 17.2 minutes a night. That was modest production, especially given the Spurs’ losing season, but it represented real wing rotation use across several months. King had been an 11.7-point scorer with Philadelphia in 1987-88; those earlier numbers were not acquired by San Antonio. Even by counting only his Spurs season, though, his return lasted far longer than Myers’s four-game Philadelphia stay.

The Team-Specific Return Explains the Revised Grades

This exchange was not a blockbuster for either club. San Antonio did not gain a future cornerstone, and King’s 1988-89 stay was his only NBA season with the Spurs. Philadelphia did acquire a legitimate professional player, but it used him for just 40 minutes and then waived him before Christmas. indiana-pacers.analysis:
New York Received Anderson While Indiana Took Stephens's Rights

The October 3, 1988 record identifies an exchange in which the Knicks received Ron Anderson and the Pacers obtained rights to Everette Stephens. It was a low-profile movement of one NBA-experienced player and another developmental asset rather than an exchange of marquee stars. Anderson had a more established professional playing background, so New York could reasonably expect an immediate roster evaluation. Indiana instead accepted the potential to develop a different guard over time. The transaction's listed counterparties and rights status matter, because acquiring someone's rights did not guarantee a signed NBA starter or the full value of that person's prior career.

Anderson's Veteran Profile Supported New York's Side

Anderson was a known perimeter player when New York pursued him, giving the Knicks a roster piece with existing professional experience. How much value he actually provided depends on his minutes after the trade and any independent subsequent transactions, not his whole résumé before arrival. He shouldn't be treated as a newly acquired franchise star or a guaranteed long-term rotation fixture. Nonetheless, trading for a veteran rather than an uncertain rights-held prospect provided New York with a more immediate personnel option. That near-term certainty supports a slight receiving-team preference, while leaving open the possibility that the rights Indiana obtained retained some developmental value.

Stephens's Rights Were a Smaller Indiana Opportunity

Indiana took the rights to Everette Stephens rather than receiving multiple first-round draft positions or an already established NBA starter. Such a player could be evaluated through training camp and roster decisions, but the transaction itself did not guarantee a large return. Later professional results, if any, must be assigned according to who signed and used the player after the exchange. The Pacers could still gain flexibility from holding the rights, though that isn't the same as receiving confirmed years of NBA scoring. Any review that skips the difference between rights and completed games will distort the practical value of the asset.

The Record Supports a Restrained New York Advantage

New York's side offered the clearer opportunity for immediate NBA service, while Indiana accepted a developmental player-rights claim with a less certain payoff. That yields a modest Knicks-winning assessment rather than a sweeping declaration of franchise victory. Neither team gained an unprotected first-round selection, and neither should be awarded later statistics from unrelated contracts. The older ledger may present brief transaction notes without all subsequent contract details, so the grades should reflect that uncertainty. Indiana wasn't empty-handed, but New York's veteran return carried more direct potential to affect its current roster.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win by a modest veteran-value edge. Neither right was an automatic multiseason contract, and the later careers of both players must be credited to the teams that actually employed them.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia received experienced forward Ron Anderson from Indiana in October 1988 for the rights to guard Everette Stephens. The Sixers gained available NBA minutes, while the Pacers accepted a prospective developmental player. The inherited Even Trade awards C+ to both clubs.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Philadelphia Preferred a Proven Forward

The 76ers acquired Ron Anderson from Indiana in October 1988, transferring the draft rights to Everette Stephens to the Pacers. Anderson had demonstrated he could contribute as an NBA forward and offered Philadelphia a clearer short-term option than a new rights acquisition. The Pacers elected to examine a prospect instead, accepting the uncertain future value of Stephens rather than keeping another veteran on their roster.

Anderson Supplied Usable NBA Experience

Anderson could fill a forward rotation role without needing to learn the league from scratch. His range and experience were useful attributes for a Philadelphia club balancing established players and younger teammates. The direct benefit was the veteran play the 76ers could use after the trade, not his statistical history from other NBA stops. He was a supporting option rather than a new franchise-leading scorer.

Stephens Offered Indiana a Developmental Chance

The Pacers received the ability to evaluate or sign Everette Stephens rather than an incoming established starter. A draft-rights acquisition gives a team control over a potential player but not a guarantee of game appearances or scoring. The player's earlier amateur successes and later opportunities should not be treated as Indiana NBA production without evidence. Indiana chose a prospect's potential and roster flexibility over known forward depth.

Equal Grades Do Not Mean Identical Player Value

The inherited C+ for each team and Even Trade result compares two different types of return. Philadelphia chose immediate experience; Indiana selected the possibility of a younger guard. Neither side acquired a highly established new star through the transaction. The balanced verdict reflects limited overall stakes instead of assuming a prospect right and a veteran contract automatically produce equal points and wins.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Philadelphia receives C+ for gaining veteran forward Ron Anderson and available rotation help. Indiana also earns C+ for the rights to Everette Stephens, a developmental guard prospect whose future was less certain. Each organization selected a different roster timeline without a decisive long-term advantage.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: The Seattle SuperSonics acquired guard Jerry Reynolds from Milwaukee on October 4, 1988 for a 1990 second-round pick that became No. 44 Steve Henson. Reynolds played 56 Seattle games in 1988-89, totaling 737 minutes and 428 points before being selected by Orlando in the expansion draft. Henson played 118 Bucks games across 1990-91 and 1991-92, totaling 1,076 minutes and 364 points. Even Trade, B both.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee Moved a Guard for Future Second-Round Flexibility

The Bucks traded Jerry Reynolds to the Seattle SuperSonics on October 4, 1988, receiving a second-round choice in the 1990 NBA draft. Reynolds was a useful reserve guard who had played three years with Milwaukee, but the club was ready to examine another backcourt option. Seattle wanted immediate wing and ball-handling help after personnel changes in the offseason. The franchises were not swapping two players ready to play that October; one side took an experienced NBA contributor while the other accepted a future draft selection.

Reynolds Provided One Season of Seattle Bench Scoring

Reynolds played fifty-six regular-season SuperSonics games during 1988-89 without starting a contest. He scored 428 points in 737 minutes, averaging 7.6 points and contributing 100 rebounds and sixty-two assists. That output made him a genuine contributor rather than an unused veteran contract. Seattle reached the playoffs, with Reynolds occupying a limited role behind its primary guards and forwards. The franchise then lost him to Orlando in the June 1989 expansion draft. His later productive Orlando seasons should not be counted as Seattle return from the Milwaukee deal.

The Future Milwaukee Pick Became Steve Henson

The 1990 selection was No. 44, used by Milwaukee to draft Kansas State point guard Steve Henson. He played sixty-eight Bucks regular-season games in 1990-91, recording 690 minutes, 214 points and 131 assists. He returned the following season for fifty games, with 386 minutes, 150 points and eighty-two assists. Across both years, Henson gave Milwaukee 118 regular-season appearances and 1,076 minutes. His later Atlanta, Charlotte and Portland NBA games belong to other clubs and must not be attributed to Milwaukee's original incoming selection.

Two Different Timetables Produced Real NBA Minutes

Seattle received its basketball production immediately during the 1988-89 campaign, while the Bucks waited until 1990 to turn the incoming pick into a player. Reynolds scored more points than Henson during his Seattle stay, but Milwaukee accumulated more games and minutes across two seasons. Both were backcourt reserves, not stars, and neither franchise gained a long-term player to build around. The separate receiving-team totals are substantial enough to support fair grades. The original even assessment correctly values the difference between quick scoring help and a longer-lived draft choice.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Milwaukee earns B because 1990 No. 44 pick Steve Henson delivered 118 Bucks regular-season games, 1,076 minutes, 364 points and 213 assists. Seattle gets B for Jerry Reynolds's 56 games, 737 minutes and 428 points before the 1989 expansion draft. Both teams received actual NBA bench work despite different timing.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston traded forward Cedric Maxwell to the Washington Bullets for Jim Grandholm in October 1988. Grandholm was waived and briefly re-signed but never logged a regular-season Rockets game. Maxwell participated in Bullets training camp but also never appeared in a Washington regular-season game, ending his NBA career after 1987-88. Contemporary reporting connects Houston's move to freeing room for Otis Thorpe. Even Trade, Houston C- for roster/cap flexibility, Washington D+ for an unused veteran.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Rockets Moved a Veteran Contract Before Pursuing Thorpe

Houston sent Cedric Maxwell to the Washington Bullets for Jim Grandholm in early October 1988. Maxwell had won championships with Boston before spending his later NBA seasons with the Rockets, but his on-court role had declined. Contemporary Washington reporting linked the transaction to Houston's attempt to reduce payroll obligations while negotiating for forward Otis Thorpe. Washington acquired an experienced championship veteran to inspect during training camp. Grandholm was not an established NBA starter, making the acquisition for Houston primarily a roster and financial decision.

Neither Incoming Forward Played a Regular-Season Game

Houston waived Grandholm on October 14, brought him back under a separate free-agent agreement on October 19 and released him again on November 1. He did not play a Rockets regular-season NBA game through this sequence. Maxwell arrived at Washington's training camp, but he also did not appear in an official Bullets game. His final NBA regular-season appearances had been for Houston during 1987-88. It would be incorrect to use Maxwell's earlier championship statistics as Washington production or to claim the Rockets obtained NBA minutes from Grandholm.

Financial Flexibility Was Houston's Documented Motivation

Washington Post coverage during the first week of camp observed that moving Maxwell's salary made it easier for Houston to pursue Thorpe within the league's salary-cap structure. Thorpe subsequently joined Houston in a separate October 11 exchange with Sacramento involving Rodney McCray and Jim Petersen. That second deal was not a direct Maxwell-for-Thorpe swap and cannot be merged into the official consideration for Grandholm. Still, payroll flexibility offers a concrete reason why the Rockets accepted a player they would quickly waive. The Bullets were instead betting a familiar veteran could still help.

A Near-Zero Basketball Trade Deserves Restrained Marks

Both franchises acquired a player who failed to enter their regular-season rotation. Washington's tryout of Maxwell did not restore his career, while Houston used Grandholm as a temporary roster contract. The salary-cap context gives Houston a more understandable indirect benefit than a simple zero-games comparison would suggest. It does not justify assigning all of Thorpe's later Rockets production to Maxwell's departure, because Thorpe required another substantial trade. The inherited Wizards-favored grades exaggerated a deal that produced no direct incoming NBA minutes for either organization.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Houston receives C- because moving Cedric Maxwell created some documented cap flexibility, although Jim Grandholm never played a Rockets regular-season game. Washington gets D+ because Maxwell likewise never appeared for the Bullets. Thorpe's later Houston career followed a separate transaction and cannot be counted as direct return from this October exchange.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Craig Hodges from Phoenix on December 14, 1988 for Ed Nealy, a 1989 second-round pick that became Ricky Blanton and cash. Hodges stayed with the Bulls through 1991-92, supplied elite three-point shooting, won three consecutive NBA Three-Point Contests and was part of the 1991 and 1992 championship teams. Phoenix received useful reserve work from Nealy, but Blanton never became a meaningful NBA contributor and the cash did not create a comparable basketball asset. Chicago did not acquire a star, yet it obtained a role player whose best skill fit a title roster for multiple seasons. That makes the Bulls the clear hindsight winner.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Chicago and Phoenix transaction records show the December 14, 1988 deal as Craig Hodges to the Bulls for Ed Nealy, a 1989 second-round pick and cash. The pick became No. 46 Ricky Blanton. This is a useful example of a trade whose importance comes from role fit rather than star power. Neither Hodges nor Nealy was a primary scorer, and the draft pick was modest. The separation appears because Chicago turned its return into a multi-year specialist on championship teams, while Phoenix's package generated mostly reserve value.

Chicago Return
Hodges immediately gave Chicago a high-level shooting specialist. His role was narrow but clear: space the floor, punish defenses from deep and provide guard minutes without needing the ball. He remained with the Bulls through the 1991-92 season and became one of the league's most recognizable perimeter shooters, winning the NBA Three-Point Contest in 1990, 1991 and 1992. More important for TradeVerdicts, he was on the roster for Chicago's first two championships. Hodges was not a core star on the level of Michael Jordan or Scottie Pippen, so the trade should not receive an A+ as if Chicago acquired a franchise player. But several seasons of specialist value during a championship window from a modest outgoing package is exactly the kind of transaction that creates meaningful surplus value.

Phoenix Return
Nealy gave the Suns legitimate reserve minutes and rebounding. He was a physical frontcourt role player and remained in Phoenix beyond the immediate post-trade stretch, so the Suns did not receive an empty return. His offensive role was limited, however, and he never became a foundational part of the club's emerging contender core. The 1989 second-round pick became Ricky Blanton at No. 46. Blanton did not develop into a durable NBA contributor, which sharply limits the draft portion of the package. Phoenix also received cash, but the available transaction record does not tie that payment to a later basketball asset, so it is recognized as consideration without inventing downstream value.

Hindsight Comparison
The deal is not a referendum on which player had the better raw box-score totals. It is about what each team needed and what each asset actually became. Phoenix received useful depth from Nealy, but the pick failed to add a second meaningful piece. Chicago received a specialist who lasted multiple seasons, had an elite repeatable skill and fit two championship rosters. That makes the Bulls' realized return stronger even though Hodges was never a full-time star.

Final Verdict
Chicago Bulls Win. Chicago earns an A- because Hodges delivered multiple seasons of high-value role fit and contributed to two championship teams at a modest acquisition cost. Phoenix earns a C+ because Nealy provided usable reserve value and the club also received cash, but the second-round pick did not become a meaningful NBA asset. The grade credits Hodges only for his Chicago tenure and does not inflate the trade with accomplishments outside that period.

sacramento-kings.summary: On February 20, 1989, Sacramento Kings acquired Wayman Tisdale; 1990 or 1991 second round pick (1990 #40-Bimbo Coles) from Indiana Pacers in exchange for LaSalle Thompson; Randy Wittman.
sacramento-kings.analysis: Neither Wayman Tisdale nor LaSalle Thompson produced enough separation to define a winner. Sacramento Kings received a usable return, and the partner did as well, but the completed careers and draft outcomes stayed broadly comparable. An even verdict is the most defensible conclusion.

summary: Win. Wayman Tisdale became a long-term primary scorer in Sacramento, while LaSalle Thompson gave Indiana legitimate frontcourt value without matching Tisdale's offensive impact. The Kings did not turn the move into team success, so A- is more appropriate than A+. Indiana's B reflects a useful return, but Sacramento captured the better player outcome.
analysis: Tisdale became the most valuable player produced by the transaction for his acquiring team. He gave Sacramento several seasons of dependable scoring, including multiple years around the 20-point-per-game level, and became one of the franchise's primary offensive options during a difficult era. The Kings did not become a contender, which keeps the grade below A+, but they clearly received the player with the highest sustained offensive value and did so without surrendering an elite asset. Indiana's return was useful rather than empty. Thompson was a rugged big who rebounded, defended and gave the Pacers frontcourt minutes across several seasons. Wittman was a smaller piece. The trade helped Indiana rebalance the roster as the franchise moved toward a new core. That functional value deserves a solid B. The Pacers simply did not receive a player who matched Tisdale's scoring burden or individual production for Sacramento. The future second-round pick did not create a transformational branch, so the evaluation remains mostly a player-for-player comparison. That simplicity helps the analysis. Sacramento kept receiving direct value from Tisdale; Indiana received several seasons from Thompson. Neither side can claim a hidden superstar downstream. The difference comes from Tisdale's higher offensive responsibility and the fact that Sacramento obtained the most difficult skill to replace in the deal: efficient frontcourt scoring.

perspectives.summary: On February 21, 1989 Dallas acquired Herb Williams from Indiana, sending Detlef Schrempf and a conditional 1990-or-1991 second-rounder that ultimately became 1990 No. 45 Antonio Davis. Indiana won the longer-term deal, though Williams gave Dallas multiple useful seasons.
perspectives.analysis: The Mavericks traded Detlef Schrempf and a future conditional second (ultimately the 1990 No. 45 choice Antonio Davis) to Indiana for center Herb Williams. The previous imported Dallas account misstated his age and playing time: he was 30 at the 1989 trade and played 30 Dallas games with 20 starts in the closing 1988-89 period. He then appeared in 81 Dallas games in 1989-90, 60 in 1990-91 and 75 in 1991-92. Williams averaged 8.6 points, 4.8 rebounds and 1.3 blocks in 1989-90, a real center return. analysis: Sacramento gets the narrow edge because Ainge was the best player in the exchange and remained a productive guard after the trade. He supplied shooting, playmaking and professionalism to a franchise searching for reliable perimeter creation. His stay was not long enough to make this a landslide, but the Kings acquired the one player capable of changing the quality of their backcourt immediately. Brad Lohaus was secondary, yet he added another usable frontcourt option. Boston did receive meaningful value. Pinckney was a credible rotation big who could rebound and defend, while Kleine gave the Celtics additional size at a time when the roster needed bodies around an aging core. The return was practical, and neither incoming player was a dead asset. Boston's grade should therefore remain in the B range. The Celtics simply exchanged the most talented and versatile player in the deal for depth rather than for a new centerpiece. The downstream branches do not create a massive hidden swing. Sacramento later moved Ainge again, preserving some value, while Boston consumed much of the return as rotation minutes. That makes the original trade a relatively clean comparison between star-adjacent guard play and frontcourt depth. Because Ainge remained marketable after his Sacramento stint, the Kings receive a little extra credit for not allowing the asset to expire without value.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State traded the 1989 first-round right later used on Dana Barros to Seattle for a 1990 first-round right later linked with Gary Payton. However, the Warriors returned that 1990 right to Seattle on August 7, 1989, to acquire Alton Lister. Payton was eventually drafted by the SuperSonics, not Golden State. The inherited Warriors Win grades Golden State A+ and Seattle C+, though that valuation needs careful rights-chain interpretation.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Exchanged a Current Pick for a Future One

On June 27, 1989, the Warriors transferred a first-round choice associated with No. 16 Dana Barros to Seattle in exchange for a 1990 first-round right. That future selection ultimately became No. 2 overall, the position at which Gary Payton was selected. At the time, Golden State was turning an immediate selection into a potentially higher-valued future opportunity. Seattle chose Barros's available draft slot to address its current roster plans, accepting the uncertainty surrounding its following-year pick.

The Crucial Second Transaction Came in August

Golden State did not retain the 1990 selection all the way to Payton's draft. On August 7, 1989, the Warriors traded the same first-round right back to Seattle for veteran center Alton Lister. The SuperSonics subsequently selected Payton at No. 2 in 1990 and received his actual on-court career. The original June rights acquisition can still be considered valuable as a tradable asset, but Golden State cannot be credited with developing or fielding Payton simply because its name appears on the earlier pick chain.

Seattle Obtained Barros and Reacquired the Future Star's Pick

The June exchange supplied Seattle with Barros's draft position; Barros went on to have an accomplished NBA career, though his later seasons outside Seattle shouldn't be attributed to the SuperSonics. By returning Lister to Golden State in August, Seattle regained control of the 1990 first-round choice and eventually selected Payton. The two transactions form a connected sequence but are distinct completed agreements with separate incoming assets. Any hindsight evaluation should make the chronology clear before comparing the teams' outcomes.

The Inherited A-Plus Is a Rights-Value Grade, Not Payton Credit

The original Warriors A+ versus Seattle C+ follows the extraordinary eventual draft position associated with the right Golden State acquired in June. That rating would overstate the Warriors' benefit if read as credit for Gary Payton's Seattle career. The proper narrower observation is that Golden State converted the No. 16 pick into a high-value future asset that it soon exchanged for Lister. Seattle ended the rights chain with both Barros's 1989 slot and Payton's eventual NBA service. The published grade should be revisited separately if direct franchise outcomes are used.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. The inherited A+ for Golden State evaluates a 1990 first-round right that ultimately became the No. 2 Gary Payton selection; Seattle receives C+ for the 1989 Dana Barros pick. Crucially, Golden State traded that future right back to Seattle for Alton Lister weeks later. Payton's actual SuperSonics playing career cannot be credited to Golden State, and the grade merits later review.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: On August 28, 1989, Philadelphia sent Maurice Cheeks, David Wingate and Christian Welp to San Antonio for Johnny Dawkins and Jay Vincent. Dawkins started 81 Sixers games in 1989-90 but suffered a serious injury the next year; Vincent played 17 Philadelphia games. philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Philadelphia Exchanged Its Longtime Guard for a Younger Starter

The 76ers traded Maurice Cheeks, David Wingate and Christian Welp to San Antonio on August 28, 1989, receiving Johnny Dawkins and Jay Vincent. Cheeks had been a cornerstone of Philadelphia's 1983 championship team, but the Sixers were changing their backcourt around Charles Barkley. Dawkins had shown scoring and playmaking talent in San Antonio yet struggled with injuries, while Vincent supplied veteran forward depth. For the Spurs, Cheeks offered an established defensive point guard and Wingate an active reserve. All five players are documented in both teams' transaction logs, so there was no extra pick or cash to grade.

Dawkins Helped Philadelphia Immediately, but His Tenure Was Brief

Dawkins started 81 regular-season games for Philadelphia in 1989-90, averaging 14.3 points and 7.4 assists. That gave the Sixers a credible starting guard during a 53-win season and a playoff run to the East semifinals. Jay Vincent, however, appeared in only 17 Philadelphia games and scored 124 points before moving on. Dawkins's contributions soon stopped as well: he managed just four appearances in 1990-91. The initial season was valuable enough to merit a respectable grade, but the new backcourt partnership did not provide several years of continuity. Neither player's production for previous teams belongs in Philadelphia's acquired return.

San Antonio Received Cheeks, Wingate and a Trade Route to Rod Strickland

Cheeks played 50 Spurs regular-season games in 1989-90, starting 49, and averaged 11.1 points and 6.2 assists before San Antonio sent him to New York in February for Rod Strickland. That second transaction was an important consequence of the original trade: a veteran received from Philadelphia became the asset used to obtain another starting-caliber guard. Wingate independently played 78 Spurs games during 1989-90 and scored 527 points as a useful reserve, then returned for part of the next season. Welp provided a smaller return and was traded to Golden State in February 1990 for Uwe Blab. Those later deals must be tracked as separate moves rather than misdescribed as direct August arrivals.

The Downstream Point Guard Matters More Than the Initial Name Count

Philadelphia got a strong first season from Dawkins and some Vincent depth. San Antonio got Cheeks's first-half starting minutes, Wingate's full-season reserve contribution and the option to convert Cheeks into Strickland in a separate February 1990 trade. The Strickland return did not happen automatically; it required New York's participation and should be treated as traceable downstream value, not as a player Philadelphia directly sent away. When the record is viewed in its real sequence, San Antonio came away with more than a short-term guard rental. That longer route gives the Spurs the advantage despite Dawkins's impressive debut season for the Sixers.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win. San Antonio earns A for 50 Maurice Cheeks games, 78 David Wingate games in 1989-90 and Cheeks's subsequent conversion into Rod Strickland. Philadelphia gets B- for 81 starts from Johnny Dawkins and 17 Jay Vincent appearances, with Dawkins's later injury limiting the return. Strickland is a downstream acquisition, not a direct piece of this August deal.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired second-year guard Steve Kerr from Phoenix on September 5, 1989 for a 1993 second-round pick that eventually became No. 49 Mark Buford. Kerr gave the Cavaliers three seasons of useful shooting and reserve guard play, including one of the league's best three-point percentages in 1989-90. He later became famous for championships elsewhere, but none of that later value belongs to Cleveland in this trade. Phoenix waited four years for the pick and ultimately received no meaningful NBA production from Buford. On realized value, Cleveland clearly won a modest transaction without turning it into a franchise-changing acquisition.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Cleveland and Phoenix transaction logs record a simple September 5, 1989 deal: Steve Kerr to the Cavaliers for a future second-round pick. The pick did not arrive until the 1993 draft, when it became No. 49 Mark Buford. That delayed return makes the hindsight comparison straightforward. Cleveland received an NBA-ready guard immediately, while Phoenix accepted a distant second-round asset whose eventual player did not establish an NBA career.

Cleveland Return
Kerr was not yet the championship role player he would later become in Chicago and San Antonio, and TradeVerdicts should not backfill that later reputation into his Cavaliers grade. What Cleveland actually received was still useful. Kerr played three seasons with the Cavaliers and became a reliable perimeter shooter off the bench. In 1989-90 he shot at an elite rate from three-point range and helped space the floor around Cleveland's established frontcourt and Mark Price. His minutes and scoring were modest, but he was available across multiple seasons and gave the club a repeatable skill at very low acquisition cost. That is real rotation value, especially for a future second-round pick four drafts away.

Phoenix Return
Phoenix received only the future pick. Because the asset conveyed in 1993, the Suns carried the opportunity cost for several years before realizing any player value. The selection became Mark Buford at No. 49. Buford did not become a meaningful NBA contributor, so the direct basketball return from the trade was effectively zero. The Suns did not receive another player, additional pick or documented downstream transaction value from this particular asset that would offset Kerr's Cleveland tenure.

Hindsight Comparison
This is a clear but appropriately scaled Cleveland win. Kerr was a reserve, not a star, and Cleveland did not benefit from the championships he later won with other franchises. His value here is limited to three Cavaliers seasons of shooting and guard depth. Phoenix's return, however, failed to produce a durable NBA player at all. When one side gets several seasons of useful rotation play and the other waits four years for a second-rounder that does not stick, the realized-value advantage is decisive even if the absolute stakes are modest.

Final Verdict
Cleveland Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns a B+ because Kerr supplied several seasons of useful role-player value at a very small acquisition cost. Phoenix earns a D because the delayed second-round pick became a player who did not generate meaningful NBA value. The grade intentionally excludes Kerr's later Bulls and Spurs accomplishments; those belong to later transactions, not to Cleveland's return.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Miami acquired Tellis Frank from Golden State on October 2, 1989, for a conditional Cavaliers second-round asset later used at No. 41 on Steve Bardo. Frank supplied 77 Heat games, 39 starts, 1,762 minutes, 735 points and 385 rebounds during 1989-90. Bardo never appeared in a Warriors NBA game; his subsequent brief NBA stints belonged to other teams. Heat Win, Miami A-, Golden State D+.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Miami Bought an Experienced Forward With a Contingent Pick

Golden State sent Tellis Frank to Miami on October 2, 1989, in return for a second-round draft asset originating with Cleveland. The transaction was described as a choice in either the 1990 or 1992 draft depending on conditions, and it ultimately resolved into the 1990 No. 41 selection. Miami was entering its second NBA season and needed adults who could play regular frontcourt minutes. Frank had two Warriors seasons behind him, including a meaningful rookie workload, while Golden State preferred another chance to draft a developmental guard.

Frank Started 39 Games for the Expansion-Era Heat

The Heat got immediate and substantial production. Frank appeared in seventy-seven games during 1989-90, starting thirty-nine and playing 1,762 minutes. He scored 735 points, pulled down 385 rebounds and averaged 9.5 points with five rebounds per game. That was one of the more productive roles on a very young team still building a professional rotation. His thirty-two Warriors games during 1988-89 were completed before the exchange and must not be folded into his Miami totals. Likewise, his brief later Minnesota appearance was not Heat production.

Golden State Drafted Bardo but Didn't Receive NBA Games

The deferred selection became No. 41 in 1990 and was used on Illinois guard Steve Bardo. He continued playing basketball professionally, including the Continental Basketball Association, and eventually reached the NBA for San Antonio, Dallas and Detroit. None of those appearances were made for Golden State, however. The Warriors therefore obtained a draft-rights asset and an opportunity to evaluate Bardo, but no direct NBA regular-season games from him. The pick was real; its conversion into meaningful Golden State rotation play did not occur.

The Receiving-Team Comparison Clearly Favors Miami

Frank delivered an entire season of frontcourt play for the Heat, while the Warriors invested the second-round pick in someone who never wore their uniform in an official NBA game. The clubs' different developmental priorities explain why they made the deal, but do not erase the difference in realized value. Miami's 77 appearances and 39 starts are much stronger evidence than the prospect's later work for unrelated organizations. The inherited Heat-win verdict was right, although the grade for the Miami receiving-team production deserved a substantial increase.

Final Verdict

Heat Win. Miami earns A- after Tellis Frank played 77 games, started 39 and contributed 735 points, 385 rebounds and 1,762 minutes in 1989-90. Golden State receives D+ because 1990 No. 41 pick Steve Bardo never made a Warriors NBA appearance. His later games with other teams are not Warriors trade return.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Hawks Bought Backcourt Help Near the Deadline

Atlanta traded Antoine Carr, Sedric Toney and a 1991 second-round pick to Sacramento for Kenny Smith and Mike Williams in February 1990. The Hawks already had a talented scoring roster but wanted a different mix at point guard. Smith had shown his ability to run an offense with the Kings, making him the leading acquisition. Sacramento took a productive veteran forward in Carr and extra guard depth in Toney, plus a future choice that would later be used near the end of the second round.

Smith's Atlanta Stay Was Valuable but Brief

Smith provided another ball-handling option for Atlanta, although he did not become a long-tenured Hawks point guard. He moved to Houston later in 1990, and his subsequent championship achievements with the Rockets belong to a separate team and series of transactions. Mike Williams offered a narrower roster role. The immediate attraction had been the chance to add a capable creator without waiting for a draft pick. The actual receiving-team result was much shorter than Smith's overall NBA career.

Sacramento Received Carr and a Draft Chance

Carr offered size and an established interior game, giving the Kings a useful forward during a period of rebuilding. Toney's role was smaller, while the incoming second-round selection eventually became No. 42 Steve Hood in the 1991 draft. That pick was a real asset, but the associated draft name should not be treated as an automatic source of Sacramento playing production. The Kings gained more individual pieces than Atlanta, yet their cumulative impact needed to be assessed against what the Hawks wanted at guard.

The Grades Reflect the Original Teams' Priorities

Atlanta obtained a guard who could make its offense function differently, but the evaluation should not borrow Smith's later Houston success. Sacramento received a known frontcourt player and additional options without adding a lasting star. The inherited Hawks advantage credits Smith's talent and roster fit during the initial acquisition, while the moderate grade for Sacramento recognizes the value of Carr and the pick. Neither team received an outcome resembling a franchise-defining championship transaction.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for adding Kenny Smith's ball handling and Mike Williams as backcourt depth, although Smith's stay was short and his later Rockets titles don't count here. Sacramento receives C for Antoine Carr, Sedric Toney and the No. 42 pick later used on Steve Hood. The Hawks acquired the more attractive immediate guard talent, while the Kings received a useful but modest package.

golden-state-warriors.summary: On February 22, 1990, Golden State acquired Chris Welp from San Antonio for Uwe Blab. Welp contributed 14 Warriors games, 142 minutes and 50 points; Blab played seven Spurs games, 50 minutes and scored 15. Slight Warriors Edge: Golden State C+, San Antonio C.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
A Straight Swap of Two Reserve Centers at the 1990 Deadline

Golden State sent Uwe Blab to San Antonio for Chris Welp on February 22, 1990. The league trade-deadline archive and both clubs’ historical transaction lists agree on the timing and the two players. No draft choice or cash was included in the documented exchange. Each team was moving a little-used big man to try a different fit late in the season. Welp had appeared only sparingly for the Spurs, while Blab had logged much more court time for Golden State before the trade. Those earlier minutes, however, belonged to the team that traded him away and cannot be credited as San Antonio’s return.

Welp Played 14 Games for the Warriors

Welp gave Golden State a measurable if limited boost across the last part of 1989-90. He appeared in 14 games with two starts, totaling 142 minutes, 50 points and 36 rebounds in a Warriors uniform. His 10.1 minutes per appearance represented a modest reserve role rather than a permanent frontcourt solution. Those numbers were better than the playing time he had accumulated with San Antonio, but that improvement does not turn Welp into a major historical acquisition. It simply gives the Warriors a concrete roster contribution to show for the exchange.

Blab’s San Antonio Return Was Seven Games

Blab played seven games for the Spurs after the trade, with no starts. He totaled 50 regular-season minutes, 15 points and nine rebounds for San Antonio. The 40 games and 481 minutes he had logged for Golden State earlier in the 1989-90 season are real NBA production, but they are not production the Spurs obtained. San Antonio waived Blab before the following season, so the February transaction did not yield a continuing rotation piece. The incoming player did contribute in a small role, which prevents the return from being treated as absolutely nothing.

Why This Is a Small Warriors Edge

Both clubs exchanged reserves, and neither acquired a starter who became important over multiple seasons. Golden State nevertheless got more from the player it received: twice the game appearances and nearly three times the minutes, with 50 points against San Antonio’s 15. Welp’s 36 Warriors rebounds also exceeded the nine Blab supplied for the Spurs. The historical source verdict had favored San Antonio despite the opposite pattern in the receiving-team splits. The revised judgment credits only the actual post-trade club totals, not full careers, earlier stops or hypothetical alternative roster roles.

Final Verdict

Slight Warriors Edge. Golden State receives C+ for 14 games, 142 minutes and 50 points from Chris Welp. San Antonio earns C for seven games, 50 minutes and 15 points from Uwe Blab. Neither player became a long-term fixture, but the Warriors got the stronger immediate reserve-center return.

minnesota-timberwolves.summary: Minnesota traded veteran center Steve Johnson to Seattle for forward Brad Sellers on February 22, 1990. Sellers played only 14 Timberwolves games, 113 minutes and 47 points in the remainder of 1989-90; Johnson gave Seattle 21 games, 242 minutes and 117 points. The imported reference to a 1991 conditional second is not supported as a conveyed pick in either contemporaneous team ledger. SuperSonics Win narrowly, Seattle C+, Minnesota D+.
minnesota-timberwolves.analysis:
Seattle Acquired an Aging Center From an Expansion Team

The Timberwolves sent Steve Johnson to the Seattle SuperSonics on February 22, 1990, receiving forward Brad Sellers. Minnesota was in its inaugural NBA season and exploring ways to assemble a frontcourt around younger talent. Johnson, previously a useful Portland center, was no longer playing heavy minutes. Seattle wanted additional veteran size during the stretch run while parting with Sellers, a bench forward it had acquired the preceding summer. Both clubs' main transaction ledgers list the direct player exchange, with no verified selection that was actually conveyed.

Johnson Played Twenty-One Regular-Season Seattle Games

Johnson gave the SuperSonics twenty-one appearances after the February trade, totaling 242 minutes, 117 points and 50 rebounds. He did not start, and his role remained that of a reserve center in a team already using several frontcourt options. Those figures should not be confused with his four Minnesota games from before the transaction or with his much more productive Portland seasons. Seattle's direct gain was modest but measurable. He later played for Golden State, which was another team and cannot be credited as the Sonics' receiving-team return.

Sellers Was Used Even Less by the Timberwolves

Sellers played fourteen Minnesota games in the remainder of 1989-90. He recorded 113 minutes, 47 points and nineteen rebounds without a start, providing only a brief look for a young expansion roster. His forty-five Seattle games earlier in the season do not count as new Timberwolves performance. Although Sellers returned to Minnesota in 1992-93 and played additional games then, that later stint occurred after another interval with a different team. It would misrepresent the 1990 trade to merge those later statistics into the original acquired role.

The Imported Conditional Pick Cannot Be Treated as Conveyed

One historical import lists a possible conditional 1991 second-round asset on Seattle's side, but neither franchise's Basketball-Reference transaction record confirms a conveyed choice in this February player-for-player swap. The pick must therefore remain an unresolved provenance note, not a basis for assigning any draft prospect to the SuperSonics. The verifiable comparison is Johnson's twenty-one Seattle games against Sellers's fourteen Minnesota games. Neither was a lasting fixture, and Seattle received only a slight advantage in playing time and output. The previous equal B grades overstated two declining veteran reserves.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win. Seattle gets C+ for Steve Johnson's 21 regular-season games, 242 minutes and 117 points after arriving in February 1990. Minnesota earns D+ for Brad Sellers's 14 games, 113 minutes and 47 points. An imported conditional 1991 pick has no verified conveying result, so it isn't awarded phantom future player value.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Clubs Rearranged Five 1990 Draft Rights

Atlanta and Golden State made a multi-pick exchange on June 27, 1990. The Hawks acquired No. 10 Rumeal Robinson and second-round choices No. 36 Trevor Wilson and No. 41 Steve Bardo. The Warriors received No. 11 Tyrone Hill and No. 28 Les Jepsen. It was not simply a trade of Robinson for Hill; adding three lower selections changes what each club hoped to accomplish. Atlanta sought more chances to find contributors, while Golden State preferred a smaller package led by Hill.

Hill Became the Strongest Player in the Package

Hill developed into a durable professional big man, with his first NBA seasons belonging to Golden State. He later produced substantial NBA work for other franchises, which helps identify his talent but cannot all be credited as Warriors receiving-team performance. His rebounding and interior style offered a different roster function from Robinson, a guard drafted one slot higher. Jepsen gave Golden State another player to evaluate, though he did not develop into a comparable contributor. The clearest realized player advantage came from selecting Hill.

Atlanta's Extra Picks Didn't Produce an Equal Centerpiece

Robinson received NBA opportunities with the Hawks but did not become a long-term lead guard who justified choosing him immediately ahead of Hill. Wilson and Bardo added legitimate second-round chances; neither developed into an Atlanta fixture capable of changing the comparison. More picks increased Atlanta's opportunities but did not guarantee better results. The team chose a specific guard and two speculative prospects, rather than the interior player Golden State took, and that selection strategy ultimately left the Hawks with less enduring value.

The Draft-Rights Choice Settled the Evaluation

The Warriors didn't acquire Hill's entire later NBA career in this transaction, and that distinction prevents overstating their direct value. They did select the most accomplished player of the group and enjoyed his early development. Atlanta had three acquired choices but did not obtain an equally useful long-term player from them. This draft-night lesson isn't that collecting extra picks was irrational; it is that the specific talent selected can outweigh a numerical advantage in selections. The grades favor the Warriors on those realized outcomes.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State earns B+ for choosing Tyrone Hill at No. 11 and adding Les Jepsen; Hill was the most successful NBA player in this draft-rights package. Atlanta gets C- for Rumeal Robinson, Trevor Wilson and Steve Bardo, none of whom matched that result. Hill's later production elsewhere isn't treated as Warriors games, but the talent decision still favored Golden State.

seattle-supersonics.summary: On June 27, 1990, Orlando delivered second-round picks for 1993 and 1995 to Seattle in exchange for the SuperSonics agreeing not to take Dennis Scott with the No. 2 pick. Seattle selected Gary Payton, while Orlando got Scott at No. 4. The consideration was Seattle's draft-day promise, not a direct trade of Scott's NBA contract or rights. The picks later resolved to No. 42 Adonis Jordan and No. 55 Michael McDonald, with the latter pick subsequently traded onward. Magic Win: Orlando A, Seattle C+.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
Orlando Paid for Seattle Not to Use Pick No. 2 on Scott

The June 27, 1990 draft-day agreement was unusual because Seattle promised not to choose a particular prospect. The SuperSonics held the second overall choice, while Orlando was picking fourth and strongly wanted Georgia Tech scorer Dennis Scott. To preserve its opportunity, Orlando committed two future second-round picks to Seattle. The arrangement did not trade Scott himself, since he had yet to be selected or sign an NBA contract. Seattle went on to choose Gary Payton at No. 2, and Orlando obtained Scott at No. 4 after Denver selected Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf third.

Scott Became a Longtime Magic Shooting Threat

Orlando's protected choice turned into one of the franchise's important early perimeter scorers. Scott joined a young expansion-era Magic team and built his reputation around high-volume three-point shooting. He remained a central offensive player through the club's ascent alongside Shaquille O'Neal and Penny Hardaway, including its run to the 1995 NBA Finals. That lasting on-court value explains why Orlando was willing to surrender future second-round opportunities to reduce uncertainty on draft night. But Scott's production is a consequence of Orlando's own draft selection, not minutes Seattle literally transferred to Orlando in a player deal.

Seattle Obtained Two Picks Rather Than Scott

The compensation given to Seattle consisted of a 1993 second-round choice later listed at No. 42, Adonis Jordan, and a 1995 second-round choice ultimately identified as No. 55, Michael McDonald. Those picks had exchange value, even though neither was equivalent to a fourth overall selection. The 1995 choice moved again in a separate 1994 transaction involving Seattle and Golden State, so attributing Michael McDonald's later draft identity as a direct Seattle development story would overstate the result. Seattle also benefited enormously from independently selecting Payton, but his future career should not be credited as a return received from the Magic.

Both Teams Achieved Different Draft-Day Goals

The SuperSonics left the 1990 draft with the player they selected second and two extra future choices. Orlando used a small stream of draft capital to protect its favored option at fourth and then acquired a player who contributed for years. The contemporary reporting and both franchise transaction ledgers support that limited structure; they do not support calling it a Scott-for-two-picks player exchange. Orlando's enduring benefit outweighs Seattle's modest additional selections, while the Sonics still deserve a fair grade for extracting value from a commitment consistent with their selection plans.

Final Verdict

Magic Win. Orlando earns A because paying two future second-round selections helped ensure it could take Dennis Scott fourth overall, a long-term perimeter contributor. Seattle gets C+ for receiving the 1993 No. 42 and 1995 No. 55 draft positions. Seattle drafted Gary Payton independently at No. 2; neither Payton's career nor a fictional direct trade of Scott's player rights should inflate the compensation from this agreement.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Los Angeles acquired Terry Teagle from Golden State on September 25, 1990, surrendering its 1991 first-round draft pick, eventually No. 25 Shaun Vandiver. Teagle appeared in 164 regular-season Lakers games over two seasons and scored 1,695 points, plus postseason minutes during their 1991 Finals appearance. Vandiver never played an NBA regular-season game for the Warriors. Lakers Win, Lakers B+, Warriors D.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Lakers Replaced Michael Cooper's Bench Scoring with Teagle

On September 25, 1990, Los Angeles acquired veteran swingman Terry Teagle from Golden State and surrendered its 1991 first-round draft selection. Contemporary Los Angeles reporting described Jerry West's search for a reserve scorer after Michael Cooper left for professional basketball in Italy. Teagle had been a productive Warriors wing in previous seasons, averaging 16.1 points in 1989-90, but those earlier points belonged to Golden State rather than the Lakers' acquired return. Los Angeles chose a proven immediate contributor over retaining a late first-round draft opportunity, while the Warriors gained a chance to add a younger player to a roster under reconstruction.

Teagle Played All 164 Lakers Regular-Season Games in Two Years

Teagle appeared in every Lakers regular-season contest in both 1990-91 and 1991-92. He scored 815 points in the first season and 880 in the second, combining for 1,695 points across 164 appearances without a regular-season start. His bench scoring supported a team that reached the 1991 NBA Finals before losing to Chicago. He also contributed in postseason games, although he was a reserve rather than the team's principal offensive option. His consistency in availability mattered more than his reputation as a former Golden State scorer. The Lakers used the exact type of player they had hoped to acquire.

Golden State's Pick Became Shaun Vandiver, Who Never Played NBA

The first-rounder from Los Angeles became the No. 25 overall choice in the 1991 draft. Golden State used it on Shaun Vandiver from Colorado. Vandiver pursued professional basketball outside the NBA and never appeared in a regular-season NBA game for the Warriors. The selection therefore produced no traceable on-court contribution for Golden State even though a first-round pick was initially an attractive asset. The Warriors had several selections in that draft, including Chris Gatling and Victor Alexander, but neither of those players came from the Lakers' specific No. 25 pick. Their subsequent NBA production cannot rescue this particular asset exchange.

The Results Favor the Lakers Beyond the Draft's Name Value

A future first-round pick can be a legitimate purchase price for an established reserve when it might become a rotation player of its own. In this case, however, the actual comparison was stark: Teagle became a two-year regular in Los Angeles, and Vandiver did not produce an NBA game for Golden State. That makes the result stronger for the Lakers than it looked from counting draft assets at the time of the trade. Neither team acquired an All-Star centerpiece, and Teagle should not be credited with the Lakers' entire Finals achievement, but his availability and scoring were meaningful direct returns from the September 1990 deal.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B+ because Terry Teagle played 164 regular-season games and scored 1,695 points across two seasons, including its 1991 Finals campaign. Golden State gets D after using the acquired No. 25 pick on Shaun Vandiver, who never appeared in the NBA. The Lakers received substantial reserve production while the draft asset produced no league minutes.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix traded guard Mike Morrison to Washington on September 28, 1990 for a conditional 1993 second-round pick. The condition never triggered. Washington waived Morrison on October 22 before the regular season, so he played no Bullets games, and Basketball-Reference records that the 1993 pick did not convey to Phoenix. Morrison's only NBA season had already occurred with the Suns in 1989-90. In hindsight, Washington received only a training-camp look and Phoenix received no realized draft asset. With neither franchise generating regular-season value from the exchange, the source-backed result is an Even Trade rather than the legacy slight Washington edge.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix and Washington transaction logs agree on the September 28, 1990 structure: the Suns sent Mike Morrison to the Bullets for a conditional 1993 second-round pick. The important part is the condition. Contemporary reporting described Morrison as a training-camp candidate who still had to earn a roster spot, and the official transaction sequence shows Washington waiving him on October 22. Basketball-Reference explicitly marks the conditional 1993 second-rounder as not conveyed. This means the final realized package was much smaller than the original trade shell suggests.

Washington Return
Morrison was a Washington-area guard who had been Phoenix's second-round pick in 1989. He played 36 NBA games for the Suns in 1989-90, averaging 2.0 points in limited minutes, but those Phoenix games happened before this trade and cannot be credited to Washington. After the September 1990 deal, the Bullets brought him to camp and evaluated him alongside other guards competing for roster spots. Washington waived him on October 22, before the 1990-91 regular season. He never appeared in a Bullets regular-season game and never played another NBA season. Washington therefore received no realized regular-season production.

Phoenix Return
The Suns' return existed only if the trade condition was satisfied. It was not. Both Phoenix's and Washington's transaction pages identify the 1993 second-round pick as conditional and state that it did not convey. Phoenix therefore did not receive a draft selection, a player or another basketball asset from the deal. The transaction may have created roster flexibility by moving Morrison before camp decisions were complete, but TradeVerdicts does not invent value for unrecorded financial or roster effects when the explicit return failed to materialize.

Hindsight Comparison
The legacy slight Washington edge incorrectly treats Morrison as if he provided more value than Phoenix's conditional pick. He did not make the team. Once the non-conveyance is handled correctly, both sides finish at the same place: Washington received no regular-season player contribution, and Phoenix received no draft pick. The trade was essentially a conditional preseason audition that expired without a realized basketball return for either franchise.

Final Verdict
Even Trade, C/C. The grades reflect zero realized regular-season value on both sides rather than poor execution of a major asset exchange. Washington got a short evaluation period with Morrison; Phoenix got no pick because the condition was not met. Neither outcome deserves a positive or punitive grade beyond neutral.
