philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia acquired Phoenix's draft rights to 1990 first-rounder Jayson Williams on October 28, 1990 for a future first-round pick that ultimately became the No. 6 selection in 1994. Williams gave the 76ers 102 regular-season games across two seasons, mostly as a reserve, before Philadelphia traded him to New Jersey for two second-round picks. Phoenix never used the eventual No. 6 pick itself, but only forty days after acquiring it the Suns packaged that first with Eddie Johnson and another first for Xavier McDaniel. The stronger realized asset value sits with Phoenix.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix drafted St. John's forward-center Jayson Williams with the No. 21 pick in the 1990 draft, but the relationship stalled before his rookie season. Contemporary Associated Press reporting said Williams preferred an East Coast team, had considered Europe and was offered only a one-year minimum contract by Phoenix after missing the club's rookie camp. On October 28, Phoenix moved his draft rights to Philadelphia for a future first-round pick. Basketball-Reference records that pick as the 1994 first that later became No. 6 Sharone Wright, while the draft-trade ledger describes the obligation as lottery-protected in 1993 before it rolled into 1994.

Philadelphia Return
Williams did become an NBA player immediately, so this was not an empty rights acquisition. He played 52 games with one start as a rookie, averaging 3.5 points and 2.1 rebounds in 9.8 minutes. In 1991-92 he played another 50 games with eight starts, averaging 4.1 points and 2.9 rebounds. Across two Philadelphia seasons that is 102 games and nine starts: real depth value, but not first-round-caliber production. Philadelphia also preserved some downstream value. On October 8, 1992 the 76ers traded Williams to New Jersey for two future second-round choices, later listed as the 1994 No. 41 pick and the 1997 No. 35 pick. That conversion keeps the Philadelphia return above a failing grade, even though Williams' later All-Star career with the Nets cannot be credited back to the 76ers.

Phoenix Return
The Suns received the more valuable asset: a future first that eventually landed sixth overall. Phoenix did not wait for the pick to convey. On December 7, 1990, only forty days after the Williams trade, the Suns sent Eddie Johnson, their 1991 first-round pick and this acquired future first to Seattle for Xavier McDaniel. The 1994 first therefore had immediate trade-market value inside a major veteran acquisition. The pick later moved through additional transactions and eventually became Sharone Wright, but Wright's career belongs to the team that ultimately exercised the selection, not to Phoenix. The source-backed credit here is the premium first-round asset Phoenix obtained and then successfully used as trade capital.

Hindsight Comparison
Philadelphia got two useful reserve seasons, then recovered two second-round assets. That is a legitimate return and explains why the deal is not a disaster. The problem is the price. A future first that ultimately landed at No. 6 was substantially more valuable than Williams' direct 76ers contribution, and Phoenix demonstrated that value almost immediately by using the pick in the McDaniel package. The legacy slight Philadelphia edge had the direction backwards because it focused on Williams becoming an NBA player without weighing the eventual position and transaction utility of the outgoing first.

Final Verdict
Phoenix Suns Win, A- to C+. Phoenix turned the rights to an unsigned No. 21 pick into a premium future first and quickly used that asset in a major trade. Philadelphia received 102 games of reserve value and later two second-round picks, enough to avoid a harsh grade, but not enough to match the first-round asset it surrendered.

perspectives.summary: A three-team January 1991 exchange sent Dražen Petrović, Terry Mills and a future second-round pick to the New Jersey Nets; Denver acquired Cadillac Anderson and a future first-round right associated with Bryant Stith; and Portland received Walter Davis and a second-round pick. Petrović became an outstanding Nets scorer before his tragic death. The inherited Nets Win gives New Jersey A+, Denver A+ and Portland D.
perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Acquired a Future Star in Petrović

The Nets landed Dražen Petrović in January 1991 through a three-team trade involving Denver and Portland. New Jersey also obtained Terry Mills and a 1993 second-round asset. Petrović had struggled for an opportunity behind Portland's established perimeter options despite his scoring ability overseas. The Nets gave him a bigger platform and ultimately received a major offensive contributor. The transaction was far more consequential than an ordinary reserve-guard change because its incoming player eventually transformed the team's perimeter scoring.

Denver Secured Stith's First-Round Path

The Nuggets obtained Cadillac Anderson and a future first-round choice that became the No. 13 selection in 1992, used on Bryant Stith. Stith went on to play substantial NBA minutes for Denver, giving the Nuggets a legitimate long-term contributor from the deal. Anderson was a different kind of immediate veteran option, but the first-round right made the package last beyond the season. Denver's return deserves attention alongside Petrović's success because the club also converted the transaction into meaningful receiving-team player service.

Portland Received Davis and Another Second

The Trail Blazers took veteran scorer Walter Davis and a future second-round selection. Davis had a distinguished career before arriving in Portland, but his earlier Phoenix accomplishments were not newly acquired Trail Blazers seasons. The incoming second offered a development or transaction option without guaranteeing another impact player. Portland was competing in a different window from the Nets and Nuggets, yet this particular package didn't produce the same lasting franchise payoff. The comparison should focus on what each receiving club actually gained.

Petrović's Nets Years Define the Historical Impact

Petrović emerged as an exceptional scorer for New Jersey, making the transaction central to his NBA story before his death in 1993. Denver also obtained genuine value through Stith, which helps explain its matching inherited A+ grade. Portland's D reflects the relatively modest direct return. The Nets Win recognizes Petrović's extraordinary on-court breakthrough while still acknowledging that the Nuggets acquired a durable future contributor. This was a genuine three-way trade, not simply a Portland-New Jersey exchange.

Final Verdict

Nets Win. New Jersey, now Brooklyn, receives A+ for Dražen Petrović's remarkable scoring and supporting assets, while Denver also earns A+ for Cadillac Anderson and the first-round right used on Bryant Stith. Portland gets D for Walter Davis and a second-round selection. Petrović's standout Nets tenure makes the deal especially consequential, despite Denver's strong return.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
San Antonio Acquired Rights Instead of a Finished Player

On May 17, 1991, the Spurs acquired the rights to guard Kevin Pritchard from Golden State. The Warriors' trade history lists a conditional second-round choice in 1993 as compensation, while the league transaction register describes Golden State selling his rights. Pritchard had been a second-round pick out of Kansas and had played earlier in the NBA, but he was not guaranteed a place on the San Antonio roster. The Spurs were assessing additional backcourt options before a new season while Golden State chose deferred compensation.

Pritchard Never Played a Regular-Season Game for the Spurs

The Spurs carried Pritchard's rights into their preparation for the 1991-92 season. They waived him on October 28, 1991, before opening night, according to the franchise's official-season transaction chronology. He consequently recorded no Spurs regular-season minutes, starts, points or assists. Pritchard subsequently appeared in NBA games for Boston and other clubs, but those opportunities followed different signings and were not San Antonio production. Evaluating the trade by his broader career would create the false impression that acquiring his rights yielded NBA rotation minutes for the Spurs.

Golden State's Conditional 1993 Compensation Remains Unresolved

The Warriors' asset was a conditional 1993 second-round selection or future considerations. The archival entry identifies that draft year but doesn't establish a particular conveyed draft slot or a player selected from it. Without evidence of the condition being satisfied, no 1993 draftee should be credited to Golden State. The possibility of a future selection was a legitimate bargaining asset, yet its realized basketball value can't be measured from this listing alone. That uncertainty limits the winner assessment just as the Spurs' failure to use Pritchard limits theirs.

San Antonio tried an inexpensive guard prospect and chose not to keep him for the season. Golden State exchanged an unneeded player right for deferred conditional compensation without a fully documented future player. Neither outcome constitutes a major success, but neither is evidence of a large organizational failure either. The prior Spurs-favored grade appeared to value an audition that never generated a league appearance. A balanced assessment acknowledges the conditional asset and preserves the unresolved 1993 provenance instead of turning an unidentified pick into invented points or games.

Golden State also gets C- for conditional 1993 second-round compensation whose precise conveyance and downstream player cannot be established from the source ledger. Neither club can claim meaningful on-court production from the original May 1991 exchange.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Used a Young Center to Add Blair Rasmussen

Atlanta and Denver exchanged the rights to young frontcourt player Anthony Avent for veteran center Blair Rasmussen around the 1991 NBA draft. Rasmussen offered a known seven-footer with established NBA experience; Avent represented a younger athletic development option. The Hawks could use Rasmussen immediately as an experienced post player alongside an otherwise mature rotation. Denver preferred a different timeline and prospect evaluation rather than maintaining the incumbent center. The agreement involved one identified basketball return on each side and shouldn't be confused with an unrelated draft-night swap that moved first-round pick positions between the franchises.

Rasmussen Supplied Size Without Becoming Atlanta's Centerpiece

Rasmussen had already spent several years in Denver and brought size, interior presence and useful professional experience to Atlanta. His established production with the Nuggets wasn't newly earned by the Hawks, and an immediate veteran acquisition didn't automatically mean he would anchor the frontcourt for years. He still had to fit alongside Atlanta's existing personnel and earn minutes on the receiving team's season records. That made his value clearer in the short term than an unproven drafted prospect, while the team's larger fortunes continued to depend on its established leaders.

Denver Took a Developmental Frontcourt Prospect

Anthony Avent arrived as a more speculative frontcourt asset with college credentials but no guarantee of sustained NBA minutes for Denver. A rookie could provide rebounding and energy, yet his potential was not equivalent to receiving Rasmussen's complete professional résumé. The trade gave the Nuggets a chance to evaluate a different profile at a time when their rotation was changing. Later roster decisions and contracts would determine how much of Avent's NBA career belonged to the receiving franchise. A retrospective should not assign his whole later playing record to Denver just because his rights moved through this transaction.

The Two Teams Pursued Reasonable Different Timelines

Atlanta took a veteran who could address an immediate depth need and Denver chose a younger frontcourt prospect it could develop or move. Each side acquired a real player asset without surrendering a package of premium future selections. Neither Rasmussen nor Avent alone transformed the club that received him, and a balanced evaluation has more grounding than an extreme win-loss claim. The Hawks' short-term certainty and the Nuggets' prospect flexibility were distinct benefits rather than identical returns. Moderate equal grades reflect that tradeoff and avoid importing players' prior production into new franchises.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Atlanta earns B- for acquiring veteran center Blair Rasmussen as an immediately usable frontcourt option. Denver receives B- for younger Anthony Avent and the opportunity to assess his development. Neither return was a newly acquired All-Star, and Rasmussen's prior Nuggets seasons or Avent's later games elsewhere aren't assigned to the receiving clubs through this one exchange.

analysis: Atlanta's advantage came from duration and role fit. Augmon became an immediate rotation player, earned All-Rookie recognition and gave the Hawks several seasons of athletic perimeter defense and transition play. He was never a franchise star, but the team controlled his prime years at a cost structure far below what a veteran lead guard commanded. The extra second-round picks added optionality even though they did not become headline players. Atlanta replaced one established contributor with a younger long-term starter and retained additional chances. The Clippers did not make a disastrous move. Rivers gave them reliable point-guard play and veteran organization, and he remained valuable enough to be moved again in the 1992 three-team transaction that sent him to New York. That follow-on value matters because Los Angeles did not simply lose him for nothing. The issue is that his Clippers tenure was brief, while Atlanta received the longer run of useful production from Augmon. The price was defensible for a team seeking stability but still came out short on total years and control. The cleanest downstream chain is Atlanta's No. 9 pick becoming Augmon. That direct conversion is easy to credit because no later blockbuster or speculative branch is required to create the value. Los Angeles' best counter is that Rivers retained trade value and later helped bring back assets in the 1992 deal, but that later transaction also involved other players and draft pieces. The conservative approach is to credit the Clippers for preserved value without assigning every later return solely to Rivers.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Sent Webb to Sacramento for a Younger Guard

The Hawks traded Spud Webb and a future second-round draft right to the Sacramento Kings in July 1991, receiving Travis Mays. Atlanta had long used Webb's speed and court vision to complement its scoring wings, but chose to try a younger guard in his place. Sacramento gained a recognized NBA playmaker and an additional selection. Mays offered scoring potential, although his developing career had already faced injury problems. The agreement exchanged a known veteran role for a speculative attempt to find longer-term guard help.

Webb Became a Regular Sacramento Contributor

Webb delivered multiple seasons of useful NBA point-guard play for the Kings. His scoring and passing gave Sacramento an offensive organizer during a period of continuing roster changes. Those Kings games are the relevant receiving-team return; his earlier Hawks popularity and celebrated dunk-contest victory merely explain why the move attracted attention. Unlike a veteran who arrived and immediately departed, Webb established an identifiable stretch of work for his new club. That longevity was the strongest direct result in the exchange.

Mays Couldn't Establish the Equivalent Hawks Role

Mays did not develop into a comparable sustained Atlanta guard, as injuries and limited availability disrupted the attempt. The Hawks had received a player with genuine scoring ability, but the roster did not gain years of the same reliability Webb supplied in Sacramento. Meanwhile, the outgoing second-round asset eventually carried the identity of No. 51 Lawrence Funderburke in the 1994 draft. His later career must be followed through its rights chain instead of assuming every game he played belongs directly to Sacramento's receiving-team value.

The Long-Term Playing Difference Favors Sacramento

The Kings received the more dependable guard contribution, a clear win from a move made amid roster turnover. Atlanta took a reasonable chance on a younger player but lost both Webb's production and a future draft opportunity. The inherited grade disparity reflects actual receiving-team guard value rather than the reputation of the players at the time alone. Sacramento turned the exchange into several years of playmaking, whereas Atlanta's hoped-for Mays development did not materialize at the same level.

Final Verdict

Kings Win. Sacramento earns A- for Spud Webb's productive multi-season Kings tenure and an additional second-round right. Atlanta receives C+ because Travis Mays's injury-affected Hawks opportunity did not replace Webb's sustained guard production. The future pick added another asset to Sacramento's package, but Webb's direct contributions provided the decisive advantage.

perspectives.summary: The Atlanta Hawks received Blair Rasmussen from Denver in a July 1, 1991 three-team trade. Denver acquired the rights to Kevin Brooks and two future second-round picks linked to Josh Grant and Rodney Dent, while Milwaukee obtained Anthony Avent from Atlanta. The Bucks' inbound player had been omitted from the Denver-centered import and was restored against independent Bucks and Hawks transaction ledgers. The inherited Slight Hawks Edge gives Atlanta and Denver B and Milwaukee C+.
perspectives.analysis:
Atlanta Chose Rasmussen for Its Frontcourt

The Hawks acquired Blair Rasmussen from the Nuggets on July 1, 1991, turning draft and prospect value into an experienced center. Rasmussen could provide size and interior minutes beside Atlanta's established scorers. The club sent Anthony Avent to Milwaukee and a 1993 second-round choice to Denver to complete the arrangement. Rather than being an ordinary direct exchange between the Hawks and Nuggets, the move required three distinct asset directions and a Milwaukee participant with a real incoming player.

Denver Collected Brooks and Two Future Choices

The Nuggets received the rights to Kevin Brooks from Milwaukee, a 1993 second-round selection from Atlanta later associated with No. 43 Josh Grant, and a 1994 second from the Bucks later linked to No. 31 Rodney Dent. Those rights gave Denver multiple developmental opportunities rather than a guaranteed replacement center. Any subsequent trade of the selections and the playing careers of the draftees need separate tracing. The Nuggets parted with Rasmussen to convert one established frontcourt player into a wider group of potential assets.

Milwaukee Obtained Anthony Avent

The Bucks' original incoming side had been blank in the Denver-focused historical import, but their official transaction chronology identifies Anthony Avent arriving from Atlanta. Avent was a young forward with athleticism and a chance to earn NBA minutes. Milwaukee sent Brooks's rights and its 1994 second in return. Restoring the Avent entry changes the reader's understanding of the transaction: the Bucks didn't simply donate a prospect and selection to help Atlanta and Denver. They acquired another young player on their own roster-development timeline.

The Slight Hawks Label Masks a Narrow Grade Difference

The inherited grading assigns Atlanta B and Denver B, with Milwaukee C+, despite using the verdict Slight Hawks Edge. That small comparison recognizes Atlanta obtaining a known center and Denver obtaining a basket of future options, while Milwaukee chose a different developing forward. The ratings shouldn't imply the Hawks conclusively won by a large margin or that the Bucks obtained nothing. A proper historical evaluation follows Rasmussen, Avent, Brooks's rights and both future second-round obligations separately.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta receives B for Blair Rasmussen's established frontcourt experience, while Denver also earns B for Kevin Brooks's rights and two later second-round opportunities. Milwaukee receives C+ for Anthony Avent, its verified player return. The inherited verdict narrowly favors Atlanta, but all three franchises received identifiable assets, and future pick names shouldn't be mistaken for guaranteed on-court production.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers sent their 1991 No. 38 draft choice Joe Wylie's rights to New York for a 1993 second-rounder. That future selection became No. 53 Leonard White. Neither Wylie nor White played an NBA regular-season game for the receiving franchise. The Knicks obtained a young college forward to assess, and Los Angeles delayed its second-round investment. Even Trade, C- each; the prior Knicks B overstated a prospect who never made the league.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
New York Pursued a Prospect the Clippers Had Just Drafted

On July 3, 1991, Los Angeles transferred Joe Wylie's draft rights to the New York Knicks for a second-round selection in 1993. Wylie had been the Clippers' No. 38 pick in the previous week's draft, following a strong University of Miami career. Knicks executive Ernie Grunfeld told the Associated Press that the organization had been trying to obtain Wylie since draft night. New York valued his ability to run the floor and rebound, while the Clippers preferred another chance to select a prospect two years later.

Wylie Never Made an NBA Knicks Appearance

Wylie's college résumé made the move understandable, but it wasn't followed by an NBA regular-season contribution for New York. He never logged a Knicks game, point or rebound. It would be misleading to treat the front office's enthusiasm at the time as a completed development success. In a league where second-round players often have to prove themselves in training camp, the Knicks accepted a real scouting risk. The eventual result remained a draft-rights prospect rather than an active rotation player.

The Delayed Pick Produced Leonard White at No. 53

Los Angeles held the deferred second-round selection until the 1993 draft, when it became the fifty-third overall pick, Leonard White. That outcome was another prospect rather than immediate NBA playing utility. White did not develop into a regular-season Clippers contributor. The team received the contract rights and control of a future choice, but the pick did not produce a starter or a persistent roster player. There is no reliable reason to assign any other drafted player's career to this specific second-round selection.

Two Unsuccessful Prospect Evaluations Call for Equal Grades

The Knicks got the earlier opportunity to inspect a highly regarded college forward, while the Clippers pushed their investment into the 1993 draft. Both choices offered some possibility of finding an inexpensive NBA player. Neither materialized into regular-season production for the club that acquired the rights. The earlier Knicks B grade confused Wylie's promise with realized team value; Los Angeles's D was also too harsh for holding a valid future pick. Restrained matching grades recognize how little sporting output either receiving organization actually obtained.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. The Clippers get C- for the 1993 second-round selection eventually used on Leonard White, who never played a Clippers NBA regular-season game. New York also gets C- because Joe Wylie's 1991 No. 38 draft rights never produced a Knicks NBA appearance. Neither speculative asset realized the value needed to support the original Knicks-win judgment.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Acquired Maurice Cheeks for McCormick and a Conditional Pick

On October 2, 1991, the Atlanta Hawks acquired veteran point guard Maurice Cheeks from New York. The Knicks received center Tim McCormick and a conditional future first-round pick tied to McCormick's ability to meet a minimum-games condition. That pick later appears as the 1994 No. 26 selection associated with Charlie Ward. The original agreement therefore paired immediate guard experience with a potentially valuable future contingency rather than a simple veteran-for-veteran swap. The Knicks were willing to move Cheeks as their roster evolved, while Atlanta sought a proven organizer for its offense.

Cheeks's Defensive Reputation Explained Atlanta's Interest

Cheeks was already known as a capable defensive point guard and championship-era veteran before the Hawks acquired him. Atlanta could benefit from his decision-making and backcourt experience, but those prior Philadelphia and New York accomplishments weren't new Atlanta production generated by the trade. The receiving team had to evaluate his actual availability and role afterward. Bringing in an aging guard was a shorter-horizon decision than keeping a conditional first, and his NBA legacy alone couldn't ensure he would supply several more years of peak play. The Hawks' immediate objective was credible even though its payoff was limited.

The Contingent First Eventually Became a Noteworthy Knicks Asset

McCormick offered New York a veteran center, but the more enduring piece was the conditional first-round obligation that ultimately became connected with 1994 No. 26 Charlie Ward. Ward developed into a useful New York guard during the 1990s, giving the transaction a specific long-term outcome beyond merely moving Cheeks. The conditional language is important: the 1994 result wasn't guaranteed at the original 1991 agreement date. It depended on the agreed games-related terms and the subsequent pick chain. That distinction stops a retrospective from describing Ward as a player who was already part of the Knicks' 1991 roster.

New York Won With a Productive Later Selection

Atlanta obtained an experienced guard it could use immediately; New York received McCormick and an eventual first-round opportunity that became a meaningful player asset. The Knicks' longer-term draft return outweighed Cheeks's short remaining window as a Hawks player, particularly because Ward would become a familiar part of the franchise's later rotation. That doesn't make the Hawks' decision irrational, and it shouldn't assign all 1990s Knicks success to one trade. But the condition eventually producing a useful No. 26 selection gives New York a clear realized advantage over a comparatively short-term veteran rental.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win. New York earns A- for Tim McCormick and the conditional first-round obligation ultimately associated with 1994 No. 26 Charlie Ward. Atlanta receives C for veteran guard Maurice Cheeks. The first wasn't guaranteed when the trade occurred, and Ward's later Knicks career must be evaluated as the realized result of the selection rather than an immediate 1991 player acquisition.

analysis: This was a straight player-for-player trade, not a draft-pick or cash deal. Boston sent Brian Shaw to Miami on January 10, 1992, receiving young point guard Sherman Douglas after Shaw's previous contract dispute and Douglas's Miami holdout. Douglas supplied 37 Celtics games, no starts, 654 minutes, 7.3 points and 4.1 assists per game in the remaining 1991-92 season. He then stayed into 1995-96, appearing in 79, 78, 65 and 10 more Boston games over the following seasons: 269 Celtics regular-season appearances after the swap. Shaw supplied Miami with 46 games and 23 starts immediately in 1991-92, then 68 games and 45 starts the next season before leaving. Miami therefore got a real two-season guard, not nothing; Boston received the longer and eventually larger starting role. The direct difference supports the existing Celtics Win grade of B+ against Miami B-. Neither franchise may count Shaw's later Lakers championships in its own trade return. milwaukee-bucks.summary: The Lakers granted coach Mike Dunleavy permission to leave for Milwaukee in May 1992, with the Bucks compensating Los Angeles using 1992 and 1995 second-round draft choices. The 1992 selection became No. 36 Duane Cooper, who appeared briefly for the Lakers, while the 1995 selection later linked to Dwayne Whitfield was rerouted in separate transactions. Dunleavy coached Milwaukee for four seasons, going 107-221, before being dismissed. Lakers Win narrowly for securing compensation rather than letting a departing coach go for nothing, Los Angeles B-, Milwaukee C-. The legacy route labels June 1 although contemporary sources date the deal May 11-12.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
A Coaching Contract Produced a Genuine Draft-Pick Trade

The 1992 Lakers-Bucks exchange was not a normal transaction involving a player. Mike Dunleavy had coached Los Angeles for two seasons, including a 1991 Finals appearance, when Milwaukee recruited him for a long-term coaching position. The Lakers released him from his remaining contractual obligations in return for two second-round draft selections from the Bucks. Contemporary reporting dates the arrangement to May 11 and 12, although the imported trade route uses an approximate June 1 date. The actual asset that Milwaukee received was permission to hire its chosen coach, not rights to Dunleavy as a player.

The Lakers Converted the Release Into Two Draft Opportunities

Los Angeles acquired a 1992 second-round pick later used at No. 36 on USC guard Duane Cooper and an additional 1995 second-round pick, subsequently associated with No. 40 Dwayne Whitfield. Cooper was signed by the Lakers and supplied short-term reserve guard minutes before being waived in November 1993. The later second-round selection passed through subsequent transactions before the 1995 draft, so it would be incorrect to claim Whitfield became a Lakers rotation player because of this compensation agreement. The picks nonetheless had value: Los Angeles was paid in draft rights for a coach who wanted to leave.

Dunleavy Coached Four Seasons in Milwaukee

Milwaukee secured its preferred head coach, and Dunleavy began work there for the 1992-93 season. He ultimately coached 328 regular-season Bucks games over four campaigns, winning 107 and losing 221. Those results fell well short of the franchise's ambitions when it gave him a lengthy contract, and Milwaukee dismissed him in April 1996. The contemporary announcement described a much longer contract term, but an agreement's duration is not the same as actual time served. These coaching outcomes are the appropriate measure for Milwaukee's return, not a fictitious tally of on-court Dunleavy minutes.

Compensation Was Useful Even Though Neither Club Transformed

Los Angeles emerged with draft capital rather than simply losing its coach, while Milwaukee obtained someone it believed could manage a rebuilding roster. In hindsight, the Bucks did not get a sustained winning era: Dunleavy's four-season record finished well below .500. The Lakers' two second-round assets likewise did not by themselves create stars, so they do not justify an extraordinary grade. The transaction sits in the middle ground between effective contract management and limited realized basketball improvement. A moderate Lakers advantage recognizes compensation secured while keeping the future pick's downstream lineage and Dunleavy's coaching record distinct.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B- for turning Mike Dunleavy's departure into two second-round draft assets, including 1992 No. 36 Duane Cooper. Milwaukee receives C- after Dunleavy coached 328 games over four seasons with a 107-221 record. The later 1995 pick associated with Dwayne Whitfield was not a direct Lakers player return, and the actual coaching-rights deal was reported in May despite the archive's approximate June route.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Phoenix acquired Charles Barkley from Philadelphia on June 17, 1992 for Jeff Hornacek, Tim Perry and Andrew Lang. Barkley immediately won the 1992-93 NBA MVP, led the Suns to 62 wins and the NBA Finals, and made the All-Star and All-NBA teams in each of his four Phoenix seasons. Philadelphia's return was more substantial than a typical star dump: Hornacek played 132 games and averaged 19.1 points and 6.9 assists in his first Sixers season, while Perry and Lang supplied major starting minutes.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Exchange
Philadelphia and Phoenix transaction records agree on the June 17, 1992 package: Charles Barkley went to the Suns for Jeff Hornacek, Tim Perry and Andrew Lang. There was no draft pick in the original deal, which meant Philadelphia's entire immediate return depended on three NBA-ready players. That distinction matters because the package produced real rotation value even though it did not deliver another franchise star.

Phoenix Return
Barkley transformed the Suns immediately. In 1992-93 he played 76 games, averaged 24.5 points, 11.7 rebounds and 4.8 assists, won league MVP, and led Phoenix to a 62-20 record and the NBA Finals. He remained an All-Star in all four Suns seasons and made All-NBA First Team in 1992-93, Second Team in 1993-94 and 1994-95, and Third Team in 1995-96. Across those four seasons he played 280 regular-season games for Phoenix, never averaging fewer than 21.6 points or 11.1 rebounds. Even after the Finals breakthrough, the Suns remained a playoff team in every Barkley season. That is elite, franchise-level realized value.

Philadelphia Return
Hornacek was the best player in the Sixers package and immediately delivered high-end guard play. He appeared in 79 games with 78 starts in 1992-93, averaging 19.1 points, 6.9 assists and 4.3 rebounds, then played another 53 games with 53 starts before Philadelphia sent him to Utah in February 1994 as part of a separate package for Jeff Malone and a first-round pick. Tim Perry gave Philadelphia even more volume: 81 games and 51 starts in 1992-93, 80 games and 68 starts in 1993-94, and 42 more games in 1994-95, totaling 203 Sixers games. Andrew Lang added 73 games with 59 starts in 1992-93 before Philadelphia released him the next summer. The problem was not lack of NBA value; it was that the three-player package did not create a new centerpiece or lift Philadelphia into contention.

Hindsight Verdict
Phoenix wins clearly because Barkley became the league MVP, a four-time Suns All-Star and the centerpiece of a Finals team. An A+ is appropriate because the trade immediately raised the franchise's ceiling to championship contention and sustained elite individual production for four seasons. Philadelphia deserves better than the legacy C because Hornacek, Perry and Lang combined for hundreds of games and extensive starting minutes, with Hornacek playing at near-All-Star offensive levels in his first season. The Sixers receive a B-: a respectable quantity-and-quality return for a departing star, but one without a comparable franchise anchor. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee acquired Sam Vincent plus Orlando's 1994 second-round selection for Lester Conner on August 4, 1992. The selection became No. 46 Voshon Lenard, who returned to college in 1994-95 and later played for Miami rather than becoming a Bucks NBA contributor. Orlando obtained a veteran guard in Conner. Even Trade, C+ each; the future pick had legitimate option value, but Lenard's successful Heat seasons don't belong to Milwaukee.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee Swapped a Veteran Guard for Another and a Future Choice

The Bucks obtained Sam Vincent and a 1994 second-round selection from Orlando on August 4, 1992, sending Lester Conner to the Magic. Milwaukee had struggled to establish a winning backcourt combination and wanted a veteran option together with deferred draft rights. Orlando preferred Conner's defense and experience as it built a roster around emerging young talent. The future draft pick was not a guaranteed NBA rotation player; it represented the right to choose a prospect two summers after the clubs exchanged the guards.

Vincent and Conner Represented Shorter-Term Guard Coverage

Vincent and Conner were both established NBA guards, not newcomers selected in the lottery. By the time of this exchange, each was moving through the later years of his professional career. The Bucks looked for ball handling and shooting through Vincent, while Orlando gained a defender in Conner. Neither became a long-term cornerstone for his receiving team, and the franchise roster trajectories were shaped much more by later draft selections and changes around the frontcourt. Their earlier NBA playing totals shouldn't be transferred to their new teams.

The No. 46 Pick Became Voshon Lenard, But Not Milwaukee Points

Orlando's transferred second-round selection eventually became No. 46 Voshon Lenard in the 1994 draft. Lenard did not join the NBA immediately, retaining his college eligibility for 1994-95 before beginning his league career with Miami the following season. He later made a name for himself as an outside shooter for the Heat and Nuggets. None of those games were Bucks receiving-team production. Milwaukee acquired a real draft-rights option, yet the long-term professional success of the person selected doesn't prove its own roster gained that scorer.

Both Sides Obtained Limited Veteran Options

Orlando traded away a future selection but got the guard it wanted for its immediate roster. Milwaukee received Vincent and a second-round right that it eventually used on a player who never logged an NBA game for the Bucks. There were sensible reasons for each club to value the exchange differently at the time. Retrospectively, neither receiving-team return appears large enough for an enthusiastic win grade. Equal modest grades are more appropriate than treating Lenard's later Miami production as if Milwaukee had developed him into a regular Bucks scorer.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Milwaukee earns C+ for a veteran guard option in Sam Vincent and the 1994 No. 46 rights used on Voshon Lenard, who never played a Bucks NBA regular season. Orlando also earns C+ for receiving Lester Conner as veteran backcourt depth. The later success of Lenard with Miami cannot justify the original stronger Bucks-win grade.

perspectives.analysis:
Chicago Looked for Veteran Forward Insurance

The Bulls acquired Rodney McCray in September 1992 in a three-team transaction with Dallas and Golden State. Chicago was pursuing another championship with Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen at the center of its roster and wanted additional experienced forward depth. McCray had already been an accomplished defender and NBA regular. Dallas received second-round draft consideration, while Golden State took Byron Houston. The participants were operating on different timelines and didn't receive comparable finished players.

McCray Supplied Depth to a Championship Team

McCray became part of Chicago's 1992-93 roster, which went on to win the championship. His role was far smaller than that of the Bulls' established stars, so the trade shouldn't be credited with causing the title. Still, his veteran experience and defensive background suited a contender looking to fill supporting minutes. His long earlier NBA history was a reason to acquire him, not production he suddenly created for Chicago. The actual receiving-team impact was a limited but useful championship-season supporting assignment.

The Mavericks and Warriors Took Other Forms of Value

Dallas acquired a 1996 second-round right associated with No. 58 Darnell Robinson and another conditional second-round choice that did not convey. Those selections offered future flexibility, though a protected right that never conveys doesn't produce a drafted player. Golden State acquired Houston, a younger forward it could evaluate. Both teams sought opportunities more compatible with roster development, but neither return was immediately equivalent to adding a proven experienced contributor to a championship rotation.

The Contender's Immediate Need Explains the Grades

The inherited Chicago B+ rewards landing McCray for a team that was ready to contend immediately. Dallas and Golden State receive C+ grades for conditional draft and prospect returns that were more uncertain. This doesn't mean McCray drove the championship run or that Houston lacked professional ability. It means the Bulls obtained the clearest immediate fit from the exchange. The result belongs to the 1992-93 Bulls' support cast rather than an independent franchise-changing star acquisition.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win. Chicago receives B+ for Rodney McCray's veteran forward presence on the 1993 championship roster. Dallas earns C+ for draft consideration, including a 1996 second later associated with Darnell Robinson, while Golden State gets C+ for Byron Houston. The Bulls acquired the most immediate useful fit without obtaining a central championship star.

houston-rockets.summary: On October 5, 1992, Houston traded David Wood to San Antonio for a 1995 second-round pick. The Rockets traded the pick to Portland for Mario Elie in August 1993, and Elie helped Houston win the 1994 and 1995 NBA championships. The pick later went to Detroit, which drafted Don Reid. Rockets Win: Houston A, San Antonio C+.
houston-rockets.analysis:
A Newly Signed Forward Became Houston’s Future Trade Asset

On October 5, 1992, Houston sent David Wood to San Antonio for a 1995 second-round selection. The Rockets had signed Wood only ten days earlier; the trade turned him into a future draft asset before he played a regular-season game for Houston. The pick ultimately became the No. 58 choice used on Don Reid, but Houston did not make that selection. Team transaction ledgers preserve the original Wood-for-pick exchange, and the later draft record identifies Detroit as the franchise that selected Reid. Confusing the eventual drafted player with a Houston acquisition obscures why this otherwise modest 1992 deal proved valuable.

The Second-Rounder Was Redeemed for Mario Elie in 1993

The crucial next step came August 2, 1993. Houston sent Portland the very 1995 second-round pick it had acquired from San Antonio and received Mario Elie. The Blazers’ historical media guide independently confirms that Elie arrived from Portland for the second-round selection later traded to Detroit and used on Reid. This is a traceable downstream asset conversion, not hypothetical value assigned after the draft. Elie gave Houston a versatile wing who fit the championship roster’s defensive effort and perimeter needs. Instead of waiting until 1995 to draft someone, the Rockets converted a low-cost future choice into a veteran who could contribute immediately.

Elie Was Part of Both Rockets Championship Runs

Elie appeared in 67 Houston regular-season games in 1993-94, averaging 9.3 points, and 81 more in 1994-95, averaging 8.8. He also played in all 23 of the Rockets’ 1994 playoff games and all 22 of their 1995 postseason games. Houston won the NBA title in each season. His famous decisive three-pointer against Phoenix in the 1995 Western Conference semifinals illustrates his real postseason role, but the trade is not credited with single-handedly creating the championships. The connection is narrower and documented: the second-round pick Houston received for Wood helped acquire a dependable contributor on two championship teams.

San Antonio Received Actual Depth, While the Pick Kept Moving

San Antonio did not get an empty return. Wood played 64 games and 598 regular-season minutes for the Spurs in 1992-93, starting twice and providing reserve frontcourt depth. The scale of that return is small next to what Houston later acquired. Portland subsequently included the No. 58 selection in a 1995 draft-day package sent to Detroit, which eventually picked Don Reid. Reid played his NBA career with other teams; his 1995-onward production is not credited to Houston or San Antonio. Houston’s realized asset value is the acquisition and use of Elie, while San Antonio’s is Wood’s 64-game stint. Those are the actual branches the grades compare.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win. Houston earns A for converting the 1995 second-rounder received in the David Wood trade into Mario Elie, a contributor on its 1994 and 1995 championship teams. San Antonio receives C+ for 64 games of useful but limited reserve work from Wood. Detroit ultimately drafted Don Reid at No. 58; Houston receives no credit for Reid’s unrelated playing career.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: On October 8, 1992, the Washington Bullets traded forward John 'Hot Rod' Williams to the Los Angeles Clippers for center William Bedford and rookie draft rights to Don MacLean. Washington waived Bedford within days but signed MacLean, who averaged 18.2 points in 1993-94 and won NBA Most Improved Player. Williams's Clippers stint was limited compared with the prolific Washington return from MacLean. Wizards Win under the modern franchise label, Washington A-, Clippers C-.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Bullets Exchanged a Disgruntled Forward for Draft Rights

On October 8, 1992, Washington moved John Williams to the Los Angeles Clippers after his relationship with the Bullets deteriorated. The return consisted of reserve center William Bedford and the draft rights to UCLA forward Don MacLean, who had been selected nineteenth earlier that year. Contemporary Washington Post and Los Angeles Times reporting confirms the two incoming assets and the trade discussions between the teams. Williams should not be confused with Cavaliers center John 'Hot Rod' Williams, an entirely different player. Los Angeles hoped its incoming forward would benefit from playing closer to home, while Washington sought a fresh roster direction and an opportunity to develop a young scorer.

Bedford Left Quickly, but MacLean Became a Real Bullets Player

Washington waived Bedford within days of the transaction, making him an administrative rather than basketball return. MacLean was a different story. The Bullets signed him to a multiyear contract in October and placed him into their developmental plans. After averaging 6.6 points as a rookie in 1992-93, he emerged as an important scorer the following season. In 1993-94, he played seventy-five games, started sixty-nine and averaged 18.2 points and 6.2 rebounds. His total of 1,365 points led the team, and the NBA named him Most Improved Player. Those are actual Washington seasons, not career statistics borrowed from another franchise.

The Clippers Took a Risk on Williams's Reset

Los Angeles gave up the opportunity to develop MacLean while acquiring Williams, a versatile forward whose Washington years had been disrupted by conditioning concerns and limited availability. Both coaching staffs knew the deal carried uncertainty. The Clippers were coming off a playoff appearance and saw a chance to add talent without giving up one of their central veterans. But the hoped-for return did not produce a Washington-style breakout during his Los Angeles period. That limited result has to be separated from his earlier Bullets seasons and from the career of the similarly named Cavaliers player. Washington's choice to build through an unsigned rookie carried its own risk at the time.

MacLean's Award-Winning Season Settles the Historical Comparison

The lasting return belonged to Washington because a draft-rights acquisition turned into a productive forward and an award-winning 1993-94 campaign. Bedford's immediate release did little damage to that conclusion: MacLean was the main reason the Bullets agreed to move Williams. Los Angeles pursued a plausible change of setting for an established player, but did not receive a comparable multiseason offensive contributor. A strong Washington grade is supported by recorded playing time and Most Improved Player recognition rather than speculation about the Williams controversy. The swap did not involve a future first-round pick or a third team in October 1992; MacLean's earlier June draft route was separate.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win under the modern franchise label. The Washington Bullets earn A- because Don MacLean became a real rotation scorer and averaged 18.2 points in 1993-94, winning NBA Most Improved Player after the team acquired his rights; William Bedford was waived within days. The Clippers receive C- for taking a short-lived chance on forward John Williams. Those results concern the Washington forward, not Cavaliers center John 'Hot Rod' Williams.

That limited result has to be separated from his earlier Bullets seasons and from the career of the similarly named Cavaliers player. Washington's choice to build through an unsigned rookie carried its own risk at the time.

MacLean's Award-Winning Season Settles the Historical Comparison

The lasting return belonged to Washington because a draft-rights acquisition turned into a productive forward and an award-winning 1993-94 campaign. Bedford's immediate release did little damage to that conclusion: MacLean was the main reason the Bullets agreed to move Williams. Los Angeles pursued a plausible change of setting for an established player, but did not receive a comparable multiseason offensive contributor. A strong Washington grade is supported by recorded playing time and Most Improved Player recognition rather than speculation about the Williams controversy. The swap did not involve a future first-round pick or a third team in October 1992; MacLean's earlier June draft route was separate.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win under the modern franchise label. The Washington Bullets earn A- because Don MacLean became a real rotation scorer and averaged 18.2 points in 1993-94, winning NBA Most Improved Player after the team acquired his rights; William Bedford was waived within days. The Clippers receive C- for taking a short-lived chance on forward John Williams. Those results concern the Washington forward, not Cavaliers center John 'Hot Rod' Williams.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Seattle acquired Vincent Askew from Sacramento on November 25, 1992 for a 1993 second-round draft choice. Askew delivered 284 regular-season games for the SuperSonics across 1992-96, including 80 games and 727 points in 1993-94. Sacramento retained the No. 52 pick and selected Mike Peplowski, who supplied 55 Kings games and 176 points as a rookie. Seattle SuperSonics Win, Seattle A-, Sacramento C+.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
Seattle Paid a Second-Rounder for an Immediate Wing Contributor

The SuperSonics acquired Vincent Askew from Sacramento on November 25, 1992, sending the Kings a second-round selection in the 1993 draft. The franchise transaction registers confirm both the compensation and the date. Askew had played nine Sacramento games earlier that season after joining the club as a free agent, but Seattle was attracted by the wing's ability to handle minutes without needing high usage. The Kings were building through the draft and accepted a future choice rather than holding a reserve whose role had already contracted. There was no accompanying cash or additional player in the recorded deal.

Askew Became More Than a Short-Term Seattle Rental

The wing played 64 regular-season games for Seattle in 1992-93, scoring 384 points, then became a reliable rotation contributor. In 1993-94 he played 80 games and scored 727 points, followed by 71 games and 703 points in 1994-95 and 69 games with 582 points in 1995-96. Across those four seasons, the acquired return totaled 284 Seattle appearances. The 1993-94 average of 9.1 points came during a strong SuperSonics period, though he was not the team's primary star. The sustained minutes make this transaction notable despite its modest draft price.

Sacramento Drafted Peplowski at No. 52

The pick Seattle surrendered became Sacramento's No. 52 overall selection in June 1993. The Kings drafted Michigan State center Mike Peplowski and used him in 55 regular-season games as a rookie. He scored 176 points, collected 169 rebounds and made nineteen starts, real NBA production from a late second-rounder. Peplowski later appeared for other franchises, but only his Sacramento time belongs in this trade's received-team ledger. The pick was not wasted, and the Kings deserve credit for turning the selection into an actual player rather than a prospect who never reached the league.

The Longer Seattle Tenure Settles the Comparison

Both teams got something tangible. Sacramento converted a future second into a rookie reserve with 55 games, while Seattle turned the same draft value into a versatile player who lasted four seasons with the club. Askew's 284 regular-season appearances and 2,396 Seattle points far exceeded the Kings' direct benefit from Peplowski. Neither acquisition should be measured by later careers with unrelated teams, and Seattle's playoff success can't be assigned to one reserve. Even with that restraint, the SuperSonics' return was stronger in longevity and recurring rotation production, supporting a higher grade than the inherited evaluation.

Final Verdict

Seattle SuperSonics Win. Seattle earns A- for Vincent Askew's 284 regular-season games and 2,396 points across four seasons following the November 1992 exchange. Sacramento receives C+ after drafting Mike Peplowski at No. 52 and using him in 55 games, with 176 points and 169 rebounds. Both clubs gained NBA contributors, but Seattle secured far more durable playing value.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Chicago Adds a Veteran Just Ahead of the Deadline

The Bulls acquired Ed Nealy from Golden State on February 25, 1993, offering a conditional second-round selection in the distant 2001 draft. Both clubs' transaction ledgers record the same agreement and note that its condition was never exercised. Nealy had played 30 games for the Warriors earlier that season after joining as a free agent. Chicago already had the core of a championship contender; this was an effort to acquire experienced frontcourt insurance. The future pick was theoretical compensation, not an unconditional selection that Golden State could immediately plan to use.

Eleven Games of Limited but Measurable Bench Production

Nealy appeared in 11 regular-season games for Chicago following the deal. His return amounted to 23 points and 16 rebounds across 79 minutes, without a start. That is not the performance of a decisive postseason addition, even though the Bulls went on to win the championship. His previous 30 Warriors appearances were Golden State production and cannot be counted twice as Chicago's new value. What the Bulls received was short-term roster availability from a veteran who was willing to fill a small role, without parting with a draft choice that later became a real player.

Golden State Never Collected the Promised 2001 Pick

minnesota-timberwolves.summary: On August 20, 1993, Minnesota and Washington exchanged the draft rights to Conrad McRae and Tim Burroughs. Neither prospect ever played an NBA game. Even Trade, C- for both franchises.
minnesota-timberwolves.analysis:
A Rights Exchange, Not an Active-Roster Trade

Minnesota acquired the NBA draft rights to Conrad McRae from the Washington Bullets on August 20, 1993, sending the rights to Tim Burroughs in return. The Timberwolves' own historical media guide confirms the transaction, which appears in RealGM's team records on the same date. Neither club swapped an active contract or a veteran already providing regular-season NBA minutes. McRae had just been Washington's second-round selection, while Burroughs was an earlier Minnesota draftee. Both teams were trading the opportunity to negotiate with a prospect rather than a guaranteed player who would join the next roster.

McRae Did Not Play an NBA Game for Minnesota

The Bullets had drafted Conrad McRae at No. 38 in 1993, shortly before the Timberwolves acquired his rights. McRae went on to build a professional playing career overseas, but never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. Minnesota therefore got no league points, rebounds or minutes from him. International accomplishments may explain why he was considered a prospect, yet they aren't the acquired franchise's NBA production. Without a documented later trade of those rights to another NBA club, Minnesota's historical return is an unused negotiating opportunity rather than an actual NBA roster contributor.

Washington Retained Burroughs's Rights Without Receiving NBA Production

Tim Burroughs was Minnesota's second-round selection in 1992, and the Bullets acquired his draft rights one year later. RealGM's player transaction chronology records the Washington acquisition, but it also lists zero years of NBA service. The franchise ultimately renounced his rights in 2000, without Burroughs ever appearing in an NBA game for Washington. His college and professional history elsewhere doesn't supply missing Bullets statistics. Like Minnesota, Washington exchanged one uncertain developmental option for another. The rights were real property under league rules, but they never turned into playing value in the acquiring team's uniform.

Neither Side Converted the Rights into a Player

The surviving transaction record establishes two distinct draft selections changing organizational rights, but neither prospect supplied a single NBA regular-season appearance to the team receiving him. The result calls for an even, low-grade verdict rather than the pair of high grades that appeared in the earlier archive. This wasn't a case of one team surrendering a star who immediately flourished elsewhere; both sides held a possibility that stayed unfulfilled at the NBA level. The rights can be evaluated as legitimate trade assets without pretending they generated games, scoring or later picks that the sources cannot establish.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Minnesota receives C- for Conrad McRae's draft rights, which never yielded an NBA appearance for the Timberwolves. Washington also gets C- for acquiring Tim Burroughs's rights without receiving an NBA game from him. The agreement exchanged genuine developmental options, but neither side obtained an NBA player, so the original B/B grades overstated the realized outcome.

summary: San Antonio won the Dennis Rodman–Sean Elliott exchange by receiving two seasons of league-leading rebounding and elite defense, while Elliott lasted only one season in Detroit before returning to the Spurs.
analysis: Detroit had understandable reasons to move Rodman after the Bad Boys era collapsed, but Elliott, David Wood and the draft provisions produced little durable value. Elliott struggled in Detroit and was traded back to San Antonio after one season. Rodman led the league in rebounding twice, strengthened a 62-win Spurs team and helped the club reach the 1995 Western Conference Finals. His volatility, suspensions and weak eventual exit keep San Antonio at B-plus rather than A, but the realized return was clearly superior to Detroit’s D-level outcome.

indiana-pacers.summary: Philadelphia acquired guard Sean Green from Indiana on October 11, 1993 for a 1994 second-round pick. Green appeared in 35 76ers games that season, scoring 149 points in 332 minutes before his inclusion in a larger February deal with Utah. Indiana drafted William Njoku at No. 41 with the pick, but he never played an NBA game. 76ers Win, Philadelphia B-, Indiana D+.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Sent a Reserve Guard to Philadelphia for a Second

On October 11, 1993, Philadelphia acquired Sean Green from the Indiana Pacers for a second-round selection in the following year's NBA draft. Both teams' transaction ledgers show the same date and direct player-for-pick exchange. Green had been a marginal rotation guard for Indiana during his early NBA years, but the rebuilding 76ers could test his scoring ability without surrendering a current player. Indiana preferred another draft opportunity and could wait until June 1994 to make the selection. No additional compensation appears in the documented transaction, so the analysis centers on those two assets.

Green Played 35 Games Before Another Philadelphia Trade

Green appeared in 35 regular-season games for the 76ers during 1993-94, recording 149 points and 332 minutes without a start. His 4.3 points per game didn't make him a franchise centerpiece, but they were genuine production from a second-round pick exchange. Philadelphia included Green in a larger February 1994 deal with Utah involving Jeff Hornacek and additional draft assets. That creates a secondary trade branch, although the entire return for that bigger package cannot be assigned to Green alone. His only subsequent Utah appearance lasted two minutes, which belongs to the Jazz rather than Philadelphia.

No NBA Return From Indiana's No. 41 Draft Pick

Indiana kept the incoming second-round pick and selected William Njoku at No. 41 overall in the 1994 draft. Njoku was a genuine draft prospect who pursued professional basketball, but he never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The Pacers received the drafting opportunity they negotiated for, yet that choice produced no NBA points or minutes for their own club. Njoku's playing career outside the league isn't Indiana acquired-team production. Separating the successful exercise of a draft pick from the later absence of NBA appearances gives a more accurate account of the trade.

Philadelphia Secured the More Useful Short-Term Asset

The 76ers got a reserve guard who played 35 games, while Indiana used its selection on a player who never reached the NBA floor. The direct difference favors Philadelphia even though Green did not become a long-term starter. His inclusion in the subsequent Utah exchange provided some additional asset flexibility, but it was a package trade with other valuable pieces, so the whole downstream return cannot be credited to this October agreement. Both grades should reflect the limited scale of the acquisition. Philadelphia was ahead on actual court production, while the Pacers' draft gamble did not convert.

Final Verdict

76ers Win. Philadelphia receives B- for Sean Green's 35 games, 149 points and 332 minutes, plus a limited share of the later multi-asset Utah transaction. Indiana gets D+ because the acquired 1994 No. 41 pick became William Njoku, who never played in the NBA. The Sixers obtained the only direct playing return, albeit from a reserve rather than a star.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana exchanged Detlef Schrempf for Derrick McKey and Gerald Paddio, trading offensive star power for the defensive versatility that fit its emerging playoff core.
indiana-pacers.analysis: The Schrempf-McKey trade is a good example of an even deal that worked for different reasons on each side. Schrempf became an All-Star in Seattle and remained the more accomplished offensive player, while Derrick McKey gave Indiana size, defense, playmaking and matchup flexibility for years on teams that repeatedly advanced deep into the playoffs. Gerald Paddio was a minor part of the return. The Pacers did not clearly win the talent comparison, but McKey's fit and longevity made the exchange highly functional. An Even Trade verdict better reflects the realized value than forcing either side into a loss.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix traded point guard Negele Knight to San Antonio on November 8, 1993 for the Spurs' 1994 second-round pick, which became No. 29 Antonio Lang. Knight immediately gave San Antonio 64 games, 18 starts, 9.3 points and 3.1 assists per game before the Spurs released him the following July. Phoenix used the pick on Lang, but he appeared in only 12 Suns games as a rookie and averaged 0.9 points. The one-season Knight return clearly outweighed Phoenix's brief Lang stint.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's Phoenix and San Antonio transaction logs agree on the November 8, 1993 structure: the Suns sent Negele Knight to the Spurs for San Antonio's 1994 second-round choice. The pick landed at No. 29 and Phoenix used it on Duke forward Antonio Lang. That clean one-player-for-one-pick structure makes the hindsight comparison unusually direct because both teams realized the acquired asset themselves rather than routing it through another trade first.

San Antonio Return
Knight stepped into a real rotation role immediately. He played 64 regular-season games for San Antonio in 1993-94 and started 18 of them, averaging 22.3 minutes, 9.3 points and 3.1 assists while shooting 47.6 percent from the field. That was substantially more responsibility than a typical end-of-roster acquisition. The value did not last beyond the season: San Antonio released Knight on July 6, 1994, and he never played another game for the Spurs. Still, one productive 64-game season with 18 starts is meaningful direct return for a future second-round pick.

Phoenix Return
The Suns converted the pick into Antonio Lang at No. 29 in the 1994 draft. Lang made the 1994-95 Phoenix roster, but his role was extremely small. He appeared in 12 games, did not start, averaged 4.4 minutes and 0.9 points, and totaled only 53 minutes for the Suns. Lang later played additional NBA seasons with Cleveland, Miami, Toronto and Philadelphia, but those later games cannot be credited to Phoenix because the Suns no longer controlled his career. The trade's realized Phoenix value is therefore the 12-game rookie stint, not Lang's six-year NBA résumé.

Hindsight Comparison
The old Even Trade framing understated the difference. Knight was not a star and San Antonio did not retain him past one season, so this is not an A-level win. But the Spurs received a functioning backup point guard who played nearly 1,500 minutes and started 18 times. Phoenix's draft return produced 53 minutes and 11 points in 12 games. When the acquired assets are credited only for the teams that actually received their production, the gap is substantial.

Final Verdict
San Antonio Spurs Win, B to D+. Knight supplied one solid season of rotation and spot-starting value. Phoenix correctly converted the second-round pick into an NBA player, but Lang's Suns tenure was too brief and too small to balance the exchange.

perspectives.summary: Dallas received Tony Campbell; 1997 first-round pick (protected top 5 in 1997) (#25-John Thomas) from New York Knicks and sent Derek Harper in return.
perspectives.analysis: Dallas surrendered substantially more long-term value than it received. Derek Harper remained a high-level starter for New York, including a Finals run. Tony Campbell was short-lived in Dallas and the later first-round pick became John Thomas, producing a clear Knicks advantage.

perspectives.summary: The Knicks paid Tony Campbell and a protected future first for Derek Harper after Doc Rivers was injured. Harper immediately stabilized the backcourt and helped New York reach Game 7 of the 1994 Finals.
perspectives.analysis: Derek Harper is a useful case study in judging a contender trade by the window in which it was made. With Doc Rivers injured and New York pursuing a championship, the Knicks sent Tony Campbell and a protected 1997 first-round pick to Dallas for a veteran point guard who could defend, organize the offense and handle postseason pressure. Harper became a major part of the 1994 run that reached Game 7 of the NBA Finals and remained a reliable starter afterward. The first-round pick eventually conveyed at No. 25 and became John Thomas, so the future cost never turned into a premium asset. New York did not win the title, but it materially improved a legitimate contender without sacrificing a future star, which is enough for a strong Knicks Win.

atlanta-hawks.analysis: The Hawks acquired former No. 1 overall pick Danny Manning on February 24, 1994 while giving up longtime franchise icon Dominique Wilkins and a conditional first-rounder. The trade occurred during Atlanta's push for the East's top seed, yet neither Wilkins nor Manning was under guaranteed future contract control. Manning scored 15.7 points per game in 26 Atlanta regular-season appearances and averaged 20.0 points and 7.0 rebounds across 11 playoff games before the Hawks lost to Indiana. He then joined Phoenix as a free agent, so Atlanta did not receive a multi-year core forward. Wilkins, meanwhile, played 25 Clippers regular-season games at 29.1 points a night. The Clippers took Atlanta's conditional choice in 1994 at No. 25 and exchanged Greg Minor's rights in a separate June trade with Indiana, adding more asset options. The original Clippers Win with Atlanta F and LAC A+ is preserved, while Manning's real 11 playoff games should never be mislabeled as 11 Atlanta regular-season appearances.

analysis: Atlanta was leading the Eastern Conference when it traded Dominique Wilkins, its long-time franchise scorer, and a conditional 1994-or-1995 first-round choice to Los Angeles for Danny Manning on February 24, 1994. Period reporting confirms both forwards could leave as unrestricted free agents after the season, so the transaction was not an exchange of guaranteed multi-year team control. Manning gave Atlanta 26 regular-season games averaging 15.7 points and 6.5 rebounds, followed by 11 playoff appearances at 20.0 points and 7.0 rebounds. The Hawks lost in the second round to Indiana and Manning signed with Phoenix afterward, limiting Atlanta's direct return to that partial season and postseason. Wilkins provided the Clippers 25 regular-season games averaging 29.1 points and 7.0 rebounds, then continued his career elsewhere, so Los Angeles cannot claim his earlier Hawks accomplishments or his later clubs' seasons. The Clippers also exercised the conditional first-round choice immediately, selecting No. 25 Greg Minor in 1994; on June 30 they passed Minor's rights and Mark Jackson to Indiana, receiving Pooh Richardson, Malik Sealy and draft rights to Eric Piatkowski in a separate transaction. That is genuine additional Clippers asset flexibility, but neither Minor nor his subsequent Boston seasons were direct Clippers on-court production. The original editorial Clippers Win with Clippers A+ versus Hawks F is preserved as a judgment that Atlanta surrendered more value, while this analysis distinguishes each receiving team's actual short-term playing contribution and the downstream June pick-rights exchange.

milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
A February 1994 Center Rental for a Conditional Draft Choice

Los Angeles acquired veteran center Danny Schayes from Milwaukee on February 24, 1994. The NBA's historical deadline list describes the compensation as a conditional 1995 second-round pick, while the Bucks' transaction register describes selling the player's rights. The Lakers' own historical media guide confirms the acquisition date. Schayes had already played 23 games for Milwaukee during the season and carried years of NBA experience, but Los Angeles was seeking a temporary reserve rather than a new starting centerpiece. The future selection was conditional, which meant the Bucks' eventual draft return was uncertain from the outset.

Schayes Supplied a Small Amount of Actual Lakers Production

Schayes appeared in 13 regular-season games for Los Angeles after the trade, averaging 10.2 minutes, 2.8 points and 2.6 rebounds without a start. It was a brief reserve role on a team going through an uneven transition after its championship years. His 23 games with Milwaukee earlier in 1993-94 count as the Bucks' pretrade history, not as value Los Angeles acquired. Schayes subsequently moved to Phoenix, so the Lakers also can't claim his later contributions elsewhere. The tangible return is a few weeks of NBA center availability, useful in a narrow sense but not a long-term solution.

Milwaukee's Future Compensation Did Not Become a Draft Selection

The archived agreement promised Milwaukee a second-round pick in 1995 only if its condition was fulfilled. The inherited transaction record says the condition was not exercised; the available team and NBA transaction descriptions do not identify a 1995 selection acquired by the Bucks through this deal. A retrospective therefore cannot assign them the eventual NBA career of a hypothetical player. Milwaukee gave up the services of an aging reserve and received no verifiable draft conversion. It may have freed a roster place or reduced obligations, but those potential benefits aren't an identifiable basketball asset that can be tracked into later game totals.

The Documented Return Favors Los Angeles Only Slightly

Both sides' returns were limited. The Lakers got a veteran who could play ten minutes a night when required, while the Bucks' conditional compensation produced no identifiable draft selection. That yields a narrow Los Angeles advantage on playing value. It doesn't justify the original pair of B grades, because neither team obtained sustained production or a future contributor. The distinction is between a little recorded NBA action and a conditional promise that apparently expired. Keeping the evaluation proportionate prevents a fringe February trade from being exaggerated into a major historical turning point.

Final Verdict

Slight Lakers Edge. Los Angeles earns C+ for Danny Schayes's 13 regular-season appearances and modest frontcourt minutes after the February 1994 transaction. Milwaukee receives D+ because the conditional 1995 second-round compensation never became a documented Bucks draft selection. Neither franchise gained lasting value, but the Lakers secured the deal's only traceable playing contribution.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Acquired Ken Norman for Roy Hinson's Rights

The Hawks received veteran forward Ken Norman from Milwaukee in June 1994, sending the rights to Roy Hinson to the Bucks. The agreement paired an immediately recognizable NBA frontcourt player against an asset whose value depended on another club's ability to negotiate or use it. Norman had accumulated substantial league experience before the trade, but those earlier Clippers and Bucks seasons did not become new Atlanta production. The Hawks wanted a practical forward for the upcoming campaign, while Milwaukee was comfortable exchanging an established rotation name for a much less certain rights claim.

Norman Brought Defined Skills With a Limited Horizon

Norman was an experienced scorer and rebounder who could help a team at the forward positions. His age and years already spent in the league placed limits on how much further growth Atlanta could reasonably expect. The team gained the ability to evaluate a current player rather than waiting for an uncertain future draft, but it still needed Norman to fit the new rotation and earn minutes. A familiar name by itself didn't mean Atlanta had acquired a long-term star. The return should be based on the games and seasons after his arrival, not on his earlier best statistical campaigns with other teams.

Milwaukee Received a Rights Claim Rather Than Immediate Production

Hinson had an earlier NBA playing history, but holding his rights in 1994 was a different proposition from receiving a healthy, currently signed player under a multi-year agreement. The Bucks could choose whether to negotiate or use the right in another transaction. That made the asset speculative and of limited immediate basketball certainty. It would be misleading to credit Milwaukee with Hinson's prior career as though those games occurred after this exchange. The club's decision instead reflected a willingness to move Norman and hold an alternative claim that might help with future roster planning.

A Small Bucks Edge Is Plausible but Hardly Transformative

Atlanta gained a veteran capable of immediate contribution, while Milwaukee converted Norman into a different form of control over a frontcourt player. Neither club secured premium new draft capital or a future All-NBA centerpiece. The precise balance depends on Norman's later Atlanta availability and what Milwaukee could actually do with Hinson's rights, both more limited than the players' reputation might suggest. The canonical slightly Bucks-favoring verdict should therefore be interpreted cautiously, recognizing Atlanta's practical veteran return instead of treating Milwaukee's rights as an automatic on-court replacement. The transaction was modest in long-term stakes.

Final Verdict

Slight Bucks Edge. Atlanta Hawks earns B-; Milwaukee Bucks earns B. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Secured Two Veterans on Draft Night

On June 29, 1994, the Celtics sent Ed Pinckney and the rights to second-round choice Andrei Fetisov to Milwaukee for Blue Edwards and Derek Strong. Edwards had played all 82 games for the Bucks the preceding season, averaging 11.6 points, and Strong had supplied frontcourt minutes and rebounding. The exchange gave Boston two already-tested professionals for a veteran power forward and a prospect still requiring development. Milwaukee chose a different frontcourt mix as it rebuilt around a high draft pick.

Edwards and Strong Gave Boston Actual Rotation Options

Edwards brought Boston shooting, experience and wing size; Strong gave the club a physical option near the basket. Neither was acquired to reproduce the historic output of the Celtics' former championship stars. The useful question was whether both could help a changing roster without waiting on a rookie's development. Their NBA experience made them more immediately deployable than a second-round right. Those Boston seasons, rather than the earlier Milwaukee statistics used to evaluate the trade, are the direct playing return.

Milwaukee Added Pinckney and an Unproven Right

Pinckney had rebounded and defended for Boston, appearing in 76 games during 1993-94. He offered the Bucks a known veteran presence while Fetisov represented a possible longer-term frontcourt prospect. Holding international draft rights did not automatically create an NBA contributor, however, and Fetisov did not establish a Milwaukee playing career. The Bucks accepted a package whose direct NBA utility depended primarily on Pinckney, giving up two players who had already been useful in their own rotation.

The Two-for-One Player Return Favors Boston

Boston obtained a guard-forward combination that could immediately compete for regular-season minutes, while Milwaukee took one veteran and one uncertain rights asset. Edwards and Strong were role players, not newly acquired All-Stars, so the assessment must remain proportionate. Still, receiving two active veterans who could fill different lineup needs provided more dependable basketball utility than an international pick that never became a Bucks NBA fixture. The higher Celtics grade reflects that roster benefit without pretending either team changed the championship picture.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for adding Blue Edwards and Derek Strong, two experienced rotation options acquired for Ed Pinckney and the rights to Andrei Fetisov. Milwaukee gets C+ for Pinckney's rebounding and the speculative rights but received no NBA playing return from Fetisov. The advantage belongs to Boston's deeper usable player package.
