golden-state-warriors.summary: Los Angeles acquired rights to Anthony 'Pig' Miller from Golden State for a 1995 second-round pick after the 1994 draft. Miller played 73 Lakers games over two seasons, producing 225 points and 177 rebounds. Golden State selected Dwayne Whitfield at No. 40 with the pick; he never played for the Warriors but later formed one of five assets sent to Toronto for B.J. Armstrong. Lakers Win, Lakers B-, Warriors C+, with only partial downstream Armstrong credit.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Draft-Night Rights Exchange with a Date Discrepancy

Golden State selected forward Anthony Miller with the 39th pick of the 1994 NBA draft, then sent his rights to the Lakers for a future second-round selection. The site's imported ledger places the transaction on June 29, while Basketball-Reference's league register dates the completed exchange to July 1. The discrepancy stays flagged rather than silently changing the canonical sort date. Los Angeles wanted a young interior reserve at a modest draft cost. Golden State accepted a later pick that could be held or traded. Neither club exchanged an established veteran NBA contract.

Two Seasons of Lakers Frontcourt Depth

Anthony Miller appeared in 46 Lakers games during 1994-95, recording 189 points and 152 rebounds. His next season brought 27 appearances, 36 points and 25 rebounds. Taken together, that was 73 Los Angeles games, 225 points and 177 rebounds. Miller played 11.5 minutes per game as a rookie but received less time during the following campaign. He never established himself as the starting power forward, and his later professional seasons for other teams don't belong to Los Angeles. The acquisition nonetheless gave the Lakers an inexpensive, usable reserve for two years.

Whitfield's Pick Later Helped Form a Package for B.J. Armstrong

The incoming Lakers second-round selection became Golden State's No. 40 choice in the 1995 draft, used on Dwayne Whitfield. He never played an NBA game for the Warriors. Nevertheless the asset wasn't entirely worthless: Golden State later included Whitfield among five outgoing players in its September 1995 transaction with Toronto for guard B.J. Armstrong. Armstrong supplied productive minutes for the Warriors, but four other players were also part of the payment. Assigning his entire Golden State season to this lone draft pick would exaggerate the asset chain. Whitfield himself eventually logged eight NBA games with Toronto, which aren't Warriors production.

A Direct Los Angeles Benefit Against Partial Warriors Trade Utility

Los Angeles received a modest two-year reserve, while Golden State converted the pick into a later trade package. The Lakers are ahead on direct, documented playing value, but the Warriors' draft choice wasn't simply discarded without a basketball use. It's fair to acknowledge the pick's role in the eventual Armstrong transaction without giving Whitfield credit for all the NBA minutes Armstrong played. Miller's 73 games make Los Angeles the more identifiable winner, although the grades stay restrained for an exchange of second-round assets. The outcome rests on the real players and asset branches rather than invented star-level returns.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win. Los Angeles keeps B- for Anthony Miller with 73 games, 225 points and 177 rebounds across two seasons. Golden State receives C+ because its No. 40 Dwayne Whitfield pick became one of five players sent to Toronto in a later trade for B.J. Armstrong. Whitfield himself played no Warriors games, and only partial downstream Armstrong trade value can be assigned to the single pick.

minnesota-timberwolves.summary: Seattle selected center Željko Rebrača at No. 54 in 1994 and sent his draft rights to Minnesota for a 1996 second-round pick, ultimately No. 35 Joe Blair. Rebrača remained overseas and made his NBA debut with Detroit in 2001, not Minnesota. Blair did not play a Seattle NBA regular-season game. Even Trade, C each, with the old Wolves-favored grades failing to separate future NBA careers from acquiring-team return.
minnesota-timberwolves.analysis:
Seattle Used a Late Draft Pick on a European Center

The SuperSonics selected Željko Rebrača with the fifty-fourth overall choice in the June 29, 1994 NBA draft and moved his rights to Minnesota. Seattle received a 1996 second-round draft selection instead. Rebrača was already developing as a big man overseas, offering the possibility of a future seven-footer without immediately consuming an NBA roster spot. The Timberwolves decided to acquire that option, while the SuperSonics preferred a later domestic scouting opportunity. The transaction was a rights-for-pick exchange, not a trade involving active NBA centers.

Rebrača's NBA Career Started Elsewhere Years Later

Rebrača continued playing professional basketball in Europe and became an accomplished international center before entering the NBA in 2001. When he finally arrived, his NBA debut was with Detroit, not the Timberwolves. He appeared in substantial regular-season action for the Pistons and subsequently played for other clubs, but none of those minutes were Minnesota production. The Wolves did hold his rights after the trade, which was a genuine asset, yet that asset did not produce a regular-season appearance for the organization that originally purchased it in 1994.

The Seattle Return Became Joe Blair at No. 35 in 1996

The 1996 second-round choice reached Seattle and became the thirty-fifth overall selection, Joe Blair. As with Rebrača, the acquiring franchise received control of a prospect rather than a finished NBA contributor. Blair did not register a SuperSonics regular-season appearance. The higher position of the future selection offered a theoretical improvement over an earlier No. 54 pick, but it did not become recorded league minutes. The subsequent Oklahoma City identity of the franchise should not be used to import the achievements of unrelated Thunder players.

Both Teams Held Prospects Without Receiving NBA Games

Minnesota gambled on a European center who eventually reached the NBA for another organization. Seattle received the right to draft again at a higher position two years later, yet the selection produced no games for the Sonics. That leaves both sides with developmental choices and no direct on-court result. The original Minnesota B+ overstated what Rebrača did for the acquiring club, and an equally elevated Seattle grade would make the same error with Blair. Matching modest grades acknowledge the draft assets without importing their other professional careers.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Minnesota receives C because the acquired rights to Željko Rebrača never produced a Timberwolves regular-season NBA game. Seattle also gets C because its 1996 second-round selection became Joe Blair, who never appeared for the SuperSonics. Rebrača's later Detroit NBA career doesn't convert this 1994 rights purchase into Minnesota playing production.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana acquired Mark Jackson and found the point guard who would organize much of the franchise's strongest 1990s and early-2000s basketball.
indiana-pacers.analysis: Mark Jackson became the central value in this deal. Indiana sent Pooh Richardson, Malik Sealy and the rights to Eric Piatkowski, then received Jackson and Greg Minor's rights. Jackson's passing, control and durability stabilized the Pacers' offense and he became a major part of multiple conference-final teams and, after a later return, the 2000 Finals club. The outgoing players had useful NBA careers, which keeps the transaction from being an empty return for the Clippers, but none produced comparable franchise impact. Indiana's fit, longevity and playoff payoff make this a clear Pacers Win.

golden-state-warriors.summary: On July 18, 1994, Golden State sent injured guard Šarūnas Marčiulionis and Byron Houston to the Seattle SuperSonics for Ricky Pierce, the draft rights to No. 11 Carlos Rogers and two 1995 second-round picks that later became No. 50 Martin Lewis and No. 55 Michael McDonald. Rogers played 49 Warriors games with 18 starts in 1994-95 and Pierce contributed 27 appearances. Seattle received a returning veteran shooter and depth but Golden State's four assets offered greater breadth. Warriors Win, Golden State B, Seattle B-; Oklahoma City is the modern franchise-history key.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Exchanged an Injured Guard for Four Assets

On July 18, 1994, the Golden State Warriors sent Šarūnas Marčiulionis and forward Byron Houston to Seattle for veteran shooter Ricky Pierce, the draft rights to Carlos Rogers and two 1995 second-round choices. Marčiulionis had missed the entire 1993-94 season with an ACL injury, making the move a gamble for Seattle despite his earlier impact in the Warriors' rotation. Pierce also carried medical risk entering his mid-thirties. Golden State obtained the eleventh pick from the 1994 draft in Rogers plus the future slots that later became No. 50 Martin Lewis and No. 55 Michael McDonald. The trade was not a simple Pierce-for-Marčiulionis exchange.

Pierce and Rogers Supplied Actual Warriors Minutes

The incoming players both appeared for Golden State in 1994-95, though neither became a long-term solution to the franchise's broader problems. Rogers played forty-nine games, started eighteen and logged 1,017 minutes in his rookie season. Pierce appeared twenty-seven times with six starts and 673 minutes, giving the Warriors some of the reserve perimeter scoring they sought. Those are direct receiving-team returns that can be counted without borrowing Pierce's previous Seattle or Milwaukee production. Rogers's career with other franchises belongs to later transactions, and his initial prospect value should be judged against the minutes Golden State actually realized.

Seattle Received a Comeback Candidate and Depth

Seattle acquired Marčiulionis with the hope that he could recover his attacking and playmaking form after missing a full season. Houston was a younger forward who offered frontcourt depth but had averaged only modest numbers in Golden State. The SuperSonics still won fifty-seven games in 1994-95, yet that club record cannot be attributed entirely to these two arrivals. The team had substantial established talent and a coach already producing winning seasons. The modern trade record's Oklahoma City Thunder key is simply the successor identity to the 1994 Seattle SuperSonics, so no analysis should describe Oklahoma City as a team involved in the agreement.

Future Second-Round Picks Added Flexibility, Not Guaranteed Stars

Golden State also received two genuine future selections that appeared in the 1995 draft ledger as Martin Lewis and Michael McDonald. The draft-choice histories trace those slots through earlier transactions, including an older Seattle arrangement involving Orlando. They represent usable capital at the time of the July agreement, not automatic Warriors NBA production by either eventually named prospect. Seattle surrendered that flexibility alongside Rogers and Pierce to pursue the potential of Marčiulionis's return. Golden State's broader asset package and actual contributions from Rogers and Pierce justify a modest edge, but the original elite grade exceeds what the receiving club turned into lasting on-court success.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State earns B after receiving 49 rookie games and 18 starts from Carlos Rogers, 27 games from Ricky Pierce and two transferable 1995 second-round selections. The Seattle SuperSonics, labeled Oklahoma City Thunder in the franchise-history database, receive B- for obtaining Šarūnas Marčiulionis and Byron Houston. Seattle's broader team success and the eventual draft identities of Martin Lewis and Michael McDonald should not be mistaken for additional direct player output in this deal.

orlando-magic.summary: Washington acquired Scott Skiles and first-round rights later associated with Todd Fuller and Vince Carter from Orlando in July 1994. The Magic received a 1996 second and 1998 first later linked with Randy Livingston and Keon Clark. Skiles brought veteran playmaking to the Bullets, while Orlando created room to pursue a different roster. The inherited Wizards Win grades Washington A- and Orlando D.
orlando-magic.analysis:
Washington Acquired an Experienced Point Guard

The Washington Bullets received Scott Skiles from Orlando on July 29, 1994, bringing a guard with established playmaking skills to a team seeking steadier organization. Skiles had been important during the Magic's early years and had produced high assist totals before Anfernee Hardaway became their primary playmaker. Washington also obtained first-round choices later associated with the selections of Todd Fuller in 1996 and Vince Carter in 1998. The package combined an immediate veteran with longer-range draft flexibility.

Orlando Reordered Its Salary and Draft Obligations

The Magic received a 1996 second-round selection later tied to Randy Livingston and a 1998 first-round choice associated with Keon Clark. Orlando was trying to clear room to pursue veteran forward Horace Grant, making the transaction as much a roster-finance decision as a one-for-one guard comparison. Skiles wasn't simply discarded for one lesser prospect; the team was selecting another roster construction strategy. Its incoming draft positions remained real rights even though the actual players' future NBA careers required additional moves.

The Famous Vince Carter Name Requires Draft-Chain Precision

Washington's incoming 1998 first-round right became linked to No. 5 Vince Carter, who was ultimately associated with a different franchise's playing career. The Bullets' 1994 acquisition should therefore not be credited with a lengthy Carter tenure in Washington. Likewise, the rights Orlando obtained through this transaction should be traced to their actual later holders before assigning player statistics. Historical picks are evidence of asset opportunities, not proof every famous eventual draftee played for the trade's initial receiving team.

The Grade Difference Recognizes Washington's Asset Package

The inherited Washington A- reflects the combination of Skiles's immediate guard utility and two high-value future choices, while Orlando's D reflects the price of giving up those options. Orlando's plan to create salary room had a separate practical rationale, but that doesn't erase what was surrendered. The deal illustrates how a team's objectives can justify a transaction even when its recorded draft compensation appears weaker in hindsight. Evaluating it requires separating financial strategy from the later accomplishments of players tied to the picks.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns A- for acquiring veteran playmaker Scott Skiles and first-round rights later linked to Todd Fuller and Vince Carter. Orlando receives D for second- and first-round choices associated with Randy Livingston and Keon Clark, plus salary flexibility. Carter's celebrated NBA career must not be assigned to Washington; the advantage concerns the opportunity represented by the acquired rights.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Atlanta acquired Tyrone Corbin and a 1995 second-round pick from Utah in September 1994, sending Adam Keefe to the Jazz. Corbin brought the Hawks defense and veteran forward minutes, while Keefe became a useful Utah frontcourt reserve during the Jazz's later Finals era. The inherited Hawks Win (B versus C-) prioritizes Corbin's Atlanta fit.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Traded Keefe for Corbin and a Pick

The Hawks acquired Tyrone Corbin from Utah in September 1994 together with a 1995 second-round selection, sending forward Adam Keefe to the Jazz. Atlanta valued Corbin's veteran defensive work and ability to play alongside its established wings. Utah accepted a younger frontcourt option who could complement Karl Malone and the Jazz's interior rotation. The future pick later became associated with No. 57 Cuonzo Martin, but the main exchange involved two active forwards with different styles and roster roles.

Corbin Offered Atlanta Perimeter and Forward Defense

Corbin arrived with NBA experience and the versatility to defend multiple forward assignments. That gave Atlanta useful depth during an era when its roster emphasized experienced competitors. His new-team contribution was not identical to the player Utah had used before the trade, and his Hawks stay was limited compared with his overall career. The acquired second-rounder provided additional flexibility but did not automatically yield a long-term NBA contributor. Corbin's direct Atlanta minutes remain the more important basketball return for that side.

Keefe Became a Useful Utah Reserve

Keefe spent additional seasons with the Jazz, contributing frontcourt minutes during their later Western Conference title and NBA Finals years. His rebounding and physical play offered a practical complement to Utah's star pairing. Those games should not be discounted merely because the inherited team grade favors Atlanta. At the same time, Keefe wasn't acquired as a first-option scorer or replacement for Malone. Utah obtained a role player whose strengths supported existing personnel, a different kind of value from Atlanta's experienced wing-forward.

Both Clubs Found Different Types of Role Players

Atlanta obtained a known defensive veteran and a late draft opportunity; Utah got a younger forward it could keep for several seasons. The inherited Hawks advantage reflects the additional pick and Corbin's usefulness, but the real comparison is closer than the grades might first imply because Keefe remained a Jazz contributor. No player in this transaction became a primary offensive star. The trade is best understood as a role-and-depth decision with benefits that differed by team, rather than a sweeping winner-take-all change.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B for Tyrone Corbin's veteran defensive contribution and the 1995 second-round right. Utah receives C- under the inherited evaluation even though Adam Keefe supplied genuine multi-year Jazz frontcourt minutes, including the team's Finals era. Corbin's immediate fit and the additional asset support Atlanta's grade, but Keefe's receiving-team work deserves acknowledgment.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: The Lakers acquired Cedric Ceballos from Phoenix on September 23, 1994 for a future first-round pick that became No. 21 Michael Finley in 1995. Both returns became unusually valuable. Ceballos averaged more than 21 points per game in each of his two full Lakers seasons, made the 1995 All-Star team, and was later part of the trade that brought Robert Horry to Los Angeles. Finley gave Phoenix an All-Rookie season and then became part of the December 1996 package that brought Jason Kidd to the Suns. With elite direct value and major downstream conversions on both sides, the source-backed result is Even Trade, A+/A+.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix sent Cedric Ceballos to Los Angeles on September 23, 1994 for a future Lakers first-round pick that could convey in 1995, 1996 or 1997. It conveyed immediately in 1995 at No. 21, where the Suns selected Michael Finley. The original trade therefore became a clean comparison between an established scoring forward and a first-round asset that Phoenix exercised itself. What makes the deal exceptional is that both acquired assets later remained valuable enough to anchor another important transaction for the same franchise.

Los Angeles Return
Ceballos delivered immediate star-level production. The Lakers' own alumni history notes that his two full Los Angeles seasons were the most productive of his career. In 1994-95 he played 58 games and averaged 21.7 points and 8.0 rebounds while making the All-Star team. In 1995-96 he played 78 games and averaged 21.2 points and 6.9 rebounds. Even before considering anything downstream, that is a strong return for one future first. The Lakers then preserved more value. On January 10, 1997 they sent Ceballos and Rumeal Robinson back to Phoenix for Robert Horry and Joe Kleine. Horry became a major playoff contributor on the Lakers' 2000, 2001 and 2002 championship teams. TradeVerdicts should not pretend Ceballos alone bought Horry, because Robinson was also in the package, but Ceballos remained a real asset in the direct conversion.

Phoenix Return
The Suns also hit on their side. Finley played all 82 games as a rookie, started 72, averaged 15.0 points, 4.6 rebounds and 3.5 assists, and earned All-Rookie recognition. He added 27 more Phoenix games in 1996-97 before the Suns used him in a major roster reset. On December 26, 1996 Phoenix sent Finley, Sam Cassell, A.C. Green and a 1998 second-round pick to Dallas for Jason Kidd, Tony Dumas and Loren Meyer. As with the Lakers' later Horry trade, Finley was not the only outgoing asset, so the original 1994 deal cannot receive all of Kidd's value. It can, however, receive credit for producing a first-round player who was good immediately and retained enough market value to be a meaningful piece of the Kidd package.

Hindsight Comparison
The legacy versions of this record disagreed sharply, with one side treating the pick as an overwhelming Phoenix victory and another giving Los Angeles a strong grade for Ceballos. The source-backed history shows why both one-sided readings are incomplete. Los Angeles received two full seasons of All-Star-caliber scoring and then carried Ceballos' remaining value into the Horry deal. Phoenix received an All-Rookie first-rounder and then carried Finley's value into the Kidd deal. Both franchises converted the original asset into another high-impact player, and both received substantial direct production before doing so.

Final Verdict
Even Trade, A+/A+. The grades are intentionally high because both teams extracted far more than ordinary value from the asset they received. The Lakers got Ceballos at his scoring peak and later used him in the Horry transaction. Phoenix drafted Finley, received a strong rookie season and later used him in the Kidd transaction. Neither side owns enough of the other's downstream package to claim a decisive winner.

miami-heat.analysis:
Atlanta Traded a Franchise Veteran for Two Established Heat Players

The Hawks sent Kevin Willis and a protected future first-round selection to Miami on November 7, 1994, receiving Steve Smith, Grant Long and a conditional second-round choice. Willis had been a highly productive Atlanta power forward for many years. Miami, hoping to improve its frontcourt immediately, was prepared to surrender two players who had both seen considerable regular-season time. Atlanta chose a younger perimeter scorer in Smith and a sturdy forward in Long. The conditional first-round obligation was the extra asset that made the deal more than a straight exchange of veterans.

Smith Became a Major Atlanta Wing Scorer

Smith took on an important offensive role with the Hawks, developing into one of their most dependable perimeter scorers over the following seasons. He supplied shooting and secondary ball-handling on playoff teams before later moves ended his Atlanta tenure. Long also served as a regular frontcourt contributor, giving the club rebounding and defense without requiring a new draft selection. Those two receiving-team careers gave Atlanta real depth at separate positions. Smith's prior Miami achievements should not be counted, but his productive Hawks seasons provide ample evidence of the trade's success.

Willis Contributed in Miami, and the First-Rounder Carried Value

Miami acquired Willis as a center and power forward who could rebound and score near the basket. He played for the Heat across parts of two seasons and was later dealt to another club, ending the direct Miami period. The protected first-round selection eventually appeared as the nineteenth pick in 1996, associated with Walter McCarty in the league's draft trade ledger. The right to the choice was a real incoming asset even if the Heat did not ultimately employ McCarty as a regular-season player. His other teams' results should not become Miami production.

Two Long-Term Atlanta Contributors Outweighed Miami's Return

The Heat acquired a reliable veteran for immediate needs and a future draft asset, so this should not be graded as a one-sided loss without any value. Atlanta, however, obtained two active rotation players who remained useful for several seasons. Smith's scoring and Long's frontcourt work supplied a broader foundation than Willis's shorter Miami stay. The historical Hawks-winning verdict was sound. A high grade for Atlanta and a moderate one for Miami recognizes both the sustained Hawks on-court value and the legitimate pick compensation the Heat received.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta gets A for acquiring Steve Smith and Grant Long as productive multi-season Hawks contributors, plus a conditional second-round selection. Miami earns B- for Kevin Willis's frontcourt playing tenure and a protected first-round pick that eventually became the 1996 No. 19 selection. Atlanta realized more sustained basketball production from its two incoming starters.

boston-celtics.summary: Boston acquired Jay Humphries and a 1995 second-round pick from Utah in February 1995 in exchange for Theodore 'Blue' Edwards. Utah obtained an experienced wing for its rotation, while Boston used Humphries for backcourt experience and received a pick later associated with Junior Burrough. The inherited Jazz Win grades Utah B+ and Boston C+.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Utah Replaced a Guard With a Bigger Wing

In February 1995 the Jazz sent Jay Humphries and a second-round draft choice to Boston for Theodore 'Blue' Edwards. Utah was already relying on John Stockton to organize its offense and Karl Malone to carry interior scoring, making another experienced wing more attractive than an additional veteran point guard. Edwards offered the flexibility to defend and score against larger perimeter opponents. Boston, meanwhile, received someone capable of handling the ball during a period of roster turnover.

Edwards Filled a Practical Jazz Rotation Need

Edwards brought established NBA wing experience to Utah and could contribute without requiring the offense to run through him. His arrival gave the Jazz another option beside their star pairing while they remained competitive in the Western Conference. The benefit should be attributed to his Jazz tenure rather than his earlier scoring elsewhere. Edwards wasn't acquired to become the team's leading scorer; the attraction was to supply an experienced and appropriately sized perimeter player.

Boston Received Humphries and a Draft Chance

Humphries gave Boston a veteran guard who understood how to run an NBA offense, although his stay wasn't a long second career there. The accompanying 1995 second-round selection was linked to No. 33 Junior Burrough. That numbered right held value whether the club used or redirected it, but Burrough's subsequent team affiliations require tracing beyond the February trade. The deal therefore offered both immediate guard depth and a chance to revisit the roster at draft time.

The Jazz Got More Directly Useful Position Depth

The inherited B+ for Utah and C+ for Boston reflect their different realized benefits. Utah addressed a wing need on a team with an established point guard, while the Celtics received a shorter-term guard option and draft compensation. The exchange did not dramatically remake either franchise, and Boston's selection prevented its package from being empty. Edwards's role in Utah nevertheless provided a clearer fit with the club's competitive plans.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win. Utah earns B+ for adding Blue Edwards as an experienced wing beside Stockton and Malone. Boston gets C+ for Jay Humphries and a 1995 second-round right later associated with Junior Burrough. The Celtics gained some guard depth and future flexibility, but Edwards's fit gave Utah the stronger directly usable rotation piece.

orlando-magic.summary: In the 1995 expansion draft, Orlando sent Vancouver a 1996 second-round pick in return for the Grizzlies choosing Rodney Dent. The selection subsequently became No. 42 Randy Livingston, but Vancouver moved the pick in a later transaction rather than receiving Livingston's NBA play. Dent did not become a lasting Vancouver contributor. The Magic protected the rest of its expansion-eligible roster, while Vancouver gained a transferable draft choice. Even Trade, C+ each for modest and distinct outcomes.
orlando-magic.analysis:
Orlando Bought Expansion-Draft Protection With a Future Second

The June 24, 1995 agreement was an expansion-draft arrangement, not an ordinary exchange of players between established teams. Orlando agreed to send the incoming Vancouver Grizzlies a 1996 second-round draft choice if they selected reserve Rodney Dent from the Magic's available list. Vancouver complied and Orlando kept the other eligible players it wanted to protect. The Grizzlies, building an inaugural roster from selections across the league, accepted a known bench piece and a future choice rather than using the expansion draft to poach a different Magic player.

Vancouver Selected Dent but Acquired a Movable Draft Asset

Rodney Dent was officially the fourth selection in the 1995 expansion draft, and the Grizzlies' selection fulfilled the agreement. Dent did not develop into a meaningful Vancouver NBA rotation player, so it would be misleading to justify the arrangement with points or starts that were never recorded. The second-round pick became No. 42 in 1996, subsequently associated with Randy Livingston. Vancouver used the rights as part of its own later transaction activity instead of turning Livingston into direct Grizzlies playing time. The pick therefore supplied trade flexibility rather than a newly developed regular.

The Magic Obtained Certainty, Not Another Star

Orlando's return was control over which member of its exposed roster would be taken. The Magic had reached the NBA Finals in 1995 with Shaquille O'Neal and Penny Hardaway leading an accomplished team. Rodney Dent had a minimal role compared with that core, so Orlando could give up a future second for the assurance that its expansion loss would be limited to him. This protection was a roster-management service rather than a box-score asset. It did not make Vancouver responsible for providing Orlando another player, cash consideration or a 1995 first-round selection.

Neither Side Realized a Major On-Court Return

Vancouver accepted a low-impact expansion player and an asset that could be deployed in subsequent deals. Orlando kept its preferred eligible roster intact and surrendered only a second-round selection. These are distinct benefits, and neither deserves to be presented as the acquisition of Randy Livingston's eventual NBA work by Vancouver. The later draft history identifies what the original pick became, not a one-step athlete transfer. Given the limited player production and small but usable flexibility, the historical even outcome and moderate C-plus grades capture the transaction's actual scale.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Orlando earns C+ because the expansion-draft arrangement directed Vancouver toward Rodney Dent and protected the Magic's preferred eligible players. Vancouver also receives C+ for obtaining a transferable 1996 second-round selection eventually identified as No. 42. Dent did not provide substantial Grizzlies NBA production, while Randy Livingston's later career cannot be credited as games played for Vancouver through this agreement.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: On June 28, 1995, Milwaukee traded draft rights to guard Eric Snow to the Seattle SuperSonics for rights to center Eurelijus Žukauskas and a 1996 second-round pick later No. 53 Jeff Nordgaard. Snow became a real NBA rotation guard for Seattle before being traded again. Žukauskas never played in the NBA, and Nordgaard's Bucks stint was brief. The existing Oklahoma City Thunder franchise label refers to the Seattle-era transaction; the winner is Seattle's side, B-, Milwaukee D+.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Seattle Bought an American Point-Guard Prospect

The Bucks used the 1995 draft night to move the rights to Eric Snow, an emerging guard from Michigan State, to the Seattle SuperSonics. Seattle gave up the rights to Lithuanian center Eurelijus Žukauskas and a 1996 second-round draft selection. Because the current franchise database uses the Oklahoma City Thunder identity for old Seattle trades, this historical record can be easy to misread. Oklahoma City did not operate an NBA club in 1995. The actual negotiation was between Milwaukee and Seattle, with both organizations exchanging developmental rights rather than established players.

Snow Became a Genuine Seattle Rotation Contributor

Unlike a merely speculative overseas selection, Snow made the Sonics and supplied real NBA minutes during the following seasons. He worked as a reserve ball handler behind Seattle's more established guards, with defensive value that later became a cornerstone of his reputation. His eventual long service with the Philadelphia 76ers cannot be assigned to Seattle, because that came following a separate franchise move. Still, the receiving team's ability to put Snow into NBA games is a concrete advantage. A modest draft-night transaction became an actual point-guard asset for the SuperSonics.

Milwaukee's Rights Return Offered Little Immediate Play

Milwaukee's initial return consisted of Žukauskas's rights and a second-round slot in the 1996 draft. Žukauskas continued a substantial international career but never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Bucks. The selection eventually resolved at No. 53 and was used on Jeff Nordgaard, who appeared in only thirteen Milwaukee games in 1997-98. That is far less direct basketball return than the Sonics obtained from Snow. Rights to a prospect and the opportunity to make a late second-round selection still have value, but neither converted into a meaningful Bucks rotation role.

The Franchise Label Must Not Distort the 1995 Outcome

The historical winner was the Seattle side of the franchise now cataloged as Oklahoma City. Snow's defense and reserve minutes outweighed the limited Milwaukee return, although assigning an elite grade for his later work in Philadelphia would overstate what Seattle directly acquired. Milwaukee made two bets on future rights but saw little NBA play from either. The source ledger identifies the draft-choice path without implying Nordgaard was ever a dependable Bucks contributor. Those limits support a Seattle advantage while keeping both grades in proportion to a late-first-and-second-round prospect exchange.

Final Verdict

Oklahoma City Thunder Win is the site's franchise-history label; the acquiring team in June 1995 was Seattle. Its side earns B- because Eric Snow became a playable SuperSonics reserve before later changing clubs. Milwaukee receives D+ because Eurelijus Žukauskas did not play NBA games and 1996 No. 53 Jeff Nordgaard appeared only briefly for the Bucks. Snow's subsequent Philadelphia years are excluded from the Seattle return.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Atlanta reacquired point guard Spud Webb from Sacramento in 1995 in exchange for veteran forward Tyrone Corbin. Webb's return gave the Hawks another experienced ball handler, while Sacramento added frontcourt depth. The inherited slight Hawks edge, B- to C+, evaluates fit rather than claiming either player was a new star.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Brought Webb Back to Its Backcourt

The Hawks reacquired Spud Webb from Sacramento in June 1995, sending Tyrone Corbin to the Kings. Webb was already well known in Atlanta for his speed, passing and years in the team's rotation. The move gave the Hawks an experienced option at point guard rather than an unfamiliar prospect. Sacramento received Corbin, a versatile forward who could defend and supply veteran minutes, in exchange for the guard it had used during its own rebuilding period.

Webb's Return Was a Familiar Short-Term Fit

Webb could organize an offense and provide energy despite his smaller stature. His return to Atlanta did not create a decade-long second stint, however, and the strongest portion of his Hawks career remained his earlier years with the franchise. The relevant return is what he offered after coming back in 1995, not his famous dunk-contest victory or his previous performances. Atlanta favored a familiar guard suited to its current personnel rather than pursuing a younger player with uncertain development.

Corbin Gave Sacramento a Veteran Forward

Corbin's value to Sacramento lay in experienced defensive work and depth, not in becoming a primary scorer. He had already played important NBA minutes elsewhere, and the Kings could use his abilities to support a roster seeking stability. Those earlier Hawks and Jazz accomplishments should not be counted as Sacramento production. His incoming role was useful in a narrower way than Webb's ball handling, making the comparison dependent on what each club wanted from its veteran acquisition.

Two Complementary Roster Needs Drove the Deal

Atlanta obtained a known playmaker while Sacramento added a veteran forward. Neither team surrendered a top draft selection or received an obvious future franchise player. The inherited slight Hawks edge gives more credit to the immediacy and familiarity of Webb's guard skills on his return. Sacramento's side remains defensible because Corbin brought real NBA experience. The exchange is best understood as roster balancing rather than a decision whose outcome can be measured by later championship rings.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta earns B- for reacquiring Spud Webb and adding an experienced point guard to its 1995 roster. Sacramento gets C+ for Tyrone Corbin's veteran forward depth. Both arrivals filled practical roles, but the inherited grading values Webb's backcourt usefulness somewhat more. Neither was a franchise-changing acquisition.

Webb could organize an offense and provide energy despite his smaller stature. His return to Atlanta did not create a decade-long second stint, however, and the strongest portion of his Hawks career remained his earlier years with the franchise. The relevant return is what he offered after coming back in 1995, not his famous dunk-contest victory or his previous performances. Atlanta favored a familiar guard suited to its current personnel rather than pursuing a younger player with uncertain development.

Corbin Gave Sacramento a Veteran Forward

Corbin's value to Sacramento lay in experienced defensive work and depth, not in becoming a primary scorer. He had already played important NBA minutes elsewhere, and the Kings could use his abilities to support a roster seeking stability. Those earlier Hawks and Jazz accomplishments should not be counted as Sacramento production. His incoming role was useful in a narrower way than Webb's ball handling, making the comparison dependent on what each club wanted from its veteran acquisition.

Two Complementary Roster Needs Drove the Deal

Atlanta obtained a known playmaker while Sacramento added a veteran forward. Neither team surrendered a top draft selection or received an obvious future franchise player. The inherited slight Hawks edge gives more credit to the immediacy and familiarity of Webb's guard skills on his return. Sacramento's side remains defensible because Corbin brought real NBA experience. The exchange is best understood as roster balancing rather than a decision whose outcome can be measured by later championship rings.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta earns B- for reacquiring Spud Webb and adding an experienced point guard to its 1995 roster. Sacramento gets C+ for Tyrone Corbin's veteran forward depth. Both arrivals filled practical roles, but the inherited grading values Webb's backcourt usefulness somewhat more. Neither was a franchise-changing acquisition.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Sacramento acquired Byron Houston and Šarūnas Marčiulionis from Seattle on September 18, 1995, for veteran forward Frank Brickowski. Marčiulionis played 53 Kings games with 10.8 points per game, while Houston played 25 games. Brickowski appeared in 63 Seattle regular-season games, then all 21 postseason games as the Sonics reached the 1996 Finals. Even Trade, B for each club, reflecting useful but different one-season returns.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Kings Preferred Two Players to One Veteran Frontcourt Reserve

The Sacramento Kings traded Frank Brickowski to Seattle on September 18, 1995, receiving Šarūnas Marčiulionis and Byron Houston in return. The deal offered Sacramento a veteran international guard capable of handling offensive possessions plus another frontcourt reserve. Seattle was constructing a deep rotation around Gary Payton, Shawn Kemp and coach George Karl, and valued Brickowski's experience as a backup big man who could handle physical matchups. Both clubs exchanged known NBA players, making this a direct roster trade rather than a speculative draft-rights arrangement. No draft selection was part of the September agreement.

Marčiulionis Became an Actual Kings Scoring Contributor

Marčiulionis played 53 Sacramento regular-season games in 1995-96, averaging 10.8 points with 2.2 assists. He also appeared in the team's four playoff games, when the Kings lost their first-round series to Seattle. Sacramento's other acquisition, Houston, made 25 regular-season appearances and logged 276 minutes, adding 86 points and 84 rebounds. The two players supplied different kinds of support, although neither remained a central long-term starter. Marčiulionis subsequently moved to Denver in a separate package transaction, so the full later value of Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf shouldn't be assigned solely to this original Seattle trade.

Brickowski Provided Seattle With Frontcourt and Playoff Depth

Brickowski appeared in 63 SuperSonics regular-season games during 1995-96, scoring 339 points and grabbing 151 rebounds in 986 minutes. Seattle went 64-18 and reached the NBA Finals against Chicago, and Brickowski played in all 21 of the club's postseason contests. He contributed 206 playoff minutes and 41 points, mainly in backup frontcourt shifts. That is useful roster service for a team that advanced through three rounds of Western Conference opponents. Brickowski's playing time shouldn't be inflated into a starting-star role, but his availability during a Finals campaign gave the acquired center direct competitive value.

Sacramento's Scoring and Seattle's Playoff Minutes Balanced Out

The Kings obtained an experienced scorer and limited reserve size, while Seattle secured a physical bench player who remained usable deep into the postseason. Neither organization gained an overwhelming advantage. Sacramento's side had stronger regular-season scoring from Marčiulionis, but Brickowski's 21 playoff appearances for a Finals team weigh heavily in the Sonics' return. The prior Kings-win verdict and unequal grades discounted Seattle's contribution too sharply. A balanced assessment rewards the meaningful receiving-team work on both sides without attributing the eventual championships or later trades to either incoming player alone.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Sacramento gets B for Marčiulionis's 53 games and 10.8 points per game, plus Byron Houston's 25 reserve appearances. Seattle also gets B after Brickowski played 63 regular-season games and all 21 postseason games during the 1996 Finals run. The two teams found useful veterans in different roles, supporting equal grades.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland sent four-time All-Star Mark Price to Washington on September 27, 1995, for the Bullets' 1996 first-round draft pick. Washington got just seven games, 127 minutes and 56 points from Price amid injuries. Cleveland used the No. 12 selection on Vitaly Potapenko, who played 177 Cavaliers games before a later trade. Cavaliers Win: Cleveland B+, Washington D+. The inherited No. 11 draft-pick label was corrected to the official No. 12.
perspectives.analysis:
Washington Bought Price's Reputation as Cleveland Started Over

On September 27, 1995, Cleveland traded Mark Price to the Washington Bullets for their 1996 first-round draft pick. Price had been a four-time All-Star and a major reason Cleveland was competitive in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Washington wanted an experienced point guard to complement Chris Webber, Juwan Howard and newly drafted Rasheed Wallace. Cleveland executive Wayne Embry was confronting Brad Daugherty's ongoing back troubles and decided to acquire a future asset rather than retain a veteran core. The Washington Post's contemporaneous coverage also documented concern about Price's health, which became central to how the exchange played out.

Price's Washington Tenure Ended After Seven Games

Washington did not acquire the durable floor general it expected. A foot injury disrupted Price's first training camp with the Bullets, and his entire 1995-96 regular-season contribution amounted to seven games and 127 minutes. He scored 56 points with 18 assists, averages of 8.0 points and 2.6 assists, without becoming the stable starter the club had sought. Washington finished 39-43 and missed the playoffs. The later years of Price's career do not count for this transaction, and his celebrated Cleveland career was already in the past when the Bullets paid a first-round selection. The club gave away a meaningful draft asset for almost no season-long production.

Cleveland Turned the Pick Into a Three-Season Center

The transferred Washington selection became the No. 12 overall pick of the 1996 draft, which Cleveland used on Vitaly Potapenko from Wright State. Older imported trade copy labeled the selection No. 11, but the Cavaliers' official draft ledger confirms No. 12. Potapenko played 80 Cleveland games as a rookie, another 80 in 1997-98 and 17 during the shortened 1998-99 season before moving to Boston. That totals 177 Cavaliers appearances, including meaningful reserve-center minutes across two full seasons. He was not a star or a permanent building block, but Cleveland's return was clearly more than a speculative paper asset.

A Clear Imbalance Despite Price's Better Overall Career

A simple career-achievement comparison would favor Price over Potapenko and miss what Washington and Cleveland actually received. Price's best work had all occurred for the Cavaliers before this deal; in a Bullets uniform he barely played. Cleveland's incoming pick yielded 177 games of center depth, including 1,238 rookie minutes and 1,412 more in his second season. The clubs were pursuing different strategies, and Washington's effort to compete immediately was understandable, but the downside of relying on an injured veteran was apparent at the time. Historical accounts of the trade should therefore reward Cleveland's realized pick return and not treat Price's former All-Star credentials as Washington's acquired basketball value.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B+ after using the acquired No. 12 pick on Vitaly Potapenko, who provided 177 regular-season Cavaliers appearances. Washington gets D+ for Mark Price's seven games and 127 minutes in 1995-96. The inherited Even Trade verdict and No. 11 draft position conflicted with official records and the receiving-team outcomes.

perspectives.summary: Chicago acquired Dennis Rodman from San Antonio on October 2, 1995 in a straight player-for-player trade for Will Perdue. Rodman led the NBA in rebounding in each of his three Bulls seasons and became a central defender and rebounder on three consecutive championship teams. San Antonio still received real value rather than a failed return: Perdue played 261 regular-season games with 87 starts across four Spurs seasons and remained on the roster for the 1999 championship.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Chicago's own historical archive and Basketball-Reference both describe the October 2, 1995 transaction as Dennis Rodman to the Bulls for Will Perdue. The legacy archive entry's vague 'other considerations' asset is not supported by those primary and high-quality transaction records and is removed rather than treated as hidden value. At the time, Chicago was specifically looking for the rebounding and defensive presence lost when Horace Grant departed, while San Antonio was ready to move on from a highly productive but difficult fit.

Chicago Return
Rodman became exactly the specialized piece the Bulls needed. He played 64 regular-season games in 1995-96 and averaged 14.9 rebounds, 55 games in 1996-97 at 16.1 rebounds, and 80 games in 1997-98 at 15.0. He led the NBA in rebounding in all three seasons, made the All-Defensive First Team in 1995-96, and started 177 regular-season games across the three-year stint. Chicago won the championship in every one of those seasons. NBA.com's Rodman retrospective describes him as the missing piece alongside Michael Jordan and Scottie Pippen, which matches the realized team result without requiring any speculative value calculation.

San Antonio Return
Perdue was not remotely as impactful as Rodman, but the legacy F grade ignores four seasons of useful center depth. He appeared in 80 games with 22 starts in 1995-96, then 65 games with 34 starts during the injury-ravaged 1996-97 season, 79 games with 30 starts in 1997-98, and 37 games in the lockout-shortened 1998-99 season. That totals 261 regular-season games and 87 starts. Perdue averaged 8.7 points and 9.8 rebounds in 1996-97 when San Antonio needed him most, then remained a reserve on the 1999 championship roster. The Spurs did not receive a star, but they did receive durable frontcourt innings and eventually a title-season contributor.

Hindsight Verdict
Chicago wins decisively because Rodman's rebounding, defense and fit were instrumental to a three-title run. The Bulls earn an A+ because a one-for-one trade turned a useful center into an elite role player whose strengths matched the roster perfectly. San Antonio earns a B rather than an F: Perdue delivered four seasons, 261 games, 87 starts and a place on the 1999 title roster. The gap is still enormous at the top end, but the Spurs return had legitimate basketball value. Final verdict: Chicago Bulls Win.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland traded Hot Rod Williams to Phoenix on October 7, 1995 for Dan Majerle, Antonio Lang and a future first-round pick that became No. 16 Brevin Knight in 1997. Phoenix received three useful Williams seasons totaling 201 games, including 154 starts. Cleveland received one productive 82-game Majerle season, two years of Lang depth, then drafted Knight, who became an All-Rookie starting point guard and played 190 Cavaliers games. Phoenix got legitimate frontcourt value, but Cleveland's multi-asset return and Knight's four-year run create the stronger outcome.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Cleveland and Phoenix transaction logs agree on the October 7, 1995 structure: the Cavaliers sent veteran big man Hot Rod Williams to the Suns for Dan Majerle, Antonio Lang and a future first-round choice. Cleveland controlled when that first would convey within the agreed window, and the asset ultimately became the No. 16 selection in the 1997 draft. The Cavaliers used it on Stanford point guard Brevin Knight. Unlike many multi-asset trades, every major component here produced NBA value for the team that acquired it, so the grades should reflect quantity and quality rather than treating Phoenix's return as empty.

Phoenix Return
Williams was 33 when the deal occurred, but he remained a useful starting center. In 1995-96 he played 62 games with 58 starts, averaging 7.3 points and 6.0 rebounds. In 1996-97 he played 68 games, started 66 and averaged 8.0 points and 8.3 rebounds. He then appeared in 71 games with 30 starts in 1997-98, averaging 6.9 points and 8.4 rebounds per 36 minutes. Across those three Phoenix seasons Williams gave the Suns 201 regular-season games and 154 starts. That is substantial realized value and is why the Phoenix grade belongs in the positive range rather than the D or C- territory found in older versions of the record.

Cleveland Return
Majerle gave Cleveland an immediate full-season veteran return. He played all 82 games in 1995-96, started 15, averaged 10.6 points and made 148 three-pointers while supplying perimeter defense and secondary playmaking. Lang added two seasons of depth: 41 games in 1995-96 and 64 more in 1996-97, mostly off the bench. Those two players alone gave Cleveland 187 regular-season appearances before the draft pick is considered.

The draft asset created the decisive separation. Knight played 80 games with 76 starts as a rookie in 1997-98, averaging 9.0 points, 8.2 assists and 2.5 steals while earning All-Rookie recognition. He remained Cleveland's primary point guard for much of the next two seasons, playing 39 games with 38 starts in 1998-99 and 65 games with 46 starts in 1999-00. He added six more Cleveland games in 2000-01 before being traded to Atlanta. In total, the pick produced 190 Cavaliers regular-season games and 160 starts, including several years of starter-level point-guard play.

Hindsight Comparison

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee acquired Kevin Duckworth from the Washington Bullets for Bob McCann on October 18, 1995. Duckworth appeared in just eight Bucks games, scoring nine points in 58 minutes. McCann contributed 62 Washington games and 653 minutes during 1995-96, with a brief waiver and re-signing sequence. Bullets Win, Washington B, Milwaukee D+; the inherited Bucks-favored assessment contradicted receiving-team use.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee Swapped a Reserve Forward for a Former All-Star Center

The Bucks received Kevin Duckworth from the Washington Bullets on October 18, 1995, sending Bob McCann back to the nation's capital. Duckworth had twice made the All-Star team during his Portland years, but he was no longer the productive offensive center of the late 1980s. Milwaukee was testing whether veteran frontcourt size could help a team with a thin center rotation. Washington wanted a player who could cover forward minutes while its roster waited for Chris Webber to return from injury. The player-for-player terms and transaction date are documented in the teams' season registers, without an attached pick or cash.

Duckworth Managed Only Eight Bucks Games

Duckworth's past recognition brought almost no 1995-96 playing return for Milwaukee. He appeared in eight Bucks regular-season games, started one and logged 58 minutes. His entire statistical contribution was nine points, seven rebounds and two assists. Milwaukee finished 25-57, but the trade cannot be blamed for that record any more than Duckworth can be credited with improving it. His Portland and earlier Washington totals are not Bucks production, and he subsequently played for the Clippers rather than remaining a useful Milwaukee frontcourt fixture. The acquired veteran had reached the end of his ability to sustain rotation minutes.

McCann Played 62 Washington Games Despite a Waiver

McCann's Washington stint was more substantial, although the club did not keep him continuously on a standard contract. He appeared in 62 regular-season games for the 1995-96 Bullets, totaling 653 minutes with no starts. Washington waived him on January 5, re-signed him to a ten-day deal January 10 and brought him back for the rest of the season February 3. That sequence matters because it explains how his roster status briefly changed without ending his 1995-96 playing return. McCann remained a deep reserve, averaging approximately 10.5 minutes per appearance, but he supplied many more usable games than Duckworth managed for Milwaukee.

Washington Got Functional Bench Coverage Instead of a Name

At the time of the exchange, Duckworth carried the stronger career reputation. Yet the actual receiving-team contribution went the other way: Washington used McCann in 62 games, while Milwaukee received eight short Duckworth appearances. McCann's temporary release and later return do not create a separate trade, and the earlier careers of both players are irrelevant to what the acquiring clubs received. The Bullets still did not secure a starter or a playoff berth, so the grade should stay measured. The difference between hundreds of frontcourt reserve minutes and a 58-minute rental is enough, however, to overturn the inherited Milwaukee-favored verdict.

Final Verdict

Bullets Win. Washington gets B for 62 Bob McCann games and 653 minutes during 1995-96, including the reserve's post-waiver return. Milwaukee receives D+ for just eight Kevin Duckworth games, 58 minutes and nine points. Duckworth's former All-Star status did not translate into Bucks playing value.

orlando-magic.summary: Vancouver acquired forward Anthony Avent from Orlando on November 1, 1995 for Kevin Pritchard and Larry Stewart. Avent played 71 Grizzlies games, starting 32 and totaling 1,586 minutes, 415 points and 355 rebounds in 1995-96. Orlando waived Pritchard the next day and Stewart November 5, both before regular-season appearances. Grizzlies Win, Vancouver B+, Orlando D+.
orlando-magic.analysis:
Vancouver Found a Forward Before Its First NBA Season

On November 1, 1995, the Vancouver Grizzlies acquired Anthony Avent from Orlando in exchange for Kevin Pritchard and Larry Stewart. The deal occurred just before the expansion franchise's inaugural regular season began, when every roster spot carried uncertainty. Avent had played NBA minutes with Milwaukee and Orlando and offered a forward with known rebounding ability. Orlando wanted to try two different players rather than keep another reserve big man on a loaded roster around Shaquille O'Neal. Neither organization exchanged a draft selection.

Avent Became an Actual Grizzlies Rotation Forward

Avent played seventy-one Vancouver regular-season games in 1995-96, starting thirty-two. He logged 1,586 minutes with 415 points and 355 rebounds, averaging 5.8 points and five rebounds a game. His field-goal accuracy was limited, and he did not become the long-term center of the expansion rebuild. Still, that volume of playing time had obvious utility for a first-year franchise. Avent also supplied forty-two blocks, giving the roster another defensive big man. His prior Orlando minutes cannot be claimed twice, but these Vancouver numbers were earned entirely after the exchange.

The Magic Released Both Incoming Players Within Four Days

Orlando's transaction ledger records that Kevin Pritchard was waived on November 2, the day after the trade. Larry Stewart was waived on November 5. Neither made a Magic regular-season appearance from this transaction, so the receiving-team statistical return was zero games. The front office had an opportunity to examine both players without keeping them, but that tryout did not yield depth for Orlando's season. The Magic did not acquire future picks or cash as part of the listed transaction to compensate for the lack of player minutes.

The Immediate Waivers Decide the Historical Verdict

The contrast isn't subtle once the two receiving-team outcomes are compared. Vancouver put Avent on the floor for more than fifteen hundred minutes and used him as a starter in thirty-two games. Orlando cut both incoming players before they could contribute to an NBA game. Avent's numbers were not franchise-changing, but they were real output for a team building from scratch. The earlier equal grades treated the Magic's unused roster auditions as comparable value. A Grizzlies win is the better conclusion, grounded in games rather than pretrade expectations.

Final Verdict

Grizzlies Win. Vancouver earns B+ for Anthony Avent's seventy-one games, thirty-two starts, 1,586 minutes and 355 rebounds in 1995-96. Orlando receives D+ because both Kevin Pritchard and Larry Stewart were waived before producing a single Magic regular-season appearance. The receiving-team production decisively favors Vancouver over the inherited even verdict.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Received Todd Day and Alton Lister in a Three-Player Exchange

On November 26, 1995, Boston acquired wing scorer Todd Day and veteran big man Alton Lister from Milwaukee in exchange for guard Sherman Douglas. The Celtics were rebuilding their identity and wanted additional options at two positions; the Bucks obtained one established ball handler instead of splitting the return across a perimeter scorer and an experienced center. All three were actual NBA players rather than speculative selections, so the immediate roster implications were more direct than a draft-rights swap. The two-player incoming package gave Boston flexibility to evaluate more than one role during the remainder of the season.

Day Offered Scoring Potential, While Lister Offered Size

Day arrived with a reputation for putting points on the board from the wing, while Lister's long career gave Boston a reserve center who could supply physical depth. Their earlier Milwaukee seasons demonstrated different skills, but couldn't be counted as Celtics production after the trade. They were also at different points in their careers, with Day still offering a chance to build on past scoring while Lister was closer to a late-career support role. Boston's return was therefore a combination of two distinct roster options, not a newly minted superstar whose previous numbers should carry forward unchanged.

Milwaukee Focused Its Return on Sherman Douglas

The Bucks acquired Douglas, a guard with meaningful prior NBA responsibilities and a history of running an offense. Milwaukee could use him to organize possessions and stabilize the backcourt rather than waiting for an unproven draft pick. The cost was giving up Day's wing-scoring profile and Lister's size, so the club sacrificed two kinds of depth for one more targeted role. Douglas's previous work for Miami and Boston could inform expectations but did not automatically guarantee peak production in Milwaukee. His real value had to come from games after the November exchange and any later deals.

Neither Team Acquired a Durable Franchise Cornerstone

Boston received two players who could fill separate needs; Milwaukee gained a veteran guard with a more defined playmaking profile. None of those benefits was a premium draft asset or a guaranteed future All-Star, and both clubs continued through broader roster changes during the middle of the 1990s. That makes an even result more appropriate than assigning an outsized win to the side that received more names. The Celtics gained flexibility and the Bucks focused on an identified guard task. Both returns were practical but limited, which supports equal modest grades.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston earns C+ for Todd Day's wing-scoring option and Alton Lister's veteran frontcourt depth. Milwaukee gets C+ for experienced guard Sherman Douglas. The Celtics' two-for-one return created options rather than two automatic starters; Douglas's previous achievements with other teams do not become new Bucks performance simply because the trade occurred.

Boston Received Todd Day and Alton Lister in a Three-Player Exchange

On November 26, 1995, Boston acquired wing scorer Todd Day and veteran big man Alton Lister from Milwaukee in exchange for guard Sherman Douglas. The Celtics were rebuilding their identity and wanted additional options at two positions; the Bucks obtained one established ball handler instead of splitting the return across a perimeter scorer and an experienced center. All three were actual NBA players rather than speculative selections, so the immediate roster implications were more direct than a draft-rights swap. The two-player incoming package gave Boston flexibility to evaluate more than one role during the remainder of the season.

Day Offered Scoring Potential, While Lister Offered Size

Day arrived with a reputation for putting points on the board from the wing, while Lister's long career gave Boston a reserve center who could supply physical depth. Their earlier Milwaukee seasons demonstrated different skills, but couldn't be counted as Celtics production after the trade. They were also at different points in their careers, with Day still offering a chance to build on past scoring while Lister was closer to a late-career support role. Boston's return was therefore a combination of two distinct roster options, not a newly minted superstar whose previous numbers should carry forward unchanged.

Milwaukee Focused Its Return on Sherman Douglas

The Bucks acquired Douglas, a guard with meaningful prior NBA responsibilities and a history of running an offense. Milwaukee could use him to organize possessions and stabilize the backcourt rather than waiting for an unproven draft pick. The cost was giving up Day's wing-scoring profile and Lister's size, so the club sacrificed two kinds of depth for one more targeted role. Douglas's previous work for Miami and Boston could inform expectations but did not automatically guarantee peak production in Milwaukee. His real value had to come from games after the November exchange and any later deals.

Neither Team Acquired a Durable Franchise Cornerstone

Boston received two players who could fill separate needs; Milwaukee gained a veteran guard with a more defined playmaking profile. None of those benefits was a premium draft asset or a guaranteed future All-Star, and both clubs continued through broader roster changes during the middle of the 1990s. That makes an even result more appropriate than assigning an outsized win to the side that received more names. The Celtics gained flexibility and the Bucks focused on an identified guard task. Both returns were practical but limited, which supports equal modest grades.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston earns C+ for Todd Day's wing-scoring option and Alton Lister's veteran frontcourt depth. Milwaukee gets C+ for experienced guard Sherman Douglas. The Celtics' two-for-one return created options rather than two automatic starters; Douglas's previous achievements with other teams do not become new Bucks performance simply because the trade occurred.

memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
The Expansion Grizzlies Exchanged Their Leading Early Scorer

Vancouver traded veteran center Benoit Benjamin to the Milwaukee Bucks on November 27, 1995, getting guard Eric Murdock and second-year big man Eric Mobley. Benjamin had been the expansion franchise's leading scorer through its first thirteen games, but the team lacked dependable point-guard direction. Milwaukee had just added Sherman Douglas to its backcourt, making Murdock more available. The Grizzlies accepted a shorter center rotation in order to address a larger organizational weakness: distributing the ball while a completely new roster learned to play together.

Murdock Provided Sixty-Four Games of Playmaking

Murdock quickly became one of Vancouver's more productive guards. He played sixty-four regular-season games after the trade, starting fourteen, and averaged 9.1 points with 4.6 assists and 2.0 steals. He brought ball pressure and a much-needed ability to run half-court sets without relying solely on inexperienced teammates. Mobley gave Vancouver a second developmental frontcourt option. Neither player made the expansion club a contender, which finished fifteen wins and sixty-seven losses, but Murdock's actual new-team minutes offer stronger evidence of value than the team's poor record alone.

Milwaukee Got a Veteran Center With a Shorter Horizon

Benjamin was a legitimate NBA center who had already played for several franchises. Milwaukee received his size and post scoring as immediate frontcourt coverage, so its end of the trade was not empty. However, the scoring that made him Vancouver's early leader occurred before the Bucks acquired him. His earlier Clippers and Nets years must also be excluded from Milwaukee's receiving-team return. The Bucks were trading two different reserve roles for a known big man who could help their interior rotation, a sensible short-term choice rather than a developmental rebuild.

The Guard Upgrade Gave Vancouver the More Durable Benefit

Expansion teams often struggle to find a player who can organize their offense, and Vancouver gained one without sending out draft picks. Murdock wasn't an All-Star, but his passing and defensive activity supplied an identifiable sixty-four-game return. Milwaukee got the center it sought, while Mobley offered an additional young option in Vancouver. The original Grizzlies-winning assessment stands, although the better grade follows specific receiving-team results rather than assuming a bad expansion season invalidated every acquisition. Vancouver bought more playable positions with its departing center.

Final Verdict

Grizzlies Win. Vancouver receives A- because Eric Murdock supplied sixty-four games, 9.1 points and 4.6 assists per outing and Eric Mobley added frontcourt depth. Milwaukee earns C+ for acquiring Benoit Benjamin as a veteran center. The Grizzlies addressed two roster needs with one outgoing scorer while the Bucks obtained a shorter-term interior option.

memphis-grizzlies.summary: Minnesota acquired guard Darrick Martin from the Vancouver Grizzlies on January 12, 1996, for a 1996 second-rounder that ultimately became No. 49 Amal McCaskill. Martin played 35 Minnesota games in 1995-96 after the trade, totaling 747 minutes, 254 points and 156 assists. Vancouver traded the incoming pick to Orlando in February alongside Kenny Gattison for Jeff Turner; Orlando, not Vancouver, drafted McCaskill. Wolves Win, Minnesota B+, Vancouver C+.
memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
Minnesota Reacquired a Guard It Had Waived Months Earlier

On January 12, 1996, the Timberwolves sent their 1996 second-round draft selection to the expansion Vancouver Grizzlies for Darrick Martin. Minnesota had waived Martin in November, after using him during the previous season, and Vancouver signed him as a free agent days afterward. The trade therefore amounted to paying a future draft choice to bring back an experienced backup guard. Minnesota needed another ball handler while Kevin Garnett was developing and Flip Saunders had only recently taken over as head coach. Vancouver chose a future scouting asset over retaining a guard it had used during its difficult inaugural months.

Martin Played 35 Games and Handled the Ball for the Wolves

Martin appeared in 35 Minnesota regular-season games during the remainder of 1995-96, starting 16. He logged 747 minutes, scored 254 points and distributed 156 assists, averages of 7.3 points and 4.5 assists in 21.3 minutes. He was not an elite scorer, but he provided tangible point-guard cover and an established relationship with the young organization. His earlier 24 Vancouver games that season should not be counted as Minnesota's new return, and his later work for the Clippers also belongs to another franchise. The incoming value was a specific 35-game second stint, rather than his entire NBA career.

Vancouver Traded the Pick to Orlando Before the Draft

The compensation selection became the 1996 second-round No. 49 pick, eventually used on Amal McCaskill. However, Vancouver did not choose McCaskill or receive his later NBA production. On February 22 the Grizzlies sent that selection and veteran Kenny Gattison to Orlando for Jeff Turner, who was soon waived in March. Orlando subsequently drafted McCaskill. The pick's movement is essential to evaluating the original deal: the Grizzlies converted it into a component of another veteran exchange, but Turner was obtained with two outgoing assets. Assigning all of Turner's arrival, or McCaskill's later career, to this January trade would exaggerate the return.

The Wolves Obtained the More Definite Playing Value

Martin's 35 appearances gave Minnesota an immediate reserve guard who could play considerable minutes and set up teammates. Vancouver received a second-round option and promptly spent it within a broader February deal, so the direct basketball benefits are harder to isolate. The Grizzlies had a reason to prefer an asset with future flexibility on an expansion roster, but neither the later Orlando pick nor the full Jeff Turner transaction should become invented Vancouver playing statistics. The modest Minnesota advantage follows the receiving-team record rather than a claim that Martin was a transformative player or that Vancouver's draft asset had no value at all.

Final Verdict

Wolves Win. Minnesota earns B+ for Darrick Martin's 35 games, 747 minutes and 156 assists after the January 1996 swap. Vancouver gets C+ for a second-round asset it later included with Kenny Gattison to acquire Jeff Turner. Orlando ultimately selected Amal McCaskill at No. 49, so the draft choice's eventual NBA career is not a Vancouver contribution.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Received Christian Laettner and Sean Rooks

At the February 22, 1996 deadline, Atlanta acquired Christian Laettner and Sean Rooks from Minnesota in exchange for veteran guard Anthony 'Spud' Webb and center Andrew Lang. The Hawks' incoming pair offered a high-profile power forward and another true frontcourt player, aligning with a desire to improve their interior rotation. Minnesota obtained an experienced small guard and an established center. This wasn't a swap involving Laettner's college rights or a still-conditional future draft selection: he had already been playing NBA seasons with the Timberwolves when the transaction occurred.

memphis-grizzlies.summary: On February 22, 1996, the expansion Vancouver Grizzlies traded veteran forward Kenny Gattison and a 1996 second-round selection to Orlando for Jeff Turner. Vancouver waived Turner on March 8, only fifteen days later. Orlando used the second-round pick at No. 49 on Amal McCaskill, who logged 17 Magic regular-season games in 1996-97, alongside the Gattison acquisition. Magic Win: Orlando B- for two usable assets and Vancouver D for a short-lived replacement; Memphis is the database successor label for Vancouver.
memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
Vancouver Exchanged Gattison and a Draft Pick for Turner

On February 22, 1996, the first-year Vancouver Grizzlies sent Kenny Gattison and a future second-round draft selection to the Orlando Magic for veteran forward Jeff Turner. In the database this franchise is listed under Memphis, but the team actually played in Vancouver at the time. The pick had reached Vancouver through a January trade sending Darrick Martin to Minnesota, so it was not an entirely new asset created in February. Orlando was a championship contender seeking reserve frontcourt options. Vancouver, still constructing a functional inaugural roster, swapped two assets for a player who had already spent years with the Magic.

Turner's Vancouver Stay Ended in Fifteen Days

The Grizzlies barely had time to evaluate their acquired veteran before moving on. Vancouver's official transaction history records the trade on February 22 and Turner's waiver on March 8, 1996. That brief stint is the clearest problem with the prior Grizzlies-favored conclusion: the side giving up a player and a draft choice did not retain its incoming veteran through the season. Turner had been an experienced Orlando reserve, but his earlier NBA contributions belong to the Magic, not to the expansion team that briefly acquired him. The swap cannot be awarded a high Vancouver grade by borrowing years of pre-trade play.

Orlando Turned the Selection Into McCaskill

The second-round choice arrived in Orlando with draft value and ultimately became the forty-ninth pick in 1996. The Magic selected Amal McCaskill, a center who appeared in seventeen regular-season games for Orlando in 1996-97, making the pick's eventual output modest but real. Gattison also supplied an experienced frontcourt option from the original transaction. This is a two-part return: one NBA veteran and a developmental selection. McCaskill's later service with San Antonio, Atlanta and Philadelphia was not Orlando production, and should never be added to its return. His seventeen Magic games are a more defensible measure of what the pick actually delivered.

The Winner Changes When the Timeline Is Followed

The move looks different when the recipient clubs' subsequent rosters are checked rather than just counting acquired names on trade day. Vancouver obtained Turner and waived him within weeks, while Orlando kept the flexibility of veteran depth and exercised a future draft choice. Even with McCaskill's limited games, the Magic realized more direct value than Vancouver did. The Grizzlies' earlier acquisition of this second-round pick from Minnesota was a separate deal and must not be treated as extra compensation in February. Correcting the old verdict recognizes the entire chain while keeping the trade anchored to the actual exchange.

Final Verdict

Magic Win. Orlando earns B- because it received veteran Kenny Gattison plus the 1996 No. 49 pick used on Amal McCaskill, who later appeared in seventeen Magic games. The Vancouver Grizzlies, identified as Memphis in the franchise database, receive D because Jeff Turner was waived on March 8, only fifteen days after the exchange. Turner's Orlando career before February and McCaskill's later games elsewhere do not count toward the wrong recipient.

summary: Win. Indiana turned Mark Jackson, Ricky Pierce and a lower first-round pick into Jalen Rose, Reggie Williams and the No. 10 pick, then later brought Jackson back in a separate transaction. Rose became a core player on the 2000 Finals team, while Denver's veteran return was short-lived. IND A+, DEN D is the appropriate completed-value spread.
analysis: Indiana's return created the best long-term value by a wide margin. Rose developed into a versatile scorer and secondary playmaker, won Most Improved Player and became a major part of the Pacers team that reached the 2000 NBA Finals. Dampier did not remain in Indiana for long, but a top-10 pick still carried meaningful asset value and became a durable NBA center. Reggie Williams was secondary. The Pacers acquired youth, size and years of control without losing Jackson permanently. Denver received a very good point guard, and Jackson's passing immediately improved organization. The problem was duration. He stayed only part of a season before Denver sent him back to Indiana, while Pierce was near the end of his career and the No. 23 pick became Efthimios Rentzias, who did not develop into an NBA contributor for Denver. The Nuggets bought experience but did not convert it into a durable competitive advantage or a comparable asset chain. The follow-on chain makes Indiana's win unusually clear. Jackson eventually returned to the Pacers, so Indiana effectively regained the veteran it had surrendered while keeping the most important young piece from the first deal. That second trade required additional outgoing value and therefore should not be treated as free, but it still demonstrates how temporary Denver's advantage became. Rose, by contrast, stayed long enough to become part of Indiana's identity during its strongest Eastern Conference run.
