Portland's stronger receiving-team performance justifies the inherited Blazers Win, Portland A and Atlanta D.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Portland acquired Steve Smith and Ed Gray from Atlanta in August 1999, giving up Isaiah Rider and Jim Jackson. Smith supplied productive shooting and helped the Trail Blazers reach the 2000 Western Conference Finals, while Rider had a turbulent Hawks stay. Portland's stronger receiving-team performance justifies the inherited Blazers Win, Portland A and Atlanta D.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Portland Targeted Smith as a Better-Fitting Veteran Wing

The Trail Blazers traded Isaiah Rider and Jim Jackson to Atlanta on August 2, 1999, obtaining Steve Smith and Ed Gray. Portland was already a strong contender and wanted another established wing whose shooting and decision-making could serve a deep rotation. Atlanta accepted two veteran scorers while changing its offensive mix. Both Rider and Smith had substantial résumés, but their reliability and likely roles with the new teams differed. The exchange became a test of whether name recognition or roster fit would produce better results.

Smith Helped Portland Reach the Conference Finals

Smith became an important Portland scorer during the 1999-2000 season and helped the Trail Blazers advance to the Western Conference Finals. They pushed the eventual champion Lakers to seven games but did not win the championship. Smith's perimeter threat complemented the team's established frontcourt, giving the offense an experienced option in high-pressure playoff games. Ed Gray was a much smaller part of the package. The direct Portland value centered on a dependable contributor to a real contender.

Rider's Hawks Tenure Was Disrupted

Rider arrived with demonstrated NBA scoring ability, but disciplinary problems and roster tension undermined his time in Atlanta. He did not become the consistent long-term offensive presence the team needed. Jackson supplied veteran minutes but could not replace everything Smith offered in Portland. It is important to distinguish Rider's achievements with earlier teams from his receiving-team production; his talent made the gamble understandable, but the Hawks did not realize the corresponding sustained benefit. The incoming players failed to establish an equivalent dependable partnership.

The Difference Emerged in Their New Uniforms

The Blazers obtained useful scoring from Smith on a team that reached the league's final four. Atlanta acquired experienced players, but their actual roles were far less stable. The comparison isn't decided by which guard had the stronger career totals before 1999, because both possessed offensive ability. It is about the performance and reliability the two organizations obtained after the trade. Portland's fit and playoff value are the clearest reasons for the large inherited gap in grades.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win. Portland earns A for Steve Smith's productive wing play during its 2000 Western Conference Finals run, with Ed Gray a minor additional piece. Atlanta gets D because Isaiah Rider's turbulent Hawks stay and Jim Jackson's temporary role did not replace Smith's dependable contribution. Portland acquired the more reliable player for its immediate competitive objectives.

boston-celtics.summary: Boston acquired Danny Fortson, Eric Williams, Eric Washington and a future first-round right from Denver in August 1999 for Ron Mercer, Ronald Jones and Dwayne Schintzius. Williams became a useful Celtics forward again while the pick eventually became No. 11 Kedrick Brown in 2001. Mercer gave Denver scoring but moved on. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Turned Mercer Into a Broader Player Package

The Celtics sent Ron Mercer, Ronald Jones and Dwayne Schintzius to Denver in August 1999. Boston received Danny Fortson, Eric Williams, Eric Washington and a future first-round selection. Mercer was a talented young scorer, making the decision to move him notable for a club still developing around Paul Pierce. Boston chose several usable pieces and draft flexibility rather than continuing with another scoring wing. Denver accepted a player who could become a central offensive option without waiting for the future pick to mature.

Eric Williams Became the Most Durable Boston Return

Williams returned to the Celtics and played meaningful forward minutes through several seasons, giving Boston a dependable perimeter defender and role player. Fortson supplied rebounding in a shorter Boston stint, while Washington had a much smaller effect. The incoming first-round right eventually became No. 11 Kedrick Brown in 2001. Brown received NBA opportunities but did not emerge as the kind of star one might expect from a lottery selection. The combination still yielded more than one useful form of roster value for the Celtics.

Denver Received Mercer's Scoring but Not Longevity

Mercer gave the Nuggets an experienced young scoring option, but his Denver tenure was short. He later continued his career with other teams, and those subsequent appearances cannot be treated as Denver production from this transaction. Jones and Schintzius did not develop into major Nuggets pieces. The club's decision emphasized the appeal of adding a recognizable guard with offensive ability, yet the realized team-specific value did not last long enough to match Boston's broader options and several seasons from Williams.

The Multiple Incoming Assets Favored Boston

Boston acquired useful short-term big-man depth, a longer-serving forward and a draft opportunity in exchange for its outgoing scoring guard. None of those components should be credited with an invented championship, and the Kedrick Brown selection was not a particularly successful use of a lottery pick. Denver still received real NBA scoring from Mercer during his brief stay. The inherited Celtics edge comes from the wider package and sustained Williams contribution rather than a claim that every Boston acquisition became a major success.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston receives B+ for reacquiring useful forward Eric Williams and collecting Fortson, Washington and the first-round choice used on Kedrick Brown. Denver gets C+ for Ron Mercer's brief scoring contribution, with Jones and Schintzius offering less enduring value. Boston obtained the broader and more lasting set of usable options, although the later lottery pick didn't become a star.

orlando-magic.summary: Orlando sent Penny Hardaway to Phoenix on August 5, 1999 for Danny Manning, Pat Garrity and two future Suns first-round picks. Hardaway still gave Phoenix 236 regular-season games, including a 16.9-point first season and a strong 2000 playoff run, but injuries prevented a return to his Orlando peak. Garrity became a 513-game Magic rotation player, while both firsts retained trade value. The second pick was eventually returned to Phoenix before the 2002 draft, so Orlando must not be credited with Amar'e Stoudemire as a player.
orlando-magic.analysis:
The Exchange
Orlando and Phoenix transaction logs agree on the core package: Hardaway went to the Suns for Danny Manning, Pat Garrity and two future Phoenix first-round choices. The draft-chain history is the first correction to the legacy archive record. The 2001 first ultimately landed at No. 18 and was used on Jason Collins, but Orlando had already routed that pick onward in a later transaction. The second Phoenix first eventually became the No. 9 selection in 2002, yet Orlando traded that pick back to Phoenix in November 2001 as part of the Bo Outlaw/Jud Buechler deal. Phoenix then used its reacquired selection on Amar'e Stoudemire. Orlando therefore received valuable draft rights, not Jason Collins or Stoudemire as realized Magic players.

Phoenix Return
Hardaway's Suns tenure was injury-limited but substantial enough that a D grade is too punitive. In 1999-00 he played 60 games, started all 60 and averaged 16.9 points, 5.8 rebounds and 5.3 assists. He then elevated his production in the postseason, averaging 20.3 points, 4.9 rebounds and 5.7 assists across nine playoff games. Knee problems reduced him to four games in 2000-01, but he rebounded to 80 games and 55 starts in 2001-02. He played 58 more games in 2002-03 and 34 in 2003-04 before Phoenix traded him to New York. Across the Suns portion created by this deal, Hardaway appeared in 236 regular-season games with 180 starts. Phoenix never got the healthy superstar pairing with Jason Kidd that it envisioned, but it did receive several seasons of starter-level guard play and one genuinely strong playoff run.

Orlando Return
Garrity became the direct long-term success. After spending his rookie season in Phoenix, he played the remaining 513 games of his NBA career with Orlando, providing shooting and frontcourt depth from 1999-00 through 2007-08. His peak came in 2001-02, when he played 80 games, started 43 and averaged 11.1 points while shooting 42.7 percent from three. Manning never played a regular-season game for Orlando. Two weeks after the Hardaway trade, the Magic packaged Manning with Dale Ellis to Milwaukee for Chris Gatling and Armen Gilliam. Gatling then played 45 games for Orlando in 1999-00 before another trade, so Manning still functioned as transaction capital even though his direct Magic value was zero. The two first-round rights also had real market value. Orlando passed the 2001 first onward during the 1999 offseason, and the 2002 first became part of the 2001 three-team trade that returned it to Phoenix. Those later transactions should be evaluated separately; the key source-backed point is that both picks remained useful assets without becoming Collins or Stoudemire for Orlando.

Hindsight Verdict
Orlando wins, but not by the enormous margin implied by treating the 2002 pick as if the Magic themselves drafted Amar'e Stoudemire. The Magic acquired nine seasons of Garrity plus two first-round assets and reusable Manning value from a star whose injuries had already become a major risk. Phoenix still received 236 Hardaway games, 180 starts and meaningful playoff production, which warrants a solid B rather than a D. Orlando earns an A- because the package produced a long-term rotation player and multiple tradable assets while avoiding Hardaway's most injury-affected seasons. Final verdict: Orlando Magic Win.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Two Future Firsts Sent Lorenzen Wright to Atlanta

The Hawks acquired center Lorenzen Wright from the Los Angeles Clippers in August 1999. Rather than surrender a single current NBA player, Atlanta committed two conditional first-round selections with separate draft years and protection formulas. The 2000 lottery-protected pick eventually matched the No. 18 position associated with Quentin Richardson; the top-four-protected 2002 choice eventually matched No. 8 Chris Wilcox. Those eventual draft slots were not certain on the original agreement date. Atlanta wanted a player it could use immediately in its interior rotation, while Los Angeles valued having two opportunities to add or move young talent across different summers.

Wright Was a Real NBA Center, Not a Guaranteed Star

Wright offered rebounding, size and experience beyond what an unknown late-first prospect might provide right away. He could compete for minutes with Atlanta's established frontcourt players and provide an accessible basketball return while the future picks remained contingent. His previous Clippers games weren't new Hawks production, and the real value of his acquired contract depended on seasons after August 1999. The deal therefore had a coherent short-term purpose, particularly for a team seeking to support its existing veterans. Yet even a useful center couldn't guarantee a long playoff breakthrough, making the price in two firsts particularly important.

Los Angeles Held Two Different Draft Opportunities

The Clippers' incoming draft rights eventually became identifiable at No. 18 in 2000 and No. 8 in 2002. Those were valuable positions for a franchise seeking roster growth, even though obtaining a future selection didn't mean a named player was under contract in 1999. Quentin Richardson and Chris Wilcox provide later landmarks for following the picks, but each player's actual NBA games belong to the franchise that ultimately signed him. The protection rules also meant the Clippers bore timing and conveyance uncertainty until the conditions resolved. Still, splitting the compensation across two first-round paths offered more development options than retaining one current center.

The Draft Capital Tips the Retrospective Toward the Clippers

Atlanta gained an available professional player, which shouldn't be dismissed simply because the Clippers later received attractive selections. Nonetheless, two first-round choices at eventual No. 18 and No. 8 represent a sizable opportunity cost for a supporting frontcourt acquisition. Los Angeles converted one center into two distinct swings at young talent, giving it greater long-term flexibility. The trade merits a Clippers-winning conclusion without falsely declaring every subsequent Richardson or Wilcox season a direct benefit of the 1999 transfer. Its main lesson is the need to value protected future picks separately rather than collapsing them into a generic late selection.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win. Atlanta Hawks earns C-; Los Angeles Clippers earns A-. orlando-magic.summary: Orlando sent Ike Austin to Washington on August 11, 1999 for Ben Wallace, Terry Davis, Tim Legler and Jeff McInnis. Wallace immediately started all 81 Magic games, averaged 8.2 rebounds and 1.6 blocks, then became part of the 2000 Grant Hill sign-and-trade. Davis and McInnis were waived before contributing, Legler never played for Orlando, and Austin gave Washington 59 games and 23 starts. The one-year Wallace return alone created a clear Orlando advantage, but Washington did receive real short-term center minutes.
orlando-magic.analysis:
The Exchange
Orlando and Washington transaction logs agree on the August 11, 1999 package: the Magic sent Isaac 'Ike' Austin to the Wizards for Ben Wallace, Terry Davis, Tim Legler and Jeff McInnis. The legacy asset ledger is directionally correct, but the original short analysis overvalues Wallace's later Detroit career as if Orlando directly realized all of it. A source-backed grade has to separate what Wallace did for the Magic from the value Orlando later carried into another transaction.

Orlando Return
Wallace was the decisive asset. In 1999-00 he played 81 games, started all 81 and averaged 4.8 points, 8.2 rebounds, 0.9 steals and 1.6 blocks in 24.2 minutes. He gave Doc Rivers' overachieving 41-41 club a full season of elite rebounding and rim protection before he had yet reached his Detroit peak. Orlando then included Wallace with Chucky Atkins in the August 3, 2000 sign-and-trade for Grant Hill. That later deal is a separate transaction and Hill's Orlando results should not be credited here, but Wallace clearly retained meaningful transaction value rather than walking away for nothing. The other three incoming players produced little direct Magic value. Basketball-Reference records Terry Davis as acquired and waived without playing in 1999-00; Orlando waived Jeff McInnis on September 16 before he appeared in a game for the club; and Tim Legler's 1999-00 regular-season action came with Golden State rather than Orlando. That makes Wallace the overwhelming source of the Magic's realized return.

Washington Return
Austin was not an empty asset. He played 59 games for Washington in 1999-00, started 23 and averaged 6.7 points, 4.8 rebounds and 1.3 assists in 19.9 minutes. Those are legitimate rotation-center minutes, and they keep Washington's grade above an F. He did not become a long-term piece, however, and the Wizards had surrendered a 25-year-old Wallace who had already shown strong defensive and rebounding indicators in Washington. The loss is especially stark because Wallace immediately became an 81-game starter in Orlando while Austin's Washington tenure lasted only that season.

Hindsight Verdict
Orlando wins comfortably, but the correct case is more disciplined than 'the Magic acquired a future Hall of Famer.' The transaction itself gave Orlando one full season of high-end defensive production from Wallace plus an asset valuable enough to be used in a major 2000 sign-and-trade. Washington got one useful season of Austin, which prevents the return from being worthless, but it surrendered the best player in the deal and three additional contracts to obtain him. An A for Orlando recognizes the 81 starts, defensive production and retained transaction value without crediting the Magic for Wallace's later Pistons championships and awards. A D+ for Washington reflects real but short-lived Austin minutes against a much more valuable outgoing centerpiece. Final verdict: Orlando Magic Win.

Orlando wins comfortably, but the correct case is more disciplined than 'the Magic acquired a future Hall of Famer.' The transaction itself gave Orlando one full season of high-end defensive production from Wallace plus an asset valuable enough to be used in a major 2000 sign-and-trade. Washington got one useful season of Austin, which prevents the return from being worthless, but it surrendered the best player in the deal and three additional contracts to obtain him. An A for Orlando recognizes the 81 starts, defensive production and retained transaction value without crediting the Magic for Wallace's later Pistons championships and awards. A D+ for Washington reflects real but short-lived Austin minutes against a much more valuable outgoing centerpiece. Final verdict: Orlando Magic Win.

orlando-magic.summary: On August 13, 1999 Philadelphia acquired veteran Billy Owens from Orlando for Harvey Grant and Anthony Parker. Orlando waived Grant before the season and played Parker sixteen regular-season games and 185 minutes before waiving him in January. Owens saw regular-season action for Philadelphia before being included in a later multiteam exchange. The older Magic-favored verdict overlooked both waivers. 76ers Win, Philadelphia B-, Orlando C-.
orlando-magic.analysis:
Philadelphia Added a Veteran Forward for Two Bench Players

The Sixers acquired Billy Owens from Orlando on August 13, 1999, surrendering veteran Harvey Grant and young guard Anthony Parker. Owens had a long record as a versatile NBA forward, and Philadelphia sought frontcourt help to complement Allen Iverson’s scoring. The Magic were reorganizing their roster and preferred to evaluate two different players rather than retain Owens. Parker was a former first-round prospect who had yet to establish himself. Grant had much more league experience but was closer to the end of his professional career.

Orlando Released Both Incoming Players Within Months

Orlando waived Harvey Grant on October 2, 1999, before the regular season began. Parker survived training camp and appeared in sixteen Magic regular-season games, totaling 185 minutes and fifty-seven points before the January 2000 waiver. That was the sum of Orlando’s direct on-court return. Parker later built an impressive career overseas and became a valuable Toronto Raptors starter years later, but none of those Toronto statistics belong to the Magic. The acquired young guard did not mature into a long-term contributor for the franchise that obtained him here.

Owens Retained Playing and Transactional Use in Philadelphia

Owens joined Philadelphia as an established forward who could provide ball movement and help around its leading perimeter star. He played for the Sixers during the early 1999-00 campaign before the franchise included him in a major three-team transaction in February involving multiple teams, contracts and established players. The subsequent exchange brought Toni Kukoč to Philadelphia but cannot be represented as a simple one-for-one Owens-for-Kukoč trade. His value as one piece of a larger package still illustrates that Philadelphia extracted some additional utility from the acquired veteran.

The Two Waivers Changed the Historical Evaluation

Neither side acquired a lasting star, and Owens did not spend several seasons in Philadelphia. However, Orlando’s two-player return evaporated quickly: Grant played no Magic regular-season games and Parker logged only a small rookie stint. By comparison Philadelphia received an available veteran and later included his contract in another trade. The original Magic-favored grade appears to have treated Parker’s later success elsewhere as potential retrospective value for Orlando. That would misallocate production between organizations. The Sixers obtained the more usable immediate roster asset.

Final Verdict

76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B- for obtaining Billy Owens as an available 1999-00 forward and later using him within a broader February trade. Orlando gets C- after waiving Harvey Grant before opening night and playing Anthony Parker for only sixteen games and 185 minutes. Parker’s later Toronto years cannot be added to the Magic’s return.

summary: Houston acquired Steve Francis and Tony Massenburg from Vancouver plus Don MacLean and Orlando's 2001 first-round pick; Vancouver received Michael Dickerson, Othella Harrington, Brent Price, Antoine Carr and draft assets; Orlando received four Vancouver players.
analysis: Houston won the deal by landing the best player by a wide margin. Steve Francis shared Rookie of the Year honors, became a three-time All-Star with the Rockets and averaged 19.3 points, 5.5 rebounds and 6.2 assists across five Houston seasons before becoming a centerpiece of the 2004 Tracy McGrady trade. Vancouver still extracted a respectable package despite Francis refusing to play there: Michael Dickerson averaged 18.2 points in 1999-00, Othella Harrington averaged 13.1 points and 6.9 rebounds, and the Grizzlies also received draft value. Orlando fared worst, surrendering a first-round pick and a second-round pick while receiving a group that produced little lasting value for the Magic.

perspectives.analysis:
Charlotte Acquired a Veteran Shooter During the 1999-2000 Season

The Charlotte Hornets brought in Dale Ellis from Milwaukee in January 2000, paying two future second-round draft choices for a player near the end of a long NBA career. Ellis had been a prolific outside shooter over many seasons, but Charlotte was buying a present-day veteran option rather than the high-scoring Seattle star of the late 1980s. Milwaukee chose draft flexibility instead of retaining an aging reserve. Historical transaction ledgers differ by approximately one day on the announcement date, but agree on the clubs and two selections. This Charlotte franchise later relocated to New Orleans, although the contemporary team name was Hornets.

The Bucks Collected Two Picks Instead of Long-Term Veteran Minutes

The first incoming selection became the forty-ninth pick of the 2000 draft, associated with guard Jason Hart. The second ultimately became the forty-seventh choice in 2002, associated with Chris Owens. Those selections provided Milwaukee with assets to exercise or move through further negotiations rather than a guarantee of two successful rotation players. Hart went on to spend time in the NBA with several franchises, and it would be misleading to credit his entire professional career to the Bucks because of this draft-rights trade. The Owens selection likewise had value as a pick without becoming evidence of years of Milwaukee on-court production.

Ellis Was a Short-Term Addition for the Hornets

Charlotte received an accomplished shooter whose prime seasons were long behind him. He appeared for the Hornets in the final stage of his NBA career, so the club should not be awarded the three-point scoring totals Ellis produced for Seattle, Denver or Milwaukee before January. Acquiring a veteran for a playoff push can still serve a club's immediate roster objectives, even when his remaining time is limited. That short horizon is central to valuing the transaction. Charlotte was not receiving draft picks or additional players back from Milwaukee, and the pick cost was not a protected future first-round obligation.

Future Options Outweighed a Brief Final Career Stint

Milwaukee's side held two chances to add inexpensive future players or deploy second-round rights in a separate transaction, while Charlotte received a veteran who did not become a lasting piece. Neither path created a star directly from the agreement, which argues against an extreme grade for the Bucks. Still, converting an aging reserve into multiple selections was more durable than Charlotte's limited end-of-career minutes. The judgment must separate what the Bucks acquired in January from the later clubs that used the selected players. Charlotte Acquired a Veteran Shooter During the 1999-2000 Season

The Charlotte Hornets brought in Dale Ellis from Milwaukee in January 2000, paying two future second-round draft choices for a player near the end of a long NBA career. Ellis had been a prolific outside shooter over many seasons, but Charlotte was buying a present-day veteran option rather than the high-scoring Seattle star of the late 1980s. Milwaukee chose draft flexibility instead of retaining an aging reserve. Historical transaction ledgers differ by approximately one day on the announcement date, but agree on the clubs and two selections. This Charlotte franchise later relocated to New Orleans, although the contemporary team name was Hornets.

The Bucks Collected Two Picks Instead of Long-Term Veteran Minutes

The first incoming selection became the forty-ninth pick of the 2000 draft, associated with guard Jason Hart. The second ultimately became the forty-seventh choice in 2002, associated with Chris Owens. Those selections provided Milwaukee with assets to exercise or move through further negotiations rather than a guarantee of two successful rotation players. Hart went on to spend time in the NBA with several franchises, and it would be misleading to credit his entire professional career to the Bucks because of this draft-rights trade. The Owens selection likewise had value as a pick without becoming evidence of years of Milwaukee on-court production.

Ellis Was a Short-Term Addition for the Hornets

Charlotte received an accomplished shooter whose prime seasons were long behind him. He appeared for the Hornets in the final stage of his NBA career, so the club should not be awarded the three-point scoring totals Ellis produced for Seattle, Denver or Milwaukee before January. Acquiring a veteran for a playoff push can still serve a club's immediate roster objectives, even when his remaining time is limited. That short horizon is central to valuing the transaction. Charlotte was not receiving draft picks or additional players back from Milwaukee, and the pick cost was not a protected future first-round obligation.

Milwaukee's side held two chances to add inexpensive future players or deploy second-round rights in a separate transaction, while Charlotte received a veteran who did not become a lasting piece. perspectives.analysis:
Philadelphia Sought Kukoč's Championship Experience

The 76ers acquired Toni Kukoč from Chicago in February 2000, adding a skilled scoring and passing forward alongside Allen Iverson. Kukoč had been part of the Bulls' championship dynasty but was playing for a franchise that had entered a lengthy rebuilding period. Philadelphia accepted his veteran contract because the team wanted another capable offensive creator before the playoffs. Acquiring him required sending useful young guard Larry Hughes and forward Billy Owens to Golden State, rather than paying only an abstract draft consideration.

Golden State Received Hughes and Owens

The Warriors obtained Hughes and Owens from Philadelphia. Hughes was a young scoring guard with potential to grow into a larger offensive role; Owens brought wing and forward experience. Golden State sent John Starks and a protected first-round right to Chicago while participating in the three-club exchange. A prior Bulls-centered ledger recorded the Warriors as receiving nothing, omitting the pair who made their participation meaningful. Hughes's later career was broader than Golden State alone, so its return should be evaluated through his actual tenure.

Chicago Acquired Starks, Bowen and a Protected First

The Bulls received Starks from Golden State and Bruce Bowen through the 76ers as part of the same transaction, plus a first-round right associated with the No. 7 selection in 2000. That pick was later linked to Chris Mihm, though subsequent draft moves determine where he actually played. Starks provided veteran guard experience, and Bowen offered wing defense but did not become a long-term Chicago foundation. Chicago was rebuilding, making draft leverage and financial flexibility more important than immediate contention.

The Grades Favor Two Different Kinds of Present Return

Philadelphia's A- reflects Kukoč's established offensive ability and postseason experience. Golden State also receives A- for acquiring Hughes and Owens as current and developmental players, while Chicago's D considers the uncertain value of its veteran stopgaps and protected pick. The slight 76ers edge is inherited, not proof that Chicago got no legitimate compensation. Accurate analysis must show the final asset paths, including the two players Golden State acquired from Philadelphia.

Final Verdict

Slight 76ers Edge. Philadelphia earns A- for Toni Kukoč's experienced scoring and passing. Golden State also earns A- for receiving Larry Hughes and Billy Owens, both previously omitted from the Bulls-only import. Chicago gets D for John Starks, Bruce Bowen and a protected 2000 first-round right linked to Chris Mihm. The three-team transaction is now evaluated with all clubs' actual returns.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Orlando Acquired a Veteran Guard for a Future Choice

Orlando acquired Anthony Johnson from Atlanta in February 2000, sending a conditional second-round selection to the Hawks. Johnson was an NBA reserve rather than an established star, but he offered the Magic additional ball-handling experience for the remainder of the campaign. Atlanta accepted a draft asset that would not provide an immediate guard replacement. The conditional terms gave the outgoing club a chance to receive value in a later draft, while Orlando could evaluate a player who had already demonstrated he could handle limited professional minutes.

Johnson Supplied the Direct Playing Opportunity

The Magic's advantage in the transaction came from receiving a real guard rather than solely a speculative future selection. Johnson could contribute spot minutes, assist with organizing the offense and offer an alternative when the primary backcourt needed relief. His later career with other franchises doesn't belong to the Orlando return, just as his previous Atlanta tenure isn't production the Magic created. The relevant advantage was access to an NBA player immediately after the February deadline. That benefit was modest, but it was more concrete than an option several drafts in the future.

Atlanta's Conditional Pick Took Years to Resolve

Atlanta's return was a conditional second that could be realized during the 2000-04 draft window. The historical record associates that line with the No. 42 selection in 2004, used on Viktor Sanikidze. Such a draft identity should not be confused with Sanikidze providing Hawks regular-season production. His professional basketball career took place outside the NBA, and the pick-rights chain can be considered separately from any games played for Atlanta. The Hawks accepted future flexibility at the cost of surrendering a reserve they could have used right away.

A Limited On-Court Advantage Favors the Magic

Neither franchise transformed its roster with this trade, and the delayed nature of Atlanta's compensation was understandable. Orlando obtained a guard it could put into competition, while the Hawks obtained a selection whose eventual basketball payoff was limited. The C+ grade for the Magic reflects that direct utility without treating Johnson as a starting-caliber acquisition. Atlanta's C- acknowledges the value of a draft chance while recognizing that the team did not secure comparable NBA minutes from the pick. A small, practical advantage belongs to Orlando.

Final Verdict

Magic Win. Orlando earns C+ for acquiring Anthony Johnson and immediate guard depth. Atlanta gets C- for the conditional future second-round pick associated with the 2004 No. 42 selection and Viktor Sanikidze, which did not turn into an equivalent Hawks NBA contributor. The Magic obtained the clearer short-term basketball return without acquiring a foundational player.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Chose One International Prospect

The Celtics acquired the rights to Croatian guard-forward Josip Sesar from the Seattle SuperSonics during the 2000 draft, sending two second-round choices for 2001. Boston was exploring overseas development instead of waiting until the following year to make its selections. Seattle preferred to add opportunities in a future draft. Sesar had professional experience in Europe and offensive skill, but his path to playing in the NBA was uncertain when the trade was completed.

Sesar Never Became a Celtics NBA Contributor

The Celtics controlled an interesting European player's rights, yet Sesar never established an NBA playing career with Boston. His achievements abroad have their own importance, but they were not minutes in a Celtics uniform. The transaction therefore supplied an opportunity that did not turn into a rotation wing. This is the central limitation of the Boston side: the club paid two later selections for a prospect it couldn't use in the NBA.

Seattle Held Two Picks in the 2001 Draft

The SuperSonics acquired second-round choices associated with No. 38 Michael Wright and No. 39 Earl Watson. Wright did not develop into a major NBA performer, but Watson built a lengthy professional career as a point guard, including time with Seattle. His subsequent work for other franchises should be evaluated separately from his original SuperSonics arrival. Even without treating both picks as successes, Seattle obtained a notably stronger practical return than an unused NBA draft right.

The Pick Trade Favored the SuperSonics

Seattle's broader draft package produced a guard capable of contributing in the league, while Boston's single rights acquisition never joined its playing roster. houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired Jason Collier's draft rights and a protected 2001 first-round choice in exchange for Joel Przybilla's rights in June 2000. Milwaukee obtained an eventual NBA starting center in Przybilla, while Houston brought Collier into its NBA rotation and used the later No. 22 pick on Jeryl Sasser. Both Rockets players reached the league, but Przybilla offered Milwaukee a longer interior run. Bucks Win, B+ versus C+.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Moved Down in the 2000 Draft to Add Another Pick

The Rockets traded the rights to Joel Przybilla to Milwaukee during the June 28, 2000 NBA draft, receiving the rights to Jason Collier and a protected future first-round selection. Milwaukee wanted a true center taken in the top ten, while Houston saw an opportunity to add two prospects instead of one. The immediate draft rights gave the Rockets a developing big man, and the protected future choice preserved another chance to select a guard or wing. The transaction was an exchange of draft capital before the players began their NBA careers.

Przybilla Developed Into a Milwaukee Interior Option

Przybilla joined Milwaukee's center group and spent several seasons with the Bucks. He offered rebounding, shot-blocking and a more traditional inside defensive role rather than a high-volume scoring game. Injuries interrupted parts of his Milwaukee tenure, but he still became a regular NBA presence and later built a long career with other franchises. Only the first Milwaukee years count toward this incoming transaction. His most durable later Portland seasons are not evidence that the Bucks retained the same center for that entire period.

Houston Got Collier and the Future Jeryl Sasser Selection

The Rockets used Collier during the early 2000s and eventually received the deferred first-round pick. That selection reached the 2001 draft as No. 22 and was used on Jeryl Sasser. Both prospects played regular-season NBA games for Houston, showing that the package was not simply a set of empty rights. Neither player established the kind of sustained frontcourt rotation role that Przybilla later supplied for Milwaukee, but the two selections offered Houston separate development paths. The inherited Rockets D- grade was too dismissive of those genuine NBA opportunities.

Milwaukee's Center Had the More Enduring Team Contribution

Both organizations received NBA players instead of leaving their acquired rights unused. Houston diversified its draft investment, while Milwaukee concentrated value in a larger center whose defensive specialty gave him a longer initial NBA role. That tradeoff was reasonable in 2000 when the players had not yet proved themselves. Retrospectively, Przybilla's years of Bucks interior duty outperformed the shorter individual Rockets stints. The result supports a Milwaukee win with positive, not extreme, grades for both sides, rather than treating Houston's extra first-round selection as worthless.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns B+ for Joel Przybilla's multi-season center presence after acquiring his draft rights in 2000. Houston earns C+ because Jason Collier played NBA games for the Rockets and the later first-round choice became No. 22 Jeryl Sasser in 2001. Houston received two real prospects, but Milwaukee obtained the steadier direct frontcourt return.

los-angeles-lakers.summary: On June 28, 2000, the Lakers bought draft rights to Cory Hightower from San Antonio for two future second-round picks, ultimately 2001 No. 56 Robertas Javtokas and 2002 No. 56 Randy Holcomb. The Lakers signed Hightower in August but waived him October 30 without a regular-season appearance. Neither later selection developed into Spurs NBA playing time, but San Antonio controlled two bona fide draft assets. Spurs Win on asset retention, C+ versus D+.
los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Lakers Spent Two Future Picks on Hightower's Rights

The Lakers obtained Cory Hightower's player rights from San Antonio during the June 28, 2000 NBA draft, sending their second-round selections in 2001 and 2002 to the Spurs. Los Angeles had just won a championship and could afford to search for an inexpensive forward without depending on him for immediate starting minutes. Hightower had played college basketball at Indian Hills and been evaluated as a physical scorer. San Antonio preferred two future chances to draft players rather than hold one prospect from the current class.

Hightower Signed but Was Waived Before Opening Night

Los Angeles signed Hightower to a multi-year agreement in August 2000, giving him a legitimate roster opportunity. The club released him on October 30, before the 2000-01 regular season began, according to its transaction archive. Hightower never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Lakers. The team went on to win another championship, but his preseason audition was not part of that playing achievement. His development and activity outside the league cannot be converted into franchise NBA games after the waiver.

San Antonio Used Both Second-Round Selections

The incoming 2001 selection landed at No. 56 overall and was used on center Robertas Javtokas. The 2002 pick became No. 56 Randy Holcomb. Those were actual draft selections, not conditional obligations that evaporated before draft night. Neither player produced a regular-season NBA appearance for San Antonio from this pair of selections. Javtokas in particular had a notable basketball career abroad, but European club performances are not Spurs NBA contributions. The genuine return was control of two draft opportunities rather than a proven NBA rotation player.

Two Draft Chances Beat a Player Who Never Reached the Roster

Both sides accepted development risks rather than trading established veterans. The Lakers' gamble on Hightower ended without a regular-season appearance, making the original high Los Angeles grade hard to defend. The Spurs did receive two picks that could have been used on different prospects, so their asset return was more tangible than an unsuccessful camp audition. Yet neither selection led to Spurs NBA playing time and the original B+ grade also overstated the final sporting outcome. A modest San Antonio win captures the asymmetry without assigning imagined contributions.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win. San Antonio earns C+ for receiving two actual future selections, 2001 No. 56 Robertas Javtokas and 2002 No. 56 Randy Holcomb, despite neither becoming a Spurs NBA contributor. Los Angeles earns D+ for Cory Hightower, who signed in August 2000 but was waived October 30 without playing a Lakers regular-season game. The former high grades exaggerated both teams' realized production.

Neither later selection developed into Spurs NBA playing time, but San Antonio controlled two bona fide draft assets. Spurs Win on asset retention, C+ versus D+.
analysis:
The Lakers Spent Two Future Picks on Hightower's Rights

The Lakers obtained Cory Hightower's player rights from San Antonio during the June 28, 2000 NBA draft, sending their second-round selections in 2001 and 2002 to the Spurs. Los Angeles had just won a championship and could afford to search for an inexpensive forward without depending on him for immediate starting minutes. Hightower had played college basketball at Indian Hills and been evaluated as a physical scorer. San Antonio preferred two future chances to draft players rather than hold one prospect from the current class.

Hightower Signed but Was Waived Before Opening Night

Los Angeles signed Hightower to a multi-year agreement in August 2000, giving him a legitimate roster opportunity. The club released him on October 30, before the 2000-01 regular season began, according to its transaction archive. Hightower never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Lakers. The team went on to win another championship, but his preseason audition was not part of that playing achievement. His development and activity outside the league cannot be converted into franchise NBA games after the waiver.

San Antonio Used Both Second-Round Selections

The incoming 2001 selection landed at No. 56 overall and was used on center Robertas Javtokas. The 2002 pick became No. 56 Randy Holcomb. Those were actual draft selections, not conditional obligations that evaporated before draft night. Neither player produced a regular-season NBA appearance for San Antonio from this pair of selections. Javtokas in particular had a notable basketball career abroad, but European club performances are not Spurs NBA contributions. The genuine return was control of two draft opportunities rather than a proven NBA rotation player.

Two Draft Chances Beat a Player Who Never Reached the Roster

Both sides accepted development risks rather than trading established veterans. The Lakers' gamble on Hightower ended without a regular-season appearance, making the original high Los Angeles grade hard to defend. The Spurs did receive two picks that could have been used on different prospects, so their asset return was more tangible than an unsuccessful camp audition. Yet neither selection led to Spurs NBA playing time and the original B+ grade also overstated the final sporting outcome. A modest San Antonio win captures the asymmetry without assigning imagined contributions.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win. San Antonio earns C+ for receiving two actual future selections, 2001 No. 56 Robertas Javtokas and 2002 No. 56 Randy Holcomb, despite neither becoming a Spurs NBA contributor. Los Angeles earns D+ for Cory Hightower, who signed in August 2000 but was waived October 30 without playing a Lakers regular-season game. The former high grades exaggerated both teams' realized production.

perspectives.summary: On August 3, 2000, Toronto completed a sign-and-trade that sent free agent Tracy McGrady to Orlando for a conditional future first-round pick. McGrady immediately became an elite scorer, won Most Improved Player in 2001 and later captured consecutive scoring titles with the Magic. Toronto did not simply hold the compensatory pick until 2005: the Raptors moved it to Detroit in February 2001 as part of the package that brought Jerome Williams and Eric Montross, so the pick's eventual use on Fran Vázquez belongs to a later chain rather than Toronto's direct return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Contemporary reporting describes the August 3, 2000 move as a sign-and-trade after Tracy McGrady chose Orlando in free agency. Toronto re-signed McGrady to a seven-year maximum contract and then sent him to the Magic for a conditional future first-round pick. Basketball-Reference later identifies that obligation as Orlando's 2005 first-round choice. The sign-and-trade context is important because Toronto was not deciding between keeping McGrady and taking the pick on ordinary trade terms; McGrady had already chosen to leave, and the mechanism allowed him a longer contract while giving the Raptors compensation.

Orlando Return
McGrady's leap was immediate. He won the 2000-01 Most Improved Player award, made the All-Star team in each of his four Orlando seasons and developed into one of the league's premier scorers. He averaged 32.1 points per game in 2002-03 and 28.0 in 2003-04, winning consecutive scoring titles, and earned repeated All-NBA recognition. The Magic did not win a playoff series during his tenure, which keeps the realized team result short of a championship-level return, but obtaining a perennial All-NBA guard for a single future first still created enormous basketball value.

Toronto Return
The legacy archive entry incorrectly compresses the compensatory pick's entire later chain into 'Fran Vázquez never played in the NBA.' Toronto did not make that 2005 selection. On February 22, 2001, the Raptors sent the same 2005 first to Detroit along with Corliss Williamson, Tyrone Corbin and Kornél Dávid for Jerome Williams and Eric Montross. Because that later trade contained several assets on both sides, it would be unsafe to assign all of Williams or Montross to the McGrady pick alone. The source-safe conclusion is narrower: Toronto recovered a real first-round asset and used it as part of a subsequent trade package, so its return was not literally zero even though it never approached McGrady's Orlando value.

Hindsight Verdict
Orlando receives an A+ for turning one future first into four seasons of elite McGrady production. Toronto receives a C- rather than the legacy F because the sign-and-trade recovered a meaningful first-round asset after McGrady had chosen to leave, and the club later used that asset in another transaction. The final verdict is Orlando Magic Win by a wide margin. This grading preserves the actual transaction context while refusing to credit Toronto with the 2005 selection itself or pretend the compensatory pick vanished without value.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland sent Shawn Kemp to Portland in August 2000 and acquired Clarence Weatherspoon, Chris Gatling, Gary Grant, a conditional first-round choice and cash. The Trail Blazers obtained Kemp while Miami received Brian Grant through a sign-and-trade. The imported Cleveland-side history had omitted Miami's incoming forward, now restored from Miami's official media guide. The inherited Cavaliers Win grades Cleveland A-, Portland C and Miami C.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Converted Kemp's Contract Into a Wider Package

The Cavaliers moved Shawn Kemp to Portland on August 30, 2000, in an agreement that also brought Miami into the exchange. Cleveland obtained forwards Clarence Weatherspoon and Chris Gatling from the Heat, veteran guard Gary Grant from the Trail Blazers, a conditional Miami first-round choice and cash considerations. The first-round selection later became associated with No. 20 Brendan Haywood in 2001. The deal addressed Cleveland's complicated frontcourt finances while allowing the franchise to examine multiple replacements rather than one incoming superstar.

Miami Acquired Brian Grant From Portland

The Heat obtained Brian Grant, the physical power forward who had played for Portland. Miami's own historical media guide explicitly describes his arrival through the three-party agreement, resolving a missing incoming side in the original Cleveland-centered archive. Grant offered rebounding, interior defense and veteran experience that Miami could use alongside its existing rotation. The franchise surrendered Weatherspoon, Gatling, a first-round obligation and cash in pursuit of that role. Grant's prior Portland numbers supplied context, not completed Miami production on the transaction date.

Portland Took a Risk on Kemp's Existing Reputation

The Trail Blazers acquired Shawn Kemp, a former All-Star whose athletic dominance in Seattle was still familiar to NBA fans. By 2000, concerns about conditioning and a substantial contract had made his remaining production much harder to forecast. Portland sent Brian Grant away and also routed Gary Grant to Cleveland, making the transaction more involved than a straight swap of power forwards. Kemp's earlier SuperSonics achievements did not automatically translate to the Blazers. The team accepted that uncertainty for the potential upside of his experience.

The Cavaliers' Grade Values Flexibility and Multiple Assets

Cleveland's inherited A- rewards the combined return of three established NBA players, draft rights and money. Portland and Miami receive C each for their decisions to invest in different veteran power forwards. The conditional 2001 first should be traced through its actual rights movement; naming Brendan Haywood doesn't mean he played his NBA career in Cleveland. The original record wrongly portrayed Miami as receiving nothing, an omission that hid the purpose of surrendering significant compensation. Restoring Brian Grant permits a fairer three-team assessment.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns A- for Clarence Weatherspoon, Chris Gatling, Gary Grant, a conditional first-round right and cash in exchange for Shawn Kemp. Portland gets C for acquiring Kemp, whose health and contract created risk. Miami also receives C for incoming Brian Grant, a proven interior forward. The first-round selection later tied to Brendan Haywood was a transferable asset, not guaranteed Cleveland playing production.

Because the Knicks had legitimate age and roster reasons to act, this is a Slight Partner Edge rather than a franchise-defining loss.

houston-rockets.summary: On September 28, 2000, Chicago acquired guard Bryce Drew from Houston, sending conditional draft compensation that ultimately became 2005 No. 51 Robert Whaley and 2006 No. 46 Dee Brown, while the Rockets obtained a $1.8 million trade exception. The contingent first-round pick protection never created an unprotected first for Houston; the second-round fallback proved to be the relevant asset. Both later selections were transferred in separate deals rather than retained as straightforward Houston draft development. Slight Rockets Edge for flexibility, Houston C-, Chicago D+.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Chicago Added Drew While Houston Accepted Conditional Future Value

On September 28, 2000, the Bulls acquired reserve guard Bryce Drew from Houston. The exchange compensated the Rockets through a complicated conditional draft arrangement rather than a conventional pick that would immediately transfer. Chicago's first-round protection in the 2003 and 2004 drafts was broad, and the fallback called for later second-round selections if the protected first never conveyed. Houston also obtained a $1.8 million trade exception, offering salary-management flexibility separate from the eventual players chosen. Both clubs were changing their rosters in the years after the Bulls' championship run and before the Rockets' next playoff core formed.

The Protected First Eventually Became Two Second-Round Choices

The future-pick record identifies the fallback as a 2005 second-round selection eventually used at No. 51 on Robert Whaley and a 2006 second eventually used at No. 46 on Dee Brown. Neither player should be treated as if Houston immediately acquired him in 2000. The Rockets subsequently transferred the conditional draft claim in a 2003 package with Glen Rice, creating another transaction in the chain. The original agreement therefore supplied a movable future asset rather than a guaranteed first-round choice or direct rotation help. Assigning those draftees' later professional statistics to this lone swap would break the provenance trail.

Drew Was Short-Term Guard Depth, Not a Franchise Reset

Bryce Drew had been drafted by Houston in 1998 and was moving from a crowded Rockets backcourt to a Bulls team that could evaluate additional guards. His role was limited compared with the established scorers the franchise had recently lost, and the trade did not create a new foundational Chicago player. The Bulls' payment became more acceptable once it was clear the pick protection would keep them from losing a high first-round slot. Drew's real contribution was an opportunity for additional NBA minutes and roster coverage, not star-level play. Chicago did not acquire the trade exception or the later Houston-side draft position.

Salary Flexibility Gives Houston a Slight Advantage

Houston's return had financial and draft optionality, while Chicago received a familiar NBA guard with a comparatively small role. The Rockets did not secure a permanent first-round player from this transaction, so the old low grade was understandable, but the transferable conditional rights and $1.8 million exception were tangible tools. The Bulls paid with future second-round value without receiving much enduring production from Drew. Those outcomes justify a narrow Rockets edge rather than a broad winner's margin. Any later results of the 2003 Rice transaction must be evaluated as part of that separate, larger exchange.

Final Verdict

Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns C- because the deal produced a $1.8 million trade exception and movable conditional draft claims that eventually resolved into two second-round selections rather than an unprotected first. Chicago receives D+ for Bryce Drew's limited veteran-guard role. The later draft names Robert Whaley and Dee Brown identify the pick chain, not direct Houston player contributions, because the relevant rights were subsequently included in another trade.

perspectives.summary: Sacramento traded Corliss Williamson to Toronto for Doug Christie, adding the elite perimeter defender and connective passer who completed the Kings’ championship-caliber starting lineup.
perspectives.analysis: Christie earned four consecutive All-Defensive selections and helped Sacramento post 55, 61 and 59 wins in his first three seasons, including the seven-game 2002 Western Conference finals. His low-usage passing and ability to guard elite perimeter scorers fit perfectly beside Chris Webber, Vlade Divac and Peja Stojakovic. Williamson was an established scorer but lasted only one season in Toronto and did not replace Christie’s broader impact. Sacramento rises to A-plus, Toronto is adjusted to D-plus and the existing Kings-win verdict is retained.

Stith offered experienced wing scoring in Boston's 2000-01 rotation, while Herren received a limited hometown opportunity. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Made a Two-for-Two Veteran Exchange Before the Season

On October 16, 2000, Boston traded Robert Pack and Calbert Cheaney to Denver for Bryant Stith and Chris Herren. The Celtics were looking for scoring and perimeter options around a roster increasingly led by Paul Pierce and Antoine Walker. Stith was an experienced NBA wing, while Herren was a former local standout trying to establish himself as a professional guard. Denver acquired Pack's backcourt experience and Cheaney's flexible wing role in return. The agreement was a conventional exchange of four player contracts, without draft selections, cash terms or future protected-pick conditions.

Stith Offered a Final Season of Useful Celtics Depth

Stith joined Boston as a veteran shooter and was part of its 2000-01 rotation. That was the final NBA season of his playing career, so it would be inaccurate to count him as a Celtic during the team's 2002 Eastern Conference Finals run. Herren also appeared for Boston, but his opportunity was brief and did not produce a long-term franchise point guard. The direct result was one year of veteran help and a smaller developmental experiment. That limited scope supports a moderate grade rather than assuming the incoming names became lasting contributors or produced championship results in subsequent seasons.

Denver Obtained Pack and Cheaney for Its Own Rotation

The Nuggets received two recognizable NBA veterans whose styles differed from Boston's incoming group. Pack could run a half-court offense when available, and Cheaney supplied length and perimeter experience as Denver assembled its early-2000s roster. Neither player became an eventual Nuggets All-Star because of this swap, and their earlier career totals elsewhere are not part of Denver's direct return. Cheaney continued to work as an NBA role player, while Pack dealt with the limitations of a veteran guard's availability. The Nuggets received real basketball options rather than empty rights, though not an enduring strategic advantage.

The Small Edge Comes From Immediate Boston Fit

Both front offices changed the mix of their reserve and supporting players ahead of a new season. Boston obtained Stith's veteran scoring in a role it could use immediately, while Denver acquired players whose experience helped fill rotation gaps. There was no young prospect who developed into a future franchise leader on either side, so extreme grades would exceed the demonstrated results. The original slight Boston edge is defensible because Stith supplied a meaningful season while Herren was at least another guard option. The judgment should be limited to those actual receiving-team contributions rather than borrowing Boston's 2002 playoff run or Denver's later Carmelo Anthony era.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B- for Bryant Stith's 2000-01 shooting and veteran minutes plus a limited Chris Herren opportunity. Denver receives C+ for Robert Pack and Calbert Cheaney as experienced roster options. Stith retired before Boston's 2002 conference-finals campaign, and neither team's later rise should be credited automatically to an October 2000 exchange of four short-term veterans.

Detroit Exchanged a Future Pick for Ceballos and Another Second

The November 26, 2000 historical transaction transferred veteran Cedric Ceballos and a future 2002 second-round selection to Miami, while Detroit received another 2002 second-round right. The incoming Pistons choice later appears in the draft ledger at No. 37, associated with Tito Maddox. The Heat's incoming later selection is associated with No. 53 Tommy Smith. These draft identities describe the rights' eventual positions, not necessarily players who reported directly to those particular teams after all subsequent transfers. Miami sought a veteran scoring option along with a further prospect chance, while Detroit preferred a different second-round position.

Ceballos Offered Experience Rather Than a New Superstar

Ceballos had been a productive NBA scorer earlier in his career, which made his name the most recognizable part of the agreement. His peak offensive seasons, however, came before the 2000 transaction and must not be counted as new Miami production. The proper benefit is whatever roster or contractual role he provided to the Heat after the agreement, including whether later team decisions changed his availability. A veteran acquisition can carry practical value even without a long new starting tenure. The Heat also obtained a separate second-round selection, so the analysis should not reduce the entire exchange to whether Ceballos replicated past All-Star output.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Atlanta acquired guard Brevin Knight from Cleveland in January 2001 for Jim Jackson, Anthony Johnson and Larry Robinson. Knight provided backcourt assistance to the Hawks, while Cleveland collected veterans at multiple positions. The inherited Cavaliers Win awards Cleveland B+ and Atlanta C-.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Consolidated Three Players Into Knight

The Hawks acquired Brevin Knight from the Cavaliers in January 2001, sending Jim Jackson, Anthony Johnson and Larry Robinson to Cleveland. Knight was a point guard known for passing and defensive activity rather than high-volume scoring. Atlanta wanted a clearer organizer for its backcourt during a difficult season. Cleveland chose the breadth of several incoming players instead of retaining the smaller guard, giving the Cavaliers options at different spots on a developing roster.

Knight Brought Passing, Not a Major Scoring Breakthrough

Knight could direct an offense and create chances for teammates, making him a plausible point-guard target for a team seeking steadier possessions. His Hawks tenure did not turn Atlanta into an immediate contender or establish him as a long-term franchise leader. The correct return is the guard work he provided in Atlanta, not his earlier Cleveland production or his later playing opportunities elsewhere. The team gained a recognizable specialist, but not a transformational player.

Cleveland Collected Three Different Player Options

Jackson offered veteran scoring experience, Johnson another option at guard and Robinson additional backcourt depth. Not every arrival became a regular Cavaliers contributor for multiple years, and the package shouldn't be evaluated as three long-lasting starters. Cleveland nonetheless gained alternative ways to distribute minutes and make subsequent moves. The versatility of the return suited a club still assessing its roster before the later LeBron James era, although these acquisitions alone did not create that future success.

The Cavaliers' Grade Reflects a More Flexible Return

Atlanta traded several pieces for one point guard whose role was useful but limited in total impact. Cleveland gained the ability to examine multiple veterans rather than rely on Knight alone. The inherited Cavaliers B+ compared with Atlanta's C- credits that broader roster value. A closer look still reveals modest receiving-team production on both sides, so the result shouldn't be confused with a deal that directly produced a future All-Star or championship centerpiece.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B+ for acquiring Jim Jackson, Anthony Johnson and Larry Robinson, a broader veteran package in exchange for Brevin Knight. Atlanta receives C- for Knight's playmaking, which provided assistance but didn't turn him into a lasting franchise point guard. Cleveland received more options, although neither side obtained a major long-term star from the exchange.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State sent Vinny Del Negro to Phoenix on January 26, 2001, receiving Corie Blount, Rubén Garcés and Paul McPherson. Blount played 38 Warriors games in 918 minutes and McPherson added 22 games and 287 minutes; Garcés was waived in February without a Warriors game. Del Negro gave Phoenix 36 games and 526 minutes. Warriors Win narrowly, Golden State B and Phoenix C+.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Warriors Exchanged a Veteran Guard for Three Suns Reserves

Golden State traded Vinny Del Negro to Phoenix on January 26, 2001, receiving forward Corie Blount, guard Paul McPherson and big man Rubén Garcés. The Warriors' official media guide records the three-for-one transaction and its exact date. The clubs were pursuing different roster adjustments: Phoenix sought a steady veteran guard who could provide some minutes behind its established perimeter players, while Golden State wanted more frontcourt bodies and a chance to evaluate a younger scoring guard. No future picks are recorded as part of this particular exchange.

Blount Supplied the Main Golden State Return

Blount played thirty-eight regular-season games for Golden State after the acquisition, logging 918 minutes and averaging 6.8 points with 8.3 rebounds per 36 minutes. His game-by-game role was more limited than those per-minute figures imply, but the Warriors needed additional size in a season affected by injuries and poor results. He was a playable power forward rather than an end-of-bench contract. McPherson also appeared in twenty-two games, played 287 minutes and averaged 6.8 points in just thirteen minutes per contest. Combined, the two players delivered 1,205 minutes of Warriors use.

Garcés Didn't Play, While Del Negro Became a Suns Backup

The third incoming player, Garcés, did not appear in a Warriors regular-season game and was waived on February 28, 2001, according to the club's transaction history. Golden State therefore should not be credited with his ten earlier Phoenix games. On the other side, Del Negro appeared in thirty-six Phoenix regular-season games after the swap, played 526 minutes and averaged 5.2 points. He gave the Suns some guard cover, but was not a major offensive contributor. His twenty-nine Golden State games before January 26 also remain pretrade Warriors statistics, not additional Phoenix value.

Two Rotation Pieces Outweighed One Veteran Guard

This exchange was not a major event for either franchise, and Golden State's season remained difficult. Nonetheless, the return was more than an unused group of contracts: Blount gave the Warriors real frontcourt minutes and McPherson a chance to handle bench possessions. Phoenix acquired a veteran guard who could help occasionally, though he logged fewer minutes than either the combined Warriors additions or Blount alone. The Suns' decision was reasonable given their need for experience, but the receiving-team records support a modest Warriors advantage rather than the imported perfectly even B grades.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State earns B for Corie Blount's thirty-eight games and 918 minutes plus Paul McPherson's twenty-two games and 287 minutes; Rubén Garcés did not play before his waiver. Phoenix receives C+ for Vinny Del Negro's thirty-six games and 526 minutes. The Warriors acquired more useful bench coverage from the January three-for-one trade.

He appeared in 17 Philadelphia games, logging 67 minutes during 2001-02, but never developed into a regular 76ers contributor. Los Angeles obtained financial consideration. Even Trade, C for each club; the earlier Sixers-win call relied on very little NBA output.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
Philadelphia Bought Selection No. 36 After Reaching the Finals

The 76ers acquired a second-round draft selection from the Clippers for cash in the summer of 2001. Philadelphia had just reached the NBA Finals and was seeking inexpensive young help behind a lineup dominated by Allen Iverson and veteran frontcourt players. The acquired slot was No. 36 overall, which the club spent on Syracuse forward Damone Brown. Los Angeles preferred a guaranteed payment rather than adding another uncertain draft candidate. No established NBA player switched clubs in this rights-and-cash agreement.

Brown Earned Only 67 Philadelphia Minutes

Brown reached Philadelphia’s roster in 2001-02 but played in just seventeen regular-season games. He logged sixty-seven total minutes without a start, a very small contribution from a second-round selection. Brown later appeared for Toronto and New Jersey, but those games belong to teams that separately obtained him and should never be rolled into the 76ers return. His college career offered a reason to draft him, not evidence that he became an important professional wing for the Philadelphia team that bought this pick.

The Clippers Banked a Financial Return Instead of a Player

Los Angeles did not acquire an NBA player in the exchange. It accepted cash for a selection whose eventual use was uncertain, leaving Philadelphia to decide which prospect was worth that draft slot. The historical transaction entries show the payment was real but do not supply an amount or a documented player later funded with those proceeds. Evaluating the Clippers as if they received nothing ignores their actual incoming asset. At the same time, the money cannot be transformed into invented wins or points for Los Angeles.

Neither Return Justifies an Aggressive Winner Grade

Philadelphia used the selection on a player who briefly reached the NBA, which gives the Sixers some measurable return for their cash payment. Yet sixty-seven minutes is not the kind of basketball result that clearly defeats a guaranteed financial receipt. Los Angeles received no on-court contribution and Philadelphia received little, so the difference comes down to low-stakes asset preferences rather than sustained roster help. Equal C grades and an even verdict correct the inherited dismissal of the Clippers return without celebrating the brief Philadelphia audition.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Philadelphia earns C for Damone Brown’s seventeen regular-season games and sixty-seven minutes as a 76ers reserve after the draft purchase. Los Angeles also earns C because it received cash rather than an uncertain second-round player. Neither club obtained lasting NBA help, making the previous Philadelphia-win verdict too strong.

During the June 27, 2001 draft, Atlanta sent the NBA rights to Jamaal Tinsley to Indiana for a protected future first-round selection. The Pacers wanted the Iowa State guard as a player who could handle their offense, while the Hawks favored retaining an additional future opportunity instead of signing that year's prospect. The conditional choice did not instantly become a player on Atlanta's roster; its terms depended on when a pick would ultimately convey. The draft-rights record later identifies the asset as the twenty-first selection of 2003, used on Boris Diaw. Both players were years away from their eventual NBA outcomes on transaction day.

Tinsley Grew Into Indiana's Regular Lead Guard

Tinsley joined the Pacers and developed into the main point guard on a team led by Jermaine O'Neal and a strong veteran rotation. His Indiana years included the 2004 Eastern Conference Finals run, making him a real multiseason contributor rather than a short-lived draft experiment. That long period of receiving-team service is the strongest argument for revising the inherited Hawks-winning assessment. Tinsley did not play for Atlanta and should never be assigned to the club that briefly controlled his rights. His later career away from Indiana likewise belongs to subsequent agreements, not additional Pacers games credited to the original swap.

The Pick Became Diaw, Then Part of a Different Trade

Atlanta eventually used the acquired draft selection on Diaw, who played for the Hawks during 2003-04 and 2004-05. His passing and all-around forward skills made him an interesting prospect, though his most acclaimed professional season came later in Phoenix. Atlanta included Diaw in the 2005 sign-and-trade package that brought Joe Johnson to the Hawks, alongside other first-round assets. It is appropriate to say Diaw retained value in another exchange, but Johnson's entire Atlanta career cannot be directly credited to the Tinsley trade. That larger transaction demanded additional compensation that this 2001 deal did not provide by itself.

The Pacers Realized More Direct Basketball Value

The trade wasn't a complete Atlanta failure, because the club turned a departing player's rights into a real first-round selection and later used that prospect in further roster construction. Indiana nevertheless got a point guard who held an important role for more seasons than Diaw played in Atlanta. Tinsley's durable contribution to a conference-finals roster gives Indiana the clearer direct basketball advantage. The trade should be judged on those team-specific seasons and asset movements rather than borrowing Diaw's standout Suns campaign or every benefit of Atlanta's eventual Joe Johnson acquisition. A moderate Hawks grade alongside a stronger Pacers grade recognizes both paths.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win. Indiana earns A- for acquiring Jamaal Tinsley, a multiseason starting guard on teams that reached the 2004 Eastern Conference Finals. Atlanta receives B for a protected future first-round selection that became 2003 No. 21 Boris Diaw and later remained useful in another trade. Diaw's best Phoenix seasons and the full Joe Johnson sign-and-trade return can't be assigned directly to the original Tinsley swap.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Hawks Sold Morris's Second-Round Rights for a First

Atlanta drafted Maryland forward Terence Morris at No. 34 in 2001, then sent his rights to Houston for a conditional future first-round selection. For the Rockets, the attraction was a player they had identified and could develop without waiting for another draft. Atlanta preferred the higher-round future asset over using a roster opportunity on Morris. The first was linked to an earlier Detroit pick obligation, so the deal's eventual pick identity required several seasons and another sequence of rights transactions to resolve.

Morris Gave Houston an NBA Forward, Not a Star

Morris joined Houston and appeared in NBA games, offering an athletic reserve forward rather than a leading scorer. The Rockets did receive a real player, so describing their side as entirely empty would be misleading. Nevertheless, Morris did not become a cornerstone whose production clearly justified surrendering a first-round asset. His Houston tenure was narrower than the careers of some other 2001 prospects. The distinction is between the immediate player whose rights Houston bought and the greater long-term flexibility the Hawks acquired.

Atlanta Used the First Before the 2003 Draft

The future first eventually became associated with No. 25 in 2003, the selection used on Carlos Delfino. Atlanta did not keep that pick until Delfino was drafted. It passed the right to Sacramento in June 2002 in a separate transaction involving draft rights to Dan Dickau. The Hawks' concrete return from the Morris exchange was therefore a movable first-round asset, not an Atlanta Delfino season. The downstream Sacramento transaction must be considered separately, including what Atlanta gave and received at that later point.

The Higher Draft Asset Made Atlanta's Decision Favorable

The Hawks converted the rights to a second-round player into a future first, giving them a chance to address a different roster need in a later draft. Houston got some NBA playing time from Morris but not enough to erase the difference between the value of those two draft tiers. Atlanta's success was largely transactional rather than a victory built on a star it drafted directly with the pick. The eventual Delfino identity clarifies the asset history without inflating the Hawks' receiving-team box-score return.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns A- for acquiring a conditional first-round asset in exchange for Terence Morris's second-round rights, later using the pick in another transaction. Houston receives C- for a playable but limited Rockets forward. The 2003 No. 25 Carlos Delfino pick is part of the rights history, not an Atlanta player's NBA production.

los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Lakers Converted Center Depth Into Backcourt Insurance

Los Angeles acquired guard Lindsey Hunter from Milwaukee for reserve center Greg Foster on June 28, 2001. The Lakers were coming off another championship and needed dependable perimeter depth for the effort to repeat. Hunter had been a regular rotation guard for Detroit before joining Milwaukee, and his defense plus outside shot offered an alternative alongside Derek Fisher and Kobe Bryant. Foster had supplied limited center minutes during the Lakers' previous title season, when Shaquille O'Neal anchored the position. The deal moved an expendable frontcourt veteran for a guard who could start when needed, while Milwaukee tested whether Foster could provide inexpensive veteran size.

Hunter Appeared in Every Regular-Season Game for Los Angeles

Hunter played all 82 regular-season Lakers contests in 2001-02, starting 47 and averaging 5.8 points in 19.7 minutes. His scoring declined from his previous Milwaukee season, but he still made enough spot starts to be a regular part of the rotation. During the playoffs he appeared in 18 games as Los Angeles advanced past Portland, San Antonio, Sacramento and New Jersey to win the 2002 NBA title. Hunter was not the primary guard or star of the championship team; Bryant, O'Neal and the starters supplied far more offense. His specific return was availability, defense and rotation cover through a title season.

Foster Played Only 24 Minutes for Milwaukee

Milwaukee's playing return was minimal. Foster appeared in six regular-season Bucks games in 2001-02, logging a total of 24 minutes and seven points, with eight rebounds. He did not start and never became a rotation fixture for the team. Foster's prior 62-game 2000-01 Lakers season does not count as Milwaukee value merely because it demonstrated he had NBA experience before the deal. He subsequently appeared with Toronto in 2002-03, outside the Bucks' return. Milwaukee was looking for a veteran big man but received only an occasional deep reserve who had no meaningful role in the club's 41-41 season.

The One-Sided Minutes Explain the Verdict

The contrast between receiving-team results is striking: Hunter made 82 appearances and 47 starts for Los Angeles, while Foster provided six Milwaukee games and almost no minutes. Hunter's role continued into a postseason championship, further distinguishing the usefulness of his stint from that of an expendable roster piece. The Lakers' win does not require claiming that Hunter was a decisive player in the Finals. His 1,616 regular-season minutes and playoff availability were actual basketball contributions from the trade. Foster's seven Bucks points did not materially change Milwaukee's lineup. That difference supports giving Los Angeles a stronger positive grade and the Bucks a much lower one than the inherited evaluation.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B+ for Lindsey Hunter's 82 regular-season appearances, 47 starts and 18 playoff appearances on the 2002 championship team. Milwaukee gets D+ after Greg Foster logged just six games and 24 minutes. The direct playing returns were sharply unequal, despite both players having useful careers elsewhere.
los-angeles-lakers.gradeRationale: The Lakers produced a modest realized-value advantage. Grades weigh realized player production, identifiable pick conversion, role, timing, contract context and downstream asset use.
