analysis:
The Lakers Converted Center Depth Into Backcourt Insurance

Los Angeles acquired guard Lindsey Hunter from Milwaukee for reserve center Greg Foster on June 28, 2001. The Lakers were coming off another championship and needed dependable perimeter depth for the effort to repeat. Hunter had been a regular rotation guard for Detroit before joining Milwaukee, and his defense plus outside shot offered an alternative alongside Derek Fisher and Kobe Bryant. Foster had supplied limited center minutes during the Lakers' previous title season, when Shaquille O'Neal anchored the position. The deal moved an expendable frontcourt veteran for a guard who could start when needed, while Milwaukee tested whether Foster could provide inexpensive veteran size.

Hunter Appeared in Every Regular-Season Game for Los Angeles

Hunter played all 82 regular-season Lakers contests in 2001-02, starting 47 and averaging 5.8 points in 19.7 minutes. His scoring declined from his previous Milwaukee season, but he still made enough spot starts to be a regular part of the rotation. During the playoffs he appeared in 18 games as Los Angeles advanced past Portland, San Antonio, Sacramento and New Jersey to win the 2002 NBA title. Hunter was not the primary guard or star of the championship team; Bryant, O'Neal and the starters supplied far more offense. His specific return was availability, defense and rotation cover through a title season.

Foster Played Only 24 Minutes for Milwaukee

Milwaukee's playing return was minimal. Foster appeared in six regular-season Bucks games in 2001-02, logging a total of 24 minutes and seven points, with eight rebounds. He did not start and never became a rotation fixture for the team. Foster's prior 62-game 2000-01 Lakers season does not count as Milwaukee value merely because it demonstrated he had NBA experience before the deal. He subsequently appeared with Toronto in 2002-03, outside the Bucks' return. Milwaukee was looking for a veteran big man but received only an occasional deep reserve who had no meaningful role in the club's 41-41 season.

orlando-magic.summary: Washington acquired center Brendan Haywood's draft rights from Orlando on August 1, 2001 for Laron Profit and a protected future first-round selection that ultimately became No. 20 in 2005. Haywood played 62 Wizards games as a rookie and 81 with 69 starts in 2002-03, beginning a long Washington tenure. Orlando's two incoming assets never produced comparable long-term NBA starts. Wizards Win, Washington A and Orlando C+.
orlando-magic.analysis:
Washington Turned an Orlando Draft-Rights Purchase Into a Center

Orlando transferred Brendan Haywood's draft rights to Washington on August 1, 2001. The Magic received wing Laron Profit and a protected future first-round selection, while the Wizards acquired a seven-footer who had impressed at North Carolina. Haywood had been the twentieth overall choice in the 2001 draft before his rights moved between franchises. Washington needed legitimate interior size and opted for a prospect with rebounding and shot-blocking ability. Orlando valued the extra future selection as well as an available young wing.

Haywood Developed From Rookie Reserve Into Long-Term Starter

Haywood appeared in sixty-two Washington games as a rookie, with two starts and averages of 5.1 points and 5.2 rebounds. His opportunity expanded quickly. In 2002-03 he played eighty-one games and started sixty-nine, and two seasons later he started all sixty-eight games in which he appeared. Haywood remained with the franchise across multiple playoff seasons, supplying size and defense next to changing groups of guards and forwards. His later Dallas championship does not belong to the Wizards, but his Washington seasons were extensive direct trade value.

Orlando Received Profit and a Protected Pick With a Long Trail

The Magic received Laron Profit and a protected first-round obligation that carried forward before finally being identified as the twentieth choice in 2005. That position eventually became associated with Julius Hodge through later transactions. It would be wrong to assume Hodge played for Orlando or to credit the Magic with the entire career of a player selected after the draft asset had moved on. Profit himself did not become an equally enduring Orlando starter. The franchise did acquire real assets, however, rather than simply losing the rights to Haywood for no compensation.

A Multi-Season Washington Center Outweighed the Deferred Assets

Orlando's package offered two potential paths to roster improvement: a young wing and a future first-rounder. Washington obtained an actual NBA center who grew into a stable starter and helped a playoff team years after the agreement. The practical difference isn't merely that Haywood was a first-rounder; it is the many seasons in which the Wizards played him. The older Wizards-winning verdict was justified but undervalued the acquired center's durability. Orlando's incoming protected choice should still be acknowledged as a useful negotiable asset rather than written off.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns A because Haywood produced sixty-two rookie games, eighty-one games with sixty-nine starts in his second season, and years of additional center depth. Orlando gets C+ for Laron Profit and a protected future first-round asset that ultimately became No. 20 in 2005. Haywood's long Wizards tenure exceeded the direct Magic playing return.

It would be wrong to assume Hodge played for Orlando or to credit the Magic with the entire career of a player selected after the draft asset had moved on. Profit himself did not become an equally enduring Orlando starter. The franchise did acquire real assets, however, rather than simply losing the rights to Haywood for no compensation.

A Multi-Season Washington Center Outweighed the Deferred Assets

Orlando's package offered two potential paths to roster improvement: a young wing and a future first-rounder. Washington obtained an actual NBA center who grew into a stable starter and helped a playoff team years after the agreement. The practical difference isn't merely that Haywood was a first-rounder; it is the many seasons in which the Wizards played him. The older Wizards-winning verdict was justified but undervalued the acquired center's durability. Orlando's incoming protected choice should still be acknowledged as a useful negotiable asset rather than written off.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns A because Haywood produced sixty-two rookie games, eighty-one games with sixty-nine starts in his second season, and years of additional center depth. Orlando gets C+ for Laron Profit and a protected future first-round asset that ultimately became No. 20 in 2005. Haywood's long Wizards tenure exceeded the direct Magic playing return.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Received McLeod and a Later First in Exchange for Moiso

Boston and Philadelphia reached an August 2001 agreement sending forward Jerome Moiso to the 76ers. The Celtics received Roshown McLeod and a future first-round draft right later associated with the 2003 No. 20 position and Dahntay Jones. The package combined a current player option with a higher-value future selection, while Philadelphia preferred to test a younger athletic big man it could bring directly into its roster. The first-round claim was not yet a selected player at the agreement date, and any later rights movement must be traced before awarding that player's NBA service to Boston.

Moiso Represented a Reclamation Opportunity for Philadelphia

Moiso had entered the league with physical and developmental upside but was still seeking a defined NBA role. Philadelphia could try him in its frontcourt after acquiring his rights from Boston, but his earlier college reputation didn't mean the 76ers had just obtained a productive NBA starter. A younger big man's path often depended on playing time and role fit, both uncertain in a roster with established contributors. The club accepted that risk by surrendering McLeod and a future first. Moiso's eventual seasons with other franchises should not be counted as Philadelphia production through this single transaction.

The Boston Pick Provided an Additional Valuable Asset

A first-round choice eventually associated with No. 20 in 2003 was a more substantial developmental asset than the late seconds in many other historical trades. Boston could use that opportunity itself or move it elsewhere, while also evaluating McLeod as a current forward. Dahntay Jones's eventual NBA career was the product of subsequent draft and contract decisions, so the fact that his name appears on the right's lineage shouldn't automatically be treated as Celtics playing time. Nevertheless, the original receiving club gained a distinct first-round claim in addition to another player asset. That combination created multiple possible routes to future value.

The Celtics' Two-Asset Return Holds the Stronger Position

Boston moved a still-unproven young big man and obtained a forward plus a future first-round selection. Philadelphia had a legitimate reason to pursue Moiso's athletic upside, but accepted a narrower future asset position to do so. This gives Boston a material advantage in expected value, even without assuming McLeod turned into a franchise centerpiece or Jones eventually played NBA games for the Celtics. The draft capital is what distinguishes this exchange from routine end-of-bench moves. Any later disposition of the acquired first requires its own transaction accounting and shouldn't be silently collapsed into the 2001 agreement.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston Celtics earns A-; Philadelphia 76ers earns D. Boston moved a still-unproven young big man and obtained a forward plus a future first-round selection. perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Scott Williams and a conditional 2004 first-round selection from Milwaukee in October 2001. Houston received Kevin Willis through the Bucks, while Milwaukee obtained Aleksandar Radojević from Denver and Houston's 2002 second-round right, later used on Dan Gadzuric. The original Nuggets Win assigns Denver A-, Houston B and Milwaukee C. Contemporary records confirm the entire three-team chain, which was incomplete in the Denver-only imported ledger.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Converted Willis and Radojević Into Williams and a First

The Nuggets sent veteran Kevin Willis and center Aleksandar Radojević to Milwaukee in October 2001, receiving Scott Williams and a conditional first-round selection. Williams was another experienced interior player who could contribute defense and rebounding, but the draft asset offered more enduring flexibility. The first later became associated with No. 17 Josh Smith in 2004. Denver's earlier transaction ledger listed the two outgoing players without correctly showing the full fate of the players across Milwaukee and Houston, obscuring why the Bucks participated.

Milwaukee Chose Radojević and a Second-Round Right

The Bucks acquired Radojević from Denver and a Houston 2002 second-round selection later used on Dan Gadzuric. In the same sequence, they routed Willis to Houston. This was also part of Milwaukee's effort to reorganize its cap situation before pursuing veteran forward Anthony Mason. The draft compensation and Radojević's contract were genuine incoming assets; describing the Bucks as getting nothing would erase the trade's structure. Radojević didn't become an established long-term star, and the selection's later player success must be evaluated through its eventual rights history.

Houston Obtained Kevin Willis as a Veteran Center

The Rockets received Willis from Milwaukee in exchange for the 2002 second-round right. Willis was a veteran big with an unusually long professional career, giving Houston an established interior reserve rather than an untested prospect. His prior years with other clubs indicated the experience the Rockets wanted, but they were not new Houston playing production on the transaction date. The move also helped Milwaukee shift its roster construction toward different frontcourt needs. The three clubs' differing objectives explain why the player and pick movements initially appeared as multiple linked transactions.

The Draft Chain Limits Who Can Claim Josh Smith's Career

Denver receives A- under the inherited grading for Williams and a first-round opportunity that eventually became associated with Josh Smith's draft slot. Houston earns B for the current veteran Willis, while Milwaukee receives C for Radojević, the Houston second and financial flexibility. Smith's eventual NBA development took place elsewhere, so his full playing career cannot be counted as a Nuggets outcome. The right itself was valuable, and its movement should be separated from the later work of the player chosen with it.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win. Denver earns A- for Scott Williams and a first-round right later linked to Josh Smith's 2004 draft position. Houston receives B for Kevin Willis's experienced center play. Milwaukee gets C for Aleksandar Radojević, the 2002 second-round right eventually used on Dan Gadzuric and roster flexibility. The transaction's three incoming packages are confirmed, but future drafted-player careers must follow their actual teams.

perspectives.analysis:
Charlotte Spread the Return Across Four Players

The Hornets sent Derrick Coleman to Philadelphia in October 2001 and received George Lynch, Jérôme Moïso and Robert Traylor from the 76ers along with Chris Porter from Golden State. Charlotte was replacing a veteran scorer with a broader group of forwards and interior players. Lynch offered defensive experience, Traylor was a physical big, and Moïso still had developmental potential. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Bought Two Veterans for Its 2002 Playoff Push

The Celtics made a February 20, 2002 deadline decision with immediate implications for a team built around Paul Pierce and Antoine Walker. Boston acquired guard Tony Delk and forward Rodney Rogers from Phoenix, giving up rookie Joe Johnson, veterans Randy Brown and Milt Palacio, plus its next first-round draft pick. The Suns were collecting younger options while Boston was trying to improve an established playoff rotation. At the time, Johnson had shown promise but was still developing. The future selection eventually became the twenty-second pick in 2002, associated with Casey Jacobsen, so the cost was much greater than the three outgoing roster spots alone.

Delk and Rogers Helped the Celtics Reach the Conference Finals

The incoming veterans had a real short-term role, which the inherited failing Boston grade overlooks. Delk offered backcourt scoring and ball handling, while Rogers was an outside-shooting frontcourt option as the Celtics advanced to the 2002 Eastern Conference Finals. The club's success was principally driven by its established stars, and those complementary minutes cannot be turned into an equivalent of Johnson's later career. Rogers left Boston after that season, and Delk was eventually included in another trade. The trade therefore delivered useful playoff depth, but not a multiyear foundational player for the Celtics.

Johnson Became the Headline Phoenix Asset

Phoenix received the rights and contract of a young guard who improved into a central member of its perimeter rotation. Johnson ultimately joined Steve Nash and Amar'e Stoudemire in the 2004-05 Suns offense, providing scoring and another ball handler during a major rise in the Western Conference. That Phoenix production is the central long-term result of the 2002 transaction. His later All-Star seasons with Atlanta followed a separate 2005 sign-and-trade and must not be credited as games he played for the Suns. Randy Brown and Milt Palacio provided additional roster options, while the No. 22 draft choice created another genuine selection for Phoenix.

The Difference Is Duration, Not Whether Boston Received Value

Boston's acquisition helped a legitimate postseason run, which prevents the F grade from meaning that Delk and Rogers were literally worthless. But the Celtics paid a steep developmental price by moving Johnson and a first-round pick for contributors whose direct Boston stays were limited. Phoenix acquired a young guard who grew into an important part of its most successful contemporary team, and the draft rights provided further flexibility. The better retrospective therefore favors the Suns strongly while acknowledging the immediate purpose of Boston's move. Neither club should receive unrelated production from Johnson's Atlanta years or a later Delk transaction.

Final Verdict

Suns Win. Phoenix receives A because Joe Johnson matured into an important Suns scorer and the club also acquired the 2002 No. 22 selection used on Casey Jacobsen. Boston gets F in the inherited long-term evaluation because Delk and Rogers couldn't match the sustained opportunity lost through Johnson. Both veterans did contribute to Boston's 2002 Eastern Conference Finals run, but that short payoff doesn't erase the eventual asset gap.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Minnesota acquired center Marc Jackson from Golden State on February 21, 2002, sending Dean Garrett and a future second-round choice that ultimately became No. 36 Jermareo Davidson in 2007. Jackson contributed Timberwolves frontcourt minutes across portions of two seasons. Garrett played five Golden State games in the remainder of 2001-02, but the future draft asset was later included in a larger 2007 Golden State exchange. Slight Wolves Edge, B versus B-.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Minnesota Took a Chance on a Former All-Rookie Center

The Timberwolves traded Dean Garrett and a future second-round selection to Golden State for Marc Jackson on February 21, 2002. Jackson had impressed as a rookie with the Warriors, but his next season had become less productive amid contract complications and a changing frontcourt. Minnesota wanted another body around Kevin Garnett without using a first-round asset. Golden State accepted an older center who could fill immediate minutes and a distant 2007 draft choice. That long delay is what makes the transaction more interesting than a straightforward swap of reserve big men.

Jackson Provided Minnesota With Frontcourt Availability

Jackson moved into Minnesota's center depth chart for the remainder of 2001-02 and spent additional time with the Timberwolves the following season. He was no longer performing at his rookie peak, so his contributions should be measured as backup or occasional starting center work, not the output of an All-Star. Still, he brought playable NBA size and rebounding to a club competing for the playoffs. His previous rookie statistics for Golden State are excluded from Minnesota's acquired return because they were earned before the trade.

Garrett's Warriors Playing Return Was Only Five Games

Golden State received very little immediate on-court production from Garrett. He appeared in five Warriors games during the remainder of 2001-02, playing thirty-one total minutes and averaging 1.6 points. He was a late-career center rather than a development prospect and did not hold a long-term position in the rotation. The Warriors had other frontcourt players drawing most of the available minutes. new-orleans-pelicans.summary: On June 25, 2002, Washington sent Courtney Alexander to the Hornets, then relocating from Charlotte to New Orleans, for draft pick No. 17, used on Juan Dixon. Dixon played 176 Wizards regular-season games during his initial three-year stint, scoring 1,441 points, and helped Washington reach the 2005 postseason. Alexander played 66 games for New Orleans in 2002-03 and scored 523 points. Wizards Win, Washington A-, Hornets D+.
new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
Washington Turned a Wing Surplus Into a Second First-Round Pick

On June 25, 2002, the Wizards traded Courtney Alexander to the Hornets for the No. 17 pick in the following day's NBA draft. The Hornets were moving from Charlotte to New Orleans, which explains why the league's season transaction log uses Charlotte while the contemporary Washington reporting already called the franchise New Orleans. Alexander had played for Washington alongside Michael Jordan and Richard Hamilton but no longer had a clear long-term place in the backcourt. The Wizards wanted a chance to select another young guard, while the Hornets were acquiring a player who had already demonstrated scoring ability in the league.

The No. 17 Selection Became Maryland Star Juan Dixon

Washington used that acquired first-round selection on University of Maryland guard Juan Dixon, who had just led the Terrapins to the NCAA championship. Dixon appeared in 42 Wizards regular-season games as a rookie, 71 in 2003-04 and 63 in 2004-05. Across those three seasons he supplied 176 appearances, 3,179 minutes and 1,441 points before leaving for Portland. He made 10 postseason appearances during Washington's 2005 playoff run, providing additional value beyond the original draft night's excitement. The franchise had not acquired a future All-Star, but it obtained three seasons of NBA wing and guard depth from the pick it received.

Alexander Provided New Orleans One Solid Reserve Season

The Hornets' return was not empty. Alexander played 66 New Orleans regular-season games in 2002-03, starting seven and delivering 523 points over 1,360 minutes. He averaged 7.9 points per contest, with 118 rebounds and 79 assists, and appeared in five postseason games as the team fell to Philadelphia in the first round. It was a serviceable reserve year for a club establishing itself in New Orleans. Alexander did not continue with the Hornets after that season, and his Washington scoring from before the exchange cannot be credited as new Hornets production. Nor can Dixon's later Portland seasons be awarded to the Wizards.

Dixon's Three-Year Stay Outpaced Alexander's One-Year Tenure

The central trade-off was immediate experience against the opportunity to select a college championship guard. Alexander could help the Hornets right away, and his 66 games are worth acknowledging. Washington nevertheless received 176 games across three seasons and used Dixon during a later postseason appearance. That extended useful life from a mid-first-round choice created more total on-court value for the Wizards, even though Dixon never became a star. The exchange should not be credited with Washington's entire roster turnaround or discounted merely because the player taken at No. 17 spent parts of his career elsewhere. The specific club-by-club record supports Washington's historical advantage.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns A- after converting Courtney Alexander into the No. 17 selection that produced Juan Dixon, who played 176 Wizards games and helped in the 2005 playoffs. New Orleans gets D+ for 66 games and 523 points from Alexander in 2002-03. Both teams received actual playing value, but Dixon offered a longer and greater return.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Exchanged an International Center's Rights for Two Seconds

In June 2002, Atlanta sent the negotiating rights to Greek center Efthimios Rentzias to Philadelphia. The Hawks received two future second-round draft selections instead of a player already signed to an NBA contract. Historical records connect those draft rights with the 2004 No. 37 selection associated with Royal Ivey and the 2006 No. 42 selection associated with Daniel Gibson. Each future opportunity carried its own eventual position and timing. The 76ers pursued a specific internationally experienced big man, while the Hawks chose flexibility over retaining a right they hadn't turned into a regular NBA contributor.

Rentzias Gave the 76ers a Prospect They Could Pursue Directly

Rentzias had established professional credentials in Europe and a traditional center's physical profile. Philadelphia could evaluate him as a possible immediate frontcourt contributor rather than wait several years to select another prospect. But overseas production isn't automatically an NBA rotation record for the team acquiring those rights. His actual availability, contract and adaptation to a different league remained uncertainties. The original price was two later seconds, so the 76ers were investing multiple development opportunities in one potential signing. This distinction makes the agreement a rights transaction rather than an exchange of proven NBA centers or an instant starting-quality upgrade.

The Hawks Acquired Distinct 2004 and 2006 Decisions

The eventual selections associated with Ivey and Gibson illuminate the value of Atlanta's compensation, but the players' later careers must be traced through the actual teams that selected or signed them. A future second is an option: the receiving club may select a player, exchange the right again or allow a prospect to develop elsewhere. Atlanta secured two such decisions in separate drafts by giving up just one incoming international right. The No. 37 position in 2004 carried different scouting conditions from the No. 42 position in 2006. Combining them into one generic asset would miss the central advantage of the return.

Two Separate Picks Offer Atlanta the Better Position

The Hawks didn't receive a guaranteed productive starter on the agreement date. They did, however, obtain two independently usable selections for a prospect right whose NBA payoff was uncertain. Philadelphia's preference for Rentzias made basketball sense if the team believed he could immediately occupy a roster spot, but that belief had to translate into actual service. The diversity and duration of Atlanta's acquired draft capital makes the Hawks-winning evaluation credible without counting every later NBA minute from Gibson or Ivey as Hawks output. The right lesson is about optionality and the difference between signed players and rights held for future negotiations.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta Hawks earns B; Philadelphia 76ers earns D. The Hawks didn't receive a guaranteed productive starter on the agreement date. They did, however, obtain two independently usable selections for a prospect right whose NBA payoff was uncertain. Philadelphia's preference for Rentzias made basketball sense These draft rights and player careers are evaluated for actual receiving-team value rather than attributed across later unrelated transactions.

perspectives.analysis: The Antonio McDyess trade is one of the harshest examples of injury risk turning a concentrated bet into a major loss. New York sent Marcus Camby, Mark Jackson and the rights to Nene to Denver for McDyess, the rights to Frank Williams and a second-round pick. Injury variance deserves context, but the combination of medical risk and outgoing talent still makes the outcome an F-level Partner Win.

memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
The Grizzlies Paid a Future Pick for an Immediate Rookie Option

During the June 26, 2002 NBA draft, Milwaukee took Chris Owens of Texas with the forty-eighth selection and sent his rights to Memphis. In exchange the Grizzlies surrendered their 2003 second-round choice. Both team transaction ledgers record the swap, and the pick eventually landed at No. 35 in the next draft. Owens gave Memphis the opportunity to evaluate a college forward without using a first-round selection. Milwaukee delayed its own prospect choice a year, betting the future position would yield something more useful than the rights it sold.

Owens Signed a Contract but Didn't Reach the NBA Rotation

The Grizzlies did sign Owens in July 2002, so the move wasn't merely a trade for paper rights left untouched. He joined their development pool and continued under contract for a period. However, the club waived him in September 2003 without a regular-season NBA appearance. His college work and later professional opportunities shouldn't be described as Memphis NBA output. The club invested a future draft selection in a player it never used during an official game. This limited the tangible basketball return to an unsuccessful roster evaluation.

Milwaukee's No. 35 Selection Became Szymon Szewczyk

The second-round selection sent to Milwaukee turned into Szymon Szewczyk, a Polish big man selected thirty-fifth overall in 2003. Szewczyk had a legitimate professional career abroad, but he never played a regular-season NBA game for the Bucks. The fact that the selection was nine spots higher than the original Owens pick offers a reason to like the timing of Milwaukee's trade. It doesn't establish that the Bucks received an actual NBA rotation contributor. His European production belongs to his overseas teams, not to Milwaukee's league ledger.

The Future Pick Was Better Positioned but Still Didn't Produce Games

Neither organization received an NBA player from this specific exchange. Memphis developed Owens briefly under contract and moved on; Milwaukee selected an overseas prospect with the future choice and did not bring him into its regular-season rotation. The Bucks may have preferred the upside of a higher subsequent pick, but the original high grade overstated a selection that didn't become an NBA contributor. At this distance the appropriate judgment is equal and restrained, with both teams credited for pursuing an understandable scouting strategy without invented player minutes.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Memphis earns C- because Chris Owens signed but never played a Grizzlies regular-season NBA game. Milwaukee also earns C- because the 2003 No. 35 selection became Szymon Szewczyk, another player with no Bucks regular-season appearances. The higher pick held developmental promise, yet neither acquiring club obtained league production.

perspectives.summary: San Antonio acquired Speedy Claxton from Philadelphia on June 26, 2002 for Mark Bryant plus the draft rights to John Salmons and Randy Holcomb. Claxton played only 30 regular-season games for the Spurs, but he became an important backup during the 2003 championship run and scored 13 points with four assists in the title-clinching Game 6. Philadelphia received the longer direct return through Salmons, who played 281 games for the 76ers across four seasons, making the trade much closer than the legacy grades suggested.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Basketball-Reference's San Antonio and Philadelphia transaction logs agree on the June 26, 2002 package: the Spurs sent veteran Mark Bryant and the rights to first-round pick John Salmons and second-round pick Randy Holcomb for Speedy Claxton. Contemporary reporting explains the roster logic. Philadelphia had Allen Iverson, Eric Snow and Aaron McKie ahead of Claxton, while San Antonio wanted a backup point guard behind Tony Parker. The trade therefore exchanged future depth for an immediate positional need.

San Antonio Return
Claxton missed much of the 2002-03 regular season and appeared in only 30 games, averaging 5.8 points and 2.5 assists in 15.7 minutes. His value rose sharply in the playoffs. He became a trusted change-of-pace guard during the championship run and was especially important in the NBA Finals. In the clinching Game 6 against New Jersey, Claxton played 23:44, scored 13 points on 5-of-8 shooting, added four assists and finished plus-21 as San Antonio closed out the title. He left for Golden State after the season, so the direct Spurs return was short but unusually leveraged.

Philadelphia Return
Salmons supplied the durable side of the package. He played 64 games as a rookie, 77 in 2003-04, 58 in 2004-05 and all 82 in 2005-06, totaling 281 regular-season games for Philadelphia. His role grew from deep reserve to a useful multi-position guard and wing, including 24 starts in 2003-04 and another 24 in 2005-06. Bryant added 11 Philadelphia games in 2002-03. Holcomb never produced meaningful 76ers NBA value, but Salmons alone makes this a legitimate return rather than a failed package.

Hindsight Verdict
This is a slight San Antonio edge rather than a one-sided win. Philadelphia received far more regular-season volume, and Salmons became a genuine rotation player over four seasons. San Antonio received only one season from Claxton, but the value of that season peaked at exactly the right time: he provided real minutes in a championship postseason and delivered one of his best performances in the title-clinching game. The Spurs earn a B+ for converting three expendable assets into immediate title-run help. Philadelphia earns a B for obtaining four seasons of Salmons plus a small Bryant contribution. Final verdict: slight San Antonio Spurs edge.

boston-celtics.summary: The Seattle SuperSonics acquired Kenny Anderson, Joseph Forte and Vitaly Potapenko from Boston in July 2002 for Vin Baker and Shammond Williams. Baker's Celtics years were disrupted by health and personal difficulties, while Potapenko provided Seattle with reserve-center production. The inherited Sonics advantage, A against Boston F, reflects the poor outcome of the Baker gamble.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Gambled on Baker's Potential Revival

In July 2002, Boston received Vin Baker and Shammond Williams from the Seattle SuperSonics, sending Kenny Anderson, Joseph Forte and Vitaly Potapenko in return. Baker had been an accomplished scoring forward earlier in his career, giving the Celtics reason to explore whether he could regain a productive role. Seattle preferred different veterans and a younger guard prospect, along with the flexibility of moving Baker's contract. The deal involved players at very different stages of their careers rather than two clubs exchanging equivalent starters.

Baker's Celtics Stay Fell Far Below Expectations

Baker was unable to establish the kind of reliable offensive role Boston envisioned, and his Celtics tenure eventually ended amid off-court and health difficulties. Those circumstances warrant accurate description without treating a player's struggles as entertainment. Shammond Williams supplied a narrower backcourt option, but he did not become a major long-term answer. Boston took on a prominent name whose previous All-Star output did not carry over into his new setting. The lack of sustained on-court production drove the low team grade.

Seattle Obtained Several Roster and Contract Options

Potapenko gave the SuperSonics center depth for multiple seasons. Anderson's Seattle stay was far shorter before he moved in another transaction, while Forte never became an established NBA guard there. The Sonics' benefit therefore wasn't that all three arrivals turned into long-serving contributors. They obtained some dependable frontcourt minutes and moved away from the Baker arrangement, improving their ability to revise the roster. That was more tangible than the outcome Boston received from its most important incoming player.

The Organization's Names Must Follow the 2002 Date

This trade occurred between Boston and the Seattle SuperSonics, even if the franchise's modern identity is listed as Oklahoma City in historical databases. Credit for the 2002 receiving side belongs to the Sonics organization at that time. Potapenko's roster service and the contract flexibility were meaningful, while Baker's Boston role proved disappointing. The inherited grade difference is substantial because the principal Celtics objective went unfulfilled while Seattle obtained more workable assets.

Final Verdict

Oklahoma City Thunder Win. The inherited franchise label refers to the Seattle SuperSonics, who receive A for Potapenko's reserve-center value and better roster flexibility after moving Baker. Boston receives F because Vin Baker's Celtics tenure did not deliver the expected productive role, while Shammond Williams offered only narrower help. The exchange favored Seattle's 2002 organization rather than the later Thunder roster.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Exchanged Three Different Assets for One Proven Scorer

The Hawks acquired Glenn Robinson from Milwaukee in August 2002, surrendering veteran Toni Kukoc, prospect Leon Smith and a conditional future first-round choice. The draft protection had multiple possible sources and conditions, with the resulting right eventually associated with the 2003 No. 8 selection and T.J. Ford. Atlanta wanted an established offensive presence immediately, while the Bucks preferred two players plus a potentially valuable draft asset. This wasn't an exchange of Robinson for one lottery pick alone, and the complicated conditional formula shouldn't be reduced to a guaranteed No. 8 position in 2002.

Robinson's Earlier Scoring Was a Reason to Acquire Him, Not the Return

Robinson had shown substantial scoring talent with Milwaukee, so Atlanta could reasonably expect him to help carry more possessions. Those Bucks performances, however, weren't newly acquired Hawks production: the receiving club needed to evaluate only his work after this agreement. His cost and roster fit were important because Atlanta gave up both a current veteran and future draft flexibility. Bringing in one familiar high-volume scorer can assist a club in the short term without automatically delivering several years of championship-level success. Later changes to Robinson's contract or team would narrow the direct return even further.

Milwaukee Gained an Experienced Forward and a Longer-Term Option

Kukoc offered NBA and international experience, while Smith represented a much more speculative player-development opportunity. The conditional first supplied another distinct way to improve the Bucks after the trade. That choice ultimately became linked with Ford, but the protection terms made its eventual draft position uncertain when signed. Ford's later games should be traced to the team actually holding his rights rather than assumed from the original wording. For Milwaukee, the attraction was variety: it could assess two players immediately and retain a future selection whose upside was greater than an ordinary low second-round pick.

The Bucks Received a More Flexible Overall Package

Atlanta acquired the most recognizable scorer but spent multiple ways to fill its roster, including a conditional first that developed into a valuable draft position. Milwaukee obtained a combination of veteran service, prospect evaluation and future draft capital. That supports a Bucks-winning result without claiming Smith became an established starter or Robinson offered Atlanta no value. Robinson's usefulness belonged to a relatively short window compared with the whole career people associated with his name. The conditional choice gave Milwaukee a meaningful later decision, which is the crucial element in explaining why the trade tilted west.

Final Verdict

perspectives.summary: In August 2002, Portland sent Steve Kerr, Erick Barkley and a 2003 second-round pick to San Antonio for Antonio Daniels, Charles Smith and Amal McCaskill. Daniels played 67 games for Portland; Kerr played 75 games for the 2003 champion Spurs and delivered four three-pointers against Dallas in the Western Conference finals. The second-rounder was subsequently traded to Detroit. Spurs Win, San Antonio B+, Portland C+.
perspectives.analysis:
Portland Bet on a Younger Guard While San Antonio Reunited with Kerr

The August 2002 deal sent Antonio Daniels, Charles Smith and Amal McCaskill to Portland, with Steve Kerr, Erick Barkley and a future second-round pick moving to San Antonio. The source ledgers disagree on the exact day: RealGM and Pro Sports Transactions record August 2, whereas Basketball-Reference places it on August 5. Neither discrepancy changes the players and pick involved. Portland wanted a younger reserve guard to supplement its veteran backcourt, while San Antonio brought back a familiar shooter with championship experience. The Spurs had previously employed Kerr during their 1999 title season, making his return a deliberate roster choice rather than an anonymous salary exchange.

Kerr Contributed in the Season That Ended with a Championship

Kerr played 75 regular-season games for San Antonio in 2002-03, averaging 4.0 points in 12.7 minutes. His greatest benefit arrived in a far more specific moment: Game 6 of the Western Conference finals against Dallas, when he hit four consecutive three-pointers in the second half and scored 12 points to help complete the series victory. The Spurs defeated New Jersey in six games in the NBA Finals. Kerr was not the driving force behind Tim Duncan's championship team, and a four-shot burst should not be treated as a season-long star turn. He nevertheless made a documented contribution to a title run.

Daniels Supplied Portland One Season of Backup-Guard Minutes

Daniels appeared in 67 Portland regular-season games in 2002-03, starting twice and playing 872 minutes. He scored 251 points with 85 assists, then appeared in six playoff games during the Trail Blazers' first-round series against Dallas. That was a real return, but Portland's use of him remained limited to 13.0 minutes per game and the franchise exited in seven postseason games. He left for Seattle in 2003, so his later success with the SuperSonics and Washington does not add value to the Portland side. McCaskill was waived in October without becoming part of Portland's regular-season rotation.

The Second-Rounder Was an Asset, Not a Spurs Draft Success

The 2003 second-round selection in San Antonio's return is often displayed with the eventual No. 58 pick and Andreas Glyniadakis's name. That should not be misread to mean the Spurs drafted and developed him. San Antonio sent the pick to Detroit in October 2002 for Mengke Bateer, transferring the draft value well before the following summer. Barkley likewise did not deliver meaningful long-term playing value for San Antonio. The decisive comparison is therefore Daniels's 67 Portland games versus Kerr's 75 San Antonio appearances and his memorable playoff shooting, with a separate low-value asset conversion on the Spurs side. The historical margin favors San Antonio without attributing Duncan's title to one trade.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win. San Antonio earns B+ because Steve Kerr supplied 75 regular-season appearances and crucial shooting during its 2003 conference-finals victory; the second-round pick also retained limited trade utility. Portland receives C+ for Antonio Daniels's 67 games and 251 points in a single season. The downstream No. 58 selection does not count as a Spurs draft outcome.

perspectives.summary: Denver sent James Posey to Houston in a December 2002 three-team deal and received Mark Bryant, Art Long and future first- and second-round rights. Houston sent Kenny Thomas to Philadelphia and received Posey. The 76ers acquired Thomas to bolster their frontcourt. The inherited Nuggets Win gives Denver A, Houston B+ and Philadelphia C, now with the missing 76ers return properly recorded.
perspectives.analysis:
Houston Acquired Posey for Its Perimeter Rotation

The Rockets received James Posey from Denver in December 2002, adding a versatile wing who could score without becoming the primary ball handler and compete on defense. Posey had developed into a useful Nuggets player, making him a meaningful acquisition for a Houston team with guards Steve Francis and Cuttino Mobley. Houston sent Kenny Thomas to Philadelphia as part of the broader transaction, trading away a productive forward to address different positional needs.

Denver Accepted Veterans and Two Future Picks

The Nuggets obtained Mark Bryant and Art Long, plus a protected first-round right from Philadelphia and a second-round right from Houston. The selections later became associated with No. 16 Joey Graham in 2005 and No. 50 Vassilis Spanoulis in 2004. Those identities describe draft lineage, not proof that both players built significant Nuggets NBA careers. Denver was exchanging Posey's immediate wing role for multiple roster and draft options while moving through a larger rebuilding stage.

Philadelphia Gained Kenny Thomas

The 76ers acquired Kenny Thomas from Houston, filling a frontcourt need with a player who could rebound and contribute points. The old Denver-only transaction record had listed Philadelphia with no incoming asset, obscuring an actual NBA forward received in the deal. Thomas's presence matters because the Sixers surrendered players and a conditional pick for a current option, not as an empty administrative participant. His eventual Philadelphia minutes are the relevant receiving-team evidence, separate from prior Rockets production.

The Nuggets Grade Rewards the Extra Draft Leverage

Denver earns A in the inherited evaluation for receiving two veterans plus a first- and second-round opportunity. Houston's B+ reflects Posey's established wing profile, while Philadelphia's C recognizes Thomas as useful but not a foundational star. That ranking shouldn't be misread as a promise the Nuggets would retain every named future draft choice. The complete three-team picture is more meaningful when the protected pick pathways and the Sixers' missing player return are both acknowledged.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win. Denver earns A for Mark Bryant, Art Long and future picks associated with Joey Graham and Vassilis Spanoulis. Houston receives B+ for versatile wing James Posey. Philadelphia receives C for Kenny Thomas, an actual forward added from Houston and previously missing from the archive. The trade turned one Denver scorer into several options while giving the other clubs immediate players.

seattle-supersonics.summary: On February 20, 2003, New Orleans traded veteran center Elden Campbell to Seattle for guard Kenny Anderson. Anderson played 23 Hornets regular-season games with 139 points and 77 assists and appeared in five postseason games. Campbell played 15 SuperSonics games, scoring 48 points in 184 minutes before leaving for Detroit. Charlotte Win is the legacy site verdict for the Hornets franchise, but the event occurred when the club was in New Orleans. The Hornets' acquired reserve minutes justify B-, Seattle D+.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
New Orleans Sought a Point-Guard Option at the Deadline

The February 20, 2003 swap brought Kenny Anderson to the New Orleans Hornets and sent veteran center Elden Campbell to the Seattle SuperSonics. Anderson had spent much of the season as a Seattle reserve after arriving in the prior Vin Baker deal. New Orleans was trying to bolster guard options as Baron Davis battled injuries, while Seattle was reshuffling its backcourt in a much larger deadline day that also involved Gary Payton and Ray Allen. This exchange was distinct from the Payton transaction and carried its own short-term frontcourt and backcourt objectives.

Anderson Played Twenty-Three Games for New Orleans

Anderson made twenty-three Hornets regular-season appearances after February 20, with one start, 446 minutes, 139 points and seventy-seven assists. He averaged six points and 3.3 assists, an appropriate depth role rather than the production of the All-Star point guard he had been years earlier. He also appeared in five New Orleans playoff games. The thirty-eight Seattle appearances earlier in 2002-03 belonged to his previous team and should not be double-counted as acquired Hornets performance. The guard's later Indiana and Atlanta seasons were separate opportunities, not benefits generated by this trade.

Campbell Supplied Fifteen Brief Seattle Appearances

Seattle received an established 6-foot-11 center in Campbell, who had already logged forty-one New Orleans games that season. His actual SuperSonics contribution was much smaller: fifteen regular-season appearances, no starts, 184 minutes, forty-eight points and thirty-nine rebounds. The Sonics did not receive Campbell's later championship-year Detroit production, because he left Seattle before the 2003-04 season. His presence at the trade deadline also did not fix Seattle's frontcourt on his own. The 2002-03 SuperSonics finished 40-42, despite acquiring Ray Allen and other players in the independent Payton deal.

The Hornets Got More Usable Minutes

Both teams acquired established veterans for the end of one campaign, but the exchange was a much more productive guard rental than center rental. Anderson played more than twice Campbell's minutes for his receiving team, helped initiate offense and remained usable in New Orleans's postseason rotation. Campbell's fifteen-game Seattle stint offered size without comparable floor time. That difference supports the inherited Hornets-winning outcome, although the original B-plus for New Orleans and C-plus for Seattle were too generous for such short and modest stays. The revised grades recognize a useful short-term guard and a largely unused veteran center.

Final Verdict

Charlotte Win is the legacy franchise verdict, referring to the New Orleans Hornets in February 2003. The Hornets earn B- because Kenny Anderson played 23 regular-season games, supplied 77 assists and appeared in five playoff games. Seattle earns D+ for Elden Campbell's 15 regular-season appearances, 184 minutes and 48 points. Campbell's subsequent Detroit career is not part of Seattle's acquired return.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Acquired Two Centers for a Guard, a Second and Cash

The February 2003 exchange between Boston and Denver sent Mark Blount and Mark Bryant to the Celtics. The Nuggets received guard Shammond Williams, $1 million and a second-round selection eventually identified as the 2003 No. 46 choice associated with Sani Becirovic. Boston was seeking available interior players for its current rotation, while Denver was ready to move two big men in exchange for backcourt depth and additional resources. No first-round right changed hands. The cash was a financial consideration rather than an NBA player, and the second-round selection remained uncertain until the next draft.

Blount Supplied the Most Tangible Boston Basketball Benefit

Blount offered a current center the Celtics could use in games without waiting for a selection or international negotiation. He would supply the main continuing basketball value in this return, with Bryant providing a more experienced but narrower reserve option. Neither player's earlier professional work belonged to Boston merely because his rights changed teams in February. The club could assess their defensive positioning and size against larger opponents, addressing a need around its established perimeter talent. The acquisition wasn't a guarantee of an elite championship center, but direct frontcourt depth carried practical value relative to the package Boston surrendered.

Denver Accepted Three Less Immediate Forms of Compensation

Williams was a known NBA guard who could help Denver organize bench possessions. The cash payment was certain, while the eventual No. 46 draft right gave the Nuggets another chance to select or transfer a prospect. Becirovic's career outside the NBA does not automatically translate into Nuggets regular-season minutes, making the choice more speculative than Blount's ability to join Boston. The original deal combined basketball depth, finances and future rights rather than returning one equally established center. Denver's rationale fit a franchise choosing to redirect its resources, even if none of the pieces yielded a major immediate NBA star.

Boston Has the Slightly Clearer On-Court Payoff

Boston obtained the type of usable size it needed, particularly through Blount's receiving-team service, while Denver's package was spread across a guard, cash and a later selection. That makes a small Celtics advantage defensible without depicting Williams or the second-round right as valueless. A lottery pick was never part of the exchange, and neither club's later franchise successes were generated solely by this move. The draft history of Becirovic needs its own attribution, separate from the team's original 2003 choice. The value here comes chiefly from targeted frontcourt help on one side and distributed compensation on the other.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. boston-celtics: B-; denver-nuggets: C+. Boston obtained the type of usable size it needed, particularly through Blount's receiving-team service, while Denver's package was spread across a guard, cash and a later selection. That makes a small Celtics advantage defensible This verdict preserves draft protections and distinguishes professional history earned elsewhere from receiving-team contributions.

analysis:
Boston Acquired Two Centers for a Guard, a Second and Cash

The February 2003 exchange between Boston and Denver sent Mark Blount and Mark Bryant to the Celtics. The Nuggets received guard Shammond Williams, $1 million and a second-round selection eventually identified as the 2003 No. 46 choice associated with Sani Becirovic. Boston was seeking available interior players for its current rotation, while Denver was ready to move two big men in exchange for backcourt depth and additional resources. No first-round right changed hands. The cash was a financial consideration rather than an NBA player, and the second-round selection remained uncertain until the next draft.

Blount Supplied the Most Tangible Boston Basketball Benefit

Blount offered a current center the Celtics could use in games without waiting for a selection or international negotiation. He would supply the main continuing basketball value in this return, with Bryant providing a more experienced but narrower reserve option. Neither player's earlier professional work belonged to Boston merely because his rights changed teams in February. The club could assess their defensive positioning and size against larger opponents, addressing a need around its established perimeter talent. The acquisition wasn't a guarantee of an elite championship center, but direct frontcourt depth carried practical value relative to the package Boston surrendered.

Denver Accepted Three Less Immediate Forms of Compensation

Williams was a known NBA guard who could help Denver organize bench possessions. The cash payment was certain, while the eventual No. 46 draft right gave the Nuggets another chance to select or transfer a prospect. Becirovic's career outside the NBA does not automatically translate into Nuggets regular-season minutes, making the choice more speculative than Blount's ability to join Boston. The original deal combined basketball depth, finances and future rights rather than returning one equally established center. Denver's rationale fit a franchise choosing to redirect its resources, even if none of the pieces yielded a major immediate NBA star.

Boston Has the Slightly Clearer On-Court Payoff

The value here comes chiefly from targeted frontcourt help on one side and distributed compensation on the other.

new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
The Hornets Needed Guard Coverage More Than a Reserve Center

The New Orleans Hornets exchanged veteran center Elden Campbell for Seattle SuperSonics point guard Kenny Anderson on February 20, 2003. New Orleans had experienced injury-related roster problems during its first season in Louisiana and wanted another experienced ball handler. Campbell had already lost much of the frontcourt responsibility he carried during earlier Charlotte Hornets seasons. Seattle, meanwhile, was making substantial deadline changes, including a separate Gary Payton transaction, and acquired another center to distribute minutes among its remaining big men. This was a direct veteran-for-veteran swap without a draft selection attached.

Anderson Delivered 23 Games and 77 Hornets Assists

After moving to New Orleans, Anderson played twenty-three regular-season games, starting once and logging 446 minutes. He scored 139 points and recorded seventy-seven assists, helping the Hornets maintain backcourt depth through their playoff push. The contribution was limited compared with Anderson's career peak, but twenty-three games and nearly nineteen and a half minutes per appearance amounted to a real reserve role. His thirty-eight Seattle appearances before the trade must remain part of his SuperSonics record rather than being added to his New Orleans return. Anderson did not become a long-term Hornets starter, leaving after the season.

Campbell Had a Smaller Seattle Role After the Swap

Campbell played fifteen regular-season games for Seattle after February 20, with no starts. His SuperSonics totals were 184 minutes, forty-eight points and thirty-nine rebounds. These figures show why it would be misleading to credit Seattle with Campbell's earlier 41 New Orleans games from the same campaign. His greatest NBA years had already passed, and the new team used him as a modest reserve center. He left after the season and later contributed to Detroit, but those Pistons games were unrelated to the Seattle acquisition. The direct return here was a brief, low-minute look at a veteran big man.

Both Clubs Got Depth, but New Orleans Used Its Player More

The trade served sensible short-term roster objectives for both franchises, yet the receiving-team record favors the Hornets. Anderson's 446 minutes more than doubled Campbell's Seattle time, and New Orleans also received more points and a useful source of assists. The SuperSonics did acquire size and had other reasons to reduce their guard allocation as they rebuilt, but this transaction alone did not generate a major frontcourt contribution. The older Seattle-favored grade put excessive weight on Campbell's previous reputation. Neither veteran stayed with his new club beyond that season, making this a narrowly defined and short-lived advantage.

Final Verdict

Hornets Win. New Orleans receives B- for Kenny Anderson's twenty-three games, 446 minutes, 139 points and seventy-seven assists in 2002-03. Seattle gets C- for Elden Campbell's fifteen games, 184 minutes and forty-eight points. The Hornets obtained the more productive short-term reserve, reversing the earlier Seattle-favored grade without counting either player's pretrade seasons.

boston-celtics.summary: Sacramento acquired the draft rights to Lithuanian forward Darius Songaila from Boston in June 2003, sending two second-round selections that became No. 56 Brandon Hunter in 2003 and No. 53 Orien Greene in 2005. Songaila developed into a useful Kings reserve, while neither Boston draftee had the same enduring team role. Kings Win, Sacramento B versus Boston C+.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Sold Songaila's Rights for Two Seconds

The Celtics transferred the rights to Darius Songaila to Sacramento in June 2003, receiving two second-round draft picks. One was tied to No. 56 Brandon Hunter in the 2003 draft, while the other became No. 53 Orien Greene in 2005. Songaila was a developing European frontcourt player who had not yet supplied Boston with NBA minutes. The Celtics chose multiple future selection opportunities rather than retaining the rights, while the Kings sought a player whose skills could complement their established frontcourt rotation.

Songaila Became a Useful Sacramento Reserve

Songaila joined the Kings and offered shooting touch, mobility and solid decision-making from a forward position. He played significant reserve minutes across Sacramento seasons before continuing his NBA career elsewhere. Those subsequent teams' games cannot be added to his Kings receiving-team return, but the initial club still acquired a dependable role player. A second-round rights acquisition becoming an active contributor is a tangible success, especially for a team already relying on an experienced competitive core.

Hunter and Greene Gave Boston Limited Returns

Boston used the two incoming second-round opportunities on Hunter and Greene. Both received NBA chances, with Hunter supplying reserve frontcourt minutes and Greene working as a backup guard, but neither became an enduring Celtics starter. The picks were genuine assets, not blank compensation, and their short-term usefulness shouldn't be erased. Nevertheless, the club surrendered rights to a player who established a more reliable position elsewhere, making the decision to split the value into two later selections less productive in hindsight.

The Strongest Long-Term Contributor Went to Sacramento

The Kings developed a recognizable rotation forward from a player Boston could have kept under contract rights. The Celtics tried to spread their chance of finding help across two second-round prospects, which was reasonable given the uncertainty surrounding Songaila before his NBA debut. Actual results favored Sacramento, whose incoming player supplied more sustained production. The grade difference is moderate rather than overwhelming because both teams received some usable depth, but the best direct player contribution belonged to the Kings.

Final Verdict

Kings Win. Sacramento earns B for securing Darius Songaila's draft rights and obtaining a useful NBA rotation forward. Boston receives C+ for the two second-round picks used on Brandon Hunter and Orien Greene, neither of whom matched Songaila's sustained Kings role. The Celtics collected more selections, but Sacramento developed the stronger single contributor.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Four Draft Rights Changed Hands on June 26

Boston and Memphis exchanged prospect rights during the June 26, 2003 draft rather than swapping signed veterans. The Celtics received the rights to No. 13 Marcus Banks and No. 27 Kendrick Perkins, sending No. 16 Troy Bell and No. 20 Dahntay Jones to the Grizzlies. The draft positions look unusual when read only by number because Boston acquired the higher of the four choices as well as a late-first-round center. Each club was pursuing specific players and valued the combinations differently. Neither group had yet produced NBA playing time, so the exchange depended on development, not established game totals.

Perkins Became the Long-Term Boston Return

Perkins developed slowly from a young big man into Boston's primary interior defender and rebounding center. His role expanded through the franchise's turnaround, and he started for the Celtics during their 2008 NBA championship season. That production stretched across years of actual Celtics basketball and gives the acquisition unusually durable value for a draft-night rights swap. Banks also played early guard minutes, although he did not become the franchise's future point guard. Perkins's later stops after leaving Boston belong to subsequent team decisions and should not be treated as more Celtics appearances acquired in June 2003.

Memphis Received Two Different Guard Outcomes

Memphis used the transaction to secure Bell and Jones, who offered very different NBA paths. Bell's short league tenure made him a limited immediate return for a first-round selection. Jones became a defense-oriented wing with subsequent professional value, though much of his best-known work came after leaving the Grizzlies for other clubs. His later appearances cannot all be counted as Memphis output. The team was making a reasonable draft-night assessment that two guards could address roster needs, and Jones supplied genuine value rather than becoming another completely unusable rights asset. That result deserves some credit even though it never matched Perkins's Boston tenure.

A Championship Starting Center Settles the Advantage

The clearest difference is that Boston obtained a player who became a long-serving defensive starter for a title winner, while Memphis did not turn either incoming guard into an equally important Grizzlies contributor. A strong Boston grade is grounded in Perkins's actual years and Banks's additional roster service, not speculation about future second-round selections. Memphis still acquired legitimate first-round rights and developed Jones into an NBA player. This wasn't a case of the Celtics simply receiving two free prospects; both teams made deliberate draft-position tradeoffs. The receiving-team outcome nonetheless puts the historical edge firmly in Boston.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns A+ because Kendrick Perkins became its long-serving starting center and contributed to the 2008 NBA championship, with Marcus Banks providing additional early guard minutes. Memphis receives C+ for Dahntay Jones's development and Troy Bell's much smaller NBA return. The acquired assets were four 2003 draft rights, not veteran player contracts; Jones's later seasons away from Memphis cannot be assigned to the Grizzlies.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Added Jones as a Versatile Forward

The Celtics acquired Jumaine Jones from Cleveland in July 2003, trading J.R. Bremer, Bruno Šundov and a future second-round right. Jones had shown the ability to contribute perimeter and rebounding minutes as a role player, giving Boston another veteran forward option. Cleveland accepted a pair of players who could be evaluated in different positions along with a later draft opportunity. The clubs were rearranging supporting pieces rather than moving a top-level franchise scorer.

Jones Supplied Boston With a Shorter-Term Role

Jones gave the Celtics an experienced wing-forward who could provide minutes in a lineup undergoing changes. His Boston stay was not the dominant phase of his broader career, and he did not become a foundational star. It is important to judge the return from his actual Celtics tenure rather than adding contributions from earlier Cleveland or Philadelphia seasons. The player was useful as depth, but the original appeal was flexibility in the forward rotation rather than transformational scoring.

Cleveland Obtained Two Players and a Draft Right

The Cavaliers received Bremer and Šundov, both of whom had limited upside as long-term starting options. The future second-round selection became linked to No. 50 Ryan Gomes in 2005, though the rights later traveled through their own sequence of transactions. Gomes's subsequent Celtics production cannot be presented as direct Cleveland playing time. The Cavaliers gained multiple possible avenues for roster value, but none of the incoming elements immediately replaced the production of a leading NBA star.

The Narrow Edge Reflects Boston's Direct Fit

Boston acquired a veteran forward who could actually play minutes, while Cleveland received broader but less certain bench and draft compensation. The inherited slight Celtics edge is reasonable on that basis, though the Cavaliers did receive a future pick and two active-player possibilities. Neither side obtained an enduring All-Star. The return should be viewed through the roles of the players when they joined, without inferring future championship value from unrelated moves.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B- for Jumaine Jones's available forward depth, while Cleveland gets C+ for J.R. Bremer, Bruno Šundov and the second-round right later associated with Ryan Gomes. The pick's subsequent route cannot be confused with Gomes playing for Cleveland. The direct roles favored Boston modestly, without creating a major star.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
Seattle Took a Second-Rounder for a Center Who Had Started 69 Games

On September 28, 2003, the Seattle SuperSonics sent Predrag Drobnjak, also known as Peja Drobnjak, to the Los Angeles Clippers for a 2004 second-round selection. The timing reflected opposite roster objectives. Seattle was opening minutes for a younger frontcourt after Drobnjak had started 69 games in the prior season. Los Angeles needed center depth following major offseason turnover, and it was willing to give up a future mid-second-round chance for someone who could join the rotation immediately. The exchange was not a deal for a pick of unknown origin: the 2004 selection became No. 35 overall.

Drobnjak Supplied One Season of Clippers Production

Drobnjak played 61 Clippers regular-season games in 2003-04, starting 14 and logging 949 minutes. He scored 382 points, grabbed 196 rebounds and made 24 blocks, averages of 6.3 points and 3.2 rebounds in 15.6 minutes per appearance. That is usable backup-center work for a team that finished 28-54, even though he did not become a starting cornerstone. He was selected by the expansion Charlotte Bobcats in June 2004, ending the direct Los Angeles stint after one season. His prior 146 appearances in Seattle and his later 71 games with Atlanta are not part of what the Clippers acquired.

Seattle Used the Pick as a Bridge to Gelabale

Seattle selected Andre Emmett with that incoming 2004 No. 35 pick, but it moved his rights to Memphis on draft night for another second-rounder in 2005. That later selection became Mickaël Gelabale, who eventually played 70 games for Seattle in 2006-07 and 39 more in 2007-08. His 109 SuperSonics games totaled 1,704 minutes and 489 points. It would be inaccurate to say Emmett played those games for Seattle; he did not. The value came through an additional trade, with a delay between the original center deal and the arrival of a useful reserve wing.

Both Clubs Eventually Found Modest Rotation Help

Los Angeles did what it set out to do: it exchanged a second-round opportunity for 61 games of immediate center depth. Seattle needed patience and another transaction, but the same draft asset later helped it obtain a player who logged more games and minutes with the SuperSonics than Drobnjak did with the Clippers. It is tempting to grade only the original Emmett selection and call the trade a Los Angeles win, yet that would ignore the documented draft-night movement of Emmett's rights. Conversely, Gelabale's contribution should not be treated as a direct 2003 return without explaining the intermediate step. The balanced result is limited but tangible value on each side.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. The Clippers earn C+ for 61 games, 949 minutes and 382 points from Predrag Drobnjak. Drobnjak gave the Clippers 61 games, 949 minutes and 382 points in 2003-04. analysis:
Seattle Took a Second-Rounder for a Center Who Had Started 69 Games

On September 28, 2003, the Seattle SuperSonics sent Predrag Drobnjak, also known as Peja Drobnjak, to the Los Angeles Clippers for a 2004 second-round selection. The timing reflected opposite roster objectives. Seattle was opening minutes for a younger frontcourt after Drobnjak had started 69 games in the prior season. Los Angeles needed center depth following major offseason turnover, and it was willing to give up a future mid-second-round chance for someone who could join the rotation immediately. The exchange was not a deal for a pick of unknown origin: the 2004 selection became No. 35 overall.

Drobnjak Supplied One Season of Clippers Production

Drobnjak played 61 Clippers regular-season games in 2003-04, starting 14 and logging 949 minutes. He scored 382 points, grabbed 196 rebounds and made 24 blocks, averages of 6.3 points and 3.2 rebounds in 15.6 minutes per appearance. That is usable backup-center work for a team that finished 28-54, even though he did not become a starting cornerstone. He was selected by the expansion Charlotte Bobcats in June 2004, ending the direct Los Angeles stint after one season. His prior 146 appearances in Seattle and his later 71 games with Atlanta are not part of what the Clippers acquired.

Seattle Used the Pick as a Bridge to Gelabale

Seattle selected Andre Emmett with that incoming 2004 No. 35 pick, but it moved his rights to Memphis on draft night for another second-rounder in 2005. That later selection became Mickaël Gelabale, who eventually played 70 games for Seattle in 2006-07 and 39 more in 2007-08. His 109 SuperSonics games totaled 1,704 minutes and 489 points. It would be inaccurate to say Emmett played those games for Seattle; he did not. The value came through an additional trade, with a delay between the original center deal and the arrival of a useful reserve wing.

Both Clubs Eventually Found Modest Rotation Help

Los Angeles did what it set out to do: it exchanged a second-round opportunity for 61 games of immediate center depth. Seattle needed patience and another transaction, but the same draft asset later helped it obtain a player who logged more games and minutes with the SuperSonics than Drobnjak did with the Clippers. It is tempting to grade only the original Emmett selection and call the trade a Los Angeles win, yet that would ignore the documented draft-night movement of Emmett's rights. Conversely, Gelabale's contribution should not be treated as a direct 2003 return without explaining the intermediate step. The balanced result is limited but tangible value on each side.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. The Clippers earn C+ for 61 games, 949 minutes and 382 points from Predrag Drobnjak. Seattle also gets C+ because its No. 35 choice was flipped for the draft selection that became Mickaël Gelabale, a 109-game SuperSonics reserve. Both teams received useful short-term or downstream contributions.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Dallas Brought Walker and Delk Into an Already Talented Offense

On October 20, 2003, Dallas acquired former Celtics All-Star Antoine Walker and reserve guard Tony Delk, sending Boston a broader package of players and a first-round choice. The Mavericks already had Dirk Nowitzki, Steve Nash and Michael Finley, so Walker added another experienced scoring and passing forward to an ambitious team. Delk offered veteran backcourt coverage. Boston was breaking apart an established Walker-Paul Pierce pairing and accepting the longer-term salary of Raef LaFrentz while receiving younger assets. This was a major change in roster direction before the season, not an isolated deadline bench swap.

Boston Received LaFrentz, Welsch, Mills and a Real First

The Celtics' incoming players were center-forward Raef LaFrentz, guard-wing Jiří Welsch and veteran Chris Mills, accompanied by a 2004 first-round selection. LaFrentz had an expensive contract and injury problems, limiting the upside of the immediate basketball return. Welsch supplied rotation minutes, while Mills contributed little because of health issues. The pick was the most flexible component: Boston eventually used No. 24 in 2004 on Delonte West. West developed into a useful Celtics guard before later being moved in the 2007 Ray Allen agreement. Boston's return cannot be dismissed as only an unwanted contract.

Walker's Dallas Tenure Was Shorter Than His Reputation

Walker brought a recognizable scoring resume to Dallas, but he spent only the 2003-04 season with the Mavericks before being traded onward. Delk likewise supplied shorter-term veteran depth rather than becoming a foundational piece. Walker's later movements are important for transaction history, especially the separate 2004 package that brought Jason Terry to Dallas, but Terry's entire subsequent Dallas career cannot be counted as a direct asset in the October 2003 swap. Evaluating the original exchange requires considering both Walker's on-court season and the ability to trade his contract again, without importing every result of that future transaction.

Different Timelines Leave Only a Moderate Winner

Dallas made a legitimate win-now move by adding two experienced offensive players, while Boston received a first-round pick, a developing guard and several contracts with very different long-term utility. West's eventual NBA contribution improves Boston's side beyond what a low grade for LaFrentz alone would suggest. Dallas did not acquire another future first or an uncredited third player through this agreement. The Mavericks hold a modest advantage for the immediate fit and flexibility surrounding Walker, but neither club should be credited with its entire later franchise trajectory from one October transaction. The correct assessment is a narrower gap than the names initially imply.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win. Dallas earns B for adding Antoine Walker and Tony Delk to its 2003-04 roster and retaining the ability to move Walker in a later transaction. Boston receives B- for Jiří Welsch's service, the 2004 No. 24 choice used on Delonte West and its other incoming contracts, offset by Raef LaFrentz's expensive and injury-affected tenure. Jason Terry arrived in a separate 2004 package and is not a direct return from this trade.

boston-celtics.analysis:
A Four-Piece Package Brought Davis to Boston

The Celtics sent Eric Williams, Tony Battie and Kedrick Brown to Cleveland in December 2003 for Ricky Davis, Chris Mihm, Michael Stewart and a future second-round pick. Boston was searching for more offensive help alongside Paul Pierce and chose Davis, a high-usage guard-forward who had not found a stable role with the young Cavaliers. Cleveland acquired veterans it could use around its own evolving group. The inclusion of the pick meant Boston also retained a path to future player development beyond the two most recognizable arrivals.

orlando-magic.analysis:
Orlando Obtained a Fringe Center Without Giving Up a Guaranteed Pick

On December 26, 2003, the Orlando Magic acquired Robert Archibald from the Phoenix Suns for a conditional 2005 second-round pick. Both franchises' transaction ledgers explicitly say the draft condition was not exercised, so Phoenix never obtained an identifiable selection from that agreement. The deal came during Orlando's difficult 2003-04 season, when the Magic were searching for inexpensive frontcourt options. Archibald had joined Phoenix earlier in a multi-player Memphis trade but had barely been used. Moving him gave Orlando a chance to evaluate another center without surrendering a guaranteed draft asset.

Archibald's Magic Playing Time Was Four Minutes

The trade produced almost no direct basketball contribution. Archibald appeared in one Magic game, against the Knicks on December 29, and played four minutes. He scored two points and had one rebound. This is important because the incoming player was not a season-long reserve, nor did he accumulate meaningful totals that explain a high grade. His earlier Phoenix appearance that December belonged to his former team, and his later Raptors games belong to Toronto. Orlando's direct playing return consisted of one short outing, followed quickly by another roster maneuver.

Orlando Used His Contract in a Larger January Exchange

On January 2, 2004, the Magic sent Archibald to Toronto together with a 2005 second-round pick in a transaction involving Mengke Bateer, the rights to Remon Van de Hare and an exchange of future second-round positions. A later record traces the swap to picks eventually used on Roko Ukić and Travis Diener. That is real transaction activity generated after the original acquisition, but it was a package trade; Archibald alone cannot be credited with everything Orlando received. His value was chiefly that of an available contractual asset in another deal, not a player who improved the Magic's regular-season rotation.

Phoenix Lost a Contract but Never Collected the Conditional Return

For Phoenix, the asset going out was a center it was not using, making the roster decision understandable. Still, the conditional second-rounder did not convey and the Suns gained no documented draft selection or player minutes from the December exchange. Orlando received minimal playing time and subsequently found use for Archibald in a separate trade, which provides a narrow receiving-team advantage. The original Magic-favored verdict can survive, but the size of that advantage should be modest. Treating the conditional choice as an exercised Phoenix pick, or the entire Toronto trade as Archibald's single-handed achievement, would distort the sequence of events.

Final Verdict

Magic Win. Orlando receives C+ for one Robert Archibald game and his later use as a piece of a larger Toronto trade. Phoenix gets D+ because the conditional 2005 second-round pick never conveyed. This was a small asset-management advantage, not the major playing return implied by the inherited Magic B grade.
