houston-rockets.summary: New York sent Clarence Weatherspoon to Houston on December 30, 2003 for guards Moochie Norris and John Amaechi. Norris played 36 Knicks games in 2003-04 and 32 in 2004-05, providing reserve point-guard minutes. Amaechi never became a meaningful Knicks contributor. houston-rockets.analysis:
Two Clubs Exchanged Surplus Depth During a Busy Season

Houston acquired Clarence Weatherspoon from New York on December 30, 2003, sending Moochie Norris and John Amaechi to the Knicks. The Rockets needed another experienced forward behind their primary frontcourt options, while the Knicks were adjusting their backcourt during a period of front-office changes. Norris had played considerable minutes as a Houston backup in prior seasons. Amaechi was a veteran center near the end of his NBA playing career. There were no draft picks included in this three-player transaction.

Norris Provided New York With Reserve Guard Minutes

Norris appeared in thirty-six Knicks regular-season games during the remainder of 2003-04, logging 446 minutes. He returned for thirty-two additional New York appearances in 2004-05 before being sent back to Houston in a later trade. That totals sixty-eight Knicks games across the two receiving-team seasons. He offered limited point-guard coverage rather than the production he had delivered in his earlier Rockets years. Amaechi never became a significant Knicks on-court contributor, so his inclusion cannot be treated as a second active regular-season player with extensive minutes.

Weatherspoon Filled Some Frontcourt Minutes for the Rockets

Weatherspoon moved into Houston's bench rotation and appeared in regular-season games across the end of 2003-04 and 2004-05. He brought rebounding and physical strength without a major offensive role. He had scored more earlier in his career with Philadelphia and other clubs, but those statistics do not belong to the Rockets. His arrival was a depth adjustment rather than a way to add a starting forward. The fact that Houston had a playable frontcourt player is still relevant when comparing what the two receiving teams actually obtained.

Neither Side Received the Star-Level Value in the Old Grades

The Knicks used Norris for dozens of games and Houston used Weatherspoon for reserve coverage, so the deal was not a basketball zero for either team. New York did not gain a dependable starting guard from the two-player package, and Houston did not acquire an elite forward. The inherited Knicks A grade overstated the transaction's competitive importance, especially when Amaechi was essentially an inactive inclusion. Modest equal grades recognize the limited but genuine playing time provided by Norris and Weatherspoon without assigning the players' earlier career achievements to new clubs.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Houston earns C+ for adding Clarence Weatherspoon as frontcourt depth during the 2003-04 and 2004-05 seasons. New York receives C+ for sixty-eight games of reserve minutes from Moochie Norris; John Amaechi offered no comparable regular-season impact. Both returns were modest, making the inherited Knicks A assessment excessive.

new-york-knicks.summary: A February 2004 three-team trade sent Michael Doleac and a future second-round pick to Atlanta, Keith Van Horn to Milwaukee, and Tim Thomas and Nazr Mohammed to New York. The Hawks' pick later became associated with No. 37 Ronny Turiaf, while the Knicks obtained immediate frontcourt and perimeter help. The inherited slight Hawks edge grades Atlanta B+, Milwaukee B and New York B-.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
New York Pursued Thomas and Mohammed

The Knicks acquired Tim Thomas and Nazr Mohammed in February 2004 through an arrangement with Atlanta and Milwaukee. Thomas offered perimeter scoring from the forward position, while Mohammed gave New York an interior presence. The Knicks were seeking greater balance among their veteran pieces in an attempt to remain competitive in the Eastern Conference. Atlanta received Michael Doleac and a future second-round selection; Milwaukee acquired Keith Van Horn. All three teams accepted actual basketball or draft assets.

Atlanta Received a Veteran Center and a Future Pick

Doleac provided the Hawks an experienced frontcourt option, though his Atlanta tenure didn't create a lasting team centerpiece. The incoming second-round right later became linked to No. 37 Ronny Turiaf in 2005. Turiaf built an NBA career through later rights and signing arrangements, so his eventual playing totals shouldn't simply be assigned to Atlanta. The club nevertheless gained a usable future selection alongside Doleac, making the package more varied than a cash-only or single-expiring-contract trade.

Milwaukee Received Van Horn's Scoring Experience

Van Horn had already spent several seasons as a starting-level NBA scorer and brought shooting from a larger forward spot. The Bucks could seek offensive production from him without developing another young prospect. His value was real but had to be judged in Milwaukee's receiving-team context rather than by his earlier New Jersey or Knicks seasons. Van Horn was a familiar name, but the inherited B grade reflects a practical veteran acquisition instead of a franchise-changing star.

Each Club Took a Different Kind of Return

The Hawks received a center and another draft opportunity, Milwaukee added a recognizable scorer, and New York chose two active veterans. The inherited slight Atlanta edge grades the future flexibility of its pick along with Doleac, although Thomas and Mohammed supplied genuine Knicks minutes. None of the three participants should be erased when reviewing the trade. The long-term rights path of the incoming selection should also be kept distinct from the eventual teams on which Turiaf played.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta gets B+ for Michael Doleac and the second-round right later associated with Ronny Turiaf. Milwaukee earns B for Keith Van Horn, an experienced perimeter scorer. New York receives B- for Tim Thomas and Nazr Mohammed, who gave the Knicks immediate rotation options. The inherited advantage rewards Atlanta's additional draft flexibility without claiming Turiaf's later games as Hawks production.

The Hawks received Chris Mills; the Pistons received Mike James. The inherited Pistons Win grades Detroit A+, Boston A- and Atlanta B+.

boston-celtics.summary: In February 2004 Boston received Lindsey Hunter, Chucky Atkins, a first-round choice later associated with Tony Allen and cash during a three-team arrangement with Atlanta and Detroit. The Hawks received Chris Mills; the Pistons received Mike James. The inherited Pistons Win grades Detroit A+, Boston A- and Atlanta B+.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Acquired Guards, a First and Cash

The Celtics entered a February 2004 three-team transaction with Atlanta and Detroit, receiving Lindsey Hunter, Chucky Atkins, a first-round choice and $3 million. The later selection became associated with No. 25 Tony Allen in the 2004 draft. Boston was adjusting its backcourt and collecting draft value rather than retaining precisely the same veteran rotation. The incoming selection provided a particularly consequential opportunity as the club rebuilt the supporting cast around Paul Pierce.

Detroit Added Mike James for a Championship Push

The Pistons received guard Mike James, giving them an experienced reserve during a season that ultimately ended with the 2004 NBA championship. James brought defensive activity and ball-handling depth behind Detroit's established starters. His role was not equivalent to the contributions of the team's leading players, but he supplied useful bench coverage when postseason guard play was valuable. That direct receiving-team value supports the inherited high Detroit grade without overstating him as the architect of the title run.

Atlanta Received Chris Mills in a Smaller Role

The Hawks acquired veteran Chris Mills as their recorded incoming asset. Mills had earlier NBA experience as a forward, but his Atlanta role did not become a substantial new on-court chapter. This side of the three-team deal is therefore different from Boston's draft selection and Detroit's championship-season guard depth. It is a roster transaction involving a veteran, not evidence that Atlanta obtained a future franchise cornerstone. Keeping the third participant visible avoids distorting the historical record into only a Celtics-Pistons exchange.

The Different Returns Explain the Three Grades

Detroit's A+ rewards the immediate usefulness of James on a contender, while Boston's A- recognizes draft capital that became connected to Tony Allen and multiple accompanying assets. Atlanta's B+ under the inherited model reflects its agreement to participate and receive Mills, though his direct playing impact was limited. These grades should be interpreted through each team's actual return rather than treating the eventual entire careers of every named player as part of one club's production.

Final Verdict

Pistons Win. Detroit earns A+ for Mike James's useful reserve play during its 2004 championship season. Boston receives A- for Lindsey Hunter, Chucky Atkins, cash and the first-round choice later used on Tony Allen. Atlanta gets B+ under the inherited grades for Chris Mills, despite his limited direct Hawks playing impact. Detroit's immediate team success supports the slight top grade.

memphis-grizzlies.summary: Seattle traded the rights to its 2004 No. 35 pick Andre Emmett to Memphis for cash and a 2005 second-round pick. Emmett played only eight NBA games for Memphis. Seattle used the following year's No. 48 choice on Mickaël Gelabale, who later appeared in 109 SuperSonics games across 2006-07 and 2007-08. SuperSonics Win, Seattle B+ and Memphis D+, owing to the greater delayed on-court return.
memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
Memphis Bought Seattle's Newly Drafted Guard

On June 24, 2004, the Memphis Grizzlies obtained the draft rights to Texas Tech wing Andre Emmett after Seattle selected him with the thirty-fifth overall choice. Memphis paid cash and surrendered a second-round selection in the 2005 draft. The Grizzlies' official historical transaction record confirms both parts of the compensation. Emmett had been a prolific college scorer, making him an attractive second-round candidate. Seattle instead preferred the financial payment and another chance to select a prospect one year later. No established NBA rotation player changed teams on draft night.

Emmett's Grizzlies Stint Lasted Eight Regular-Season Games

Emmett signed with Memphis during July 2004 and joined the organization for his rookie season, but his NBA opportunities were limited. He appeared in eight Grizzlies regular-season games in 2004-05 and never became a dependable rotation wing. He later left the team in a separate multi-club transaction and pursued opportunities elsewhere in basketball. His college points and professional performances after Memphis are not receiving-team output created by this exchange. The club got a genuine player audition, though an extremely small number of NBA appearances for the rights it had purchased.

Seattle Turned the 2005 Selection Into Gelabale

The 2005 second-rounder arrived at No. 48, and Seattle selected French forward Mickaël Gelabale. He continued overseas for another season before joining the SuperSonics, then appeared in 70 games in 2006-07 and 39 more in 2007-08. His 109 Seattle appearances were a delayed but measurable return on the incoming pick, alongside the money the team had already collected. The timing matters: Gelabale was selected in 2005 and debuted in the NBA in 2006, not as an immediate piece of the 2004 Memphis trade. That chain is fully documented by draft records.

The Sonics Won Through a More Useful Follow-Up Pick

Memphis acquired a scorer worth investigating but did not find a lasting NBA contributor. Seattle accepted the risk of a future second-round selection and received a reserve wing who eventually played far more games in a SuperSonics uniform than Emmett did for Memphis. Neither athlete became a star, and Gelabale's later appearances outside the Seattle franchise aren't part of this return. Still, a 109-game reserve plus cash was a better outcome than an eight-game audition. The original equal grades overlooked the delayed draft pick and should favor Seattle without exaggerating either side's value.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win. Seattle earns B+ for the cash payment and the 2005 No. 48 pick that became Mickaël Gelabale, who played 109 SuperSonics regular-season games. Memphis receives D+ because Andre Emmett played only eight Grizzlies games after the rights purchase. The original 2004 draft choice was less valuable than the delayed selection Seattle acquired.

He continued overseas for another season before joining the SuperSonics, then appeared in 70 games in 2006-07 and 39 more in 2007-08. His 109 Seattle appearances were a delayed but measurable return on the incoming pick, alongside the money the team had already collected. The timing matters: Gelabale was selected in 2005 and debuted in the NBA in 2006, not as an immediate piece of the 2004 Memphis trade. That chain is fully documented by draft records.

The Sonics Won Through a More Useful Follow-Up Pick

Memphis acquired a scorer worth investigating but did not find a lasting NBA contributor. Seattle accepted the risk of a future second-round selection and received a reserve wing who eventually played far more games in a SuperSonics uniform than Emmett did for Memphis. Neither athlete became a star, and Gelabale's later appearances outside the Seattle franchise aren't part of this return. Still, a 109-game reserve plus cash was a better outcome than an eight-game audition. The original equal grades overlooked the delayed draft pick and should favor Seattle without exaggerating either side's value.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win. Seattle earns B+ for the cash payment and the 2005 No. 48 pick that became Mickaël Gelabale, who played 109 SuperSonics regular-season games. Memphis receives D+ because Andre Emmett played only eight Grizzlies games after the rights purchase. The original 2004 draft choice was less valuable than the delayed selection Seattle acquired.

philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Cleveland Sought a Defensive Guard Beside LeBron James

The Cavaliers acquired Eric Snow from Philadelphia on July 20, 2004, giving up young forward Kedrick Brown and guard Kevin Ollie. Snow had helped the 76ers reach the 2001 NBA Finals and had years of starting experience. Cleveland wanted an experienced defender and organizer to share the backcourt with rising star LeBron James. Philadelphia was adjusting its roster under a new coaching staff and moved a veteran contract for two players. The deal paired an established starter against younger or more limited rotation options.

Snow Became a Dependable Cavaliers Starter

Snow's most influential Cleveland season came in 2005-06, when he started all eighty-two regular-season games and all thirteen postseason contests. His scoring totals were modest, but he handled difficult defensive matchups while James took much of the offensive responsibility. Cleveland returned to the playoffs that year, establishing a new competitive era for the franchise. Snow also appeared in all eighty-two regular-season games in 2006-07, when the Cavaliers advanced to the NBA Finals. His sustained availability far exceeded a short veteran audition.

Philadelphia Did Not Obtain an Equivalent Starting Guard

The Sixers received Brown, a young forward who struggled to secure a consistent long-term NBA role, along with Ollie, a veteran guard who was better suited to reserve responsibilities. Philadelphia got immediate roster flexibility and backcourt cover, but neither incoming player replaced the combination of defense, starts and leadership that Snow delivered in Cleveland. Snow's previous 76ers accomplishments should not be counted as a Cavaliers return, yet the clubs' subsequent records show the acquisition paid off over multiple seasons. The difference became apparent once the Cavaliers made repeated playoff trips.

The Multi-Year Starter Clearly Beat the Return Package

The old even grade treated a functioning Cleveland starting point guard as equivalent to a pair of Philadelphia reserves. The season-by-season receiving-team evidence supports a different conclusion. Brown and Ollie were NBA professionals and helped fill positions, but Snow took on higher responsibility for a contending team for several years. He was not an elite scorer and did not replace James as a primary playmaker. Still, the Cavaliers received a stable defensive guard at the time their competitive identity was being established, giving Cleveland a distinct advantage.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland gets A- for Eric Snow's multi-season defensive and organizing role, including all eighty-two starts and thirteen playoff starts in 2005-06. Philadelphia gets C+ for Kedrick Brown and Kevin Ollie as roster options without comparable sustained starting responsibilities. Snow's years as an established Cavalier support replacing the inherited even verdict.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Dallas Traded Walker Back Out and Secured Terry

The August 4, 2004 deal sent Antoine Walker and Tony Delk to Atlanta while giving Dallas Jason Terry, Alan Henderson and a conditional future draft consideration that ultimately resolved to cash. Walker had spent one season in Dallas after arriving from Boston, so the Mavericks were changing a major forward role again. Atlanta, meanwhile, accepted an established scorer who could handle significant possessions for a team trying to establish a new rotation. The conditional first-round term should not be turned into a draft prospect who never actually reached Dallas; its protection ultimately changed the practical compensation.

Terry Became a Genuine Long-Term Dallas Contributor

Terry was the decisive asset. He joined the Mavericks as a guard who could score, handle the ball and play alongside Dirk Nowitzki, and remained part of the team's core through its 2011 NBA title. In the championship-clinching Game 6 against Miami, Terry scored twenty-seven points and led Dallas in scoring. His actual Mavericks tenure lasted well beyond the short season Walker had just spent with the organization. Henderson provided further veteran frontcourt depth, but the scale of the victory comes from Terry becoming a trusted postseason player. No later Terry appearances with Boston or other teams need to be borrowed for this conclusion.

Walker and Delk Were Short-Term Atlanta Options

Atlanta obtained recognizable NBA offense in Walker and backcourt coverage in Delk. Walker supplied points and rebounds during the 2004-05 season, but the club did not make him a permanent part of its rebuild. It later returned him to Boston in another transaction rather than building several playoff runs around him. Delk also supplied roster minutes without becoming the Hawks' long-term answer in the backcourt. Their value was real, so a failing grade for Atlanta would be unfair, but neither outgoing Mavericks veteran matched what Terry later delivered in Dallas. The follow-up Boston exchange had its own players and draft costs.

The Original 2004 Exchange Created a Title-Team Foundation Piece

The central comparison is between a long-serving championship guard for Dallas and shorter-term veteran contracts for Atlanta. The Mavericks paid an established scorer and another guard but received a player who could stay through multiple roster iterations. Atlanta's front office obtained immediate scoring and flexibility for additional trades, not a useless return. The protected future pick did not produce an identifiable first-round NBA player for Dallas and must remain a cash-resolution item. Even after assigning proper value to Walker's Atlanta minutes, the difference in direct receiving-team production is large and favors Dallas strongly.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win. Dallas earns A+ for Jason Terry's eight-season tenure and central role in the 2011 NBA championship, with Alan Henderson offering additional depth. Atlanta receives C+ for Antoine Walker's short-term scoring and Tony Delk's veteran service before both moved on. The future first-round condition resolved to cash, not a drafted Mavericks player, and Terry's later seasons elsewhere are excluded.

boston-celtics.analysis:
An Amended Trade Changed the Actual Outgoing Players

The Celtics agreed to acquire Gary Payton, Rick Fox, a conditional first-round choice and cash from the Lakers on August 6, 2004. The initial terms sent Chris Mihm, Chucky Atkins, Marcus Banks and a second-round pick to Los Angeles. One week later, Boston and the Lakers amended the agreement: Jumaine Jones replaced Banks, and the second-round choice was removed. The corrected final terms are essential. Evaluating the superseded announcement as if it were completed would attribute assets to the wrong club.

Payton Played While Fox Retired Before His Celtics Debut

Payton supplied veteran guard minutes for Boston during the 2004-05 season, although he was later part of another trade and subsequently returned. Fox, in contrast, retired without becoming a Celtics regular-season contributor. Their previous Lakers careers explain why the names drew attention, but only their receiving-team outcome belongs in the Boston assessment. The Celtics had acquired experienced personnel during a roster reworking, yet the two veterans did not deliver the same level of actual playing utility.

The Conditional First Was Valuable Across Later Trades

The incoming first-round right eventually became associated with the 2006 No. 21 selection used on Rajon Rondo. That does not mean Rondo arrived directly in Boston from this 2004 agreement. The pick passed through later transactions involving Atlanta and Phoenix before the Celtics obtained Rondo's rights in a separate draft-day move. Boston initially received a useful and movable draft asset, and its later identity demonstrates why the Lakers' surrender of a first was more consequential than sending away aging veterans alone.

Los Angeles Got Immediate Depth but Gave Up Draft Value

Mihm offered the Lakers a center option, Atkins gave them backcourt experience and Jones joined the forward group under the revised agreement. Those were genuine roster pieces, not empty compensation. Still, Los Angeles parted with a conditional first and financial considerations to make the roster change. The Celtics obtained a veteran guard plus an asset with significant downstream draft value, while the Lakers got depth rather than a major long-term replacement for their departing stars. The higher Boston grade reflects that broader return.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns A- for Gary Payton's veteran contribution and the movable conditional first-round asset, with Fox providing no Celtics regular-season games. Los Angeles gets C+ for Chris Mihm, Chucky Atkins and Jumaine Jones under the amended final terms. Banks and Boston's second-round pick were removed; Rajon Rondo's eventual No. 21 identity belongs to a later chain of transactions.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Looked for Frontcourt Experience

The Hawks acquired Predrag Drobnjak from the expansion Charlotte Bobcats in August 2004, giving up a second-round choice in the following draft. Atlanta had an unsettled roster and needed a veteran center capable of taking minutes while younger players developed. Drobnjak had already played NBA seasons with Seattle and the Clippers, giving him a more established professional background than an unknown prospect. Charlotte chose a future draft opportunity rather than keeping another veteran big in its expansion roster.

Drobnjak Supplied a Short-Term Hawks Option

Drobnjak was a capable perimeter-shooting big for his era, but his Atlanta stay did not evolve into a long run as the franchise's starting center. His prior NBA scoring belongs to his earlier employers and shouldn't be carried into the Hawks' evaluation. The acquired center gave the club immediate depth during a transitional season. He did not provide the type of lasting production that would make surrendering a valuable second-round selection an automatic success.

Charlotte Secured a 2005 Second-Round Selection

The incoming choice became associated with No. 37 Ronny Turiaf in the 2005 draft. Turiaf eventually established an NBA career, but the rights chain passed through other transactions before his playing time elsewhere; Charlotte should not be credited with all those later games. The pick was still a useful tradable asset for a newly formed club collecting ways to construct its roster. Charlotte chose flexibility over an immediate center who wasn't essential to its development.

The Draft Asset Favored the Expansion Team

Atlanta obtained veteran availability for the season but no enduring new centerpiece, while Charlotte acquired a selection with more long-term maneuvering potential. The inherited Charlotte B+ reflects the future right rather than a claim that Turiaf personally became a Bobcats star. Atlanta's C- follows from the limited duration of Drobnjak's Hawks tenure. This is a small but revealing example of a rebuilding team paying draft capital for short-term depth.

Charlotte Win. perspectives.analysis:
Houston Acquired Mutombo for Three Supporting Players

On September 8, 2004, Houston acquired veteran center Dikembe Mutombo from Chicago for Eric Piatkowski, Adrian Griffin and Mike Wilks. Mutombo had arrived in Chicago during an earlier multiteam roster change and was not part of the Bulls’ intended young frontcourt. Houston had Yao Ming as its starting center and sought an experienced backup who could anchor defensive possessions, rebound and protect the rim. The Rockets acquired a known specialist instead of several different rotation candidates.

Mutombo Provided Multiple Seasons of Defensive Insurance

Mutombo became a valuable backup for Yao across five Houston seasons. In 2004–05 he supplied about 5.3 rebounds and 1.3 blocks in limited minutes, and later played a larger role when Yao was injured. His defensive positioning, rebounding and shot-blocking allowed Houston to maintain a credible interior presence. This was more than a one-season rental: Mutombo’s usefulness persisted long after the individual Chicago acquisitions had become minor depth players or left the roster.

Chicago Did Receive Some Real Guard-and-Wing Minutes

Piatkowski played 68 games for Chicago in 2004–05, averaging 4.8 points in about twelve minutes a night while spacing the floor. Griffin appeared in 69 games and supplied defensive wing depth. Wilks was waived before the season began. Those were legitimate modest contributions to a Bulls team that made the playoffs, but the three-player total does not automatically equal the multi-season value Houston received at center. Chicago’s return was useful but not the stronger package.

The Recorded Winner and Grades Needed a Source Correction

The earlier inherited canonical verdict favored Chicago with a B-plus while giving Houston C-plus, despite its own Houston perspective acknowledging Mutombo’s longevity. That grading overvalued a count of three incoming players against one veteran. The completed results instead support Rockets Win, Houston A-minus and Chicago C-plus. Houston acquired a lasting defensive insurance policy while Chicago received smaller, largely short-lived role-player contributions. This correction updates the canonical verdict and perspectives together rather than leaving contradictory descriptions live in the archive.

Rockets Win — Houston A-minus, Chicago C-plus. Mutombo provided five seasons of defensive help behind Yao, including important minutes when the starting center was unavailable. Chicago obtained usable 2004–05 minutes from Piatkowski and Griffin, but waived Wilks before opening night. The Rockets’ longer and more consequential return outweighs Chicago’s depth, reversing the old template-based Bulls verdict.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Teams Exchanged Very Different Backcourt Specialists

On December 23, 2004, Atlanta acquired Tyronn Lue from Houston for Jon Barry in a straightforward two-player exchange. Lue was a point guard whose role involved initiating possessions and steadying an inexperienced offense. Barry was a veteran shooting guard known for moving the ball and punishing open perimeter looks. The Hawks needed more minutes from a conventional ball handler as they rebuilt, while the Rockets sought an additional shooter around Tracy McGrady and Yao Ming. Both teams made clear near-term decisions rather than exchanging future lottery assets or international draft rights.

Lue Supplied Atlanta with Actual Guard Minutes

Lue joined the Hawks for the remainder of 2004-05 and continued to play meaningful backcourt minutes across later Atlanta seasons. His steady ball handling brought experience to a team cycling through younger scorers and searching for its next successful core. The guard was not a future All-Star for Atlanta, and the earlier championships he won as a Lakers reserve did not become Hawks achievements through this trade. Those distinctions keep the grade within a moderate range. Atlanta received a usable point guard, but it did not obtain the playoff offense that Barry might have provided to an already established contender.

Barry Fit Houston's Immediate Perimeter Needs

Barry supplied veteran outside shooting after arriving from Atlanta and was part of Houston's 2004-05 roster during its postseason push. His playing career already included stops with several clubs, so only his Houston games should count toward what the Rockets bought in December. He could operate without requiring the offense to run through him, making his skill set compatible with McGrady and Yao. He did not remain a major Houston contributor for many years, and his prior scoring elsewhere should not inflate his Rockets tenure. The agreement delivered a useful specialist rather than an enduring franchise centerpiece.

Each Team Received a Player Suited to Its Timetable

Atlanta's benefit was a veteran point guard who could direct younger players during a rebuild, while Houston added a familiar shooter to a better-positioned team. Lue's longer direct Hawks service offsets the Rockets' more immediate playoff utility from Barry. Neither club surrendered an incoming first-round selection, and neither acquired a foundational star in this exchange. As a result, a balanced judgment is more credible than transferring Barry's earlier seasons or Lue's Los Angeles championship achievements to their new teams. Both front offices had a specific basketball objective and obtained at least part of it.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Atlanta receives B- for Tyronn Lue's point-guard service over multiple Hawks seasons, and Houston earns B- for Jon Barry's shooting and veteran postseason contribution. The incoming guards answered different immediate needs without becoming either franchise's long-term star. Lue's earlier Lakers championships and Barry's production for past clubs belong to those earlier teams, not the direct 2004 transaction returns.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Exchanged McCarty for a Future Selection

The Celtics sent veteran forward Walter McCarty and cash to Phoenix in February 2005, taking back a second-round right in the 2007 draft. McCarty had been a familiar Boston rotation player whose outside shooting and defensive size helped him fill different roles. Phoenix was assembling depth for a competitive Western Conference season and could use a veteran with those qualities. Boston chose the possibility of a younger player later instead of keeping McCarty on the roster through the rest of that campaign.

McCarty's Phoenix Contribution Was Limited

McCarty supplied veteran depth for the Suns, but the trade did not create a major new scoring option or a long-term starter in Phoenix. His greatest playing history had already been established elsewhere, so those past Celtics minutes cannot become Suns production simply by changing his uniform. The appeal for Phoenix was the opportunity to use him as a reserve in a roster already led by other stars. The incoming cash was part of the deal but not an additional on-court contributor.

Boston Held a Pick Later Linked to Aaron Gray

Boston's incoming second-round right was eventually associated with the 2007 selection at No. 49, used on Aaron Gray. Draft-rights ownership changed through later transactions, so Gray's subsequent NBA career should not be presented as several seasons of Celtics center play from this agreement. The pick still had potential trade value and represented a chance to revise the roster when the draft arrived. It was a future option, not a direct substitute for McCarty's immediate forward minutes.

The Equal Grades Fit a Smaller Transaction

Phoenix got a veteran who could play a supporting role during a competitive season, while Boston received a later draft right instead of direct playing time. Neither side acquired an enduring centerpiece from the agreement, and the value depended on very different team priorities. The original Even Trade judgment awards both teams C+ for modest rather than transformative returns. That assessment doesn't require pretending McCarty became a key Suns star or crediting Boston with Gray's career on other clubs.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston receives C+ for the future second-round selection later linked to Aaron Gray, a movable draft asset whose later player production shouldn't be credited automatically to the Celtics. Phoenix also gets C+ for Walter McCarty's veteran depth and cash during its competitive 2005 season. Neither incoming package created a major lasting advantage.

golden-state-warriors.summary: New Jersey sent Golden State second-round selections in 2005 and 2007 for veteran Clifford Robinson on February 14, 2005. The picks became Chris Taft at No. 42 and Stéphane Lasme at No. 46, while Robinson supplied New Jersey with depth through the 2006-07 season, including playoff minutes. Neither Warriors draftee established a comparable sustained rotation role. Nets Win: New Jersey A- and Golden State C.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Nets Spent Two Second-Round Picks on a Veteran Big Man

New Jersey acquired Clifford Robinson from Golden State on February 14, 2005, surrendering second-round choices in the 2005 and 2007 drafts. The Nets had a competitive core featuring Jason Kidd, Vince Carter and Richard Jefferson and wanted a defender who could switch between forward and center responsibilities. Robinson was a proven veteran but past his peak scoring years. Golden State chose two future chances to add lower-cost prospects rather than carrying the rest of the center's contract. The trade was recorded before the February deadline.

Robinson Contributed Across Several Nets Playoff Seasons

Robinson played the remainder of 2004-05 for New Jersey and stayed with the team through 2006-07, giving the Nets years of frontcourt defensive experience. He was useful as a veteran reserve and occasional starter when the club needed more size or a matchup option. The Nets reached the postseason in each of those years, although Robinson was not their primary scorer and his contribution varied with age and injuries. That practical availability was meaningful for a team focused on advancing past the opening playoff rounds.

The Draft Selections Became Taft and Lasme

The 2005 choice given to Golden State became Chris Taft, taken forty-second overall, while the 2007 choice became Stéphane Lasme at No. 46. Both were legitimate attempts to find athletic defensive big men late in the draft. Neither developed into a sustained Warriors rotation fixture. Taft made only a short series of NBA appearances, and Lasme's Warriors opportunity was even briefer before he later played for Miami. Golden State cannot use Lasme's other-team career or international seasons as evidence that its 2005 acquisition produced a dependable contributor.

The Nets Realized Their Role-Player Investment

New Jersey exchanged two uncertain second-round slots for frontcourt depth it could actually deploy on playoff teams. Golden State obtained the right to develop two younger athletes, which wasn't valueless, but the realized league production stayed limited. Robinson did not make the Nets championship contenders by himself, and his earlier Phoenix and Portland accomplishments should not be included. His sustained receiving-team presence nevertheless exceeded the combined Warriors careers of the two drafted players. The existing Nets-winning verdict was supported by the asset outcomes, not merely the reputation of the veteran.

Final Verdict

Nets Win. New Jersey earns A- for Clifford Robinson's defensive rotation work spanning the balance of 2004-05 through 2006-07 and multiple playoff appearances. Golden State receives C for the two second-round picks that became Chris Taft and Stéphane Lasme, neither of whom developed into sustained Warriors depth. The Nets secured the more useful direct return.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Celtics Reunited With Walker at the Deadline

Boston acquired Antoine Walker from Atlanta in February 2005, sending Gary Payton, Tom Gugliotta, Michael Stewart and a protected first-round selection. Walker had been a familiar offensive centerpiece for the Celtics before his earlier departure, so the reunion was intended to add immediate scoring and passing to the frontcourt. Atlanta was changing direction and preferred multiple pieces and draft capital over retaining Walker. The deal combined an emotional reunion with a consequential future pick.

Walker Helped Boston's Immediate Rotation

Walker gave the Celtics another experienced forward for their 2005 playoff push, contributing size, passing and shot creation in a team already centered around Paul Pierce. His presence had a clear near-term basketball purpose even though it was not a long-term championship solution. Payton's trajectory was unusual: after arriving in the Hawks' package, he was released and returned to Boston. That sequence should not be misreported as a long productive Atlanta point-guard stint or as an asset Boston received directly in the original exchange.

Atlanta Received a First-Round Right With a Long Trail

The Hawks' incoming draft asset was a protected first that eventually became linked to No. 21 Rajon Rondo in 2006. Rondo's later Celtics career was outstanding, but the rights passed through other trades before he played in Boston. His seasons cannot be counted as Hawks production from this 2005 move. Gugliotta and Stewart were also part of the incoming package, though their immediate Hawks value was limited compared with the pick's potential.

Both Teams Had Reasonable Time Horizons

Boston wanted known offensive help immediately and got Walker for a return stint. Atlanta preferred flexibility and rights that could be exchanged or developed later. The absence of extended Hawks playing time from Payton lowers the immediate value of its package, but the first-round asset prevents it from being empty. The inherited Even Trade verdict reflects different benefits rather than matching player statistics. It also requires tracing the Rondo selection honestly instead of claiming the future Celtics star played for Atlanta.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston earns B for reacquiring Antoine Walker and gaining immediate frontcourt offense for its 2005 playoff push. Atlanta also receives B for the veterans and protected first-round right later associated with Rajon Rondo, although Payton soon returned to Boston and Rondo didn't play for the Hawks. Each organization pursued a different timeline with a recognizable benefit.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Converted Welsch Into Draft Flexibility

The Celtics sent Jiří Welsch to Cleveland at the February 2005 deadline, acquiring a future first-round pick and an agreement altering protection on a previous Cavaliers first-round obligation. Boston was trying to balance its current playing group against the ability to make moves in later drafts. Cleveland wanted another wing who could handle the ball and contribute on the perimeter. The two parts of Boston's compensation gave the deal unusual value beyond a straightforward single pick for a reserve.

Welsch Did Not Establish a Long Cavaliers Career

Welsch had shown versatility in Boston, but Cleveland did not receive years of established rotation production after acquiring him. His Cavaliers stay was limited and he moved on during another transaction. The intended appeal was a guard with size and some passing ability, yet the immediate playing result was comparatively modest. His past Celtics numbers cannot substitute for the smaller receiving-team output in Cleveland, which helps explain why the team's inherited grade is only C.

The Boston First Eventually Became No. 24

The future first-round selection was later associated with No. 24 Rudy Fernández in the 2007 draft. Rights to the player followed additional transactions before Fernández became an NBA contributor, so his later career should not be represented as playing time in a Celtics uniform. The first-round asset still held value because Boston could direct its future draft strategy around it. Removing protection on a separate Cavaliers obligation was another practical improvement in Boston's draft position.

Two Draft Benefits Outweighed a Brief Wing Trial

The Celtics obtained a first-round opportunity and improved terms on another existing selection without surrendering a central player. Cleveland received Welsch but lacked the substantial on-court return needed to justify that compensation. The B+ Boston grade reflects the breadth of its draft leverage, while Cleveland's C reflects a short-lived wing acquisition. Those results don't require imagining either pick immediately became a Boston All-Star.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for a 2007 first-round right associated with Rudy Fernández and removal of protection on an earlier Cavaliers pick obligation. Cleveland receives C for Jiří Welsch, who had a brief and limited Cavaliers stint. The draft leverage Boston secured proved more useful than the guard Cleveland added, without treating Fernández's later teams' performances as Celtics production.

houston-rockets.analysis:
Milwaukee Collected Two Second-Round Chances for Immediate Guard Help

Houston acquired Mike James and Zendon Hamilton from the Bucks at the February 24, 2005 deadline. Milwaukee took back guard Reece Gaines and the Rockets' second-round selections in 2006 and 2007. James had played for multiple teams but offered the Rockets an experienced scorer behind Tracy McGrady. The Bucks, not positioned for a deep postseason run, chose more future player options. At the time there was little reason to know that the later of those draft selections would produce a useful NBA point guard.

James Was a Short-Term Houston Playoff Contributor

James played for Houston through the end of the 2004-05 regular season and the club's postseason series against Dallas. His scoring ability was useful for a team that needed more backcourt offense, even when his minutes fluctuated. Hamilton provided another reserve body but did not become a lasting rotation player. Houston then traded James in October 2005 for Rafer Alston in a separate transaction, which ended the direct playing period from this February exchange. His later Toronto, Minnesota and Houston years should not be attached to the initial acquisition.

The Bucks Used Their Picks on Noel and Sessions

Milwaukee used the 2006 second-round selection on David Noel at No. 39, then selected Ramon Sessions at No. 56 in 2007 with the later pick. Noel was a short-term Bucks reserve, but Sessions developed into a useful ball handler who earned substantial regular-season minutes in 2007-08 and 2008-09. That delayed return gave Milwaukee more than a speculative foreign draft-rights asset. Sessions' later work for Minnesota and other franchises is not part of Milwaukee's direct return, but the seasons he actually played for the Bucks are meaningful.

The Later Draft Choice Changes the Historical Verdict

Houston's side was not a failure. James provided real guard scoring during a playoff push, and the Rockets obtained the opportunity to trade his contract again later that year. Milwaukee nonetheless turned the two outgoing veterans into multiple NBA players, most importantly Sessions. The inherited Bucks win was sensible and becomes clearer when the draft selections are traced to the players who occupied them. An A- for Milwaukee rewards the useful point-guard development without counting every later stop in Sessions' career or assuming his original selection was a first-round pick.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns A- for turning the trade into the 2006 No. 39 David Noel selection and the 2007 No. 56 Ramon Sessions pick, later a useful Bucks guard. Houston gets B- for Mike James's immediate 2005 regular-season and playoff depth, plus Zendon Hamilton. The delayed draft return outweighs the shorter Rockets acquisition stint.

Houston gets B- for Mike James's immediate 2005 regular-season and playoff depth, plus Zendon Hamilton. The delayed draft return outweighs the shorter Rockets acquisition stint.

summary: Houston received Mike James and Zendon Hamilton from Milwaukee on February 24, 2005 for Reece Gaines and second-round picks in 2006 and 2007. The 2007 pick became No. 56 Ramon Sessions, who played for the Bucks during the following two seasons, while the 2006 pick became David Noel. James gave Houston an immediate guard during its 2005 playoff run but did not stay long. Bucks Win, Milwaukee A- versus Rockets B-.
analysis:
Milwaukee Collected Two Second-Round Chances for Immediate Guard Help

Houston acquired Mike James and Zendon Hamilton from the Bucks at the February 24, 2005 deadline. Milwaukee took back guard Reece Gaines and the Rockets' second-round selections in 2006 and 2007. James had played for multiple teams but offered the Rockets an experienced scorer behind Tracy McGrady. The Bucks, not positioned for a deep postseason run, chose more future player options. At the time there was little reason to know that the later of those draft selections would produce a useful NBA point guard.

James Was a Short-Term Houston Playoff Contributor

James played for Houston through the end of the 2004-05 regular season and the club's postseason series against Dallas. His scoring ability was useful for a team that needed more backcourt offense, even when his minutes fluctuated. Hamilton provided another reserve body but did not become a lasting rotation player. Houston then traded James in October 2005 for Rafer Alston in a separate transaction, which ended the direct playing period from this February exchange. His later Toronto, Minnesota and Houston years should not be attached to the initial acquisition.

The Bucks Used Their Picks on Noel and Sessions

Milwaukee used the 2006 second-round selection on David Noel at No. 39, then selected Ramon Sessions at No. 56 in 2007 with the later pick. Noel was a short-term Bucks reserve, but Sessions developed into a useful ball handler who earned substantial regular-season minutes in 2007-08 and 2008-09. That delayed return gave Milwaukee more than a speculative foreign draft-rights asset. Sessions' later work for Minnesota and other franchises is not part of Milwaukee's direct return, but the seasons he actually played for the Bucks are meaningful.

The Later Draft Choice Changes the Historical Verdict

Houston's side was not a failure. James provided real guard scoring during a playoff push, and the Rockets obtained the opportunity to trade his contract again later that year. Milwaukee nonetheless turned the two outgoing veterans into multiple NBA players, most importantly Sessions. The inherited Bucks win was sensible and becomes clearer when the draft selections are traced to the players who occupied them. An A- for Milwaukee rewards the useful point-guard development without counting every later stop in Sessions' career or assuming his original selection was a first-round pick.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns A- for turning the trade into the 2006 No. 39 David Noel selection and the 2007 No. 56 Ramon Sessions pick, later a useful Bucks guard. Houston gets B- for Mike James's immediate 2005 regular-season and playoff depth, plus Zendon Hamilton. The delayed draft return outweighs the shorter Rockets acquisition stint.

miami-heat.summary: Miami sent Malik Allen and cash to Charlotte on February 24, 2005, reacquiring former Heat draft choice Steve Smith. Smith played 13 Miami games, totaling 114 minutes and 23 points, while Allen played 22 Charlotte games, 271 minutes and 111 points. The Bobcats gained extra frontcourt coverage and money; Miami obtained a brief veteran reunion. Bobcats Win, Charlotte B- and Miami C.
miami-heat.analysis:
Miami Brought Steve Smith Back to His Original NBA Team

On February 24, 2005, the Heat reacquired veteran swingman Steve Smith from Charlotte, giving the Bobcats forward Malik Allen and cash. Smith had originally been selected fifth overall by Miami in 1991 and spent several productive early years there. By 2005 he was near the end of his playing career, so the reunion served a different purpose: perimeter experience for a team built around Shaquille O'Neal and Dwyane Wade. Charlotte preferred a younger frontcourt player and additional financial compensation to retaining its veteran scorer.

Smith Supplied Limited Depth Rather Than His Former Star Form

Smith appeared in thirteen Miami regular-season games following the move, totaling 114 minutes and only twenty-three points. A back injury restricted his early availability after the trade, and his roster role remained small. He did not regain the offensive responsibility he had enjoyed in his first Miami stint or during later years with other teams. His 2004-05 Charlotte scoring and earlier career totals belong to the teams that employed him at the time. The Heat acquired a veteran voice and occasional bench shooting, not an everyday rotation guard.

Allen Played Twenty-Two Bobcats Games and Brought Cash

Allen stepped into a more active Charlotte reserve role. He appeared in twenty-two regular-season games after the transaction, totaling 271 minutes and 111 points, along with forty-seven rebounds. He started once and played much of his time as a power forward. The Bobcats also received cash, according to the league's historical deadline list and detailed transaction tracking. That additional consideration explains why their side should not be scored solely on the modest player's performance. Allen's fourteen Miami games before the trade do not count as Charlotte production.

Charlotte Obtained More Playing Time From Its Incoming Veteran

The Heat's interest in a former franchise player was understandable, particularly for a club building toward playoff basketball, but Smith's direct contributions were minimal. Charlotte used Allen for more than twice as many minutes and received a payment alongside him. Neither player became a long-term cornerstone, and Miami should not be credited with Smith's 1990s All-Star-level performances. On the documented team-specific totals, the Bobcats obtained the better immediate return. That supports replacing an overly neutral verdict with a modest Charlotte win, not a sweeping criticism of Miami's roster decision.

Final Verdict

Bobcats Win. Charlotte gets B- because Malik Allen supplied twenty-two regular-season games, 271 minutes, 111 points and cash after the exchange. Miami earns C for Steve Smith's thirteen games, 114 minutes and twenty-three points in his brief return. Smith's earlier Heat years aren't part of his 2005 incoming value, and Charlotte obtained more playing utility.

summary: 76ers Win. Rogers gave Philadelphia usable veteran minutes, while Mashburn’s contract and health situation were absorbed without producing on-court value. analysis: Philadelphia acquired Jamal Mashburn and Rodney Rogers. New Orleans acquired Glenn Robinson. The names suggested a veteran-for-veteran exchange, but health and availability quickly made the actual outcomes far less balanced than the announcement-day reputations. Rogers gave Philadelphia usable veteran minutes, while Mashburn’s contract and health situation were absorbed without producing on-court value. Even that limited contribution exceeded New Orleans’ result because Robinson was waived only days after the trade and never appeared for the franchise. New Orleans was trying to move salary and unavailable veterans, so the transaction had financial and roster-management logic. Still, Robinson’s immediate waiver meant the basketball return was effectively nonexistent, making it hard to defend the old even-trade framing. There is little downstream basketball chain to inflate on either side. Mashburn never played for Philadelphia and later retired, while Robinson never played for New Orleans. Rogers’ actual minutes are therefore unusually important because they are one of the few realized pieces in the trade details. Both clubs were dealing with older players, injuries and expiring competitive windows rather than building around young cornerstone assets. That context lowers the ceiling of the transaction, but it does not erase the difference between receiving some usable play and receiving none. Philadelphia B, New Orleans D. New Orleans falls to D because Robinson was waived almost immediately and created no meaningful court value.

new-orleans-pelicans.summary: New Orleans acquired Speedy Claxton; Dale Davis; cash from Golden State Warriors for Baron Davis.
new-orleans-pelicans.analysis: New Orleans lost the Baron Davis trade because the outgoing star still had far more prime value than the return package. Davis became an All-NBA-caliber lead guard in Golden State and was the centerpiece of the Warriors' 2007 playoff breakthrough. Speedy Claxton was useful for New Orleans and cash created some flexibility, but Dale Davis never supplied comparable basketball value. The context matters because the relationship with Baron Davis had deteriorated and his injury history complicated leverage, so this was not a clean voluntary giveaway. Even with that context, the realized gap is too large to call the deal anything other than a major partner win.

perspectives.summary: Utah moved from No. 6 to No. 3 in the 2005 draft by sending Portland the No. 6 and No. 27 picks plus a protected 2006 first-rounder. The Jazz used No. 3 on Deron Williams, who played 439 regular-season games for Utah, made two All-Star teams and two All-NBA Second Teams, and led the 2007 club to the Western Conference finals. perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Utah's official all-time transaction history confirms the June 28, 2005 deal: Portland sent the No. 3 pick, which became Deron Williams, for No. 6 Martell Webster, No. 27 Linas Kleiza and a conditional 2006 first-round pick that ultimately became No. 30 Joel Freeland. Basketball-Reference's Portland transaction log independently matches the package. The trade was not simply Williams for Webster; Portland received three first-round assets and immediately used one of them in another draft-night move.

Utah Return
Williams became the franchise-level point guard Utah was paying to reach. He appeared in 439 regular-season games for the Jazz from 2005-06 through the 2011 trade to New Jersey, became a full-time starter in his second season, and developed into one of the league's top playmakers. atlanta-hawks.summary: Atlanta acquired Joe Johnson from Phoenix through an August 2005 sign-and-trade that sent Boris Diaw and two first-round picks to the Suns. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Paid Two Firsts and Diaw for Johnson

The Hawks acquired Joe Johnson from Phoenix in August 2005 in a sign-and-trade arrangement. Atlanta sent Boris Diaw and two future first-round selections to the Suns, committing real draft capital to acquire a young, versatile guard who had played a supporting role in Phoenix's highly productive offense. The Hawks needed a primary creator who could handle the ball, score efficiently and grow with their roster. Phoenix chose a forward with multiple skills plus long-term draft options rather than matching the same financial and roster commitment to Johnson.

Johnson Became the Hawks' Offensive Centerpiece

Johnson emerged as Atlanta's leading scorer and a six-time All-Star during his Hawks tenure. He helped move the team from a rebuilding franchise into a regular playoff participant, taking on late-game shot creation and heavy offensive responsibility. Those seasons are the defining direct return, not his earlier Phoenix production. Johnson was far more than a short-term rental: Atlanta used his skill set to establish a competitive identity over multiple years before moving him to Brooklyn in another transaction.

Phoenix Still Collected Real Value From the Package

Diaw flourished with the Suns, winning the 2005-06 Most Improved Player award and providing passing, versatility and frontcourt play. The 2006 first-round right later became associated with No. 21 Rajon Rondo, and the other choice became No. 15 Robin Lopez in 2008. Their draft and trade paths differed, so all of Rondo's subsequent Celtics accomplishments cannot be added to Phoenix's received production. Lopez contributed to the Suns, while Diaw supplied the most immediately important player value.

One High-End Star Outweighed Several Smaller Pieces

The Suns obtained an award-winning role player and useful draft capital, making their return genuine rather than worthless. Johnson nevertheless developed into the franchise player Atlanta was trying to acquire. His years as the primary offensive option supplied sustained value that Atlanta had lacked. This comparison must account for Phoenix's compensation without treating the Celtics' later Rondo championship as a Suns achievement or ignoring the two first-round choices spent by Atlanta. The Hawks' long-term scoring return drives the winner.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for acquiring Joe Johnson, who became a six-time Hawks All-Star and led multiple playoff teams. Phoenix receives C for Boris Diaw's Most Improved Player season and two valuable draft rights, one later tied to Rajon Rondo and the other to Robin Lopez. The Suns received real assets, but Johnson delivered the stronger single-player return to Atlanta.

analysis:
Atlanta Paid Two Firsts and Diaw for Johnson

The Hawks acquired Joe Johnson from Phoenix in August 2005 in a sign-and-trade arrangement. Atlanta sent Boris Diaw and two future first-round selections to the Suns, committing real draft capital to acquire a young, versatile guard who had played a supporting role in Phoenix's highly productive offense. The Hawks needed a primary creator who could handle the ball, score efficiently and grow with their roster. Phoenix chose a forward with multiple skills plus long-term draft options rather than matching the same financial and roster commitment to Johnson.

Johnson Became the Hawks' Offensive Centerpiece

Johnson emerged as Atlanta's leading scorer and a six-time All-Star during his Hawks tenure. He helped move the team from a rebuilding franchise into a regular playoff participant, taking on late-game shot creation and heavy offensive responsibility. Those seasons are the defining direct return, not his earlier Phoenix production. Johnson was far more than a short-term rental: Atlanta used his skill set to establish a competitive identity over multiple years before moving him to Brooklyn in another transaction.

Phoenix Still Collected Real Value From the Package

Diaw flourished with the Suns, winning the 2005-06 Most Improved Player award and providing passing, versatility and frontcourt play. The 2006 first-round right later became associated with No. 21 Rajon Rondo, and the other choice became No. 15 Robin Lopez in 2008. Their draft and trade paths differed, so all of Rondo's subsequent Celtics accomplishments cannot be added to Phoenix's received production. Lopez contributed to the Suns, while Diaw supplied the most immediately important player value.

One High-End Star Outweighed Several Smaller Pieces

The Suns obtained an award-winning role player and useful draft capital, making their return genuine rather than worthless. Johnson nevertheless developed into the franchise player Atlanta was trying to acquire. His years as the primary offensive option supplied sustained value that Atlanta had lacked. This comparison must account for Phoenix's compensation without treating the Celtics' later Rondo championship as a Suns achievement or ignoring the two first-round choices spent by Atlanta. The Hawks' long-term scoring return drives the winner.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for acquiring Joe Johnson, who became a six-time Hawks All-Star and led multiple playoff teams. Phoenix receives C for Boris Diaw's Most Improved Player season and two valuable draft rights, one later tied to Rajon Rondo and the other to Robin Lopez. The Suns received real assets, but Johnson delivered the stronger single-player return to Atlanta.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Took Dan Dickau for a Future Second-Round Right

Boston's September 2005 transaction sent a future 2006 second-round selection to the New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets in exchange for guard Dan Dickau. The original club was in a temporary Oklahoma City arrangement after Hurricane Katrina, and its franchise history is indexed under today's New Orleans Pelicans. The selection later appeared as No. 56, associated with Edin Bavcic. Boston favored a player who had NBA guard experience and could compete for a near-term role, while the Hornets accepted a lower-round development opportunity. This was not a multi-player veteran package or a guaranteed first-round future asset.

Dickau Arrived as an Experienced Guard, Not a Long-Term Promise

Dickau had already played NBA minutes and established a reputation for outside shooting and passing. Boston could use him as backcourt depth without waiting for the following summer's draft, but his earlier performances for other teams did not instantly become Celtics production. A player approaching a new roster had to earn his own playing time and could be affected by health or subsequent roster changes. Dickau's recognizable name shouldn't be treated as evidence of an All-Star arrival. The deal's immediate purpose was to give Boston a practical guard option for an evolving rotation.

The Future Pick Carried a Specific Late-Second Outcome

The Hornets acquired a 2006 second-round pick later associated with No. 56 Edin Bavcic. That draft slot offered an opportunity to obtain or use the rights to an international prospect, but it wasn't equal to a signed NBA player ready for the opening tip. Any later Bavcic career outside the league could be useful contextual evidence without being credited as actual Hornets game production. The 2005 agreement did not automatically place Bavcic on the club's active roster in 2006. Draft-rights control and professional minutes are distinct outcomes when evaluating this type of exchange.

A Balanced Return for Different Roster Horizons

Boston sought an immediate reserve guard while the Hornets prioritized an additional future selection during a period of organizational disruption. Dickau's NBA experience supplied more current certainty, but the 2006 pick preserved the possibility of selecting or moving a different player later. Neither side obtained a franchise-altering contributor, and the agreed assets were too small to justify sweeping conclusions about either team's next decade. Equal moderate grades recognize the value of near-term guard depth and speculative later draft flexibility without awarding unrelated career achievements to either receiver.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston Celtics earns C+; New Orleans Pelicans earns C+. Picks became Aldridge (7-time All-Star) and Noah (DPOY, All-NBA). Even though Bulls traded Aldridge for Thomas on draft night, the asset haul was massive. One of best heists of 2000s.

perspectives.summary: New York surrendered premium first-round value and a future swap for Eddy Curry. Chicago ultimately controlled the picks tied to LaMarcus Aldridge and Joakim Noah, while Curry never reached star-level impact.
perspectives.analysis: The Eddy Curry trade became damaging because New York accepted both player risk and unusually dangerous draft exposure. The Knicks acquired Curry and Antonio Davis from Chicago while sending Tim Thomas, Michael Sweetney, Jermaine Jackson, a 2006 first, a 2007 first-round swap and additional second-round picks. New York's poor records turned those mechanisms into premium assets: the 2006 first landed at No. 2, in the LaMarcus Aldridge slot, and the 2007 swap allowed Chicago to pick at No. 9, where it selected Joakim Noah. Curry could score in the post, but he never supplied the two-way star impact needed to justify that price. The protections were not strong enough to shield New York from its own downside, making this a clear F-level Partner Win.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired Rafer Alston from Toronto for Mike James on October 4, 2005. James gave the Raptors one exceptional scoring season, averaging 20.3 points across 79 starts. Alston became Houston's starting point guard for parts of four seasons, totaling 267 regular-season Rockets games after the deal. Slight Rockets Edge, Houston B+, Toronto B.
houston-rockets.analysis:
A Straight Guard Swap Recast Two Backcourts

On October 4, 2005, Toronto exchanged Rafer Alston for Houston's Mike James. Both clubs recorded the deal as a direct player-for-player trade, with no draft selection or money attached to the transaction. Toronto wanted a different point-guard fit while Houston sought someone to handle substantial minutes next to Tracy McGrady and Yao Ming. James had already played for the Rockets during the preceding season after arriving from Milwaukee. Alston had spent 2004-05 as Toronto's main point guard. The unusual feature was not the package size, but how differently the two veterans' subsequent tenures would unfold.

James Had a Career Year for Toronto, but Only One

James was an outstanding short-term acquisition. He started all 79 of his regular-season appearances with the 2005-06 Raptors, averaging 20.3 points and 5.8 assists. He shot 46.9 percent from the field and 44.2 percent from three-point distance, an exceptional scoring year for a guard acquired in a straightforward swap. Toronto nevertheless finished 27-55 and missed the playoffs. James departed for Minnesota as a free agent in 2006. His later years with other clubs cannot be counted toward Toronto's return, which was productive but lasted only that single season.

Alston Became Houston's Longer-Term Starting Point Guard

Alston played 63 games for the Rockets in 2005-06 and started all 63. He then started all 82 games in 2006-07 and 74 more in 2007-08. Before Houston traded him to Orlando during 2008-09, he made another 48 starts. That totals 267 regular-season Houston appearances and 267 starts after the 2005 exchange, with more than three full seasons' worth of court time. His shooting was frequently inefficient, but he gave the Rockets a continuing ball handler while the roster revolved around McGrady and Yao. He also played in Houston's 2007 and 2008 postseason series, whereas James had no Toronto playoff appearances.

Peak Output Versus Longevity Makes the Verdict Close

Toronto received the single best scoring season either new team got from this trade. James's 1,604 points in 2005-06 were an immediate offensive return, not an empty expiring contract. Houston instead acquired a long-serving starting point guard who contributed across multiple seasons and playoff appearances. Comparing only the first season makes the Raptors look stronger; comparing all games played for the receiving teams favors the Rockets' much longer return. The verdict gives Houston the modest edge without dismissing James's breakout year or assigning later Magic postseason production to the Rockets.

Final Verdict

Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns B+ for 267 regular-season starts from Rafer Alston and multiple seasons of point-guard continuity. Toronto gets B for Mike James's 20.3-point season across 79 games, followed by his free-agent departure. The Raptors acquired the sharper single-season scorer; the Rockets acquired the longer-lived starter.

Magloire started all 82 Bucks games in 2005-06 and averaged 9.5 rebounds; Mason and Simmons gave New Orleans several roster options, although Simmons never became a star. new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
Milwaukee Swapped Wing Depth and a Pick for a Starting Center

The Bucks acquired Jamaal Magloire on October 26, 2005, transferring Desmond Mason and a future first-round draft choice to the New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets. The first-round selection became No. 15 Cedric Simmons in 2006, and the imported transaction ledger also records cash on the Hornets side. Magloire had been an All-Star with the Hornets, but Milwaukee was purchasing a center whose most productive season had already occurred. The move was designed to pair proven interior size with a Bucks roster that included rookie Andrew Bogut.

Magloire Immediately Started All Eighty-Two Bucks Games

Magloire fulfilled the immediate starting-center requirement. He appeared in every Milwaukee regular-season game in 2005-06 and started all eighty-two, averaging 9.2 points and 9.5 rebounds. He supplied rebounding, physical post defense and consistent lineup availability as Milwaukee made the postseason. Those eighty-two starts represent substantial real value and shouldn't be discarded because the Bucks traded him again after one season. His previous years in New Orleans and the All-Star selection earned there, however, remain outside this receiving-team return.

The Hornets Added Desmond Mason and the Fifteenth Pick

New Orleans received Mason as an established forward who could attack the basket and provide athletic perimeter defense. The following summer the Hornets used the acquired draft choice on Cedric Simmons at No. 15. Simmons had promise as an interior defender but did not establish a sustained starting role for the franchise. Neither return matched the volume of Magloire's entire earlier Hornets career, yet the transaction gave New Orleans two separate basketball assets instead of one veteran under contract. The possible cash component should be recognized without assigning an unsupported dollar amount.

The Two-Asset Return Barely Outweighed One Productive Year

Milwaukee obtained exactly what it wanted for the 2005-06 campaign: an available starting center who rebounded at a high level. New Orleans added wing minutes through Mason and invested another first-round choice in the future. The Hornets carried more developmental uncertainty, while the Bucks got a shorter but more certain return. Neither side should receive an extreme grade, and the comparison is closer than the inherited Bucks B- might suggest. The wider two-asset package gives New Orleans a small advantage over a single season of dependable Bucks starting production.

Final Verdict

Pelicans Win narrowly. The Hornets earn B+ for receiving Desmond Mason and the 2006 No. 15 pick used on Cedric Simmons, with cash also listed in the original ledger. Milwaukee gets B because Jamaal Magloire started all eighty-two 2005-06 Bucks games and averaged 9.5 rebounds. Both teams realized meaningful, different returns.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Sent Several Veterans for Szczerbiak

The Celtics and Timberwolves exchanged sizeable packages in January 2006. Boston acquired Wally Szczerbiak, Michael Olowokandi, Dwayne Jones and a future first-round obligation. Minnesota received Ricky Davis, Marcus Banks, Mark Blount, Justin Reed and two second-round choices. The Celtics wanted Szczerbiak's shooting alongside Paul Pierce, while the Timberwolves revised their rotation around Kevin Garnett. Multiple players and future picks meant neither club's return could be evaluated from the most recognizable names alone.

Szczerbiak Provided Boston Perimeter Scoring

Szczerbiak gave Boston another experienced outside scorer, though his Celtics tenure was relatively short and injuries limited his longer-term effect. Olowokandi offered frontcourt size without becoming a major new defensive anchor, while Jones contributed very little. The incoming first-round right later became associated with the No. 6 selection used on Jonny Flynn in 2009, but that pick's rights moved again. Flynn's NBA career in Minnesota must not be misrepresented as Boston playing production generated by the 2006 agreement.

Minnesota Received Players and Productive Picks

Davis supplied some veteran scoring with the Timberwolves, while Banks, Blount and Reed had varying roles. The more interesting long-term value came from the second-round choices: No. 36 Craig Smith in 2006 and No. 31 Nikola Peković in 2008. Both developed into Timberwolves contributors, with Peković later becoming a substantial interior presence. Those Minnesota seasons are tangible receiving-team payoff from the draft rights, not merely eventual names attached to picks traded elsewhere.

A Narrow Advantage Reflects the Second-Round Results

The Celtics obtained useful shooting in Szczerbiak and additional trade flexibility, while Minnesota found multiple roster contributors and unusually productive second-round value. Both teams had credible objectives at the time. Boston didn't receive a permanent star to pair with Pierce, and Minnesota's veteran additions alone wouldn't have decided the comparison. The inherited slight Timberwolves edge rests on the combination of Davis's immediate output and the longer-term success of the Smith and Peković selections, rather than treating every asset as equally valuable.

Final Verdict

Slight Wolves Edge. Minnesota receives B+ for Ricky Davis's scoring and the useful second-round outcomes of Craig Smith and Nikola Peković, alongside other veteran depth. Boston gets B for Wally Szczerbiak's shooting and additional assets, but the stay was shorter and the future first's rights changed hands again. Jonny Flynn's later Minnesota games are not credited to the Celtics.

new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
The Hornets Acquired a Veteran Center in a Disrupted Season

On January 31, 2006, the New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets received Aaron Williams from Toronto for two second-round draft selections. The club was playing home games in Oklahoma City following Hurricane Katrina, and Williams offered immediate backup size during an unusual season. Toronto was restructuring its frontcourt and chose future draft flexibility instead of retaining an aging reserve. The agreement was not an exchange of two NBA players: the Raptors received one selection for 2006 and another for 2009, giving them more options for later negotiations.

Williams Supplied Thirty-Four Hornets Games

Williams made thirty-four New Orleans/Oklahoma City regular-season appearances after the trade, starting twice. He logged 692 minutes, scored 197 points and collected 166 rebounds while functioning as a backup center. Those were useful frontcourt minutes for a team working around Chris Paul and David West, though the role never resembled Williams's most productive earlier years in New Jersey. His fourteen Toronto games before January 31 remain Raptors statistics and must not be added to his incoming Hornets totals. He moved to the Clippers afterward rather than developing into a long-term Hornets starter.

Toronto Obtained Two Picks That Followed Different Paths

The 2006 selection became No. 56 Edin Bavčić. Toronto selected him and promptly sold his draft rights to Philadelphia, yielding a separate asset transaction rather than playing Bavčić in a Raptors uniform. The later pick eventually became No. 51 Jack McClinton in 2009, but Toronto had included its rights in a wider trade with San Antonio for Rasho Nesterović in 2006. Consequently, neither draftee's career can be counted as a direct Raptors playing return. Both second-round choices nevertheless had real use in subsequent decisions, and their paths need to be explained.

Immediate Center Minutes Versus Two Movable Assets

New Orleans received exactly the sort of veteran support it wanted during the remaining months of the 2005-06 season. Toronto gave up a little-used forward-center and received two draft assets it could move in separate arrangements. Those trades created financial and roster flexibility, even without a productive player selected and retained from either choice. Comparing only Williams's scoring with the draftees' nonexistent Toronto minutes would ignore what the Raptors actually did with the assets. The original even verdict remains sensible because each organization realized a different and documented category of value.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. New Orleans earns B for Aaron Williams's 34 appearances, 692 minutes, 197 points and 166 rebounds in 2005-06. Toronto also receives B because it acquired two usable second-round picks, selling Edin Bavčić's No. 56 rights and later transferring the 2009 selection within the Nesterović package. No later player's entire career is assigned to this single swap.
