houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Replaced a Familiar Reserve Guard With a Younger Center

On February 13, 2006, the Rockets sent Moochie Norris to the New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets for Maciej Lampe. Houston already had its primary backcourt responsibilities allocated and was looking for another inexpensive interior prospect. Lampe, still in his early twenties, had not secured a regular NBA role despite prior opportunities in Phoenix and New Orleans. The Hornets were coping with a disrupted season after Hurricane Katrina and could use experienced guard coverage. Both organizations' transaction ledgers record a direct one-for-one swap rather than a separate draft asset.

Lampe's Rockets Tenure Consisted of Four Brief Appearances

Lampe played only four regular-season games for Houston during the rest of 2005-06. The NBA's team-specific player statistics show that he averaged three minutes and one point in those appearances, making his direct Rockets return twelve minutes and four points. His earlier two games for the Hornets during the same season cannot be combined into a Houston total. He never established himself in the Rockets' frontcourt rotation after arriving. The experiment was inexpensive, but the club found little evidence in NBA games that he could supply sustained center minutes.

Norris Played Sixteen Hornets Games After Leaving Houston

Norris received a somewhat larger opportunity with New Orleans/Oklahoma City. He appeared in sixteen regular-season games for the Hornets following the exchange, logging approximately 11.4 minutes and 3.8 points per game. His experience as a ball handler brought limited veteran coverage during a difficult season. The rest of his forty-five combined 2005-06 NBA appearances had been in a Rockets uniform before the deal, so those cannot be attributed to his receiving club. Neither the frequency nor the production suggests that Norris became a long-term answer at point guard.

The More Active Bench Player Produced a Narrow Hornets Advantage

The trade gave each franchise a reserve it could use for a short period, but neither addition changed a team's competitive fortunes. Houston got four very small center outings from Lampe, while the Hornets used Norris sixteen times in meaningful backup minutes. Those are clearly unequal incoming returns even without pretending Norris was a starting guard or Lampe had no basketball value outside the league. The older New Orleans B and Houston F grades overstated the stakes for a swap between peripheral veterans and prospects. A slight Hornets advantage with restrained grades better matches the actual NBA playing record.

Final Verdict

Hornets Win. New Orleans/Oklahoma City receives C+ because Moochie Norris supplied sixteen reserve games and approximately 182 minutes after the February transaction. Houston receives D+ for Maciej Lampe's four games, twelve minutes and four points. Both clubs acquired bench depth, but Norris furnished more actual receiving-team playing time than the young center did.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers acquired Vladimir Radmanović from Seattle for Chris Wilcox on February 14, 2006. Radmanović played 30 regular-season games for Los Angeles, totaling 885 minutes and 320 points, and appeared in 12 playoff games that spring. Wilcox gave Seattle 29 games and 408 points immediately, then remained a Sonics starter in 2006-07 and 2007-08, including 82 games in 2006-07. SuperSonics Win: Seattle A-, Clippers B.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
Seattle Surrendered Shooting to Acquire a Younger Power Forward

The Los Angeles Clippers traded Chris Wilcox to the Seattle SuperSonics on February 14, 2006, receiving Vladimir Radmanović in return. The two forwards had different profiles. Radmanović could spread the floor with three-point shooting, a skill Los Angeles needed alongside Elton Brand and Chris Kaman. Wilcox was a younger athlete whose rebounding and finishing around the basket could complement Seattle's perimeter scorers. The straight exchange did not include draft picks. It came with the Clippers positioned for their first playoff appearance in several years and the SuperSonics looking for a more dependable frontcourt option.

Radmanović Helped Los Angeles During One Playoff Push

Radmanović played 30 regular-season Clippers games after the swap, starting 11 and logging 885 minutes. He scored 320 points and made 66 three-point field goals, offering bench scoring and floor spacing. The Clippers reached the 2006 Western Conference semifinals, and Radmanović appeared in all 12 postseason games. Those appearances were legitimate short-term value and explain why the Clippers' side should retain a positive grade. However, he signed with the Los Angeles Lakers in the summer, ending the Clippers return after those months. His later Lakers years cannot be credited to the club that traded for him.

Wilcox Turned Into a Multi-Year Seattle Starter

Wilcox quickly gained a larger role with Seattle than he had held with the Clippers. After the February 2006 exchange he started 23 of 29 SuperSonics games, averaging 14.1 points and 8.2 rebounds. He then appeared in all 82 regular-season games in 2006-07 and started 81, averaging 13.5 points and 7.7 rebounds. He added 62 games and 55 starts in 2007-08 with averages of 13.4 points and 7.0 rebounds. Wilcox continued with the franchise after its move to Oklahoma City before leaving for the Knicks. The long run of starts and scoring was a larger, more enduring contribution than a short rental.

An Immediate Clippers Win Became a Long-Term Seattle Gain

The Clippers achieved their near-term objective. Radmanović gave them spacing and was available during a meaningful playoff run, so calling the exchange a one-sided failure would overlook the context of 2006. Seattle, though, received more than a short-term adjustment: Wilcox was a regular starter for two full seasons and remained in the organization through its relocation. The franchise's move to Oklahoma City makes the modern trade ID look unusual, but the acquiring club was the Seattle SuperSonics in February 2006. Judging the two actual receiving-team stints rather than the players' later careers gives Seattle a distinct edge.

Final Verdict

SuperSonics Win. Seattle earns A- because Chris Wilcox became a multi-season starter after arriving in 2006, beginning with 29 games and 408 points that spring and carrying through two productive Sonics seasons. Los Angeles receives B for Vladimir Radmanović's 30 regular-season appearances and 12 playoff games during the Clippers' postseason run. Seattle enjoyed the longer, greater return.

summary: New York acquired Steve Francis from Orlando for Trevor Ariza and Penny Hardaway's expiring contract. Francis duplicated Stephon Marbury's ball-dominant role, struggled with injuries and fit, and lasted little more than a season. Orlando cleared long-term salary and added a young wing, making this a clear Magic win.
analysis: The Knicks chased name recognition instead of roster complementarity. Francis and Marbury both needed the ball, neither solved the team's defense, and Francis carried substantial guaranteed money. Orlando had suspended Francis earlier in the season and used the trade to reset around Dwight Howard, accepting Hardaway's expiring salary and a 20-year-old Ariza. Ariza did not reach his eventual peak in Orlando, so the Magic grade stops at A-minus, but the club escaped the worse contract and recovered a useful young asset. New York receives an F because the fit problem was visible before the deal and the on-court return was brief.

perspectives.analysis:
Seattle Chose Watson and Draft Flexibility

The SuperSonics reacquired Earl Watson from Denver in February 2006, also receiving Bryon Russell and a 2008 second-round selection later associated with No. 50 DeVon Hardin. Watson offered a defined backup point-guard profile and already knew Seattle from an earlier stop in his career. Russell brought veteran experience, though his immediate playing role was more limited. The combination gave Seattle an experienced ball handler and a future draft opportunity in exchange for moving Reggie Evans and Vitaly Potapenko.

Denver Targeted Rebounding and Defensive Energy

houston-rockets.summary: On February 23, 2006, Houston sent Derek Anderson to Miami for Gerald Fitch and a trade exception. Anderson played 23 Heat regular-season games, totaling 465 minutes, and appeared in eight playoff games as Miami won its first NBA title. Fitch played no Rockets regular-season games and was assigned to their development affiliate, though the trade exception remained a valid financial tool. Heat Win, Miami B- and Houston C-.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Miami Acquired an Experienced Guard for a Contending Roster

The Heat acquired Derek Anderson from Houston on February 23, 2006, sending young guard Gerald Fitch in exchange. Houston also received a trade exception that could provide additional financial flexibility under league roster rules. Miami was pursuing a championship around Dwyane Wade and Shaquille O'Neal, and Anderson had prior playoff experience as a guard with size. Houston was having a disappointing, injury-affected season and decided to adjust its backcourt options. The trade involved two players plus a financial mechanism, not draft rights.

Anderson Played Twenty-Three Regular-Season Games for Miami

Anderson appeared in twenty-three Miami regular-season games after arriving, starting three and recording 465 minutes. He averaged 5.8 points and offered ball-handling experience behind the Heat's main guards. Anderson also appeared in eight postseason games that spring, although his shifts were generally limited. Miami went on to win the 2006 NBA championship, but Anderson did not play in the Finals and should not be credited as the principal cause of that title. His acquired role was useful guard depth rather than star production.

Fitch Never Played a Regular-Season Game for Houston

Fitch had previously appeared in eighteen NBA games for Miami before the February transaction, but that playing time belongs to the Heat. Houston assigned him to the Austin Toros in the Development League during March, then recalled him. He did not make a Rockets regular-season NBA appearance as a result of this trade. His earlier Miami scoring cannot be transferred to Houston in a team-specific evaluation. The Rockets did obtain a trade exception alongside Fitch, which has value as a salary-cap tool even when no player minutes immediately follow.

Miami Realized Its Veteran Depth; Houston Retained Flexibility

Anderson gave Miami occasional regular-season and playoff guard minutes on a team that won the championship. Houston never used its new player in an NBA game, so its immediate basketball return was essentially absent. The trade exception prevents treating the Rockets side as entirely empty, though it does not justify inventing a subsequent acquisition without a documented link. The original Heat win was directionally correct, and the team-specific evidence supports a larger distinction than the inherited grades showed. It was still a small supporting transaction rather than a championship-defining blockbuster.

Final Verdict

Heat Win. Miami receives B- for Derek Anderson's twenty-three regular-season games, 465 minutes and eight postseason appearances during the 2006 title season. Houston gets C- for a trade exception and Gerald Fitch, who played no Rockets regular-season NBA games. The direct on-court advantage belongs to Miami without assigning Anderson credit for the team's full championship run.

perspectives.summary: Toronto acquired Kris Humphries and Robert Whaley from Utah on June 8, 2006 for Rafael Araujo. Humphries became the only meaningful Raptors return, playing 159 regular-season games across three seasons as a reserve big before leaving Toronto in 2009; Whaley was waived less than two weeks after the trade. Utah received only 28 games and no starts from Araujo in 2006-07, the final NBA season of his career.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Toronto's official June 8, 2006 announcement confirms the simple player package: Kris Humphries and Robert Whaley came from Utah for Rafael Araujo. That matters because secondary transaction databases sometimes attach exceptions or cash mechanics to the cap treatment; those accounting details should not be promoted into player-value assets unless a reliable team source identifies them as consideration. Toronto general manager Bryan Colangelo framed the move as a positive change for both teams, but the basketball outcome quickly separated.

Toronto Return
Humphries gave the Raptors three seasons of usable reserve minutes. He appeared in 60 games in 2006-07, 70 in 2007-08 and 29 in 2008-09, totaling 159 regular-season games for Toronto. He averaged 3.8 points and 3.1 rebounds in his first Raptors season, then 5.7 points and 3.7 rebounds in 2007-08 before injuries reduced his third-year role. Those numbers are modest, and his later breakout as a double-double starter in New Jersey should not be credited to Toronto. The value here is that Toronto turned an unproductive former lottery pick into a younger reserve who remained useful for three seasons. Whaley added no on-court value: Toronto's own June 21 announcement says the club waived him less than two weeks after acquiring him.

Utah Return
Araujo's Jazz stint lasted one season and 28 games, all off the bench. Basketball-Reference records 248 total minutes, no starts and a .415 field-goal percentage. He did not appear in the 2007 playoffs and never played another NBA regular-season game after that year. For a Utah team that won 51 games and reached the Western Conference finals, he was a fringe depth piece rather than a rotation solution.

Hindsight Verdict
Toronto wins because Humphries supplied 159 games of legitimate reserve value while Utah received only 28 low-minute games from Araujo. The gap is clear, but the original A-minus grade overstates how much Toronto actually captured: Humphries did not become a starter or high-impact player until after leaving the Raptors, and Whaley never played for them. Toronto earns a B for converting a struggling asset into three seasons of usable depth. Utah earns a D+ because Araujo filled a small bench role for one year but provided no durable return. Final verdict: Toronto Raptors Win.

perspectives.summary: San Antonio acquired Matt Bonner, Eric Williams and Toronto's 2009 second-round pick on June 21, 2006 for Rasho Nesterovic and cash. Bonner became the long-term prize, playing 632 regular-season games across 10 Spurs seasons and appearing on the 2007 and 2014 championship teams. Toronto still received a solid direct return: Nesterovic played 151 games with 112 starts over the next two seasons, giving the Raptors dependable center minutes before he left for Indiana.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Toronto's official June 21, 2006 release confirms the full package: the Raptors acquired Rasho Nesterovic and cash from San Antonio for Matt Bonner, Eric Williams and a 2009 second-round pick. The future pick eventually became No. 51 Jack McClinton. This was partly a roster-fit deal: Toronto president Bryan Colangelo described Nesterovic as an experienced center who could address the club's defensive needs without changing its cap position.

San Antonio Return
Bonner created nearly all of the Spurs' long-term value. From 2006-07 through 2015-16 he appeared in 632 regular-season games for San Antonio and made 106 starts. He developed into a durable floor-spacing big, shooting above 40 percent from three in multiple seasons and leading the league at 45.7 percent in 2010-11. Bonner remained in the rotation through two championship seasons, 2007 and 2014, and his ten-year tenure made the acquisition much more valuable than a short-term depth swap. Eric Williams contributed only 16 Spurs games before San Antonio traded him to Charlotte during the 2006-07 season. The Toronto second-rounder became McClinton, whom San Antonio selected 51st in 2009 and waived before he played an NBA regular-season game.

Toronto Return
Nesterovic gave the Raptors meaningful immediate value. In 2006-07 he played 80 games with 73 starts, shot 54.6 percent and helped Toronto win 47 games and the Atlantic Division. He followed with 71 games and 39 starts in 2007-08, shooting 55.0 percent. Across the two seasons created by this trade, Nesterovic totaled 151 regular-season games and 112 starts, plus playoff minutes in both years. He was not a star and did not remain beyond the 2008 offseason, but that is a substantial direct return and makes the legacy C-minus/D view of Toronto too harsh. The cash consideration adds value even though it does not need to be quantified to recognize the on-court contribution.

Hindsight Verdict
San Antonio wins because Bonner supplied a decade of continuity, shooting and championship-roster value while the other Spurs assets were mostly minor. Toronto's side was still successful in its narrower objective: Nesterovic started 112 games over two playoff seasons and filled the center role the club targeted. The Spurs receive an A- because a role player acquired in a secondary trade became a ten-year contributor on two title teams. Toronto receives a B because Nesterovic gave two productive seasons and significant starting volume. Final verdict: San Antonio Spurs Win, but by a much smaller margin than the legacy grades implied.

analysis: Portland's strongest asset chain is unusually clean. The No. 7 rights to Foye were exchanged directly for Brandon Roy's rights, and Roy became Rookie of the Year, a three-time All-Star and the centerpiece of Portland's return to relevance before knee injuries shortened his career. That is franchise-level realized value from an asset acquired in this transaction. Boston did not receive nothing. Telfair played one season, Ratliff's expiring salary became useful in the 2007 Kevin Garnett blockbuster, and the second-round pick later became Trent Plaisted. Ratliff and Telfair were both included in the Garnett package, so they retained transactional utility. But Garnett required Al Jefferson, Gerald Green, Ryan Gomes and multiple first-round picks as well, making it inappropriate to credit Boston with Garnett's full value here. Portland's chain requires no speculative step: Foye's rights became Roy's rights on the same night. Boston's chain is real but diluted because Ratliff and Telfair were secondary pieces in a much larger offer for Garnett. TradeVerdicts gives credit for preserved value without pretending every later superstar acquisition came from one salary slot.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Celtics Turned a Future First Into Draft Rights

Boston acquired the rights to Rajon Rondo from Phoenix on June 28, 2006, receiving Brian Grant and cash while surrendering a protected future first-round selection. Rondo had been drafted at No. 21, making the move an attempt to acquire a defensive-minded young guard with unusually strong instincts. The Celtics were not buying an established starting point guard; they were wagering that his passing, speed and pressure defense would translate to NBA competition. Grant's contract played a supporting role in the transaction rather than serving as the principal basketball prize.

Rondo Developed Into the 2008 Championship Floor General

Rondo became Boston's starting point guard and helped the Celtics win the 2008 NBA championship beside Paul Pierce, Kevin Garnett and Ray Allen. His court vision and disruptive defense grew into All-Star-level skills, and he remained an important part of Boston's playoff identity for years. Those accomplishments belong directly to the receiving Celtics and make the initial price look extraordinarily low. The transaction yielded a long-tenured high-impact guard, not a draft prospect who supplied only a brief trial season.

Phoenix Received Another Draft Opportunity

The protected first obtained by Phoenix became associated with the 2007 No. 24 selection used on Rudy Fernández. That pick had its own subsequent rights history; Fernández's later playing career with other franchises cannot simply be counted as Suns minutes from this agreement. Phoenix received a potentially useful draft asset but didn't develop a player directly comparable to Rondo through the original transaction. The difference is between movable future rights and a guard who became a prominent starter for the acquiring team.

The Contrast Was Particularly Clear in the Playoffs

Boston turned one future first and a willingness to take on an additional contract into an essential member of its next championship roster. Phoenix chose roster and draft flexibility, which may have been understandable on trade night but delivered far less realized value than Rondo. The Boston guard's limitations as a shooter were meaningful, yet his command of the offense and defense made his overall effect large. The Celtics received the best player and kept that value through multiple contention seasons.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston receives A+ for Rajon Rondo's championship contribution, repeated All-Star appearances and years as a leading point guard. Phoenix gets F because the future first-round right it acquired did not produce a comparable direct Suns return. Brian Grant and cash were secondary components; Rondo's outstanding Celtics career defines the judgment.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Bought a Second-Round Forward's Rights

Boston and Denver completed a small but historically important draft-rights swap on June 28, 2006. The Celtics acquired the rights to California forward Leon Powe, selected forty-ninth overall, and the Nuggets received a future 2007 second-round choice that eventually resolved to No. 49 Aaron Gray. The exchange involved an unsigned rookie and a future pick, not two established NBA players. Boston was seeking useful interior talent beyond the lottery positions, while Denver retained the opportunity to select or trade a player in the following draft. Neither team could know the full value of Powe's postseason contribution at the time.

Powe Turned a Late Selection Into Championship Bench Value

Powe joined Boston and earned reserve frontcourt minutes during the seasons that followed. His most famous performance came against the Lakers in Game 2 of the 2008 NBA Finals, when he scored twenty-one points and delivered a timely scoring burst for the eventual championship team. That was a concrete Celtics contribution from a pick outside the first round. His career was later affected by injuries, so he wasn't a decade-long Boston starter, but the direct value was still notable. Boston did not buy the rights to Aaron Gray or another future first-round pick through this transaction.

Denver Kept a Future Second-Round Asset

The Nuggets' return was the 2007 second-round selection, not Powe's eventual NBA career. That choice became associated with Gray at No. 49, though its draft rights moved again before producing later playing time elsewhere. Denver therefore obtained a piece of transferable draft capital instead of a ready-made rotation player. That modest return had value when the agreement was signed, but it did not bring the club an equivalent Finals contributor. Counting Gray's later Chicago or New Orleans NBA appearances as Denver games would exaggerate the benefit from this particular swap. The lineage of the pick and the player receiving team must stay separate.

Boston's Playoff Return Was Decisive Without Being a Star Acquisition

Powe was a role player rather than a franchise centerpiece, which keeps the score below the highest conceivable grade for a championship-changing superstar. Yet the Celtics obtained genuine NBA minutes and a memorable Finals performance with a modest draft-day payment. Denver chose the flexibility of a future second and did not convert it into similar direct Nuggets production. The original direction of the verdict therefore holds. It is possible to give the Nuggets credit for moving a late draft asset without treating the eventual Gray draft identity as if he had already signed with Denver. Powe's actual Boston years drive the outcome.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns A- because Leon Powe developed into a useful reserve on the 2008 title team and scored 21 points in Game 2 of the NBA Finals. Denver receives C+ for the future 2007 second-round right that became No. 49 Aaron Gray. The Nuggets did not acquire Powe's later Boston performances or Gray's NBA minutes with other franchises directly through this rights exchange.

houston-rockets.summary: On June 28, 2006, Orlando drafted Israeli forward Lior Eliyahu No. 44 overall and sent his rights to Houston for cash. Eliyahu developed a long professional basketball career overseas but never logged a Rockets regular-season NBA appearance. Orlando received immediate financial compensation; Houston obtained international development rights with no realized NBA playing time. Magic Win, Orlando C+, Houston D+.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Magic Monetized Their Mid-Second-Round Selection

Orlando used the forty-fourth choice of the June 28, 2006 NBA draft on Israeli forward Lior Eliyahu, then transferred his rights to the Houston Rockets for cash considerations. The move was a way for Orlando to obtain immediate compensation from a selection late enough that it would not necessarily produce a roster player. Houston was willing to take a longer view on a skilled international forward who could continue developing outside the NBA. The trade involved rights and money, not an active NBA player swapping uniforms.

Eliyahu's European Career Was the Development Bet

Eliyahu became a recognized forward in Israeli and European professional basketball, including important seasons with Maccabi Tel Aviv and appearances for his national team. That career supports why Houston found the second-round prospect worth a financial investment. It does not mean the Rockets received his points or rebounds on an NBA floor. Eliyahu never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for Houston. This distinction between ownership of draft rights and actual NBA playing value is crucial when evaluating overseas prospects years after their original selection.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Utah acquired Derek Fisher from Golden State in July 2006 for Devin Brown, Keith McLeod and Andre Owens. Fisher appeared in all 82 Jazz games and started 61 in 2006-07, helping Utah reach the Western Conference finals. McLeod played 26 Warriors games and became part of Golden State's four-player exchange with Indiana. Slight Jazz Edge: Utah A-, Golden State B+.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
A Financial Reset for Golden State, a Veteran Starter for Utah

Golden State traded Derek Fisher to Utah on July 12, 2006 for Devin Brown, Keith McLeod and Andre Owens. The Jazz were pairing a veteran with Deron Williams in a backcourt supporting Carlos Boozer and Mehmet Okur. Fisher had extensive playoff experience and could lead the second unit or play beside Williams. The Warriors wanted relief from Fisher's remaining contract and took back three guards as less expensive roster options. The four-player exchange therefore combined a meaningful basketball acquisition for Utah with a different type of value for Golden State, beyond a simple comparison of the numbers of players moved.

Fisher Played Every Game on a Western Conference Finals Team

Fisher suited up for all 82 Utah regular-season games in 2006-07 and started 61, averaging 10.1 points and 3.3 assists in 27.9 minutes. He supplied reliable guard minutes in a 51-win season when Williams was establishing himself as the team's primary ball handler. Utah reached the Western Conference finals after beating Golden State in the second round, and Fisher appeared in 16 postseason games. His stay lasted only one season before a return to Los Angeles. Still, the Jazz received a documented season of starting-caliber play on a deep postseason run, not merely a veteran name on the roster.

McLeod Offered Minutes and Became Part of the Indiana Transaction

Of the three acquired guards, Keith McLeod was the only one who played a Golden State regular-season game. He appeared in 26 games, logging 379 minutes with averages of 5.3 points and 1.7 assists. The Warriors waived Devin Brown on October 3 and Andre Owens on October 26 before either played for the team. McLeod later moved with Ike Diogu, Mike Dunleavy and Troy Murphy to Indiana in January 2007. Golden State obtained Al Harrington, Stephen Jackson, Sarunas Jasikevicius and Josh Powell in that separate four-for-four transaction. McLeod was one ingredient in that larger deal, rather than the source of all four returning players.

Utah's Direct Return Was Larger, Though Both Teams Gained

A championship-tested guard who started 61 games and contributed in the postseason gave Utah the clearest on-court benefit. Golden State did not come away empty: it reduced a sizeable salary obligation, received reserve minutes from McLeod and later included him in the asset package that reshaped its playoff roster. Those advantages help explain the Warriors' favorable grade. But the other two guards never joined their regular-season rotation, and the subsequent Indiana trade also required three separate Warriors assets. Fisher's direct contribution to Utah remains more easily attributable to the July 2006 exchange, warranting a narrow rather than overwhelming Jazz advantage.

Final Verdict

Slight Jazz Edge. Utah earns A- for Fisher's 82 games, 61 starts and real 2007 conference-finals contribution. Golden State receives B+ for contractual flexibility, 26 McLeod appearances and his limited role in the separate Indiana transaction. Golden State cannot claim all of that later package as value from Fisher alone.

McLeod was one ingredient in that larger deal, rather than the source of all four returning players.

Utah's Direct Return Was Larger, Though Both Teams Gained

A championship-tested guard who started 61 games and contributed in the postseason gave Utah the clearest on-court benefit. Golden State did not come away empty: it reduced a sizeable salary obligation, received reserve minutes from McLeod and later included him in the asset package that reshaped its playoff roster. Those advantages help explain the Warriors' favorable grade. But the other two guards never joined their regular-season rotation, and the subsequent Indiana trade also required three separate Warriors assets. Fisher's direct contribution to Utah remains more easily attributable to the July 2006 exchange, warranting a narrow rather than overwhelming Jazz advantage.

Final Verdict

Slight Jazz Edge. Utah earns A- for Fisher's 82 games, 61 starts and real 2007 conference-finals contribution. Golden State receives B+ for contractual flexibility, 26 McLeod appearances and his limited role in the separate Indiana transaction. Golden State cannot claim all of that later package as value from Fisher alone.

indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Hornets Used a Sign-and-Trade to Add a Veteran Shooter

In July 2006 the New Orleans/Oklahoma City Hornets secured forward Peja Stojaković from Indiana in a sign-and-trade that sent Andrew Betts's rights to the Pacers. Stojaković had been a high-volume outside scorer in Sacramento, while his brief Indiana tenure was interrupted by injuries. New Orleans was building around Chris Paul and needed a veteran who could space the floor. Indiana moved on from a player it had acquired only months earlier and accepted draft rights instead of a comparable active NBA contributor.

A Difficult First Season Gave Way to Real Hornets Production

Stojaković's 2006-07 campaign was cut short by a serious back problem, delaying the value of his new contract. He responded with a far more productive 2007-08 season, appearing in seventy-seven games and averaging 16.4 points. He scored 1,263 regular-season points and made 231 three-pointers while helping New Orleans finish near the top of the Western Conference. He also started all twelve Hornets playoff games that year. Those are direct New Orleans achievements, unlike Stojaković's earlier All-Star seasons with Sacramento.

Andrew Betts Never Appeared for the Pacers

Indiana received the draft rights to Andrew Betts, an English center whose NBA path had never materialized despite being selected years earlier. Betts did not log a regular-season NBA game for the Pacers. That distinction matters because international rights can have bargaining or developmental value even when the prospect never joins an active roster. The Pacers avoided carrying the full Stojaković salary, but this particular incoming player asset did not replace his scoring or create any documented Indiana NBA minutes. No later rights-holder team games should be credited to the Pacers.

Stojaković's Useful Years Establish the Winner

New Orleans incurred real contract risk and lost much of its first season with Stojaković. The long-term result nonetheless included several seasons of veteran perimeter shooting during the best Chris Paul Hornets years. Indiana collected a deferred rights asset without on-court return. Evaluating only the summer transaction, rather than Stojaković's eventual championship season with Dallas after a separate move, gives New Orleans a pronounced advantage. The original Hornets-winning verdict was sound, but the sustained production justifies a high grade while Indiana's receiving-team return was extremely limited.

Final Verdict

Pelicans Win. New Orleans earns A for securing Stojaković, including seventy-seven games, 1,263 points and twelve playoff starts in 2007-08. Indiana gets D+ because Andrew Betts never played a Pacers NBA regular-season game. The initial Hornets injury disappointment does not erase later direct scoring, and his Dallas championship is excluded.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Turned Harrington's Departure Into a Future First

On August 22, 2006, the Atlanta Hawks sent forward Al Harrington and center John Edwards to the Indiana Pacers in an agreement that returned a protected future first-round selection and cash. Harrington was rejoining a franchise he had played for earlier, while Atlanta chose draft capital over extending its immediate commitment to the veteran scorer. The pick's protections mattered because Atlanta did not acquire a player on the spot. The right ultimately conveyed in the 2007 draft, when the Hawks used the eleventh overall selection on guard Acie Law IV. This was not a direct trade of Harrington for an established NBA guard.

Indiana Received a Familiar Rotation Forward

Harrington supplied Indiana with immediate veteran scoring and frontcourt flexibility during the 2006-07 season. His return stint was relatively brief, because the Pacers later included him in a larger trade involving Golden State and several other prominent players. That later agreement had its own incoming and outgoing assets, so the full future contributions of Mike Dunleavy or Troy Murphy cannot simply be assigned to the 2006 Atlanta transaction. John Edwards added another roster piece, but he was not the primary reason for Indiana's interest. The Pacers obtained a player who could help immediately and could subsequently be moved again as part of a broader redesign.

Jackson did not develop into a durable Celtics wing, while Jones provided a chance at frontcourt depth in Cleveland. The inherited Even Trade assigns C+ to each team.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Took a Chance on Jackson's Shooting

The Celtics acquired Luke Jackson and cash from the Cavaliers in October 2006, sending Dwayne Jones and a trade exception in the other direction. Jackson had been a high draft choice whose NBA career had been disrupted by injuries and limited opportunity. Boston could attempt to evaluate his outside shooting without surrendering a prominent starter. Cleveland preferred a frontcourt prospect and additional flexibility over retaining the wing at that stage of his development.

Jackson Did Not Become a Celtics Fixture

Jackson's acquisition offered Boston a prospect with recognizable draft pedigree, but the hoped-for long-term NBA role did not follow. His earlier Cleveland games and college scoring reputation could not substitute for Celtics production. The team's direct return was an opportunity to examine his availability and fit, alongside cash considerations. The move did not produce a new core wing and should not be retrospectively elevated because Jackson had once carried a high draft selection.

Cleveland Received Jones and a Financial Mechanism

Dwayne Jones gave the Cavaliers a big man who could compete for reserve minutes and rebounding assignments. His ceiling was limited compared with established starting centers, but he represented an active player option. The trade exception offered another route to manage transactions without obligating the club to acquire a particular future player. Those are genuine roster tools, though the exception should not be counted as guaranteed production until its later use is verified.

Both Sides Pursued Modest Upside

Boston took a low-cost opportunity on an injury-affected wing, while Cleveland accepted frontcourt depth and roster flexibility. Neither incoming package became an enduring core solution. The inherited Even Trade makes sense because both clubs gained possibilities rather than a decisive proven contributor. The analysis should focus on the assets actually exchanged and their limited realized roles, not on hypothetical healthy seasons for Jackson or an invented star developed from the trade exception.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston receives C+ for acquiring Luke Jackson and cash at a small basketball cost, although the wing did not become a lasting Celtics contributor. Cleveland also earns C+ for Dwayne Jones and a trade exception, gaining depth and flexibility without a major on-court breakthrough. Neither side received a transformative long-term player.

houston-rockets.summary: On February 13, 2007, Houston acquired center Jake Tsakalidis from Memphis for forward Scott Padgett. Tsakalidis played 13 Rockets regular-season games, logging 132 minutes and averaging 2.3 points and 3.1 rebounds; he also made one short playoff appearance. Padgett appeared in seven Grizzlies games, logging 33 minutes and scoring two points before the team waived him April 4. Rockets Win, Houston C+, Memphis D+.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Obtained a Big Center for Its Bench

The Rockets acquired Jake Tsakalidis from Memphis on February 13, 2007, sending Scott Padgett in the other direction. Houston was a 52-win club built around Yao Ming and Tracy McGrady, with a need for emergency size behind its frontline starters. Tsakalidis stood over seven feet and had previously been part of the Memphis center rotation. The Grizzlies were headed for another losing season and opted to try the perimeter-oriented forward Padgett instead. The teams exchanged only these two veterans, without a draft choice or cash reported in their official seasonal transaction records.

Tsakalidis Made Thirteen Houston Regular-Season Appearances

Tsakalidis did not become a central component of Houston's playoff rotation, but he supplied thirteen regular-season appearances after the February trade. He played 132 minutes, averaging 2.3 points and 3.1 rebounds in just over ten minutes per game. He also appeared once against Utah during the Rockets' first-round postseason series, recording two points and four rebounds in three minutes. His earlier 23 Memphis games in 2006-07 were completed before he joined Houston and should not be counted toward the Rockets' return. His contribution was modest, but it was actual center depth for a playoff club.

Padgett's Memphis Tenure Ended After Seven Games

Memphis used Padgett only seven times in the remainder of the season. Those appearances totaled 33 minutes, two points and nine rebounds, and he never started. The Grizzlies waived him on April 4, 2007, well before the season's final games. Padgett had played 24 games for Houston before being dealt, but those cannot be transferred to his Memphis record. The team effectively acquired a briefly available veteran forward who never established a place in the rotation. His earlier NBA career contained more useful seasons, yet they offer no direct justification for grading this Grizzlies acquisition highly.

Limited Return on Both Sides, With Houston Ahead

Neither team found a player it would build around. Tsakalidis was a deep backup, and Padgett's tenure was shorter still. The historical question is what the receiving teams got for the assets exchanged, rather than who carried the better pretrade reputation. Houston played its new center for 132 regular-season minutes plus a brief postseason outing; Memphis got 33 minutes before releasing its forward. That is not a dramatic team-changing difference, but it is a verifiable advantage. The inherited Memphis-favored verdict reversed the evidence and assigned the higher grade to the side with virtually no playing return.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win. Houston earns C+ because Jake Tsakalidis logged thirteen regular-season games, 132 minutes and a short playoff appearance in 2007. Memphis receives D+ for Scott Padgett's seven games, 33 minutes and two points before the April waiver. Both returns were small, but the Rockets obtained more actual playing utility.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia sent Alan Henderson, cash and unspecified draft considerations to Utah on February 22, 2007, receiving the right to swap 2007 second-round picks. The swap went unused, and Utah waived Henderson March 2 without a Jazz game. Philadelphia removed a seldom-used veteran and obtained draft flexibility that it did not exercise; Utah received cash of an undisclosed amount. Slight 76ers Edge, Philadelphia C+, Utah C.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Philadelphia Paid Utah to Take Alan Henderson

The February 22, 2007 deadline exchange was unusual because Philadelphia traded veteran forward Alan Henderson, cash and draft considerations to Utah and received the right to exchange 2007 second-round picks. The NBA's official historical deadline ledger lists the pieces in that direction. Utah's own media guide separately confirms that the Jazz received Henderson and cash from Philadelphia. The published cash amount is not specified, and the draft considerations should not be assumed to represent a confirmed high-value pick. Philadelphia wanted options for the 2007 draft and fewer commitments to a veteran who had little place in its young roster.

The Jazz Cut Henderson Ten Days Later

Utah did not acquire useful frontcourt minutes from Henderson. The club requested waivers on March 2, ten days after the transaction, without him appearing in a regular-season Jazz game. Before being traded, Henderson had played 34 Philadelphia games in 2006-07, including five starts, with averages of 3.5 points and 3.1 rebounds. Those 34 games are not production Utah received. The incoming player's on-court contribution was therefore zero. Utah's tangible gain was financial: cash considerations supplied by Philadelphia, with the precise sum absent from the public official record.

Philadelphia's Pick-Swap Right Was Not Used

The 76ers received a conditional option rather than an immediate draft selection or a player. The right to swap 2007 second-round picks was not exercised, so it did not produce a better draft position or drafted contributor from this February deal. The transaction nonetheless could provide Philadelphia with roster and draft flexibility by moving Henderson off its books. A separate June 2007 arrangement in which Philadelphia received Herbert Hill's draft rights and Utah received Kyrylo Fesenko should not automatically be assigned to the earlier swap. The different 2007 transactions need to be assessed independently unless their assets are explicitly linked.

The Small Advantage Is Administrative, Not On-Court

No new NBA playing value came directly to either club from this particular exchange. Utah waived Henderson, and Philadelphia did not exercise its pick right. The 76ers can claim a modest benefit from shedding a veteran contract and retaining an optional route to a later draft decision; the Jazz can claim the cash it received, but its value cannot be quantified from the available documents. Neither outcome merits a top grade or a claim of major basketball improvement. The resulting assessment is intentionally narrow, and the stale partner aggregate is corrected to agree with the published team grades.

Final Verdict

Slight 76ers Edge. Philadelphia gets C+ for moving Henderson and briefly holding a draft-swap option, even though it was unused. Utah earns C for receiving cash while waiving Henderson before he played. Neither side gained on-court production from this exchange. The undisclosed cash amount prevents a stronger comparative claim.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston traded Juwan Howard to Minnesota for Mike James and Justin Reed on June 11, 2007. Minnesota waived Howard on October 29 before he played a Timberwolves regular-season game. James returned to Houston and provided backcourt appearances during 2007-08; Reed was a fringe addition. Rockets Win, Houston B- versus Minnesota D+. Howard's later Dallas career wasn't a Minnesota return.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Reacquired a Veteran Guard From Minnesota

The Rockets obtained Mike James and Justin Reed from the Timberwolves on June 11, 2007, sending veteran power forward Juwan Howard in return. Houston was changing its support around Yao Ming and Tracy McGrady and wanted more guard scoring behind its leading players. Minnesota was preparing for a broad roster overhaul and took on Howard's frontcourt experience. James had previously played for Houston during the 2004-05 season, so the trade also brought him back to an organization that knew his playing style and off-bench strengths.

Howard Never Reached Minnesota's Regular-Season Floor

Howard looked like a plausible veteran presence for a young Minnesota roster, but that forecast never became actual team output. The Timberwolves waived him on October 29, 2007, before the regular season began. His career continued elsewhere, but Minnesota received zero games, points and rebounds from the veteran acquired in June. His earlier productive Rockets seasons and later appearances with Dallas must be excluded from the Timberwolves return. The waived contract is central to understanding why the inherited Minnesota-winning evaluation was not supported by actual basketball production.

James Provided the Rockets With Another Guard Option

James did play for Houston in 2007-08, giving the team additional backcourt scoring and ball-handling coverage. He had been a stronger offensive player in Toronto and Minnesota than he would be during this brief Rockets reunion, but he remained a usable NBA guard. Reed also moved to Houston in the transaction, without establishing an equally substantial role. The organization later traded James again as part of a separate deal, so his following years should not be counted as the June 2007 return. Unlike Minnesota, Houston received regular-season participation from its incoming principal player.

The Waiver Makes the Verdict Hard to Defend for Minnesota

On paper the Timberwolves acquired a respected veteran frontcourt player, and Houston accepted smaller guards in return. The practical results diverged quickly once Howard was waived. Minnesota's side never yielded an appearance, while Houston put James on the floor during a season when it sought to compete in the Western Conference. The Rockets weren't getting their future franchise point guard, and the original deal was not high stakes. Yet the receiving-team evidence is not close enough to call a Minnesota victory. A modest Rockets advantage better describes the transaction.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win. Houston earns B- for receiving Mike James as a playable 2007-08 backcourt option alongside Justin Reed. Minnesota receives D+ because it waived Juwan Howard in October 2007 without one Timberwolves regular-season game. Howard's NBA appearances for other franchises cannot rescue the Timberwolves' original trade return.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Sent a Top-Five Selection for Elite Shooting

Boston traded Wally Szczerbiak, Delonte West, the rights to No. 5 Jeff Green and a future second-round pick to the Seattle SuperSonics in June 2007. The Celtics received Ray Allen and the rights to LSU forward Glen Davis at No. 35. Allen was an accomplished perimeter scorer who could give Paul Pierce another elite offensive partner immediately. Seattle was rebuilding and had already selected Kevin Durant, so acquiring Green and additional roster options aligned with its longer timetable.

Allen Helped Deliver the Celtics' 2008 Title

Allen's three-point shooting, off-ball movement and ability to thrive alongside other stars were essential to Boston's 2008 championship. The Celtics later added Kevin Garnett in a separate trade, completing a veteran core that fit Allen's particular strengths. Davis also developed into a useful reserve on playoff teams. Those direct receiving-team contributions gave Boston both top-end production and depth. The outcome justified moving a high draft choice rather than waiting for Green to mature on a younger timeline.

Seattle Used the Deal to Support Its Rebuild

The SuperSonics obtained Green as a promising forward to develop beside Durant, while West and Szczerbiak added experience and roster flexibility. Green's later years after the franchise relocated to Oklahoma City belong to its successor organization's history rather than the final Seattle season alone. The package provided developmental options but could not immediately reproduce Allen's established offense. The extra second-round right also carried possible future use, making the trade more than a straight exchange of Allen for one rookie.

The Two Clubs Prioritized Different Championship Windows

Boston's decision produced an immediate contender and ultimately a title, while Seattle assembled young talent for a longer rebuilding cycle. Both strategies were coherent, and Green became a real NBA contributor, so Seattle's return should not be described as worthless. Allen was nonetheless the crucial acquisition in a championship-winning roster. The addition of Davis at the second-round price widened Boston's advantage. A title in the very next season is a decisive outcome when the outgoing assets had been primarily future-oriented.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns A+ for Ray Allen's championship impact and Glen Davis's productive reserve tenure. Seattle receives B for Jeff Green's draft rights, Delonte West, Wally Szczerbiak and a second-round pick, which served its rebuilding plans. The trade favored Boston because Allen became an essential starter on the 2008 NBA champion.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Charlotte acquired Jason Richardson and Jermareo Davidson's draft rights from Golden State in 2007 for Brandan Wright's rights. Richardson started all 82 Bobcats games in 2007-08 and averaged 21.8 points, producing 1,788 points and 243 made three-pointers before a 2008 Phoenix trade. Wright played 98 Golden State games across 2007-08, 2008-09 and 2010-11. Charlotte Win: A- versus C+.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Bobcats Bought an Established Scorer With a Top-Ten Pick

Charlotte acquired shooting guard Jason Richardson and second-round prospect Jermareo Davidson's rights from Golden State on June 28, 2007. Golden State received the rights to Brandan Wright, selected eighth overall after a promising North Carolina freshman season. Richardson had already built a strong offensive résumé with the Warriors and came with a larger contract. Charlotte accepted that expense to secure immediate perimeter scoring. Golden State bet the younger big man could develop while opening space in its backcourt.

Richardson Gave Charlotte an 82-Game Scoring Season

The centerpiece played every game for Charlotte in 2007-08, starting all eighty-two and averaging 21.8 points. He scored 1,788 points, made 243 three-pointers and also averaged 5.4 rebounds. Those were meaningful results from a team that had lacked a consistent high-volume wing scorer. Richardson began the following season with the Bobcats before being traded to Phoenix in December 2008. His later Suns and Magic production cannot be charged to the Charlotte acquisition, but the fully productive first season is sufficient evidence of substantial value.

Wright's Warriors Development Was Interrupted by Injuries

Wright appeared in thirty-eight Golden State games as a rookie, then thirty-nine the following season as his role expanded. A shoulder problem cost him the entire 2009-10 campaign. He returned for twenty-one Warriors games in 2010-11 before the club sent him to New Jersey in a separate trade. His total direct Golden State return was ninety-eight regular-season appearances rather than the lengthier NBA career he eventually assembled with other franchises. He showed finishing ability but never matched Richardson's offensive responsibility for their receiving teams.

The Proven Starter Beat the Prospect Gamble

Charlotte got a player who immediately led its scoring attack for an entire season. Davidson's rights were a secondary sweetener rather than the decisive asset. Golden State received a top-ten prospect who played in shorter stretches and lost a season to injury, an outcome that made the transaction disappointing despite Wright's later NBA usefulness. The older Charlotte-winning assessment was directionally correct. Richardson's 1,788-point campaign supports a stronger Bobcats grade, while the Warriors still deserve credit for acquiring a player who did reach their rotation.

Final Verdict

Charlotte Win. The Bobcats earn A- after Richardson started all eighty-two 2007-08 games and produced 1,788 points with 243 made threes. Golden State gets C+ for ninety-eight games from Brandan Wright across three partial seasons. Wright's injuries and later career elsewhere limit the original Warriors payoff while Charlotte realized a proven scorer.

houston-rockets.summary: Orlando selected Australian guard Brad Newley with pick No. 54 in the June 28, 2007 NBA draft and sold his draft rights to Houston for cash. Newley built a long professional career in Australia and Europe but never played an NBA regular-season game for the Rockets. Houston later moved the rights to New York. Magic Win on realized NBA production, Orlando C+, Houston D+; the transaction chiefly exchanged international development rights for money.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Orlando Sold a Second-Round Draft Stash on Draft Night

On June 28, 2007, Orlando selected Australian guard Brad Newley with the 54th pick in the NBA draft and sent his rights to Houston for cash considerations. The Rockets' official media guide confirms both the selection and the exchange. Newley was already an established scorer in Australia's National Basketball League and offered the possibility of signing an international prospect later rather than immediately using a roster place. Orlando accepted a guaranteed payment instead of retaining a player whose NBA arrival was uncertain. This was a draft-rights purchase, not a trade of an active Magic player.

Newley Built His Career Outside the NBA

Newley continued competing in Australia and European leagues after the draft. He represented Australia internationally, developed a long career overseas and became an accomplished NBL veteran. Houston monitored him as an asset, but he never made an NBA regular-season appearance for the Rockets. The distinction is essential: Newley's international scoring and honors are his own achievements, not Houston points or assists. NBA and club records show why the move was plausible in 2007, when late draft selections often served as overseas investments that did not take up an immediate roster position.

Houston Eventually Transferred the Rights Again

Although the Rockets never obtained on-court NBA production from Newley, the contract rights did retain some transactional use. In 2021, Newley himself discussed the NBA rights moving to the New York Knicks, after Houston had held them for years. That onward movement prevents a simplistic assertion that the Rockets received absolutely nothing from the original purchase. It does not establish the monetary or sporting value of the later transaction in isolation, however. Without a documented specific Houston roster player created solely by this transfer, the defensible primary finding is that the incoming rights never produced an NBA game for Houston.

The Cash Return Was More Certain Than the Overseas Option

Orlando received financial compensation immediately and avoided the waiting period that Houston chose to accept. The Rockets acquired a potential future player who prospered internationally but did not join their NBA rotation. Rights that can be moved later have some value, even when that option never turns into a player wearing the acquiring team's uniform. Therefore the exchange deserves modest grades on both sides rather than an extravagant judgment based on Newley's Australian career. Orlando gets the benefit of the known cash payment, while Houston's deferred player-development bet never produced league playing time.

Final Verdict

Magic Win. Orlando gets C+ for receiving cash immediately when it sold the 54th pick's rights. Houston receives D+ because Brad Newley never played an NBA regular-season game for the Rockets, although the rights later moved to New York and retained limited transaction potential. His successful international career should not be counted as Houston on-court value.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston purchased Carl Landry's No. 31 draft rights from Seattle on June 28, 2007 for cash and a 2008 second-round pick, later No. 56 Sasha Kaun. Landry played 163 Rockets regular-season games from 2007-08 through his 2009-10 midseason departure, totaling 1,819 points and 2,178 minutes in his first two seasons alone. Seattle gained cash and a pick but no Kaun NBA appearances for the franchise. Rockets Win, Houston A, Seattle C.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Seattle Selected Landry and Sold His Rights to Houston

Seattle drafted Purdue forward Carl Landry with the thirty-first choice in 2007, then traded his rights to Houston. The Rockets sent cash and a future 2008 second-round selection that would eventually become No. 56 Sasha Kaun. Seattle had just drafted Kevin Durant second overall and made several other major roster moves, while Houston wanted an inexpensive power forward who could compete for minutes alongside its established stars. Unlike a speculative cash-only deal, the Rockets were acquiring a player who quickly developed into a useful NBA reserve.

Landry Became an Efficient Houston Scorer

Landry played forty-two Houston games as a rookie in 2007-08, scoring 342 points and converting more than sixty percent of his field-goal attempts. He appeared in sixty-nine games in 2008-09, contributing another 638 points and 343 rebounds. Landry wasn't a high-volume star, but he finished around the rim and brought important energy off the bench. The two seasons gave Houston 111 regular-season appearances, 980 points and 2,178 minutes of direct frontcourt production, an especially strong outcome for rights to an early second-round draft selection.

Another Fifty-Two Games Arrived Before His Next Trade

Landry started 2009-10 with the Rockets and appeared in fifty-two games, scoring 839 points while averaging more than sixteen per game. Houston subsequently traded him to Sacramento within a much larger exchange. That departure marks the end of the direct Rockets receiving-team return: 163 regular-season games and 1,819 points across the first two-and-a-half seasons. His later Kings and Hornets appearances should not be added to Houston's totals. The club nonetheless received a sustained contributor for a modest draft-night purchase and ultimately retained a tradeable contract in a more complex deal.

The Future Pick Never Produced a Seattle Franchise Player

Seattle obtained cash plus the 2008 second-round choice, which was used on Sasha Kaun at No. 56. Kaun later played NBA games for Cleveland after a separate set of rights and contract decisions, not for the SuperSonics or their Oklahoma City successor. Cash and an additional choice are legitimate assets, but their direct contribution fell well short of Landry's substantial Houston minutes. This is a clear draft-rights success for the Rockets, and the original modest C+ Houston grade undervalued the actual receiving-team production. Seattle's compensation deserves credit without invented Kaun playing time.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win. Houston earns A after getting 163 regular-season games and 1,819 points from Carl Landry before his 2010 trade to Sacramento. Seattle earns C for cash and the 2008 No. 56 draft selection, later Sasha Kaun, who never played a game for the Seattle/Oklahoma City franchise. The acquired player created far more NBA value for Houston.

That departure marks the end of the direct Rockets receiving-team return: 163 regular-season games and 1,819 points across the first two-and-a-half seasons. His later Kings and Hornets appearances should not be added to Houston's totals. The club nonetheless received a sustained contributor for a modest draft-night purchase and ultimately retained a tradeable contract in a more complex deal.

The Future Pick Never Produced a Seattle Franchise Player

Seattle obtained cash plus the 2008 second-round choice, which was used on Sasha Kaun at No. 56. Kaun later played NBA games for Cleveland after a separate set of rights and contract decisions, not for the SuperSonics or their Oklahoma City successor. Cash and an additional choice are legitimate assets, but their direct contribution fell well short of Landry's substantial Houston minutes. This is a clear draft-rights success for the Rockets, and the original modest C+ Houston grade undervalued the actual receiving-team production. Seattle's compensation deserves credit without invented Kaun playing time.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win. Houston earns A after getting 163 regular-season games and 1,819 points from Carl Landry before his 2010 trade to Sacramento. Seattle earns C for cash and the 2008 No. 56 draft selection, later Sasha Kaun, who never played a game for the Seattle/Oklahoma City franchise. The acquired player created far more NBA value for Houston.

seattle-supersonics.summary: On July 20, 2007, Phoenix sent Kurt Thomas and its 2008 and 2010 first-round picks to Seattle for a conditional 2009 second-round pick, while Phoenix received an $8 million trade exception. Seattle used the 2008 first on Serge Ibaka and the 2010 first on Quincy Pondexter, then later traded Thomas for additional assets. The combination of usable veteran value, two first-rounders and Ibaka's long-term impact makes this one of the strongest returns in the Seattle-to-Oklahoma City transition.
seattle-supersonics.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix's official announcement and Basketball-Reference agree on the July 20, 2007 structure. The Suns sent Kurt Thomas plus their own 2008 and 2010 first-round picks to Seattle for a conditional 2009 second-round pick. Phoenix also received an $8 million trade exception, not the $9 million figure carried by the legacy archive entry. The Suns openly framed the move around salary relief and roster flexibility, while Seattle was rebuilding around Kevin Durant and Jeff Green.

Seattle Return
The first 2008 pick became No. 24, Serge Ibaka. That alone creates substantial realized value: Ibaka developed into a long-term defensive anchor for the Oklahoma City core and played 14 NBA seasons. Basketball-Reference credits the No. 24 pick to Seattle, and the Thunder's own historical profile describes the organization selecting Ibaka at No. 24 after scouting him internationally. The 2010 first became No. 26, Quincy Pondexter, adding another first-round asset to the return.

Kurt Thomas also was not dead salary from Seattle's perspective. He gave the club part of the 2007-08 season and was then traded to San Antonio on February 20, 2008 for Brent Barry, Francisco Elson and a 2009 first-round pick. Seattle waived Barry, but the ability to turn Thomas into another first shows that the veteran component retained transaction value beyond his short stay. The original deal therefore produced both immediate optionality and multiple draft assets rather than relying entirely on one lucky pick outcome.

Phoenix Return
The Suns received the conditional 2009 second-round pick that Basketball-Reference later maps to No. 57, Emir Preldžić, along with the $8 million trade exception and the intended financial relief. Contemporary Associated Press reporting described the move as a salary-cutting decision after Phoenix signed Grant Hill and while the team was already carrying a high payroll. That context explains the transaction, but financial flexibility does not erase the basketball assets surrendered.

Hindsight Verdict
Seattle receives an A+ because it converted cap capacity into Thomas, two first-round picks and eventually Ibaka, then extracted more value from Thomas in a later trade. Phoenix receives a D+ because the club achieved the intended salary relief but surrendered the best long-term basketball asset and an additional first to do it. The verdict remains Seattle SuperSonics Win. The grade credits only traceable assets from this transaction and its direct downstream chain rather than unrelated Oklahoma City success.

boston-celtics.summary: Boston acquired Kevin Garnett from Timberwolves in exchange for Al Jefferson; Gerald Green (b. 1986-01-26); Theo Ratliff; Ryan Gomes; Sebastian Telfair; 2009 first-round pick (#6 Jonny Flynn); 2009 first-round pick (#28 Wayne Ellington); cash.
boston-celtics.analysis: Garnett won Defensive Player of the Year in 2008, changed Boston's culture, and anchored the 2008 championship. Jefferson became a 20/10 big, but Minnesota missed on Flynn (#6) and never contended. A franchise-altering superstar trade that delivered Banner 17.

minnesota-timberwolves.summary: Minnesota began its post-Kevin Garnett rebuild with Al Jefferson, Ryan Gomes, Gerald Green, Sebastian Telfair, Theo Ratliff, two firsts and cash.
minnesota-timberwolves.analysis: The Kevin Garnett trade requires separating process from realized franchise outcome. Minnesota was dealing a superstar who wanted a path to contend and did receive a substantial rebuilding package: Al Jefferson became a high-level scorer, Ryan Gomes was useful, and the deal included two first-round picks plus additional young players and salary structure. That was meaningful leverage under difficult circumstances. Boston nevertheless received the defining asset and immediately won the 2008 championship with Garnett as its defensive and emotional centerpiece. Minnesota never turned the return into a comparable team-level result. The D+ grade is therefore a hindsight verdict on what the assets became, not an argument that the Wolves had an obvious better offer available in July 2007.

new-orleans-pelicans.summary: Cleveland acquired forward Cedric Simmons from New Orleans on September 29, 2007 for veteran David Wesley, with cash noted in the historical ledger. Simmons played seven Cavaliers games in 2007-08, totaling roughly 68 minutes, before becoming part of a February three-team trade. new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
Cleveland Acquired a Former Mid-First-Round Forward

The Cavaliers received Cedric Simmons from the Hornets on September 29, 2007, sending veteran guard David Wesley to New Orleans. Simmons had been selected fifteenth overall in the 2006 NBA draft, and Cleveland saw an opportunity to evaluate a younger power forward with defensive potential. The original imported transaction also lists cash on the New Orleans side, although club transaction histories describe the player swap without specifying a payment. This was a roster and financial adjustment for both teams, not an exchange of established frontcourt starters.

Simmons Played Seven Cleveland Games Before Another Trade

The Cavaliers gave Simmons only seven regular-season appearances in 2007-08, without a start. He averaged 9.7 minutes and 0.6 points, a total of roughly sixty-eight minutes and four points. Cleveland also assigned him to its developmental affiliate while looking for ways to use its deep bench. He was then included in a larger February 2008 three-team deal that brought multiple veterans to the Cavaliers. His contract was one of several outgoing assets, so the later exchange's entire return cannot be credited to Simmons alone.

Wesley Never Played a New Orleans Regular-Season Game

Wesley was a familiar Hornets veteran from years earlier in his career, but the September 2007 acquisition did not become a playing reunion. On October 29, before the regular season, New Orleans sent his contract to New Jersey for Mile Ilić and Bernard Robinson. The Hornets waived both incoming players that same day. That onward transaction illustrates limited use as a movable contract, not a route to NBA points or starts. Wesley's earlier Hornets career and Cleveland experience both belong to periods before this particular trade.

Small Playing Return Versus Brief Contract Flexibility

Cleveland got a former first-round forward and tried him in seven games before using his contract in a later transaction. New Orleans received a veteran contract it could immediately move, while the two players in the next exchange were waived. Neither side gained lasting rotation depth. The original B grades appear too generous given the minimal direct basketball results. It would be equally misleading to award Cleveland a decisive win for Simmons's handful of outings or to invent an amount for the disputed cash component. Matching modest grades reflect the evidence.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Cleveland receives C+ for Cedric Simmons's seven games and roughly sixty-eight minutes before another transaction. New Orleans earns C+ for briefly using David Wesley's contract in a subsequent October exchange, with the originally recorded cash component unquantified. Neither team received an enduring rotation player, so the inherited matching B grades overstated both sides.

miami-heat.analysis: By February 2008, the championship core had run its course, and Miami moved Shaquille O’Neal to Phoenix for Shawn Marion and Marcus Banks. O’Neal still produced useful basketball in Phoenix, but Marion gave Miami a younger, more versatile two-way player and a contract that became important to the franchise’s roster flexibility. Marion’s Heat tenure lasted only about a year, so this was not a transformational acquisition. The value came from resetting the roster while extracting a prominent asset for an aging star. Phoenix received real production, but Miami’s combination of on-court usefulness and flexibility creates a modest hindsight edge.

Bibby became the Hawks' starting organizer during their return to the playoffs and remained with the club for several seasons. Sacramento's multiple incoming veterans proved less enduring. Hawks Win, Atlanta B+ versus Sacramento D.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Consolidated Depth Into a Starting Guard

The Hawks acquired Mike Bibby from Sacramento at the February 2008 deadline, sending Anthony Johnson, Tyronn Lue, Shelden Williams, Lorenzen Wright and a second-round pick. Bibby brought playmaking, outside shooting and years of experience organizing a high-level Kings offense. Atlanta already had Joe Johnson and emerging forwards but needed a dependable starting point guard. Sacramento accepted a package of veterans and a future selection rather than continuing with a guard who had been central to its earlier playoff teams.

Bibby Helped Atlanta Reenter the Postseason

The Hawks reached the 2008 playoffs and pushed the eventual champion Boston Celtics to seven games in the first round. Bibby provided a veteran lead guard who could direct possessions and space the floor for Johnson, Josh Smith and Al Horford. He stayed in Atlanta for multiple seasons, making this a meaningful roster addition rather than a temporary deadline rental. His earlier Sacramento postseason achievements shouldn't be counted as Hawks value, but his role in Atlanta's own playoff return is a strong direct result.

Sacramento's Numerous Arrivals Had Limited Longevity

The Kings obtained four players and the No. 42 pick later associated with Sean Singletary. None became a long-running foundation comparable with Bibby's Atlanta tenure. Sacramento waived Lue shortly after the trade, and the other arrivals filled narrower roles or moved on. The selection gave the club a prospect opportunity, but its eventual development did not balance the transaction. The number of players acquired looked impressive on the ledger; their receiving-team NBA production and continued usefulness were much less substantial.

One Good Fit Outweighed Several Smaller Pieces

Atlanta traded quantity for a position-specific veteran who helped a developing team build continuity. Sacramento got several roster options but not a replacement point guard with equal impact. That judgment does not mean every incoming Kings player provided zero minutes or that Bibby alone produced Atlanta's first playoff berth in years. He did, however, help an existing core function more effectively and remained useful beyond the initial season. The gap in lasting roles supports the large difference in team grades.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta receives B+ for Mike Bibby's immediate playoff help and multiple seasons as its starting point guard. Sacramento gets D for Anthony Johnson, Tyronn Lue, Shelden Williams, Lorenzen Wright and the pick used on Sean Singletary, whose combined impact did not match Bibby's Hawks tenure. The team that acquired the reliable organizer got the better return.

seattle-supersonics.summary: Seattle moved veteran Kurt Thomas to San Antonio for two expiring veterans and a protected first, converting a short-term player into additional draft capital during the rebuild.
seattle-supersonics.analysis: By February 2008, Seattle’s priority was accumulating future assets rather than maximizing the current roster. Moving Kurt Thomas to San Antonio brought back Brent Barry, Francisco Elson and a protected first-round pick that ultimately landed at No. 25. The veteran contracts were not the point of the transaction; the first-round asset was. Thomas helped a contender immediately, so San Antonio received useful win-now value, but Seattle turned an older center into another first during an intentional rebuild. The protection reduced the pick’s ceiling and prevents an elite grade, yet the asset conversion was favorable enough to support a clear Seattle win and an A- evaluation.

perspectives.summary: At the February 2008 deadline Chicago acquired Larry Hughes, Drew Gooden, Shannon Brown and Cedric Simmons in a three-team trade involving Cleveland and Seattle. Cleveland gained Ben Wallace and Joe Smith, while the SuperSonics acquired Adrian Griffin. Wallace and Smith helped address Cleveland's immediate frontcourt needs. The inherited slight Cavaliers edge grades Cleveland B+, Seattle B+ and Chicago C+.
perspectives.analysis:
Chicago Rebuilt Multiple Rotation Spots

The Bulls acquired Larry Hughes, Drew Gooden, Shannon Brown and Cedric Simmons in a three-team February 2008 transaction with Cleveland and Seattle. Hughes and Gooden offered experience in the backcourt and frontcourt, while Brown and Simmons represented younger player possibilities. Chicago was reshuffling a roster that had struggled to meet expectations. Rather than secure one obvious star, the club received several pieces whose roles and later destinations would require individual assessment. Each acquisition brought a different kind of potential value.

Cleveland Added Wallace and Joe Smith for a Playoff Push

The Cavaliers received Ben Wallace and Joe Smith, gaining veteran frontcourt defense and interior depth around LeBron James. Wallace's reputation had been built in Detroit, where he was a dominant defender; Cleveland needed to evaluate the version it received in 2008 instead of assuming all those earlier accomplishments transferred automatically. Smith brought another experienced big with midrange offense. Both could contribute to a team targeting deep playoff runs, giving the Cavaliers a more direct immediate rationale than a purely developmental roster swap.

Seattle Acquired Griffin Near the End of Its Era

The SuperSonics received Adrian Griffin, a veteran perimeter player, in the arrangement. The trade occurred during Seattle's final NBA season before the franchise's relocation to Oklahoma City, so referring to its destination at the time matters historically. Griffin's role was limited, and his earlier seasons elsewhere do not create substantial new SuperSonics production. Even so, the club gained an experienced player within a larger transaction involving teams pursuing different competitive goals.

Cleveland's Frontcourt Fit Explains Its Edge

The inherited slight Cavaliers advantage rewards the immediate relevance of Wallace and Smith to a team relying on veteran defensive support. Chicago received more names, but four pieces didn't automatically create more combined long-term value. Seattle's B+ under the inherited grades reflects participation in the deal despite Griffin's relatively small direct return. The correct review compares the three receiving packages and their actual roles rather than merely totaling prior career accomplishments.

Final Verdict

Slight Cavaliers Edge. Cleveland earns B+ for Ben Wallace and Joe Smith's veteran frontcourt help. Seattle also receives B+ under the inherited grading for Adrian Griffin, though his direct impact was limited. Chicago gets C+ for Larry Hughes, Drew Gooden, Shannon Brown and Cedric Simmons. The Cleveland return best matched an immediate playoff need.
