houston-rockets.summary: Houston traded Kirk Snyder, cash and a 2010 second-round pick to Minnesota for Gerald Green on February 21, 2008. Green played one Rockets game, four minutes and six points before being waived March 8. Snyder made 27 Timberwolves appearances, including 18 starts, scoring roughly 8.4 per game and logging 680 minutes. The pick was used on No. 45 Paulo Prestes, who never played Minnesota NBA games. Wolves Win, Minnesota B+, Houston D+.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Took a Brief Chance on Gerald Green

At the February 21, 2008 trade deadline, the Rockets acquired Gerald Green from Minnesota for wing Kirk Snyder, cash and a future second-round selection. Green was a young, athletic former first-rounder whose raw tools had not developed into a dependable role with the Timberwolves. Houston could give him a short evaluation while its veteran players chased a playoff berth. Minnesota chose a more experienced defender and another chance to draft a prospect in 2010. The pick later settled at the forty-fifth position, making this more than a simple guard exchange.

Green Played Just Four Rockets Minutes

Green appeared in one Houston regular-season game after the trade, making all three field-goal attempts and scoring six points in four minutes. The surprising shooting line should not disguise the tiny sample. The Rockets waived Green on March 8, before he could become part of their playoff rotation. His twenty-nine Minnesota games earlier in 2007-08 were completed before this trade and do not contribute to Houston's acquired value. His subsequent more successful NBA seasons with other franchises were also separate contracts, not delayed Rockets performance.

Snyder Contributed Twenty-Seven Minnesota Games

Snyder found a larger role with the Timberwolves. He appeared in twenty-seven 2007-08 regular-season games after his arrival, started eighteen and played 680 minutes. He averaged 8.4 points and 4.2 rebounds while serving as a physical perimeter player on a rebuilding roster. That contribution was useful even though he was not retained as a franchise fixture. perspectives.summary: On June 25, 2008, Charlotte's Bobcats acquired the No. 20 draft selection used on Alexis Ajinça from Denver in exchange for a protected future first-round pick. Ajinça appeared in 31 Charlotte games in 2008-09 and six in 2009-10, totaling 37 games and ten career NBA points the latter season. The protected pick conveyed in 2010 as No. 16 Luke Babbitt but Denver had moved the right through Minnesota before Portland eventually selected Babbitt. Denver gained a transferable first-round asset, not Babbitt's playing time. Nuggets Win, Denver B-, Charlotte C.
perspectives.analysis:
Charlotte Acquired a Center Prospect at No. 20

On June 25, 2008, the Charlotte Bobcats obtained Denver's twentieth overall draft pick and used the selection on French seven-footer Alexis Ajinça. The Nuggets received a protected future first-round pick in exchange. Charlotte was buying immediate access to a prospect with developmental upside, while Denver preferred to hold a later asset that could be deployed as its roster needs changed. This was a draft-choice deal rather than a trade of existing NBA player contracts. The site uses the current Charlotte Hornets team name, but the franchise was called the Bobcats when this agreement was completed.

Ajinça's Charlotte Career Produced Thirty-Seven Games

Ajinça entered the NBA with Charlotte and appeared in thirty-one regular-season games during 2008-09, starting four. He then played six more games for the Bobcats in 2009-10 before continuing his professional career elsewhere. Those thirty-seven appearances, totaling eighty points, were the direct NBA playing return from the No. 20 choice for Charlotte. The center later played for other franchises, including much more productive seasons with New Orleans, but that later career cannot be credited to Charlotte as though the Bobcats retained him. A grade for this trade must use the actual short Charlotte tenure rather than his eventual career total.

Denver's Future Pick Traveled Through Two More Franchises

The protected first-round selection Charlotte sent to Denver eventually became the sixteenth overall pick in the 2010 draft, associated with Luke Babbitt. The Nuggets' own media guide explains that the future pick moved through Minnesota and ultimately to Portland before Babbitt was selected. This route gives Denver credit for receiving a transferable first-round asset, not for any NBA minutes Babbitt played with the Trail Blazers. The deal's protective terms were spread across several possible draft years before the selection conveyed. They gave the incoming pick legitimate flexibility, but a transaction chain still has to distinguish the original buyer from the final drafting club.

Denver Did Better With an Asset Than Charlotte With the Player

Charlotte got a young center at a first-round price, but thirty-seven NBA appearances were a limited direct result. Denver did not get a player who would become an on-court Nuggets contributor through the selection; it instead acquired a first-round right that could be moved again and eventually conveyed as a real pick. The transaction therefore favors Denver's asset management while acknowledging the modest nature of the benefit. Calling it a franchise-changing win would overstate the eventual right's importance, just as using Ajinça's later New Orleans games would flatter Charlotte. The revised grades measure each receiving team's actual opportunity and direct output.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win. Denver earns B- for converting the 2008 No. 20 selection into a protected future first that ultimately conveyed in 2010 and was transferable through other transactions. Charlotte receives C because Alexis Ajinça appeared in only thirty-seven Bobcats games over two seasons. Luke Babbitt's later Portland career was not Denver playing production, while Ajinça's subsequent NBA seasons elsewhere were not part of Charlotte's short return.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Purchased a Second-Round Prospect's Rights

The Celtics acquired the draft rights to Bill Walker from Washington on June 26, 2008, paying cash rather than exchanging a roster player or future first-round selection. Boston had just won the championship and could afford to explore a developmental wing without counting on immediate major rotation minutes. Walker had shown athletic scoring ability in college despite injury questions. The Wizards preferred a cash return to signing the player they had selected in the second round.

Walker Joined the Celtics as a Developmental Wing

Walker received some NBA opportunities with Boston, offering a look at his athleticism and perimeter potential, but he was not a driving contributor to the championship the Celtics had already won. His stay was relatively short, and he later played a larger role after changing teams. Those subsequent games should not be counted as Celtics production from the original rights purchase. The direct result for Boston was a low-cost roster prospect with some playing exposure.

Washington Received Cash Without Incoming Minutes

The Wizards took a financial return rather than acquiring a player to join their team. Cash can help a franchise manage operating choices, but it cannot be treated as a reserve scorer or defender on the court. The draft right that Washington surrendered had some potential value because Walker was able to reach the NBA, though it was not an established first-round talent. The exchange was an example of monetizing a late selection instead of dedicating a roster place to a prospect.

The Draft Cost Was Small Enough to Favor Boston

Boston obtained a player it could evaluate and eventually use in further roster decisions, while Washington settled for cash. Walker never became a central Celtics star, preventing an inflated assessment of the deal. Yet the price was modest and did not require giving up another contributor or an important selection. The inherited narrow Celtics advantage reflects securing an NBA-capable prospect at relatively little basketball cost, not an assertion that Walker carried the club through its postseason runs.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston receives B- for purchasing Bill Walker's rights and gaining a low-cost developmental wing who played limited Celtics minutes. Washington gets C for accepting cash instead of retaining the second-round prospect. Walker's more substantial later work elsewhere isn't credited to Boston, but the Celtics secured the only incoming NBA player.

perspectives.summary: Chicago obtained the draft rights to Turkish center Ömer Aşık through a June 2008 three-team agreement involving Portland and Denver. Denver received draft rights to Sonny Weems from Chicago, while the Trail Blazers acquired two Bulls future second-round rights and a 2009 Nuggets second later used on Patty Mills. Aşık later played meaningful defense for Chicago. The inherited Bulls Win grades Chicago B+ and both Denver and Portland B-.
perspectives.analysis:
Chicago Chose Aşık's Interior Defense

The Bulls acquired the draft rights to Ömer Aşık from Portland in a June 2008 multiteam draft transaction. Aşık was a Turkish center prospect with size and a defensive profile that distinguished him from the perimeter prospects involved in the deal. Chicago was willing to surrender future second-round opportunities and rights to another drafted player to obtain him. Aşık would later supply actual rebounding and rim protection for the Bulls, giving this move a direct receiving-team payoff beyond the abstract value of a draft-rights exchange.

Denver Received Sonny Weems in the Same Agreement

The Nuggets acquired the draft rights to Sonny Weems from Chicago. Weems was a young wing with athletic ability, making him a prospect Denver could evaluate as part of its broader perimeter depth. This incoming player-rights leg had been missing from the previous Bulls-focused archive, falsely presenting Denver as an empty participant. Weems's future NBA minutes are a separate measure from the simple fact of acquiring his rights. The correction also keeps Denver's outgoing future second-round selection distinct from the two selections Chicago sent to Portland.

Portland Collected Three Second-Round Rights

The Trail Blazers received second-round selections associated with No. 38 Jon Brockman in 2009 and No. 44 Jerome Jordan in 2010 from Chicago, along with a separate Denver 2009 second tied to No. 55 Patty Mills. Those links describe the draft-rights chain; they don't mean all three eventual NBA players stayed with Portland. Accurately recording the Nuggets-originated selection matters because omitting it reduces Portland's compensation and makes the transaction look like an ordinary two-team swap. All three incoming choices carried potential but required later scouting and roster decisions.

Aşık's Chicago Tenure Supports the Inherited Edge

Chicago receives B+ for obtaining Aşık, whose defensive contributions proved tangible in the Bulls' rotation. Denver and Portland each earn B- for their draft-rights packages. Weems had value as an athletic prospect, while the Blazers received several chances to draft or trade for later talent. The Bulls' grade shouldn't be based on assigning all of Aşık's later career with other franchises to Chicago, but his Bulls appearances supply more direct evidence than speculative draft outcomes. perspectives.summary: Detroit traded first-round pick No. 29 D.J. White on June 26, 2008 to Seattle in exchange for the rights to Walter Sharpe (No. 32) and Trent Plaisted (No. 46). White eventually played NBA games for the relocated Oklahoma City club, while Sharpe made just eight Detroit regular-season appearances totaling 20 minutes and Plaisted never played in the league. The original Detroit-winning verdict overstated two unused assets. Thunder Win in the franchise model, Oklahoma City B-, Detroit D+.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Converted One Late First Into Two Second-Round Chances

On June 26, 2008, the Pistons drafted Indiana forward D.J. White with the twenty-ninth overall selection and promptly traded his rights to Seattle. Their return was a pair of second-round draft rights: Walter Sharpe at No. 32 and Trent Plaisted at No. 46. Detroit was seeking two developmental possibilities rather than one late first-rounder. The trade is sometimes labeled Oklahoma City in contemporary data products because the SuperSonics relocated soon afterward. On draft night, however, Seattle still held the acquiring side, and White would enter the league as an Oklahoma City player.

White Actually Played for the Relocated Franchise

White was a productive collegiate big man at Indiana, and the Sonics' successor organization put him into NBA games after the franchise's 2008 move. He was not a superstar and did not turn this swap into one of the defining transactions of that first Oklahoma City season. But his actual regular-season availability made the No. 29 choice more than a paper asset. Subsequent games with other franchises were produced through different agreements, so they cannot be counted as if Seattle had kept him forever. The relevant comparison is the early Oklahoma City playing contribution against Detroit's two developmental selections.

Sharpe and Plaisted Offered Almost No Detroit Production

Detroit's more favorable-looking pair of draft selections never developed into equivalent NBA value. Sharpe made eight regular-season Pistons appearances, totaling twenty minutes and eight points before his NBA playing career ended. Plaisted, the other player acquired through the draft-rights exchange, never appeared in an NBA regular-season game. The two selections provided training-camp rights and the possibility of uncovering an inexpensive rotation player, yet that possibility did not materialize. Replacing a first-round pick with two near-unused second-round assets explains why the original Pistons-favored assessment required review.

A Real NBA Contributor Beats Two Unconverted Draft Rights

The choice faced the usual late-draft uncertainty: Detroit could spread its risk across two prospect evaluations, while Seattle could concentrate on the player it preferred. With hindsight, the distribution did not work for the Pistons. White supplied a genuine roster contribution in Oklahoma City, whereas one Detroit acquisition never debuted and the other appeared only eight times. Seattle's transition to Oklahoma City should be noted to prevent miscrediting games to a city that did not host the team on draft night. Those modest but measurable returns give the franchise's incoming White side the better grade.

Final Verdict

Thunder Win under the site's successor-franchise identity. The draft-night buyer was Seattle, which secured No. 29 D.J. White for the club that soon moved to Oklahoma City and earns B-. Detroit receives D+ because Walter Sharpe contributed only eight games, twenty minutes and eight points, while Trent Plaisted never played an NBA regular-season game. Two acquired draft-rights slots did not outweigh the first-round choice sent away.

new-orleans-pelicans.summary: On June 26, 2008, the New Orleans Hornets sold the rights to No. 27 Darrell Arthur to Portland for cash. Portland immediately used those rights in a three-team exchange involving Houston and Memphis to acquire Nicolas Batum's rights, with additional players and picks changing hands. Arthur played his NBA career for other franchises rather than Portland. The Blazers benefited from the transferable draft rights but the Batum result cannot be attributed solely to this cash purchase. Blazers Win, Portland B+, New Orleans C.
new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
New Orleans Sold the Twenty-Seventh Pick for Cash

The New Orleans Hornets used the twenty-seventh selection of the 2008 NBA draft on Kansas forward Darrell Arthur but did not plan to keep his rights. On June 26, New Orleans sold that draft asset to the Portland Trail Blazers for cash. The sale offered immediate financial value rather than a prospect the Hornets would develop, and it did not transfer an existing roster player in the ordinary sense. New Orleans's use of the selection happened as the franchise was coming off a strong Western Conference season. The current database calls the club the Pelicans, although the 2008 transaction belonged to the Hornets.

Portland Immediately Moved Arthur's Rights Again

Arthur's rights did not stay in Portland long enough to become an NBA playing contribution. On the same draft night, Portland joined a three-team agreement involving Houston and Memphis. The Blazers sent Arthur's rights to the Grizzlies and Joey Dorsey's rights to the Rockets, while Houston sent the rights to Nicolas Batum to Portland. Memphis supplied other draft rights and a future second to Houston as part of the larger transaction. The chain matters because Arthur was not literally traded for Batum in a standalone two-team agreement. Portland needed the multi-party structure and other assets to end up with the player it wanted.

Neither Original Buyer nor Seller Got Arthur's Playing Minutes

Arthur went on to a substantial NBA career, principally with Memphis and Denver. He did not provide regular-season games for either the Trail Blazers or the Hornets through this first rights sale. New Orleans instead realized financial consideration; the amount should not be invented in the absence of a verified figure. Portland's reward was the ability to deploy a draft-rights asset immediately toward another prospect. Batum later became an important Portland wing, but that fact is a downstream result of a different transaction containing multiple additional pieces, not a direct player transfer from New Orleans in the cash sale.

The Draft Rights Had More Utility for the Buyer

New Orleans obtained cash for a pick it had chosen to monetize rather than retain, making its return real but limited. Portland received draft rights that could immediately be used in a more ambitious exchange, helping the club reorganize its draft-night portfolio. Giving Portland every minute Batum eventually played without accounting for the three-team deal would overstate this original purchase. Giving New Orleans an automatic failure because it received no roster player would ignore the purpose of the cash sale. The Blazers nonetheless hold the stronger asset-utility result, justifying an advantage grounded in the short draft-night chain rather than imagined Arthur appearances.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win. Portland earns B+ because the Darrell Arthur rights purchased from New Orleans became one useful component of its same-night multi-team deal that delivered Nicolas Batum's rights. The New Orleans Hornets receive C for cash consideration with no incoming player. Arthur never supplied games to either original participant. Batum's subsequent NBA contribution belonged to Portland's distinct three-team agreement and cannot be credited solely to the cash sale.

The Blazers sent Arthur's rights to the Grizzlies and Joey Dorsey's rights to the Rockets, while Houston sent the rights to Nicolas Batum to Portland. Memphis supplied other draft rights and a future second to Houston as part of the larger transaction. The chain matters because Arthur was not literally traded for Batum in a standalone two-team agreement. Portland needed the multi-party structure and other assets to end up with the player it wanted.

Neither Original Buyer nor Seller Got Arthur's Playing Minutes

Arthur went on to a substantial NBA career, principally with Memphis and Denver. He did not provide regular-season games for either the Trail Blazers or the Hornets through this first rights sale. New Orleans instead realized financial consideration; the amount should not be invented in the absence of a verified figure. Portland's reward was the ability to deploy a draft-rights asset immediately toward another prospect. Batum later became an important Portland wing, but that fact is a downstream result of a different transaction containing multiple additional pieces, not a direct player transfer from New Orleans in the cash sale.

The Draft Rights Had More Utility for the Buyer

New Orleans obtained cash for a pick it had chosen to monetize rather than retain, making its return real but limited. Portland received draft rights that could immediately be used in a more ambitious exchange, helping the club reorganize its draft-night portfolio. Giving Portland every minute Batum eventually played without accounting for the three-team deal would overstate this original purchase. Giving New Orleans an automatic failure because it received no roster player would ignore the purpose of the cash sale. The Blazers nonetheless hold the stronger asset-utility result, justifying an advantage grounded in the short draft-night chain rather than imagined Arthur appearances.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win. Portland earns B+ because the Darrell Arthur rights purchased from New Orleans became one useful component of its same-night multi-team deal that delivered Nicolas Batum's rights. The New Orleans Hornets receive C for cash consideration with no incoming player. Arthur never supplied games to either original participant. Batum's subsequent NBA contribution belonged to Portland's distinct three-team agreement and cannot be credited solely to the cash sale.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston traded Steve Novak to the Clippers on August 6, 2008 for the right to swap 2011 second-round selections. The resulting exchange placed No. 38 Chandler Parsons with Houston and No. 47 Travis Leslie with Los Angeles, per Pro Sports Transactions and ShamSports; Basketball-Reference conflictingly labels it 'not exercised.' Parsons became a multi-season Rockets starter after a separate draft-night rights transfer via Minnesota. Novak played 125 Clippers regular-season games in two years. Rockets Win, Houston A-, Clippers B.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Moved Novak for a Right to Exchange Future Draft Slots

The Rockets traded reserve three-point shooter Steve Novak to the Los Angeles Clippers on August 6, 2008. In exchange, Houston obtained the right to swap second-round selections in the 2011 NBA draft. This was not an immediate player-for-player transaction; the Clippers got a known shooting specialist while the Rockets acquired a potentially more favorable future draft position. The arrangement has a notable source conflict: Basketball-Reference's summary says the swap was not exercised, while detailed draft-pick ledgers and ShamSports trace the exercised rights to specific 2011 selections.

The 2011 Pick Ledger Shows No. 38 Reaching Houston

Pro Sports Transactions records the Clippers' No. 38 choice, used on Chandler Parsons, as transferred to Houston through the 2008 option. Houston's No. 47 pick, used on Travis Leslie, moved to the Clippers side. A separate 2011 draft-night transaction briefly routed Parsons's rights through Minnesota before Houston bought them back for cash, so it would be wrong to treat the player's entire subsequent Rockets career as a straight uninterrupted transfer from Los Angeles. The origin of the advantageous No. 38 draft position, however, is traced to the Novak exchange.

Parsons Became an Everyday Rockets Forward

Parsons reached Houston's rotation as a rookie in 2011-12 and played sixty-three games. He followed with seventy-six regular-season appearances in 2012-13 and seventy-four in 2013-14, a total of 213 Rockets games over three seasons. His offense, rebounding and outside shooting became central to the club's lineups before he left for Dallas. The intermediate Minnesota cash transaction must be recognized when assigning causation, but the swap's improved draft position was a necessary part of the selection path. The Rockets ultimately extracted far more on-court utility from their later choice than a generic unexercised-option label suggests.

Novak Also Played a Useful Two-Year Clippers Role

Los Angeles wasn't empty-handed. Novak appeared in seventy-one Clippers games during 2008-09, starting three and logging 1,161 minutes while shooting 41.6 percent from beyond the arc. He returned for fifty-four more games in 2009-10 and 362 additional minutes. His 125 total Clippers appearances offered genuine perimeter spacing, especially in the first season. The No. 47 selection was a separate future asset, but Leslie did not become a comparably productive NBA player. Houston benefited more in the long term through the higher pick, while the Clippers acquired real near-term shooting depth.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win. Houston earns A- for obtaining the improved No. 38 draft slot later used on Chandler Parsons, a 213-game Rockets contributor after an additional Minnesota rights transaction. Los Angeles gets B because Steve Novak supplied 125 games and 1,523 minutes. Detailed 2011 pick ledgers show the swap was exercised despite Basketball-Reference's conflicting abbreviated label, which should not be silently repeated.

The resulting exchange placed No. 38 Chandler Parsons with Houston and No. 47 Travis Leslie with Los Angeles, per Pro Sports Transactions and ShamSports; Basketball-Reference conflictingly labels it 'not exercised.' Parsons became a multi-season Rockets starter after a separate draft-night rights transfer via Minnesota. Novak played 125 Clippers regular-season games in two years. Rockets Win, Houston A-, Clippers B.
analysis:
Houston Moved Novak for a Right to Exchange Future Draft Slots

The Rockets traded reserve three-point shooter Steve Novak to the Los Angeles Clippers on August 6, 2008. In exchange, Houston obtained the right to swap second-round selections in the 2011 NBA draft. This was not an immediate player-for-player transaction; the Clippers got a known shooting specialist while the Rockets acquired a potentially more favorable future draft position. The arrangement has a notable source conflict: Basketball-Reference's summary says the swap was not exercised, while detailed draft-pick ledgers and ShamSports trace the exercised rights to specific 2011 selections.

The 2011 Pick Ledger Shows No. 38 Reaching Houston

Pro Sports Transactions records the Clippers' No. 38 choice, used on Chandler Parsons, as transferred to Houston through the 2008 option. Houston's No. 47 pick, used on Travis Leslie, moved to the Clippers side. A separate 2011 draft-night transaction briefly routed Parsons's rights through Minnesota before Houston bought them back for cash, so it would be wrong to treat the player's entire subsequent Rockets career as a straight uninterrupted transfer from Los Angeles. The origin of the advantageous No. 38 draft position, however, is traced to the Novak exchange.

Parsons Became an Everyday Rockets Forward

Parsons reached Houston's rotation as a rookie in 2011-12 and played sixty-three games. He followed with seventy-six regular-season appearances in 2012-13 and seventy-four in 2013-14, a total of 213 Rockets games over three seasons. His offense, rebounding and outside shooting became central to the club's lineups before he left for Dallas. The intermediate Minnesota cash transaction must be recognized when assigning causation, but the swap's improved draft position was a necessary part of the selection path. The Rockets ultimately extracted far more on-court utility from their later choice than a generic unexercised-option label suggests.

Novak Also Played a Useful Two-Year Clippers Role

Los Angeles wasn't empty-handed. Novak appeared in seventy-one Clippers games during 2008-09, starting three and logging 1,161 minutes while shooting 41.6 percent from beyond the arc. He returned for fifty-four more games in 2009-10 and 362 additional minutes. His 125 total Clippers appearances offered genuine perimeter spacing, especially in the first season. The No. 47 selection was a separate future asset, but Leslie did not become a comparably productive NBA player. Houston benefited more in the long term through the higher pick, while the Clippers acquired real near-term shooting depth.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win. Houston earns A- for obtaining the improved No. 38 draft slot later used on Chandler Parsons, a 213-game Rockets contributor after an additional Minnesota rights transaction. Los Angeles gets B because Steve Novak supplied 125 games and 1,523 minutes. Detailed 2011 pick ledgers show the swap was exercised despite Basketball-Reference's conflicting abbreviated label, which should not be silently repeated.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Mo Williams from Milwaukee in an August 2008 multi-team trade, with Milwaukee receiving Damon Jones and the Seattle SuperSonics franchise gaining Joe Smith. Williams became an NBA All-Star playing alongside LeBron James and supplied sustained Cavaliers backcourt scoring. The inherited Cavaliers Win grades Cleveland A, Milwaukee D and the Seattle/Oklahoma City franchise D.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Targeted a Scoring Partner for James

The Cavaliers acquired Mo Williams from the Bucks in August 2008 in a transaction also involving the Seattle franchise's transition to Oklahoma City. Milwaukee received Damon Jones, while the third participant obtained Joe Smith. Cleveland wanted more reliable perimeter creation alongside LeBron James and preferred a guard already capable of scoring in the NBA. The trade was built around immediate basketball fit rather than the prospect of waiting for a late draft selection to develop.

Williams Became a Major Cavaliers Contributor

Williams provided Cleveland with shooting and playmaking that complemented James's ability to attack defenses. His performance during the 2008-09 season earned an All-Star selection and helped support one of the league's strongest regular-season teams. Those Cavaliers minutes and honors are direct receiving-team evidence, making this trade easier to evaluate than an exchange in which the incoming prospect never played. Williams was not solely responsible for Cleveland's success, but his arrival improved the offense in a visible way.

The Bucks and Third Team Took Smaller Returns

Milwaukee acquired Jones, an experienced outside-shooting guard whose role was not a replacement for Williams's broader creation abilities. Joe Smith joined the franchise now identified with Oklahoma City, providing veteran frontcourt possibilities without delivering the same lasting contribution as Williams did for Cleveland. The deal happened during a relocation period, so historical references to Seattle and the Thunder can appear in descriptions of the same organization. Their incoming packages had narrower direct competitive impact.

The Cavaliers Received the Clearest Immediate Upgrade

The inherited Cleveland A rewards a productive All-Star season and tangible backcourt chemistry with James. Milwaukee and the Oklahoma City franchise each receive D for less consequential direct returns. Williams's actual Cleveland success is more informative than a hypothetical case that one of the outgoing veterans might have had a similar offensive role. The Cavaliers traded to help a contender immediately and secured a player who fit that goal.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns A for Mo Williams, whose scoring and 2009 All-Star selection supplied a valuable backcourt complement to LeBron James. Milwaukee receives D for Damon Jones, and the Seattle/Oklahoma City franchise receives D for Joe Smith. The Cavs obtained the only standout long-term receiving-team contribution among the incoming players.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston sent the rights to Patrick Ewing Jr. to New York on August 29, 2008, receiving the long-held draft rights to French center Frédéric Weis. The Knicks released Ewing Jr. after preseason competition without a regular-season Knicks appearance; Weis never played in the NBA for Houston. Ewing Jr. subsequently debuted in the league with New Orleans in 2011. Even Trade, D+ each, overturning the unsupported Knicks A grade.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Knicks Acquired an NBA Prospect With a Famous Surname

New York received Patrick Ewing Jr. from Houston on August 29, 2008, in exchange for the rights to French center Frédéric Weis. Ewing Jr., whose father was the Knicks' Hall of Fame center, had been drafted earlier that summer and passed through Houston in a separate trade. New York had retained Weis's rights since taking him in the first round in 1999, but he had never signed an NBA contract. This deal swapped two very different prospects whose financial and roster situations were far removed from their original draft-night expectations.

Ewing Jr. Played in the Knicks Preseason but Never the Regular Season

Ewing Jr. took part in New York's 2008 preseason competition and attracted interest as a developmental forward. The Knicks nevertheless waived him before the regular season. His name and connection to Madison Square Garden were not a substitute for an NBA roster role, and his subsequent NBA appearances came with the New Orleans Hornets in 2011. An official Hornets announcement recounts the Knicks preseason and subsequent waiver. The Knicks therefore received no regular-season games, points or rebounds from the player acquired in this particular transaction.

Weis Remained an International Rights Holder's Asset

Weis had been the nineteenth overall selection in the 1999 NBA draft and continued his career overseas rather than joining the Knicks. Houston obtained his rights in 2008, but he never played an NBA game for the Rockets either. The rights might theoretically have been exchanged again, although no incoming Rockets rotation player is established by this deal alone. Weis's European basketball accomplishments should not be attributed to Houston's NBA record. This was an asset exchange with little realized basketball output for either franchise, not a route to a new starting center.

The Former Knicks-Favored Grade Was Built on Potential, Not Games

The inherited verdict awarded New York an A despite the absence of regular-season appearances by Ewing Jr. and almost no direct evidence of value returned through the exchange. Houston did not receive NBA production from Weis, either. Ewing Jr. and Weis had distinct reasons to be considered developmental or international assets, but the historical scoring of a trade should start with what the acquiring teams actually received. New York's preseason tryout and Houston's unexercised draft rights leave neither side with a persuasive sporting advantage. Modest equal grades avoid overstating an unusual transaction.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Houston receives D+ for holding Frédéric Weis's draft rights without an NBA appearance, and New York also receives D+ because Patrick Ewing Jr. was waived before the Knicks regular season. His eventual Hornets games in 2011 are not New York production. Neither return supports the previously recorded Knicks A assessment.

houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Sent a Former All-Star and Returned a Memphis Draft Pick

In December 2008, Houston traded Steve Francis, cash and a 2009 second-round choice back to the Memphis Grizzlies for a conditional 2011 second-round selection. Memphis's official announcement describes the 2009 selection as its own pick, which Houston had acquired through an earlier draft-night transaction. Francis had once been drafted by Vancouver but had never played for the Grizzlies franchise. By 2008 injuries had curtailed his career, so the central basketball asset in this package was the future draft selection rather than his famous name.

The Grizzlies Used the Pick on Sam Young

Memphis selected Pittsburgh forward Sam Young at No. 36 in the 2009 NBA draft. He played eighty regular-season games as a rookie and scored 595 points in 1,321 minutes. In 2010-11 Young appeared seventy-eight more times, started forty-six contests and contributed 572 points in 1,577 minutes. He added twenty-one Memphis games in the shortened 2011-12 season before leaving for Philadelphia. Those 179 regular-season appearances were real value from the reacquired second-rounder. His subsequent Sixers career should not be included in Memphis's return.

Francis Never Played, and Houston's Conditional Return Expired

The Grizzlies' January 2009 release announcement confirms that Francis was waived without making a Memphis appearance. The veteran's earlier Houston, Orlando and New York playing totals therefore offer no additional value to this deal. Houston's return also failed to generate an active asset. The protected 2011 second-round choice did not convey, as the franchise transaction register explicitly notes. It would be wrong to assign any 2011 draftee to the Rockets through this agreement. Houston had moved cash and a genuine eventual NBA player for a contingent right that expired.

A Long-Lived Second-Round Reserve Created the Difference

The Grizzlies did not acquire productive Steve Francis minutes, and the deal was not a veteran revival. Its success instead came from recovering a second-round position and using it on a forward who contributed over multiple seasons. Houston might have benefited from removing Francis's remaining roster obligation, but the specific compensation received never became a pick or player. The on-court contrast is stark: Young accumulated extensive Memphis minutes, while the Rockets recorded no NBA production from the incoming conditional second. That supports Memphis's favorable historical grade.

Final Verdict

Grizzlies Win. Memphis earns A- because the reacquired 2009 No. 36 selection became Sam Young, who played 179 Grizzlies games and started 46 in 2010-11. Steve Francis was waived without playing. Houston gets D because the conditional 2011 second-round pick never conveyed despite sending cash and the productive future draft asset.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Los Angeles Clippers acquired Hassan Adams from Toronto on January 1, 2009, sending cash and a conditional 2015 second-round pick that never conveyed. Adams was waived January 7 without appearing in a Clippers NBA game. The imported January 7 identifier reflects the waiver date, not the transaction date. Raptors Win, Toronto C+ for the cash return and Los Angeles D+ for an unused player contract.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Sent Toronto Cash for a Wing Audition

The actual trade took place on January 1, 2009, when the Clippers acquired Hassan Adams from the Raptors. Los Angeles sent cash and a conditional 2015 second-round choice to Toronto. The later January 7 date in the imported trade identifier is the date Adams was waived, not when the clubs agreed to the exchange. Both franchises' seasonal transaction histories clarify that distinction. Adams had been a second-round pick in 2006 and offered a low-cost possibility for wing depth, but the opportunity did not last a week.

Adams Never Appeared in a Clippers Regular-Season Game

Adams was released by Los Angeles on January 7, before he could take the floor in a Clippers regular-season contest. His earlier NBA appearances were with New Jersey and Toronto, and no portion of those statistics can be credited to the receiving Los Angeles team. This trade therefore delivered no player minutes, points or rebounds to the Clippers. That outcome is different from acquiring a reserve who spends even a few games on the active roster. Los Angeles paid to examine a player whose opportunity ended almost immediately.

The Conditional 2015 Draft Pick Did Not Transfer

The agreement also listed a 2015 second-round pick with restrictive protections, described in the archived record as top-50 and No. 56–60 protected. The selection was not exercised. Toronto accordingly did not receive a draftee from that obligation, and the trade must not be traced to an unrelated 2015 second-round player. Toronto's tangible documented compensation was the cash the Clippers paid, not a pick it later deployed. This was the source of an additional imported-data problem: an earlier version of the trade incorrectly showed the cash going from Toronto to Los Angeles.

Correcting the Cash Direction Changes the Evaluation

Once the assets are placed with the proper receiving teams, the retrospective is straightforward. Toronto moved a player it was not using and received money. Los Angeles obtained no regular-season production from Adams and did not retain him through the next week, while the potential future pick never conveyed. The Raptors did not obtain a transformative basketball asset, so their positive grade should remain restrained. The Clippers' loss was a small failed audition rather than a devastating roster move. Preserving the existing private slug avoids creating a duplicate route while accurately reporting the January 1 trade date.

Final Verdict

Raptors Win. Toronto earns C+ because it received cash when Hassan Adams was sent to Los Angeles on January 1, 2009. The conditional 2015 second-round selection never conveyed. The Clippers earn D+ because Adams was waived January 7 without playing a single Clippers regular-season game. The legacy January 7 slug records the waiver, not the actual trade date.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Moved a Veteran Guard and Cash

The Celtics sent Sam Cassell and cash to the Sacramento Kings in February 2009 in exchange for a conditional second-round right in 2015. Cassell had been part of Boston's 2008 championship roster, but the club was no longer counting on him for a major playing role in the following season. Sacramento accepted the contract and financial consideration while maintaining its own rebuilding options. The distant conditional pick was not expected to replace Cassell with an immediate contributor.

Sacramento Did Not Use Cassell as a Rotation Player

Cassell did not establish a Kings playing stint after the transaction; Sacramento waived the veteran rather than asking him to organize its backcourt. His earlier All-Star-level career and Celtics championship membership could not be counted as playing value for the Kings. The practical benefit for Sacramento was the financial side of the arrangement and the ability to move on without keeping him long term. The exchange functioned as a roster and contract decision, not a trade to acquire a new on-court leader.

The Conditional Pick Never Became a Celtics Draftee

Boston obtained a 2015 second-round right that was never exercised under its protection terms. No drafted player or subsequent NBA production should be attributed to that pick. The Celtics' immediate benefit instead came from removing a contract and creating flexibility for other roster decisions. The transaction was small relative to Boston's larger championship-era activity, but that does not justify inflating its impact. It supplied roster management rather than a measurable new player contribution.

A Slight Edge Reflects Different Administrative Benefits

The Kings received cash while Boston cleared a player it wasn't using and held a possible future pick. Neither club gained a substantial incoming performer, and the condition prevented the selection from becoming a completed draft asset. The inherited narrow Celtics advantage recognizes the modest flexibility gained in a constrained roster, without asserting that Sacramento suffered a major basketball loss. Both teams treated the arrangement as an administrative step rather than a significant rebuilding exchange.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston gets C+ for gaining roster flexibility and a conditional 2015 second-round right, although that pick never conveyed. Sacramento receives C for taking Sam Cassell and cash without establishing him in its rotation. Neither team acquired durable playing production from the deal, so the advantage was modest and primarily administrative.

The 2014 second-round selection recorded as Boston's incoming asset was never exercised. That distinction is important: the Celtics did not receive a new drafted player through this particular conditional right. The trade could still serve roster and financial aims, but the basketball payoff from a nonconveyed selection was not equivalent to a successful draft prospect. Describing the transaction as Boston acquiring an immediate productive reserve would misrepresent the canonical asset direction.

Sacramento obtained cash, a finite return that can support financial management without itself providing minutes on the court. Toronto received O'Bryant's development opportunity, though the center's prior NBA appearances didn't become Raptors production retroactively. Neither club gave up a proven new All-Star to accomplish these objectives. The deal's modest scale and contractual context help explain why the actual return was less exciting than transactions involving immediate starters.

The original grading favors the club's ability to rearrange roster obligations and retain contingent flexibility. Toronto chose a center evaluation, while Sacramento took cash. None of the three returns supports a major championship-credit narrative.

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B under the inherited grading for conditional draft and roster flexibility, although its 2014 second-round right did not convey. perspectives.summary: On June 24, 2009, Dallas sent pick No. 22 (Victor Claver) to Portland for pick No. 24 (B.J. Mullens), pick No. 56 (Ahmad Nivins) and a 2010 second-rounder (No. 51, Magnum Rolle). Dallas immediately traded Mullens to Oklahoma City for the rights to Rodrigue Beaubois and an additional 2010 second; Beaubois played 182 games for Dallas. Portland eventually received 80 games from Claver. Mavericks Win, Dallas B, Portland C+.
perspectives.analysis:
Dallas Moved Down Two First-Round Slots and Added Two Seconds

On June 24, 2009, the Mavericks traded the No. 22 draft position to Portland, receiving No. 24, No. 56 and a future second-rounder. Portland used No. 22 on Spanish forward Victor Claver; Dallas initially took B.J. Mullens at No. 24 and Ahmad Nivins at No. 56. The additional 2010 second-round selection eventually landed at No. 51, where Magnum Rolle was selected after the choice moved again. This was not initially a straight Claver-for-Beaubois deal. The draft ledger shows a sequence of rights and picks that Dallas converted into other assets within the following day.

Dallas Quickly Turned the Mullens Pick Into Beaubois

The day after the Portland swap, Dallas sent Mullens's draft rights to Oklahoma City in exchange for the rights to Rodrigue Beaubois at No. 25 and another future second-rounder. Beaubois ultimately played four NBA seasons for the Mavericks, totaling 182 regular-season appearances, 54 starts and 1,286 points. He wasn't a long-term franchise answer, but he was a genuine NBA contributor acquired through a traceable second transaction involving the pick Portland had sent Dallas. The distinction matters: Beaubois was not part of the original Portland package, but Dallas's ability to redeploy that package made him part of the downstream value.

The Other Selections Were Real Rights, Not Automatic Production

Dallas also secured No. 56 in 2009, used on Ahmad Nivins, whose career did not produce a Mavericks regular-season appearance. The additional 2010 second was traded to Minnesota on June 25, 2009 for the draft rights to Nick Calathes. That later transfer means Dallas never used that specific second-rounder to select Magnum Rolle; it merely owned the pick for part of its chain. Beaubois provided the team's most tangible return from the sequence, while the Nivins and Calathes rights did not provide comparable on-court minutes for the Mavericks. Counting all the eventual draftees as Dallas players would overstate the transaction.

Claver Played in Portland, but Less Than Beaubois in Dallas

Portland kept Claver's rights and brought him to the NBA for the 2012-13 season. Over three Trail Blazers seasons he played 80 regular-season games with 16 starts and scored 258 points. That was a legitimate reserve return from pick No. 22, although his North American role remained smaller than the team's draft investment might have suggested. Dallas had turned the downtrade into Beaubois's 182 games and additional developmental rights. It would be wrong to credit those 182 games solely to Portland because Oklahoma City was essential to the intermediate exchange. Still, tracing the pick's actual movement explains why the Mavericks' original downtrade created more realized on-court value than Portland's selection.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win. Dallas earns B because the Portland-supplied No. 24 pick helped obtain Rodrigue Beaubois, who played 182 Mavericks games, plus extra draft rights. Portland gets C+ for 80 games from Victor Claver. Dallas needed a separate Oklahoma City trade to reach Beaubois, so the verdict credits the asset chain rather than falsely listing him as a direct Portland acquisition.

minnesota-timberwolves.summary: Minnesota acquired the No. 5 pick used on Ricky Rubio plus three veterans from Washington for Randy Foye and Mike Miller.
minnesota-timberwolves.analysis: The 2009 Washington trade gave Minnesota the premium asset in the deal: the No. 5 pick used on Ricky Rubio. Rubio's delayed arrival complicated the timeline, but once he joined the Wolves he became a long-term starting point guard, elite passer and important defensive organizer. Randy Foye and Mike Miller were established NBA players and gave Washington immediate competence, so this was not a cost-free win. The difference is that neither became a franchise-level building block for the Wizards, while Rubio supplied Minnesota with years of distinctive on-court value and eventually retained trade value of his own. The A- grade reflects that meaningful long-term advantage while accounting for the uncertainty and patience required to realize it.

analysis: The Wizards traded a premium lottery pick to accelerate around Gilbert Arenas, Antawn Jamison and Caron Butler, but injuries and dysfunction destroyed the win-now plan. Foye and Miller were gone after one season. Minnesota had to wait two years for Rubio to arrive from Spain, yet received years of elite passing, disruptive defense and credible starting play. The Wolves did not maximize the broader 2009 draft, but that separate criticism does not erase the value secured in this transaction. Minnesota wins, and Washington’s F reflects that the incoming veterans did not justify surrendering No. 5.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Hawks Win. Atlanta Hawks earns A; Golden State Warriors earns B-. The Hawks obtained the strongest continuing basketball contributor in Crawford, whose on-court role was measurable
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Acquired Jamal Crawford for Law and Claxton

On June 25, 2009, Atlanta traded guard Acie Law and veteran Speedy Claxton to Golden State in exchange for Jamal Crawford. The Hawks obtained a proven NBA perimeter scorer with several seasons of experience, while the Warriors accepted two guards on different career trajectories. The agreement was a direct player exchange, not an additional lottery selection or conditional first. Crawford could provide Atlanta with offense from a reserve role without immediately replacing every member of its starting backcourt. Golden State pursued roster flexibility and opportunities for the incoming guards, rather than keeping Crawford's existing scoring contract.

Crawford Became an Important Atlanta Bench Scorer

Crawford's subsequent Hawks seasons provided the strongest identifiable return of the transaction. His scoring ability and ball handling translated into a productive supporting role, including major recognition for his performance off the bench. That was actual receiving-team basketball value rather than a projection built entirely on his earlier years elsewhere. The Hawks didn't need to claim that Crawford alone created their playoff progress; their starting core contributed heavily as well. But adding a reliable second-unit offensive creator in exchange for expendable guard depth was a tangible personnel improvement that can be traced directly to this deal.

Golden State Took Back Two Less Proven Alternatives

Acie Law arrived still searching for a stable NBA guard role, while Claxton's injury and late-career circumstances limited the certainty of his immediate usefulness. Neither should be credited with Crawford's prior scoring just because Golden State surrendered him. The Warriors may have valued contract and roster options, but they did not receive a player who matched Crawford's later Atlanta bench production. Law's potential could be assessed in a new environment, though a second attempt at development wasn't guaranteed to work. The return was therefore more speculative and less immediately productive than the Hawks' established scorer.

Atlanta Won on Clear Receiving-Team Production

The Hawks obtained the strongest continuing basketball contributor in Crawford, whose on-court role was measurable in Atlanta rather than relying on another club's statistics. Golden State received two legitimate contract assets but lacked comparable sustained court results from the exchange. That supports a decisive Hawks-winning verdict without pretending Claxton and Law were valueless at the transaction date. The agreement wasn't a complicated draft-rights chain, making the retrospective relatively straightforward. Its value lies in the distinction between a proven offensive reserve and two players whose subsequent fit remained much less certain.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta Hawks earns A; Golden State Warriors earns B-. houston-rockets.summary: On July 14, 2009, Atlanta traded David Andersen's NBA draft rights to Houston for cash, future considerations and a conditional second-round choice eventually used at No. 50 in 2013 on James Ennis III. Andersen signed with Houston and played 63 games in 2009-10, totaling 367 points and 891 minutes. Atlanta later traded the No. 50 rights to Miami for another future selection instead of retaining Ennis as an NBA regular. Rockets Win, Houston B for immediate actual production, Atlanta B- for monetizing unused international draft rights.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Acquired International Draft Rights Instead of a Signed NBA Player

The Rockets arranged a July 14, 2009 agreement with Atlanta for the NBA rights to Australian forward-center David Andersen. Atlanta had originally drafted him in 2002, but he had spent the intervening seasons with successful professional clubs in Europe. Houston paid cash, future considerations and a future conditional second-round draft selection to bring those rights under its control. Atlanta's own official announcement identifies all three components of the return. With Yao Ming unavailable during the 2009-10 season, Houston was searching for size and shooting from other sources. The trade offered a possible immediate rotation player rather than simply a speculative overseas prospect.

Andersen Converted His Rights Into Sixty-Three Houston Games

Houston signed Andersen after obtaining his rights, and he appeared in sixty-three regular-season Rockets games in 2009-10. He played 891 minutes, scored 367 points and contributed 208 rebounds, coming off the bench every time. His average of 5.8 points and 3.3 rebounds shows useful reserve depth rather than a star-level replacement for an injured center. Even at that level, the return was concrete NBA production from rights that had not been exercised by Atlanta for years. Andersen later played for Toronto and New Orleans in different transactions, and those appearances should not be assigned to Houston's direct acquisition.

Atlanta's Pick Became Ennis Rights and Was Moved Again

The conditional second-round selection eventually conveyed in 2013 at No. 50, a pick associated with James Ennis III. The Hawks did not receive Ennis's subsequent NBA minutes from this 2009 transaction. Their 2013 draft-night activity sent his rights to the Miami Heat for another future second-round selection. Miami publicly announced that acquisition, confirming the pick was a transferable asset rather than a player Atlanta retained. The additional 2009 cash and future consideration helped make the deal useful to the Hawks even without an immediate NBA player. Still, the later Miami outcome requires recognition as a separate trade with its own compensation.

On-Court Use Gives Houston the Narrower but Clearer Victory

Houston obtained an experienced international big man who played most of a season, while Atlanta converted previously dormant rights into cash and a pick it could move. Neither team suffered an overwhelming loss, so the inherited failing grade for Houston exaggerates the cost and ignores the direct contribution. Andersen's sixty-three appearances are a stronger immediate basketball return than assigning Atlanta Ennis's eventual career would allow. At the same time, the Hawks received valid financial and draft value and deserve more than a token grade. The better retrospective is a Houston advantage based on realized playing time without misattributing another team's later draft development.

Final Verdict

Rockets Win. Houston receives B because David Andersen delivered sixty-three Rockets games, 891 minutes and 367 points after his rights arrived in July 2009. Atlanta earns B- for cash, future considerations and the conditional second-round pick later identified as 2013 No. 50 James Ennis III. The Hawks sold Ennis's rights to Miami through a subsequent trade, so Ennis's later NBA games cannot be claimed as Atlanta production.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Memphis acquired Zach Randolph from the Clippers for Quentin Richardson, turning a distressed veteran contract into the two-time All-Star and cultural centerpiece of the Grit-and-Grind era.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis: Randolph averaged 20.8 points and 11.7 rebounds in his first Memphis season, earned two All-Star selections with the franchise and powered the 2011 upset of top-seeded San Antonio for the Grizzlies first playoff-series victory. Richardson was quickly rerouted, and Los Angeles realized little direct incoming value, although moving Randolph created frontcourt and financial room around No. 1 pick Blake Griffin. That reset logic supports a C rather than a failing grade for the Clippers, while Randolphs eight-year franchise impact warrants A+ and a clear Grizzlies Win.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers sent Quentin Richardson to Minnesota on July 20, 2009, receiving Craig Smith, Sebastian Telfair and Mark Madsen. Smith played 75 Clippers games in 2009-10, averaging 7.8 points and 3.8 rebounds; Telfair played 39 games, averaging 4.3 points and 2.9 assists, before another trade. Madsen was waived in August. Richardson played no Timberwolves regular-season game and was flipped to Miami for Mark Blount. Clippers Win, Los Angeles A-, Minnesota C+.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Quickly Recycled Quentin Richardson Into Three Players

Los Angeles acquired Quentin Richardson in a separate Zach Randolph trade and moved him again on July 20, 2009, receiving Craig Smith, Sebastian Telfair and Mark Madsen from Minnesota. Richardson had not become a regular-season Clipper. The team preferred inexpensive frontcourt and guard cover over carrying another established wing. Minnesota accepted Richardson as a transferable veteran contract while reorganizing its own roster. This was a three-for-one agreement with no immediate new draft pick, but the individual playing returns ended up very different.

Craig Smith Gave Los Angeles Seventy-Five Productive Games

Smith appeared in 75 Clippers regular-season games during 2009-10, starting twice and averaging 7.8 points with 3.8 rebounds. His 16.4 minutes per appearance supplied dependable scoring around the basket for a team with several young interior players. Telfair also played 39 Clippers games, including one start, averaging 4.3 points and 2.9 assists in 14.9 minutes. He eventually moved to Cleveland during a separate February transaction. Their subsequent contributions for other organizations do not belong to this Los Angeles trade, but the Clippers already received a useful collection of bench appearances.

Madsen Was Waived, and Richardson Never Played for Minnesota

The third incoming Clipper, Madsen, was waived August 21 before the season. Minnesota did not keep Richardson long enough to receive league minutes from him either. On August 13, it traded the forward to Miami in return for Mark Blount, an agreement confirmed by the Heat's contemporaneous announcement. Blount's contract was a financial and roster-management asset, but his earlier Miami statistics are not Timberwolves basketball production. Richardson's 2009-10 appearances were made with the Heat, so they cannot be assigned to Minnesota merely because it briefly held his contract.

Los Angeles Received Actual Minutes While Minnesota Continued Rearranging Contracts

The Clippers clearly benefited from securing two players who could participate in their rotation, even though a third incoming veteran was released before opening night. Minnesota viewed Richardson as a short-term contract asset and converted him into another veteran's contract within weeks. That onward transaction was real rather than a total loss, but it did not result in the immediate playing contributions Los Angeles obtained from Smith and Telfair. The inherited Clippers-favored winner remains appropriate. Its advantage rests on the 114 combined Clippers appearances, not Richardson's later Miami performances or an imagined Minnesota season.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win. Los Angeles retains A- after Craig Smith supplied 75 games and 7.8 points per game, while Sebastian Telfair added 39 games and useful reserve ball handling. Minnesota receives C+ for using Quentin Richardson's contract in the later Mark Blount transaction, but Richardson played zero Timberwolves regular-season games. Mark Madsen was waived before contributing for Los Angeles.

perspectives.analysis: New Orleans Hornets realized more from Emeka Okafor than Charlotte did from Tyson Chandler. The result supports a slight partner edge at this tier.

perspectives.summary: New Orleans acquired Emeka Okafor from Charlotte Hornets franchise for Tyson Chandler.
perspectives.analysis: New Orleans comes out slightly ahead in the Emeka Okafor-for-Tyson Chandler trade when the transaction is judged by what each franchise directly realized. Okafor gave the Hornets three seasons of durable starting-center production and helped stabilize the frontcourt. Charlotte received Chandler, but injuries limited his lone Bobcats season and the franchise moved him again the next summer for a weak return. Chandler later became a championship anchor in Dallas, but that value was created after a separate Charlotte transaction rather than captured by the Bobcats themselves. The direct New Orleans return was more dependable, making this a narrow Hornets edge rather than a major win.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers acquired Rasual Butler and cash from New Orleans in August 2009 for a protected 2016 second-round selection that never conveyed. Butler started 64 of 82 Clippers games in 2009-10 and averaged 11.9 points, then returned for 41 more games in 2010-11. The Hornets never received the conditional draft pick. Clippers Win, Los Angeles A- for 123 games of wing production and New Orleans D+ for unloading a contract without the contemplated selection.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
Los Angeles Acquired a Veteran Shooter With a Conditional Pick

On August 11, 2009, the Clippers acquired Rasual Butler from the New Orleans Hornets along with cash considerations. The payment going the other direction was a conditional second-round selection in 2016. Butler had started regularly for New Orleans in the preceding season and was known for shooting from the perimeter. Los Angeles needed an experienced wing who could fill substantial minutes during a difficult roster transition. New Orleans, by contrast, was managing its player contracts and future flexibility. The incoming pick was protected rather than guaranteed, an important detail for what eventually happened.

Butler Played and Started Throughout His First Clippers Season

Butler appeared in all 82 Los Angeles regular-season games during 2009-10, starting 64. He averaged 11.9 points in 33.0 minutes and served as one of the Clippers' principal outside shooters. This was not a deep-bench contract or a short preseason audition; the club acquired a regular starter capable of playing heavy wing minutes. His previous Hornets production cannot be counted as part of Los Angeles's return, but the full season that followed the August trade supplies ample evidence that the new team received immediate value. The Clippers obtained a known player rather than waiting for an uncertain prospect.

The Clippers Kept Another Forty-One Games of Production

Butler returned for 2010-11, when his Clippers role declined to 41 appearances, two starts and 744 minutes, averaging 5.0 points. He later finished that season with Chicago, a separate team whose numbers should not inflate the acquisition. Across his Los Angeles stint, the original trade brought 123 regular-season games and 3,446 minutes of wing depth. Although his second year was weaker, it adds genuine roster use beyond a one-year rental. The first-season starting role remains the most important part of the return.

The Hornets Never Collected the Protected 2016 Selection

The conditional 2016 second-rounder did not convey under its protections, so New Orleans received no draftee or replacement selection from this deal. Shedding Butler's contract may have served financial objectives, but a precise payroll benefit is not independently established by the trade ledger. Los Angeles received a full-time starter for one year and a reserve for part of another, plus cash. Those outcomes are markedly more valuable than the old modest Clippers grade suggested. The comparison doesn't require blaming the Hornets for all of Butler's earlier salary or asserting that a phantom second-round pick turned into another NBA player.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win. Los Angeles earns A- for Rasual Butler's 123 games and 3,446 minutes across two Clippers seasons, including 64 starts and an 11.9-point average in 2009-10. New Orleans gets D+ because its conditional 2016 second-round pick never conveyed. The receiving-team playing and cash return favored Los Angeles decisively.

minnesota-timberwolves.summary: On September 9, 2009, Minnesota moved forwards Darius Songaila and guard Bobby Brown to New Orleans for veteran Antonio Daniels and New Orleans' 2014 second-round pick, later No. 40 Glenn Robinson III. The Hornets received 75 games and 543 points from Songaila plus 22 games and 145 points from Brown. Minnesota ultimately used the 2014 choice on Robinson III, who played 25 games and scored 29 points for the Wolves in 2014-15. New Orleans Hornets Win, B, Minnesota B-. Simplified team transaction ledgers omit the pick, but official Pelicans history and RealGM identify it.
minnesota-timberwolves.analysis:
The 2009 Hornets Sent Daniels and a Future Pick to Minnesota

The September 9, 2009 trade moved Antonio Daniels from the New Orleans Hornets to Minnesota. In return, New Orleans received Darius Songaila and Bobby Brown. An important part of the consideration is easy to miss in brief transaction summaries: the Hornets also transferred their own 2014 second-round draft selection to Minnesota. The current site stores New Orleans franchise history under a Charlotte Hornets label for this legacy record, but the team involved in September 2009 played in New Orleans. The Pelicans' official later media guide explicitly includes the draft pick, independently corroborated by a 2014 draft-rights history and RealGM's contemporary transaction archive.

Songaila and Brown Gave New Orleans Immediate NBA Minutes

Songaila played seventy-five regular-season games for the Hornets during 2009-10, producing 543 points across 1,410 minutes. His steady reserve-frontcourt role offered more than a paper asset or expiring contract. Brown appeared in twenty-two New Orleans games, adding 145 points and 46 assists before moving again in January. Those are receiving-team contributions tied directly to this swap, not earlier playing time in Minnesota. The Hornets traded Brown to the Clippers in a later deal for a different 2014 second-round asset, so that transaction should not be confused with the 2014 pick the team had already delivered to the Timberwolves in September.

The Future Selection Really Did Become Glenn Robinson III

Minnesota acquired the Hornets' 2014 second-round pick in addition to Daniels. That choice ultimately became No. 40, used by the Timberwolves to draft Glenn Robinson III out of Michigan. The club's own media guide reports twenty-five Minnesota appearances, 108 minutes and twenty-nine points in the 2014-15 season before it waived Robinson in March. The pick was a real draft return even though the later player output was modest, and its existence is confirmed by franchise materials despite being omitted from simplified Basketball-Reference transaction lines. Treating the selection as nonexistent would misstate Minnesota's compensation and produce a misleading verdict.

Immediate Hornets Production Slightly Outweighed the Draft Benefit

The Hornets received ninety-seven combined games from Songaila and Brown during the season after the exchange, with Songaila becoming a useful rotation reserve. Minnesota's eventual value was a future second-round choice and an incoming veteran contract rather than comparable direct playing production. Glenn Robinson III's later career with other organizations cannot be treated as if all those appearances were Timberwolves games. Conversely, New Orleans did not keep its own 2014 selection and should not be awarded the pick's downstream rights. Evaluating both sides with the valid draft term and actual recipient seasons produces a modest New Orleans advantage rather than the inherited Minnesota win.

Final Verdict

Hornets Win. The historical New Orleans side, represented by the site's Charlotte franchise key, earns B for Darius Songaila's 75 games and 543 points plus Bobby Brown's 22 games and 145 points in 2009-10. Minnesota receives B- for Antonio Daniels and the legitimate New Orleans 2014 second-round pick, ultimately No. 40 Glenn Robinson III, who played 25 Wolves games. Both clubs' receiving-team returns are counted without importing later careers or unrelated picks.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey acquired a 2011 second-round right and a protected future first-round right from Golden State in September 2009, sending Marcus Williams to the Warriors. The Nets' rights were later associated with Darius Morris and Gorgui Dieng in subsequent draft chains; the Warriors obtained another guard prospect. The inherited Nets Win grades New Jersey B+ and Golden State C.
perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Exchanged Williams for Future Draft Choices

The Nets traded guard Marcus Williams to Golden State in September 2009 for a 2011 second-round right and a protected future first-round obligation. New Jersey was willing to move a guard who had struggled to establish a lasting role in order to collect future roster-building options. Golden State received a player it could evaluate immediately, while the Nets accepted the uncertainty associated with selections not yet made.

The Picks Required Multiple Years of Conditions

The second-round selection became linked to No. 41 Darius Morris in 2011. The first-round right carried protection conditions across several years before being associated with No. 21 Gorgui Dieng in 2013. Those later draft identities were part of the rights history, not proof that Morris or Dieng spent those seasons in New Jersey. Following the actual rights transfers is essential when judging an old pick-heavy transaction, especially when the protected obligation could have changed form.

Golden State Took a Young Guard With Some NBA Experience

Williams had shown passing ability in New Jersey but hadn't established himself as a consistent lead guard. The Warriors acquired an opportunity to test his skills with a new roster. His earlier Nets assists and appearances weren't Golden State production, and the club was surrendering future selection flexibility for the current developmental chance. That made the receiving-team payoff more dependent on one player than on a broad menu of later draft rights.

The Nets' Advantage Was the Future Asset Package

The inherited New Jersey B+ to Golden State C reflects the value of a second-round right plus a conditionally protected first-round path. The eventual pick recipients and selected players still have to be traced separately. Williams was a legitimate prospect to evaluate, but the Nets obtained multiple chances to build later without assuming that every linked selection became an impact NBA player in a Nets uniform.

Final Verdict

Nets Win. New Jersey, now represented by the Brooklyn franchise, receives B+ for a 2011 second-round right and a protected first-round asset later associated with Gorgui Dieng. Golden State earns C for Marcus Williams as a guard prospect. The original Nets advantage reflects two future opportunities rather than a false claim that the later named draftees played directly for the Nets.

golden-state-warriors.summary: On November 16, 2009, Charlotte acquired Stephen Jackson and Acie Law from Golden State for Raja Bell and Vladimir Radmanović. Jackson started all 72 of his Bobcats games during 2009-10 and averaged 21.1 points, helping Charlotte earn the franchise's first NBA playoff berth. Bell appeared once for Golden State amid a wrist injury; Radmanović offered reserve frontcourt minutes but no comparable star scoring. Charlotte Win, Bobcats A-, Warriors C+.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Charlotte Took a Risk on a Proven High-Usage Scorer

The Charlotte Bobcats acquired Stephen Jackson and Acie Law from Golden State on November 16, 2009, sending veterans Raja Bell and Vladimir Radmanović to the Warriors. Charlotte needed another player who could create his own offense alongside Gerald Wallace, while Golden State was moving away from Jackson after a difficult relationship with its organization. The four-player deal involved no promised future draft selection. Acquiring an established scorer represented a more ambitious change than swapping interchangeable reserves, especially for a young franchise still seeking its first postseason appearance.

Jackson Became Charlotte's Leading Scorer in Its First Playoff Season

Jackson played 72 regular-season games with the Bobcats after the exchange, starting every one and averaging 21.1 points in 39.3 minutes. He also added 5.1 rebounds, 3.6 assists and 1.6 steals per game. The combination with Wallace helped Charlotte reach the 2010 playoffs for the first time in the franchise's history. Jackson remained an important offensive player beyond that initial campaign. His Golden State appearances earlier in 2009-10 are not part of Charlotte's acquired value; the 72 games and ensuing Bobcats seasons provide the proper evidence.

Golden State Obtained Depth but Little from Raja Bell

Bell arrived with a reputation for defending perimeter stars, yet he played only one regular-season game for Golden State in 2009-10 because of a wrist injury and related roster decisions. Radmanović provided frontcourt and wing reserve minutes during the same season and continued with the Warriors afterward. He brought shooting size but did not replace Jackson's workload as a primary offensive option. Law's Charlotte stay was likewise a supporting part of the package, not the main reason the Bobcats succeeded. The receiving-team comparison should keep all four players in view without implying Bell reproduced his earlier Suns scoring and defense for Golden State.

The Scoring Upgrade Was Worth More Than Golden State's Depth Return

Golden State's motivation was understandable: moving Jackson offered a change in roster direction, while Radmanović's experience and Bell's contract could serve different needs. Charlotte, however, received an immediate twenty-point scorer who stayed healthy enough to start 72 games and help deliver the franchise's first postseason trip. No reserve contributions by the two incoming Warriors equaled that impact. The old Charlotte-favored verdict was right but too conservative about its primary player. A strong Bobcats grade reflects actual 2009-10 contributions without assigning the later success of other franchises to this exchange.

Final Verdict

Charlotte Win. The Bobcats earn A- because Stephen Jackson started 72 regular-season games, averaged 21.1 points and helped the franchise reach its first NBA playoffs in 2010. Golden State receives C+ for reserve Vladimir Radmanović and a largely unavailable Raja Bell, who played just one Warriors game. Jackson delivered the greater receiving-team value by a decisive margin.

oklahoma-city-thunder.summary: Oklahoma City acquired Eric Maynor and Matt Harpring’s contract for the rights to Peter Fehse, adding a useful backup point guard at almost no basketball cost.
oklahoma-city-thunder.analysis: Eric Maynor quickly became a trusted backup behind Russell Westbrook and gave Oklahoma City competent second-unit play during the franchise’s early rise. Peter Fehse never played in the NBA, so the outgoing basketball value was effectively negligible. Harpring’s contract was part of the transaction mechanics rather than the on-court return, which limits how high the grade should climb. Still, acquiring a real rotation guard for a dormant draft-rights asset is exactly the kind of low-cost depth move that creates surplus value. Oklahoma City receives a clear win.
