new-orleans-pelicans.summary: On January 11, 2010 New Orleans traded reserve center Hilton Armstrong to Sacramento for cash and a conditional 2016 second-round selection. The pick never conveyed. Armstrong played six Kings games, logging 56 minutes and ten points before being sent onward as part of a separate three-team transaction. New Orleans received the cash; Sacramento obtained a brief player contract and occasional minutes. Even Trade, C+ for New Orleans and C for Sacramento.
new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
The Hornets Accepted Cash and a Protected Future Pick

The New Orleans Hornets traded Hilton Armstrong to the Sacramento Kings on January 11, 2010. Sacramento sent cash and a conditional second-round selection in the 2016 draft. Armstrong had been a first-round pick but no longer enjoyed a dependable role behind the Hornets frontcourt starters. New Orleans could reduce a roster obligation while Sacramento investigated a taller reserve center. The distant draft obligation had protections, so it should not be treated as an unconditional future draft pick or an immediately realized player asset.

Armstrong Played Only Six Regular-Season Games for Sacramento

Armstrong appeared in six Kings games after the January transaction, logging fifty-six minutes and ten points. He started none of them and had little time to change the team’s frontcourt rotation. In February, Sacramento included his contract in a much larger three-team exchange with Houston and New York. That later deal involved several players, so Armstrong cannot be credited with the entire return produced by those many assets. His previous Hornets appearances also do not become Sacramento production. The direct playing value was limited to six short outings.

The Conditional Second-Rounder Never Conveyed

The Hornets were owed a possible pick in the 2016 second round, but the protection terms prevented the choice from being transferred. Both franchise transaction histories mark the conditional obligation as unexercised. No 2016 draftee can therefore be assigned to New Orleans from this agreement. The club still received immediate cash, a legitimate financial asset. Because the public source ledger does not establish an amount or a direct player acquired with the proceeds, the retrospective should value it without inventing extra NBA points, minutes or an additional draft selection.

Two Small Returns Do Not Produce a Decisive Winner

Sacramento bought a brief center tryout and made use of Armstrong’s contract in a later package transaction. New Orleans secured a cash payment and avoided carrying the player, while its protected pick never arrived. Those are modest but recognizable forms of value. The original Kings-win grade gave excessive weight to six games and did not distinguish the subsequent multi-team trade from this small January exchange. Treating Sacramento’s six appearances and New Orleans’s cash fairly supports an even assessment, with neither side credited for assets beyond the documented incoming compensation.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. New Orleans earns C+ for the cash it received, although the protected 2016 second-round selection never conveyed. Sacramento earns C for Hilton Armstrong’s six appearances, fifty-six minutes and brief use as a tradable roster contract. Neither acquired a lasting NBA contributor through this stand-alone deal, and the earlier strong Kings-win grade lacked support.

new-orleans-pelicans.summary: On January 25, 2010, Chicago sent center Aaron Gray to the New Orleans Hornets for guard Devin Brown. Brown played 11 Bulls games, 93 minutes and scored 20 points after the exchange. Gray played 24 Hornets games in the rest of 2009-10 and another 41 in 2010-11, totaling 65 appearances, 792 minutes and 215 points. Hornets Win: New Orleans B, Chicago D+.
new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
A January Trade Rebalanced Two Different Depth Charts

On January 25, 2010, Chicago acquired Devin Brown from New Orleans in exchange for Aaron Gray. The Bulls announced the one-for-one agreement in an official release, explaining that Brown's shooting and defensive versatility fit their perimeter rotation. He had started 37 of 39 Hornets games before the exchange, while Gray had appeared in only eight Bulls games during the first half of the season. New Orleans needed another available center who could supply minutes behind Emeka Okafor and David West. Both clubs were chasing roster utility rather than exchanging their primary scorers.

Brown's Chicago Playing Return Lasted Only Eleven Games

Brown's earlier 39 New Orleans starts made him look like a potential upgrade for Chicago, but that form never carried over. He appeared in 11 Bulls regular-season games after the trade, playing only 93 minutes and scoring 20 points. He attempted 17 three-pointers and made four, and did not start a game for his new club. Chicago went to the 2010 playoffs, but Brown did not emerge as a prominent postseason contributor. His 379 Hornets points from before January belong to the team that traded him away and cannot be added to Chicago's acquired return.

Gray Supplied Sixty-Five Hornets Games Over Two Seasons

Gray produced limited offense for New Orleans, but he stayed in use much longer. In the remainder of 2009-10 he made 24 regular-season appearances, totaling 261 minutes, 86 points and 90 rebounds. He returned in 2010-11 for 41 more appearances, six starts, 531 minutes, 129 points and 171 rebounds. That made 65 regular-season games, 792 minutes, 215 points and 261 rebounds for the Hornets as the direct result of the deal. He was still a backup center, not a replacement for the main frontcourt, yet his availability offered real rotation insurance across two seasons.

The Receiving-Team Comparison Favors New Orleans

Both transactions made sense on paper. Chicago wanted a veteran guard whose production earlier that season suggested he could contribute quickly, while New Orleans accepted a slower, more specialized interior reserve. Their actual receiving-team results went in opposite directions: Brown barely played for the Bulls and Gray accumulated two years of center minutes for the Hornets. The difference does not turn Gray into a star or make the deal central to New Orleans's record. It does mean the inherited close grades were too generous to Chicago when judged by what its acquired player provided after January 25.

Final Verdict

Hornets Win. New Orleans earns B for Aaron Gray's 65 games, 792 minutes, 215 points and 261 rebounds across the balance of 2009-10 and 2010-11. Chicago receives D+ because Devin Brown managed just 11 Bulls games, 93 minutes and 20 points. The Hornets secured durable center coverage from a player Chicago seldom used.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers acquired guard Bobby Brown from the New Orleans Hornets on January 26, 2010, surrendering a top-55-protected second-round selection in 2014. Brown played 23 Clippers games with 191 minutes, 70 points and 42 assists. The pick ultimately conveyed at No. 58, becoming Jordan McRae, but New Orleans subsequently transferred it to San Antonio in the separate Curtis Jerrells trade. Hornets Win, New Orleans B- for a valuable tradable pick and Clippers C for brief guard depth.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
A Protected Future Pick Brought Brown to Los Angeles

The Clippers traded a conditional second-round selection in the 2014 NBA draft for Bobby Brown on January 26, 2010. New Orleans had used the guard earlier that season but accepted the possibility of a future selection rather than keeping him in its backcourt. The pick was protected through No. 55, meaning the Hornets would receive it only if it landed among the last five places of the second round. The Clippers needed another inexpensive reserve behind their more prominent ball handlers while moving through a difficult season.

Brown Gave the Clippers Twenty-Three Games

Brown appeared in 23 Los Angeles regular-season games following the deal, logging 191 minutes and 70 points. He added 42 assists with no starts, averaging roughly eight minutes per appearance. This was legitimate reserve point-guard work, though hardly a long-term solution. The 22 games and 145 points he produced for New Orleans earlier in 2009-10 belong to the franchise that sent him away. His later professional career abroad and eventual return to Houston several seasons afterward are likewise separate from the value Los Angeles purchased in January 2010.

The Conditional Selection Ultimately Became No. 58

The future choice eventually became the No. 58 pick in 2014, after its top-55 protection allowed it to transfer. Historical draft-chain records identify Jordan McRae as the player selected at that position. New Orleans, however, did not retain the pick until the draft: later in 2010 it transferred the selection to San Antonio as payment for Curtis Jerrells. McRae therefore was not a Hornets draft acquisition from this transaction, and his NBA playing record cannot be treated as New Orleans production. The receiving club's real benefit was the tradable pick it obtained.

A Short Guard Rental Compared With a Transferable Draft Asset

Los Angeles paid an eventual draft selection for a few months of backup-guard availability. Brown played only 191 minutes, and he did not return as a lasting Clippers contributor. New Orleans turned him into a pick that retained value and could be spent in another transaction, rather than letting the opportunity evaporate. The initial Hornets B+ grade may overstate an eventual late-second-round asset, but the franchise did realize a concrete pick and then put it to use. A smaller Hornets advantage survives when both receiving-team outcomes are weighed carefully.

Final Verdict

Pelicans Win. The New Orleans Hornets receive B- for a 2014 second-round pick that ultimately conveyed at No. 58 and could be moved again. Los Angeles receives C for Bobby Brown's 23 games, 191 minutes and 70 points. Jordan McRae was selected only after New Orleans traded the pick onward, so his NBA career is not Hornets return.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Antawn Jamison from Washington and Sebastian Telfair from the Clippers on February 17, 2010. Washington obtained Zydrunas Ilgauskas, Al Thornton, Emir Preldžić's rights and a 2010 first-round pick. Los Angeles acquired Drew Gooden from Washington. The inherited Even Trade assigns Cleveland, Washington and the Clippers B, with important differences in each team's goals.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Added Jamison for a Championship Push

The Cavaliers acquired Antawn Jamison from Washington in February 2010 while also receiving Sebastian Telfair from the Clippers. Cleveland was trying to add a veteran scoring forward to a lineup led by LeBron James, giving the offense another source of midrange and perimeter shots. Jamison brought a long record of points and rebounds, although those earlier Wizards seasons weren't themselves production for Cleveland. Telfair offered guard depth but wasn't the central reason for structuring a three-team agreement.

Washington Replaced a Veteran With Prospects and Options

The Wizards received Zydrunas Ilgauskas from Cleveland, Al Thornton from the Clippers, Emir Preldžić's draft rights and a 2010 first-round selection later tied to No. 30 Lazar Hayward. The club was moving away from an expensive veteran centerpiece and collecting assets for future roster decisions. Ilgauskas's contract path required separate attention, and the draft pick was a rights opportunity rather than guaranteed Washington playing production. Thornton had already shown his ability to score from the wing in Los Angeles.

The Clippers Received Gooden From Washington

Los Angeles acquired forward Drew Gooden from the Wizards and sent Telfair to Cleveland plus Thornton to Washington. Gooden was an experienced rebounder and interior scorer, offering a more immediate frontcourt option than another speculative draft asset. His receipt is confirmed in both the Cavaliers' and Wizards' official announcements. Without that directed Gooden entry, the transaction misleadingly reads as though the Clippers paid two players to serve as an administrative participant. They had a concrete incoming player and made a real roster decision.

Three Equal Grades Shouldn't Obscure Different Outcomes

All three franchises get B under the inherited Even Trade evaluation. Cleveland was choosing a veteran scorer to help compete immediately, Washington was changing its long-term roster commitments, and Los Angeles acquired a frontcourt player it could use without a draft delay. The decision to trade Jamison had financial and rebuilding implications for Washington that were distinct from Cleveland's title aspirations. A balanced account must preserve each club's incoming package and the separate histories of later transactions involving these players.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Cleveland receives B for Antawn Jamison and Sebastian Telfair as current roster pieces. Washington also earns B for Zydrunas Ilgauskas, Al Thornton, Emir Preldžić's draft rights and a first-round selection. The Clippers receive B for Drew Gooden, a verified incoming veteran omitted from the former source view. Each club had different competitive or financial objectives, making a narrow tie defensible.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Celtics Added Robinson to a Contending Bench

At the February 18, 2010 deadline, Boston sent Eddie House, J.R. Giddens and Bill Walker to New York for Nate Robinson and Marcus Landry. A conditional 2014 second-round right was also part of the Knicks' compensation, though it never conveyed. Boston's veteran core had championship ambitions, and Robinson offered a reserve who could create his own scoring chances when the usual ball handlers were off the floor. New York was still revising its rotation before an important summer of roster decisions, making the exchange a way to test several younger options.

Robinson Helped During Boston's Long Playoff Run

Robinson didn't become an every-night Celtics starter, but he could supply sudden offense and energy. His contributions during the 2010 postseason were especially useful as Boston reached the NBA Finals against the Lakers. Landry, the other incoming player, did not develop into a meaningful Celtics rotation piece. The relevant benefit was Robinson's ability to alter stretches of games behind Rajon Rondo, not his earlier Knicks scoring totals. Boston got more immediate help for a contending roster than it might have expected from the three players it surrendered.

New York Received Depth and a Walker Development Chance

House gave the Knicks experienced shooting in a temporary role, while Giddens had limited impact. Walker was the most interesting longer-term addition, gaining regular-season opportunities after moving from Boston. He didn't develop into an All-Star, but the Knicks could evaluate a young wing while reorganizing around future personnel plans. The conditional second-round asset never supplied a new draft selection. New York's return therefore included some useful playing time, though not an equivalent to Robinson's well-timed playoff bursts for a Finals-bound team.

A Targeted Playoff Addition Outweighed a Modest Return

Robinson's Boston tenure was relatively short, but the Celtics were paying for help when the games were most important, and he contributed to a deep postseason run. The Knicks got real evaluation opportunities and some backcourt depth without obtaining a decisive future star. The narrow grade difference recognizes that the trade wasn't a landslide; Walker's development mattered, and Boston did not acquire a permanent successor to its established veterans. Still, Robinson's immediate fit in a championship-contending bench role provided the clearer practical result.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B+ for Nate Robinson's timely reserve scoring during the 2010 Finals run, while Marcus Landry contributed little. new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Celtics Added Robinson to a Contending Bench

At the February 18, 2010 deadline, Boston sent Eddie House, J.R. Giddens and Bill Walker to New York for Nate Robinson and Marcus Landry. A conditional 2014 second-round right was also part of the Knicks' compensation, though it never conveyed. Boston's veteran core had championship ambitions, and Robinson offered a reserve who could create his own scoring chances when the usual ball handlers were off the floor. New York was still revising its rotation before an important summer of roster decisions, making the exchange a way to test several younger options.

Robinson Helped During Boston's Long Playoff Run

Robinson didn't become an every-night Celtics starter, but he could supply sudden offense and energy. His contributions during the 2010 postseason were especially useful as Boston reached the NBA Finals against the Lakers. Landry, the other incoming player, did not develop into a meaningful Celtics rotation piece. The relevant benefit was Robinson's ability to alter stretches of games behind Rajon Rondo, not his earlier Knicks scoring totals. Boston got more immediate help for a contending roster than it might have expected from the three players it surrendered.

New York Received Depth and a Walker Development Chance

House gave the Knicks experienced shooting in a temporary role, while Giddens had limited impact. Walker was the most interesting longer-term addition, gaining regular-season opportunities after moving from Boston. He didn't develop into an All-Star, but the Knicks could evaluate a young wing while reorganizing around future personnel plans. The conditional second-round asset never supplied a new draft selection. New York's return therefore included some useful playing time, though not an equivalent to Robinson's well-timed playoff bursts for a Finals-bound team.

A Targeted Playoff Addition Outweighed a Modest Return

Robinson's Boston tenure was relatively short, but the Celtics were paying for help when the games were most important, and he contributed to a deep postseason run. The Knicks got real evaluation opportunities and some backcourt depth without obtaining a decisive future star. The narrow grade difference recognizes that the trade wasn't a landslide; Walker's development mattered, and Boston did not acquire a permanent successor to its established veterans. Still, Robinson's immediate fit in a championship-contending bench role provided the clearer practical result.

perspectives.analysis: Milwaukee won this deal because John Salmons immediately became a major part of the 2010 playoff push while the draft mechanics also produced useful future value. The Bucks sent Hakim Warrick and Joe Alexander to Chicago, acquired Salmons, improved their first-round position through a swap and added second-round capital. Salmons averaged strong scoring numbers after the trade and helped Milwaukee surge into the postseason before the seven-game series with Atlanta. The first-round swap ultimately helped the Bucks land Larry Sanders, and the extra seconds retained value. For a midseason move, Milwaukee received both immediate impact and future assets without giving up a core player.

summary: Win. Milwaukee acquired a scorer who immediately transformed its 2010 playoff push and also gained favorable draft mechanics. Chicago created useful flexibility, but Warrick and Alexander did not replace Salmons' basketball value and the cap benefit was more indirect. Milwaukee solved an urgent roster need without sacrificing a core asset, earning an A to Chicago's C.
analysis: Salmons became one of the most important midseason additions in the league that year. Milwaukee's offense stabilized after his arrival, the Bucks surged into the playoffs and pushed Atlanta to seven games despite losing Andrew Bogut late in the season. Salmons gave the team creation on the wing without requiring a core young player in return. The draft mechanics added another layer because Milwaukee improved its position and retained additional future value beyond the immediate playoff boost. Chicago achieved a real objective by moving Salmons' contract and creating additional flexibility for the summer of 2010. Warrick supplied temporary frontcourt minutes, while Alexander was a reclamation project rather than a long-term piece. The Bulls later used their cap space aggressively and remained a strong team, so the trade did not derail the franchise. Still, those broader roster results cannot be credited entirely to this transaction, and the direct return did not approach what Milwaukee received on the court. The draft side strengthens Milwaukee's case. The swap mechanics were associated with the pick that became Larry Sanders, a high-impact defensive big before his career changed course. The additional second-round value also had a tangible endpoint. Chicago's return was primarily cap-oriented, which is legitimate but harder to value when the outgoing player immediately becomes a major contributor elsewhere. Milwaukee therefore received both present production and future optionality from the same move.

summary: Rockets Win: The transaction is remembered as a McGrady salary-clearing deal, but that shorthand understates Houston's work. The Rockets turned an ending into Martin, a prospect, a first and swap control, while New York purchased flexibility and Sacramento reset its backcourt. analysis: Houston captured the best combination of immediate production and controllable value. Martin became a high-volume scorer for the Rockets, Hill gave them several seasons of frontcourt minutes, Jeffries later returned to the rotation, and the protected first conveyed in 2012 at No. 16. The 2011 swap was not exercised and the pick became Royce White, so the draft side did not produce a star, but Houston still converted a relationship that had run its course into multiple usable assets. New York achieved the narrow financial objective: Jeffries' money came off the future books and McGrady expired, preserving room for the 2010 free-agent class. McGrady played only a short stretch and Rodríguez was temporary. The Knicks did sign Amar'e Stoudemire that summer, but the trade itself did not directly deliver the transformational free agent the cap strategy targeted, and surrendering Hill plus a first made the clearing cost meaningful. The cleanest downstream chain is Houston's. Martin remained valuable enough to become a central outgoing salary-and-talent piece in the 2012 James Harden trade. That later deal required substantial additional assets, so Harden cannot simply be credited to this trade, but Martin's retained market value matters because Houston did not consume its return immediately. The Knicks' main downstream benefit was cap flexibility rather than a directly tied player chain.

Maggette played 67 Bucks games in 2010-11, while Bell appeared in 19 Warriors games and Gadzuric in 28 before being moved again. Milwaukee sold Jerome Jordan's rights to the Knicks after the draft. golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Moved Maggette's Long Contract Before the Draft

On June 22, 2010, the Warriors traded Corey Maggette and the No. 44 choice in the upcoming draft to Milwaukee for Charlie Bell and Dan Gadzuric. Maggette was coming off a high-scoring Golden State season, but his multiyear contract tied up money a franchise under financial pressure wanted to redirect. Bell and Gadzuric carried shorter commitments, including Gadzuric's expiring deal. Milwaukee was trading away depth to get another proven scorer, hoping to help a young Brandon Jennings-led group that had just reached the playoffs. The second-round selection gave the Bucks a separate draft asset.

Maggette Played Sixty-Seven Games for Milwaukee

Maggette was the only player in the original exchange who became a sizable regular-season contributor for his receiving team. He appeared in sixty-seven Bucks games during 2010-11, started eighteen and logged 1,401 minutes. His ability to draw fouls and produce shots offered Milwaukee a reliable bench scoring option, although the team finished outside the playoffs that season. The No. 44 choice became Jerome Jordan, but the Bucks sold his rights to the New York Knicks after making the selection. No future Jordan minutes can be recorded as Milwaukee output because the center did not play an NBA game for the Bucks.

Bell and Gadzuric Supplied Only Spot Duty

Bell's Warriors stay included nineteen regular-season games in 2010-11, all as a reserve, with an average of just nine minutes per appearance. Gadzuric provided twenty-eight Golden State games, four starts, 297 minutes and seventy-nine points before a February move to New Jersey. These limited totals help explain why the Bucks hold the narrow immediate basketball advantage. But treating Gadzuric only as a reserve center also misses the fact that his expiring contract remained tradable. The Warriors had accepted less player production in exchange for different roster economics and a contract they could move again.

A Later Warriors Draft Pick Required an Additional Trade

On February 23, 2011, Golden State sent both Gadzuric and Brandan Wright to the Nets for Troy Murphy and a 2012 second-round selection. That choice eventually became No. 35, used on Draymond Green. The draft-pick chain makes Gadzuric part of an important later transaction, but it would overstate this June deal to say the Warriors simply traded Maggette for Green. They also contributed Wright in the intervening exchange, and the pick did not arrive until months afterward. The trade grades therefore weigh Milwaukee's direct scoring gain against Golden State's salary relief and the tangible ability to use Gadzuric in another asset package.

Final Verdict

Slight Bucks Edge. Milwaukee gets B+ because Corey Maggette supplied 67 games and 1,401 minutes in 2010-11, although Jerome Jordan's draft rights were promptly sold. Golden State earns B because moving Maggette's contract met a financial purpose and Dan Gadzuric later helped bring in a 2012 second-round pick through a package that also cost Brandan Wright. Charlie Bell's nineteen games and Gadzuric's twenty-eight weren't major direct returns, and Draymond Green must not be assigned solely to this one trade.

perspectives.summary: Atlanta acquired the rights to Jordan Crawford and Tibor Pleiss from the New Jersey Nets for the rights to Damion James during the 2010 NBA Draft. The Hawks then sent Pleiss's rights to Oklahoma City for cash. The ledger now marks Atlanta's holding of Pleiss as temporary, avoiding a duplicate final owner. The inherited Slight Hawks Edge grades Atlanta B, the Thunder B and the Nets C.
perspectives.analysis:
Atlanta Turned James's Rights Into Two Opportunities

On draft night in 2010, the Hawks traded the rights to No. 24 selection Damion James to the New Jersey Nets for the rights to Jordan Crawford and Tibor Pleiss. Crawford was the No. 27 pick, while Pleiss was selected at No. 31. Atlanta was balancing the value of a specific scoring guard against another team's desire for James. The initial acquisition was not the entire story, however, because Atlanta had another arrangement ready for one of the two incoming players.

Pleiss's Rights Immediately Moved to Oklahoma City

The Hawks sent Pleiss's rights to the Thunder for cash consideration in a separate draft-night step. An official Thunder release confirmed the receipt, and Atlanta's own contemporaneous announcement traced both phases. Pleiss had been briefly acquired from New Jersey but was not a second permanent Hawks draft asset alongside Oklahoma City's final rights. The corrected ledger identifies that interim status and restores the spelling of Tibor's name. Cash was Atlanta's compensation for giving up those rights, not an additional player arriving from Oklahoma City.

Crawford and James Followed Different NBA Paths

Atlanta retained Crawford's draft rights and could evaluate his offensive scoring potential. New Jersey received James as its incoming prospect, while Oklahoma City acquired the developmental rights to an international center. Each club was buying a different kind of opportunity; none obtained a current veteran star. Crawford's later appearances for other NBA teams and Pleiss's eventual career should be assigned to the franchises for which they occurred. One prospect's future elsewhere can't be used as retroactive Hawks or Nets playing minutes.

The Grades Should Follow Final Ownership

The inherited Atlanta B, Oklahoma City B and Nets C value Atlanta's guard prospect and cash, the Thunder's center rights and the Nets' single first-round acquisition differently. The Slight Hawks Edge label is modest rather than a claim that every Hawks draft decision succeeded. The important provenance repair is recognizing that Pleiss passed through Atlanta on the way to Oklahoma City. Without that step, the same prospect can appear to belong to two final recipient teams in the archive.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta gets B for Jordan Crawford's rights and cash received after promptly forwarding Tibor Pleiss's rights. Oklahoma City also earns B for acquiring Pleiss, and New Jersey receives C for Damion James. Atlanta held Pleiss only temporarily, so the complete 2010 rights chain doesn't award the same permanent prospect to both the Hawks and Thunder.

Slight Oklahoma City Thunder Edge is retained but graded B for Thunder and B- for the Hornets' successor franchise.
oklahoma-city-thunder.analysis:
Oklahoma City Obtained the Higher Draft Choice

The July 8, 2010 draft-rights trade sent Kansas center Cole Aldrich, selected eleventh, and veteran wing Morris Peterson from the New Orleans Hornets to the Oklahoma City Thunder. New Orleans received the rights to forwards Craig Brackins at No. 21 and Quincy Pondexter at No. 26. The Thunder wanted a young defensive center and experienced perimeter presence around Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook. New Orleans traded down to acquire two distinct first-round rights. The site's old Charlotte Hornets franchise key refers to the historical New Orleans club, not a 2010 trade with the Charlotte Bobcats.

Aldrich Provided Limited Thunder Playing Time

Aldrich appeared in eighteen Oklahoma City regular-season games during his 2010-11 rookie season and twenty-six more in 2011-12, totaling forty-four Thunder appearances before he moved elsewhere. His defensive and rebounding potential made him a reasonable prospect to obtain, but he never developed into a major Thunder starter. Peterson did not become a long-term veteran cornerstone either. In February 2011 Oklahoma City included Peterson and D.J. White in a separate trade for Nazr Mohammed. That transaction demonstrated the veteran contract's utility, although Mohammed's entire contribution cannot be credited solely to having acquired Peterson the previous summer.

New Orleans Turned Two Picks Into Separate Roster Options

The Hornets had two first-round selections instead of one higher pick. Pondexter went on to record NBA appearances for New Orleans, establishing a direct playing return from the draft-night agreement. Brackins did not remain with the Hornets for the season. The club later packaged his rights with Darius Songaila and sent them to Philadelphia for Willie Green and Jason Smith. Those incoming veterans were obtained through an additional agreement requiring Songaila, so crediting both entirely to this exchange would overlook the later price. The original return is best described as two movable first-round assets with different developmental outcomes.

The Slight Edge Is an Asset-Chain Judgment

Both organizations received usable options but neither produced a star directly from this one transaction. Oklahoma City got a frontcourt prospect who played forty-four Thunder games and a movable veteran contract. New Orleans collected a pair of first-round rights that supplied some playing time and separate trade flexibility. Comparing only eventual NBA careers without checking ownership changes would give misleading credit for Pondexter's later teams or Mohammed's full Thunder service. The old high grades are more generous than those direct returns justify. A modest Thunder edge recognizes the higher selection and Peterson's later flexibility without transforming either into a franchise-defining acquisition.

Final Verdict

Slight Oklahoma City Thunder Edge. Oklahoma City earns B for Cole Aldrich's forty-four regular-season Thunder games and the ability to include Morris Peterson in a subsequent deal. The historical New Orleans Hornets receive B- under the site's Charlotte franchise identifier for Quincy Pondexter's playing contribution and Craig Brackins's transferable rights. Nazr Mohammed and Willie Green arrived through later packages that required additional assets, not directly in the original July 2010 exchange.

new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
Oklahoma City Moved Up for Cole Aldrich

The July 8, 2010 agreement sent the draft rights to center Cole Aldrich, taken eleventh overall, and veteran Morris Peterson to Oklahoma City in exchange for the rights to Craig Brackins and Quincy Pondexter. New Orleans held the rights to two later first-round prospects rather than focusing on a single lottery-position center. Oklahoma City was looking for defensive size alongside a young core that featured Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook. Peterson's veteran contract was part of the larger financial and roster calculation. The clubs were exchanging different packages of prospect rights and a veteran, not one NBA player for another on equal contracts.

Pondexter Was the More Useful Initial New Orleans Return

Pondexter entered the New Orleans rotation as a young wing during the 2010-11 season and played NBA minutes before a later trade took him to Memphis. Brackins did not produce an extended Hornets tenure and was moved separately to Philadelphia. That leaves New Orleans with some direct player value and additional flexibility to redirect the other prospect rights. Pondexter returned to the franchise years later through another transaction, and that second stint should not be automatically attributed to the 2010 Thunder deal. His original receiving-team service is the important performance to include here.

Aldrich Did Not Become Oklahoma City's Long-Term Center

The Thunder obtained Aldrich as a developmental interior defender, but he never established himself as the team's full-time long-term center. He supplied limited reserve minutes, and the team later used his contract in another transaction when restructuring its roster. Peterson also did not bring Oklahoma City a major stretch of new NBA playing production. His previous New Orleans seasons and earlier Toronto scoring belonged to those prior receiving teams. The trade still gave the Thunder a legitimate young NBA big and a veteran asset, but the on-court output was smaller than a No. 11 draft position might have implied.

Neither Club Turned Its Return Into a Franchise Centerpiece

New Orleans gained a wing who actually appeared for the organization and another prospect it could move, while Oklahoma City received a lottery-selected center whose role remained limited. This supports a modest New Orleans advantage, but there is no basis to credit either club with every later transaction involving those players. The Thunder's eventual rise to championship contention owed far more to its existing stars and other acquisitions. The Hornets' receiving-team return was tangible without being transformative. The July 8, 2010 agreement sent the draft rights to center Cole Aldrich, taken eleventh overall, and veteran Morris Peterson to Oklahoma City in exchange for the rights to Craig Brackins and Quincy Pondexter. New Orleans held the rights to two later first-round prospects rather than focusing on a single lottery-position center. Oklahoma City was looking for defensive size alongside a young core that featured Kevin Durant and Russell Westbrook. Peterson's veteran contract was part of the larger financial and roster calculation. Brackins did not produce an extended Hornets tenure and was moved separately to Philadelphia. That leaves New Orleans with some direct player value and additional flexibility to redirect the other prospect rights. Pondexter returned to the franchise years later through another transaction, and that second stint should not be automatically attributed to the 2010 Thunder deal. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Phoenix Brought Childress Back From Greece

In July 2010, the Suns arranged a sign-and-trade for Josh Childress, who had spent the previous two seasons with Olympiacos after leaving Atlanta. Phoenix sent the Hawks a 2012 second-round selection and created a trade-exception opportunity for the outgoing club. Childress had been an athletic multi-position forward during his first Hawks tenure. The Suns hoped that experience would translate into another productive NBA reserve. Atlanta decided to take future draft compensation rather than retain the rights of a player returning on a new contract.

Childress Didn't Establish a Major Phoenix Role

Childress joined a Suns roster trying to adjust after its own major changes, but his playing time and production did not become an essential part of the next competitive cycle. His earlier Hawks statistics and successful season in Greece were reasons Phoenix considered him, not direct Suns output. The signing involved a substantial new commitment without yielding an equally important role. That gap between expectation and actual receiving-team performance is the primary weakness of Phoenix's side of the transaction.

Atlanta's Pick Eventually Produced Mike Scott

The 2012 second-round choice became No. 43, which Atlanta used on forward Mike Scott. Scott developed into a valuable bench scorer during the Hawks' later playoff seasons, providing a tangible basketball payoff from the sign-and-trade. The trade exception also had roster-management utility, although it was not a player and cannot be counted as guaranteed scoring or defense. Atlanta acquired an inexpensive development path rather than a well-known veteran, and that route produced a contributor who stayed longer than the Suns' Childress experiment.

A Second-Round Success Made the Exchange Work

Phoenix received a recognizable forward with NBA experience but did not obtain the impact it wanted under the new arrangement. Atlanta used the delayed pick to add useful frontcourt scoring and preserved financial flexibility. The trade was not a major star swap, but second-round choices rarely turn into dependable rotation players; Scott's development gave the Hawks unusually good value for surrendering the outgoing rights. That clear receiving-team result supports Atlanta's advantage without pretending the trade exception itself played NBA games.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B for the 2012 second-round pick used on Mike Scott and additional roster flexibility. Phoenix receives D because Josh Childress's return to the NBA delivered less Suns production than anticipated. Scott's later Hawks rotation career gave the draft compensation a concrete payoff that outweighed the incoming veteran's limited Phoenix tenure.

golden-state-warriors.summary: New Jersey received sharpshooter Anthony Morrow from Golden State on July 13, 2010, for a conditional 2011 second-round selection that never conveyed. Morrow played 120 Nets games during 2010-11 and 2011-12, averaging 13.2 and 12.0 points, respectively, including 65 starts across the two seasons. The pick never transferred to Golden State. Nets Win, New Jersey B+, Warriors D+.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
New Jersey Used an Uncertain Pick to Add a Proven Shooter

Golden State sent Anthony Morrow to the New Jersey Nets on July 13, 2010, in return for a conditional 2011 second-round draft pick. Morrow had already established himself as a high-percentage three-point shooter with the Warriors, including a 45.6 percent season from distance in 2009-10. The Nets were rebuilding a backcourt around Devin Harris and wanted reliable floor spacing without giving up a guaranteed first-round asset. The Warriors were reshuffling their wings and treated the return as a possible draft opportunity. Both clubs' transaction ledgers explicitly state that the condition was never met and the pick did not convey.

Morrow Supplied Two Full Seasons of Nets Scoring

Morrow played 58 New Jersey regular-season games in 2010-11, starting 47 and averaging 13.2 points in 32.0 minutes. He made 42.3 percent of his three-point attempts, giving the Nets a credible spot-up scoring option. In the shortened 2011-12 season he appeared 62 more times with 18 starts and averaged 12.0 points. Across those two years, his 120 games and 65 starts amounted to sustained rotation value. The franchise was still called the New Jersey Nets throughout this stint; referring to Brooklyn as the modern successor should not obscure the original club's name or dates.

Golden State Received No Actual Draft Selection

The Warriors were offered a conditional second-round selection in the 2011 draft, but the obligation was not exercised. That means Golden State did not receive a pick it could use on a player or trade again. It would be misleading to assign the franchise any 2011 second-rounder's NBA games merely because a choice was listed as possible compensation. The return was a contingent right that expired without producing a documented selection. Morrow's own earlier 136 Golden State games, including his 2009-10 scoring season, were Warriors contributions made before the deal rather than value created by acquiring the Nets' potential pick.

The Nets Acquired a Real Starter for a Nonconveyed Asset

New Jersey clearly benefited more from the arrangement. A guard capable of scoring in double figures appeared in 120 games while the club surrendered no exercised draft selection. The two seasons were not enough to turn the Nets into a contender, and Morrow moved on before the team's first Brooklyn campaign, so the result should not be exaggerated into a franchise-changing acquisition. But the alternative side is straightforward: Golden State parted with a useful shooter and realized no pick from the agreement. That imbalance justifies a favorable Nets grade grounded in actual receiving-team minutes, points and starts.

Final Verdict

Nets Win. New Jersey earns B+ after Anthony Morrow provided 120 regular-season games, 65 starts and double-digit scoring in both seasons. Golden State receives D+ because the conditional 2011 second-round pick never conveyed. The Nets acquired two years of effective perimeter shooting without delivering an actual draft selection.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Chicago acquired C.J. Watson from Golden State on July 22, 2010, for the second-round pick ultimately used on Charles Jenkins and a traded-player exception. Watson played all 82 Bulls games in 2010-11 and 49 in 2011-12, scoring 879 points across 131 games. Jenkins gave Golden State 98 games across 2011-12 and part of 2012-13, including 28 rookie starts. Bulls Win, Chicago B+ and Golden State B-; both teams got NBA playing value.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Chicago Bought Point-Guard Depth With a Future Second-Round Pick

The Bulls acquired C.J. Watson from Golden State on July 22, 2010, sending a 2011 second-round selection in return. The Warriors also obtained a traded-player exception, a salary-cap mechanism that could help with later moves. Chicago wanted a dependable backup to Derrick Rose as it built a stronger playoff rotation under Tom Thibodeau. Golden State chose a future draft opportunity and financial flexibility over continuing Watson's reserve contract. This was not an exchange of two active NBA guards on the same day.

Watson Covered 131 Chicago Regular-Season Games in Two Years

Watson appeared in all eighty-two Bulls games in 2010-11, providing 1,091 minutes, 405 points and 186 assists. During the shortened 2011-12 campaign he played forty-nine more games and started twenty-five, recording 474 points and 200 assists in 1,159 minutes. Combined, his Chicago stint produced 131 regular-season games, 2,250 minutes and 879 points. His role was especially useful when the team needed additional ball handling behind Rose. The Nets and Pacers seasons from later in Watson's career do not belong to this Chicago acquisition.

Golden State Used the Pick on Charles Jenkins

The second-round selection reached Golden State as No. 44 in the 2011 draft, when the Warriors selected Hofstra guard Charles Jenkins. Jenkins played fifty-one Warriors regular-season games during the shortened 2011-12 season, starting twenty-eight and logging 893 minutes with 297 points. He returned for forty-seven Warriors appearances in 2012-13 before moving to Philadelphia, where his final twelve games of that year must be kept separate. That is an actual player return rather than a pick that never conveyed, which justifies credit for Golden State's side.

The Bulls Obtained More Consistent Guard Cover, Though Both Clubs Benefited

Chicago had Watson available through two competitive regular seasons and playoff runs, collecting more minutes and veteran experience than Golden State received from Jenkins. But Jenkins was also a usable young guard, and the trade exception had value in roster accounting even without crediting an unverified later player to it. The earlier slight Chicago edge recognized the correct direction while underselling the duration of Watson's reserve service. A clearer Bulls advantage with positive grades for both teams reflects what their respective incoming assets actually delivered in NBA games.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win. Chicago earns B+ after C.J. Watson supplied 131 games, 2,250 minutes and 879 points during two seasons as a reserve and occasional starter. Golden State gets B- because No. 44 Charles Jenkins played 98 Warriors games, including 28 rookie starts, and the club also obtained a trade exception. Both returns were real, but Chicago secured more sustained NBA guard coverage.

The second-round selection reached Golden State as No. 44 in the 2011 draft, when the Warriors selected Hofstra guard Charles Jenkins. Jenkins played fifty-one Warriors regular-season games during the shortened 2011-12 season, starting twenty-eight and logging 893 minutes with 297 points. That is an actual player return rather than a pick that never conveyed, which justifies credit for Golden State's side.

Chicago had Watson available through two competitive regular seasons and playoff runs, collecting more minutes and veteran experience than Golden State received from Jenkins. The earlier slight Chicago edge recognized the correct direction while underselling the duration of Watson's reserve service. A clearer Bulls advantage with positive grades for both teams reflects what their respective incoming assets actually delivered in NBA games.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win. Chicago earns B+ after C.J. Watson supplied 131 games, 2,250 minutes and 879 points during two seasons as a reserve and occasional starter. Golden State gets B- because No. 44 Charles Jenkins played 98 Warriors games, including 28 rookie starts, and the club also obtained a trade exception. perspectives.summary: Indiana acquired point guard Darren Collison and forward James Posey in the August 2010 four-team exchange that brought Troy Murphy to New Jersey, Courtney Lee to Houston, and Trevor Ariza to New Orleans. Collison gave the Pacers a young lead guard with actual receiving-team production. The inherited Pacers Win grades Indiana A-, Houston B, New Orleans B and New Jersey C.
perspectives.analysis:
Indiana Acquired a Young Starting Guard

The Pacers received Darren Collison and James Posey through an August 2010 four-team trade involving the Nets, Rockets and New Orleans Hornets. Collison had impressed as a rookie guard in New Orleans when asked to run the offense, giving Indiana an identifiable young backcourt target. Posey provided experienced wing depth. New Jersey acquired veteran big Troy Murphy, Houston secured Courtney Lee, and New Orleans added Trevor Ariza. All four teams obtained an actual player rather than purely conditional draft rights.

Collison Delivered a Tangible Pacers Return

Collison gave Indiana a guard capable of running the offense and creating opportunities for teammates. His size and scoring limitations were part of the evaluation, but his early Pacers tenure provided real starting-caliber minutes instead of the uncertain promise of an unsigned prospect. Posey contributed veteran experience in a narrower role. Collison later played elsewhere and returned to Indiana again, but the first stretch following this trade alone was enough to establish meaningful receiving-team value.

Houston and New Orleans Found Useful Wings

Courtney Lee offered Houston perimeter defense and outside shooting, filling a role different from Murphy's interior abilities. Trevor Ariza joined the then-New Orleans Hornets as a wing capable of guarding opponents and working without requiring constant offensive touches. Their B grades recognize legitimate fits without claiming either became an immediate franchise centerpiece. New Jersey's Murphy acquisition delivered a shorter and less impactful return than the longer-term guard and wing options obtained by the other participants.

The Four-Team Structure Matters to the Verdict

The transaction was not simply a swap of Collison for Ariza; Houston and New Jersey also took parts of the same arrangement. Indiana's A- is supported by Collison's immediately usable backcourt role. Houston and New Orleans each receive B for accomplished wings, while the Nets get C for Murphy's limited stay. Comparing only draft position or career scoring elsewhere would miss the actual receiving-team roles these four franchises gained during the following seasons.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win. Indiana earns A- for Darren Collison's early lead-guard contribution and James Posey's veteran depth. Houston gets B for Courtney Lee, and New Orleans also receives B for Trevor Ariza's wing defense. The Nets receive C for Troy Murphy's shorter impact. The Pacers obtained the most durable direct roster solution from this four-team exchange.

new-orleans-pelicans.summary: New Orleans traded Julian Wright to Toronto for Marco Belinelli on August 11, 2010. Belinelli gave the Hornets 80 games in 2010-11, made 134 threes at 41.4 percent, and returned as a key reserve in the lockout-shortened 2011-12 campaign. Wright played one Raptors season and never acquired a lasting role. Hornets Win, New Orleans A-, Toronto D+.
new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
New Orleans Exchanged a Forward for Outside Shooting

On August 11, 2010, New Orleans sent Julian Wright to the Toronto Raptors for Marco Belinelli. The Hornets were preparing for head coach Monty Williams's first season and needed dependable shooting around Chris Paul and David West. Belinelli had struggled to secure a long-term starting job during earlier stops with Golden State and Toronto, but his shot gave New Orleans a clear reason to experiment. Toronto took a chance on Wright, a former Kansas forward whose athleticism had never turned into a steady offensive role. There was no draft pick involved in the straight player swap.

Belinelli Became a Reliable Hornets Starter Immediately

Belinelli started regularly for the 2010-11 Hornets and appeared in 80 of 82 regular-season games. He made 134 three-point attempts at a 41.4 percent conversion rate, the best team percentage among major rotation shooters. The franchise's official season review credited him with its highest three-point total and noted that he missed only two games because of an ankle sprain. His work gave Paul an outside option during a playoff season, and Belinelli made his first NBA postseason appearances when the Hornets faced the Lakers. The team obtained much more than a fringe reserve in the first year of the exchange.

Toronto Did Not Find a Long-Term Fit for Wright

Wright played 52 games for the Raptors in 2010-11, averaging fewer than four points in a limited reserve role. He did not become the versatile wing Toronto had hoped might develop from his earlier promise with New Orleans, and that single season was the entirety of his Toronto NBA tenure. The club later moved to a different group of forwards. Wright's prior college achievements and his Hornets appearances before August 2010 are not Toronto receiving-team production. By contrast, Belinelli also returned to the New Orleans rotation in the shortened 2011-12 season, extending the value of the initial acquisition beyond his first productive year.

One Team Solved an Immediate Need and Kept the Benefit

For New Orleans, the trade addressed an identifiable roster problem: it transformed a rarely used forward into an accurate three-point shooter capable of starting and contributing in the playoffs. Toronto's gamble on Wright never yielded comparable minutes or production, even though the cost of acquiring him was a player the Raptors had not fully developed. Belinelli's later success elsewhere in the NBA does not belong to the Hornets, but their own two seasons provide ample evidence that the original decision worked. New Orleans won this exchange through on-court usefulness rather than headline value or hypothetical potential.

Final Verdict

Hornets Win. New Orleans earns A- for Marco Belinelli's 80-game 2010-11 season, 134 made three-pointers at 41.4 percent and another year in the rotation. Toronto gets D+ after Julian Wright played 52 games with limited scoring and did not stick beyond one season. Belinelli gave the Hornets the shooting they acquired him to provide.

new-orleans-pelicans.summary: On October 18, 2010, New Orleans sent the Clippers-origin protected 2014 second-round pick to San Antonio for reserve guard Curtis Jerrells. Jerrells was waived by the Hornets October 24 without a regular-season NBA appearance. The choice ultimately conveyed at No. 58 and was used on Jordan McRae after subsequent transactions. Spurs Win, San Antonio B- for a real transferable pick, New Orleans D+ for a short camp audition.
new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
The Hornets Spent a Future Clippers Pick on a Guard

New Orleans acquired Curtis Jerrells from San Antonio on October 18, 2010. The Hornets surrendered a conditional second-round selection in the 2014 draft, originally obtained from the Clippers earlier that year in the Bobby Brown trade. The pick was top-55 protected, making it valuable only if it ended near the bottom of the second round. Jerrells had experience with the Spurs' developmental program and overseas basketball, offering the Hornets another guard to evaluate as the new season approached. The transaction was an exchange of a future draft asset for a present roster audition.

Jerrells Was Released Before Playing a Hornets Game

The trial lasted less than a week. New Orleans waived Jerrells on October 24, 2010, before the regular season began. He consequently appeared in no NBA regular-season games for the Hornets and contributed no minutes, points or assists to the receiving club. His extensive subsequent overseas career was genuine professional basketball work but did not count as New Orleans production. Nor do prior developmental-league appearances for the Spurs become Hornets statistics. The acquisition served only a short-term attempt to inspect another backcourt option.

The Conditional Pick Ultimately Conveyed as No. 58

The draft choice sent to San Antonio was the same Clippers-origin pick that the Hornets had acquired in January 2010. It eventually landed at No. 58 in the 2014 draft, satisfying its top-55 protection and retaining genuine draft value. Historical pick-chain records associate it with Jordan McRae, though the pick subsequently moved through other transactions. McRae did not become a Spurs regular-season player by virtue of this particular trade. The benefit San Antonio received here was a future second-round selection that it could keep or use as part of another deal, not his later scoring statistics.

A Real Future Pick Was Better Than a Camp Cut

San Antonio converted a player it was prepared to move into a selection that ultimately became real draft compensation. The Hornets traded away that option and received a guard who never appeared in an NBA game for them. This disparity explains the favorable Spurs verdict. Yet an A- grade for San Antonio is too high when the return was one late second-round pick rather than a long-term starter. Recognizing the selection's successful conveyance and the lack of Hornets playing time supports a solid but limited San Antonio advantage.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win. San Antonio earns B- for a Clippers-origin 2014 second-round pick that ultimately conveyed at No. 58 and retained trade value. New Orleans receives D+ because Curtis Jerrells was waived October 24, 2010, before making a Hornets regular-season appearance. Jordan McRae's eventual NBA career happened after later pick movements and cannot be assigned directly to San Antonio's incoming player production.

new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
New Orleans Replaced Two Departing Players With Guard Depth

The November 20, 2010 deal was a five-player exchange between the New Orleans Hornets and Toronto Raptors. New Orleans sent former All-Star shooter Peja Stojaković and young guard Jerryd Bayless north, receiving Jarrett Jack, David Andersen and Marcus Banks. Toronto's own announcement also disclosed cash considerations accompanying the incoming players. New Orleans was off to a strong start and wanted another established guard to relieve Chris Paul without abandoning its competitive plans. Andersen provided additional frontcourt coverage, while Banks was largely a contract piece. The historical franchise is now labeled Pelicans in the site, but it still played as the Hornets in 2010.

Jack's New Orleans Tenure Was More Than a Rental

Jack played seventy New Orleans regular-season games after the November trade in 2010-11, then forty-five more in the lockout-shortened 2011-12 season. His Hornets totals across the two campaigns were 115 games and 468 assists, with his second year featuring thirty-nine starts as the guard rotation changed. That production is specific to the club that acquired him in this exchange. The thirteen Toronto games he played before the deal and the years he later spent with Golden State or Brooklyn cannot be credited to the Hornets. Jack's direct ability to play significant minutes made him the lasting and useful return from this package.

Toronto Received a Prospect and Limited Peja Time

The Raptors were seeking younger talent and future payroll flexibility, not an immediate veteran star to replace Jack's full contribution. Bayless was twenty-two at the time and continued to receive Toronto backcourt opportunities, giving the club a genuine player rather than just cash savings. Stojaković, despite his long-standing reputation as a shooter, barely figured in Toronto's games and eventually moved on before joining Dallas. His previous scoring years in New Orleans are not acquired Toronto performance, nor is his championship run with Dallas. The incoming cash consideration reinforced the financial motive but cannot be represented as another player or first-round draft selection.

Different Objectives Yielded Different Basketball Returns

New Orleans wanted a rotation guard during a period of immediate contention and received one who played meaningful minutes over two seasons. Toronto was retooling and prioritized Bayless's development along with relief from longer-term obligations. Both sides could reasonably defend their intentions, but the guard depth and subsequent playing record favor the Hornets' side. The original grade underrates Toronto if it treats Stojaković's short stay as the full return, since Bayless continued to play for the franchise. A high New Orleans grade is better grounded in Jack's 115 Hornets appearances than in any unrelated future NBA stops or historic Peja statistics.

Final Verdict

Pelicans Win is the site's franchise label; the receiving team was the New Orleans Hornets. New Orleans earns A- because Jarrett Jack played 115 games and recorded 468 assists across the rest of 2010-11 and 2011-12, with Andersen adding depth. Toronto receives B- for acquiring younger guard Jerryd Bayless and some financial flexibility. Stojaković's later Dallas success and Jack's post-Hornets work belong to separate transactions and cannot inflate the return.

perspectives.summary: New Jersey obtained Sasha Vujačić and two protected first-round draft assets in a December 2010 three-team trade. Houston received Terrence Williams and the Lakers took Joe Smith plus second-round rights. The Nets prioritized future flexibility and a veteran perimeter role, whereas Houston bet on Williams's athleticism. The inherited slight Nets edge grades New Jersey B+, Houston B and Los Angeles C+.
perspectives.analysis:
New Jersey Took a Veteran and Protected First-Round Rights

The Nets acquired guard Sasha Vujačić and two protected first-round selections in a December 2010 deal involving Houston and the Los Angeles Lakers. The picks were linked to later draft identities including JaJuan Johnson and Shane Larkin, although each one's final player destination depended on subsequent moves. New Jersey was willing to give up Terrence Williams to gain several assets it could retain or trade. Houston chose the younger wing, while the Lakers accepted Joe Smith and future second-round consideration.

Vujačić Provided an Immediate Backcourt Option

Vujačić had experience playing on championship-level Lakers teams and brought perimeter shooting to New Jersey. His arrival did not turn the Nets into a contender, but it gave them a recognizable veteran guard while the organization rebuilt. The associated draft assets were important because they could be exchanged even if the eventual draftees never played for the Nets. The transaction should not attribute every later JaJuan Johnson or Shane Larkin season to New Jersey without tracking those subsequent rights transfers.

Houston and Los Angeles Pursued Different Timelines

The Rockets acquired Williams, an athletic young perimeter player who had shown potential with New Jersey but struggled to establish a stable role. Houston could evaluate that upside in its own system. The Lakers received Smith as a veteran frontcourt option and second-round assets later tied to Darius Morris and Robert Sacre. Smith's earlier success for other teams was not new Los Angeles production, and draft rights carry their own later histories. The packages mixed short-term veterans and longer-term developmental possibilities.

The Nets' Asset Breadth Explains the Narrow Edge

New Jersey received a current NBA guard and multiple future first-round opportunities in exchange for parting with Williams. Houston obtained the younger player it preferred, and the Lakers gained frontcourt depth and lower-round draft options. The inherited Nets B+ compared with Houston B and Los Angeles C+ reflects the relative flexibility of the incoming rights. This isn't a claim that New Jersey secured two first-round stars or that either other club obtained no basketball value.

Final Verdict

Slight Nets Edge. New Jersey earns B+ for Sasha Vujačić and two protected first-round rights later associated with JaJuan Johnson and Shane Larkin. Houston gets B for acquiring Terrence Williams as a developmental wing. The Lakers receive C+ for Joe Smith and two later second-round opportunities. The broader future draft package gives the Nets their inherited edge.

perspectives.summary: Denver sent Carmelo Anthony, Chauncey Billups and supporting players to New York in a three-team blockbuster, receiving a deep player package, draft assets, cash and the 2016 pick-swap right later used to select Jamal Murray.
perspectives.analysis: Denver produced the strongest realized return despite negotiating after Carmelo Anthony requested a move. Gallinari, Chandler, Felton, Mozgov and the rest of the player package preserved immediate competitiveness, while the future draft control extended the transaction into another era. New York still received an extended superstar who won a scoring title and led a 54-win team, so its side deserves a solid grade rather than dismissal. The decisive separator is Denver's combination of short-term depth and the 2016 swap that became Jamal Murray, a foundational player on the franchise's championship roster.

summary: Washington traded Kirk Hinrich and Hilton Armstrong to Atlanta in February 2011 for Mike Bibby, Jordan Crawford, Maurice Evans and a first-round pick. Hinrich gave the Hawks useful playoff guard defense, but Crawford played a more sustained scoring role for Washington and the pick became Chris Singleton. Wizards Win, Washington A and Atlanta C-.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Washington traded Kirk Hinrich and Hilton Armstrong to Atlanta in February 2011 for Mike Bibby, Jordan Crawford, Maurice Evans and a first-round pick. Hinrich gave the Hawks useful playoff guard defense, but Crawford played a more sustained scoring role for Washington and the pick became Chris Singleton. Wizards Win, Washington A and Atlanta C-.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Targeted Hinrich for Backcourt Defense

The Hawks sent Mike Bibby, young guard Jordan Crawford, Maurice Evans and a 2011 first-round selection to Washington on February 23, 2011, receiving Kirk Hinrich and Hilton Armstrong. Atlanta was trying to improve its defense at point guard around Joe Johnson, Josh Smith and Al Horford. Hinrich had a more disciplined defensive reputation than Bibby, and Armstrong offered situational size. Washington was rebuilding and preferred Crawford's developmental upside alongside a first-round choice rather than relying on another veteran backcourt combination.

Hinrich Helped Atlanta During the 2011 Playoffs

Hinrich became a useful member of the Hawks rotation and gave the team another experienced ball handler during its postseason push. His perimeter defense helped Atlanta compete against Orlando before the Hawks were eliminated by Chicago in the next round. Armstrong supplied much less direct value. The trade did meet a short-term need, but Hinrich was not an enduring Hawks point-guard answer whose production justified every outgoing component. His useful playoff performance deserves acknowledgment without stretching it into several seasons of Atlanta success.

Crawford and a First-Rounder Improved Washington's Return

Crawford developed into an important young scoring guard for the Wizards, providing more lasting playing opportunities than several other players in the transaction. Washington used the first-round choice at No. 18 in 2011 on forward Chris Singleton, adding another player to its rebuilding roster. The veteran Bibby did not become a Wizards cornerstone; he was waived shortly after arriving. Evans also represented a transitional piece. The team's longer-term benefit rested on Crawford's development and control of a relatively valuable selection.

A Short-Term Defensive Fix Cost Atlanta Two Young Assets

Atlanta improved its immediate playoff guard rotation but surrendered a rookie scorer and a first-round pick to do it. Washington accepted the uncertainty of young-player development and obtained enough value for its timeline to justify the exchange. This wasn't a total failure for Hinrich's Hawks tenure, nor was Singleton automatically a star because he was drafted in the first round. Crawford's scoring and the additional draft chance nevertheless gave Washington a larger combination of realized and potential value than Atlanta received.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns A for acquiring Jordan Crawford and the No. 18 selection used on Chris Singleton, with Mike Bibby and Maurice Evans as transitional veterans. Atlanta gets C- despite Kirk Hinrich's useful 2011 playoff defense, because the acquisition cost a developing scorer and first-round pick. The Wizards secured the stronger overall return for their rebuilding roster.

new-orleans-pelicans.summary: New Orleans acquired Carl Landry from Sacramento on February 23, 2011 for Marcus Thornton and cash. Landry played 23 Hornets games in 2010-11 and another 41 in 2011-12, scoring 783 points in 64 regular-season games. Thornton broke out immediately in Sacramento, averaging 21.3 points in 27 post-trade games and 18.7 points over 51 games in 2011-12. Kings Win, Sacramento A- and New Orleans B.
new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
New Orleans Chose Frontcourt Help Over a Young Scoring Guard

The Hornets acquired Carl Landry from Sacramento on February 23, 2011, sending Marcus Thornton and cash to the Kings. New Orleans was looking for reliable bench offense and rebounding as Chris Paul's team prepared for a playoff push. Landry already had several seasons of productive interior scoring. Thornton was a younger guard who could create shots but had not secured a permanent starting role with the Hornets. Sacramento was rebuilding and could offer him more offensive opportunities. The deal was about immediate frontcourt help versus a longer scoring-guard investment.

Landry Contributed Sixty-Four Hornets Games Across Two Seasons

Landry played twenty-three regular-season games after joining New Orleans, scoring 272 points and grabbing ninety-four rebounds over 602 minutes. He returned during the shortened 2011-12 campaign for forty-one appearances, 511 points and 214 rebounds. In total he provided sixty-four Hornets games, 783 points and 308 rebounds in 1,601 minutes. That is a solid rotation return for the team that acquired him. His earlier Rockets and Kings points do not belong to New Orleans, and his subsequent Golden State work arose after another move.

Thornton Immediately Produced Twenty-Point Scoring in Sacramento

Thornton's scoring rose dramatically once the Kings put the ball in his hands. He played twenty-seven Sacramento games in the rest of 2010-11, starting twenty-three and averaging 21.3 points. In 2011-12 he started all fifty-one appearances and averaged 18.7 points. He was still a double-digit scorer in the following season. These are not hypothetical projections of what he might have become with New Orleans; they are actual Kings performances after the February trade. The cash arriving alongside him made Sacramento's side of the agreement stronger.

Both Teams Received Basketball Value but Sacramento Got More

New Orleans addressed a real need and Landry remained useful through the following year, so this was not an empty return or an obviously irrational deadline deal. Sacramento, however, transformed an interior veteran into an active scoring guard who rapidly became one of its primary offensive options. The difference was apparent immediately and lasted beyond the initial post-deadline schedule. The Hornets' 2011 playoff run does not automatically turn Landry into a franchise-altering acquisition. A stronger Sacramento grade reflects the production in the uniforms that the respective teams acquired.

Final Verdict

Kings Win. Sacramento earns A- for Marcus Thornton's 21.3-point average in his first twenty-seven Kings games and 18.7 points over fifty-one starts the next season, plus cash. New Orleans gets B because Carl Landry played sixty-four Hornets games and scored 783 points across two seasons. Both players helped, but Thornton provided the greater offensive return.

Both incoming Cavaliers had limited roles, and the pick's later rights chain did not produce Withey's NBA career in Boston. Both sides earned C+ under the inherited Even Trade verdict.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Cleveland Added Two Young Frontcourt Options

The Cavaliers acquired Semih Erden and Luke Harangody from Boston at the February 2011 deadline, sending the Celtics a future second-round pick. Cleveland wanted to examine younger reserve big men while rebuilding the roster after LeBron James's departure. Erden offered size and experience from playing in Boston, while Harangody brought energy and outside-shooting potential. Boston chose another future draft opportunity over keeping both players as the team pursued more immediate rotation options in other transactions.

Erden and Harangody Supplied Limited Cavaliers Minutes

Both players joined Cleveland and received NBA chances, but neither became a durable starting frontcourt answer for the franchise. Their earlier college profiles and brief Boston performances explained the appeal, not proof of what the Cavaliers actually obtained. The pair gave Cleveland additional depth and player evaluations during a rebuilding season. The organization eventually continued to change the frontcourt, showing that the two-player return served more as an experiment than a long-term solution.

Boston Held a Pick Later Tied to Jeff Withey

The Celtics acquired a second-round right eventually associated with the 2013 No. 39 selection used on Jeff Withey. The choice had movable draft value, but Withey's subsequent NBA minutes cannot be counted as Boston production without tracing the intervening rights transfers. Boston did not receive an active player at the 2011 deadline in this particular swap. It held a future opportunity instead, trading away two reserve players with limited immediate responsibilities on its roster.

Neither Team Gained an Enduring Centerpiece

Cleveland got two young big men to evaluate and Boston received one second-round asset. Both sides had understandable reasons for making the exchange, though neither immediate outcome became an obvious franchise success. Erden and Harangody failed to establish lasting Cavaliers roles, while the draft choice did not translate into a long-tenured incoming Celtics player. That limited realized value on both sides supports equal grades rather than inventing a major winner from a marginal deadline trade.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston earns C+ for the 2013 second-round asset later linked to No. 39 Jeff Withey, without claiming his later NBA games as Celtics production. Cleveland also gets C+ for Semih Erden and Luke Harangody, two reserve frontcourt options whose Cavaliers roles remained limited. Neither side acquired a lasting core contributor, leaving a modest tie.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Moved Daniels While Its Rotation Changed

The Celtics traded Marquis Daniels and cash to Sacramento in February 2011, receiving a conditional second-round selection tied to the 2017 draft. Daniels had been a versatile wing reserve but suffered an injury before the agreement, complicating his immediate value to another team. Boston was managing its roster during a deadline with several personnel changes. Sacramento accepted the incoming contract and financial considerations without expecting a fully healthy high-usage scorer to transform its backcourt.

Daniels Did Not Become a Kings Rotation Fixture

Daniels never established a productive Sacramento playing stint from this transaction. His prior work with Boston and other teams was part of his veteran résumé, but that reputation could not substitute for games actually played for the receiving Kings. His medical situation also limited what the club could reasonably expect upon acquiring him. Sacramento's practical benefit concerned the financial arrangement rather than a new wing who could materially change its results during the season.

The Celtics' Draft Condition Was Never Exercised

Boston's incoming 2017 second-round right did not convey, leaving no draftee to credit to this trade. The club instead gained a way to reorganize part of its bench and contractual obligations. Subsequent Celtics roster moves and any later employment of Daniels need to be treated as separate basketball events. An unexercised conditional selection has a clear recordable disposition even though it produces no on-court return, which helps distinguish this move from exchanges of completed picks.

Neither Club Received Substantial Court Production

The Kings did not acquire an active long-term wing, and Boston did not receive a draft selection that produced an incoming player. Cash and roster flexibility were the tangible benefits. That narrow outcome supports the modest difference in inherited grades rather than a claim of major strategic success for either franchise. Boston was able to move a limited-availability reserve, while Sacramento obtained financial compensation but no enduring playing contribution. The exchange was chiefly administrative.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston gets C+ for roster flexibility and a conditional 2017 second-round right that ultimately never conveyed. Sacramento receives C for Marquis Daniels and cash without gaining a meaningful Kings playing stint. Neither franchise added a durable on-court contributor, so the inherited advantage is small and grounded in contractual value.

analysis: Charlotte received Corey Maggette and the draft rights to Bismack Biyombo. Milwaukee received Stephen Jackson, Shaun Livingston, Beno Udrih and the draft rights to Tobias Harris. Sacramento received John Salmons and the draft rights to Jimmer Fredette. The transaction was built around draft-night slot movement and veteran salary, so a fair retrospective grade must follow both the rookies and the later uses of the veterans rather than treating the pick numbers as the entire story. Charlotte's return aged best because both incoming pieces created value tied directly to the deal. Biyombo became a useful defensive center during his initial Charlotte tenure, and Maggette was not merely a one-year scorer: in 2012 Charlotte moved him to Detroit for Ben Gordon and a future first-round pick. That first eventually conveyed as a top-10 selection. The combination of a long-lived rotation big, a productive veteran season and a future first produced more durable value than the announcement-day reaction suggested. Milwaukee collected the flashier four-piece package but converted it unevenly. Jackson played only part of one season before being included with Andrew Bogut in the Monta Ellis trade. Livingston was later used in another deal, and Harris plus Udrih became part of the 2013 package for J.J. Redick, Gustavo Ayon and Ish Smith. Those follow-on moves preserved some value, but Milwaukee moved Harris before his prime and did not capture his long career. Sacramento's Fredette and Salmons return supplied much less durable impact. Charlotte's Maggette-to-Gordon-and-first sequence is the clearest downstream chain because Maggette alone was the outgoing player in that 2012 exchange. Milwaukee's chains are more mixed: Jackson shared the outgoing side with Bogut, and Harris/Udrih were packaged with Doron Lamb. Those later returns count, but only proportionally; the original 2011 trade cannot be awarded the full value of Monta Ellis or Redick. That narrower attribution still favors Charlotte. Charlotte was rebuilding and needed young upside, so Biyombo plus a future value created by those assets fit its timeline. Milwaukee was attempting to remain competitive around Brandon Jennings and Andrew Bogut and preferred veteran depth with Harris as a developmental bonus. Sacramento wanted shooting and a familiar veteran in Salmons. The different timelines explain the structure, but completed value still matters: Charlotte retained the best blend of controllable youth and later draft capital. Milwaukee receives B because Jackson, Livingston, Udrih and Harris all had value, but the club did not keep Harris long enough to realize his peak and later conversions were mixed.
