golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State bought the rights to Jeremy Tyler, the No. 39 choice in the June 2011 draft, from the Charlotte Bobcats for cash. Tyler appeared in 42 Warriors games as a rookie, starting 23 with 568 minutes and 205 points; the following season he added 20 games and 63 minutes before moving to Atlanta. Warriors Win, Golden State B-, Charlotte C. Both sides received a real asset.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Charlotte Sold the Rights to a Center With an Unusual Development Path

Golden State obtained Jeremy Tyler's draft rights from the Charlotte Bobcats for cash during the June 23, 2011 NBA draft. Tyler had taken an uncommon route to the league by leaving high school early and playing abroad rather than following the standard American college path. He was selected thirty-ninth overall, meaning the investment involved second-round rights rather than a guaranteed high draft choice. Charlotte chose immediate cash while Golden State sought a young, athletic center capable of growing into an inexpensive frontcourt reserve.

Tyler Started Twenty-Three Warriors Games in His Rookie Season

The Warriors gave Tyler genuine regular-season work in 2011-12. He appeared in 42 games, started 23, played 568 minutes and scored 205 points, while grabbing 140 rebounds. He was inconsistent offensively and seldom looked like a dependable long-term starter, yet those appearances gave the club a chance to evaluate his size and activity against NBA opposition. This was not a draft selection that sat unused overseas or a prospect who never reached the active roster. Golden State obtained actual center depth during a transitional season.

The Second Warriors Season Was Much Shorter

Tyler returned for 20 Golden State appearances in 2012-13, but his playing time declined to only 63 total minutes and 22 points. He was subsequently moved to Atlanta, making his cumulative Warriors contribution 62 games, 631 minutes, 227 points and 23 starts. Tyler also played for New York later in his NBA career, but those Knicks appearances belong to a different acquisition. A source-conscious evaluation credits Golden State for the two seasons it actually employed him without pretending that every later roster opportunity was part of the original Charlotte deal.

Both Teams Got Something, but Golden State Obtained Basketball Utility

The Bobcats received cash consideration, which was a legitimate financial asset even though the amount is not established in the available transaction summaries. Golden State received a young center who logged hundreds of minutes and nearly two dozen starts. That is useful second-round production, although Tyler did not become a permanent rotation fixture for the Warriors. The older grade of D for Golden State and F for Charlotte missed both forms of return. A stronger Warriors grade follows the on-court contribution, while Charlotte deserves acknowledgment for selling a low pick without taking a new roster obligation.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State earns B- for Jeremy Tyler's 62 games, 631 minutes and 23 starts over two seasons after the cash-for-rights transaction. Charlotte earns C for a real financial return, without a player contribution. Tyler's later appearances for Atlanta and New York are excluded from Golden State's acquired production.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Converted International Rights into Immediate Backcourt Depth

Boston completed a December 9, 2011 exchange with Milwaukee, acquiring veteran guard Keyon Dooling and a conditional second-round selection for the rights to Albert Miralles. The additional pick ultimately did not convey, so the value rested on Dooling's work as a Celtics player rather than hypothetical draft capital. Boston was keeping an experienced roster supplied with secondary guards during a compressed season. Milwaukee preferred to move a reserve guard for a set of international rights, an asset it could retain without requiring an NBA roster place immediately.

Dooling Supplied Forty-Six Celtics Games

Dooling appeared in 46 regular-season games for Boston in 2011-12, logging 662 minutes and averaging 4.0 points. His role was limited behind the primary guards, but he gave the Celtics another defender and ball handler for lineups that did not call for a major offensive creator. The club advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals and could call upon its reserves as the season progressed. Dooling's previous Orlando and Milwaukee seasons aren't Boston return value; those 46 games are the direct contribution of the player acquired in this particular transaction.

The Bucks Held Rights Rather Than Obtaining NBA Rotation Minutes

Albert Miralles's rights gave Milwaukee an option involving an international big man, but the transaction never turned into a sustained Bucks playing tenure. Those rights can have organizational value because they may be retained or moved later, yet they are not equivalent to thirty or forty appearances by a rostered player. Milwaukee also surrendered a veteran whose future role with the Celtics was modest, not a star the team built around. The conditions attached to the pick moving to Boston expired without the club gaining another actual draft selection.

A Measured Advantage Favors Boston's Usable Minutes

The advantage belongs to Boston because Dooling filled a real backup role during a deep playoff season. That outcome isn't large enough to turn a minor personnel deal into a franchise-changing transaction, especially with the extra second-round pick never conveying. Milwaukee's Miralles rights had flexibility value but did not generate comparable NBA time with the Bucks. The transaction demonstrates why a rights-only return must be evaluated separately from the games played by an incoming guard. Boston received exactly the kind of modest short-term depth it sought.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B- for Keyon Dooling's 46 regular-season games and backup guard work during its 2012 Eastern Conference Finals season. Milwaukee gets C+ for Albert Miralles's international rights, which offered optionality but no comparable Bucks NBA rotation production. The conditional pick to Boston did not convey, so the result is a limited direct-use advantage rather than a major talent windfall.

perspectives.summary: New York acquired Tyson Chandler in a three-team deal for a modest outgoing package. Chandler immediately became Defensive Player of the Year and anchored the best Knicks team of the 2010s.
perspectives.analysis: Tyson Chandler was exactly the kind of complementary star the Knicks needed after acquiring Carmelo Anthony. New York received Chandler and draft rights from Dallas, sent Andy Rautins and a trade-exception mechanism to the Mavericks, and routed Ronny Turiaf, cash and a second-round pick to Washington. Chandler immediately transformed the defense, won the 2011-12 Defensive Player of the Year award, earned All-NBA recognition and became the back-line anchor of the 54-win 2012-13 team. The outgoing assets were real but modest relative to that impact, and neither partner received a player or pick that approached Chandler's value in New York. Because the move addressed a roster weakness without stripping the remaining core or premium draft capital, it stands as one of the strongest Knicks trades of the era.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Brandon Bass Arrived for Glen Davis and Von Wafer

Boston and Orlando completed a December 2011 exchange that sent Brandon Bass to the Celtics and Glen Davis plus Von Wafer to the Magic. Bass and Davis were both experienced frontcourt players but offered different offensive habits; Wafer added an additional perimeter option for Orlando. The Celtics wanted a dependable midrange and rebounding contributor capable of fitting around their older championship core. The Magic obtained a more physical interior player with an existing personality and a wing whose place in the rotation remained uncertain. There were no draft picks or contingent future protections to track in this direct player transaction.

Bass Found a Useful Role With Boston's Veterans

Bass could hit open jump shots, compete on the glass and operate within Boston's established offensive structure. His ability to supply dependable frontcourt minutes helped the Celtics maintain depth without expecting a new focal-point scorer. Those are real receiving-team contributions that can be assessed after the trade, rather than copying his earlier Orlando numbers into Boston's record. The exchange was particularly practical because the Celtics already had veterans taking most of the primary shot-creation responsibilities. Bass's skills complemented that approach and eventually gave the team more flexible combinations at power forward than simply retaining an incumbent reserve.

Orlando Took Davis's Interior Physicality and Wafer's Shooting

Davis had a recognizable track record as a Celtics rotation big man and could offer strength, screens and occasional interior offense. Wafer's arrival added a second piece, giving Orlando another choice on the wing instead of restricting the return to one player. However, neither acquisition guaranteed improvement equal to the sustained fit Bass found in Boston. Davis's previous playoff moments with the Celtics did not count as Magic accomplishments, and Wafer's existing professional history likewise needed fresh receiving-team evaluation. Orlando was trading a useful but comparatively understated forward for a package whose value depended on finding stable roles for both incoming players.

Boston's Better Fit Supports the Winning Verdict

The Celtics took the more coherent single-player return in Bass, whose scoring and rebounding worked alongside the remaining veteran core. Orlando acquired two named NBA personnel options, so the Magic were not left without compensation, but their combined value was less certain. The lack of future picks or trade exceptions keeps the transaction easy to judge from actual rotation outcomes. A Celtics-winning assessment rests on the frontcourt fit rather than treating Davis's previous Boston contributions as new Orlando value or describing Bass as an All-Star. The trade was useful for Boston precisely because the expectations were specific and attainable.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston Celtics earns B+; Orlando Magic earns C. The Celtics took the more coherent single-player return in Bass, whose scoring and rebounding worked alongside the remaining veteran core. Boston and Orlando completed a December 2011 exchange that sent Brandon Bass to the Celtics and Glen Davis plus Von Wafer to the Magic. Bass and Davis were both experienced frontcourt players but offered different offensive habits; Wafer added an additional perimeter option for Orlando. Bass could hit open jump shots, compete on the glass and operate within Boston's established offensive structure. los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers acquired Chris Paul and two second-round picks for Eric Gordon, Chris Kaman, Al-Farouq Aminu and the unprotected 2012 first that became Austin Rivers, creating the Lob City era.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis: Paul transformed the Clippers into a perennial playoff team, organized Blake Griffin and DeAndre Jordan, won the franchise's first two division titles and established sustained relevance in Los Angeles. New Orleans received a credible quantity-based package, but injuries limited Gordon, Kaman stayed briefly, Aminu's best role came later and Rivers did not become the replacement cornerstone the franchise needed. The Clippers never advanced beyond the second round during Paul's first stint, which limits the championship case, but six winning seasons and a complete organizational transformation vastly exceeded the realized return. The grades remain Clippers A-plus, New Orleans D-plus, with Clippers Win.

golden-state-warriors.summary: In December 2011 Golden State received Brandon Rush from Indiana for Lou Amundson and a 2015 second-round pick. Rush played 65 games, 1,717 minutes and scored 634 points in his first Warriors season, shooting 45.2 percent from three. A subsequent knee injury restricted his next season to two appearances. Indiana acquired a working reserve and a late second-round asset. Warriors Win, B+ versus C+.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Paid for a Wing Who Could Shoot and Defend

Golden State acquired Brandon Rush in December 2011, sending Indiana forward Lou Amundson and a future second-round draft selection. Rush was a former first-round guard-forward who had played regular minutes for the Pacers but was not essential to their plans. The Warriors valued his shooting and defensive versatility as they adjusted their backcourt rotation. Indiana received a physical rebounding forward and a future asset rather than another scoring wing. Unlike a straight player exchange, the 2015 second-round selection formed a separate component of the Pacers return.

Rush Gave the Warriors an Efficient and Busy First Season

During the shortened 2011-12 season Rush played sixty-five Warriors regular-season games and logged 1,717 minutes. He scored 634 points and made ninety-nine of 219 three-point attempts, a 45.2 percent shooting rate. He was a useful reserve who could defend multiple perimeter positions and offer outside spacing without a large number of possessions. Those totals belong to the Warriors after this specific trade, not to his prior years in Indiana. It was a genuine season-long contribution from an acquired player.

A Knee Injury Sharply Reduced the Following Year

Rush returned in 2012-13 but suffered a serious knee injury after only two regular-season appearances. That limited his initial Warriors spell to sixty-seven games across two seasons. He later played for Utah before returning to Golden State through a separate roster transaction, so it would be inaccurate to attribute his eventual later Warriors work directly to the December 2011 purchase. The significant return from this trade was his accurate perimeter shooting in the first season. The injury reduced his future value without wiping out those already-earned minutes.

Indiana Obtained an Actual Veteran and a Future Pick

Amundson supplied Indiana with physical backup frontcourt play during the same shortened season. The accompanying second-round asset later reached the 2015 draft as a very late selection associated with Luka Mitrović, rather than a proven Pacers NBA contributor. Indiana did receive something useful, so the exchange should not be evaluated as if Rush departed for nothing. Still, Golden State acquired considerably more offensive production from the 2011-12 wing than the Pacers acquired from the separate pick option and a brief reserve forward stint. The original Pacers-favored verdict was too strong.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State earns B+ for Rush’s 65-game, 634-point first Warriors season and efficient 45.2 percent three-point shooting. Indiana gets C+ for Amundson’s backup minutes and a 2015 second-round asset. Rush’s later return after a separate Utah season does not count toward the 2011 trade return, which already favors Golden State.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Golden State Bought a Late Second-Round Selection

Atlanta sent a conditional 2012 second-round choice to Golden State for cash at the March 15 deadline. The obligation concerned the less favorable of the relevant Hawks and Suns second-round positions, making the eventual draft slot dependent on the standings and prior pick rights. Golden State wanted additional chances to identify low-cost talent, while Atlanta accepted an immediate financial return. The agreement did not move a signed NBA veteran in either direction, so the eventual draft result is a better place to assess Golden State's basketball return than the date of the trade alone.

The Selection Became Center Ognjen Kuzmić

The second-round right resolved as pick No. 52, used on Ognjen Kuzmić in the 2012 draft. He later joined Golden State and appeared in regular-season games, though he did not develop into a dependable starting center. The Warriors' success during his broader time with the organization doesn't make him a driving force behind that success. His contribution was a limited developmental roster role. That was at least tangible NBA activity, but it fell short of the kind of breakthrough that would make a purchased late second-rounder a major personnel achievement.

Atlanta Took the Certainty of Cash

The Hawks received money rather than a future prospect to develop. Cash was directly valuable to the organization, but it should not be described as on-court production or conflated with the team's other 2012 draft transactions. Atlanta accepted a known return instead of holding a selection near the end of the draft where the probability of finding a durable NBA contributor was limited. The club's side of the bargain involved reducing uncertainty rather than trying to win the individual-player-development comparison.

The Outcome Remained Small for Both Franchises

Golden State produced some NBA minutes from Kuzmić, which means the pick wasn't simply wasted, but he did not become an essential part of its frontcourt. Atlanta received a guaranteed payment and avoided the commitment of scouting, signing or developing another player. The inherited Hawks advantage reflects that certain return against an underwhelming long-term pick outcome, not a claim that Atlanta acquired an NBA contributor. The C and D+ grades recognize limited consequences relative to larger roster moves around the same period.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns C for accepting cash in exchange for a late second-round choice. Golden State receives D+ after using No. 52 on Ognjen Kuzmić, who logged some Warriors minutes but never became a core center. Neither team acquired a major difference-maker; Atlanta's payment was more certain than the Warriors' modest developmental outcome.

perspectives.summary: Portland sent Gerald Wallace to the Nets for Mehmet Okur, Shawne Williams and a 2012 first-round pick protected only in the top three; the pick conveyed at No. 6 and became Damian Lillard.
perspectives.analysis: Wallace supplied Brooklyn with credible veteran wing play and later became salary in the Kevin Garnett-Paul Pierce transaction, but the Nets exposed most of the lottery while still near the bottom of the standings. Portland correctly prioritized a future asset over an aging veteran and selected Lillard, who became Rookie of the Year, a seven-time All-Star, an NBA 75 selection and the franchise’s defining player for eleven seasons. The protection structure and realized star outcome make this a decisive Trail Blazers win.

perspectives.summary: Washington received Nenê from Denver plus Brian Cook and a 2015 second-round right from the Clippers in a March 2012 three-team trade. Denver obtained JaVale McGee, Ronny Turiaf and conditional second-round consideration. Los Angeles acquired scoring guard Nick Young. Contemporary official Nuggets and Wizards releases verify all three incoming packages. The inherited Wizards Win grades Washington B+, Denver C+ and Los Angeles C.
perspectives.analysis:
Washington Pursued Nenê and a More Experienced Interior Core

The Wizards traded young center JaVale McGee and reserve Ronny Turiaf to Denver in March 2012, obtaining veteran big man Nenê in return. Nenê had been a productive and versatile Denver frontcourt contributor, offering inside scoring, rebounding, passing and positional toughness. Washington also received Brian Cook and a future second-round selection from the Clippers, assets absent from the simplified Denver-centered original. The franchise chose a more established center even though Nenê carried his own availability and contract considerations.

Denver Accepted McGee's Defensive Potential

The Nuggets took McGee and Turiaf, along with conditional second-round consideration from the Clippers that could instead settle in cash. McGee was younger than Nenê and had shown unusual athleticism and shot-blocking ability during his Washington tenure. Denver could evaluate whether its coaching staff and existing roster would help him develop a more reliable role. Turiaf supplied an additional veteran reserve big. Neither acquisition immediately guaranteed the sort of offensive polish that Nenê had demonstrated, but the move changed Denver's frontcourt timeline.

The Clippers Received Nick Young, Not an Empty Transaction

Los Angeles obtained Nick Young from the Wizards, an experienced scoring guard with the ability to generate his own shot. The Clippers gave up Brian Cook and future second-round consideration in the exchange. Their incoming player mattered: the original Denver-only archive omitted Young, inaccurately presenting Los Angeles as a team that received nothing. A contemporary Nuggets release and the Wizards' official statement independently identify Young's destination. His previous Washington shooting totals were evidence of skill rather than games already played for his new club.

The Inherited Washington Advantage Accounts for Proven Value

The model's original grades give Washington B+, Denver C+ and Los Angeles C. Nenê's established two-way frontcourt role provides a coherent reason to favor the Wizards, with extra compensation strengthening their package. Denver's decision to take a younger shot blocker was a defensible developmental bet, and the Clippers sought a current bench scorer. The separate conditional draft obligations require careful handling; naming one future second twice could falsely inflate the return. With every incoming player restored, this is a meaningful three-team comparison rather than only a center swap.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns B+ for experienced center Nenê plus Brian Cook and a Clippers-linked 2015 second-round right. Denver receives C+ for JaVale McGee, Ronny Turiaf and separate conditional draft or cash compensation. Los Angeles gets C for acquiring Nick Young as immediate perimeter scoring depth. All three clubs received real assets, and the two future second-round references must be tracked separately.

houston-rockets.summary: On March 15, 2012, the Lakers acquired Jordan Hill from Houston for Derek Fisher and Dallas's protected first-round pick. Fisher never appeared for the Rockets and was waived March 19, but Houston later included the Dallas-origin selection in its October James Harden package to Oklahoma City; the pick eventually became No. 21 Mitch McGary in 2014. Hill played 178 Lakers regular-season games across four seasons with 91 starts and 1,764 points. Lakers Win, Los Angeles B+ for direct frontcourt output and Houston B- for the consequential later use of a movable draft asset.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Los Angeles Paid a Dallas-Origin First to Replace an Aging Guard

At the March 15, 2012 deadline, the Lakers sent Derek Fisher and a protected first-round draft choice originally acquired from Dallas to Houston for Jordan Hill. The Lakers' own announcement confirmed both pieces of the return, making it inaccurate to describe the transaction as Fisher straight up for Hill. Los Angeles was simultaneously reworking its point-guard situation with Ramon Sessions arriving in a separate Cleveland deal. Hill, a former No. 8 overall selection, supplied size and rebounding behind the team's veteran frontcourt. Houston's main prize was the protected Dallas-origin choice rather than a long-term plan to use Fisher.

Hill Delivered Four Seasons of Lakers Frontcourt Minutes

Hill appeared in seven Lakers regular-season games after the 2012 trade and returned for another twenty-nine in 2012-13. His workload rose to seventy-two appearances and thirty-two starts in 2013-14, then seventy games and fifty-seven starts in 2014-15. Across those four Lakers seasons he totaled 178 regular-season appearances, ninety-one starts and 1,764 points. His rebounding gave Los Angeles a dependable inside contributor during roster turnover, and his 2014-15 season brought a career-high scoring average of 12.0 points. Those totals are specific to Los Angeles, excluding his earlier New York and Houston games and his later years with Indiana and Minnesota.

Fisher Never Played for Houston, but the First-Rounder Traveled

Fisher did not suit up for Houston. The Rockets waived him on March 19, only four days after receiving his contract, and he signed with Oklahoma City on March 21. Houston still held the protected Dallas first-round pick acquired in this deal. In October 2012 the Rockets packaged that selection with other picks and players in the much larger transaction that brought James Harden from the Thunder. The Dallas-origin choice finally conveyed in 2014 as No. 21, when Oklahoma City selected Mitch McGary. McGary was never a Rockets draft-pick development story, and Harden cannot be credited solely to this one smaller trade.

The Grade Difference Reflects Direct Production and Trade-Asset Utility

The Lakers obtained a frontcourt player who eventually started ninety-one regular-season games and scored more than seventeen hundred points for their franchise. Houston received no games from Fisher, which makes the player portion look one-sided. Yet grading the Rockets purely on Fisher's immediate departure would erase the protected first-rounder that later helped complete their Harden acquisition. The 2014 McGary pick belonged to Oklahoma City by draft night, and its contribution to a multi-piece October agreement is evidence of the asset's importance rather than proof that Houston acquired McGary. Los Angeles has the stronger direct-player return, while Houston deserves more credit than a near-failing grade for the draft asset it secured.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B+ because Jordan Hill produced 178 regular-season games, 91 starts and 1,764 points from 2012 through 2015. Houston gets B- rather than the inherited D+; Derek Fisher never played a Rockets game, but the Dallas-origin first-round selection helped form the October 2012 James Harden package. Oklahoma City ultimately drafted Mitch McGary at No. 21 in 2014, not Houston.

new-orleans-pelicans.summary: Washington acquired Emeka Okafor and Trevor Ariza from New Orleans on June 20, 2012 for Rashard Lewis and the No. 46 pick that became Darius Miller. Lewis never played for the Hornets and was waived June 30. Miller appeared in 102 games in his first New Orleans stint through 2014-15; his later 2017 return was a separate free-agent signing. Okafor played 79 Washington games and Ariza played 133 in two seasons. Wizards Win, Washington A- for starting-caliber defense and wing play, New Orleans B- for the pick and financial reset.
new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
New Orleans Sent Two Established Starters to Rework Its Books

On June 20, 2012, the New Orleans Hornets sent Emeka Okafor and Trevor Ariza to Washington in return for Rashard Lewis and the No. 46 selection in that summer's draft. The Hornets had just won the lottery and were preparing to select Anthony Davis, so moving the salaries attached to their veteran center and wing created room for a younger roster. Washington, by contrast, wanted established players who could defend alongside its developing backcourt. The transaction did not involve Davis's No. 1 selection; its draft consideration was a much later second-round pick.

Washington Received a Full Season From Okafor

Okafor made seventy-nine regular-season appearances for the Wizards in 2012-13, starting seventy-seven, playing 2,052 minutes and averaging 13.4 points with 12.1 rebounds per thirty-six minutes. His actual per-game rebounding average was 8.8, making him a sturdy interior option for Washington. A neck injury kept him off the court in 2013-14, so the center's direct Washington return ended after one season. Ariza gave the Wizards another 56 games in 2012-13, then played seventy-seven and started every appearance in 2013-14. That second year included 14.4 points per game and 40.7 percent shooting from three.

Lewis Was Waived, but Miller Became a Real Hornets Draftee

Lewis did not record an official New Orleans appearance. The team announced his release on June 30, ten days after the trade, which means his prior All-Star numbers and later Miami career were not incoming Hornets production. The No. 46 pick was used on Kentucky forward Darius Miller, who played fifty-two games as a rookie in 2012-13, forty-five in 2013-14 and five in 2014-15. Those first 102 games were direct development of the acquired selection. Miller subsequently spent time overseas and returned in 2017 under another agreement, so his later 151 New Orleans games should not inflate the immediate draft-return accounting.

A Salary Reset Could Not Equal Two Starting Contributors

The franchises received different kinds of value. New Orleans exchanged expensive established contracts for a veteran it could waive and a second-round player who served as a young reserve, which fit a rebuild around its incoming No. 1 pick. Washington obtained a dependable center for one year and a productive defensive wing for two, including Ariza's strong 2013-14 campaign. Those actual starting jobs were more than a marginal asset win. The trade therefore favors Washington even after crediting Miller's early development and the salary flexibility New Orleans pursued. Okafor's later absence still prevents an exaggerated multi-year center valuation.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns A- because Emeka Okafor started 77 games in 2012-13 and Trevor Ariza supplied 133 Wizards appearances across two seasons, with his 2013-14 shooting and defense proving especially valuable. New Orleans receives B- for contract flexibility and No. 46 selection Darius Miller, who played 102 games during his first Hornets/Pelicans stint. Rashard Lewis was waived without playing; Miller's later return followed another signing.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Danny Ferry Reassigned an Established Frontcourt Contract

The Hawks sent Marvin Williams to Utah for Devin Harris in July 2012 as part of their new front office's effort to alter an expensive roster. Williams had spent seven seasons with Atlanta after being picked second in the 2005 draft, but his production hadn't matched that draft position. Harris gave the club an experienced ball handler on a shorter contractual horizon. This was a direct swap, separate from the much larger Joe Johnson transaction announced during the same period. Atlanta wanted more room to redesign the team rather than continuing with its former starting small forward.

Harris Played a Useful One-Season Atlanta Role

Harris joined Jeff Teague in the Hawks' backcourt during 2012-13, providing secondary scoring, playmaking and a second experienced guard in varying lineups. He appeared in the postseason as Atlanta faced Indiana in the first round. The contribution wasn't franchise-defining, and Harris departed after the season, but it satisfied the need for immediate guard depth while the Hawks evaluated the shape of their next roster. The club didn't acquire an All-Star version of Harris from his earlier New Jersey years; its value came from what he actually provided in Atlanta.

Utah Got a Familiar Wing Without a Major Breakthrough

Williams gave the Jazz more size and versatility on the wing, playing in Utah across the next two seasons. His role differed from the heavy expectations of his Atlanta draft history: he could handle forward assignments and finish possessions without demanding the offense be organized around him. The Jazz didn't suddenly acquire a perennial twenty-point scorer. Utah's receiving-team output was genuine, but it also inherited the remaining financial commitment attached to a player whose ceiling had already become clearer. That made the exchange defensible without handing the Jazz the stronger overall value.

Contract Timing Tilted the Comparison Toward Atlanta

Atlanta converted Williams's longer commitment into a serviceable guard and reached the summer of 2013 with greater ability to adjust its personnel. Utah got forward minutes but less opportunity to reset its roster immediately. Harris wasn't a perfect long-term solution for the Hawks, yet he filled the desired position during a playoff season. The verdict therefore turns on Atlanta's combination of playing value and flexibility, not on Williams being unusable or Harris reproducing his peak earlier-career statistics. Both incoming veterans helped, but their contracts led the teams in different directions.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta receives B- for Devin Harris's playable 2012-13 guard season and the shorter commitment it acquired by moving Marvin Williams. Utah earns C because Williams provided real forward minutes across two seasons but didn't unlock comparable roster flexibility. This was a modest, rational personnel change, with the Hawks getting the more useful combination of role and contract timing.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Moved Its Leading Scorer in a Large Deal

The Hawks sent Joe Johnson to Brooklyn in July 2012, accepting Anthony Morrow, Jordan Farmar, Jordan Williams, DeShawn Stevenson and Johan Petro together with draft compensation. Johnson had become a multi-time All-Star in Atlanta, but his expensive contract influenced the franchise's decision to change direction. The Nets wanted an established perimeter scorer who could help a newly ambitious team compete quickly. Atlanta prioritized financial flexibility and additional ways to maneuver through future drafts instead of receiving a direct replacement of equal star power.

Johnson Gave Brooklyn Real Star-Level Minutes

Johnson became an important Nets scoring option and helped the franchise reach the playoffs in multiple seasons. His half-court creation and ability to make difficult shots gave Brooklyn a recognizable centerpiece beside other established veterans. Those Brooklyn contributions must count, even if the inherited grade for the Nets is much lower than Atlanta's. The transaction did not deliver a championship, and the financial commitment was considerable, but Johnson was not an unused acquisition. His Nets tenure is the strongest direct player return on that side.

Atlanta Received a Complicated Set of Draft Rights

The Hawks collected a protected first later linked to the 2013 No. 18 selection, swap rights in 2014 and 2015, and a second-round asset later associated with No. 31 in 2017. Some rights weren't exercised and others followed separate draft-night trades. A player's later NBA production elsewhere should not be attributed automatically to Atlanta just because a pick appeared in this package. The main organizational benefit was freeing the franchise to redirect assets and rebuild its roster around a different financial plan.

new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
New Orleans Accepted Miller and Two Future Seconds

On July 13, 2012, Minnesota transferred veteran center Brad Miller and two future second-round draft choices to the New Orleans Hornets. The return was a 2017 second-round selection with top-fifty-five protection. The pick never conveyed, which made the long-term compensation small for Minnesota, although moving Miller's remaining obligation still advanced its payroll objective. New Orleans received the rights to what would ultimately be the fifty-second selection in 2013 and the thirty-fifth selection in 2016. Those later slot identifications trace the selections, not immediate contracts with Lorenzo Brown or Rade Zagorac.

Brad Miller Was an Asset for Another Transaction, Not a Hornets Regular

Miller was nearing the end of his NBA career, and New Orleans did not obtain an extended playing contribution from him. Instead, the Hornets used him in a subsequent three-team transaction on July 27 involving the Phoenix Suns and Minnesota. That agreement moved Miller, Jerome Dyson and future pick rights while bringing Robin Lopez, Hakim Warrick and cash to New Orleans. The later deal also required additional consideration beyond what the Hornets acquired in this July 13 swap. Any Lopez games should be credited to the separate three-team agreement rather than presented as Miller's direct playing return.

The Future Picks Followed Different Downstream Paths

The 2013 second-round selection associated with Lorenzo Brown returned to Minnesota as part of the July 27 transaction, while the 2016 choice later associated with Rade Zagorac was directed into the wider three-team arrangement. Neither prospect became an immediate Hornets draft success through the July 13 exchange. That chronology prevents the original deal from receiving inflated grades based on career totals earned elsewhere. The choices were valuable primarily because New Orleans could redeploy them quickly. Minnesota, meanwhile, obtained a conditional 2017 second that did not convey, so the exchange's residual draft return was weaker than the two outgoing pick rights initially appeared.

The Hornets Had More Flexibility, but the Later Deal Had Costs

The original trade favored New Orleans because it assembled an expiring veteran contract and two second-round assets at the cost of a protected selection that ultimately delivered nothing. Minnesota reduced a salary commitment but gave up rights that would have been useful in its own future draft planning. The July 27 trade demonstrated that New Orleans could use the received pieces, though that later package had its own outgoing assets and counterparties. The judgment should neither credit the Hornets with every subsequent player's career nor call the Wolves' salary objective imaginary. A moderate New Orleans advantage best captures the original asset value without overstating the deal.

Final Verdict

Pelicans Win under the modern site label; New Orleans was still the Hornets in July 2012. analysis:
New Orleans Accepted Miller and Two Future Seconds

On July 13, 2012, Minnesota transferred veteran center Brad Miller and two future second-round draft choices to the New Orleans Hornets. The return was a 2017 second-round selection with top-fifty-five protection. The pick never conveyed, which made the long-term compensation small for Minnesota, although moving Miller's remaining obligation still advanced its payroll objective. New Orleans received the rights to what would ultimately be the fifty-second selection in 2013 and the thirty-fifth selection in 2016. Those later slot identifications trace the selections, not immediate contracts with Lorenzo Brown or Rade Zagorac.

Brad Miller Was an Asset for Another Transaction, Not a Hornets Regular

Miller was nearing the end of his NBA career, and New Orleans did not obtain an extended playing contribution from him. Instead, the Hornets used him in a subsequent three-team transaction on July 27 involving the Phoenix Suns and Minnesota. That agreement moved Miller, Jerome Dyson and future pick rights while bringing Robin Lopez, Hakim Warrick and cash to New Orleans. The later deal also required additional consideration beyond what the Hornets acquired in this July 13 swap. Any Lopez games should be credited to the separate three-team agreement rather than presented as Miller's direct playing return.

The Future Picks Followed Different Downstream Paths

The 2013 second-round selection associated with Lorenzo Brown returned to Minnesota as part of the July 27 transaction, while the 2016 choice later associated with Rade Zagorac was directed into the wider three-team arrangement. Neither prospect became an immediate Hornets draft success through the July 13 exchange. That chronology prevents the original deal from receiving inflated grades based on career totals earned elsewhere. The choices were valuable primarily because New Orleans could redeploy them quickly. Minnesota, meanwhile, obtained a conditional 2017 second that did not convey, so the exchange's residual draft return was weaker than the two outgoing pick rights initially appeared.

The Hornets Had More Flexibility, but the Later Deal Had Costs

The original trade favored New Orleans because it assembled an expiring veteran contract and two second-round assets at the cost of a protected selection that ultimately delivered nothing. Minnesota reduced a salary commitment but gave up rights that would have been useful in its own future draft planning. The July 27 trade demonstrated that New Orleans could use the received pieces, though that later package had its own outgoing assets and counterparties. The judgment should neither credit the Hornets with every subsequent player's career nor call the Wolves' salary objective imaginary. A moderate New Orleans advantage best captures the original asset value without overstating the deal.

Final Verdict

Pelicans Win under the modern site label; New Orleans was still the Hornets in July 2012. The Hornets receive B for acquiring Brad Miller's transferable contract and two future second-round choices, subsequently deployed in another deal. Minnesota gets C- for reducing an obligation, while the protected incoming 2017 second never conveyed. The 2013 pick returned to Minnesota in a later transaction, so the eventual draft names aren't automatic New Orleans player production.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Atlanta acquired Kyle Korver from Chicago on July 16, 2012, sending the Bulls cash and a trade exception. Korver became a central shooter in the Hawks' ball-movement system and earned an All-Star selection with the 60-win 2014-15 club. Atlanta's sustained on-court gain dwarfed Chicago's financial return.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Acquired an Elite Shooter for Financial Consideration

Chicago sent Kyle Korver to Atlanta on July 16, 2012, receiving cash and a trade exception instead of a player in return. The Bulls were managing their salary obligations, while the Hawks saw a chance to obtain a proven three-point specialist without surrendering a draft choice or established member of their rotation. Korver had already supplied two reliable shooting seasons in Chicago. The deal also aligned with Atlanta's broader summer of roster changes, but its compensation must be kept distinct from the separate Devin Harris and Joe Johnson trades.

Korver Became a Building Block for a Sixty-Win Offense

Korver's value in Atlanta went beyond occasional bench shooting. He became one of the defining floor spacers in coach Mike Budenholzer's motion offense, forcing defenders to track his off-ball movement and opening driving lanes for teammates. In 2014-15, he shot nearly fifty percent from three, earned an All-Star selection and helped the Hawks win sixty regular-season games. His presence was fundamental to how that roster created good looks without relying exclusively on one isolation scorer. That extended Atlanta return made the original price strikingly small.

Chicago Obtained Savings Rather Than Replacing His Production

The Bulls' return served financial and roster-planning purposes. A trade exception could assist with a future signing or transaction subject to its rules, and the cash created immediate value, but neither asset directly replaced Korver's shooting on the court. Chicago still had a strong core and its own guards and forwards, so dealing a specialist was defensible in the context of payroll decisions. What the club didn't get was another reliable wing with Korver's accuracy and movement. The difference in direct basketball output grew as Korver thrived in Atlanta.

The Long-Term Hawks Payoff Made the Outcome Decisive

The Hawks received several seasons of elite perimeter spacing, not a short-term rental. Korver became an emblem of a collective offense and a crucial part of one of the franchise's best regular seasons. Chicago acquired budget tools whose utility shouldn't be treated as nonexistent, but the gap between those tools and an All-Star shooting campaign is substantial. Atlanta achieved exactly what a smart low-cost veteran acquisition should: it found a skill that fit its system, retained it through multiple seasons and received far more competitive value than the nominal outgoing compensation implied.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns A+ for Kyle Korver's multi-season shooting impact, 2015 All-Star selection and essential role on a sixty-win team. Chicago receives D because its cash and trade exception addressed financial priorities without supplying a comparable on-court replacement. Few minor veteran trades gave the receiving franchise such an enduring and productive fit.

The Rockets received Sean Williams, E'Twaun Moore, JaJuan Johnson and a future second-round right linked to Alex Abrines; the Trail Blazers received Sasha Pavlovic and picks later tied to Jeff Withey and Marko Todorović, plus cash. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Filled a Perimeter Need With Lee

The Celtics acquired Courtney Lee in July 2012 through a multi-team sign-and-trade involving Houston and Portland. Lee had played significant NBA minutes as a capable perimeter defender and shooter. Boston wanted a reliable guard who could operate alongside established veterans as the roster shifted after an extended playoff era. Rather than obtain a draft pick, the Celtics accepted a known NBA player with a role they could define. The package required cooperation from two other franchises.

Houston Received Players and a Second-Round Right

The Rockets accepted Sean Williams, E'Twaun Moore and JaJuan Johnson, plus a 2013 second-round selection associated with No. 32 Alex Abrines. Those names offered different kinds of possible return: Moore had backcourt potential, while Williams and Johnson were frontcourt prospects still seeking consistent roles. Not all incoming players became lasting Rockets rotation contributors. The future pick provided another option to trade or draft, and Abrines's later career should be attributed to its actual rights destination rather than automatically to Houston.

Portland Added a Veteran and Additional Draft Options

The Trail Blazers received Aleksandar 'Sasha' Pavlović, second-round rights later associated with No. 39 Jeff Withey and No. 45 Marko Todorović, and cash. Portland's interests were different from Boston's immediate need for Lee: it could evaluate veteran depth and several development possibilities. Those draft numbers did not guarantee that the named players would spend their careers in Portland. The cash component supplied financial value, while the draft rights made the return broader than a single veteran.

Three Teams Evaluated Different Kinds of Assets

Boston got a guard ready for NBA minutes, Houston collected players and a future selection, and Portland obtained a veteran plus multiple draft options. The inherited slight Rockets edge assigns the highest grade to its combined return even though individual players had uncertain direct impact. Boston's C recognized Lee's useful but limited tenure, while Portland's B rewarded added draft flexibility. None of the three receiving packages should be assessed by simply counting another team's later player statistics.

Final Verdict

Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns B+ for Sean Williams, E'Twaun Moore, JaJuan Johnson and a second-round right later connected to Alex Abrines. Portland gets B for Pavlović, two additional second-round rights and cash. Boston receives C for Courtney Lee's immediate wing-guard role. Each club obtained a different kind of return, with Houston's wider package earning the inherited edge.

Cunningham gave the Wolves 161 games over 2012-13 and 2013-14, contributing 1,205 points and 738 rebounds. memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
Minnesota Opted for Defensive Frontcourt Depth

The Minnesota Timberwolves traded guard Wayne Ellington to Memphis for forward Dante Cunningham on July 24, 2012. Memphis wanted additional shooting around its paint-heavy offense and had seen Ellington develop a usable perimeter jumper during his first three seasons with Minnesota. The Timberwolves, meanwhile, sought a mobile forward who could defend, rebound and spell Kevin Love in the frontcourt. Cunningham had established himself with Memphis after earlier stints in Portland and Charlotte. This was a direct one-for-one swap with no attached pick, allowing both clubs to address different weaknesses without adding long-term contractual complexity.

Cunningham Became a Two-Year Minnesota Regular

Cunningham appeared in 80 Timberwolves games in 2012-13, scoring 695 points and grabbing 408 rebounds in 2,010 minutes. He was a regular part of the rotation even when the team was disrupted by injuries. The next season, he played 81 more games, adding 510 points and 330 rebounds over 1,635 minutes. Across his two years after the trade, that made 161 appearances, 1,205 points and 738 rebounds for Minnesota. Cunningham was not a major offensive creator, but his availability and defensive work brought exactly the kind of complementary production that Minnesota had been seeking.

Ellington Gave Memphis Half a Season of Shooting

Ellington played 40 regular-season games for the Grizzlies in 2012-13, starting four and logging 676 minutes. He scored 218 points and made 41 three-pointers, shooting 42.3 percent from beyond the arc. That percentage was genuinely valuable for a team that often leaned on interior scoring, but his minutes declined as Memphis searched for other wing combinations. The Grizzlies traded Ellington to Cleveland in January 2013, so his later 38 Cavaliers games and subsequent NBA shooting career do not count as Memphis performance from this exchange. The direct stint offered useful shooting but relatively few games.

The Wolves Collected More Value From the Same One-for-One Deal

Memphis's decision was defensible because Ellington did what a spacing specialist is supposed to do when he was on the floor. Minnesota nevertheless received a player who stayed for two seasons and logged over five times as many minutes in the receiving uniform. The contrast is not simply a comparison of a forward's rebounds with a guard's three-pointers; it is about how long each player was useful to the organization that acquired him. The Wolves turned a fringe guard into reliable frontcourt rotation coverage while Memphis viewed Ellington as movable after four months. That produces a clearer Minnesota advantage than the inherited slight edge suggested.

Final Verdict

Wolves Win. Minnesota earns A- for Dante Cunningham's 161 games, 3,645 minutes, 1,205 points and 738 rebounds across two seasons. Memphis gets C+ for Wayne Ellington's 40 games, 218 points and accurate three-point shooting before his January trade. The Wolves gained substantially more sustained roster value from the exchange.

Memphis wanted additional shooting around its paint-heavy offense and had seen Ellington develop a usable perimeter jumper during his first three seasons with Minnesota. The Timberwolves, meanwhile, sought a mobile forward who could defend, rebound and spell Kevin Love in the frontcourt. Cunningham had established himself with Memphis after earlier stints in Portland and Charlotte. This was a direct one-for-one swap with no attached pick, allowing both clubs to address different weaknesses without adding long-term contractual complexity.

Cunningham Became a Two-Year Minnesota Regular

Cunningham appeared in 80 Timberwolves games in 2012-13, scoring 695 points and grabbing 408 rebounds in 2,010 minutes. He was a regular part of the rotation even when the team was disrupted by injuries. The next season, he played 81 more games, adding 510 points and 330 rebounds over 1,635 minutes. Across his two years after the trade, that made 161 appearances, 1,205 points and 738 rebounds for Minnesota. Cunningham was not a major offensive creator, but his availability and defensive work brought exactly the kind of complementary production that Minnesota had been seeking.

Ellington Gave Memphis Half a Season of Shooting

Ellington played 40 regular-season games for the Grizzlies in 2012-13, starting four and logging 676 minutes. He scored 218 points and made 41 three-pointers, shooting 42.3 percent from beyond the arc. That percentage was genuinely valuable for a team that often leaned on interior scoring, but his minutes declined as Memphis searched for other wing combinations. The Grizzlies traded Ellington to Cleveland in January 2013, so his later 38 Cavaliers games and subsequent NBA shooting career do not count as Memphis performance from this exchange. The direct stint offered useful shooting but relatively few games.

The Wolves Collected More Value From the Same One-for-One Deal

Memphis's decision was defensible because Ellington did what a spacing specialist is supposed to do when he was on the floor. Minnesota nevertheless received a player who stayed for two seasons and logged over five times as many minutes in the receiving uniform. The contrast is not simply a comparison of a forward's rebounds with a guard's three-pointers; it is about how long each player was useful to the organization that acquired him. The Wolves turned a fringe guard into reliable frontcourt rotation coverage while Memphis viewed Ellington as movable after four months. That produces a clearer Minnesota advantage than the inherited slight edge suggested.

Final Verdict

Wolves Win. Minnesota earns A- for Dante Cunningham's 161 games, 3,645 minutes, 1,205 points and 738 rebounds across two seasons. Memphis gets C+ for Wayne Ellington's 40 games, 218 points and accurate three-point shooting before his January trade. The Wolves gained substantially more sustained roster value from the exchange.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Clippers Turned International Rights into a Guard

Los Angeles acquired veteran Willie Green from Atlanta on July 30, 2012, while sending the rights to Greek center Sofoklis Schortsanitis and trade-exception consideration the other way. Green could provide shooting and backcourt depth behind the Clippers' established ball handlers. Atlanta was managing a summer of wider roster changes and preferred financial flexibility over keeping another veteran guard. The incoming rights had an identifiable basketball prospect attached, but Schortsanitis had never established an NBA role. This made the transaction a trade between immediate playing help and organizational optionality.

Green Delivered Meaningful Minutes to the Clippers

Green became a usable rotation guard for Los Angeles across the following seasons, contributing perimeter shooting and occasional starts. The club had Chris Paul controlling the offense, so it didn't need Green to serve as a primary creator. His value came from being available for specific lineup needs while the Clippers were trying to contend in the West. Those games were a direct return from this transaction and should not be minimized. Atlanta's future flexibility was real, but the Hawks did not receive an incoming player with comparable NBA appearances.

Atlanta Held Rights Without Receiving an NBA Center

Schortsanitis had a long international résumé and was recognizable to followers of European basketball. Holding his rights nevertheless did not give Atlanta a center who actually played regular-season NBA minutes. The trade exception also had restrictions and potential future uses; it wasn't an additional player with an existing statistical record. The Hawks were entitled to view the transaction through contract and roster planning rather than immediate floor production, particularly while restructuring around younger pieces. That practical rationale explains the club's interest in moving Green even though Los Angeles obtained the only direct playing return.

The Existing Verdict Reflects Non-Playing Benefits

The canonical Slight Hawks Edge must be read narrowly because the Clippers undeniably obtained more court time from their acquired asset. Atlanta's advantage, to the extent the grade credits one, rests on trade flexibility and a low-cost international-rights option rather than a superior NBA roster contributor. Los Angeles made a useful short-term pickup without giving away a star or a prime draft selection. Neither side had a blockbuster outcome, but the comparison should make the difference between contractual utility and actual playing minutes explicit instead of claiming a fictional Schortsanitis Hawks tenure.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta receives C+ for trade-exception flexibility and Schortsanitis's international rights, though neither yielded comparable NBA minutes. The Clippers receive C because Willie Green did become a genuine reserve and occasional starter. Los Angeles enjoyed the clearer on-court payoff, while the inherited narrow Hawks advantage rests on Atlanta's financial and roster-planning interests rather than playing production.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired James Harden before his age-23 season for Kevin Martin, Jeremy Lamb and draft assets, then developed him into an MVP and the engine of eight seasons of contention.
houston-rockets.analysis: Houston correctly projected that Harden's efficiency, passing and creation would scale from a sixth-man role to a franchise offense. He won the 2018 MVP, led the Rockets to a franchise-record 65 wins and drove conference-finals runs in 2015 and 2018. Oklahoma City's return was not empty: Martin scored efficiently for one season, Lamb became a rotation player and a first-round pick produced long-term starting center Steven Adams. That useful package still fell far short of replacing a future MVP or preserving the Durant-Westbrook-Harden core. Houston's A-plus and Oklahoma City's D support an unambiguous Rockets Win.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Exchanged Two Veterans for Crawford's Scoring

The Celtics acquired Jordan Crawford from Washington at the February 21, 2013 deadline, sending Jason Collins and Leandro Barbosa to the Wizards. Barbosa had suffered a season-ending ACL injury before the trade, leaving Washington with little chance of immediately replacing Crawford's offense through him. Collins was an experienced reserve center rather than a high-volume scorer. Boston had been dealing with injury-related holes in its backcourt and wanted another player capable of creating a shot without depending entirely on its established veterans.

Crawford Offered Scoring and Later Trade Utility

Crawford could handle the ball and make difficult shots, sometimes at the expense of offensive efficiency. Boston used him through the final part of 2012-13 and into the following season, when his role expanded during the club's transition after its veteran core broke up. He didn't become the Celtics' long-term starting guard, but they were able to use him in competitive games and later include him in another transaction. That was considerably more basketball utility than Boston could have expected from retaining an injured Barbosa and a seldom-used Collins.

Washington's Return Didn't Deliver Much Immediate Offense

Washington had its own reason for moving Crawford: his shot-first approach no longer fit the guard rotation as John Wall returned from injury. Collins could add situational size and veteran guidance, but he was not acquired to replace the outgoing guard's points. Barbosa remained unavailable to play because of his knee injury, making his receiving-team production effectively zero. The trade helped the Wizards shift their roster structure and priorities, yet their return was weaker in terms of active contributors than the one Boston obtained.

The Specific Player Situations Explain the Grade Gap

A transaction involving two veterans for one scorer may look balanced by head count, but the context of those contracts changes the analysis. One Washington arrival was injured for the season; the other had a narrow reserve role. Boston actually obtained usable perimeter offense and held Crawford as an asset for later maneuvering. This wasn't a franchise-changing trade, and Crawford's inconsistent shot selection came with costs. Still, the Celtics received the clearer combination of playing minutes and future flexibility, supporting the verdict without overstating the player's ceiling.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for acquiring Jordan Crawford, whose scoring and subsequent trade utility helped a backcourt facing injuries and transition. Washington receives C for Jason Collins's limited reserve value and Leandro Barbosa's inability to play after his ACL injury. The Wizards achieved a roster reset, but the Celtics obtained the stronger direct player return.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta and Dallas Swapped Perimeter Specialists at the Deadline

At the February 21, 2013 trade deadline, the Hawks acquired Dahntay Jones from Dallas in exchange for Anthony Morrow. The swap paired a more defensive-minded wing with a player whose main appeal was his outside shooting. Atlanta sought a different perimeter role for the rest of the season, while the Mavericks wanted more three-point offense. Neither club obtained draft capital or a multi-year contingent right through the transaction. It was a direct adjustment to how bench minutes might be distributed, not a change in the league's top scoring hierarchy. Both players had established NBA experience but limited overall roster control.

Jones Gave Atlanta Defensive Wing Depth

Jones brought energy, physical perimeter defense and an ability to compete for minutes without demanding many offensive possessions. That profile could be useful beside Atlanta's primary shot creators, particularly when the team needed to protect a lead or handle an athletic opposing wing. His previous games for other franchises were scouting context rather than Atlanta performance, and the limited late-season window constrained how much the team could gain. A defender could help a rotation even without posting impressive raw scoring numbers. However, that value needed to be evaluated alongside the loss of Morrow's perimeter shooting and potential offensive spacing.

Morrow's Shooting Was Dallas's Targeted Return

Morrow had built his reputation as a long-range shooter, a skill that could create space around Dallas's established veterans. The Mavericks weren't receiving an elite all-around starter, but they acquired a player capable of making defenses respect the three-point line. His existing percentages from earlier teams provided evidence of the trait rather than guaranteed new Mavericks results. Dallas paid with Jones's defensive versatility and accepted a narrower offensive specialist. That difference gave the two clubs complementary motives: Atlanta wanted another defender, Dallas another shooter. Neither team needed the exchange to determine its entire season or franchise direction.

The Mavericks Have the Modest Advantage in Role Value

Both clubs acquired an NBA-caliber reserve, but Morrow's distinctive outside shooting supplied a clearer single offensive function to Dallas than Jones's brief defensive stint did for Atlanta. That supports the Mavericks-winning verdict in the existing record while recognizing the Hawks' legitimate desire for wing defense. This wasn't a transaction that produced a major draft pick or future team cornerstone. The best evaluation compares the incremental role each side could fill after the February deadline. Morrow's earlier years outside Dallas and Jones's earlier defensive accomplishments belong to their prior clubs, not to the respective receiving franchises.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win. Atlanta Hawks earns C+; Dallas Mavericks earns B. Both clubs acquired an NBA-caliber reserve, but Morrow's distinctive outside shooting supplied a clearer single offensive function to Dallas than Jones's brief defensive stint did for Atlanta. That supports the Mavericks-winning verdic The results assess NBA value acquired after the transaction rather than prior-player output or later rights-only careers.

golden-state-warriors.summary: On February 21, 2013, Philadelphia acquired guard Charles Jenkins and cash from Golden State in return for a protected second-round selection. Jenkins played 12 76ers games, starting once and totaling 150 minutes; the pick never conveyed. golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Used a Deadline Trade to Adjust Payroll

The Warriors sent Charles Jenkins and cash considerations to Philadelphia on February 21, 2013, in exchange for a protected second-round selection. Golden State was trying to move below the luxury-tax line while preserving the main roster that would later reach the playoffs. Jenkins had been a second-round pick in 2011 and had played a considerable number of games during his first season. Philadelphia was willing to audition another point guard for the final part of the schedule, particularly because the incoming deal also brought cash.

Jenkins Played a Dozen Games in Philadelphia

After joining the 76ers, Jenkins appeared in twelve regular-season games, with one start and 150 minutes of playing time. He averaged about two points per game, a very small offensive return even for a backup guard. His earlier 98 NBA appearances for Golden State were completed before the trade and cannot be allocated to Philadelphia. The stint did at least provide an actual NBA player to the receiving team, but Jenkins left the league for overseas basketball that summer. There was no sustained Philadelphia development success.

Golden State's Protected Pick Was Never Exercised

Contemporary coverage described the compensation as a protected second-round choice. The 2013 pick carried restrictive protection and never conveyed, according to later player-contract and trade histories. It would therefore be wrong to assign the Warriors a particular drafted player's production through this agreement. The tangible Golden State objective was financial flexibility from moving a reserve contract, even though the team also sent cash along with Jenkins. That makes the deal different from a straightforward pick-for-player exchange and explains why salary context belongs in the verdict.

Philadelphia Gained a Brief Guard Option Without a Pick Cost

Philadelphia received twelve appearances and cash while surrendering a draft obligation that did not become a selection for Golden State. That is a modest but identifiable advantage. Golden State achieved part of its payroll objective and could devote its active roster spots to other players, so an extremely punitive grade would overlook why the trade was made. Neither side added a major contributor or secured meaningful lottery compensation. The older Sixers-favored outcome holds, but the appropriate margin is modest rather than a declaration that one front office discovered a hidden star.

Final Verdict

76ers Win. Philadelphia earns C+ for Charles Jenkins's twelve NBA games, one start and 150 minutes plus incoming cash. Golden State receives C for managing its payroll even though the protected second-round choice never conveyed. The trade produced a brief backup-guard audition rather than substantial on-court value for either organization.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
A Salary-Management Deal Sent Tyler to Atlanta

The Warriors traded Jeremy Tyler to the Hawks on February 21, 2013, receiving cash and future considerations. Golden State was trying to reduce payroll obligations around the trade deadline as it built a playoff roster. Tyler was a young forward-center who had found limited opportunities behind other Golden State big men. Atlanta accepted the possibility of developing a mobile reserve at relatively low acquisition cost. The arrangement was part of the same day's roster reshuffling that also sent Charles Jenkins to Philadelphia, but the transactions involved different counterparties and must be evaluated separately.

The Hawks Gave Tyler a Single Five-Minute Game

Atlanta's official March 6 announcement is unusually precise about Tyler's direct return. He appeared once for the Hawks, on March 4 at Denver, recording three rebounds in five minutes. The Hawks then waived him. That is the entirety of his NBA playing record for Atlanta after the trade. His previous 62 games in Golden State uniforms and later appearances elsewhere cannot be added to the Hawks return. A single short appearance does not support a high player-development grade, although Atlanta had a defensible reason to inspect a young center.

The Warriors Received Financial Consideration

Golden State's team transaction register identifies cash and unspecified future considerations as the assets acquired for Tyler. The actual amount of cash and any later exercised draft choice are not established by the named entries in the imported ledger, so those should not be invented. Contemporary reporting connected the Tyler and Jenkins transactions with reducing the team's financial commitments below the luxury-tax line. That context provides a reason for the club to part with an inexpensive player without demanding another regular-season contributor in return. Roster flexibility was the intended benefit.

Measured Value Was Primarily on the Selling Side

The Hawks obtained a player they briefly tested and then released, while Golden State received some financial consideration and payroll relief. Atlanta's NBA output was one game and no scoring, which puts the incoming basketball return near the bottom of the scale. Golden State's payment cannot be converted to fictional wins, but it was a concrete reason to complete the deal. The earlier Hawks-favored judgment put too much weight on the possibility of Tyler developing rather than what Atlanta actually received. A narrowly favorable Warriors result recognizes the tangible financial benefits without overstating the stakes.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State receives C+ for cash, future consideration and financial flexibility from trading Jeremy Tyler. Atlanta gets D+ because Tyler played one Hawks regular-season game, collecting three rebounds in five minutes before his March 6 waiver. The club's earlier Tyler appearances elsewhere are not Hawks production, and no unverified later draft selection is credited to Golden State.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Sold Neto's Rights for a Later Selection

The Hawks sent the draft rights to Raul Neto to Utah in June 2013, receiving a second-round selection for 2015. Neto was a Brazilian point guard whose path to the NBA would require further development and an eventual contract. Utah was prepared to wait for a potential rotation guard, while Atlanta chose a future pick rather than hold his rights. The trade was about how each team valued an uncertain prospect, not an exchange of established NBA starters.

Neto Eventually Became an NBA Guard in Utah

Neto did not immediately join the Jazz after the rights transaction, but he later played real NBA minutes for Utah as a guard. That receiving-team production deserves acknowledgment despite the inherited lower Jazz grade. His passing and ball-handling offered reserve and occasional starting options, although he never developed into a franchise lead scorer. His later NBA career elsewhere must be treated separately from what Utah received directly from acquiring his rights.

The Atlanta Pick Carried a Later Draft Identity

Atlanta obtained the 2015 second-round asset later associated with No. 41 Pat Connaughton. As with other future selections, the trade trail and eventual holder of the rights are important before attributing the draftee's playing career to the Hawks. Connaughton's later years as an NBA wing cannot simply be transferred onto Atlanta's ledger. The original benefit for the Hawks was a movable future selection that could help complete another transaction or support a new prospect.

The Verdict Rewards Different Types of Value

Utah ultimately produced an NBA contributor from Neto's rights, while Atlanta collected a future pick that acquired a recognizable draft identity. The inherited Hawks Win favors the additional draft flexibility, although the practical return deserves a careful qualification because Neto did appear for the Jazz. Neither side received an immediate star. The correct assessment distinguishes actual Utah guard minutes from draft-rights value held by Atlanta, rather than treating eventual third-team careers as direct results of this two-team deal.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta gets B+ for acquiring the second-round right later associated with No. 41 Pat Connaughton and preserving draft flexibility, without claiming his NBA production. Utah receives C- under the inherited evaluation for Raul Neto's rights, even though he later gave the Jazz actual guard minutes. The grading favors Atlanta's movable pick but requires acknowledging Utah's genuine contributor.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Dallas Targeted Shane Larkin in a Draft-Night Deal

Atlanta acquired a multi-part package from Dallas while transferring the rights to Shane Larkin and cash during the 2013 draft. The Hawks received guard Jared Cunningham alongside the rights to Lucas Nogueira and Mike Muscala. Dallas was placing value on Larkin as a prospective young point guard. Atlanta preferred several distinct player opportunities, including a center it could develop and international or draft-rights flexibility, rather than using the incoming value on only one guard. Each incoming asset had a different path to possible NBA production.

Muscala Became the Most Durable Hawks Contributor

Muscala eventually gave Atlanta several seasons of rotation help as a frontcourt player with a developing outside shot. That long tenure became the strongest receiving-team basketball return from the package. Cunningham did not develop into a lasting Hawks guard, while Nogueira's NBA appearances came principally with Toronto after another transaction. Those Raptors minutes should not be counted as Hawks production. The Hawks nonetheless received an opportunity to develop Muscala and additional rights they could use in later deals, giving the acquired package substance beyond the initial draft-night paperwork.

Larkin's Dallas Tenure Was Brief

Larkin entered the league as a young point guard with quickness and playmaking potential, but his time with the Mavericks did not become a sustained multi-season starting opportunity. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Purchased a Late Second-Round Opportunity

Boston obtained the rights to Colorado State center Colton Iverson from Indiana on June 27, 2013, sending cash in return. The Pacers had used the fifty-third selection on Iverson, so the Celtics acquired his rights rather than a player who had already signed an NBA contract. For Boston, the appeal was a low-cost chance to assess a large college center while reworking its roster after several years of contention. Indiana could turn a late draft opportunity into an immediate payment without occupying a regular-season roster spot.

Iverson's Rights Never Became Celtics NBA Games

Iverson offered size and rebounding potential, but he did not develop into a regular-season contributor for Boston. His subsequent basketball activity took place outside the league, while the Celtics retained the capacity to evaluate his rights under the applicable rules. This distinction limits the outcome: an overseas career, a workout or a summer exhibition isn't equivalent to an NBA appearance earned through this trade. Boston received the prospect's rights, not a proven rotation center. The acquisition therefore stayed an option rather than becoming a lasting part of its frontcourt.

Indiana Received Money Rather Than a Replacement Player

The Pacers didn't receive a veteran, another selection or a rookie through this particular exchange. Their consideration was cash, which carried direct organizational value even though it could not block a shot or score a basket on the floor. Indiana still had a competitive roster, reducing the need to hold every late draft right indefinitely. Selling a second-round selection can be defensible when a club doesn't have a clear use for the player, but that decision shouldn't be reframed as an incoming player who supplied Pacers minutes.

A Small Draft Rights Deal Produced Limited Basketball Change

Neither side got a long-term NBA player directly from this transaction. Boston spent money on the prospect of developing Iverson, and Indiana accepted the payment rather than keeping his rights. The absence of a subsequent NBA Celtics role is the clearest limitation on the basketball payoff; the Pacers' financial return was more certain but less visible in game statistics. With no major player lost or acquired, the trade is best understood as a minor draft-night adjustment. The matching C+ grades reflect modest costs and narrow effects rather than equal on-court contributions.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston receives C+ for taking a low-cost look at Colton Iverson's draft rights, although they never produced Celtics regular-season minutes. Indiana also gets C+ for converting a late second-round selection into cash without losing an established player. Neither franchise obtained a meaningful basketball breakthrough from this small 2013 rights transaction.
