atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Miami Used a Future Second for Ennis's Draft Rights

The Heat obtained the rights to James Ennis III from Atlanta following the 2013 draft in return for a future second-round selection with protection conditions. The Hawks had drafted Ennis late in the second round, creating an asset they could move without committing an immediate roster place. Miami saw athleticism and energy in a developing wing who might eventually provide depth around its established stars. The transaction was a prospective-player exchange rather than a direct trade of two signed NBA veterans. Neither side was guaranteed meaningful production on draft night.

Ennis Eventually Played for Miami's Senior Team

Ennis spent time developing before becoming a Heat regular-season player in 2014-15. His athleticism and willingness to run the floor offered Miami an option on the wing, even if he didn't grow into a long-term high-usage scorer. These appearances are the key receiving-team value because they turned a late draft-right acquisition into actual NBA minutes. His later seasons with other franchises cannot all be attributed to Miami, but his Heat stint was tangible return. The waiting period is also relevant: the club did not obtain immediate 2013 NBA rotation help.

The Hawks' Future Choice Had a Separate Draft Path

Atlanta's incoming pick ultimately became the No. 46 selection in 2017, associated in the draft record with Sterling Brown. That identity alone does not mean Brown played NBA games for the Hawks. The selection and its rights later passed through other transactions, so Brown's subsequent seasons elsewhere have to remain separate from this Ennis exchange. Atlanta obtained future flexibility and could redirect the pick according to its roster needs. That was a legitimate asset, but it did not produce a receiving-team wing directly comparable with Ennis's appearances for Miami.

A Late Draft Investment Produced Real Heat Minutes

Miami's ability to turn a second-round-right purchase into a playable wing explains its advantage. Ennis was not a superstar, yet the Heat obtained something many late draft picks never provide: an actual rotation audition at the NBA level. Atlanta received a future selection it could use or move but did not reap the same direct court-time benefit. Both clubs operated within ordinary late-second-round uncertainty, and the result shouldn't be exaggerated into an essential championship-era transaction. It was a productive low-cost prospect decision for Miami.

Final Verdict

Heat Win. Miami earns B+ because James Ennis III developed into an NBA contributor during the 2014-15 Heat season. Atlanta gets C for the future protected second-round pick that eventually became the No. 46 selection in 2017. Brown's later career with other teams isn't Hawks production from this trade, leaving Miami with the clearer direct return.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Celtics Moved Three Slots Up to Select Kelly Olynyk

Boston obtained the No. 13 selection in the 2013 NBA Draft from Dallas so it could take Gonzaga big man Kelly Olynyk. The Mavericks received the rights to No. 16 choice Lucas Nogueira and two future second-round selections. Danny Ainge's interest was tied to Olynyk's unusual combination of size, outside shooting and passing vision, which offered a different frontcourt option as Boston's veteran core changed. Dallas, by contrast, was gathering draft flexibility rather than committing to a specific player at No. 13. The second-round obligations meant Boston paid more than a simple exchange of adjacent picks.

Olynyk Became a Four-Season Rotation Player

Olynyk spent four seasons in Boston and gave the Celtics a versatile reserve who could space the court and keep the ball moving. He did not become the sort of traditional dominant center that a team could build an offense around, but his skill mix had practical value in Brad Stevens's lineups. That contribution was especially visible in the deciding seventh game against Washington during the 2017 playoffs. Olynyk scored 26 points as Boston advanced to the Eastern Conference Finals, an important playoff moment that flowed directly from its acquired draft choice.

Dallas Used the Incoming Rights as Trading Inventory

Nogueira did not become a long-term Mavericks frontcourt player. Dallas moved his draft rights onward as part of another transaction involving Atlanta and the rights to Shane Larkin, so his later playing career cannot simply be credited as Mavericks production. The two future seconds made the initial package deeper, although each later draft right has to be followed separately before assigning any NBA minutes to Dallas. The original exchange provided flexibility and additional assets rather than a direct player with four consecutive Dallas seasons. Evaluating those rights as if they all developed in Dallas would exaggerate the realized return.

The Known Boston Contribution Breaks the Tie

Dallas's rationale for trading down was understandable because it obtained more selections and flexibility. However, Boston received the particular frontcourt prospect it wanted, used him for years and benefited in a decisive postseason game. The extra second-round choices were genuine costs, not bookkeeping details that disappear from the evaluation, but none independently offsets the measured on-court role Olynyk played in Boston. This is a Celtics win built on useful lineup minutes rather than superstar expectations. Nogueira's subsequent career elsewhere and Dallas's later use of his rights should be represented as separate asset movements.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for acquiring Kelly Olynyk, whose four seasons of regular frontcourt work and 26-point Game 7 in 2017 directly helped the franchise. Dallas receives C+ for Lucas Nogueira's rights and two future second-round selections, giving it options without equivalent direct playing production. The Mavericks' later rights transactions are distinct from the first exchange and shouldn't be double-counted.

golden-state-warriors.summary: Golden State took Malcolm Lee and No. 26 Andre Roberson rights from Minnesota on June 27, 2013, for its 2014 second-rounder and cash. The Warriors immediately sent Roberson to Oklahoma City for Archie Goodwin's rights plus cash and then sent Goodwin and Lee to Phoenix for No. 30 Nemanja Nedović. Nedović played 24 NBA games for Golden State. Minnesota used its 2014 No. 53 selection on Alessandro Gentile and then sold his rights to Houston for cash. The direct modest outcomes support Even Trade, C+ both.
golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Minnesota Moved Draft Rights and Malcolm Lee for a Future Pick

On June 27, 2013, Minnesota gave Golden State the rights to No. 26 first-round selection Andre Roberson and guard Malcolm Lee. The Timberwolves received the Warriors' 2014 second-round pick and cash. Roberson was a Colorado prospect, while Lee had been a Minnesota roster guard whose development was interrupted by injuries. Golden State valued the incoming rights as an asset to move again on draft night. The cash and later selection gave Minnesota resources it could use without committing to another rookie guaranteed a first-round contract. This was a draft-asset transfer, not the start of Roberson's Warriors playing career.

Two More Transactions Produced Nedović for the Warriors

Golden State immediately passed Roberson's rights to Oklahoma City in exchange for the rights to No. 29 Archie Goodwin and cash. It next moved Goodwin and Lee to Phoenix for the rights to No. 30 Nemanja Nedović. The Warriors' own media guide documents all three transactions on the same day, distinguishing the original Minnesota deal from the follow-on swaps. Nedović eventually appeared in twenty-four NBA games for Golden State during 2013-14. Roberson later established himself as a defender with Oklahoma City, but none of those Thunder games should count as Golden State return from keeping his rights.

Minnesota Turned Its Second-Round Pick Into Another Cash Deal

The 2014 second-round selection Minnesota received became No. 53, used to select Alessandro Gentile. Minnesota did not develop him into a regular Wolves rotation player. Instead, the franchise sold the rights to Houston for cash in a separate June 2014 transaction. That later move is evidence that Minnesota's original compensation was transferable; it is not evidence of Gentile playing NBA games for the Timberwolves. The 2013 agreement contained cash in addition to the draft pick, and each amount belongs to the relevant step in the trade chain. The NBA draft ledger supports both dates and the pick identity.

Modest Returns on Both Sides Support an Even Verdict

Neither club produced a lasting homegrown regular through this one transaction. Golden State's connected sequence yielded Nedović and limited NBA minutes, while Minnesota collected financial value and a second-round asset it moved again. The original strong Warriors grade would depend too heavily on Roberson's later career for Oklahoma City, where he arrived through a separate exchange. Minnesota likewise cannot claim an influential NBA player because Gentile's rights eventually bore that name. Judging the first trade by what each franchise genuinely received and could deploy supports a modest even assessment. The exact dates and intermediate assets are more informative than a winner's label alone.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Golden State receives C+ because Roberson and Malcolm Lee were exchanged again that night, ultimately yielding Nemanja Nedović and his twenty-four Warriors games. Minnesota also receives C+ for cash and the 2014 No. 53 pick, later used on Alessandro Gentile and sold for additional cash. Neither Roberson's Thunder career nor a fictional Minnesota playing contribution from Gentile is assigned to the wrong team.

new-york-knicks.analysis: The Andrea Bargnani trade was a poor use of both draft capital and roster flexibility. New York sent Steve Novak, Marcus Camby, Quentin Richardson, a 2014 second, a 2016 first-round mechanism and a 2017 second to Toronto for a player who never became the spacing or secondary scoring solution the Knicks expected. Bargnani appeared in only 71 games across two injury-filled seasons and did not provide enough rebounding, defense or availability to justify the cost. Toronto eventually benefited from the first-round structure that produced the No. 9 position in the 2016 draft, while the Knicks had already fallen out of contention. Even without pretending New York would have made the same downstream selection, a first plus additional assets for limited production is an F-level Partner Win.

houston-rockets.summary: On July 13, 2013, Houston sent Royce White, Furkan Aldemir's draft rights and cash to Philadelphia for a heavily protected 2014 second-round pick that never conveyed. Houston wanted room for its Dwight Howard signing and disposed of White's salary, while Philadelphia obtained a prospect that later gave it 41 games and nine starts in 2014-15. White did not appear in a Sixers regular-season game and was waived in October 2013. Slight 76ers Edge, Philadelphia B- for Aldemir and cash, Houston C for cap space rather than nonexistent pick production.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Moved White and Rights to Create Salary-Cap Flexibility

The July 13, 2013 exchange sent Royce White, the draft rights to Turkish big man Furkan Aldemir and cash from the Houston Rockets to Philadelphia. The 76ers offered a conditional 2014 second-round selection that would not convey if its protective terms were met. Houston was creating financial room during its pursuit of Dwight Howard, who signed as a free agent rather than arriving through this trade. White had not appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Rockets following disputes over his availability and team arrangements. Moving his guaranteed contract was a tangible financial purpose even without a player returned to Houston.

The Protected Pick Never Supplied Houston a Player

The second-round obligation eventually expired without conveying, so Houston cannot claim a drafted prospect or NBA appearances from the incoming pick. That doesn't make the transaction wholly valueless to the Rockets: eliminating salary and a difficult roster fit opened flexibility during a major free-agency period. The price was the rights to Aldemir and cash alongside White, a real resource cost that should be included in the analysis. The original failing grade treats the absent pick as proof of no benefit, ignoring the cap-management objective. Yet Houston's later Howard seasons remain the consequence of a separate signing, not direct on-court trade compensation.

Philadelphia Got Forty-One Games From Aldemir, None From White

Philadelphia waived White in October 2013 before he played an NBA regular-season game for the franchise. Aldemir's contribution arrived later: the Sixers signed him in December 2014, and he appeared in forty-one games during 2014-15. He started nine times, totaled 540 minutes and scored ninety-three points while averaging 4.3 rebounds. That is a modest but measurable return for the overseas draft rights the team acquired in 2013. The Sixers did not receive a future first-round pick or immediate rotation cornerstone, and White's eventual professional stops elsewhere cannot be used to improve their trade grade.

Short-Term Financial Goals and Later Reserve Minutes Both Count

Houston exchanged prospect rights and cash to clear an unwanted contract, while Philadelphia accepted the risk and collected a young player's rights with no effective draft-pick payment. Aldemir's later NBA minutes make the Sixers' side the stronger tangible basketball return, though his single 41-game season doesn't justify star-level grading. Houston still advanced a reasonable salary-cap objective when pursuing a major free agent. The separation between those two forms of value matters: the Rockets' protected second never arrived, and the 76ers' Royce White asset never produced court time. A modest Philadelphia edge recognizes actual reserve appearances without dismissing Houston's financial outcome.

Final Verdict

Slight 76ers Edge. Philadelphia earns B- because Furkan Aldemir eventually played 41 Sixers games and made nine starts, and the team also received cash; Royce White was waived without an NBA appearance. Houston gets C for removing White's contract during its free-agency planning even though the incoming conditional 2014 second-round pick never conveyed. Dwight Howard signed separately, so his Houston career isn't a direct player return from this trade.

memphis-grizzlies.summary: On July 22, 2013, Dallas sent the rights to point guard Nick Calathes to Memphis in exchange for removal of the protection on a 2016 second-round pick previously owed by the Grizzlies. Calathes signed with Memphis and played 71 games in 2013-14 and 58 more in 2014-15, totalling 129 regular-season appearances and 590 points. Dallas improved the certainty of collecting a future second but acquired no immediate rotation player. The measurable return favors Memphis, B+, while Dallas receives C+ for its draft-asset protection adjustment.
memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
Memphis Purchased Rights to Calathes by Changing a Pick Obligation

The July 22, 2013 transaction brought Nick Calathes's NBA rights from Dallas to Memphis. The Grizzlies did not send the Mavericks an existing rotation player or a newly issued first-round selection. Instead, they lifted the protection on a 2016 second-round choice already owed to Dallas through an earlier chain involving Denver. Dallas thereby improved the certainty of receiving a lower-value draft asset, while Memphis acquired a guard who had been playing professionally overseas since being drafted in 2009. The trade has to be evaluated as an exchange of draft rights and protection terms, not as an ordinary swap of two signed players.

Calathes Converted His Rights Into Two Actual NBA Seasons

Memphis signed Calathes in August 2013, and he appeared in seventy-one regular-season games as a rookie during 2013-14. He made seven starts and scored 347 points. The following season he played fifty-eight more games, adding 243 points. His direct Memphis tenure therefore yielded 129 appearances and 590 points before he returned to European basketball. The Grizzlies' official media guide confirms both seasonal lines and identifies the Dallas transaction as the way his rights arrived. Those numbers offer a firmer valuation than speculation about what an unprotected second might eventually become, and they cannot be awarded to Dallas.

Dallas Secured the Value of an Existing Second-Round Claim

Dallas entered the arrangement already entitled to a conditional 2016 second-round selection, with restrictions that could have prevented the pick from conveying. Memphis removed the top-fifty-five protection, converting the obligation into one less vulnerable to disappearing because of draft position. That is a legitimate form of compensation: draft certainty has value even when a club does not receive a player. The Mavericks did not receive Calathes's later NBA minutes, and the protection adjustment should not be mistaken for the transfer of a lottery pick. The earlier transaction that created the debt also needs to remain distinct from this July 2013 negotiation.

A Real Two-Year Reserve Outweighs the Pick-Term Adjustment

Both franchises achieved something they wanted. Dallas obtained stronger rights to a future selection, while Memphis turned a conditional obligation into an NBA-ready guard. With hindsight, Calathes's 129 Grizzlies appearances made the latter outcome more substantial than the modest pick-protection benefit can demonstrate on its own. The original Mavericks-winning result undervalued the actual basketball return and relied too heavily on the abstract importance of an unprotected future pick. Memphis did not obtain an All-Star, and Dallas did not give away a proven NBA veteran. More moderate grades recognize a credible reserve contributor on one side and useful draft certainty on the other.

Final Verdict

Grizzlies Win. Memphis earns B+ because Nick Calathes produced 129 games and 590 points across 2013-14 and 2014-15 after the club acquired his rights. Dallas receives C+ for removal of top-fifty-five protection on a previously owed 2016 second-round pick, strengthening a future draft claim without adding immediate playing time. The July 2013 exchange involved rights and protection terms, not a first-round selection or Calathes's already completed NBA service.

boston-celtics.summary: Boston and Memphis exchanged Donte Greene and Fab Melo in August 2013. Greene never established a regular-season Celtics role, while the Grizzlies waived Melo without a substantive Memphis playing tenure. Both clubs exchanged fringe center/forward opportunities but received almost no on-court result. Even Trade, C+ for both.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston and Memphis Swapped Two Fringe Roster Bets

Boston sent Fab Melo to Memphis in exchange for Donte Greene in August 2013. Melo had been drafted in the first round one year earlier, but his NBA opportunities were already limited. Greene was a forward with several seasons of Sacramento experience, yet he was also trying to establish the next stage of his career. The transaction took place while the Celtics were reshuffling their roster after the departure of major veterans, and Memphis could explore a younger center without sacrificing one of its established rotation players.

Greene Never Turned the Deal Into Celtics Production

Greene's prior NBA appearances were mostly with Sacramento, not Boston. Although that experience gave the Celtics a reason to assess him, he never became a lasting regular-season contributor through this exchange. The value of acquiring an NBA veteran shouldn't be measured by carrying across statistics from teams he had left. Boston's practical benefit was limited to roster evaluation and flexibility as it continued moving away from its previous championship-era core. For a franchise that needed more dependable players, the trade did not solve an immediate on-court need.

Melo Was an Unfulfilled Grizzlies Development Attempt

Memphis acquired a large developmental center rather than an established interior starter. Melo had shown some shot-blocking traits but remained raw, and the Grizzlies moved on without gaining a substantive NBA tenure from him. His earlier games in a Celtics uniform belong to Boston's pre-trade history and are not Memphis receiving-team production. The organization may have considered the trade a chance to take a look at a recent first-round selection, but that opportunity did not turn into a persistent backup-center role.

The Result Was Smaller Than Either Player's Résumé Suggested

Both players brought recognizable professional histories, but those records should not obscure the limited returns in their new organizations. Boston did not secure reliable forward minutes from Greene, and Memphis did not develop Melo into a regular. Neither side was giving away a player who later became a major star for the other club, and the bargain carried relatively little lasting cost. An Even Trade grade recognizes the symmetry of two unsuccessful roster auditions. It is not a claim that either team transformed its depth with this minor summer move.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston and Memphis each receive C+ because the Donte Greene–Fab Melo exchange amounted to a short-lived roster evaluation, not a productive NBA acquisition for either side. Greene's Sacramento career and Melo's earlier Boston appearances can't be counted as incoming contributions. Neither franchise extracted a lasting basketball advantage from the transaction.

perspectives.summary: On December 9, 2013, Toronto acquired John Salmons; Greivis Vasquez; Patrick Patterson; Chuck Hayes from Sacramento Kings in exchange for Rudy Gay; Aaron Gray; Quincy Acy.
perspectives.analysis: On December 9, 2013, Toronto acquired John Salmons, Greivis Vasquez and Patrick Patterson from Sacramento Kings in exchange for Rudy Gay, Aaron Gray and Quincy Acy. Patrick Patterson, Greivis Vasquez and the supporting veterans helped launch a sustained winning era, while Sacramento's Rudy Gay package did not create comparable team value.

summary: Raptors Win: The deal is a classic example of a trade where the team receiving the famous scorer did not necessarily receive the better total package. Gay was good in Sacramento, so the Kings deserve a positive grade. Toronto improved its chemistry, added useful depth and later converted Vasquez into assets that helped define the franchise's next era. That cumulative value makes the Raptors the winner.
analysis: Toronto's direct basketball response was immediate. The Raptors surged after the trade, won the Atlantic Division and began a multi-year run of playoff appearances. Patterson became a dependable reserve forward, Hayes supplied veteran interior minutes and Vasquez handled backup creation. Salmons was later moved in another transaction, preserving additional flexibility. Sacramento also received real value. Gay averaged around 20 points per game across multiple seasons, gave Cousins a credible scoring partner and re-signed on terms that avoided an immediate asset loss. The Kings did not make the playoffs, however, and Gay eventually left in free agency after an Achilles injury, so the acquisition did not create a durable team-level breakthrough or a major outgoing return. Vasquez created the most important downstream value for Toronto. In 2015 the Raptors traded him to Milwaukee for the draft rights to Norman Powell and a future first-round pick that became OG Anunoby. That direct asset conversion significantly expands Toronto's return because both players later became high-level contributors. The chain is directly tied from a player acquired in this deal, not a hypothetical draft choice.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Chose Draft Flexibility Over Crawford's Scoring

The Celtics traded Jordan Crawford and MarShon Brooks to Golden State on January 15, 2014, accepting Joel Anthony, draft consideration and cash from Miami. Crawford had provided usable offense during an injury-affected season, but Boston was developing a longer-term roster and chose to turn two perimeter contracts into several future options. Anthony was an experienced reserve center who had played on Miami championship teams, yet his on-court role in Boston was secondary to the draft rights obtained alongside him.

The Protected Selection Ultimately Became Two Seconds

Part of Miami's compensation was a Philadelphia-origin protected first-round right that later converted into second-round selections. Those were associated with No. 33 Jordan Mickey in 2015 and No. 31 Deyonta Davis in 2016. Miami also sent a separate 2016 second tied to No. 51 Ben Bentil. The historic ledger should identify all three as second-round outcomes rather than misleadingly calling Mickey and Davis first-round selections. The rights may have moved again, so a named draftee doesn't establish a full Celtics playing career.

Golden State Took Two Guards While Miami Added Douglas

Golden State acquired Crawford and Brooks for backcourt and wing depth around its established offense. Crawford offered immediate shot creation; Brooks was a developmental scoring option whose place in the rotation was less certain. The Heat received Toney Douglas from Golden State, a meaningful incoming guard who had been omitted from the previous Boston-only asset record. Miami's aim included roster and tax flexibility, with Anthony's salary leaving the books. Neither receiving team obtained a proven new long-term franchise star through the agreement.

The Celtics Received the Wider Collection of Future Choices

The inherited Boston B+ rewards the conversion of two relatively short-term guard assets into a reserve center, cash and multiple draft rights. Golden State's B reflects Crawford's immediate perimeter utility, while Miami's C- corresponds with Douglas and financial considerations. These choices were made on different competitive timelines: Boston could hold or use selections, while the other two teams sought near-term roster changes. The corrected Miami incoming player and the second-round classifications make this three-party comparison more faithful to the real transaction.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B+ for Joel Anthony, cash and the rights eventually associated with second-round picks Jordan Mickey, Deyonta Davis and Ben Bentil. Golden State receives B for adding Jordan Crawford and MarShon Brooks. Miami gets C- for Toney Douglas and improved roster flexibility. The Celtics acquired the broadest future package without actually receiving first-round players through the converted pick.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: On February 20, 2014, Los Angeles traded Antawn Jamison and cash to Atlanta for the draft rights to Turkish guard Cenk Akyol. Atlanta waived Jamison the next day before any Hawks regular-season appearance. Akyol, a 2005 second-round selection whose rights the Clippers acquired, never logged an NBA game for Los Angeles. Hawks Win narrowly, Atlanta C+ for cash received, Clippers D+ for unexercised overseas rights and flexibility.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
Los Angeles Exchanged a Veteran for Unused International Rights

On February 20, 2014, the Clippers sent Antawn Jamison and cash to Atlanta for the draft rights to Cenk Akyol, a Turkish guard picked in the second round in 2005. The Clippers' official deadline announcement identified Akyol as an international prospect already playing professionally in Turkey. Jamison, a veteran former All-Star, had appeared in 22 Clippers games during the first part of the season. By moving him, Los Angeles was managing a roster role it no longer needed while acquiring a rights asset that would not require an immediate NBA contract.

Atlanta Released Jamison the Day After the Transaction

The Hawks did not obtain Jamison as an active rotation veteran. Their transaction archive records his waiver on February 21, one day after the trade. As a result he never played an Atlanta regular-season NBA game. Jamison's earlier Clippers scoring and his substantial accomplishments with Golden State, Dallas, Washington and Cleveland belong to those clubs, not to the receiving Hawks. The principal documented Atlanta return was therefore the cash included in the exchange, not the former twenty-point scorer's career totals. This distinction is essential to grading the small deadline arrangement fairly.

Akyol's Draft Rights Did Not Become Clippers Minutes

Akyol was the 59th selection in the 2005 draft and had played in the Turkish professional league rather than signing with Atlanta. Los Angeles obtained those dormant NBA rights in February 2014, but he never joined the Clippers for a regular-season NBA game. His overseas numbers and competitions are not NBA points earned for the Los Angeles franchise. The rights still represented a negotiable asset with theoretical value, and the deal could free roster room for other moves. Neither possibility demonstrates that the Clippers obtained a regular-season player from Akyol.

A Cash Receipt Provides the Small Atlanta Advantage

Both teams were solving roster problems rather than pursuing a marquee star. Atlanta agreed to take Jamison's contract and immediately waived him, receiving cash consideration as part of the exchange. Los Angeles moved a little-used veteran and acquired a foreign prospect whose rights were never exercised into a Clippers playing career. Without a documented dollar figure or a player tied solely to the money, Atlanta's return should not be exaggerated. Nevertheless, it acquired a realized payment, while the Clippers' direct playing return from Akyol was zero. The inherited Hawks-favored verdict is defensible with modest grades.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns C+ for cash received when it acquired and promptly waived Antawn Jamison, who played no Hawks regular-season games. Los Angeles gets D+ because the rights to Cenk Akyol never produced a Clippers NBA appearance, despite offering a limited speculative asset. This was a minor financial and roster-management transaction rather than a major basketball win.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Milwaukee Traded Patterson's Draft Rights for a Future Second

The Bucks used No. 48 in the 2014 draft on Lamar Patterson but moved his rights to Atlanta in return for a 2015 second-round selection. Milwaukee preferred future flexibility instead of holding Patterson's rights while deciding whether to bring him over. Atlanta took a developmental wing with college scoring and passing skills, betting that a low second-round choice could become a usable reserve. The recorded trade date follows the draft-night rights activity, and the precise player and pick directions matter because the 2015 selection did not remain in Milwaukee's possession indefinitely.

Patterson Eventually Played Thirty-Five Hawks Games

Patterson appeared in 35 regular-season games for Atlanta in 2015-16, averaging 2.4 points in a small role, and also saw brief playoff action. The Hawks therefore obtained an actual player from the rights they acquired, although he never became the kind of durable wing who could reshape the rotation. His Atlanta contribution took time to arrive, reflecting the gap between acquiring rights and using the player on an NBA roster. Thirty-five games were real value from a late second-round swing, but the minutes and production don't support treating the pick as a major talent discovery.

Milwaukee Used the Future Pick in a Different Deal

The Bucks traded their incoming 2015 second-round pick onward with another selection in the transaction that brought Jason Kidd to Milwaukee as head coach. The pick eventually became No. 41 in 2015, associated with Pat Connaughton, but it would be misleading to claim this 2014 Hawks exchange directly supplied Connaughton as a Bucks player. His eventual return to Milwaukee came through a later free-agent signing. The draft right's role as part of a subsequent coaching transaction is the actual utility Milwaukee obtained from this original deal. Pick provenance matters more here than a later name in the ledger.

The Verdict Depends on Asset Use, Not Retroactive Player Credit

Milwaukee's grade recognizes that the future second became movable draft inventory in an important organizational transaction. Atlanta secured a reserve with modest NBA appearances, not a lasting starter. Neither side should receive an invented multi-season Connaughton playing return from the 2014 rights swap; those later events involved other transactions and contractual decisions. The Bucks' decision to move Patterson's rights offered them flexibility as they assembled a new coaching and roster plan. Atlanta got a usable but limited prospect, supporting a measured rather than definitive victory analysis.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns A for the 2015 second-round asset it subsequently used in a separate transaction associated with hiring Jason Kidd; Atlanta receives C- for Lamar Patterson's 35 regular-season games and limited development as a Hawks reserve. The 2015 pick later carried Pat Connaughton's draft identity, but his eventual Bucks career began through free agency and must not be attributed directly to this rights trade.

houston-rockets.summary: Minnesota selected Italian forward Alessandro Gentile No. 53 in the June 26, 2014 NBA draft and sent his rights to Houston for cash. Gentile was an accomplished Italian national-team player and Milan standout, but never appeared in a regular-season NBA game for Houston. The Timberwolves obtained the immediate cash payment; the Rockets acquired a speculative international draft stash with no realized NBA minutes. Wolves Win, Minnesota C+, Houston D+.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Minnesota Converted the No. 53 Draft Pick Into Cash

The Timberwolves selected Alessandro Gentile of Italy with the 53rd overall pick in the June 26, 2014 NBA draft and traded his rights to the Houston Rockets for cash. Minnesota's transaction register and Houston's own media guide both confirm the direction of the exchange. Gentile was a promising young wing who had already shown a combination of physical strength and playmaking ability in Italy. Houston saw him as an overseas asset it could possibly sign later. Minnesota preferred an immediate financial payment rather than carrying a long-range rights position with an uncertain NBA timeline.

Gentile's 2014 Success Was Real but Wasn't Houston Production

Gentile helped Olimpia Milano win Italy's championship around the time of the draft. FIBA reported on his prominent role and his reaction to having his rights acquired by Houston. He continued his career in European basketball and with the Italian national team, but did not join the Rockets for an NBA regular season. It is tempting to treat his professional success abroad as proof that Houston secured a productive rotation player; that would confuse leagues and clubs. His draft rights had possible future value, while Houston's actual NBA statistical return from Gentile remained zero games.

Houston Held International Rights Rather Than a Roster Spot

The Rockets' 2016-17 media guide listed Gentile among the organization's international rights players. That archival detail shows the club still viewed him as an asset after the initial draft night, even though he was not taking minutes away from Houston's NBA rotation. The roster was being built around James Harden and its immediate competitive needs, so buying an overseas prospect for cash was a relatively inexpensive option. The downside was that the organization could wait without ever receiving player minutes. Gentile's league accomplishments in Milan and elsewhere were not convertible into Houston points or rebounds.

The Teams Received Different Kinds of Low-Stakes Value

For Minnesota, cash was guaranteed at the time of the swap. Houston obtained the chance that Gentile might cross the Atlantic and become a useful NBA forward, a possibility that did not materialize during the club's period holding his rights. Neither side surrendered a first-round player or a central starter, and the public transaction records do not establish a large payment that justifies an exceptional Timberwolves grade. The favorable Minnesota verdict remains defensible as a realized-versus-speculative comparison, but the appropriate difference is modest. An unknown cash amount is not evidence of a franchise-altering return.

Final Verdict

Wolves Win. Minnesota receives C+ for immediate cash on the 2014 No. 53 selection, a certain financial outcome. Houston earns D+ because Alessandro Gentile's rights remained a speculative international asset and did not result in regular-season Rockets appearances. His successful European career supports the scouting rationale but cannot be credited as NBA production for the franchise.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana drafted French forward Louis Labeyrie No. 57 in 2014 and sold his draft rights to New York for cash, with the transaction recorded June 27 following the June 26 draft. Labeyrie maintained a substantial European professional career but never appeared in an NBA regular-season game for the Knicks. Pacers Win on realized return, Indiana C+, New York D+; the earlier Knicks B grade lacked an on-court basis.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
The Pacers Used a Late Draft Pick as a Cash Asset

Indiana selected French forward Louis Labeyrie at No. 57 in the June 26, 2014 NBA draft and agreed to transfer his rights to the New York Knicks for cash considerations. Indiana's transaction ledger dates the formal trade June 27, one day after the selection, which clarifies why draft-night summaries can display a different date. The Pacers already had an established playoff roster and were not committing a guaranteed rotation position to a late international prospect. New York accepted the option of negotiating with a developing French forward instead of paying for a proven NBA veteran.

Labeyrie's Professional Work Remained Outside the Knicks

Labeyrie enjoyed a legitimate professional career in France and European competition, establishing himself as a mobile power forward with rebounding and interior scoring skills. The Knicks retained interest in his rights at different points, but he never appeared in a New York regular-season NBA game. His accomplishments in Paris, Strasbourg, Valencia or other professional settings remain player achievements, not recorded Knicks wins, points or rebounds. For this trade, the question is whether the international draft option produced a usable NBA player for the organization that acquired it.

Indiana Collected a Guaranteed Return Without Waiting

The Pacers received cash when they sold the pick's rights, avoiding the expense and uncertainty of tracking a prospect who might never enter the NBA. The public records confirm the kind of consideration, not a dollar figure that would justify ranking this deal among the franchise's greatest financial wins. Indiana cannot claim any NBA games from Labeyrie, because it no longer owned the rights after the transaction. The value it received was straightforward payment for a second-round position that otherwise could have remained a non-roster investment for several years.

A Good International Prospect Does Not Equal Knicks Production

New York's reasoning was understandable. At No. 57, an overseas forward with European experience offered a reasonable developmental gamble, particularly because the rights need not consume an NBA roster place. The payoff never reached the Knicks' regular-season rotation. That makes the inherited Knicks-win grade of B misleading if it implies actual acquired basketball production. Indiana received immediate cash, while New York held speculative rights without on-court realization. The relative advantage is modest, not a dramatic failure of the Knicks' talent evaluation or a high-value sporting triumph for the Pacers.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win. Indiana earns C+ for obtaining immediate cash from the No. 57 selection in 2014. New York earns D+ because Louis Labeyrie never played a Knicks regular-season NBA game, although his international career supplied some reason for the gamble. The earlier Knicks B assessment was not supported by receiving-team playing production.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Raptors Obtained a Scoring Guard and Center Prospect

Toronto acquired Lou Williams and the rights to Lucas Nogueira from Atlanta on June 30, 2014, while sending the Hawks veteran John Salmons and a 2015 second-round choice. Williams offered precisely the type of second-unit scoring that Toronto needed beside Kyle Lowry and DeMar DeRozan. Nogueira, meanwhile, gave the franchise a developmental center whose rights could be held and evaluated over multiple seasons. Atlanta was rearranging its roster around a different mix of guards and forwards, with Salmons and future draft compensation providing flexibility rather than an immediate replacement for Williams's shot creation.

Williams Delivered an Award-Winning Toronto Season

Williams flourished as a reserve scorer with Toronto in 2014-15, providing instant offense and winning the NBA Sixth Man of the Year award. The Raptors reached the playoffs, and the veteran guard's offensive bursts were important when the starting unit needed relief. The successful season didn't turn into a lengthy Williams tenure in Toronto; he left in free agency afterward. Even so, the award and his contribution were concrete returns for the team that received him, unlike estimates based on earlier Atlanta statistics. Toronto acquired a player whose particular skill fitted an immediate roster need.

Nogueira Added Depth While Atlanta Released Salmons

Nogueira eventually appeared in Raptors games and remained an athletic reserve with rim-protection potential. His offensive limitations prevented a major breakout, yet his multi-year presence added value beyond the Williams rental. Salmons, Atlanta's incoming veteran, did not become a Hawks rotation fixture because the club waived him soon after the transaction. The second-round pick ultimately associated with Marcus Eriksson supplied a future asset, but that draft identity must be distinguished from any NBA games actually played for Atlanta. The player return was far more compelling on Toronto's side.

The Bench-Scoring Payoff Justified the Deal

Toronto acquired a Sixth Man of the Year and a prospective reserve center for a player the Hawks did not retain and a later second-round selection. That is a strong basketball outcome for the Raptors even though the team did not enjoy a deep playoff run that spring. Atlanta's financial flexibility and extra draft right had some utility, but neither replaced Williams's production. The contrast also explains why this should be evaluated as a Toronto win rather than a mutually beneficial short-term reshuffle with equal court contributions. The key outcomes were rooted in the receiving franchises.

Final Verdict

Raptors Win. Toronto earns A- for Lou Williams's Sixth Man of the Year season and the additional development opportunity with Lucas Nogueira. Atlanta gets C- for John Salmons, whom it waived, and a 2015 second-round choice associated with Marcus Eriksson. The Toronto backcourt received immediate, award-winning offense that the Hawks' compensation couldn't match.

Brooklyn received Jarrett Jack and Sergey Karasev from Cleveland, while the Cavaliers acquired overseas draft rights to Edin Bavčić and İlkan Karaman alongside a conditional second. The inherited Cavaliers Win grades Cleveland A, Boston B+ and Brooklyn C-. The missing Nets and Cavaliers incoming assets have been restored from the official transaction ledger.

boston-celtics.summary: Boston acquired Tyler Zeller, Marcus Thornton and a future first-round right in a July 2014 three-club transaction. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Collected a Center, a Guard and a First

The Celtics acquired Tyler Zeller from Cleveland and Marcus Thornton from Brooklyn in July 2014, together with a protected future first-round selection from the Cavaliers. Boston could use Zeller as an interior rotation option and Thornton as a perimeter scorer while retaining another path to a future draft prospect. The deal made use of roster and trade-exception flexibility that Boston had accumulated through earlier decisions. The incoming first later became associated with No. 28 Skal Labissière in 2016, but the rights required their own subsequent history.

Brooklyn Received Jack and Karasev

The Nets added Jarrett Jack and Sergey Karasev from Cleveland, a pair omitted from the earlier Boston-only transaction import. Jack had experience directing offenses and supplying guard scoring, while Karasev was a younger wing whose professional role was still developing. Their acquisition gave Brooklyn actual players to evaluate rather than merely clearing a contract for another team. The franchise had to decide how much each could contribute within its current roster rather than assume their previous Cavaliers minutes would transfer unchanged.

Cleveland Reworked the Books and Took Overseas Rights

The Cavaliers sent Zeller, Jack, Karasev and the future first-round right out as part of an offseason roster strategy. Cleveland obtained rights to Edin Bavčić and İlkan Karaman from Brooklyn, plus a heavily protected future second-round consideration from Boston. Those rights weren't equivalent to two proven NBA starters and did not automatically become Cavaliers game appearances. The larger purpose was gaining flexibility during an important period of free-agent roster reconstruction. Financial room was an important part of the motivation, although the inbound overseas assets were legitimate records.

The Original High Cavaliers Grade Requires Explanation

The inherited Cavaliers A favors its flexibility and restructuring possibilities over a direct comparison of player box-score results. Boston earns B+ for recognizable frontcourt and guard help plus a first, while Brooklyn receives C- for Jack and Karasev. The grades don't mean Cleveland obtained a better immediate scoring player than Boston; they reflect the broader strategic context in which it chose to shed contracts. The corrected complete three-team ledger makes that distinction clear rather than inventing a player return for the Cavaliers.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives A under the inherited evaluation for salary and roster flexibility, overseas rights to Edin Bavčić and İlkan Karaman and a protected second. Boston earns B+ for Tyler Zeller, Marcus Thornton and a first-round selection. Brooklyn gets C- for Jarrett Jack and Sergey Karasev. The Cavaliers' high grade reflects financial strategy, not imagined NBA minutes from overseas prospects.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Turned a Sign-and-Trade into a Defensive Addition

Atlanta acquired Thabo Sefolosha through a July 2014 sign-and-trade with Oklahoma City, also receiving the rights to Giorgos Printezis and cash. The Thunder took the rights to Sofoklis Schortsanitis and a trade exception. This structure made the move more than a simple free-agent signature while leaving its actual basketball value heavily dependent on Sefolosha. The Hawks were building a lineup that could defend opposing wings and move the ball around multiple contributors. The Thunder accepted rights and roster flexibility after years of using Sefolosha as a starting-caliber perimeter defender.

Sefolosha Gave the Hawks Real Defensive Rotation Work

Sefolosha joined an Atlanta team that won 60 games in 2014-15 and reached the Eastern Conference Finals. His perimeter defense and willingness to play without heavy shot volume complemented a group built around Jeff Teague, Paul Millsap and Al Horford. His season was interrupted by an off-court injury, limiting his playoff availability during that run, so he should not receive credit for playing in the conference finals he missed. But his earlier Hawks minutes and his subsequent seasons with Atlanta created a much longer receiving-team return than an unused international draft right.

The Thunder Acquired Rights Instead of an NBA Replacement

Schortsanitis was a highly recognizable international center, yet holding his NBA rights did not produce an Oklahoma City rotation player who could directly replace Sefolosha. The trade exception offered the Thunder a separate avenue for managing the roster and later transactions, but should not be written up as an incoming player who already scored NBA points. Atlanta's Printezis rights and cash likewise contributed less to its on-court product than Sefolosha's signed contract. Keeping those categories distinct prevents an international rights exchange from appearing equal to an experienced wing who actually filled NBA minutes.

The Multi-Year Atlanta Wing Return Decides the Verdict

Atlanta converted a complicated rights-and-cash package into a proven wing who could defend and occupy minutes for multiple seasons. Oklahoma City's compensation retained potential business utility, and a sign-and-trade can serve financial goals that aren't visible in a box score. Nonetheless, the Hawks had more direct basketball value from the transaction, especially given Sefolosha's contribution to a team that became a top seed in the East. This evaluation doesn't rely on claiming the Hawks acquired Schortsanitis or that an overseas career instantly became Thunder NBA production. The enduring playable wing makes Atlanta the winner.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ because Thabo Sefolosha provided real defensive wing minutes across multiple seasons, beginning with the 60-win 2014-15 campaign. Oklahoma City receives C for Schortsanitis's international rights and trade-exception flexibility, which did not yield a comparable direct on-court player from the exchange. Printezis's rights and cash helped complete the Hawks' package, but Sefolosha's NBA contribution is the decisive difference.

summary: Slight Rockets Edge. Houston landed Trevor Ariza, who became a four-year starter, plus the 2015 first-round pick that became Sam Dekker. New Orleans got a strong first season from Ömer Aşık but limited long-term return, while Washington salvaged Ariza's free-agent departure into Melvin Ely and a trade exception it soon used to help acquire Kris Humphries.
analysis: Houston came out ahead because the two assets that mattered most aged well. Ariza immediately became a full-time starter and held that role for four seasons, including Houston's runs to the Western Conference Finals in 2015 and 2018. The protected first-round pick also conveyed at No. 18 and became Sam Dekker, giving the Rockets another useful asset. New Orleans did get real short-term value from Aşık: he started 76 games, averaged 9.8 rebounds and helped a 45-win Pelicans team reach the 2015 playoffs. The return faded after that first season, however, and Aşık was later included with another first-round pick in the 2018 Nikola Mirotić trade. Washington deserves a strong grade too. Rather than lose Ariza in free agency with nothing coming back, the Wizards generated a trade exception and Melvin Ely; that exception was then used to help acquire Kris Humphries. This was not a one-team rout, but Houston received the best combination of immediate fit, multi-year production and first-round value.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Washington Added Humphries to Its Frontcourt

The Wizards acquired Kris Humphries from Boston in a July 2014 sign-and-trade. Washington wanted another veteran big man who could rebound and contribute behind its established frontcourt, and Humphries had already shown that he could handle an NBA rotation role. The Celtics received a conditional second-round pick and a trade exception instead of a player ready to take the floor. The conditional selection was never exercised, leaving the exception as the concrete planning benefit for Boston.

Humphries Provided the Wizards With Useful Minutes

Humphries played a real role in Washington's frontcourt after the trade, providing rebounding and physical interior depth. He wasn't expected to replace the Wizards' leading scorers or change the offense by himself. The usefulness was more straightforward: an experienced forward-center could absorb regular-season assignments and reduce the demand on other big men. boston-celtics.analysis:
The Celtics Received a Broad Package

Boston took Dwight Powell, Erik Murphy, Malcolm Thomas and John Lucas III from Cleveland in September 2014. The transaction also brought two future second-round selections and a trade exception, while the Cavaliers received Keith Bogans and conditional draft rights. Boston was gathering assets during a roster transition, whereas Cleveland wanted to streamline contracts around a new contender. The incoming players had very different potential roles and career stages.

Few Arrivals Became Longtime Boston Players

Powell offered genuine developmental potential as a young big, but his substantial later playing career occurred elsewhere after another transaction. Murphy, Thomas and Lucas didn't establish long stretches as central Celtics rotation players. Boston therefore shouldn't value the agreement as four newly acquired lasting starters. The more durable benefit lay in the extra draft options and financial flexibility, with the initial players available to evaluate or redirect.

Draft Rights Later Had Specific Identities

Boston's selections were later associated with No. 58 Abdel Nader in 2016 and No. 53 Kadeem Allen in 2017. The organization could choose to draft, use or move those assets, and Nader eventually provided NBA minutes. The Cavaliers' incoming conditional second-round rights are recorded as not exercised, so Cleveland received no automatically attributable future draftee through them. This difference explains part of the gap in the two teams' realized returns.

Cleveland Sought Roster Management Benefits

Cleveland obtained Bogans and took a different approach to roster consolidation and financial planning. Boston could accept multiple contracts in exchange for future choices. The inherited Celtics B+ recognizes two additional selections and a trade exception; Cleveland's C reflects a narrower administrative benefit. The deal wasn't primarily about a high-scoring star moving cities, and its value should be read through the actual rights and players acquired.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for the package of players, second-round rights later tied to Abdel Nader and Kadeem Allen, and a trade exception. Cleveland receives C for Keith Bogans and conditional seconds that didn't convey. Boston gained the more useful future asset collection despite short tenures for most incoming players.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Swapped a Reserve Center for a Reserve Guard

The October 17, 2014 agreement sent Joel Anthony to Detroit and Will Bynum to Boston. Detroit's announcement identified Anthony as an experienced depth center, while the Celtics had already built a crowded frontcourt around younger options. Bynum had played six previous seasons for the Pistons, but Boston wasn't buying that historical output as if it had happened in Massachusetts. The guard also arrived at a time when the Celtics were sorting through several backcourt candidates in training camp. The exchange offered both sides a way to rearrange minor roster commitments before the season began.

Bynum Never Supplied Regular-Season Celtics Minutes

The Boston portion was especially brief. Bynum did not establish himself in the Celtics' regular-season guard rotation and was gone before an appearance that could be credited to this trade. His scoring records and assist totals in Detroit show why Boston might have considered a look, but none count as a contribution to the receiving franchise. This was a speculative preseason personnel move rather than a successful acquisition of immediate help. That distinction is important because a trade-history page can otherwise overstate the return by carrying over a player's entire career résumé.

Anthony Filled a Small but Measurable Detroit Role

Anthony did play for Detroit. He appeared in 49 games during the 2014-15 season, averaging only 8.3 minutes and 1.8 points, with his more recognizable contribution coming from defense and shot blocking. The Pistons weren't getting the athletic Miami-era version of a championship reserve, but they could use him in spot frontcourt minutes. His 49 appearances are real receiving-team value, yet limited playing time keeps the outcome from becoming a substantial roster gain. Detroit also retained him briefly beyond that first season, without making him a central building block.

A Minor Personnel Transaction Deserves a Modest Assessment

The deal didn't decide either team's season. Boston acquired flexibility in evaluating a guard but never extracted court time from Bynum. Detroit obtained a veteran center for emergency minutes, accepting a narrow rather than transformative basketball return. Both teams' C+ grades can be understood as reflecting a small preseason transaction with little financial or talent risk rather than equal numbers of NBA appearances. The on-court comparison leans Detroit, but the existing Even Trade verdict recognizes that neither side surrendered a foundation piece or gained a long-term starter.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston receives C+ because Will Bynum was a short-lived preseason acquisition rather than a regular-season contributor. Detroit also gets C+, with Joel Anthony appearing in 49 games in 2014-15 but producing only modest reserve numbers. The Pistons got more direct minutes, while the overall consequences were too small to treat the swap as a decisive franchise win.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Dallas Paid a Large Package for Rajon Rondo

The Mavericks acquired Rajon Rondo and Dwight Powell from Boston on December 18, 2014, seeking an experienced point guard to help their offense in a competitive Western Conference. Boston received Brandan Wright, Jae Crowder and Jameer Nelson, plus a 2016 first-rounder, a second-rounder and a sizeable trade exception. The deal represented a major decision for both organizations. Dallas wanted a proven playmaker immediately, while the Celtics were moving on from an established member of their previous title-winning core and collecting more options for their next roster.

Rondo's Dallas Fit Broke Down Before the Playoffs Ended

Rondo had a strong reputation from his Celtics years, but his Dallas tenure was disappointing. His role and relationship with the Mavericks' staff became strained, and the team did not retain him as the long-term point guard it had hoped to acquire. Powell was the more lasting Mavericks return, developing into a useful frontcourt contributor over several seasons. Ignoring Powell would overstate Dallas's loss, yet the original reason for surrendering so much value was the expectation that Rondo would improve a contender. That central expectation was not fulfilled.

Crowder and Draft Assets Strengthened Boston's Reset

Crowder became a valuable defensive wing for Boston and played an important role as the Celtics rebuilt into a playoff team. Wright and Nelson were more temporary acquisitions, eventually used in further personnel moves. The 2016 first-round selection became No. 16 Guerschon Yabusele, while the second-rounder became No. 45 Demetrius Jackson. Those choices were real draft capital, though neither should be credited with nonexistent star careers in Boston. The additional trade exception also gave the club a planning tool that Dallas did not retain.

The Main Bet Failed Even With Powell's Later Growth

Dallas obtained a long-tenured reserve in Powell, but that unanticipated benefit did not offset the unsuccessful Rondo acquisition and the multiple pieces surrendered. Boston gained a proven future rotation player in Crowder, draft opportunities and additional flexibility as its roster evolved. The deal's strong grade disparity reflects the differing overall outcomes while still acknowledging the Mavericks got some tangible value. Boston's return was built from several separate assets rather than one spectacular season by an incoming superstar.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns A+ for Jae Crowder's productive years and the additional players, picks and trade exception obtained for Rajon Rondo. Dallas receives D because Rondo's short tenure fell far below expectations, although Dwight Powell later became a useful longtime Maverick. The Celtics received a broader collection of durable roster tools, making the overall trade heavily favorable to Boston.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers moved Jared Cunningham, the rights to Cenk Akyol and cash to Philadelphia for the rights to Serhiy Lishchuk. Los Angeles saved nearly $400,000 against the cap, reduced luxury-tax exposure and opened a roster spot; Philadelphia waived Cunningham the same day and kept the cash and Akyol rights. Neither side created meaningful direct NBA player value, so the practical return was financial and roster flexibility on both sides.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis: Los Angeles was facing a guarantee decision on Cunningham, who was likely to be waived. Trading him instead saved a cap charge, reduced the related luxury tax and opened a roster spot while bringing back Lishchuk rights that were not expected to become NBA value. Philadelphia accepted Cunningham, cash and Akyol rights, then waived Cunningham. Akyol later appeared as the nominal return in the JaVale McGee salary-dump deal, but the first-round pick Philadelphia received in that later transaction reflected the cost of absorbing McGee and should not be credited to this trade. The original deal was a small financial transaction in which both teams accomplished a limited objective without producing lasting on-court value.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Quickly Converted Wright Into More Picks

The Celtics moved center-forward Brandan Wright to Phoenix in January 2015, accepting two future draft selections instead of another established player. Wright had joined Boston in an earlier deal and was not being retained as a central long-term frontcourt piece. Phoenix wanted an athletic interior option for the remainder of its season. Boston's rebuilding direction made multiple future opportunities more attractive than Wright's immediate reserve minutes. The draft returns later acquired the identities of No. 35 in 2016 and No. 37 in 2017.

Wright Gave Phoenix Only a Short Trial

Wright was an efficient finisher who could provide vertical spacing and rebounding, making him a sensible reserve target for the Suns. His actual stay in Phoenix was limited, however, and he later played for other clubs. Those other teams' statistics aren't part of the Suns' incoming production from this transaction. Phoenix obtained the playing option it wanted at the time, but did not secure a long-term center to anchor the roster. That limited tenure weakens its side of the inherited evaluation.

The 2017 Selection Became the Better Boston Return

The later pick associated with No. 37 Semi Ojeleye became a useful contributor in Boston's rotation. The other selection, linked to No. 35 Rade Zagorac, followed its own draft-rights path and did not produce comparable Celtics minutes. Both numbered selections were second-round slots; the unusual terminology in some transaction imports shouldn't lead a reader to describe No. 35 or No. 37 as a literal first-round draft position. The value came from the future options and what Boston eventually realized from the second of them.

Boston Found More Durable Depth Through the Draft

Phoenix accepted a short-term center it could use immediately, while Boston converted that veteran into multiple opportunities to add future contributors. Ojeleye's Celtics tenure supplied measurable receiving-team work and made the return more lasting than Wright's Phoenix stay. Neither asset by itself was a franchise cornerstone. The inherited Celtics advantage fits the practical difference between a temporary rotation big and a future pick that became a long-serving role player, without implying that every Boston selection succeeded.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for turning Brandan Wright into two later draft selections, especially the No. 37 choice associated with Semi Ojeleye, who became a usable Celtics wing. Phoenix receives C for Wright's relatively short center stint. The other choice, No. 35 Rade Zagorac, did not supply equivalent Boston minutes; the longer-term payoff came primarily from Ojeleye.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Moved a Veteran Guard for a Familiar Name

On January 13, 2015, the Celtics shipped Jameer Nelson to Denver and received Nate Robinson, who had already played in Boston earlier in his career. Nelson had joined the Celtics only weeks before in a separate trade and was not firmly established in their evolving guard rotation. Robinson brought prior familiarity with the franchise, but he was not acquired as a future franchise cornerstone. Both organizations were managing veteran contracts in a season of roster turnover, making the immediate practical value dependent on whether either newcomer would actually remain with the team.

Robinson's Second Boston Stint Produced No New Games

Robinson's earlier Celtics performances were real, but they belonged to a different tenure several seasons before this exchange. Boston waived him shortly after the January deal, without a regular-season appearance during his return. That means the receiving-side basketball payoff was negligible. His previous Denver production also cannot be transferred retroactively to Boston. The Celtics' opportunity was principally to manage the rotation and contract commitments, not to obtain a guard who played a meaningful second stretch in green. A trade assessment should not combine his first Boston spell with this aborted comeback.

Nelson Gave Denver Useful Veteran Guard Minutes

Denver retained Nelson and used him as a veteran ball handler beyond the initial 2014-15 campaign. His passing, experience and occasional outside scoring supplied stability for a developing backcourt, and he remained involved through parts of multiple Nuggets seasons. He wasn't a replacement for an All-NBA star, but the team received real games and rotation work where Boston got none from its incoming guard. Any Nelson appearances with Orlando or Dallas before January 2015 are separate from this value. His Denver tenure is the meaningful receiving-team result of the transaction.

The Nominal Tie Masks Unequal Actual Playing Value

Denver's actual on-court payoff was much stronger, but this still was a low-cost exchange of veteran guards during a complicated Celtics roster reset. The Celtics had reasons to free a spot or facilitate further moves, even though Robinson never helped them win a game after this transaction. The canonical Even Trade verdict and matching C+ grades should therefore be read as a restrained historical assessment, not as a claim that Robinson and Nelson logged equivalent minutes with their new teams. Denver benefited most in basketball terms without making the trade pivotal to either franchise.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston receives C+ for a low-stakes roster reshuffle, but Nate Robinson never supplied another Celtics game after the deal. Denver also receives C+ in the canonical evaluation, despite obtaining significantly more direct value from Jameer Nelson's multi-season reserve and starting minutes. This is an ordinary veteran transaction with a real Denver playing edge, not a major asset transfer.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Clippers Targeted Rivers for Their Backcourt

Los Angeles acquired Austin Rivers from Boston on January 15, 2015, completing a three-team arrangement that also involved Phoenix. Rivers had recently moved from New Orleans to Boston and was searching for a more stable NBA role. The Clippers saw an opportunity to develop a younger reserve guard in a rotation already led by established stars. Boston received Chris Douglas-Roberts, Shavlik Randolph and a 2017 second-round right, while Phoenix secured Reggie Bullock from the Clippers.

Rivers Became a Real Clippers Rotation Player

Rivers spent multiple seasons with Los Angeles, playing guard minutes during regular seasons and playoff series. He offered the team ball handling and defensive energy, even if his scoring efficiency varied from year to year. That direct receiving-team contribution is what makes the Clippers' side more than an exchange of contracts. His earlier Pelicans statistics aren't part of his Clippers production, and his arrival didn't make the club an automatic title favorite. It did give the team an identifiable role player who lasted longer than a brief deadline stop.

Boston's Compensation Was More Than a Cash Adjustment

Douglas-Roberts and Randolph offered veteran depth at positions where Boston could evaluate alternatives, while the second-round right later became associated with No. 56 Jabari Bird in 2017. That draft link created another prospect opportunity without guaranteeing a successful player. The Celtics also created a trade exception as part of the deal, a useful roster-building mechanism distinct from receiving a new active player. Their package mixed immediate contracts with future draft flexibility rather than acquiring one replacement guard of Rivers's age.

Phoenix Obtained Bullock in the Same Transaction

The Suns acquired Reggie Bullock from the Clippers, a detail absent from the original Boston-only team import but confirmed by both clubs' official announcements. Bullock was a young wing with three-point shooting potential, though his later NBA accomplishments with other organizations shouldn't be credited automatically to Phoenix. The inherited grades are B+ for both the Clippers and Celtics and C for Phoenix. The narrow Clippers victory reflects Rivers's multi-season usefulness rather than denying that the Celtics obtained several legitimate assets.

Final Verdict

Slight Clippers Edge. Los Angeles earns B+ for Austin Rivers, whose multi-season guard role supplied direct receiving-team production. Boston also receives B+ for Chris Douglas-Roberts, Shavlik Randolph, the 2017 selection associated with Jabari Bird and roster flexibility. Phoenix gets C for young shooter Reggie Bullock, who was a genuine part of the full three-team deal. The Clippers gained the longest-lived direct roster fit.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Found a Scorer at the Deadline

The Celtics acquired Isaiah Thomas from Phoenix on February 19, 2015, sending guard Marcus Thornton and a protected 2016 first-round selection that Boston had previously obtained from Cleveland. Thomas had been one of several guards competing for roles in Phoenix, while the Celtics sought an offensive creator for Brad Stevens's developing group. Boston wasn't receiving the older All-Star version of a declining veteran. It was taking a chance on a still-productive guard whose scoring instincts had not yet found a permanent home with a playoff contender.

Thomas Became the Center of Boston's Offense

Thomas gave Boston the late-game shot creation it lacked and developed into the club's leading scorer. He earned consecutive All-Star appearances in 2016 and 2017, finished fifth in the 2017 MVP vote and helped the Celtics reach the Eastern Conference Finals. His fourth-quarter scoring earned him the King of the Fourth reputation and made a relatively modest deadline acquisition unusually memorable. The club's eventual decision to move Thomas in another major deal did not erase what it had received in the interim. These achievements belong to his Celtics tenure.

Phoenix Took a Guard and a Future Draft Right

Thornton was a veteran scoring guard who could play immediately, but his Phoenix stint did not become a multi-year foundation. The protected first-round selection eventually conveyed as No. 28 in 2016, a pick later associated with Skal Labissiere in the draft's transaction history. That rights path is distinct from whether the Suns directly developed Labissiere. The deal gave Phoenix something tangible for a guard squeezed into a crowded rotation, but the return never approached the All-Star-level production Thomas provided after moving to Boston.

The Scoring Peak Makes the Winner Unambiguous

Boston obtained an elite offensive season and a deep postseason run for the price of a reserve guard and a later first-round choice. Thomas's height was a persistent defensive challenge and his physical situation became complicated near the end of his stay, but those costs don't cancel out what he accomplished. Phoenix made an understandable guard-allocation decision during the transaction window, yet its compensation offered less comparable upside. This is a clear Celtics win rooted in Thomas's on-court Boston career rather than his fame before or after the exchange.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns A+ for turning Marcus Thornton and a future first-rounder into Isaiah Thomas, a two-time Celtics All-Star who carried elite scoring responsibility during the 2017 conference-finals run. Phoenix receives D because Thornton and the conveyed selection produced far less realized return. The value is based on Thomas's remarkable Boston peak, not on unrelated later stops.

perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Acquired a Guard Seeking a Larger Role

The Pistons traded for Reggie Jackson in February 2015 after his opportunities in Oklahoma City had been limited behind Russell Westbrook. Detroit wanted a guard able to take on more responsibility in the offense and direct a young roster. The multi-team arrangement also gave Oklahoma City D.J. Augustin, Kyle Singler and a future second-round right, while Utah acquired another future selection. The Pistons' decision depended heavily on whether Jackson could convert an expanded role into regular production.

Jackson Became a Major Pistons Contributor

Jackson did play extensive minutes for Detroit and provided scoring and playmaking in the seasons after the deal. He helped the team reach the playoffs, although injuries and variable efficiency complicated the longer-term assessment. Those Pistons games are a direct receiving-team payoff rather than hypothetical value from the guard's Oklahoma City reserve seasons. He did not become the greatest point guard in franchise history, but he gave Detroit a recognizable offensive identity at a position the club had been searching to stabilize.

Oklahoma City and Utah Took Smaller Assets

Augustin brought veteran backup-point-guard experience to the Thunder and Singler offered wing depth. The associated 2019 second-round right became linked to No. 45 Isaiah Roby, whose subsequent rights and NBA appearances need separate tracing. Utah's incoming 2017 selection was associated with No. 42 Thomas Bryant; that draft association didn't automatically make Bryant a long-serving Jazz player. Both clubs gained options, but neither directly acquired a high-usage scorer comparable to Jackson's first Pistons years.

Detroit's Player Production Was the Clearer Return

Detroit's A- reflects Jackson's multi-season backcourt contribution. Oklahoma City's B and Utah's B+ recognize useful veterans and later selection rights without pretending those picks all turned into direct roster contributors. The difference between the two sides of the comparison is not simply total draft position. It is whether an incoming player became central to the receiving team's play. Jackson did so for Detroit, making this a good example of a trade that changed a player's role and produced actual results.

Final Verdict

Slight Pistons Edge. Detroit earns A- for Reggie Jackson's substantial backcourt role and subsequent playoff contribution. Oklahoma City gets B for D.J. Augustin, Kyle Singler and an asset later tied to Isaiah Roby, while Utah earns B+ for a second-round right associated with Thomas Bryant. Jackson's direct Detroit production supplies the clearest outcome despite useful draft flexibility elsewhere.

Detroit wanted a guard able to take on more responsibility in the offense and direct a young roster. The multi-team arrangement also gave Oklahoma City D.J. Augustin, Kyle Singler and a future second-round right, while Utah acquired another future selection. The Pistons' decision depended heavily on whether Jackson could convert an expanded role into regular production.

Jackson Became a Major Pistons Contributor

Jackson did play extensive minutes for Detroit and provided scoring and playmaking in the seasons after the deal. He helped the team reach the playoffs, although injuries and variable efficiency complicated the longer-term assessment. Those Pistons games are a direct receiving-team payoff rather than hypothetical value from the guard's Oklahoma City reserve seasons. He did not become the greatest point guard in franchise history, but he gave Detroit a recognizable offensive identity at a position the club had been searching to stabilize.

Oklahoma City and Utah Took Smaller Assets

Augustin brought veteran backup-point-guard experience to the Thunder and Singler offered wing depth. The associated 2019 second-round right became linked to No. 45 Isaiah Roby, whose subsequent rights and NBA appearances need separate tracing. Utah's incoming 2017 selection was associated with No. 42 Thomas Bryant; that draft association didn't automatically make Bryant a long-serving Jazz player. Both clubs gained options, but neither directly acquired a high-usage scorer comparable to Jackson's first Pistons years.

Detroit's Player Production Was the Clearer Return

Detroit's A- reflects Jackson's multi-season backcourt contribution. Oklahoma City's B and Utah's B+ recognize useful veterans and later selection rights without pretending those picks all turned into direct roster contributors. The difference between the two sides of the comparison is not simply total draft position. It is whether an incoming player became central to the receiving team's play. Jackson did so for Detroit, making this a good example of a trade that changed a player's role and produced actual results.

Final Verdict

Slight Pistons Edge. Detroit earns A- for Reggie Jackson's substantial backcourt role and subsequent playoff contribution. Oklahoma City gets B for D.J. Augustin, Kyle Singler and an asset later tied to Isaiah Roby, while Utah earns B+ for a second-round right associated with Thomas Bryant. Jackson's direct Detroit production supplies the clearest outcome despite useful draft flexibility elsewhere.
