houston-rockets.analysis:
The Rockets Added a Veteran Guard to a Contending Team

Houston's February 19, 2015 trade brought Pablo Prigioni from the New York Knicks in exchange for Alexey Shved and two future second-round draft selections. The Rockets were preparing for a postseason run behind James Harden and Dwight Howard and wanted an experienced ball handler who could manage possessions alongside their main creators. Prigioni was thirty-seven and had been part of the Knicks' guard rotation before the deadline. This was distinct from Houston's separate acquisition of K.J. McDaniels from Philadelphia on the same day. New York, meanwhile, was collecting future opportunities for a struggling roster, a very different timetable from Houston's immediate competitive objectives.

Prigioni Had a Defined Houston Rotation Role

Prigioni appeared in twenty-four Rockets regular-season games after the trade in 2014-15 and did not start any of them. He nevertheless provided veteran handling and defensive activity to a second unit that needed decisions made without the ball stopping. His role continued into the postseason, where he played in seventeen games while Houston advanced to the Western Conference Finals. Those appearances are the appropriate direct return for the deadline acquisition. His earlier Knicks career and any subsequent free-agent movements do not belong in Houston's 2015 trade totals. A grade based only on his limited scoring would miss the purpose of obtaining a reliable veteran reserve.

New York Received Shved and Two Future Draft Assets

The Knicks added Shved plus Houston's second-round selections for 2017 and 2019. Shved was a wing-sized ball handler who could take shots and minutes on a roster short of established options, but he was not a long-term franchise centerpiece. The picks carried value through their ability to be selected or traded later, rather than guaranteeing that either eventually named prospect would wear a Knicks uniform. The selection lineages ultimately connect them to Ognjen Jaramaz at No. 58 in 2017 and Kyle Guy at No. 55 in 2019. Those identities track the choices, not automatic Knicks playing production, and any subsequent draft-rights transactions require separate attribution.

Asset Flexibility Gives New York a Narrow Edge

Houston gained useful immediate minutes from Prigioni and reached the conference finals, which improves on the inherited near-failing grade. New York obtained one short-term player and two distinct future selections for someone who would otherwise have supplied veteran depth during a rebuild. The quantity and flexibility of those assets justify the Knicks' advantage without treating two late seconds as guaranteed NBA starters. This comparison needs to preserve Houston's actual twenty-four regular-season appearances and seventeen playoff appearances from Prigioni rather than borrow unrelated years. It also needs to keep Houston's McDaniels trade separate, because that involved an additional second-round pick and another outgoing player.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win. New York earns B for Alexey Shved's short-term roster service and Houston's 2017 and 2019 second-round selections, later associated with Ognjen Jaramaz and Kyle Guy. Houston receives B- rather than D+ because Pablo Prigioni contributed twenty-four regular-season games and seventeen playoff appearances during the 2015 Western Conference Finals run. Neither future draft identity should be assigned Knicks playing minutes merely because the pick was once owned by New York.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Pelicans drafted Michigan State defender Branden Dawson at No. 56 in 2015 and sold his rights to the Clippers for cash. Dawson played six Clippers games totaling 29 minutes and five points in 2015-16, after which he made no further NBA appearances. New Orleans obtained a financial return without a player; neither outcome justified a decisive winner. Even Trade, Los Angeles C, New Orleans C+.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
New Orleans Sold a Late Second-Round Defensive Prospect

The Pelicans used the fifty-sixth overall selection in 2015 on Branden Dawson from Michigan State and transferred his draft rights to Los Angeles for cash. Dawson had earned attention as a tough college rebounder and defender, not as a polished NBA offensive player. For the Clippers, an inexpensive second-round audition fit behind established big men and veteran wings. New Orleans instead accepted money immediately. The official franchise announcement identifies a sale of rights, not the transfer of a player already under NBA contract.

Dawson Reached the Clippers Bench, but for Six Games

Dawson appeared in six Los Angeles regular-season contests in 2015-16. Those appearances totaled twenty-nine minutes, five points and four rebounds, with no starts. The Clippers saw enough to give him a short professional audition, but the small amount of time cannot be inflated into a rotation season. His college defensive credentials and later work outside the league do not count as Clippers NBA output. The acquired player never earned another regular-season NBA appearance after those six games.

The Pelicans Received Immediate Cash, Not Player Minutes

New Orleans obtained cash considerations for the draft selection and avoided spending a roster slot on Dawson. This was a real financial return, but no reliable source in the transaction file establishes an exact amount. The Pelicans cannot be assigned hypothetical players purchased with that money, and they cannot count the six Dawson appearances made for Los Angeles. The known result is simply payment for an uncertain second-round prospect. That makes the selling club rational without demonstrating an exceptional basketball gain.

A Brief Tryout and a Cash Receipt Support Balanced Grades

Both organizations got what their small transaction was designed to provide: the Clippers inspected a college defender in actual NBA games while New Orleans converted a late draft option into money. Neither side collected enough sporting value to claim a major victory. In particular, six games and fewer than thirty minutes do not warrant an aggressive Clippers grade, but an unknown cash amount cannot support the inherited Pelicans B either. The appropriate historical judgment is an even low-stakes exchange with restrained grades.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Los Angeles earns C because Branden Dawson played six Clippers regular-season games, totaling twenty-nine minutes and five points. New Orleans earns C+ for accepting cash in return for a late second-round selection. Neither receiving-team result supports an emphatic winner, and the previously recorded Pelicans B grade overstated the known return.

new-york-knicks.summary: The Hawks received Tim Hardaway Jr. from the Knicks and a future Washington second during the June 2015 draft. New York acquired the draft rights to Jerian Grant through Atlanta, while Washington received Kelly Oubre Jr.'s rights. The inherited Hawks Win gives Atlanta A+, New York F and Washington C. The repaired ledger now includes the previously absent Wizards player rights and Hawks second-round asset.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
Atlanta Turned Grant's Draft Rights Into Hardaway

The Hawks acquired Tim Hardaway Jr. from New York during the 2015 NBA Draft, using the rights to No. 19 Jerian Grant as the outgoing piece. Atlanta had first obtained Grant's rights from Washington after selecting Kelly Oubre Jr. at No. 15. Hardaway was a young guard with NBA scoring experience, making the acquisition more than a speculative draft selection. The Hawks also received a future second-round right from Washington as part of the rights routing.

New York Chose Grant as a Guard Prospect

The Knicks obtained the rights to Grant, a Notre Dame guard with college playmaking credentials, in exchange for Hardaway. New York was evaluating whether Grant's passing and defensive tools could contribute within its developing backcourt. The trade didn't guarantee he would match every aspect of Hardaway's future NBA scoring career. Grant's eventual seasons at other organizations have to be distinguished from his immediate Knicks contributions, which is especially important when a draft-rights transaction gets graded years later.

Washington Received Oubre's Rights, Not an Empty Entry

The Wizards obtained the rights to Oubre from Atlanta, an actual first-round wing prospect. Their later NBA development of Oubre should be attributed to Washington and its subsequent receiving teams, not to the Hawks simply because Atlanta made the initial No. 15 selection. Washington surrendered the No. 19 rights and second-round consideration to obtain the higher pick's player. The old Knicks-centered record had mistakenly left Washington's incoming side blank, obscuring why the franchise took part in the three-team arrangement.

The Inherited Grades Give Atlanta a Large Advantage

Atlanta earns A+ for acquiring Hardaway and an additional future second, New York receives F for surrendering an established young shooter to draft Grant, and Washington gets C for Oubre's rights. The Hawks advantage is the original record's verdict; Washington's actual Oubre acquisition and later career deserve separate recognition. This transaction demonstrates why rights-routing chronology is essential: the player selected by a franchise on draft night may ultimately belong to another team.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta receives A+ for Tim Hardaway Jr. and future second-round rights. New York gets F under the original grading for sending Hardaway away to acquire Jerian Grant. Washington receives C for the rights to Kelly Oubre Jr., which were omitted from the old ledger. Oubre's eventual Wizards games should be credited to Washington, not Atlanta's temporary selection rights.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Targeted a Championship-Experienced Center

The Hawks acquired Tiago Splitter from San Antonio on July 9, 2015, after a sixty-win season that had exposed some frontcourt limitations in the playoffs. Splitter brought size, screening and familiarity with coach Mike Budenholzer's Spurs-influenced system. Atlanta exchanged the rights to Giorgos Printezis and a heavily protected future second-round pick rather than an established rotation player. San Antonio was creating flexibility for its own roster plans, while the Hawks hoped a traditional center could complement Al Horford and Paul Millsap instead of forcing smaller lineups into every difficult matchup.

Splitter's Availability Limited His Atlanta Impact

Splitter could set solid screens, defend interior possessions and understand the spacing concepts that Atlanta prized. His Hawks tenure was nevertheless hampered by injuries, preventing him from establishing a stable multi-season frontcourt role. He was not the version of the player who had contributed to San Antonio's 2014 championship for a full healthy season, and those earlier accomplishments aren't Atlanta receiving-team production. Even in a curtailed spell, the Hawks gained actual veteran NBA minutes and a player with a clearly defined basketball skill set rather than only international rights.

The Spurs Collected Rights and Contract Flexibility

Printezis was a well-established European forward, but his NBA rights did not turn into Spurs regular-season games. The conditional second-round component carried strong protection and ultimately did not convey as an additional pick. San Antonio's primary rationale was roster and financial management rather than replacing Splitter's screening directly with a new rotation center. The club had other frontcourt plans, including a major free-agent pursuit that summer. That context makes the deal understandable even though its incoming basketball return was thin. International success for Printezis cannot be added to the Spurs' NBA totals.

Atlanta's Edge Was Real but Narrower Than Expected

Atlanta paid relatively little in playable talent and obtained a veteran center, justifying an advantage over a package of unused draft rights and a nonconveying pick. At the same time, Splitter's injuries stopped the trade from generating the durable interior presence the Hawks initially wanted. The B+ grade reflects value relative to the price paid, not a claim that the move transformed a contender into a Finals team. San Antonio's cap goals were legitimate, but the Hawks held the clearer immediate on-court asset from the specific transaction.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ because Tiago Splitter provided usable veteran frontcourt help at a low player cost, though injuries sharply limited the payoff. San Antonio gets C- for the international rights to Giorgos Printezis and a protected second that did not convey. This was a worthwhile Hawks acquisition by price, not the lasting center solution initially envisioned.

indiana-pacers.summary: On July 9, 2015, the Pacers sent former All-Star center Roy Hibbert to the Lakers for a 2019 second-round draft choice. Hibbert started all 81 Lakers regular-season games in 2015-16, totaling 481 points, 398 rebounds and 110 blocks. Indiana traded the incoming pick to Cleveland two weeks later for rights to Rakeem Christmas, who played 30 Pacers games. The 2019 pick ultimately became No. 41 Eric Paschall through later transactions but was drafted by Golden State, not Indiana. Even Trade, B- for each.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Moved On From a Former All-Star Center

The Pacers sent Roy Hibbert to the Los Angeles Lakers on July 9, 2015, receiving a future second-round selection. Indiana's official statement acknowledged Hibbert's seven years with the club, including two All-Star appearances, but the franchise was changing how it built its frontcourt. The Lakers were looking for experienced center depth while Kobe Bryant's era was drawing to a close. Hibbert was no longer producing his best Indiana numbers, yet he could still start and defend the rim. Indiana preferred roster and payroll flexibility plus a delayed pick over committing to another year of the veteran center.

Hibbert Started Eighty-One Games During His Lakers Season

Hibbert started all 81 regular-season games in which he appeared for Los Angeles in 2015-16. His averages declined to 5.9 points, 4.9 rebounds and 1.4 blocks in 23.2 minutes, with 481 points, 398 rebounds and 110 blocks in total. That is genuine NBA playing value from the Lakers' side, even though the team struggled badly and did not reach the postseason. Hibbert left after one season. His two Indiana All-Star selections and earlier playoff performances belong to his career before the trade and cannot be credited to the Lakers as if they acquired his prime years.

The Pacers Spent the Incoming Pick on Rakeem Christmas Rights

Indiana did not wait until 2019 to use the incoming selection. On July 23, 2015, the Pacers sent that second-round pick to Cleveland for the draft rights to Rakeem Christmas, an athletic Syracuse forward. Christmas appeared in one Indiana game in 2015-16 and 29 more in 2016-17, totaling 30 appearances, 225 minutes and 63 points before being waived. The original 2019 pick kept moving after it left the Pacers, passing through Cleveland and Atlanta before Golden State acquired it. It eventually became No. 41 Eric Paschall, but the Warriors drafted Paschall and received his playing career. Indiana cannot claim Paschall's Golden State stats as its trade return.

The Lakers Got Starts; Indiana Got Flexibility and a Small Asset

Los Angeles received more immediate on-court minutes, because Hibbert was its starting center for nearly an entire season. Indiana received contract and roster flexibility along with a draft asset that it quickly converted into an actual, if little-used, reserve. Neither organization obtained a long-term cornerstone. The Lakers' 81 starts should not be waved away because their season was unsuccessful, and the Pacers' side should not be inflated by the eventual NBA achievements of a player selected with a pick they no longer owned. An even judgment with restrained grades reflects the different ways each team used the exchange.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. The Lakers earn B- for Roy Hibbert's 81 starts, 481 points, 398 rebounds and 110 blocks in 2015-16. Indiana also receives B- for salary and roster flexibility plus the 2019 second-round pick it converted into Rakeem Christmas's 30 games. Eric Paschall was drafted by Golden State after later pick trades, so his career is not Pacers return.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: Philadelphia used cap space on July 9, 2015 to absorb Nik Stauskas, Carl Landry and Jason Thompson from Sacramento while also receiving 2016 and 2017 first-round swap rights and a future Kings first. The 2017 swap moved the 76ers from No. 5 to No. 3, and the future first ultimately conveyed in 2019 at No. 14. Sacramento received only the draft rights to Arturas Gudaitis and Luka Mitrovic while clearing salary for a free-agent push.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
The Exchange
Philadelphia's media guide, Sacramento's transaction history and Basketball-Reference all resolve the package. The 76ers received Nik Stauskas, Carl Landry, Jason Thompson, the right to swap first-round picks in 2016 and 2017, and a future Sacramento first-round pick. Sacramento received the draft rights to Arturas Gudaitis and Luka Mitrovic. The 2016 swap was not exercised. The 2017 swap was exercised after Sacramento's lottery position landed at No. 3 and Philadelphia's at No. 5, giving the 76ers the No. 3 draft asset and sending No. 5 back to the Kings. The future first was top-10 protected in 2018 and unprotected in 2019, when it conveyed at No. 14.

Philadelphia Return
The trade delivered value in two different forms. Stauskas became a real rotation guard for Philadelphia, and Landry contributed productive minutes during the 2015-16 season. Thompson was moved again before playing a regular-season game for the 76ers, so his direct value was mainly transactional flexibility. The much larger return was draft control. The 2017 swap improved Philadelphia's own selection from fifth to third before the club later used that No. 3 asset, together with the future Sacramento first, in the separate trade with Boston for the No. 1 pick. Boston ultimately used No. 3 on Jayson Tatum and the Sacramento first eventually conveyed at No. 14 in 2019, when Romeo Langford was selected. Those later Boston selections should not be credited as Philadelphia players, but they demonstrate the market value of the draft assets Philadelphia obtained for taking on salary.

Sacramento Return
The Kings' immediate objective was cap room. NBA.com's later review of the move noted that Sacramento unloaded Stauskas, Landry and Thompson to create flexibility for its 2015 free-agent plan, which soon included Rajon Rondo, Kosta Koufos and Marco Belinelli. Rondo led the league in assists in his one Sacramento season, so the cap space was not literally worthless. The problem is the price. Gudaitis and Mitrovic never produced NBA value for Sacramento, the 2017 swap cost the Kings two draft positions, and the additional first remained outstanding until 2019. Sacramento gained short-term flexibility but surrendered unusually valuable long-term draft control without reaching the playoffs.

Hindsight Verdict
Philadelphia wins by a wide margin. The 76ers earn an A+ because they converted unused cap space into playable veterans plus two pieces of premium first-round leverage, including a swap that actually improved their 2017 position and a future unprotected first. Sacramento earns a D rather than an F because the salary relief was intentional and helped fund a roster that included a productive Rondo season, but the short-term benefit did not come close to the future draft value surrendered. The grade is based on the assets created by the original trade, not on Philadelphia's later choice to package those assets for Markelle Fultz. Final verdict: Philadelphia 76ers Win.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Celtics Received Jones and a Future Pick

Boston acquired Perry Jones III, a 2019 second-round right and cash from Oklahoma City in July 2015. The Thunder received a separate second-round choice tied to the 2018 draft. Jones had once been an intriguing forward prospect, but his role in Oklahoma City had narrowed. Boston took the contract and additional draft compensation while deciding which young wings deserved roster spots. The structure emphasized future flexibility instead of a proven player swap.

Jones Did Not Become a Celtics Rotation Fixture

Although Jones had NBA experience with the Thunder, he did not establish a regular playing role in Boston after the transaction. The Celtics' main basketball return was therefore not his earlier scoring or defensive potential but the extra pick and resources accompanying him. That distinction keeps the evaluation grounded: a prospect can carry a recognizable name without generating substantial new-team production. Boston chose to move on from Jones rather than build its future rotation around him.

The Picks Later Acquired Different Draft Identities

Boston's 2019 second-round right was linked to No. 45 Isaiah Roby, while Oklahoma City's incoming 2018 choice was associated with No. 57 Kevin Hervey. The players' later rights transfers and professional paths must be followed before attributing any NBA appearances to the first team that held a selection. Both assets offered opportunities to develop or trade prospects rather than guaranteed starting-caliber performers. Boston also received cash, giving it another concrete component of the deal.

The Celtics Gained a Little More Flexibility

The inherited slight Boston edge values the future draft right and cash obtained in exchange for a later second, despite Jones's failure to contribute meaningfully on the court. Oklahoma City gained a different pick and room to manage its roster after releasing a former prospect from its plans. Neither side secured a franchise-changing player. The modest B- to C+ gap is better understood through the asset terms than through imagined contributions by Jones in a Celtics uniform.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B- for taking Perry Jones III along with cash and the 2019 second-round right later associated with Isaiah Roby, although Jones didn't become a Celtics rotation player. Oklahoma City receives C+ for the 2018 choice linked to Kevin Hervey and roster flexibility. The result was chiefly a modest draft-and-financial gain for Boston.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The July Agreement Became Official on July 27

Boston completed its David Lee acquisition from Golden State on July 27, 2015, sending Gerald Wallace and Chris Babb to the Warriors. The clubs had agreed to the framework earlier in July, explaining why some transaction databases carry an earlier date, but Golden State's official log records July 27 as completion. Boston wanted a proven scoring and rebounding big to test in its developing frontcourt. Golden State had shifted its power-forward responsibilities toward Draymond Green and could move the veteran's substantial contract. It was an immediate player-and-salary exchange rather than a trade involving direct first-round draft compensation.

David Lee Played Thirty Games for Boston

Lee averaged 7.1 points and 4.3 rebounds across 30 Celtics appearances in 2015-16, producing useful but limited reserve minutes. He had once been an All-Star and a central Golden State frontcourt piece, yet those accomplishments belonged to his previous team and did not automatically carry into Boston's rotation. As Brad Stevens leaned on other combinations, Lee's playing time declined. The Celtics waived him in February 2016. Boston's receiving-team return therefore ended after part of one season, but at least consisted of measurable on-court production rather than a purely financial paper transaction.

Golden State Sent Wallace Along in a Separate Deal

Gerald Wallace didn't become a new Warriors rotation fixture, and Chris Babb didn't establish a playing role there. Golden State moved Wallace again on July 31 in a separate exchange with Philadelphia, receiving Jason Thompson while also sending cash and draft consideration. That follow-up made sense as roster management, but the Thompson transaction cannot be merged into the direct list of players Boston sent to Golden State. Treating Thompson's later Warriors appearances as if Boston had directly traded him would confuse two distinct deals. The original Lee swap provided the Warriors contract flexibility, not a comparable replacement veteran who played thirty games for them.

The Result Was an Advantage, Not a Boston Windfall

The Celtics received more direct on-court production from their incoming player than Golden State received from Wallace or Babb. That observation supports a small Boston edge without overstating the impact of a brief Lee experiment. Golden State had strategic reasons to move Lee, particularly its existing frontcourt depth and budget, and subsequently used the Wallace contract in another deal. The trade did not by itself decide the 2015-16 championship picture or add a long-term rotation anchor for either club. Boston's modest grade acknowledges useful minutes while the Warriors' grade recognizes financial and roster utility rather than imagined on-court output.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston gets B- for David Lee's 30 games and 7.1 points per game before his February 2016 exit. Golden State receives C+ because Wallace and Babb provided no comparable playing contribution, though the franchise used Wallace's contract in a separate trade and opened frontcourt flexibility. Neither the Warriors' prior championship with Lee nor Thompson's later arrival should be mistaken for direct production acquired in this exchange.

houston-rockets.summary: On January 22, 2016, the Clippers traded Josh Smith back to Houston along with cash and the rights to Sergei Lishchuk for the Rockets' draft rights to Maarty Leunen. Smith had appeared in 32 Clippers games that season but played 23 regular-season games for Houston after his return. Neither Lishchuk nor Leunen became an NBA regular for the receiving team. The Rockets obtained a short-term playing contributor for rights they could relinquish, whereas the Clippers largely cleared a role and roster space. Slight Rockets Edge, Houston B-, Clippers C-.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Clippers Sent Smith Back to the Rockets

On January 22, 2016, Los Angeles returned Josh Smith to Houston after a difficult partial season with the Clippers. The exchange also sent cash and the draft rights to Ukrainian big man Sergei Lishchuk to the Rockets, while Los Angeles acquired the rights to Maarty Leunen. Smith had joined the Clippers in the preceding offseason after playing for Houston during its 2015 playoff run. He averaged only 5.7 points in thirty-two Clippers appearances, and his minutes were disappearing as the team shifted more playing time to Cole Aldrich. The agreement therefore solved a roster-management problem for Los Angeles while offering Houston a familiar veteran.

Smith Played Another Twenty-Three Houston Games

Smith's second Houston stint in 2015-16 consisted of twenty-three regular-season games after the January transaction. Those appearances, rather than the fifty-five Rockets regular-season games from his separate 2014-15 signing, are the direct playing return of this trade. He offered size and a known style of passing from the frontcourt but did not reproduce the larger impact of the previous season's Western Conference Finals run. Even so, getting NBA minutes from a veteran player was more measurable than simply holding distant draft rights. Houston did not have to send a current rotation player back to Los Angeles to make this deal work.

Two Rights Assets Had Little Direct NBA Output

Lishchuk's rights moved to Houston, and Leunen's rights moved to Los Angeles, but neither player became an NBA rotation regular because of the transaction. Rights to an overseas prospect can retain administrative or negotiating value without ever converting into court time. The cash accompanying Smith belonged to Houston, not to the Clippers, and should not be reversed when recording who received which part of the package. The Clippers gained flexibility to continue with their other frontcourt reserves, having traded away a player who had fallen out of the main rotation. That benefit differs from a typical asset-based return involving draft picks with defined selection dates.

The Direct Player Return Gives Houston the Edge

Houston acquired a veteran with a useful history in the franchise and obtained a limited but genuine twenty-three-game contribution. Los Angeles moved away from a signing that was not working and avoided retaining another out-of-rotation contract. Those practical outcomes favor the Rockets, although a stronger victory would exaggerate what Smith actually accomplished after January. His past Houston success is relevant background, not earned minutes from this new transaction. Likewise, Leunen's and Lishchuk's international records do not equal NBA games for the clubs receiving their rights. The grading should reflect a narrow playing-value advantage rather than treating the rights swaps as major roster upgrades.

Final Verdict

Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns B- for acquiring Josh Smith's twenty-three 2015-16 regular-season games along with Sergei Lishchuk's rights and cash. Los Angeles receives C- for moving a reserve who had fallen out of favor and taking Maarty Leunen's rights, without any resulting Clippers NBA games from those rights. Smith's fifty-five Houston appearances in 2014-15 came from an earlier free-agent signing and cannot be credited to this January 2016 trade.

perspectives.analysis:
Charlotte Added Lee for a More Immediate Wing Role

The Hornets acquired Courtney Lee in February 2016 through a transaction involving Memphis and Miami. Lee had established himself as a perimeter defender and capable shooter, skills Charlotte needed as it pursued a postseason berth. The team also received cash. Memphis obtained P.J. Hairston, Chris Andersen and second-round draft assets, while Miami received Brian Roberts. The deal brought together clubs with different needs, from immediate guard depth to future draft flexibility.

Lee Supplied Charlotte With Actual Rotation Minutes

Lee joined Charlotte's backcourt and provided an experienced presence without needing a large share of offensive possessions. His defensive versatility helped the team match up against opposing perimeter scorers, while his outside shooting was useful alongside the Hornets' established playmakers. He wasn't acquired as a franchise-leading scorer, and his earlier NBA production shouldn't be assigned to Charlotte before he arrived. The trade supplied a tangible short-term rotation fit even if the club didn't retain him for an extended tenure.

Memphis and Miami Took Different Packages

Memphis received Hairston, a young wing with an uncertain development path, and Andersen, a veteran center known for defensive energy and rebounding. Its incoming second-round rights in 2018 and 2019 provided other ways to build the roster. Miami accepted Roberts, a guard who could provide ball handling without implying a long-term starting role. These incoming assets had distinct purposes. Draft selections and players could be moved again, so every subsequent NBA season should be attributed to the correct receiving club.

The Close Grades Reflect Mixed Results

The inherited slight Grizzlies edge gives Memphis B for acquiring multiple player options and future selections. Miami also earns B for adding Roberts, while Charlotte's C+ recognizes Lee's useful but shorter wing tenure. The top grade doesn't mean every Memphis draft choice became a successful NBA player or that Charlotte received nothing important. Rather, the framework favors the breadth of Memphis's compensation while acknowledging that Lee gave Charlotte an immediate basketball benefit.

Final Verdict

Slight Grizzlies Edge. Memphis earns B for P.J. Hairston, Chris Andersen and two second-round assets, receiving several roster and draft choices. Miami also gets B for Brian Roberts as guard depth. Charlotte receives C+ for Courtney Lee's veteran defense and shooting plus cash. The inherited margin favors Memphis's broader package, although Lee provided the Hornets with direct rotation value.

summary: Utah acquired Shelvin Mack in a February 2016 three-team trade that sent Kirk Hinrich to Atlanta and Justin Holiday plus a future second-round selection to Chicago. Mack stepped into a useful backcourt role for the Jazz while the other clubs received shorter-term guard options and draft flexibility. The inherited Jazz Win grades Utah B+, Atlanta C- and Chicago D.
analysis:
Utah Pursued a Guard Who Could Actually Handle the Ball

The Jazz acquired Shelvin Mack in February 2016 through a three-team arrangement with the Hawks and Bulls. Utah wanted another point guard option and was willing to move away from assets that didn't satisfy that immediate roster need. Atlanta took veteran Kirk Hinrich, while Chicago obtained Justin Holiday and a future second-round pick. The three different returns reflected Utah's more urgent backcourt problem compared with the Bulls' interest in future flexibility and Atlanta's familiarity with Hinrich.

Mack Had a Tangible Receiving-Team Role

Mack could distribute the ball, organize possessions and play minutes when Utah's other guards were unavailable. His Jazz appearances offered a measurable return rather than merely an overseas rights claim or an unsigned prospect. That doesn't mean he transformed Utah into an instant championship contender, but the fit was unusually direct. The Jazz acquired a player whose immediate role was readily identifiable in a division of the roster where depth mattered. His earlier NBA minutes elsewhere shouldn't be counted as Utah production.

Atlanta and Chicago Took Different Alternatives

Hinrich brought Atlanta established defensive experience and some familiarity with the organization, but his second Hawks stint was not a long-term backcourt answer. Chicago received Holiday as a wing option and a second-round right later associated with No. 47 Svi Mykhailiuk in 2018. That draft identity carries value without proving Mykhailiuk spent his eventual NBA career with the Bulls. The two receiving teams gained plausible assets of shorter duration or more uncertain draft return than Mack's Utah playing time.

The Jazz Won the Immediate Need Comparison

The inherited B+ for Utah reflects Mack's usable guard role following the deadline. Atlanta receives C- because Hinrich was a limited veteran acquisition, and Chicago's D reflects the uncertain results of its broader package. Those grades should not erase Holiday's individual ability or the long-term tradability of a future pick. They compare each club's direct benefit from this particular exchange. Utah entered seeking backcourt help and acquired a player who could occupy those minutes.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win. Utah earns B+ for Shelvin Mack's immediate guard play and the clearer receiving-team fit. Atlanta gets C- for a brief return from Kirk Hinrich. Chicago receives D for Justin Holiday and the second-round right later tied to Svi Mykhailiuk, with later rights movements limiting what can be credited directly to Chicago. Mack's visible Jazz contribution supplies the main edge.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland added shooting forward Channing Frye at the February 2016 deadline as part of a three-team deal. Orlando acquired Jared Cunningham; Portland accepted Anderson Varejão and a protected future first-round selection. Frye became a useful Cavaliers reserve on the team that won the 2016 championship. The inherited Cavaliers Win grades Cleveland B+ and both Orlando and Portland B-.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Added a Veteran Stretch Big

The Cavaliers acquired Channing Frye from Orlando in a February 2016 transaction involving Portland. Frye offered an established perimeter shot from a frontcourt position, giving Cleveland another way to create offensive room around LeBron James and Kyrie Irving. Orlando took Jared Cunningham, while Portland received Anderson Varejão and a protected future first-round right. The trade was rooted in different timelines: the Cavaliers sought another contributor for an immediate championship effort, while the other clubs accepted more speculative packages.

Frye Fit the Cavaliers' Championship Rotation

Frye's outside shooting could pull defenders away from the basket and offer a different approach from the team's more traditional interior combinations. He contributed during Cleveland's successful 2016 championship campaign, which gives the transaction direct receiving-team evidence. The veteran wasn't the team's central star, and his contribution should not be overstated as the decisive reason for the title. Still, the Cavaliers acquired a player able to fill a recognizable role in their playoff roster rather than simply adding a contractual placeholder.

Orlando and Portland Received Limited Immediate Production

Cunningham gave Orlando a guard to evaluate, but the Magic did not acquire an established long-term star in the exchange. Portland accepted Varejão's contract and a protected future first-round selection that later became associated with No. 25 Moritz Wagner in 2018. Varejão's subsequent playing history with other teams should not be assigned to the Trail Blazers. The draft right had potential transactional value, even though the identity of the eventual player and where he later played required additional moves.

The Cleveland Outcome Is Much Easier to Trace

The Cavaliers' B+ reflects Frye's identifiable shooting role on a title-winning roster. Orlando and Portland receive B- for guard and draft-contract returns with less obvious direct on-court payoff. A protected first is a meaningful piece, so Portland's side was not empty. Nevertheless, Cleveland targeted a specific frontcourt skill and gained it at a moment when it could be used immediately. Evaluating the transaction through that real contribution explains the inherited outcome without treating Frye as the sole author of the 2016 championship.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns B+ for adding Channing Frye's perimeter shooting to its eventual 2016 championship rotation. Orlando receives B- for Jared Cunningham, while Portland also gets B- for Anderson Varejão's contract and a protected first-round right later linked to Moritz Wagner. The Cleveland fit provided the clearest direct basketball value, though Frye was a supporting piece rather than the team's leading star.

Memphis signed and played Davis, while Boston later routed the Thybulle rights to Philadelphia in a separate 2019 trade. Boston's gain was draft flexibility, not a Celtics Thybulle playing career.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Turned Two Second-Round Rights Into a Future First

In the 2016 NBA Draft, Boston selected Deyonta Davis at No. 31 and Rade Zagorac at No. 35, then sent both sets of draft rights to Memphis. The Celtics received a protected future first-round selection, seeking a potentially more valuable future pick rather than retaining both young prospects. Memphis wanted Davis badly enough to trade the protected first and could also explore Zagorac as an international option. The exchange was a wager on the relative value of timing and pick position, with Boston choosing to consolidate two second-round opportunities into one later, higher-round asset.

Memphis Actually Signed Davis and Used Him

Memphis signed Davis in July 2016, giving him regular-season playing opportunities over the following two seasons. His role was primarily developmental: he provided size and occasional shot blocking but never established himself as a dependable starting center. Zagorac's overseas experience offered another possible route to future talent, though it did not translate into a stable Grizzlies NBA career. The receiving-team result wasn't zero, because Davis did play in Memphis. But two second-round acquisitions failed to become the kind of core depth that would erase the value of giving up a future first-round choice.

The Protected First Eventually Landed at No. 20

The future first conveyed as the No. 20 selection in the 2019 draft. That was the pick used on Matisse Thybulle, but he shouldn't be listed as a Celtics rotation player from this transaction. Boston dealt his rights to Philadelphia in a separate draft-night exchange, taking a different group of picks back. The distinction is essential: this 2016 trade gave the Celtics a first-round asset they could spend, not Thybulle's subsequent defensive production for the Sixers. The ability to move that right again is the concrete outcome of Boston's multi-year asset strategy.

A First-Round Asset Outweighed Two Incomplete Development Bets

Boston's side is best evaluated by the future pick's draft position and trade utility. It turned two selections early in the second round into a pick in the top twenty in 2019, a meaningful upgrade in flexibility. Memphis, meanwhile, received a young center that actually appeared but didn't achieve a lasting frontcourt breakthrough, plus rights to a prospect whose NBA future remained uncertain. This is not a judgment that second-round picks are always less useful; Davis had genuine opportunities. The outcome nevertheless supports Boston's stronger grade on the value of the eventual asset.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for converting the rights to Deyonta Davis and Rade Zagorac into a future first that landed at No. 20 in 2019 and became useful draft-night trade capital. Memphis receives C- for Davis's limited NBA tenure and Zagorac's undeveloped rights. Thybulle's later NBA production came in Philadelphia, so it cannot be counted as a direct Celtics playing return.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers traded the rights to No. 33 Cheick Diallo to New Orleans on June 23, 2016 for No. 39 David Michineau and No. 40 Diamond Stone. Diallo supplied 133 Pelicans regular-season games and 1,676 minutes between 2016 and 2019. Stone played just seven Clippers games and 24 minutes, while Michineau never joined the Clippers' NBA regular-season roster. Pelicans Win, New Orleans B+ and Los Angeles D+.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Split One Second-Round Selection Into Two Prospects

During the June 23, 2016 draft, the Clippers selected Kansas forward Cheick Diallo at No. 33 and sent his rights to New Orleans. They received two later second-round selections, No. 39 David Michineau and No. 40 Diamond Stone. The Clippers' official announcement confirms the exact transaction and draft positions. Diallo offered energetic rebounding and interior defense. Michineau was a young guard playing in France, and Stone was an American center coming out of Maryland. Los Angeles preferred two chances to develop talent instead of retaining the higher-ranked forward.

Diallo Earned Three Pelicans Seasons of NBA Frontcourt Work

Diallo made seventeen New Orleans regular-season appearances as a rookie, then fifty-two in 2017-18 and sixty-four in 2018-19. He totaled 1,676 minutes across those 133 games, with his most active season coming in his third year. His rebounding and finishing made him useful as a young reserve, even though he was not a regular starter. A draft pick in the early second round producing three years of NBA appearances is a measurable success. His later Phoenix games are not New Orleans output from this specific rights acquisition.

The Clippers Got Seven Games From Stone and None From Michineau

Stone reached the NBA with Los Angeles but appeared in only seven regular-season games in 2016-17, logging twenty-four minutes and ten points. He did not secure a second Clippers season or become a frontcourt rotation fixture. Michineau continued his professional career outside the NBA and never supplied Clippers regular-season minutes. Their overseas and developmental achievements should not be retroactively credited as Clippers league production. Two draft rights offered more potential paths to success, but neither generated the kind of sustained contribution that Diallo gave New Orleans.

The Higher Pick Produced the More Substantial NBA Return

Los Angeles had a reasonable drafting philosophy: exchanging one early second-round pick for two later prospects created additional options without using first-round capital. New Orleans simply chose the player it valued more and invested in his development. The result favors the Pelicans because they actually played their acquired center for three seasons, while the Clippers received only a handful of NBA appearances from Stone. Neither side acquired a star, so the outcome should be graded as a strong reserve return rather than a defining roster transaction.

Final Verdict

Pelicans Win. New Orleans gets B+ for Cheick Diallo's 133 regular-season games and 1,676 minutes over three seasons after the No. 33 rights purchase. Los Angeles receives D+ because Diamond Stone played just seven games and twenty-four minutes, while David Michineau never appeared for the Clippers. One higher draft choice delivered far more NBA production than the two incoming prospects.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix traded the rights to Bogdan Bogdanovic, the No. 13 and No. 28 picks in the 2016 draft and a future second-round choice to Sacramento for the rights to No. 8 pick Marquese Chriss. Chriss started 124 games across two Suns seasons and made the 2017 All-Rookie Second Team, but Phoenix moved him after only 154 games. Sacramento received three seasons and 209 games from Bogdanovic, 106 games from Skal Labissiere and 38 from Georgios Papagiannis, giving the Kings the stronger aggregate return.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Phoenix's official draft-night account and Sacramento's draft history resolve the package cleanly. The Kings selected Marquese Chriss eighth overall and sent his rights to Phoenix. In return, Sacramento received the rights to No. 13 pick Georgios Papagiannis, No. 28 pick Skal Labissiere, the rights to Bogdan Bogdanovic and a future second-round selection. The Suns had drafted Bogdanovic in 2014 and still controlled his NBA rights while he played for Fenerbahce. Phoenix therefore consolidated four assets into the one prospect its front office had targeted near the top of the 2016 class.

Phoenix Return
Chriss did provide real rotation value. As a 19-year-old rookie he played all 82 games, started 75, averaged 9.2 points and 4.2 rebounds and earned All-Rookie Second Team recognition. He followed with 72 games and 49 starts in 2017-18, averaging 7.7 points and 5.5 rebounds. Across two Suns seasons that is 154 games and 124 starts, so the legacy F grade is too harsh. The problem is that the expected development never arrived in Phoenix. His efficiency remained below league average, his role did not expand in year two, and the Suns moved him to Houston before the 2018-19 season. Phoenix received a legitimate young starter for two years, but not the long-term cornerstone the aggressive draft-night price implied.

Sacramento Return
Bogdanovic became the best player in the package. After one more season in Europe, he joined Sacramento in 2017 and played 209 games over three seasons, averaging 14.1 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.5 assists in his final Kings season. He earned All-Rookie Second Team honors as a 25-year-old rookie and became a reliable secondary creator and high-volume three-point shooter. Labissiere added 106 Kings games across parts of three seasons, including 29 starts in 2017-18. Papagiannis was the miss: Sacramento used the No. 13 rights on him, got only 38 games across two seasons and waived him in 2018. The future second-round asset remained another piece of draft capital even though it was not the centerpiece of the return.

Hindsight Verdict
Sacramento wins because the Kings received the best realized player in Bogdanovic plus additional NBA rotation value from Labissiere and a second-round asset. Phoenix's two seasons of Chriss keep the deal from being a disaster, and his All-Rookie recognition shows why the gamble was defensible at the time. The source-backed grades should therefore be less extreme than the legacy F/A+ split. Sacramento earns an A- for turning one draft slot into multiple assets and getting three productive seasons from Bogdanovic. Phoenix earns a C+ for 154 Chriss games and 124 starts without the development or retention needed to justify the consolidation price. Final verdict: Sacramento Kings Win.

summary: Cleveland acquired the draft rights to diminutive point guard Kay Felder from Atlanta in June 2016 in exchange for cash. Felder joined the Cavaliers' roster during their championship-defense season, though his role was limited. Atlanta preferred a direct financial return to carrying another developmental guard. The inherited Even Trade assigns C to both franchises.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Cleveland acquired the draft rights to diminutive point guard Kay Felder from Atlanta in June 2016 in exchange for cash. Felder joined the Cavaliers' roster during their championship-defense season, though his role was limited. Atlanta preferred a direct financial return to carrying another developmental guard. The inherited Even Trade assigns C to both franchises.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Cleveland Purchased a Second-Round Guard

The Cavaliers acquired the draft rights to Kay Felder from Atlanta in June 2016, paying $2.4 million for the opportunity. Felder had scored heavily in college despite being far shorter than most NBA guards. Cleveland had just won the championship and could explore another small backcourt prospect behind its established stars. Atlanta valued the direct cash return more than using a roster position on a second-round developmental player.

Felder Entered a Deep Cleveland Roster

Felder played NBA minutes for the Cavaliers during the 2016-17 season, offering quickness and scoring attempts in a limited role. He was not a major contributor to the 2016 championship, which Cleveland had won before the draft-night rights purchase. His smaller stature created defensive challenges and made it difficult to establish a consistent place behind more experienced guards. The Cavs obtained a legitimate chance to evaluate him without surrendering a player or a future pick.

Atlanta Took Cash Instead of a Draft Experiment

The Hawks received a specific financial payment instead of another draft choice. Cash had value for the organization but didn't directly deliver point-guard play or future rights. Atlanta's roster already required decisions about how to allocate minutes to other prospects and veterans. Selling this selection gave the club a certain return in exchange for bypassing the possibility that Felder developed into an NBA regular. That opportunity cost was real even if his Cavaliers role proved limited.

Neither Side Found a Lasting Competitive Advantage

Cleveland received a rookie it could use in games, while Atlanta received cash without taking on a developmental contract. Felder did not grow into an enduring Cavaliers starting guard, so the team did not find a hidden star through the purchase. Atlanta likewise didn't acquire a new performer. The inherited equal C grades fit the small return: a modest trial of a second-round prospect for one organization and a defined financial benefit for the other.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Cleveland gets C for purchasing Kay Felder's rights and giving him a limited NBA guard role in 2016-17. Atlanta also receives C for collecting $2.4 million rather than keeping the second-round prospect. Felder wasn't on Cleveland's already-completed 2016 championship roster, and neither team obtained an enduring core player from the deal.

summary: In July 2016 Atlanta received the draft rights to Taurean Prince, Indiana acquired Jeff Teague, and Utah received George Hill in a three-team guard-and-draft exchange. The deal provided Atlanta with a developing wing, Indiana with a proven playmaking guard, and Utah with a veteran floor general. The inherited slight Hawks edge assigns Atlanta A-, Indiana B+ and Utah B+.
analysis:
Atlanta Turned Teague Into a First-Round Wing

The Hawks joined a three-team transaction involving Indiana and Utah in July 2016. Atlanta sent Jeff Teague to the Pacers and received the draft rights to Taurean Prince. The move reflected a willingness to transition the Hawks' backcourt while adding a longer-term perimeter prospect. Prince had shown size, shooting potential and versatility in college, making him a credible developmental choice. The trade also opened opportunities for Atlanta to reorganize its remaining guard responsibilities.

Indiana Acquired a Proven Point Guard in Teague

The Pacers received Teague, an established NBA playmaker who had become an All-Star in Atlanta. Indiana valued his ability to run offense and create shots during a period of roster change. His receiving-team role should be judged from the season he actually spent with the Pacers, not all of his prior Hawks career. Teague gave Indiana an immediate option at a demanding position, though his eventual tenure was shorter than a long-term franchise rebuilding cycle.

Utah Took George Hill to Stabilize Its Backcourt

The Jazz acquired Hill from Indiana, gaining a guard with defensive size and an ability to shoot beside the team's young core. Hill's veteran profile suited a Utah group trying to advance in the Western Conference. He supplied a different kind of value from Prince's long-term developmental appeal and Teague's higher-volume ball handling. Any subsequent Hill transactions need to remain separate from the immediate Jazz benefit. The original trade placed one legitimate incoming asset with each franchise.

Three Viable Returns Made This More Than a Two-Sided Deal

Atlanta obtained a younger wing who could grow within the organization, Indiana added an experienced playmaker, and Utah secured an established two-way guard. The inherited slight Hawks edge reflects the upside Prince represented and the possibility of developing him beyond the veteran guards' shorter timelines. The B+ grades for Indiana and Utah still recognize real receiving-team benefits. A complete review must include all three clubs rather than comparing only the Hawks and Pacers and omitting Utah.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta earns A- for securing Taurean Prince's draft rights and beginning a wing-development pathway. Indiana receives B+ for adding Jeff Teague as a proven point guard, while Utah also gets B+ for George Hill's veteran defense and ball handling. The inherited edge values Prince's longer timeline, but all three franchises received meaningful assets.

philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Two Second-Round Picks Made This More Than a Center Dump

On August 26, 2016, the Utah Jazz sent center Tibor Pleiss and two future second-round selections to Philadelphia for the rights to guard Kendall Marshall. Utah’s official announcement confirmed all four components, and each franchise’s transaction register records the same exchange. houston-rockets.summary: Milwaukee acquired forward Michael Beasley from Houston for reserve guard Tyler Ennis on September 22, 2016. Beasley contributed 56 regular-season Bucks games, six starts, 935 minutes and 528 points at 53.2 percent shooting; he also appeared in four playoff games. houston-rockets.analysis:
Milwaukee Turned an Extra Point Guard Into a Scoring Forward

On September 22, 2016, the Bucks acquired Michael Beasley from Houston in exchange for Tyler Ennis. Milwaukee was reshaping its frontcourt around Giannis Antetokounmpo and Jabari Parker, while retaining several options at point guard. Beasley had been a productive scorer in short stretches for the Rockets and earlier clubs, and the Bucks could use someone who would create shots from the bench. Houston was preparing for Mike D'Antoni's first season as coach and saw Ennis as inexpensive additional ball-handling depth behind James Harden and the other guards. The deal involved no draft picks or cash.

Beasley Scored 528 Bucks Points and Played in the Playoffs

Beasley appeared in 56 regular-season games for Milwaukee in 2016-17, starting six and totaling 935 minutes. He scored 528 points, a 9.4-point average in 16.7 minutes, shooting 53.2 percent from the field. He also added 193 rebounds and made four postseason appearances when the Bucks faced Toronto in the first round. Milwaukee did not acquire a defensive anchor or a full-time starter, but Beasley was capable of supplying offense in limited stretches. His strong percentage and genuine playoff roster participation make the one-year return meaningfully more useful than a low-minute spare guard.

Ennis Played 31 Rockets Games Before Leaving

Ennis appeared in 31 Houston regular-season games before his departure for the Lakers in February 2017. His Rockets stint totaled 196 minutes, 58 points and 34 assists, with no starts. He played 22 more games for Los Angeles later that same season, but those numbers belong to the Lakers and cannot be merged into Houston's acquired value. The Rockets already had significant backcourt responsibilities allocated elsewhere, which helps explain why Ennis struggled to earn minutes. His 31 appearances showed he was at least available as a deep reserve, yet he never became a central part of Houston's attack.

The Bucks Found Bench Offense Without Sacrificing a Main Contributor

The teams made different small bets. Milwaukee moved a guard without a secure role and received a forward who provided over five hundred points plus playoff minutes. Houston acquired affordable ball-handling insurance and got a short stint before trading that player onward. Beasley's experience with other teams should not be used to inflate the Bucks' grade, and his own single Milwaukee season was not a long-term acquisition. Still, the measurable difference in 2016-17 playing time and scoring favors Milwaukee by a clear margin. Houston's return was not literally zero, which is why its inherited F warrants a less punitive evaluation.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win. Milwaukee retains B+ for Michael Beasley's 56 regular-season games, 528 points, efficient shooting and four playoff appearances. Houston receives D+ for Tyler Ennis's 31 games and 196 minutes before his transfer to Los Angeles. The Bucks secured a useful scoring reserve while the Rockets received only marginal guard depth.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Cleveland Sought a Specialist Around Its Stars

The Cavaliers traded for Kyle Korver in January 2017 to add catch-and-shoot ability beside LeBron James and Kyrie Irving. Korver had been a notable perimeter threat in Atlanta, and Cleveland could use that skill without asking him to initiate most possessions. The Hawks received Mike Dunleavy Jr., Maurice Williams, cash and second-round compensation. The move matched a contender's immediate desire for shooting with Atlanta's interest in reshuffling its roster.

Korver Delivered Real Cavaliers Playing Value

Korver contributed perimeter gravity and reserve shooting for Cleveland, helping its offense create space around the players who handled the ball. He joined a team capable of reaching the NBA Finals, although neither his earlier Atlanta All-Star season nor every subsequent Cleveland achievement belongs exclusively to this trade. The direct receiving-team return was an experienced shooter with a clear role, not merely a recognizable name who never appeared.

Atlanta Collected More Fragmented Compensation

Dunleavy was an experienced wing, while Williams had a narrower potential role following the move. The Hawks also obtained cash and a future second-round right. That pick's later description in the canonical archive has unresolved formatting and rights-chain ambiguity; it should not be credited as the career of a particular NBA player without checking the intervening transactions. Atlanta received several possibilities, but fewer immediately productive minutes than Cleveland acquired.

The Grades Reflect the Difference in Timelines

Cleveland's B+ credits the direct benefit of adding a high-level outside shooter to an already competitive lineup. Atlanta's C records smaller veteran and future-asset returns that could provide flexibility but were less influential on the court. Korver was not a primary scoring star for the Cavaliers, yet his specialist function was unusually well aligned with their roster. The inherited Cavaliers Win follows from that practical fit.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland receives B+ for Kyle Korver's shooting and spacing around its leading scorers. Atlanta earns C for Mike Dunleavy Jr., Maurice Williams, cash and a second-round component with a complicated rights history. Korver supplied the more direct on-court contribution to his new team.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Added Shooting for Its Playoff Frontcourt

The Hawks acquired Ersan Ilyasova from Philadelphia in February 2017, also arranging a second-round pick-swap option. Atlanta wanted an experienced stretch forward who could shoot from outside and complement its existing big men during a playoff push. The 76ers received Tiago Splitter and draft compensation, choosing additional asset flexibility while building around a younger roster. The transaction combined immediate playing help with multiple draft conditions, not a direct exchange of comparable full-time starters.

Ilyasova Gave Atlanta a Useful Rotation Option

Ilyasova offered the Hawks perimeter spacing, rebounding and experience in the frontcourt. His ability to draw defenders away from the basket made him a practical player for the remaining 2016-17 season. That immediate Atlanta role is the direct basketball benefit of this trade, not his earlier time with Milwaukee or later stints elsewhere. He did not become the franchise's primary scorer, and his relatively short Atlanta tenure limits the long-term value attributable to this particular acquisition.

Philadelphia Received Draft Rights and an Injured Veteran

Splitter brought a recognized NBA career, but physical limitations reduced what Philadelphia could expect from him as an active center. The 76ers also obtained a second-round asset associated with No. 46 Sterling Brown and rights connected with the pick-swap framework. Other related picks were tied to different names, including Mathias Lessort and Alpha Kaba, depending on the side of the swap. Following those rights accurately is important; their later NBA careers cannot all be claimed by the original receiving franchise without tracing additional moves.

The Grades Favor Philadelphia's Future Options

Atlanta secured usable frontcourt minutes for a team seeking an immediate playoff contribution. Philadelphia received wider draft flexibility and compensation that could support future roster decisions, while Splitter was not an important long-term playing answer. The inherited 76ers edge credits those options over a comparatively brief veteran stint. It does not require claiming that Ilyasova failed in Atlanta or that every eventual draftee played productive NBA seasons for the Sixers.

Final Verdict

76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B for Tiago Splitter and second-round draft compensation, including the right later associated with Sterling Brown, despite Splitter's limited on-court role. Atlanta gets C+ for Ersan Ilyasova's useful stretch-forward minutes and an associated pick-swap option. The inherited verdict favors Philadelphia's additional future assets over Atlanta's relatively short-term frontcourt upgrade.

houston-rockets.summary: On February 23, 2017, the Lakers acquired Tyler Ennis and the draft rights to Australian wing Brad Newley from Houston for Marcelo Huertas. Ennis appeared in 22 Lakers games that spring and 54 more the following season, totaling 76 games and 1,075 minutes. Houston waived Huertas without a Rockets regular-season appearance. Newley never played in the NBA. Lakers Win, Los Angeles B and Houston D+.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Los Angeles Acquired a Guard With More Development Time

The Lakers obtained Tyler Ennis and the draft rights to Australian wing Brad Newley from Houston on February 23, 2017, sending Marcelo Huertas to the Rockets. Los Angeles's official release and the league's deadline tracker list both incoming assets. Ennis had appeared in 31 Rockets games earlier in the season but hadn't secured a regular role behind the main scorers. The Lakers had just reshuffled their basketball leadership, giving the organization reason to evaluate another young point guard. Newley's rights offered a theoretical additional option, although he was continuing a successful international career.

Ennis Immediately Played Twenty-Two Lakers Games

Ennis took advantage of the Los Angeles opening and appeared in 22 regular-season games to close 2016-17, starting twice. He averaged 7.7 points and 2.4 assists while totaling 392 minutes for his new club. Those games were enough to persuade the Lakers to re-sign him in July, according to an official NBA announcement. That extension is important because the February acquisition was not simply a brief roster shuffle. Ennis was a real point-guard option rather than an unused expiring contract, and his 31 earlier Rockets games should not be included in his Lakers return.

Another Fifty-Four Games Followed Before Ennis Left

Ennis returned for 2017-18 and played 54 more Los Angeles regular-season games, including eleven starts and 683 minutes. His scoring average decreased to 4.1 points in a shorter nightly role, but he remained available behind other young guards. Across both receiving-team seasons, the original trade yielded 76 Lakers games and 1,075 minutes. Brad Newley continued playing overseas and never joined an NBA Lakers rotation, so his rights shouldn't be credited with extra league statistics. Ennis was the meaningful on-court asset Los Angeles acquired.

Houston's Incoming Player Didn't Make a Regular-Season Contribution

Huertas had provided veteran point-guard play to the Lakers earlier in his NBA career, appearing in 76 games across the preceding season. That work belonged to Los Angeles before the deal. After Houston acquired him, the Rockets did not use Huertas in a regular-season game and moved on from the contract. The difference between an unused incoming guard and two partial seasons of Ennis is enough to justify a decisive Lakers win. The original Lakers grade of D treated a legitimate 76-game return too harshly, while Houston's poor basketball return remained a minor reserve acquisition rather than a major franchise error.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B because Tyler Ennis played 76 regular-season games and 1,075 minutes across two seasons after the deal; Brad Newley's international rights never produced NBA appearances. Houston receives D+ because Marcelo Huertas played no Rockets regular-season games. The Lakers found a useful reserve while Houston's player return went unused.

houston-rockets.summary: The Rockets acquired Lou Williams from the Lakers on February 23, 2017, sending Corey Brewer and a first-round choice later used at No. 28 on Tony Bradley. Williams appeared in 23 Houston regular-season games, scoring 343 points in 591 minutes, plus the playoffs, before he was moved onward in a different multi-player transaction. The Lakers received Brewer's veteran depth and a real first-round draft asset. Slight Rockets Edge for the immediate playoff scoring, Houston B, Los Angeles B-.
houston-rockets.analysis:
Houston Added an Established Sixth-Man Scorer for Its Push

Houston sent Corey Brewer and its 2017 first-round pick to the Lakers on February 23, 2017 in exchange for Lou Williams. The Rockets were surrounding James Harden with additional ball handlers and shooters in Mike D'Antoni's high-volume offense. Williams had been leading Los Angeles in bench scoring, while Brewer's role in Houston had narrowed. For the Lakers, recently reorganized under Magic Johnson, the trade exchanged a veteran scorer for an additional chance to draft a prospect. Both teams clearly valued different timelines, one focused on the imminent postseason and the other on rebuilding.

Williams Gave Houston Twenty-Three Games and More Scoring

Williams appeared in twenty-three regular-season Rockets games after the move, all as a reserve. He totaled 591 minutes and 343 points, an average of 14.9 per game, while contributing fifty-six assists. His ability to generate offense without Harden helped Houston's second unit ahead of the playoffs. The sample was shorter and his shooting less efficient than the stretch he had just completed for the Lakers, so the return should be judged by those Houston games, not by his 58 earlier appearances in purple and gold. His subsequent scoring years with the Clippers also belong to a separate acquisition.

Los Angeles Received Brewer and a Usable First-Round Choice

The Lakers took in Brewer's veteran contract and, more importantly for their rebuilding timetable, Houston's 2017 first-round pick. The selection ultimately landed at No. 28, later associated with Tony Bradley, although its draft-rights trail continued beyond the original agreement. That history is why Bradley should not simply be listed as a long-term Lakers player acquired from Houston. Brewer supplied another experienced perimeter option during an unsettled roster period, while the pick created an opportunity to trade or select a younger player. Los Angeles obtained genuine draft capital rather than just discarding its leading bench scorer.

The Value Difference Is Short-Term Offense Versus Future Choice

Houston got exactly the kind of bench scoring the club sought during a playoff push, with Williams making an immediate impact in a defined rotation role. The Lakers accepted fewer short-term points in exchange for an extra first-round selection and a player contract that could fill minutes while the roster changed. Houston later used Williams in a much larger multi-asset deal with the Clippers, but the entire eventual return from that transaction cannot be attributed to this February swap. The original slight Houston edge remains plausible for instant on-court utility, with more measured credit than the inherited low grades gave either side.

Final Verdict

Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns B because Lou Williams supplied 23 games, 591 minutes and 343 points during its 2016-17 playoff push. Los Angeles receives B- for Corey Brewer's depth and the first-round pick ultimately listed as No. 28 Tony Bradley, a transferable draft asset. Williams's later Clippers scoring and the full return of subsequent unrelated transactions are excluded from Houston's direct NBA performance.

The selection ultimately landed at No. 28, later associated with Tony Bradley, although its draft-rights trail continued beyond the original agreement. That history is why Bradley should not simply be listed as a long-term Lakers player acquired from Houston. Brewer supplied another experienced perimeter option during an unsettled roster period, while the pick created an opportunity to trade or select a younger player. Los Angeles obtained genuine draft capital rather than just discarding its leading bench scorer.

The Value Difference Is Short-Term Offense Versus Future Choice

Houston got exactly the kind of bench scoring the club sought during a playoff push, with Williams making an immediate impact in a defined rotation role. The Lakers accepted fewer short-term points in exchange for an extra first-round selection and a player contract that could fill minutes while the roster changed. Houston later used Williams in a much larger multi-asset deal with the Clippers, but the entire eventual return from that transaction cannot be attributed to this February swap. The original slight Houston edge remains plausible for instant on-court utility, with more measured credit than the inherited low grades gave either side.

Final Verdict

Slight Rockets Edge. Houston earns B because Lou Williams supplied 23 games, 591 minutes and 343 points during its 2016-17 playoff push. Los Angeles receives B- for Corey Brewer's depth and the first-round pick ultimately listed as No. 28 Tony Bradley, a transferable draft asset. Williams's later Clippers scoring and the full return of subsequent unrelated transactions are excluded from Houston's direct NBA performance.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Moved Down Two Spots and Secured Another First

On June 19, 2017, Boston sent the first selection in that week's NBA Draft to Philadelphia for the third pick and a future first-round selection subject to detailed protections. The Sixers wanted Washington guard Markelle Fultz and paid for the right to select him without waiting. Boston's front office believed it could move down, retain access to a favored prospect and gain another meaningful draft asset. The extra pick wasn't automatically a 2019 selection at the time: the agreement first tested a protected 2018 Lakers pick, with an alternative 2019 path if those conditions weren't met.

The Third Pick Became Jayson Tatum and a Championship Cornerstone

Philadelphia used No. 1 on Fultz, but Boston selected Duke forward Jayson Tatum at No. 3. Tatum developed into a principal scorer, an All-NBA-level forward and the centerpiece of repeated Celtics playoff runs. He led the team's scoring during the 2024 championship season and scored 31 points in the Finals-clinching win over Dallas. Those are concrete Boston outcomes from the pick obtained in the swap, not merely a scouting projection preserved from draft night. Selecting Tatum despite trading down is what makes the deal unusually valuable in hindsight.

Philadelphia's Fultz Return Ended After Just 33 Games

Fultz's Philadelphia tenure never produced the long-term lead guard the Sixers imagined when they moved up. He played 14 regular-season games as a rookie and 19 more in 2018-19, with health and shooting difficulties disrupting his time alongside Joel Embiid and Ben Simmons. Philadelphia moved him to Orlando in a separate February 2019 transaction. His later NBA progress with the Magic belongs to that franchise's record, not Philadelphia's return for the 2017 pick swap. The original gamble was understandable because Fultz was a highly regarded prospect, but the resulting 33-game Sixers stint left an enormous opportunity cost.

The Conditional Extra First Eventually Became Romeo Langford

Boston also realized the conditional second component of its return when the first-round obligation conveyed in 2019. That selection landed at No. 14 and was used on Romeo Langford, who became a Celtics depth prospect rather than a star matching Tatum. The smaller return is still a genuine additional draft opportunity Philadelphia surrendered to climb from third to first. Boston's advantage isn't based on pretending Langford enjoyed Tatum's career or that the second pick was fixed in the initial deal. The central comparison is a future championship leader plus a separate first-round chance against Fultz's very brief Philadelphia tenure.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns A+ because moving from No. 1 to No. 3 still yielded Jayson Tatum, a driving force behind the Celtics' 2024 NBA title, and another first-rounder eventually used on Romeo Langford. Philadelphia receives F because its 2017 No. 1 choice, Markelle Fultz, appeared in just 33 regular-season Sixers games before a separate trade to Orlando. The protected extra pick increased the cost of an already unfortunate Philadelphia outcome.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Charlotte traded Marco Belinelli, Miles Plumlee and the No. 41 pick to Atlanta for Dwight Howard and the No. 31 pick in June 2017. Howard started 81 Hornets games in 2017-18 and averaged a double-double, while Atlanta gained short-term wing shooting and center depth plus a second-rounder used on Tyler Dorsey. Hawks Win in the canonical record, Atlanta B+ and Charlotte C-.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Charlotte Took Howard While Atlanta Reset Its Roster

The Hornets acquired Dwight Howard and the No. 31 draft pick from Atlanta in exchange for Marco Belinelli, Miles Plumlee and the No. 41 selection in June 2017. Howard was returning to a coach, Steve Clifford, familiar with his earlier career as an elite rebounder and interior defender. Atlanta, which had acquired Howard only a year earlier, was shifting direction under new management. The club accepted two veterans and a lower pick to alter a frontcourt contract and make room for different lineup combinations. This was not a straight one-player swap.

Howard Produced One Strong Individual Charlotte Season

Howard gave Charlotte legitimate center production, starting 81 games in 2017-18 and averaging roughly 16.6 points and 12.5 rebounds. That volume is important when weighing the trade: the Hornets did receive a productive player, not a failed acquisition with no games. But he was not retained as the team's long-term solution. Charlotte moved him again after the season while adjusting its roster and finances. The exchange brought impressive individual counting statistics without delivering a sustained second phase of Howard's Hornets career.

Belinelli, Plumlee and Dorsey Gave Atlanta Multiple Paths

Belinelli added perimeter shooting and reserve scoring, though he spent only part of the season with Atlanta before departing. Plumlee provided another veteran center option, with his contract and minutes contributing to the club's subsequent planning. The No. 41 pick became guard Tyler Dorsey, giving the Hawks a prospect to develop rather than merely a veteran salary swap. None of these incoming pieces alone matched Howard's statistical output in Charlotte. Their collective utility and Atlanta's decision to reset an expensive center commitment explain the club's side of the transaction.

The Different Time Horizons Define the Result

The Hornets received the best single-season player, but their acquisition ended after one campaign. Atlanta acquired three separate assets and gained control over the direction of its frontcourt and reserve guard development. Neither outcome should be exaggerated: Belinelli was temporary, Plumlee wasn't a star and Dorsey didn't establish himself as a franchise guard. Still, the Hawks obtained multiple usable elements without carrying Howard through another long stint. The canonical Atlanta advantage weighs those roster options against Charlotte's brief burst of center production.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for Marco Belinelli, Miles Plumlee and No. 41 pick Tyler Dorsey, a package that also helped the franchise reset its center commitment. Charlotte receives C- despite Dwight Howard's strong 81-game double-double season, because his Hornets stint lasted only one year. The judgment favors Atlanta's broader flexibility over an impressive but temporary individual return.
