golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Bought the No. 38 Pick From Chicago

The Bulls selected Jordan Bell from Oregon with the 38th overall pick in the 2017 NBA draft and immediately sent his rights to the Golden State Warriors for $3.5 million in cash. Golden State already had a title-contending roster anchored by Stephen Curry, Kevin Durant, Klay Thompson and Draymond Green, but it needed affordable athletic big men on rookie deals. Bell's rebounding, help defense and mobility fit that requirement better than another veteran contract. Chicago chose immediate cash instead of investing a roster position in the second-rounder. The financial amount was real and documented, even though it did not improve the Bulls' basketball roster.

Bell Gave the Warriors Two Postseason-Useful Seasons

Bell appeared in 57 regular-season Warriors games as a rookie in 2017-18, starting 13 and playing 809 minutes. He used his athleticism around the rim and contributed as a reserve during the team's successful championship defense. He returned for 68 games in 2018-19, adding another 788 minutes and three starts as Golden State reached the Finals again. Across those two seasons, Bell totaled 125 appearances and 1,597 regular-season minutes. He was not the principal player responsible for either Finals run, but that is an appreciable contribution from an inexpensive second-round center.

Chicago Received Cash but Passed on a Useful Rotation Option

The Bulls received $3.5 million, a tangible payment that could support the organization's finances or broader transactions. It is not correct to describe their return as literally nothing. However, the club did not receive another player or draft selection from the rights swap. Bell provided the Warriors minutes while Chicago was rebuilding following the Jimmy Butler trade. A salary-cap or payroll analysis would have to consider how the Bulls used the money, but there is no reason to invent a specific later draft or player acquisition funded solely by this deal. The known immediate return was cash, not on-court production.

The Cost of Buying Rotation Depth Was Well Worth It

Golden State gave up a cash payment rather than future player assets to acquire two years of inexpensive frontcourt contributions. Bell's defense fit a switchable system built around proven stars, and his rookie-season minutes helped a team seeking a fourth championship in five years. Chicago had a rational financial reason to accept the offer, but a prospect who could play 125 games for a contender had more sporting value than the money alone demonstrates. The Warriors did not discover another All-Star at No. 38, and Bell's role declined in his second year, yet this was a favorable return on a draft-rights purchase.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State keeps B+ for Jordan Bell's 125 regular-season games and 1,597 minutes across two Finals seasons, including the 2018 title. Chicago gets C because it received the documented $3.5 million payment but sacrificed the opportunity to use Bell itself. The player contribution gave the Warriors the better basketball result.

indiana-pacers.summary: On June 22, 2017, Indiana paid New Orleans $1 million for the rights to second-round pick Edmond Sumner. The Xavier guard played 108 Pacers regular-season games across 2017-18 through 2020-21, including 29 starts, and averaged 7.5 points across 53 games in 2020-21. An Achilles injury interrupted the following season, and his later Nets games belong to Brooklyn. Pacers Win, Indiana B+, New Orleans C.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Purchased a Late Second-Round Guard Prospect

During the June 22, 2017 NBA draft, the Pacers purchased Edmond Sumner's draft rights from the New Orleans Pelicans for $1 million. The transaction is recorded in Indiana's season history and in the front-office ledger for president Kevin Pritchard. Sumner had shown athletic defensive ability at Xavier but faced injury concerns, reducing his draft position. The Pacers did not have to surrender a player or future selection to take the chance on him. New Orleans accepted guaranteed financial compensation rather than carrying another development guard on its own roster.

Sumner's Indiana Development Took More Than a Season

Sumner played only one regular-season game during 2017-18, logging two minutes. His next two seasons involved limited but growing assignments: 23 Pacers games and two starts in 2018-19, then 31 appearances and three starts in 2019-20. The improvement was gradual, reflecting the difficulties of establishing a late second-round guard in a rotation led by established veterans. This stretch is important because a short-term draft-night grade would have written the purchase off before Indiana actually received a usable player. The franchise held the rights long enough for that development period to pay off.

The 2020-21 Season Delivered His Main Return

In 2020-21 Sumner appeared in 53 Indiana regular-season games and started 24, averaging 7.5 points on 52.5 percent shooting from the field. His increased role lifted the cumulative Pacers return from a speculative G League development story to 108 NBA appearances and 29 starts across four seasons. The club had purchased his rights for cash rather than sacrificing future picks. An Achilles injury kept him from playing during 2021-22, and he later appeared for Brooklyn in 2022-23. Those Nets games should not be added to Indiana's acquired-team performance.

New Orleans Received Cash, Indiana Received Rotation Games

The Pelicans got the agreed $1 million, and that is a documented financial result rather than an empty asset. There is no identified subsequent player or draft choice that can be directly assigned to that payment alone, however. Indiana got a guard who eventually started nearly half his games in one season and delivered a sustained stretch of NBA availability. Sumner was not a star and his injury history capped the investment, but 108 appearances from a low second-round rights purchase is meaningful. The basketball result therefore favors Indiana more distinctly than the earlier slight-edge grade suggested.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win. Indiana earns B+ for Edmond Sumner's 108 regular-season games, 29 starts and useful 2020-21 reserve-and-starter minutes following the $1 million draft-rights purchase. New Orleans gets C because its compensation was guaranteed cash but produced no direct player minutes. Sumner's later Brooklyn seasons do not contribute to the Pacers' trade return.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: On June 22, 2017, Milwaukee sold the rights to No. 48 draft pick Sindarius Thornwell to the Clippers for about $2 million. Thornwell played 73 Clippers games as a rookie, scoring 282 points in 1,156 minutes, and another 64 games in 2018-19, totaling 137 appearances and 1,469 minutes in two years. Clippers Win, Los Angeles B, Milwaukee C+: the Bucks received cash, but the Clippers acquired a usable reserve.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Bought Thornwell's Rights on Draft Night

Milwaukee selected South Carolina guard Sindarius Thornwell with the 48th overall pick of the 2017 NBA draft and immediately sent his rights to Los Angeles for cash considerations. Both clubs issued official announcements. Thornwell was the SEC Player of the Year as a senior, with defensive toughness and enough ball-handling skill to merit a look as a professional wing. The Clippers were managing changes in their backcourt, while Milwaukee was willing to take roughly $2 million instead of keeping a late second-round player. This was a draft-rights sale, not a swap of two active NBA players.

Thornwell Earned 73 Clippers Games as a Rookie

Thornwell appeared in 73 Los Angeles regular-season games in 2017-18, starting 17 and playing 1,156 minutes. He scored 282 points, grabbed 140 rebounds and made 48 steals, mostly while defending perimeter players and filling reserve minutes. That is a substantive rookie workload for the No. 48 pick, especially on a club that was adjusting to its post-Chris-Paul roster. Thornwell did not emerge as a consistent high-volume scorer; his 3.9 points per game show how narrow his offensive role remained. Still, the team acquired a real contributor rather than an unused prospect.

His Second Season Added Games but Far Fewer Minutes

Thornwell returned in 2018-19 for 64 regular-season Clippers appearances, totaling 313 minutes and 62 points. He started once, and his reduced playing time showed that he had slipped below other guards in the rotation even as the team reached the postseason. Across two seasons, Thornwell supplied 137 regular-season games, 1,469 minutes and 344 points in a Clippers uniform. His later NBA appearances for New Orleans and Orlando came after the original Los Angeles stint and must be kept separate. The Clippers received a useful rookie and then a deep reserve, which is still considerable draft-rights value.

Milwaukee Received Cash While Los Angeles Obtained a Player

The Bucks acquired a real financial asset through the cash payment, so it would be wrong to treat the receiving side as completely empty. But the money did not itself record minutes or points, and Milwaukee was surrendering a player who ultimately earned a lengthy rookie role. Los Angeles got two seasons of bench coverage from a late draft selection without giving up another player or future pick. That does not make Thornwell a star or prove Milwaukee's front office made a disastrous decision. It does mean the earlier Bucks-favored evaluation gave the cash return too much weight relative to 137 actual Clippers appearances.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win. Los Angeles earns B for Sindarius Thornwell's 137 regular-season games, 1,469 minutes and 344 points in two seasons. Milwaukee gets C+ for approximately $2 million in cash. The Bucks' financial return was legitimate, but the Clippers received the stronger on-court result from the No. 48 selection.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: At the June 22, 2017 draft, Philadelphia acquired the No. 25 draft rights to Latvian center Anžejs Pasečņiks from Orlando, sending a conditional 2020 first-round pick and a 2020 second-round pick. The assets eventually became No. 21 Tyrese Maxey and No. 47 Yam Madar, but Orlando did not keep the No. 21 pick until 2020: it returned to Philadelphia as part of the Markelle Fultz deal in 2019. Pasečņiks played no NBA games for the 76ers. Magic Win, Orlando A- for movable first/second rights and their leverage, Philadelphia D+.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Philadelphia Paid Two Future Choices for a Late First-Round Center

The June 22, 2017 NBA draft produced a rights trade that sent Anžejs Pasečņiks from Orlando to Philadelphia. Orlando had used the twenty-fifth overall selection on the Latvian center, whose European development made him a longer-term prospect. The 76ers offered a conditional 2020 first-round pick and a 2020 second-round choice tied to the less favorable of Brooklyn and New York's selections. The first carried protection terms rather than being an unqualified top selection. Philadelphia was wagering that a specific international prospect would be worth more than the future draft flexibility, while Orlando preferred two later assets.

The Sixers Never Obtained Pasečņiks NBA Minutes

Pasečņiks did not become a Philadelphia regular-season player through the 2017 rights acquisition. He remained overseas while the organization continued developing other frontcourt options and ultimately moved on without turning the draft choice into a Sixers rotation appearance. His subsequent NBA time in Washington belongs to a different franchise agreement and cannot retroactively rescue Philadelphia's original return. A low Sixers grade is appropriate because the club surrendered a future first and another second without receiving direct on-court production. The situation differs from drafting a useful reserve who played for several seasons before being moved again.

Orlando Converted the First Into a Later Trade Asset

The protected first-round pick eventually conveyed as No. 21 in 2020, which was used to select Tyrese Maxey. However, Orlando did not draft or develop Maxey. The Magic included that future pick in the February 2019 transaction that sent Markelle Fultz from Philadelphia to Orlando. The second-round choice eventually became No. 47, associated with Yam Madar, and followed its own series of later rights transfers. Those are genuine values from the original 2017 trade, but the later pick names are a record of what the selections became, not proof of Magic minutes by Maxey or Madar.

The Magic Retained Leverage, Not the Players Drafted Years Later

Orlando exchanged an overseas prospect for two draft assets and later used the first as part of a package to acquire a young guard in Fultz. Philadelphia received Pasečņiks's rights and did not convert them into any NBA contribution, even though the same organization eventually drafted Maxey using the pick returned in a separate deal. The multiple transactions need to remain independent: Fultz had his own asset price in 2019, and Maxey's Sixers career cannot be credited directly to the 2017 Orlando trade. The Magic's advantage is substantial in terms of pick leverage, although the revised grade stops short of claiming all later returns as a single one-step victory.

Final Verdict

Magic Win. Orlando receives A- for obtaining a future first and second in exchange for No. 25 Anžejs Pasečņiks, retaining assets it could later trade. Philadelphia gets D+ because Pasečņiks never played an NBA game for the Sixers. The first eventually became 2020 No. 21 Tyrese Maxey but returned to Philadelphia through the separate 2019 Markelle Fultz trade; Orlando must not be credited with Maxey's Sixers production or Yam Madar's subsequent rights path.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Exchanged Ryan Kelly for Cash

In late June 2017, Atlanta traded forward Ryan Kelly to Houston for cash. Kelly had already played for the Lakers and spent time with the Hawks, making him a familiar reserve with enough outside shooting ability to interest another club. Atlanta was beginning a larger roster transition and could use the transaction to move a peripheral contract without sacrificing a key player. Houston received the chance to consider Kelly as a possible depth option rather than a proven piece of its next starting group.

The Hawks Obtained Financial Flexibility Instead of Another Player

Atlanta's return was a payment rather than a draft choice or a direct replacement for Kelly. That is an appropriate outcome to evaluate financially, not through imagined minutes from a player who never arrived. The franchise had other decisions to make after moving Dwight Howard earlier that summer, and smaller transactions helped manage the roster around its evolving priorities. Trading a reserve for cash is a limited move, but it can still serve a purpose when the outgoing player's opportunity to contribute is declining.

Kelly Did Not Establish a Houston Regular-Season Role

Kelly's previous NBA experience explained why Houston might have considered him, yet the move did not produce a continuing Rockets role. His earlier Los Angeles and Atlanta minutes must remain attached to those franchises, not transferred into the receiving-side value calculation. Houston's opportunity was an inexpensive personnel look, one that did not turn into a dependable shooting forward on its roster. The absence of sustained court time matters more to a trade review than whether the new organization briefly held the player's contractual rights.

Neither Side Expected a Franchise-Altering Return

Houston's assessment of a marginal forward and Atlanta's receipt of cash were narrow operational decisions. This was not a deal that altered the playoff balance in either conference or moved a future lottery asset. Atlanta obtained something certain, while Houston accepted a chance that ultimately delivered little visible NBA impact. The grades remain modest because the risk and ceiling were both small. Calling the exchange Even Trade doesn't mean both sides enjoyed equal scoring production; rather, neither side gave up a central piece or secured a major gain.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Atlanta receives C+ for converting Ryan Kelly's fringe roster place into cash, and Houston also receives C+ for a low-cost opportunity to evaluate a forward without obtaining durable Rockets minutes. The transaction helped with roster housekeeping but did not yield a meaningful basketball contributor for either side. Earlier Kelly production elsewhere isn't a Rockets return.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis: The Clippers received Patrick Beverley, Lou Williams, Montrezl Harrell and a first-round pick, a strong reset package. Houston received Chris Paul and reached a 65-win, title-level peak, giving the Rockets the narrow realized edge. The Clippers franchise received Patrick Beverley; Sam Dekker; Montrezl Harrell; Darrun Hilliard; DeAndre Liggins; Lou Williams; Kyle Wiltjer; first-round pick (protected top 3 in 2018-23, unprotected in 2024) (2018 #30-Omari Spellman); $661K cash and surrendered Chris Paul. The counterpart's realized return was better, but the Clippers' incoming package was meaningful enough to keep this below a full Partner Win. Because this was a franchise-level transaction, the evaluation gives extra weight to star-level production, years of control, playoff impact and identifiable downstream draft conversion rather than treating the assets as interchangeable.

summary: Houston acquired Chris Paul for a deep Clippers package, creating a 65-win title contender, while Los Angeles converted an outgoing star into Patrick Beverley, Lou Williams, Montrezl Harrell and a successful bridge roster.
analysis: Paul gave Houston the best regular season in franchise history and a 3-2 conference-final lead over Golden State before his hamstring injury. The partnership lasted only two seasons and never reached the Finals. Los Angeles recovered three major contributors, won 48 games during its transition and preserved flexibility for its next star cycle. Houston achieved the higher peak, but the Clippers generated broader and more durable transition value. A-minus on both sides and an Even Trade verdict best capture the outcome.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston sent cash to Portland on June 28, 2017 for guard Tim Quarterman, then waived him October 13 without a Rockets regular-season appearance. Quarterman briefly signed again with Houston in spring 2018 but still supplied no league game during the initial trade stint. Portland banked cash for a player who didn't fit its roster. Blazers Win, Portland C+ for a realized payment and Houston D+ for a nonproductive audition.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Rockets Bought a Young Reserve Guard From Portland

On June 28, 2017, Houston acquired Tim Quarterman from the Trail Blazers for cash considerations. The move took place during a busy Rockets offseason and was among several small transactions surrounding the arrival of Chris Paul. Quarterman had spent his first NBA season with Portland, earning an opportunity as a young guard with size. Houston wasn't paying for a proven starter; it was securing another option to evaluate in camp. The official NBA trade tracker explicitly lists the receiving player and outgoing cash, without identifying a specific dollar amount.

Quarterman's First Houston Stay Ended Before Opening Night

The Rockets carried Quarterman through the offseason, but they released him on October 13, 2017, prior to the start of regular-season play. He consequently logged no Houston NBA points, assists or official games as the direct first-stint return from this June trade. His 2016-17 Portland statistics don't transfer to his new organization merely because Houston acquired his contract. The distinction prevents a misleading grade based on a rookie season that belonged entirely to the club which sold him. It was an unsuccessful Rockets tryout.

A Separate Spring Signing Doesn't Alter the Trade's Return

Quarterman's professional record includes a later Rockets contract in March 2018 followed by another April waiver. That was a fresh free-agent move rather than a second stage of the original Portland cash sale. Separating the two transactions avoids crediting the June 2017 trade with anything Quarterman might have done after rejoining under a different agreement. The main historical result remains that the player originally acquired for cash never became part of Houston's regular-season rotation during the contract bought from Portland.

Portland Received the Only Realized Compensation

The Trail Blazers collected cash for an end-of-bench prospect, which was a valid financial return even though the amount wasn't publicly specified in the official trade summary. Houston obtained the right to examine a guard who didn't survive the roster cut. Neither side lost a central player, and the dollar value shouldn't be exaggerated. The imported F grades dismissed both forms of value: Portland actually received payment, and Houston's developmental risk was modest. Still, the difference between a realized cash receipt and a player who logged zero official games favors the seller.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win. Portland gets C+ for receiving cash when it moved Tim Quarterman to Houston. The Rockets get D+ because their June 2017 acquisition was waived before the season without any team-specific NBA appearance. His later March 2018 return was a distinct contract, not a league contribution produced by the original cash purchase.

houston-rockets.summary: Houston acquired Shawn Long from Philadelphia on June 28, 2017, sending a 2018 second-round pick and $100,000 cash according to the NBA trade tracker and contemporary Rockets reporting. Long was waived September 26 without playing a Rockets regular-season game. The 2018 selection became No. 60 Kostas Antetokounmpo after later rights movement. Philadelphia received transferable compensation; Rockets received a short camp opportunity. 76ers Win, Philadelphia B- and Houston D+.
houston-rockets.analysis:
The Rockets Paid Cash and a Future Second for a Camp Prospect

Houston acquired forward-center Shawn Long from Philadelphia on June 28, 2017, during the roster movement surrounding the Chris Paul trade. The NBA's own offseason tracker lists a 2018 second-round selection and cash as the 76ers return. Other transaction histories list the cash payment as $100,000. Long had shown scoring and rebounding ability in limited 2016-17 appearances for Philadelphia, but he was not a proven Houston rotation player. The Rockets were taking a low-cost developmental look rather than acquiring a starting frontcourt option.

Long Left Houston Without a Regular-Season Appearance

The Rockets waived Long on September 26, 2017, before their opening regular-season game. His NBA games during the prior spring were for Philadelphia and cannot be carried over into Houston's incoming production. After signing Long in the summer, Houston used the preseason period to evaluate its frontcourt candidates and ultimately retained other players. The player it purchased in this agreement gave the Rockets zero regular-season minutes, points and rebounds. That result should control the on-court side of the verdict instead of Long's earlier 76ers statistics.

The Draft-Pick Records Need an Explicit Source Caveat

There is a documented discrepancy in how the outgoing asset appears across reference sites. Basketball-Reference's Philadelphia season ledger names only the $100,000 cash, while the official NBA trade tracker and independent transaction histories include a 2018 second-round pick. The later draft-chain database identifies the selection as No. 60, associated with Kostas Antetokounmpo. Such disagreement should be disclosed rather than silently choosing a version that inflates the score. Philadelphia held tradeable value from the deal, but Antetokounmpo's later NBA career was for other organizations, not the Sixers.

Philadelphia Obtained Assets, Houston Got a Short Audition

Philadelphia moved a marginal forward and accepted a cash payment with draft consideration documented by the league's transaction tracker. Houston obtained a chance to evaluate a young big man but released him before a regular-season appearance. Neither transaction created an NBA star, and the uncertainty about the precise draft-pick history warrants a tempered grade for the selling club. Still, the disparity in actual outcomes favors Philadelphia more than a pure player-for-player comparison would suggest. The Rockets' first objective was developmental optionality, which simply did not translate into on-court production.

Final Verdict

76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B- for cash reported at $100,000 and a 2018 second-round pick identified in the NBA's official trade tracker, subject to the disclosed discrepancy with Basketball-Reference's cash-only ledger. Houston receives D+ because Shawn Long was waived September 26, 2017, without a Rockets regular-season appearance. No subsequent NBA games by the eventual draft recipient are credited to Philadelphia.

perspectives.summary: The Clippers acquired Danilo Gallinari in a July 6, 2017 three-team deal. Denver received the 2019 Washington-origin second-round selection via Atlanta, while the Hawks acquired Jamal Crawford, Diamond Stone, the protected 2018 Houston-origin first-round right and cash. The original slight Clippers edge grades Los Angeles A-, Atlanta B+ and Denver C. A prior Denver-only source view had omitted Atlanta's incoming package.
perspectives.analysis:
Los Angeles Selected a Proven Scoring Forward

The Clippers acquired Danilo Gallinari from Denver through a July 2017 sign-and-trade that required Atlanta's participation. Gallinari had been a productive scoring forward with the Nuggets and could offer shooting, size and the ability to create offense outside the paint. The Clippers were seeking another established player after substantial changes to their veteran roster. Giving up Jamal Crawford, young center Diamond Stone and future draft consideration was a meaningful price for a forward with a recognizable NBA role.

Atlanta Collected a Wider Package Than the Original Import Showed

The Hawks obtained Crawford, Stone, a protected 2018 first-round right originating with Houston and cash from the Clippers. The complete official Hawks release independently confirms these incoming assets. Crawford brought extensive bench-scoring experience, Stone offered a young center to evaluate, and the future first gave Atlanta additional draft flexibility. Crawford's lengthy past NBA career wasn't new Hawks performance, while the protected selection's eventual value depended on its actual conveyance and later rights path. The package was real, not an empty facilitating-team return.

Denver Accepted One Second-Round Right

The Nuggets received Atlanta's 2019 second-round selection originating with Washington. Denver was losing a player who had been an important scoring option over multiple seasons, but it chose a draft asset rather than matching his offensive contribution with another established forward. The right's eventual selection history needed separate tracing; it wasn't automatically an NBA player who spent a season in Denver. The exchange also occurred while the Nuggets were changing the composition of their frontcourt and the offensive responsibilities of other players.

The Grades Compare Immediate Fit With Asset Breadth

The inherited slight Clippers edge gives Los Angeles A- because Gallinari supplied a current scoring profile, Atlanta B+ for multiple incoming assets, and Denver C for the more limited second-round return. Those grades don't prove the Clippers received uninterrupted star production or that Atlanta kept every future drafted player. The real difference is the distribution of value: one established forward for Los Angeles, several contracts and draft rights for Atlanta, and a comparatively small future opportunity for Denver.

Final Verdict

Slight Clippers Edge. Los Angeles receives A- for the established scoring and size of Danilo Gallinari. Atlanta gets B+ for Jamal Crawford, Diamond Stone, a protected 2018 first-round right and cash. Denver receives C for a 2019 second-round selection originating with Washington. The Hawks' four confirmed assets must be included to assess the full three-team return accurately.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana traded Paul George to Oklahoma City for Victor Oladipo and Domantas Sabonis, creating two exceptional asset chains that later reached Tyrese Haliburton on one side and Shai Gilgeous-Alexander plus extensive draft control on the other.
indiana-pacers.analysis: Indiana operated with reduced leverage after George signaled his intention to leave and still received two future All-Stars. Oladipo produced an immediate All-NBA season, Sabonis became a multi-time All-Star, and the Sabonis asset later brought Tyrese Haliburton. Oklahoma City also realized A-plus value: George re-signed, delivered an MVP-caliber season, and was later traded to the Clippers for Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Danilo Gallinari, five first-round picks and two swaps. Both franchises converted pressure into durable contender-building value, making equal A-plus grades and an Even Trade verdict more accurate than a slight edge.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
Philadelphia Sold the Rights to an Oklahoma State Point Guard

Philadelphia used the 39th overall choice in the 2017 draft on Jawun Evans, a quick Oklahoma State guard, before transferring his draft rights to the Los Angeles Clippers for cash considerations. The move was formally recorded in the clubs' summer transaction histories. The 76ers already had a heavily stocked young roster and opted for a financial return from a second-round selection. Los Angeles wanted another affordable ball handler with enough defensive quickness to compete for reserve minutes. This was a pick-rights purchase, not a swap of two active NBA guards.

Evans Played Meaningful Rookie Minutes for the Clippers

Evans appeared in 48 Clippers regular-season games in 2017-18, starting four and totaling 778 minutes. He averaged 4.8 points and 2.1 assists and spent much of the year learning how to operate a professional offense. The percentages and scoring totals were not remarkable, but those appearances represented a real roster contribution from a player picked late in the second round. The Clippers had altered their guard rotation after moving Chris Paul, creating more opportunities for fringe players. Evans was not an eventual franchise starter; he was inexpensive injury and backcourt cover with actual playing time.

His Clippers Career Ended Before a Second Regular Season

The following October, Los Angeles waived Evans while finalizing its opening-night roster, a decision reported alongside the Wesley Johnson and Alexis Ajinça transaction. Evans later made NBA appearances for Oklahoma City and Phoenix in 2018-19, but none of those games should be counted as Clippers return. That cutoff limits the grade: the Clippers did not find a long-term second-round steal. Their direct return was one 48-game rookie season with a handful of starts. Philadelphia, for its part, acquired no player or replacement selection from the cash sale, only the cash consideration.

The Receiving-Team Return Reverses the Older Winner

A second-round cash transaction is low stakes compared with a blockbuster, and Philadelphia was under no obligation to keep every prospect it drafted. Still, the older Sixers-favored verdict treated the money as superior to the actual NBA utility that Evans provided in Los Angeles. The Clippers invested in a modest guard and got hundreds of rotation minutes in return. Philadelphia collected an undisclosed financial payment, which has value but cannot be credited with basketball production without documented use of the funds. The more defensible retrospective gives Los Angeles the modest sporting edge while retaining a fair acknowledgment of Philadelphia's financial rationale.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win. Los Angeles earns B- because Jawun Evans supplied 48 regular-season appearances, four starts, 778 minutes and a rookie-season reserve guard option. Philadelphia gets C for the cash it received when selling the No. 39 draft rights. Evans did not stick beyond one Clippers season, but those actual NBA minutes outweigh the Sixers' unquantified on-court return.

milwaukee-bucks.summary: Milwaukee acquired No. 46 pick Sterling Brown's draft rights from Philadelphia for about $1.9 million in cash on July 6, 2017. Brown played three Bucks seasons, logging 54, 58 and 52 regular-season appearances from 2017-18 through 2019-20, 164 games in all, plus 15 postseason games. Bucks Win, Milwaukee A-, Philadelphia C. Brown's 164-game contribution outweighed Philadelphia's immediate cash return.
milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee Paid Philadelphia Cash for a Second-Round Guard

On July 6, 2017, the Bucks acquired the draft rights to Sterling Brown from the Philadelphia 76ers for cash considerations. Philadelphia had selected the SMU guard at No. 46 in June, and Milwaukee's official release confirmed the rights purchase. The Bucks needed affordable two-way wing development behind Khris Middleton, Giannis Antetokounmpo and their other main options. Brown brought defensive size, rebounding and a promising three-point shot. Philadelphia received about $1.9 million rather than adding another rookie to an already young roster. This was a cash-for-rights exchange, not a trade in which an established player moved from one active rotation to another.

Brown Stayed With Milwaukee for Three Regular Seasons

Brown played 54 regular-season Bucks games during his 2017-18 rookie year, making four starts and logging 776 minutes. He followed with 58 appearances and 1,034 minutes in 2018-19, averaging 6.4 points, then appeared 52 more times in 2019-20 with 767 minutes. In total, Milwaukee received 164 regular-season games and 2,577 minutes from the acquired selection. His shooting and defensive roles fluctuated, but he became a useful bench option during Milwaukee's rise in the Eastern Conference. Brown was not a franchise star, yet a 46th pick that plays for three years is an appreciable outcome.

The Bucks Also Used Brown in Three Postseasons

Brown appeared in three playoff games during Milwaukee's first-round loss to Boston in 2018, then played eleven during the Bucks' 2019 Eastern Conference Finals run. He was available for one postseason appearance during the disrupted 2020 playoffs. Those 15 games were mainly reserve minutes, not evidence he was a primary factor in the team's success. They nevertheless extended the usefulness of the original draft-rights purchase beyond the regular-season totals. Brown moved to Houston for 2020-21, and his later performances with the Rockets and other clubs should not be credited to Milwaukee's acquisition.

Philadelphia's Cash Return Had No Comparable Basketball Production

The 76ers received money they could use for organizational flexibility, so their side did have real financial value. But they did not keep the draft rights and therefore collected none of Brown's on-court contributions. Milwaukee effectively purchased three seasons of reserve guard depth and playoff availability for a comparatively small cash payment. That is the kind of outcome teams hope for when buying second-round selections from clubs with too many prospects. The result is not equivalent to adding an expensive free-agent starter, but the Bucks received more enduring sporting value than Philadelphia's known return, supporting a stronger favorable grade.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns A- after Sterling Brown supplied 164 regular-season games, 2,577 minutes and 15 playoff appearances over three years. Philadelphia gets C for its approximately $1.9 million cash consideration. The Bucks obtained real multi-season bench production from the purchased No. 46 draft rights.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Acquired Marcus Morris While Detroit Got Bradley and a Second

In July 2017, Boston traded Avery Bradley and a 2019 second-round selection to the Detroit Pistons for forward Marcus Morris. The later second is associated with No. 45 Isaiah Roby in the 2019 draft ledger. Boston wanted another versatile forward who could score and cover several frontcourt matchups; Detroit wanted an established perimeter defender and a future development option. The incoming pick for the Pistons was not an immediately signed 2017 NBA player, and its final slot was not known on the agreement date. The trade offered each team a different way to balance offensive creation with defensive assignments.

Morris Added Scoring and Positional Flexibility in Boston

Morris provided the Celtics with a forward capable of making outside shots, creating some offense against mismatches and defending larger wings. His future Boston seasons gave the club a sustained player contribution rather than a right that might never convey. The team could use him alongside other versatile defenders without requiring him to become its sole scoring leader. His previous Detroit production explained the interest but wasn't the same as new Boston output. The acquisition had added value because the Celtics' personnel needs were changing as the franchise rebuilt its top of the roster around different offensive and defensive combinations.

Detroit Acquired Bradley's Defense and an Additional Draft Chance

Bradley arrived with a reputation as a determined perimeter defender and an established starter, which gave the Pistons a usable guard instead of a speculative rights claim alone. The accompanying 2019 second offered another opportunity to select or move a prospect. That selection's eventual association with Isaiah Roby doesn't automatically mean Roby spent his career playing for Detroit, particularly if rights changed hands later. Bradley's own receiving-team tenure needed to be evaluated after the trade rather than through his preceding years in Boston. Detroit traded one starting-caliber forward for a guard and a future asset, a defensible alternative team-building approach.

Boston's Longer Forward Return Provides the Edge

Morris's ongoing contribution in Boston offers a stronger realized asset than the brief window associated with Detroit's use of Bradley. The extra second-round pick gave the Pistons meaningful optionality, so the return shouldn't be described as a single-for-single loss without qualification. Still, Boston acquired a durable frontcourt scorer and defender suited to its developing identity. This supports a Celtics-winning verdict without treating Morris as a franchise superstar or crediting Detroit with all later games played by the prospect connected to its incoming draft right. The trade's value came from fit, available minutes and an appropriately measured use of future assets.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston Celtics earns B+; Detroit Pistons earns C+. Morris's ongoing contribution in Boston offers a stronger realized asset than the brief window associated with Detroit's use of Bradley. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Exchanged a Broad Package for Irving

The Celtics acquired Kyrie Irving from Cleveland in an August 2017 blockbuster, sending Isaiah Thomas, Jae Crowder, Ante Žižić and a future first-round choice. After questions about Thomas's hip injury, the teams amended the package to include another second-round selection. Boston wanted a younger elite offensive guard who could create late-game shots and fit with its developing wings. Cleveland chose additional players and draft assets after Irving requested a different team, hoping to retain competitive depth while preparing for roster changes.

Irving Delivered Scoring but Only a Two-Year Stay

Irving was an All-Star-level offensive talent for Boston, creating difficult shots and helping the Celtics remain competitive. His tenure also came with a serious limitation: knee problems kept him out of the team's 2018 playoff run, and he departed for Brooklyn after the 2018-19 season. Boston therefore received two regular seasons rather than a long-term franchise guard. Those Celtics contributions were real and often impressive, but they must be measured against the cost of several players and a valuable first-round right.

Cleveland Obtained Sexton After Shorter Veteran Returns

Thomas's injury prevented him from reproducing his peak Boston scoring in Cleveland, while Crowder and Žižić were more limited fits. The most enduring Cavaliers asset became the 2018 No. 8 draft selection, used on Collin Sexton. Sexton developed into a productive young scorer during his Cleveland seasons and gave the club value beyond the initial veteran experiments. The 2020 second-round selection had its own draft-rights path and should not be treated as proof the Cavaliers developed Skylar Mays's later NBA career.

The Narrow Edge Recognizes Two Real Returns

Irving offered Boston the highest immediate level of offensive creation in the package, even though his exit shortened the payoff. Cleveland collected a productive young guard from the draft choice after several incoming veterans failed to establish longer careers there. That makes the trade far less one-sided than Irving's superstar profile might imply. The inherited modest Celtics advantage weighs Irving's All-Star seasons against the risk of using a top-eight pick and multiple players to obtain only a short window with the guard.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston receives B+ for two seasons of Kyrie Irving's elite offensive skill, tempered by his 2018 postseason absence and eventual departure. Cleveland gets B for Collin Sexton's productive young-guard tenure and other acquired assets, even though Thomas and Crowder had disappointing stays. Both franchises received value; the Celtics gained the stronger immediate star while the Cavaliers retained more future flexibility.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Hawks Received a Player and Cash for a Protected Pick

Atlanta acquired DeAndre Liggins and cash from the Los Angeles Clippers in September 2017. In return, the Clippers were due a 2018 second-round selection protected through the fifty-fifth choice. The terms meant Atlanta was unlikely to surrender a pick unless it landed near the very end of the second round. Liggins brought a defensive reputation from earlier NBA stops, but the more reliable part of Atlanta's package was the cash attached to the transaction. This was a roster-financing move rather than a bet on another starting guard.

Liggins Did Not Become a Hawks Rotation Fixture

Liggins had enough NBA experience to offer a temporary evaluation opportunity, particularly as a perimeter defender. Nevertheless, he did not establish a continuing Atlanta playing role after arriving. His earlier appearances for other franchises cannot be added to the Hawks' return from this transaction. Atlanta was more interested in the contract and financial structure than in changing its defensive identity around one reserve guard. That distinction prevents the receipt of a recognizable player's name from being mistaken for substantial new game production.

The Conditional Pick Never Became a Clippers Selection

The Clippers accepted rights to a heavily protected future second-round choice, but the condition was not met and the selection did not convey. As a result, they didn't obtain a player drafted with that asset from this specific exchange. The terms were understandable for a modest September deal, but the eventual outcome gave Los Angeles little direct basketball value. The team had effectively attached cash to moving Liggins's contract for an opportunity dependent on a narrow draft condition that ultimately failed to materialize.

Atlanta Kept Its Draft Asset and Took the Guaranteed Return

The Hawks came out ahead in a transaction with limited stakes. They received cash, evaluated a player and ultimately avoided losing the protected second-round selection. That didn't build a championship roster or generate an important Hawks guard season, but it was favorable relative to what the Clippers received. The F grade for Los Angeles reflects the failure of the incoming condition rather than a claim that every small cap transaction must produce a new star. Atlanta's B- recognizes a useful financial outcome secured at little actual draft cost.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B- for obtaining cash and DeAndre Liggins without surrendering a conveyed 2018 second-round pick, though Liggins produced no lasting Hawks rotation role. The Clippers receive F because their heavily protected draft compensation never became a usable selection. The deal provided Atlanta a tangible financial benefit while yielding essentially no direct basketball return for Los Angeles.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Absorbed Two Veterans for Asset Compensation

The Hawks agreed to take Richard Jefferson and Kay Felder from Cleveland in October 2017, receiving cash and future second-round rights. In return, the Cavaliers took draft rights to Sergiy Gladyr and Dimitrios Agravanis. The deal mainly served roster-management objectives after Cleveland reconfigured the fringes of a veteran contender. Atlanta was prepared to accept contracts in exchange for additional draft and financial value.

The Players Did Not Become Hawks Mainstays

Jefferson had extensive experience as a wing and had won a championship in Cleveland, while Felder was a young point guard whose role had been limited. Neither arrived to anchor Atlanta's rotation for several years. Their prior Cavaliers appearances should not be credited to the Hawks. The more meaningful compensation was the accompanying cash and pick rights rather than an invented stretch of productive Atlanta starting minutes.

Two Future Rights Had Different Outcomes

The incoming 2019 second-round choice was later associated with No. 41 Eric Paschall, but any rights moves must be considered before counting his NBA career as Atlanta production. The 2020 conditional second-round right did not convey. Atlanta also received three million dollars in the recorded agreement. Cleveland acquired two overseas-player rights, not immediate veteran NBA players, making the return predominantly administrative for both franchises.

Atlanta's Advantage Was in Extra Compensation

The inherited A- Hawks grade favors taking on contracts in return for draft and financial compensation. Cleveland's C- reflects a smaller direct asset return but the benefit of freeing roster flexibility. Because the incoming veterans did not become Atlanta core players, the transaction's value should not be described as a major on-court upgrade. It was a creative use of trade capacity during two clubs' different roster stages.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns A- for receiving Richard Jefferson, Kay Felder, cash and second-round assets, especially the 2019 right later tied to Eric Paschall. Cleveland gets C- for rights to Sergiy Gladyr and Dimitrios Agravanis, alongside roster flexibility. The Hawks' advantage was financial and draft-related rather than sustained playing production from either veteran.

milwaukee-bucks.analysis: Milwaukee won the Eric Bledsoe trade because it acquired a high-level starting guard for a package that did not contain a core player. The Bucks sent Greg Monroe, a heavily protected first-round pick and a protected second-round pick to Phoenix. Bledsoe became a major regular-season contributor, earned All-Defensive recognition and helped Milwaukee make the jump to elite team status under Mike Budenholzer. His later playoff limitations are part of the evaluation, and the first-round pick eventually became a real asset, but Milwaukee still received several seasons of strong starter-level production at a price appropriate for the team’s stage of development.

atlanta-hawks.summary: Atlanta exchanged Luke Babbitt for Okaro White at the February 2018 deadline. The Hawks waived White on the same date rather than using him, while Babbitt returned to Miami to provide perimeter-shooting depth. Miami obtained the practical playing benefit; Atlanta primarily handled roster needs.
atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Miami Brought Back a Familiar Shooting Forward

The February 8, 2018 deal sent Luke Babbitt from Atlanta to Miami and Okaro White the other way. Babbitt had played for the Heat in the previous season, so the club knew what kind of spacing it could expect from him. Miami wanted another forward willing to take open perimeter shots with injuries testing its rotation. Atlanta's motive was different: the Hawks were reworking a rebuilding roster and weren't necessarily seeking immediate production from White. The two players' recent résumés gave each club a reason to exchange rather than retain its original forward.

Atlanta Waived White Instead of Using Him

White's time on the Hawks' roster effectively ended when it began. Atlanta waived him on February 8, the same date the transaction was completed, so no regular-season Hawks appearances resulted from the acquisition. His earlier time with Miami and in its development system is not Atlanta playing value. The decision may have helped manage a roster spot and available contracts, but those benefits should be described honestly instead of treated as rebounds or defensive minutes that never occurred. The receiving player did not become a piece of the Hawks' on-court rebuilding effort.

Babbitt Returned as a Narrow but Usable Miami Option

The Heat brought back a specialist rather than a foundational starter. Babbitt's willingness to shoot from outside could help when Miami required spacing around its primary ball handlers, though his defensive limitations restricted his value. He was familiar with the organization and had been playing for Atlanta before the deal, averaging 6.1 points in 37 Hawks games that season. Those Atlanta games belong to the Hawks' outgoing résumé; only his subsequent Miami time counts as incoming Heat production. Even a short spell of actual rotation depth outperformed Atlanta's nonexistent White playing return.

The Outcome Favors Miami Without Rewriting the Trade's Scale

Miami got the player it wanted for an identifiable tactical reason, and Atlanta did not convert White into on-court help. The difference is enough for the Heat edge, but it doesn't merit a claim that Babbitt transformed Miami's competitive standing. His value was situational, tied to perimeter spacing and limited reserve minutes. Atlanta's move should instead be understood as a roster decision during a rebuilding season. Distinguishing those purposes produces a fair comparison rather than assigning star-level importance to a minor deadline exchange.

Final Verdict

The Heat received the only tangible on-court return, although Babbitt's contribution remained limited reserve support rather than a decisive roster upgrade.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Accepted an Injured Guard and Cash

The Hawks acquired Sheldon Mac and cash considerations from Washington in February 2018, sending a conditional second-round choice tied to the 2019 draft. Mac had been a Wizards reserve, but an Achilles injury had prevented him from building a current-season playing role. Atlanta was rebuilding and able to handle a small contract transaction. Washington gained roster and financial flexibility without demanding a proven NBA rotation player in return. The selection's eventual outcome depended on the specific protections attached.

Mac Didn't Supply Hawks Rotation Minutes

Mac's name in the transaction shouldn't be treated as evidence of productive Atlanta guard play. His injury affected his availability, and he did not establish a lasting Hawks role after joining the deal. The player had shown some potential in earlier Washington appearances, but those minutes belong to his previous club. Atlanta's benefit was therefore driven more by the incoming cash and terms of the agreement than by immediate basketball contributions from Mac.

The Conditional Wizards Pick Did Not Convey

Washington's conditional 2019 second-round asset was never exercised. No 2019 draftee can be assigned to the Wizards as a return from this trade on that basis alone. The organization obtained the opportunity to alter roster obligations and open a spot, while Atlanta received cash with a player whose current playing availability was limited. These are real administrative benefits, though they are not directly comparable to a player arriving and contributing to a winning rotation.

The Small Difference Is About Transaction Value

The inherited Hawks Win and B- grade do not imply Mac became a useful Atlanta starter. They recognize the value of receiving cash in a transaction whose outgoing pick never became a completed selection. Washington earned C for its portion of the maneuver, but also received no usable draft player from the conditional right. Neither side acquired a long-term core component. The deal illustrates how minor deadline trades can generate financial benefits without producing a substantive change in either team's basketball lineup.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta gets B- for the cash accompanying Sheldon Mac, though the injured guard did not provide meaningful Hawks playing minutes. Washington earns C for taking a conditional 2019 second-round right that never conveyed. The edge reflects minor financial and roster-management benefits, not an invented Atlanta contribution from Mac or a Wizards draftee.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired George Hill, Rodney Hood and overseas rights through a February 2018 three-team deal with Sacramento and Utah. The Kings received Iman Shumpert, other rights, draft assets and cash; the Jazz obtained Jae Crowder and Derrick Rose. Cleveland sought immediate help around LeBron James, while the other clubs reshuffled veteran rosters. The inherited Even Trade gives all three B.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Added Hill and Hood for an Immediate Playoff Need

The Cavaliers acquired George Hill and Rodney Hood in a February 2018 three-team transaction involving the Kings and Jazz. Cleveland was adjusting its roster around LeBron James and needed guard and wing support that could contribute during an imminent postseason run. Hill brought experienced playmaking and defense, while Hood offered perimeter scoring. The Cavaliers also obtained overseas draft rights and a possible later second-round swap, reflecting how complicated trade-deadline balancing can become across several clubs.

Sacramento Received Shumpert and Draft Flexibility

The Kings acquired Iman Shumpert, the rights to Dimitrios Agravanis, a future second-round asset associated with No. 50 Skylar Mays in 2020, and cash. Shumpert could contribute perimeter defense, while the rights and pick represented different kinds of future optionality. The asset list shouldn't be reduced to Shumpert alone, nor should Mays's later playing statistics for other teams be automatically counted for Sacramento. The incoming package fit a club considering both current role players and its future roster.

Utah Acquired Crowder and Rose Under Different Conditions

The Jazz received Jae Crowder and Derrick Rose, whose careers and immediate roles were not interchangeable. Crowder could defend multiple forward matchups and became a useful Utah perimeter contributor. Rose did not establish an equivalent Jazz playing tenure from the transaction, illustrating why a famous name is not the same as receiving-team production. The agreement also involved a conditional second-round swap; the final value depends on subsequent rights conditions, rather than any invented automatic selection transfer.

Different Immediate Fits Produced Equal Inherited Grades

Cleveland added Hill and Hood to support a contender, Sacramento gathered Shumpert and assets, and Utah obtained Crowder as a useful wing. The inherited B on each side acknowledges those distinct benefits without treating all names as long-term stars for their new teams. Cleveland still needed to integrate its acquisitions quickly, and Utah's Rose component was not itself a major court payoff. The deal's real outcome is better understood as three separate roster decisions than a single glamorous exchange.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Cleveland earns B for George Hill, Rodney Hood and additional rights in a playoff-oriented roster reset. Sacramento also gets B for Iman Shumpert, future draft consideration and cash. Utah receives B for Jae Crowder's useful wing contribution plus Derrick Rose's contract, though Rose didn't create a comparable Jazz playing tenure. All three clubs received a plausible form of value.

The Jazz received Jae Crowder and Derrick Rose, whose careers and immediate roles were not interchangeable. Different Immediate Fits Produced Equal Inherited Grades

Cleveland added Hill and Hood to support a contender, Sacramento gathered Shumpert and assets, and Utah obtained Crowder as a useful wing. The inherited B on each side acknowledges those distinct benefits without treating all names as long-term stars for their new teams. Cleveland still needed to integrate its acquisitions quickly, and Utah's Rose component was not itself a major court payoff. The deal's real outcome is better understood as three separate roster decisions than a single glamorous exchange.

Even Trade. Cleveland earns B for George Hill, Rodney Hood and additional rights in a playoff-oriented roster reset. Sacramento also gets B for Iman Shumpert, future draft consideration and cash. Utah receives B for Jae Crowder's useful wing contribution plus Derrick Rose's contract, though Rose didn't create a comparable Jazz playing tenure. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Traded One Premium Pick for Two Chances

Atlanta selected Luka Doncic third in the 2018 NBA Draft, then sent his rights to Dallas for the rights to fifth choice Trae Young and a protected future first-round pick. The extra selection eventually conveyed at No. 10 in 2019, when Atlanta took Cam Reddish. Hawks management valued Young's shooting and passing enough to move down, while Dallas regarded Doncic as worth sacrificing another draft asset. The two clubs used the same night to make different decisions about the type of player who would drive their rebuilds.

Young Earned His Own Atlanta Playoff Accomplishments

Young became a major scorer and distributor for Atlanta rather than a cautionary tale who never justified the fifth pick. He directed an offense that reached the 2021 Eastern Conference Finals, establishing real on-court value for the Hawks. Reddish offered another lottery development opportunity with positional size, though his uneven Atlanta career and subsequent movement limited that component's direct payoff. Those facts distinguish the deal from a situation in which one team got a star and the other got nothing. Young gave Atlanta recognizable leadership and production even as the comparison with Doncic intensified.

Doncic Produced a Finals Appearance for Dallas

Doncic became the central creator in Dallas, generating his own scoring and passes for teammates while attracting a high volume of defensive attention. His repeated All-NBA selections and the Mavericks' 2024 NBA Finals appearance demonstrate the rare receiving-team outcome of the trade. The acquisition did not depend upon a draft-night prediction surviving years of uncertainty: Dallas saw the player it targeted become the centerpiece of a contender. That evaluation stops with his Mavericks tenure. Production with a different club after a later transaction is not an additional Dallas return from the 2018 swap.

The Second Pick Did Not Close the Talent Gap

Atlanta's return deserves a respectable grade because Young played like a legitimate star and the added first created a second lottery selection. But the Reddish component did not develop into the durable supporting cornerstone that might have offset the distance between the lead prospects. Dallas traded away an extra first and received the higher individual ceiling, with a Finals run as a tangible team result. The Hawks' own conference-finals appearance prevents an absolute condemnation of the deal. The Mavericks' larger peak and longer high-end creation still make them the stronger beneficiary of the exchange.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win. Dallas earns A+ for acquiring Luka Doncic, an All-NBA offensive engine who led its 2024 Finals run. Atlanta gets B because Trae Young became an All-Star and powered the 2021 Eastern Conference Finals trip, while the additional lottery pick became Cam Reddish. That added piece fell short of bridging the difference between the principal players, but the Hawks obtained a real star.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Charlotte Purchased Graham's Second-Round Rights

The Hornets acquired the draft rights to Devonte' Graham from Atlanta during the 2018 draft. The Hawks received two future second-round selections, later linked to the 2019 No. 44 and 2023 No. 34 picks. Charlotte identified Graham as an inexpensive guard with strong shooting and playmaking potential despite his second-round status. Atlanta preferred to spread its return over two future drafts rather than sign Graham immediately. The deal exchanged one identifiable prospect for multiple delayed opportunities whose eventual team destinations would depend on later transactions.

Graham Developed Into a Productive Hornets Guard

Graham grew into a leading Charlotte backcourt contributor, most notably during the 2019-20 campaign when he averaged more than eighteen points and seven assists per game. His three-point shooting and ability to organize an offense gave the Hornets direct on-court value far beyond a typical second-round selection. The guard eventually moved to another franchise, but his Charlotte seasons remain a concrete return from this trade. Those achievements distinguish the transaction from speculative moves whose acquired rights never produce meaningful NBA games.

Atlanta's Later Pick Names Belong to Other Chains

The incoming second-round selections became associated with No. 44 in 2019, eventually used on Bol Bol, and No. 34 in 2023, associated with Colby Jones. Atlanta did not simply retain both players as Hawks rotation pieces. The choices passed through other deals, making the eventual drafted names part of the asset history rather than direct NBA production credited to Atlanta. The rights had potential trade value, yet neither delivered anything comparable to the reliable Hornets playmaking Graham provided for Charlotte.

An Outperforming Second-Round Guard Decided the Deal

Charlotte acquired a player whose production became unusually strong for the cost of two later second-round choices. Atlanta gained extra draft flexibility and could redirect those assets as its roster plans changed, but the opportunity to develop Graham was the more valuable result. The trade should not be judged by pretending both 2019 and 2023 selected players played for Atlanta. Its decisive contrast is between the useful Hornets guard and future picks whose realized Hawks return was less direct and less productive.

Final Verdict

Charlotte Win. The Hornets earn B+ for Devonte' Graham's productive seasons as a scoring and playmaking guard. Atlanta gets D+ for two future second-round rights, eventually associated with Bol Bol and Colby Jones but redirected through later transactions rather than producing those players' Hawks careers. Graham's direct Charlotte contribution was the clearest lasting basketball value in this draft-night swap.

perspectives.summary: Phoenix acquired the rights to No. 10 pick Mikal Bridges from Philadelphia on 2018 draft night for the rights to No. 16 pick Zhaire Smith and Miami's unprotected 2021 first-round pick. Bridges played every possible Suns regular-season game before his 2023 trade, totaling 365 games, 298 starts, an All-Defensive First Team selection and a starting role on the 2021 NBA Finals team. Smith played only 13 games for Philadelphia, but the Miami first retained major trade value and became part of the 2019 Tobias Harris package.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
NBA.com's draft tracker and Phoenix's official release agree on the package. Philadelphia selected Mikal Bridges at No. 10 and traded his rights to Phoenix for the rights to No. 16 pick Zhaire Smith plus Miami's unprotected 2021 first-round selection, an asset Phoenix had acquired earlier in the Goran Dragic trade. The 2021 pick was especially notable because it carried no protection. It later landed at No. 18 and ultimately became Tre Mann after moving through additional transactions, but Philadelphia had already used the asset in a different trade long before draft night 2021.

Phoenix Return
Bridges became one of the NBA's most durable two-way wings. He played all 82 games as a rookie, all 73 in the shortened 2019-20 season, all 72 in 2020-21, all 82 in 2021-22 and all 56 Suns games before the 2023 deadline. That is 365 regular-season games and 298 starts without missing a Suns game. He grew from a low-usage defender into a 13-to-17-point scorer, started all 22 playoff games during Phoenix's 2021 run to the NBA Finals and earned All-Defensive First Team in 2022 while finishing second in Defensive Player of the Year voting. Phoenix then retained significant exit value. In February 2023, Bridges was one of the central players sent to Brooklyn in the Kevin Durant trade. Durant's entire acquisition cannot be credited to Bridges because Phoenix also sent Cam Johnson, Jae Crowder and a large draft package, but Bridges' inclusion shows that the 2018 asset remained premium currency after four and a half productive Suns seasons.

Philadelphia Return
Smith's career never developed. He suffered a foot fracture before his rookie season and then a severe food-allergy complication during recovery. He eventually appeared in six games as a rookie and seven more in 2019-20, finishing his Philadelphia tenure with only 13 NBA games and two starts. The 2021 Miami first was the meaningful portion of the return. In February 2019, Philadelphia included that unprotected pick in the multi-asset package that acquired Tobias Harris, Boban Marjanovic and Mike Scott from the Clippers. The Sixers also sent Landry Shamet, Wilson Chandler, Mike Muscala, their own protected 2020 first and two second-round picks, so the Harris return cannot be assigned entirely to the Miami selection. Still, the pick demonstrably carried enough market value to function as a major component of a win-now trade.

Hindsight Verdict
Phoenix wins clearly because Bridges delivered 365 consecutive regular-season appearances, elite defense, a Finals run and premium downstream trade value. That supports an A+ grade. Philadelphia's player outcome was poor, but grading the Sixers as a D ignores the unprotected Miami first and the leverage it supplied in the Harris deal. A B- better reflects a return consisting of one failed prospect plus one genuinely valuable first-round asset that Philadelphia converted into veteran help. Final verdict: Phoenix Suns Win.

perspectives.summary: Charlotte acquired 2019 second round pick (#52-Jalen McDaniels); cash from Oklahoma City Thunder for rights to Hamidou Diallo.
perspectives.analysis: Charlotte moved its freshly obtained 2018 No. 45 Hamidou Diallo rights to Oklahoma City in exchange for a 2019 Thunder second and cash, confirmed July 6 by the official Thunder release. That future choice became 2019 No. 52 Jalen McDaniels. The Hornets developed McDaniels for 174 NBA games (41 starts) through February 2023; the 2023 exchange of McDaniels and a separate incoming-from-New York 2024 second was part of a multi-team deal that returned draft choices to Charlotte, so those rights are not free compensation for the July 2018 deal. The original cash receipt and longer player service are valuable. Diallo gave Oklahoma City 129 games and won the Dunk Contest, then brought Svi Mykhailiuk and 2027 second via Detroit, a real Thunder return rather than an empty pick. Modest Slight Charlotte Edge, Charlotte B, Oklahoma City B-.

perspectives.summary: Oklahoma City acquired Hamidou Diallo rights from Charlotte for its 2019 second-round pick and cash. Diallo played 129 Thunder games before a separate 2021 deal returned Svi Mykhailiuk and a later second; Charlotte used the conveyed pick on Jalen McDaniels, who played 174 Hornets games. The existing source-backed B Charlotte and B- Thunder grades support only a slight Charlotte edge.
perspectives.analysis: The Thunder acquired the rights to Brooklyn drafted No. 45 Hamidou Diallo from Charlotte for a 2019 second-round pick and cash on July 6, 2018. Diallo contributed 129 Oklahoma City regular-season games, 11 starts and 6.9 points per contest before the March 13, 2021 trade to Detroit for Svi Mykhailiuk and a Houston-origin 2027 second. The later trade is a realized downstream asset return but cannot be represented as original July 2018 compensation; Diallo Detroit 136-plus career games belong only to Detroit. Charlotte spent the conveyed pick on 2019 No. 52 Jalen McDaniels, who appeared in 174 Hornets games with 41 starts through the February 2023 trade, and also received immediate cash. Each organization got a practical rotation contributor and a later asset opportunity. The extra cash and more Charlotte player games justify only Slight Charlotte Edge, Charlotte B and Oklahoma City B-, NOT inherited Oklahoma City Thunder Win B+ against C+ nor an unsupported claim McDaniels never played.

summary: On July 6, 2018, Charlotte transferred Hamidou Diallo 2018 No. 45 draft rights to Oklahoma City for the Thunder 2019 second-round pick and cash. The 2019 selection became Charlotte No. 52 Jalen McDaniels. Diallo played 129 Thunder games before being traded to Detroit for Svi Mykhailiuk and a 2027 second; McDaniels played 174 Charlotte games before entering a 2023 multi-team transaction that delivered additional future draft rights to Charlotte alongside another outgoing Charlotte pick. Both teams obtained NBA players and further options; Charlotte cash and extra on-court time produce only a slight Hornets edge, Charlotte B and Oklahoma City B-.
analysis: Oklahoma City acquired No. 45 Hamidou Diallo NBA rights from Charlotte July 6 2018 for its own 2019 second and cash (2018-19 transaction ledger reports $243,000). Diallo actually played 51, 46 and 32 Thunder regular-season games over three partial seasons — 129 total, 11 starts, 6.9 points per game — and won the 2019 Dunk Contest. In March 2021 OKC exchanged him for Svi Mykhailiuk and a Houston-origin 2027 second, a separate later trade that should not be counted as direct 2018 terms. The second-round pick sent to Charlotte became 2019 No. 52 Jalen McDaniels, who played 174 Charlotte games and made 41 starts across 2019-23; his later Philadelphia career cannot be attributed to Charlotte. McDaniels then participated in Charlotte 2023 multi-team exchange to Philadelphia involving additional Hornets 2024 pick and incoming rights. Charlotte received cash plus longer direct NBA forward service, while Oklahoma City got useful Diallo time and a separate later draft right. Slight Charlotte Edge, Charlotte B, Thunder B-.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Added Lin With Future Draft Sweeteners

The Hawks acquired Jeremy Lin from Brooklyn in July 2018, also receiving a future second-round right and a potential 2023 second-round swap. Brooklyn obtained the rights to Isaia Cordinier and a conditional second-round selection. Atlanta wanted an experienced guard who could support a backcourt in transition while young players developed. The Nets sought greater flexibility after injuries and roster changes had limited Lin's role. The draft conditions made the agreement more involved than simply moving one veteran guard for another.

Lin Gave Atlanta Temporary Backcourt Depth

Lin played part of the 2018-19 season with the Hawks, offering ball handling and scoring off the bench. He did not remain a long-term starter in Atlanta and subsequently joined Toronto after being waived. His later association with the Raptors' 2019 championship must not be counted as a Hawks achievement. The relevant Atlanta payoff was the veteran guard play it received while developing a different long-term backcourt. The move answered a short-term need without asking Lin to be the franchise centerpiece.

The Pick Rights Added Another Atlanta Opportunity

The future second-round asset later became associated with a 2025 selection, while the 2023 swap was not exercised. Those are separate forms of compensation, and neither should be counted as immediate 2018-19 on-court production. Brooklyn acquired Cordinier's rights and a conditional second that ultimately did not convey. The Nets therefore obtained relatively little directly measurable NBA playing value from the incoming package, although their roster and salary flexibility remained relevant to their plans.

The Moderate Edge Does Not Depend on Future Titles

Atlanta had an active veteran for part of a season and another draft opportunity to use or redirect later. Brooklyn received rights whose immediate NBA contribution was limited. That is enough to explain the inherited Hawks advantage without inflating Lin's half-season stint into a long-term breakthrough. The trade primarily managed guard availability, roster planning and conditional assets. The better direct basketball return on the initial teams' rosters came from Lin's actual Hawks minutes.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta receives B+ for Jeremy Lin's useful short-term backcourt contribution and future second-round rights, including a 2025 pick, while its 2023 swap went unused. Brooklyn gets C for Isaia Cordinier's rights and a protected second that never conveyed. Lin's later Toronto championship is not credited to Atlanta; the Hawks' actual veteran minutes and extra asset define the edge.

perspectives.summary: On July 18, 2018, Toronto acquired Kawhi Leonard, Danny Green and the cash consideration recorded in transaction ledgers from San Antonio for DeMar DeRozan, Jakob Poeltl and a protected 2019 first-round pick that conveyed at No. 29 and became Keldon Johnson. Leonard won 2019 Finals MVP as Toronto captured the first championship in franchise history, while San Antonio received three separate pieces that produced multi-year value. The title makes Toronto the clear hindsight winner, but the Spurs' return was substantial rather than empty.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
San Antonio and Toronto officially announced the July 18, 2018 deal as Kawhi Leonard and Danny Green to the Raptors for DeMar DeRozan, Jakob Poeltl and a protected 2019 first-round pick. Basketball-Reference's transaction ledgers additionally record $5 million in cash going to Toronto. The official releases do not foreground that cash term, so it should be treated as administrative consideration rather than a reason for the grade. The protected first conveyed at No. 29 in 2019 and San Antonio selected Keldon Johnson.

Toronto Return
Leonard delivered the highest possible one-season outcome. He averaged 26.6 points and 7.3 rebounds in 60 regular-season games, then 30.5 points and 9.1 rebounds across 24 playoff games. Toronto defeated Golden State in six games for the 2019 NBA championship, and Leonard was named Finals MVP after averaging 28.5 points in the series. Green started 80 regular-season games, shot 45.5 percent from three and remained a useful two-way starter throughout the title run. Both left after one season, but the transaction's realized value in Toronto is not hypothetical: the franchise converted the package directly into its first championship.

San Antonio Return
DeRozan gave the Spurs three productive seasons, appearing in 206 regular-season games and averaging 21.6 points, 5.3 rebounds and 6.2 assists over that span. Poeltl developed into the club's starting center and later became valuable enough that San Antonio traded him back to Toronto in 2023 for Khem Birch, a protected 2024 first-round pick and two future second-round picks. The original 2019 first became Keldon Johnson, who developed into a long-term Spurs starter and scorer. That combination of immediate production, development value and another traceable downstream return explains why San Antonio's side should not be graded like a failed salvage package.

Hindsight Verdict
Toronto receives an A+ because Leonard and Green were central to a championship in the season immediately following the trade. San Antonio receives a B: DeRozan was productive, Poeltl became a starting center with later trade value, and the first-round pick became Keldon Johnson. The final verdict is Toronto Raptors Win because one championship season from the transaction's best player outweighs a strong multi-year return. The grade does not penalize Toronto for Leonard leaving in free agency after the title, and it does not credit San Antonio with value beyond the directly traceable assets acquired in this deal.
