boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Used Rodney Purvis to Reduce a Salary Obligation

Boston sent Abdel Nader and $450,000 in cash to Oklahoma City on July 23, 2018, receiving Rodney Purvis in return. Purvis had a non-guaranteed contract, which made him a convenient way for the Celtics to move salary before their offseason obligations became more expensive. Oklahoma City took on a wing it believed could supply depth behind its established rotation. The deal therefore had two different aims: Boston wanted contract flexibility, while the Thunder were willing to give a roster spot to a player who had already seen NBA action with the Celtics.

Purvis Did Not Appear in a Celtics Game

Boston waived Purvis on July 30, only a week after the trade. He never delivered regular-season playing time to the Celtics through this acquisition. His earlier minutes with Orlando are not Boston production, nor can the non-guaranteed contract be treated as a hidden scorer. The move still gave the Celtics a genuine financial advantage by avoiding more of Nader's guaranteed salary and associated tax exposure. That value explains the deal's logic without disguising the absence of an incoming Boston rotation contributor. The cash Boston sent was a distinct cost of obtaining the contract flexibility.

Nader Became a Playable Reserve for Oklahoma City

Nader remained with Oklahoma City and played as a reserve wing during the following two seasons. His minutes weren't those of a franchise centerpiece, but the Thunder did receive an NBA player who could defend multiple perimeter positions and supply occasional outside scoring. That actual roster use contrasted sharply with Purvis's absence from Boston's lineup. Nader's 48 rookie appearances before July 2018 belonged to the Celtics and shouldn't be added to the Thunder side. His later work outside Oklahoma City also falls outside the direct receiving-franchise result being graded here.

The Distinct Team Objectives Explain Both Grades

Oklahoma City obtained sustained rotation assistance from Nader and a cash payment, giving it more immediate basketball value. Boston achieved the salary and tax relief it sought, so a Celtics grade that recognizes financial utility remains reasonable despite receiving no games from Purvis. Both outcomes need to be kept visible instead of assigning all value to box-score totals or pretending the deal was purely a salary dump with no Thunder benefit. The edge belongs to Oklahoma City because it combined financial compensation with an actual reserve contributor across more than one campaign.

Final Verdict

Oklahoma City Thunder Win. The Thunder earn B for adding Abdel Nader as a playable reserve over the next two seasons along with $450,000 in cash. Boston receives C+ for the salary and tax flexibility made possible by Rodney Purvis's non-guaranteed deal, although Purvis was waived without a Celtics appearance. The winner is determined by Nader's direct Thunder contributions while preserving Boston's financial motive.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
Los Angeles Used a Trade to Reach the Opening-Night Roster Limit

The Clippers sent Wesley Johnson to New Orleans on October 15, 2018, and received Alexis Ajinça. The timing, one day before the regular season began, is central to understanding the deal. Los Angeles was trimming its roster to fifteen players and could save approximately $850,000 by moving Johnson's larger expiring salary for Ajinça's smaller one. The Clippers waived Ajinça the same day, alongside guard Jawun Evans, so they were not trading for a new frontcourt contributor. Their objective was administrative and financial rather than basketball production from the arriving center.

Johnson Gave New Orleans Twenty-Six Games of Wing Depth

The Pelicans were willing to take Johnson because they needed help on the wing. He played 26 New Orleans regular-season games during 2018-19, logging 377 minutes, 95 points and 54 rebounds. His limited offense and three made three-pointers show that he was not a high-volume scorer, but he was available during the opening months. The franchise's official media guide confirms the October acquisition and those New Orleans totals. Johnson's prior Clippers career does not become a Pelicans accomplishment just because the organizations swapped him, nor do his later Washington appearances belong to this incoming stint.

The Pelicans Converted Johnson Into Another Transaction

On February 7, 2019, New Orleans traded Johnson to the Washington Wizards for Markieff Morris, cash considerations and a future second-round selection. Contemporary team reporting documents that second move. The Pelicans waived Morris shortly afterward, so it would be inaccurate to suggest they received a productive Morris season from Johnson. The second-round compensation nonetheless shows why an expiring veteran with a limited scoring role retained transaction value. That downstream agreement was a separate trade involving more than one asset, and its full eventual draft outcome should not be assigned mechanically to the original Ajinça swap.

Both Sides Met Different Objectives but New Orleans Received Minutes

The Clippers achieved a predictable roster and salary result: Johnson's contract left, Ajinça was waived and the payroll reduction was real. New Orleans obtained short-term wing minutes and a player it could exchange again. On a strict on-court comparison, the Pelicans got 26 games while Los Angeles got none from the incoming center. The Clippers' cash savings prevent an F-type grade, but they did not acquire a roster contributor. The original Pelicans-favored decision holds because the club derived both immediate and later transactional use from Johnson, rather than merely moving salary out of the way.

Final Verdict

Pelicans Win. New Orleans retains B for Wesley Johnson's 26 games, 377 minutes and subsequent use in the February Washington deal. Los Angeles gets C because it saved approximately $850,000 in salary but waived Alexis Ajinça before any Clippers regular-season appearance. The teams had different objectives, but the Pelicans received the stronger basketball and asset return.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland obtained Matthew Dellavedova, John Henson and draft compensation in a December 2018 three-team trade. Milwaukee acquired George Hill and Washington acquired Sam Dekker and a second-round right. Cleveland secured future flexibility, including selections associated with MarJon Beauchamp, Sandro Mamukelashvili and Bryce McGowens, although those later players followed separate rights paths. perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Collected Players and Several Draft Rights

The Cavaliers received Matthew Dellavedova, John Henson and multiple future draft rights in a December 2018 exchange with Milwaukee and Washington. Dellavedova was familiar to Cleveland from its earlier championship-period backcourt, while Henson offered veteran frontcourt depth. The bigger rebuilding appeal was the combination of selection rights that could be used in subsequent roster decisions. Milwaukee acquired George Hill, and Washington received Sam Dekker plus a separate future second-round right.

Milwaukee Added Hill's Experienced Guard Play

Hill had established himself as a steady guard capable of playing with or without the ball, making him a useful acquisition for the Bucks' developing contender. His defense and shooting were the relevant basketball skills, not the immediate prospect of creating a future All-Star through the draft. Milwaukee's C grade under the inherited model is modest despite Hill's usefulness in meaningful playoff situations. His subsequent work must be evaluated during his Bucks tenure rather than credited through unrelated franchises.

Washington Received Dekker and a Separate Selection

The Wizards acquired Dekker and a future second-round right associated with No. 43 Greg Brown III in 2021. Dekker offered a forward option, but he didn't become the lasting centerpiece of Washington's roster. The pick was a form of future flexibility whose actual player destination depended on subsequent rights transactions. That distinction is also important for Cleveland's own collection of selections later associated with names such as MarJon Beauchamp and Sandro Mamukelashvili: the original receiving franchise did not necessarily keep every resulting player.

The Cavaliers' Broader Package Explains the Lead

Cleveland obtained multiple draft chances while accepting two veteran contracts, a useful approach during a period of roster change. Milwaukee gained Hill's more immediate guard experience, while Washington collected a forward and future draft possibility. The inherited Cavaliers A- values the breadth of long-range compensation, compared with C for each partner. The grade does not mean all of Cleveland's later numbered selections produced NBA stars in a Cavaliers uniform. It recognizes flexible rights and players acquired for the club's rebuilding needs.

Final Verdict

Cavaliers Win. Cleveland earns A- for Dellavedova, Henson and several future draft rights, even though the resulting player paths require separate attribution. Milwaukee gets C for George Hill's veteran guard play, while Washington receives C for Sam Dekker and a future second-round right. Cleveland collected the broadest rebuilding package rather than a guaranteed new star.

Dallas still acquired the best basketball asset at the time, so Slight Partner Edge remains the most defensible verdict.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Boston Sent Bird and Cash to Atlanta

The Celtics traded Jabari Bird and cash considerations to the Hawks at the February 2019 deadline, receiving a conditional second-round selection for 2020. Bird was not an active part of Boston's playing rotation, and the transaction gave the franchise another opportunity to manage its roster. Atlanta agreed to accept the player's contract and accompanying payment. This was not an exchange of two established contributors, so its main impact belonged to the financial and roster side of team operations.

Atlanta Did Not Obtain New Guard Production

Bird did not become a regular Hawks player after the transaction. His previous NBA appearances for Boston were not Atlanta production and cannot be used to justify an on-court gain. The incoming cash supplied the Hawks with a tangible benefit for accommodating the move. Its value is different from adding a player who helps a rebuilding team's guard rotation, so the trade's result should be recorded without inventing games or shot creation that the receiving club did not receive.

The Celtics' Conditional Pick Never Materialized

The 2020 second-round right was protected and did not convey under the recorded terms. Boston therefore did not acquire a drafted prospect from this transaction. Its benefit was administrative flexibility from moving a contract and creating a roster opening. Later Celtics draft picks and player signings need to be connected to their actual transaction chains rather than treated as automatic consequences of the Bird move. The exchange remains meaningful as a roster decision even when no new Celtics player arrived.

The Small Difference Fits a Salary Transaction

The inherited slight Celtics advantage measures the practical effect of clearing an unused roster arrangement while Atlanta accepted cash. Neither franchise obtained a long-term basketball performer in the immediate deal. Both had reasons to proceed: Boston could focus its playing group and Atlanta could receive financial consideration without surrendering a meaningful active contributor. That is enough for modest grades but not a sweeping claim of winning a blockbuster talent exchange.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston gets B- for moving Jabari Bird's contract and gaining roster flexibility, though the conditional 2020 second never conveyed. Atlanta receives C+ for cash considerations and a player who did not become a Hawks rotation contributor. Neither side obtained a meaningful new on-court player, making the grade difference narrow and administrative.

Its value is different from adding a player who helps a rebuilding team's guard rotation, so the trade's result should be recorded without inventing games or shot creation that the receiving club did not receive.

The Celtics' Conditional Pick Never Materialized

The 2020 second-round right was protected and did not convey under the recorded terms. Boston therefore did not acquire a drafted prospect from this transaction. Its benefit was administrative flexibility from moving a contract and creating a roster opening. Later Celtics draft picks and player signings need to be connected to their actual transaction chains rather than treated as automatic consequences of the Bird move. The exchange remains meaningful as a roster decision even when no new Celtics player arrived.

The Small Difference Fits a Salary Transaction

The inherited slight Celtics advantage measures the practical effect of clearing an unused roster arrangement while Atlanta accepted cash. Neither franchise obtained a long-term basketball performer in the immediate deal. Both had reasons to proceed: Boston could focus its playing group and Atlanta could receive financial consideration without surrendering a meaningful active contributor. That is enough for modest grades but not a sweeping claim of winning a blockbuster talent exchange.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston gets B- for moving Jabari Bird's contract and gaining roster flexibility, though the conditional 2020 second never conveyed. Atlanta receives C+ for cash considerations and a player who did not become a Hawks rotation contributor. Neither side obtained a meaningful new on-court player, making the grade difference narrow and administrative.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Two Guards Went Opposite Ways at the Deadline

Memphis announced the acquisition of Tyler Dorsey from Atlanta on February 7, 2019, in exchange for veteran Shelvin Mack. The Grizzlies could give a younger shooting guard a longer look during their transition, while the Hawks were already arranging a rotation around rookie Trae Young. Mack wasn't a stranger to Atlanta: he had previously played for the franchise and could theoretically provide experienced guard depth. The transactions were modest compared with the deadline's major deals, but they still affected which player each team had under contract heading into the season's final weeks.

The Hawks Declined to Keep Mack

Atlanta didn't retain Mack for a second extended stint. It waived him on February 8, one day after the trade, and he subsequently joined another team. Those later appearances cannot be counted as part of the Hawks' return, nor can the 172 Atlanta games from his earlier tenure. Instead, the exchange helped Atlanta exit Dorsey's roster obligation while it explored other personnel options. Any assessment based on Mack's earlier assists or scoring for Memphis would confuse the outgoing résumé with the incoming contribution. The new Hawks stint produced no sustained basketball minutes.

Dorsey Had a Real Receiving-Team Opportunity in Memphis

Dorsey moved into a Grizzlies environment that needed young guards to prove themselves. The official release noted his first 83 NBA appearances with Atlanta, which informed Memphis's decision but weren't yet Grizzlies output. After the deadline he played for Memphis and could supply scoring from a reserve role. His connection with former Oregon teammate Dillon Brooks gave the club another familiar developmental pairing. Even if Dorsey didn't become a long-term Memphis starter, the team obtained playable depth, unlike Atlanta's very short experience with Mack following the exchange.

This Modest Swap Did Not Change Either Franchise's Future

The trade gave Memphis a usable audition for a young player and let Atlanta proceed with its backcourt reset. Neither incoming guard became a defining piece of his receiving franchise, and both teams were operating within ordinary deadline roster constraints. The canonical Even Trade verdict and identical B- grades reflect that limited overall importance rather than identical minutes played. The real court-time comparison favors Memphis, while Atlanta's practical motivation involved clearing a place in a roster increasingly built for the next phase.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Atlanta receives B- for the low-stakes decision to exchange Tyler Dorsey, although Shelvin Mack was waived a day later without establishing a new Hawks role. Memphis also earns B-, gaining a young guard it could use for the final portion of the season. The Grizzlies obtained more direct playing value; neither club acquired a durable core player.

perspectives.summary: At the February 2019 deadline Cleveland acquired Brandon Knight, Marquese Chriss and draft rights from Houston, while Houston received Nik Stauskas, Wade Baldwin IV and a second-round asset. Sacramento acquired Alec Burks. The incoming Cavaliers picks later became associated with Dylan Windler and Andrew Nembhard, but those rights require individual tracing. The inherited Even Trade grades all three clubs C+.
perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Took Two Players and Extra Draft Opportunities

The Cavaliers accepted Brandon Knight and Marquese Chriss in a February 2019 three-team exchange with Houston and Sacramento. They also gained rights tied to a 2019 first-round selection and a future second. Knight was a veteran guard whose availability had been affected by injuries, while Chriss remained a young big seeking a stable NBA role. The Cavaliers' rebuilding strategy made draft flexibility at least as important as the short-term playing contributions of either incoming player.

The Cavaliers' Picks Developed Separate Rights Histories

One selection became associated with No. 26 Dylan Windler in the 2019 draft, and another later with No. 31 Andrew Nembhard in 2022. Those names provide identities for incoming rights but don't establish that every player later starred for Cleveland. Nembhard's eventual NBA development with a different organization must remain separate from this original trade. The Cavaliers received options to develop or redirect selections in addition to evaluating Knight and Chriss. That is a meaningful asset package despite limited immediate roster improvement.

Houston and Sacramento Received More Direct Returns

Houston acquired Nik Stauskas, Wade Baldwin IV and a future second-round right associated with No. 54 Sandro Mamukelashvili. Stauskas and Baldwin offered depth possibilities rather than guaranteed long-term starters, while the draft pick represented another separate future option. Sacramento obtained Alec Burks, an established perimeter scorer who could provide useful bench minutes. The Kings' side had the most straightforward active-player identity, but a single veteran's tenure could also be comparatively short.

The Equal Grades Recognize Three Different Approaches

Cleveland acquired two players plus draft flexibility, Houston received guard options and a future choice, and Sacramento selected an experienced wing. The inherited C+ grades on all three sides reflect modest potential rather than a decisive new franchise player. The analysis shouldn't erase the future draft rights because they didn't immediately become rotation minutes. It also shouldn't exaggerate them by transferring Nembhard's later success at another club to the Cavaliers. Each participant obtained a plausible but limited return.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Cleveland gets C+ for Brandon Knight, Marquese Chriss and future draft assets associated with Dylan Windler and Andrew Nembhard. Houston also receives C+ for Stauskas, Baldwin and a second-round right, while Sacramento earns C+ for Alec Burks. The three packages offered different kinds of value without a decisive direct franchise-changing result.

perspectives.summary: In a February 2019 three-team trade, Milwaukee acquired Nikola Mirotić, Detroit received Thon Maker, and New Orleans took Stanley Johnson, Jason Smith and four future second-round selections. The original Pelicans Win grades New Orleans B+, Detroit C+ and Milwaukee C+. The Pistons-only imported ledger had omitted Mirotić and the additional Pelicans compensation, now restored using the official Bucks transaction record.
perspectives.analysis:
Milwaukee Acquired a Shooting Forward for Its Contender

The Bucks traded for Nikola Mirotić in February 2019, bringing a frontcourt scorer with reliable three-point range to a team building around Giannis Antetokounmpo. His ability to stretch defenses offered an immediate offensive option alongside Brook Lopez and other Milwaukee forwards. The price included Thon Maker going to Detroit and Jason Smith plus future draft choices going to New Orleans. Mirotić was a genuine incoming Bucks player, not an omitted administrative side of a two-team exchange.

Detroit Took Maker as a Young Frontcourt Project

The Pistons received Maker, a former lottery pick whose size and mobility had intrigued Milwaukee. Detroit was willing to evaluate whether the big man could earn a larger role with a different set of teammates. It sent Stanley Johnson to New Orleans rather than retaining the young wing. Maker's earlier Bucks minutes could help establish his experience but were not games automatically delivered for the Pistons. The exchange replaced one developmental forward with another type of uncertain frontcourt upside.

New Orleans Collected Two Players and Four Seconds

The Pelicans acquired Johnson from Detroit and Smith from Milwaukee, plus four future second-round selections from the Bucks. That package was broader than the single Johnson entry preserved in the old Detroit-centered source. Smith brought veteran interior experience, while Johnson offered an opportunity to evaluate a former high draft choice. The second-round rights provided additional flexibility, although their final player outcomes and any subsequent transfers required individual tracing. Four picks shouldn't be described as four immediately productive NBA players.

The Preserved Pelicans Grade Emphasizes Asset Volume

The inherited model grades New Orleans B+ for collecting several players and selections, with Detroit and Milwaukee both C+. That result differs from the contemporary appeal of Mirotić to a leading Eastern contender, and the article should acknowledge his real shooting value. The source-complete record gives each team a defined return and lets readers distinguish Milwaukee's current basketball need from the Pelicans' future-option strategy. A retrospective grade revision is separate from restoring the correct assets.

Final Verdict

Pelicans Win. New Orleans receives B+ for Stanley Johnson, Jason Smith and four future second-round choices. Milwaukee earns C+ under the inherited model despite acquiring established shooter Nikola Mirotić, while Detroit also receives C+ for developmental big Thon Maker. All three returns are real, and the original Pelicans advantage primarily credits the larger package of future assets.

houston-rockets.analysis:
Indiana Collected Four Assets in a Deadline Contract Move

At the February 7, 2019 deadline, Indiana obtained the contracts of Nik Stauskas and Wade Baldwin IV, draft rights to overseas forward Maarty Leunen and a future 2021 second-round selection from Houston. The Rockets received cash, a financial consideration that reflected their desire to adjust roster and payroll commitments. The 2021 choice later appeared in the draft ledger at No. 54, associated with Sandro Mamukelashvili. Indiana was not acquiring four established Pacers starters; it was taking short-term contracts and assets it could hold or move. The teams' different roster and financial motivations are critical to understanding why the exchange occurred.

Stauskas and Baldwin Were Contract Opportunities, Not Core Pacers

Stauskas and Baldwin had NBA experience with earlier clubs, but their incoming Indiana contracts did not create an extended Pacers rotation career. Both had moved through other deadline transactions during the same period, and roster decisions soon followed. Counting their earlier seasons with Brooklyn, Portland or other teams as Indianapolis basketball would greatly exaggerate the deal's impact. Instead, the Pacers obtained a set of contractual and developmental options while focusing their active rotation elsewhere. Leunen's overseas-rights status should be treated similarly: the team held an NBA entitlement, not an instantly available big man playing regular-season games.

The Later Second-Round Identity Is a Rights Trail

The 2021 second-round selection became associated with the No. 54 draft slot and Mamukelashvili, but the forward's NBA career followed additional rights movements and contracts. The future pick was legitimate compensation to Indiana even if the Pacers didn't themselves employ its eventual namesake for years. A source-backed review needs to distinguish the incoming right from the player later selected by another NBA organization. Houston, meanwhile, didn't get an NBA player or draft choice in the original move; its direct return was cash and the organizational flexibility associated with outgoing contracts.

A Collection of Options Outweighs Only Cash

Indiana acquired several potential assets at relatively modest basketball cost, while Houston pursued a narrower cash-and-payroll result. The Pacers have a reasonable edge for retaining a second-round opportunity and several contracts to evaluate, but their grade cannot imply all four arrived as meaningful on-court contributors. The Rockets should not receive a failing grade for obtaining cash through a deal designed around resource management. Neither club's later postseason performance can be attributed principally to this minor deadline swap. A moderate assessment gives Indiana credit for draft flexibility while respecting what Houston actually wanted from the transaction.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win, modestly. Indiana earns B- for acquiring Nik Stauskas, Wade Baldwin IV, Maarty Leunen's rights and a 2021 second-round asset later associated with No. 54 Sandro Mamukelashvili. Houston receives C for cash and payroll flexibility. Incoming Pacers contracts didn't automatically create long NBA tenures, and Mamukelashvili's later career wasn't direct Indiana playing output.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: Ivica Zubac for Mike Muscala became one of the Clippers' cleanest modern wins: Zubac developed into a long-term starting center and valuable two-way asset at minimal acquisition cost.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis: Los Angeles acquired Ivica Zubac and Michael Beasley from the Lakers for Mike Muscala, then retained Zubac as a durable starting center for years. Zubac developed from a young rotation big into a high-level rebounder, interior defender and efficient finisher, eventually becoming valuable enough to headline another major trade package in 2026. Muscala's Lakers tenure was brief, and Beasley was not the reason for the Clippers' win; the decisive asset was Zubac. Given the tiny acquisition cost and the years of production and later trade value, A+ is justified.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: On February 7, 2019, the Clippers exchanged Avery Bradley for Memphis veterans Garrett Temple and JaMychal Green. Temple played 26 regular-season Los Angeles games after the deal while Green played 24, then returned to the Clippers for 63 more games in 2019-20. Bradley played 14 games for Memphis before leaving the organization after the season. Clippers Win, Los Angeles A- and Memphis C+, with Green supplying the sustained return.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Turned One Veteran Guard Into Two Experienced Reserves

Los Angeles sent Avery Bradley to Memphis on February 7, 2019, acquiring Garrett Temple and JaMychal Green in return. The Clippers were playing toward a playoff berth while also adjusting their longer-term roster, and adding a forward who could rebound and shoot fit their frontcourt needs. Temple offered perimeter defense and secondary guard minutes. Memphis was reshaping its personnel after moving away from parts of its established veteran core. Bradley gave the Grizzlies a known defensive guard, but this was a short midseason transaction rather than a trade built around a franchise cornerstone.

Both New Clippers Played Through the 2019 Playoff Push

Temple appeared in 26 Clippers regular-season games after the trade, including six starts. Green added 24 games and averaged 8.7 points and 6.5 rebounds while making better than 41 percent of his three-point shots. The two also appeared in Los Angeles's six-game first-round playoff series against Golden State. Green provided a particularly useful small-ball frontcourt option against a difficult opponent, while Temple offered dependable defensive possessions. Their 2018-19 Memphis statistics before February do not belong to the Clippers, but their posttrade games supplied the depth Los Angeles had sought.

Green Stayed Another Year While Bradley Did Not Remain in Memphis

Green returned to the Clippers for 2019-20 and appeared in 63 more regular-season games, adding another 1,307 minutes. Across his first two Clippers seasons, the direct result was 87 regular-season appearances and a recurring reserve role. Temple departed after the initial spring, so only his 26 Los Angeles games count. Bradley, meanwhile, played 14 games for the Grizzlies after arriving in February. He was an active contributor during that stretch, but moved to the Lakers the following summer. His later Los Angeles Lakers work is not Memphis production, and Green's subsequent Denver seasons are likewise separate.

The Multi-Season Forward Return Gave Los Angeles the Advantage

Memphis obtained a competent guard for the remainder of 2018-19, which explains why the deal cannot fairly be scored as zero on its side. Los Angeles acquired two rotation-capable veterans, then retained one through the next season. The deciding difference was not the number of people named in the trade but Green's continued rebounding, floor spacing and postseason utility in a Clippers uniform. This was a practical roster win for a team pursuing playoff success, not evidence that Memphis gave up a future All-Star. The inherited Clippers-favored result remains valid, with a modest reduction of the Memphis grade.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win. Los Angeles earns A- for Temple's 26-game stint and Green's 24-game spring followed by another 63 regular-season games in 2019-20. Memphis receives C+ for Bradley's 14 games before he left. The Clippers obtained the longer-lasting player and better postseason frontcourt flexibility from the exchange.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Sold the Forty-Fourth Selection to Miami

Atlanta agreed to send its No. 44 selection in the 2019 draft to Miami for $1.9 million and a heavily protected future second-round pick. The transaction gave the Hawks an immediate cash return on a choice they did not intend to keep. Miami purchased the chance to select or redirect a player at that spot. This was a trade of draft inventory, not an established center moving directly into a new rotation. The pick later became associated with Bol Bol, one of the night's more recognizable developmental prospects.

Miami Used the Pick as a Subsequent Trade Asset

Miami's control of the acquired selection allowed it to select Bol and then move his rights in a separate draft-related deal involving Denver. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Golden State Bought the Forty-First Selection

Ahead of the June 20, 2019 draft, the Warriors secured pick No. 41 from Atlanta by offering $1.3 million in cash and a 2024 second-rounder. The Hawks were collecting future assets while reshaping a roster full of draft choices, whereas Golden State wanted another prospect immediately. The agreement didn't guarantee which player the Warriors would select, and the future pick wasn't a present-day rotation player for Atlanta. The teams made opposite calculations about time: Golden State paid to act in 2019, while the Hawks accepted a distant chance and the immediate money.

Paschall Supplied an Unusually Productive Rookie Return

Golden State used No. 41 to draft Villanova forward Eric Paschall. Injuries and roster turnover created playing time for him in 2019-20, and he averaged 14.0 points and 4.6 rebounds in 60 games. He was selected to the NBA All-Rookie First Team, an unusually strong opening outcome for a mid-second-round selection. That performance is a concrete Warriors return created by the purchased pick, not a projected value assigned to whoever Atlanta might have picked. Paschall's later career was shorter than his rookie promise, but the original receiving franchise benefited immediately.

Atlanta's Cash and Deferred Draft Right Were Different Assets

The Hawks received a meaningful cash payment and a second-round choice five years in the future. The pick eventually resolved at No. 44 in 2024, associated with Pelle Larsson in the draft's rights history. That doesn't prove Larsson's subsequent NBA career was played for Atlanta; the selection's later movements need to be treated independently. The financial return and future optionality did have value, yet neither delivered the same kind of direct immediate player production as Paschall's first Warriors season. Atlanta accepted that timing trade-off deliberately rather than misplacing a prospect already on its roster.

The Outcome Shows Why Second-Round Picks Can Be Valuable

The Warriors found a real contributor and award-winning rookie with an acquired second-round choice, validating their willingness to pay an added cash cost. Atlanta's return offered money and another future selection but less measurable on-court output from this precise transaction. Paschall never became an enduring franchise cornerstone, so the trade should not be exaggerated into a dynasty-making acquisition. Nevertheless, sixty rookie appearances and 14 points a night constitute a more tangible payoff than most purchased second-round picks yield. The Golden State edge is grounded in his receiving-team performance.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State earns C+ for purchasing the pick used on Eric Paschall, who averaged 14.0 points over 60 games and reached the All-Rookie First Team. Atlanta gets C- for $1.3 million and a future second-round choice that ultimately became the No. 44 selection in 2024. That draft asset had its own later routing, but it didn't match Paschall's immediate Warriors contribution.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Sold a Yale Prospect for a Known Two-Million-Dollar Payment

Golden State selected Yale guard-forward Miye Oni at No. 58 during the June 20, 2019 NBA draft and transferred his rights to Utah for $2 million in cash. The Warriors had limited guaranteed roster places and converted a late selection into a clearly documented financial return. Utah liked Oni's size, perimeter defensive tools and prospect of growing into a rotation wing. Transaction ledgers date the processing June 21, immediately after the draft-night selection. The trade wasn't a player-for-player swap, and no other NBA player formed part of the consideration.

Oni Developed Into an Occasional Utah Regular

Oni played ten Jazz regular-season games in 2019-20, fifty-four in 2020-21 and sixteen in 2021-22. Across those three seasons he totaled eighty league appearances, 672 minutes, 145 points and 108 rebounds. His best year for Utah came in the middle, when he played more than nine minutes a game and sometimes helped cover wing defensive assignments. Those numbers establish real NBA value from a second-round purchase. They don't imply he became a permanent starter or an offensive centerpiece, and the Jazz eventually moved on.

The Playoffs Added Ten Brief Appearances

Oni also appeared in ten postseason games for Utah across two playoff runs, mostly for short shifts. That playing time supplements the direct eighty-game regular-season return, though it shouldn't be used to exaggerate his responsibility for the team's playoff results. His one career regular-season start came in his first year. The Jazz had bought the opportunity to develop a late draft choice, then used that player on their bench while competing in a crowded Western Conference. Unlike overseas stashes that never arrive, Oni gave the receiving club actual NBA minutes.

Two Different Realized Returns Keep the Grades Close

Golden State collected $2 million without carrying another second-round rookie contract, a more clearly quantified cash receipt than most trades of this type. Utah received three seasons of limited wing coverage and a player who appeared in the playoffs. Neither benefit was transformative, so it would be unreasonable to label the transaction a runaway basketball success or a terrible cash sale. Utah gets a modest edge because it acquired playable NBA depth with development time, while the Warriors deserve a solid grade for the confirmed money rather than an assumed zero return.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win. Utah earns B for Miye Oni's eighty regular-season games, 672 minutes, 145 points and ten playoff appearances after the second-round rights purchase. Golden State gets B- for its verified $2 million cash receipt. Both organizations obtained value; Utah earned the slight basketball edge because its incoming asset actually played for three NBA seasons.

Across those three seasons he totaled eighty league appearances, 672 minutes, 145 points and 108 rebounds. His best year for Utah came in the middle, when he played more than nine minutes a game and sometimes helped cover wing defensive assignments. Those numbers establish real NBA value from a second-round purchase. They don't imply he became a permanent starter or an offensive centerpiece, and the Jazz eventually moved on.

The Playoffs Added Ten Brief Appearances

Oni also appeared in ten postseason games for Utah across two playoff runs, mostly for short shifts. That playing time supplements the direct eighty-game regular-season return, though it shouldn't be used to exaggerate his responsibility for the team's playoff results. His one career regular-season start came in his first year. The Jazz had bought the opportunity to develop a late draft choice, then used that player on their bench while competing in a crowded Western Conference. Unlike overseas stashes that never arrive, Oni gave the receiving club actual NBA minutes.

Two Different Realized Returns Keep the Grades Close

Golden State collected $2 million without carrying another second-round rookie contract, a more clearly quantified cash receipt than most trades of this type. Utah received three seasons of limited wing coverage and a player who appeared in the playoffs. Neither benefit was transformative, so it would be unreasonable to label the transaction a runaway basketball success or a terrible cash sale. Utah gets a modest edge because it acquired playable NBA depth with development time, while the Warriors deserve a solid grade for the confirmed money rather than an assumed zero return.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win. Utah earns B for Miye Oni's eighty regular-season games, 672 minutes, 145 points and ten playoff appearances after the second-round rights purchase. Golden State gets B- for its verified $2 million cash receipt. Both organizations obtained value; Utah earned the slight basketball edge because its incoming asset actually played for three NBA seasons.

Brantley appeared in NBA games for Utah during the 2019-20 and 2020-21 seasons, but never became a regular starter. Indiana received both cash and a later selection, ultimately No. 60 in 2021. Even Trade, Indiana B- and Utah C+ for different modest asset returns.
indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Sold the No. 50 Rights for Cash and an Unconditional Pick

The Pacers selected Jarrell Brantley from the College of Charleston with the fiftieth choice in the 2019 NBA draft, then traded his rights to Utah. Indiana's official announcement, released June 21, identifies the return as cash considerations plus an unconditional second-round selection in 2021. That is stronger compensation than cash alone because the club secured another chance to draft a player without needing a protected condition to be met. Utah wanted an athletic forward it could develop within its own system, while the Pacers collected two modest future-building assets.

Brantley Reached the Utah Roster as a Deep Reserve

Brantley made his NBA debut for the Jazz and remained under their control across the next two seasons. He played nine regular-season games in 2019-20, followed by 28 appearances in 2020-21, totaling 37 NBA games for Utah. His role was limited, mostly behind established playoff contributors, and he did not become a reliable starting forward. The Jazz also developed him through their minor-league program. Those developmental assignments can help explain why the club valued the rights, but only the actual Utah NBA appearances should count as acquired league output.

The Pacers Received a Later Draft Choice Without a Protection Risk

Indiana's return included the unconditional 2021 second-rounder, providing a guaranteed selection independent of Utah's eventual win total or draft position. The choice reached the late second round in 2021. The Pacers also secured cash at the time of the exchange, though the official news release did not state a dollar amount. It would be an error to credit Indiana with the professional accomplishments of every player who later held the pick or of another team that may have acquired the rights. The asset's immediate importance was a real future draft position plus a financial payment.

The Clubs Chose Different Forms of Second-Round Value

The Jazz acquired a fringe NBA forward they could develop and briefly deploy, giving them actual playing minutes from a late draft pick. Indiana preferred flexibility: cash immediately and another second-round choice two years later. Neither organization uncovered a cornerstone, and Brantley's relatively short NBA stint doesn't justify a decisive Utah victory. Conversely, Indiana's pick and payment should not be dismissed because the Pacers didn't receive an established veteran on draft night. The best retrospective treats the exchange as broadly balanced, with a slightly stronger Indiana asset grade and the Jazz credited for getting Brantley into games.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Indiana earns B- for obtaining cash plus an unconditional 2021 second-round selection when it sold Jarrell Brantley's draft rights. Utah earns C+ because Brantley reached the Jazz rotation for 37 games across two seasons but did not hold a regular starting role. Both teams received limited but genuine value from a late second-round agreement.

boston-celtics.summary: Philadelphia moved the No. 24 and No. 33 draft rights to Boston in June 2019 to acquire the No. 20 rights to Matisse Thybulle. Boston retained Carsen Edwards from the second round but moved Ty Jerome's rights to Phoenix in a separate draft-night transaction. Thybulle developed into an All-Defensive wing with substantial 76ers minutes. 76ers Win, Philadelphia B and Boston D.
boston-celtics.analysis:
Philadelphia Traded Two Picks to Reach Matisse Thybulle

Philadelphia targeted Washington defender Matisse Thybulle in the 2019 draft and sent Boston the rights to No. 24 Ty Jerome and No. 33 Carsen Edwards for the No. 20 rights to Thybulle. The Sixers preferred an immediately usable defensive wing over two opportunities further down the board. Boston accepted a later first and an additional second, giving itself the choice to develop players or reroute one of the selections. Both teams were acquiring draft rights rather than an established NBA veteran, and the ultimate value depended on which rights became useful rotation work.

Thybulle Became a Recognized Defensive Specialist

Thybulle spent multiple seasons with Philadelphia and established himself as a disruptive perimeter defender. He earned All-Defensive Second Team recognition, supplying steals, deflections and unusual recovery ability in a role that didn't demand high offensive usage. The Sixers could put him alongside their more prolific scorers and rely on his ball pressure. His limitations as a shooter affected how he was deployed, particularly in certain postseason matchups, but he played genuine rotation minutes over several years. That direct Philadelphia contribution gives the receiving team considerably more than a theoretical prospect or unused contract.

Boston's Rights Returned a Short-Term Reserve and Another Trade

Carsen Edwards became a Celtics guard but did not establish a permanent rotation role before leaving Boston. Ty Jerome's draft rights had an even more complicated path: Boston forwarded them to Phoenix in a separate transaction rather than developing Jerome as a Celtic. His later work for the Suns and other teams therefore cannot be credited as Boston playing production from the Thybulle swap. The additional second-round opportunity was real draft value at the time, yet Edwards did not provide sustained contribution comparable to the defender Philadelphia acquired. Boston's short direct return is the decisive limitation.

The Defensive Contributor Outweighed the Two-Pick Package

Boston's logic was defensible on draft night because two selections offer more chances to discover useful talent than one. The eventual returns did not justify giving up the player Philadelphia chose. Thybulle helped the Sixers over several seasons, while Edwards remained a modest reserve and Jerome was moved in another deal before suiting up in Boston. Philadelphia's win rests on the actual defensive specialist it used rather than pretending he became an elite two-way scorer. The Boston grade reflects missed opportunity, not a belief that having extra draft choices is inherently poor strategy.

Final Verdict

76ers Win. Philadelphia earns B for Matisse Thybulle's years as an NBA rotation defender and his All-Defensive honors. Boston gets D because Carsen Edwards provided limited reserve value and Ty Jerome was moved again before he could produce Celtics playing minutes. Jerome's subsequent career at other clubs cannot be added to Boston's direct return from this June 2019 draft-rights exchange.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
The Hawks and Blazers Exchanged Veteran Wings

Atlanta acquired Evan Turner from Portland on June 24, 2019, sending Kent Bazemore to the Trail Blazers. Both veterans had been playing meaningful roles in their old cities, but their skills differed. Turner preferred to initiate secondary offense, rebound and move the ball, while Bazemore supplied catch-and-shoot potential and defensive activity. Atlanta was beginning a youth-oriented roster transition and could evaluate a different kind of veteran. Portland wanted wing help after a Western Conference Finals season. The agreement contained no direct new draft choice in this two-player exchange.

Turner Played Only a Short Atlanta Stretch

Turner had previously been useful as a ball-handling reserve in Portland, but his Atlanta role didn't develop into a season-long rotation fixture. He appeared in only 19 Hawks games in 2019-20 before becoming part of a different multi-team transaction. The Hawks therefore got limited actual court value despite the intention of giving their young group a veteran passer. His earlier 73 games for the Blazers are the outgoing player's background, not part of his new Atlanta return. The transaction was more about short-term experimentation than creating a core piece.

Bazemore's Portland Stay Was Also Brief

Bazemore moved to a Trail Blazers roster that needed reliable wing bodies. He played 43 games for Portland during 2019-20 before the team traded him again as its personnel needs shifted. His long Atlanta record, including 355 games and a visible community role, explains why the Hawks valued him but must not be credited as Portland production. In his new city he provided minutes and some defense, though his offensive efficiency failed to lift the team in the way hoped. Portland's return was real, yet it too lasted only part of a campaign.

Neither Veteran Turned the Deal Into a Lasting Upgrade

Atlanta received fewer games than Portland did from its incoming player, but Turner's expiring-contract utility and ball-handling role gave the Hawks a different kind of option while rebuilding. Portland added a wing it could use immediately and subsequently moved again. The canonical slight Hawks edge is therefore not an argument that Turner outperformed Bazemore on the court. Instead, it reflects the Hawks' strategic reset and financial timetable. Both organizations ultimately treated the acquired players as movable short-term pieces rather than foundations for future seasons.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta gets B- because Evan Turner fitted its short-term contract and roster-planning approach, although he played only 19 Hawks games. Portland receives C+ for Kent Bazemore's 43 appearances before another trade. The Blazers obtained more direct minutes, but neither veteran became an enduring difference-maker, leaving this a narrow overall judgment.

boston-celtics.analysis:
A Sign-and-Trade Replaced Two Teams' Starting Point Guards

Boston brought Kemba Walker from Charlotte on July 6, 2019, in a sign-and-trade that sent Terry Rozier the other way. The agreement also exchanged protected 2020 second-round rights, later associated with Yam Madar for Boston and Grant Riller for Charlotte. Walker had become the Hornets' franchise scoring leader, but the teams were heading toward different roster timelines. The Celtics needed an established offensive star after the departure of Kyrie Irving. Charlotte saw a chance to give Rozier the responsibility and minutes he had wanted behind Boston's veterans.

Walker Helped Boston Reach the 2020 Conference Finals

Walker made the All-Star team during his first Boston season and combined with Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown as the Celtics reached the 2020 Eastern Conference Finals. His quickness, pull-up shooting and ball handling made him a valuable fit initially. Knee problems increasingly complicated his availability and effectiveness, however, and he left Boston in another transaction after only two seasons. Walker's eight earlier Charlotte seasons explain his reputation at acquisition, but Boston's direct return consists of those Celtics seasons, including the strong opening year and diminished follow-up.

Rozier Became a Longer-Term Charlotte Starter

Rozier did what Charlotte hoped a new starting guard might: he expanded his scoring and ball-handling responsibilities over multiple seasons. His growth gave the Hornets a productive backcourt presence alongside emerging teammates, and he was still contributing years after Walker had departed Boston. Rozier was not necessarily the better individual player when the deal occurred; the comparison concerns what each receiving franchise actually obtained afterward. The draft-pick exchange also offered secondary value, but neither team's roster direction was determined mainly by the two late second-round rights.

Longer Availability Favors Charlotte's Side

The Celtics enjoyed a real conference-finals campaign with Walker, making it incorrect to call the acquisition worthless. Nonetheless, health problems shortened the return from an expensive guard who was expected to anchor multiple seasons. Charlotte received a younger player who grew into a dependable starter and remained useful much longer. That durability, rather than a retrospective dismissal of Walker's prime career, supports the Hornets' advantage. Both teams filled a vacant backcourt role on trade day; the outcomes diverged as the months of actual receiving-team production accumulated.

Final Verdict

Charlotte Win. The Hornets earn B+ for Terry Rozier's longer productive starting tenure after the sign-and-trade. Boston receives C- despite Kemba Walker's All-Star opening season and contribution to the 2020 Eastern Conference Finals, because knee trouble cut short his expected run. The 2020 second-round selections are included without attributing other teams' later players to either franchise.

analysis:
Atlanta Took Crabbe and Two First-Round Rights Paths

Atlanta traded Taurean Prince and a 2021 second-round selection to Brooklyn in a July 6, 2019 transaction involving guard Allen Crabbe, the rights to 2019 first-round pick Nickeil Alexander-Walker and another protected first-round asset. The future selection eventually appeared in the 2020 draft as No. 17, associated with Aleksej Pokuševski. The Hawks were trading an established wing for a mix of current veteran salary and developmental options, while Brooklyn wanted another shooter and defender during a major free-agent offseason. Multiple draft-rights paths made this deal more complex than a simple Prince-for-Crabbe exchange.

Crabbe Played in Atlanta, But the Pick Rights Moved Again

Crabbe made NBA appearances for the Hawks during the 2019-20 season, providing some immediate perimeter depth. The more important long-run flexibility came from the two first-round rights, not from treating every player eventually associated with them as an Atlanta roster member. Alexander-Walker's rights moved in another transaction before he established his NBA career with New Orleans. Likewise, Pokuševski's NBA career developed with Oklahoma City after additional rights transfers. Their subsequent games elsewhere are evidence that the choices had trade value, not that the Hawks enjoyed the full players' production on the court.

Brooklyn Received Prince as a Regular Rotation Wing

Prince joined Brooklyn and played substantial wing minutes during the 2019-20 season, providing size, defense and three-point shooting for a team preparing to integrate new star talent. The Nets also received an incoming future second-round selection that later appears in the draft ledger as No. 49 Marcus Zegarowski in 2021. That choice and Prince's direct appearances are real benefits. Prince's later seasons with other franchises should not be counted as extra Nets production. Brooklyn was paying a meaningful price in first-round rights to gain a player it expected to use immediately rather than a guaranteed multi-year All-Star.

Two Tradable First-Round Assets Favor Atlanta

The Hawks acquired usable veteran minutes and two important draft opportunities, which helped support the organization's larger roster-building effort. Brooklyn received a proven young wing and a second-round choice, so its side was not empty. The difference is the extra value carried by the first-round rights Atlanta could later move in independent deals. The verdict favors the Hawks without assigning every performance of Alexander-Walker or Pokuševski to Atlanta, and without treating Brooklyn's big free-agent moves as direct consequences of a single exchange. A fair retrospective weighs immediate Prince production against the Hawks' wider asset base.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for Allen Crabbe's short-term playing time and the transferable rights tied to Nickeil Alexander-Walker and the later No. 17 Aleksej Pokuševski draft slot. Brooklyn receives B for Taurean Prince's wing minutes and a 2021 second-round asset associated with Marcus Zegarowski. Alexander-Walker and Pokuševski's NBA games with other franchises aren't assigned to Atlanta.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Phoenix Acquired Baynes and Jerome's Draft Rights

The Suns received Aron Baynes and the rights to Ty Jerome from Boston in July 2019, while the Celtics gained a future first-round selection and a trade exception. Phoenix wanted another experienced center to support its young lineup, and Jerome represented a guard prospect with draft-day potential. Boston prioritized flexibility rather than retaining Baynes, whose established NBA role had given the Celtics useful defensive and interior minutes. The move exchanged immediate rotation assets for future roster maneuvering.

Baynes Had a Real Impact With the Suns

Baynes became a useful Phoenix center during the 2019-20 season, offering screens, interior physicality and improved outside shooting. Jerome had a smaller NBA role, but the incoming package was not devoid of court value. That is important because Phoenix's inherited D grade looks severe alongside the actual contribution of Baynes. The trade did not produce a Suns championship or long-serving All-Star through these players. It did provide a productive veteran for a season, which needs to be counted rather than ignored.

Boston's Pick Later Became No. 30 Desmond Bane

The Celtics' incoming first-round asset was associated with the No. 30 selection used on Desmond Bane in the 2020 draft. The draft rights then changed hands, and Bane became a high-level NBA guard with a different franchise, not a Boston rotation player. His subsequent breakout cannot be credited directly to Boston's on-court return. The selection still had meaningful asset value because Boston could use it in later deals, and the trade exception offered a separate way to adjust the roster.

The Pick's Upside Contrasted With Phoenix's Immediate Help

Boston received a valuable future first and financial flexibility, while Phoenix got a veteran center capable of playing meaningful minutes plus a developing guard. The original Celtics advantage rewards the potential of a strong draft asset, but there is a legitimate qualification: Baynes played well for Phoenix and Bane's major career achievements came after another rights transaction. A fair reader-facing analysis distinguishes draft value from the NBA games each receiving team actually obtained.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for obtaining a first-round right later tied to No. 30 Desmond Bane and a trade exception, without claiming Bane's later Memphis performances. Phoenix receives D under the inherited grades despite legitimate Aron Baynes production and Ty Jerome's development opportunity. The selection gave Boston leverage, but Phoenix's actual player return deserves more credit than the letter alone suggests.

perspectives.summary: Washington acquired Davis Bertāns from San Antonio during a July 2019 three-team transaction in which the Spurs received DeMarre Carroll and Brooklyn took the rights to Aaron White and Nemanja Dangubić. Bertāns became an important outside shooter for the Wizards, giving Washington the strongest direct on-court return. The inherited slight Wizards edge grades Washington A-, Brooklyn B+ and San Antonio C-.
perspectives.analysis:
Washington Acquired a Proven Stretch Forward

The Wizards landed Davis Bertāns in July 2019 through a three-team arrangement with San Antonio and Brooklyn. Bertāns was already a dangerous outside shooter from a frontcourt position, an appealing skill for a Washington team seeking new scoring options. The Spurs took DeMarre Carroll, a veteran wing, and the Nets received the draft rights to Aaron White and Nemanja Dangubić. The clubs weren't all trying to add a similar player: Washington sought an offensive fit, while the others adjusted contracts and overseas rights.

Bertāns Produced a Clear Washington Breakout

Bertāns substantially expanded his offensive role with the Wizards and became an especially effective high-volume three-point shooter. His Washington production was direct receiving-team value rather than a projection based only on earlier Spurs minutes. The success also led to additional contractual decisions after the season, which should be evaluated separately from the 2019 exchange. His limitations as a defender and interior finisher meant he wasn't an all-purpose star, but the shooting role supplied Washington with an obvious, measurable benefit.

Brooklyn and San Antonio Received Different Kinds of Assets

Brooklyn acquired the overseas rights to White and Dangubić, which could be retained or moved without guaranteeing either would become a Nets rotation player. San Antonio took Carroll as a veteran wing option. Carroll did not develop into a major extended Spurs tenure through the deal, making its basketball return less compelling than Washington's immediate scoring upgrade. The Nets' rights offered transactional flexibility, but later player careers or club movements must be tracked before assigning them direct Nets production.

The Wizards Got the Most Tangible On-Court Upside

Washington's A- grade reflects Bertāns's successful adaptation to a larger shooting role. Brooklyn receives B+ for a pair of transferable overseas rights, while San Antonio's C- corresponds with Carroll's limited direct Spurs tenure. These grades shouldn't be treated as proof that overseas rights became NBA stars or that the Wizards solved every roster problem through one shooter. They recognize the different types of compensation, with Washington realizing the clearest identifiable offensive improvement.

Final Verdict

Slight Wizards Edge. Washington earns A- for Davis Bertāns's outstanding perimeter shooting after arriving from San Antonio. Brooklyn gets B+ for the rights to Aaron White and Nemanja Dangubić, which offered future flexibility. San Antonio receives C- for DeMarre Carroll's limited tenure. The Wizards secured the most direct and sustained offensive benefit from the three-team arrangement.

indiana-pacers.summary: Indiana acquired Malcolm Brogdon in a sign-and-trade and received several seasons of starting guard play before converting him into another productive asset package.
indiana-pacers.analysis: The Pacers paid a protected first-round pick, two second-round picks and a trade exception to acquire Malcolm Brogdon from Milwaukee. Brogdon immediately became a high-usage starter, gave Indiana three productive seasons and was later traded to Boston in the deal that brought Aaron Nesmith and additional draft value. Milwaukee's compensation was meaningful, particularly the first-round pick, so this was not a free acquisition. Still, Indiana received the best established player in the transaction and later preserved value when it moved him. That combination of production and downstream conversion supports a Pacers Win.

new-orleans-pelicans.analysis: The 2019 draft-night deal with Atlanta produced one of the better asset chains of the Pelicans' post-Anthony Davis reset. New Orleans moved the rights to De'Andre Hunter and other pieces, then received the rights to Jaxson Hayes, Nickeil Alexander-Walker and Didi Louzada plus future draft compensation. Hayes never justified his lottery slot and Hunter became a solid NBA starter, which keeps the trade from being a runaway. The key swing is the downstream draft value: the future-pick structure eventually helped produce Herb Jones, an elite defensive role player on a second-round contract. Alexander-Walker also became a useful NBA guard. Taken together, the Pelicans extracted the stronger total package.

philadelphia-76ers.analysis:
Atlanta Traded Several Picks for Bruno Fernando's Rights

The July 6, 2019 exchange gave Atlanta the draft rights to Maryland big man Bruno Fernando, selected thirty-fourth in 2019. Philadelphia received guard Jordan Bone's draft rights and two later second-round selections whose historical draft slots became associated with Theo Maledon in 2020 and Colby Jones in 2023. The choice allowed Atlanta to concentrate its resources on one identifiable center prospect, while Philadelphia preferred several chances and tradable future assets. The listed draft names represent the lineage of each choice, not proof that all three ever signed a 76ers NBA contract. Both teams were making decisions about developmental timing rather than swapping veterans.

Fernando Became a Genuine Hawks Reserve

Fernando played NBA games for Atlanta during the following seasons and had a chance to develop behind more established frontcourt options. His contribution was limited compared with the team's key scorers and rim protectors, but it was real receiving-team playing time. He did not become the franchise's long-term centerpiece solely through this move, and his subsequent seasons elsewhere must be separated from the trade. Atlanta's incoming asset was a player who could be tested in an NBA rotation rather than merely stored in a draft ledger. That deserves a stronger evaluation than assuming Fernando contributed nothing.

Philadelphia Retained Multiple Paths to Future Value

The 76ers held a package including Jordan Bone's rights and two future second-round opportunities. Bone's path later led through other NBA organizations, while Maledon became associated with Oklahoma City and Jones with Sacramento after further transactions. Philadelphia could use the selections as trade components or developmental choices, but those external NBA games weren't 76ers production. The asset package was still genuine compensation: three chances or transactions provided more flexibility than a single second-round prospect. Counting all subsequent careers as Philadelphia players would be as misleading as dismissing the draft options entirely because the team later moved them.

Multiple Rights Versus an Actual Atlanta Contributor

Philadelphia acquired broader draft flexibility and retained several opportunities to move or use secondary assets, which supports the winning direction. Atlanta nevertheless received a center who made actual NBA appearances and shouldn't be given a failing grade. A fair comparison looks beyond the raw total of three incoming names on the 76ers side, because each choice carried specific later conveyance paths. The Hawks received immediate access to an identifiable roster prospect, while the Sixers pursued a collection of smaller assets over time. Neither outcome resembles a franchise-changing star trade, and the grades should stay in a moderate range.

Hill played 48 Memphis games in 2019-20 and averaged 5.7 points with defensive wing minutes before another trade. Memphis waived Plumlee before he played a regular-season game. memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
The Hawks and Grizzlies Exchanged Expiring Forward Contracts

Memphis moved Chandler Parsons to Atlanta in a July 2019 transaction, taking Solomon Hill and Miles Plumlee in return. The trade was recorded in the team ledgers on July 8, while some draft and roster chronologies place negotiations a day earlier. Both organizations were moving veterans with sizable contracts rather than swapping emerging stars. Memphis sought players who might actually provide wing or interior depth during its young rebuilding season. Atlanta accepted an opportunity to examine Parsons, whose Grizzlies tenure had been limited by recurring injuries.

Hill Supplied Forty-Eight Regular-Season Games for Memphis

Hill became the meaningful basketball return for Memphis. In the first portion of 2019-20 he appeared in 48 regular-season games, starting three, and averaged 5.7 points while playing 18.8 minutes per night. His outside shooting and defensive coverage provided veteran support around a young rotation. The Grizzlies later included Hill in a different multi-team deadline transaction, so his games after leaving Memphis belong to another franchise. The club also acquired Plumlee in the July deal, but waived him in October before he could play a regular-season Memphis game.

Parsons' Atlanta Career Lasted Five Brief Appearances

Parsons remained an NBA player on Atlanta's books during the 2019-20 season, but his availability was severely limited. He appeared in five Hawks games without a start, logging only 54 total minutes and averaging 2.8 points. His injury history and previous productive Houston and Dallas seasons offered a reason Atlanta might have been interested in a low-risk roster option. Those earlier accomplishments weren't transferred to the Hawks. With only five short outings, Atlanta received virtually no on-court production from the forward acquired in exchange for two veterans.

A Useful Wing Stint Beat a Little-Used Former Scorer

Neither franchise landed a long-term star, and the deal shouldn't be celebrated as a decisive rebuilding achievement. But Memphis did get forty-eight games of wing depth and could use Hill within a later separate roster move. Atlanta got an injured veteran who played only a handful of minutes. The value gap is larger than the inherited comparison suggested for the Hawks, although the Grizzlies' original B+ is also strong for a player they kept only part of one season. An adjusted Memphis win credits the real production while acknowledging that Plumlee contributed no NBA games.

Final Verdict

Grizzlies Win. Memphis earns B for Solomon Hill's 48 regular-season games and 5.7 points per game, while Miles Plumlee was waived before appearing. Atlanta receives D+ because Chandler Parsons played only five Hawks games and 54 minutes. The club-specific record supports a clear Memphis edge without counting other teams' later player production.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Acquired a Center and a Distant Second

The Hawks acquired Damian Jones and a 2026 second-round pick from Golden State on July 8, 2019, sending Omari Spellman to the Warriors. Jones had won championship rings as part of Golden State's earlier roster, but Atlanta was interested in his ability to fill minutes at center rather than taking credit for those rings. Spellman, a recent first-rounder, offered Golden State a young big who could stretch the floor. The additional future second gave Atlanta more value than a direct player swap on paper, although the pick's eventual conveyance and use must be tracked separately from the players.

Jones Became a Regular Hawks Rotation Option

Jones appeared in 55 Atlanta games during the 2019-20 season, averaging 5.6 points and 3.7 rebounds. He wasn't a foundational center, but he provided genuine size and finishing around the basket for a rebuilding club. That season is the appropriate window for measuring the player Atlanta received: his earlier Warriors games and championship history are background, not part of the Hawks' direct on-court return. The team could try him alongside younger guards and assess whether his athletic tools justified a longer commitment. Even without a breakout, 55 appearances produced tangible short-term utility.

Spellman Played for Golden State During a Difficult Year

Golden State also received real on-court minutes from its incoming player. Spellman appeared across the injury-hit 2019-20 Warriors campaign and showed some ability to hit outside shots from a frontcourt position. His time there ended in another transaction, so he wasn't an enduring piece of the team as its established stars returned. The contrast with Jones isn't a win-by-default argument: both teams used their acquired players. Atlanta's extra second-round obligation tipped the package toward greater overall flexibility, while the Warriors mainly received a brief developmental audition for Spellman.

The Second-Round Asset Breaks a Modest Player Comparison

This is a smaller deal whose player returns were measured in reserve minutes rather than postseason star power. Jones gave Atlanta solid but replaceable center depth; Spellman likewise contributed in Golden State without turning into a lasting rotation answer. The Hawks received an additional 2026 pick that might be used in later draft or trade planning. Its value shouldn't be inflated by an unverified future outcome. Atlanta's slight edge reflects a comparable short-term player plus an extra asset, not an assertion that either newcomer permanently changed the receiving club's competitive fortunes.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta receives B- for Damian Jones's 55 appearances and a 2026 second-round pick, giving it both usable center minutes and another asset. Golden State earns C+ because Omari Spellman played during 2019-20 but did not become a lasting Warriors frontcourt option. Both teams got real short-term NBA contributions, with the added selection tilting the package toward the Hawks.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Traded Two Veteran Contracts and Cash

In early July 2019, Golden State moved guards Shabazz Napier and Treveon Graham, along with cash, to Minnesota in exchange for the NBA draft rights to overseas forward Lior Eliyahu. The transaction followed a complicated Warriors offseason with salary and roster needs around their reconfigured backcourt. Minnesota wanted additional veterans who could play immediately, while Golden State preferred the room and administrative flexibility created by moving two contracts. Eliyahu's rights were held as an asset, not acquired as an active NBA starter or as a prospect newly drafted in 2019.

Napier Gave Minnesota a Usable Guard

Napier played meaningful backcourt minutes for Minnesota during the 2019-20 season, providing playmaking and a secondary scoring option. He was not a long-term franchise answer, but the Timberwolves had tangible use for an NBA-experienced guard at a time when their roster was changing. Graham also supplied wing defense and reserve opportunities before being moved again in another transaction. The cash consideration brought a financial benefit independent of either player's on-court role. Minnesota's direct post-trade games are the proper return; the players' previous Portland, Brooklyn and Charlotte seasons aren't newly created Timberwolves contributions.

Eliyahu's Rights Didn't Mean Warriors NBA Minutes

Golden State received the rights to a player who had established a professional career internationally rather than a contract guaranteed to bring him to the NBA. Eliyahu did not become an identifiable Warriors rotation regular as a result of the exchange. The trade was still useful for roster accounting and the future possibility of assigning or holding international draft rights, but those possibilities should not be treated as actual NBA points or games. Golden State's subsequent return to championship contention was driven by several other personnel and health developments rather than directly by Eliyahu's acquisition.

One Season of Guards Outweighed Dormant Rights

The Timberwolves obtained real guard and wing options plus money, while Golden State collected an overseas-rights asset and freedom to adjust its salary structure. That difference makes Minnesota the more productive receiving team. It doesn't warrant attributing every Napier or Graham NBA season to Minnesota or assuming the Warriors were obligated to bring Eliyahu into camp. A moderate Minnesota-winning grade recognizes that both newcomers were temporary, even if their contribution was clearer than the rights Golden State held. The original transaction was chiefly about two teams valuing immediate depth against financial flexibility.

Final Verdict

Wolves Win. Minnesota earns B+ for Shabazz Napier's usable 2019-20 guard minutes, Treveon Graham's short-term wing service and cash. Golden State receives C for international rights to Lior Eliyahu and salary flexibility, not a guaranteed NBA player. Neither receiving team is awarded games that occurred before the agreement or through later independent deals.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers acquired Paul George to secure Kawhi Leonard and created a contender, but Oklahoma City received Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Danilo Gallinari, five first-round picks and two swaps that became a championship foundation.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis: George produced meaningful value in Los Angeles, including All-NBA play and the franchise's first Western Conference finals appearance. Oklahoma City's return nevertheless became overwhelming. Gilgeous-Alexander developed into a two-time MVP, 2025 Finals MVP and championship centerpiece, while the Clippers' 2022 first-round pick became Jalen Williams and the remaining draft control supplied additional flexibility. The Clippers' strategy was coherent because Leonard's commitment was tied to acquiring George, but the realized outcomes now create a decisive gap. Oklahoma City earns an A-plus, Los Angeles a C-plus, and the explicit verdict is Thunder Win.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Teague Returned to the Hawks in a Three-Player Swap

On January 16, 2020, Atlanta acquired Jeff Teague and Treveon Graham from Minnesota for wing Allen Crabbe. Teague had previously played several seasons for the Hawks, including a long stretch as their primary point guard, so the trade was a homecoming rather than a debut. Atlanta needed another ball handler alongside its young offensive core, while Minnesota could use a different perimeter player and adjust its guard rotation. This was a direct exchange of three established NBA contracts; the parties did not add a future first-round selection or an overseas prospect.

Atlanta Received a Familiar Point Guard

Teague supplied an experienced point guard presence for the Hawks during the remainder of 2019-20. He could run an offense when Trae Young sat and help newer teammates understand routine NBA possessions. Graham added defensive and wing depth but did not become a lasting Atlanta regular. The club’s benefit was therefore limited yet real. Teague’s earlier All-Star season in Atlanta belonged to his original Hawks stint and must not be added to the return from January 2020. The pandemic-shortened season also restricts how much accumulated playing time any receiving team could generate.

Minnesota Tried a Different Wing Option

The Timberwolves took Allen Crabbe, a shooter who had moved through several teams before the exchange, in hopes of getting more perimeter spacing. He did not become a durable Minnesota piece, and his direct Timberwolves service proved short. Minnesota’s broader roster overhaul continued through other deals that season, but those later moves had their own assets and cannot automatically be credited to acquiring Crabbe. The team did not receive a new draft selection in this swap, so a review must focus on the guard and wing minutes the actual incoming players supplied rather than imagined draft flexibility.

The Shortened Season Favors Atlanta Slightly

Neither team landed a cornerstone, and the disrupted 2019-20 schedule makes a large winning margin inappropriate. Atlanta obtained a familiar guard who could play a useful reserve role during the rest of the season, whereas Minnesota failed to build a long-term plan around Crabbe. Graham’s limited involvement reduces Atlanta’s advantage without erasing it. The old slight Minnesota edge seems to place too much weight on acquiring a different shooter and not enough on what the Hawks’ returning guard actually did. A modest Hawks win better reflects receiving-team service and realistic roster expectations.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta receives B- for Jeff Teague’s usable point-guard minutes after his return and the added option of Treveon Graham. Minnesota gets C because Allen Crabbe supplied only a brief wing opportunity and no long-term core contribution. Teague’s earlier Atlanta All-Star years and later Minnesota roster trades are not direct additional value from the January 2020 exchange.
