Atlanta found the best long-term fit, Minnesota extracted meaningful young-player value, Houston gained a useful specialist and later assets, and Denver chose a conservative path that produced the least upside.
analysis: Atlanta received the cleanest long-term basketball return. Capela became its starting center for five seasons, supplied elite rebounding and vertical spacing, and was part of the 2021 team that reached the Eastern Conference finals. The Hawks paid a first-round pick and secondary draft value rather than a core young player, then extracted multiple seasons of starting production. Houston's bet worked tactically for a short window. Covington fit the switch-heavy scheme and was useful in the 2020 postseason. More importantly, Houston preserved value when it later moved Covington to Portland for draft capital. The Rockets still surrendered Capela and a first to execute a strategy that lasted only months, so the direct basketball return was narrower than Atlanta's. Covington's later trade to Portland is relevant because Houston converted him back into additional assets rather than losing him for nothing. Minnesota also preserved value through Beasley and Vanderbilt, although later blockbuster transactions required other major pieces and should not be credited wholesale to this deal. Atlanta's chain was simpler: Capela himself supplied the value over a long tenure.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Obtained a Guard and Cash From the Clippers

Atlanta acquired Derrick Walton Jr. and about $1.3 million in cash consideration from the Los Angeles Clippers at the February 6, 2020 deadline. The Clippers received a 2022 second-round selection protected through No. 55. The Hawks were moving through a broader roster reset and could evaluate a young guard while collecting financial compensation. Los Angeles wanted a smaller contract off its books as its veteran-heavy roster pursued the postseason. The incoming pick was conditional, not a guaranteed future second-round selection.

Walton Was a Short-Term Addition, Not a Hawks Cornerstone

Walton's NBA opportunity with Atlanta was brief rather than the beginning of a long stretch as the Hawks' lead point guard. The club had Trae Young carrying its offensive workload and other guards seeking rotation opportunities, which limited what the new contract could reasonably provide. His earlier Clippers and Miami appearances were not newly generated Hawks games. For Atlanta, the immediate combination of roster flexibility and the cash payment was the central value. Neither the existing player nor cash can be mistaken for a major first-round prospect.

The Clippers' Conditional Pick Did Not Convey

The second-round choice Atlanta owed was protected through the fifty-fifth position in 2022. The condition was not met, and the choice did not convey to the Clippers. Los Angeles therefore did not use this trade to draft a player or add a usable pick for another acquisition. The franchise still achieved a modest short-term payroll and roster adjustment, which has value, but the missing selection cannot be graded as successful draft development. Any later Clippers guard production originated from other contracts and moves rather than from Walton's departure.

Cash and Flexibility Make This a Limited Atlanta Advantage

The Hawks secured cash while taking a look at Walton, whereas the Clippers obtained only salary-management benefit because the conditional pick expired. Neither side received an NBA star, and a dramatic judgment would exaggerate a low-profile deadline move. Atlanta's return was more concrete financially, supporting the historical Hawks-winning direction. The revised Clippers grade avoids treating payroll relief as entirely worthless, while excluding a second-round prospect that was never delivered. Distinguishing the actual pick protection from an ordinary future second is essential to an accurate record.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B- for securing Derrick Walton Jr. and cash in the deadline exchange. Los Angeles gets C- for payroll flexibility; its protected 2022 second-round pick never conveyed, so there was no Clippers draft player from this agreement. Walton's previous NBA seasons and later unrelated roster transactions aren't counted as Atlanta or Clippers returns.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Reacquired Dedmon and Two Second-Round Picks

On February 6, 2020, the Hawks sent Alex Len and Jabari Parker to Sacramento for Dewayne Dedmon and two future second-round selections. Dedmon had been a productive Atlanta center in 2017-19 but had struggled to settle into the Kings' frontcourt rotation that season. The Hawks wanted another look at a familiar defensive big and were willing to take on the associated contract. Sacramento obtained two veterans who could join its rotation, while Atlanta also gathered draft opportunities from Houston's 2020 second-round right and Miami's 2021 second-round right.

Dedmon's Return Was Shorter Than His First Hawks Tenure

Dedmon could screen, rebound and defend in ways that suited Atlanta's young perimeter roster. His return after the February trade lasted only a short portion of the suspended 2019-20 season, however, and he was moved again later in the year. The club did not get to count his earlier two full Hawks seasons as fresh production from the reacquisition. This was a limited immediate center experiment, but the two second-round picks made it much more than a one-for-two veteran swap. Their later draft outcomes offered independent paths to find help.

Sacramento Received Len and Parker for Depth

Len gave Sacramento another traditional center with size and rim protection, while Parker arrived as a forward who had shown scoring ability earlier in his career. Neither became the long-term reason for the franchise to make this deal. Parker's Kings availability was especially limited, reducing the club's direct receiving-team basketball benefit. The pair also didn't yield a lasting developmental asset comparable to the two choices Atlanta collected. The Kings' motivation to move Dedmon's remaining contract and revise their rotation explains their willingness to accept two veterans for one.

The Picks Made the Atlanta Package More Interesting

The 2020 second-rounder became No. 50 Skylar Mays, and the 2021 selection became No. 48 Sharife Cooper. Neither selection turned into an unquestioned Hawks star, so the package shouldn't be evaluated as if both were successful first-round talents. Still, Atlanta acquired two concrete draft opportunities along with a familiar center in exchange for players it had decided to move. Sacramento got serviceable but temporary veterans. The Hawks' multiple ways to obtain a player contribution or another transaction asset give them the stronger overall return.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B+ for the combination of Dewayne Dedmon's short return and two draft selections, ultimately used on Skylar Mays and Sharife Cooper. Sacramento receives C+ for Alex Len and Jabari Parker, whose Kings impact was limited. The additional picks, rather than an invented long second Dedmon tenure, provide the central advantage for Atlanta.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
The Warriors Sold Two Veterans for Three Second-Round Assets

Golden State sent guards Alec Burks and Glenn Robinson III to Philadelphia at the February 6, 2020 deadline in exchange for three future second-round selections. The move came during a difficult Warriors season without the availability of their familiar championship backcourt, making later draft opportunities more valuable than retaining two expiring veteran contributors. Philadelphia wanted capable perimeter depth while preparing for the postseason. The draft ledger subsequently links the three selections to No. 48 Nico Mannion in 2020, No. 55 Aaron Wiggins in 2021 and No. 51 Tyrese Martin in 2022. Those eventual names represent draft histories, not three guaranteed Warriors roster players.

Philadelphia Received Actual Playable Perimeter Depth

Burks supplied scoring and guard creation to the 76ers after the trade, while Robinson offered additional size and shooting on the wing. Their Philadelphia work extended through the unusual, pandemic-interrupted 2019-20 season and the playoff restart in the Orlando bubble. Neither arrival turned into a long-term franchise cornerstone, but both players were real veteran options for a club already relying on Joel Embiid and Ben Simmons. That immediate utility deserves a fair grade. Assigning Burks's later production with other organizations to Philadelphia, however, would make the transaction seem more durable than it was.

Not Every Draft Name Became a Warriors Contributor

Golden State's first incoming selection became Mannion, who played NBA games for the Warriors before continuing his professional career overseas. The later selections had additional transaction histories: Wiggins became an Oklahoma City player, and Martin was selected by Atlanta, rather than providing Golden State with corresponding multiseason rotations. Those later draftees illustrate why future choices must be tracked through each conveyance and separate deal. A list of three names printed beside the original trade doesn't establish that the Warriors employed all three. The real return combined Mannion's limited direct playing time with the ability to move later draft capital.

Long-Term Flexibility Gives Golden State the Narrower Advantage

Philadelphia obtained a short-term shooting and backcourt package that helped complete its roster, while Golden State converted veteran contracts into several opportunities across subsequent drafts. The latter produced some on-court value and draft maneuverability, but not three established stars. A stronger grade for the Warriors is defensible because the team recouped assets during a rebuilding season and avoided making a long commitment to departing veterans. The 76ers still got useful contributors in the period they needed them. Neither club's complete championship history can be explained through one 2020 deadline exchange.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State earns B+ for three transferable second-round assets, including the No. 48 right that became Nico Mannion, but the later Aaron Wiggins and Tyrese Martin draft identities weren't automatically Warriors NBA players. Philadelphia receives B- for actual Alec Burks and Glenn Robinson III rotation minutes after the deadline. Both teams gained usable value, and downstream transactions are evaluated separately.

analysis:
The Warriors Sold Two Veterans for Three Second-Round Assets

Golden State sent guards Alec Burks and Glenn Robinson III to Philadelphia at the February 6, 2020 deadline in exchange for three future second-round selections. The move came during a difficult Warriors season without the availability of their familiar championship backcourt, making later draft opportunities more valuable than retaining two expiring veteran contributors. Philadelphia wanted capable perimeter depth while preparing for the postseason. The draft ledger subsequently links the three selections to No. 48 Nico Mannion in 2020, No. 55 Aaron Wiggins in 2021 and No. 51 Tyrese Martin in 2022. Those eventual names represent draft histories, not three guaranteed Warriors roster players.

Philadelphia Received Actual Playable Perimeter Depth

Burks supplied scoring and guard creation to the 76ers after the trade, while Robinson offered additional size and shooting on the wing. Their Philadelphia work extended through the unusual, pandemic-interrupted 2019-20 season and the playoff restart in the Orlando bubble. Neither arrival turned into a long-term franchise cornerstone, but both players were real veteran options for a club already relying on Joel Embiid and Ben Simmons. That immediate utility deserves a fair grade. Assigning Burks's later production with other organizations to Philadelphia, however, would make the transaction seem more durable than it was.

Not Every Draft Name Became a Warriors Contributor

Golden State's first incoming selection became Mannion, who played NBA games for the Warriors before continuing his professional career overseas. The later selections had additional transaction histories: Wiggins became an Oklahoma City player, and Martin was selected by Atlanta, rather than providing Golden State with corresponding multiseason rotations. Those later draftees illustrate why future choices must be tracked through each conveyance and separate deal. A list of three names printed beside the original trade doesn't establish that the Warriors employed all three. The real return combined Mannion's limited direct playing time with the ability to move later draft capital.

Long-Term Flexibility Gives Golden State the Narrower Advantage

Philadelphia obtained a short-term shooting and backcourt package that helped complete its roster, while Golden State converted veteran contracts into several opportunities across subsequent drafts. The latter produced some on-court value and draft maneuverability, but not three established stars. A stronger grade for the Warriors is defensible because the team recouped assets during a rebuilding season and avoided making a long commitment to departing veterans. The 76ers still got useful contributors in the period they needed them. Neither club's complete championship history can be explained through one 2020 deadline exchange.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State earns B+ for three transferable second-round assets, including the No. 48 right that became Nico Mannion, but the later Aaron Wiggins and Tyrese Martin draft identities weren't automatically Warriors NBA players. Philadelphia receives B- for actual Alec Burks and Glenn Robinson III rotation minutes after the deadline. Both teams gained usable value, and downstream transactions are evaluated separately.

new-york-knicks.summary: The Knicks sent Marcus Morris to the Clippers in February 2020 and took Moe Harkless plus draft-rights compensation in a three-team exchange. Washington received Jerome Robinson from Los Angeles for Isaiah Thomas and rights to Yusuf Sanon; the Clippers added Thomas alongside Morris. The inherited Knicks Win assigns New York A, the Clippers B and Washington C.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
New York Converted Morris Into Several Assets

The Knicks moved Marcus Morris to the Los Angeles Clippers in February 2020 and received Moe Harkless, the rights to Yusuf Sanon and future draft considerations. Washington also played a basketball role: the Wizards acquired Jerome Robinson from the Clippers while sending Isaiah Thomas and Sanon's rights into the broader exchange. The Clippers obtained Morris and Thomas. New York prioritized a package of draft flexibility, the Clippers sought an immediate playoff wing, and Washington decided to evaluate a young guard.

The Picks Followed Separate Draft-Rights Paths

New York's package included a 2020 first-round right associated with No. 27 Udoka Azubuike and a 2021 second-round right associated with No. 32 Jeremiah Robinson-Earl. The first-round swap option involving the Clippers in 2021 was protected and wasn't exercised. Those draft identities do not mean both players ultimately spent their NBA careers with the Knicks. Their rights required additional moves, while the selections themselves provided transactional flexibility. Harkless was another veteran wing option in the immediate return.

The Clippers Added a Proven Two-Way Forward

Morris had already shown physical wing defense and perimeter scoring that suited Los Angeles's contending roster. The Clippers also received Isaiah Thomas from Washington, although they did not retain him as a major rotation contributor. Washington obtained Jerome Robinson, a former lottery guard whose developmental potential appealed to its front office. The Wizards' receipt is distinct from the Knicks' picks and Harkless return; ignoring Robinson would make the transaction look like a two-team exchange and incorrectly leave Washington with no incoming asset.

New York's Grade Emphasized Asset Flexibility

The inherited Knicks A compared with Clippers B credits the draft options and roster flexibility New York acquired. Washington's C recognizes a genuine opportunity to evaluate Jerome Robinson in its backcourt. The unexercised 2021 first-round swap should not be counted as a completed new Knicks draft choice, and the eventual players tied to other selections may have moved again. The trade was a multi-club redistribution of a veteran wing, prospect guard, contracts and several rights, not merely a Morris-for-Harkless swap.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win. New York earns A for Moe Harkless, Yusuf Sanon's rights, draft picks and added flexibility after dealing Marcus Morris. Los Angeles gets B for Morris's immediate wing play plus Isaiah Thomas's contract. Washington receives C for acquiring young guard Jerome Robinson, who came from the Clippers for Thomas and Sanon's rights. The protected 2021 pick swap went unexercised.

orlando-magic.summary: Orlando acquired defensive wing James Ennis III from Philadelphia on February 6, 2020, for a 2020 second-round pick owed originally by the Lakers. Ennis helped the Magic immediately and returned in 2020-21. Philadelphia used the selection at No. 58 on Paul Reed, who grew into a regular reserve center and appeared in more than 200 Sixers games through 2023-24. 76ers Win, Philadelphia A- and Orlando B; both teams received real basketball value.
orlando-magic.analysis:
Orlando Purchased Wing Help at the 2020 Trade Deadline

On February 6, 2020, the Magic sent a second-round draft selection to Philadelphia for James Ennis III. Orlando's official team announcement identified the outgoing choice as a 2020 second-rounder originally owed by the Los Angeles Lakers. At the time, the Magic wanted someone with defensive length and enough perimeter shooting to support a roster whose scoring had lagged behind the league average. Ennis was a veteran who had appeared in 49 games for the 76ers earlier that season. The arrangement was a straightforward veteran-for-pick swap, not a multi-player salary dump.

Ennis Helped Orlando Immediately and Returned the Next Season

Ennis joined Orlando's wing rotation during the last stretch of the 2019-20 schedule, including the interrupted season's restart, and was available for its postseason series. He was neither the main scorer nor a franchise centerpiece, but provided the toughness, athleticism and floor spacing cited by the Magic's front office when it made the deal. Ennis also played for Orlando in 2020-21, extending the return beyond a one-month rental. His 49 Philadelphia games before February belong to the Sixers, while the games he played after joining Orlando are the Magic's proper acquired-team contribution.

Philadelphia Turned the Incoming Selection Into Paul Reed

The 76ers used the acquired 2020 second-round pick at No. 58 to select Paul Reed, a DePaul forward-center. Reed began as an end-of-bench option, appearing 26 times in 2020-21 and 38 times in 2021-22. His role grew to 69 games in 2022-23 and 82 games in 2023-24, totaling 215 Philadelphia regular-season appearances over those four seasons. He also supplied playoff frontcourt minutes as a reserve behind Joel Embiid. This is the documented pick's basketball payoff, not an unrelated draft choice credited to the same year.

The Pick's Long-Term Return Edged Orlando's Short-Term Defense

Orlando achieved a reasonable immediate objective by adding a veteran wing for a playoff push, and Ennis stayed available in its rotation beyond that season. Philadelphia, however, received an inexpensive center whose NBA usefulness expanded for several years after the trade. Reed's growth from a late second-round selection into a regular defensive and rebounding reserve gave the Sixers a more enduring outcome. The deal isn't a failure for Orlando because the Magic actually used Ennis; it is a Philadelphia win because the transferred selection became a player the club employed through multiple playoff cycles.

Final Verdict

76ers Win. Philadelphia earns A- for the No. 58 pick that became Paul Reed, who played 215 regular-season games over four Sixers seasons and developed into an active playoff reserve. Orlando gets B for Ennis's immediate wing minutes and additional work in 2020-21. Philadelphia secured the more durable basketball result, while Orlando did receive meaningful short-term help.

oklahoma-city-thunder.summary: Phoenix acquired Chris Paul and Abdel Nader for Ricky Rubio, Kelly Oubre Jr., Ty Jerome, Jalen Lecque and a protected first-round pick, then reached the 2021 NBA Finals in Paul's first season.
oklahoma-city-thunder.analysis: Phoenix received the superior realized outcome because Chris Paul immediately organized a young core, elevated Devin Booker and Deandre Ayton, and helped end the franchise's 28-year Finals drought. Oklahoma City also executed a strong rebuilding strategy: it had restored Paul's market value during one successful season, then converted him into younger players, movable contracts and another first-round pick. Both sides deserve high grades, but an A-plus for Phoenix and an A-minus for Oklahoma City require a narrow separation. The Finals run and Paul's direct competitive impact support Slight Suns Edge rather than an Even Trade verdict.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Obtained an Early Second-Round Center

Los Angeles acquired the draft rights to Daniel Oturu, taken thirty-third in 2020, from Minnesota on November 18. The Timberwolves collected overseas center Mathias Lessort's NBA rights and a future second-round selection eventually associated with the thirty-first position in the 2023 draft. Both clubs were managing young interior prospects rather than swapping established rotation centers. The Clippers wanted an inexpensive player with college rebounding credentials and a path to developmental NBA minutes. Minnesota preferred more flexible rights spread across two players and different draft years, giving itself further roster-building options without spending a first-round selection.

Oturu's Clippers Career Was Brief

Oturu appeared in NBA games for the Clippers during his rookie season, but was a reserve behind an established group of frontcourt veterans. His playing time did not establish him as an everyday starting center or a key contributor to the team's 2021 postseason. The immediate return was the chance to evaluate a young big and obtain limited NBA minutes. His later movements to other organizations came through separate roster decisions and do not increase what Los Angeles received from Minnesota. Nor do Oturu's strong performances at the University of Minnesota count as Clippers NBA statistics after the draft-night exchange.

Minnesota Acquired Separate International and Draft Options

Lessort's NBA draft rights belonged to Minnesota after the trade, but his established career overseas should not be mistaken for Timberwolves games. The future second eventually entered a draft-rights path associated with James Nnaji at No. 31 in 2023. That player's later destination and playing record must be traced through subsequent transactions rather than treated as direct Minnesota NBA production. The incoming pair of rights offered different kinds of optionality, including the ability to trade the assets. This makes Minnesota's benefit more about retained prospect flexibility than about a rotation player immediately joining the Timberwolves in 2020.

Future Assets Give Minnesota a Small Edge

The original Minnesota-winning result is sensible when measured by what each team obtained and how long those assets could remain useful. Oturu's direct Clippers tenure was short, while Minnesota gained two possible opportunities across different development paths. Still, neither incoming Wolves right guaranteed an NBA starter, and their eventual draft identities shouldn't be counted as finished Timberwolves careers. Los Angeles deserves more than a failing grade because it acquired and briefly used an actual NBA player. A narrower Minnesota edge gives realistic weight to both the brief on-court return and the uncertainty inherent in future draft rights.

Final Verdict

Wolves Win, narrowly. Minnesota receives B- for the rights to Mathias Lessort and a future second-round selection ultimately associated with No. 31 James Nnaji. Los Angeles earns C+ after Daniel Oturu, selected thirty-third in 2020, supplied only brief reserve NBA minutes. Later Nnaji roster destinations and Lessort's overseas career are not counted as Timberwolves NBA games.

milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee Purchased Rights to the Forty-Fifth Pick

At the November 18, 2020 draft, Milwaukee acquired the No. 45 selection that became forward Jordan Nwora from Orlando. The Magic received two future second-round rights in return, including a choice later identified as 2022 No. 35 Max Christie and another later tied to a 2026 second-round position. This was a transaction in unsigned draft rights rather than a swap of established NBA player contracts. Milwaukee was looking for an inexpensive perimeter forward who could develop behind a contending veteran core, while Orlando chose to spread the value of one mid-second-round selection over later drafts.

Nwora Played for a Championship Bucks Team

Nwora joined the Bucks as a rookie and supplied reserve wing opportunities while Milwaukee won the 2021 NBA championship. His contributions were not equivalent to those of Giannis Antetokounmpo or Khris Middleton, and he did not become the decisive Finals scorer. Nonetheless, he appeared for an eventual championship organization and continued to play NBA minutes for Milwaukee in subsequent seasons. Those are direct receiving-team benefits from an inexpensive draft choice. Nwora's later NBA opportunities after leaving Milwaukee must not be added to his Bucks production, and he was not acquired from Orlando as a veteran with an existing NBA record.

Orlando Secured Two Distinct Future Selection Assets

The Magic's benefit was draft flexibility rather than an immediate reserve player. One future choice later entered the 2022 No. 35 rights chain associated with Christie, while the other became a later 2026 second-round slot. Orlando could keep or exchange either asset under the relevant conveyance terms; that did not mean Christie necessarily played NBA games for the Magic. The later draft identities need to follow the true recipient clubs after any additional trades. Counting NBA performances elsewhere as Orlando production would overstate what the original agreement itself delivered, but dismissing two future choices as useless would also be unreasonable.

A Useful Bucks Reserve Against Two Chances for Orlando

Milwaukee succeeded in selecting a forward who reached its roster during a title-winning period. Orlando gained two genuine draft opportunities and could decide separately how to realize their value over time. The Magic's flexibility earns a small retrospective edge over the Bucks' modest individual playing contribution, although it isn't a runaway win. A fair assessment distinguishes Nwora's real Bucks minutes from the championships won by the team's much larger core and from later players associated with Orlando's traded selections. The draft-rights exchange was a developmental investment on both sides rather than a roster-defining transaction.

Final Verdict

Magic Win, narrowly. Orlando earns B+ for obtaining two future second-round choices in exchange for the rights to No. 45 Jordan Nwora, including a selection later associated with Max Christie. Milwaukee receives B because Nwora actually played reserve minutes for its 2021 championship team. Draft assets later moved through other deals mustn't be credited as Orlando NBA playing seasons.

perspectives.summary: A November 2020 three-team draft-week transaction distributed Landry Shamet, Bruce Brown and Reggie Perry's rights to Brooklyn; Saddiq Bey's rights and other assets to Detroit; and Luke Kennard and additional rights to the Clippers. Brown became an important Nets role player, while Bey developed with the Pistons. The inherited slight Nets edge grades Brooklyn A- and both Detroit and Los Angeles B+.
perspectives.analysis:
Brooklyn Collected Multiple Perimeter Contributors

The Nets acquired Landry Shamet, Bruce Brown and rights to Reggie Perry during a November 2020 three-team deal involving Detroit and the Los Angeles Clippers. Brooklyn was constructing a contender around high-usage stars and needed wings capable of filling smaller offensive roles. Shamet offered outside shooting, while Brown brought energetic defense, rebounding and movement without the ball. Perry's rights were a separate prospect opportunity. The multiple incoming players allowed the Nets to address immediate lineup needs and retain developmental flexibility.

Detroit's Package Was Built Around Bey and More

The Pistons acquired Dzanan Musa, Rodney McGruder, the rights to Saddiq Bey and Jaylen Hands, plus future draft consideration linked to No. 37 J.T. Thor in 2021. Bey became an identifiable Detroit scoring forward, giving that part of the return real receiving-team production. The other players and selections had less uniformly direct impact, and subsequent rights movements need to be distinguished from Detroit playing time. The organization was trying to strengthen its developing roster rather than maximize the immediate output of one veteran.

The Clippers Obtained Kennard and Other Options

Los Angeles added Luke Kennard, an accomplished perimeter shooter, along with rights involving Jay Scrubb and later second-round assets. Justin Patton was another part of the package. Kennard supplied useful shooting for the Clippers, but not every accompanying asset evolved into a lasting rotation contributor. His style offered a clear role beside the team's more prominent wing scorers. The incoming pick considerations remained tradable rather than automatically producing future Clippers players without further decisions.

The Nets' Versatile Pair Explains Their Lead

The inherited Brooklyn A- recognizes that Brown and Shamet supplied real supporting value in the Nets' lineup. Detroit and the Clippers each receive B+ for productive elements such as Bey and Kennard. The margin is modest because all three clubs obtained an identifiable useful player, while additional rights carried uncertain outcomes. The trade's three-sided structure matters: reducing it to only a Brooklyn-Detroit exchange would overlook the Clippers' receiving-player benefit and the complications of the accompanying draft rights.

Final Verdict

Slight Nets Edge. Brooklyn earns A- for Bruce Brown's versatile role and Landry Shamet's shooting, with Reggie Perry's rights as another option. Detroit gets B+ for a package featuring Saddiq Bey and additional assets, while the Clippers also receive B+ for Luke Kennard and draft rights. All three teams realized useful returns, but the Nets' combined supporting players justify their narrow inherited lead.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Moved Poirier During an Offseason Reshuffle

The Celtics sent Vincent Poirier and cash to Oklahoma City in November 2020 in exchange for a conditional 2021 second-round pick. Poirier had not become a regular Boston center, and the club was revising its roster after the 2019-20 season. Oklahoma City accepted the contract and financial component as it engaged in broader player and draft-asset transactions. The trade did not include an established Thunder scorer heading to Boston, and the incoming draft right was subject to conditions.

Poirier Did Not Establish a Thunder Playing Role

Poirier's stay with Oklahoma City was transitional, and he did not create a sustained regular-season rotation contribution for the Thunder. His earlier Celtics appearances are not direct Oklahoma City return. The receiving club could still use the contract in its sequence of transactions, but a player's movement through a roster does not mean that he supplied basketball value on the court. The practical benefit came from contractual maneuvering and cash rather than an established center.

The Conditional 2021 Choice Failed to Convey

Boston's future second-round right was never exercised, preventing the club from selecting a player through this particular transaction. That distinction matters when comparing teams' results: the Celtics can't claim the development of an unrelated 2021 draftee simply because a conditional pick was listed in the original terms. The more immediate Boston payoff was the reduction of roster obligations and creation of flexibility for other decisions, while the Thunder's benefits involved cash and the ability to move the acquired contract.

Neither Team Acquired a Major Player Return

Oklahoma City received financial compensation and a center it could redirect; Boston parted with a reserve who lacked an established role and held an unexercised conditional pick. Neither organization gained an important new performer directly from the deal. The inherited small Boston advantage credits its ability to manage roster obligations with little outgoing playing cost, while recognizing the Thunder's different financial objectives. The move should be evaluated as a modest administrative trade rather than as a contest involving future stars.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston gets B- for moving Vincent Poirier and gaining roster flexibility, though the conditional 2021 second-round selection never conveyed. Oklahoma City receives C+ for Poirier's contract and cash without a substantial Thunder playing stint. The outcome involved financial and roster mechanics rather than meaningful direct on-court production.

los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
Los Angeles Bought a Sixth-Man Guard After Its Title

The Lakers acquired Dennis Schröder from Oklahoma City on November 19, 2020, sending Danny Green, the draft rights to Jaden McDaniels and associated transaction flexibility to the Thunder. Los Angeles had just won the NBA title and wanted more shot creation and ball handling alongside LeBron James and Anthony Davis. Schröder had excelled as a reserve guard with Oklahoma City, making him a logical target. The Thunder were following a different timetable and preferred the veteran contract and movable draft capital over extending their commitment to the same backcourt combination.

Schröder Delivered Real Lakers Backcourt Work

Schröder became a regular part of the Lakers’ 2020-21 rotation, starting games and supplying scoring plus point-guard responsibility while injuries disrupted the roster. Los Angeles did not repeat as champion, but the incoming guard plainly had direct basketball value, and the inherited grade underrates a full season of meaningful minutes. His later free-agent movements, Boston stint and subsequent return to the Lakers came through separate decisions. Those future contracts should not be treated as an uninterrupted 2020 trade return. This was a useful one-season acquisition rather than a guaranteed permanent backcourt solution.

Oklahoma City Used Green and Draft Rights as Assets

Oklahoma City did not bring Danny Green in to become a long-term franchise veteran; it retained the ability to redistribute his contract. The Thunder subsequently sent Green to Philadelphia as part of a different agreement, while the McDaniels draft rights moved through further transactions and eventually became associated with Minnesota. Neither Green’s later Sixers games nor McDaniels’s Timberwolves career was direct Thunder on-court production. They were tradable assets in a rebuilding strategy, and accounting for the additional participants and compensation in each later deal is essential when evaluating the original trade.

The Thunder Created More Long-Range Flexibility

The Thunder’s longer-range asset flexibility deserves the edge, though the comparison is closer than a purely theoretical draft-capital verdict would suggest. The Lakers acquired a real guard who played significant minutes during a difficult title-defense campaign, making their outcome more than an empty short-term swing. Oklahoma City converted a player at a high point in his market into contracts and rights that could be reused. Neither club got a new first-round player who immediately started for it solely from this exchange, and the trade’s value needs to be separated from later free-agent and draft-rights choices.

Final Verdict

Oklahoma City Thunder Win. The Thunder receive B+ for Danny Green’s tradable veteran contract and Jaden McDaniels draft rights, both used in additional roster transactions. Los Angeles earns B- because Dennis Schröder gave the Lakers substantial guard minutes in 2020-21. McDaniels’s later Timberwolves production and Schröder’s later free-agent return to the Lakers were separate developments, not direct player returns from this deal.

Oklahoma City converted a player at a high point in his market into contracts and rights that could be reused. Neither club got a new first-round player who immediately started for it solely from this exchange, and the trade’s value needs to be separated from later free-agent and draft-rights choices.

Final Verdict

Oklahoma City Thunder Win. The Thunder receive B+ for Danny Green’s tradable veteran contract and Jaden McDaniels draft rights, both used in additional roster transactions. Los Angeles earns B- because Dennis Schröder gave the Lakers substantial guard minutes in 2020-21. McDaniels’s later Timberwolves production and Schröder’s later free-agent return to the Lakers were separate developments, not direct player returns from this deal.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Sent Out a Veteran Center for Wing Shooting

Atlanta moved Dewayne Dedmon to Detroit on November 20, 2020, acquiring Tony Snell and Khyri Thomas. The Hawks were revising their supporting cast around Trae Young and wanted perimeter help while reducing an obligation tied to Dedmon's contract. Snell arrived with established shooting and defensive experience, whereas Thomas was more of a low-cost option than an assumed rotation regular. Detroit received a veteran center and associated flexibility. The two clubs were not exchanging equivalent long-term starters; much of the decision depended on how they would handle the incoming contracts and whether those players actually appeared.

Snell Supplied Forty-Seven Games and Exceptional Accuracy

Snell became a real member of Atlanta's 2020-21 rotation. He played 47 games, starting 23, and shot 56.9 percent on three-point attempts. His role was modest in scoring volume, but reliable spot-up accuracy made him useful beside Young's creation. The Hawks then reached the Eastern Conference Finals that spring, giving Snell's receiving-team contribution a meaningful postseason context without claiming he led the run. His earlier Detroit production wasn't Atlanta value. Thomas, the other incoming guard, was waived days after the transaction, so the basketball return was essentially Snell rather than two functioning rotation pieces.

Detroit Did Not Get Games From Dedmon

The Pistons waived Dedmon shortly after the November transaction. He therefore provided no Detroit regular-season production through this acquisition, regardless of what he had done in Atlanta before the swap or for his next teams. That distinction is unusually important when assessing a deal whose outgoing player had a recognizable résumé. Detroit could have roster and financial reasons for processing the contract, but a bookkeeping result is not an additional frontcourt rotation contribution. Likewise, the trade exception in the record is flexibility subject to its actual later use, not a player who already played games for Detroit.

The Real On-Court Return Came Only to Atlanta

The Hawks obtained one reliable wing whose shooting helped a playoff lineup, while Detroit did not use its incoming veteran center in competition. Snell's limited volume prevents the swap from earning an extravagant grade, and the waiving of Thomas narrows Atlanta's return. Nevertheless, forty-seven games of exceptionally accurate outside shooting are plainly more than Detroit received on the court from Dedmon. The verdict also respects the deal's cap and roster context without trying to assign unrelated later careers to either team. Atlanta made better use of the player it actually kept.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B for Tony Snell's 47 regular-season games and 56.9 percent three-point shooting on a team that reached the 2021 Eastern Conference Finals. Khyri Thomas was waived without becoming a rotation contributor. Detroit receives C+ chiefly for contract flexibility because it waived Dewayne Dedmon without any Pistons games. The Hawks secured the trade's measurable receiving-team production.

new-york-knicks.summary: The Knicks acquired the rights to Immanuel Quickley and Mathias Lessort, plus a 2023 second, in a three-team 2020 draft transaction. Minnesota gained Leandro Bolmaro, Ricky Rubio and Jaden McDaniels's rights; Oklahoma City received James Johnson, Aleksej Pokuševski's rights and a future second. Quickley became a valuable Knicks contributor. The inherited Knicks Win grades New York A, Minnesota C- and Oklahoma City D.
new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Knicks Targeted Quickley on Draft Night

New York obtained Immanuel Quickley's draft rights in a November 2020 three-team transaction, along with rights to Mathias Lessort and a later second-round selection. Minnesota received Leandro Bolmaro's rights from the Knicks, plus Ricky Rubio and Jaden McDaniels's rights from Oklahoma City. The Thunder acquired James Johnson, Aleksej Pokuševski's rights and a future Minnesota second-round right. Each team pursued a different draft strategy, with New York zeroing in on a guard prospect it could develop immediately.

Quickley Became a Real Knicks Development Success

Quickley evolved from a rookie guard with a reliable perimeter shot into an important creator and scorer for New York. He supplied substantial receiving-team playing value before moving elsewhere through a later trade. That Knicks tenure is central to judging this 2020 exchange; his future work for another club should be treated separately. The incoming rights to Lessort and a 2023 second associated with No. 31 James Nnaji offered additional options without guaranteeing either resulting player had a lasting Knicks rotation role.

Minnesota Took Bolmaro's Rights

Minnesota added experienced point guard Rubio and the draft rights to two young forwards, McDaniels and Bolmaro. McDaniels eventually developed into an important defensive wing for the Timberwolves, which complicates a simplistic reading of their inherited C- grade. Oklahoma City received the rights to Pokuševski, who also played NBA minutes for the Thunder, plus veteran James Johnson and a future second-round selection. Those were actual incoming assets, not just an administrative appearance in a three-team draft exchange.

The Grade Gap Follows Direct Playing Production

New York's inherited A follows Quickley's strong development as a Knicks guard and the future flexibility from the additional rights. Minnesota's C- and Oklahoma City's D were preserved from the canonical evaluation, but both clubs received real players or meaningful prospects. A proper historical comparison must acknowledge McDaniels's sustained Timberwolves defense and Pokuševski's Thunder opportunities, rather than treating New York as the only franchise that acquired anyone. The eventual grade model merits later reconsideration without falsifying the asset directions.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win. New York earns A for acquiring and developing Immanuel Quickley, plus Lessort's rights and a future second. Minnesota receives C- under the inherited grading, despite also acquiring Ricky Rubio, Jaden McDaniels and Leandro Bolmaro. Oklahoma City gets D despite receiving James Johnson, Aleksej Pokuševski and a future pick. Quickley supplied substantial Knicks value, but the other teams' actual returns must remain visible.

analysis: The November 2020 transaction linked four distinct packages. Milwaukee received Jrue Holiday and the draft rights to Sam Merrill; New Orleans received Steven Adams, Eric Bledsoe, Milwaukee's 2025 and 2027 first-round picks and 2024/2026 swap rights; Oklahoma City received George Hill, Denver's protected first, Zylan Cheatham, Josh Gray, Darius Miller, Kenrich Williams and two second-round picks; Denver received R.J. Milwaukee's title outcome remains the strongest direct result; New Orleans and Oklahoma City retained broad asset value, and Hampton later provided Denver partial downstream utility in the Aaron Gordon trade.

oklahoma-city-thunder.analysis:
Gallinari Joined Atlanta Through a Sign-and-Trade

Atlanta acquired Danilo Gallinari from Oklahoma City in a November 24, 2020 sign-and-trade, alongside the recorded cash consideration. The Thunder received a protected future second-round selection, with the terms later modified and the draft lineage eventually appearing as No. 44 in 2025, associated with Brooks Barnhizer. The Hawks had playoff aspirations built around Trae Young and wanted another reliable perimeter scorer who could play forward. Oklahoma City chose to recoup a draft option for a veteran leaving its rebuilding timeline. The pick's protections mattered: this was not an unrestricted first-round prospect awarded immediately to the Thunder.

Gallinari Helped a Real Atlanta Conference-Finals Team

Gallinari supplied bench scoring, spacing and additional shooting during Atlanta's 2020-21 campaign. The Hawks reached the Eastern Conference Finals that season, and the veteran had a genuine role in the playoff rotation. His time with the franchise continued into the next season, giving the transaction a multiyear on-court return beyond a small deadline cameo. None of Gallinari's earlier Clippers or Thunder scoring should be assigned to the Hawks, and the team's playoff success had important contributions from several other players. But his actual Atlanta minutes are powerful evidence for a strong original acquisition grade.

Oklahoma City Kept a Protected Future Right

The Thunder obtained a second-round claim that was initially protected through No. 55 and later had its terms changed through a separate transaction. The draft record eventually associates it with a 2025 No. 44 selection, but the change in protection must be reflected before declaring that all future draft outcomes were known in 2020. Barnhizer's eventual draft identity is a useful ledger fact, not proof that the original deal itself brought a long-serving Thunder player to the floor. Oklahoma City was managing an asset-oriented rebuild, and collecting any additional draft value for Gallinari was a legitimate objective.

Atlanta's Two Seasons Were the Clearer Basketball Return

The Hawks obtained an experienced forward who contributed directly to a deep playoff run, while the Thunder accepted conditional future flexibility that could be used later. This favors Atlanta on observed receiving-team performance, but it does not make the pick worthless simply because it was years away. The agreement was a sign-and-trade, not a conventional one-for-one player swap, and its usefulness to Oklahoma City was partly financial and transactional. A strong Hawks grade and a moderate Thunder grade capture the difference between confirmed playoff minutes and a protected draft asset without borrowing unrelated seasons or inventing the future player's output.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns A- for Gallinari's real scoring and veteran contributions during the 2021 Eastern Conference Finals run and his following Hawks season. Oklahoma City gets B- for the protected future second-round asset ultimately associated with No. 44 Brooks Barnhizer in 2025. The revised pick protections and any later draftee appearances are tracked separately, not assumed to be 2020 Thunder games.

perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Took a Chance on Tucker's Athleticism

The Cavaliers acquired Rayjon Tucker from Utah during the November 2020 offseason, giving a young wing another NBA opportunity. Tucker was an athletic player with an emerging professional résumé, not an established scorer expected to lead a new franchise. Cleveland's objective was to evaluate his defensive effort and transition play while managing roster spots around a larger rebuilding plan. The trade also delivered a future second-round selection, giving the Cavaliers an asset whose eventual use would require separate accounting.

The 2027 Selection Was a Conditional Future Asset

Cleveland's incoming draft consideration was associated with the 2027 second round. The canonical record identifies the outcome as pending, so a retrospective writer should not invent a drafted player or assume the selection conveyed exactly as originally anticipated. Second-round picks can be retained, swapped or affected by protection conditions before draft night. Its value at the time of the trade was flexibility rather than an immediate lineup contribution. Any eventual evaluation needs to separate this right from Tucker's direct Cavaliers tenure.

Utah Received Cash Rather Than a Rotation Replacement

The Jazz acquired cash considerations in the exchange, a legitimate financial return but not a player able to absorb Tucker's minutes. Utah had other choices for its bench and could decide to convert a roster contract into financial flexibility. Cash has a fixed form of value even when fans prefer a prospect or another draft pick. The trade was therefore asymmetrical in the kinds of assets exchanged: Cleveland emphasized a player opportunity and future rights, while Utah accepted compensation not measured through box scores.

The Historic Record Does Not Establish a Winner

Both clubs receive N/A under the inherited grading because the canonical record does not establish a decisive overall value comparison. Tucker's actual receiving-team role and the eventual handling of the second-round right should be considered before making claims about which organization benefited more. A small offseason transaction can be useful to both sides even without producing a recognized star. The financial return for Utah and developmental return for Cleveland also don't lend themselves to a simple immediate statistical comparison.

Final Verdict

Insufficient Evidence. Cleveland gets N/A for Rayjon Tucker's developmental opportunity and a future 2027 second-round right whose recorded outcome remains pending. Utah also gets N/A for cash considerations. The two teams exchanged different forms of value, and the source history does not support a confident winner without further evidence about playing contributions and the eventual pick settlement.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Charlotte Committed to Hayward in a Sign-and-Trade

The Hornets added Gordon Hayward from Boston in November 2020, along with two future second-round selections. The Celtics received a conditional 2022 second that never conveyed and obtained a sizeable trade exception. Charlotte wanted an experienced forward who could score, pass and support its developing guards. Boston chose not to retain Hayward on the new contract terms, instead opening opportunities for later roster transactions. The pick exchanges and financial mechanics were part of the package, not proof that each selection became an incoming NBA player.

Hayward Delivered Several Hornets Seasons

Hayward became an important Charlotte forward, offering shooting and half-court creation when available. Injuries interrupted multiple stretches, preventing the club from enjoying an uninterrupted high-level run. Even with that limitation, he played substantial minutes for the team that acquired him and provided leadership to its young perimeter group. His earlier Jazz and Celtics achievements explain his reputation, but only the Hornets years belong to Charlotte's direct transaction return. He was not merely a name attached to a salary deal.

Boston Collected Flexibility Rather Than a Drafted Player

The Celtics' conditional 2022 second-round right was not exercised, meaning it produced no incoming Boston draft selection under the recorded terms. The trade exception was a more meaningful planning tool, potentially facilitating a separate later acquisition. That capability is useful but shouldn't be equated automatically with the production of whichever player Boston may have acquired through unrelated roster moves. Meanwhile, Charlotte's extra seconds later acquired draft identities through additional rights chains; those eventual players' NBA games cannot be assigned to the Hornets without following each transaction.

The Modest Grade Difference Reflects Different Payoffs

Charlotte received the active veteran forward it sought, albeit with health-related limits. Boston obtained financial flexibility and avoided committing to the same long-term contract. Both objectives were defensible, and a sign-and-trade has different practical benefits from an ordinary player swap. The narrow Hornets edge reflects the years of direct Hayward contribution against Boston's less tangible incoming package, rather than treating the Celtics' exception as worthless or the Hornets' experience as fully successful.

Final Verdict

Slight Charlotte Edge. Charlotte gets B for Gordon Hayward's scoring and playmaking contributions during several Hornets seasons, tempered by injuries, plus two incoming second-round picks. Boston receives B- for a substantial trade exception and a conditional second that never conveyed. The Hornets enjoyed the more visible immediate court return, while the Celtics gained contractual flexibility.

houston-rockets.analysis:
The Wizards Swapped Wall for a Former MVP

Washington sent John Wall and a heavily protected future first-round pick to Houston for Russell Westbrook on December 2, 2020. Wall had missed a long stretch because of injury, so the Rockets were betting on a comeback rather than acquiring a guaranteed All-Star at his previous peak. Washington was seeking an experienced star guard to pair with Bradley Beal immediately. The associated draft asset carried stepped protections over several seasons, making its eventual value conditional rather than an unrestricted first-round choice. These were two major guard contracts with very different availability and competitive implications.

Westbrook Made Washington a Playoff Team for One Season

Westbrook spent the 2020-21 season with the Wizards and provided high-volume playmaking, rebounding and transition offense alongside Beal. He recorded another season of triple-double production and helped Washington reach the NBA postseason through the play-in tournament. His tenure was only one season, however, before he moved again in a separate agreement involving the Lakers. The Wizards received real on-court performance at a difficult time for the franchise, but his later Lakers and Clippers careers are not additional Washington games. Nor should every subsequent Washington asset be credited solely to the Houston swap.

Wall's Rockets Comeback Was Short and Complicated

Wall returned to NBA action with Houston after his injuries and contributed guard minutes during 2020-21. His involvement did not produce a lasting Rockets playoff partnership, and the organization later kept him out of games while exploring roster alternatives. The contract was eventually resolved through later personnel decisions. Houston also held the protected future first-round opportunity, which must be evaluated according to the actual protections and conveyance, not as if a top lottery prospect had already been delivered. Wall's earlier all-star performances in Washington were history, not newly created value for Houston.

The Clearer Immediate Basketball Return Belonged to Washington

Washington secured a productive starting point guard and a postseason appearance, while Houston got a comeback season from Wall and a conditional draft asset that could support its reset. Both sides were responding to changes in their core roster, and neither created a long dynasty from the exchange alone. An inherited Rockets-winning score understates Westbrook's actual Wizards performance and overweights the theoretical upside of the protected selection. The better retrospective favors Washington, while preserving meaningful credit for Wall's NBA return and Houston's future flexibility. Every downstream trade involving these expensive contracts must be considered separately.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns B+ for Russell Westbrook's one season of substantial playmaking and its 2021 playoff appearance. Houston receives B- for John Wall's limited comeback season and the conditional first-round asset, with the protection schedule preventing any invented guaranteed lottery return. Westbrook's later teams and Wall's previous Wizards achievements aren't counted as newly acquired production.

oklahoma-city-thunder.summary: Oklahoma City absorbed Al Horford, acquired a future first and additional rights, and later restored Horford’s trade value; Philadelphia received immediate cap and roster relief.
oklahoma-city-thunder.analysis: The Horford deal worked because Oklahoma City was willing to use cap flexibility as an asset. The Thunder took on Al Horford and received the rights to Théo Maledon and Vasilije Micić, a future first-round pick and cash, while sending Danny Green, Terrance Ferguson and Vincent Poirier to Philadelphia. Horford played well enough in Oklahoma City to rebuild his market value before the franchise moved him again, and the attached first remained meaningful draft capital. Philadelphia achieved its own objective by reshaping an awkward roster fit, so the trade was not one-sided. The combination of restored player value and extra assets gives Oklahoma City a modest but real edge.

philadelphia-76ers.summary: On December 8, 2020, the Philadelphia 76ers acquired Danny Green, Terrance Ferguson and Vincent Poirier from the Oklahoma City Thunder in exchange for Al Horford, rights to Theo Maledon, rights to Vasilije Micić, and 2 additional assets.
philadelphia-76ers.analysis: Philadelphia moved Al Horford, draft rights, cash, and a protected first for Danny Green, Terrance Ferguson, and Vincent Poirier. Green helped restore lineup balance on the 2021 top seed, but the first-round cost was real. The basketball fit improved while Oklahoma City gained premium future value, leaving an even result.

perspectives.analysis: Harden played at an MVP level in Brooklyn, but the Durant-Irving-Harden trio never reached the Finals and broke apart after thirteen months. Brooklyn paid a championship-level price without completing the championship objective, making Houston the clearest winner.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Added Fournier for a Short Playoff Push

The Celtics acquired Evan Fournier from the Magic at the March 25, 2021 deadline, sending guard Jeff Teague and two future second-round selections to Orlando. Boston wanted another perimeter scorer to support Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown during an uneven season. Fournier had been a reliable offensive option in Orlando for years, but his Boston role would depend on a rapid adjustment to a different roster. The Magic chose future flexibility instead of retaining a veteran guard whose contract was approaching free agency.

Fournier's Celtics Tenure Lasted Only a Few Months

Fournier supplied outside shooting and scoring in his limited Boston appearances and participated in the 2021 playoffs, when the Celtics were eliminated by Brooklyn in the opening round. He was not an incoming star who stayed for several seasons: he departed in free agency to the Knicks that summer. His Orlando career established his ability and explained the Celtics' interest, but it could not be treated as new production in Boston. The team received a short-term offensive option without a sustained postseason payoff.

Orlando Received Draft Capital and a Trade Exception

The Magic acquired rights to two future second-round selections, later linked to a 2025 No. 57 pick and a still-future 2027 choice, plus salary-cap flexibility through the transaction. Teague did not establish an Orlando playing role, so the veteran's NBA history elsewhere cannot count as Magic minutes. The draft assets offered a chance to add prospects or participate in later deals, while the trade exception could help facilitate separate roster moves. Those were tangible organizational tools even without an immediate replacement for Fournier's scoring.

The Rental's Short Duration Favored Orlando

Boston obtained a player who could shoot, but the brief stay and first-round postseason exit limited the return on the outgoing assets. Orlando chose to stockpile future options during a rebuild rather than watch Fournier's contract expire without compensation. Not every second-round pick develops into a strong NBA player, and the still-unresolved selection cannot be given a fictional future outcome. The grade difference reflects the Celtics' limited window against the Magic's retained flexibility, not a claim that Fournier was ineffective during every Boston game.

Final Verdict

Magic Win. Orlando receives B+ for turning Evan Fournier into two future second-round choices and financial flexibility while Jeff Teague contributed no meaningful Magic minutes. Boston gets D because Fournier was a short-term rental who left after the 2021 playoffs. The Celtics enjoyed some useful shooting, but their brief return did not match the future assets surrendered.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Brought Lou Williams Back for the Playoff Push

The Hawks traded Rajon Rondo to the Clippers at the March 25, 2021 deadline, receiving Lou Williams, cash and two second-round selections. Williams was returning to Atlanta, where he had played earlier in his career, and offered scoring from the bench alongside Trae Young. The Clippers wanted another veteran who could organize the offense during the postseason. Atlanta obtained more distinct assets in addition to the shooting guard, while Los Angeles was effectively committing its return to whether Rondo could provide valuable playoff direction.

Williams Delivered a Real Atlanta Bench Contribution

Williams joined a Hawks team that soon made an unexpected run to the Eastern Conference Finals. His scoring and ability to make difficult shots gave the roster another option when Young was resting or when the offense stalled. Williams returned for the following season before ending his NBA career. Those Atlanta minutes are the appropriate receiving-team payoff, distinct from his earlier achievements as a prolific Clippers reserve. The player was older, but the Hawks got useful production at a moment when their postseason aspirations were growing.

Rondo Was a Short-Lived Clippers Acquisition

Rondo brought championship experience and a reputation for playoff decision-making, but his Clippers tenure did not last long. He participated in their 2021 postseason run and then moved to another team in a separate transaction. The club did not receive a durable new floor general from the swap. Meanwhile, Atlanta held two second-round rights, including a 2023 selection associated with No. 35 Julian Phillips and a 2027 choice. Phillips's subsequent playing career must be traced through later draft-night transactions, not treated as games earned directly for the Hawks.

The Additional Picks Broke a Veteran-for-Veteran Tie

Each team acquired a guard who could help during the 2021 playoffs, so the trade should not be judged solely by comparing Williams and Rondo at their peaks. Atlanta added a useful reserve and multiple future assets while sending away a player whose role had become limited. The Clippers received some immediate playoff utility but no lasting starting solution. That asymmetry supports the Hawks' higher grade without implying Williams alone transformed the club into a contender. The draft rights and cash were meaningful additions to the transaction.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta receives A- for Lou Williams's postseason bench scoring, cash and two future second-round picks. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Reworked Its Bench Big-Man Options

The Celtics acquired Luke Kornet and Moritz Wagner in March 2021 through a transaction involving Chicago and Washington. Kornet was a center with outside shooting potential, while Wagner offered a more mobile offensive frontcourt profile. Boston's goal was to evaluate alternatives behind its main rotation rather than secure a marquee star. The transaction also sent Daniel Theis and Javonte Green to Chicago, two players whose defensive and athletic contributions were already familiar to Boston.

The Bulls Received a Recognizable Defensive Center

Chicago acquired Daniel Theis and Javonte Green from Boston, Troy Brown Jr. from Washington, and cash considerations. Theis offered dependable frontcourt positioning and postseason experience, Green supplied athletic defensive energy, and Brown added a younger perimeter option who could switch across matchups. All three were real basketball pieces rather than a single aggregated salary entry. The package allowed Chicago to add depth around its newly acquired frontcourt stars without giving up a comparable high-usage scorer in the same transaction.

Kornet and Wagner Had Different Boston Timelines

Kornet provided Boston with center depth and eventually became associated with subsequent Celtics rotations, although later contractual moves should be distinguished from the 2021 exchange. Wagner's first Celtics stint was much shorter. It would be misleading to add their entire later NBA careers together as a guaranteed return for one deadline transaction. Washington participated in the three-club arrangement, but this particular canonical entry does not list an active player or selection coming directly to the Wizards.

The Grade Difference Is Narrower Than the Verdict

The inherited slight Bulls edge is narrow because Boston also received two playable frontcourt options, while Washington acquired center Daniel Gafford and wing Chandler Hutchison from Chicago. Gafford's rim protection and interior finishing gave the Wizards a tangible return; Hutchison provided another perimeter evaluation. Washington's C+ shouldn't be described as a grade for receiving nothing. Chicago and Boston each retain B+, and the three clubs' different post-deadline needs explain why the transaction cannot be reduced to a one-for-one center swap.

Final Verdict

Slight Bulls Edge. Chicago earns B+ for Daniel Theis, Javonte Green, Troy Brown Jr. and cash, a useful combination of defense and wing depth. Boston also receives B+ for Luke Kornet and Moritz Wagner. Washington gets C+ for Daniel Gafford and Chandler Hutchison, with Gafford providing genuine interior value. The slight Chicago advantage follows its broader immediate rotation return, not an invented empty Wizards package.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Charlotte Added Wanamaker at the 2021 Deadline

The March 25, 2021 exchange sent veteran point guard Brad Wanamaker from Golden State to Charlotte together with cash and a 2022 second-round selection protected through No. 54. The Warriors took back a conditional 2025 second-round right protected through No. 55. Charlotte sought a backup guard while dealing with injuries in a young team built around LaMelo Ball and Terry Rozier. Golden State was resetting bench responsibilities and could free roster space by moving Wanamaker. The precise protections are important because neither incoming draft right guaranteed a selected player.

Wanamaker Played Real Hornets Games

Wanamaker offered Charlotte an experienced ball handler for the remainder of the 2020-21 season, with some ability to steady reserve possessions. His direct Hornets service was short and did not establish him as the franchise's long-term point guard. Still, those games were an actual receiving-team return, unlike an unexercised pick. Wanamaker's earlier Celtics years and his time with Golden State before the deadline belong to those teams. Cash consideration also provided the Hornets an economic benefit separate from how many minutes he played after arriving in North Carolina.

Both Protected Second-Round Rights Failed to Convey

The pick Golden State received was protected through No. 55 in 2025 and did not convey. Charlotte's inbound 2022 second was protected through No. 54 and likewise did not result in an exercised pick. Oklahoma City took Austin Rivers; Philadelphia received Ignas Brazdeikis. A pick ultimately connected to No. 58 Jericho Sims produced the clearest direct Knicks return. new-york-knicks.analysis:
New York Used the Deadline to Secure Future Center Depth

The Knicks acquired Terrance Ferguson, Vincent Poirier, the overseas rights to Emir Preldžić and two conditional second-round rights in March 2021. Oklahoma City received Austin Rivers, while Philadelphia acquired Ignas Brazdeikis. The trade was an exercise in reorganizing reserve contracts and draft assets rather than an exchange of multiple current starters. For New York, the incoming 2021 second-round right would prove more identifiable than either incoming reserve guard.

Jericho Sims Turned a Late Pick Into Real Knicks Minutes

The 2021 second-round selection became associated with No. 58 Jericho Sims, who went on to supply athletic center minutes in New York. His rebounding and finishing gave the Knicks an actual receiving-team contribution from an otherwise modest draft asset. Ferguson and Poirier did not establish lasting prominent Knicks roles, while Preldžić's rights remained a separate international asset. The additional protected 2024 second did not convey, so it shouldn't be counted as another NBA player.

The Thunder and Sixers Received Narrower Player Options

Rivers had NBA experience as an active guard, but his Oklahoma City transaction path didn't produce the extended Thunder playing role his previous career could imply. Brazdeikis offered Philadelphia a young wing with a less established skill set. Those were real incoming assets, though neither produced a substantial long-term replacement for an established starter through this transaction. Their earlier performances for other franchises shouldn't be retroactively attributed to these receiving teams.

The Late Pick Explains the Inherited Knicks Advantage

New York's B+ values the opportunity created by Sims alongside flexibility from other rights. Oklahoma City's C+ and Philadelphia's B- recognize contracts and developmental options that proved less durable. The draft lineage is especially relevant because picks near No. 58 often don't produce reliable NBA contributors. Here New York found an actual center, while the nonconveyed conditional selection added no fictional later value.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win. New York earns B+ for its player and rights package led by the second-round choice used on Jericho Sims, who became a usable Knicks center. Oklahoma City gets C+ for Austin Rivers, whose Thunder tenure was limited, and Philadelphia receives B- for Ignas Brazdeikis. The separate protected pick that did not convey cannot be credited as a selected player.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Reacquired a Veteran It Already Trusted

The Celtics obtained Al Horford, Moses Brown and a future second-round asset from Oklahoma City in June 2021. They sent Kemba Walker, a 2021 first-round selection and a 2025 second-round right to the Thunder. Horford had previously played a major role in Boston, so the club understood his defensive communication, passing and ability to fit beside its wing scorers. Oklahoma City took additional draft inventory while managing a roster designed to develop younger players rather than depend on an expensive veteran point guard.

Horford Supplied an Immediate and Lasting Return

Horford returned as a central frontcourt contributor for Boston, helping the Celtics reach the 2022 NBA Finals and ultimately win the 2024 championship. His passing and defense allowed the roster to function with different lineup combinations, and his experience carried particular value in postseason basketball. This is actual receiving-team production created by the trade, not credit borrowed from his first Boston stint. Brown's stay was shorter, but Horford alone supplied a substantial basketball benefit during multiple contention seasons.

Oklahoma City Redirected Its Draft Capital

Walker did not become a Thunder regular-season contributor, making the picks the more important Oklahoma City return. The 2021 first-round choice was linked to No. 16 Alperen Şengün, but the Thunder subsequently moved his draft rights to Houston, where his NBA playing production occurred. The additional 2025 second-round selection and outgoing 2023 right belonged to separate stages of the draft-asset ledger. Oklahoma City gained options to rearrange its future roster without treating Şengün's Houston achievements as Thunder games.

Boston Got the Clearer Immediate Court Impact

Both sides pursued coherent strategies. Oklahoma City accepted future selections and the opportunity to reshape contract commitments, while Boston sought a veteran big man already suited to its stars. The Thunder's draft rights had genuine value even when later moved elsewhere. Yet Horford's sustained return to the Celtics included deep playoff runs and an NBA championship, giving Boston a much more direct measure of success. The higher grade follows from that multiyear performance, not a claim that every pick Oklahoma City received failed.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns A- for Al Horford's productive second stint, including an essential role on its 2024 championship team, with Moses Brown and a future pick as smaller assets. Oklahoma City gets B for Kemba Walker's contract and two draft selections, but Walker didn't become an active Thunder contributor. The first later associated with Alperen Şengün moved to Houston, so Boston's proven Horford return was the stronger direct outcome.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Obtained Draft Rights to Jason Preston

Los Angeles acquired the rights to Ohio University guard Jason Preston, picked thirty-third in the 2021 draft, from Orlando on July 29. The Magic received cash and a future 2026 second-round selection. The Clippers were making a relatively inexpensive developmental bet on a creative guard coming out of college, while Orlando chose financial compensation and later draft flexibility. No veteran NBA starter changed teams, and Preston had not yet signed the professional contract that would begin his Clippers career. The deal was a draft-night rights transfer rather than a midseason rotation swap.

Preston Had an Interrupted Path to NBA Games

Preston's first season was affected by a foot injury that kept him from regular action, delaying the Clippers' evaluation of their new draft choice. He eventually appeared in NBA games for Los Angeles, but never established the sort of major playing role that would convert a second-round gamble into a clear franchise success. The real return was a modest amount of developmental and reserve guard work. His college scoring and assists illustrated why he appealed on draft night, but those performances aren't NBA production gained by the Clippers. The team did receive an identifiable prospect rather than merely a future selection.

Orlando Accepted Cash and a Deferred Draft Chance

The Magic's compensation was an immediate cash payment and the right to a later second-round pick. Such an asset could help replenish the organization's pool of prospects or be moved again in another trade, but its protections and final 2026 destination must be verified before assigning a specific NBA career. Orlando did not acquire Preston and should not be credited with his subsequent Clippers appearances. Likewise, the cash payment was a real financial return rather than an incoming guard who could play for the Magic that season. The two sides chose different risk profiles for the same draft slot.

Two Small Returns Don't Establish a Decisive Winner

Los Angeles got the opportunity to develop a drafted guard, though injuries limited the immediate payoff. Orlando collected cash and draft flexibility without requiring a current roster spot. Neither club spent a first-round choice or added an established two-way starter, and neither direct return clearly dominated the other. A broadly even verdict remains appropriate while the grades improve slightly from the inherited low assessments, reflecting tangible value without inventing star outcomes. The 2026 selection should be analyzed on its actual rights chain and not on speculative future results.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. The Clippers receive C+ for Jason Preston's draft rights and limited eventual NBA playing time following an injury delay. Orlando also earns C+ for cash and a future 2026 second-round choice. Neither side acquired a proven starter, and no unverified 2026 draftee is treated as an Orlando player without checking the final pick lineage.
