The Magic received cash and a future 2026 second-round selection. The Clippers were making a relatively inexpensive developmental bet on a creative guard coming out of college, while Orlando chose financial compensation and later draft flexibility. No veteran NBA starter changed teams, and Preston had not yet signed the professional contract that would begin his Clippers career. The deal was a draft-night rights transfer rather than a midseason rotation swap.

Preston Had an Interrupted Path to NBA Games

Preston's first season was affected by a foot injury that kept him from regular action, delaying the Clippers' evaluation of their new draft choice. He eventually appeared in NBA games for Los Angeles, but never established the sort of major playing role that would convert a second-round gamble into a clear franchise success. The real return was a modest amount of developmental and reserve guard work. His college scoring and assists illustrated why he appealed on draft night, but those performances aren't NBA production gained by the Clippers. The team did receive an identifiable prospect rather than merely a future selection.

Orlando Accepted Cash and a Deferred Draft Chance

The Magic's compensation was an immediate cash payment and the right to a later second-round pick. Such an asset could help replenish the organization's pool of prospects or be moved again in another trade, but its protections and final 2026 destination must be verified before assigning a specific NBA career. Orlando did not acquire Preston and should not be credited with his subsequent Clippers appearances. Likewise, the cash payment was a real financial return rather than an incoming guard who could play for the Magic that season. The two sides chose different risk profiles for the same draft slot.

Two Small Returns Don't Establish a Decisive Winner

Los Angeles got the opportunity to develop a drafted guard, though injuries limited the immediate payoff. Orlando collected cash and draft flexibility without requiring a current roster spot. Neither club spent a first-round choice or added an established two-way starter, and neither direct return clearly dominated the other. A broadly even verdict remains appropriate while the grades improve slightly from the inherited low assessments, reflecting tangible value without inventing star outcomes. The 2026 selection should be analyzed on its actual rights chain and not on speculative future results.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. The Clippers receive C+ for Jason Preston's draft rights and limited eventual NBA playing time following an injury delay. Orlando also earns C+ for cash and a future 2026 second-round choice. Neither side acquired a proven starter, and no unverified 2026 draftee is treated as an Orlando player without checking the final pick lineage.

oklahoma-city-thunder.analysis:
Utah Paid Oklahoma City to Absorb Favors's Contract

Utah traded Derrick Favors and a heavily protected future first-round obligation to Oklahoma City at the end of July 2021. The Jazz received cash and the right to a later second-round pick, described as the least favorable among several eligible franchises in 2027. The Thunder were rebuilding and had room to take on the experienced big man's contract, while Utah needed financial flexibility around its established roster. The incoming first was conditional: it couldn't simply be counted as a lottery selection until the relevant protection periods passed. The timing of Utah's earlier obligation to Memphis added further complexity to the right.

Favors Played for the Thunder Without Becoming a Long-Term Fixture

Favors appeared in Oklahoma City during the 2021-22 season and supplied veteran frontcourt minutes, rebounds and screening when available. He was not the centerpiece of the Thunder's developing rotation, and his earlier seasons alongside Rudy Gobert in Utah were not newly created Oklahoma City NBA production. Later health and roster-management decisions reduced his continuing role, preventing the trade from delivering a durable starting center. The contract absorption nevertheless had a rational asset purpose because it initially came with a protected first-round path. For this transaction, actual receiving-team games and the uncertain future selection must be considered separately, rather than combining Favors's full NBA career into one club's return.

The Protected First Never Conveyed in the Early Windows

The Utah draft obligation could become a first only if the choice fell outside specified protections in later years. The pick was protected inside the top ten in 2024 and 2025 and the top eight in 2026, with a later second-round fallback if no first conveyed. Utah received the No. 2 position in the 2026 draft, so the selection remained with the Jazz rather than transferring to Oklahoma City under the original condition. That fact eliminates an assumed 2026 Thunder first-round draftee from the retrospective. The fallback rights still possessed future value, but the franchise cannot be credited for an actual first-round star that it never selected through this obligation.

Both Teams Achieved Part of Their Salary-and-Asset Objectives

Oklahoma City gained veteran depth and a conditional future claim in exchange for handling a contract, while Utah received financial relief and a separate later second-round right. Neither side enjoyed the full idealized outcome: Favors's Thunder tenure was modest, and the protected first failed to become a premium pick for Oklahoma City. The Jazz's opportunity to keep its high 2026 draft choice was real, yet that retention resulted from the agreed protections rather than a new asset received from the Thunder. Balanced grades reflect the trade's cap logic and actual draft mechanics without assigning unearned NBA minutes or future picks to either side.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Oklahoma City receives B- for Favors's limited frontcourt minutes and a protected obligation that did not convey as a first through 2026, leaving later second-round fallback value. Utah earns B- for cash and roster flexibility while retaining its top-eight-protected 2026 selection. Neither side is awarded an invented Thunder lottery pick or Favors's earlier Jazz production.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Chose a Veteran Wing Over a Developmental Center

On July 31, 2021, Boston traded Moses Brown to Dallas for Josh Richardson, with transaction records showing trade exceptions for the two teams. Richardson had already worked as a defensive-minded guard and occasional secondary scorer for other franchises. Boston wanted a more established perimeter contributor alongside its young stars, while Dallas obtained a big man with size and rebounding upside. The deal was not a draft-night rights exchange or a promise that Richardson would become a permanent Celtics starter. It was a rotation adjustment in which both clubs received an actual player under contract.

Richardson Supplied Boston Depth Before a Separate Trade

Richardson became part of Boston's guard and wing rotation during the first half of 2021-22, providing perimeter defense and occasional scoring. The Celtics could use him around their primary forwards without demanding that he direct the offense. Boston later sent Richardson to San Antonio as a component of the February 2022 Derrick White transaction, converting the experienced reserve into a piece of another roster decision. White was not sent by Dallas in July, so he cannot be listed as a direct asset in the earlier exchange. Richardson's actual Boston games and his availability as subsequent trade capital explain the Celtics' benefit.

Moses Brown Was Not a Lasting Dallas Center

Dallas received a young rebounder who had shown flashes of production in Oklahoma City but remained a developmental player. Brown spent only part of the season with the Mavericks and did not establish a durable starting or major reserve role before leaving. His prior Thunder performances provided a reason Dallas was willing to acquire him; they were not Mavericks production acquired in this swap. Similarly, the bookkeeping value of the trade exceptions has to be assessed on its own rather than treated as a second star in either direction. The player contrast favors the team that used its veteran wing.

The First Trade Worked Better for the Celtics

Boston got an experienced player it could actually use, then possessed a useful component for a later trade as the roster shifted. Dallas acquired a plausible prospect but did not receive a comparable stretch of reliable contribution. The Mavericks' cap flexibility still deserves recognition, which is why the return should not be described as completely worthless. Yet the Celtics received the more functional player for the needs of that season. Evaluating the July transaction separately from Richardson's earlier Mavericks year and from the subsequent Spurs deal produces a measured Boston-winning assessment.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ because Josh Richardson provided useful guard and wing minutes before becoming part of a separate trade package later in the season. Dallas receives C+ for acquiring Moses Brown and flexibility through the transaction exception, but Brown never developed into a durable Mavericks rotation piece. Derrick White's eventual arrival came from another deal and isn't a direct July 2021 Dallas asset.

perspectives.summary: An August 2021 five-team agreement involved Washington, the Lakers, Brooklyn, Indiana and San Antonio. Washington obtained Spencer Dinwiddie and a broad package including Kyle Kuzma, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Montrezl Harrell; the Lakers acquired Russell Westbrook; Indiana took Isaiah Jackson's rights. The inherited slight Wizards edge grades Washington B+, Indiana B, Spurs B, Nets C- and Lakers D.
perspectives.analysis:
Washington Used a Five-Team Structure to Add Depth

Washington joined the Lakers, Nets, Pacers and Spurs in a complicated August 2021 transaction that sent Russell Westbrook to Los Angeles. The Wizards acquired Kyle Kuzma, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Montrezl Harrell and Spencer Dinwiddie among a wider collection of players and rights. Their goal was to replace a high-usage star with several different contributors rather than merely swap him for a single guard. The deal required several clubs to exchange selection options and roster contracts.

The Lakers Acquired Star Credentials but Faced Fit Problems

Westbrook had an extraordinary NBA career before moving to Los Angeles, but combining his style with the Lakers' established stars was a different challenge. His receiving-team tenure fell short of expectations and created offensive spacing questions. The club also received second-round rights through the broader agreement. Those draft possibilities do not erase the limitations of Westbrook's actual Lakers fit, nor do his previous MVP achievements count as new production earned after the 2021 move.

The Other Three Clubs Received Distinct Assets

Indiana acquired Isaiah Jackson's draft rights and could develop a young athletic big. Brooklyn received the rights to Nikola Milutinov and future second-round selection and swap opportunities, assets that did not automatically translate to Nets playing time. San Antonio obtained Chandler Hutchison and a 2022 second-round right, choosing a smaller player-and-pick package. Each of those franchises belonged to the same official five-team structure and should not disappear from an assessment centered entirely on the headline Westbrook trade.

Washington's Multiple Contributors Explain the Verdict

The inherited Wizards B+ reflects the combination of Kuzma's forward play, other established veterans and added rights. Indiana and San Antonio each receive B for more specialized returns, Brooklyn C- for future-rights value and the Lakers D for the difficult Westbrook fit. The Wizards didn't receive five All-Stars, and every later draft selection needs tracing. They did obtain several practical player options instead of relying on the production of one departing guard.

Final Verdict

Slight Wizards Edge. Washington earns B+ for Kyle Kuzma, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Montrezl Harrell, Spencer Dinwiddie and additional assets. Indiana gets B for Isaiah Jackson's rights, San Antonio B for Chandler Hutchison and a pick, Brooklyn C- for overseas and future rights, and Los Angeles D for Russell Westbrook's difficult fit. The Wizards' broader usable return justifies the inherited lead.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Reconfigured a Veteran Center Contract

The Celtics sent Tristan Thompson to Sacramento in August 2021 through a three-team arrangement also involving Atlanta. In return Boston received defensive-minded guard Kris Dunn, young big Bruno Fernando and a 2023 second-round selection originally coming through Portland. The deal gave the organization a mix of immediate depth and future rights instead of one like-for-like starting center. Thompson had brought playoff experience to Boston but no longer fit every part of its developing roster strategy.

Atlanta Received Delon Wright, Not an Empty Return

The Hawks acquired point guard Delon Wright from Sacramento as part of the same agreement. Wright had proved useful as a secondary ball handler, defender and spot-up shooter, making him a plausible backup behind Trae Young. The official Hawks announcement explicitly confirms the incoming guard, correcting a missing Atlanta-side leg in the original Celtics-only ledger. His previous experience with other teams established the skill set Atlanta was buying; his later career elsewhere cannot simply be assigned to the Hawks.

Sacramento Chose Thompson's Veteran Frontcourt Experience

The Kings obtained Thompson, a proven rebounder and screen setter with extensive Cleveland playoff experience. The frontcourt addition gave Sacramento another experienced option as its guard rotation changed following the draft. He was not expected to replace the long-term upside of a lottery prospect, but his presence could help younger teammates manage difficult interior matchups. Sacramento sent Wright away in the process. Boston's incoming 2023 second was later associated with No. 35 Julian Phillips, but subsequent draft-rights movement needs separate tracing.

A Small Celtics Edge Reflects Varied Returns

The inherited Celtics B+ recognizes Dunn, Fernando and the future second-round right as a broad package. Atlanta's B rewards Wright's credible guard skills, while Sacramento earns C+ for acquiring Thompson. Those grades don't imply Dunn immediately became Boston's lead scorer or that Atlanta participated without a return. Each club acquired a different kind of asset, and the original verdict gives Boston only a narrow advantage because no single incoming player transformed a franchise.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston receives B+ for Kris Dunn, Bruno Fernando and a 2023 second-round right. Atlanta earns B for Delon Wright, a real backup playmaker acquired from Sacramento. The Kings receive C+ for Tristan Thompson's veteran frontcourt experience. The Celtics' package offers several options, but Atlanta's confirmed incoming guard prevents the transaction from being described as a Boston-Sacramento deal with an empty third party.

perspectives.summary: Charlotte, Memphis and New Orleans redistributed veterans, prospects and draft rights in an August 2021 transaction. Charlotte's package included Wes Iwundu and a protected first later used on Mark Williams; Memphis acquired Steven Adams and multiple draft assets; New Orleans took Devonte' Graham, Jonas Valančiūnas and rights linked to Trey Murphy III. The inherited slight Charlotte edge grades Charlotte A, New Orleans A- and Memphis D.
perspectives.analysis:
Charlotte Collected a Wide Set of Assets

The Hornets participated in a 2021 arrangement with Memphis and New Orleans, acquiring Wes Iwundu, a protected 2022 first-round right later associated with Mark Williams, cash and the rights to Tyler Harvey. The draft component gave Charlotte an opportunity to add a center on a different timeline from the veteran wing. Its package wasn't limited to the first player named in the transaction, and the protected selection required its own later draft-rights accounting.

Memphis Acquired Veterans and More Draft Options

The Grizzlies received Steven Adams and Eric Bledsoe, along with rights to Ziaire Williams and Jared Butler and a protected future Lakers first-round selection. Adams later supplied valuable rebounding and screens in Memphis, a real receiving-team benefit that should not be ignored simply because the inherited grading awards the Grizzlies D. Bledsoe and the prospect rights followed different paths. The package mixed established interior skills with longer-term draft development.

New Orleans Received Multiple Frontcourt and Wing Pieces

The Pelicans obtained Devonte' Graham and Jonas Valančiūnas plus draft rights associated with Trey Murphy III and Brandon Boston Jr. Valančiūnas offered a proven center with interior offense, while Murphy developed into a useful perimeter forward. These represent more direct New Orleans basketball value than a single abstract pick. Graham supplied another guard option, although his arrival did not ensure a long-term starting role. Rights later routed elsewhere shouldn't automatically be counted as Pelicans production.

The Inherited Winner Label Needs Context

Charlotte's A and New Orleans's A- reward substantial rights and player returns, while Memphis receives D under the original model. That Memphis grade sits uneasily beside Adams's actual contributions, so the review should not suggest its roster received nothing. The proper historical account notes several teams obtaining useful pieces and avoids treating this complicated arrangement as a simple one-for-one player exchange.

Final Verdict

Slight Charlotte Edge. Charlotte earns A for an asset package including the protected pick later used on Mark Williams. New Orleans receives A- for Jonas Valančiūnas, Trey Murphy III's rights and other perimeter options. Memphis gets D under the inherited grade, although Steven Adams's real Grizzlies contribution deserves explicit acknowledgment. The multi-asset structure makes this closer than a simplistic reading of the grade gap.

golden-state-warriors.analysis:
Golden State Exchanged a Reserve Forward for a Protected Pick

On August 7, 2021, Golden State moved forward Eric Paschall to Utah in exchange for a protected 2026 second-round draft selection. The pick's protection covered positions thirty-one through forty-two, meaning the Warriors were not assured an ordinary unrestricted second-round choice. Paschall had been an energetic frontcourt option for Golden State, but the club was adjusting its depth while preparing for a season with championship ambitions. Utah sought a young, physical forward who could contribute without requiring a high draft expenditure. This was a one-player-for-conditional-pick exchange.

Paschall Provided a Direct One-Season Jazz Return

Paschall joined Utah's rotation during 2021-22 and offered reserve frontcourt offense, energy and size. He was not an All-Star or a permanent Jazz cornerstone, and his one-season role should not be exaggerated into a long-term franchise outcome. Still, the team obtained actual NBA appearances for an obligation involving only a future protected second. Those games belonged to Utah rather than Golden State, and Paschall's earlier breakout Warriors rookie season was not a newly acquired Jazz achievement. His later career path must also remain separate from what Utah received through this agreement.

The Pick's Protections Limited Golden State's Certainty

Golden State collected future draft rights that could become useful if the protection terms permitted conveyance, but that possibility was not equal to a guaranteed draftee in the trade's immediate aftermath. The original record identifies 2026 and the thirty-first through forty-second pick condition; an audit should not assign a future NBA player without a verified resolution. The Warriors also freed a roster opportunity as they adjusted their mix of young players and veterans. That management value is real even if Utah received the more tangible immediate playing contribution. Neither club obtained additional cash or a first-round asset in this particular exchange.

Utah's Immediate Minutes Outweighed Conditional Future Value

The Jazz acquired a reserve who could play throughout the next season, while Golden State gained restricted draft flexibility and a different use for Paschall's roster slot. Both teams' objectives were legitimate, especially given Golden State's existing frontcourt priorities. A revised modest Jazz edge best reflects actual receiving-team minutes without claiming Paschall stayed for years or that the Warriors' protected pick was automatically worthless. The condition may still determine future asset value, so the verdict avoids inventing its final destination. One contract and one restricted pick made this a limited rather than historic trade.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win. Utah receives B- for Eric Paschall's usable 2021-22 reserve frontcourt games. Golden State gets C+ for roster flexibility and a protected 2026 second-round right whose terms did not guarantee a selection. Paschall's earlier Warriors output belongs to Golden State before the trade; no unverified future draftee is assigned to the Warriors' incoming asset.

memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
Memphis Paid a Package of Second-Round Assets for Aldama

The Grizzlies obtained the draft rights to Spanish forward Santi Aldama, selected thirtieth overall in 2021, while Utah received the rights to Baylor guard Jared Butler and two second-round draft assets. Those future selections included a 2022 pick later associated with Jabari Walker and a protected 2026 second. The clubs were trading different collections of prospects and choices, not established starters. Memphis wanted Aldama as a potential modern frontcourt contributor. Utah preferred spreading its opportunity across a guard prospect and multiple selections.

Aldama Became Real Rotation Value in Memphis

Aldama developed into a genuine Memphis rotation forward, contributing floor spacing, rebounding and interior versatility after beginning as a project. His role expanded when the Grizzlies needed additional playable size around their developing core. That output is a direct Memphis return, distinct from any overseas performance he recorded before entering the NBA. The club benefited from selecting a specific player rather than assuming every late first would produce equivalent minutes. Aldama's development is the strongest concrete evidence supporting the longstanding Grizzlies-winning verdict.

The Jazz Obtained Butler and More Draft Flexibility

Utah acquired Butler's rights along with two second-round picks, but the final draft names do not all represent seasons of actual Jazz production. Butler had a limited NBA role with Utah, and the 2022 selection associated with Jabari Walker followed a rights path of its own. The 2026 protected obligation requires verification of the eventual conveyance before anyone can claim a particular NBA player through it. The asset package was real, and it would be wrong to dismiss the Jazz as receiving nothing, but the direct receiving-team results were more limited than Aldama's development.

A Reliable Grizzlies Forward Outweighed Dispersed Options

Memphis concentrated multiple smaller assets into a player who earned NBA minutes and became a useful part of its frontcourt. Utah chose flexibility that could make sense for a team seeking additional draft opportunities, yet its incoming guard and pick package did not reproduce Aldama's specific on-court return. The trade's value is grounded in observed receiving-team performance rather than in a claim that every future pick was worthless or guaranteed. Memphis wins decisively on player development, with Utah retaining reasonable credit for the prospect and selections it controlled.

Final Verdict

Grizzlies Win. Memphis earns A after the No. 30 rights to Santi Aldama became a productive NBA rotation forward. Utah receives C+ for Jared Butler's rights and two future second-round selections, including the 2022 No. 57-linked pick and a protected 2026 asset. los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Consolidated Three Contracts Into Bledsoe

On August 16, 2021, Los Angeles sent Patrick Beverley, Rajon Rondo and Daniel Oturu to Memphis in exchange for veteran guard Eric Bledsoe. The Clippers were reorganizing their backcourt after an injury-affected postseason and chose to combine multiple contracts into a player who could defend and handle the ball. Memphis had less reason to retain Bledsoe for its developing roster and accepted a varied package of older guards and a young big man. The recorded agreement did not involve a fresh first-round selection; its appeal rested on immediate roles and potential later trades.

Bledsoe Supplied a Season of Guard Minutes

Bledsoe played a meaningful share of the Clippers’ 2021-22 schedule, offering backcourt defense and a second ball handler. He was not a long-term franchise star and eventually moved again in another multi-player agreement, but his receiving-team appearances were a genuine return from this transaction. The Clippers had to consider fit with Paul George and their other wing options, so the player’s role was narrower than his earlier Phoenix or Milwaukee years might suggest. His past All-Defensive recognition was background, not a new award earned for Los Angeles after August.

Memphis Moved Beverley Again and Did Not Keep Rondo

Memphis treated the package differently. Beverley arrived with immediate market value and was soon traded to Minnesota for Jarrett Culver and Juancho Hernangómez. That was a separate agreement, and Beverley’s Timberwolves playoff games did not occur in Memphis. Rondo was not retained as a long-term Grizzlies rotation guard, and Oturu failed to become a central frontcourt player there. The value on this side therefore came largely from the ability to reuse or clear incoming contracts rather than direct NBA games by all three players. Their prior Clippers appearances must remain attributed to Los Angeles.

Short-Term Contract Utility Decides the Close Call

Both organizations used the trade to manage depth rather than acquire their next franchise leader. Los Angeles obtained a playable guard for the current season, while Memphis recovered assets and options it could redistribute, most notably Beverley’s value in another negotiation. A close Clippers edge is justified by Bledsoe’s tangible service, without transferring all the benefits of his later move to the original agreement. Memphis earned some consideration for a useful contract package but not the inflated grade that would come from treating Beverley’s subsequent Minnesota period as a Grizzlies success.

Final Verdict

Slight Clippers Edge. Los Angeles earns B for Eric Bledsoe’s 2021-22 guard service and later contract mobility. Memphis receives C+ for obtaining Patrick Beverley, Rajon Rondo and Daniel Oturu, with Beverley quickly moved to Minnesota in a separate exchange. The later Wolves season and any additional players acquired by the Clippers in 2022 are not automatic direct returns from the August transaction.

boston-celtics.analysis:
New York Added Fournier in a Sign-and-Trade

New York completed a deal with Boston on August 17, 2021, to bring in Evan Fournier after agreeing to terms with the free-agent guard. The transaction also directed a conditional 2022 second-round selection and a separate 2023 second-round right toward the Knicks. Boston received cash and created a trade exception rather than taking back another established guard. Fournier had provided shooting and secondary creation during a brief Celtics spell the previous spring. The Knicks sought to make him a fuller part of their offense as they tried to build on a playoff appearance.

Fournier Supplied a Full First Season in New York

Fournier started all 80 games in which he appeared for the Knicks in 2021-22 and averaged 14.1 points while shooting 38.9 percent from three. Those figures provide an unmistakable receiving-team basketball return. He could space the floor and generate occasional offense, even though the team didn't achieve the consistent improvement hoped for from its new perimeter combination. His role contracted markedly in later seasons, limiting the longer-term success of the contract. Still, the first season alone gave New York far more court time than Boston obtained from the cash consideration in this particular exchange.

Boston Got Flexibility, Not a Replacement Shooter

The Celtics' direct listed compensation was cash, with a trade exception arising from the sign-and-trade structure. That flexibility could support later roster planning, but it is not another player who logged NBA appearances on the date of this exchange. Boston also parted with draft assets alongside Fournier. The protected 2022 component did not convey in its initial form, while the later second was associated with No. 41 in 2023, ultimately used on Amari Bailey. Treating Bailey's career as a Boston return would reverse the direction of that outgoing right.

A Real Knicks Shooting Season Outweighs the Contract Drawbacks

The signing proved less durable than New York initially hoped, and Fournier eventually fell out of the regular rotation. His contract also created an opportunity cost as the Knicks revised their backcourt. Nevertheless, the transaction delivered a full starting season and a high volume of made threes for the club that actually received him. Boston made a logical cap-management choice after Fournier's short stay, but its compensation did not replace those Knicks minutes. The trade's on-court value goes to New York, tempered by the later decline of his role.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win. New York earns B because Evan Fournier started 80 games and averaged 14.1 points in 2021-22, even though the contract's long-term value faded. Boston receives C+ for cash and sign-and-trade flexibility while sending conditional second-round rights away. memphis-grizzlies.analysis:
Minnesota Sought Beverley for Backcourt Defense

The August 25, 2021 transaction brought Patrick Beverley to Minnesota from Memphis in exchange for Jarrett Culver and Juancho Hernangómez. Beverley had been acquired by the Grizzlies in a different trade only days earlier, so this was effectively a quick redistribution of a veteran guard rather than the end of a long Memphis playing tenure. Minnesota wanted defensive intensity and experience alongside a developing roster built around Karl-Anthony Towns and Anthony Edwards. Memphis accepted two players who might fit different frontcourt and wing roles without receiving a new first-round selection.

Beverley Supplied Leadership and Playoff Minutes

Beverley played a meaningful role during Minnesota’s 2021-22 season and its return to the NBA playoffs. His aggressive defense and willingness to set a competitive tone added a veteran element to a young backcourt. That contribution was specific to the Timberwolves and should not be confused with his earlier Clippers reputation or his later stops after leaving Minnesota. A grade for the receiving club should use the fact that the guard played real, high-leverage games for the Wolves rather than assuming every passionate leadership story was itself a statistic.

Memphis Took Two Players Instead of a Current Guard

Memphis obtained Culver, a former Minnesota lottery selection trying to rebuild his role, and Hernangómez, a forward with shooting experience. Hernangómez did not become a long-term Grizzlies regular and was moved again, while Culver saw limited NBA opportunities in Memphis. The two incoming contracts created optionality in a transaction that did not require another premium pick, but their direct receiving-team production was not comparable to Beverley’s playoff involvement. Culver’s earlier Timberwolves games and Hernangómez’s time in other cities cannot be reassigned as Grizzlies minutes to improve the result.

The Wolves Received the Direct Basketball Payoff

Minnesota made the clearer basketball gain because the acquisition helped an actual playoff roster at a specific point in its development. Memphis avoided retaining an unwanted veteran and gathered two younger pieces, a reasonable strategy in the moment, but neither provided an equivalent long-term payoff with the team. The deal should not be credited with all of Minnesota’s improved performance or any future transactions that later sent Beverley elsewhere. The direct 2021-22 contribution is enough to sustain a strong Wolves verdict while permitting a modest grade for the Grizzlies’ roster flexibility.

Final Verdict

Wolves Win. Minnesota earns A- for Patrick Beverley’s defensive guard minutes and contribution to its 2022 playoff season. Memphis receives C for Jarrett Culver’s limited opportunity and the short-lived rights to Juancho Hernangómez, who moved again. Beverley’s prior Clippers years and Culver’s original Timberwolves tenure are excluded; the exchange is judged by what each receiving team actually obtained.

analysis: Cleveland acquired Lauri Markkanen in a sign-and-trade. Portland acquired Larry Nance Jr. Chicago received Derrick Jones Jr., a protected Cleveland second and Portland's lottery-protected first-round pick, which remained alive through multiple seasons before ultimately conveying. The deal redistributed three forwards with different contract situations and gave Chicago draft compensation for facilitating Markkanen's exit. Cleveland earns the narrow edge because Markkanen supplied useful size and shooting immediately and then remained valuable enough to become a central player component of the 2022 Donovan Mitchell trade. Cleveland cannot credit this 2021 move with the entire value of Mitchell because the later package also included Collin Sexton, Ochai Agbaji, multiple firsts and swaps. Jones contributed as a rotation athlete, and the Portland first remained protected for years before conveying as a mid-first-round selection in 2026. That delayed conversion rewarded the Bulls for insisting on draft value rather than letting Markkanen leave for nothing. Portland received one season of Nance and then included him in the 2022 C.J. McCollum trade with New Orleans, preserving some downstream value even though his direct Portland tenure was brief. Each team has a legitimate asset chain. Cleveland's Markkanen-to-Mitchell connection is the strongest, though it must be shared with the many other assets in that blockbuster. Portland's Nance-to-McCollum package is also directly tied but mixed with McCollum and Tony Snell, so only part of the later return belongs to Nance. Portland wanted a versatile defender for a win-now roster around Damian Lillard. No team made an irrational bet. The historical edge comes from how well Cleveland preserved Markkanen's value after his first season. Cleveland receives A for useful direct production and a strong role in the later Mitchell acquisition. Chicago earns A- for Jones plus a first-round pick that eventually conveyed. los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
Los Angeles Transferred Gasol and a Future Second

The Lakers sent veteran center Marc Gasol, cash consideration of approximately $250,000 and a 2024 second-round pick to Memphis on September 10, 2021. In return Los Angeles obtained the NBA draft rights to Chinese center Wang Zhelin, an overseas prospect who did not immediately join its rotation. Gasol's contract was the primary financial issue for the Lakers as the franchise rearranged its veteran roster. Memphis accepted both the veteran's obligation and a future draft asset, giving it flexibility even without expecting him to play a full new Grizzlies season.

Gasol's Return to Memphis Was Not a Second Long Tenure

Although Gasol had previously become one of the greatest players in Memphis franchise history, the 2021 transaction did not revive that earlier run. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston and Memphis Reshuffled Fringe Backcourt Pieces

Boston traded Kris Dunn and Carsen Edwards to Memphis in September 2021 for Juancho Hernangómez, with reciprocal rights involving a 2026 second-round pick swap included in the arrangement. The Celtics wanted another forward who could offer rebounding and positional flexibility, while the Grizzlies were balancing roster places ahead of camp. Dunn had already moved through several teams, and Edwards was seeking an opportunity to earn more guard minutes. This was an exchange of roster options rather than one involving established NBA starters.

Hernangómez Had a Short Celtics Assignment

Hernangómez arrived with experience playing forward for Denver and Minnesota, but that earlier résumé was not the immediate value Boston received. His Celtics stretch was brief and produced limited regular-season time before he was moved again. The club never built an enduring frontcourt partnership around him, and his later activity elsewhere cannot be counted toward Boston's return. The Celtics obtained another player to evaluate during a season of rotation decisions, but the trade didn't become an important driver of their on-court development.

Memphis Didn't Establish Either Guard as a Core Piece

Dunn had defensive strengths and prior point-guard experience, while Edwards offered shooting potential from a smaller guard position. Neither became a lasting feature of Memphis's primary rotation as a result of this transaction. The incoming guards were ultimately less important than the club's established backcourt, and the Grizzlies continued adjusting their depth. The 2026 pick-swap provisions are part of the recorded assets, but their specific eventual settlement requires separate source verification. They should not be converted into an invented Memphis draft selection.

The Equal Grade Reflects Limited Realized Impact

Boston obtained a forward for a short assessment, and Memphis took back guards whose immediate utility proved limited. Neither player package produced a clear long-term starter. The swap rights created a contractual possibility, but the visible basketball comparison offers little reason for a strong winner. The matching B- evaluations account for a sensible personnel exchange under ordinary roster constraints. An Even Trade result is more defensible than pretending either franchise acquired a new pillar of its rotation from these marginal pieces.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston and Memphis each earn B- for a modest roster exchange that delivered little sustained playing value. Juancho Hernangómez was only briefly with the Celtics; Kris Dunn and Carsen Edwards did not become long-term Grizzlies rotation players. The 2026 second-round swap terms are recognized without assigning an unverified final pick outcome to either organization.

perspectives.summary: Cleveland acquired Rajon Rondo from Los Angeles in a January 2022 three-team trade. The Lakers received Louis Labeyrie's draft rights from New York. The Knicks obtained Denzel Valentine from Cleveland and rights to Wang Zhelin and Brad Newley plus cash from the Lakers. perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Targeted an Experienced Backup After Injuries

The Cavaliers acquired Rajon Rondo from the Lakers in January 2022, seeking experienced ball handling during a season when guard injuries had depleted their rotation. Rondo had spent many years directing NBA offenses and working through difficult playoff possessions. He wasn't being acquired as the franchise's new offensive centerpiece, but he could help younger teammates organize lineups and manage possession decisions. Cleveland sent Denzel Valentine toward New York rather than replacing Rondo with another Lakers player in a simple two-club swap.

Los Angeles Received Overseas Draft Rights

The Lakers obtained draft rights to Louis Labeyrie from New York. Those were rights to a player selected in 2014, not an immediate new Lakers roster addition. Los Angeles had given Rondo limited minutes and could free a roster spot while preserving another option in its rights inventory. The exchange was primarily a practical roster management decision for a club trying to optimize its veteran rotation, which helps explain why the inherited B- grade is lower than Cleveland's B despite the Lakers obtaining a genuine asset.

New York Took Valentine, Two Rights and Cash

The Knicks received Denzel Valentine from Cleveland and rights to Wang Zhelin and Brad Newley plus cash considerations from the Lakers. The two international prospects had been drafted in earlier years, meaning New York gained negotiating rights, not NBA seasons already completed in its uniform. Valentine's deal created another roster decision, and he wasn't guaranteed a lengthy Knicks tenure simply because his contract passed through the transaction. The official Knicks announcement confirms the complete package that the original Cleveland-centered ledger had reduced to Valentine alone.

The Close Grades Reflect Different Kinds of Value

Cleveland and New York receive B under the inherited model, while Los Angeles gets B-. The Cavaliers acquired a recognizable veteran playmaker with a defined short-term need. New York assembled a broader set of rights and financial compensation, and the Lakers opened a roster place while obtaining Labeyrie's rights. This isn't evidence that all three clubs received equivalent immediate on-court talent. The slight Cavaliers edge follows Rondo's fit on an injury-affected roster, not a claim that he began another championship-caliber prime.

Final Verdict

Slight Cavaliers Edge. Cleveland earns B for Rajon Rondo's experienced backup guard play during an injury-affected season. New York receives B for Denzel Valentine, Wang Zhelin and Brad Newley's rights and cash. Los Angeles gets B- for Louis Labeyrie's rights and roster flexibility. The official three-team agreement included real incoming assets for every team, though overseas rights don't guarantee future NBA production.

oklahoma-city-thunder.analysis:
The Jazz Transferred Oni and a Future Pick to Oklahoma City

Utah traded guard Miye Oni and a future 2028 second-round selection to Oklahoma City on January 4, 2022, receiving cash in return. The Thunder were collecting potential draft assets during a long-term roster rebuild, while Utah had greater immediate pressure to manage a competitive team and its roster obligations. Oni had already spent time as a Jazz reserve before the deal but was not arriving in Oklahoma City as an established high-volume scorer. The incoming second was a future opportunity, not a known NBA player or an unrestricted first-round pick, and the cash moved to Utah rather than in the other direction.

Oni Did Not Become a Regular Thunder Guard

Oni's NBA playing history with Utah was part of his earlier contract, not basketball production newly purchased by Oklahoma City. The Thunder acquired his contract as part of the asset structure and did not develop him into a long-serving rotation guard. This distinction is important because simply listing his name as incoming could misleadingly imply meaningful Thunder playing time. The transaction's potential basketball value lay mostly in the attached 2028 second-round position and the team's freedom to handle the contract as needed. Later roster decisions involving Oni were separate steps rather than a guarantee of future output.

Utah Chose Immediate Financial Consideration

The Jazz received cash and could reduce a player or contract obligation at a time when they were concentrating on their current rotation. That financial return was real even without an incoming draft prospect, and the original transaction wasn't a straight trade for nothing. However, it also required surrendering a future second-round right that could be used or transferred later. The actual 2028 draft is necessary to establish the resulting pick position and any player associated with the right. Assigning an invented player to Oklahoma City now would distort the evaluation, just as assigning Oni's earlier Jazz games to the Thunder would.

Draft Flexibility Supports Only a Small Thunder Edge

The Thunder gained a future draft option and a veteran contract they could address within their rebuilding plan, while Utah received immediate cash and roster relief. The inherited strong Oklahoma City grade overstates the assured result because the pick had not produced a documented future player and Oni supplied no established Thunder rotation contribution. A modest edge is more appropriate for the team that gained possible draft utility at a limited current cost. Utah should retain credit for the economic objective it achieved, and neither side can claim star performances through this low-profile agreement.

Final Verdict

Oklahoma City Thunder Win by a limited draft-flexibility edge. The Thunder receive B- for the future 2028 second-round right and an incoming Miye Oni contract that did not become a lasting Oklahoma City NBA rotation role. Utah earns C+ for cash and roster flexibility. The future pick isn't assigned an unverified draftee, and Oni's earlier Jazz games remain Utah history.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Exchanged Hernangómez for Two Injured Players

The Celtics acquired Bol Bol and P.J. Dozier from Denver in January 2022, sending Juancho Hernangómez and cash to San Antonio. Boston was operating under financial and roster constraints as the trade deadline approached. Bol had foot surgery planned, and Dozier was recovering from an ACL injury, so neither acquisition should be portrayed as an instant frontcourt or wing upgrade. The transaction created roster flexibility while allowing Boston to assess the value of two player contracts before further deadline decisions.

Denver Added Shooting Through Bryn Forbes

The Nuggets received Bryn Forbes from San Antonio, a rotation guard with an established reputation as a three-point shooter. Forbes had hit more than forty percent of his attempts from beyond the arc during portions of his NBA career and could support Denver's offense without monopolizing possessions. The club surrendered Bol, Dozier and a protected second-round selection along with cash considerations. Its aim was a more immediate bench shooting option, while Boston accepted injured players and the Spurs received a flexible package.

San Antonio Obtained Hernangómez, Cash and a Future Pick

The Spurs received Hernangómez and cash from Boston, as well as a protected 2028 second-round pick and additional cash from Denver. San Antonio's official transaction announcement independently identifies both cash directions, which makes them more than an inferred balancing entry. Hernangómez had played limited games for Boston that season but offered some rebounding and forward depth. The second-round right could eventually acquire a prospect or be traded again, though it wasn't a player San Antonio could use during the 2022 playoff chase.

The Three Equal Grades Represent Different Objectives

The inherited B grades for Boston, Denver and San Antonio reflect different practical returns. Boston gained roster-management options through Bol and Dozier, Denver acquired Forbes's actual shooting profile, and San Antonio collected a veteran forward, cash and future rights. Both injured incoming Celtics players were later included in a separate trade with Orlando, so crediting their subsequent Magic playing time to Boston would distort this move's direct result. The equal grades are more defensible with the complete three-team ledger than with the original missing Denver return.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston earns B for obtaining Bol Bol and P.J. Dozier as roster assets despite their injuries. Denver receives B for Bryn Forbes's bench shooting, and San Antonio earns B for Juancho Hernangómez, a protected 2028 second-round right and cash from two teams. The official league and Spurs records confirm the full three-party return, not an empty Nuggets package.

los-angeles-clippers.summary: The Clippers won the 2022 Portland deal by acquiring Norman Powell and Robert Covington for a package led by Eric Bledsoe, Justise Winslow, Keon Johnson and a second-round pick.
los-angeles-clippers.analysis: Norman Powell became the centerpiece of this win. He provided multiple seasons of high-level scoring and later retained enough value to become part of another meaningful Clippers transaction, while Robert Covington added useful two-way depth. Portland received Eric Bledsoe, Justise Winslow, Keon Johnson and draft compensation, but the realized production from that package did not match what Los Angeles received. The displayed team grades for LA Clippers and Portland Trail Blazers reflect the realized value of the players, draft assets and transaction context that ultimately materialized.
los-angeles-clippers.gradeRationale: Los Angeles acquired Norman Powell and Robert Covington for Eric Bledsoe, Justise Winslow, Keon Johnson and a second. Powell became a major scorer and later another trade asset, creating a clear value win.

portland-trail-blazers.summary: On February 4, 2022, Portland acquired Eric Bledsoe; Justise Winslow; Keon Johnson; 2025 second round pick (Pistons pick) (#47-Bogoljub Markovic) from Los Angeles Clippers in exchange for Norman Powell; Robert Covington.
portland-trail-blazers.analysis: The Blazers’ incoming side was Eric Bledsoe and additional draft assets; the outgoing side was Norman Powell and additional consideration. The deal’s realized value separated sharply against Portland once the core assets were resolved. The full transaction history therefore supports a clear partner win.

summary: Clippers Win: The trade has aged as one of the clearest talent-for-flexibility swaps of the early 2020s. Portland can defend the financial logic, especially the repeater-tax reset, but financial logic is not the same as equal trade value. Los Angeles got multiple seasons of high-end scoring, useful Covington minutes and a still-movable Powell contract. That is a decisive basketball return.
analysis: Los Angeles received by far the strongest realized player value. Powell became one of the league's most efficient high-volume secondary scorers, remained productive through multiple seasons and reached a career-best 21.8 points per game in 2024-25. Covington supplied versatile defense and shooting before later leaving in another trade. Powell then retained enough value to be moved in 2025 as part of the three-team transaction that brought John Collins to the Clippers. Portland achieved its financial objective but received little direct basketball return. Bledsoe never played for the Blazers, Winslow's tenure was limited by injuries, Johnson did not develop into a long-term rotation piece, and the 2025 second-round pick became Bogoljub Markovic. The cap savings were real and helped reset the repeater-tax clock, so the deal should not be graded as if Portland received literally nothing. The Clippers' value chain remained alive after Powell's best season. In July 2025, Los Angeles sent Powell into a three-team deal and received John Collins from Utah while also sending a second-round pick. Collins required an additional asset and a third team, so his full future value should not be credited to the 2022 trade, but Powell's ability to anchor that exchange shows the original acquisition retained market value.

perspectives.analysis: The balance tilts away from Cleveland without becoming a major loss. Cleveland received Caris LeVert and 2022 second round pick (#56-Luke Travers) and sent Ricky Rubio, 2022 second round pick (#31-Andrew Nembhard), draft picks (first round pick protected top 14 in 2022-23, else 2025 second round pick, 2026 second round pick) (2023 #26-Ben Sheppard) and 2027 second round pick (outcome pending). The outgoing side produced somewhat greater long-term utility, though Cleveland still obtained legitimate rotation, draft or financial value and avoided a franchise-level loss. perspectives.analysis: The LeVert trade produced useful value for both sides. Cleveland received a proven scorer in Caris LeVert plus the second-round pick that became Luke Travers. Indiana received Ricky Rubio's contract, the No. 31 pick used on Andrew Nembhard, the draft mechanism that yielded Ben Sheppard and an additional future second-round pick whose outcome remains pending. Nembhard and Sheppard became important rotation players for Indiana's next contender, while LeVert contributed in Cleveland. The completed Cavaliers evaluation supports a B+ Pacers grade versus C+ for Cleveland, making this a Slight Pacers Edge rather than a runaway win.

indiana-pacers.analysis: Indiana received the higher-end long-term outcome because Haliburton became an All-NBA lead guard and the offensive engine of teams that reached the 2024 Eastern Conference finals and 2025 NBA Finals. Sacramento also succeeded: Sabonis became an All-NBA center, formed a productive partnership with De'Aaron Fox, and helped end a sixteen-year playoff drought. The Kings therefore deserve an A-minus rather than a middling grade. Haliburton's age, positional value and Finals-level ceiling give Indiana the narrow separation, making Slight Pacers Edge more accurate than a broad Pacers Win.

miami-heat.analysis:
Miami Restructured a First-Round Obligation With Oklahoma City

The February 9, 2022 transaction sent forward K.Z. Okpala and a revised first-round draft obligation from Miami to Oklahoma City. In return, the Heat gained greater flexibility around a 2023 first-round selection and an associated 2026 second-round right. This was fundamentally a pick-protection and obligation restructuring, not a straightforward exchange of two already drafted players. The outgoing protected first later appears in the 2025 draft lineage as No. 15 Thomas Sorber. Meanwhile, Miami retained the freedom to use its 2023 No. 18 choice, eventually selecting Jaime Jaquez Jr. The timing of those different drafts is central to evaluating the deal.

The Heat's Draft Flexibility Produced Jaquez

Miami used the 2023 eighteenth selection on Jaquez, who provided immediate wing and forward minutes as a rookie. His NBA play was real value to the Heat, although the underlying first-round position also depended on their existing team record and the terms of the obligation before it was amended. The trade didn't magically create an extra first-round pick; it changed which years were available and which liability remained outstanding. The second-round piece later passed through additional transactions associated with the Max Strus sign-and-trade, so its future draft identity cannot automatically be treated as another Miami roster contributor.

Oklahoma City Converted Future Protection Into a Pick

The Thunder received Okpala's contract and the altered right to a Miami first-round selection, which eventually conveyed in the 2025 draft as the fifteenth choice associated with Sorber. Okpala didn't become a long-term Oklahoma City rotation figure through this agreement, so the important value was the pick obligation and its eventual resolution. The 2025 selection was genuine draft capital, not an invented future lottery asset beyond what Miami had promised. The difference between lottery-protected and later unprotected years affected the risk both teams accepted when they restructured the arrangement.

Both Clubs Benefited From Different Draft Timing

The Heat retained an earlier first-round opportunity that became a useful NBA player in Jaquez, while Oklahoma City eventually obtained a later first-round selection for its developing roster. That makes the deal more balanced than a simple declaration that one club gave away its draft future. Miami receives a narrow edge based on already observed Jaquez production, not because the 2025 Thunder selection lacked value. The transaction also allowed both front offices to clarify their pick obligations for other roster decisions. Each later player must be credited to the team that actually acquired and used the draft right.

Final Verdict

Slight Heat Edge. Miami receives B+ for securing draft-year flexibility that allowed use of its 2023 No. 18 pick on Jaime Jaquez Jr., a genuine Heat contributor. Oklahoma City earns B for the modified first-round obligation eventually associated with 2025 No. 15 Thomas Sorber. Okpala's brief contractual presence and later second-round rights are treated distinctly from the main pick-protection adjustment.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Orlando Took a Chance on Two Reserve Players

The Magic acquired Bol Bol, P.J. Dozier, cash and a conditional 2028 second-round right from Boston at the February 2022 deadline. The Celtics received a conditional 2023 second-round selection that ultimately did not convey. Boston was adjusting the bottom of its roster and its salary obligations during a wider deadline reshuffle. Orlando, which was prioritizing young-player development, had more room to evaluate a tall skilled prospect such as Bol without requiring him to become an immediate starting center.

Bol Eventually Became an Active Orlando Contributor

Bol's move did not produce an immediate healthy run, but he later logged meaningful NBA minutes for Orlando, displaying an unusual combination of height, ball handling and finishing ability. His Magic playing time belongs to the receiving team and provides a clear point of comparison with Boston's outcome. Dozier's contribution to Orlando was much smaller, so the successful portion of the package centered on Bol. His earlier Denver appearances and later career elsewhere should remain distinct from the Magic development period.

Boston Received No Realized Selection From the Condition

The conditional 2023 second-round asset did not convert into an incoming Celtics pick under the recorded terms. Boston's benefit was therefore largely the financial and roster effect of moving the two players and associated obligations, not a drafted prospect who later performed for the club. The Celtics had other deadline trades that reshaped their rotation; those separate incoming veterans should not be attributed to this Orlando transaction. The Magic also received a conditional future right whose eventual resolution has to be traced independently.

Orlando Gained More Direct Playing Value

The Magic obtained a young big who proved capable of taking real NBA minutes for them, while the Celtics received no conveyed pick and moved on from reserve roster spots. Boston's desire for flexibility was understandable for a contender, but it produced less readily measurable basketball value here. Orlando's gamble had a positive playing outcome without requiring Bol to become an All-Star. The inherited grade gap reflects the difference between an active developmental contributor and an unexercised conditional selection.

Final Verdict

Magic Win. Orlando receives B+ for acquiring Bol Bol, who later played useful Magic minutes, along with P.J. Dozier and conditional future compensation. Boston earns C- because its conditional 2023 second-round right never conveyed and the benefit was primarily roster flexibility. Bol's actual Orlando playing time supplied the clearest direct basketball value from this trade.

Dinwiddie supplied useful Mavericks guard scoring during their 2022 conference-finals run, while Porziņģis produced a strong 2022-23 Wizards season. washington-wizards.analysis:
Dallas Ended Its Porziņģis Experiment at the Deadline

On February 10, 2022, the Mavericks sent Kristaps Porziņģis and a 2022 second-round selection to Washington for Spencer Dinwiddie and Davis Bertans. Dallas had been looking for a more dependable offensive balance around Luka Dončić, while Porziņģis had struggled to provide the expected pairing because of changing roles and health interruptions. The Wizards received a skilled scoring big man capable of protecting the rim and shooting from distance. Dallas took two veterans whose immediate use depended on how well they fit the guard and forward rotation.

Dinwiddie Helped Dallas in a Deep Playoff Run

Dinwiddie gave the Mavericks another capable ball handler and scorer, providing important minutes as the club reached the 2022 Western Conference Finals. He could attack as a secondary creator without requiring every offensive possession to run directly through Dončić. Bertans gave the team an outside-shooting option, but his contribution was narrower and more intermittent. That success matters when judging Dallas's compensation: the outgoing center was not exchanged for two players who supplied nothing. Dinwiddie was a genuine contributor to a particularly successful Mavericks postseason.

Porziņģis Became a Productive Wizards Center

Porziņģis returned to a prominent offensive role in Washington and enjoyed a strong 2022-23 season, averaging more than twenty points per game while supplying interior length and perimeter shooting. His contribution gave the Wizards a major frontcourt player they otherwise lacked. The club later moved him to Boston in a separate transaction, so his Celtics championship career cannot be credited to Washington's return from Dallas. The second-round asset added another possible benefit, but the main player was easily the defining part of Washington's package.

The Trade Had Different Successful Outcomes

Washington obtained the most accomplished individual incoming talent, and his strong season gives substance to the higher grade. Dallas, though, reshuffled its attack in a way that contributed to a conference-finals trip, largely through Dinwiddie's fit. The Wizards Win verdict is therefore not a claim that Dinwiddie failed or that the Mavericks had no reason to move Porziņģis. It credits Washington's larger long-term talent return while acknowledging that Dallas extracted real short-term playoff utility from the exchange.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns A for a productive Kristaps Porziņģis tenure and an additional second-round asset. Dallas receives C, even though Spencer Dinwiddie provided useful 2022 playoff scoring and Davis Bertans filled a narrower shooting role. The Wizards obtained the better individual talent return, while the Mavericks' successful postseason fit prevents the swap from being a complete Dallas failure.

boston-celtics.analysis:
The Celtics Reacquired a Familiar Frontcourt Defender

Boston reacquired Daniel Theis from Houston at the February 10, 2022 trade deadline. The Rockets received Dennis Schröder, Enes Freedom and Bruno Fernando, creating an exchange of one rotation big man for three contracts with different playing prospects. Theis had previously played multiple seasons for the Celtics, so Brad Stevens' front office understood his defensive habits and role. Boston was preparing for a postseason push under Ime Udoka. Houston pursued contract flexibility and potential short-term guard help during a rebuild rather than needing Theis as a veteran starter.

Theis Supplied Actual Postseason Center Minutes

Theis quickly joined Boston's frontcourt mix and gave the coaching staff another player who understood its defensive rotations. During the Celtics' 2022 run to the NBA Finals, he was available as a reserve option and helped absorb minutes when injuries or foul situations affected the main rotation. The team did not acquire a new primary offensive scorer, and his contribution was smaller than the work of Jayson Tatum, Jaylen Brown or Robert Williams III. Yet the incoming player's usefulness was real. His previous Boston seasons should not be double-counted as output generated by the 2022 reacquisition.

Houston's Incoming Contracts Had Uneven Outcomes

Schröder provided Houston some veteran guard minutes following his departure from Boston, but he did not become a long-term starting centerpiece. Freedom was released rather than producing an extended Rockets playing stint. Fernando could supply frontcourt depth in the organization's developmental timeline, although his later NBA moves need to be judged on their own terms. The three-player return provided personnel options and salary flexibility, but treating it as three fully realized rotation contributors would be inaccurate. Houston was trading a veteran who no longer matched its competitive timetable for multiple possible uses of roster space.

A Familiar Fit Helped Boston More Than a Three-Contract Return

Boston's advantage came from Theis contributing to a Finals-bound team when the club specifically needed reliable backup size. Houston wasn't attempting to win that postseason with the newly obtained veterans, and should receive reasonable credit for turning Theis into several roster and contract choices. Still, Boston realized more direct high-leverage basketball value from its incoming player. The trade wasn't the sole reason the Celtics reached the Finals, and the grade shouldn't claim that Theis alone solved their defense. Keeping the distinct transaction histories for Freedom and Fernando avoids inventing playing contributions.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns B+ for reacquiring Daniel Theis and obtaining meaningful frontcourt depth during its 2022 Finals run. Houston receives C+ for Dennis Schröder's guard minutes, Bruno Fernando's developmental value and the flexibility of the incoming contracts; Enes Freedom was released without becoming a Rockets regular. Previous Theis Celtics seasons aren't counted as new trade output.

perspectives.summary: Detroit acquired Marvin Bagley III from Sacramento in the February 2022 four-team trade. The Kings received Donte DiVincenzo, Josh Jackson, Trey Lyles and David Michineau rights. Milwaukee acquired Serge Ibaka, second-round rights and cash. The Clippers obtained Rodney Hood, Semi Ojeleye and Vanja Marinković rights. The inherited slight Kings edge grades Sacramento B, Milwaukee B-, Detroit C and the Clippers C.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Took a Developmental Chance on Bagley

The Pistons acquired Marvin Bagley III from Sacramento, wagering that the former No. 2 selection could have a more productive role away from the Kings. His interior finishing and rebounding potential made him an appealing young frontcourt player, but injuries and uneven playing time had limited his earlier progress. Detroit gave up Josh Jackson, Trey Lyles and a second-round right as part of the wider deal. The purpose was to evaluate Bagley's future fit, not to acquire an already established top-tier center.

Sacramento Combined a Guard With Two Forwards and Rights

The Kings received Donte DiVincenzo from Milwaukee, Jackson and Lyles from Detroit, plus the draft rights to David Michineau from the Clippers. DiVincenzo had contributed to Milwaukee's championship-era rotation before injury, while Lyles offered size and outside shooting. Jackson supplied another wing option. Michineau's rights were a distinct international asset rather than a guaranteed active Sacramento player. The package provided the Kings with several roster and rights possibilities in return for a prospect whose Sacramento tenure had become difficult to sustain.

Milwaukee and Los Angeles Exchanged Veteran Depth

The Bucks obtained Serge Ibaka from the Clippers, cash from Los Angeles and future second-round selections, including one already recorded from Detroit and another from Sacramento. Ibaka's shot-blocking history and championship experience offered a veteran interior option. Los Angeles received Rodney Hood and Semi Ojeleye from Milwaukee plus Sacramento's rights to Vanja Marinković. Neither side exchanged a star entering his prime, but both obtained measurable assets. The original Detroit-only ledger had omitted the Clippers' entire return and much of Milwaukee's.

The Kings Grade Favors Multiple Immediate Options

Sacramento receives B under the inherited ranking, Milwaukee B-, and Detroit and the Clippers C. The Kings' collection of three usable NBA players plus rights explains their narrow lead, while the Bucks addressed frontcourt experience around a contending roster. Detroit's C reflects Bagley's uncertain ceiling and the price of testing it. The Clippers' C recognizes a smaller and more speculative return. The transaction should not be evaluated as Bagley for Jackson alone, because the other two teams had meaningful roles.

Final Verdict

Slight Kings Edge. Sacramento earns B for Donte DiVincenzo, Josh Jackson, Trey Lyles and David Michineau's rights. Milwaukee gets B- for Serge Ibaka, two future second-round rights and cash. Detroit receives C for Marvin Bagley III, while the Clippers earn C for Rodney Hood, Semi Ojeleye and Vanja Marinković's rights. The Kings obtained the broadest current player package in the verified four-team trade.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Moved Back Seven Picks and Took Cash

The Hawks used the 2022 draft to exchange the rights to No. 44 Ryan Rollins for the rights to No. 51 Tyrese Martin and cash from Golden State. The deal was struck on June 23 and described in Atlanta's early-June-24 draft release. Both players were college guards, with Rollins offering a scoring profile and Martin bringing rebounding and physicality from the wing. Golden State spent cash to choose earlier; Atlanta accepted a later pick and financial compensation. Neither party was acquiring an established NBA starter at this stage of the draft.

Martin Received a Short Hawks Audition

Martin appeared in 16 regular-season games for the Hawks in 2022-23, playing only a small number of minutes. His strongest work came as a developmental prospect rather than a consistent Atlanta rotation contributor. The receiving club nonetheless got an actual player it could evaluate in NBA competition, plus the cash included in the draft-rights exchange. Martin's 16 appearances shouldn't be inflated into a long-term solution at the wing. The value of the move for Atlanta rests as much on extracting a cash return from the small move down as on the immediate performance of its second-round selection.

Rollins Had Twelve Warriors Games Before Surgery

Golden State signed Rollins and gave him a limited NBA opportunity, but he played only 12 regular-season games as a rookie before undergoing foot surgery. He averaged 1.9 points in 5.2 minutes across those appearances. Those numbers document a genuine, though very small, Warriors return. His subsequent moves and later play for Milwaukee cannot be counted toward Golden State's original 2022 transaction. The Warriors paid to choose earlier in the second round but did not receive an enduring rotation guard from the pick while he was with that franchise.

Cash Made the Hawks' Return More Reliable

The two guards produced comparably brief first-franchise playing résumés, so this deal is more about the additional consideration and what each team hoped to develop. Atlanta received Martin and cash for dropping seven positions, while Golden State assumed the downside of paying to move up for Rollins. The Hawks' return was modest but included value that did not depend on the guard becoming a regular. The Warriors' acquisition didn't yield much on-court help. That contrast supports the configured Hawks advantage without claiming either player became a franchise-changing prospect in his receiving city.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta earns B for extracting cash and the rights to Tyrese Martin while moving seven spots down; Martin appeared in 16 Hawks games. Golden State receives D because Ryan Rollins logged only 12 brief Warriors appearances before injury interrupted his rookie season. Later production with other franchises is outside this trade's receiving-team return, leaving Atlanta with the sturdier package.

perspectives.summary: Charlotte received a package of future first- and second-round draft rights from New York in a June 2022 draft-rights exchange for the rights to Jalen Duren. The package later linked to selections including Nick Smith Jr., Mouhamed Gueye, Amari Bailey, Jaylen Clark and Cam Spencer. Duren's rights continued through additional moves rather than producing Knicks center minutes. The inherited Knicks Win grades New York B+ and Charlotte D+.
perspectives.analysis:
Charlotte Collected Multiple Future Selections

The Hornets acquired a protected first-round right connected to Denver and several second-round selection rights in a June 2022 exchange with New York. The Knicks received the rights to Jalen Duren, a young center prospect selected in the lottery. Charlotte preferred to distribute the value across several possible later drafts rather than retain that single top prospect. The first-round obligation carried protection conditions, so its exact outcome depended on later standings and rights movements.

The Pick Package Produced Several Named Draft Links

Charlotte's incoming rights became associated with selections such as No. 27 Nick Smith Jr., No. 39 Mouhamed Gueye, No. 41 Amari Bailey, No. 53 Jaylen Clark and another later No. 53 Cam Spencer. Those names describe a draft-rights chain, not an assertion that every player spent his NBA career with the Hornets. Some prospects were retained, while others moved through separate agreements. The package's value depended on those decisions and the players' later development.

The Knicks Controlled Duren's Rights, Not His Career

Duren had the physical traits of a potential NBA starting center, giving New York an identifiable high-end prospect right. However, the Knicks did not simply add multiple seasons of Duren's eventual NBA production to their own roster. His rights moved in subsequent transactions and he developed with another franchise. The inherited New York advantage must therefore reflect the leverage and trade value of acquiring his rights, not imaginary Knicks games or points.

Both Grades Should Be Read Through Rights Movements

New York receives B+ for obtaining the rights to a lottery-level center, while Charlotte's D+ is a relatively low inherited grade for a substantial multi-pick package. That difference requires caution because the Hornets did secure genuine later selections. The outcome shouldn't be simplified into Duren producing directly for New York while Charlotte received nothing. The meaningful comparison is the trade value of Duren's rights against the set of protected and lower-round options.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win. New York earns B+ under the inherited evaluation for obtaining Jalen Duren's high-value draft rights, subsequently moved in another transaction rather than converted into Knicks center minutes. Charlotte gets D+ for multiple protected and second-round assets linked to Nick Smith Jr. and other later picks. The label reflects rights leverage, not a claim that Duren's later NBA production belonged to New York.

indiana-pacers.analysis:
Milwaukee Purchased an Overseas Prospect's Draft Rights

The June 23, 2022 draft produced a small transaction between Indiana and Milwaukee. The Bucks obtained the rights to French guard Hugo Besson, the fifty-eighth overall choice, with the Pacers receiving approximately $1 million in cash consideration. Neither club was dealing an established NBA contract or sacrificing a protected first-round pick. Milwaukee was making a low-cost developmental bet on a prospect who had shown scoring ability abroad. Indiana chose guaranteed cash instead of occupying a future-rights slot with another second-round player.

The Draft-Rights Investment Had a Longer Horizon

Besson's immediate path was overseas rather than straight into Milwaukee's NBA rotation. The Bucks could retain the selected player's rights while he continued his professional career elsewhere, but rights alone were not equivalent to NBA contributions. That distinction limits the value of the acquisition. A later NBA appearance with another organization, if any, should not be automatically awarded to Milwaukee unless it actually occurred under a Bucks contract. The team accepted uncertainty for the possibility of an inexpensive player arriving after further development.

Indiana Converted a Late Choice Into Certain Cash

The Pacers' side was a straightforward financial return from one of the last picks in the draft. Receiving roughly $1 million let Indiana turn a speculative No. 58 selection into immediate resources without allocating a roster position to the incoming prospect. The money did not score points or create an additional draft choice, yet it was tangible consideration at the trade's completion. Indiana had its own collection of young players to evaluate, and cash could be used to support that broader program rather than creating a new future pick obligation.

Neither Club Acquired an Established Rotation Player

This exchange should not be graded as if Milwaukee acquired a proven guard who began scoring immediately, nor as if Indiana received nothing because its compensation was financial. The Bucks controlled a draft-rights prospect with potential but no immediate on-court return; the Pacers obtained certainty. The inherited Milwaukee-winning verdict depended on projected development, whereas Indiana received documented cash immediately. The practical edge belongs to the Pacers unless Bucks NBA playing production materializes from the rights. A moderate verdict better fits an end-of-draft transaction than an aggressive grade based on an imagined completed NBA career.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win. Indiana earns B- for receiving approximately $1 million in cash when it sold the No. 58 draft rights to Hugo Besson. Milwaukee gets C+ for a speculative international prospect whose rights had not generated established Bucks NBA rotation production. Indiana's guaranteed payment was a more concrete result than an unrealized development possibility; no subsequent unrelated NBA career is assigned to Milwaukee.
