los-angeles-lakers.analysis:
The Lakers Bought the Thirty-Fifth Pick From Orlando

Los Angeles acquired the thirty-fifth overall choice in the June 23, 2022 NBA draft from Orlando and used it on Michigan State guard Max Christie. The Magic obtained approximately $2.15 million in cash and a future 2028 second-round selection, subject to which of two associated picks would be more favorable. This was not an established NBA player swap. The Lakers wanted to take a chance on a young perimeter defender and shooter; Orlando converted an early-second-round slot into financial compensation and another chance in a later draft.

Christie Developed Into a Usable Los Angeles Guard

Christie entered the Lakers organization as a teenage second-round prospect and earned opportunities across multiple seasons. His responsibilities included learning to defend opposing guards, spacing the floor and contributing to lineups centered on LeBron James and Anthony Davis. Progress was not immediate or linear, but the club secured actual NBA minutes from a selected player at a modest draft cost. His later move to another franchise is part of a subsequent agreement and cannot erase the service Los Angeles received. Nor should any future team production be projected backward as more Lakers games.

Orlando Received Cash and a Conditional Future Asset

The Magic's incoming compensation included a specified cash amount and a 2028 second-round selection tied to the favorable position of eligible picks. That future asset had tradable value without guaranteeing a particular athlete or playing season for Orlando. Because the choice was years away, assigning an eventual player or NBA performance prematurely would distort the historical record. Orlando was also managing a deep collection of young prospects at the time of the 2022 draft. Selling the No. 35 choice was an understandable roster and resource decision even though the Lakers later realized a more tangible basketball return.

Low Draft Cost and Real Playing Time Favor Los Angeles

The deal illustrates how teams can value the same draft slot differently. The Lakers identified Christie, signed him and developed him into a rotation option, while Orlando preferred cash and deferred draft flexibility. Neither side surrendered a first-round selection, and an exaggerated championship-level score for the agreement alone would be inappropriate. Nevertheless, demonstrated NBA contributions from Christie carry greater weight than a future conditional right whose player outcome cannot yet be established. Orlando deserves credit for the guaranteed payment and the asset, but Los Angeles had the clearer on-court benefit over the first seasons after the swap.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns A- because the purchased No. 35 pick became Max Christie, who logged real rotation minutes for the franchise. Orlando receives C+ for roughly $2.15 million and the future 2028 second-round right. Any later Christie seasons outside Los Angeles and the eventual identity of the Magic's conditional future selection are not invented as direct trade returns.

new-york-knicks.analysis:
The Thunder Chose Dieng Over Multiple Future Rights

Oklahoma City acquired the draft rights to Ousmane Dieng during the 2022 NBA Draft, sending New York a package of conditional future first- and second-round choices. Dieng was an athletic young forward whose long-term development appealed to a Thunder team building around versatile talent. The Knicks took a different strategy, preferring the ability to use several selection rights in later drafts or move them to other clubs.

New York's Assets Had Different Protections

The incoming package included rights originating with Denver, Detroit and Washington, each carrying its own conditions. Some future picks would convey as first-round selections only if the protection requirements were met; otherwise later seconds or other outcomes could follow. Rights connected in later draft records with names such as Nick Smith Jr., Joan Beringer and Bruce Thornton did not automatically mean those players became Knicks rotation contributors. Additional pick transfers were relevant to the actual return.

Oklahoma City Received a Specific Player to Develop

Dieng offered length and ball-handling potential at forward, making him a prospect the Thunder could evaluate within an existing youth-focused development program. His NBA outcome couldn't be assumed from draft slot alone. That player-specific bet contrasted with New York's broader but more complicated package of draft obligations. Either approach could eventually pay off, but a drafted player's future belongs to the franchise where he actually plays rather than the team that once held his rights.

The Inherited Knicks Grade Rewards Flexibility

New York's A compared with Oklahoma City's B- values the number of future options acquired in exchange for one prospect. The grade should not erase the risk that protected rights fail to convey in their initially advertised form. The Thunder gained a clear player to develop, while the Knicks gained several pieces that could be useful in future deals. The historical decision is about multiple conditional choices versus a specific young forward.

Final Verdict

Knicks Win. New York earns A for multiple protected future first- and second-round rights tied to Denver, Detroit and Washington, creating valuable options with differing conveyance conditions. analysis:
The Thunder Chose Dieng Over Multiple Future Rights

Oklahoma City acquired the draft rights to Ousmane Dieng during the 2022 NBA Draft, sending New York a package of conditional future first- and second-round choices. Dieng was an athletic young forward whose long-term development appealed to a Thunder team building around versatile talent. The Knicks took a different strategy, preferring the ability to use several selection rights in later drafts or move them to other clubs.

New York's Assets Had Different Protections

The incoming package included rights originating with Denver, Detroit and Washington, each carrying its own conditions. Some future picks would convey as first-round selections only if the protection requirements were met; otherwise later seconds or other outcomes could follow. Rights connected in later draft records with names such as Nick Smith Jr., Joan Beringer and Bruce Thornton did not automatically mean those players became Knicks rotation contributors. Additional pick transfers were relevant to the actual return.

Oklahoma City Received a Specific Player to Develop

Dieng offered length and ball-handling potential at forward, making him a prospect the Thunder could evaluate within an existing youth-focused development program. His NBA outcome couldn't be assumed from draft slot alone. That player-specific bet contrasted with New York's broader but more complicated package of draft obligations. Either approach could eventually pay off, but a drafted player's future belongs to the franchise where he actually plays rather than the team that once held his rights.

The grade should not erase the risk that protected rights fail to convey in their initially advertised form. The Thunder gained a clear player to develop, while the Knicks gained several pieces that could be useful in future deals. The historical decision is about multiple conditional choices versus a specific young forward.

summary: Atlanta acquired Dejounte Murray and Jock Landale from San Antonio on June 30, 2022 for Danilo Gallinari, Charlotte's protected first, Atlanta's unprotected 2025 and 2027 firsts, and a 2026 first-round swap. Murray gave the Hawks two productive seasons but the Young-Murray pairing never advanced beyond the 2023 first round, and Landale was moved for cash days later. San Antonio turned the package into No. 14 Carter Bryant in 2025, No. 20 Jayden Quaintance through the exercised 2026 swap, retained the unprotected 2027 Atlanta first, and used the Charlotte asset in the 2025 De'Aaron Fox trade.
analysis:
The Exchange
Atlanta's and San Antonio's official releases agree on the core deal: the Hawks received Dejounte Murray and Jock Landale; the Spurs received Danilo Gallinari, a protected Charlotte first, Atlanta's unprotected 2025 and 2027 first-round picks, and the right to swap 2026 firsts. That package looked expensive in 2022 and has become easier to value because two of the Atlanta-controlled draft mechanisms have now converted into actual Spurs selections.

Atlanta Return
Murray was productive. He played 74 games in 2022-23 and 78 in 2023-24, averaging 20.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 6.1 assists in his first Hawks season and 22.5 points, 5.3 rebounds and 6.4 assists in his second. Atlanta reached the 2023 playoffs but lost to Boston in the first round, then lost in the 2024 Play-In Tournament. The Murray-Trae Young pairing therefore supplied high-level individual production without producing the contender jump the trade was designed to create. Landale never played for Atlanta; the Hawks sent him to Phoenix for cash on July 6, 2022. Murray did retain substantial transaction value. In July 2024 Atlanta traded him to New Orleans for Dyson Daniels, Larry Nance Jr., E.J. Liddell, Cody Zeller and two future first-round picks. That later trade should be judged separately, but it prevents the original Hawks return from being treated as a dead-end asset.

San Antonio Return
Gallinari was waived, so the Spurs' basketball value was always in the draft package. The 2025 unprotected Atlanta first became No. 14, which San Antonio used on Carter Bryant. The 2026 swap also became real value: San Antonio ended up with Atlanta's No. 20 slot and selected Jayden Quaintance. The protected Charlotte first never became a Spurs draft selection, but San Antonio preserved its market value and included that conditional first in the February 2025 package for De'Aaron Fox. The largest unresolved piece is still ahead: Atlanta's 2027 first remains unprotected and belongs to San Antonio. That means the Spurs have already realized two first-round selections plus transaction value from the Charlotte asset while another unprotected first remains outstanding.

Hindsight Verdict
San Antonio wins clearly. Atlanta did not receive nothing: Murray delivered 152 regular-season games of high-level guard play and later brought back a meaningful package from New Orleans. That makes a D-range grade too harsh. But the Spurs converted one outgoing All-Star into a long asset runway that has already produced Carter Bryant, Jayden Quaintance and a piece of the De'Aaron Fox trade, with the unprotected 2027 Atlanta first still to come. An A+ for San Antonio reflects both realized and remaining draft value. A B- for Atlanta recognizes Murray's strong individual production and retained resale value while accounting for the lack of team-level breakthrough and the extraordinary draft cost. Final verdict: San Antonio Spurs Win.

His movement without the ball and quick-release shooting complemented the team's creators. Those games were legitimate Sacramento receiving-team value, not statistics borrowed from Atlanta. His later career changes belong to separate transactions, but the initial deal already produced a useful starter during a defining Kings season. That outcome deserves emphasis despite Sacramento's lower inherited team grade.

The protected first-round selection carried greater future flexibility and eventually became associated with the 2025 No. 13 choice linked to Derik Queen. That numbered pick is a real asset, but any later rights transfers should be followed before crediting the resulting player's games to Atlanta. The incoming package was broader than a single veteran swap and could help the Hawks make subsequent moves.

Sacramento obtained a player who immediately helped improve its offense and reach the playoffs. The inherited slight Hawks advantage reflects the pick and additional personnel, but the direct court-value comparison strongly supports Huerter's contribution. This is not a case in which the team receiving the recognizable player gained nothing: Sacramento got substantial production during its first playoff season in years.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Phoenix Acquired Landale Without Giving Up a Player

The Suns obtained Jock Landale from Atlanta in July 2022 in exchange for cash considerations. Landale had shown that he could contribute reserve frontcourt minutes, and Phoenix was looking for additional center depth behind its main interior options. Atlanta chose a financial return rather than incorporating the big man into its own rotation. With no draft picks or active Suns players included on the outgoing side, the transaction carried limited acquisition risk for Phoenix.

Landale Provided Useful Suns Reserve Minutes

Landale joined Phoenix for the 2022-23 season and saw regular-season and postseason playing time as a backup big. His willingness to work around the basket, rebound and bring energy made him a usable rotation option in specific matchups. That Suns work is the direct basketball value of the trade; his earlier Spurs appearances and later career elsewhere are separate. Phoenix did not buy an elite starting center but obtained a player who could fill a needed supporting role.

Atlanta Received Cash Instead of Incoming Depth

The Hawks accepted a cash payment, leaving them without a direct incoming player or additional draft selection from the agreement. Cash can serve organizational goals, especially when a team does not expect to use an acquired player's roster spot. It is not equivalent to NBA minutes, however, and the Hawks did not gain a comparable on-court contributor through this specific transaction. Their side of the exchange must therefore be assessed as an asset-management outcome rather than a basketball rotation upgrade.

A Modest Price Produced the Suns' Better Return

Phoenix obtained a useful reserve on a relatively inexpensive transaction and gave up no established player. Atlanta received money and had reasons to prefer that outcome to adding another center. Neither side took part in a franchise-altering swap, so the inherited grades remain moderate. The Suns' advantage lies in converting cash into real frontcourt minutes during a competitive season, while the Hawks' benefit was financial and did not carry the same immediate playing value.

Final Verdict

Slight Suns Edge. Phoenix earns B- for Jock Landale's useful backup-center minutes during the 2022-23 season and playoffs. Atlanta receives C+ for cash considerations without an incoming player or draft pick. The transaction was small, but Phoenix converted its financial outlay into an active rotation contributor, creating the clearer on-court return.

washington-wizards.analysis:
Denver Traded Two Guards to Rebalance Its Rotation

On July 6, 2022, Denver sent Will Barton and Monte Morris to Washington and received Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Ish Smith. The Nuggets had Nikola Jokić directing much of their offense and were planning around the returns of Jamal Murray and Michael Porter Jr., making off-ball defense and perimeter shooting important considerations. Caldwell-Pope had already established those skills during previous stops, while Smith offered experienced backup-point-guard coverage. Washington, seeking more immediate backcourt scoring and playmaking, obtained two veterans rather than draft picks or future conditional rights.

Caldwell-Pope Became a Championship Starter

Caldwell-Pope quickly became a core role player for Denver, defending opposing guards and spacing the floor without demanding the ball. He started during the Nuggets’ 2023 championship postseason and helped the team win its first NBA title. Smith also supplied reserve minutes and eventually shared in the championship run. Those are direct receiving-team results from the July 2022 exchange, not retroactive credit for Caldwell-Pope’s earlier Lakers title or Smith’s prior work around the league. Denver improved its fit around Jokić while keeping the main creators in place.

Washington Collected Established Backcourt Depth

Washington acquired two genuine NBA players, and the inherited failing grade obscures that fact. Morris could handle point-guard duties, while Barton supplied veteran wing scoring, even though his Wizards stay proved shorter than the team might have preferred. Barton’s productive years with Denver before the transaction did not transfer as new Washington minutes, and Morris’s later destinations must be evaluated independently. The Wizards did not receive additional first-round compensation in this deal. Their return was a present-day veteran backcourt, useful on paper but less durable than Denver’s new starting wing.

One Club Found a Title Fit and the Other Found Temporary Roles

This is a particularly clear example of fit producing more value than the combined reputations of the outgoing veterans. Denver paired Caldwell-Pope’s defense and shooting with Jokić’s playmaking and took a direct step toward championship-level lineup balance. Washington made a reasonable attempt to stock its guard rotation, though neither acquired player became a permanent cornerstone. A substantial Denver edge follows from actual 2022-23 play and the NBA title, while an upgraded Wizards grade acknowledges real player acquisitions rather than portraying Barton and Morris as empty consideration.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win. Denver earns A+ because Kentavious Caldwell-Pope started on the 2023 championship team and Ish Smith supplied veteran reserve depth. Washington receives C+ for legitimate, if shorter-lived, Will Barton and Monte Morris guard minutes. Caldwell-Pope’s previous Lakers title and the departing Nuggets players’ earlier Denver seasons are excluded from the respective receiving-team returns.

A substantial Denver edge follows from actual 2022-23 play and the NBA title, while an upgraded Wizards grade acknowledges real player acquisitions rather than portraying Barton and Morris as empty consideration.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win. Denver earns A+ because Kentavious Caldwell-Pope started on the 2023 championship team and Ish Smith supplied veteran reserve depth. Washington receives C+ for legitimate, if shorter-lived, Will Barton and Monte Morris guard minutes. Caldwell-Pope’s previous Lakers title and the departing Nuggets players’ earlier Denver seasons are excluded from the respective receiving-team returns.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Purchased a Sixth-Man Candidate With Depth

Boston acquired Malcolm Brogdon from Indiana in July 2022, sending Aaron Nesmith, Daniel Theis, Malik Fitts, Juwan Morgan, Nik Stauskas and a 2023 first-round pick. The Celtics had reached the NBA Finals and needed another guard to reduce the creative burden on their established stars. Brogdon offered an experienced ball handler with the ability to score and distribute off the bench. Indiana prioritized a younger wing, additional roster options and future draft inventory while adjusting the direction of its personnel around a developing backcourt.

Brogdon Produced an Award-Winning Celtics Season

Brogdon became a valuable reserve for Boston in 2022-23, averaging substantial bench scoring and earning the NBA Sixth Man of the Year award. His ball handling gave the Celtics flexibility when their primary creators needed rest, and the club again advanced deep into the playoffs. The incoming guard supplied the immediate quality Boston wanted. His stay was nevertheless short, ending in another trade in 2023. That limitation is part of the eventual evaluation: Boston got a high-end one-season reserve, not a long-term lead guard who stayed through every subsequent campaign.

Nesmith Became a Stronger Long-Term Pacers Asset

Nesmith found a larger role after joining Indiana, adding wing defense and outside shooting as his confidence grew. His development into a regular starter supplied more sustained roster value than many of the other outgoing Boston pieces. Theis gave the Pacers temporary center depth, while Fitts, Morgan and Stauskas were not the principal basketball payoff. The 2023 pick became associated with No. 29 Julian Strawther through its later rights chain; Strawther's subsequent NBA games elsewhere cannot simply be treated as Indiana production from this transaction.

The Grade Gap Is Small Because Both Teams Benefited

Boston received a major award-winning reserve for a season when it was competing to win the title. Indiana got a younger player who developed into a durable rotation piece and accepted an additional first-round selection. These are different kinds of successful return, not a deal with one obvious failure. The inherited slight Pacers edge reflects a longer horizon and the package of assets, while Boston's B+ recognizes genuine near-term payoff. The appropriate comparison preserves both outcomes instead of claiming that Brogdon was unsuccessful merely because he later changed teams.

Final Verdict

Slight Pacers Edge. Indiana earns A- for Aaron Nesmith's development into a key wing and an additional first-round asset, while Boston receives B+ because Malcolm Brogdon won Sixth Man of the Year during his single Celtics season. Both teams obtained meaningful value; the Pacers' longer-running player contribution narrowly outweighs Boston's immediate postseason-focused success.

perspectives.analysis:
New York Sent Two Contracts and Draft Compensation to Detroit

The July 11, 2022 exchange sent Alec Burks and Nerlens Noel from New York to Detroit, along with second-round draft compensation and cash. The Knicks received the NBA rights to overseas prospect Nikola Radičević and a protected future second-round obligation. New York was creating room for a larger roster redesign, with its subsequent pursuit of Jalen Brunson among the important surrounding developments. Detroit was willing to take veteran contracts while accumulating draft options. The deal should be evaluated as a roster and financial transaction rather than two clubs simply swapping equally important on-court starters.

Burks Provided Usable Pistons Minutes

Burks contributed to Detroit's rotation in the seasons after the trade, offering bench scoring and perimeter versatility around a young core. He was a genuine receiving-team contributor, not merely an unwanted contract that sat unused. Noel had a much smaller on-court role for the Pistons and moved out of the team's plans, limiting the value of that incoming veteran piece. Detroit also held the draft compensation, with a 2023 second later associated with No. 31 James Nnaji and another future second contingent on its conveyance terms. Those later rights and player destinations require separate accounting before being counted as Pistons NBA playing production.

The Knicks Gained Cap Flexibility, Not a Starting Overseas Guard

New York's principal benefit was the ability to clear existing contracts and pursue different personnel. Radičević's international rights did not become an immediate Knicks NBA rotation player, while a protected future second-round possibility carried more limited value than a guaranteed first. The cap benefit mattered because the franchise soon added Brunson, but his full later career was achieved through a separate free-agent agreement with its own salary commitment. Crediting every Brunson point to the Detroit trade would grossly overstate its direct on-court return. The Knicks did, however, achieve an important financial objective through the contract movements.

Distinct Benefits Make the Trade Broadly Balanced

Detroit received an experienced guard who could play and several assets tied to picks and cash. New York gained room to reshape its roster without holding the same veteran obligations. Those are different types of value, and neither should be forced into a purely box-score comparison. The inherited even verdict is reasonable because Detroit's real Burks service balances against New York's contract flexibility. Moderate high marks for both teams are more defensible than treating both as automatic A-grade successes from a trade involving mostly supporting veterans and conditional rights. Each later pick and free-agent decision must stand on its own.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Detroit earns B+ for Alec Burks's real veteran scoring and the added second-round compensation, with Nerlens Noel's shorter stay limiting the return. New York also gets B+ for clearing substantial contracts and acquiring international rights plus a protected future second. Brunson joined through a separate free-agent deal and isn't treated as a direct Pistons-trade player.

perspectives.analysis:
New York Sent Two Contracts and Draft Compensation to Detroit

The July 11, 2022 exchange sent Alec Burks and Nerlens Noel from New York to Detroit, along with second-round draft compensation and cash. The Knicks received the NBA rights to overseas prospect Nikola Radičević and a protected future second-round obligation. New York was creating room for a larger roster redesign, with its subsequent pursuit of Jalen Brunson among the important surrounding developments. Detroit was willing to take veteran contracts while accumulating draft options. The deal should be evaluated as a roster and financial transaction rather than two clubs simply swapping equally important on-court starters.

Burks Provided Usable Pistons Minutes

Burks contributed to Detroit's rotation in the seasons after the trade, offering bench scoring and perimeter versatility around a young core. He was a genuine receiving-team contributor, not merely an unwanted contract that sat unused. Noel had a much smaller on-court role for the Pistons and moved out of the team's plans, limiting the value of that incoming veteran piece. Detroit also held the draft compensation, with a 2023 second later associated with No. 31 James Nnaji and another future second contingent on its conveyance terms. Those later rights and player destinations require separate accounting before being counted as Pistons NBA playing production.

The Knicks Gained Cap Flexibility, Not a Starting Overseas Guard

New York's principal benefit was the ability to clear existing contracts and pursue different personnel. Radičević's international rights did not become an immediate Knicks NBA rotation player, while a protected future second-round possibility carried more limited value than a guaranteed first. The cap benefit mattered because the franchise soon added Brunson, but his full later career was achieved through a separate free-agent agreement with its own salary commitment. Crediting every Brunson point to the Detroit trade would grossly overstate its direct on-court return. The Knicks did, however, achieve an important financial objective through the contract movements.

Distinct Benefits Make the Trade Broadly Balanced

Detroit received an experienced guard who could play and several assets tied to picks and cash. New York gained room to reshape its roster without holding the same veteran obligations. Those are different types of value, and neither should be forced into a purely box-score comparison. The inherited even verdict is reasonable because Detroit's real Burks service balances against New York's contract flexibility. Moderate high marks for both teams are more defensible than treating both as automatic A-grade successes from a trade involving mostly supporting veterans and conditional rights. Each later pick and free-agent decision must stand on its own.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Detroit earns B+ for Alec Burks's real veteran scoring and the added second-round compensation, with Nerlens Noel's shorter stay limiting the return. New York also gets B+ for clearing substantial contracts and acquiring international rights plus a protected future second. Brunson joined through a separate free-agent deal and isn't treated as a direct Pistons-trade player.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Targeted Krejčí's Development

The Hawks acquired Vit Krejčí from Oklahoma City in September 2022, looking at a young player with positional size and ball-handling potential. The Thunder received veteran Maurice Harkless and second-round draft considerations, including a change to protections on an existing obligation. Atlanta chose a developmental wing rather than preserving those draft rights. The deal was largely about future options for teams evaluating the margins of their rotations.

Krejčí Offered a Young Atlanta Roster Option

Krejčí had experience from Oklahoma City's rebuilding period, but his previous Thunder minutes could not be treated as Atlanta contributions. The Hawks obtained the opportunity to evaluate his shooting and passing alongside an established core. His developmental path was not a guarantee of a permanent starting job. The player could supply useful depth, but the trade itself didn't turn him into the franchise's leading creator.

Oklahoma City Improved Its Draft Position

The Thunder received a future 2029 second-round right and a modification of protection on a previously traded 2025 second, changing it from top-55 protection to top-40 protection. Those adjustments could make a selection more likely to convey, depending on the final draft position. Harkless was another incoming contract, but his veteran reputation shouldn't be interpreted as years of new Thunder on-court production. The main attraction was asset flexibility.

The Difference Is a Prospect Versus More Chances

Atlanta acquired a young wing with a possible development trajectory; Oklahoma City received multiple ways to improve its future draft position and manage the roster. The inherited Thunder B compared with Atlanta's C+ values those picks and protection changes. Neither club acquired a proven star. Proper evaluation distinguishes actual playing time gained through Krejčí from rights whose eventual selection outcomes require later verification.

Final Verdict

Oklahoma City Thunder Win. The Thunder receive B for Maurice Harkless, a 2029 second-round right and improved protection terms on a 2025 second. Atlanta gets C+ for Vit Krejčí, whose development remained a more uncertain immediate return. Oklahoma City gained broader draft flexibility, while Atlanta acquired a prospect to evaluate in its rotation.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Traded a Reserve Big and Cash

The Celtics sent Noah Vonleh and cash to San Antonio in January 2023, receiving a conditional 2024 second-round right. Vonleh had joined Boston as a reserve frontcourt option but wasn't part of the team's most important playing group. The Spurs were rebuilding and willing to accommodate a transaction involving an expiring or movable roster spot. The Celtics used the exchange to manage their bench and financial obligations rather than to acquire a new active player.

Vonleh Did Not Enter the Spurs' Rotation

San Antonio did not retain Vonleh as a long-term frontcourt contributor after the acquisition. The veteran was waived instead of establishing a Spurs regular-season role, so his earlier NBA career could not supply direct receiving-team minutes. The incoming cash consideration had real financial value and helps explain why San Antonio accepted the deal. It would be incorrect to assess the transaction as though the Spurs had received several months of on-court center production.

The Draft Condition Produced No Incoming Celtics Pick

Boston's conditional 2024 second-round right did not convey under the recorded terms. That means the Celtics did not acquire a draftee through the selection, and no later player's statistics should be attributed to this trade. The organization's gain concerned roster flexibility and the ability to direct resources toward other needs. Those advantages are harder to translate into points or rebounds than the output of an incoming player, but they are legitimate reasons to make a small transaction.

A Minor Administrative Edge Fits the Result

Neither team added a lasting basketball contributor from this exchange. Boston moved an out-of-rotation big man while San Antonio received cash and did not keep the player for meaningful games. The inherited slight Celtics advantage reflects the relative usefulness of clearing obligations rather than a belief that an unexercised second-round choice became a valuable prospect. This trade is best recorded as a modest roster-management step with financial benefits, not a major competitive inflection point.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns C+ for moving Noah Vonleh and obtaining roster flexibility, while its conditional 2024 second never conveyed. San Antonio gets C for Vonleh and cash but did not receive a lasting on-court contributor. The two teams gained limited administrative value; there was no significant incoming player performance to credit on either side.

washington-wizards.analysis:
Los Angeles Added Hachimura Ahead of Its Playoff Push

The Lakers acquired Rui Hachimura from Washington in January 2023, sending Kendrick Nunn and three second-round selections to the Wizards. Hachimura was a former lottery pick whose combination of size and midrange offense gave Los Angeles another forward option. Washington chose additional draft capital rather than extending its investment in him. The Lakers were attempting to improve the rotation around LeBron James and Anthony Davis, making immediate playable frontcourt depth more valuable than several distant second-round possibilities.

Hachimura Became a Useful Lakers Playoff Forward

Hachimura helped the Lakers reach the 2023 Western Conference Finals, offering scoring and the ability to handle difficult defensive assignments in the postseason. He wasn't the sole reason for the run, but his role was a genuine improvement over a rotation with fewer large wings. He also remained with the Lakers after that first season, extending the value beyond a brief trade-deadline trial. Those Los Angeles games, rather than his earlier Washington statistics, provide the strongest direct evidence for the winning grade.

The Wizards Acquired Picks and a Short-Term Guard

Washington received Nunn, whose stay was not a lasting backcourt solution, and second-round choices spread across 2023 and later drafts. The 2023 right was used on Tristan Vukčević at No. 42, giving the team a developmental possibility. The 2028 and 2029 selections are separate rights whose final value cannot be assumed from the initial trade alone. The Wizards made an asset-management decision, but the immediate incoming guard production was modest compared with Hachimura's contributions after moving west.

Los Angeles Won the More Tangible Basketball Return

The Lakers got a rotation forward who played meaningful minutes during a deep playoff run. Washington retained additional chances to draft or trade young talent, though future picks do not guarantee contributors. That difference in realized output explains the inherited grades. Hachimura did not transform the franchise single-handedly, and the Wizards' draft package was not empty. Los Angeles nevertheless converted an outgoing reserve and three second-round choices into a player who repeatedly affected its games.

Final Verdict

Lakers Win. Los Angeles earns B+ for Rui Hachimura's useful scoring and defensive contributions during its 2023 Western Conference Finals run and subsequent seasons. Washington gets C- for Kendrick Nunn and three second-round choices, including the pick used on Tristan Vukčević. The Wizards gained draft flexibility, but the Lakers obtained a substantially more productive immediate rotation player.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Exchanged Expiring Veterans for Two Familiar Roles

The Hawks obtained Garrison Mathews and Bruno Fernando from Houston at the February 9, 2023 deadline. The Rockets received Justin Holiday, Frank Kaminsky and two future second-round selections. Atlanta wanted additional perimeter shooting and an athletic center behind its primary frontcourt options. Houston was prioritizing roster adjustments and draft assets as it continued building around young players. Mathews had developed a reputation as a willing outside shooter, while Fernando offered size and rim-running. The exchange was a multi-asset depth move rather than a transaction involving an established star.

Mathews Provided Shooting While Fernando Added Size

Mathews joined Atlanta as a floor-spacing reserve and received real playing opportunities over the following seasons. His willingness to shoot could help bench lineups that lacked perimeter options. Fernando also returned to a franchise that had previously employed him, offering interior depth and rebounding in a narrower role. Neither newcomer became a primary creator, but both supplied NBA minutes that belonged to the receiving Hawks. Their contributions were practical and role-specific, which is the kind of payoff a team can reasonably seek from a deadline exchange of veterans.

Houston's Player Return Was Primarily Transitional

Holiday and Kaminsky were veteran arrivals for the Rockets, but neither developed into a lasting core player as a direct result of this deal. Houston's second-round rights were therefore particularly relevant to its side of the compensation. The eventual draft identities associated with the two choices included No. 57 in 2024 and No. 59 in 2025. Those identities must be tracked through any later rights movements rather than crediting the eventual draftees' NBA careers automatically to Houston. The club's objective was flexibility more than immediate veteran production.

The Hawks Found Two Usable Bench Options

The exchange gave Atlanta two players whose roles were easy to understand, while Houston collected marginal draft inventory and roster options. The Hawks' return wasn't transformative, but Mathews and Fernando offered actual minutes in identifiable lineup situations. Houston's additional selections had possible future worth yet did not automatically outweigh that present contribution. The grades reflect a sensible advantage for Atlanta without implying that either reserve became a championship cornerstone. This was an ordinary trade that succeeded by supplying specific types of depth at a manageable player cost.

Final Verdict

Hawks Win. Atlanta receives B for Garrison Mathews's perimeter shooting and Bruno Fernando's interior reserve minutes. Houston earns C+ for Holiday, Kaminsky and two second-round choices whose later draft identities require separate rights-chain accounting. The Rockets gained flexibility, but the Hawks got the more visible receiving-team basketball contribution from this February 2023 deal.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Acquired Muscala for Bench Shooting

The Celtics traded Justin Jackson and two second-round selections to Oklahoma City for Mike Muscala at the February 2023 deadline. The picks included a 2023 choice later associated with No. 50 Keyontae Johnson and an additional 2029 second. Boston was a contender looking for an experienced big man who could stretch the floor with his outside shooting. Oklahoma City was building around younger talent and preferred retaining draft flexibility rather than extending Muscala's veteran reserve assignment.

Muscala Had a Specific Role in Boston

Muscala joined Boston's frontcourt as a shooting option who could be used when the offense needed additional space. He gave the Celtics regular-season minutes during a competitive season, although he was not one of the stars who carried their postseason runs. His stay proved brief and ended in a later roster change. Those Boston appearances are the actual playing return, not Muscala's longer history in Atlanta or Oklahoma City. The addition made basketball sense even without creating a permanent frontcourt pairing.

Oklahoma City Collected Two Draft Opportunities

The Thunder received Jackson, whose incoming veteran tenure did not become the main source of value, along with selections from separate drafts. The 2023 pick was used at No. 50 on Keyontae Johnson, while the 2029 second remains a future asset. Their worth depends on player development and subsequent rights transactions rather than an automatic guarantee of starting-level NBA minutes. Oklahoma City exchanged a reserve with a limited long-term role for more chances to identify young contributors.

Two Sensible Strategies Produced a Narrow Difference

Boston addressed an immediate matchup need during a contender's season, while Oklahoma City took the longer-term route through draft inventory. Muscala was usable but stayed only a short period, limiting the total playing value the Celtics could claim. The Thunder received multiple opportunities at relatively little present competitive cost. That modest advantage fits the inherited grades; it would be misleading to call Muscala a complete failure or treat a still-future 2029 selection as a finished NBA success story.

Final Verdict

Slight Oklahoma City Thunder Edge. Oklahoma City earns B+ for Justin Jackson and the 2023 and 2029 second-round assets received for Mike Muscala. Boston gets B because Muscala provided useful outside shooting but only during a short Celtics stay. The Thunder's additional draft options narrowly outweigh the limited-term veteran bench contribution.

oklahoma-city-thunder.analysis:
The Thunder Obtained Šarić and Future Consideration

At the February 9, 2023 deadline, Oklahoma City obtained veteran forward Dario Šarić from Phoenix, along with roughly $1 million in cash and a future 2029 second-round draft asset. The Suns received Darius Bazley in the exchange. Oklahoma City was building a young roster and could use an experienced frontcourt player for the remainder of the season. Phoenix was adjusting depth around a separate, much larger roster transformation. This was a stand-alone two-team swap, and its assets should not be collapsed into any other deadline trade involving the Suns.

Šarić Supplied a Short Thunder Veteran Stint

Šarić joined Oklahoma City as a forward who could move the ball and stretch the floor with outside shooting. His stint was brief rather than a multiyear starting role, but the club received actual NBA minutes from him after the agreement. Those games are distinct from his earlier Phoenix recovery from injury and his subsequent career stops. The Thunder also held cash and a future conditional asset, allowing the team to realize some financial and draft flexibility even if the veteran did not stay long. Evaluating those three incoming pieces together captures why the trade made sense.

Phoenix Took a Chance on Bazley's Athletic Profile

Phoenix acquired Bazley as a younger forward with NBA experience and defensive versatility, hoping he could add reserve depth around its established stars. He did not become the defining frontcourt presence in the Suns' next postseason, and his later team movements must be separated from this initial opportunity. The Suns did not obtain a new first-round draft choice or immediate cash consideration in this trade. Their direct return consisted of one player whose ceiling depended on finding a usable role. That was a credible depth gamble, but it offered less flexibility than Oklahoma City's player-plus-assets package.

The Cash and Draft Right Favor Oklahoma City

The original slight Thunder edge is defensible because Oklahoma City received a veteran it could actually use, financial consideration and a future second-round asset. Phoenix obtained a player with a developmental possibility that did not become a long-term foundation for the club. Neither return was large enough to explain either franchise's subsequent fortunes, and the 2029 selection should not be turned into a named prospect years before its verified final conveyance. A moderate advantage to Oklahoma City accounts for more types of incoming value while keeping both players' actual team-specific appearances in view.

Final Verdict

Slight Oklahoma City Thunder Edge. The Thunder earn B for Dario Šarić's brief veteran minutes, approximately $1 million and a future 2029 second-round asset. Phoenix receives C+ for Darius Bazley's reserve opportunity. The protected future choice isn't credited as a drafted player, and Šarić's later NBA seasons outside Oklahoma City don't inflate this February 2023 outcome.

Warren; cash considerations.
perspectives.analysis: Brooklyn converted Kevin Durant into Mikal Bridges, Cameron Johnson, four Phoenix first-round picks, a swap and additional draft assets. The later Bridges trade multiplied that return and gave the Nets the stronger long-term position.
perspectives.reviewStatus: Final Reconciled - Hold for Canonical Gate

summary: Win. Phoenix acquired the best player, but Brooklyn acquired the better total portfolio: Bridges, Johnson, four first-round picks, a swap and additional value. Durant's excellence kept the Suns competitive, yet the contender never reached the level required to justify surrendering so much long-term control. Brooklyn's package stayed useful across multiple timelines, which is the decisive advantage.
analysis: Brooklyn received both playable talent and an unusually deep draft portfolio. Bridges immediately proved he could handle a larger offensive role, Johnson remained a starting-caliber wing, and the first-round package extended far enough into the future to preserve upside even after Phoenix's initial contender window. The Nets later retained the ability to convert individual pieces again rather than being locked into a single aging star timeline. That combination is exactly what a rebuilding seller wants from a superstar trade. Phoenix did receive elite basketball. Durant remained an efficient high-volume scorer and gave the Suns a legitimate top-end playoff weapon. The problem is proportionality: the roster never reached the conference finals during the Durant era, depth became increasingly difficult to maintain, and the franchise had surrendered a huge amount of future control. A superstar can still be worth an aggressive price, but the team that pays that price needs either sustained contention or a title-level payoff to justify an outgoing package this large. The draft chain is the central reason Brooklyn earns the stronger grade. Long-dated firsts and a swap are not abstract when the acquiring team also receives players with independent trade value. Bridges and Johnson could contribute, be retained, or be moved again, while the Suns' future picks remained separate upside. Phoenix's downstream chain was narrower because Durant's value had to carry a roster with limited trade flexibility. When the original star is later moved, that later return helps but does not erase the opportunity cost of the initial package.

perspectives.summary: Josh Hart has already delivered championship-level value for New York, but the full multi-team return still needs more time before the transaction receives a permanent overall verdict.
perspectives.analysis: The Knicks have already received far more than a short-term rental from Josh Hart. He became a core rotation player immediately, re-signed, developed into a connective rebounder and playmaker beside Jalen Brunson, and later contributed to New York's 2026 championship. The direct Portland leg cost Cam Reddish, Ryan Arcidiacono, the rights to Ante Tomic and the protected 2023 first-rounder that became Kris Murray; Charlotte separately received Svi Mykhailiuk, while Philadelphia had no direct Knicks asset edge. That price looks favorable from New York's side, and the Knicks-side grade is already A+ caliber. The overall verdict remains Incomplete Evidence, however, because Grok's reconciliation standard requires more partner-side outcome maturity before the trade is locked permanently.

summary: Knicks Win. New York earns A+ because Hart became a championship starter acquired for a manageable package. Portland receives B+ for Thybulle, Reddish and a first, a useful rebuilding return. Charlotte earns B- for second-round capital and a short-term player, while Philadelphia receives C+ because McDaniels did not become a durable playoff solution. Knicks Win is the completed-value verdict. New York clearly created the highest value. Hart became a foundational rotation player, then a starter-level connector whose rebounding, defense, transition play and chemistry with Jalen Brunson helped shape the Knicks' identity. He remained part of the starting group that won the 2026 championship. The acquisition cost was a protected first plus Reddish and Arcidiacono, a reasonable price for a player who became a durable postseason contributor and championship starter.
analysis: New York acquired Josh Hart in a four-team transaction. Portland received Cam Reddish, Matisse Thybulle, Ryan Arcidiacono and a 2023 first-round pick. Philadelphia received Jalen McDaniels plus second-round assets, while Charlotte received Svi Mykhailiuk and two second-round picks. This four-team transaction is presented in full so Josh Hart's role is visible alongside the McDaniels/Mykhailiuk portion rather than splitting one event into artificial duplicates. New York clearly created the highest value. Hart became a foundational rotation player, then a starter-level connector whose rebounding, defense, transition play and chemistry with Jalen Brunson helped shape the Knicks' identity. He remained part of the starting group that won the 2026 championship. The acquisition cost was a protected first plus Reddish and Arcidiacono, a reasonable price for a player who became a durable postseason contributor and championship starter. Portland received a respectable package. Thybulle gave the Blazers defensive value, Reddish was a reclamation swing, and the first-round pick preserved real future capital. Philadelphia's McDaniels addition was short-lived and did not become a long-term piece, though the seconds added modest value. Charlotte's Mykhailiuk-and-seconds return was similarly limited but defensible for facilitating and moving McDaniels before free agency. Those returns keep the deal from being a one-team robbery, even though Hart's outcome towers over them. The Knicks' value is overwhelmingly direct because Hart stayed and became part of the title core. Portland's first-round pick and Thybulle represent the strongest countervailing assets. Philadelphia and Charlotte relied more on second-round optionality and short-term rotation minutes. The list of assets therefore separates into one premium realized player outcome, one solid future-value package, and two smaller facilitator returns. New York was trying to turn a rising playoff team into a more physical, resilient group and targeted a player whose skills matched Tom Thibodeau's style. Portland was beginning to reconfigure around Damian Lillard's uncertain future and wanted draft capital. Philadelphia was chasing immediate wing depth for a contender, while Charlotte could monetize a player it did not plan to retain long term. The strategies make sense; New York simply executed the best conversion. New York earns A+ because Hart became a championship starter acquired for a manageable package. Portland receives B+ for Thybulle, Reddish and a first, a useful rebuilding return. Charlotte earns B- for second-round capital and a short-term player, while Philadelphia receives C+ because McDaniels did not become a durable playoff solution. Knicks Win is the completed-value verdict.

perspectives.summary: Denver acquired Thomas Bryant in a February 9, 2023 four-club trade. The Clippers obtained Bones Hyland; the Lakers received Mo Bamba, Davon Reed and two second-round picks; and Orlando acquired Patrick Beverley, cash and a 2024 Denver second-round selection that was later rescinded. The inherited Slight Clippers Edge grades the Clippers B+, Denver B, Orlando B- and the Lakers C-.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Obtained Bryant While Sending Out Two Guards

The Nuggets acquired Thomas Bryant from the Lakers on deadline day in February 2023. Bryant had been providing interior scoring and rebounding for Los Angeles, making him a plausible backup option behind Denver's established frontline. The Nuggets sent Davon Reed to the Lakers and Bones Hyland to the Clippers as part of the same four-team construction. Bryant's prior Lakers statistics did not become new Nuggets production, and the team still needed to determine how his role would work behind Nikola Jokić.

The Clippers Added an Energetic Scoring Guard

Los Angeles acquired Bones Hyland, a younger guard with outside shooting and shot-creation ability. His first two seasons in Denver had already shown that he could contribute points in reserve lineups, although defensive questions limited his reliability. The Clippers surrendered two second-round selections as part of the structure. The resulting opportunity was more immediate than keeping those future rights, but it also depended on whether Hyland earned regular minutes alongside established Los Angeles perimeter players.

The Lakers Took Bamba, Reed and Two Future Picks

The Lakers acquired center Mo Bamba from Orlando and guard-forward Davon Reed from Denver, plus the two Clippers second-round selections. The picks were associated with the 2024 and 2025 drafts in historical transaction records, but any draftee's eventual NBA career must be traced through subsequent rights moves. Bamba provided an option for size and shooting in a reserve frontcourt role. Reed offered bench depth, though neither was guaranteed a long-term starting position through this agreement.

Orlando's Conditional Pick Was Later Rescinded

The Magic obtained Patrick Beverley and cash from the Lakers and a 2024 Denver second-round right that was subsequently rescinded. Orlando waived Beverley soon after the exchange, meaning his later NBA games should not be credited to a long Magic tenure. The original ratings give the Clippers B+, Denver B, Orlando B- and the Lakers C-. That view values Hyland's upside above the other immediate returns, but the real outcome requires recording the pick's cancellation and the Lakers' complete incoming package.

Final Verdict

Slight Clippers Edge. The Clippers earn B+ for acquiring Bones Hyland. Denver receives B for Thomas Bryant, Orlando B- for Patrick Beverley, cash and a later-rescinded draft right, and the Lakers C- for Mo Bamba, Davon Reed and two second-round selections. The record should not award Orlando a player from a pick that was rescinded or omit the Lakers' full return.

perspectives.summary: In February 2023 Detroit acquired James Wiseman from Golden State, Atlanta obtained Saddiq Bey from Detroit, and Portland received Kevin Knox II and a package of second-round selections. Golden State received Gary Payton II and conditional draft consideration from Atlanta. The inherited slight Hawks edge grades Atlanta A-, Detroit D, Golden State B and Portland B+.
perspectives.analysis:
Detroit Took Another Chance on Wiseman

The Pistons acquired James Wiseman from Golden State in a February 2023 four-team transaction that also involved Atlanta and Portland. Wiseman had been the No. 2 selection in the 2020 NBA Draft but had struggled to establish a reliable role with the Warriors. Detroit chose to evaluate his size, finishing and potential as a young center. Sending Saddiq Bey away was a meaningful price because Bey had produced points and outside shooting from the wing in Detroit.

Atlanta Acquired Bey for Its Wing Rotation

The Hawks received Bey from Detroit, gaining an established NBA scorer who could handle forward minutes and stretch the floor. His ability to work as a complementary option alongside guards and other wings gave Atlanta a direct current roster benefit. The team also committed future second-round rights as part of the wider exchange. Bey's earlier Pistons performance was the basis for his appeal, not a claim that he had already matched those numbers in Atlanta before the trade.

Golden State Reunited With Payton and Reworked Its Future Picks

The Warriors acquired Gary Payton II from Portland, bringing back a defensive guard who had contributed to their 2022 championship team. League transaction records also describe conditional second-round rights associated with Atlanta in Golden State's return. Payton's point-of-attack defense and off-ball movement fit a specific role alongside the Warriors' stars. His incoming player entry had been absent from the prior Detroit-only ledger, making the full deal appear to give Golden State no basketball return at all.

Portland Received Knox and Draft Consideration

Portland acquired Kevin Knox II from Detroit and a group of future second-round selections in the same multiclub arrangement. Knox brought size and a developmental wing skill set, although his career had already included several stops. The draft bundle supplied flexibility, not guaranteed future Trail Blazers rotation players. Published contemporaneous accounts differ in how they break out conditional selections flowing through Golden State and Atlanta, so bundle totals should not be interpreted as eight already-selected individuals. The inherited Hawks A- leads Portland B+, Golden State B and Detroit D, while every team obtained real assets.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta receives A- for Saddiq Bey's established perimeter scoring. Portland earns B+ for Kevin Knox II and future second-round draft rights. Golden State gets B for reuniting with Gary Payton II and gaining conditional draft consideration. Detroit receives D for its developmental gamble on James Wiseman. The four-party exchange has concrete returns on every side, not an empty Golden State record.

The Warriors acquired Gary Payton II from Portland, bringing back a defensive guard who had contributed to their 2022 championship team. League transaction records also describe conditional second-round rights associated with Atlanta in Golden State's return. Payton's point-of-attack defense and off-ball movement fit a specific role alongside the Warriors' stars. His incoming player entry had been absent from the prior Detroit-only ledger, making the full deal appear to give Golden State no basketball return at all.

Portland Received Knox and Draft Consideration

Portland acquired Kevin Knox II from Detroit and a group of future second-round selections in the same multiclub arrangement. Knox brought size and a developmental wing skill set, although his career had already included several stops. The draft bundle supplied flexibility, not guaranteed future Trail Blazers rotation players. Published contemporaneous accounts differ in how they break out conditional selections flowing through Golden State and Atlanta, so bundle totals should not be interpreted as eight already-selected individuals. The inherited Hawks A- leads Portland B+, Golden State B and Detroit D, while every team obtained real assets.

Final Verdict

Slight Hawks Edge. Atlanta receives A- for Saddiq Bey's established perimeter scoring. Portland earns B+ for Kevin Knox II and future second-round draft rights. Golden State gets B for reuniting with Gary Payton II and gaining conditional draft consideration. Detroit receives D for its developmental gamble on James Wiseman. The four-party exchange has concrete returns on every side, not an empty Golden State record.

new-orleans-pelicans.analysis:
San Antonio Collected Graham and Four Future Seconds

The February 9, 2023 deadline brought Josh Richardson to New Orleans in exchange for guard Devonte' Graham and four second-round selections routed to San Antonio. The incoming pick package included a 2024 choice eventually associated with No. 41 Adem Bona, plus conditional selections in 2026, 2028 and 2029. The Spurs were willing to absorb a veteran guard contract in return for additional draft flexibility, while New Orleans sought an established perimeter defender who could join its active rotation. This was a player-and-picks exchange involving two teams with different priorities, not a simple swap of guards with the same contract profile.

Richardson Provided New Orleans With Defensive Depth

Richardson had played meaningful NBA minutes for several organizations before arriving in New Orleans. He offered the Pelicans an experienced wing defender and reserve offensive option after the deadline, although his direct tenure with the team was short. The club missed the main 2023 playoff bracket after a play-in elimination, so this trade should not be credited with carrying it through a successful playoff series. Richardson's earlier career in Miami, Philadelphia and San Antonio also did not become new Pelicans games. The real return was a temporary player who could defend opposing wings while the front office reassessed its longer-term perimeter options.

The Spurs Traded Immediate Veterans for More Draft Chances

Graham joined the Spurs as a backcourt option during a roster rebuild, playing NBA minutes while the organization shifted toward younger players. The four second-round rights offered additional opportunities to select inexpensive players or make other trades. The 2024 choice entered the draft lineage that included Adem Bona, but his later NBA team and playing record should not be assumed to be direct San Antonio production. Future 2026, 2028 and 2029 selections require separate verification of their final protections and destinations. The Spurs' benefit was the quantity and transferability of these assets rather than four already developed NBA rotation players.

Longer Asset Flexibility Favors the Spurs

New Orleans gained an NBA-ready defender, but Richardson did not stay long enough to justify a top-tier grade for the Pelicans. San Antonio used its willingness to take Graham's contract to acquire a deeper collection of future draft rights. That is valuable even if particular picks later move again or don't produce long-term starters. The outcome favors the Spurs without counting every subsequent NBA player associated with a draft position as if he had been signed by San Antonio. A fair retrospective recognizes Richardson's legitimate direct Pelicans minutes while assigning the stronger organizational flexibility to the Spurs.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win. San Antonio earns B+ for acquiring Devonte' Graham and four future second-round assets, including the 2024 No. 41-linked choice, in exchange for Josh Richardson. New Orleans receives B- for Richardson's short-term defensive and reserve wing minutes. Adem Bona's eventual draft identity and the later outcomes of the other seconds don't automatically become Spurs NBA performances.

perspectives.summary: On February 9, 2023, Toronto reacquired Jakob Poeltl from San Antonio for Khem Birch, Toronto's 2023 and 2025 second-round picks and a top-six-protected 2024 first-round pick. The first conveyed at No. 8 in 2024; San Antonio selected Rob Dillingham and immediately traded his draft rights to Minnesota for an unprotected 2031 first and a top-one-protected 2030 pick swap. Poeltl has remained a productive Toronto starter, but the Spurs converted the package into more long-term draft equity than the original shorthand suggests.
perspectives.analysis:
The Exchange
Toronto's official release and the NBA trade tracker confirm the February 9, 2023 package: Jakob Poeltl to the Raptors for Khem Birch, Toronto's 2023 second-round pick, its 2025 second-round pick and a protected 2024 first. The first was protected 1-6 and conveyed in 2024 when Toronto landed at No. 8. Basketball-Reference maps the two seconds to No. 44 in 2023 and No. 37 in 2025, but those pick labels should not be confused with players who necessarily stayed with San Antonio. The transaction has to be graded through the actual asset chain.

Toronto Return
Poeltl immediately returned to a starting-center role and gave Toronto the interior size and screening the roster had lacked. The Raptors re-signed him in July 2023, so the return was not a short rental. His value is real and multi-year: Toronto acquired a proven center who already understood the organization and remained part of the core beyond the trade-deadline season. The cost became much steeper once the protected first conveyed at No. 8. Toronto did not surrender an abstract future first; it surrendered a top-ten selection after a 25-win 2023-24 season.

San Antonio Return
The 2023 second became No. 44, which San Antonio used on Sidy Cissoko. The 2024 first became No. 8. The Spurs selected Rob Dillingham and immediately traded his rights to Minnesota for an unprotected 2031 first-round pick and a 2030 first-round swap protected only for the No. 1 pick. That draft-night conversion is the most important downstream result because it turns the original Toronto first into two pieces of distant first-round equity. The 2025 Toronto second later became No. 37, but San Antonio had already routed that pick to Dallas in the 2023 Grant Williams transaction; Detroit eventually selected Chaz Lanier after another trade. That later player should not be counted as Spurs value from the Poeltl deal.

Hindsight Verdict
San Antonio receives an A- because it turned a veteran center into a top-eight first, two seconds and additional future first-round leverage through the Dillingham draft-night trade. Toronto receives a C+ because Poeltl has provided legitimate multi-year starter value, but the No. 8 pick was a high price for a team that did not become a contender after the acquisition. The final verdict is San Antonio Spurs Win. The grade recognizes that the 2030 and 2031 assets remain future value as of 2026 and therefore stops short of treating them as already realized star production.

milwaukee-bucks.analysis:
Milwaukee Used Orlando's Draft Position on Andre Jackson Jr.

On June 22, 2023, the Milwaukee Bucks acquired the draft rights to Connecticut wing Andre Jackson Jr., selected thirty-sixth overall, from Orlando. The Magic received cash considerations and a 2030 second-round selection. Milwaukee targeted an athletic and versatile defender who could contribute without dominating possessions or costing a first-round slot. Orlando preferred deferred draft flexibility and a cash payment, likely reflecting the club's other young players under development. This was a trade in prospect rights immediately after the pick, not a deal in which Jackson had already accumulated NBA appearances or established a veteran contract.

Jackson Earned Actual Bucks Rotation Opportunities

Jackson joined the Bucks and showed defensive energy, rebounding and passing as a reserve wing during his first NBA seasons. He played real regular-season minutes for Milwaukee, giving the franchise a tangible use for an early second-round selection. His effectiveness depended on the lineup: he could guard opposing perimeter players and help the offense without requiring frequent isolation shots. He was not the primary scorer on a team featuring Giannis Antetokounmpo and Damian Lillard, and his acquisition alone did not guarantee another championship. The direct value was a rotation contributor whose defensive profile matched a clear roster need.

The Magic Received Financial and Future-Draft Flexibility

Orlando got immediate cash and a second-round opportunity years down the line. The 2030 selection could eventually supply a prospect or be traded again, but it would be false to claim an identifiable NBA player through that choice long before the actual draft. The cash payment also mattered even though it produced no NBA box-score statistics. Orlando had a different developmental timetable and did not necessarily require another second-round wing in 2023. The Magic's financial return was real, yet it didn't deliver a player who contributed NBA rotation minutes directly in the seasons after this agreement.

Observed Defense Beats Hypothetical Future Production

The Bucks obtained a useful NBA wing from an inexpensive draft-rights acquisition, while Orlando secured legitimate financial and long-dated draft value. Both objectives make sense, but Jackson's direct Milwaukee minutes support the stronger current grade. It would overstate the result to project him as a guaranteed star or to value the 2030 pick as a franchise-changing player before anyone has been selected. The historical record is stronger when each asset is counted only for the club that actually received and used it. That leaves Milwaukee with the clearer demonstrated basketball payoff.

Final Verdict

Bucks Win. Milwaukee earns A- because Andre Jackson Jr., the No. 36 selection, became a useful defensive wing and logged real NBA rotation minutes for the Bucks. Orlando receives B- for cash and a 2030 second-round right. The future draft option is not a guaranteed Magic NBA player, and Jackson's collegiate Connecticut achievements aren't counted as Milwaukee playing production.

analysis: Boston turned Marcus Smart and secondary pieces into Porzingis plus draft leverage, then immediately received championship-level value. Porzingis gave the Celtics interior scoring, rim protection and spacing that diversified an already elite roster. Boston won the 2024 championship with Porzingis producing important Finals minutes despite injuries, and the draft capital created additional flexibility for subsequent roster construction. The move upgraded Boston's ceiling without sacrificing Jayson Tatum or Jaylen Brown. Memphis acquired the former Defensive Player of the Year and a proven organizer, but Smart's tenure was repeatedly interrupted by injuries and never became the stabilizing multi-year bridge the Grizzlies hoped to buy. Washington did reasonably well given Porzingis' leverage and contract situation: Jones started for a season, Gallinari and Muscala were movable veterans and the draft piece had some value. Still, neither side matched Boston's championship return. The most important downstream value belongs to Boston because the transaction was not merely a one-for-one player swap. The Celtics received draft control alongside Porzingis, preserving the ability to redirect value into later roster moves. Memphis paid both a starting point guard and draft capital for Smart, so his abbreviated tenure carries a real opportunity cost. Washington's return was more about liquidity than a single centerpiece, which is understandable for a rebuilding team but lowers the realized ceiling.

washington-wizards.analysis:
The Final Pick Became a Real NBA Big

On June 23, 2023, Golden State acquired the draft rights to Indiana big man Trayce Jackson-Davis, the fifty-seventh selection, from Washington for cash. The Warriors wanted a player who could give them energy around the rim, screen for their guards and rebound without demanding a high usage rate. Washington chose financial compensation for the last selection it controlled in this part of the draft. This was a rights purchase involving the same 2023 selection, not a first-round swap or a trade of a veteran on an established contract.

Jackson-Davis Joined an Active Warriors Rotation

Jackson-Davis signed with Golden State and soon showed why the relatively low draft position understated his ability to contribute. He earned regular-season appearances as a rookie in 2023-24, blocked shots and provided a vertical finishing option when the Warriors needed more size. The key return is actual NBA work in the Warriors uniform, not projections about what an unsigned late second might become. The player was a direct product of the rights purchase; there was no additional blockbuster transaction required to bring him into the club after Washington transferred the selection.

The Wizards Received Cash Instead of a Prospect

Washington accepted cash rather than taking Jackson-Davis into its own developmental program. Cash can be a sensible return for a late draft pick when a team has roster-space or budget priorities, and the recorded trade should respect that objective. However, no Washington player games resulted from the compensation, and the exact cash amount should not be invented without a primary transaction disclosure. The Wizards did not own later Warriors appearances by the prospect they selected and immediately sent elsewhere. Their benefit was financial consideration received at the point of transfer.

Late-Second-Round Return Strongly Favors Golden State

The difference between a late second-round selection that becomes a playable frontcourt piece and one that is sold for cash gives Golden State the clear hindsight advantage. That conclusion does not require portraying Jackson-Davis as an All-Star or claiming he transformed the franchise. The Warriors created NBA roster value from an inexpensive draft right, while Washington fulfilled a different, narrower transaction objective. Treating the sale as an automatic failure misses the limited cost of the original pick; treating the outcomes as equally valuable ignores the actual playing contribution on one side.

Final Verdict

Warriors Win. Golden State earns A- after acquiring Trayce Jackson-Davis at No. 57 and converting his rights into meaningful Warriors frontcourt minutes. Washington receives C+ for securing cash, a legitimate financial return with no direct NBA player attached. The exact cash amount is not asserted, and Jackson-Davis’s later Warriors production belongs to Golden State rather than to the club that sold his rights.

perspectives.summary: Denver used a June 23, 2023 four-team draft-rights exchange to obtain Julian Strawther, Jalen Pickett, Hunter Tyson and a 2024 second-round choice. Indiana received Mojave King's rights, a protected 2024 Oklahoma City first and cash; the Lakers gained Maxwell Lewis; and the Thunder took a conditional future Denver first. The original Nuggets Win grades Denver A+, Indiana B, the Lakers C+ and Oklahoma City B+.
perspectives.analysis:
Denver Converted Future Rights Into Three Draft Prospects

The Nuggets acquired Julian Strawther, Jalen Pickett and Hunter Tyson through a June 2023 four-team draft agreement, along with a 2024 second-round selection. Denver had just won the NBA title, but these players were drafted after that championship and should not be credited with its 2023 postseason run. Strawther brought shooting from a wing position, Pickett offered guard size and ball-handling experience, and Tyson provided another forward prospect. The deal concentrated several current selections on a team seeking affordable talent around its established core.

Indiana Received a Real Package in Return

The Pacers obtained the rights to No. 47 Mojave King from the Lakers, a conditional 2024 first-round right from Oklahoma City and cash considerations routed from Los Angeles. The first-round selection later became associated with No. 29 Isaiah Collier, but that draft identity doesn't establish Collier as a long-term Indiana player. The original Denver-focused source had left the Pacers' incoming asset list empty, a problem corrected against NBA's official draft tracker and the teams' transaction records. Indiana gave up Strawther and Pickett in exchange for a distinct package of its own.

Los Angeles and Oklahoma City Took Different Rights

The Lakers received Maxwell Lewis's No. 40 draft rights from Denver, enabling them to evaluate a developing wing prospect. Oklahoma City acquired a conditional first-round selection originating with Denver, tied to 2029 with later protection and conversion language. The imported record had split that single obligation into two partial asset strings, which risked overstating the Thunder's return. The consolidated right is a conditional pick, not two guaranteed future first-round selections. These side deals made the full four-team movement possible.

The Original Nuggets Grade Reflects Prospect Concentration

Denver's inherited A+ rewards the quantity of near-term prospects and an additional future second; the Thunder receive B+ for longer-range flexibility, Indiana B for its combination of draft rights and cash, and Los Angeles C+ for Lewis. The strength of Denver's return still depended on later player development. None of the future selections could be counted as a current rotation contributor before the receiving franchise actually drafted or acquired an NBA player. The grades provide an initial evaluation, not a substitute for the full rights chain.

Final Verdict

Nuggets Win. Denver earns A+ for acquiring Strawther, Pickett, Tyson and an additional second-round asset. Oklahoma City gets B+ for one conditional Denver first-round obligation, Indiana B for Mojave King's rights, a 2024 protected first and cash, and the Lakers C+ for Maxwell Lewis. The complete official asset directions prevent Indiana from appearing empty and the Thunder's single conditional first from being counted twice.

washington-wizards.summary: The Bulls obtained Julian Phillips's draft rights from Washington in June 2023 for two future second-round selections, due in 2026 and 2027. Phillips joined Chicago's young wing pipeline, while Washington collected additional chances to draft or trade prospects later. The inherited slight Wizards edge gives Washington B- and Chicago C+.
washington-wizards.analysis:
Chicago Traded Future Seconds for Phillips's Rights

The Bulls acquired the draft rights to Julian Phillips from Washington during the 2023 draft, sending second-round selections for 2026 and 2027. Chicago wanted to evaluate a young athletic wing rather than defer both chances to later drafts. Washington was willing to spread the return over two future years instead of retaining Phillips's rights. The deal was a classic draft-night decision between a known current prospect and multiple later opportunities, without established veterans changing teams.

Phillips Became a Developmental Bulls Player

Phillips joined Chicago and received NBA development opportunities as a defensive-minded forward. His size and athletic ability offered possibilities on the wing, although his early role was not comparable to the output of a settled starting scorer. Those Chicago appearances are the actual receiving-team benefit. Phillips's college performance explains why the club wanted him, but the transaction should be judged by his subsequent Bulls role rather than by projecting an unearned All-Star future.

Washington Retained Two Draft Opportunities

The Wizards received rights to selections in 2026 and 2027. Each pick offered a future possibility to add a prospect or participate in a subsequent trade. These rights are not equivalent to immediate Washington NBA playing time; no specific draftee should be assigned to the original deal unless the selection and any intervening rights movements are traced. The package spread value across two drafts, providing the rebuilding club with flexibility without requiring it to sign another young wing in 2023.

A Slight Wizards Edge Reflects Extra Chances

Chicago preferred the certainty of evaluating Phillips, while Washington accepted two later second-round opportunities. Neither strategy guaranteed a star. The inherited slight Wizards advantage rewards the broader draft inventory, though Phillips did become an active developmental piece for the Bulls. The proper comparison is a present prospect against future flexibility rather than a claim that Chicago acquired nothing or that Washington had already developed two NBA rotation players from the selections.

Final Verdict

Boston Moved Back Into a Different Draft Package
