Boston chose to split its return between a younger wing prospect and another selection rather than keep the original guard prospect. Sacramento preferred Jones, whose college experience and perimeter skills appeared useful for backcourt depth. This was a modest rights exchange rather than a trade of players already established as NBA starters.

Walsh Entered Boston's Development Pipeline

Walsh came to Boston as a wing whose defensive activity and length were part of his appeal. He received NBA opportunities with the Celtics, although he was not a central playoff contributor on the club's 2024 championship run. Evaluating his actual work requires separating the team's overall achievements from the individual minutes this transaction produced. The trade provided Boston with a player it could develop over time, not an immediate star with a guaranteed role in the championship rotation.

Sacramento Took Jones While Boston Held Another Pick

Jones was a guard prospect who received a limited chance to establish himself with Sacramento. The Celtics' additional 2024 second-round right became associated with No. 54 Anton Watson. That identity was another draft opportunity, not a promise that Watson would become an NBA regular or that every future appearance belonged to the Celtics. The Kings obtained the single player they preferred from the rights sequence, while Boston gained two possible developmental paths rather than one.

Neither team obtained an established offensive leader directly from this deal. Sacramento had a reasonable case for targeting Jones, but his early Kings role was limited. Boston obtained Walsh and a subsequent pick, making its side somewhat broader despite a modest immediate basketball return. The inherited narrow Celtics advantage credits that added selection and flexibility without turning Walsh's roster membership into credit for every game won by Boston's veterans. This was a gradual development move judged on limited realized evidence.

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston receives B- for Jordan Walsh's developmental opportunities and the 2024 second-round asset associated with Anton Watson. The transaction gave Detroit a player it had identified as a potential source of shooting and backcourt depth alongside its young guards. That contribution belongs directly to the receiving Pistons, not to Boston, which had traded his rights before he played an NBA game. The guard's development is the strongest Detroit argument in the evaluation. He was not acquired as an immediate star, however, and the team still needed to decide how large a role he could earn as the roster evolved.

Boston Held Rights and Two Separate Draft Chances

The two future second-round choices added separate opportunities to select or trade other players. Their later draft identities must be tracked through additional transactions instead of declaring every eventual draftee a Boston regular-season player. In Boston's case, the useful return was flexibility and multiple pieces of draft capital for a single outgoing first-round prospect.

Detroit obtained the player who actually appeared in NBA games for his acquiring club, while Boston chose international rights and future inventory. Both approaches had a reasonable basketball rationale. The inherited Celtics advantage assigns higher value to receiving multiple movable assets, but it should not hide that the Pistons enjoyed the clearer immediate on-court return from Sasser. The comparison is about the price paid for that rotation chance and what Boston could retain or exchange later, not an invented Celtics Nnaji season.

minnesota-timberwolves.analysis:
The Timberwolves Acquired Rights to Leonard Miller

Minnesota obtained the draft rights to forward Leonard Miller, selected thirty-third overall in 2023, from San Antonio in exchange for two future second-round selections. The obligation included a 2026 choice connected with Utah and a 2028 second. Minnesota was acquiring a young frontcourt project it could develop alongside a team built around Anthony Edwards and Rudy Gobert. San Antonio chose to hold more future draft capital rather than keep that particular early-second-round prospect. These were draft-rights and pick obligations, not an exchange of established veterans.

Miller Entered an Already Crowded Frontcourt

Miller offered size, rebounding and developmental potential when he joined Minnesota, but the Timberwolves' depth chart did not give him an uncontested starter's role. Gobert and Karl-Anthony Towns consumed important frontcourt minutes during the early part of his tenure, and the team's competitive ambitions required immediate reliability. Limited NBA playing time is still a genuine receiving-team return, but it cannot be inflated into the production of a lead scorer. The draft pick paid for the possibility of future growth rather than instant proof of a successful starter acquisition.

San Antonio Prioritized Two Future Second-Round Options

The Spurs received two separate draft assets, one associated with 2026 and another with 2028. Those rights could provide future inexpensive players or be incorporated into additional personnel moves. The deal should not assign later NBA games to San Antonio simply because a selection eventually bears another player's name. The protections and final conveyance paths determine whether either right actually supplies an asset. San Antonio was developing its own group of young talent and could plausibly prefer spreading its draft opportunities across multiple seasons rather than retaining Miller's specific rights.

Future Flexibility Against Developmental Playing Time

The clubs pursued opposite timelines: Minnesota wanted one identified prospect in hand, while San Antonio chose multiple future second-round chances. By itself, Miller's limited early playing time doesn't establish a major Timberwolves victory, and two later selections are not equivalent to two guaranteed rotation players for the Spurs. The inherited San Antonio edge can be retained at a moderate grade based on flexible capital. Minnesota still received a legitimate young player who reached its roster, which is more than a speculative placeholder. A faithful retrospective separates actual games, protected rights and possible future outcomes.

Final Verdict

Spurs Win by a narrow draft-flexibility margin. San Antonio earns B for two future second-round selections, including the Utah-linked 2026 choice and a 2028 choice. Minnesota gets B- after acquiring Leonard Miller's No. 33 rights and developing him as a depth forward. Neither side is credited with unknown future draftees or hypothetical star-level NBA production.

washington-wizards.analysis:
Detroit Targeted a Veteran Point Guard

The Pistons acquired Monte Morris from Washington on July 6, 2023, sending a conditional 2027 second-round selection. The obligation was linked to the more favorable of Brooklyn and Dallas picks controlled through Detroit's asset history. Morris had shown he could organize an offense and protect the ball, making him an appealing veteran for a young Pistons backcourt. Washington took a longer-term option rather than retaining another guard as it reshaped its roster. The transaction looked like a simple exchange of a playable veteran for a future draft right.

Injury Kept Morris From Establishing a Detroit Role

Morris's ability to contribute was heavily limited by a persistent injury during the 2023-24 season. He made only a handful of regular-season appearances for Detroit before being sent to Minnesota in a separate move. His earlier work with Denver and Washington explained why Detroit wanted him, but those productive seasons cannot be included as Pistons minutes from the transaction. The club didn't get the dependable guard organizer it originally envisioned for a meaningful stretch. That outcome sharply reduced the immediate payoff from giving up a future second-round obligation.

Washington Held an Unresolved Future Asset

The Wizards received a conditional second-round right tied to the 2027 draft. Because that draft is in the future relative to this evaluation, there is no realized selection or player whose games can legitimately be assigned to Washington. The right still carries possible trade and scouting value, even though its precise destination will depend on the terms and applicable standings. Washington sacrificed a veteran it was prepared to move and accepted that uncertainty. Describing the pick as a future asset is more accurate than inventing a draftee or retroactively crediting games played elsewhere.

A Brief Player Tenure and a Future Pick Leave a Tie

Detroit's approach was reasonable because Morris had a record of filling a useful role, but the injury meant it did not receive sustained guard play. Washington took on draft uncertainty and did not obtain an incoming contributor in 2023-24. The subsequent Morris trade is a different transaction whose return should not be folded into the original exchange without following the asset chain. The matching C+ grades reflect limited realized value and modest initial costs. Neither side received a definitive win from this narrow guard-for-pick arrangement.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Detroit gets C+ after Monte Morris's injury-shortened Pistons tenure produced only brief playing time before another trade. Washington also earns C+ for a conditional 2027 second-round asset whose outcome isn't yet known. The original swap gave both sides reasonable options but little established receiving-team value, making a modest tie more defensible than a decisive winner.

perspectives.analysis:
Cleveland Pursued a Proven Playoff Shooter

The Cavaliers acquired Max Strus through a July 2023 multiclub sign-and-trade involving the Heat and Spurs. Cleveland's young core needed another wing who could space the floor and make opponents defend the perimeter. Strus had contributed to Miami's deep playoff run earlier that year, giving the Cavaliers an identifiable player profile rather than an untested draft-rights option. Cleveland was investing in a complementary starting-caliber shooter, not another ball-dominant star.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Utah Bought Collins at a Discounted Trade Cost

The Jazz acquired John Collins from Atlanta in July 2023, sending Rudy Gay and a conditional 2026 second-round selection to the Hawks. Collins had been an established scoring and rebounding forward alongside Trae Young, although his role and salary had become harder to balance with Atlanta's plans. Utah saw an opportunity to add a capable NBA starter without giving up one of its central younger players. The Hawks prioritized moving his contract and taking a much smaller direct package.

Collins Provided the Jazz With Real Frontcourt Production

Collins played substantial minutes with Utah, adding interior finishing, rebounding and an outside-shooting option. His Jazz work, rather than his earlier years in Atlanta, is the receiving-team value that defines the transaction. The club eventually moved him in a separate deal, but the initial acquisition delivered an active contributor rather than an unused roster right. Collins was not an immediate franchise-changing All-Star, yet he provided enough dependable frontcourt play to make the modest outgoing compensation attractive.

Atlanta Did Not Receive an Active Player From Gay

Gay was a recognizable veteran with a long scoring career, but Atlanta waived him before he played a regular-season game for the Hawks. His accomplishments with earlier teams therefore cannot be counted as Atlanta playing production. The conditional 2026 second-round right carried possible draft value, though its protections limited what could be assumed and require separate confirmation of the eventual resolution. The Hawks' tangible benefit primarily concerned salary and roster flexibility rather than an incoming player ready to replace Collins.

One Team Obtained the Established Contributor

Utah added a forward who immediately became part of its lineup, while Atlanta took financial flexibility and a conditional asset. The Hawks may have had reasons to move Collins's contract, but that decision did not deliver equivalent court production from Gay. The verdict distinguishes a practical salary-management purpose from the basketball value of what each franchise actually received. Utah's superior direct player return supplies the clearest reason for the wide inherited gap in grades.

Final Verdict

Jazz Win. Utah earns B+ for acquiring John Collins and receiving meaningful forward production during his Jazz tenure. Atlanta gets C- because Rudy Gay was waived before playing for the Hawks and the conditional second-round choice provided uncertain additional return. Salary flexibility had value, but Utah obtained the only significant receiving-team on-court contributor.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Targeted Mills During a Busy Offseason

The Hawks acquired Patty Mills from Oklahoma City in July 2023, sending the Thunder TyTy Washington Jr., Usman Garuba, Rudy Gay and a future second-round choice tied to 2026. Mills had won a championship earlier in his career and remained a recognizable veteran point guard. Atlanta wanted an experienced bench presence while adjusting younger roster players. Oklahoma City accepted multiple contracts and a draft asset as it continued reshaping the fringes of its roster.

Mills Filled a Narrow Hawks Guard Role

Mills gave Atlanta veteran ball-handling experience and a reliable professional presence, though his playing opportunities were limited compared with his earlier years in San Antonio and Brooklyn. The Hawks didn't acquire him as a replacement for their leading scorer or an unquestioned new starter. His leadership and availability mattered more than a major boost in box-score totals. The relevant receiving-team value is the period he actually spent in Atlanta, not championships won for another franchise.

The Thunder Acquired Contracts and a Future Choice

Oklahoma City took Washington, Garuba and Gay, with the veteran and younger players each having different roster possibilities. Their arrivals did not all translate into sustained Thunder playing roles, which makes the incoming second-round asset an important piece. The 2026 choice was a future right at the time and depended on subsequent transactions to determine its final effect. The club also gained opportunities to manage contracts and create space for its younger core through follow-on moves.

The Grade Gap Reflects Oklahoma City's Flexibility

Atlanta obtained a short-term veteran guard who could support a developing roster, whereas Oklahoma City received multiple movable components and a draft chance. The inherited Thunder B+ credits those combined options over Mills's comparatively small Hawks stint. It would exaggerate the deal to assume Washington, Garuba and Gay all became important Thunder rotation players. The more reliable conclusion is that Oklahoma City generated flexibility and extra draft value in a transaction aimed largely at roster management.

Final Verdict

Oklahoma City Thunder Win. Oklahoma City receives B+ for TyTy Washington Jr., Usman Garuba, Rudy Gay and a future 2026 second-round asset, primarily useful as roster and draft flexibility. Atlanta gets C for veteran Patty Mills, whose Hawks playing role was limited. The Thunder collected a broader package even though not every acquired player established a lasting rotation position.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Dallas Obtained Williams to Support Its Stars

The Mavericks acquired Grant Williams from Boston in July 2023 through a sign-and-trade involving San Antonio. Williams had played valuable defensive forward minutes for the Celtics and could stretch the floor, which made him a plausible complementary option beside Dallas's lead ball handlers. He entered on a multiyear contract rather than as a one-season rental. The receiving-team question was whether his defensive skills and outside shooting would translate into the Mavericks' rotation, not whether his previous playoff appearances with Boston could be retroactively counted as Dallas success.

Boston Chose Three Different Second-Round Options

The Celtics obtained a 2024 second-round choice routed through San Antonio, a 2025 second-round swap with Dallas and another second-round selection from Dallas in 2030. The 2024 right became associated with No. 41 Adem Bona, but that historical selection reference doesn't mean the Celtics received his eventual playing career. The team was converting a restricted free agent's departure into future draft flexibility while limiting longer-term roster expense. The different years and conditional mechanics should be traced independently rather than presented as three immediately selected players.

San Antonio and Dallas Exchanged More Than Williams

Bullock offered veteran perimeter defense and shooting; the future first-round swap had substantial potential but no guaranteed draft position when executed. Dallas also acquired 2025 and 2028 second-round selections routed from San Antonio. Those incoming Mavericks picks are part of the same official three-team deal even though the earlier Boston-only record omitted them. Each receiving team's actual contract and pick obligations must be kept intact.

The Celtics Grade Favors Flexibility Over Immediate Minutes

The inherited Celtics B+ reflects the collection of future rights from allowing Williams to move. Williams did not stay with the Mavericks for the full initial contract term, which limits direct team value, but the Spurs and Dallas packages weren't empty. The narrow Boston edge is a judgment about total compensation and not a claim that second-round selections guaranteed franchise stars.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns B+ for three future second-round opportunities after trading Grant Williams. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Paid Players and Picks for a Two-Way Guard

The Celtics acquired Jrue Holiday from the Trail Blazers in October 2023, sending Robert Williams III, Malcolm Brogdon, a 2024 first-round selection and another first due in 2029. Holiday had joined Portland as part of the separate Damian Lillard transaction, but Boston quickly acted to acquire his defense and playmaking. The deal cost two NBA veterans and real draft capital, making it more consequential than a salary shuffle. The Celtics wanted a starter who could fit beside Jayson Tatum and Jaylen Brown without monopolizing offensive possessions.

Holiday Became Part of Boston's Championship Core

Holiday supplied perimeter defense, ball handling and timely scoring during the 2023-24 season as Boston won the NBA championship. His ability to work without the ball and guard difficult assignments complemented the Celtics' other starters. That title is direct receiving-team value, not credit assigned from Holiday's earlier championship in Milwaukee. Boston invested heavily, but the decision produced a player who was integral to the lineup at the precise moment the franchise captured its next title.

Portland Obtained Both Veterans and Future Options

The Trail Blazers acquired Brogdon and Williams, two established players whose long-term roles would depend on health and subsequent roster plans. They also secured first-round draft capital. The 2024 selection became associated with No. 14 Carlton Carrington, although its later draft-night route cannot be mistaken for Carrington playing a Portland season. The additional 2029 first gave the rebuilding organization another future opportunity. Those are meaningful assets even if they did not produce a championship for Portland immediately.

Different Timelines Produced Two Strong Returns

Boston converted depth and picks into a title-winning starter, a direct payoff that justified a substantial acquisition cost. Portland took a broader package suited to a rebuild after the Lillard era. The inherited high grade on both sides acknowledges that Williams, Brogdon and the selections had real value. Boston receives the edge because Holiday's specific Celtics contribution is unusually clear: he filled an essential position on a championship team rather than merely promising to help at some later date.

Final Verdict

Slight Celtics Edge. Boston earns A+ for Jrue Holiday's immediate two-way contribution to its 2024 championship, paying with Malcolm Brogdon, Robert Williams III and two first-round choices. Portland gets A for acquiring veterans and valuable draft flexibility, including the right later associated with Carlton Carrington. Both clubs obtained real value, but Boston converted the deal directly into a title-winning starter.

los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Exchanged Petrusev's Contract for Overseas Rights

Los Angeles sent forward Filip Petrušev and cash to Sacramento on November 9, 2023, acquiring the draft rights to Serbian forward Luka Mitrović. Petrušev had only recently moved through several NBA organizations and was not established as a regular Clippers contributor. Sacramento took a chance on evaluating an available young big man, while the Clippers preferred a rights-held overseas prospect who did not immediately occupy an NBA roster spot. The deal contained no new first-round selection and was far smaller in basketball impact than the headline trades both California teams had executed around this period.

Sacramento Received an NBA Player Contract and Cash

The Kings acquired Petrušev's contract, providing the ability to assess his short-term place in their frontcourt or make another roster decision. His Sacramento opportunity was brief and did not develop into an extended NBA career with the Kings. The incoming cash was a distinct benefit, but the team did not gain a long-serving center by simply processing the agreement. Petrušev's previous playing time with Philadelphia and future professional seasons abroad aren't Sacramento statistics. The direct return was the rights to a roster evaluation and financial consideration rather than guaranteed on-court production.

Mitrović Was a Long-Held International Draft Asset

The Clippers received the rights to Mitrović, who had established his professional reputation outside the NBA. Retaining the rights did not produce a season of Clippers frontcourt minutes, nor did it require him to come to Los Angeles immediately. The franchise could hold or further trade the asset, a small form of flexibility during a season when its veteran NBA roster was already crowded. It would be inappropriate to convert his European club accomplishments into NBA games or to assign him a current Clippers role without evidence of an NBA contract. That limits the tangible impact of the incoming return.

A Small Financial Edge Rather Than a Major Kings Win

Neither side converted its acquired player rights into a recognized long-term NBA rotation piece during the immediate period. Sacramento's cash payment and ability to evaluate Petrušev offered slightly more concrete value than the Clippers' dormant overseas rights. The difference is narrow, making modest grades a better fit than claims of a lopsided trade victory. This is the kind of transaction where cap and roster management outweigh box-score performance. Both clubs should be judged on the actual assets exchanged rather than on unrelated postseason results or the full careers of players who appeared elsewhere.

Final Verdict

Slight Kings Edge. Sacramento receives C+ for Filip Petrušev's short-lived roster opportunity and cash considerations. Los Angeles gets C for the international draft rights to Luka Mitrović, with no implied NBA Clippers games. Neither acquisition became a verified long-term starting player for its new club, so the difference is modest and largely based on contract and financial flexibility.

washington-wizards.summary: Washington acquired Marvin Bagley III, Isaiah Livers and two second-round assets from Detroit in January 2024, sending Danilo Gallinari and Mike Muscala to the Pistons. Bagley supplied interior scoring and rebounding in Washington, while Detroit took veteran contracts. The inherited Wizards Win grades Washington B+ and Detroit C.
washington-wizards.analysis:
Washington Acquired Bagley and Extra Draft Chances

The Wizards obtained Marvin Bagley III and Isaiah Livers from Detroit in January 2024, along with two second-round draft rights. The Pistons received veterans Danilo Gallinari and Mike Muscala. Washington was looking for more frontcourt options and future selections during its rebuild, while Detroit sought to alter an uneven roster. Bagley had already shown NBA scoring ability near the basket, so this was not solely a speculative draft-rights deal. The extra picks added a separate long-term element.

Bagley Provided Washington With Actual Interior Play

Bagley had stretches of productive scoring and rebounding with the Wizards, supplying a mobile interior option rather than merely occupying a roster slot. His availability and defense limited how much that contribution could transform the team, but his receiving-team minutes are part of the trade's actual return. Livers offered another developmental forward possibility with health and performance questions. Washington did not obtain an established franchise center, though it acquired players and picks with recognizable roles.

Detroit's Incoming Veterans Offered Shorter-Term Options

Gallinari and Muscala were experienced shooters who could, in theory, provide frontcourt spacing. Their Detroit tenures did not become lengthy central playing roles, and later stops elsewhere should not be counted as Pistons production. The club also gave up second-round assets that could be used by Washington in later drafts. One of those selections became associated with No. 47 Bogoljub Marković in 2025, while the other was tied to 2026. Rights and player destinations still require tracing.

The Wizards' Return Was More Durable

Washington obtained the more obvious direct court contributor in Bagley and retained two future opportunities through the acquired selections. Detroit received veterans whose practical tenure was comparatively limited. The inherited B+ for Washington and C for Detroit follows the combination of on-court big-man minutes and draft flexibility. The conclusion shouldn't be inflated into a claim that Bagley became an All-Star, or that the later draft players all logged Washington minutes.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington receives B+ for Marvin Bagley III's interior production, Isaiah Livers and two second-round assets. Detroit earns C for Danilo Gallinari and Mike Muscala, who did not establish long, central Pistons roles. The Wizards gained a more usable frontcourt piece plus draft opportunities, while Detroit's veteran return was brief.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Paid Two Seconds to Add Tillman

Boston acquired center-forward Xavier Tillman from Memphis on February 7, 2024, sending Lamar Stevens and two second-round choices slated for 2027 and 2030 to the Grizzlies. The Celtics already possessed an elite starting lineup but wanted another versatile interior defender for matchup-based postseason rotations. Memphis was dealing with an injury-hit season and prioritized additional selections over retaining a player in a reserve role. The deal did not involve a first-round pick or a core Celtics starter, allowing Boston to improve depth without abandoning its principal championship group.

A Defensive Reserve Found Playoff Minutes

Tillman could switch defensively, defend physical forwards and give Boston short bursts of dependable minutes behind its more prominent big men. During the 2024 NBA Finals against Dallas, he even made a notable three-pointer in Game 3, illustrating how a reserve obtained months earlier could contribute to a decisive championship series. That limited but actual Finals participation should be credited to this acquisition. It should not be conflated with all of Boston’s 2024 success, which depended on a much larger roster assembled through many previous transactions and signings.

Memphis Bought Flexibility After Injuries

Memphis received Lamar Stevens, a serviceable forward whose NBA career had already included other teams, plus two future second-round draft assets. Those selections offered opportunities to add inexpensive players or to become components of later trades, even if no specific receiving-team NBA minutes existed on deadline day. Stevens was not a replacement for the team’s injured stars, and his earlier Boston appearances belonged to the Celtics. Memphis nevertheless gained legitimate long-term flexibility during a difficult 2023-24 campaign without surrendering a first-round prospect.

The Title Run Adds Direct Boston Value

The strongest measurable result belongs to Boston because Tillman contributed to a championship rotation and cost only secondary assets. Memphis cannot be marked as losing an invaluable cornerstone, because it converted a useful reserve into a player and two selections that could support future moves. That balanced asset context is why the trade merits a strong Boston grade but not an exaggerated claim that Tillman single-handedly decided a championship. The Finals performance establishes direct value; the future pick outcomes must still be evaluated separately when they actually occur.

Final Verdict

Celtics Win. Boston earns A- for adding Xavier Tillman, a useful defensive reserve who supplied minutes and a memorable Game 3 three-pointer during the 2024 NBA Finals. Memphis receives B- for Lamar Stevens plus 2027 and 2030 second-round choices. Those picks are future assets rather than established NBA contributors, and the Celtics’ entire championship cannot be credited to one depth trade.

washington-wizards.analysis:
Dallas Upgraded Its Center Rotation at the Deadline

On February 8, 2024, Dallas acquired Daniel Gafford from Washington while the Wizards took Richaun Holmes and a first-round draft asset arranged through Oklahoma City. The incoming selection was later associated with the twenty-sixth overall position in the 2024 draft and Dillon Jones, though the right was routed through another transaction rather than becoming Jones’s NBA service in Washington. Dallas sought a more athletic interior presence alongside Dereck Lively II and the Luka Dončić–Kyrie Irving backcourt. Washington chose a veteran contract and future selection as it continued a broader rebuilding process.

Gafford Became a Real Playoff Rim Finisher

Gafford changed Dallas’s frontcourt rotation by providing vertical finishing, offensive rebounding and shot blocking. He and Lively offered the Mavericks two playable centers who could run to the rim as passing targets for Dončić and Irving. That pairing was part of Dallas’s run to the 2024 NBA Finals. The new center’s direct impact is not merely the reputation he had built in Washington; his Dallas games following February demonstrate the receiving team’s actual basketball return. The trade supplied a role that the Mavericks needed without requiring an expensive long-term star acquisition.

Washington Received Holmes and a First-Round Right

Holmes entered a rebuilding Wizards organization and was not asked to become the central offensive engine. The draft asset was the more important longer-range element, though it traveled through a chain of rights and cannot be evaluated as if Washington directly developed Dillon Jones. The relationship with Oklahoma City and the later draft identity should remain distinct from the initial Dallas-Washington exchange. Washington gained some flexibility, but it also surrendered an established rim protector who immediately helped another club. Neither Holmes’s earlier Sacramento years nor Jones’s later destination games belong to the Wizards’ direct return.

The Finals Run Exposes the Return Gap

The Mavericks achieved an immediate roster improvement that translated into meaningful postseason minutes. Washington acquired a veteran and an asset that could be deployed as part of its long-term plans, an understandable strategy for a team in a different competitive phase. Yet Gafford’s value as a dependable center on a Finals participant outweighs the limited immediate Wizards production. The conclusion holds without crediting all Dallas wins solely to Gafford or dismissing the first-round right as nonexistent. It is a strong present-day fit against a more uncertain future package.

Final Verdict

Mavericks Win. Dallas receives A because Daniel Gafford became a major center-rotation contributor during its 2024 NBA Finals run. Washington earns C+ for Richaun Holmes and a transferable 2024 first-round asset whose later No. 26 Dillon Jones identity followed a separate rights chain. boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Moved a Reserve Guard at the Deadline

The Celtics sent Dalano Banton and cash to Portland in February 2024, receiving a conditional second-round choice due in 2027. Banton had seen limited opportunities in Boston's crowded backcourt, while the Trail Blazers could offer more room for player evaluation. The Celtics were building toward a title push with an established rotation and chose to clear a spot rather than retain another developmental guard. The future pick remained conditional, so it could not be treated as a guaranteed new Celtics player.

Banton Received a Larger Trial in Portland

Banton saw increased playing opportunities after joining the Trail Blazers, showing his ability to handle the ball and create offense with a younger roster. His previous Toronto and Boston performances explain why Portland took the chance, but the minutes in a Blazers uniform are the return that belongs to this trade. Portland did not acquire a proven All-Star or a guaranteed long-term starter. It obtained a relatively inexpensive opportunity to see how an athletic guard performed with more responsibility.

The Celtics Preferred Roster Flexibility

Boston received a conditional second-round right rather than an active replacement for Banton. That future opportunity might create value depending on its protections and later transactions, but there was no immediate draft pick ready to help the 2024 team. The Celtics ultimately won the NBA title that season, yet that success cannot be assigned directly to a deal whose main outgoing asset was a reserve guard. Their practical benefit was the ability to adjust personnel and salary commitments.

Two Modest Benefits Support the Even Grade

Portland secured useful evaluation minutes from a young guard; Boston gained flexibility and a possible later second-round asset. Those results are different and difficult to compare as if one side received the same type of compensation. Neither organization surrendered a central contributor or made a bet on a transformational player. The inherited even grade reflects the modest scale of the agreement, recognizing that both teams achieved aspects of their separate roster-management goals without a decisive long-term result.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Boston receives C+ for clearing a reserve role and acquiring a conditional 2027 second-round right, without claiming a guaranteed draftee. Portland also earns C+ because Dalano Banton provided increased guard minutes after arriving with cash considerations. Both sides gained modest flexibility or player development value, rather than a franchise-changing transaction.

boston-celtics.analysis:
Boston Added a Defensive Guard Prospect

The Celtics acquired Jaden Springer from Philadelphia at the 2024 deadline, sending the 76ers a future second-round choice. Springer was a young guard known more for his defensive potential than for established high-volume NBA scoring. Boston could evaluate him behind an experienced backcourt during a title push. Philadelphia preferred a draft opportunity over keeping a prospect whose immediate rotation role had been limited. The trade involved a developmental player and a selection rather than two starting-level veterans.

Springer Was Not a Central Championship Contributor

Springer joined Boston in the season the Celtics went on to win the 2024 championship, but he was not a major source of postseason playing production. Membership on the title roster should not be mistaken for the minutes provided by players who anchored the run. His Boston stint offered some defensive development opportunities and later ended with another transaction. His earlier 76ers games and later work elsewhere must stay separate from the value acquired by Boston in February 2024.

Philadelphia Used the Incoming Pick on Adem Bona

The 76ers' acquired second-round selection became associated with No. 41 Adem Bona in the 2024 draft. Bona offered an athletic interior prospect who later received NBA opportunities in Philadelphia. Those receiving-team appearances gave the choice a concrete player identity and an emerging frontcourt role. No selection guarantees a successful career, and Bona's long-term ceiling should not be treated as settled. Yet the immediate return was more durable than the limited role Springer filled for Boston.

The Grades Follow the Realized Playing Opportunities

Boston obtained a young guard it could try in a competitive roster, while Philadelphia turned the outgoing player into a new big-man prospect. Springer's limited Celtics responsibilities restrict the amount of championship credit attributable to this deal. Bona's development gave the Sixers an active path to roster value from the pick. The inherited Philadelphia advantage is therefore grounded in the different receiving-team opportunities, not in a claim that Springer had no NBA ability or that Bona had become an established franchise star.

Final Verdict

76ers Win. Philadelphia gets B for the second-round right used on Adem Bona, who became a developmental frontcourt contributor. Boston earns C- for Jaden Springer, whose Celtics playing role remained limited despite the franchise's 2024 championship. The Sixers converted the outgoing guard into another young player with clearer receiving-team minutes, while Boston's acquisition had modest direct impact.

analysis: The February deal itself was straightforward: Golden State moved Cory Joseph, cash and a protected 2025 Charlotte second to Indiana for a 2024 second. Joseph was waived by Indiana the same day, and Basketball-Reference records that the protected Charlotte pick did not convey. The acquired 2024 second became No. 52. oklahoma-city-thunder.analysis:
Oklahoma City Took the Fortieth Pick Rights, Portland the Fifty-Second

On June 27, 2024, Oklahoma City received draft rights associated with Marquette forward Oso Ighodaro from Portland. The Blazers obtained the rights to Boston College center Quinten Post along with cash. The transaction redistributed second-round prospects rather than swapping established NBA players. The Thunder preferred an earlier pick that could be held or used in another deal, while Portland moved back and received direct financial consideration. The difference between the No. 40 and No. 52 draft positions created a modest edge for the team holding the higher pick, though either choice's actual future roster impact depended on later transactions.

Ighodaro Became a Phoenix NBA Player After Additional Rights Moves

Ighodaro's draft-night rights passed through more than one club before he began his NBA career, and his playing opportunities developed with Phoenix rather than as an Oklahoma City regular. His athletic, mobile frontcourt profile helped explain why the draft position was valuable, but that scouting upside should not turn Suns games into Thunder games. The proper Oklahoma City return was a transferable early-second-round asset. A team can gain value from moving such a right in another transaction, yet the outcome must be traced rather than treating the eventual player's career as the original receiving team's direct production. No guaranteed Thunder center emerged from the single Portland exchange alone.

Post Developed With Golden State, Not Portland

Portland received the later selection associated with Post and cash. The rights to Post subsequently moved again, and his NBA career developed with Golden State rather than through a long Blazers stint. The draft position and immediate financial return were real, even though his subsequent shooting and frontcourt minutes elsewhere weren't Portland production. This is especially important for draft-night packages in which multiple teams may briefly hold the same player's rights before signing rights finally settle. The Blazers got a lower choice plus money and retained the option to redirect their acquired asset, which is a legitimate but limited return relative to Oklahoma City's incoming higher selection.

A Higher Pick Creates Only a Narrow Initial Advantage

The Thunder acquired the earlier draft-rights slot in a transaction whose direct value was largely about dealing options, while the Blazers accepted a lower slot and cash. Oklahoma City has a modest advantage when comparing the nominal draft positions, but both clubs' later outcomes depended heavily on other moves. Neither can honestly claim the full Phoenix or Golden State NBA careers of Ighodaro and Post under this single trade. A limited Thunder-winning verdict maintains that distinction and avoids grading an unsettled draft asset as if the team had already secured a regular starting center.

Final Verdict

Oklahoma City Thunder Win by a limited draft-position edge. The Thunder earn B- for the earlier No. 40 rights to Oso Ighodaro, while Portland receives C+ for No. 52 Quinten Post rights and cash. Ighodaro's Phoenix and Post's Golden State NBA production occurred after other rights transfers and is not assigned to these original receiving teams.

washington-wizards.analysis:
Washington Targeted George in the 2024 Draft

The Wizards acquired Kyshawn George's draft rights from the Knicks during the June 2024 draft, sending the rights to Dillon Jones and Melvin Ajinça in return. Washington identified George as a wing prospect who fit its younger roster plan and chose to concentrate the incoming value in one player. New York took two separate draft-rights assets it could retain or redirect through subsequent transactions. The agreement exchanged choices and prospect identities, not proven NBA veterans.

George Became an Active Wizards Wing

George entered Washington's development program and gained NBA playing opportunities. His length, passing and willingness to handle multiple wing assignments gave the rebuilding Wizards another player to evaluate alongside their young core. He was not a finished star when acquired, so the value lies in actual developmental minutes and future potential rather than an invented immediate playoff transformation. His on-court work with Washington is the direct return that belongs in the initial trade evaluation.

The Knicks Held Two Different Rights Packages

New York received Jones and Ajinça's draft rights, providing separate choices in how to manage the roster and future transactions. Subsequent rights transfers complicate any simple claim that both players became Knicks rotation contributors. A draft-night exchange can have value even when a player never appears in the receiving team's NBA lineup, because the rights themselves are tradable assets. The Knicks' direct playing return from these specific names must be distinguished from what other franchises did with them later.

The Grade Edge Comes From a Known Developing Player

Washington obtained an identifiable wing it could put into games and develop over time. New York gained a broader collection of rights but did not derive an equivalent direct Knicks playing role from the transaction. The inherited Wizards advantage captures the appeal of consolidating value into George, while recognizing that Jones and Ajinça had their own prospect value. The outcome should not be exaggerated into a verdict on either player's entire eventual career so early in development.

Final Verdict

Wizards Win. Washington earns B+ for securing Kyshawn George and developing him as an NBA wing. New York receives C+ for the rights to Dillon Jones and Melvin Ajinça, assets whose subsequent destinations must be tracked separately rather than counted automatically as Knicks playing time. The Wizards acquired the clearer direct player contribution from the draft-night exchange.

summary: Golden State sent the draft rights to No. 52 pick Quinten Post to Oklahoma City for Lindy Waters III. The Thunder immediately rerouted Post's rights and cash through Portland and New York in the draft-night chain that produced Ajay Mitchell. Golden State separately reacquired Post from Portland for cash. Post later became a useful two-season Warriors rotation big, while Mitchell developed into an important Thunder rotation player. analysis: The original exchange was Lindy Waters III to Golden State for the draft rights to Quinten Post. Oklahoma City then sent Post's rights and cash to Portland for Oso Ighodaro's rights and used Ighodaro in the path to Ajay Mitchell. Golden State separately sent cash to Portland to reacquire Post. NBA.com's draft-night reporting explicitly ties the broader sequence to Oklahoma City getting Mitchell and Golden State keeping Post, but those later moves should not be collapsed into the initial bilateral ledger. Hindsight is strong for both sides: Post became a Warriors rotation big for two seasons and averaged 7.7 points and 4.0 rebounds over 67 games in his final Golden State season, while NBA.com described Mitchell as an important part of Oklahoma City's rotation in 2025-26. Waters also gave Golden State rotation depth before leaving in the 2025 Jimmy Butler transaction. The C-level grades therefore understate the value created by both front offices.

washington-wizards.analysis:
Portland Purchased an Emerging Two-Way Forward

The Trail Blazers acquired Deni Avdija from Washington in July 2024, surrendering Malcolm Brogdon, the 2024 No. 14 draft right, a future first and two second-round choices. Avdija had grown as a versatile Washington forward capable of defending, rebounding and initiating offense. Portland was willing to spend multiple draft assets for a player still early in his career. Washington instead accepted Brogdon and additional opportunities to add younger talent through its rebuilding process.

Avdija Became an Important Portland Contributor

Avdija gave the Blazers a forward who could handle the ball, attack the basket and contribute across several statistical categories. His size and versatility made him useful in different lineups as the franchise sought a new competitive core. Those Portland seasons are the direct benefit of the acquisition, not his earlier development in Washington. The team invested heavily, but its return was a player who could grow into a central role rather than an older rental approaching the end of his contract.

Washington Received Carrington and More Draft Capital

The No. 14 choice became Carlton Carrington, known as Bub Carrington, whom Washington could develop in its backcourt. Brogdon offered veteran experience but did not become an enduring Wizards centerpiece. The additional 2029 first-round right and two later second-round choices increased the club's flexibility for subsequent draft decisions. Their exact future basketball impact depends on later selections or trades; no unplayed pick should be credited with fictional NBA minutes. Washington took a broader package instead of keeping one proven versatile forward.

The Grade Gap Reflects the Quality of the Main Player

Portland's reward was a developing forward capable of playing a substantial role in its rotation and offense. Washington gained a young guard and several draft chances, which have value but require further development to match the outgoing player. The inherited Blazers advantage is not a claim that Carrington lacks promise. It credits a more immediately identifiable high-level contributor while acknowledging the uncertainty of future picks and the relatively short Washington role of the veteran Brogdon.

Final Verdict

Blazers Win. Portland earns A+ for acquiring Deni Avdija, who became an important versatile forward and creator for the Blazers. Washington gets C+ for Malcolm Brogdon, Bub Carrington's draft rights and additional first- and second-round assets. The Wizards received meaningful rebuilding opportunities, but Avdija provided the stronger realized player value to his new franchise.

summary: Atlanta sent Dejounte Murray to New Orleans on July 6, 2024 for Dyson Daniels, Larry Nance Jr., E.J. Liddell, Cody Zeller, the Lakers' 2025 first-round pick and a conditional 2027 first. Daniels immediately became the 2025 Most Improved Player, All-Defensive First Team and Defensive Player of the Year runner-up, then remained a full-season Atlanta starter in 2025-26. Murray produced 31 Pelicans games before a ruptured Achilles ended 2024-25 and returned for only 14 games in 2025-26. The 2025 pick retained trade value rather than becoming a Hawks player, while the 2027 first remains pending.
analysis:
The Exchange
Atlanta's official July 6, 2024 release confirms the package: Dejounte Murray went to New Orleans for Dyson Daniels, E.J. Liddell, Larry Nance Jr., Cody Zeller, the Lakers' 2025 first-round pick and a conditional 2027 first-round choice that is the least favorable of Milwaukee and New Orleans, protected in the top four. The legacy archive record gets the core exchange right, but the source-backed version has to distinguish Atlanta's actual value from downstream draft outcomes. The 2025 Lakers pick became the No. 22 slot, where Drake Powell was drafted, but Atlanta routed those draft rights to Brooklyn in the 2025 three-team Kristaps Porzingis transaction. Powell should not be credited as a Hawks player from this deal.

Atlanta Return
Daniels has already made the trade valuable on his own. In 2024-25 he played 76 games and averaged 14.1 points, 5.9 rebounds, 4.4 assists and an NBA-leading 3.01 steals. He won Most Improved Player, finished second in Defensive Player of the Year voting and made the All-Defensive First Team. Atlanta then signed him to a multi-year extension. In 2025-26 he again played 76 games, averaging 11.9 points, 6.8 rebounds and 5.9 assists, reinforcing that the first season was not a one-year availability spike. Nance supplied 24 games of useful frontcourt depth in 2024-25, averaging 8.5 points and 4.3 rebounds, before leaving in the 2025 offseason. Liddell and Zeller did not become comparable long-term pieces. The Lakers first was still meaningful transaction capital: the No. 22 draft rights were later moved to Brooklyn during the three-team deal that brought Kristaps Porzingis to Atlanta. That later transaction should be judged separately, but the pick clearly retained market value. Atlanta also still owns the conditional 2027 first from the original Murray trade, so part of the return remains unresolved.

New Orleans Return
Murray's Pelicans tenure has been productive when available but heavily interrupted. He broke his left hand in his New Orleans debut, later returned, and finished 2024-25 with 31 starts while averaging 17.5 points, 6.5 rebounds, 7.4 assists and 2.0 steals. His season then ended with a ruptured right Achilles tendon, requiring surgery in February 2025. He returned in 2025-26 but appeared in only 14 games, averaging 16.7 points, 5.4 rebounds and 6.4 assists. Through two seasons New Orleans has therefore realized 45 regular-season games from a player acquired to organize a veteran core. The production is real enough to keep the Pelicans out of the bottom grade range, but the availability and team-level impact have fallen far short of what the two-first-plus-Daniels price required.

Hindsight Verdict
Atlanta wins clearly on realized value while still holding future upside. Daniels became one of the league's premier perimeter defenders, an award winner and a durable starter, and the Hawks also extracted useful Nance minutes, preserved the 2025 first as transaction capital and still have the 2027 first pending. New Orleans received only 45 Murray games across the first two seasons because of major injuries. Those injuries were not foreseeable as certainties on trade day, so the verdict is about realized hindsight value rather than process blame. An A for Atlanta recognizes the Daniels breakthrough plus the two first-round assets without pretending the pending 2027 choice has already produced a player. A C for New Orleans recognizes Murray's solid per-game production but reflects the limited availability and lack of a postseason payoff. Final verdict: Atlanta Hawks Win.

Valančiūnas provided Washington with veteran interior minutes before moving again, while the Pelicans accepted future asset flexibility. The inherited Even Trade assigns C+ to both teams.
washington-wizards.analysis:
Washington Added a Veteran Center Through a Sign-and-Trade

The Wizards acquired Jonas Valančiūnas from the Pelicans in July 2024, sending New Orleans a conditional second-round selection due in 2027. Valančiūnas had been a productive rebounder and interior scorer, giving Washington an experienced big man to support a roster undergoing change. The Pelicans elected not to retain him under a new agreement and accepted a future draft opportunity instead. The player and conditional pick represented very different timelines.

Valančiūnas Played Real Minutes for the Wizards

Valančiūnas became an active Washington center, supplying rebounding and inside scoring. His tenure did not last for several seasons; he was moved again in a subsequent transaction. That shorter stay still generated actual receiving-team playing value and shouldn't be erased merely because he wasn't part of a long-term rebuild. At the same time, his previous Pelicans, Memphis and Toronto performances cannot be treated as newly earned Washington production. The trade supplied a veteran for a defined period.

New Orleans Received a Protected Future Choice

The Pelicans acquired a conditional second-round right tied to the 2027 draft and originating with Chicago. Its protections limit what can be assumed about eventual conveyance and value. No specific 2027 rookie or successful rotation player should be assigned to the club before tracing the choice's final status. New Orleans' return was a future option, not an active replacement center. The organization accepted that distinction while adjusting its frontcourt personnel and contract commitments.

The Even Grade Reflects Contrasting Purposes

Washington received a veteran center capable of helping immediately, whereas New Orleans retained an opportunity in a future draft without committing to Valančiūnas's new contract. Neither club exchanged an established top-level star for another. The inherited equal grades recognize that each side achieved its selected type of value, though Washington had the more visible on-court return during the months after the trade. The Pelicans' final pick payoff remains conditional on later events.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Washington receives C+ for Jonas Valančiūnas's useful interior production during his shorter Wizards stint. New Orleans also gets C+ for a conditional 2027 second-round pick and the roster flexibility that came with moving the veteran. The Wizards obtained active center minutes, while the Pelicans acquired a future asset whose final value cannot be assumed.

indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Targeted Furphy's Size and Shooting

Indiana and San Antonio completed a 2024 draft-rights agreement finalized in early July. The Pacers received the rights to Kansas wing Johnny Furphy, selected thirty-fifth overall, while the Spurs obtained the rights to guard Juan Núñez and cash consideration. Both teams were managing second-round prospects with distinct playing styles and developmental paths. Indiana wanted a tall, mobile wing who could operate within its up-tempo offense. San Antonio was willing to retain overseas guard rights and cash rather than immediately use a rotation spot on Furphy.

Furphy Joined the Pacers as a Developing Wing

Furphy entered Indiana's organization as a rookie with an opportunity to develop his defense and long-range shooting around Tyrese Haliburton and an established playoff-caliber roster. The club was not acquiring a guaranteed starting forward; it was taking a calculated chance on a prospect selected early in the second round. Any minutes Furphy logged for Indiana were legitimate team output, unlike speculative projections about his ceiling. His collegiate experience at Kansas described his profile, but did not create NBA wins by itself. That distinction keeps the grade modest even while recognizing the value of an acquired roster player.

Núñez and Cash Gave San Antonio Another Kind of Option

The Spurs obtained Núñez's draft rights and cash rather than a signed veteran or an additional NBA first-round pick. His international background suggested playmaking and developmental possibilities, though the rights did not guarantee that he would immediately join the Spurs for regular-season action. The cash consideration supplied more certain value while the organization could assess when to use the prospect. San Antonio's broader roster overhaul involved many other transactions, and any later playing time by unrelated guards should not be counted as production from this single rights trade.

An NBA-Ready Path Gives Indiana the Early Edge

A comparison of the receiving-team outcomes favors Indiana slightly because Furphy was a player the club could bring into its developmental rotation, while San Antonio's rights-based upside remained more remote. That doesn't make the Spurs' overseas prospect or cash meaningless. Both teams exercised reasonable discretion over a pair of young players selected outside the first round. The inherited even verdict discounts the practical difference between an arriving wing and an overseas-rights prospect, so a limited Indiana edge is appropriate without assuming either athlete will become a star.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win by a small development advantage. Indiana earns B- for acquiring Johnny Furphy's No. 35 rights and gaining an NBA roster prospect suited to its wing rotation. San Antonio receives C+ for Juan Núñez's international draft rights and cash. Neither pick was a first-rounder, and future NBA performances beyond the actual recipient team are not assumed.

perspectives.summary: Sacramento acquired DeMar DeRozan in a July 2024 sign-and-trade with Chicago and San Antonio. The Bulls received Chris Duarte, RaiQuan Gray, two future second-round rights and cash. The Spurs acquired Harrison Barnes and a future Sacramento first-round selection associated with 2031. The inherited Bulls Win grades Chicago B and Sacramento and San Antonio C+ each.
perspectives.analysis:
Sacramento Pursued DeRozan's Offensive Creation

The Kings added DeMar DeRozan in a July 2024 three-team sign-and-trade, obtaining a six-time All-Star guard and forward who had been an important offensive option for Chicago. DeRozan's ability to create midrange attempts and draw fouls gave Sacramento a distinct scoring threat. The decision also required giving up Chris Duarte, Harrison Barnes, draft rights and cash across the other two teams. The Kings were choosing a proven scorer on a competitive timeline rather than waiting for a rookie to grow into that role.

Chicago Converted a Departing Veteran Into Flexibility

The Bulls received Chris Duarte and a package including RaiQuan Gray, two second-round selections and cash considerations. Duarte had NBA wing experience with Indiana and Sacramento, giving Chicago an option to evaluate beside its younger perimeter players. The second-round rights were associated with the 2025 and 2028 drafts, with their eventual player identities subject to further transactions. Chicago didn't replace DeRozan's scoring with one equally established star, but it obtained multiple forms of value instead of allowing the departure to produce no return.

San Antonio Added Barnes and a Future First

The Spurs acquired Harrison Barnes from Sacramento along with a future first-round selection tied to the Kings, associated with 2031 in the team's later transaction history. Barnes was a veteran wing who could supply outside shooting and experience beside San Antonio's developing core. A first-round asset also offered future flexibility, but its precise eventual value depended on conditions and where the selection landed. The original Bulls-centered ledger had recorded San Antonio as receiving nothing, a mistake corrected through the official announcement and Sacramento's transaction record.

Why the Model Slightly Favors Chicago

The inherited grades assign Chicago B and both Sacramento and San Antonio C+, even though Sacramento acquired the best established scorer at the moment of the agreement. The Chicago advantage reflects the breadth of Duarte, draft choices and cash relative to its circumstances. Barnes and a first-round asset are still substantial Spurs compensation, while Sacramento gained the targeted veteran. A responsible retrospective review considers actual receiving-team outcomes and doesn't treat the original grade as proof the other teams got no useful players.

Final Verdict

Bulls Win. Chicago earns B for Chris Duarte, RaiQuan Gray, second-round draft rights and cash. Sacramento receives C+ for DeMar DeRozan's veteran scoring, while San Antonio also gets C+ for Harrison Barnes and a future Sacramento first-round asset. The inherited result recognizes Chicago's outgoing free-agent compensation, but the complete record confirms that the Spurs obtained meaningful assets.

Utah receives C+ for Russell Westbrook's contract, Balsa Koprivica draft rights, cash and a conditional 2030 second-round swap option. Westbrook's later Denver seasons weren't Jazz games, and the future swap isn't assumed to have yielded a drafted Utah player. Los Angeles acquired defensive guard Kris Dunn from Utah on July 18, 2024 in a transaction that sent Russell Westbrook, the rights to Serbian prospect Balsa Koprivica and cash consideration to the Jaz
los-angeles-clippers.analysis:
The Clippers Acquired Dunn Through a Multi-Asset Agreement

Los Angeles acquired defensive guard Kris Dunn from Utah on July 18, 2024 in a transaction that sent Russell Westbrook, the rights to Serbian prospect Balsa Koprivica and cash consideration to the Jazz. The agreement also included a conditional option related to swapping second-round picks in 2030. Dunn was a veteran with a defined defensive reputation, which suited the Clippers' perimeter needs following other offseason changes. Utah pursued financial and asset flexibility rather than treating Westbrook as the new franchise point guard. The future swap must be described as an option whose eventual value depends on 2030 draft ordering, not as an immediate extra selection.

Dunn Played Real Rotation Defense in Los Angeles

Dunn joined the Clippers and contributed defense at the point of attack, an area that mattered for lineups built around experienced offensive players. He was not a high-volume scorer or the team's primary offensive initiator, but his ability to pressure guards and support perimeter matchups gave the franchise useful NBA minutes. That direct playing return supports a relatively strong grade. Dunn's earlier Timberwolves, Bulls and Jazz games belong to those earlier clubs and cannot be counted as Clippers production. Likewise, the club's wider season outcomes depended on more than this one defensive acquisition.

Westbrook's Utah Stop Was Primarily Transactional

Utah received Westbrook's contract but did not begin a lengthy new Jazz playing career with the former MVP. The veteran soon reached another roster arrangement and later played for Denver, making his Nuggets games the consequence of a separate move rather than a Utah on-court return. Koprivica's international draft rights and cash were additional assets with legitimate potential or financial utility. The 2030 swap provision created possible future value for the Jazz but had not been determined as of the agreement and shouldn't be counted as a drafted player. Utah's benefit was consequently flexibility rather than a proven incoming NBA starter.

An Active Defensive Guard Beats Uncertain Future Rights

The Clippers gained an identifiable rotation defender while Utah received a veteran contract to process, cash, international rights and conditional second-round flexibility. Each organization pursued a different timeline, making the deal understandable from both perspectives. A Clippers advantage rests on Dunn actually playing useful NBA minutes for his receiving club. Utah's compensation wasn't empty, but much of it was indirect or could only be valued after future transactions. Avoiding Westbrook's earlier All-Star history and any still-unknown 2030 draft position keeps the retrospective properly tied to the assets delivered in July 2024.

Final Verdict

Clippers Win. Los Angeles earns B+ for Kris Dunn's useful defensive guard minutes after July 2024. Utah receives C+ for Russell Westbrook's contract, Balsa Koprivica draft rights, cash and a conditional 2030 second-round swap option. Westbrook's later Denver seasons weren't Jazz games, and the future swap isn't assumed to have yielded a drafted Utah player.

analysis:
Atlanta and Phoenix Exchanged Two Developing Forwards

On July 29, 2024, Atlanta acquired forward David Roddy from Phoenix for E.J. Liddell in a straight player exchange. Both athletes were young frontcourt prospects who had already experienced changes of team early in their careers. Atlanta had space to evaluate a physical wing, while Phoenix hoped the incoming forward could help its reserve group or offer developmental flexibility. The transaction did not include a first-round selection, a cash purchase or a future protected pick. It was an attempt by two teams with different roster circumstances to use an unsettled prospect in a different environment.

Roddy Was an Opportunity Rather Than a Guaranteed Starter

Roddy came to Atlanta with experience in Memphis and Phoenix but still needed to prove he could hold a regular NBA role. His strength and versatility created a possible niche, yet this trade did not suddenly turn him into a long-term Hawks starter. Only his actual time after the July transaction belongs on Atlanta’s side of the ledger; his previous Grizzlies seasons cannot be credited as new Hawks production. A moderate result is appropriate for a club that bought another look at a developing player rather than trading for a proven scorer or defensive anchor.

Liddell Faced a Similar Challenge in Phoenix

Phoenix received Liddell, whose earlier career had been interrupted by injury and limited NBA playing opportunities. The Suns did not acquire an established veteran with dependable postseason minutes or additional draft picks to offset the change. They acquired a young player whose physical tools made him worth evaluating, but whose position on a competitive roster was uncertain. His prior Pelicans draft position was background, not a separate incoming asset. Phoenix could move or waive him later in another personnel decision; those future moves need to remain separate from what the Roddy agreement directly delivered.

The Modest Retrospective Reflects Both Timelines

The small-scale trade gave both front offices a chance to reassess similar types of NBA prospects without sacrificing major assets. A retrospective should resist giving either organization a headline grade just because one player had a higher profile when drafted. Neither return produced evidence of a franchise-changing contributor through the immediate exchange, and neither club assumed a new long-dated first-round obligation. This is a case where a broadly even judgment captures the modest opportunity cost better than an invented outright victor or the original overoptimistic assessments of two reserve possibilities.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Atlanta receives C+ for a fresh evaluation of David Roddy, while Phoenix also gets C+ for taking a developmental chance on E.J. Liddell. Neither player was acquired as a proven long-term starter and no draft pick changed hands. Earlier playing time with other clubs cannot be used to enlarge either franchise’s direct return from this July 2024 exchange.

atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta and Phoenix Exchanged Two Developing Forwards

On July 29, 2024, Atlanta acquired forward David Roddy from Phoenix for E.J. Liddell in a straight player exchange. Both athletes were young frontcourt prospects who had already experienced changes of team early in their careers. Atlanta had space to evaluate a physical wing, while Phoenix hoped the incoming forward could help its reserve group or offer developmental flexibility. The transaction did not include a first-round selection, a cash purchase or a future protected pick. It was an attempt by two teams with different roster circumstances to use an unsettled prospect in a different environment.

Roddy Was an Opportunity Rather Than a Guaranteed Starter

Roddy came to Atlanta with experience in Memphis and Phoenix but still needed to prove he could hold a regular NBA role. His strength and versatility created a possible niche, yet this trade did not suddenly turn him into a long-term Hawks starter. Only his actual time after the July transaction belongs on Atlanta’s side of the ledger; his previous Grizzlies seasons cannot be credited as new Hawks production. A moderate result is appropriate for a club that bought another look at a developing player rather than trading for a proven scorer or defensive anchor.

Liddell Faced a Similar Challenge in Phoenix

Phoenix received Liddell, whose earlier career had been interrupted by injury and limited NBA playing opportunities. The Suns did not acquire an established veteran with dependable postseason minutes or additional draft picks to offset the change. They acquired a young player whose physical tools made him worth evaluating, but whose position on a competitive roster was uncertain. His prior Pelicans draft position was background, not a separate incoming asset. Phoenix could move or waive him later in another personnel decision; those future moves need to remain separate from what the Roddy agreement directly delivered.

The Modest Retrospective Reflects Both Timelines

The small-scale trade gave both front offices a chance to reassess similar types of NBA prospects without sacrificing major assets. A retrospective should resist giving either organization a headline grade just because one player had a higher profile when drafted. Neither return produced evidence of a franchise-changing contributor through the immediate exchange, and neither club assumed a new long-dated first-round obligation. This is a case where a broadly even judgment captures the modest opportunity cost better than an invented outright victor or the original overoptimistic assessments of two reserve possibilities.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Atlanta receives C+ for a fresh evaluation of David Roddy, while Phoenix also gets C+ for taking a developmental chance on E.J. Liddell. Neither player was acquired as a proven long-term starter and no draft pick changed hands. Earlier playing time with other clubs cannot be used to enlarge either franchise’s direct return from this July 2024 exchange.

indiana-pacers.analysis:
Indiana Bought Veteran Frontcourt Insurance

Indiana acquired Thomas Bryant from Miami on December 15, 2024, when frontcourt injuries had tested the Pacers’ supply of available big men. Miami received the right to swap second-round draft positions with Indiana in 2031 rather than an established roster player or an immediate selection. The difference between a swap right and ownership of a future pick matters: the Heat could only benefit if the specified draft ordering made the option useful. The Pacers, by contrast, could put an NBA-experienced center into their rotation immediately after the transaction.

Bryant Provided a Real Rotation Option

Bryant brought screen setting, interior finishing and rebounding to a team built around Tyrese Haliburton’s pace and passing. His Indiana service extended into the club’s deep 2025 playoff run, giving the franchise a real return during a period when depth behind its main frontcourt contributors was valuable. Bryant did not suddenly become the team’s best player, but his presence reduced the need to depend entirely on emergency options. Every game credited here belongs to his time after joining Indiana, not his earlier seasons with the Lakers, Wizards, Nuggets or Heat.

Miami Retained a Narrow Future Pick-Swap Right

Miami gave up a player who was not commanding an indispensable role in its own rotation. The distant 2031 second-round swap could offer some value, but it was not a guaranteed extra pick, and it was years away from producing any player when this deal occurred. That allowed the Heat to manage a smaller present-day roster obligation while retaining a limited upside claim. It would be misleading to award Miami the full future career of any eventual second-round player before the draft position, exercise terms and recipient are known.

The Immediate Need Outweighed the Distant Return

The Pacers received identifiable NBA center minutes while Miami collected conditional future flexibility. This was a useful depth acquisition rather than a franchise-changing trade, so Indiana’s grade should be solid without being inflated. The Heat should not be treated as getting literally nothing simply because the incoming right could not play in December. But an active contributor during an important playoff period is stronger evidence of a successful exchange than an unresolved second-round option. The original Indiana-winning direction therefore remains the defensible judgment.

Final Verdict

Pacers Win. Indiana earns B+ for acquiring Thomas Bryant as an available rotation center who contributed during the 2024-25 season and playoff run. Miami gets C+ for the conditional right to swap 2031 second-round picks, not a guaranteed extra selection. Bryant’s previous NBA seasons and any hypothetical future draft player are excluded from the direct transaction return.

washington-wizards.analysis:
Sacramento Sought Immediate Frontcourt Experience

The Kings acquired Jonas Valančiūnas from Washington in February 2025, sending the Wizards Sidy Cissoko and two future second-round selections. Sacramento wanted a proven center who could rebound and score inside without needing an extended developmental period. Washington, still restructuring its roster, was willing to part with a veteran acquired the previous offseason. The deal reflected a direct choice between present big-man availability and future draft flexibility rather than two players at comparable career stages.

Valančiūnas Was an Established Interior Contributor

Valančiūnas had produced useful NBA scoring and rebounding for multiple clubs before reaching Sacramento. The Kings received an experienced center, giving them an immediate alternative in the frontcourt. His earlier production with Washington and New Orleans is relevant background but not new Kings statistics. The trade offered a way to strengthen a specific position during the season, though an incoming veteran center by himself could not guarantee a deep playoff run.

Washington Received a Wing Prospect and Two Picks

Cissoko was a young athletic wing whose immediate role in Washington was less certain than Valančiūnas's existing NBA pedigree. The Wizards also obtained 2028 and 2029 second-round rights, spreading the possible payoff across future roster decisions. Those draft choices were not current Washington players, and no eventual draftee can be named without following the later rights history. atlanta-hawks.analysis:
Atlanta Exchanged Bogdanović for Two Guards

The Hawks sent Bogdan Bogdanović and several second-round assets to the Clippers in February 2025, receiving Terance Mann and Nah'Shon 'Bones' Hyland. Atlanta acquired a bigger defensive-minded wing in Mann and a younger guard with scoring potential in Hyland. Los Angeles wanted another experienced outside shooter to support a playoff-oriented rotation. The exchange mixed immediate team fit with draft compensation instead of replacing one identical backcourt role with another.

Mann Offered Atlanta an Established Wing

Mann had shown he could defend across perimeter positions and contribute without being his team's leading scorer. That made him a practical addition for a Hawks group attempting to balance skill sets around its primary creators. Hyland offered a more uncertain young guard option. Their previous Clippers numbers explain why Atlanta wanted them but are not automatically new Hawks output. The incoming players had distinct roles rather than one shared substitute for Bogdanović.

The Clippers Added Shooting and Draft Rights

Bogdanović brought proven spacing, playmaking and experience to Los Angeles. The Clippers also obtained rights associated with a 2025 second-round choice tied to No. 51 Mohamed Diawara and additional conditional future selections. Later rights movements must be traced before a particular draftee's entire NBA career is credited to the Clippers. These multiple assets gave the receiving club additional choices after securing a veteran with a clear offensive skill.

Both Teams Had Plausible Immediate Benefits

Atlanta collected a defender and another possible scoring guard, while Los Angeles received Bogdanović's shooting and broader draft flexibility. The inherited B grades on both sides reflect a balanced assessment even though the packages differed in number and playing roles. The long-term results depend on player fit and the actual conveyance of the picks. This was a meaningful rotation adjustment, not a completed trade for a franchise centerpiece.

Final Verdict

Even Trade. Atlanta earns B for Terance Mann's wing skills and an additional chance to develop Bones Hyland. The Clippers also get B for Bogdan Bogdanović's outside shooting and second-round draft compensation. Both clubs addressed different perimeter needs, and the future pick values require careful tracking.
